Re: 
EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01—Office of Water – National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)  
  
Dear Mr. Goldberg,  
  
Denver Water submits this comment letter in response to the U.S. Environmental Protection 
Agency’s (EPA) request for comments on the proposed National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations for Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).   
Denver Water is committed to delivering safe water to our customers. In 2012, Denver Water’s 
Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) sampling results exceeded the action level measuring the amount 
of lead present in a customer’s tap water under the LCR. After years of public education and 
study, in 2018, the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) 
designated orthophosphate as Optimal Corrosion Control Treatment (OCCT) for Denver Water’s 
potable drinking water system. Denver Water and many other regional partners came together 
with concern regarding the designation due to downstream impacts that would affect natural 
streams and rivers, source water for drinking water plants, wastewater treatment plants, 
stormwater water providers, and other ecological impacts. These stakeholders assessed the 
loading and cost impacts from the introduction of additional phosphorus to municipalities and 
watershed as compared to a pH adjustment. Denver Water put forth a plan using filters, 
accelerated lead service line (LSL) replacements and pH adjustment for corrosion control, 
providing statistical evidence that this approach was at least as effective at lowering lead levels 
and protecting the health of the community as using orthophosphate for corrosion control 
treatment to protect public health.  
As a result of this stakeholder effort, in 2019, Denver Water became the first in the nation to 
receive approval from the EPA, as well as the CDPHE, for a variance from Rule 40 C.F.R. § 
141.82(e) Subpart I of the LCR. The variance has enabled Denver Water to chart a new path 
with the Lead Reduction Program, one that permanently addresses lead exposure in drinking 
water through an accelerated lead service line replacement program that will remove all LSLs 

Letter From. Denver Water ―  
Docket No. EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW  
February 5, 2024 
 
Page 2 of 9 
 
within 15 years beginning in 2020. Since 2020, Denver Water has met all metrics of its variance. 
A new variance was granted to Denver Water in 2022 under the Lead and Copper Rule 
Revisions (LCRR). 
The Lead Reduction Program includes five key elements: 1) the development of an online, 
publicly accessible LSL inventory; 2) the replacement of all LSLs in our service area within 15 
years at a 7% annual replacement rate; 3) a filter distribution program to customers who may 
have an LSL; 4) comprehensive communications, outreach and education efforts; and 5) the 
incorporation of equity principles (referred to as health equity and environmental justice, or 
HE&EJ, in official reporting) in all aspects of the program.1 
 
Through the Lead Reduction Program, over the last four years Denver Water reduced lead 
exposure to levels below what was initially projected at the time of the original variance 
approval, and what could be achieved under the LCRR. Denver Water has created a 
comprehensive LSL inventory that is continually being updated, has successfully replaced over 
22,000 customer-owned LSLs, maintained a long-term pitcher filter distribution program, and 
lowered regulatory lead sampling results to below 5 parts per billion through the maintenance of 
pH and alkalinity. Based on the performance under the variance metrics and the results from the 
lead equivalency model, the variance and Lead Reduction Program are objectively more 
effective at lowering lead levels at customers’ taps compared to the use of orthophosphate 
treatment under the LCRR. In addition, the Lead Reduction Program has incorporated HE&EJ 
principles to help prioritize areas and specific properties within Denver Water’s service area to 
investigate and replace LSLs, as well as to maximize outreach efforts with vulnerable 
populations as well as disproportionately affected communities and neighborhoods. 
 
Denver Water appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed LCRI and supports the 
efforts to protect public health and the potential exposure of lead in drinking water. Among the 
listed developments in the LCRI, Denver Water supports accelerating the replacement of LSLs, 
lowering the Action Level threshold to 10 parts per billion, the incorporation of connectors or 
lead goosenecks into system inventories, and increasing consumer communication and 
outreach efforts. 
Comments on Costs of LSL Replacement Programs: 
1. 
EPA should consider assuming a higher average cost for LSL 
replacements than is currently assumed. The cost for Denver Water to fully replace an LSL 
can range from $5,000-$12,000 per replacement, which includes required exterior restoration. 
Cost efficiencies are gained when combining LSL replacement with a water main replacement 
project or by grouping hundreds of properties in a single work package. Costs can increase 
when it is a larger diameter pipe, construction activities are occurring in a major roadway, and 
also with the restoration of landscape and hardscape surfaces. Based upon Denver Water’s 
experience, the average cost for contractors to replace LSLs in geographically concentrated 
work areas is $9,600, not including the administrative, management and outreach costs. 
Additionally, Denver Water has found that covering exterior restoration costs (e.g., asphalt

repair, concrete, landscape) is a necessary cost to comply with permits required to do the work, 
including stormwater and street occupancy permits.  
 
2. 
Financial funding guidance is needed to assist water providers to 
understand what funding options are available to replace LSLs. Denver Water is replacing 
customer-owned LSLs and providing pitcher filters to customers until six months after their LSLs 
are replaced at no direct charge to the customer notwithstanding the fact that customers own 
their service lines from the main to their properties. Protecting the public from the potential 
impacts of customer-owned LSLs that were installed during the first half of the 20th century will 
cost hundreds of millions of dollars over the life of the program. With its variance, which 
approved an alternative treatment technique that Denver Water is required to perform, Denver 
Water was able to use ratepayer resources and bond financing to spread the costs across all 
ratepayers, similar to other water treatment costs. Additionally, Denver Water followed 
accounting standards to capitalize the cost of LSL replacements and pitcher filter distribution. 
The ability to capitalize the cost of LSL replacements and pitcher filters has allowed Denver 
Water to spread the costs for the program with rate increases over time rather than incurring 
them all at once. This has kept rates affordable for Denver Water customers while undertaking 
this important public health effort. 
 
3. 
Federal funding is essential to the successful implementation of the LCRI. 
In 2022, Denver Water received $76,123,628 from the Colorado Drinking Water State Revolving 
Fund, thanks in part to the federal bipartisan Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act signed into 
law by President Joe Biden in November 2021. The state approved allocation of funds to 
Denver Water in October, and the Denver Board of Water Commissioners formally accepted the 
funds Dec. 7, 2022. The funding Denver Water received is a low-interest loan that the utility will 
repay, with $40 million of the loan’s principle forgiven immediately, as allowed by the legislation. 
The money is being spent 2023 through 2025 and will support the replacement of 6,800 more 
LSLs than we originally planned. Thanks to the new funding, 2,000 lines were replaced in 2023 
— on top of the nearly 5,000 lines completed last year. Denver Water complies with all the 
federal requirements and absorbs the 10%-15% non-reimbursable costs (e.g., meters and 
meter pit fittings) through the program’s normal funding mechanisms. 
 
4. 
Water Providers need additional tools to finance replacement of LSLs. Even 
with existing federal funding, water providers will need additional financing tools to close the 
substantial gap between the costs to undertake this work and available funding sources.  Water 
providers face particular challenges in finding ways to finance the replacement of privately-
owned LSLs.  In Denver Water’s case, we had to obtain a private letter ruling from the Internal 
Revenue Service (I.R.S.) to confirm our ability use tax-exempt debt to pay for replacement of 
LSLs owned by our customers due to the “private use” limitations generally applicable to tax-
exempt bonds.  The Financing Lead Out of Water Act (H.R. 6985) would amend the private use 
test to exempt LSL replacement, allowing other water providers to utilize this important funding 
tool without having to seek costly individual determinations from the I.R.S.  Financing private 
lines over the life of the asset significantly reduces the impact to customers’ bills. EPA’s support

of this, or revenue ruling to accomplish the same objective, could be instrumental in reducing a

Comments and Recommendations on the Proposed LCRI Requirements: 
The last four years of implementing the Lead Reduction Program have brought many 
successes and challenges. The replacement of LSLs is a permanent solution to addressing a 
major contributor to lead in drinking water, but it is also a heavy cost burden on water utilities, 
and the replacement at individual properties can be a very difficult task. Denver Water has 
evaluated these experiences and submits the following comments and suggested modifications 
to clarify and improve the LCRI:  
5. 
Denver Water supports the proposed lead action level of 0.010 mg/L. 
Denver Water prioritizes public health and the removal of lead in drinking water and 
believes 0.010mg/L is an appropriate action level for the LCR. The action level is a level at 
which water providers must take additional steps to try to reduce lead levels in their system and 
raise customer awareness. The action level was never intended to be a maximum contaminant 
level. Denver Water is concerned that if the action level is set too low, many water providers will 
exceed the action level on a frequent or constant basis. This may have the unfortunate effect of 
reducing the effectiveness of certain actions triggered by an action level exceedance, such as 
customer education. If water providers are communicating with customers on a relatively 
constant basis that they are above the action level, this has the potential to cause customers to 
become desensitized to this important public notice. Water providers may also have to expend 
valuable resources that could be used for LSL replacement programs on OCCT and re-
optimization studies. For these reasons, Denver Water supports an action level of 0.010 mg/L.  
 
6. 
Denver Water is concerned that the proposed maximum replacement 
requirement of 10,000 LSLs per year is not feasible for many water providers and 
recommends EPA instead adopt a maximum limit of 8,000 LSL replacements per year. 
Denver Water supports the proposed minimum LSL replacement rate and replacement 
deadlines, although replacement of all LSLs within 10 years will be difficult for water providers 
that have large numbers of LSLs. Denver Water’s program is a 15-year program, which requires 
the replacement of nearly 64,000 total LSLs at a rate of 7% per year. This is an accelerated 
program that has required additional staffing, contractors, and extensive resources to 
accomplish. Between 2020 and 2024, Denver Water has spent $2.4M on additional staffing to 
administer the program and $308M on the LSL replacements themselves. It has also required 
careful coordination with the City and County of Denver’s transportation department as well as 
other utilities to avoid conflicts related to road construction, utility work, and street paving. A 
program on the magnitude of 10,000 LSLs per year may approach the level where traffic and 
transportation, and general construction is affected. Medium to large systems with large 
quantities of LSLs will have a difficult time replacing all LSLs within a 10-year period and 
reducing the time frame for such systems to less than 10 years would likely not be feasible. For 
water providers that are managing massive capital infrastructure projects and challenges, a 
large 10-year LSL replacement program will be especially difficult to sustain. For these reasons, 
Denver Water believes an annual 8,000 LSL replacement requirement is more realistic, 

Letter From. Denver Water ―  
Docket No. EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW  
February 5, 2024 
 
Page 5 of 9 
 
although 2024 will be the first year it has attempted to reach this number through its 
replacement program.  
 
7. 
For water providers with a significant number of LSLs, EPA should 
consider excluding the first two years of the LSL replacements from the three-year 
rolling average to give water providers a buffer to gain experience with LSL 
replacements. In Denver Water’s experience, it would have likely failed to replace 10,000 LSLs 
in the first year of its variance. During the first year of its variance, Denver Water achieved 4,800 
LSL replacements which was a monumental effort and a significant learning experience. While 
EPA proposes to adopt a three-year rolling average, if a water provider that has a significant 
number of LSLs only achieved 4,800 LSL replacements in its first year, it would be extremely 
difficult to recover in subsequent years.   
 
8. 
EPA should provide states with the authority to waive the requirement to 
re-optimize again following an action level exceedance regardless of meeting their 
optimal water quality parameters and to provide the state with the authority to waive this 
requirement.  Corrosion control treatment studies can be resource-intensive, costly, and time-
consuming. Denver Water believes that if water providers are able to meet certain metrics, such 
as an accelerated LSL replacement effort or pitcher filter distribution program, resources 
expended toward these efforts can be better utilized to advance public health. Prior to the Lead 
Reduction Program approval, Denver Water, state and local regulators and other stakeholders 
evaluated the downstream impacts and cost that would affect natural streams, rivers and 
wastewater treatment plants associated with using orthophosphate as corrosion control 
treatment.2 The estimated costs of orthophosphate implementation to the Front Range were 
higher than the estimated costs of implementing the Lead Reduction Program, which offered a 
more permanent solution to addressing lead in drinking water by replacing LSLs at an 
accelerated rate. By having the option to implement the Lead Reduction Program in lieu of 
orthophosphate treatment, Denver Water was able to invest resources in the permanent 
removal of lead as opposed to a treatment method that would have required the downstream 
investment in new clean water nutrient treatment removal technologies and contirbuted 
additional phoshorous loading to already nutirent-stressed waters throughout the region.

9. 
EPA should adopt clear regulatory pathways that would allow a system to 
defer OCCT using orthophosphate by implementing an alternative treatment technique 
program. Such an option is desirable for water providers in parts of the country with nutrient-
stressed waterways, climate-impacted streams, and strict nutrient-based water quality 
regulations. However, the system should not be required to implement orthophosphate as 
OCCT at the end of its program, as this would eliminate the incentive to adopt such a program. 
Additionally, EPA has requested comment whether, as a condition of deferring OCCT, a system 
should commit to replacement of at least 20 percent removal per year and must have no LSLs, 
galvanized service lines requiring replacement (GRR) , or lead status unknown service lines 
remaining at the end of the five-year period. Denver Water believes that such a level of 
replacement is not a realistic option for most water providers. A 10% removal rate is a much 
more realistic option, coupled with a pitcher filter distribution program.  
 
 
10. 
Denver Water supports the definition of reasonable effort under § 
141.84(d)(3)(i) as four attempts to obtain property owner consent. Water providers should 
be required to make at least four attempts to obtain customer consent for LSL replacement. 
Denver Water was one of the first utilities in the country to adopt a standard operating 
procedure to follow up with customers multiple times to obtain their consent to an LSL 
replacement. Through the first four years of Denver Water’s Lead Reduction Program, Denver 
Water has a consent rate average of 95% with 3-4 attempts at contact. In Denver Water’s 
experience, more than four attempts could become burdensome for utilities to track and 
implement and counterproductive with customers.  
 
11. 
EPA should broaden § 141.84(d)(3)(i)-(ii) by revising references to “property 
owner consent” to “property owner or tenant consent, as applicable.” EPA may want to 
consider making similar changes to §§ 141.85(a)(vi)(E) and (F) as well. Under the common 
law in most states, property owner consent is not required or effective to conduct an LSL 
replacement in a single-family residential property because a landlord has surrendered control 
of the property to the tenant, who has exclusive use over the property, subject to the terms of 
their lease. An exception to this would be situations where systems require access to a common 
area over which the landlord retains exclusive control. This does not mean that a tenant is 
necessarily responsible for the LSL replacement, as in many states, landlords, not tenants can 
be held responsible for upgrades to property required by government action unless the tenant’s 
particular use of the leased space triggers the government order.   
 
12. 
Denver Water supports the proposed requirement to ban partial lead and 
GRR service line replacement unless it is conducted in accordance with emergency or 
planned infrastructure work under § 141.84(g)(1) (excluding planned infrastructure work 
solely for the purposes of replacing lead and GRR service lines as part of a service line 
replacement program). If a system can obtain customer cooperation, a partial LSL 
replacement should never be performed. However, there are times when partial LSL 
replacements are unavoidable, such as when a customer’s property cannot be accessed. 
During both emergency work and planned work, where a customer’s consent cannot be 

Letter From. Denver Water ―  
Docket No. EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW  
February 5, 2024 
 
Page 7 of 9 
 
obtained or property cannot be accessed, for the sake of protecting and completing work on a 
distribution system, a partial LSL replacement cannot be avoided. Fortunately, in Denver 
Water’s experience, the instances where customers do not provide consent, or their property 
cannot be accessed are few in number. 
 
13. 
Inventory Validation Requirements. Denver Water recommends that EPA 
clarify whether systems currently complying with inventory validation requirements adopted by 
EPA or primacy states under the LCRR will need to be revalidated under §§ 141.84(b)(5)(i)-(ii) 
of the LCRI, or whether validation decisions made under the LCRR will control over the new 
LCRI requirements, i.e., clarify that systems do not have to repeat validation requirements under 
the LCRI where primacy agencies have approved of inventory decisions under the LCRR. The 
LCRI has the potential to create confusion for systems relying on current EPA and state 
guidance to validate randomly sampled pools of customer properties prior to the compliance 
date for the LCRI. The requirement to have a random sample and exclusion of previously 
developed data from the validation pool is also problematic for water providers that are already 
developing inventories through inspections, water quality tests and potholing. Alternatively, EPA 
should make the inventory requirements effective in 2024 to avoid confusion over whether 
validation work done now, will have to be repeated when the LCRI goes into effect.  
  
14. 
EPA should include alternative requirements for systems to validate their 
inventories using predictive modeling to determine the probability of LSLs within a 
service area. Predictive modeling seeks to determine the probability of a location of LSLs within 
geographic areas in a service area, not through a minimum number of random samples, but 
instead through an abundance of samples, and other forms of evidence, such as record 
reviews, water quality testing, potholing, and interior investigations. Some systems, such as 
Denver Water, are already using predictive models developed through abundant data that has 
already been collected. If systems that use predictive modeling are required to meet the same 
data and validation requirements as proposed under Rule §§ 141.84(b)(5)(i)-(ii), such systems 
will be forced to invest resources unnecessarily to develop new data and collect random 
samples where they may already have a reliable model capable of predicting the location of 
LSLs in their service area. For systems that use predictive modeling, EPA should instead 
require their model have a confidence level of at least 95%.  
 
15. 
EPA should reconsider the deadlines for systems to provide sampling 
results to customers. Rules §§ 141.85(d)(2) and (4) would require systems to deliver sampling 
results to consumers within three days of learning of the sampling results. Where systems are 
managing large numbers of consumer tap sample requests, a three-day timeline is not feasible. 
If systems utilize a contract lab, there is typically a 1-2-day timeline to receive results and 
another few days to review, authorize and confirm results. Once that review is completed, a 
letter will need to be mailed, which can take up to 10 days if the mailing service is managed out 
of state. An additional consequence of requiring three days to provide notice is that water 
providers will need to focus on meeting short deadlines to distribute lead water quality results, 
which may detract from attention to other pressing water quality concerns that cause more 

Letter From. Denver Water ―  
Docket No. EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW  
February 5, 2024 
 
Page 8 of 9 
 
acute health impacts. Denver Water recommends that EPA instead adopt a 14-day time frame 
from when systems learn of sampling results to deliver the results to customers. 
 
16. 
Denver Water supports conducting all public education activities related to 
an exceedance within 30 days. A prescriptive time period to complete all activities may result 
in rushed completion of activities that does not create the greatest opportunity for educating the 
public. Flexibility should be provided to water providers, through consultation and approval with 
the state, to develop an appropriate timeline to complete public education activities. 
 
17. 
Denver Water recommends that EPA keep the requirement for systems to 
provide notice to customers whether their LSL is made of lead, GRR, or unknown 
material to no more than once a year. For large systems, issuing such notices more 
frequently than once a year can become costly and have a desensitizing effect on customers.  
  
18. 
Translation of educational materials. For the Lead Reduction Program, 
Denver Water used local and state information to identify languages spoken within its service 
area. For example, Denver Water was able to incorporate (along with state data), the City and 
County of Denver neighborhood demographics along with language preferences from Denver 
Public Schools to identify language preferences in addition to limited English proficiency. To the 
extent possible, states should support the development of these needs for smaller utilities 
requiring assistance. Denver Water also recommends that EPA require state primacy agencies 
to provide translation services to support systems that are unable to do so for consumers with 
limited English proficiency. For Denver Water’s Lead Reduction Program, translation and 
interpretation costs are ongoing and borne by the utility to ensure access to program information 
and meeting resources. These costs are upwards of $10,000 annually, and the ongoing nature 
of these costs could be burdensome for smaller systems. Denver Water wholeheartedly 
supports states providing resources to meet water providers interpretation and translation 
needs. 
 
19. 
Definition of service line. Denver Water encourages EPA to consider the 
American Water Works Association’s suggested revision to the definition of a service line, as 
shown below: 
Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe 
which directly connects the community water system’s water main to the building 
inlet first fitting inside the building (i.e., connecting the service line to the building 
water system). Relevant service lines are those that supply water for drinking and 
cooking in the building.  The term service line does not include private water mains. 
Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water main to the 
outlet. Where a private main exists between the community water system main 
and a building, associated service lines are not subject to subpart I. (§ 141.2 of 
LCRI) 
Systems should not be responsible for (1) diagraming on-site distribution system piping 
networks or (2) taking responsibility for “distribution systems” maintained by others and only

Docket No. EPA–HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW  
February 5, 2024

connected to the water system by virtue of the sale of water through a mass meter. Many, if not 
most, of these situations either are state-recognized public water systems or are public water 
systems as defined by the Safe Drinking Water Act. Their status as unregulated (or less 
regulated) public water systems (PWSs) should not lead to a burden on regulated PWSs. 
20. 
State Waivers for Previously Performed School and Child Care Sampling. 
To avoid a duplication of efforts and unnecessary cost impacts, EPA should immediately 
implement the proposed rule to allow states to issue waivers to systems from the requirement 
for lead sampling in schools and child care facilities during the five-year period after the LCRI 
compliance date if the facility was sampled for lead after Jan. 1, 2021, but prior to the LCRI 
compliance date and the sampling otherwise meets the waiver requirements of § 141.92(h). 
Colorado has adopted a school testing program that meets the requirements of the LCRR and 
LCRI, and is already performing testing of schools and child care facilities under the program. 
However, because the LCRR does not currently provide a waiver for such a testing program, 
testing in Colorado will need to be repeated. EPA should accelerate the compliance date for this 
rule to avoid a duplication of resources, as without an accelerated compliance date, Colorado 
school districts and possibly water systems will need to repeat testing.  
Once again, Denver Water appreciates the opportunity to comment on the proposed LCRI and 
supports the efforts to protect public health and the potential exposure of lead in drinking water. 
Replacing LSLs within a 10-year timeframe is an ambitious and proactive approach, and we 
strongly encourage EPA to provide additional funding mechanisms to assist utilities with this 
work. 
Thank you for the opportunity to submit public comments on the questions posed. If you have 
any questions regarding this comment letter, please do not hesitate to contact me.

Dear Sir or Madam: 
The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) is providing the enclosed comments 
regarding the proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, as requested by February 5, 2024.  
TCEQ recognizes the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) important role in managing 
and protecting the nation’s drinking water under the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and 
supports EPA’s efforts to revise the federal Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). TCEQ 
recognizes that control of lead in drinking water is a significant public health issue. We 
understand that these proposed improvements are an opportunity to control lead in drinking 
water and increase public health protection. 
TCEQ appreciates EPA’s efforts to simplify and address many of the comments on the Lead and 
Copper Rule Revisions. TCEQ urges EPA to continue to work with primacy agencies to develop 
data management tools to reduce the significant time, effort, and financial resources necessary 
to implement, administer, and enforce this rule. 
If you have any questions concerning the enclosed comments, please contact Ms. Michele Risko, 
Water Supply Division Deputy Director, at (512) 239-1689 or michele.risko@tceq.texas.gov. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Kelly Keel 
Executive Director 
Texas Commission on Environmental Quality 
 
Enclosure 
 

Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) Comments on National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Rule Improvements 
(LCRI) Proposed by the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 
Docket ID Number EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801  
 
I. 
General Comments 
TCEQ appreciates EPA’s efforts to simplify and address many of the comments on the 
Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). TCEQ fully supports allowing the use of  
Water Infrastructure Improvement for the Nation (WIIN) grant testing to be used 
toward school and child care required testing. 
 
II. 
Specific Concerns with Lack of Implementation Resources, Proposed 
Requirements and Regulatory Language, and Funding 
TCEQ has concerns with some of the proposed regulatory language that would govern 
how these concepts are implemented and enforced. The most concerning issues with 
the proposed requirements are as follows:  
A. Lack of Tools  
TCEQ recommends EPA provide or complete data management tools prior to 
finalizing the rule, including timely data entry instructions and updating 
database applications to ensure the ability to make reliable compliance 
determinations. Without adequate data management tools, requirements cannot 
be effectively implemented. Existing EPA data tools do not have the functionality 
to implement the proposed rule and additional tools are needed to facilitate the 
LCRI. The current version of the Safe Drinking Water Information System-State 
(SDWIS/State) database does not have the functionality to calculate compliance 
reliably and consistently for the complex tiering updates and 90th percentile 
calculations required under the LCRI. For example, data management tools are 
needed in order to implement requirements in 40 Code of Federal Regulations 
(CFR) Section 141.86(a)(1)(I) and 40 CFR Section 141.86(b)(1)(i). Without proper 
data management tools, states like Texas will be unable to consolidate its more 
than 155,615 historic lead and copper sample sites (and associated materials 
evaluation data) with the proposed sample site tiering criteria and will be unable 
to confirm which samples (1st liter, or 1st and 5th liter) are utilized in the 90th 
percentile calculations. EPA’s modernization of SDWIS/State has been in the 
process for more than a decade and primacy agencies still do not have a reliable 
database to be able to implement the requirements of several newly 
promulgated National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWRs). Without 
an adequate data management solution, primacy agencies would have to 
perform manual compliance determinations. This will increase the potential for 
errors and delays in timely compliance determinations and communications to 
the public, and potentially impacting public health.  
If EPA cannot provide the necessary updates to SDWIS/State before finalizing 
the LCRI, TCEQ recommends the Drinking Water State Federal Tribal 
Information Exchange System (DW-SFTIES) be completed and supersede 
SDWIS/State with an adequate structure to accommodate compliance 

determination requirements of the LCRI. Updates to SDWIS/State or DW-SFTIES 
are needed by the rule compliance date, to ensure effective implementation of 
the LCRI. 
B. 10-year Replacement Timeline  
TCEQ recommends EPA remove “Lead Status Unknown Service Lines” from 
replacement rate calculations or create an alternative replacement rate 
calculation for systems reporting a significant amount of Lead Status Unknown 
Service Lines. As proposed, the 10-year time period for Lead Service Line 
Replacement creates a “one-size-fits-all” approach that many public water 
systems (systems) in states like Texas will not be able to meet. TCEQ notes that 
if a system has limited records there may not be options available to determine 
the material of service lines other than digging. TCEQ has identified systems 
who have lost historical records due to natural disasters and struggle to identify 
service line materials under the methods approved by EPA. Unless alternative 
means for identification are provided, these systems will likely be forced to 
report a majority of their service lines as Lead Status Unknown in their initial 
service line inventory. The proposed LCRI will create additional challenges for 
these systems as they will likely not be able to meet a replacement rate based on 
their number of Lead Status Unknown Service Lines.  
C. Service Line Ownership and Replacement Liability  
As proposed, liability issues could arise if systems are responsible for customer’s 
service line replacement, or if they require or manage funding for customers to 
replace their lines. The proposed rule requires full lead service line replacement 
regardless of ownership. TCEQ continues to caution that liability issues could 
arise if systems are responsible for the customer’s service line replacement, or if 
they require or manage funding for customers to replace their lines. The 
possibility that lead service line replacement could cause damage to 
foundations, premise plumbing, and landscaping and yard disturbances should 
be addressed.  
D. Pipe Loop Study Requirements  
TCEQ recommends pipe loop studies be required only for large systems (i.e., 
>50,000 in population) who are better equipped to accomplish the study, and for 
guidance to be developed to accomplish the studies. 
Proposed revisions to 40 CFR Section 141.81(d)(1) that require pipe loop studies 
to be conducted for systems with a population of 10,000 or more, a lead action 
level exceedance (ALE), and lead service lines will impose a huge financial 
burden on systems. These systems, due to lack of scale, may not be equipped to 
meet this requirement themselves and will need to hire consultants. TCEQ is 
concerned that this requirement diverts resources from the goal of getting the 
lead out of water supply systems, and recommends the study requirement be 
focused on systems that may have more resources to comply with the 
requirement.  
Additionally, an official guidance for pipe loop studies has not been developed. 
At a minimum, a pipe loop study will require the ability to design a protocol, 
develop piping materials to simulate the piping environment, measure corrosion 
activity, analyze data, test secondary impacts and maintain quality control of 

the testing program. Many groundwater system operators do not have the 
training to develop a pipe loop study. In states like Texas, groundwater systems 
are approximately 94% of systems subject to the LCRI. Pipe loop studies also 
require several months or years to obtain accurate comparisons and would 
likely require a system to dedicate one operator full time to the endeavor. Only 
large systems with many operators are likely to have the personnel with the 
expertise to design and perform a pipe loop study. Small and most medium 
systems, regardless of source type and operator training, are unable to perform 
pipe loop studies due to the amount of time that must be dedicated to 
collecting and analyzing the data. Systems will be forced to spend thousands of 
dollars to hire consultants to conduct the studies, but the impact of these 
requirements will be most detrimental to small and medium groundwater 
systems.  
The LCRI should include guidance with flexibility on study approaches - with all 
studies being maintained as valid options. Desk-top, coupons, and pipe loop 
studies all have value and can provide different types of information in 
different timeframes. It would also be beneficial to provide some options that 
are faster to implement, especially if lead is considered an acute contaminant 
since pipe rigs and loop studies can take years to complete. Time, resource, and 
cost intensive studies divert valuable resources from the stated goal of “getting 
the lead out.” 
E. Consecutive System Requirements  
TCEQ recommends removing wholesaler optimal water quality parameter 
(OWQP) requirements for consecutive systems. Proposed language in 40 CFR 
Section 141.82(g) suggests that if a system operates under OWQP ranges, any 
system that purchases from that system must also operate under the same 
ranges. Many water systems in states like Texas are intertwined and use 
comingled water. 
TCEQ recommends removing OWQP requirements due to the inability to directly 
apply OWQPs developed for the wholesaler to each consecutive system’s unique 
characteristics or limit the scope of the requirement. The existing definition of 
consecutive system indicates that a “consecutive system is a system that 
receives some or all of its finished water from one or more wholesale systems. 
Delivery may be through a direct connection or through the distribution system 
of one or more consecutive systems.” If a consecutive system receives all of its 
finished water, unaltered from a wholesale system, the monitoring of optimal 
corrosion control treatment through OWQPs could provide valuable information 
regarding the protection of the downstream customer. However, if a consecutive 
system only receives some of its water from a wholesaler, receives water from 
multiple wholesalers, receives water through multiple consecutive systems or 
alters the water upon receipt, the OWQPs of the originating wholesale system 
would not be optimized to the unique characteristics of the consecutive 
system’s blended, augmented, or altered water. TCEQ continues to recommend 
removal of this requirement. Should the requirement be retained, its scope 
should be limited to situations where the water characteristics of the 
consecutive system and wholesale system can be documented as equivalent due 
to the wholesaler being the sole source to the consecutive system and no 
additional treatment is being performed. 

Without revision, it may not be possible to implement and comply with the 
requirements. Should the provision not be altered, some states like Texas may 
be unable to implement this aspect of the proposed rule due to the 
interconnected nature of many of our systems. Systems have taken significant 
efforts to expand resilience and enable the flow of water within their region 
through interconnections, symbiotic contractual relationships, and joint 
partnerships. As an example, one large system in Texas is directly connected to 
more than 100 unique community and non-transient, non-community systems. 
These first-tier consecutive systems then serve more than 200 interconnected 
second-tier systems that also serve more than an additional 250 systems. Many 
of these systems receive water from more than one wholesale provider, 
therefore, under the LCRR they could be required to monitor and comply with 
different OWQPs associated to the unique wholesalers. The ability for each 
consecutive system to monitor OWQPs and the expectation that these 
parameters would accurately represent the water quality of the wholesaler, first- 
or second-tier system and the implied protection of public health lacks 
continuity. 
TCEQ requests EPA provide specific information regarding consecutive systems 
that do not currently have constructed treatment facilities, and any options that 
may be available, including requiring cooperation with the wholesale provider. 
Many consecutive systems within states like Texas receive water under direct 
pressure from one or multiple wholesale providers and do not already have 
constructed production, treatment, storage, or pressure facilities. It is unclear if 
EPA intends to require consecutive systems without current treatment facilities 
to install corrosion control treatment (CCT), and make capital improvements 
(including constructing facilities to house and administer this CCT). 
Additionally, for systems who receive water under direct pressure at multiple 
locations, is it EPA’s intention for treatment facilities to be constructed and CCT 
to be installed at each location the consecutive system receives water? The 
requirement to have consecutive systems install CCT when they do not already 
have facilities where treatment may be administered will place a very heavy 
burden on these systems, both financially and relating to operator training and 
education. The operators for these consecutive systems may only have 
experience in managing distribution systems, and no experience with treatment. 
F. Loss of Funding 
TCEQ requests EPA emphasize the importance of funding to the Drinking Water 
State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) to restore allocations to historic levels and 
maintain the intent and impact of the DWSRF. In state fiscal year 2023, Texas’ 
Base Capitalization grant experienced a new loss of $31 million due to 
congressional earmarking. Although there is funding currently available through 
the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, this funding is limited and will not remain 
available in perpetuity. Therefore, it is important to protect the long-term 
viability of the DWSRF base program funding for the additional resources 
needed to implement the LCRI and other newly promulgated federal regulations, 
to ensure equitable funding access to all eligible systems and safeguard the 
intended self-sustaining nature of the DWSRF.  
 

III. 
Carryforward of Concerns with the LCRR 
In addition to the issues named above, TCEQ raised many concerns with the proposed 
LCRR which still remain with the proposed LCRI. These concerns include the following: 
A. Burden of New Requirements 
TCEQ remains concerned about the significant burden of new requirements put 
forth in the proposed LCRI. These changes create additional burden to the 
primacy agency as well as the systems. A recent data review projects that 
lowering the lead action level to 10 ppb will increase Texas’ ALEs by 50%. As a 
result, this increase in ALEs will lead to an increase in corrosion control 
activities (e.g., corrosion control studies (CCST), optimal corrosion control 
treatment (OCCT), source water treatment (SOWT), etc.) by systems as well as 
associated reviews by the primacy agency. 
TCEQ recommends removal of the requirement to provide pitcher filters. TCEQ 
remains concerned that systems who conduct lead service line replacements are 
required to provide customers a pitcher filter certified to remove lead and 
replacement cartridges. Filter efficacy is dependent on proper installation, 
cartridge age, and storage conditions. Many manufacturers recommend unused 
cartridges be stored in a cool, dry place prior to use. The homeowner being 
provided the filter may not use it or may feel it is an inconvenience and throw it 
away. TCEQ recommends removing this requirement. The Safe Drinking Water 
Act (SDWA) public notification requirements are intended to allow consumers to 
make informed decisions regarding the use of water. Informed consumers may 
choose to use filters, obtain bottled water, or seek alternative treatment options. 
It is outside the intent of the SDWA for the state to determine consumer action. 
TCEQ recommends requirements to issue notices of potential elevated lead be 
revised in order to improve communication with customers and reduce confusion. 
States like Texas routinely experience natural disasters (i.e., hurricane, tornado, 
flood, drought, fire, etc.) where water systems work diligently against difficult 
situations to provide potable water. Often, systems will issue a boil water notice 
out of an abundance of caution for protection of public health. TCEQ is 
concerned that issuing the “potential for elevated lead” notification when 
pressure and capacity decline, or when water is turned off due to emergency 
work, will confuse customers if the notice is required to contain language that 
encourages flushing and opposes boiling. TCEQ proposes that notice of 
potential for elevated lead only be issued to customers if a water system turns 
off water at a customer’s meter and not if emergency or routine maintenance is 
conducted affecting more than one customer. If EPA determines a “disturbance” 
includes emergency maintenance on service lines in accordance with 40 CFR 
Section 141.84(h)(1)(i-iv), it may be impractical to require systems to maintain a 
surplus of filter pitchers and cartridges in the event of emergency repair. 
B. “Designation” versus “Review and Approval”  
 
TCEQ recommends changing the “state designates” language in the proposed 
rule to “the state will either designate or review and approve treatment proposed 

by the system.” TCEQ continues to request that EPA recognize that many states, 
including Texas, review and approve a system’s treatment recommendations 
and OWQPs, and do not “designate” treatment or OWQPs based on the state’s 
own analysis of the system.  
 
C. Re-optimization 
 
TCEQ requests that EPA provide a definition for “re-optimization.” This definition 
is important because the proposed rule requires re-optimization when a system 
has already installed corrosion control treatment and then has an action level 
exceedance. The definition should clarify that re-optimization is only applicable 
for treatment that has been reviewed and approved (or designated) by the state. 
A guidance document should be developed by EPA that would aid a system in 
troubleshooting problems with their treatment such as proper dosing or 
changes in the treatment product or method itself. In addition, this term will 
need to be added to SDWIS and DW-SFTIES for documenting the “deeming” of 
each system under milestones.  
 
IV. 
Recommended Revisions  
TCEQ proposes revisions to several areas of the proposed LCRI to streamline activities, 
standardize information, or add clarity. These areas include:  
A. Premise Plumbing Replacement 
TCEQ recommends expanding flexibility afforded in the LCRR. In the LCRR, TCEQ 
concurred with and appreciated the premise plumbing replacement option for 
lead exceeding non-transient non-community systems. TCEQ recommends 
expanding this flexibility option to address copper exceedances. 
B. Service Line Replacement 
TCEQ recommends revising language within 40 CFR Section 141.84(d)(3)(ii) to 
state that water systems must offer full service line replacement once the water 
system becomes aware of an ownership change. As proposed, requirements 
would put an undue burden on water systems to continuously obtain data on 
property ownership which is outside their purview. TCEQ’s recommendation to 
revise the proposed language is underlined below:  
“Within six months of becoming aware of any change in ownership of the 
property, the water system must offer full service line replacement to any new 
property owner and make a “reasonable effort” to obtain the property owner’s 
consent…” 
C. Optimal Water Quality Parameters (OWQPs) 
TCEQ recommends a definition be added to 40 CFR Section 141.2 for the term 
“optimal water quality parameters” to allow for standardization of the term, and 
to consider TCEQ’s recommended definition. Currently the term is noted more 
than 10 different ways within rule language, without being clearly defined. 
Definition of and consistent use of the term will ensure systems and primacy 
agencies are clear on specific citations related to OWQPs and their associated 
obligations. TCEQ’s recommendation for the definition is underlined as follows:  

“Optimal water quality parameters (OWQPs) for the purpose of subpart I of this 
part only, means water quality parameters reflecting optimal corrosion control 
treatment that is approved or specified by the state.” 
TCEQ recommends that additional information be provided on Step 6 described 
in 40 CFR Section 141.82(j)(6). Current language does not indicate a timeline for 
water systems to submit OWQP recommendations to the state. TCEQ 
recommends sampling results and corresponding recommendations be 
submitted to the state within six months of completing the requirements of Step 
6 described in 40 CFR Section 141.82(j)(6). 
D. Distribution System and Site Assessment 
TCEQ recommends that additional information be provided on Step 3 described 
in 40 CFR Section 141.82(j)(3) regarding the Distribution System and Site 
Assessment (DSSA). Current language does not address how this step and 
subsequent steps apply to systems with no existing CCT. TCEQ recommends 
EPA revise this portion of the rule to acknowledge that site specific actions, 
beyond installing CCT, are available to systems which trigger the DSSA but do 
not currently utilize CCT.  
E. Replacement Program Year 
TCEQ recommends that EPA define “program year” as it relates to the 
mandatory service line replacement schedule within 40 CFR Section 141.84 and 
40 CFR Section 141.90, and consider TCEQ’s suggestion for a definition. TCEQ 
suggests defining “program year” as the 12-month period that starts from the 
promulgation of the final rule. This will allow the inventory updates to be made 
at the same time as the replacement rates are being calculated. Such a revision 
would streamline activities by both the state and systems.  
F. Sample Collection Methods 
TCEQ recommends revising language in 40 CFR Section 141.86(b)(1) to specify 
the maximum amount of time water can stagnate before sampling. Current 
language does not encourage best management practices by residents, 
especially when combined with the requirement that “if a system allows 
residents to perform sampling, the system cannot challenge the accuracy of 
sampling results based on alleged sample collection errors.” If residents are 
expected to collect samples properly, additional information must be provided 
to ensure their success. TCEQ’s recommended revision is underlined below:  
“Sample collection instructions provided to customers cannot direct the 
customer to remove or clean the aerator or flush taps prior to the start of the 
minimum six-hour (not to exceed 24 hours) stagnation period.” 
TCEQ recommends allowing preapproved backup sites within tiered categories. 
40 CFR Section 141.86(b)(2) sets requirements for water systems to collect 
samples from the same sampling sites in consecutive monitoring periods. With 
property ownership changes or current residents being unwilling to continue to 
participate, TCEQ recommends that the rule be revised to allow systems to 
request preapproved backup sites within each tiering category. 
 

G. Standard Monitoring 
TCEQ requests EPA allow certain water systems to continue tap monitoring 
schedules under certain conditions. The requirement within 40 CFR Section 
141.86(c)(2)(i) for all systems with lead, galvanized requiring replacement, 
and/or lead status unknown service lines to begin standard tap monitoring 
poses a burden on laboratories and may lead to the potential exceedance of 
laboratory capacity. Increased sample frequency, combined with increased 
sampling requirements (i.e., 1st and 5th liter sampling) creates an increased 
workload for laboratories and demand for limited supplies. TCEQ requests EPA 
allow water systems currently on reduced monitoring to continue that schedule, 
unless increased monitoring is prompted by objective events (e.g., due to an 
ALE, change in source, change in treatment, etc.). This change will enable 
laboratories to accommodate the rule modifications without outpacing the 
ability to expand capacity and allow systems to concentrate efforts on sampling 
warranted through objective evidence.  
H. Seasonal Sampling 
TCEQ requests revising proposed language for seasonal sampling, and to 
consider TCEQ’s recommendation to increase clarity. TCEQ finds the proposed 
language in 40 CFR Section 141.86(d)(3)(iii), which allows states flexibility in 
seasonal sampling, to be unnecessarily long and confusing. TCEQ recommends 
the entire citation be revised as follows: 
“Systems who alter the seasonality of their reduced sampling period must 
receive written pre-approval by the State. Sampling for the approved period 
must be completed during the next scheduled sampling period.” 
I. 90th Percentile Calculations 
TCEQ recommends revising 40 CFR Section 141.80(c)(3)(i)(A) to clarify that 
concentrations of lead and copper are treated separately when ranking sites for 
calculation of 90th percentile concentrations. These revisions can be simply 
made adding the word “respectively” at the end of the first and second 
sentence. Proposed language is underlined below:  
“The results of all lead or copper samples taken during a tap sampling period 
must be placed in ascending order from the sample with the lowest 
concentration of lead or copper to the sample with the highest concentration of 
lead or copper, respectively. Each sampling result must be assigned a number, 
in ascending order beginning with the number 1 for the sample with the lowest 
concentration of lead or copper, respectively. The number assigned to the 
sample with the highest concentration level must be equal to the total number 
of samples taken.” 
TCEQ requests EPA provide options for systems who have locations served by lead 
lines, but whose residents are unwilling to participate in sampling. The 
requirement for systems with enough Tier 1 or Tier 2 service lines in their 
inventory to meet their minimum sampling requirements to only use these sites 
for calculating their 90th percentile is overly burdensome for systems. It is 
often a challenge for water systems to find homeowners/residents who are 
willing to participate in sampling. TCEQ requests EPA provide options for 

systems who have locations served by lead lines, but whose residents are 
unwilling to participate in sampling. 
J. Typographical Error 
TCEQ requests EPA correct typographical errors with certain tables. The table 
referenced in the narrative of 40 CFR Section 141.87 is Table 5, while the Table 
provided is labeled “Table 1.” TCEQ requests EPA correct this typographical 
error. 
K. Implementation Dates 
TCEQ requests EPA review compliance dates within the LCRI, in order to ensure 
dates are consistent and implementation is achievable. Several provisions in the 
proposed LCRI reference implementation prior to the LCRI compliance date in 
the rule narrative, but are not cited for earlier implementation. For example, 
inclusion of written service line inventory statements in the Consumer 
Confidence Report (40 CFR Section 141.153(d)(4)(xi)) and Tier 2 lead public 
education requirements (40 CFR Section 141.85(a)(1)(ii)) are not included in 40 
CFR Section 141.80(a)(4). TCEQ requests EPA review if these citations should be 
included within the 40 CFR Section 141.80(a)(4) language for implementation 
prior to the LCRI compliance date. Consistency is needed between the rule 
narrative and associated citations. 
 
V. Request for Additional Information 
TCEQ is concerned that several areas of the proposed LCRI do not contain sufficient 
information for understanding subsequent implementation. TCEQ requests EPA 
provide additional information in the following areas: 
A. Service Line Replacement 
TCEQ requests additional and updated information on the definition of “service 
line” as proposed in 40 CFR Section 141.2 Definitions, in order to account for 
EPA’s alternative configurations provided in guidance. In EPA’s guidance 
document “Developing and Maintaining a Service Line Inventory: Small Entity 
Compliance Guide” (https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-
06/Final%20Small%20System%20Entity%20Inventory%20Guide_508.pdf), exhibits 
3 and 4 (pages 7 and 8 of the document) illustrate examples of service line 
configurations for community water systems and non-transient non-community 
water systems. However, these configurations do not conform with the 
definition “…a portion of pipe which connects the water main to the building 
inlet…” in the proposed rule. TCEQ requests the definition of a service line be 
updated to account for EPA’s alternative configurations. 
B. Corrosion Control Treatment  
TCEQ requests that EPA provide additional information to clarify inconsistent 
requirements. TCEQ also requests that EPA remove the requirement for a system 
to establish OWQP ranges in response to a DSSA, and instead allow the system to 
correct the issue on a site-specific basis. 40 CFR Section 141.81(a)(2)(ii) 
establishes requirements for medium sized systems to set OWQP ranges when a 
system exceeds the practical quantitation limit (PQL). 40 CFR Section 141.82(j) 

requires systems to also set OWQP ranges as part of the DSSA. Requiring 
establishment of OWQP ranges in response to a DSSA is not consistent with the 
requirement to establish those ranges in response to a 90th percentile result 
exceeding the PQL. The requirement in 40 CFR Section 141.81(a)(2)(ii) is based 
on a system’s entire set of tap sample data, while a DSSA is triggered by a single 
data point. Additional information is needed to clarify these requirements and 
reconcile these inconsistencies. TCEQ request that EPA remove the requirement 
for a system to establish OWQP ranges in response to a DSSA, and instead allow 
the system to correct the issue on a site-specific basis. 
TCEQ requests additional information on the timelines outlined under 40 CFR 
Section 141.81(e)(2). Specifically, TCEQ requests that EPA include additional 
information on the following: 
• 
40 CFR Section 141.81(e)(2) Step 2 states, “within one year after the end 
of the tap sampling period during which a water system exceeds the lead 
or copper action level….” TCEQ requests EPA provide additional 
information if this refers to the timeframe in which water systems must 
perform corrosion control activities, or the timeframe in which the state 
must notify them of the requirement.  
• 
40 CFR Section 141.81(e)(3)(ii) states, “the water system must complete 
the studies […] and recommend OCCT within 18 months after the end of 
the tap sampling period during which it exceeds the lead or copper action 
level, or the State notifies the system in writing that such studies must be 
conducted.” TCEQ requests EPA provide additional information on which 
timeline takes precedence: the tap sampling period, or the date the state 
notifies the system. 
C. Sample Site Tiering Criteria 
TCEQ requests additional information regarding the new sample site tiering 
criteria. Specifically, regarding the following items: 
• 
40 CFR Section 141.86(a)(4)(i) amends the definition of a Tier 1 sample 
site to include premise plumbing made of lead. While 40 CFR Section 
141.84 describes the steps to verify/validate service line materials, EPA 
must provide additional information on what is needed to document 
verification of premise plumbing material.  
• 
40 CFR Section 141.86(a)(4)(iv) Tier 4 references sites served by copper 
lines with lead solder but does not discuss premise plumbing which was 
proposed in the criteria outlined for Tier 1, 2, and 3 sites. TCEQ requests 
EPA not include premise plumbing in the site tiering criteria, but if 
retained, TCEQ requests that language regarding premise plumbing be 
included consistently across all tiers. 
D. Service Line Inventory 
TCEQ requests additional information on what constitutes a “two point 
verification” as referenced in 40 CFR Section 141.84(b)(5)(i). Specifically, TCEQ 
asks if a visual investigation in the meter pit, examining the material of the 
system portion of the service line, as well as the material of the customer owned 
portion of the service line constitutes a two-point verification. 

 
E. Reduced Monitoring 
TCEQ requests EPA provide additional information and maintain the current 
pathway for systems to qualify for reduced tap monitoring. The pathway(s) 
described in 40 CFR Section 141.86(d)(2) for systems to qualify for reduced 
annual and triennial tap monitoring contradict each other and are unclear. The 
pathway from initial six-month, non-action level exceedance six-month/annual, 
action level exceedance six-month to annual and after installation of optimal 
corrosion control treatment unnecessarily adds complexity to an already 
complex rule and stands to only confuse systems.   
F. 90th Percentile Calculations 
TCEQ requests additional information to clarify 40 CFR Section 141.86(e), 
pertaining to the number and tiering of samples used to calculate the 90th 
percentile lead and/or copper levels for systems with lead service lines (LSLs). 
Additional information is needed to clarify this section, in order to improve the 
assessment of corrosion control treatment efficacy. Specifically, more 
information is needed to determine whether samples from non-LSL sites that 
have higher lead concentrations (rather than samples from LSL sites), should be 
included in the 90th percentile calculation; and whether these higher values 
should replace lower values from LSL sites in the 90th percentile 
calculation. TCEQ requests that EPA specify the highest values, regardless of 
location tier, be used. 
G. Alternative School and Child Care Lead Sampling Programs 
TCEQ requests additional information regarding the requirements of 40 CFR 
Section 141.92(h)(1)(v), and consider TCEQ’s request to retain the existing schema 
in grant programs. Specifically, TCEQ asks whether the frequency and protocol 
of outlets described in 40 CFR Section 141.92(f) are required for sampling under 
a WIIN grant awarded in accordance with Section 1464(d) of the SDWA, or if 
grant programs may retain their existing sampling schema. TCEQ requests grant 
programs retain their existing schema.  
TCEQ requests EPA provide flexibility for water systems to re-apply when waivers 
expire. 40 CFR Section 141.92(h)(2) describes criteria that would cause lead 
testing in school and child care facility waivers to expire. Current language is 
not clear as to whether a water system could re-apply for, and be granted, 
another waiver once a waiver has expired. TCEQ requests allowing systems the 
ability to reapply to encourage mutually beneficial relationships with state’s 
voluntary Lead Testing in Schools and Child Care Facilities programs.

Re:  Comments to National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (Docket

Dear Mr. Goldberg, 
The Suffolk County Water Authority (SCWA) is pleased to present our comments on the above referenced 
Federal LCRI regulation. As the largest water supplier on Long Island, serving over 1.2 million people, we are 
pleased to see that the EPA, through these regulatory changes, is making improvements and attempting to 
streamline what was already a very complex rule (the LCRR). We are concerned however, that some of the 
details of these changes may have the unintended consequences of undermining confidence in the water supply 
and those on the front lines that work tirelessly to uphold that confidence. While our comments are unique to our 
utility, through our contacts with other suppliers and those within our industry, we recognize that this rule and 
the implementation of it will have vastly different impacts on suppliers based upon their size, the age of their 
infrastructure and the economic circumstances of their customer base. It is because of this that we urge the EPA 
to exercise caution in the rule making process as one size clearly does not fit all. We remain confident however, 
that if thoughtfully crafted, this rule can have a profound impact on the quality of our nations drinking water.  
We have carefully reviewed the proposed regulations and offer the following comments and recommendations: 
 
Service Line Inventories 
 
- 
EPA was looking for comments on the requirement to document all previously replaced LSLs and 
connectors. It is not feasible for SCWA as we have only partial paper records of these previous activities. 
 
- 
In the SCWA service territory we have over one thousand private communities with private distribution 
networks and service lines. The community water supply (CWS) should not be responsible for inventorying 
private piping networks and service lines on the customer side of master meters. 
 
- 
Remove fire service lines from inventory and replacement requirements providing there is a clear safeguard 
to prevent potable use of them. 
 
SUFFOLK COUNTY WATER AUTHORITY 
Joseph M. Pokorny, P.E. 
Deputy CEO for Operations  
4060 Sunrise Highway, Oakdale, New York 11769
(631) 563-0202
Fax:  (631) 563-0358

 
 
 
 
 
- 
Since records for connectors and their length are very limited and since the rule requires them to be changed 
out when they are encountered, there seems to be little benefit to inventorying them. Our suggestion would 
be to remove any requirement to inventorying connectors.  
 
- 
The as-drafted rule language to include connectors in the inventory does not align with the past inventory 
requirements. As such, water utilities that have expended significant efforts to complete their inventories 
may not have collected the service line connection data in a manner that complies with the proposed 
regulatory requirement. Furthermore, the distinction between “never lead” and “no connector” is unclear, as 
copper services do not have connectors, and thus are both. Significant rework is likely required for those who 
proactively began their inventory. 
 
Service Line Replacement 
 
- 
The LCRI maintains the requirement that when replacing a connector, the customer is notified, provided 
educational materials and a pitcher with 6 months of cartridges. This is onerous especially when SCWA 
performs main replacements. Entire streets and all the homes could require pitchers. In a system such as the 
SCWA, where there has never been a documented exceedance, a better approach would be to provide 
educational materials to the homeowner related to flushing of their service lines after construction has been 
complete and flushing stagnant water from their service line as a matter of routine practice for some period 
of time following a main replacement project or a simple connector replacement. 
   
- 
What happens if a connector is disturbed or replaced during an emergency or main break at night? Is the  a 
supplier expected to wake customers and provide them with pitchers? This is not practical. How does the 
EPA envision this being managed? 
 
- 
The LCRI indicates that the simple disturbance of a lead connector the replacement of a meter or meter 
setting on a galvanized service line with a lead connector will require the provision of a filter and educational 
materials to the customer? As is above, this provision seems onerous and should be replaced with the 
requirement to simply provide educational materials. 
   
- 
Like much of the rest of the country, many SCWA customers already have refrigerator filters that meet 
NSF/ANSI 53 requirements and will not want pitchers in their refrigerators. If the EPA determines that there 
are circumstances where pitchers are required to be distributed, why not offer an alternative to a pitcher for 
these customers such as a credit on their water bill for replacement refrigerator cartridges in lieu of a pitcher? 
 
- 
The minimum average annual lead service line replacement rate is calculated by counting the number of 
replaced service lines divided by the “replacement pool.” However, a Utility that is acting in good faith to 
comply with the rule could identify large quantities of unknown service lines as non-lead, which would not 
contribute towards the calculated compliance percentage. This could result in the rolling average for 
replacements dropping below compliance through no fault of the utility and despite progress identifying 
unknowns. 
 
Action Level and Trigger Level 
 
- 
We appreciate the efforts of the EPA to simplify compliance with the LCRI. The use of a single 0.010 mg/L 
action level, rather than using an action level and a separate trigger level, improves the rule by reducing 
complexity. 
 
Lead and Copper Tap Monitoring 
 
- 
A three day turn around on notification of sample results to customers is unreasonable. The SCWA 
anticipates that due to laboratory internal processes, working hours and staffing, we will need more time and 
flexibility in the method of notification. A more realistic approach would be to allow for 3 to 5 business days 
for the notification of sample results. We believe this is an acceptable alternative as there is little, short-term 
threat to the public. 
  

 
 
 
 
 
- 
It is unclear whether supplemental and “distribution system and site assessment” samples count toward the 
90th percentile calculations. This should be clarified. 
 
- 
The LCRI includes several instances where the CWS is assumed to know the premise plumbing material in 
consumer’s homes. This is included in revisions to sampling sites, “EPA is proposing to correct the 
definition for Tier 1 and Tier 2 sites to include sites with premise plumbing made of lead due to the high risk 
of lead exposure associated with premise plumbing made of lead.” Requiring utilities and/or water suppliers 
to enter consumer’s homes to identify pipe material extends likely extends beyond their authority and would 
be difficult, or impossible, to comply with. 
- 
Aligned with the previous comment, the LCRI does not provide instruction regarding how water systems 
would continue to sample after lead and galvanized requiring replacement (GRR) service lines are replaced. 
Would only samples with homes where the pipe materials are confirmed as lead or galvanized only be used 
for premise plumbing material? 
 
Corrosion Control (CCT) and Water Quality Parameters (WQPs) 
 
- 
We are pleased to see that EPA is providing suppliers more latitude with respect to requiring reoptimization 
of previously OCCT in the event of an exceedance. We feel strongly that systems that have voluntarily 
optimized their corrosion control treatment and demonstrated 90th percentile lead concentrations below 
0.005 mg/L should be recognized and given the opportunity to have an extended schedule for identifying 
unknowns and service line replacement.  
 
Public Education and Outreach 
 
- 
Public education and notification efforts required to comply will be significant. More should be done to 
streamline and reduce this burden. 
 
- 
The rule does not provide guidance or instruction related to sample delivery other than postal mail. Many 
utilities and water suppliers find mail an unreliable method to effectively delivering communications and 
information to their customers and consumers. Sample result delivery options such as customer emails or text 
messaging should be allowed. Water utilities have found these methods to be more effective at delivering 
information and are often preferred by consumers. 
 
- 
Hard copy mailings of results should be limited to samples that exceed the lead action level to prevent 
overwhelming consumers with frequent mailings. Notification of other sample results should be made 
available through other means as mentioned above. 
 
Public Notification 
 
- 
Requiring annual notification of customers served by a lead connector is excessive. Requiring notification for 
unknown service materials is also unreasonable. This is because all customers are exposed to lead and copper 
from their homes plumbing system (especially those with lead solder plumbing) a better approach would be 
to educate all customers on methods they can take to reduce their lead exposure. The record keeping and 
systems needed to notify a select group of customers would be more complicated than simply delivering 
educational information to all customers on an annual basis. 
   
- 
Requirement to notify all customers when AL is exceeded in a system like SCWA’s is unreasonable. SCWA 
has over 40 pressure zones and 250 entry points. A localized lead and copper problem should not require 
notification of every customer.  
  
- 
Providing pitchers to every household after three AL exceedances is excessive. The SCWA has thirty plus 
years of LCR data showing our CCT works for households without LSLs or GRRs. Pitchers should only be 
offered to households with lead service lines of galvanized lines requiring replacement.  
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Lead in Schools and Childcare Facilities 
 
- 
Within the text of the LCRI, the EPA acknowledges that States are better prepared to apply for and receive 
funding for programs that impact these facilities. In addition, the rule encourages states to develop their own 
testing programs for these facilities. Why burden water suppliers with this requirement especially when the 
rule only covers facilities served by the CWS. In our service territory, there are many of these facilities that 
operate their own water supply systems and as a result, those facilities would have their testing performed 
and reported through some other mechanism. This will bifurcation of sampling and reporting can only lead to 
regulatory confusion. 
 
- 
It is our understanding that Schools and Day Care Facilities are beyond EPA’s authority. As such, how can 
these regulations apply to these facilities? 
 
The Suffolk County Water Authority appreciates that we have been given the opportunity to comment on this 
proposed rule. We appreciate your attention to these important matters and the opportunity to provide our input.  
We strongly encourage the development of regulations that strike a balance between protecting public health and 
the practical challenges faced by us. 
 
Thank you for your time and consideration. We look forward to continued collaboration and the opportunity to 
contribute to the development of effective and scientifically lead and copper rule regulations. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Joseph M. Pokorny P.E 
Deputy CEO for Operations
