Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
RE: Comments by the Corix on EPA National Primary Drinking Water Proposed Regulations for Lead and 
Copper Improvements; Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801.   
 
 
Corix Infrastructure Inc., (Corix) on behalf of itself and its operating subsidiaries, respectfully submits 
this comment letter regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed National Primary 
Drinking Water Regulation Rulemaking published in the Federal Register on December 6, 2023, and 
referred to as the Lead and Cooper Rule Improvements (LCRI).   
 
Through its operating subsidiaries, Corix provides drinking water to approximately 800,000 people in 
18 states and two Canadian provinces. Corix is a member of the National Association of Water 
Companies (NAWC) and agrees with the NAWC in its support for the EPA taking action to the health risk 
posed by the presence of lead in drinking water supplies.  Corix supports EPA’s commitment in the 
proposed rule to improving public health and reducing lead exposures in drinking water by requiring the 
replacement of all lead service lines regardless of the lead levels occurring in taps. We believe that 
several important adjustments are necessary as discussed below to make implementation of the rule 
achievable and workable for water systems, without compromising the protections afforded to consumers 
under the proposed rule. 
 
Generally, it can be acknowledged that setting a standard does not protect public health. It is the 
implementation of the standard that does. The implementation must be feasible for water systems to 
adequately comply. The proposed LCRI addresses many concerns and confusion found in the LCRR, 
however it still has remaining requirements that are complex and overly burdensome with no clear sign 
those requirements address the risk posed to consumers.   
 
Corix works on a daily basis to protect our customers and communities by providing high quality 
drinking water that is compliant with the Safe Drinking Water Act.  Corix respectfully submits the following 
comments in response to the EPA’s request in addition to a request to review and revise elements of the 
proposed rulemaking to ensure the rule is feasible for all water providers. It is important that the EPA 
carefully tailors its approach to reducing the levels of lead in water supplies without imposing 
unnecessary costs and restrictions because the costs and the impacts of reducing the presence of lead in 
the water supply will be substantial and will place a heavy burden on communities, households and 
ratepayers at a time when other new regulatory measures addressing contaminations such as PFAS will 
be adding to the financial burden on communities. 
 
Corix urges the EPA to ensure that this rulemaking and other actions related to removing 
contaminants from the water supply treat all water systems be treated equally regardless of whether the 
systems are publicly or privately owned or operated.  All water providers should have equal access to any 
and all federal and state funding related to removing lead from the water network.  
 
 
Comments  

500 West Monroe Street, Suite 3600 
Chicago, Illinois  
USA 60661 
 
T 847.498.6440 
 
www.corix.com  
 
 
 
1. Most urgently, EPA must extend compliance deadlines under the LCRR so that water utilities can focus 
on the requirements of the LCRI.  
 
EPA’s proposal creates confusion about compliance deadlines under the LCRR due to the 
uncertainty of when the LCRI will be “promulgated.”  (88 Fed. Reg. 84881).  Even so, extended 
deadlines are necessary under the LCRR for several reasons.  CWS’s are now investing time and 
resources into programs that may be delayed or revised and efforts are better focused now on 
the requirements of the proposed LCRI.  Additionally, adding connectors to the inventory is 
problematic and will require more time because states do not have the connectors in the 
computer inventories for LCRR and water systems will need additional time to develop new ways 
to submit inventories compared to LCRR. 
  
 
2. The proposal to require water systems to replace service lines “under the control of the water system” 
should be changed to “owned by the water system.”  
 
EPA’s proposal to require water systems to replace service lines “under the control of water 
systems” is vague and subject to different interpretations.  EPA states that it intends to treat a line 
as under the control of a water system “whenever a water system has adequate access” to 
conduct replacement but declines to delineate the prerequisites or elements of access.  (88 Fed. 
Reg. 84920).  “Adequate access” is too vague a standard for regulated parties to know their 
requirements under the proposed rules.  Regulated parties need a clearer and predictable 
standard to make important decisions regarding access.  Corix proposes that a better, clearer 
standard for which lines are to be replaced would be when the lines are “owned by the water 
system.”  This standard is clear, predictable and allows the regulated parties to understand the 
regulatory requirements. 
 
3. The service line replacement rate requiring ten percent (10%) of service lines of unknown composition is 
not feasible due to the expected large number of lines of unknown composition.  An approach that 
requires 10% of known lead lines first, followed by 10% of unknown lines is preferable.  
 
EPA’s proposed approach to identify and replace service lines of unknown composition in parallel 
with the replacement of known service lines.  EPA states it is proposing to consolidate these 
deadlines for identifying all lead status unknown service lines and replacing all LSLs and GRR 
service lines.  (88 Fed. Reg. 84934).  This approach would pose implementation difficulties 
because it is expected that there will be large number of lines of unknown composition and doing 
both replacements simultaneously would present an unreasonable burden on water systems and 
further stretch limited labor and material resources.  Focusing on each category individually would 
allow water systems to set realistic and achievable goals for replacement and at the same time 
reduce the number of unknown service lines.  
 
 
4. EPA’s proposed approaches present difficult implementation issues and rely too heavily on homeowners 
or residents to collect data and grant access.  
 
Several of the approaches EPA proposes rely heavily on homeowners or residents to achieve the 
goals of the proposed approach.  EPA’s updated tap sampling protocols, for example, rely on 
homeowners or residents to fill five (5) liter bottles and maintain them in a certain order, which will 
almost certainly lead to some confusion and inaccurate results.   
 
It is an ongoing challenge in every Corix facility, even with ongoing education and incentives, to 
get customer participation and the additional demands on the customer for sampling which, in 

500 West Monroe Street, Suite 3600 
Chicago, Illinois  
USA 60661 
 
T 847.498.6440 
 
www.corix.com  
 
 
addition to causing confusion, may place a strain on customer relations, and will pose even 
greater challenges in complying with the proposed sampling requirements. EPA needs to 
consider other approaches for the tap sampling such as requiring the use of a timed approach for 
sampling.   
 
EPA also needs to define the following terms: customer; consumer; resident; and non-owner 
resident – and be careful in their use.  The LCRI should not require notification to an owner of a 
property since water systems may not have that information. 
 
 
5. EPA’s proposed approach should recognize the limits of the authority of private water companies to carry 
out replacement programs and inventories in some instances when local authorities refuse to provide 
access.  
 
Because private water companies do not own or manage the streets where their water mains are 
located, they may be prevented by local laws or authorities from conducting the actions required 
under the LCRI.  EPA must recognize this issue and state its intention not to penalize private 
water companies when those companies are prevented by local governments from taking actions 
to comply with the LCRI.   For the same reason, EPA’s proposal to add connectors to the 
inventory requirement is problematic because some communities will not permit private water 
companies to dig up street to determine whether connectors are present. 
 
In addition, not every property owner may be amenable to replacing a service line, even when the 
water system bears partial or full cost. In many states, water systems do not have legal authority 
to access private property without the owner’s permission and lack clear authority to spend 
ratepayer funds to remove lines on private property. In other places, water systems will face 
logistical challenges as they coordinate lead service line replacement with street improvement 
projects or incorporate it into large capital projects. Lining up trained contractors in a tight labor 
market and acquiring necessary materials introduces additional complications.  
 
Corix requests that EPA provide more guidance on how to access private property and allow 
flexibility to meeting replacement deadlines when constraints beyond the control of the water 
system (e.g. access to property, available skilled labor or necessary materials) are present. 
 
 
6. EPAs proposed requirement to publish the replacement plan should be clarified to reduce confusion and 
promote education to the consumer. 
 
The replacement plan is constructed and built to be an internal planning document that is shared 
with and approved by the state. Without context and training, the material is very likely to cause 
confusion with the customer and potential frustrations in how the plan is being implemented. The 
proposed CCR requirement to publish information about the availability and description of the 
replacement plan could be modified to ensure relevant and necessary information is provided to 
consumers in an easily understood format, without having the need to provide a more technical 
document to the customers, which may not serve the purpose of customer education as intended. 
 
7. EPA’s proposed requirement for water systems must deliver consumer notice of lead and copper tap 
sampling results to consumers whose tap was sampled as soon as practicable but no later than 3 days 
after receiving the results creates unnecessary burden to the water system without reducing risk to 
consumers. 
 
Corix agrees that the requirement to send results to customers is essential to reduce the potential 
health risk of consuming lead in drinking water. However, if there is no risk (e.g., there is no 
detects) or very minimal risk (low copper levels) then the 3-day requirement would not serve the 

500 West Monroe Street, Suite 3600 
Chicago, Illinois  
USA 60661 
 
T 847.498.6440 
 
www.corix.com  
 
 
purposes as intended by EPA and would only add additional administrative burden to water 
systems. Corix proposes the proposed rule be modified to allow more time to send the 
information where there is no lead detection.  
 
8. EPA’s proposed requirement that water systems with multiple lead action level exceedances (at least 3 
action level exceedances in a 5-year period) must conduct additional public outreach activities, submit a 
filter plan to the State and make filters available to all consumers should be reconsidered or modified. 
 
The 3-action level exceedance over a 5-year period measurement is not a true representation of 
risk and the associated requirements are unnecessary.  The number of exceedances should be 
based on the number of customers.   If this requirement is included in the final rule, then Corix 
proposes that filters be provided only to consumers that may be exposed to lead, those 
downstream from the lead exceedance.  
 
9. EPA’s proposed requirement that water systems validate the accuracy of the non-lead service line 
category in their inventory no later than 7 years after the compliance date should be clarified, as it could 
cause confusion and potentially non-productive efforts. 
 
The proposed rule requires that all service lines be identified by the deadline of the replacement 
(10 years after the rule is finalized). It is not clear how the 7-year validation requirement would 
apply in cases where a significant number of unknown lines remain and if, in that case, the efforts 
would serve the stated purpose of the validation activity.  
 
States are providing guidance on what information and efforts are acceptable with regards to 
determining material of service lines.  Validation efforts should not be required where there is no 
risk of lead lines, particularly where there is evidence that the building was built after the state 
implementation of the Federal Lead Line ban of 1986.  
 
In addition, and potentially most burdensome, validation efforts such as potholing would trigger 
the proposed addition of notification and filter distribution under the expanded definition of 
disturbance with “inventorying efforts”. Where water systems have reduced capacity to complete 
identification of unknown service lines before the 7-year deadline to validate non-lead service 
lines, this would create a significant and potentially untenable burden to notify and provide filters 
to customers as validation efforts are underway. The inventorying efforts should not be included 
in the definition of ‘disturbance’ that triggers notification and filter distribution and/or clarification is 
needed on how this cyclical process is to be handled that will not overwhelm water system 
resources.    
 
Conclusion 
 
Corix appreciate EPA’s efforts to protect public health and the environment from the harmful impacts 
of lead in drinking water that poses a risk to many individuals.  We support EPA’s proposal requiring the 
replacement of all lead service lines regardless of the lead levels occurring in taps but urge EPA to 
consider these comments to ensure that the agency produces a rule that is protective, feasible and 
affordable.   
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Kendra Rose 
Director, Health, Safety & Environment

COMMENTS OF THE LABORERS’ INTERNATIONAL UNION OF NORTH 
AMERICA ON THE ENVIRONMENTAL PROTECTION AGENCY’S PROPOSED 
NATIONAL PRIMARY DRINKING WATER REGULATIONS FOR LEAD AND 
COPPER: IMPROVEMENTS (LCRI) 
 
Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
On behalf of the more than 500,000 members of the Laborers’ International Union of 
North America (“LIUNA”), we submit these comments in support of the Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) proposal to reduce copper and lead exposure in drinking water, 
both for our members who are affected and the communities that they serve.1 The EPA’s 
proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (“LCRI”) will protect children and adults from 
lead contamination in drinking water with the ultimate goal of 100% lead service line (“LSL”) 
replacement within the next 10 years. This aggressive goal will not only accelerate local lead line 
replacement programs, but will also provide valuable job opportunities for LIUNA members 
who are trained for this work. We encourage the implementation of these changes as quickly as 
possible, and we support the EPA and Biden Administration in making lead abatement a top 
public health priority. 
 
LIUNA SUPPORTS THE REDUCED ACTIONABLE LEVEL FOR LEAD 
REPLACEMENT AND THE TEN-YEAR REPLACEMENT REQUIREMENT 
 
LIUNA supports the EPA proposal to lower the lead action level from 0.15mg/L to 0.010 
mg/L as it will ensure that we are setting a higher standard for what we allow in our 
communities’ drinking water. EPA Administrator Michael S. Regan has plainly stated, “There is 
no safe level of exposure to lead.”2 Even at low levels, lead particles in the environment can 
cause developmental delays and other health issues to our nation’s children. The negative effects 
of lead in drinking water on overall health are well known. Small children and pregnant women 
are especially at risk of being harmed by lead exposure from water lines. Permanent cognitive 
                                                
1 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Cooper: Improvements (LCRI), 88 Fed. Reg. 84878

2 U.S. Envtl. Protection Agency, EPA and HHS Encourage States to Utilize Federal Resources for Lead Detection 
and Mitigation in Early Care and Education Settings, (Mar. 28, 2023).

impairment and cancer have been linked to overexposure to lead particles.34 Additionally, there 
are significant health and safety concerns in the handling of LSLs for the workers involved in 
pipe replacement activities.5 
Protecting LIUNA members who reside in areas with lead lines, as well as everyone in 
the communities they serve, is a priority for our union. The available data on lead service line 
inventories are notably incomplete and state-by-state LSL estimates vary significantly – a gap 
which this proposed rule intends in part to remedy.6 Nonetheless, we know the number of union 
Laborers directly affected by LSLs is significant. The EPA’s 2021 needs assessment survey 
produced an estimate of 9.2 million lead service lines.7 This number is consistent with an earlier 
survey conducted by the National Resources Defense Council (“NRDC”) which arrived at an 
estimated range of 9.7 million to 12.8 million LSLs, albeit with significant differences in 
respective state-by-state numbers.8 There are a combined thirteen states that appear on one or 
both of the EPA and NRDC “top ten” lists for existing LSLs inventory estimates.9 In these 
thirteen states, LIUNA represents 189,663 active members.10 Given the direct consequences to 
our members, we support all reasonable efforts to address the health threat caused by lead 
contamination in drinking water.

LIUNA supports complete lead service line removal as the preferred public health 
strategy to reduce lead exposure in drinking water. Determining lead levels in household 
drinking water remains difficult and imprecise. Removing lead lines remains the safest and surest 
method to eliminate the risk of lead exposure from this source. EPA’s proposed ten-year 
requirement for water systems to remove lead lines is an appropriately aggressive yet practical 
goal. As EPA notes in its preamble, there are numerous examples of water systems that have 
successfully implemented LSL replacement programs with aggressive timelines and exceptional 
results. 88 Fed. Reg. 84911-84913. Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, and Rhode Island have 
required replacement of LSLs through state law, and the latter two states require systems to 
conduct such replacements in ten years unless granted an extension. The proposed rule is 
therefore consistent with the trend in legislative action among states with the highest lead line 
inventories.  
The feasibility of implementing a complete removal of LSLs in ten years is evidenced in 
part by the individual systems that have successfully undertaken removal programs. EPA offers 
notable examples of water systems that have replaced LSLs in a ten-year window. The large 
systems that responded to crises – Newark, New Jersey and Flint, Michigan – have successfully 
removed nearly all of the lead lines in their systems, in four years and seven years, respectively. 
During its peak, Newark replaced several hundred lines per day for 4-5 days per week. Other 
systems that took leadership on lead include Madison, Wisconsin and Lansing, Michigan, which 
successfully inventoried lead lines, developed a program, and successfully contracted the work 
for thousands of LSL in just over a ten-year period (11 and 12 years, respectively). 88 Fed. Reg. 
84912.  
LIUNA has been at the forefront of lead service removal across the country. On nearly all 
of the water system examples of successful LSL programs described in the NPRM, the relevant 
construction work was performed predominately or exclusively by union craft labor. Each 
residential LSL replacement project is generally performed by a composite construction crew 
comprised of Laborers and other crafts. In Newark, New Jersey and Flint, Michigan, local 
LIUNA leaders established job pathways for local workers that included training programs for 
the applicable skills need to perform underground and pipelaying activities for LSL, as well as 

4 
 
health and safety instruction related to the work.11 12 In Milwaukee, LIUNA Local 113’s 
apprenticeship program was incredibly successful in generating interest in LSL removal and 
prepared a well-trained workforce ready to implement the program rapidly.13 This collaboration 
with employers and water systems to train and employ Laborers to replace LSLs continues in St. 
Paul, Minnesota where its Regional Water Services (SPRWS) is implementing its portion of 
$240 million in the state’s dedicated LSL funding by partnering with LIUNA Local 363 on a 
training program tailored for entry-level jobseekers.14 In Wassau, Wisconsin the city recently 
entered a public-private partnership to remove approximately 8,000 lead lines from its system. 
Wassau’s collaboration includes LIUNA’s national training program to address contractor 
capacity issues and ensure an adequate local and skilled workforce to replace LSLs.15

PROGRAMS

and have access to common curricula covering the broad range of tasks performed by 
construction laborers. The requisite skills required for LSL replacement include pipelaying 
basics, OSHA safety training, and in some cases lead awareness. These classes are commonly

public health crisis. Numerous water systems have demonstrated the EPA’s proposed timelines 
are feasible at both the small and large-scale system level. LIUNA’s own experience in this

I am writing on behalf of the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments (COG) Chesapeake 
Bay and Water Resources Policy Committee (CBPC) to provide our committee’s comments on the 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI). 
COG is a nonprofit association, with a membership of 300 elected officials from 24 local 
governments, the Maryland and Virginia state legislatures, and U.S. Congress. Every month, more 
than 1,500 officials and experts connect through COG to develop solutions to the region’s major 
challenges and plan for the future. Established in 1998, the CBPC is comprised of local elected 
officials and representatives from COG's member governments and water and wastewater utilities in 
the metropolitan Washington region. The CBPC recommends water resources policies to the COG 
Board of Directors, addressing issues related to water and wastewater treatment, local water quality, 
stormwater management, flooding, and more.

government, including strong support for environmental regulations based on sound science and 
equity. We share the same goal as EPA to ensure the delivery of clean, safe drinking water to the 
public. Considering the continuing challenges of lead in drinking water and the known human health 
effects, COG supports EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. COG believes 
wholeheartedly in EPA’s shared objective to swiftly identify, remove, and replace lead service lines 
with the ultimate goal of complete removal of all lead service lines. 
 
The replacement of lead service lines from the main, to the residence, including connectors such as 
goosenecks is vital to the success of this rule. Additionally, we believe that partial service line 
replacement must become a practice of the past and should be rectified under the revised LCRI.  
 
Changing the lead action level from 15 μg/L to 10 μg/L is an important step toward improving public 
health protections. Furthermore, COG is pleased with the increased public education and public 
notification (PE/PN) requirements. This component is essential for our residents to understand the 
rule and participate in our efforts to remove lead in drinking water.

To Whom it May Concern,
Save the Dunes, on behalf of itself and its members, strongly supports U.S. Environmental
Protection Agency’s (EPA) revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation
(NPDWR) for lead and copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA).
We support the agency requiring water systems to replace lead service lines, remove the lead
trigger level, reduce the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling
procedures. We also support the many other improvements to public health protection and
simplifications to the rules relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR).
Although our organization is grateful for these new changes, we also offer these changes in
addition to the rules. We recognize that even low levels of lead present a risk to our drinking
water and the public health, and request that the current level of remediation decrease from 10
ppb to 5 ppb. We also ask for the agency to establish more long-term multi-year grants that
focus on lead service line replacement, especially in smaller communities such as the ones in
our region of Northwest Indiana.
Due to the large amount of industrial activity in Northwest Indiana and our organization’s leading
role in creating a culture of pollution prevention in our region, we know with certainty that this
regulation is an absolute necessity to ensure environmental protections. We hope to see this
rule go into effect as soon as possible. We believe that this will address public health concerns
that affect our organization and our membership who live, work, and recreate in Northwest
Indiana. Thank you for considering these comments. If you have any questions, please contact
Advocacy Coordinator Harshini Ratnayaka at 219-879-3564 ext. 101 or
harshini@savedunes.org.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0925 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
February 5, 2024 
Michael S. Regan

1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W.

Administrator Regan, 
San Antonio Water System (SAWS) is grateful for the opportunity to comment on the proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). SAWS is, has been, and always will be an advocate for any rule or 
regulation that will provide the safest water to the community in the most cost-effective and affordable 
manner. SAWS stands with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in safeguarding our water quality 
and safety for future generations by updating necessary infrastructure. As one of the largest public water 
systems (PWS) in the country with over 650,000 service lines supplying over 2 million residents, we strive 
to be a leader in customer service and protection of public health.  
The new LCRI makes great strides in accomplishing its goals of a lead-free system, and many of the 
proposed rules not only put the health and safety of American citizens at the forefront, but also take into 
consideration some of the capabilities and limitations of the PWS.  
• 
The lowering of the lead action level to 10 ppb is a perfect example of finding a balance. This 
benchmark will improve the health and safety of the community while keeping the capabilities 
and limitations of a PWS in mind.  
• 
SAWS would also like to applaud the EPA for updating language throughout the LCRI; 
specifically, the change from “find-and-fix” to “distribution system and site assessment” due to 
its accurate depiction of the legal restraints on a PWS.  
• 
The clarity of street addresses to be included within the public facing inventory to make a 
consistent and transparent product for all PWS and their rate payers. 
• 
Including sampling waivers for school sampling taking place ahead of the proposed 2027 
deadline. This allows PWS and schools to be proactive with their programs to better ensure the 
water quality within their facilities. 
Although there are many proposed rules of which SAWS approves, there are also aspects that will inhibit 
the PWS and ultimately put rate payers at a financial disadvantage. The main topics of concern are listed 
below with specific examples from the SAWS inventory, current contracts, and real-world experiences 
within our distribution system. 
Feasibility of 10-year deadline and deferment eligibility categories 
SAWS has over 650,000 service connections within our system. The current estimation of unknown 
service lines categorized in our inventory is greater than 380,000. While the majority of the publicly 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
owned side is identified and has shown no presence of lead, there are many locations which will 
require investigations on both sides of the meter. 
Under the LCRI, SAWS will be faced with determining the material for all of these service lines within 
10 years. Over 50,000 inspections will need to be completed annually or approximately 150 
inspections every day. This effort would require at least five potholing crews working every day for 
this 10-year period. Additional staff will be needed to obtain right of entry to private property ahead 
of the potholing crews. Based on the disappointing customer participation SAWS has had to date, we 
do not anticipate we will be able to gain access at a rate to support 150 daily inspections.   
The customer participation rate is also an indicator that we will likely have low participation and 
willingness for private property owners to agree to replace their existing service lines if lead is found. 
Requiring investigation and assessment of private property service lines and saddling a PWS with 
responsibility for replacement of private service lines that are not within its control or ownership is 
inconsistent with the legal authority given to SAWS and creates an impossible and unrealistic burden. 
If EPA persists in the requirement for investigation of private service lines, each investigation will cost 
$2,000 on average taking into consideration all the above-mentioned tasks. This anticipated cost will 
ultimately be passed on to our customers and ratepayers within our service area in an estimated 
amount of $1 billion over 10 years. The considerable cost and practicality of having enough manpower 
and materials for this one daily task is unfeasible.  
EPA states that the 10-year deadline is feasible for 96-99% of the systems in the United States. In the 
proposed rule, the two categories eligible for deferred deadlines are supposed to encompass the less 
than 5% of systems not able to meet this deadline.  SAWS believes this is likely true but considers that 
systems with substantial unknowns also fall in the estimated 5%. SAWS strongly suggest another 
category for deferred deadline eligibility be created for systems with substantial unknowns. This 
would allow for systems of any size and situations to meet the compliance goals established in LCRI.   
Formal acceptance of predictive modeling by EPA 
In the validation pool section of the LCRI, EPA provides a pathway that would help validate 
alternative methods for determining service line material types. SAWS applauds EPA for taking a step 
in the right direction to make the strict LCRI timelines potentially feasible. However, the clarity of the 
methods that can be used prior to this validation step are vague. SAWS strongly encourages EPA to 
clearly support the use of predictive models. 
Prior to the inception of San Antonio Water System, an effort was made to remove all utility owned 
lead service lines in the distribution system. Through our records review and initial inspections, we 
have yet to uncover any documentation of a lead line within our system that has not already been 
replaced. While this effort was very successful in removing the lead within the SAWS system, its 
intent was not to record all pipe materials. This is a large data gap within the SAWS inventory leaving 
the system with the burden of proof. A predictive model is a cost-effective method to fill in these 
gaps. While the conditions of a predictive model should be carefully stipulated, the research supports 
it as a valuable statistical approach. 
In the case of SAWS, the application of predictive modeling to complete our non-lead service lines is 
the only feasible or economical way a 10-year inventory deadline may be reached. With over 380,000 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
unknowns in the SAWS service area, it has the potential to save the rate payers of San Antonio an 
estimated $800 million dollars. The primacy of the state agencies should be respected; however, a 
clear approval from the EPA will give state agencies the confidence to accept modeled inventory 
results. 
Separate Replacement Rate and Unknown Rate 
As it currently stands, SAWS has over 380,000 unknown service line material identifications. The 
previous section discussed the feasibility of uncovering these unknowns, but an additional factor is the 
use of these unknowns in the replacement rate calculation. This approach skews the required 
calculation by over-inflating the denominator. Per this calculation, SAWS would have to replace over 
38,000 complete services lines a year. At present, SAWS has no identified lead service lines that need 
to be replaced.  Nonetheless, the use of unknowns as a driver for replacement rates would require this 
excessively high number of line replacements when there is no supporting evidence that anywhere 
near that number of service lines require replacement.   
Aside from the lack of a tangible connection between unknowns and replacements, the negative 
impact of the current requirements is compounded because deferment of this requirement is not 
available despite the fact that the replacement rate value is greater than 10,000 lines. SAWS would not 
be eligible for deferment as these lines are unknown rather than lead service lines (LSL) or galvanized 
requiring replacement (GRR). Given how this calculation is currently completed, SAWS will be required 
to expend considerable time and resources to needlessly replace service lines in a futile effort to chase 
an unattainable goal.  
EPA should consider separate calculations for uncovering unknowns and replacement rates. The latter 
should be calculated annually from those lines with known material to give PWS a potentially 
achievable goal. Including unknown service lines does not incentivize larger PWS, but instead further 
diminishes our resources to complete a service line inventory and raise rates for the customer. 
Penalizing a PWS for failing to replace a service line that may not need replacing is counterproductive.  
Acceptance of Partial Replacement 
EPA’s changing of “partial service line replacement” to not include partial replacements towards the 
LCRI replacement rate is a roadblock backed by property rights and laws beyond the control of many 
PWSs and will result in a PWS not maintaining a compliant replacement rate. In the case of Texas 
utilities, private property is legally protected by the Texas Private Real Property Rights Preservation 
Act. As a municipal entity, SAWS does not have the legal standing to complete a full replacement of 
service lines to include both the public and private side without homeowner consent. In the event a 
customer refuses or does not respond, a partial replacement should count towards the PWS 
replacement rate as long as the PWS has done their due diligence to engage the property owner. SAWS 
can provide all the necessary information to inform its customers of the dangers of a LSL and the 
importance of replacement, but ultimately the decision belongs solely to the property owner. 
Customer Response Attempts 
In the LCRI, EPA made progressive efforts towards recognizing where the legal rights of a PWS end and 
the rights of the property owner begin. SAWS applauds the proposed language describing the aspects 
of a service line which are under the control of the system. However, the use of the word “control” 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
lacks in clarity where the word “ownership” or “access” may be more appropriate. In fact, an 
argument can be made that the shift to “control” has lessened the ability to access meter boxes and 
public service lines that are located within the bounds of someone’s private property as a PWS does 
not technically “control” that private property. Reverting to “own” or “access” would provide a clearer 
means to identify and acknowledge that through established easements or rights of entry, a PWS 
could inspect meters or PWS lines within that private property that are owned by the PWS. 
Notwithstanding the above, service line inspections cannot be conducted without the property 
owner’s consent. Under the LCRI, a PWS is required to make a “reasonable effort” to gain property 
owner’s consent. SAWS has concerns about what dictates a “reasonable effort”. Four contact 
attempts, by any means, may be overzealous to a customer. Additionally, the time and expense in 
attempting communication through various means could be substantial.  Spam and malicious calls or 
messages are a prevalent nuisance for many. It is our concern that four calls or messages to our 
customers would only irritate them and could lead to more ignored attempts and even build a 
mistrust in future communication efforts.  
Tap Sampling Protocols 
EPA requested comment on whether in-home sampling is the most appropriate method to identify 
situations where the water is too corrosive. SAWS recommends EPA consider a sampling protocol that 
does not rely on residents. First liter sampling is already a challenge to complete due to the locations 
requiring the cooperation of the homeowner and are strictly on a volunteer basis.  Updating the 
sampling protocol to include 5th liter sampling along with 1st liter sampling could realistically 
compromise the quality of a sample collection and will likely increase the cost of sampling supplies 
that must be provided.  Although homeowners are given instructions their lack of experience may 
compromise the quality of the samples taken by introducing contamination, incorrectly filling out the 
paperwork or not disclosing water treatment within their home that influences the results.   
A resident does not have an obligation to respond to a PWS’s questions on their internal plumbing nor 
is there any means for a PWS to validate a resident’s material. In many cases, a resident may not have 
an accurate assessment of their internal plumbing or may give a false declaration to become eligible 
for further sampling at no cost.  
In either of these cases, the results taken by the resident would inaccurately skew the sampling pool 
as well as the intent behind tap sampling. This is further complicated by the use of whole house filters 
and water softeners. Both systems are very prevalent within customer homes in the SAWS distribution 
system. They alter the chemistry of the water and its corrosivity. This is yet another process with 
which the PWS does not have any right to be involved. However, based on the tiered sampling the 
PWS is being held accountable for the water quality results sampled under these conditions.  
SAWS has previously completed sampling efforts to determine the potential corrosivity influence of 
water softeners given their prevalence in San Antonio. Water quality samples were taken inside and 
outside of a residence with a water softener in use. The water quality results of the water going into 
the home were just as would be expected for the water source at that time with minimal metal 
concentrations. While the customers were not noticing any discolored water, the chemistry results 
after the water softener had substantial increases in metals concentrations. This specific home was 
built in the latter 1990s with copper plumbing throughout.  

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
We also have water samples from customers with full plastic-based service lines as well as elevated 
lead concentrations due to their choice in fixtures. While the U.S. has strict lead concentration limits 
for the manufacturing of fixtures, those produced in other countries do not. When they are imported, 
the potential lead concentrations are not known, and the risk is then passed onto the customer. These 
types of fixtures, with or without a water softener, could easily skew the tap sampling results by 
highlighting a problem that can never be fixed by the PWS.  
All the above situations could lead to an action level exceedance (ALE) resulting in increased sampling 
schedules, potential systemwide treatment and increased communications effort as outlined in the 
proposed LCRI. Introducing sample results impacted by customer private property leads to inaccurate 
representation of a whole system’s water quality. The associated costs would increase a ratepayer’s 
bill while not necessarily improving the condition of their water or health risks. 
Premise Plumbing included in tiering 
The overall goal of including premise plumbing in the tap sampling protocols is admirable, however, it 
is not feasible for a water system to be held accountable for the customer’s private property that it 
does not own nor for which it does not have control. We have strict private property laws here in 
Texas.  We are having difficulty gaining access for simple pothole inspections of private service lines 
and anticipate access will be exponentially more difficult to obtain for assessing internal plumbing to 
private homes. In the event a lead-based component is in place, the LCRI does not give the PWS any 
authority to have it removed. This means that if a customer exercises their right not to replace a lead-
based pipe or fixture, the PWS and its rate payers may be forced to pay for more frequent sampling, 
as well as systemwide treatment solutions for personal decisions regarding their private property. 
SAWS strongly suggests that EPA reconsider holding the water system accountable for private 
property without legal access or authority over a customer’s decision. 
Distribution of filters after Action Level Exceedance 
With the proposed LCRI rules, SAWS strongly feels the requirement for filter distribution to all PWS 
customers in the event of an ALE is unfeasible, inefficient, and financially irresponsible. Typical PWS 
infrastructure framework includes pressure zones and the ability to isolate portions of the distribution 
as needed to meet demand requirements and address emergency conditions of all kinds including 
suspected water contamination. A current regulatory example in Texas exists within the Revised Total 
Coliform Rule (RTCR). This rule allows a system with a positive bacterial sample to look at water sources, 
pressure zones and all available resources to resolve the issues without unessential expenses. 
This is a Tier 1 notification of a contaminant with acute exposures risks which allows the flexibility for 
the system to use all the tools it has at its disposal to isolate the areas with potential risk. The LCRI 
describes distributing filters to the entire city under a Tier 1 notification for a contaminant with chronic 
exposure risks. SAWS urges the EPA to consider consistency within their water regulatory programs. 
This would reduce the complexity of all the regulatory rules a PWS must manage for overall compliance.   
In the event of a lead ALE, SAWS would be able to conduct the same procedures as outlined in RTCR to 
isolate the point of potential contamination, collect appropriate samples, and if needed disperse filters 
and cartridges to customers within that service area and/or pressure zone only. Under the proposed 
sampling requirements in the LCRI, premise plumbing could trigger a lead ALE. Premise plumbing is an 
issue that lies solely in control of the homeowner. If for any reason that private citizen decides to not 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
correct any lead issues within their home, it should not pass the burden of cost onto the PWS and 
ultimately all other rate payers.   
Under the proposed LCRI, if a lead ALE were to occur, it could cost SAWS an estimated $32.5 million to 
distribute filters where the vast majority of these filters would go to customers without potential risk. 
In order to comply with a potential distribution of filters within the currently established timeframe, it 
would likely require the purchasing, warehousing, and periodic replacement of a stockpile of pitchers 
and filters that may never be used.  Considering the other added costs attached to the LCRI, this is 
another financial burden that will ultimately trickle down to the customer and would be an 
unconscionable waste of resources. As an alternative to the EPA’s proposal, SAWS suggests limiting filter 
and cartridge issues to customers within an isolated service area, customers identified as having a lead 
service line awaiting replacement of that service line, or customers whose household meets a certain 
criterion. By limiting the dispersal of filters, EPA would not only ensure sufficient supplies for those who 
need the filters but would also greatly reduce the costs of the overall filter proposal. 
Sample Results Notification Timeline 
Following a tap sampling event, it is important to provide the results in a timely manner. The proposed 
rule requires notification to residents within three calendar days of the PWS receiving the results from 
the lab. This timeline is not practical nor is it feasible. Despite a PWS maintaining operations every day 
of the week, most staff work a traditional work week and hours. If sample results are received Friday, 
this leaves a small window of time to process and prepare for the customer notifications. Additionally, 
with this proposed timeframe, employee requested time off and city, state, and federally recognized 
holidays would leave a PWS vulnerable to LCRI violations. EPA should consider expanding this to a more 
achievable and reasonable timeframe such as five business days.  
Risk mitigation and disturbances 
Risk mitigation on disturbances to unknown service line investigations is impractical and built upon a 
fundamental assumption that lead is present throughout system service lines that does not appear to 
be supported by any data.  This misconception underlies multiple requirements of the LCRI and presents 
repeated scenarios where a PWS is required to expend considerable resources to establish that lead is 
not present in its system.  This approach does not make the best use of resources and is not based on a 
true mitigation of risk.   
SAWS is a very large system with multiple departments performing various functions on the distribution 
system including dead-end main flushing, water quality sampling from various fire hydrants, main 
repairs, flushing for water quality complaints, opening and shutting of valves, and other daily system 
maintenance.  These essential duties in addition to disturbances from external sources such as fire 
department hydrant checks, and outside contractor’s use make it difficult to track system impacts back 
to any single one of these activities. It is unfeasible for a PWS to manage all potential disturbance 
sources and correlate them back to the everchanging service line inventory.  
This is further complicated by the vague definition provided in the LCRI for a disturbance. SAWS suggests 
that EPA clarify all potential activities that would constitute a disturbance as well as the specific 
conditions around the disturbance that would trigger a filter distribution. 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
An example of how difficult and costly this provision will be for the PWS can be found during main 
break season. In San Antonio, main break season runs from about April to October every year with an 
average of 400 main breaks a month. On average, SAWS repairs 2,500 main breaks every year with 
approximately 40 residences without water per main break. This is in a city with over 7,000 miles of 
potable water mains over more than 470 square miles. A PWS is not given any advanced notice before 
a break occurs but has become efficient at fixing the problem quickly to restore the needed water 
back to their customers. Through the LCRI, filters would then need to be supplied in all of these 
instances. This would further delay the return of water service to our customers and dramatically 
increase our costs. If we assume 40 residences without water due to the average water main break, at 
the 60% unknown rate for SAWS, that will equate to 60,000 filters supplied annually. While most 
events will vary depending on the area of town and distribution of unknowns, at a cost of $50 each, 
this is an additional $3,000,000 for which our rate payers will be responsible. Additional 
considerations include the PWS’ ability to have enough filters on hand, store them until they are 
needed, tracking the filters distributed as well as the physical activity of filter distribution. While the 
intent behind this section of the LCRI is noteworthy, it is not feasible for a PWS to complete this task 
from multiple points of view.  
Distribution system and Site Assessment 
SAWS supports the renaming of this section within the LCRI. This change gives a more accurate and 
realistic representation of the required actions. However, the half mile radius for a water quality 
parameter sampling location may not be realistic for very large systems as well as rural systems 
whose distribution covers a large area. These site locations must be approved by the state. Within 
our distribution area, we would be required to have over 100 established sites. Expanding this radius 
would make this requirement more attainable for systems of all sizes and configurations.   
Consumer Confidence Report increased frequency 
In regard to the Consumer Confidence Report (CCR), we support the EPA’s effort to update the health 
effects language about lead in the CCR to improve completeness and clarity.  However, issuing the CCR 
twice per year is not significant in advancing the goal of protecting children and adults from the 
irreversible health effects of lead in drinking water.  Customers have already been receiving an annual 
CCR.  The increased frequency merely adds unnecessary costs of materials and manpower to our 
already stretched resources. Increased communications and a second annual report could inundate 
our customers with notifications and increase distrust in the water systems’ ability to provide safe 
drinking water.   
Requirements for PWS’s to accommodate customer requests  
The LCRI allows customers to request both reinvestigations of their service line material and 
individual tap sample collections. However, the EPA’s proposal for any customer-initiated request is 
not feasible for SAWS. These events will put a burden on the PWS outside already strict timelines 
proposed in other areas of this rule.  
The 60-day timeframe for a customer-initiated service line reinvestigation is disorganized and 
uneconomical. SAWS supports the intent behind this stipulation; however, this aspect will greatly 
hinder a PWS’s ability to reach the inventory and replacements deadlines within the LCRI. The PWS 
will be actively making plans for unknown identification efficiently using system resources. In the 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
event a customer requests a check of their service line, the PWS will have to redirect crews to a single 
location. This will reduce the efficiency of this crew and would not be an economical use of rate-
payers funds. The PWS should be allowed to accommodate the customer request within the existing 
investigation schedule outside of a 60-day window to make this additional work as feasible and 
economical as possible.  
Additionally, SAWS recommends EPA consider allowing a PWS to provide documentation and 
pictures of the inspection to the customer prior to completing another inspection. A PWS should be 
held accountable by their customers to the accuracy of their inventory, but at the same time the 
existing data should be provided and reviewed with a customer before requiring the scheduling of 
additional work. By approving this additional option for compliance, a system would be able to satisfy 
this requirement without compromising the investigation schedule and allowing for an economical 
alternative.  
The LCRI also requires a PWS to collect a water quality sample on request from a customer with an 
unknown, GRR or lead service line. While it is important the customer feels confident in the quality of 
the water, a PWS is likely to be over-whelmed with sampling requests especially when updates to the 
inventory are made. SAWS currently sits at 385,000 unknown service lines. If EPA enforces this aspect 
of the rule, it will further stress a system’s resources including manpower, time, laboratory 
capabilities and capital.  
As the cost of this sampling efforts will fall on the PWS, this is a potentially large budgetary item 
without any means of control or planning. Based on the average cost of these tests, the rate payers in 
San Antonio could pay multiple millions of dollars depending on response. SAWS suggests that EPA 
reconsider this requirement to make it feasible for all systems which may face a flood of these types 
of requests. 
Lack of large system flexibility 
Just as EPA has accommodated small systems and some of their cost and operational challenges, we 
encourage the EPA to consider large systems as well for these same challenges.  SAWS serves a 
population over 30 times larger than what is defined as a large system under the LCRI yet is still in the 
same category as a large system that serves only 50,000 customers.  A system of our magnitude with 
few expected lead lines estimates it will cost well over $1 billion dollars over ten years to maintain 
compliance.  Ultimately our rate payers would carry the burden of this unreasonable cost. The EPA 
fails to acknowledge the practical impact of the rule and the fact that our budgets, which may be 
larger than a small system, also carry proportionately larger costs.  
Small systems serving 3,300 or less under the LCRI have been given flexibilities to have options after 
ALEs and exemptions from conducting pipe loop studies because they often lack the technical 
expertise and could better focus limited resources on replacing their LSLs.  We urge the EPA to 
include flexibilities for very large systems as well, including acceptance of predictive modeling and 
incorporating another category for deferred deadline eligibility. These supplements would help SAWS 
meet the requirements of the LCRI more efficiently and would save the citizens of San Antonio 
substantial funds.  
LCRI Costs and Funding 

2800 U.S. Hwy 281 North • P.O Box 2449 • San Antonio, TX • 78298-2449 • www.saws.org 
 
The cost estimates listed in the LCRI appear to be underestimated based on our experience with the 
current costs from existing SAWS contracts as well as communications with other PWSs. We 
estimated the cost of LCRI compliance for SAWS will be between $1.5 and $2 billion. As an unfunded 
mandate, this burden falls on the rate payers of San Antonio resulting in multiple rate increases over 
the next decade to fund these efforts.  
We understand there have been efforts to make governmental funds available, but unfortunately 
due to our superior size we do not qualify for those funding and grant initiatives. Rate payers across 
the country have clearly stated they do not wish to pay for these required LCRI activities through rate 
increases and the citizens of San Antonio are not any different. In order to ease the burden on our 
residents, funding needs to become more available to larger systems as well as smaller.  
SAWS values the effort and resources the EPA has placed towards developing this proposed rule. The 
LCRI attempts to correct the mistakes of the past and to secure a safe and healthy future. Many of the 
proposed rules in the LCRI will update our nation’s infrastructure placing the health and safety of its 
citizens as the priority. However, there are many aspects of this proposal that will divide a PWS’ loyalties 
between its customers and the EPA. SAWS appreciates the consideration that the EPA will give to these 
comments and all others presented. Thank you for your time and attention. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
______________________________________ 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Scott R. Halty 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Director 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Resource Protection and Compliance 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
San Antonio Water System

Dear Administrator Regan,
The Missouri State Conference of the NAACP submits the following comments
regarding the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) proposed “National
Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”).
The NAACP Missouri State Conference provides leadership for local branches, youth
councils, and college chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in Missouri.
The NAACP and its Center for Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding
interest in ensuring that issues of community engagement and environmental justice
center Black communities and frontline communities most impacted, including
communities throughout Missouri.
The Missouri State Conference applauds EPA for proposing stronger regulations to
protect communities from lead in drinking water. Lead in drinking water has been a
historically prevalent issue in Black communities, posing extreme risks to the health of
young people, mothers, and their families. In Missouri, estimates suggest that there are
as many as 330,000 lead service lines, threatening families across our state with
exposure to a potent and irreversible neurotoxin which even at low levels of exposure is
linked to damage to the brain and nervous system, learning disabilities, shorter stature,
impaired hearing, and harm to blood cells. In Missouri we would derive more than 7
billion dollars in public health cost savings from full lead service line Replacement.
4002-SC Missouri State Conference of the NAACP
111 W High St. • Jefferson City, MO 65101 • 573.616.2537 • www.monaacp.org

In Missouri, a strong rule is especially needed. In our state, 82% of children have
detectable lead levels in their blood.
For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong
elements of the proposed LCRI such as the requirement for the removal of all lead
service lines in ten years, the requirements for water systems to sample both the first
and fifth liter of water passing through lead pipes and a lower action level; but also
ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which undermine their goals and
ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule
does not leave black communities in Missouri behind:
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a fundamental
injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 or
more years to fix this issue.
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: Removal
can cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted
communities will result in mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service
lines replaced. Removal and replacement do not make up major proportions of utility
budgets, and utilities should be expected to maximize the use of available federal water
infrastructure funds and other non-ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize solving this
crisis.
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many hours
there daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead
exposure when compared with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing
program does not differ from past ineffective programs, and EPA should move towards
incentivizing the installation of filters and protecting children.
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would
allow for environmental injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline
communities have long suffered from disinvestment and lack of resources. Past
NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had the
strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA of any
4002-SC Missouri State Conference of the NAACP
111 W High St. • Jefferson City, MO 65101 • 573.616.2537 • www.monaacp.org

sociodemographic characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to make
significant changes in the lives of millions of people in [state], and to provide a measure
of environmental justice which these families are owed, and we encourage this
administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by strengthening the
final rule further.

RE: 
Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) for Regulations for Lead and Copper:

Public Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
To United States Environmental Protection Agency,  
 
The Ohio Section of the American Water Works Association (OAWWA) represents over 4,500 water utilities that serve 
Ohio’s population of 11.5 million.  The Ohio Water Utility Council (OWUC) of the OAWWA has a primary purpose of 
advocating on matters that affect the water industry, treatment and delivery of safe, clean drinking water.   
The OWUC appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed drinking water standards for Regulations 
for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) during this 
comment period of the rulemaking process.  We recognize the importance of a collaborative effort between the EPA and 
the water utilities in United States and Ohio when evaluating the impacts of these rules.  OWUC is focused on providing 
operational context to the regulatory requirements being proposed by EPA.   
The OWUC would like to acknowledge the efforts the EPA has made to address the potential lead exposure in drinking 
water.  There are several positive elements in the proposed rules that the OWUC supports including:  
• 
Maintaining the treatment technique regulatory framework for the control of lead and copper in drinking water.  
• 
Establishing a program for lead service line replacement rather than based on triggered requirements.  
• 
Recognizing that public water systems (PWSs), specifically community water systems (CWSs), continue to face 
legal constraints outside of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) that limit our access to customer properties.  
• 
Delaying changes to the optimized corrosion control treatments until lead services line materials (LSLs) and 
galvanized requiring replacement service lines (GRRSLs) are replaced as directed by the LCRI are completed.  
Eliminating potentially redundant work.  
• 
Importance of customer education, especially in lead risk reduction of PWSs customers.  
• 
A goal of simplifying the rule for effective implementation.   
  
 

 
 
 
 
400 W. Wilson Bridge Rd, Ste. 120 | Worthington OH 43085 | 844.766.2845 
www.oawwa.org | oawwa@assnoffices.com  
 
There are, however, critical revisions to this rule that need to be addressed prior to the final version becoming 
promulgated.  Without these modifications the PWSs of Ohio would be subject to regulations that are not legally sound, 
as they would be beyond the scope of the SDWA.   
• 
EPA must act to immediately extend the compliance date for the provisions under the LCRR that will not be 
continued 
in 
the 
LCRI. 
 
The 
PWSs 
in 
Ohio 
continue 
to 
work 
towards 
meeting 
the  
requirements of the LCRR, including service line inventory, tap sample monitoring, etc.  But our PWSs should not 
be expending resources on compliance requirements with no guarantee from EPA that the LCRI final rule will be 
published prior to the compliance date of the LCRR. 
• 
In the LCR revisions in 2000 the definition of “control” was based on ownership.  With the proposed change of 
this definition, the EPA is creating access issues for PWSs in Ohio to meet the requirements of the LCRI. The 
definition of what is “under the control” of water systems as described in SDWA does not include piping not owned 
by the water system, even when the actual owner uses their “control” to grant “access” to a water system.  
• 
The EPA needs to simplify the compliance path for systems with no or few LSLs and/or GRRSLs.  There are a number 
of PWSs within Ohio that have no known LSLs on the public side, which have been certified to the state agency, 
Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (OEPA) and based on predictive modeling, have completed to comply with 
the LCRR deadline of October 16th, 2024, a very low probability of LSLs on the private side.  The proposed rule 
does not allow for an alternative method for PWSs to have a second path to compliance that focuses primarily on 
(1) having a procedure for the rare occurrence of a LSL or GRRSL is discovered and (2) the validation study to 
assure the initial characterization of the system’s inventory is correct. 
EPA has requested comment on the feasibility of a 10-year replacement period for all PWSs.  Based on the experience of 
Ohio PWSs and what has been presented by EPA in this rulemaking this timeframe is not feasible.  A shorter timeframe, 
as a possible option for systems, is not feasible either with the potential for expanding requirements in the proposed rule.  
Should a 10-year timeframe be finalized in the rule it would create a strain on utilities; financially, skilled labor wise and 
physical resources.  The supply chain would be strained as more than 4,500 public water systems in Ohio, not to mention 
the thousands of other PWSs in the United States, who would be working towards meeting the same goal, in the same 
time period, using the similar if not the exact same materials.  The final LCRI should have mechanisms for water systems 
to extend past the 10-year time period for their LSL replacement programs dependent on that particular water systems 
circumstances. The examples given in the proposed rule all were completed outside of the proposed regulations of the 
LCRI and did not have the concerns detailed above that systems under this new rule would encounter.  Therefore, it is 
hard to rationale the use of those examples to justify the feasibility of the 10-year timeframe.  
Funding continues to be a major concern to PWSs as increased regulations are placed on Ohio PWSs.   The ratepayers of 
our systems are ultimately the payers of these regulatory changes, whether through direct charges or through increased 
water rates.  With the majority of water infrastructure funding available coming in loans, this means that the upfront cost 
is again, coming from the ratepayers.  The Ohio Section’s parent organization, American Water Works Association as 
estimated that the average cost for full lead service line replacements as defined in the proposed rule would be $12,000-
$15,000 per service line.  This cost is a significant burden that will require more than reimbursement loans and the 
Administration should seek Congressional appropriations to support the LSLR programs.

Re: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801) 
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
We the People of Detroit (WPD) submits the following comments on U.S. EPA’s proposed Lead 
and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The state of Michigan has, and continues to see, some 
of the worst impacts of lead-poisoned water. From Flint to Benton Harbor, our most vulnerable 
Michiganders are still reeling from lead catastrophes that will have lasting impacts in the years to 
come. As a result of one of these unfortunate, and preventable, crises the Great Lakes State 
adopted the strongest lead and copper regulations on drinking water at the time in 2018 to protect 
its residents and we applaud the U.S. EPA’s work to prioritize this issue nationwide. We seek to 
further strengthen the rule with the nation’s most lead-burdened communities in mind and look 
forward to supporting the administration to a lead-free future. To that end, we hope to see the 
following: 
 
Prioritizing the most impacted, low-wealth communities. 
 
The final rule should mandate that water utilities are responsible for paying the full cost of lead 
service line replacement (LSLR). The inability to pay for full LSLR may put an already 
vulnerable household in further debt or inhibit the removal itself, given the loose definition of 
“Water System Access to Full Service Line”. Both of these outcomes would lead to furthering 
the social, financial, and health gap between low- and high-wealth communities and ultimately 
fail to meet the nation’s goal to remove all lead service lines in an equitable way. We must 
maximize the combined benefits of federal and state programs and initiatives like the Bipartisan 
Infrastructure Law, State Revolving Funds, Justice40, and more to make the necessary funds 
available for full LSLR at no direct cost to the resident. 
 
Supporting and incentivizing equitable workforce development in accelerating lead service 
line removals. 
 
As stated in the proposed rule, stakeholders have cited concerns of limited workforce. This 
should not be seen as an insurmountable obstacle but rather an opportunity for the EPA rapidly 
expand its partnerships and incentivize participation under the Lead Service Line Replacement 
Accelerators. The newly launched American Climate Corps is a recognition that updating the 

We the People of Detroit 
P.O. Box 7033 
wethepeopleofdetroit.com 
 
Detroit, MI 48207 
nation’s infrastructure to protect against climate change through equitable workforce 
development is essential and the approach to LSLRs are no different. Cities and states across the 
country have already adopted workforce development plans to recruit, hire, and train their own 
residents to develop the skilled workforce needed to meet the demands of nationwide lead 
removal and this effort should be elevated nationwide.  
 
Ensuring the nation meets the 10-year timeline goal. 
 
While we recognize the EPA’s effort to address certain stakeholder concerns of feasibility, it is 
clear that this administration believes the timeline and process are achievable for 96-99 percent 
of community water systems nationwide. However, rather than providing deadline extensions for 
those 1-4% of systems, EPA should remove the extension options and work closely with systems 
of concern to find solutions that will meet the 10-year timeline rather than potentially allowing 
full lead pipe removal to be pushed out by decades.  
 
Better protections for children. 
 
Lead is a highly dangerous neurotoxin, widely accepted as having no safe level of exposure. In 
late 2023, Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer signed bipartisan bills to prevent lead 
contamination in schools and childcare centers. These institutions are now required to install 
filtered-faucets certified for lead removal, develop a drinking water management plan, and 
conduct routine sampling and testing to ensure safe and accessible drinking water for children. 
This effort should be elevated across the country to protect all children to bring immediate 
protections against lead in schools.

Detroit Community Research Collective 
(CRC) demonstrates the breadth and 
concentration of lead risk across metro 
Detroit in the map to the right. And WPD’s 
work with communities has found that 
catastrophic contamination can lead to a 
distrust in the water utility and supply, 
making it very difficult for impacted 
households to return to the tap. It is critical 
that we move aggresively and thoroughly to 
remove this dangerous toxin from our water 
supply.  
 
We commend the administration’s plans and actions to remove lead from our infrastructure once 
and for all. The proposed rule builds on the layers of work this administration has done to 
prioritize environmental justice and brings us a step closer to realizing a healthy, lead-free future. 
We must now ensure that there is no room for technicalities that allow lead pipes to remain in the 
ground and in our homes. Thank you for the opportunity to comment. 
 

We the People of Detroit
