Louisville Water requests further consideraƟon and ﬂexibility for galvanized service line 
replacements. Replacing galvanized service lines that connect to older mains (especially cast iron) and 
older galvanized premise plumbing carries much more risk to the customer and is more diﬃcult to 
manage for the water system. Many systems have reported addiƟonal costs associated with main 
replacement when aƩempƟng targeted replacement of galvanized service lines. Louisville Water has 
had several cases where customers experienced water loss and failure of premise plumbing materials 
aŌer service line replacement. The agency should consider that most galvanized pipes will fail or be 
replaced over the next 20 years regardless of the requirements of this rule.  
 
EPA should focus the ﬁrst 10 year schedule exclusively on replacing lead service lines, not galvanized; 
and consider requiring replacement of galvanized service lines over the next 20 years in coordinaƟon 
with main-replacement projects where construcƟon crews are beƩer able to miƟgate upstream and 
downstream risks. Requiring both lead and galvanized replacement in 10 years does not properly 
account for the diﬀerent risk levels associated with the two diﬀerent types of plumbing materials. 
Louisville Water’s 90P for LSL is an order of magnitude higher than the 90P for galvanized SLs. In most 
cases, lead release from galvanized pipe can be eﬀecƟvely managed with opƟmized corrosion control. 
EPA recognizes the disƟncƟon between lead risk and galvanized risk in the sample Ɵering framework, 
but that same logic doesn’t carry forward to other areas of the rule, namely the 10-year replacement 
schedule and calculaƟon of replacement rates.  
 
Furthermore, EPA should consider the costs related to main replacement and post-replacement 
ﬂushing damage to premise galvanized pipe associated with targeted replacement of galvanized 
service lines. These costs may be compounded by the accelerated 10-year schedule and lead to 
addiƟonal ﬁnancial liabiliƟes for water systems.

Whether the proposed LCRI appropriately interprets “control” for the purposes of the mandatory 
replacement provision (i.e., require systems to conduct full service line replacement in situaƟons where 
the system has access to conduct the full replacement). 
 
In addiƟon to removing all known lead service lines in its distribuƟon system, Louisville Water has 
undertaken signiﬁcant eﬀorts to idenƟfy and replace lead and GRR private service lines and is 
subsidizing 100% of the costs via customer reimbursement or using our plumbing contractors to 
conduct the replacement. However, Louisville Water recognizes that the SDWA does not allow 
regulaƟon of private property outside of public water systems and maintains that “control” cannot be 
equated with “access.” EPA’s proposed deﬁniƟon is not supported by the statutory text. The SDWA 
regulates public water systems but does not provide EPA authority to regulate other enƟƟes, such as 
businesses, landlords, or private residences. Similarly, it does not give EPA authority over private 
property or other persons, and therefore cannot be used to compel removal of lead in private lines or 
plumbing ﬁxtures that are private property. By requiring public water systems to inventory and 
conduct LSR replacements on property that is not part of the public water system, the LCRI exceeds 
the scope of EPA’s authority under the SDWA and is therefore contrary to law.

Louisville Water requests that EPA decouple GRR replacements from LSL replacements in the 
calculaƟon of replacement rate – i.e., have separate calculaƟons for GRR replacement rate than for LSL 
replacement rate. There is scant data demonstraƟng that a GRR service line poses the same risk as a

A system’s exisƟng authority to access the service line and complete the full service line replacement 
might provide the system with the legal authority to conduct the service line replacement over the 
objecƟon of the property owner or resident. However, as some stakeholders noted, requiring service

safety concerns for uƟlity staﬀ. EPA is seeking comment on whether the proposed LCRI should either 
allow systems to treat those service lines as not under the control of the system and forego 
replacement of the lines or require systems to conduct full service line replacement in situaƟons where 
the system has legal access to conduct the full replacement, but property owners or residents deny 
physical access. 
 
Louisville Water recognizes that the SDWA does not allow regulaƟon of private property outside of 
public water systems and “control” cannot be equated with “access.” EPA’s proposed deﬁniƟon is not 
supported by the statutory text. --The SDWA regulates public water systems but does not provide EPA 
authority to regulate other enƟƟes, such as businesses, landlords, or private residences. Similarly, it 
does not give EPA authority over private property or other persons, and therefore cannot be used to 
compel removal of lead in private lines or plumbing ﬁxtures that are private property. By requiring 
public water systems to inventory and conduct LSR replacements on property that is not part of the 
public water system, the LCRI exceeds the scope of EPA’s authority under the SDWA and is therefore 
contrary to law.

COMMENTS ON THE PROPOSED LEAD & COPPER RULE IMPROVEMENTS 
MAYOR DANENE SORACE | CITY OF LANCASTR, PENNSYLVANIA 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. The 
City of Lancaster PA submits the following comments.  
  
The City of Lancaster is comprised of approximately 58,000 people within 7.3 square miles. More than 
¾ of the city’s census tracks have been designated as overburdened and underserved according to the 
Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool.  
  
The City of Lancaster owns and operates two water treatment plants serving approximately 58,000 
people in the city and 62,000 outside its municipal boundaries. Additionally, the city operates a 
wastewater treatment facility that is currently under an EPA consent decree for combined sewer 
overflows. City rate payers pay the highest property taxes and pay the only stormwater fee in the 
county. Additionally, the largest exposure to lead in the city is paint.   
 
The City is among the top ten cities for the highest rates of childhood lead poisoning in Pennsylvania, 
primarily due to our aged housing stock (over 80% of the homes in Lancaster City were built before 
1978) and exposure to lead paint. On September 26, 2019, the City of was awarded a $9.1 million Lead 
Hazard Reduction Grant through the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD), plus 
an additional $600,000 of Healthy Homes supplemental funding. The Lead Hazard Reduction Grant will 
systematically make 710 housing units lead safe in Lancaster city. The Healthy Homes supplemental 
funding will enable the City to address other health hazards such as radon, mold and tripping hazards 
in 120 homes. Matching funds from the City and property owners bring the total funding to $11.1 
million. 
 
The focus area for the grant is four census tracts (9, 10, 14, and 147) south of King Street where 16,000 
residents live. The majority of houses in the area were built prior to 1940, many of which have lead-
based paint present. These census tracts are among the highest for children with elevated blood lead 
levels in the city. Data from the PA Department of Health indicates that between 2015-2018, 18.3% of 
children under the age of six who resided within those four census tracts and were tested for lead had 
elevated blood lead levels (over 5 μg/dL).  
 
In April 2022, City Council adopted an ordinance to enhance lead safety protections in rental housing 
and childcare facilities. This ordinance requires all rental properties and childcare facilities built before 
1978 to meet lead safety requirements every two to four years. The City has strengthened its support 
of children with elevated blood lead level (EBLL) cases by requiring homeowners and landlords to more 
quickly respond to potential exposure to lead in homes and giving City Health Officers more tools to 
address exposure. These changes went into effect in January 2023. The City is committed to improving 
the health of its youngest citizens.  
 
 
 
 

 
2 
 
On the water side, we have been methodically removing lead laterals throughout the city’s water 
distribution system – only 1% of City lead lines remain (519) and we are committed to removing these 
as expeditiously and cost effectively as possible while also maintaining our corrosion control program.  
Our comments focus on the practicality of the regulations, the affordability, and the fact that the lead 
that is poisoning our children is predominately found in paint.  
 
1. Timeline  
The reduced time period to replace all lead lines in ten years will place a financial burden on cities such 
as Lancaster. The timeline does not factor in existing corrosion control, historical efforts to eliminate 
lead lines, and water quality. The City has provided corrosion control since April 1, 1997, and has 
replaced at least 274 water laterals dating back to 2012, when we started tracking replacements in an 
electronic database. However, Lancaster’s replacement efforts started after the lead ban of 1991. We 
are extremely proud that our water quality has tested under the 15 ppb threshold and data indicates 
that we will be under the proposed 10 ppb limit. Water providers should be given more time if water 
quality is in compliance and providers have shown a strong track record of eliminating lead pipes.  
 
2. Affordability  
The City’s water distribution system is comprised of city customers and outside city customers with 
median incomes of 60,000 and 80,000 respectively. Within our Water Bureau, the City is in the midst of 
generational upgrades to our distribution system, namely a 42” main, circa 1956, that needs to be 
replaced at an estimated cost of $44 million in addition to replacement of approximately 1.5 miles of 
transite pipe annually, at an approximate cost of $2 million a year. Moreover, the City will be replacing 
plant assets such as pumps, membranes, and tanks as part of its capital plan over the next 20 years. 
Maintaining water infrastructure is extremely capital intensive, and providing water at an affordable 
rate to the community is harder to do each year, with increasing regulations and little grant funds.  
 
Our water fund current debt burden is now 34% of the operating budget and 15% of its inside city 
accounts are in delinquent status. Adding the unknowns into the replacement pool continues to add to 
that debt burden, even though the replacement pool can be updated annually. Targeting unknowns 
will reduce the number of lines to replace, but identifying the unknowns will take significant resources 
too.  
 
The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission regulations already place an undue burden on the City 
requiring that the customer line also be replaced. These costs can be recovered in the rate setting 
process. Treating inside City customers different than outside suburban customers is not equitable, so 
the City will also be replacing the customer side within the City limits. However, most City rate payers 
cannot afford increased rates in the Justice 40 areas.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
3 
 
3. Inventory  
The City has deployed an online form for customers to self-identify and take a picture of their line. To 
date 7,365 customers have responded. Of these responses, 600 customers have asked for help and 
1,200 customers identified lead or galvanized on their side. These customers all must be verified too. 
The City does not believe that all of the customers who identified lead service lines are lead as data has 
shown customers taking pictures of lines that are not water service and have copper lines that they 
think are lead. But this will increase the costs of replacement too.  
 
For inside city customers, we have also deployed codes and housing inspectors to collect data from 
approximately 2,950 properties by October during their systematic inspections. In total, we expect 
these efforts to yield information for about 5.9% of customers in our water distribution service area. To 
gather data for the remainder of homes, we will have to hire staff or contract with a third party to 
collect data. Moreover, PA DEP also requires two forms of identification for the service line, including 
the customers’ side.   
 
The City has already contracted with Trinnix to use machine learning as a second form of identification. 
With 49,763 customers and about 9,706 lines installed after the January 6, 1991, lead ban, there still 
will be significant unknowns on the customer side. Homes will have to be entered or potholing 
conducted on both sides to identify the unknowns, and to correct the pictures of customers who 
identified the wrong line. Potholing costs about $750 per hole. If we have a 20% response rate for 
customer pictures, and remove the lines installed after the lead ban and homes from code and housing 
inspections, the City could still have 30,000 homes to pothole. That is an expense of $22.5 million with 
no lead lines replaced if potholing is used. The City is currently evaluating costs to hire consultants to 
enter homes, provided permission is granted. If a customer refuses entry, then potholing is a last 
resort.   
 
4. Inventory Validation  
The proposed requirement to validate non-lead lines by year seven is excessive. The City’s known lead 
lines are at 519 and we do not expect that number to climb exponentially when the inventory on the 
customer side is done. The City has been replacing lead lines for years. If the City ends up with 48,000 
to 49,000 non-lead lines, the inventory will require another 381 inspections by potholing. If the City has 
to pothole to identify unknowns, it should not have to do more to verify the inventory. This will 
provide no additional value.   
 
5. Financing Lead Line Replacements  
Lancaster has availed itself of state revolving funds via PENNVEST on several occasions and we have 
benefited from low interest rates for our water and sewer projects. At PENNVEST’s direction, the City 
applied to replace 27 known City lead lines as well as any lead service lines of the property owner and 
determine the material of unknown lines in a subset of 379 properties in the City’s Jewels 
neighborhood in an effort to maximize grant dollars focused on overburdened and underserved areas 
in the city.  
 
 

 
4 
 
As part of the application, we also asked for funds to include lead line inventory of 115 lines of 
unknown material on both the City and the property owner’s side as a pilot. The City also intended to 
complete an inventory of the 238 copper lines on the property owner’s side and to replace any that 
were incorrectly identified. The City was directed to revise the application as PENNVEST was not able 
to use its funds for inventory upfront. We were told that we could inventory and then make an 
application to request reimbursement.   
  
After we revised our application to exclude funds for inventory, we were awarded a loan of $430,934 
and a grant of $441,406 an approximate 50% grant/50% loan funding solution, with the expectation 
that we would continue to apply for small areas throughout the city. (We estimate that we would need 
to submit at least 17 separate applications to PENNVEST to cover ¾ of the city that is EJ designated.) 
The City reluctantly turned down the funding because of the costs it would incur for this small 
borrowing, multiplied by 17. The incurred financing costs do not replace lead lines.  
 
We are planning to submit another application for lead line replacement for the entirety of the City’s 
overburdened and underserved census tracks, in an attempt to get better grant funding. However, 
PENNVEST has not specifically allocated funding or prioritized high need census tracks statewide. 
PENNVEST informed us that the lead line replacement program was oversubscribed in PA so we could 
not get 100% grant funding. Regardless of the promises of federal funding to replace lead lines, it is not 
fully funded and ultimately will impact our low- and moderate -income households, at about the same 
time when we will be increasing rates to pay for a new distribution transmission main, transite 
replacement, as well as future mandates related to PFOA/PFAS.   
 
In June of 2023, the City also attempted to apply for a $9 million in CDBG grant funding through HUD 
to replace any lead lines in the City’s low-income census tracks. The City was not eligible for these 
funds because we were told that we had to verify the income level of each individual household in the 
tracks. We did not have this level of detail for each household, and we were advised that we would not 
be grant eligible. The City is estimating that it will spend $14 million on its 519 known lead lines 
($27,000 each for both the City and the customer portion of the line). This does not include the 
significant effort and cost that we are incurring now to complete the inventory, and the funds needed 
to verify lines that customers have identified as lead.  
 
6. Compliance Monitoring  
The new regulations will cause increased monitoring costs. Again, there is no flexibility in evaluating 
lead data to determine if monitoring needs to increase. Increased monitoring needs to be driven by 
data.  
 
The proposed sampling requirements and customer requests increase under the new proposed 
regulations. The City would have to offer lead sampling for all lead lines and galvanized lines, and 
unknowns. Consideration should be given to remove the unknowns. Moreover, if the new action level 
of 10 ppb is exceeded, compliance sampling would have to be offered to all customers. 
 
 

 
5 
 
Under the new regulations, in 2028, if the action level of 10 ppb is exceeded, additional sampling must 
be offered which will strain operating budgets. In 2028, all systems will have semi-annual system lead 
sampling for two years. If we are under the action level for all four rounds, only then could we 
potentially go back to reduced monitoring. These additional requirements would also have to be 
initiated while starting lead sampling for all elementary schools and daycares in our system that must 
be completed within five years. All these samples will also be under the new 1st and 5th Liter sampling, 
which essentially means two lead samples for one location. Consideration should be given to the 
efficacy of the additional cost to benefit.  
  
7. Notifications and Outreach  
The proposed regulations place an undue burden on staff to provide results to customers in three 
calendar days. We propose this be amended to 5 business days. Please note that if a child tests positive 
for lead in the bloodstream, a five-business day notification is allowed by HUD.   
 
The public notifications are burdensome and will result in no lead reductions. The multiple 
notifications for routine work and even emergency work also place an undue burden on staff. In 
addition, the regulations need to be clear on the notifications required for these specific maintenance 
activities.  We will have to hire another staff member just to keep track of all of the notifications, 
including the requirement of contacting at risk customers. Water providers will now have to act as a 
public health agency to make all the contacts. This is not the role of public water. Moreover, the tier 
one notification in 24 hours is not realistic. Water providers will not have the resources to notify and 
mail customers in such a short time period. Again, this serves to set up the water provider for non-
compliance.  
 
Thank you for this opportunity to comment.  
  
Sincerely,  
 
Danene Sorace, Mayor  
City of Lancaster, Pennsylvania

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0782 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
AMERICAN WATER WORKS ASSOCIATION  
ORAL COMMENT  
at 
NATIONAL DRINKING WATER ADVISORY COUNCIL  
on the  
NATIONAL PRIMARY DRINKING WATER REGULATIONS FOR LEAD AND COPPER: IMPROVEMENTS 
PROPOSED RULE  
January 31, 2024 
Good morning.  Thank you for the opportunity to speak to the Council.  My name is Steve Via. I would 
like to offer the following comments on behalf of the American Water Works Association (AWWA).   
AWWA’s members have a continuing interest in the provision of safe drinking water and in building on 
our success to-date reducing exposure to lead through drinking water.  AWWA shares EPA’s 
commitment to both effective use of corrosion control and reducing the remaining sources of lead in 
contact with drinking water.  AWWA supports the continued regulation of lead in drinking water 
through a treatment technique and supports the proactive replacement of lead service lines as an 
element of the treatment technique. 
AWWA is preparing comments on the proposed rule reflecting the experience of our members, 
including those with lead service line replacement programs that operate without substantial federal 
subsidies. AWWA would like to draw several recommendations from our review to the Council’s 
attention as it prepares its own recommendations to EPA:  
1. Service Line Inventory and Replacement – EPA should better focus rule requirements to realize 
risk reduction and simplify implementation by 
• 
Not penalizing water systems when property owners do not collaborate in service line 
replacement  
• 
Eliminating the proposed annual replacement rate as unnecessary and unnecessarily 
complicated to implement 
• 
Prioritizing replacement rather than overemphasizing potential misclassification of 
service line materials and administrative oversight 
2. Public Education – EPA should revise customer / occupant notifications to reflect practical 
implementation considerations by 
• 
Allowing use of modern electronic communication tools in lieu of written notification 
when possible 
• 
Clarifying and focusing notification requirements so that target audiences are reached 
and expectations for timely notification are feasible 
3. Compliance Monitoring – EPA should phase in the transition to new lead and copper compliance 
monitoring requirements by system size 

• 
Assuring states will be able to adequately administer compliance requires reducing the 
number of systems that will have to immediately transition to the new tap sample 
monitoring requirements. Implementation can be crafted to assure a smooth transition 
to a revised monitoring framework 
4. Reassess Feasibility – EPA should review the available data and consider more carefully the 
feasibility and risk reduction advantage sought through proposed rule requirements including 
the pace of service line replacement, lowering the action level, and provision of filters in the 
wake of any recurring lead action level exceedance 
5. Involve Other Federal Offices – Engage other federal offices to assure that determinants of 
success for the proposed requirements are in place 
• 
Internal Revenue Service – Clarify that publicly funded service line replacements are not 
taxable income for individual households 
• 
White House – Determine the feasibility of obtaining funding support necessary to 
alleviate the financial pressure associated with full lead service line replacement on 
individual households and community water systems.  EPA cannot assume current 
drinking water revolving loan funds are more than an initial start on the federal funding 
required for the cost of service line replacement envisioned in the proposed rule. 
Thank you for your attention and consideration. 
 
Who is AWWA 
The American Water Works Association (AWWA) is an international, nonprofit, scientific and educational 
society dedicated to providing total water solutions assuring the effective management of water. Founded 
in 1881, the Association is the largest organization of water supply professionals in the world. Our 
membership includes more than 4,000 utilities that supply roughly 80 percent of the nation's drinking 
water and treat almost half of the nation’s wastewater. Our 50,000-plus total membership represents the 
full spectrum of the water community: public water and wastewater systems, environmental advocates, 
scientists, academicians, and others who hold a genuine interest in water, our most important resource. 
AWWA unites the diverse water community to advance public health, safety, the economy, and the 
environment.

US EPA’S Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)

Dear Mr. Goldberg: 
The Texas Chemistry Council (TCC) submits the following comments on EPA’s proposed rule for National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) (88 FR 84878, December 6, 2023, EPA Docket ID No. EPA-
HQ-OW-2022-0801), hereafter “Proposed Rule.”   
 
TCC is a statewide trade association of chemical manufacturers representing more than 60 member companies who own 
and operate over 200 manufacturing and research facilities across Texas. The business of chemistry provides employment 
for approximately 500,000 Texans and its products are the state’s top non-energy export with more than $50 billion in 
state exports annually to customers around the world. TCC’s member companies have industrial facilities throughout the 
United States, of which some are also registered Non-Transient Non-Community Public Water Systems (NTNCWSs).  Our 
membership is committed to the safety of our employees, including the protection of their health when consuming 
drinking water in the workplace.   
 
When assessing the requirements of the Proposed Rule and considering the competing priorities of the proposed PFAS 
regulations for Drinking Water, TCC echoes the comments of the American Petroleum Institute (API) and American 
Chemistry Council (ACC) in identifying the following opportunities for EPA to provide additional flexibility and clarity to 
NTNCWSs.  Specifically, TCC requests EPA allow the option for NTNCWSs to install point-of-use devices in lieu of lead 
service line (LSL) replacement for NTNCWSs and to provide bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or POU devices 
following disturbances.  Additionally, TCC requests that EPA provide clear and timely guidance to all PWSs, including 
NTNCWSs on expectations associated with the final rule and the definition of Service Line.  Finally, TCC argues that EPA 
has underestimated the cost burden to NTNCWSs, and TCC formally requests that EPA consider feedback on assumptions 
that EPA has made on NTNCWSs when considering compliance alternatives. 
 
TCC offers the recommendations in these comments to inform EPA’s consideration in advance of any future regulatory 
action and support the separate comments submitted to this docket from API and ACC.  The following points highlight key 
elements of our detailed comments: 
• 
EPA should allow Point-of-Use Devices in lieu of LSL replacement for NTNCWS that do not supply water to 
sensitive populations, such as schools or child-care facilities. 
• 
EPA should add alternative options and sample validation as an option for risk mitigation after disturbances for 
NTNCWSs. 

Comments of TCC on EPA Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations

February 5, 2024

• 
EPA should provide clear and timely guidance for industrial facility NTNCWSs. 
• 
EPA should clarify the definition of Service Line. 
• 
EPA’s assumptions result in an underestimated Cost Burden to NTNCWSs. 
• 
Sample Tiering based on Premise Plumbing presents undue burden to Public Water Systems. 
 
TCC’s specific comments are included below.  
 
1. EPA should allow Point-of-Use Devices in lieu of LSL replacement for NTNCWS that do not supply water to 
sensitive populations, such as schools or child-care facilities – The Proposed Rule contains Small System Flexibility 
provisions that allow NTNCWSs to leverage Point-of-Use (POU) systems in lieu of the corrosion control treatment 
requirements as described in the Proposed Rule § 141.93.  TCC echoes API and ACC’s appreciation of EPA’s 
inclusion of Small System Flexibility and encourages EPA to consider additional applications for flexibility. TCC 
proposes that EPA allow any NTNCWSs regardless of sizes that do not supply water to sensitive populations (e.g., 
schools or child-care facilities) the option to use POU devices as an alternative to conducting Lead Service Line 
Inventories or Lead Service Line Replacements on the portion of the service line onto which the POU is installed.  
This arrangement would allow NTNCWSs to outfit specific segments of their service lines with POU systems while 
replacing other lines if identified as LSLs. TCC echoes the comments of API and ACC that this additional flexibility 
would further EPA’s objectives of the proposed rule by addressing both service lines and premise plumbing as 
potential lead sources. 
 
The Proposed Rule was issued in the same year as the proposed per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR).  The proposed PFAS NPDWR identified Granular 
Activated Carbon (GAC) and Reverse Osmosis (RO) amongst the possible treatment technologies capable of 
removing PFAS from drinking water.  GAC and RO are also identified and certifiable via NSF / ANSI standards1 for 
the removal of lead from drinking water.  Where a single solution can achieve removal of both PFAS and Lead, 
EPA should allow NTNCWSs the flexibility to use a single solution instead of both removing LSLs and adding 
treatment for PFAS.  
 
Under the Proposed Rule, systems must make annual updates to service line inventories, tracking both changes 
in service lines and connector materials and systems would be required to identify service lines of unknown 
materials.  TCC proposes PWSs that use POU devices be exempt from the requirement to identify the material of 
connectors and unknown service lines.  A resulting LSL inventory would thus identify either the service line 
material or the presence of a POU system.  Expanding flexibility for NTNCWS compliance with the Proposed Rule 
will maintain alignment with EPA’s goals in the Proposed Rule of protection of human health and transparency to 
the NTNCWS water consumers. 
 
2. EPA should add alternative options and sample validation as an option for risk mitigation after disturbances for 
NTNCWSs – EPA is maintaining the Lead and Copper Rule Revision (LCRR) requirement that water systems provide 
pitcher filters or point-of-use devices for six months following partial and full LSL replacement, replacement of a 
lead connector, and other scenarios.  At NTNCWSs that serve at workplace, employers may find it feasible to 
supply employees with bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or POU devices.  Some workplace 
 
1 The Proposed Rule’s provisions for use of a POU device specify that the device must be independently certified by a third party to 
meet the American National Standards Institute standard applicable to the specific type of POU unit to reduce lead in drinking water.  
EPAs’ Consumer Tool for Identifying Point of Use (POU) Drinking Water Filters Certified to Reduce Lead specifies NSF/ANSI Standard 
53.

February 5, 2024 
Page 3 
 
environments are staged with water coolers that contain large (e.g., 5 gallon) bottles of water, in which case 
allowing continued use of that water supply would prevent waste of pitcher filters that would not be used. API 
requests that the flexibility to use bottled water be added for NTNCWSs in addition to the options of providing 
pitcher filters or POU devices.   
 
EPA specified a six-month period of time to provide pitcher filters or POU devices on the basis of a 2008 study2, 
which referenced that one site in the study suggested the potential for lead accumulated in the system to be 
released for months following disturbance, while most detected releases in systems took place in the first several 
days following LSL replacement.  The reason why one system was impacted for a lengthy period was not specified 
in the preamble.  The source document summarized elevated lead concentrations following LSL replacement as 
occurring in many cases for the first three days after replacement.  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have the ability 
to control flushing of service lines and premise plumbing within buildings as well as the ability to conduct their 
own sampling following disturbances.   As such, industrial facilities are capable of monitoring taps.  TCC agrees 
with API’s proposal that EPA allow NTNCWSs the option to sample taps after a minimum of 96 hours following a 
disturbance and eliminate the use of mitigations upon receipt of analytical results confirming that lead 
concentrations are below the lead action level.    
 
3. Clear and timely guidance for industrial facility NTNCWSs is requested – EPA has concluded “the overwhelming 
majority of NTNCWSs that do have LSLs and Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRR) service lines are expected 
to have relatively few of these service lines requiring replacement over the proposed 10-year deadline” (88 FR 
84912).  EPA’s position is based upon several assumptions, namely: 
• 
That responses from just 147 NTNCWSs to the 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey 
Assessment3  indicating that lead service lines are rarely used are representative of all 17,418 NTNCWSs 
in the Safe Drinking Water Information System, 
• 
That responses from three states estimating the number of LSLs at NTNCWSs in 20174 are accurate and 
representative across the country, and 
• 
That NTNCWSs have no stand-alone lead connectors and no GRR service lines since NTNCWSs are unlikely 
to replace only the upstream portion of an LSL and leave a galvanized service line in place, because they 
own the entire service, and galvanized lines have a high failure rate given age and disturbance like that 
produced by removing a section of LSL.5  
 
The assumption that few NTNCWSs have lead service lines cannot be confirmed until the October 2024 deadline 
to submit Lead Service Lines inventories.  Furthermore, piping makeup and configuration of NTNCWSs at industrial 
facilities could be influenced by the specific sector in which the piping is used.      
 
Conducting Lead Service Line Inventories is a complex undertaking.  NTNCWSs at industrial sites that attempt to 
leverage guidance documents that are developed for Community Water Systems are left to interpret guidance 
 
2 Sandvig, A., Kwan, P., Kirmeyer, G., Maynard, B., Mast, D., Trussell, R.R., Trussel, S., Cantor, A., and Prescott, A. (2008). Contribution 
of service line and plumbing fixtures to lead and copper rule compliance issue. AWWA Research Foundation, 523. 
3 88 FR 84912: Regarding NTNCWSs, Needs Survey responses from 147 NTNCWSs showed LSLs are rarely used in these systems since 
132 of them did not report any lead, GRR, or unknown service lines. 
4 Economic Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement, 2023. In August 2017, EPA disseminated a questionnaire 
to nine states asking for the estimated number or percentage of NTNCWSs with one or more LSLs and the total number of LSLs in 
NTNCWSs.  EPA received responses from seven states.  Four states did not provide any estimate.  The remaining three states 
provided estimates ranging from five to zero percent.  Based upon this data, EPA assumed 2.5% of NTNCWSs would have LSLs. 
5 Economic Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement, 2023 

Comments of TCC on EPA Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations  
for Lead and Copper Improvements 
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4 
 
written for systems that provide water to homes.   EPA Issued "Guidance for Developing and Maintaining a Service 
Line Inventory" in August 2022, and guidance tailored for small CWSs and NTNCWSs was not issued until June of 
2023.  TCC echoes the comments of API and ACC that, although EPA developed guidance tailored for smaller 
systems, the guidance was issued after LSL inventory development was underway.  Accordingly, TCC echoes the  
requests of API and ACC that EPA provide timely and clear guidance for NTNCWS with examples applicable to 
NTNCWSs at Industrial facilities. Furthermore, TCC would comment that eyewash stations should be included as 
active connections and therefore lines servicing them should be counted in the initial inventory. TCC comments 
that the “human consumption” definition does not list eyewash stations (skin absorbtion) and guidance 
documents should inform affected NTNC entities that they are to be included in the count.  
 
4. Clarity to the definition of Service Line is requested – EPA has added a definition of “Service Line” to the Proposed 
Rule, which states “Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe which 
connects the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water 
main to the outlet."  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have service lines that do not enter buildings and are used 
for purposes other than drinking or cooking.  TCC comments that EPA has the opportunity to add clarity and reduce 
ambiguity by specifying whether outlet in the definition is intended to mean all possible water uses or is specific 
to uses associated with cooking and drinking. 
 
TCC joins API and ACC in requesting that EPA clarify the definition of "Service Line" as follows: “Service line, for 
the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe that connects the water main to the building 
inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water main to an outlet used for cooking or 
drinking."  
 
5. EPA’s assumptions for Cost Burden to NTNCWSs is an underestimate – EPA’s Economic Analysis of the Proposed 
Rule has assumed that NTNCWSs will not incur burdensome  costs to update their inventories since they own their 
own service lines and are not expected to have any unknowns.  This assumption is not accurate.  NTNCWSs at 
industrial facilities that have been developing their inventories have incurred costs to field-identify service lines 
in advance of the October 16, 2024 submission deadline.  Unknown service lines can occur through a variety of 
reasons including age of a facility and loss of drawings. Furthermore, NTNCWSs are unlikely to have customer 
meters, thus unlikely to have water meter readings or replacements as an opportunity to collect service line data.  
Further, EPA has assumed NTNCWSs are able to rely on drawings as a means to identify connectors and service 
line materials of construction; however, due to the age of some facilities, this is not consistently applicable to 
NTNCWSs. TCC proposes PWSs that use POU devices be exempt from the requirement to identify the material of 
connectors and unknown service lines and/or alternative options for connector identification if information is 
difficult to maintain in a system with no lead concerns. 
 
Cost will be a significant challenge in replacing all lead service lines, especially when considered alongside 
competing priorities such as PFAS removal. The average cost to fully replace a single lead service line is estimated 
to be between $6,507 and $8,519 per the Proposed Rule’s Economic Analysis; however, for NTNCWSs at Industrial 
facilities, these costs are likely higher due to line length maintenance and safety practices required within 
industrial facilities and the possibility that piping may run adjacent to or through process units. While the federal 
Bipartisan Infrastructure Act has allocated funding for lead service line replacement, this funding will not be 
available to industrial facilities.  Similarly, the NTNCWSs at commercial facilities are not eligible for other funding 
mechanisms described in Section IV.G of the Proposed Rule’s preamble.  EPA should consider these realities for 
NTNCWSs when considering the additional flexibilities proposed by TCC, API, and ACC.  
 

Comments of TCC on EPA Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations  
for Lead and Copper Improvements 
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5 
 
6. Sample Tiering based on Premise Plumbing presents undue burden to Public Water Systems – The Proposed 
Rule maintains the tiering structure established by the original Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) and updated by the 
LCRR. In the Proposed Rule, EPA is proposing to adjust the definition for the highest priority tiers (Tier 1 and Tier 
2) to include sites with premise plumbing made of lead.  EPA specifies that by premise, plumbing made of lead, 
EPA means premise plumbing that consists of pure lead pipes, like the pipes used for LSLs, rather than pipes 
made from metal alloys which may contain lead content.  EPA further proposes galvanized premise plumbing to 
be an element of Tier 3. 
 
EPA has not requested that Lead Inventories include premise plumbing material construction.  TCC echoes the 
concern of API and ACC that identifying the premise plumbing material of construction includes additional time 
and cost that EPA has not considered in the Economic Analysis.  TCC joins API and ACC in commenting that EPA 
should not assume that NTNCWSs are likely to have previous knowledge of the premise plumbing present in 
buildings that are in their control.  
 
Conclusion:  
 
TCC appreciates the opportunity to file comments in this letter concerning the Proposed Rule.   EPA has requested 
feedback as to whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the regulatory approach used to 
address lead in drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique rule in section 
1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA. TCC joins API and ACC in proposing that the LCRI could be simplified and burden could be 
reduced without affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects by allowing 
NTNCWSs additional flexibility as described within these comments. 
 
Please contact me at (512) 646-6403, pearson@texaschemistry.org, when you wish to discuss these comments or if you 
would like any additional information concerning the issues raised in these comments.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Shea Pearson 
General Counsel & Director of Regulatory Affairs 
Texas Chemistry Council

Thank you for your recently announced proposal to replace 100% of lead pipes for the vast majority of water systems by
2037 and strictly limit partial replacements. Recognizing that there is no safe level of exposure to lead, EPA must adopt
strong standards that help our nation address one of the biggest environmental injustices of our time—exposure to toxic
lead pipes. That is why I’m writing to show my support.
The numerous public health and socioeconomic benefits this proposed rule would bring—such as prioritizing
replacements for those who are disproportionately impacted by lead and lowering the action level—are a strong step in
the right direction.

equitable, and expedited way possible. I encourage you to act with urgency to protect public health by finalizing the

(Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801) I support strong regulations to rapidly replace
100% of lead service lines and protect public health.
Caution: This email originated from outside EPA, please exercise additional caution when deciding whether to open
attachments or click on provided links.
Dear Administrator Michael Regan,
Thank you for your recently announced proposal to replace 100% of lead pipes for the vast majority of water systems by
2037 and strictly limit partial replacements. Recognizing that there is no safe level of exposure to lead, EPA must adopt
strong standards that help our nation address one of the biggest environmental injustices of our time—exposure to toxic
lead pipes. That is why I’m writing to show my support.
The numerous public health and socioeconomic benefits this proposed rule would bring—such as prioritizing
replacements for those who are disproportionately impacted by lead and lowering the action level—are a strong step in
the right direction.
Please continue to engage with communities and adopt strong standards that address lead pipes in the most transparent,
equitable, and expedited way possible. I encourage you to act with urgency to protect public health by finalizing the
most ambitious rule possible by October 2024.
Sincerely,
Mrs. Edna Anderson
812 Moore St  Beloit, WI 53511-5038
chaplainmamabear@aol.com

lead pipes. That is why I’m writing to show my support.
The numerous public health and socioeconomic benefits this proposed rule would bring—such as prioritizing
replacements for those who are disproportionately impacted by lead and lowering the action level—are a strong step in
the right direction.
Please continue to engage with communities and adopt strong standards that address lead pipes in the most transparent,
equitable, and expedited way possible. I encourage you to act with urgency to protect public health by finalizing the
most ambitious rule possible by October 2024.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0843 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Water Treatment Plant    603-225-8696   
 
 
The Honorable Michael Regan  
 
 
 
 
 
February 5, 2024 
Administrator  
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency  
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW  
Washington, DC 20460  
 
For electronic delivery to the docket via https://www.regulations.gov/  
  
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (Docket 
Id#: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801)  
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
On behalf of the City of Concord New Hampshire, I am pleased to provide the following 
comments to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI).  Our organizations represent drinking water professionals throughout the 
New England states.  
Our organization applauds the U.S. EPA for its efforts in developing a rule that will provide 
important, positive changes that will lead to further reduction of lead in the nation’s drinking 
water. Doing so will involve substantial, collaborative efforts between state and federal agencies, 
utilities, and the general public, where all will need to work together and conduct due diligence 
to minimize lead exposure. We recognize that while significant progress has been made over the 
past several decades in reducing children’s exposure to lead in their environment, that even small 
exposures may result in detrimental health effects. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
offer the opportunity to make further progress in reducing potential lead exposure from drinking 
water.   
Upon review, our organization offers the following comments to the below key items within the 
proposed rule, and endorse the much more detailed comments being offered by the American 
Water Works Association. In addition to our comments on the substance of the proposed rule, we 
wish to focus your initial attention on an important issue of rule scheduling and compliance that 
should be resolved immediately.  
EPA must immediately provide regulatory clarity and certainty about LCRR requirements 
and deadlines.  We support EPA’s approach of eliminating confusion and unnecessary 
expenditures of resources by deferring compliance with many aspects of the LCRR until the 
compliance date of LCRI.  However, until the LCRI is finalized, water systems have no 
assurance of what will be in it, and there is concern that even if we assume that the final rule will 
City of Concord, New Hampshire 
GENERAL SERVICES DEPARTMENT 
Water Supply Division 
53 Hutchins Street 
CONCORD, NH   03301 

contain the deferral of LCRR deadlines, any delay in issuance leaves systems vulnerable to non-
compliance. New England Water Works will be providing training and guidance on the LCRI in 
upcoming courses and at their spring and fall conferences. At present, we cannot in good faith 
provide specific advice on whether systems should continue to assume compliance with LCRR 
by October 2024.  
COMMENTS ON THE LCRI PROPOSAL:  
The following sections provide specific recommendations on the proposed rule provisions and 
responses to some of the related EPA requests for comments. Concord participated in the 
development of the American Water Works Association and Association of Metropolitan Water 
Agencies’ comments, and we urge you to carefully consider those as well. 
 
LCR AS A TREATMENT TECHNIQUE:  
CONCORD supports the continued use of the Safe Drinking Water Act’s (SDWA’s) 
Treatment Technique framework for reducing the risk of lead in drinking water.  
  
LEAD SERVICE LINE REPLACEMENT REQUIREMENTS:  
EPA has overstepped its authority in saying that access equals control: CONCORD 
supports the timely full removal of all lead service lines (LSLs1). However, we have serious 
concerns that EPA has overstepped its authority under the Safe Drinking Water Act.  EPA has 
presented contorted logic in attempting to demonstrate that having an owner allow access equals 
actual control. We do not agree that this is the case. Many of our water systems are actively 
working with their customers to voluntarily replace service lines on private property, often with 
substantial local funding, but the emphasis in those programs is that participation is voluntary. 
Water systems are not asserting that they have control, but rather are requesting access from the 
owner who has control over their property. Water systems do not control customer-owned 
portions of their plumbing and therefore cannot force customers to remove lead fixtures or 
plumbing materials without major changes to terms and condition agreements and methods to 
address legal liability implications.  
Federal Funding is Essential: EPA must make additional targeted funding available if 
communities across the nation are to succeed in eliminating LSLs within a decade. Concord has 
serious concerns that the federal government’s financial commitment falls far short of the funds 
needed to complete the job nationwide, and that much of EPA’s  public rhetoric on funding 
deliberately understates what a small fraction of the total cost will be covered by current federal 
commitments. Failure of the federal government to step up and provide adequate resources will 
either result in communities being unable to meet the deadlines in the LCRI, or will affect their 
ability to meet other regulatory requirements and system maintenance needs.  Proposed PFAS 
standards, suggested changes in the disinfection byproducts rules, and concerns about aged 
infrastructure will all require attention and funds at many of our member’s systems. Many 
systems are already challenged by existing state rules for PFAS, and will be further challenged if 
EPA finalizes its PFAS rule as proposed. New England has many of the oldest water systems in 
the U.S., and much of the oldest infrastructure in need of the most resources is in our poorest 
communities.  EPA’s own estimates2 of need for Drinking Water State Revolving Fund-eligible 
                                                 
1 Unless specifically stated, for simplicity we are referring to both lead service lines and galvanized requiring 
replacement as LSL.  
2DRINKING WATER INFRASTRUCTURE NEEDS SURVEY AND ASSESSMENT 7TH REPORT TO CONGRESS – September 
2023:  https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-09/Seventh%20DWINSA_September2023_Final.pdf 

infrastructure projects that are necessary over the 20-year period for water systems in New 
England to continue to provide safe drinking water to the public exceeds $28 billion. Unless the 
federal government increases its support, the burden of resolving the decades or centuries old 
issue of lead service lines will be borne by our most vulnerable ratepayers. 
Accelerated Replacement and CCT: CONCORD supports EPA’s use of incentives to 
accelerate LSL replacement, particularly the provision to defer construction or re-optimization of 
corrosion control treatment if a system can replace all its LSLs within 5 years of exceeding the 
proposed new lead Action Level. Both the LCRR and the LCRI recognize that lead service lines 
represent the most significant source of lead when they are present, and emphasize this by 
requiring that salvaged lead service lines be included in any evaluation of corrosion control.  
Requiring a focus on modifying carefully balanced treatment objectives, even as LSLs are 
beinging replaced, is inappropriate. CONCORD believes that EPA has struck an appropriate 
balance with this provision of encouraging that LSL replacement be conducted faster.  
Ten Year Deadlines: EPA should separate the metrics for replacing LSLs from those for 
resolving lead status unknown services. The current combined 3-year rolling average metrics 
for monitoring compliance with LSL replacement and resolution of unknowns are unworkable, 
and will almost inevitably result in unavoidable non-compliance for many if not most water 
systems. Systems with many more unknowns than confirmed LSLs, which appears to be the case 
for many systems in the preliminary inventories we have seen, will quickly exhaust the pool of 
LSLs to replace. And even if that were not an issue (for example, in a system with mostly 
confirmed LSLs and relatively few unknowns), the 3-year rolling average may discourage efforts 
to initially replace LSLs quickly. Replacing or resolving more than 10 percent for several early 
years will prevent compliance in later years with the proposed 3-year rolling average mechanism.  
CONCORD recommends that EPA revise this requirement by instead requiring a cumulative 
10 percent average beginning in year three for replacement of LSLs and a separate cumulative 10 
percent average for resolving unknowns.  
Counting Refusals: CONCORD also recommends that the final rule clarify how homes with 
LSLs where the owner has refused access to their private property and declined participation in 
the system’s LSL replacement program are accounted for in progress reporting. It is clear that 
some owners will simply refuse access, even at no cost, leaving some properties with a LSL in 
place. EPA’s proposal provides an appropriate provision that refusal after four attempts indicates 
that the property is not within the control of the water system. What is left unclear is whether a 
system can count that towards its annual 10 percent progress, and more importantly, whether the 
system would be in compliance at the end of 10 years (or five in the case where a system is 
availing itself of the incentivized deferral of corrosion control treatment provision). The final rule 
must make it clear that the replacement obligations are only applicable to those LSLs where the 
owner has allowed access.   
Partial Replacements: CONCORD supports the provision to allow partial replacements 
when they are conducted as part of an emergency repair or in coordination with planned 
infrastructure work. While the proposed exclusion of partial replacements during planned 
infrastructure work relative to LSL replacement projects is intended to prevent systems from 
intentionally conducting partial replacements, it does not account for customer refusal and further 
impedes lead removal. If a system is implementing a LSL replacement project in a neighborhood 
and a customer refuses to participate, prohibiting a partial replacement prevents the removal of 
the public-portion of the LSL and would require remobilization and additional costs to conduct 
the replacement in the future. EPA should remove this prohibition or at a minimum include 
language permitting partial replacements in these cases. 

SYSTEMS WITH MULTIPLE ACTION LEVEL EXCEEDANCES:  
Requiring filters: EPA should revisit the requirement to offer filters to all customers if a 
system has multiple Action Level (AL) exceedances.  With the lower proposed AL and the 
changes in sampling and reporting protocols, many systems will likely exceed the AL. Even in 
our older region, for many of the systems that have lead service lines, they account for less than 
one percent of the total number of service lines in the system.  If filters are needed at all, the 
focus should be on those buildings with LSLs.  Providing filters to buildings without a LSL will 
confuse the public and dilute the focus on replacing LSLs where they exist.  Providing them to 
buildings with LSLs could reduce the owner’s impetus to replace the LSL. EPA should 
eliminate this provision in its entirety, or at a minimum focus the offer on only those buildings 
with LSLs. 
Availability of certified filters:  There are likely to be substantial issues with availability of 
appropriately certified filters if this becomes a nationwide mandate. We have already heard from 
systems that are proactively making filters available as part of LSL investigations and 
replacements that they are having difficulty purchasing even lots of a few hundred filters, let 
alone the thousands that would be needed for larger systems if this requirement were to be 
implemented.  
If EPA chooses to retain any part of this requirement, it must clarify what the term “make 
filters available” means in practice, as the preamble states that the system must only make them 
available at “no direct cost” for low-income customers which implies that for all others, they 
could be offered to the customer at cost3.  EPA should consider the feasibility of creating a 
national program, similar to the COVID test kit program, where EPA would directly provide the 
certified filters to consumers.  This would simplify the requirement and make it nationally 
uniform. 
We also believe there will need to be an aggressive public outreach campaign conducted by EPA 
on the proper maintenance of POU filters.  Filters need to be regularly changed to ensure that 
water quality is maintained.  Our members are concerned that improperly maintained filters could 
lead to unintended negative public health impacts due to biological growth, etc.      
 
SAMPLING AND RESULTS REPORTING REQUIREMENTS:  
Rejecting inappropriate samples: EPA should further clarify when a system can reject an 
inappropriately collected sample. The rule preamble discusses ways a system can identify and 
avoid analyzing inappropriately collected samples, but there is no parallel rule. EPA should 
either provide additional language in the rule itself, or at a minimum develop explicit 
guidance that buildings that are not currently occupied or samples with stagnation times in 
excess of 12 hours should be discarded and new samples collected.  
Sample reporting requirements:  Requiring that sample results be provided to the sampler 
within three calendar days presents systems with the substantial risk of inadvertent and 
potentially unavoidable non-compliance.  Analysis and reporting of results typically takes several 
weeks from when the sample is collected - one or two additional days to provide the results is not 
a crisis. Monday holidays and shortened Friday work hours mean that when results are received 
on a Friday, there may well be no one to receive and respond to the data during that entire three-
calendar-day period.  Water system staff have many varied responsibilities to actively and safely 
manage their systems; there is not a dedicated staff person awaiting results, ready to jump into 
                                                 
3 This requirement is clearly distinguished for the language related to replacement of LSL or disturbances of LSL 
which requires that the system “provide filters and replacement cartridges”.  

action to immediately generate and distribute letters. EPA should change the rule to allow at a 
minimum, 5 business days and more ideally 7 business days, and limit rapid data 
transmittal to samples over the Action Level, retaining the current 30-day notification for all 
other samples.  Requiring as EPA proposes in the LCRI that all samples receive rush delivery 
notification defeats the purpose of quickly delivering elevated results.  When a result is over the 
AL, water system staff should be able to prioritize directly connecting with and educating those 
samplers (and beginning the process of working with the resident to begin the required 
Distribution System and Site Assessment).  
Sampling schedules: EPA should consider staggering implementation of standard monitoring. 
In prior rules, EPA has staggered certain requirements for monitoring with larger systems going 
first, and smaller systems staggered behind.  This allows for some lessons to be learned, and 
mitigates overload of laboratory capacity and primacy agency attention.  
Sample Collection Frequency: Systems with no LSLs with current sampling results below the 
AL that have qualified for reduced monitoring for many consecutive years should have a means 
to continue on reduced monitoring as deemed appropriate by the Primacy Agency. 
 
INVENTORY REQUIREMENTS:   
EPA should remove fire services and other non-potable service lines from inventory and 
replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to prevent potable 
uses. Similarly, there has been confusion about system obligations for piping downstream of the 
recognized service line.  A service line is clearly defined as connecting the system’s main with 
the building.  Additional piping connecting buildings, or connecting buildings with 
appurtenances on private property are not service lines. It should not be the responsibility of the 
water system to try to decipher materials beyond the service line, in facilities such as trailer parks 
or office or condo complexes.  
 
EPA should remove service lines serving abandoned properties from inventory and 
replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to assure 
construction of appropriate service line materials prior to the property receiving service. If the 
system has the appropriate administrative safeguards in place, this serves no useful propose and 
diverts resources from achieving LSL replacement at occupied locations.  
 
EPA should retain the LCRR requirement that systems must only replace lead connectors as 
they are encountered.  EPA should not include the replacement of connectors in the mandatory 
LSL replacement requirements because in many cases connector material records are not 
available, and field investigating all connector material in the absence of records would not be 
feasible or practical for most systems. Lead connectors should only be included in service line 
inventories for the purpose of identifying potential sampling locations, and only where existing 
records indicate their presence.  
Galvanized service lines: While CONCORD supports the inclusion of galvanized service lines 
downstream of a LSL in the inventory and replacement mandates of the proposed rule, we do not 
support the inclusion of those galvanized services that ever were downstream of a LSL or are 
currently downstream of unknown service lines in the inventory and replacement mandates. 
Including them in the mandate increases the total cost of replacement programs, with limited 
benefit. In addition, as EPA is requiring that all unknowns be resolved within 10 years, any 
galvanized service lines downstream of unknowns will be either identified as needing 
replacement because the upstream line was positively identified as lead, or the upstream service 

line will be positively identified as not lead. In the case of the latter, EPA should remove its 
requirement for systems to demonstrate that the upstream portion was never a LSL, as this is not 
possible given the previously unknown nature of the material, and instead reclassify the service 
line as non-lead and remove it from the replacement pool.  
Use of state laws or regulation prohibiting lead: EPA should be explicit that service lines 
without recorded material can  be classed as non-lead if state law or regulation extant at the time 
of construction prohibited the use of lead.  For example, the 1926 Maine State Law Lead Pipe 
ban should be allowed to qualify homes built in or after 1927 to be classified as Non-Lead.  
 
Simplifying Inventory Updates:  Systems with online inventories should be able to simply 
notify their state primacy agency annually with summary statistics on any changes and provide 
instructions on how to access their online inventory. There is no need for these systems to 
annually re-submit the complete inventory to the state.  
 
Validation Requirements: EPA should reconsider the content and timing of the proposed 
inventory validation requirement. The validation requirement will represent a distraction and 
unnecessary resource drag for many systems. The requirements are overly prescriptive, and the 
deadline overlaps with the most important time when systems will be working to make real 
progress at LSL replacement. Validation should only be necessary if the state primacy agency 
finds that the methods used to develop the inventory are unreliable. States should be given the 
latitude to review and approve validation work done prior to the LCRI implementation date.  
CONCORD also recommends that the validation language explicitly state that only one point 
on the private side and one point on the public side need validation.  EPA should also state that 
service lines that have been identified by a record on one side of the service and physical 
inspection on the other side do not need to be included in the validation pool.  
 
ELIMINATION OF THE TRIGGER LEVEL AND LOWERING THE ACTION LEVEL  
CONCORD supports the efforts that EPA has made to slightly simplify the rule by 
eliminating the Trigger Level.  However, EPA has failed to adequately analyze and document 
the synergistic impacts of lowering the Action Level, changes to the sampling site selection 
focusing on LSLs, and new sampling and reporting protocols using the highest of 1st and 5th liter 
samples. These proposed changes combined with the 24-hour public notice requirement will do 
unnecessary damage to public confidence as more systems exceed the Action Level, not because 
water quality is worse, but because the goal posts and game rules have been changed.  
 
OUTREACH AND EDUCATION REQUIREMENTS:  
Flexibility to improve coordinated outreach: EPA should carefully review all outreach 
activities for consistency, and design them as an integrated public education program. The 
outreach requirements must allow sufficient flexibility so that they can be thoughtfully 
integrated into a cohesive whole, helping consumers make good choices rather than unnecessarily 
scaring or confusing them. As currently proposed, customers in systems over the Action Level 
would receive the following outreach during a 12-month period:  
1. Two consumer confidence reports, with additional information on LSLs;  
2. an annual notice that they have a LSL or unknown (perhaps 4 additional times if their 
street is in a current LSL replacement program);  
3. exposure to the 24 hour Public Notice, and  

4. a lead education brochure with information on LSLs and replacement efforts (potentially 
twice that year).   
As part of that cohesive education program, for systems with LSLs, EPA should ensure that the 
24-hour Public Notice template emphasizes the following:  
1. That the samples were taken at homes with LSLs,  
2. That customers would have received information about the presence of a LSL or 
unknown, and  
3. A focus on actions the system and residents can take to replace  LSLs and identify 
unknowns.  
The goal should be to encourage consumer action to permanently reduce their potential exposure 
through drinking water by replacing their LSL if they have one.   
The current 60-day delivery requirement should be retained for Public Education after an 
Action Level exceedance. Especially with all the lead-related outreach efforts described above, 
including the new 24-hour Public Notice, there is no need to unnecessarily rush delivery of the 
public education brochures.  
CORROSION CONTROL TREATMENT: 
Corrosion control treatment: Any required changes to treatment and water quality parameters 
needs to be system specific. A one size fits all approach to establishing Optimum Corrosion 
Control Treatment presents real risk to what is often a carefully crafted balancing of objectives 
for simultaneous compliance. Rule text and guidance must make this clear.  
 
 
SIMPLIFYING REQUIREMENTS FOR SYSTEMS WITH FEW OR NO LSLs: 
 
EPA should consider simplifying the compliance and reporting path for systems with no LSLs or 
unknowns. If a system has no identified LSLs or GRR, and no specific indication that they  were 
used historically, there should be no need to conduct extensive potholing or other validation 
efforts, nor should service lines currently inventoried as unknown require risk mitigation efforts 
after disturbances. In cases where there are no known LSLs and no documented history that any 
had ever been installed, the likelihood of unknowns being lead is slight, and the primacy agency 
should have the flexibility to reduce the level of required effort.  
Systems with no LSLs and unknowns or connector updates should be able to submit a statement 
to their Primacy Agency to certify that no inventory updates are currently required.  
 
SCHOOL SAMPLING:  
CONCORD agrees that EPA has offered some additional flexibility for systems that have worked 
with schools and/or childcare facilities on lead testing, but believes the changes do not go far 
enough.  Primacy agencies should have the flexibility to exempt (or reduce the scope of testing 
for) systems with recent past or ongoing school and childcare facility lead testing programs, even 
if they are not exactly congruent with the specific requirements in the proposed rule.  
 
 
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this complex and important effort to further 
reduce potential lead exposures to consumers from drinking water and premise plumbing.  

 
 
 
 
 
 
Marco Philippon 
Water Treatment Superintendent 
General Services Department | City of Concord 
53 Hutchins Street, Concord, NH 03301 
MPhilippon@concordnh.gov 
(603) 230-3951

The Honorable Michael Regan

Administrator  
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency

RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (Docket 
Id#: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801)  
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
On behalf of the New England Water Works Association (NEWWA), in conjunction with the 
state associations Green Mountain Water Environment Association, Maine Water Utilities 
Association, Massachusetts Water Works Association, New Hampshire Water Works 
Association, and Rhode Island Water Works Association, we are pleased to provide the 
following comments to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements (LCRI).  Our organizations represent drinking water professionals 
throughout the New England states.  
Our organizations applaud the U.S. EPA for its efforts in developing a rule that will provide 
important, positive changes that will lead to further reduction of lead in the nation’s drinking 
water. Doing so will involve substantial, collaborative efforts between state and federal agencies, 
utilities, and the general public, where all will need to work together and conduct due diligence 
to minimize lead exposure. We recognize that while significant progress has been made over the 
past several decades in reducing children’s exposure to lead in their environment, even small 
exposures may result in detrimental health effects. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
offer the opportunity to make further progress in reducing potential lead exposure from drinking 
water.   

2 
 
Upon review, our organizations offer the following comments to the below key items within the 
proposed rule, and endorse the much more detailed comments being offered by the national 
water associations. In addition to our comments on the substance of the proposed rule, we wish 
to focus your initial attention on an important issue of rule scheduling and compliance that 
should be resolved immediately.  
EPA must immediately provide regulatory clarity and certainty about LCRR requirements 
and deadlines.  We support EPA’s approach of eliminating confusion and unnecessary 
expenditures of resources by deferring compliance with many aspects of the LCRR until the 
compliance date of LCRI.  However, until the LCRI is finalized, water systems have no 
assurance of what will be in it, and there is concern that even if we assume that the final rule will 
contain the deferral of LCRR deadlines, any delay in issuance leaves systems vulnerable to non-
compliance. NEWWA will be providing training and guidance on the LCRI in upcoming courses 
and at our spring and fall conferences. At present, we cannot in good faith provide specific 
advice on whether systems should continue to assume compliance with LCRR by October 2024.  
COMMENTS ON THE LCRI PROPOSAL:  
The following sections provide specific recommendations on the proposed rule provisions and 
responses to some of the related EPA requests for comments. A number of NEWWA members 
participated in the development of multiple national water association’s comments, and we urge 
you to carefully consider those as well. 
LCR AS A TREATMENT TECHNIQUE:  
NEWWA supports the continued use of the Safe Drinking Water Act’s (SDWA’s) Treatment 
Technique framework for reducing the risk of lead in drinking water.  
LEAD SERVICE LINE REPLACEMENT REQUIREMENTS:  
EPA has overstepped its authority in saying that access equals control: NEWWA supports 
the timely full removal of all lead service lines (LSLs1). However, we have serious concerns 
that EPA has overstepped its authority under the Safe Drinking Water Act.  EPA has presented 
contorted logic in attempting to demonstrate that having an owner allow access equals actual 
control. We do not agree that this is the case. Many of our water systems are actively working 
with their customers to voluntarily replace service lines on private property, often with 
substantial local funding, but the emphasis in those programs is that participation is voluntary. 
Water systems are not asserting that they have control, but rather are requesting access from the 
owner who has control over their property. Water systems do not control customer-owned 
portions of their plumbing and therefore cannot force customers to remove lead fixtures or 
plumbing materials without major changes to terms and condition agreements and methods to 
address legal liability implications.  
 
1 Unless specifically stated, for simplicity we are referring to both lead service lines and galvanized requiring 
replacement as LSL.  

3 
 
Federal Funding is Essential: EPA must make additional targeted funding available if 
communities across the nation are to succeed in eliminating LSLs within a decade. NEWWA 
members have serious concerns that the federal government’s financial commitment falls far 
short of the funds needed to complete the job nationwide, and that much of EPA’s public rhetoric 
on funding deliberately understates what a small fraction of the total cost will be covered by 
current federal commitments. Failure of the federal government to step up and provide adequate 
resources will either result in communities being unable to meet the deadlines in the LCRI, or 
will affect their ability to meet other regulatory requirements and system maintenance needs.  
Proposed PFAS standards, suggested changes in the disinfection byproducts rules, and concerns 
about aged infrastructure will all require attention and funds at many of our member’s systems. 
Many systems are already challenged by existing state rules for PFAS, and will be further 
challenged if EPA finalizes its PFAS rule as proposed. New England has many of the oldest 
water systems in the U.S., and much of the oldest infrastructure in need of the most resources is 
in our poorest communities.  EPA’s own estimates2 of need for Drinking Water State Revolving 
Fund-eligible infrastructure projects that are necessary over the 20-year period for water systems 
in New England to continue to provide safe drinking water to the public exceeds $28 billion. 
With respect to cost estimates to address the replacement of lead service lines, EPA estimated in 
the same report that “Based on the findings from the 7th DWINSA, the total projected number of 
LSLs in the United States is 9.2 million for the states, U.S. territories, Puerto Rico, and the 
District of Columbia…. The estimated cost to replace these LSLs ranges from approximately $50 
billion to $80 billion (2021 dollars).”  This estimate does not account for the cost to replace 
Galvanized Requiring Replacement lines.  Unless the federal government increases its support, 
the burden of resolving the decades or centuries old issue of lead service lines will be borne by 
our most vulnerable ratepayers. 
Accelerated Replacement and CCT: NEWWA supports EPA’s use of incentives to 
accelerate LSL replacement, particularly the provision to defer construction or re-optimization of 
corrosion control treatment if a system can replace all its LSLs within 5 years of exceeding the 
proposed new lead Action Level. Both the LCRR and the LCRI recognize that lead service lines 
represent the most significant source of lead when they are present, and emphasize this by 
requiring that salvaged lead service lines be included in any evaluation of corrosion control.  
Requiring a focus on modifying carefully balanced treatment objectives, even as LSLs are 
bringing replaced, is inappropriate. NEWWA believes that EPA has struck an appropriate 
balance with this provision of encouraging that LSL replacement be conducted faster.  
Ten Year Deadlines: EPA should separate the metrics for replacing LSLs from those for 
resolving lead status unknown services. The current combined 3-year rolling average metrics 
for monitoring compliance with LSL replacement and resolution of unknowns are unworkable, 
and will almost inevitably result in unavoidable non-compliance for many if not most water 
systems. Systems with many more unknowns than confirmed LSLs, which appears to be the case 
for many systems in the preliminary inventories we have seen, will quickly exhaust the pool of

LSLs to replace. And even if that were not an issue (for example, in a system with mostly 
confirmed LSLs and relatively few unknowns), the 3-year rolling average may discourage efforts 
to initially replace LSLs quickly. Replacing or resolving more than 10 percent for several early 
years will prevent compliance in later years with the proposed 3-year rolling average mechanism.  
NEWWA recommends that EPA revise this requirement by instead requiring a cumulative 
10 percent average beginning in year three for replacement of LSLs and a separate cumulative 10

system would be in compliance at the end of 10 years (or five in the case where a system is

Partial Replacements: NEWWA supports the provision to allow partial replacements when
