finds that the methods used to develop the inventory are unreliable. States should be given the 
latitude to review and approve validation work done prior to the LCRI implementation date.  
NEWWA also recommends that the validation language explicitly state that only one point on 
the private side and one point on the public side need validation.  EPA should also state that 
service lines that have been identified by a record on one side of the service and physical 
inspection on the other side do not need to be included in the validation pool.  
ELIMINATION OF THE TRIGGER LEVEL AND LOWERING THE ACTION LEVEL  
NEWWA supports the efforts that EPA has made to slightly simplify the rule by eliminating 
the Trigger Level.  However, EPA has failed to adequately analyze and document the 
synergistic impacts of lowering the Action Level, changes to the sampling site selection focusing 
on LSLs, and new sampling and reporting protocols using the highest of 1st and 5th liter samples. 
These proposed changes combined with the 24-hour public notice requirement will do 
unnecessary damage to public confidence as more systems exceed the Action Level, not because 
water quality is worse, but because the goal posts and game rules have been changed.  
OUTREACH AND EDUCATION REQUIREMENTS:  
Flexibility to improve coordinated outreach: EPA should carefully review all outreach 
activities for consistency, and design them as an integrated public education program. The 
outreach requirements must allow sufficient flexibility so that they can be thoughtfully 
integrated into a cohesive whole, helping consumers make good choices rather than 
unnecessarily scaring or confusing them. As currently proposed, customers in systems over the 
Action Level would receive the following outreach during a 12-month period:  
1. Two consumer confidence reports, with additional information on LSLs;  

8 
 
2. an annual notice that they have a LSL or unknown (perhaps 4 additional times if their 
street is in a current LSL replacement program);  
3. exposure to the 24 hour Public Notice, and  
4. a lead education brochure with information on LSLs and replacement efforts (potentially 
twice that year).   
As part of that cohesive education program, for systems with LSLs, EPA should ensure that 
the 24-hour Public Notice template emphasizes the following:  
1. That the samples were taken at homes with LSLs,  
2. That customers would have received information about the presence of a LSL or 
unknown, and  
3. A focus on actions the system and residents can take to replace  LSLs and identify 
unknowns.  
The goal should be to encourage consumer action to permanently reduce their potential exposure 
through drinking water by replacing their LSL if they have one.   
The current 60-day delivery requirement should be retained for Public Education after an 
Action Level exceedance. Especially with all the lead-related outreach efforts described above, 
including the new 24-hour Public Notice, there is no need to unnecessarily rush delivery of the 
public education brochures.  
CORROSION CONTROL TREATMENT: 
Corrosion control treatment: Any required changes to treatment and water quality parameters 
needs to be system specific. A one size fits all approach to establishing Optimum Corrosion 
Control Treatment presents real risk to what is often a carefully crafted balancing of objectives 
for simultaneous compliance. Rule text and guidance must make this clear.  
 
SIMPLIFYING REQUIREMENTS FOR SYSTEMS WITH FEW OR NO LSLs: 
 
EPA should consider simplifying the compliance and reporting path for systems with no LSLs or 
unknowns. If a system has no identified LSLs or GRR, and no specific indication that they were 
used historically, there should be no need to conduct extensive potholing or other validation 
efforts, nor should service lines currently inventoried as unknown require risk mitigation efforts 
after disturbances. In cases where there are no known LSLs and no documented history that any 
had ever been installed, the likelihood of unknowns being lead is slight, and the primacy agency 
should have the flexibility to reduce the level of required effort.  
Systems with no LSLs and unknowns or connector updates should be able to submit a statement 
to their Primacy Agency to certify that no inventory updates are currently required.  
SCHOOL SAMPLING:  
NEWWA agrees that EPA has offered some additional flexibility for systems that have worked 
with schools and/or childcare facilities on lead testing, but believes the changes do not go far 
enough.  Primacy agencies should have the flexibility to exempt (or reduce the scope of testing 

9 
 
for) systems with recent past or ongoing school and childcare facility lead testing programs, even 
if they are not exactly congruent with the specific requirements in the proposed rule.  
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this complex and important effort to further 
reduce potential lead exposures to consumers from drinking water and premise plumbing.  
 
Kirsten King, CEO 
New England Water Works Association, Inc. 
Representing 2,000 Water Professionals Across New England 
 
Joseph Duncan, President 
Green Mountain Water Environment Association 
Representing 450 Vermont Water Professionals

Maine Water Utilities Association

FOR ELECTRONIC DELIVERY  
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper Improvements (Docket ID#:  
EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801)  
 
Dear Administrator Regan,  
Seattle Public Utilities (SPU) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).   SPU would like to express our support for the Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements in general.  Public health protection should be a top priority for the US 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), including the reduction of exposure to lead. 
 
There are a number of areas of the rule that we have concerns about or would like clarification. 
 
1. School and Childcare testing requirements as written in the LCRI and LCRR could result in 
an increased burden on utilities with little to no public health improvement for some 
utilities, especially if the utility has very low lead levels (<lead PQL) in routine testing and is 
producing water meeting the optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT) requirements.  
Limiting the use of lead testing results from schools to only those completed after 2021 
seems unnecessarily restrictive.  Any lead results from testing done at schools and 
childcare facilities that meets the proposed sampling criteria should be allowed as long as 
the utility can show that water quality conditions have been consistently meeting the OCCT 
requirements during the time of testing, the utility’s 90th percentile level is consistently 
below the 5 ppb, and the facilities are not connected to the system by a lead service line or 
GRR.  Please clarify if the school testing requirements include privately operated schools. 
 
2. Please clarify that utilities with no known lead service lines or galvanized requiring 
replacement (GRR) can remain on reduced monitoring even if there are some unknown 
service lines in the system. 
 
3. Including connector materials (i.e. lead goosenecks) in the inventory should be a much 
lower priority than service line materials.  Many utilities do not document the materials 
used for connectors, and determining the materials used for connectors could be a huge 

700 Fifth Avenue |  PO Box 34018  |  Seattle, WA 98124-4018  |  206-684-3000  |  seattle.gov/util 
 
burden with very little public health benefit, especially for those utilities with no known lead 
service lines or GRR.   We agree with the requirement to replace lead connectors when 
encountered in the course of regular work. 
 
4. If LCRI is requiring utilities to inventory all service line materials within 10 years of 
implementation (this needs clarification), there should be a clause allowing systems with 
no known LSLs or GRR to stop updating the inventory when a certain level of “knowns” is 
reached.  For example, if the utility has documented a minimum of 10% (or whatever a 
statistically representative number is) of their service lines, and no lead service lines were 
found, it should be assumed that the remaining service lines are also not lead. 
 
5. Please clarify if utilities with no known lead service lines on the public side, but a significant 
portion of unknowns on the private side:  
 
o Will be subject to the requirement of replacing “unknowns” at a rate of 10% per 
year. 
 
o Will need to provide filter pitchers to the customers with unknown materials. 
 
o Will need to offer tap sampling to those customers with unknown service lines. 
 
6. Please clarify the start date for distributing pitchers when lead connectors are found and 
replaced. 
 
7. Please clarify if utilities with no known lead service lines on the public side, but with lead 
connectors, will need to change sampling locations if the location of the lead connectors is 
unknown.   
 
8. Reporting results to customers within 3 days of receiving the results from the laboratory 
may be a burden for those utilities with results <5 ppb.  This requirement should only apply 
to those customers with results > 5 ppb. 
 
Thank you for this opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements.  If you have any questions regarding these comments, please contact Seattle 
Public Utilities at lynn.kirby@seattle.gov or 206-684-0216. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Lynn Kirby 
SPU Water Quality Engineer 
 
 
Cc: 
Alex Chen, SPU Water Line of Business Deputy Director  
Winsome Robinson Williams, SPU Drinking Water Quality Division Director

Dear Administrator Regan,
Enclosed you will find the names of 865 individuals who commented on your proposed regulations to
establish emissions standards for heavy-duty vehicles such as delivery trucks, garbage trucks,
day/sleeper cabs, and school/transit buses. These standards aim to reduce greenhouse gas emissions
starting in model year 2027. The rule sets vehicle emission standards for new heavy-duty trucks and
buses.
The signers below agree that:
Thank you for your recently announced proposal to replace 100% of lead pipes for the vast majority of
water systems by 2037 and strictly limit partial replacements. Recognizing that there is no safe level of
exposure to lead, young people want the EPA to adopt strong standards that help our nation address one
of the biggest environmental injustices of our time—exposure to toxic lead pipes. That is why I’m writing
to show my support.
The numerous public health and socioeconomic benefits this proposed rule would bring—such as
prioritizing replacements for those who are disproportionately impacted by lead and lowering the action
level—are a strong step in the right direction.
Please continue to engage with communities and adopt strong standards that address lead pipes in the
most transparent, equitable, and expedited way possible. I encourage you to act with urgency to protect
public health by finalizing the most ambitious rule possible by October 2024.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Kyli Wagner
Director, Defend Our Future

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0818 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
unleadedkids.org
1
 
 
February 4, 2024 
 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, EPA Docket Center 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Mail Code 28221T, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW 
Washington, DC 20460 
Submitted to Docket ID Number: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. 
 
Re: Comments on Proposed Improvements to Lead and Copper Rule:  
 
 
To Whom It May Concern:  
 
Unleaded Kids enthusiastically supports EPA’s proposed 
improvements to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) published 
in the December 6, 2023, Federal Register. If finalized as 
proposed, the rule should virtually eliminate the estimated 9.2 
million lead service lines (LSLs) from our public water systems 
with the vast majority replaced by 2037.1 This would be a major 
achievement in the effort to reduce children’s and adult’s exposure 
to lead in drinking water. 
 
We applaud EPA for investing the three years since the 2021 LCR 
revisions to dramatically improve the rule by: 
 
Ensuring the estimated socioeconomic benefits of the rule include: 1) reduced deaths from 
cardiovascular disease (CVD) from adult exposure to lead; 2) fewer cases of Attention-
Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) from early childhood exposure to lead; and 3) fewer 
cases of babies born with low birth weight from exposure to lead during the pregnancy. The 
agency’s investment in rigorously evaluating the scientific evidence and developing peer-
reviewed quantitative models demonstrates the tremendous benefits of reducing people’s 
exposure to lead, not just from drinking water but from all sources. Specifically, the 
socioeconomic benefits from the proposed rule vastly outweigh the cost and range from $17.3 to 
$34.8 billion per year – a whopping 8 to 12 times the annual cost of replacement. 
 
Requiring replacement of all LSLs as an integral part of a safe drinking water compliance 
program instead of as a last resort when the lead action level is exceeded. By uncoupling full 
LSL replacement from lead action level exceedances, Americans can have real hope that they will 
not be drinking water through a lead pipe.  
 
Refining the public notice and transparency provisions based on feedback from impacted 
communities. These improvements enable communities to better track progress, identify 
problems, and more effectively engage in helping the water system succeed. As a result, water 
systems are more likely to comply with the rule. 
 
Basing water systems responsibility to fully replace LSLs on their control of the service line 
instead of ownership and then defining control based on access. This change addresses problems 
that have plagued LSL replacement since the 1990s by enabling water systems to simply redirect 
 
1 Based on publishing a final rule in October 2024, compliance would be required in late 2027. 
Unleaded Kids is the only 
national organization focusing 
on reducing the cumulative 
impact of all sources of 
children’s exposure to lead. 
For more information see 
www.unleadedkids.org.  

 
 
Page 2 
 
responsibility to customers to address safe drinking water concerns with LSLs on private 
property.  
 
Fixing various implementation challenges so that the water systems would have significant 
incentives to replace LSLs, lead connectors, and service lines that are galvanized requiring 
replacement (GRR). When incentives are properly aligned, water systems and customers have 
greater reason to replace LSLs in a cost-effective manner.  
 
After providing our specific recommendations to improve the proposal in Part I, we will respond to 
selected EPA requests for comments in Part II. 
 
 
Part I: Specific Recommendations to Improve the Proposal 
 
As we reviewed the proposal closely, we identified several areas where it could be improved. The primary 
areas where those improvements are needed consist of: 
1. Amending the definition of “service line” to clearly include both the portions owned by the 
property owner and the water system; 
2. Providing criteria to establish when a water system has “access” to LSLs; 
3. Eliminating deferred deadline limiting mandatory full LSL replacements to 10,000 per year; 
4. Modifying the deferred deadline for 0.039 replacements so it is based on the number of service 
lines and not the number of households; and 
5. Reducing the lead action level to 5 parts per billion (ppb) but continuing to use the 10 ppb as a 
trigger for greater corrosion control.  
 
  
1. 
Amending the definition of “service line” to clearly include both the portions owned by the 
property owner and the water system. 
 
The proposal modifies 40 C.F.R. § 141.2 by simplifying the definition of “lead service line,” removing 
the definition of “full lead service line replacement,” and adding a definition of “service line.” These 
changes address significant problems with circular and confusing definitions created by the 2021 
revisions to the LCR, especially in the final three sentences of the definition of “lead service line.”2 
 
However, the changes go too far when they eliminate a reference to property ownership in the definition 
of the lead service line. Specifically, a key sentence proposed for deletion says: “A lead service line may 
be owned by the water system, owned by the property owner, or both.”3  
 
Without this sentence, water systems could define the service line as if it were in multiple parts based on 
ownership. Yet, the pipe is an integral unit designed to move drinking water from the main to the home or 
building. The service line’s function does not change based on ownership. EPA clearly – and justifiably – 
did not intend that outcome based on its reasoning in the preamble to the proposed rule and the changes 
made to § 141.84(d).  
 
2 The proposal would change the definition of lead service line at 40 C.F.R. § 141.2. as follows: “Lead service line 
means a portion of pipe that is made of lead, which connects the water main to the building inlet. A lead service line 
may be owned by the water system, owned by the property owner, or both. For the purposes of this subpart, a 
galvanized service line is considered a lead service line if it ever was or is currently downstream of any lead service 
line or service line of unknown material. If the only lead piping serving the home is a lead gooseneck, pigtail, or 
connector, and it is not a galvanized service line that is considered a lead service line the service line is not a lead 
service line. For purposes of § 141.86(a) only, a galvanized service line is not considered a lead service line.”  
3 Id. 

 
 
Page 3 
 
 
We strongly encourage EPA to restore the sentence by adding it to the end of the definition of “service 
line” so it reads:  
 
Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe which connects 
the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the 
water main to the outlet. A service line may be owned by the water system, owned by the property 
owner, or both. 
 
The definition of a “lead service line” would remain as proposed to read: 
 
Lead service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a service line that is made 
of lead or where a portion of the service line is made of lead. 
 
 
2. 
Providing criteria to establish when a water system has “access” to LSLs.  
 
According to the preamble of the proposed rule, the improvements to the LCR are intended to require that 
water systems conduct full LSL replacement without regard to ownership, as long as they are under the 
control of the water system. In the proposal, “control” is based on “access” to the service lines, and the 
proposal provides “requirements and flexibilities to increase access and expedite full service line 
replacement . . .”4  
 
Unfortunately, the proposal does not establish criteria that water systems can follow to determine whether 
they have access to a service line. Without clear criteria, water systems are likely to narrowly define 
“access” so that an LSL that is owned by a private property owner, in part or in whole, is not the system’s 
responsibility. This issue has plagued progress on LSL replacement and undermined efforts to reduce lead 
in drinking water since 1991. 
 
Instead of providing useful criteria to establish if access is present, EPA takes the unusual - and 
unnecessary – step of stating at § 141.84(d)(2)(i) that “[t]his rule does not establish the criteria for 
determining whether a system has access to conduct full service line replacement.” Nonetheless, § 
141.84(d)(2) hints at criteria with a confusing parenthetical example - “(e.g., legal access, physical 
access).”  
 
The resulting ambiguity is likely to make one of the most important provisions of the proposed rule 
difficult to enforce – an unfortunate outcome that undermines the public health goal of the Safe Drinking 
Water Act (SDWA) because it all-to-often leaves environmental justice communities that lack the 
resources, political clout, or access to lawyers most at risk.  
 
In the preamble, EPA explained that it was silent “because of the wide variation of relevant State and local 
laws and water tariff agreements as well as the potential for these to change over time.”5 We recognize 
that there is a wide variation in laws and that they change over time, but that is hardly justification to 
avoid establishing criteria that would avoid confusion and endless legal disputes. 
 
4 88 Federal Register 84920 stating that “EPA is proposing to treat a service line as under the system’s control 
wherever a water system has adequate access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full service line 
replacement. This means that a water system would be in violation of the rule if the system fails to replace a service 
line in accordance with the proposed requirements even though it has adequate access to conduct a full service line 
replacement.”  
5 Id. 

 
 
Page 4 
 
 
From our perspective, SDWA’s purpose is to protect public health. This is a public purpose that empowers 
government agencies at the federal level and in every State to act even if it involves private property.  
 
In this case, we suggest that the criteria be added to § 141.84(d)(2) that sets forth a process that water 
systems should follow to determine if they have sufficient access, and, therefore, control. The process 
should be based on the provisions of the proposed rule that require water systems to seek access by 
engaging with the owner of property under which the service line is buried. If the property owner 
provides access and gives a green light to the water system to replace the service line, the water system 
has control. If the property owner refuses to provide access, the water system lacks the control needed to 
trigger the full service line replacement provisions. In addition, the proposed rule recognizes that property 
owners change by requiring water systems to provide notice of the LSL to new customers with the 
language inviting the new owner to have the service line replaced.  
 
Therefore, we recommend the following changes6 to proposed § 141.84(d) regarding mandatory full 
service line replacement: 
 
(1) All water systems must replace all lead and galvanized requiring replacement service lines 
under the control of the water system unless the replacement would leave in place a partial lead 
service line.  
 
(2) Where a water system has access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full service 
line replacement, the service line is under its control, and the water system must replace the 
service line regardless of ownership of the line or the property it is on. Where a water system 
does not have access to conduct full service line replacement, the water system is not required by 
this rule to replace the line, but the water system must document the reasons that the water system 
does not have access and include any specific laws, regulations, and/or water tariff agreements 
that affect the water system’s ability to gain access to conduct full replacement of lead service 
line or a and galvanized requiring replacement service line replacement identified pursuant to 
paragraph (c)(1)(viii) of this section. The water system must provide this documentation to the 
State pursuant to § 141.90(e)(10).  
 
(i) This rule does not establish the criteria for determining whether a system has access to 
conduct full service line replacement. The criteria for determining whether a system has 
access to conduct full service line replacement include: whether the system can safely 
enter the property; whether the system can safely conduct the replacement; and whether 
the system has obtained the property owner’s consent, if consent is required for access. 
Presence of a lead service line on private property does not, by itself, determine whether 
a system has access to conduct full service line replacement for purposes of this rule. Any 
State or local laws or water tariff agreement requirements to gain access to conduct full 
service line replacement must be identified in the service line replacement plan as 
described in paragraph (c) of this section and in the notification provided to persons 
served by lead, galvanized requiring replacement, and unknown service lines as described 
in § 141.85(e).  
 
(3) Where a water system has legal access pursuant to § 141.84(d)(2)(i) to conduct full service 
line replacement only if property owner consent is obtained, the water system must make a 
‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain property owner consent or written waiver documenting refusal of 
access for the purpose of full lead service line replacement. If such a water system does not obtain 
 
6 Changes are in red font. Underlined text indicates text to be added. Strikethrough text indicates text to be deleted. 

 
 
Page 5 
 
consent after making a ‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain it from any property owner, then the water 
system is not required by this rule to replace any portion of the service line at that address.  
 
As noted above, we also recommend: 
 
Removing from § 141.84(d)(1) the confusing phrase “unless the replacement would leave in 
place a partial lead service line.” As written, it makes little sense to us since it implies that full 
replacement would not be required if a partial would remain.  
 
Adding to the first sentence in § 141.84(d)(2) the phrase “regardless of ownership of the line or 
the property it is on” to reinforce that ownership of the line is not the controlling factor. This 
phrase is in the current definition of “full LSL replacement” at § 141.2 that EPA proposes to 
delete as confusing.7  
 
Revising the text in the third sentence of § 141.84(d)(2) to avoid saying “galvanized requiring 
replacement service line replacement.” While accurate, the use of the word “replacement” twice 
so close together is awkward. 
 
Deleting the word “legal” in § 141.84(d)(3) since it is unnecessary. 
 
 
3. 
Eliminating deferred deadline limiting mandatory full LSL replacements to 10,000 per year. 
 
Unleaded Kids wants LSLs to be removed from service as soon as possible. EPA’s proposal giving ten 
years for the vast majority of water systems to remove LSLs is a significant step towards that goal. 
 
We also understand EPA’s concerns about affordability as well as the disruption to the community. 
Therefore, we are not opposed to giving a few more years to those water systems such as Chicago Water 
that have a huge number of LSLs.  
 
However, we oppose deferring the ten-year deadline based on an absolute number of LSLs – whether 
8,000 or 10,000 – replaced each year as EPA proposes at § 141.84(d)(5)(i). Unlike many major 
infrastructure projects such as installing a water treatment plant, replacing LSLs is completely scalable; 
each additional crew can increase the number of LSLs replaced. The only limit is finding crews to do the 
work – a situation that will change based on local conditions. The examples EPA provides to justify that 
limit do not address whether the water system had a reason or the capacity to go faster.  
 
In addition, EPA acknowledges that only a few cities, such as Chicago, Cleveland, or New York have so 
many LSLs that they could benefit from the deferral. In Chicago Water’s case, they will be allowed to 
defer completely full service line replacement for more than 40 years – until 2067 – to remove the LSLs. 
This is unacceptably long.  
 
We also think that writing a rule for a few water systems is inappropriate. Instead of building a deferral 
based on an absolute number into the rule, those water systems with more than 100,000 LSLs should 
pursue a variance or consent decree that is tailored to their situation much as Denver Water has done. That 
process includes public participation and periodic reviews. 
 
For these reasons, we recommend that EPA delete § 141.84(d)(5)(i).  
 
 
 
7 The current rules says” “full lead service line replacement means the replacement of a lead service line (as well as 
galvanized service lines requiring replacement), as defined in this section, that results in the entire length of the 
service line, regardless of service line ownership, . . .” (emphasis added). 

 
 
Page 6 
 
4. 
Modifying the deferred deadline for 0.039 replacements/year so it is based on the number of 
service lines and not the number of households. 
 
We see EPA’s logic in granting a deferral for water systems with a high percentage of LSLs. It is a more 
rational approach to considering affordability. 
  
Therefore, we are not opposed to the provision at § 141.84(d)(5)(i) that would defer the ten-year full 
service line replacement deadline a few years if a water system would be required to replace each year 
more than 3.9% of the number households it serves. Based on EPA’s calculations in Exhibit 4 of the 
Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI),8 5 to 17 
large systems, 141 to 420 medium systems, and 570 to 1,737 small systems may exceed this 3.9% 
threshold based on a ten-year replacement deadline. And almost all those systems would have LSLs 
replaced in 17 years.  
 
However, we recommend that EPA base the deferral on the number of service lines instead of households 
and adjust the percentage accordingly. We make this recommendation because: 
 
Determining the number of households served by a water system with confidence is difficult, 
even under the best of circumstances. For example, single family homes are often subdivided into 
multiple households and the number of homes in manufactured housing communities can change 
year-to-year. Most communities lack a solid inventory of households. 
 
Unlike households, water systems know with confidence the number of service lines because they 
use it for billing purposes.  
 
The number of service lines is an essential part of the inventory. As a result, relying on service 
lines would simplify compliance assurance and enforcement. 
 
In addition, basing the deferral for LSL replacement on the number of households creates a number of 
complications that EPA did not appear to consider. For example, multi-family properties with more than 
20 households are unlikely to have LSLs because their service lines are typically larger than 2” in 
diameter – a size that is uncommon for lead pipe. As a result, water systems with significant numbers of 
large multi-family properties would be differently affected than those large percentages of single-family 
homes. 
 
We understand that switching from households to service lines may require that EPA increase the 3.9% 
number. But the change is warranted.  
 
 
5. 
Reducing the lead action level to 5 ppb but continuing to use the 10 ppb as a trigger for 
greater corrosion control.  
 
We fully support EPA’s proposal to reduce the lead action level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb. Based on Exhibit 
4 of the preamble, 95% of water systems without LSLs can achieve 15 ppb. If they have LSLs, between 
73% and 80% can meet 15 ppb. Dropping the level to 10 ppb would mean 91% of water systems without 
LSLs can achieve it. If they have LSLs, the percentage drops to 59% to 65% depending on the 
effectiveness of corrosion control technology (CCT).  
 
8 https://www.regulations.gov/document/EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0709.  

 
 
Page 7 
 
 
 
The challenge is that the lead action level is generally considered by the public to be health-based and is 
commonly used to indicate that the water has acceptable levels of lead and poses no significant risk. 
Given what we know about the risks of lead, we think that the message from a lead action level of 10 ppb 
is a problem.  
 
EPA should consider lowering it to 5 ppb – the practical quantification limit.9 This would be consistent 
with EPA August 2023 proposal10 to tighten the lead dust hazard standard for lead-based paint to a level 
that is “greater than zero.”  
 
As we reviewed EPA’s reasoning in the preamble for not adopting a lead action level of 5 ppb, it is largely 
based on the burden to water systems and States to adequately assess the proper corrosion control 
treatment. The agency also references limited technical capacity to conduct the assessment. Furthermore, 
EPA properly points to the need to focus water systems and States on LSL replacement given its 
significant impact on lead contamination of drinking water.  
 
EPA’s reasoning did not appear to consider the positive implications of a more protective level on the 
public education requirements. From our experience, a lower action level would strengthen community 
engagement and avoid implying that 10 ppb were somehow safe or without hazard. 
 
For these reasons, we suggest that, just as it did with LSL replacement, EPA should consider loosening the 
connection between lead action level exceedances and corrosion control treatment. The corrosion control 
treatment can still be conditioned on the 90th percentile exceeding 10 ppb. 
 
 
 
 
 
9 EPA sets the practical quantification limit is ‘‘the minimum concentration of an analyte (substance) that can be 
measured with a high degree of confidence that the analyte is present at or above that concentration.’’ 40 C.F.R. § 
141.2. We think EPA should also consider revising the PQL to reflect current methods but understand that the issue 
is beyond the scope of this immediate rulemaking. 
10 See August 1, 2023 Federal Register at page 50444. See also Docket No. EPA–HQ–OPPT–2023–0231 at 
https://www.regulations.gov/document/EPA-HQ-OPPT-2023-0231-0001.

Part II: Responses to Selected EPA Requests for Comment 
 
A. Requests for Comment on General Matters 
Whether the proposed revisions to the LCR revision’s treatment technique are effective to prevent 
known or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible in accordance with the SDWA. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: Yes, the proposed revisions should reduce anticipated adverse health 
effects from exposure to lead in drinking water. However, we provide specific recommendations 
in Part I above where the proposal should be improved in feasible and practical ways to further 
reduce those anticipated adverse health effects.  
Whether the proposed requirements of the rule are enforceable and promote compliance without the 
need for State or Federal enforcement action. EPA also solicits comment on ways the rule could be 
modified to better promote compliance. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: Yes, the proposed revisions are enforceable and should promote 
compliance without the need for State or Federal enforcement action by providing greater 
transparency and public education to impacted communities than the current version of the 
LCR. However, in Part I we provide five specific recommendations in which the proposal could 
be improved to make the rule more enforceable and promote compliance.  
 
Specifically, EPA should: 1) provide criteria to establish when a water system has sufficient 
access to conduct full service line replacements; 2) use the number of service lines instead of 
households to determine whether the water system is eligible for a deferred deadline under § 
141.84(d)(5)(i); and 3) clarify the definition of “service line” to avoid confusion about whether 
a service line can be defined by ownership rather than its function.  
B. Requests for Comment on Service Line Replacement
All aspects of the proposed scope of the replacement requirements, including the criteria used to define 
a full service line replacement (e.g., cutting the pipe at abandoned properties, replacing the entire service 
line) and which lead sources are subject to replacement under the mandatory program. EPA is seeking 
comment on whether to prohibit reconnection of any disconnected LSL or GRR service line. EPA is 
requesting comment on whether the Agency should include lead connectors or galvanized service lines 
that are or were downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory replacement. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: We enthusiastically support EPA’s proposed improvements to the 2021 
Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) published in the December 6, 2023 Federal Register. In 
particular, we support the provisions:  
1) Requiring replacement of all LSLs as an integral part of a safe drinking water 
compliance program instead of as a last resort when the lead action level is exceeded. 
By uncoupling full LSL replacement from lead action level exceedances, Americans can 
have real hope that they will not be drinking water through a lead pipe.   
2) Refining the public notice and transparency provisions based on feedback from 
impacted communities. These improvements enable communities to better track 
progress, identify problems, and more effectively engage in helping the water system 
succeed. As a result, water systems are more likely to comply with the rule. 
3) Basing water systems responsibility to fully replace LSLs based on control instead of 
ownership and defining control based on access. This change addresses problems that 
have plagued LSL replacement since the 1990s by enabling water systems to simply 

 
 
Page 9 
 
redirect responsibility to customers for fixing the issue of service lines on private 
property.  
4) Fixing various implementation challenges so that the water systems would have 
significant incentives to replace LSLs, lead connectors, and galvanized service lines 
requiring replacement. 
 
Unleaded Kids supports a prohibition on reconnection of any disconnected LSL or GRR service 
line. We also support EPA’s inclusion of lead connectors or galvanized service lines that are or 
were downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory replacement. 
Whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should be more than four times (e.g., five, 
six, or seven times). 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: Four times using multiple mechanisms as provided in the proposed 
rule represents a reasonable effort. While more is always better, EPA has established a practical 
minimum. 
Whether the proposed LCR improvements appropriately interprets “control” for the purposes of the 
mandatory replacement provision (i.e., require systems to conduct full service line replacement in 
situations where the system has access to conduct the full replacement). 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: Yes, the proposed improvements to the LCR appropriately interprets 
control based on access. However, EPA needs to provide criteria for water systems to use to 
determine access. We recommend in Part I, Section 2 specific changes to address those 
shortcomings. 
The proposed minimum replacement rate and replacement deadlines. EPA is seeking comment on 
whether it is feasible for systems across the nation to complete service line replacement in a shorter 
timeframe than ten years, such as in six, seven, or eight years.  
 
Unleaded Kids comment: We want to see the timeframe be as short as possible, especially if EPA 
is to provide deferred deadines. In many cases, seven years would be practical. Or the 
timeframe for complying with the rule could be shortened from three years to one since 
compliance is based on a three-year rolling average, giving the water system an opportunity to 
ramp up. 
 
We recommend that EPA drop the deferrable deadline at § 141.84(d)(5)(i) based on an absolute 
maximum. Unlike many major infrastructure projects, such as installing a water treatment 
plant, replacing each LSL is a unit operation that can be scaled up with no real limit; each 
additional crew increased the capacity of the water system to replace LSLs. The only limit is 
finding crews to do the work – a situation that will change based on local conditions. With only 
a handful of water systems having more than 100,000 LSL, EPA should rely on the other 
deferral at § 141.84(d)(5)(ii) or use the variance provisions in SDWA as it did for Denver Water 
or use a consent decree. 

 
 
Page 10

Unleaded Kids comment: We support EPA’s proposed approach.

progress sooner than three years after the compliance date. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: We think EPA should seriously consider requiring compliance with a

EPA is requesting comment on the expansion of the inventory reporting to include lead connectors and

Unleaded Kids comment: We support the expansion of the inventory reporting to include lead 
connectors and non-lead service lines.

Whether it is practicable for water systems to implement notification and risk mitigation provisions after

Unleaded Kids comment: We support earlier alternative compliance dates for the LCRI. 
L. Questions from within Preamble 
A system’s existing authority to access the service line and complete the full service line replacement 
might provide the system with the legal authority to conduct the service line replacement over the 
objection of the property owner or resident. However, as some stakeholders noted, requiring service line 
replacement at properties where customers object to their replacement could create potential safety 
concerns for utility staff. EPA is seeking comment on whether the proposed LCRI should either allow 
systems to treat those service lines as not under the control of the system and forego replacement of the 
lines or require systems to conduct full service line replacement in situations where the system has legal 
access to conduct the full replacement but property owners or residents deny physical access. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: In Part I Section 2, we provide criteria by which a water system would 
establish it has sufficient control to conduct full service line replacement. The criteria for should 
include:  
 
Whether the system can safely enter the property;  
 
Whether the system can safely conduct the replacement; and  
 
Whether the system has obtained the property owner’s consent, if consent is required for 
access. 
 
The process should be based on the provisions in the proposed rule that require water systems to 
seek access by engaging with the owner of the property under which the service line is buried. If 
the property owner provides access and gives a green light to the water system to replace the 
service line, the water system has control. If the property owner refuses to provide access, the 
water system lacks the control needed to trigger the full service line replacement provisions.  
 
In addition, the proposed rule recognizes that property owners change by requiring water 
systems to provide notice of the LSL to new customers with mandatory text inviting the new 
owner to have the service line replaced.  
A deadline for inventory completion that precedes the deadline for mandatory service line replacement 
could reduce the possibility of non-compliance with the replacement deadline, but it would not have the 
advantages of a consolidated deadline as described above. EPA seeks comment on its rationale for the 
consolidated deadline approach as compared to an earlier deadline for identifying unknown service 
lines. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: We support EPA’s proposed approach. The benefits of a consolidated 
deadline are not sufficient to warrant a different approach.

distribution of filters for this type of disturbance. 
 
Unleaded Kids comment: We think filters certified to reduce lead and replacement cartridges 
should be provided for disturbances. The releases of lead from these disturbances are too

EPA can modify the rule.

As a water operator in the State of Michigan, we have been working under the strictest 
lead and copper rule of any state since 2019.  
EPA will be utilizing much of Michigan’s L/C rule to finalize their revised rule.  
The Michigan rule has several flaws, and the state refuses any discussion.  
Now these flaws will be nationwide.
Water providers were not included in developing the Michigan rule.  People that 
were making the decisions did not perform this kind of work for a living.  It is easy to put 
something on paper and say do this and create deadlines…however, if you have not 
performed this kind of work or understand cost of pipe material, cement, topsoil, 
plumbing, customer outreach, and the manpower that will be needed, you are creating a 
financial burden that will only be passed on in water rate cost.
Residential Compliance.    Anytime a municipality pointed out that the rule’s actions 
were not lawful, or residents would not cooperate…we were told to shut the water off to 
the home.  Regardless if the water bill is paid up to date, we are to force the issue on 
the resident.  Leaving the municipality to deal with the fall-out, not the State.
Public vs Private Property.  There are strict rules/laws regarding municipalities 
working on private property.  Municipalities do not perform upgrades to private property.  
However, the new rule mandates municipalities replace the lead service line all the way 
to the water meter inside the private home.  The Michigan rule conflicts with Bolt vs. City 
of Lansing.  The State of Michigan is forcing municipalities to perform work on private 
property.  (Municipalities do not replace leaky roofs that cause mold issues, remediate 
lead paint, fix sewers that back up, correct electrical issues, cut private trees, fix private 
driveways…etc.)
Soon enough, a law firm will bring a class action lawsuit against a municipality that used 
public funding on private property, regardless of intentions.   
We have already seen this occur in Michigan with Stormwater Utilities, and it cost 
municipalities millions of dollars.  
If the lead service line needs to be replaced, then the homeowner should be provided a 
grant to have private work performed and keep municipalities protected from a lawsuit. 
Municipalities could use there ordinances to oversee the work is performed correctly.
Sampling Method.  The 1st and 5th liter sampling are intended to check the water 
quality throughout the residential water service line.  However, the aerators on faucets
utilized to take the sample MUST stay in place during the sampling.  
An aerator screen will trap particles and other debris.  This debris can cause false 
positives on water samples.  
Aerators are part of private plumbing that requires regular maintenance and cleaning.  
Michigan list aerators a health issue for lead exposure because of particulates can be 
trapped, its in all their documentation, yet municipalities are forbidden to remove or 
clean an aerator before taking a 1st or 5th liter sample…we must take the sample with a 

dirty aerator in place.  Only if the sample fails can the aerator be cleaned for 
resampling.
If we are to be sampling water quality in the service line, the aerator needs to be 
removed.  
No other type of water sample is taken with an aerator in place, this includes Chlorine
Residual, Bacteriological, or Disinfection By-Product sampling to name a few.
Funding.  Since 2019, there has been little to no funding to combat the lead service line 
replacements.  Historically, no municipality ever budgeted for lead service line removal 
and lead service lines exist in some of the oldest and the most financially challenged 
communities.
The recommended EPA revision may cost an additional $ 600,000.00 per year, if a 
funding source is not found.  That could be up to a $ 12.00 increase per unit of water 
per customer, for many customers who already are financially challenged.  (A home that 
uses an average of 4 units per month will pay an additional $48.00 monthly.)
Where do municipalities get the funding to meet compliance?
The only offering is “State Revolving Funds (SRF).”  This is a loan that must be paid 
back with interest.  Paying “interest” is another payment made with public funding for 
private property work.
A SRF will be another added expense to already stretched budgets, which will only 
result in water rate hikes nationwide.
Red Tape.  Funding red tape needs to be loosened to allow a greater number of 
qualified contractors to be utilized.  There are only so many contractors that meet the 
funding standards to be awarded work.
EPAs New 10-year Timeframe.  EPA needs to reconsider their 10-year replacement 
rule.
With this nationwide revision, will there be enough contractors available to complete the 
work in EPAs timeframe? This shortened timeframe will cause contractor costs to
skyrocket, and any funding will not go as far as planned.
Aside from that, there are only so many suppliers that can supply the materials needed 
to properly address water service line replacements. How will the supply chain keep up 
with demand, which will result in municipalities not meeting compliance.  
Since Covid, our general materials and supplies that took only days to receive, are now 
taking months, with high-cost increases.
Is this a Crisis or Not?  The State and Federal agencies allowed “lead” to be an 
approved material for water service lines over seventy years ago.
Current operators are tasked/mandated with remediating the problem without a funding 
source.

I ask this…If this is such a “Public Health Crisis,” why is proper funding so 
scarce?

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0765 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
The regulations set by the EPA aimed to protect public health by establishing 
standards for the allowable levels of lead and copper in drinking water. The 
Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) is a specific regulation under the NPDWR that 
addresses these contaminants.
Improvements to the regulations may include updates to standards, testing 
requirements, monitoring procedures, and public notification protocols. 
Improvements are often driven by advances in scientific understanding, 
technological developments, and experiences gained from incidents of water 
contamination.
Possible areas of improvement could include:
•
Lowering Action Levels: The EPA might consider lowering 
the action levels for lead and copper in drinking water to reflect updated health 
risk assessments.
•
Enhanced Monitoring: Improved methods of monitoring and 
testing for lead and copper could be implemented to ensure more accurate 
and timely identification of water quality issues.
•
Public Education and Notification: Strengthening 
requirements for public education and notification about lead and copper 
levels in drinking water can help raise awareness and empower communities 
to take action.
•
Lead Service Line Replacement: Regulations might be 
updated to accelerate the replacement of lead service lines, which are a 
significant source of lead contamination in drinking water.
•
Infrastructure Investment: Increased emphasis on funding 
and support for water infrastructure projects to address aging pipes and 
mitigate the risk of lead and copper leaching into the water supply.
•
Compliance and Enforcement: Strengthening measures for 
ensuring water systems' compliance with regulations and enhancing 
enforcement mechanisms to hold non-compliant entities accountable.
•
http://vexanshop.com

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1139 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
By way of background, Women for a Healthy Environment (WHE) is a nonprofit in 
Pennsylvania that addresses environmental exposures that impact public health. Our organization 
uses a scientific approach to achieve equitable lives free of environmental hazards through 
advocacy and community-based programs. 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide public comment on the proposed revisions to the Lead 
and Copper Rule, an issue WHE has directly been engaged with since its formation in 2009. Our 
three main program areas are Healthy Homes, Healthy Schools and Healthy Early Learning 
Centers. Each of these programs has provided support and assistance to the community to 
respond to lead in drinking water by distributing water pitchers that remove lead in drinking 
water; holding community education sessions that address lead in drinking water; providing 
funding and technical assistance to test and remediate for lead in drinking water; and advocating 
for policy change to better protect public health at the local, state and federal levels of 
government. 
Following are our organization’s comments regarding the proposed National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements.  
 
Public Education: 
EPA must provide updated educational resources so that the public knows and understands how 
to protect themselves from lead in drinking water exposures. To achieve the public health goals 
of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), the following components of public education are 
referenced and relied upon: corrosion control, source water treatment, lead service line 
replacement, and public education. These components separately must introduce an effective 
layer of consumer protection, and all these components together must produce a system of 
consumer protections that maximizes the Lead and Copper Rule’s (LCR) public health protective 
capacity as a whole. For this to happen, the four components must be based on:  
• the best available, peer-reviewed science, as well as  
• robust understanding about how water utilities implement (or don’t) the LCR, how oversight 
agencies enforce (or don’t) the LCR, and how consumers are empowered (or not) to make 
health-protective decisions in relation to lead in water and the LCR. 

National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements – Women 
for a Healthy Environment 
 
2 | P a g e  
 
 
As an example, oftentimes we hear from residents that their water system didn’t exceed the 
15ppb reference level so their drinking water is lead-free and safe, without understanding that 
indeed their home could have lead service lines and premise plumbing that contains lead, both of 
which may be contributing to contaminated drinking water. The EPA website and educational 
materials must make this information clear for the public and that currently does not exist. 
Residents across the country need to know how to make informed decisions about such things as 
testing (which is practically useless due to the high variability in testing protocol and results), 
lead service line replacement (i.e., full is better than partial), filtering options and how to 
interpret the Consumer Confidence Report (e.g., the 90th percentile value says little about lead 
levels at people's individual taps). 
Public education is critical; it must be understandable and consistent. In WHE’s Something’s in 
the Water report published in 2021, we surveyed the 36 water systems across Allegheny County. 
Of those that responded, 41% indicated their system does not provide notice to consumers if 
partial lead line replacements are about to occur. 
Public versus Private Lead Service Line Replacements: 
In PA the Municipal Authorities Act of 1945 posed significant challenges to water systems 
seeking to conduct full lead service line replacements. The law, at the time, stated that 
municipalities could only utilize these funds to remediate public lines. To amend this, several 
water systems petitioned the state legislature and the Pennsylvania Public Utilities Commission 
(PUC) to allow systems to use funds for private line replacement. In March 2017, the PA PUC 
and York Water Company set a precedent by permitting the use of these funds for private lines.  
Will this state action be required across the country? Will other state legislatures be willing to 
take this action to ensure clarity of the system’s ability to conduct a full lead service line 
replacement? We have been in conversations with one water system that conducted partial lead 
service line replacements in the 1970s, and now, knowing more about the potential health 
impacts that may exist from that action, want to do better; however, they cannot access the funds 
necessary to replace the private side that was left intact. This leads to frustration amongst all – 
the water system and community it serves. 
According to our findings in the Something’s in the Water report, most water systems do not offer 
lead testing, and of those that do, only three systems of the 36 confirmed they can offer testing 
free of charge. This, again, points to an issue of capacity and resources within each water system. 
We are asking EPA for the following: 
1. Require water utilities to cover the full cost of lead service line replacement. This will 
prevent the financial burden from being placed on low-income homeowners and renters, 
whose landlords are unlikely to pay the cost of lead pipe replacement. This is especially 
important in environmental justice communities that already face disproportionate lead 
contamination. 

National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements – Women 
for a Healthy Environment 
 
3 | P a g e  
 
 
2. Ensure water utilities do not take more than a decade to remove lead service lines. We do 
not want another generation of our kids to be harmed by lead-contaminated tap water, or to 
expose adults with cardiovascular disease to additional risk of heart attack or death. 
Consumer Confidence Report: 
We have many instances where a smaller water system purchases its water from a larger system 
and, as such, does not conduct or oversee the water treatment process. Therefore, the corrosion 
control evaluation component for systems in exceedance, as mandated by the LCR, does not 
apply to them and they have little control. How will this situation be addressed in the revisions? 
In addition, our analysis looked at water system violations. From 2016 to March 2020, there 
were five instances where the water system failed to submit its Consumer Confidence Report, as 
well as failures to issue public notice. In fact, one water system failed to submit for at least three 
years in a row and then two violations were issued in 2022 due to failure to submit a timely CCR 
after all that time. Additionally, 6% of the water systems didn’t have the CCR posted on their 
website and perhaps never will due to staff capacity issues. How will regulations related to CCR 
compliance be enforced and support provided to the smaller water systems?  
Schools and Childcare Centers: 
Communication and direction for schools and childcare centers is lacking in the proposed 
revisions. As a result, there continues to be inconsistencies with states passing legislation that 
does not protect public health, such as was done in PA. Our organization manages a program that 
provides funding to test and remediate for lead in all sources in schools and early learning 
centers. We have tested over 200 learning environments for lead in drinking water. What we have 
found is that when you test for lead in drinking water, you find lead in drinking water. And this is 
not just the result of lead service lines entering the buildings but includes premise plumbing, as 
well as kettles in cafeterias and drinking water fountains. We know lead is present, we test for it, 
and then there is no remediation plan to address it. We are failing our school children who drink 
that water over 180 days a year.   
Our interaction with schools has informed us that personnel still believe that the school should 
only be concerned if their lead testing results (or their local water system’s CCR) exceeds the 15 
ppb, the reference level for water systems. Our State of Environmental Health in PA Schools 
report examines environmental factors such as lead in drinking water in schools. Reviewing 2019 
data, we noted that of the 99 school districts in southwestern PA: 
• Only 66.7% of the districts who tested performed these tests in all their school buildings  
• Of the school districts with lead levels exceeding 15 ppb, 43.8% sent remediation records 
(there were no records present for the remaining districts) 
• Lead testing in one district revealed concentrations on “1st draw” samples reached 
alarming levels of 1,920 ppb

for a Healthy Environment 
 
4 | P a g e  
 
 
In our statewide sample of the 164 districts sampled: 
• Only 82% of school districts reported testing for lead in drinking water, despite the statewide 
requirement which notably had a large loophole to not test by providing public notice. And of 
those that reported an exceedance of 15 ppb which is atrocious, one-third did not indicate that 
they had taken any corrective action. 
We know with the variability of testing that one day you could take a sample from a sink in a 
classroom and it could provide one reading and you can go back the following day and get a 
completely different lead level reading. And there is a significant disconnect between EPAs 3T 
for Reducing Lead in Drinking Water guidance and these revisions.  
This is all to say that the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements is completely silent regarding regulations for schools and childcare centers, which 
is a critical misstep and not health protective for our most vulnerable. Clearly this is a needed 
space to focus time, attention and resources. If you go to the EPA’s general fact sheet on the 
proposed revisions, there is no mention of schools and childcare centers because it wasn’t 
addressed in these revisions. Again, a shortcoming, so that means it goes back to the previous 
administration’s lead and copper rule revisions.  
Both Michigan and Washington, D.C., now have “filter first” policies that require schools and 
childcare centers to install filters at every tap that’s used for drinking or cooking. This approach 
would require all childcare centers and schools to install filtered drinking water devices, develop 
a “drinking water management plan”, test the filtered water regularly, and communicate with 
families about the improved water quality. We need to protect children’s health in all spaces, 
especially where they spend their days in the learning environment.  
In closing, this is an opportunity to correct the outdated EPA narrative and to provide consistent, 
accurate education and messaging regarding lead in drinking water. Right now, nonprofits such 
as WHE and other community members are filling this gap, using best available science, to better 
inform residents and it appears contradictory to EPA’s communications. That confusion is unfair 
to the general public. This is an opportunity to right the wrongs. Investment in improved public 
education would result in greater public health protection.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1128 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 1st, 2024
Indiana Lead Coalition/Hoosier Environmental Council
3951 N Meridian St #100
Indianapolis, IN 46208
Re: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements, Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801,
The Indiana Lead Coalition, hosted by Hoosier Environmental Council, consists of
over 50 individuals dedicated to ending childhood lead poisoning. The group meets
monthly to discuss lead and healthy housing related policies. The Indiana Lead
Coalition is action oriented and has advocated for policies, both at the state and
federal level, to improve the lives of families at risk of lead poisoning. Members of
the group hail from various institutions, including but not limited to academia, local
government, not-for-profits, philanthropy, and advocacy.
Though not directly responsible for LSL, the Indiana Lead Coalition shares the EPA’s
goal of reducing lead exposure through drinking water and preventing lead
poisoning through policy change, like the the proposed Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements (LCRI)
The Indiana Lead Coalition’s comments focus on the following issues:
●
Lead Pipe Identification and Replacement
●
Tap Sampling and Corrective Action
●
Outreach and Prevention
Lead Pipe Identification and Replacement
While we commend the EPA for its goal of 100% Lead Pipe Replacement within 10
years, the Coalition seeks clarity with regards to (a) prioritization of lead pipe
identification and (b) next steps following the identification. The Coalition recognizes
that certain cities/areas/census tracts are at higher risk of lead exposure. This is, in
part, due to high levels of lead in children who are tested and/or low childhood lead
testing rates in these areas.
In addition, the Lead Coalition desires the LCRI to provide further clarity around the
parties responsible for lead service line (LSL) identification and replacement.
Though water systems are responsible for the identification of LSLs, they ultimately
rely on homeowners and property owners to submit information on their respective
service lines.
Water systems in the state of Indiana have come across issues with identifying and
replacing LSLs due to unresponsive and/or out of state property managers. This,

along with relying on homeowners to voluntarily submit information on their service
lines, could prevent the EPA from achieving its goal of LSL replacement within 10
years.
It is unclear if the LSL replacement ultimately falls under the responsibility of the
homeowner or the water system. In addition, the proposed rule change does not
state the qualifications or type of professional needed to replace LSL. As we’ve seen
in the case of HUD related Lead Remediation grants available in the state of
Indiana, contractors who are qualified and willing to do the work of lead remediation
and abatement are limited.
Tap Sampling and Corrective Action
The proposed LCRI would require water systems to collect first and fifth liter
samples at sites with LSL. The higher of the two values would be used to determine
compliance. In addition, the LCRI would lower the lead action level to 10 µg/L.
The Indiana Lead Coalition strongly encourages the LCRI to include guidance on the
prioritization of tap sampling and remediation for LSL sites. Tap sampling should first
be conducted at sites that present the highest risk to the community, such as
schools and daycares. In addition, the Indiana Lead Coalition strongly recommends
sampling be performed during/after events that disturb chemical treatment that
prevents corrosion in the pipes.
Following tap sampling procedures, the Indiana Lead Coalition believes that the lead
action level should be as low as technically feasible. This should be guided by
exposure level for babies who get water from formula. If a baby drinks 2 pints of
formula per day, that’s about 10 micrograms of lead, which poses severe health risks
to the child.
Outreach and Prevention
While the Indiana Lead Coalition acknowledges outreach as a valuable tool to alert
homeowners of potential lead risk and exposure, the LCRI does not specify what
types of public notification (PN) or public education (PE) should be utilized in the
case of tap results that exceed the action level. Public notice and education is most
effective when an individual can be contacted directly or by multiple channels.
Relying on one method, such as a mailer or postcard, can be ineffective, especially
for groups that do not rely on mail for communication. The Indiana Lead Coalition
suggests that the LCRI indicates effective forms of PN and PE to improve outreach
and education of the general public.
The Indiana Lead Coalition also requests clarification when it comes to providing
water filters to those with LSL. “Making water filters available” is not very clear

guidance. It would be more straightforward to require the non-complying water
systems to deliver a faucet-mount water filter to each customer’s porch. In addition,
they should supply replacement cartridges every ~3 months, depending on the
recommended filter change cycle for the product purchased.
In conclusion, the Indiana Lead Coalition thanks the EPA for the opportunity to
provide comments on the LCRI. The group acknowledges that remediating leaded
infrastructure is a complex issue and appreciates the work of the EPA to reduce lead
in drinking water. The Indiana Lead Coalition kindly asks the EPA to consider these
comments in an effort to further support this work.
Sincerely,
Jocelyn Keranen, Environmental Health Project Manager, Hoosier Environmental
Council

especially on those who may be disproportionately impacted financially.  
To help our customers who require financial assistance with the costs for the basic 
necessities, such as clean water, Citizens is proud to offer and partner in several programs such as 
the Warm Heart Warm Home Foundation1 (“WHWH Foundation”).  WHWH Foundation is a 
residential customer payment assistance fund - funded by Citizens’ donations, Utility Shield 
proceeds, and customer donations – to help customers in need to prevent disconnection or to 
reconnect service.  Citizens also encourages customers needing assistance to contact 211 Connect 
– a program of the Indiana Family and Social Services Administration2. However, it is important 
to note that these assistance programs alone do not fully ease the potential burden of the rising 
rates that could result to comply with the requirements of this proposed rule. 
 
As a member of the American Water Works Association (AWWA), Citizens supports and 
endorses the AWWA’s comments submitted on this proposed rule.  To substantiate the points made 
by the AWWA, Citizens offers the following supplemental comments and observations in addition 
to giving the perspective as the owner and operator of water systems that will be charged with the 
implementation of the requirements in the proposed LCRI rule if it is finalized.

LSL Replacement Time Frame and Minimum Replacement Rates Must Recognize Constraints 
Beyond the Control of Water Systems 
 
Citizens has a history of supporting the implementation of a lead service line3 (LSL) 
replacement program and, following Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission (IURC) approval, 
has proactively initiated an LSL replacement program for the Citizens Water – Indianapolis system. 
Citizens advocated for Indiana legislative changes to allow water systems to seek approval from 
the IURC to implement the rate-funded LSL replacement programs4.  In this current 2024 session 
of the Indiana General Assembly, Citizens supports Senate Bill 55 that will allow a utility operating 
under an IURC-approved LSL Replacement Plan the access needed to conduct full LSL 
replacements if the owner is not responsive to requests to enroll in the LSL replacement program 
or does not elect to replace the LSLs on their own within a specified timeframe.   
 
As it relates to the proposed LCRI and the minimum LSL replacement rate that a water 
system must meet, the three-year rolling average 10% compliance obligation provides water 
systems some (although limited) protection against factors that may influence year-over-year 
success in replacing LSL, but does not protect water utilities if the threshold is not achieved due 
to factors outside the water utilities control, such as the ability to timely procure materials or skilled 
labor.   
 
Implementing a strict minimum replacement rate in the first three (3) years of the LSL 
program to “…give States an opportunity to enforce replacement rate progress sooner than three 
years after the compliance date[.]6” does not take into account the time that water systems may 
need to get an LSL program in place or to overcome the very real supply chain barriers that limit 
the ability for water utilities to timely procure critical materials. Since 2020, Citizens, like other 
water utilities throughout the nation, has first-hand experience with supply chain issues, such as 
ever-changing lead times that extend delivery dates far beyond what may have been planned and 
abnormally high cost escalations. 
 
Most recently, Citizens’ rate-funded LSL replacement program was approved by the IURC 
in March of 2022.  This approval was the culmination of over four years of efforts developing the 
inventory of lead service line locations, developing plans, promoting enabling legislative changes, 
submitting an LSL Replacement Plan to the IURC, subsequently obtaining IURC Plan approval, 
separately filing for funding authorization and ultimately obtaining funding approval.  While 
Citizens is appreciative of the legislative tools now available in Indiana, there are significant timing 
elements that must be considered to fully implement programs of the scale proposed in this rule.

For example, over the next three years, water systems will stand up the LSL replacement 
programs needed to address the estimated 9.2 million LSLs across the nation.    Because these new 
programs will be coming together at the same time, material and skilled labor shortages are more 
than likely7 to develop across the supply chain, creating a barrier to timely implementation of this 
proposed rule.   
 
Citizens’ experiences with the lead time to fulfill brass valve orders – items critical to LSL 
replacements – is six (6) months or more due to limited manufacturing capacity.  Although new 
manufacturing facilities are proposed for construction and additional capacity is being added at 
existing manufacturing facilities8, including at Indiana-based manufacturer The Ford Meter Box 
Company, Inc., this increased capacity is not forecasted to be available until late 20279.  While this 
forecasted increase in supply will result in a less constrained market in approximately three (3) 
years, orders for brass valves and other components needed to support the LSL replacement 
programs will continue to be placed in the interim; it will take some time to fully relieve the 
anticipated logjam of orders for this material. 
 
Stated in another way, Citizens anticipates longer lead times as demand increases for the 
various brass components utilized by water systems across the U.S., at least until the brass 
manufacturing capacity adjusts for market conditions. This anticipated increase in brass 
component lead times (of unpredictable lengths) stands to further delay the ability of LSL 
replacement programs nationwide to meet the ambitious goals set forth in the LCRI.  
 
The increased demand for these brass components coupled with the limited availability 
likely will cause the price for these brass components to rise, having the unfortunate and 
unintentional impact of raising the overall anticipated cost of the LSL replacement program for 
water systems nationwide.  As described later in these comments, most water systems will then be 
forced to make very complex and difficult decisions, working to balance the mandatory LSL 
replacement program with the existing programs that water systems are implementing to address 
the nation’s aging water infrastructure and to support growth.
