Additionally, many older homes in communities like Indianapolis with lead service lines 
have ‘inside set’ meters (water meters that are located inside a basement or cellar of a home).   Like 
a number of other communities, Citizens, through its Water Standards Manual that dictate 
construction specifications, no longer permits the installation of new inside meter sets and requires 
existing inside meter sets to be replaced if the service line is modified.  Citizens is using LSL 
replacement projects as an opportunity to install a new water meter in an exterior location 
(typically a meter pit) that is accessible to the utility without entering the customer’s premise.  This 
relocation of the customer’s water meter is funded through the LSL replacement project. 
Unfortunately, supply chain constraints and delays also exist for residential water meters and for 
the components required to equip meters with automatic meter reading (AMR) capabilities.  Lead 
times for standard residential water meters have ranged between 12 and 24 weeks over the last two 
years, and the reported lead time is approximately 37 weeks for the electronic components that 
support the AMR technology.   Unfortunately, and in Citizens experience, it is common for 
materials to be received beyond promised ship dates, making it challenging for water systems to 
plan for shifting lead times.  
 
These cumulative impacts of the volatile supply chain delays must be factored in as water 
systems, including Citizens, develop schedules for implementation of LSL replacement projects.  
While there are strategies, including building a stock of supplies and materials through bulk 
procurement far in advance, as available, these strategies must be balanced against and with other 
needs by water systems.  These materials must be paid for, which means the water system must 
have available funds to support the advanced purchase while ensuring sufficient space is available 
for the storage of these materials - whether it be within each water utility’s own facilities, rental of 
a secure location or ensuring that a materials supplier will maintain stock reserved solely for the 
use of that water system.  The uncertainty in reported lead times only complicates the efforts to 
adequately plan and prepare for the deployment of LSL replacement projects.  Finally, as water 
systems across the U.S. contemplate how to deliver the LSL replacements required by the proposed 
LCRI no later than 2037, these advanced purchasing strategies will place additional burden on the 
supply chain.   
 
Challenges with Access Can Create Delays Beyond the Control of a Water System 
 
As EPA notes in the preamble, ownership of the LSL in many jurisdictions resides with the 
customer, not the water system; for those water systems, these LSLs are not “under the control” of 
the water system10.  While water systems have sufficient legal authority to replace the portion of 
the LSL that lies within the right-of-way, the LCRI prohibits partial service line replacements 
except in emergency situations, and then only in rare conditions.  The failure to obtain access (from 
the owner) is not, at least not in LCRI as proposed, a condition that would warrant a partial 
replacement of the LSL.  Thus, at present, a water system MUST have the customer’s permission 
to access private property to complete the full service line replacement.  In Citizens’ limited 
experience with our rate-funded LSL replacement program, obtaining the customer’s permission 
 
10 88 Fed Reg 84,923 

Comments of Citizens Energy Group 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations 
Lead and Copper Rule:  Improvements Proposed Rule 
February 5, 2024 
Page 6 of 10 
 
has taken extensive time to accomplish if able to be accomplished at all. In neighborhoods that are 
predominantly owner-occupied, enrolment in the LSL replacement program averages 90%; 
however, in neighborhoods that are predominantly rentals, enrollment falls to approximately 60%.   
Without permission, accessing the property could be considered trespass and place our employees 
in harm’s way. 
 
Partial Lead Service Line Replacements Should Be Permitted  
 
 
Citizens appreciates the concerns expressed by EPA in the preamble discussion regarding 
partial lead service line replacements. In addition to our comments above regarding delays that can 
be created because of limits on access to private property, based on our experiences, Citizens 
believes that partial replacement of LSLs for neighborhood projects creates public benefits that 
should be realized.  Notwithstanding our current efforts in the Indiana General Assembly regarding 
access to an owner’s property for the purposes of implementing the LSL replacement project to a 
home, owners would need to enroll into the program, but still, several do not.  Our experience is 
not novel.   
 
A neighborhood-wide LSL replacement project involves numerous street cuts and 
excavation to facilitate the replacement of the LSLs; once the neighborhood project is complete, 
restoration of customer’s properties and the public right of way is placed back to the condition 
prior to the replacement project.  Without allowing for partial replacement of the LSL in the right 
of way, a portion arguably under the control of the water system, the water system would need to 
go back into a neighborhood to complete a “one-off” LSL replacement after the original 
neighborhood-wide project is complete.  
 
These “one-off” projects create disruptions for the entire neighborhood as the street cut is 
made to address the individual replacement and, in many cases, into a newly paved street which 
reduces the integrity, and resulting asset life, of the street itself. Newly paved roads are an 
important piece of infrastructure serving the highly urbanized communities within Citizens’ 
service territory. Further, this adds additional costs to the overall project that can be avoided if the 
final LCRI rule allows for a portion of the service line, namely within the utility the right of way, 
to be replaced (as a “partial” LSL replacement).  Based on Citizens’ experience with its own LSL 
replacement program, the cost of performing one-off service line replacements is nearly double 
the cost of the programmatic replacements, in large part as a result of the repaving and penalties 
incurred for cutting into pavement within the 3-year warranty period, as well as inefficiencies with 
labor to support the work. 
 
Citizens believes that following these partial service line replacements, it would make 
common sense, as an option, for a water system to leave behind a pitcher filter and replacement 
cartridges, as well as (yet again) information on how to contact the water system in order to enroll 
in the LSL replacement program (i.e., grant the water system access to the owner’s property) for 
purposes of replacing the customer-owned portion of the service line located on private property 
at a later time.

Page 7 of 10 
 
 
Another example of a circumstance where a partial LSL replacement would be most 
efficient and least disruptive, Citizens often coordinates with the City of Indianapolis and other 
utilities to minimize the impact that infrastructure projects (including road widening, intersection 
projects, and road resurfacing projects) have on the local communities.  On January 29, 2024, 
Citizens and the City of Indianapolis Department of Public Works announced a targeted LSL 
replacement project ahead of a planned road construction project11.  The intent is to enroll every 
eligible owner in the LSL replacement project to maximize the public benefit through coordination 
with the City of Indianapolis.  This specific project was highlighted in local media stories12 to raise 
public awareness of the intent to implement an LSL replacement project as a strategy to increase 
enrollment in the program. However, despite Citizens’ and the City of Indianapolis’ best efforts to 
highlight this project, there will inevitably be some properties where Citizens is unable to obtain 
property owner approval to conduct the work.   Should LCRI be finalized as proposed, it would 
limit Citizens ability to conduct partial LSL replacements, which, as previously noted, creates 
impacts in future years for the neighborhood should customers who did not enroll in the LSL 
replacement program opt into the program, or as the water system implements its mandatory LSL 
replacement program (such as the one proposed in the LCRI). 
 
Water Systems Must Balance Multiple Priorities when Funding the LSL Replacement Program 
 
In the preamble to the LCRI, EPA indicates a preference that a water system’s LSL 
replacement program be offered to the owner without incurring a separate cost, which Citizens 
believes is the most effective way to implement the LSL replacement program.  However, many 
water utilities are highly leveraged and challenged in issuing further debt to fund their existing 
capital improvement programs, even if at zero- or low-interest borrowing.  Providing water 
systems with federal funding through grants specifically for LSL replacements would provide 
greater financial flexibility versus zero or low interest federal funding. Grants would provide 
significant benefits to most water system, increasing their ability to meet the 10-year replacement 
timeline while also helping to address affordability issues.  EPA’s position in the preamble seems 
straight forward but does not consider the existing constraints on funding.  
 
“EPA does, however, strongly encourage customer-side service line replacement to 
be offered at no direct cost to the customer wherever possible to achieve higher 
customer participation rates and reduce potential environmental justice impacts that 
may result where customers cannot afford to replace their portion of the line.  EPA 
anticipates the proposed requirements and flexibilities to incentivize systems 
obtaining access, as described above in section V.B.5., would also incentivize water 
systems to fund customer-side service line replacement. Furthermore, significant 
Federal funding is available for service line replacement (discussed in section

IV.G.), some of which is directed to disadvantaged communities least likely to 
afford full service line replacement. Additionally, Federal civil rights laws, 
including Title VI as described in sections IV.H. and V.B.9., incentivize systems to 
achieve full replacement outcomes that do not discriminate on the basis of race, 
color, or national origin.”13  
 
The funding mechanisms for water system capital programs (like a system-funded LSL 
replacement program) are complex.  Water systems that use the “pay-go” funding model to finance 
capital programs seek to balance both maximizing the funding that can be achieved through 
customer rates while minimizing rate shock to those customers who can least afford it.  Citizens 
adopted this approach in framing its IURC-approved rate-funded LSL replacement program.   
 
Water systems like Citizens Water – Indianapolis can issue debt to fund capital programs 
but must carefully manage the debt coverage obligations to protect customers from rate shock - 
rate funds will be required to cover both principal and interest payments over the course of the 
debt repayment.  Further, incurring additional debt to support the implementation of an LSL 
replacement program does not relieve the water systems of obligations to cover not only routine 
Operations & Maintenance expenses but also existing debt repayment needs through customer 
rates that are unrelated to the LSL replacement programs.  Thus, incurring debt through a federal 
loan (even if the federal loan carries zero interest) is simply another funding option available to 
communities that may or may not be better for customers compared to a fully rate funded pay-go 
funding program. 
 
Importantly, while the preamble to the proposed LCRI rule speaks of federal funding 
available to water systems, it does not guarantee this funding to water systems at any set level in 
any calendar year, nor is this federal funding guaranteed in future federal budget cycles. Further, 
the distribution of funding to states does not guarantee a minimum distribution to each water 
system with LSLs in any calendar year.  Therefore, it is difficult to budget and plan the LSL 
replacement work over the course of the proposed 10-year replacement program. Without funding 
guarantees, this adds another potential financial burden on the water utility – that, in turn, may 
need to adjust rates for its customers to fund these much needed projects.  Citizens does not take 
making rate changes, especially if the rates are to rise, lightly; further, granting approval for a rate 
case is no easy task when a water utility is under the jurisdiction of a state public utility 
commission, like the IURCA formula for the allocation of federal funds by the states that would 
ensure states distribute (on an annual basis) a minimum percentage of the funds to small systems 
and a minimum percentage to each water system in a state that accounts for 10% or more of the 
LSLs statewide would help to alleviate some of the uncertainty water systems face when 
considering funding for the LSL replacement program. 
 
 
As indicated above, the IURC oversees the regulatory activities of Citizens through its state 
statutes and authority requiring a level of formality and approval “to make decisions that are in the 
 
13 88 Fed. Reg. 84923 – 84924

public interest to ensure the utilities provide safe and reliable service at just and reasonable rates.”14  
Compliance with the IURC orders creates a level of responsibility and accountability that is higher 
than municipal water systems with rates set by a town council or local public works board.  
 
 
Finally, in addition to ensuring that adequate funding is made available for the LSL 
replacement program that balances the financial obligations of a water system, water systems must 
also prioritize the demands on the pool of funds available.  The EPA released its Seventh Report 
to Congress of Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs in September 202315 (Infrastructure Needs 
Report).   The Infrastructure Needs Report highlights the estimated $625 billion in infrastructure 
investment needs by water systems across the U.S., including over $11 billion in Indiana alone 
over the 20 year forecast period.  While these investments reflect the needs of the LSL replacement 
program (estimated as a need of $50 billion to $80 billion), the Infrastructure Needs Report also 
reflects much needed investments in other water system infrastructure, including over $100 billion 
investment in treatment plants, nearly $25 billion in source of supply, and over $55 billion in 
storage.  Furthermore, the Infrastructure Needs Report highlights the more than $420 billion in 
distribution/transmission needs for water systems, a figure that includes the LSL replacement 
program. 
 
 
These infrastructure demands require that water systems plan for and procure the necessary 
skilled labor and materials to complete the much-needed projects to protect the drinking water 
delivered to our communities.  The skilled trades and many of the materials and components that 
will be needed to support an LSL replacement program are also required to deliver many of the 
other infrastructure projects identified in the Infrastructure Needs Report.  This competition for 
skilled trades labor may create an additional challenge that we believe can consequently further 
escalate the costs for implementation of this replacement program. 
 
Restoration of Water Service Should Not Be Unnecessarily Delayed as a Result of Disturbances 
Described at § 141.85(g) 
 
Notification to customers of potential health risks is an extremely important aspect of 
public health protection.  The proposed LCRI incorporates multiple requirements to enhance 
existing requirements for CWS to provide these notifications.  A specific area of additional 
notification in the proposed LCRI relates to lead service line disturbances and the requirement to 
provide notification to customers before a lead service line that has been shut off is returned to 
service.  Citizens supports communications to customers in these events to provide awareness of 
potential risks. However, water utilities operate on a 24 hour per day, 7 day per week schedule that 
can often result in actions occurring during late-night or early-morning hours that are not amenable 
to customer notification, and that could even provide safety risks to utility employees attempting

to make notifications at these hours of the day.  Alternatively, delaying the re-establishment of

For disturbances that do not require that water service be shut off, such as activities that 
cause vibration of the service line, the proposed LCRI requires notifications be made as soon as 
possible, but not to exceed 24 hours following the disturbance.  Citizens believes that customers 
will be best served by requiring a similar notification approach for all types of disturbances, and 
this approach should not delay restoration of water service or pose a safety risk to utility 
employees. Adopting a process to require notification of all disturbances as soon as possible but 
not to exceed 24 hours would achieve this goal.

‭blood pressure, kidney or nervous system problems, and cancer.‬‭1‬‭These dangers also manifest‬

‭annually.‬‭2‬‭Further analyses based on the Harvard study show that removing lead service lines‬
‭would accrue at least 14 times more monetizable health benefits than costs.‬‭3‬‭The benefits‬

‭line.” The rule then defines “control” as legal access or physical access without further definition,‬
‭essentially leaving determinations of “control” up to states, water systems and localities to‬
‭determine whether the utility has access.‬
‭4‬‭https://www.nrdc.org/resources/watered-down-justice‬
‭2‬

‭As a result, a water system could “comply” with its requirement to replace all lead service lines‬
‭yet leave vast quantities of lead service lines in the ground by asserting a lack of access to any‬
‭portions of lead service lines under private property. This interpretation is a huge risk, and is‬
‭unnecessary. EPA should affirmatively state that water systems have control over all portions of‬
‭lead service lines, since they generally require or approve use of lead pipes, retain physical‬
‭access to them in an emergency, and ultimately can shut off water through them.‬
‭Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines:‬
‭The proposed rule fails to mandate that water systems pay for removal of the entire lead service‬
‭line, but it is imperative that the final rule does.  Removal of lead pipes can cost thousands of‬
‭dollars. Putting a disproportionate financial burden on impacted low-wealth homeowners and‬
‭renters by allowing utilities to bill property owners individually will result in mostly wealthy and‬
‭white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced, particularly when combined with the‬
‭aforementioned “access” loophole.‬‭5‬‭There are enough‬‭financing solutions, rate structures, and‬
‭funding streams available that EPA should ensure replacements be made at no direct cost to‬
‭individual consumers. This would achieve more equitable implementation, better protect‬
‭children’s health, and is essential to meet EPA’s statutory mandate to protect public health to the‬
‭extent feasible.‬
‭Public Education about Protection from Lead in Water:‬
‭Right to know reports, public notifications, and public education materials should include‬
‭language that is clear about the possibility of lead exposure from drinking water even when the‬
‭system as a whole is in compliance. Information should include annual messaging about not‬
‭only the risks of contamination from lead service lines but also lead plumbing, which is‬
‭ubiquitous. It should also include information about the effectiveness of lead-certified point of‬
‭use filters as a way for families to reduce lead levels in their drinking water. EPA should forbid‬
‭messaging that states or suggests that tested lead levels below the action level are "safe," and‬
‭emphasize that there is no safe level of lead exposure.‬
‭Incentivize utilities to install filters in schools and child care facilities and ensure that‬
‭children who spend many hours in these settings daily are not at risk of exposure:‬
‭EPA’s proposed provisions related to protections in schools do not meaningfully differ from the‬
‭inadequate Trump administration proposal. EPA should require water systems to either install‬
‭filters certified to remove lead or to conduct thorough, frequent tap testing at all taps with full‬
‭public disclosure of the test results for all schools and child care facilities. Where a school or‬
‭childcare’s lead levels exceed the action level (which we urge be set at 1 ppb per the American‬
‭Academy of Pediatrics recommendation), the water system should be required to remediate by‬
‭installing certified filters.‬

‭Lower the action level to no higher than 5 parts per billion:‬
‭Lowering the action level from 15 to 10 ppb is an important improvement, but still less strict than‬
‭the 5 ppb standard urged by health experts, recommended by Canadian and European‬

‭Prevent regrettable substitutions and pollution from removed lead pipes:‬

CLARKSBURG WATER BOARD 
    A Municipal Corporation Serving Clarksburg Since 1887

By Electronic Submission: Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
To Whom It May Concern: 
 
The Clarksburg Water Board (“Board”) is a public water system located in 
Clarksburg, West Virginia providing water service to approximately 17,500 people 
through approximately 8,000 service connections in central West Virginia.  Like 
most utilities in the region, the Board’s system is over 100 years old and contains 
a significant amount of lead service lines.  Just under fifty percent (50%) of the 
Board’s system includes lead or galvanized service lines.  As the agency is aware, 
the Board has been the subject of state and federal enforcement and is facing 
lead contamination issues head on.  Since 2021, the Board has aggressively 
worked to achieve and maintain compliance with the current LCR and is working 
diligently to design phased projects and secure funding so that its pending lead 
service line replacement projects will achieve compliance with USEPA’s proposed 
revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead 
and copper. 
 
This work has highlighted some of the significant issues with the new proposed 
rule as described below.  From the Board’s perspective, which is shared by other 
utilities and associations representing those who produce and deliver the nation’s 
drinking water, the proposed rule ignores critical legal, financial and scheduling 
hurdles that will likely place the majority of public water systems in 
noncompliance with the proposed rule.  The Board feels strongly that this will be 
more prevalent in the Appalachian region due to the prevalence of small and 
medium sized water systems serving rural and disadvantaged communities.  The 
resources available to these critical service providers are already extremely limited 
and the recent environment of increased costs, supply chain delays and limited  
 

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
February 5, 2024 
Page Two 
 
 
construction and engineering services have hit these communities particularly 
hard. 
 
The Board hopes that EPA will consider the comments submitted by utilities and 
associations representing them.  No one is in a better position to articulate the 
impracticality and challenges that the requirements of the rule, as proposed, 
could present to the systems that supply our nations water.  The Board 
specifically supports and echoes the content and concerns articulated by the 
West Virginia Municipal Water Quality Association, the Washington Association of 
Sewer and Water Districts, the Illinois Municipal League, and comments on prior 
rules submitted by the American Water Works Association.  The Board is 
currently dealing with some of these significant issues and has serious concerns 
with how these requirements will play out as the Board’s lead service line 
replacement work progresses. 
 
On December 6, 2023, EPA issued for public comment further proposed revisions 
to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), found in 40 C.F.R. § 141.80.91), known as 
the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).  The Board generally supports 
improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule, but believes that, with the best 
intentions, the Agency has gone too far on a number of requirements as described 
below.  Accordingly, we submit these comments because the proposed LCRI 
requirements will create an unfeasible regulatory obligation for both public water 
systems and their ratepayers.  As noted in other comments, we believe that the 
inventory obligations and the manner in which LSL removal is tracked and 
credited to LCR removal benchmarks will be unachievable for many water 
systems.  As noted by others, this will create significant conflict between EPA, 
State agencies, and water utilities as they work to complete the mandated 
replacements. 
 
I. 
The Full Lead Service Line Replacement Requirements in the Rule 
Ignore the Legal Rights and Authority of Public Water Systems. 
 
In the Board’s view, the most significant and problematic requirements of the 
proposed rule are those regarding LSL replacements, inventories, and removal 
goals that expose utilities to potential liability for customer owned service lines.  
Put simply, most public utilities have no rights to access, let alone remove and 
replace, customer owned service lines.  In most jurisdictions, each and every 
customer must specifically consent and grant such access to the public water 
system.  Based on decades of experience, this is going to create a huge issue 
across the country especially in West Virginia and other rural areas.  No level of 
diligence will result in access to 100% of customer-owned infrastructure.  The 
Board has already experienced these refusals during its response to EPA and 
DHHR orders concerning lead contamination in the system over the last two and  

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
February 5, 2024 
Page Three 
 
 
a half years.  A troubling percentage of customers, even after numerous written, 
telephonic, and in person outreach still refuse access even for completely free 
sampling purposes.  This outreach has included and continues to include all 
available public education materials concerning the risks associated with lead. 
 
In West Virginia, it is well established law that the customer service line1 is 
privately owned and maintained; W. Va. Code R. 150-7-3.  The customer service 
line is private property, located outside of the right-of-way held by the water 
system.  The Board does not have a right-of-way to access the customer service 
line to complete a replacement or repair as required by the Proposed Rule.  
Further, entering a service location and modifying private property without 
permission of the private property owner would be an “unreasonable practice” 
under West Virginia Code § 24-2-7 and would clearly expose the utility to liability.  
As such, we urge EPA to reconsider the “reasonable effort” standard for 
attempting to engage private property owners to allow for a full service line 
replacement and the resulting implications for failure to obtain property owner 
consent.  Indefinite obligations for locations after reasonable efforts to secure 
access is not practical or reasonable and provides no clear path to compliance 
with the rule. 
 
As noted by other commenters, EPA lacks the authority to require public water 
utilities to replace privately-owned water infrastructure located on private 
property.  There are significant legal questions about whether public entities can 
even spend public funds for this private purpose.  Historically, at least in West 
Virginia, this has been clearly forbidden.  The Board and its consultants are 
currently working through these issues with West Virginia funding agencies. 
 
EPA cannot and should not withhold credit for a public side lead service line 
replacements where access to private property is denied.  EPA needs to address 
the legality of requiring public water systems to replace private lead service lines 
before imposing such a requirement in the LCRI.  The proposed rule attempts to 
punt this requirement to state programs yet still hold utilities accountable for 
compliance with the federal rule, which in West Virginia, is incorporated by 
reference into the State rules. 
 
Rather than illegally seeking to force public water systems to make improvements 
to private outdoor and indoor plumbing, EPA should give water utilities a benefit 
for each LSL replacement that is performed.  We also share other commenter’s 
concerns regarding whether EPA’s assumed cost to implement the proposed rule 
has included private side LSL replacement costs.  If such an analysis has been  
 
1 Defined as “that portion of the service pipe from the point of service to the structure or premises supplied” in W. Va. 
Code R. 150-7-3.7. 

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
February 5, 2024 
Page Four 
 
 
performed, details should be provided which include an analysis of the varying 
regional costs for this work. 
 
Additionally, 
the 
proposed 
LCRI’s 
definition 
and 
discussion 
regarding 
infrastructure that is “Under the Control of the Water System” is flawed and 
ignores the practical realities of private ownership described above.  This 
definition as proposed attempts to expand the longstanding definitions in the 
SDWA in a way that ignores basic property law and vaguely equates “legal access” 
and “physical access”.  It is arguable that any person or entity has “physical 
access” to private property if they are willing to trespass.  EPA also makes vague 
reference to “data and anecdotes” about limited access to customer property.  The 
Board can attest that these issues are not mere anecdotes, but regularly 
occurring challenges that the Board has experienced and continues to experience.  
Customers routinely refuse access for free lead sampling and some have even 
refused free filters despite repeated in person delivery and outreach. 
 
The Board agrees strongly with other commenters who have noted that the 
definition of “Control” must clarify that water utilities are not obligated to replace 
customer-owned LSLs as EPA cannot legally require public utilities to make 
changes to private property.  The key determination for compliance and inventory 
goals should be based on actual ownership.  The proposed requirements are 
written for a complete replacement so that water systems do not get credit for LSL 
replacement if it doesn’t include the customer’s side.  The Board believes that this 
is an illegal provision.  The Board strongly supports full replacements when and 
wherever possible, but utilities cannot be exposed to liability and noncompliance 
for failing to replace plumbing that it does not own.  Those private side 
replacements should instead be driven by federal funding efforts and partial 
replacements should be given the credit they are due, considering they take 
considerable resources to locate and complete. 
 
II. 
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement Within 10 Years is not 
Reasonable or Achievable for Most Public Water Systems. 
 
The proposed LCRI would require water utilities to complete 100% lead service 
line replacement (LSLR) within 10 years.  While there are alternative timelines for 
(1) systems with a high proportion of lead and GRR service lines in their 
distribution system relative to their total number of households served and (2) 
systems that would otherwise be required to replace greater than 10,000 service 
lines per year under the proposed 10-year replacement requirement, in the vast 
majority of cases, the ten-year timeframe is woefully inadequate.  Using the 
Board’s system as an example, the currently proposed alternative timelines would 
only provide approximately two (2) additional years for the Board to achieve these 
goals and the system includes nearly 50% lead service lines. 

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
February 5, 2024 
Page Five 
 
 
EPA estimates that there are more than 50,000 water systems nationwide.  An 
untold number of these systems are already struggling to meet financial 
obligations and lack adequate staffing and resources to meet this requirement as 
currently set forth in the proposed rule. 
 
III. 
The Service Line Inventory Obligations In The Proposed LCRI Will Be 
Overly Burdensome, Especially For Medium And Small Utilities. 
 
The proposed revisions fail to consider the burden that establishing and 
maintaining a service line inventory creates on medium and small water systems.  
EPA should consider that with less resources and less staffing, it will be a 
challenge to update the service line inventory on an annual basis and should 
reduce or eliminate these requirements for small and medium sized systems.  
This exercise will likely yield little benefit to the overall goals of the LCRI and after 
the establishment of a lead service line inventory will have limited benefit.  The 
rule should simply require that inventories be updated as needed as lead service 
line replacement projects progress. 
 
The Board also takes issue with the requirements related to a validation pool of 
non-lead service line locations and echoes the comments presented by the West 
Virginia Municipal Water Quality Association.  The proposed regulation instructs 
water systems to develop a “validation pool” consisting of all lines categorized as 
non-lead minus the non-lead lines that already replaced LSL or GRR lines, non-
lead lines already visually inspected at two points along the line, or non-lead lines 
with documentation demonstrating their composition.  The rule would require 
water systems to randomly and visually inspect as many service lines in the 
validation pool as necessary to ensure a “95% confidence level” that the observed 
proportion of non-lead lines validated is representative of the larger validation 
pool within ten years of the rule’s publication and seven years of submitting 
baseline inventories. 
 
This requirement is an unnecessary and arguably duplicative administrative task 
that will be very resource intensive to comply with.  It also ignores the practical 
implications of the data and document review that is conducted to complete a 
lead service line inventory.  It is unclear how EPA believes that a service line will 
be designated as “non-lead” without documentation or visual inspection.  For 
those locations where records are available describing the materials used for 
service connections, these locations should be specifically excluded from any 
“validation pool” requirements.  This is not currently clear. 
 
Another key factor that should exclude certain locations from validation is the age 
of the service line.  The use of lead in new plumbing systems was officially banned 
in 1986, but its use had been significantly phased out for a number of years  

U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
February 5, 2024 
Page Six 
 
 
before that.  At a minimum any service line constructed or replaced after 1986 
should be specifically excluded from validation requirements. 
 
IV. 
Public Disclosure of LSL Addresses 
 
The Board has serious concerns about the public disclosure of individual 
addresses in its lead service line inventory and has received considerable negative 
feedback from its customers regarding the public availability of this information.  
As noted by other commenters, the LCRR includes location identifiers (street, 
intersection, landmark, etc.) served by each LSL, but the LCRI states utilities 
must include a street address with each service line and connector.  Utilities face 
potential liability for the disclosure of this information publicly and the Board 
asserts that this level of specificity in a public database is unnecessary.  Not 
surprisingly, the Board has experienced customer refusal to grant access for pot 
holing and other lead related investigative work because customers do not want 
their addresses identified in the Board’s lead service line inventory.  Each 
customer served by a lead service line will receive annual outreach regarding the 
presence of a lead service line and will also receive other public education and 
outreach as required by the rule.  Additionally, any home that tests for lead will 
receive the sampling results. 
 
The Board and its employees work tirelessly to provide clean, reliable, and safe 
drinking water to its customers and we appreciate the opportunity to comment on 
this critically important EPA rulemaking.  Please contact me if you have any 
questions or if I can provide any additional information related to these 
comments. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Jason L. Myers 
General Manager

Re: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801,   
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements  
  
Michael S. Regan, Administrator   
US Environmental Protection Agency   
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW

Dear Administrator Regan,  
  
The South Carolina State Conference of NAACP Branches submits the following comments 
regarding the US Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”). The South Carolina State 
Conference of NAACP State provides leadership for local branches, youth councils, and college 
chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in the state of South Carolina. The NAACP 
and its Center for Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring 
that issues of community engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and 
frontline communities most impacted, including communities in South Carolina.   
  
The South Carolina State Conference of NAACP Branches applauds EPA for proposing stronger 
regulations to protect communities from lead in drinking water. Lead in drinking water has been 
a historically prevalent issue in Black communities, posing extreme risks to the health of young 
people, mothers, and their families. In South Carolina, estimates suggest that there are as many 
as 44,000 lead service lines, threatening families across our state with exposure to a potent and 
irreversible neurotoxin which even at low levels of exposure is linked to damage to the brain and 
nervous system, causes learning disabilities, shorter stature, impaired hearing, and harm to 

blood cells. In South Carolina, we would derive $968,000,000.00 in public health cost savings 
from full lead service line replacement.  
  
In the south, the most vulnerable communities are low income, impoverished, under-resourced, 
and overburdened. When you see these communities they are almost always black 
communities.  Black communities have a greater risk of being exposed to environmental 
injustices. Within the black demographic, populations like pregnant mothers, and children from 
birth to five are impacted the most. These populations are at greater risk of health effects like, 
damage to the brain and nervous system. In black communities, most people don't know what 
to look for or even know that they are impacted so their trust is placed in the hands of agencies 
who are supposed to protect people. Most are unaware of all of the contaminants that are 
consumed and water should be safe for all. Black families should not have to be exposed to 
injustices because everyone should have the right to access to clean drinking water no matter 
where they live. In the black community there are cumulative impacts that we are burdened 
with. Our air is polluted, water polluted, our food is contaminated and we are at higher risks.  We 
deserve a healthy livable environment to live, grow, and thrive in.  Environmental justice should 
be for all, not just those who can afford it.  South Carolina deserves better and we should have 
a people first approach to making sustainable changes for our black communities.   
For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the 
proposed LCRI such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the 
requirements for water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through 
lead pipes and a lower action level; but also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes 
which undermine their goals and ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.  
 
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not 
leave black communities in South Carolina behind:  
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a fundamental 
injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 or more 
years to fix this issue.   
● 
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: Removal can cost 
thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted communities will result in 
mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced. Removal and 
replacement do not make up major proportions of utility budgets, and utilities should be 
expected to maximize the use of available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-
ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize solving this crisis.   
  
● 
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many hours there 
daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead exposure 
when compared with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing program does not 
differ from past ineffective programs, and EPA should move towards incentivizing the 
installation of filters and protecting children.  

  
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would allow for 
environmental injustice to persist.  Black communities and frontline communities have long 
suffered from disinvestment and lack of resources.  Past NAACP analysis has demonstrated 
that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had the strongest relationship to slow and inadequate 
enforcement of the SDWA of any sociodemographic characteristic analyzed.  The final LCRI is a 
rare opportunity to make significant changes in the lives of millions of people in South Carolina, 
and to provide a measure of environmental justice which these families are owed, and we 
encourage this administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by 
strengthening the final rule further.  
  
 
  
Brenda Murphy 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
       
 
                                                                                                                
 
 
 NAACP SC State Conference

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0778 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
The Water Collaborative of Greater New Orleans
1433 N. Claiborne Ave, Suite 201
New Orleans, LA 70116
January 31, 2024
Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
RE: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Dear Administrator Regan,
The Water Collaborative of Greater New Orleans (TWC) is a non-profit organization dedicated to
sustainable urban water management, serving as a leader in rights-based water governance in the region.
In alignment with our mission, TWC has played a leading role in the Biden-Harris 'Get the Lead Out'
partnership in New Orleans. Collaborating with the Sewerage and Water Board and two community
organizations, we played a key role in developing an extensive lead awareness program and replacement
plan. Our ongoing efforts aim to contribute to a resilient and equitable water management system,
ensuring the well-being of our communities and the longevity of our shared natural resources.
In the state of Louisiana, there are approximately 266,984 lead service lines. Although the exact
count of lead lines in New Orleans remains unknown, the city's historical age and infrastructure suggest a
substantial presence. Economic challenges in New Orleans may exacerbate this issue, as older and
economically disadvantaged neighborhoods often bear a disproportionate burden of aging infrastructure,
including lead pipes. This underscores the urgent need for comprehensive measures to ensure the safety
and well-being of residents that make the city a cultural hub.
We commend the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) for advancing water quality
measures and building upon the progress initiated by the LCR Revisions. The efforts to protect the quality
of our drinking water are crucial, and we appreciate the agency's commitment to this cause.
The initiative to establish a 10-year timeline for the nationwide replacement of lead service lines
marks a proactive step toward addressing a longstanding issue affecting public health. While
acknowledging these positive strides, it is crucial to strengthen the LCRI to the fullest extent and to
uphold the EPA’s unwavering commitment to public safety. Removing exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe
removal mandate is crucial to prevent communities with the most lead service lines from having
additional decades to address this issue, ensuring fairness and avoiding further injustice. We applaud the
EPA for decisive actions such as removing the lead trigger level, reducing the lead action level, and
adopting a more thorough water testing procedure. Under this procedure, water systems would be
required to collect first and fifth liter samples at sites with lead service lines and use the higher of the two
values when determining compliance with the rule.
However, the recently set limit of 10 parts per billion (ppb), though a step forward, lacks
alignment with health-based scientific considerations, resembling the detached nature of the prior
standard at 15 ppb. Notably, bottled water standards have maintained a 5 ppb limit since 1994. In
alignment with global leaders such as Canada and the European Union, we strongly recommend lowering
the action level to 5 ppb.
1

Additionally, the LCRI should prohibit partial service line replacements. Construction
disturbances during these replacements risk lead leaching into drinking water from nearby lines,
potentially contaminating incoming water for weeks. We also advocate for the immediate availability of
filters in known affected areas, recognizing that residents in disadvantaged communities may face
challenges in affording the replacement of their own lead service lines or the purchase of certified filters.
Residents currently experiencing impacts should swiftly access mitigation measures. Immediate
limitations on their exposure are crucial to preventing further harm.
To meet the ambitious goals of the LCRI, it is crucial to confront a stark reality: placing the
burden of private service line replacement solely on individual ratepayers would force those unable to
afford it to endure ongoing lead exposure. This scenario presents a glaring disparity, disproportionately
affecting the financial and health well-being of the lowest-income customers. Strengthening these efforts
necessitates urgent action from the EPA to mandate utilities cover the entire cost of replacement and
extend their rights to private service lines. This may involve superseding varying state laws and
advocating for the rights of renters. These proactive steps are essential to streamline the process, ensuring
uniformity in addressing the lead pipe issue and maintaining an equitable approach to replacement.
Unfortunately, the LCRI proposal fails to capitalize on the critical opportunity to enhance
regulations for protecting children in educational facilities, lacking improvements upon the provisions set
forth in the LCRR. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises that drinking water provided to children
should not exceed 1 ppb of lead. The current approach of relying on schools for independent water testing
introduces significant challenges, as these institutions may face potential deficiencies in expertise,
resources, and standardized procedures. This reliance raises concerns about the consistency and accuracy
of water testing practices across various educational facilities, which is vital for ensuring the health and
safety of students and staff.
In addressing the critical issue of water safety in educational facilities, the implementation of
lead-certified filters or regular comprehensive tap testing is imperative. To ensure the well-being of
students and staff, the immediate necessity lies in introducing health-protective measures such as filters or
rigorous testing protocols. Unfortunately, the existing rule falls short of safeguarding this need. It lacks a
mandatory stipulation requiring notification to parents, students, or faculty about lead test results, creating
a significant gap in transparency. Moreover, the absence of a requirement for remediation when lead is
detected, combined with a limited testing scope, adds to the deficiencies. This underscores the urgency of
adopting a more extensive approach and extending these increased protections to secondary schools.
Recognizing the paramount importance of prioritizing children's health, we strongly advocate for the
adoption of the Filter First approach, similar to what was recently enacted in Michigan. This
health-protective strategy stands out as a consistent approach, ensuring the well-being of children in
educational environments.
Recognizing that effective communication is paramount in ensuring the success of lead service
line replacement initiatives, we advocate for the EPA to mandate utilities, especially those utilizing
federal funds such as State Revolving Funds, to implement sufficient outreach strategies. This should
include a mix of communication strategies such as mailings, community events, and possibly text
notifications, particularly in areas where lead service lines are being replaced. The goal is to not only
2

inform residents about ongoing projects but also to educate them about the potential risks of lead
exposure and the available resources for mitigation and risk reduction.
Lastly, we recommend the EPA establish a national service line inventory, consolidating all
state-reported progress on a publicly accessible platform. A centralized repository would serve as a
valuable resource for communities, advocacy groups, policymakers, and concerned citizens seeking
up-to-date and accurate information on the nation’s progress. This commitment to outreach and
transparency aligns with the EPA's dedication to meaningful public involvement and fosters
accountability among state agencies, ensuring a well-informed and empowered public.
Recommendations
●
Lower the action level to 5 ppb to better align with health-based scientific considerations.
●
Prohibit partial service line replacements to streamline the process and avoid disturbing the
remaining lead lines.
●
Mandate utilities to cover the costs of full replacement, advocating for uniformity and renters'
rights.
●
Implement enhanced regulations to safeguard children in educational facilities, extending to
secondary schools.
●
Require utilities to perform consistent outreach to engage communities nationwide.
●
Establish a national service line inventory for transparency, accountability, and public access.
In offering these recommendations, our goal is not just to suggest but to demand the
establishment of a comprehensive and equitable water safety framework, in line with The Water
Collaborative's enduring commitment to ensuring communities have access to safe drinking water. By
advocating for strengthened regulations and transparent initiatives, we aspire to transcend mere
compliance, creating lasting improvements in water quality and management. Our aspirations extend
beyond immediate changes, envisioning a future where communities thrive in harmony with their water
resources. Through collaborative efforts and a united pursuit of responsible management practices, we
hope to contribute to a legacy of health and resilience for generations to come.
Sincerely,
The Water Collaborative of Greater New Orleans Team

RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements 
(LCRI), Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
On behalf of the National Conference of State Legislatures (NCSL), the bipartisan organization representing the 
legislatures of our nation’s states, commonwealths and territories, we appreciate the opportunity to provide input on the 
proposed improvements to the national primary drinking water regulations for lead and copper. While we vigorously 
applaud the agency’s efforts to address lead in the drinking water of vulnerable populations, we oppose the creation of 
new unfunded mandates. We look forward to working with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to further 
strengthen the state-federal partnership to ensure clean and safe drinking water for all Americans. 
 
Continue State Consultation 
We are encouraged by the administration’s actions to make improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) and the 
Lead Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), especially given ongoing lead contamination in drinking water systems. As states 
currently possess the ability to obtain and retain primary enforcement responsibilities (primacy) for public water system 
supervision under the Safe Drinking Water Act, we urge the EPA to work in tandem with primacy states on the proposed 
revisions to water testing, service line inventorying and record keeping, actionable lead levels, public notification and 
education, and other compliance requirements to develop the most effective methods and systems in the most cost-
effective manner. We applaud the willingness the EPA has already demonstrated in engaging with primacy states in the 
development and implementation of best testing practices, many of which are already being utilized on the ground. 
Additionally, we urge the EPA to reject all potential new conditions for state primacy as suggested in the proposed Lead 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) rule. Furthermore, to ensure the protection of human health, we also urge the EPA to 
base all potential revisions on scientifically sound principles.  
 
Avoid Unfunded Mandates and Facilitate New Federal Funding Support  
The implementation of LCRI is estimated to cost billions of dollars. By the EPA’s own admission, implementation and 
administrative costs will likely be significant for various state activities related to the rule. The EPA indicates that even 
considering currently available federal funding opportunities, costs could exceed $174 million per year. While NCSL 
recognizes the availability of additional federal funds outlined and recommended for utilization in LCRI, such as allocated 
funds from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, these funding sources are in no way guaranteed to all individual water 
systems. In fact, certain water systems may experience relatively disproportionate cost burdens due to a lack of expertise 
and capacity necessary to apply for or meet the conditions of supplemental funding. The LCRI’s proposed unfunded 
requirements may also result in disproportionate cost burdens. Some requirements such as the full-service line 
replacement of all lead service lines (LSL) and galvanized requiring replacement service lines (GRR) under a water 
system’s control or the requirement to make water systems serving a minimum population publish their service line 

replacement plans on a publicly available and accessible platform may be prohibitively expensive and technically 
infeasible.  
 
As the EPA moves forward in finalizing the LRCI, we urge the EPA to avoid creating new unfunded federal mandates, 
enable state flexibility and request sufficient funds from Congress to properly fund all existing mandates and 
requirements. Additionally, we ask the EPA to consult with states and confirm they have a clear understanding of any 
potential new costs as existing funding mechanisms are not sufficient to implement this rule.  
 
Consider State Statutory Timelines and Revise Compliance Deadlines 
NCSL strongly encourages the EPA to consider states’ legislative session schedules while working to finalize the LCRI. 
The suggested revisions are substantial, and states must have adequate time to make any needed legislative changes to 
comply with new mandates. State legislatures and state administrators need to be given ample time to restructure their 
compliance approach to follow the potentially confusing EPA proposed plan of having water systems transition from 
compliance with LCR to compliance with LCRI, while simultaneously meeting interim LCRR inventory requirements. 
While NCSL applauds the streamlining of compliance requirements, we advocate for an appropriate timeline for states 
and water system entities to reorient, and, if needed, redesign their compliance plan, especially given the limited number 
of compliance extensions that are expected to be issued for this 10-year objective.  
 
State legislatures’ in-session dates vary significantly across the nation. Although special sessions may be held post 
adjournment, such sessions are often limited in scope and can cost tens of thousands of dollars per day. Depending on the 
timeline for finalizing the proposed rule, many states will not be able to address the rule until the start of their next 
legislative session. Many of these would not start until January 2025. For additional information on state legislative 
calendars and processes for special legislative sessions, please visit NCSL’s website or contact NCSL staff member 
Selena Saucedo (303-856-1529 or selena.saucedo@ncsl.org) 
 
NCSL looks forward to continuing dialogue as the EPA works to finalize LCRI. If you have any questions, please do not 
hesitate to contact NCSL staff members Ben Nasta (202.624.3597 or benjamin.nasta@ncsl.org) or Megan Bland 
(202.624.3569 or megan.bland@ncsl.org).

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1103 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
BlueGreen Alliance 
Harley Stokes, Senior Policy Advisor 
1020 19th St., NW | Suite 750 
Washington, DC 20036 
Hstokes@bluegreenalliance.org 
 
February 5, 2024 
Docket ID Number: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 
BlueGreen Alliance’s Comments on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements  
The BlueGreen Alliance unites labor unions and environmental organizations 
to solve today’s environmental challenges in ways that create and maintain 
quality jobs and build a clean, thriving, and equitable economy. Our 
partnership is firm in its belief that we don’t have to choose between a good 
job and a clean environment—we can and must have both. We are excited to 
offer our comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI) and specifically on proactive and equitable lead service line replacement 
(LSLR). LSLR represents a significant and scalable opportunity to support and 
create good, union jobs, improve the health of communities, and address 
environmental injustice by prioritizing those communities that have been 
disproportionately impacted by toxic legacy substances like lead. 
The proposed rule makes several key improvements in how lead in drinking 
water is regulated. However, our recommendations include revisions to key 
provisions, as well as new provisions to ensure the final rule results in long-
lasting and equitable public health benefits and supports the creation of good 
jobs. 
 
As stated in the Biden-Harris Lead Pipe and Paint Action Plan, replacing lead 
pipes “will put American plumbers and pipefitters to work replacing all of America’s 
lead pipes and service lines and making other critical upgrades. All families, 
children, and Americans should be able to turn on the faucet at home or school and 
drink clean water—including in low-income communities and communities of color 
that have been disproportionally affected by dangerous lead pipes...”i We couldn’t 
agree more. Below are recommendations to ensure the final rule delivers 
exactly that. 
• Remove exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate. Lead in 
water is an urgent public health matter and replacing all lead service 
lines (LSL) within ten years is not only feasible, but necessary. As 
written, the proposed rule only requires most water systems to replace 

 
 
lead lines within ten years. This leaves behind large municipalities—such 
as New York City and Cleveland—with some of the highest densities of 
LSLs and allows a much slower replacement timeline that will continue 
to impact generations of children. It is a fundamental injustice that 
communities with the most lead service lines would be subject to lead 
exposure for decades more than the rest of the country. For example, 
in Chicago the proposed rule would allow 40+ years to fully replace 
LSLs with the current exception in the proposed rule. A second 
provision would allow close to 2,100 water systems across the country 
that have a relatively high percentage of lead pipes to take 20+ years to 
replace lead pipes.ii It is unnecessary to build such exceptions into the 
proposal itself and the BlueGreen Alliance urges the U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency (EPA) to require all LSLs to be replaced within ten 
years without exception.  
 
• Ban cost sharing and mandate water systems fully pay for removal of 
lead service lines. While the proposed rule requires full LSLR (both 
public and private side), it does not require the utility to pay for the 
private side. Therefore, any property owner who will not or cannot 
afford to pay for their side could end up with a partial lead service line 
replacement even though only full LSLR will count towards the 
mandate. At best, partial replacements are a waste of money because 
they do not reduce lead in water; at worst, they substantially increase 
lead levels for months if not years.iii Not only are partial replacements a 
predictable consequence contradictory to the intent of requiring full 
LSLR, but it is also an environmental justice (EJ) issue. Both in theory 
and in practice, lower-income communities suffer because property 
owners cannot afford to replace the pipes, or in the case of renters, 
landlords refuse to pay for replacement. This is what happened in 
Washington D.C. when the utility was not required to pay for the full 
replacement and lower-income neighborhoods and individuals were left 
with lead in their pipes. A study conducted by the Environmental 
Defense Fund (EDF) found lower rates of full LSLR in wards and census 
tracts with lower median household incomes and a higher percentage 
of residents self-identified as African American/Black.iv We recommend 
EPA follow the example of Michigan’s Lead and Copper Rule and 
require full LSLR at no cost to the property owner to ensure maximum 
uptake.v 

 
 
 
• Lower the action level to 5 parts per billion (ppb). We are happy to see 
that trigger levels were eliminated in the proposed rule and that the 
action-based level was lowered from 15 to 10 ppb. However, as stated 
in the Lead Pipe and Paint Action Plan the EPA, Centers for Disease 
Control and Prevention (CDC), and countless experts “agree that there 
is no known safe level of lead in a child’s blood.”vi Therefore, we 
continue to advocate lowering the action-based level to a maximum of 
5 ppb. EPA’s sister agency, the Federal and Drug Administration, 
already sets 5 ppb as the allowable limit for lead in bottled water and 
EPA—at minimum—should set the action level to do the same for tap 
water. Ideally, the EPA should move to a Maximum Contaminant Level 
(MCL) which sets a limit on the amount of lead in drinking water. Action 
levels are appropriate when it is not technically or economically feasible 
to determine the level of a contaminant in the water, but it is feasible to 
determine the amount of lead in water. Both the LCRI and past EPA 
regulations direct utilities to determine the level of lead in the water. In 
the LCRI the action level rests on water sampling for lead, and 
previously EPA did set an MCL for lead in 1975. Given the feasibility of 
measuring lead in water and the similarities between dynamics of lead 
in water and other substances for which EPA has established MCLs, the 
agency should set a stringent limit. Moving away from an action level 
will offer clarity and greater protection from this harmful substance. 
 
• Incentivize prevention measures for schools and daycares. The 
proposed rule only requires water systems to offer very limited testing 
for most schools and childcare centers: a single lead test at just five 
locations in each school and just two locations in a childcare center—
once in the first five years—with no mandatory retesting or required 
notice to parents and staff.  Even federally regulated schools and 
childcare centers would only have to remediate taps where tests show 
lead concentrations at 10 ppb or more. This is beyond insufficient to 
detect lead let alone prevent lead exposure. In cases where full 
abatement of lead pipes will take many years—such as in schools and 
childcare centers—we recommend that the new rule facilitate plans to 
ensure that appropriate water filters are installed in taps used for 
cooking and drinking water. These devices are relatively quick and 

 
 
inexpensive to install and offer vital interim assistance in preventing 
lead contamination. 
 
In addition to the above proposed revisions to the proposed LCRI, we 
continue to advocate for the following elements that were entirely absent 
from the proposed rule: 
 
• Discourage or disqualify use of polyvinyl chloride (PVC) pipes to 
replace lead pipes. We cannot replace one harmful pipe material with 
another. Vinyl chloride is a known human carcinogen and PCV pipes are 
considered the most hazardous pipe materials by the Healthy Building 
Network (HBN). HBN research shows that, of available potable water 
pipe materials, PVC contains “the highest levels of chemicals of 
concern.” In addition, they are typically installed using hazardous 
solvents.vii Furthermore, EPA’s Office of Chemical Safety and Pollution 
Prevention recently included vinyl chloride as a high priority substance 
for risk evaluation under the Toxic Substances Control Act.viii 
 
• 
Provide guidance on choosing the safest, most durable pipe materials. 
Other plastic piping materials can also leach estrogenic substances and 
other chemicals of concern and are more permeable to gasoline and 
other solvents.ix In addition to the problems with plastic water pipes, 
the information on lead in solders and fluxes and the problem of low 
PH water causing copper leaching should be part of an EPA education 
package on replacing lead service lines.x The EPA should provide 
guidance on choosing the safest and most durable option to prevent 
future health risks. 
 
• Recycle old lead pipes at U.S. facilities. Currently, there are no 
provisions in the proposed rule regarding disposal of lead pipes. It is 
important to ensure that addressing environmental injustices in the U.S. 
does not create environmental injustice elsewhere in the world. Most 
of the lead scrap from the U.S.—including LSLs—is exported to 
countries with weaker environmental standards for recycling. In 2021, 
50% of lead scrap exports went to India and Mexico for recycling. The 
other half went to more than 40 other countries including China, 
Ecuador, Guatemala, Bangladesh, and Indonesia. These countries have 
much weaker pollution controls for air emissions, occupational 

 
 
exposures, and few resources for enforcement. The removal of old lead 
pipes in the U.S. should not contribute to environmental injustices in 
other countries that have weaker environmental standards. Because 
U.S. standards are more stringent, it is important that EPA require all 
LSLs to be recycled at a U.S. facility.xi 
 
We urge EPA to finalize a strong LCRI that contributes to the Biden-Harris 
vision of a lead-free future by replacing ALL lead service lines in the U.S. in the 
next decade and look forward to working alongside the EPA to make that 
vision a reality.

through drinking water. Both bold and achievable, this proposal is a very important step toward 
eliminating the blight of lead in the country’s drinking water system.  
 
Public Citizen’s founder, Ralph Nader, and his Nader’s Raiders were instrumental in creation of 
consumer protection agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and passage of its 
seminal regulatory authorities like the Clean Water Act and the Safe Drinking Water Act.1 Our 
organization also has a long history of working to reduce harmful contaminants in drinking water 
like arsenic,2 and to ensure water infrastructure remains a public good and fighting against 
“multinational corporations [that] exploit shrinking fresh water resources for profit.”3 Public 
Citizen appreciates this opportunity to comment on these Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI or proposal) since ensuring safe, clean drinking water in Americans’ homes and 
businesses is one of the most essential actions undertaken by the government in support of 
meeting the basic needs of the nation’s populace.  
 
 
1 PUBLIC CITIZEN FOUNDATION, PUBLIC CITIZEN THE SENTINEL OF DEMOCRACY, at 25 (Doyle Printing) (2016).

While this proposal will provide significant movement toward getting the lead out of drinking 
water, as discussed below, the proposal should be strengthened in several critical areas. For 
example, the EPA must ensure that all communities’ lead service lines are replaced within the 
10-year window outlined through the basic framework of the LCRI since exemptions to that

historically underinvested areas of the country who have disproportionately been affected by lead 
pollution, are not made to pay out of their pockets to get the lead out of their water.  
 
 
Background  
 
It is well understood that there are no safe levels of lead exposures for humans, which causes 
negative effects on our bodies’ neurological, developmental, reproductive, cardiovascular, and 
renal systems even at very low levels of exposure.4 Despite lead exposure being completely 
preventable and decades of policies seeking to reduce the threat it poses to humans-- especially 
among vulnerable populations-- detectable levels of lead continue to be found in blood samples 
representing a majority of the nation’s children.5 This is deeply disheartening since children are 
particularly vulnerable to lead’s damaging neurological and developmental impacts because their 
brains and bodies are still growing.6  
 
Though the dangers of lead exposure have been known for many years, over time the body of 
medical research showing the harmful impacts of lead at very low levels of exposure has greatly 
expanded.7 This underscores the need to tackle all remaining sources of lead exposure in 
people’s lives, including from drinking water infrastructure like service lines. The LCRI is 
clearly aligned with the goals encapsulated by the Biden-Harris Administration’s whole-of-
government approach to eliminating the pathways of lead exposure in Americans’ lives, as 
outlined in the Lead Pipe and Paint Action Plan.8

The EPA’s charge, as authorized by the Safe Drinking Water Act, is to create standards for 
drinking water systems (National Primary Drinking Water Regulations or NPDWRs), that, 
among other safeguards, require removal of known threats to the “extent feasible.”9 When not 
possible to meet the Maximum Containment Load Goal, treatment options must be undertaken 
toward achieving the health-based standard.  
 
 
The Expanding Evidence of Lead’s Toxicity 
 
The United States government first started taking action toward elimination of lead in consumer 
products in the 1970s, even though lead’s harmful impacts of human health had been known for 
decades prior.10 Recent medical research continues to add to the ever-growing scientific 
understanding that even very low levels of lead concentrations in the human body can be linked 
to health impacts. For example, lead levels “as low as 2.5 μg/dL have been found to produce 
diminished cognitive function and maladaptive behavior in humans.”11 Yet, today there are still 
in excess of 9 million homes that are receiving their water via lead service lines.12 
 
Low concentrations of lead (below 10 micrograms per deciliter) in the bloodstream of children 
have been found to cause neurological effects like lower test scores, compromised attention, 
declining IQ, impaired coordination, and other cognitive deficits.13 Young adults exposed to lead 
were found to engage in violent and delinquent behaviors in higher proportions, and links to 
increased rates of ADHD diagnosis in children have also been shown.14 Nor is lead’s 
neurotoxicity confined to the young, increased risk of diseases that impact the elderly like 
Alzheimer’s and Parkinsons have been linked to lead exposure earlier in life.15  
 
Numerous studies have shown significant permanent adverse health effects on adults from lead 
exposure that go beyond neurological toxicity such as reproductive, pregnancy and fetal health 
impacts.16 Low levels of lead detected in the human body have also been linked to cardiovascular 
problems like hypertension and renal effects like chronic kidney disease.17

Racial Equity Considerations 
 
While there have been high-level instances of lead contamination of drinking water, such as the 
Flint, Michigan tragedy,18 lead service lines exist in communities across the country—from the 
most rural to the most urban. However, despite lead being a ubiquitous threat across America, 
there is a racial justice component to lead abatement policies as disparities based on race have 
been shown to exist regarding adverse health impacts due to lead exposure.19 
 
Given that communities of color disproportionately live in areas with higher all-around lead 
exposure20 (such as from older, more affordable but deteriorating housing) it is important for the 
government to ensure that all sources of lead exposure that can be feasibly addressed are 
eliminated to better address these historical systemic inequities that are currently burdening the 
health of Black and Brown communities. Additionally, given the unfortunate persistence of a 
correlation between BIPOC populations and poverty,21 to achieve an equitable outcome and 
ensure 100 percent of lead service lines are replaced, the cost associated with replacement must 
not be borne by individuals and rather should be paid for by water utilities.  
 
 
Overview of Proposal 
 
Unlike the 2021 revision to the Lead and Copper Rule, which did not take adequate action 
toward the EPA’s goal of totally removing lead from drinking water,22 this proposal would 
require removal of all lead service lines, most within a ten-year timeline. This is a monumental 
step forward as lead pipes running underneath our homes and businesses are a lurking threat, 
exposing millions of people every day to a toxic substance that is endangering both adults as well 
as vulnerable children.  
 
In addition, under this proposal the Lead Action Level—the concentration of lead above which 
additional remediation and information-sharing with the public is required has been reduced 
from 15 micrograms per liter to 10 micrograms per liter. While some organizations have called

for an even lower Lead Action Level threshold23 and we urge the agency to continue to evaluate

proposed Lead Action Level standard is an important move toward a drinking water safeguard 
more closely based on health. This element of the proposal is also a recognition that to achieve a 
future where drinking water lead contamination shrinks closer toward the EPA’s goal of a 
Maximum Contaminant Level of zero, additional action and public disclosures must come into 
play at lower levels of lead concentration in water. 
 
Moreover, this proposal’s requirement for drinking water customer outreach and the provision of 
effective lead-removing filters when there have been multiple instances of the Lead Action Level 
threshold having been surpassed is an important move to protect communities most impacted by 
the scourge of lead in drinking water. Other protections included in the proposal to require water 
systems to better understand and track the location and replacement of lead service lines over 
time and to undertake more representative water sampling methods are most welcome as these 
requirements will help the agency more accurately target and respond to the threat of lead in 
drinking water in specific localities.  
 
 
Needed Strengthening of the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements Proposal 
 
Public Citizen believes that the central elements of the LCRI proposal represent a concerted 
effort from the EPA to better align the Lead and Copper Rule with the irrefutable body of 
science that has clearly demonstrated the irreversible toll that lead wreaks on the human body, 
even at very low doses of exposure, and must be commended. However, Public Citizen urges the 
EPA to finalize a rule that is even more protective of human health than the LCRI as currently 
proposed.   
 
Because no level of lead exposure can be considered safe, it is imperative the EPA strive to 
comprehensively remove all known vectors of lead contamination, like drinking water pipes, as 
soon as possible. It follows from this reasoning that no communities should receive an 
exemption from the proposal’s overarching requirement to replace all lead service lines at least 
within the next decade.  
 
The EPA has known for decades that lead exposure is unsafe at any level and drinking water 
utilities and municipalities have sat on their hands in many cases without addressing the threat. 
To give a longer timeline for replacement of lead service lines threatens further inaction when 
the science is clear that lead is potentially permanently and significantly impacting the health of 
millions of Americans at this very moment. It would be unconscionable to allow citizens of our

country to be exposed to a known health hazard beyond that already very long window, when
