Equity considerations must be given strong weight in the EPA’s proposal since lead exposure 
and its detrimental health impacts has a disparate impact on communities of color. This racial 
justice lens is especially critical as the agency hopefully reexamines who should pay for line 
replacement—the equitable solution means that water utilities should be required to pay rather 
than homeowners and renters in communities that have few resources to spare.24  
 
It also follows from equity considerations that implementation of this rule be prioritized based on 
putting into place stronger protections for areas that have seen historic and systemic under- and 
dis-investment in water infrastructure such as low-income areas and communities of color. 
Additionally, to ensure the rule is maximally protective of human health, provision of remedial 
protections like filters must be prioritized based on reaching areas where vulnerable persons like 
children or pregnant people are currently drinking water that contains lead, like in schools or 
childcare facilities.   
 
 
Conclusion 
 
Public Citizen commends the EPA for taking seriously its remit to work toward its goal of 
reaching the level of zero lead contamination in the nation’s drinking water. With further 
improvements to the proposal as outlined in this comment and in those of our allied 
organizations, we believe the rule would be more equitable and more protective of human health. 
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this important revision to strengthen the 
EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule.

RE: Comments on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-
OW-2022-0801 
The San Diego County Water Authority (Water Authority) appreciates the opportunity to 
provide input on the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The Water Authority is a regional wholesale water agency 
that provides a significant amount of the water used in San Diego County, and in partnership 
with its member agencies, sustains a $240 billion economy and quality of life for 3.3 million 
residents.  
The Water Authority’s mission is to provide a safe and reliable water supply to its member 
agencies. We appreciate the EPA’s efforts to protect public health by reducing lead exposure in 
drinking water. To improve the effectiveness of the regulation and consider previous efforts by 
community water systems (CWS) to address lead and copper concerns, we ask the EPA to 
consider the following comments on the proposed rule.  
WAIVER REQUIREMENTS FOR LEAD SAMPLING IN SCHOOLS AND CHILDCARE FACILITIES  
The proposed LCRI includes a provision that allows states to issue waivers to CWS from the 
requirement for lead sampling in schools and childcare facilities during the initial sampling 
period if the facility was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021, but prior to the LCRI 
compliance date. 
California Assembly Bill (AB) 746 required CWS to test lead levels by July 1, 2019, in drinking 
water at all California public K-12 school sites that were constructed before January 1, 2010. 
Additionally, AB 2370 required licensed childcare facilities located in buildings constructed 
before January 1, 2010, to test for lead between January 1, 2020, and January 1, 2023. The 
waiver requirements should be revised to permit sampling conducted in 2017 and beyond, and 
in accordance with AB 746 and AB 2370, to qualify for a waiver during the initial five-year 
sampling cycle in schools and childcare facilities. 
 
 

 
 
4677 OVERLAND AVE, SAN DIEGO, CA 92123 | (858) 522-6600 | SDCWA.ORG 
 
PARTIAL LEAD SERVICE LINE REPLACEMENT 
The EPA requested comment on whether partial service line replacement should be prohibited 
during planned infrastructure work or with certain types of planned infrastructure work.  
Partial service line replacement should continue to be allowed during emergency or planned 
infrastructure work. Requiring customer-side service line replacement for planned 
infrastructure projects would cause considerable delay as CWS must obtain a property owner’s 
approval, plan the additional work (including possible budget and contractual changes), acquire 
additional materials, and perform the work. Many infrastructure projects are either facilitating 
essential water deliveries or performed as preventative maintenance to avoid future water 
emergencies, and delays to these projects should be avoided to protect water supply reliability. 
The LCRI should allow CWS to use their discretion to determine if the customer-side 
replacement can be incorporated into planned infrastructure work.  
CUSTOMER-SIDE SERVICE LINE REPLACEMENT COSTS 
The Water Authority appreciates that there is funding available to assist CWS in their lead 
service line replacement programs; however, the anticipated cost to replace all lead service 
lines is expected to be much higher than the funding that was allocated. Because water 
affordability is a concern for communities nationwide, it is important that rate impacts are 
minimized as a result of implementation of the LCRI. Further, California’s Proposition 218 (Prop. 
218) limits how CWS can set fees, and raising rates to pay for customer-side service line 
replacement at select properties likely violates Prop. 218.  
We acknowledge that the proposed LCRI does not mandate CWS to pay for customer-side 
service line replacement costs. At the same time, we recommend that those costs are not 
shifted onto customers. Rather, we urge the EPA to continue to advocate for additional federal 
funding that can be accessed directly by households at all income levels.    
INCLUSION OF LEAD CONNECTORS IN BASELINE INVENTORY 
Previously, the EPA has recognized the challenges of inventorying lead connectors. Unlike 
service lines, connector materials are often difficult to identify without excavation, which 
disturbs road pavement and potentially customer property. Furthermore, records of lead 
connectors are often limited or non-existent. Including lead connectors in the baseline 
inventory would create an unnecessary additional burden on water systems and introduce 
inconsistencies between the initial Lead and Copper Rule Revisions inventory already underway 
and the baseline LCRI inventory. Therefore, we ask that the EPA remove the requirement that 
lead connectors be included in the LCRI baseline inventory.  
 

 
 
4677 OVERLAND AVE, SAN DIEGO, CA 92123 | (858) 522-6600 | SDCWA.ORG 
CONSUMER NOTICES OF TAP SAMPLING RESULTS 
The EPA requested comment on the proposed determination that water systems can provide 
consumer notices of tap sampling results within three calendar days, or if a longer time frame is 
needed. The Water Authority is concerned that three calendar days will not be sufficient time 
to notify customers of their results in some situations. For example, a CWS could receive 
sampling results on the eve of a three-day holiday weekend which limits the feasibility of 
meeting the notification requirement. We support the requirement to deliver tap sampling 
results that indicate a lead or copper action level exceedance within three calendar days. 
However, we request that the notification requirements be revised to allow CWS seven 
calendar days to deliver tap sampling results that do not indicate an action level exceedance. 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this very important rulemaking. If you have any 
questions regarding our comments, please contact Jesica Cleaver, Water Resources Specialist, 
at JCleaver@sdcwa.org.  
Sincerely, 
 
Jeff Stephenson 
Director of Water Resources

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1134 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Public Comment Submission on
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI)
February 5, 2024
The EPA estimates there are 9.2 million lead service lines in the United States, with other
research estimating as many as 12 million lead service lines bringing water to 22 million
people.[1,2] While the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement (LCRI) requires lead service
lines be replaced within 10 years—barring rule exemptions—many families will still have toxic
lead in their water for many years during the rules implementation and line replacement. Cities
currently eligible for timeline extensions, such as Chicago, will be without lead-free water for as
many as 40 years.[3]
World health experts agree there is no safe level of lead.[4] Even low levels of lead exposure can
cause children and those still in the womb to develop brain and nervous system damage,
learning disabilities, reduced physical growth, and impaired hearing and speech abilities.[5] The
EPA must establish requirements in the proposed rule that will ensure families have access to
safe drinking water as soon as possible with the proactive distribution of filters, not plastic water
bottles.
Mitigating the Distribution of Single-Use Plastic Water Bottles
The EPA should strongly discourage the use of single-use plastic water bottles during the lead
service line replacements, as single-use plastic water bottles have significant environmental
impacts over their lifecycle. Supplying all of the impacted communities with single-use plastic
bottled water for drinking for 6 months would take an estimated 32 billion bottles. The removal of
all lead pipes will take decades and could result in hundreds of billions of water bottles ending
up in landfills and in the surrounding environment.
Single-use plastic bottles can leach dangerous contaminants into the water they hold, resulting
in health consequences for consumers. Many single-use plastic water bottles are made from
polyethylene terephthalate (PET), which can “yield endocrine disruptors under conditions of
common use, particularly with prolonged storage and elevated temperature.”[6] Plastic water
bottles can also break down into microplastics, with recent research from Columbia University
and Rutgers finding at least 240,000 plastic particles, primarily nanoplastics, in the average liter
of bottled water.[7] Over the past several years, scientists have detected the presence of tiny
plastic particles all throughout people’s bodies, including in our hearts, bloodstreams, veins,
lungs, placentas, feces, testes/semen, breast milk, and brains, with more worrying research on
the way.[8]

Plastics are made of fossil fuels.[9] We should not continue or increase our reliance on these
materials, driving ourselves deeper into the climate crisis. Plastic production releases highly
toxic chemicals that contaminate air, soil, and water. This harms primarily low-income, rural, and
BIPOC frontline/fenceline communities, contributing to elevated rates of asthma, cardiovascular
disease, and cancer.[10] Most plastic water bottles, like all plastics, are not recycled.[11] Instead,
they are most commonly sent to landfills or incinerators, are shipped overseas, or are dumped
and open-burned. This plastic poses health risks to communities near these facilities.[12]
Furthermore, a recent EPA memo makes clear that pursuant to the Safe Drinking Water Act,
single-use plastic water bottles are not eligible for State Revolving Funds (SRF). Both pitchers
and filters are eligible for this funding.[13] That is smart policy and encourages the EPA to take
further steps to mitigate unnecessary plastic pollution.
Strengthened Filter Requirements Needed
We were pleased to see that the proposed LCRI includes language to require water systems
with consistently high levels of lead to make available to customers filters certified to remove
lead from water.[14] However, this language needs to be strengthened with the following
measures to ensure expedient access to clean drinking water.
EPA should require water systems to fund the purchase and distribution of filters to customers
while also providing education materials and training on filter efficacy and maintenance. Proper
distribution and education is critical to ensuring customers can access, trust, and properly use
their filter, as seen in Denver, Colorado where, with advanced distribution and education
measures, the city achieved 80% filter adoption rates.[15]
The EPA needs to minimize the period families must wait for a filter by reducing the time and
number of lead level exceedances required to constitute “consistently high levels of lead” and
expedite filter program implementation. A “filter first” approach will ensure families have access
to clean, safe drinking water in the many years to come as the LCRI is implemented and lead
service lines are replaced.
We recognize that in certain unusual circumstances, such as where a system’s water chemistry
results in the substantial production of nanoparticles of lead that may escape standard point of
use filtration, or where there are ongoing microbial contamination risks in a water system that
could result in growth of microbes in such filters, that alternative methods of ensuring safe water
may be necessary, such as water buffaloes or reusable water bottles.
Recommending Safe Replacement Pipe Materials
Additionally, Plastic Pollution Coalition calls on the EPA to provide recommendations for safe
replacement pipe materials, such as recycled copper and stainless steel, and advise against
dangerous alternatives, such as PVC and CPVC plastic pipes, that introduce another source of
plastic pollution. These materials are an environmental injustice nightmare to produce, as
evidenced by the derailment of a train carrying vinyl chloride a year ago in East Palestine, Ohio,
and can leach dangerous contaminants into the water they carry such as vinyl chloride and
microplastics. Communities need to understand the potential health risks associated with
different water pipe materials so that they do not select alternatives that turn out to be just as
bad, if not worse, as the original option. EPA needs to weigh in on this.
Support for Filtered Not Bottled Water and Plastic Free Pipes

In September of 2023, Plastic Pollution Coalition submitted a letter to EPA Administrator Regan,
signed by 23 leading organizations, calling for the distribution of filtered, not bottled, water, and
the selection of non-toxic, non-plastic pipes during Lead Service Line Replacement. In the
following year, this letter has been adapted to a campaign letter with signatures representing
over 70 groups, including Black Millennials For Flint, Greenpeace, Hip Hop Caucus, Green
Latinos, Safer States, Beyond Plastics, Society of Native Nations and more. There is also a
public petition with 1,800 signatures and counting. We urge the EPA to hear the calls of
impacted communities and public health experts and use the Lead and Copper Rule
Improvement to advance filtered not bottled water and plastic free pipes, and ensure lead pipes
are not replaced with plastic pollution. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Dear Administrator Regan: 
New Jersey Future is pleased to submit comments on the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–
0801. 
New Jersey Future believes every New Jerseyan deserves to live with a prosperous, fair 
economy, thriving communities, and healthy neighborhoods. As a smart growth organization, we 
promote policies for cost-effective, sustainable water systems in New Jersey and support policies 
promoting access to clean drinking water nationwide. New Jersey Future played a pivotal role in 
crafting the comprehensive New Jersey lead service line replacement statute (P.L. 2021, c.183) 
enacted in 2021 and is proud that our work and partners' work show our collective leadership on 
this public health issue. 
Overview 
New Jersey Future acknowledges the dedication and commitment of the US Environmental 
Protection Agency (EPA) to protecting the public's health and delivering clean, safe drinking 
water to the nation. However, we offer comments on the equity, efficiency, and cost-
effectiveness of the proposed 10-year goal of total lead service line (LSL) replacement, the 
COMMENTS 

proposed reduction in the lead action level from the current 15 ppb to 10 ppb, requirements, 
treatment, sampling and distribution of lead-certified filters and the requirements for school and 
childcare facilities. 
NJF supports, in addition to recommendations, the following key improvements on EPA’s 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)
Inventory Validation Requirements
Definitions
●
Building Outlet: EPA should clarify the definition of a service line and clearly 
define the term “outlet” with specific clarification regarding hydrants. 
●
Building Inlet: In some cases, the lead service line portion may extend into the 
property at a minimum of three (3ft) feet after the inlet.
Annual 10% replacement requirement 
●
Water systems with few LSLs but many unknowns will not be able to meet the 
10% replacement per year. Including unknowns in the total count without 
including verification for non-lead as “credit” means water systems will fail to 
meet the requirement. EPA should consider the following equity issues for 
calculating the replacement rates. 
○
Identification and Verification: EPA should consider counting the 
verification of unknowns (not lead) towards the 10% rate. 
○
Replacement: EPA should consider only counting the 10% replacement 
of the water systems' known lead based on the count of known LSLs. 
○
Prior to the establishment of the first year’s replacement rate, EPA should 
allow utilities to use random sampling of the service lines with completely 
(both sides) unknown materials to the 95% confidence (300-400 sites) to 
establish a percentage of lead that would be used for setting a realistic 
10% replacement rate goal.
Verifications, Records, and Inspections 
●
Validation pool: EPA should clarify the requirements for “two points of 
verification” and clearly state whether the verification requires: (a) two points on 
each side or (b) two points total - one on each side to be verified non-lead. 
●
Records: The EPA should clarify what counts as a “record” and what counts as 
an “inspection.” Meter installation records are listed as a record. However, meter 
installation records account for pipe material information during a meter 
replacement—which may be inside and only account for the interior customer 

side. In that case, the EPA should clarify whether other types of inspections 
recorded in a database are also considered records.
●
Filters: EPA should clarify which inventory activities require a post-disturbance 
filter.
●
Minimum % accuracy: EPA should guide random sampling of each type of 
record (or overall set if the type of record is not known) to clarify a minimum 
percent accuracy that is acceptable, less than 100%, and with an obligation to 
replace LSLs whenever they are encountered. 
●
Inspections by emerging methods: EPA should guide how an emerging method 
can be deemed acceptable at the water system level, such as comparing the 
emerging method results against another type of physical verification. If the 
emerging method has no false negative results for lead/galvanized and/or an 
accuracy greater than 90% with a 95% confidence, it can be valid for use by the 
water system. Also, if this guidance is followed and meets acceptance criteria for 
a particular emerging method as a valid inspection tool for the water system, the 
non-lead results from this method can be excluded from the validation pool. 
Lead Service Line Replacements
   Cost-Sharing
●
EPA should encourage states to provide statutory authority for water 
systems to access private property. LSLs are typically jointly owned: the water 
system owns the portion from the water main to the curb stop, and the property 
owner owns the portion from the curb stop to the home. The places nationwide 
with the highest concentrations of LSLs tend to be lower-income communities 
and communities of color, where a majority of residents are renters. As such, 
many residents must rely on absentee property owners to consent to make their 
properties available for work and to coordinate LSL replacements. 
●
In addition, removing the access to private property barriers is essential for 
water systems to comply with the proposed ban on partial replacements.
The ban on partial replacements introduces coordination challenges for the water 
system as they work with paving jurisdictions when access to private property is 
limited. The water systems face difficulties in coordinating the replacement of the 
private portion with these barriers. Without removing the access to private 
property barriers,  the water systems would have to remove the street portion and 
then return and do the customer side later, or consequently, the water system will 
be hemmed in by road opening moratoriums (5 years after paving in many areas). 
The water system may lose the autonomy and cost savings of being able to 

coordinate with other large-scale capital projects or, most importantly, delay 
replacement until the moratorium expires. 
●
EPA should prohibit water systems from charging a customer cost-share. 
To remove the barrier property owners pose to replacing LSLs, we recommend a 
provision prohibiting a customer cost share, enabling all customers to participate 
in the program. Water systems will only achieve the goal of replacing all LSLs 
efficiently and cost-effectively within ten years if it is at no cost to customers. 
Many LSLs will need more funding for private side replacements since many 
families in disadvantaged areas cannot pay for private side replacements. 
Regardless of whether the water system serves an underserved community, an 
urban area with an abundance of absentee landowners, or a more affluent 
neighborhood, investor and government-owned water utilities encounter a high 
percentage of property owners who simply refuse to participate if they are 
required to pay a cost share. Consequently, water utilities waste time on outreach, 
replacing far fewer pipes at a significantly higher cost.
●
EPA should recommend that states allow water systems to use ratepayer 
funds to remove private-side LSLs.
In most states, water systems believe they need to find a way to use the 
Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, also known as the Bipartisan 
Infrastructure Law, loan money for private-side replacements since they must 
repay the loan with ratepayer funds. A federal or state law may be needed to allow 
water systems to use ratepayer funds to remove private-side LSLs in the interest 
of public health for the greater public good. Without free LSL replacements for 
water customers, the only LSLs remaining will be those in lower-income areas, 
exacerbating equity concerns.
●
EPA should re-evaluate the proposed 10,000 lines per year criterion for LSL 
replacements.                           
Achieving 10,000 LSL replacements per year can only occur under the best 
circumstances. This only happened in one year of the Newark program and under 
the most optimal of conditions, i.e., high level of media attention, an emergency 
declaration due to the high lead levels, city council and mayor aligned and 
supportive of the program, a smaller city that was able to pause their own rules 
and regulations regarding permitting and fees; delay of other priorities and paving 
programs and ignoring moratoriums; funding of the private side from a timely 
settlement with the Port Authority, such that ratepayer funds weren’t used; two 
mild winters allowing for work to progress year-round service lines that are only 
3 feet deep that do not require a trench box/excavation support; and a densely 

populated area with significant contractor capacity. If any of the conditions 
described regarding Newark’s LSL Replacement Program are not met year after 
year, the water system will not achieve this high LSL replacement rate. 
Furthermore, reduction of the barriers discussed above must occur, such as 
mandating replacement, no cost to customers, access to private sides, and 
assurance of funding through the end of the water system’s LSL replacement 
program.                                                                                                                                      
●
EPA should propose 8,000 lines per year as a more realistic replacement 
criterion for time extensions of LSL replacements. 
Under typical circumstances that most cities will face, 8,000 LSL replacements 
per year is a more reasonable and realistic goal. However, it is still very 
challenging to meet even under the most ideal conditions. Cities and towns with 
harsh winters, deeper service lines requiring trench boxes, or less contractor 
capacity would likely be able to meet the 8,000/year target if they also try to 
replace the private side of the line.
●
EPA should consider removing the requirement for utilities to replace the 
utility side of the service line within 45 days of a customer-side replacement.
This requirement undermines the Environmental Justice component of the work 
because wealthier customers can change their own line, report it to the water 
company, and then essentially "jump the line" to the front of the scheduled utility 
side replacements because the water company has a limited time to respond by 
changing the utility side. The scenario could arise where LSL replacements are 
planned in a poorer community first, and wealthier customers begin changing 
their lines. This introduces chaos into the LSL replacement project planning if 
water systems have to continually accommodate customers who just changed their 
side of the service line. 
Disturbances
Definitions
●
EPA defines the replacement of a water meter as a major disturbance 
activity requiring a filter to be provided to the consumer along with 
educational materials and flushing instructions. The EPA should consider 
defining only water meter replacements that connect to service lines made of 
lead or galvanized materials as major disturbances.
The portion of a service line that does not connect to a meter experiences much 
less of a disturbance/vibration. For example, in many locations throughout NJ, the 
water meter is inside the building and only connects to the customer side of the 
service line. Removal and replacing the meter only vibrates the customer side of 

the service line. If the customer side of the service line is not lead or galvanized, 
requiring replacement, and the meter is only connected to the customer side, 
consider reducing this scenario to a minor disturbance that does not include 
providing the customer with a water filter. Similarly, if the curb valve and exterior 
meter are separated from each other by the length of the pipe, then the meter 
replacement would only vibrate the customer side and the short pipe between the 
meter and the curb valve. The utility side beyond the curb valve would not be 
affected. If the only portion of the lead service line is the utility side upstream of 
the curb valve, consider reducing this scenario to a minor disturbance that does 
not include providing the customer with a water filter.
Water Quality and Sampling
●
EPA should specify that electronic notification be provided within three 
business days, not calendar days.
The logistics of reporting a result to a customer by postmarked letter within three 
calendar days will be very challenging within water systems, particularly smaller 
systems with less full-time staff. If the person who handles this procedure goes on 
vacation, the notification will be delayed. If the water system receives the results 
on a Thursday or Friday during a busy time, the notification timing will extend 
beyond three days, especially if post offices are closed for weekend days and/or 
holidays. As an unintended consequence of this three-day requirement, water 
systems will instruct their outside laboratories to only report their results on 
Mondays and Tuesdays. If using an in-house laboratory, the analyses of water 
samples for lead will only be conducted on Mondays and Tuesdays. Both of these 
scenarios will extend the time that samples are analyzed after collection and/or the 
time that the results are reported to the water system staff.
As a replacement for the three-day notification requirement, the EPA should 
consider reducing the hold time between sample collection and sample 
submission to the laboratory and/or sample analysis to provide more timely 
results to consumers. Currently, samples collected from customer taps can be 
held for weeks or months before being delivered to the laboratory in a batch.
Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT)
Sodium Silicate
●
EPA should prohibit the use of sodium silicate as a corrosion control 
treatment option for the control of lead.  
●
Lack of Evidence: No evidence has demonstrated that silicates form insoluble (or 
low solubility) phases with lead to immobilize lead into protective pipe scales. 

The likely benefit of silicates is the resulting boost in pH, which promotes the 
formation of lead carbonate scales or a dense silica scale to form a barrier against 
lead release.
●
Newark, NJ: CDM Smith’s 2019 study for Newark, New Jersey, found a silica 
crust (SiO2) on all three lead service lines examined from a portion of the system 
that had utilized sodium silicate (varying dose range of 8 – 15 mg/L) as its CCT 
for many years (since the mid-1990s). The silica crust was relatively porous and 
did not act as an effective barrier against the outward flux of lead released from 
the pipe as the passivating lead layers (mainly plattnerite and hydrocerussite) 
were found behind the silica crust.
●
Alkalinity: Because silicates are highly alkaline, the primary corrosion protection 
offered by silicates is believed to be the increase in pH that comes from adding 
the chemical, particularly in low alkalinity waters. When pH was controlled for as 
a variable in studies that evaluated sodium silicate as a corrosion inhibitor, most 
studies showed no benefit for sodium silicate beyond its increase in pH (Li, 
Trueman, Dore, & Gagnon, 2021). One exception was a recent study with pipes 
that had an appreciable aluminum-rich layer of the pipe scale overlying lead-rich 
layers. The action of the silicate in that study may have been to make the 
aluminum-rich layer a better barrier and still did not involve any direct interaction 
of the silicate with the lead materials in the pipe or its scale (Mishrra, Wang, 
Sidorkiewicz, & Giammar, 2021). Increased pH is beneficial as it promotes the 
formation of low-solubility lead carbonate mineral phases, as discussed above. 
However, increasing pH using standard chemicals such as lime or sodium 
hydroxide would be more economical. 
●
EPA should consider the findings of the recent studies below to re-evaluate 
the use of sodium silicate as a corrosion control treatment option for lead 
control.  
○
Mishrra et al. (Water Res. 2021) tried to isolate the effect of silicate 
from pH increase in a pipe loop study. Sodium silicate was added to the 
water, and then acid was immediately added to adjust pH to 7.7, the level 
before the sodium silicate addition. Silicate mass balance and scale 
analysis were conducted, and the data showed a reduction in concentration 
for both dissolved and total lead. The authors speculated that the reduced 
lead release may be caused by silicate reacting with lead or aluminum to 
form an amorphous compound or precipitating as amorphous silica within 
the scale layer. Further studies would be needed to confirm these findings. 
If some benefits of silicate were to be confirmed, it would have limited 
applicability as it would be unrealistic in actual water treatment practice to 
lower pH after silicate application.                                                                                         

○
Li et al. (Environ. Sci. Technol. 2021) critically reviewed the data from 
11 peer-reviewed studies on silicate-based corrosion inhibitors, including 
the Mishrra et al., 2021 research mentioned above. The review concluded 
that pH increase resulting from silicate addition appears to be the primary 
mechanism of controlling lead release. Based on current understanding, 
silicate is not an effective corrosion control inhibitor for lead. Including 
the LCRI as an acceptable CCT technology will only lead to continued 
confusion and misunderstanding by water utilities and some consultants. 
Compliance Dates and Timelines 
Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR)
●
EPA should clarify the compliance timelines for the LCRR.                                           
If the final LCRI is delayed beyond October 16, 2024, water systems will need 
time for implementation, including the preparation of the Lead Service Line 
Replacement Program Plan. EPA should consider extending the compliance 
deadline for the LCRR if there is a delay.
●
EPA should restate, in a separate Federal Register action, the delay of 
milestones described in the proposed LCRI.
Schools and Childcare Centers
Lead Action Level
●
EPA should strengthen the requirements for schools and childcare centers, 
including lowering the lead action level to 5 ppb.
EPA should further reduce the action level for lead in drinking water for schools 
and childcare facilities to 5 ppb. The current action level of 15 ppb and 
subsequent proposal for 10 ppb set by the federal LCR and proposed by the LCRI 
is not a health-based standard but rather a technology treatment measure that 
gauges the effectiveness of corrosion control treatment, which minimizes lead 
leaching. Since exposure to small amounts of lead can seriously impact children’s 
health and cognitive development, and current science cannot identify a safe level 
of exposure, lead concentrations in drinking water at schools and childcare 
facilities should be kept as low as reasonably achievable.
Sampling
●
EPA should encourage schools and childcare facilities to do voluntary 
sampling immediately. Children are most vulnerable to lead health effects, so 
timely water sampling and remediation are important. There are many great free 
or reduced-cost water sampling and remediation programs available to schools 
and childcare facilities through voluntary programs, such as those funded by 
EPA’s Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act grant program. 

Starting in 2025, the EPA should require water systems to notify schools and 
childcare facilities of voluntary water sampling programs available to them. To do 
so, the EPA should also require water systems to develop a list of schools and 
childcare facilities served by them with available contact information by October 
16, 2024.
●
EPA should include registered and/or listed childcare facilities in the 
childcare facility sampling requirements.
States regulate childcare facilities in different ways using different nomenclature. 
By only including “licensed” childcare facilities, many childcare facilities are left 
off future sampling lists. No childcare facility should be skipped because it is 
registered instead of licensed, such as church-based childcare facilities in the State 
of Virginia, where the licensing status has to do with curriculum oversight, not 
health oversight. 
Filters
●
EPA should strengthen the filter provisions for schools and childcare 
facilities.
There is no safe level of lead exposure. Though lead exposure poses a risk to 
people of all ages, children are most vulnerable. Even in small doses, infants, 
toddlers, and pre-schoolers up to age six are particularly susceptible, as their 
growing bodies absorb lead much faster than adults. For children, prolonged 
exposure can cause irreversible damage to the brain and nervous system, slowing 
growth and development and prompting behavioral, hearing, and speech 
problems. And the long-term damage is not just physical. Lead exposure can also 
trigger severe learning disabilities, as well as emotional and social health impacts. 
EPA should mandate point-of-use filters to reduce lead and particulate at all 
fixtures intended to supply water for drinking, food preparation, or baby formula 
in schools and childcare facilities.
Deandrah Cameron, MPH
Policy Manager, New Jersey Future

Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 (Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, LCRI) 
 
The East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) appreciates the opportunity to comment on 
the above referenced proposal. EBMUD provides water service to 1.4 million residents of the 
eastern part of the San Francisco Bay Area. Our service area covers 332 square miles and 
includes 20 cities and 15 unincorporated areas in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. 
 
Overall, we agree with these regulatory changes and believe they will result in significant public 
health improvements in many parts of the country. Removal of lead service lines, regardless of 
tap sample results, is undoubtedly beneficial and will result in lower exposure to lead for 
consumers. EBMUD removed its lead service lines years ago for this reason. In addition, we 
agree that good operational practices such as informing customers, providing filters during 
disturbance of lead materials, and offering free lead testing, should be required. Such practices, 
which are already implemented at EBMUD, have been demonstrated to reduce consumers’ 
exposure to lead.  
 
However, where lead service lines were removed long ago, one aspect of the new regulations is 
not likely to improve public health and will result in unnecessary expenditures, confusion, and 
distrust of water utilities. The treatment of certain galvanized customer-owned service lines 
(galvanized requiring replacement or GRRs) as equally harmful as lead service lines, with no 
exceptions and in perpetuity, is unwarranted. The LCRI would require complete replacement of 
all GRRs within 10 years, regardless of tap sample results and regardless of how long ago the 
lead service line was removed. EBMUD does not own or have access to customer-side service 
lines, nor do we have legal authority to pay for private plumbing replacement. 
 
Classification of a service line as a GRR has no “sunset”. Even if the public-side lead was 
removed decades ago, and water samples indicate no significant lead release at present, EPA still 
considers the GRR to be a source of lead. In the LCRI preamble EPA states “While one 
stakeholder recommended that galvanized lines that were downstream of an LSL should be 
classified as non-lead after a period of time, stating that these lines eventually stop being a lead 
source, EPA disagrees with this stakeholder because the scientific literature does not support a 
timeline for these GRR service lines to cease contributing lead into drinking water.” 
 

February 2, 2024 
Page 2 
 
 
In the LCRI preamble, EPA cites several published studies documenting elevated lead in 
drinking water resulting from GRRs1,2,3,4. Each of these papers contains a discussion regarding 
possible mechanisms that may have occurred. Most of the case studies cited use orthophosphate 
for corrosion control. Each paper includes language describing how this lead accumulation-and-
release phenomenon is highly variable and water system specific. It does not occur in all cases.  
 
Indeed, EBMUD is conducting a pre-compliance study to better understand the implications of 
the LCRR and LCRI. We estimate that there are about 4,000 customers currently served by 
galvanized lines that were formerly downstream of LSLs (GRRs) in our system. We are using 
the 1st and 5th liter sampling protocol described in the rule proposal, although we are analyzing 
all five one-liter samples. Of the 39 GRR data sets analyzed to date (195 individual samples), 
none has exceeded the detection limit for reporting (DLR) of 5 ppb, and the ninetieth percentile 
(P90) for both the 1st liter set and the 5th liter set is less than 1 ppb (0.40 ppb and 0.22 ppb, 
respectively). For comparison, since 2017, EBMUD has had a program in which any customer 
can have their water tested for lead for free. Upon request, customers are mailed a kit with a 1-L 
bottle, instructions for stagnation and first-draw sampling, and a return mailing address with pre-
paid postage. The service line materials for this pool of results are not tracked. However, since 
94% of EBMUD service lines are copper and 3% are plastic, it is likely that these results are 
from non-lead services. Of the 1,743 samples analyzed to date, the P90 is less than 1 ppb, 
indistinguishable from the GRR samples. Our ongoing study also includes sequential samples 
from galvanized service with lead connectors (pigtails), and analysis of the scale inside extracted 
galvanized service lines, both with and without exposure to upstream lead. We expect the work 
to be completed by mid-2024. 
 
A recent Water Research Foundation study by Edwards et al (2022)5 called Evaluating Key 
Factors that Affect Lead Accumulation and Release of Lead from Galvanized Pipes, was not 
among the references included in the LCRI publication. This study was the basis for an article 
published in the AWWA Water Science in 20236. The authors suggest a decision tree whereby 
utilities can classify their galvanized iron pipes (GIP) as “low risk” or “high risk” of lead release 
based on various factors. The AWS paper includes several case studies and states “A summary of 
case studies reveals that some systems may have no GIP corrosion problems while other systems 
can be classified as having either short- or long-term problems”.

The WRF report details how metal co-occurrence is a way to distinguish sources of lead in 
drinking water. For example, the presence of trace cadmium in water can indicate that galvanized 
pipe is the source of lead because the galvanized coating often uniquely contains a small amount 
of cadmium in addition to zinc and lead. Lead‐tin solder was commonly used to join copper 
pipes and fittings up until 1986. Therefore, the presence of tin in water often indicates that 
corrosion of lead‐tin solder is occurring. The lead from lead pipe can sometimes be distinguished 
by higher levels of lead without co‐occurring cadmium, tin, copper, or zinc. Particulate lead (Pb) 
in galvanized pipes is important: “Profile sampling results at multiple sites reinforced the 
contribution of particulate Pb release to overall Pb in drinking water. The vast majority (92‐
100%) of the Pb in water was particulate, indicating that Pb in scale can be a significant 
contributor to Pb risk. Also, not surprisingly, higher amounts of Pb were detected at elevated 
flow rate, further signifying the importance of particulate Pb release, as the scale can be 
increasingly scoured from pipe walls at higher flow”.  
 
Under the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), GRRs must be identified, included in the 
inventory, and included in the sample pool for compliance monitoring. This makes sense given 
the potential for lead release from these pipes. The LCRI goes much farther and requires their 
removal regardless of any demonstrated lead release. In cases where the water system does not 
have control over the GRRs (e.g., customer-side services in California), the LCRI requires the 
water system to request permission of the property owner to conduct the replacements. 
Permission must be requested annually, numerous times, using more than one communication 
method, and very specific language must be included about the adverse health effects of lead.  
 
Undoubtedly, when a lead service line is replaced, if it is connected to a galvanized line, that 
galvanized line should be replaced at the same time. However, if the lead service line was 
removed years ago, removal of the galvanized line may or may not be warranted today. Without 
the authority to pay, EBMUD will need to request access/consent for replacement but will 
inform these customers they will need to pay for the replacement. Continued, persistent customer 
notification using alarming language about the health effects of lead, with no corresponding lead 
in their water, is likely to undermine confidence in the safety of the water for no reason. After a 
few rounds of such false alarms, customers may disregard future notifications, even those with 
legitimate warnings about the safety of the water. Excessive and unjustified warnings could also 
cause actual psychological harm, or cause consumers to spend thousands of dollars on home 
filtration systems to deal with an insignificant health risk7.  
 
In contrast to EPA’s statement in the preamble, there is more than “one stakeholder” impacted by 
this never-ending GRR requirement. As EPA noted, many water agencies have already removed 
most or all of their lead service lines. The cities of Tucson and Spokane were listed as examples 
in the preamble; EBMUD and the city of San Francisco can be included in this list; collectively

removing more than 17,000 LSLs decades ago. Presumably many of these early LSL removal 
efforts inadvertently created GRRs. The cost for replacement of GRRs is in the tens of millions 
for EBMUD alone (approximately 4,000 GRRs at $5,000 to $10,000 each). 
 
Water utilities should determine whether their site-specific conditions create this phenomenon. 
As Edwards et. al noted: “This research provides methods for utilities to identify and classify 
their unique scenario using profile sampling, scale analysis, lead isotope ratios, and element co‐
occurrence within water samples and pipe scale.” The decision tree in the WRF report and the 
AWS paper rightfully makes a distinction between “Low Pb Risk” public education and “High Pb 
Risk” public education.  
 
The LCRI should include a regulatory mechanism to allow water utilities with older GRRs to 
conduct a study to determine if their GRRs are a source of lead today. Such studies could include 
a review of historical corrosion control treatment, sequential tap sampling, measurement of co-
occurring metals, measurement of particulate vs. dissolved lead, analysis of scale in excavated 
pipes, or other tools that may become available. If the conclusion of the study is that the 
galvanized pipes are not a source of lead, then the water system should be permitted to cease 
notifying their GRR customers and recommending replacement. 
 
Two additional issue requires comment: First, EPA is proposing to require all consumer notices 
of lead tap sampling results to be delivered within three calendar days after the system learns of 
the results, regardless of whether the results exceed the lead action level. EBMUD’s laboratory, 
and many others, batch the samples and run them once per week for maximum efficiency. The 
batch is often run late in the week. If an individual result is high, the laboratory technician makes 
a phone call to the program manager for follow-up, and the program manager contacts the 
consumer as soon as possible. Batches of samples are often not complete and confirmed until late 
in the day on Friday and therefore special measures (e.g., overtime, supervisor notification, 
outlier reports) are needed to notify customers quickly. Such special measures are warranted in 
the case of high results since there is a potential risk to the consumer. However, for low results, 
such measures are not justified. The three calendar day notification requirement cannot be met 
over holiday weekends without special measures, it is overly burdensome without any public 
health benefit. A more reasonable timeframe such as two weeks should be required for results 
below the Action Level. 
 
And lastly, we recommend that EPA expand the window allowable for waivers from the school 
sampling requirements. Section 141.92 (h) “Alternative school and child care lead sampling 
programs” paragraph 5 says that states may issue waivers only when schools were sampled 
between January 1, 2021 and the compliance date of the LCRI. There is no technical basis for a 
2021 cutoff date for school sampling. EBMUD and most other water system in California 
conducted sampling for all schools in our service area during 2018-2019 using the 3Ts protocol 
and specific instructions provided by our state regulatory agency. Individual school site plans 
were developed, over 7,000 samples were collected and transmitted to the schools, numerous 
endpoint devices were mitigated, and follow-up samples were collected. There have been no 
changes in analytical methods or plumbing codes regarding lead materials since 2018, and 

February 2, 2024

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1860 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 7, 2024 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 
EPA Docket Center 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Mail Code 28221T 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20460 
Re: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
Dear Administer Regen, 
I appreciate the opportunity to comment on the lead portion of the National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-
0801. The medical community has stated in various publications that there is no useful purpose for 
lead in the human body, i.e., the body does not need it to function. The contribution of lead from 
drinking water to the total body burden needs to be controlled since it one of the routes of entry 
into the body. The most vulnerable group with the greatest health risk from all sources of lead are 
infants, children, and women of child bearing age (WOCBA). This most vulnerable population 
deserves a health-based protection level from the contributions caused by drinking water to their 
total lead body burden. We, as a society, owe it to current and future generations to not continue 
condemning them to the known lifetime ill effects lead can produce and by controlling this one 
source of lead, we can achieve a level of protection for those at greatest risk. 
The following comments are provided for consideration to further improve the LCR.  
A. Mandating Replacement of Lead and Galvanized Service Lines. The mandate to replace lead 
and some galvanized service lines over a specified timeframe places a financial burden upon 
all water systems (WSs) across the country may not achieve the intended outcome in all 
instances, and may not be fully supported by data based upon Flint Michigan’s Sentinel 
Monitoring and Flint CLEAR monitoring programs [CLEAR (Confirming Lead Elimination 
After Replacement) Program is a study to obtain data over a period of time to help determine 
what impact service line replacement has on lead levels in the home.]. Link: Flint Water - Test 
Results (michigan.gov). Currently there are WSs with lead and galvanized pipe in use in their 
distribution system but the water transiting those waterlines is hopefully not corrosive and may 
contain chemicals that coat the pipe putting a barrier between the lead and the water. This 
barrier protects those consumers with copper water lines where lead solder was used. Why 
require WSs to replace waterlines if the WS can provide verifiable data that the consumer is 
drinking water at the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) maximum level for lead in bottled 
water of 5 parts per billion (ppb) [micrograms/ liter (µgm/L)] or less? Before placing this 
economic burden upon all WSs, which in turn places an economic burden upon the WS 
customers by way of rate increases and tax payers across the country as funds are released at 
the federal level, a revision to the requirement should be made to enable WSs to analyze their 
data, with competent regulatory oversight, and then prioritize identified replacement needs. 
This would allow WSs to address the needs of the most vulnerable: infants, children, and 
WOCBA. 
B. Reviewing the timelines and the cost to implement the changes in the regulation, it is critical 
that the most important protective measure to take is to continue to limit chemical changes in 
a systems water chemistry that increases the corrosivity. When chemistry changes occur that 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
2 | P a g e  
 
prompt any coating on the inside of the pipes to slough off and expose lead in the pipes or 
solder, then increases in lead will occur. Flint Michigan appears to not have had a problem 
until the water chemistry was changed causing the lead to leach from all lead sources. 
Replacing lead service lines and certain galvanized service lines is a costly process that will 
reduce the potential for lead exposure to those at greatest risk. However, after reviewing many 
rounds of sampling data from Flint MI, it may not be the sole answer to correcting the problem 
and may provide a false sense of security to the consumers. On Nov 17,2016, a copper service 
line had a lead concentration of 5986 ppb (sample FS 9063) which appears to be the highest 
recorded reading collected during the Sentinel Sampling program. Thus, the push to replace 
all the lead pipes may not protect those with copper service lines unless corrosion inhibitors 
are added to coat the pipes. When the system was providing bottled water to its consumers, it 
was providing water that by FDA regulation shall not contain more than 5 parts per billion 
(ppb) [micrograms/ liter (µgm/L)]. When the consumer began drinking water from the system 
again with the system in compliance with the 90th percentile action level of 15 ppb, then that 
consumer may have been drinking water at or above 15 ppb since there is no maximum lead 
level that can come from a consumer’s faucet. 
C. Deleting the trigger level and changing the action level to 10 parts per billion (ppb) is definitely 
a positive action in protecting those at greatest risk: infants, children, and women of child 
bearing age (WOCBA). However, further clarification on the term “action level” is needed to 
convey to all that it is not a Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) and is not a cutoff level 
between safe and not safe to drink. Over the years the term action level has become 
misinterpreted, misunderstood, and misused. One reason for this misunderstanding could be 
that the Occupational Safety and Health Administration, the Food and Drug Administration 
(FDA) and other health agencies provide the term and numerical value using a health-based 
determination and one could easily assume that when the EPA uses the action level term for 
lead it is also health- based. A very important action the EPA can undertake is to revise the 
LCR definitions to clearly identify that “15 (10) ppb is only a level that water systems need to 
begin to take specified actions to reduce the risk to their consumers and not a level between 
drink and not to drink. This clarification will hopefully reverse the trend of water system 
officials, government officials, and private entities interpretating it as a quasi MCL, and in 
some cases, stating it is an MCL. This could be accomplished by incorporating the words 
“treatment technique” in the definition and discussion in the applicable LCR and CCR 
sections. The Treatment Technique Action Level definition should specifically state that it is 
only a “treatment technique action level (TTAL) and should not be considered or referenced as 
an MCL. With the clarification must come enforcement requirements with violations attached. 
When entities do not have to be held accountable for misrepresentation, there is no reason to 
achieve accuracy. Failing to make and enforce changes will only continue to perpetuate the 
concept that the proposed 10 ppb is the new quasi MCL and allow misinformation to be spread 
potentially harming the consumer who believes what is written such as a treatment technique 
action level is an MCL. [See the ACTION LEVEL MISINTERPRETATION, 
MISUNDERSTANDING, AND MISUSE section later for examples verifying the 
misunderstanding and demonstrating the need for specific clarification and renaming the action 
level term. 
D. The League of Women Voters - Corpus Christi Area conducted a study (“Potential for Lead 
Contamination in Our Communities’ Drinking Water”) from 2016 – 2021 and developed a 
position statement to establish a health-based, early intervention, “Further Evaluation Level 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
3 | P a g e  
 
(FEL)” at 5 ppb for lead. The EPA could adapt this concept into the actions that WSs take 
once their sampling results are received. The FEL allows for early intervention into causation 
of a level above the FDA limit of 5 ppb and would be an excellent public health proactive 
measure. Developing a FEL at 5 ppb in which a LCR regulated water system informs the 
sampled consumer that their result was greater than 5 ppb which is the established maximum 
allowable FDA level for lead in bottled water and not reference the treatment technique action 
level of 15 ppb. The regulated water system would assist the consumer in evaluating the cause 
of the level above 5 ppb such as doing a repeat sample to verify the initial result. This would 
not create an undo economic burden on a regulated water system in that the system could assist 
with any additional resampling and determining if the system or the consumers system was the 
cause for the elevation above 5 ppb. This would allow the consumer to evaluate their lead 
reduction options based upon their perceived risk. For example, if the customer was a WOCBA 
with/without infants or children regularly consuming the tap water from the kitchen faucet and 
ice from the refrigerator ice maker, they may take immediate actions such as flushing, using 
Point of Use (POU) filters on the faucet and ice maker to immediately begin reducing their 
health risk while trying to determine if their service line and internal plumbing was 
contributing the levels above 5 ppb. 
E. Suggest modifying the wording in the education portion of the LCRs (141.85(a)(1)(i), 
“IMPORTANT INFORMATION ABOUT LEAD IN YOUR DRINKING WATER. [INSERT 
NAME OF WATER SYSTEM] found elevated levels of lead ….” The use of the words 
“elevated levels” is definitely open for interpretation. Suggest modifying to read “…found lead 
levels above 5 parts per billion (ppb) which is the FDA maximum limit for lead in bottled 
water, in the drinking water in some homes/buildings.…” If the 15 (10) ppb treatment 
technique action level value is included, an explanation that it is not a health-based level, but 
it is just a level in which specific actions are required by the water system. As required in the 
notification section 40 CFR 141.85(d) each sampled consumer wants to know what is coming 
from their faucet to help them make informed decisions about their health. It could be assumed 
that no one wants to be in that 10% category that may be above the current 15 ppb action level 
and know that the water system has no further responsibility. 
F. Suggest modifying CFR 141.85(b) Delivery of public education materials. Today, most water 
systems are not required to disseminate a paper copy of the Consumer Confidence Report 
which would provide such lead required information. Modifying to allow for distribution via 
social media and/or posting on the system’s internet site would afford consumers the needed 
information electronically for faster distribution. For example, the City of Plano Texas, on their 
internet site provides visual lead sampling result information. Link: Drinking Water Quality 
Information | Plano, TX - Official Website. Regarding the information provided in Consumer 
Confidence Reports, a violation with penalties needs to b established when WSs do not provide 
verifiably correct information regarding lead and other chemical constituents. Currently no WS 
is held accountable when verifiably incorrect is provided on lead to the consumers. 
G. Reference 40 CFR 141.86(86(b)(2) “First draw samples from residential housing must be 
collected from the cold-water kitchen or bathroom sink tap. First draw samples from a 
nonresidential building must be one liter in volume and collected at a tap from which water is 
typically drawn for consumption.” The use of bathrooms/restrooms as sampling points should 
be deleted because from a total body burden perspective, very few infants, children and 
WOCBA or others daily/regularly/typically consume water from these faucets Kitchen and 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
4 | P a g e  
 
cafeteria faucets and drinking fountains are typical drinking water locations. Allowing 
bathroom faucets may statistically be relevant but it is not a major source for consumption. For 
example, Naval Air Station Corpus Christi (NASCC) (ID # TX1780017) in 2013 sampled 
about 50% residential structure faucets but by December 2019, only about 15% of LCR 
samples came from residential structures. The LCR sample locations had shifted to faucets in 
industrial/administrative type facilities. From 2013 through 2019, 73 of 200 (36.5%) LCR 
samples collected were from Men’s restrooms and in June 2014, 45% of all the LCR samples 
were from Men’s restrooms. During this same 2013 – 2019 period, only four of 200 (2.0%) 
LCR samples came from Women’s restrooms. This strong bias toward Men’s restroom faucets 
brings into question if NASCC station officials understand who is the group at greatest risk: 
infants, children, and WOCBA. It appears that NASCC was striving for “compliance with the 
letter” of the regulation and missed “the intent of protecting” those at greatest risk, their 
infants, children and WOCBA. 
H. The sampling allowance for schools and child care facilities of 20 percent per year, should be 
modified and accelerated to identify those location where our children are at greater risk. By 
allowing a water system to perform its sample collection in compliance with the LCRs to 
sample mainly just schools and child care facilities in one of their early compliance sampling 
rounds. We need to initially focus on protecting those at greatest risk as soon as possible to 
reduce this potential source of total lead body burden. Priority should be included in the LCRs 
that collection from child care facilities and elementary schools are the first priority followed 
by middle and then high schools. Without setting priorities, a child entering school 
kindergarten could be consuming water with levels above the EPA’s 3Ts (Training, Testing, 
and Taking Action) for reducing lead in drinking water in schools’ level of 5 ppb for four years 
before their school was tested and a possible elevated level identified.

8. U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Interim Reference Level (IRL) for lead. The 
FDA assesses whether the amount of lead in a food product is high enough to raise a 
person’s blood lead level to a point of concern. To do this, the agency calculated a 
maximum daily intake for lead from food, called the Interim Reference Level (IRL). In 
determining the IRL, the FDA takes into account the amount of a particular food a person 
would need to consume daily, as well as other factors, that would result in blood lead levels 
of 5 ug/dL, the level at which the CDC recommends clinical monitoring of lead exposure 
in children. In 2018, the FDA calculated an IRL at 3 µg per day for children and 12.5 µg 
per day for adults. These levels allow for differences across human populations and are set 
nearly ten-times less than the actual amount of lead intake from food that would be required 
to reach the CDC’s blood reference level. The adult level is particularly important for 
women of childbearing age, to protect against possible fetal exposure in women who are 
unaware that they are pregnant, and against infant exposure during nursing. The FDA will 
continue to research and evaluate the health effects and dietary exposure to lead and will 
update the IRL as appropriate. In 2021, the CDC updated its BLRV to 3.5 μg/dL. To align 
with the CDC's updated BLRV, the FDA is updating its interim reference levels (IRLs) for 
lead from food to 2.2 μg/day for children and 8.8 μg/day for females of childbearing age. 
Citation: “Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology Volume 133, August 2022, 105202, 
Brenna M. Flannery , Karlyn B. Middleton, Copyright © 2024 Elsevier Inc.” 
9. 2018 Edition of the Drinking Water Standards and Health Advisories, EPA 822-F-
18-001, Office of Water, U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, March 2018. Lead is 
listed as “B.2 Probable human carcinogen; indicates sufficient evidence in animals and 
inadequate or no evidence in humans.” 
BASIS FOR COMMENTS 
The following provide verifiable examples that were used to develop the some of the comments. 
I. ACTION LEVEL MISINTERPRETATION, MISUNDERSTANDING, AND MISUSE 
A. Action Level Misinterpretation, Misunderstanding, And Misuse. The trigger action level 
term only added to the existing confusion surrounding the “action level” term. Deleting the 
trigger level term and reducing the action level for lead to 10 parts per billion (ppb) is better 
than the 15 ppb level. The term “Action Level” needs further clarification in the standard 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
6 | P a g e  
 
to reverse the existing misunderstanding outside of the regulatory community of the term 
“Action Level.” Nowhere in the definition of this term are the words “safe to drink” used. 
The term provides a way for Water Systems (WSs) to limit their cost by meeting specific 
requirements mandated by the LCR regulations. The LCR is mandated by the Safe 
Drinking Water Act but nowhere in the LCR is a concentration linked with the words “safe 
to drink”. The only concentrations used are those that are economic for the WS when the 
Action Level or waiver level at the 90th percentile is not exceeded.  
B. The use of just the term action level at the 90th percentile contaminant level concentration 
of 15 µg/l, aka ppb, has created over the years a misperception among consumers, water 
department personnel, some health department personnel, and even some government 
officials that there is no health risk, read as “SAFE”, to consuming water at 15 ppb. In the 
Consumer Confidence Reports required by the Safe Drinking Water Act, in the Lead and 
Copper Table the table column heading reads: Number of samples over the Action Level of 
15 ppb. Medical journals, media, governmental entities and others in discussing lead, 
reference their data/statements to the EPA federal standard for lead in drinking water of 15 
ppb – implying a health-based standard [de facto MCL]. Over the years the “Action Level” 
of 15 ppb appears to have become a de facto MCL. As referenced in the California Public 
Health Goal documentation, April 2009. Page 26: “Therefore, for all practical purposes 
the standard described in the lead and copper rule is equivalent to an MCL.” Clarification 
of this term must be provided with enforcement and violations attached. The Action Level 
definition must specifically state that it is not health-based and is only a “treatment 
technique action level (TTAL).” The misconception that 15 ppb (changed to 10 ppb under 
these revisions) is “safe” for consumers must not be allowed to continue to be perpetuated 
especially as it pertains to infants, children, and WOCBA. To quote from an EPA internet 
page “Background: Lead in Drinking Water and the LCR: No safe level of lead exposure 
has been identified, and it is especially harmful to children and pregnant women.” 
Link: Proposed Revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule | Ground Water and Drinking Water 
| US EPA  
C. Regulators and experienced environmental professionals hopefully are aware that there is 
no regulatory established Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) for lead but that there is 
a Maximum Contaminant Level Goal (MCLG) of 0. Reference: 40 CFR 141.141. Yet, 
commercial entities advertise the action level of 15 ppb as an MCL. WSs use the 15 ppb 
Action Level as comparisons with an individual customer’s specific faucet results. In Flint 
Michigan, monitoring results posted in the 2017 CLEAR Sampling data tables show the 
background color as red when a result is 16 ppb and above while no background color is 
used for 15 ppb and below. The following are instances where the action level of 15 ppb at 
the 90th percentile level has become a implied/perceived “safe level” to drink and that WSs 
appear to have misconceptions about 15 ppb and the impact upon their customers 
understanding about lead in drinking water. 
1) The City of Flint internet site (as of Feb 4, 2024) provides the following graph in which 
Flint marks its 7th year in compliance with lead standards. Cite: Flint marks 7th year of 
compliance with lead standards - City of Flint. Note that the term “LEVELS ABOVE 
15 PPB REQUIRE ACTION PER FEDERAL STANDARDS” implies to the residents 
that the water is at a safe to drink level. There were 11 of the 15 sampling events in 
which the 90th percentile was above the FDA bottled water 5 ppb maximum level. 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
7 | P a g e  
 
When the residents were drinking bottled water supplied by the city, they were at less 
risk than they may be being supplied water from the current water distribution system. 
 
 
2) Pace Analytical internet site. On their “Lead & Copper in Water” page, in “The Lead 
and Copper Rule” tab, the following statement is made: “In 1991, the EPA issued the 
Lead and Copper Rule, which requires public water systems to control water 
corrosivity and to monitor for lead and copper levels in their distribution systems. The 
EPA has set Maximum Contaminant Levels (MCLs) of 1.3 ppm (parts per million) for 
copper and 15 ppb (parts per billion) for lead in drinking water.” This is clearly an 
incorrect statement since there is no MCL just a treatment technique action level. 
However, unless a WS customer is knowledgeable of its inaccuracy, a WS customer 
will probably accept this as a correct statement and perpetuate it in their discussions 
with their consumers. Link: Lead & Copper In Water- Pace Analytical (pacelabs.com) 
3) San Antonio Water System (SAWS) (ID # TX0150018) Internet site. On the SAWS 
Water Quality FAQs page, SAWS responds to the question: Should I be concerned with 
lead in the water? The answer provided was: “In an effort to reduce lead and copper 
levels in public drinking water supplies, the lead and copper rule was adopted by EPA 
on May 7, 1991. If sample monitoring indicates that lead exceeds 15 parts per billion 
(0.015 PPM) in 10 percent or more of the samples taken, then the water system must 
take a prescribed action to minimize lead contamination. Lead is not used in SAWS 
production facilities or distribution system. There is a concentration of 0.0015 PPM 
found in the water or one-tenth of the amount necessary before prescribed action is 
required.  *PPM – parts per million” The SAWS answer causes confusion in it last 
sentence to the reader on the significance of actions to be done if 15 ppb (1/10 th of the 
amount necessary?). This implies that 150 ppb is the necessary amount to get to 15 
ppb. They use the word action and not actions, which indicates that there is only one 
action to take. This is probably a typographical error, at least one would hope so, but 
indicates a lack of knowledge about the health risk of lead and a lack of quality control 
in the releasing of information to the public about the lead drinking water standard. 
Finally, SAWS never addresses the question regarding “should a customer be 
concerned about lead in the water?” From a consumer point of view, the consumer 
wants to know about what is coming from their faucet and not what is in the entire 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements

system that serves more than 724,000 residential connections. Link: Water Quality 
FAQs - San Antonio Water System (saws.org) 
4) In a May 19, 2021, letter from the Corpus Christi Water Utilities Department (ID # 
TX1780003) to one of its consumers who participated in a special lead in water testing 
program, in the Your Results section, the letter stated “Lead results in parts per billion 
(ppb): 1.4.” In the “What Does This Mean?” section, the statement was: “The level of 
lead in your tap water sample was under the federal and state action level of 15 ppb.” 
This response implies that the department is (mistakenly) attempting to establish the 
Action Level as a Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) at 15 ppb in the mind of the 
consumer. A consumer is not interested in the regulations governing the actions a WS 
is obligated when an action level exceedance occurs under the Lead and Copper Rule 
(LCR). Simply put, the citizen consumer sits outside the perimeters of the LCR. The 
ordinary citizen is not equipped to understand the regulatory obligation of a water 
system’s distribution system, which in turn has no remedial obligation to the citizen’s 
household system. A consumer is only interested in what is coming out of their faucet 
and not what actions a water system must take when the 90th percentile concentration 
exceeds 15 ppb. No one want to be in that 10th percentile group where a WS does not 
have to do any further action. In this case, the value was low but there was no 
documentation available for review from any customer who may have exceeded the 15 
ppb level to determine what the water department stated. 
5) U.S. Navy, OPNAV M-5090.1, Environmental Readiness Program Manual. 3 Sep 
2019, page 21-21, paragraph 21-5.1. Defines Action Level (AL) as “the concentration 
of lead or copper in water that is used to determine compliance with the lead and 
copper rule. Under the lead and copper rule, ALs have replaced lead and copper 
MCLs.” The U.S. Navy appears to use the Action Level of 15 ppb as a “safe level” for 
infants and children to drink. Naval Air Station Corpus Christi (NASCC) (ID # 
TX1780017) in an October 4, 2019, Commanding Officers letter (5900 Serial N00/265) 
to NASCC Parents and Staff, the commander informed them of the lead in priority 
areas water monitoring results. There were three monitored fixtures with 
concentrations of 16 ppb and one at 150 ppb. Those fixtures were immediately taken 
out of service. After those four fixtures were replaced and resampled, all fixtures at 15 
ppb (1) and lower (3) were returned to service per U.S. Navy guidance. Thus, it appears 
that the U.S. Navy uses the EPA Action Level of 15 ppb as a safe or not safe to drink 
level for infants and children. NOTE: One fixture that was taken out of service had a 
concentration of 16 ppb and after replacement the monitoring result was 15 ppb and 
placed back into service. A difference of one part per billion in lead between being out 
of service and being in service with a new fixture indicates that this Naval Station 
personnel believe water at 16 ppb is not safe and that water at 15 ppb is safe.
