II. ESTABLISHMENT OF A HEALTH-BASED “FURTHER EVALUATION LEVEL” AT 
5 PPB [MICROGRAMS / LITER (µgm/L)]. 
Establishment of a health-based, early intervention, “Further Evaluation Level (FEL)” at 5 ppb 
for lead. This FEL would allow an early intervention into the cause of a lead in water issue 
with the goal of preventing further consumption of water containing lead. Currently there is no 
maximum contaminant level (MCL), a health based developed concentration, for lead. The 
EPA’s 3T (Training, Testing, and Taking Action) program for Reducing Lead in Drinking 
Water in Schools and Child Care Facilities, [Revised Manual, Office of Water (4606M) EPA 
815-F-18-017 October 2018] uses 5 ppb as the concentration where a further evaluation for the 
cause of lead in the facilities water should be accomplished. Establishing this level to further 
evaluate will begin to afford protection to those 10% consumers who are not currently 
protected by the LCR requirements. This will also minimize the resource burden on the tens 
of thousands of water systems (WSs) across the United States who can demonstrate through 
their source and system monitoring that the water they deliver at their consumers 
drinking/cooking water faucets is below the proposed Treatment Technique Action Level of 10 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
10 | P a g e  
 
ppb. There is an extensive database available that indicates that over 90% of all WSs across 
the country have concentrations of 5 ppb or lower at the 90th percentile level and sometimes at 
the 95th percentile level (States of Arizonia and Missouri compute this value) for lead. The 
basis for this statement comes from data reported by the WSs Consumer Confidence Reports 
(CCRs) and in several instances verified by reviewing various state’s Drinking Water Watch 
(DWW) internet site. 
The establishment of a health-based 5 µgm/L (ppb) as a further evaluation level (FEL) would 
allow WSs to assist their customers in evaluating the source of any elevated level of lead and 
if the source was determined to be the service line, then the WS must include the replacement 
in their operations and maintenance activities. The WS should develop a prioritization ranking 
for replacement with waterlines servicing locations where infants, children and WOCBA reside 
being the top priority. The health-based FEL would be a level that demonstrates the EPA is 
concerned about the lead exposure consumers of a WSs water and would debunk the 
misconception that the proposed treatment technique action level of 10 ppb is “safe to drink.” 
The 5 ppb level currently exists in the LCR and other EPA documents. By establishing it as 
the FEL, it would then comport with other governmental agency lead levels that are health-
based. 
A. The City Corpus Christi Texas Water Utilities Department (ID # TX1780003) from 2005 
through 2020 took 413 LCR required water samples with only 23 sample concentrations 
with lead results > 5 ppb.  Five of 23 locations accounted for 14 of the 23 sample results 
>5 ppb. Site LCR038 had 5 of 6 results >5 ppb and the average concentration from 2005 – 
2017 was 7.4 ppb. If a Further Evaluation Level (FEL) at 5 ppb had been in place, early 
intervention may have prevented the average being 7.4 ppb and may have achieved a level 
below the FDA bottled water limit of 5 ppb. 
B. In 2008, Scottsdale Arizona (ID # AZ0407098) had lead concentrations of 93.7 ppb and 
55.1 ppb at two separate locations in their distribution system out of 50 locations sampled. 
These two results were respectively 18.7 and 11 times the FDA bottled water allowable 
lead level of 5 ppb. The 90th percentile contaminant level was below 15 ppb and thus, no 
further actions were required beyond eventually notifying the individual residences of the 
results. If a FEL had been instituted, those customers who have had assistance in 
determining the causation of such concentrations. 
C. The EPA established a 0.005 mg/L (5 ppb) level for systems at the 90th percentile for 
monitoring waivers for small systems. “Lead levels. To qualify for a full waiver, or a lead 
waiver, the system must demonstrate that the 90th percentile lead level does not exceed 
0.005 mg/L.” Reference: 40 CFR 141.86(g)(2)(i) 
D. The EPA established the 0.005 mg/L (5 ppb) level in reference to continued eligibility for 
waiver renewal: “A system with a full waiver or a lead waiver no longer satisfies the 
materials criteria of paragraph (g)(1)(i) of this section or has a 90th percentile lead level 
greater than 0.005 mg/L.” Reference: 40 CFR 141.86(g)(5)(i) 
E. The EPA established the Practical Quantitation Level, or PQL for lead at 0.005 mg/L (5 
ppb). Reference: 40 CFR 141.89(a)(1)(ii)(A). 
F. The EPA’s 3T (Training, Testing, and Taking Action) program for Reducing Lead in 
Drinking Water in Schools and Child Care Facilities, uses 5 ppb, as the concentration 

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
11 | P a g e  
 
where a further evaluation for the cause of lead in the facilities water should be 
accomplished. Reference: EPA 3T Revised Manual, Office of Water (4606M) EPA 815-
F-18-017 October 2018. 
G. When a WS is required by regulatory agencies or chooses to provide bottled water to its 
customers because of an issue with the water quality or with a distribution system 
disruption, the WS is providing water to those affected customers that can only have 5 ppb 
of lead per liter and not a 10 ppb Treatment Technique Action Level. 
H. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) established a health-based not to exceed 
level of lead in bottled water at 0.005 milligrams/liter (mg/L) [5 parts per billion (ppb)]. 
This level was established after “Having consulted with EPA as required by section 410 of 
the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, the Food and Drug Administration has 
determined that bottled water, when a composite of analytical units of equal volume from 
a sample is examined by the methods listed in paragraphs (b)(4)(iii)(E) through 
(b)(4)(iii)(F), and (b)(4)(iii)(G) of this section, shall not contain the following chemical 
contaminants in excess of the concentrations specified in paragraphs (b)(4)(iii)(A) through 
(b)(4)(iii)(D) of this section.” Reference: 21 CFR 165.110(b)(4) (iii). 
The FDA uses an “interim reference level (IRL)” in assessing whether the amount of lead 
in a food product, including bottled liquids, is high enough to raise a person’s blood lead 
level (BLL) to a level of concern. To do this, the FDA established a maximum daily intake 
for lead called the IRL. In determining the IRL, the FDA considers the amount a person 
needs to ingest daily, as well as other factors, that would result in the Centers for Disease 
Control and Prevention (CDC) 2012 established reference BLL of 5 micrograms/deciliter 
(µg/dl). This is the whole blood lead level at which the CDC recommends clinical 
monitoring of lead exposure in children. The FDA applied a safety factor of 10 to the CDC 
level in their evaluation process which indicated the BLL of concern the FDA used in its 
models would be 0.5 µg/dl. The FDA established the IRL at 3 µg per day for children and 
12.5 µg per day for women of child bearing age (WOCBA) which can also be used as the 
IRL for all adults. These levels were set to yield ten-times less than the amount of daily 
ingestion required to reach the CDC’s blood reference level. [U.S. Food and Drug 
Administration's interim reference levels for dietary lead exposure in children and women 
of childbearing age, Regulatory Toxicology and Pharmacology, Volume 111, March 2020, 
104579.] 
In April 2021 the U.S. FDA developed an initiative called “Closer to Zero: Action Plan for 
Baby Foods,” to identify actions the agency will take to reduce exposure to toxic elements 
from foods eaten by babies and young children—to as low as possible. The FDA prioritized 
babies and young children because their smaller body sizes and metabolism make them 
more vulnerable to the harmful effects of the contaminants to be considered, one being 
lead. In this process the FDA stated they will develop “Action Levels” in their regulations 
of the contaminants. The FDA stated “Action levels are a level of contamination at which 
a food may be regarded as adulterated within the meaning of section 402(a)(1) of the 
Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The FDA considers action levels, in addition to 
other factors and scientific evidence, when considering whether to bring enforcement 
action in a particular case.” Link: Closer to Zero: Action Plan for Baby Foods | FDA 
I. According to the additional requirements for a Consumer Confidence Report (CCR):  

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
12 | P a g e  
 
“(iii) In order to ensure that tap water is safe to drink, EPA prescribes regulations which 
limit the amount of certain contaminants in water provided by public water systems. FDA 
regulations establish limits for contaminants in bottled water which must provide the same 
protection for public health.” Reference: 40 CFR141.153(h)(1)(iii). 
If the FDA bottled water limits must provide the same protection for public health as the 
EPA prescribed regulations which limit the amount of certain contaminants provided by 
public water systems and if the FDA consulted with the EPA on its bottled water limit of 5 
ppb, then by implication, the EPA tacitly acknowledged the 5 ppb as presenting a lower 
risk to health than its Treatment Technique Action Level of 15 (10) ppb, especially to 
infants, children, and pregnant and nursing women, or as the FDA uses women of child 
bearing age (WOCBA). 
SUMMARY COMMENTS. 
WSs along with federal and state environmental regulatory agencies focus on achieving 
compliance with the “letter of the law,” e.g., statute, rule, code and not on the “intent to 
protect” those at greatest risk – infants, children, and WOCBA. Over the years the main 
attention by WSs has been on meeting the regulatory Action Level (AL) number of 15 ppb at 
the 90th percentile contaminant level in order to not have an exceedance and to not have to 
accomplish additional actions. When regulatory agencies do not thoroughly review and verify 
documentation submitted from the WSs, the enforcement of federal and state LCR regulations 
by regulators on WSs can deteriorate to a point where WSs no longer due their due diligence 
on their submissions and information provided to consumers. When a WSs seeks only 
compliance and does not understand the intent to protect, it can arrange its monitoring sites 
and procedures to yield concentrations that will keep it compliant with the LCR requirements. 
If there are no violations with penalties attached, then there is no initiative for WSs to strive to 
meet the intent and do their due diligence in how they set up their program and how they report 
the information to government officials and to their customers. 
I hope the comments promote discussion on how to further improve the LCR requirements that 
will protect those at greatest risk. We want future generations to be able to say that we took actions 
that did not continue to condemn them from the adverse effects of lead. We need enforced 
regulations that provide drinking water that minimizes its contributions to the total body burden to 
all consumers. 
Thank you for your attention to my comments. 
Sincerely, 
 
RONALD L. SCHILLER, CIH (1978 – 2020, Retired)

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1384 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
The Honorable Michael S. Regan, Administrator

Washington, DC 20460
RE: Ensuring Safe Drinking Water at School - Proposed Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements (Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801)
Dear Administrator Regan,
As medical and public health professionals, we urge you to strengthen the proposed Lead &
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) to ensure safe drinking water for all Americans - especially
for children at schools and child care centers.
Lead contamination of drinking water is a serious, longstanding and widespread public health
threat. Even at low levels, this toxic substance impairs the way that children learn, grow and
behave and is linked to cardiovascular disease in adults. As the EPA’s own website duly notes,
“In children, low levels of [lead] exposure have been linked to damage to the central and
peripheral nervous system, learning disabilities, shorter stature, impaired hearing and impaired
formation and function of blood cells.”
Lead contamination of drinking water is a serious, longstanding and widespread threat to public
health. A key reason this problem persists is that federal policy has only required action when
highly variable testing detects lead. To finally ensure safe drinking water for all Americans, the
EPA must transform that “test and fix” policy to one that prevents lead contamination at every
drinking water tap.
A perfect example of this preventative approach is the LCRI’s requirement that water utilities
replace all lead service lines within 10 years. These 9+ million toxic pipes are the single greatest
source of lead contamination for buildings served by them. We wholeheartedly support turning
President Biden’s goal of eliminating these lead pipes within a decade into an enforceable
reality.
We need similarly bold policies to stop lead from contaminating the water where
America’s children go to learn and play each day. Even low levels of lead can damage
children’s health - including learning disabilities, behavior problems, and more. Yet national
standards have allowed the fountains, faucets, pipes and plumbing in our schools to contain a
significant amount of lead. (Even some post-2014 faucets can cause contamination.) As a
result, lead contamination of schools’ drinking water is now widespread.
Yet for most schools and child care centers, the proposed rule only requires testing (and very
limited testing at that). Even federally regulated schools and child care centers would only have
to remediate taps where tests show lead concentrations at 10 parts per billion (ppb) or more.
These proposed policies will fail to secure safe water for kids and educators. Because lead
testing is highly variable, the water from a fountain or faucet can be “highly hazardous” even if

several samples fail to detect lead. Moreover, the 10 ppb action level means that no remediation
will be required for a huge proportion of taps where some level of lead is detected. This weak
policy is also contrary to EPA’s own 3Ts Guidance, which urges schools to reduce lead levels “to
the lowest possible concentrations.”1
America’s kids and educators deserve better. Just as we must replace every lead service line,
federal policy should aim to prevent lead contamination at every tap at schools. Except where a
school district or child care facility affirmatively opts out, the LCRI should require Community
Water Systems (which serve 90% of schools) to implement one of the following options at
schools and child care facilities:
a) Prevent lead contamination at every tap, including:
1.
Filter first: Install and maintain certified point of use filters certified to remove lead on
every tap used for drinking water, cooking or beverage preparation. As fountains contain
lead and cannot accept filters at the point where water comes out, they should be
replaced by new water stations with filters. A growing number of jurisdictions have
already adopted some version of this “filter first” policy - Including Michigan,
Philadelphia, Portland (OR) and the District of Columbia;
2.
A health-based limit on lead: Limit lead in schools’ water to 1 ppb, as recommended
by the American Academy of Pediatrics.2 Schools and child care centers are particularly
well-situated to meet this low lead concentration because they have full control of their
water delivery systems - all the way to the tap. Taps should be tested after filter
installation to ensure this standard is being met; and
3.
Get the lead out: To stop the cycle of lead contamination at school, new and
replacement taps and plumbing should meet the Q≤1 standard recently adopted by
California, where lead leached into water is less than or equal to 1 ppb; or
b) Test every drinking water tap at least once every 6 months, and then replace taps and install
filters whenever lead concentrations exceed 1 ppb. While not ideal, this much more robust “test
and fix” option would be more effective at reducing the likelihood of lead-contaminated water at
school than the infrequent testing and no required remediation in the proposed rule.
For the roughly 10% of schools and child care facilities that are federally regulated as
Non-Transient Non-Community Water Systems, the EPA can and should simply require the
much more protective Option a) above in the LCRI rule.
Right to Know: To counter the strong likelihood of a false sense of safety from inherently
variable testing, the LCRI should also require all water utilities to regularly communicate
(including online) the following to families, educators and the public regarding schools and child
care facilities: full test results showing any level of lead at each tap; that tests are variable and
can fail to detect lead; that there is no safe level of lead; prevention/remediation measures taken
2 “The science is clear that there is no known safe level of exposure to lead in drinking water,
especially for children,” as EPA notes in the proposed rule. The AAP-recommended 1 ppb is a
measurable, attainable limit for schools that is closest to the Maximum Contaminant Level Goal of
zero.
1 U.S. EPA, 3Ts for Reducing Lead in Drinking Water in Schools and Child Care Facilities (2018) at Module
4, page 36, accessed on January 10, 2024.

at each tap; and any school districts or child care facilities opting out of their Community Water
System’s measures outlined above.
In addition to these requirements for schools and child care centers regulated as NTNCWS,
EPA should also incorporate policy changes that will better prevent lead contamination at all
other schools and child care facilities:
●
Establish a clear preference for awarding grants aimed at prevention - such as replacing
fountains with filter-equipped water stations - rather than funding more testing. Condition
grants on adhering to the Right to Know provisions outlined above.
●
Change the name of EPA’s 3 Ts Guidance to “Preventing Lead Contamination at Every
Tap” and replace its “test-and-fix” recommendations with the prevention-oriented
measures outlined above for LCR-regulated schools.
America’s children and educators need safe drinking water to thrive and be healthy. We urge the
EPA to act more boldly to get the lead out at school.
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0876 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Page 1 
 
Safe Water Engineering, LLC 
 
Elin Betanzo

February 5, 2024

Re: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
 
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
I am writing to submit my public comment on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, and 
to provide my perspectives on the LCRI based on my experience in implementing the Michigan Lead and 
Copper Rule. As a member of the National Drinking Water Advisory Committee, I have already 
participated in an advisory session for EPA during the public comment period. I shared several 
perspectives at that meeting, and I am submitting my data analysis here in writing.  
My comments follow, and two attachments, “What Michigan Lead and Copper Rule Compliance Tell Us 
About the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements,” and “January 11, 2023 Benton Harbor 
Corrosion Control Study Letter to EGLE” provide additional analysis.  
 
Comments: 
1. The proactive LSLR requirement is a massive improvement. The requirements and circumstances 
around requirements need to be strengthened to achieve all the intended outcomes. 
 
2. The way to simplify implementation, which is critical for achieving the intended public health 
outcomes, is to make a lead action level exceedance a meaningful intervention for protecting public 
health and providing an incentive for water systems to be as proactive as possible regarding 
corrosion control treatment.  Delivering certified lead reducing filters should be mandatory with 
every lead action level exceedance. For every LALE, EPA should require delivery of filters for two 
sampling periods for every one exceedance. This is the ultimate motivator to get good CCT installed 
and maintained.  Accelerated lead service line replacement (LSLR) is recommended in response to a 
lead action level exceedance, especially if EPA maintains the option for deferring LSLR deadlines in 
the final rule.  
 
3. Using the 90th percentile to measure compliance with the lead action level means there’s minimal 
incentive for water utilities to use corrosion control to minimize lead in all homes. It ensures that, in 

Page 2 
 
Safe Water Engineering, LLC 
 
absence of true OCCT, there will always be up to 10% of households that are at increased risk of 
exposure to lead in drinking water and they will never know who they are. The attached analysis 
shows that 111 Michigan Community Water Systems (CWSs) do not exceed the LAL but still have 
results between 10 and 790 ppb. In most cases residents of these water systems would not get 
improved public health protection under the LCRI. Further analysis is provided in the attachment.  
 
4. Further, Benton Harbor, Michigan had a 90th percentile result of 1 ppb, yet they still had a 
compliance sample at 28 ppb even after all LSLs were removed. Improved CCT will do nothing to 
address the 10% of systems remaining in Benton Harbor with risk of exposure to lead in water 
unless a different measure is used to evaluate a lead action level exceedance. If the maximum lead 
result were measured against the lead action level, we could rely on several provisions of the LCRI to 
achieve a lot of self correcting at PWSs. As long as the 90th percentile is used, it provides an out for 
PWSs to dismiss all valid concerns about lead in water.  
 
5. The requirement to remove all LSLs in 10 years will protect public health if it actually requires all 
public water systems to replace all LSLs in 10 years.  
a. The definition of an LSL must extend into the house, (e.g., from the discharge of the 
corporation fitting to the building plumbing at the first shut-off valve inside the building, or 
18 inches inside the building, whichever is shorter) and connectors goosenecks must be 
considered LSLs.  
b. Strengthen inventory and validation. To be validated as a non-lead service line, there needs 
to be checks on the public side, building side, and inside the building. Goosenecks or 
connectors can be assumed to be present unless there is a control establishing that they 
were never used, or the PWS can validate that there is no lead connector present. See the 
Michigan Distribution System Materials Inventory guidance for more information.  
c. The non-lead validation process must have clear requirements for what to do if one or more 
non-lead services is found to be lead or GRR through the validation process. This should 
trigger re-opening the entire inventory process because it puts all non-lead records in 
question.  
d. Allowing the validation timeline to year 7 will waste LSLR money. If the non-lead data set is 
confirmed to have lead or GRR pipes, the utility would essentially have to start over the LSLR 
program which could effectively double the cost of the program.  
e. Provide an inventory/replacement option where a water utility can commit to, and prove 
they have the resources to, verify every service line as they work through their LSLR 
program to meet the LSLR deadline and avoid the non-lead validation step. There needs to 
be an option to comply as Newark, NJ and Benton Harbor, MI were able to successfully 
remove all LSLs and verify all non-lead service lines. Note that both cities were able to do 
this for all their service lines in less than 3 years.  
 
 
6. Under the proposal, the places with the most lead service lines or high concentrations of these lead 
pipes would potentially have decades of compliance extensions available. Chicago, for example, 
would have 45 to 56 years to remove all of their lead service lines. It is a fundamental injustice that 
communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed extra decades to fix this issue, and it 
is unnecessary to build such extraordinary exceptions into the rule. There should be no extensions 
beyond 10 years; Newark was able to replace 120 lead pipes a day, and there is no reason other 

Page 3 
 
Safe Water Engineering, LLC 
 
cities cannot meet a 10-year deadline. Clearly, no extensions can allow backsliding from the 1991 
Lead and Copper Rule’s requirement that a minimum of 7 percent of lead pipes must be replaced 
annually–a replacement rate EPA long ago determined is feasible. 
 
7. EPA’s mandate states that water systems must replace all lead service lines within their control, but 
EPA’s definition could leave out large numbers of lines and leave them in the ground in perpetuity. 
While the proposed rule is headlined by a requirement for removal of all lead service lines in ten 
years, it actually requires removal only of those service lines that are “under the control of the 
water system unless the replacement would leave in place a partial lead service line.” The rule then 
defines “control” as legal access or physical access without further definition, essentially leaving 
determinations of “control” up to states, water systems and localities to determine whether the 
utility has access. As a result, a water system could “comply” with its requirement to replace all lead 
service lines yet leave vast quantities of lead service lines in the ground by asserting a lack of access 
to any portions of lead service lines under private property. This interpretation is a huge risk, and is 
unnecessary. EPA should affirmatively state that water systems have control over all portions of lead 
service lines, since they generally require or approve use of lead pipes, retain physical access to 
them in an emergency, and ultimately can shut off water through them. 
 
8. The proposed rule fails to mandate that water systems pay for removal of the entire lead service 
line, but it is imperative that the final rule does.  Removal of lead pipes can cost thousands of 
dollars. Putting a disproportionate financial burden on impacted low-wealth homeowners and 
renters by allowing utilities to bill property owners individually will result in mostly wealthy and 
white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced, particularly when combined with the 
aforementioned “access” loophole. There are enough financing solutions, rate structures, and 
funding streams available that EPA should ensure replacements be made at no direct cost to 
individual consumers. This would achieve more equitable implementation, better protect children’s 
health, and is essential to meet EPA’s statutory mandate to protect public health to the extent 
feasible. 
 
9. Most corrosion control studies should focus on lead in premise plumbing. Only water systems with 
more than 2,500 potential LSLs should focus on CCT for lead service lines. Looking at Michigan data, 
this would apply to up to 14% of CWS with potential LSLs. CCT requirements should focus as much 
as possible on expediting better corrosion control treatment that will reliably achieve all lead 
compliance samples at or below 10 ppb. That may or may not include pipe loop studies. Universal 
distribution of certified lead reducing filters could be allowed at all potential LSL and GRR homes as 
an alternative to pipe loop studies for any water system that is expediting LSLR. This would allow a 
protective option to match the Denver Water approach to addressing lead in drinking water.   
 
10. Corrosion Control studies in the LCRI read more like a paperwork and consultant project that 
focuses more on process than outcomes. The purpose of a corrosion control study must be to 
reduce the lead levels in the public water system.  
a. The LCRI should focus on incentives to get the lead as low as possible rather than focusing 
on CCT study requirements that lengthen the CCT timeline. A max lead level of 10 ppb would 
be an appropriate incentive with the requirement to deliver filters if the max lead is greater 
than 10 ppb. Low lead levels should always be the outcome of the CCT study.  
b. Studies take too long and don’t offer public health protection while they happen. 
c. Requiring filters provides immediate, reliable protection against lead in drinking water. 

Page 4 
 
Safe Water Engineering, LLC 
 
d. The CCT requirements of the LCRI provide huge potential to waste time, money and public 
health protection opportunity.  
e. Rather than focusing on study process, the LCRI should consider leaving the CCT process up 
to PWS to do a study that meets their needs to not have an LALE. Low lead compliance 
sampling results in properly collected samples at appropriately tiered sampling sites should 
be the primary measure of CCT success, not the study methodology. If the treatment 
doesn’t result in low lead levels, the PWS should have to start over. 
f. A memo reviewing the corrosion control study process in Benton Harbor is attached. It 
demonstrates the limitations of corrosion control studies and a wide range of issues that can 
go wrong while a community is waiting for public health protection.   
 
11. If corrosion control is not working to reduce maximum lead compliance sampling results below 10 
ppb there should be a requirement for a third-party review of the CCT study to identify more 
effective strategies for reducing lead levels.  
 
12. After a LALE that triggers filter distribution, the final LCRI could allow an end to filters if 100% 
samples are below a revised PQL of 0.002 mg/L.  
 
13. If a PWC wants to stop corrosion control treatment after all LSLs are removed, they should be 
required to conduct a study to determine whether lead levels will rise if they stop CCT treatment. 
 
14. Consecutive system CCT treatment must be explicitly addressed in final LCRI. These issues are 
described in more detail in the attachment “What Michigan Lead and Copper Rule Compliance Data 
Tell Us About the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements.” 
 
15. There are no copper provisions in the LCRI. To avoid backsliding, the final LCRI should include a 
separate sampling pool of new copper sites, preferably locations after LSLR, to measure the 
adequacy of CCT for controlling copper corrosion.  
 
16. School sampling as appears in the draft LCRI is not scientifically defensible, misleading, and is a 
waste of money and implementation burden with a negative public health result. A filter first 
approach like the one instituted in Michigan is a far more direct approach to providing public health 
protection that should not increase burden on public water systems and primacy agencies. EPA 
should explore an “all of government approach” to ensure certified lead reducing filters are used in 
all school and childcare settings even if it is not through regulating public water systems.  
 
17. Distribution system water quality is most effective for corrosion control if consistency is maintained 
in water quality parameters. More frequency of sampling, more parameters, and setting both a 
lower and upper bound for water quality parameters will help ensure water quality consistency and 
better corrosion control.  
 
18. Right to know reports, public notifications, and public education materials should include language 
that is clear about the possibility of lead exposure from drinking water even when the system as a 
whole is in compliance. Information should include annual messaging about not only the risks of 
contamination from lead service lines but also lead plumbing, which is ubiquitous. It should also 
include information about the effectiveness of lead-certified point of use filters as a way for families 
to reduce lead levels in their drinking water. EPA should forbid messaging that states or suggests 

Page 5 
 
Safe Water Engineering, LLC 
 
that tested lead levels below the action level are "safe," and emphasize that there is no safe level of 
lead exposure. The attachment, ““What Michigan Lead and Copper Rule Compliance Data Tell Us 
About the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” describes how more than 100 Michigan 
CWS have confirmed elevated lead levels even when they are in compliance with the 10 ppb lead 
action level using the 90th percentile measurement. These lead levels go as high as 6,000 ppb even 
while the CWS is in full compliance with the LCRI. If the final LCRI is to continue using the 90th 
percentile for measurement against the lead action level, it is imperative that all public education 
materials be revised to notify all consumers that they are all at risk of exposure to elevated lead at 
any time. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to express my views on this important matter. I trust that you will 
carefully consider the feedback provided by the public during this comment period, as it represents the 
collective voice of concerned citizens who share a common commitment to our drinking water. 
 
Sincerely, 
Elin Betanzo 
President and Founder, Safe Water Engineering, LLC

National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper:            
 
Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801  
  
  
Dear Administrator Regan: 
  
On behalf of the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation (hereinafter “RWJF”), we are pleased to submit 
comments on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s proposed National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–
0801, published in the Federal Register on December 6, 2023.  
 
RWJF is committed to improving health and health equity in the United States. In partnership with others, 
we are working to develop a Culture of Health rooted in equity that provides every individual with a fair 
and just opportunity to thrive, no matter who they are, where they live, or how much money they have. 
This includes supporting the development of the physical, economic, and social conditions in communities 
that enable all residents to reach their best possible health and wellbeing.   
  
Health is more than an absence of disease. It is a state of physical, mental, and emotional wellbeing. It 
reflects what takes place in our communities, where we live and work, where our children learn and play, 
and where we gather to worship. That is why RWJF focuses on identifying, illuminating, and addressing 
the barriers to health caused by structural racism and other forms of discrimination, including sexism, 
ableism, xenophobia, and prejudice based on sexual orientation.  
  
We rely on evidence to advance health equity. We cultivate leaders who work individually and collectively 
across sectors to address health equity. We promote policies, practices, and systems change to 
dismantle the structural barriers to wellbeing created by racism. We work to amplify voices to shift 
national conversations and attitudes about health and health equity.  
  
Safe, affordable water is fundamental to good health. While most water systems in the U.S. deliver safe 
drinking water, in every state, there are communities that lack access to safe water they can afford. Often, 
these are places where people with lower income, Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous people, and other 
people of color live. A long legacy of discriminatory policies and structural racism, including the lack of 
historic investment in communities of color, has created these inequities. Yet this water crisis can be 
solved. By upgrading our aging infrastructure and making water more affordable, we can make sure 
everyone, everywhere can turn on the tap without a second thought.  

 
2 of 11 
 
  
Our comments on the Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) are grounded in the perspectives and 
expertise of our grantees, who include policy experts, advocates, and organizers with deep expertise in 
public health, lead poisoning prevention, and environmental and water justice. Our comments also are 
based on the findings of RWJF-funded research. This includes a comprehensive 2017 report (known as 
the “10 Policies Report”) by the Health Impact Project, a collaboration of the Pew Charitable Trusts and 
RWJF, on evidence-based policies to prevent and respond to childhood lead exposure, including lead in 
drinking water.i 
  
We highlight here some of the relevant public health and clinical experience of the co-signatories of this 
comment letter: Dr. Richard Besser, RWJF’s president and CEO, and Dr. Julie Morita, RWJF’s executive 
vice president. Dr. Besser worked at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for 13 years, 
including serving as the acting director of the agency in 2009. He practiced as a volunteer pediatrician at 
community clinics across the U.S. for more than 30 years. Dr. Morita is also a pediatrician and helped 
lead the Chicago Department of Public Health for nearly two decades, first as a medical director, then as 
chief medical officer, and ultimately as commissioner where she oversaw the public health needs of 2.7 
million residents in the nation’s third largest city.   
  
RWJF’s Commitment to Water Equity and Reducing Lead Exposure  
  
Building on the water justice efforts sparked by the Flint, Michigan water crisis that began in 2014, RWJF 
has made more than $15 million in grants and investments in the past several years to advance water 
equity and reduce lead exposure. RWJF and our grantees have coordinated with EPA on the Lead 
Accelerator initiative, the more recent Get the Lead Out initiative, and the implementation of the $15 
billion set aside of Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding for lead service line (LSL) replacement. Some 
examples of these investments include funding to:  
  
• 
The Environmental Policy Innovation Center to support multiple communities in implementing LSL 
replacement programs and to make recommendations for improving the Consumer Confidence 
Reports; 
  
• 
The Natural Resources Defense Council to pursue stronger federal, state, and local lead policies 
as well as policies that advance water affordability; 
  
• 
New Jersey Future, which has helped to galvanize support for some of the most aggressive LSL 
replacement programs in the country; 
  
• 
The Little Village Environmental Justice Organization to advocate for more effective LSL program 
implementation for historically marginalized communities, including entire neighborhoods in 
Chicago that have been disproportionately burdened by lead;  
 
• 
The National Center for Healthy Housing to build local capacity to reduce childhood lead 
exposure in homes and to advance evidence-based lead poisoning prevention efforts through 
policy and systems change. 
  
Recognizing that water is one of many sources of lead exposure, RWJF also has supported the National 
Center for Healthy Housing to support a cohort of cities around the country in advancing policies to 
prevent exposure from lead-based paint hazards. As a member of the Lead Action Funders Network—a 
collaborative of philanthropic organizations committed to reducing childhood lead exposure—we have 
developed several tools and resources for financing lead remediation. We have also funded Altarum 

 
3 of 11 
 
Institute to create the Value of Lead Prevention website, which enables state and community leaders and 
the public to easily calculate the cost of lead exposure in their state and the economic benefits of key 
interventions to reduce lead exposure.  
  
Comments on the LCRI  
  
As outlined here, RWJF’s comment on the LCRI presents research that underscores the importance of 
LSL replacement and key provisions of the LCRI; documents the unequal burden of lead on people with 
lower incomes, Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous people, and other people of color; and makes 
recommendations to strengthen the LCRI.  
  
I. 
The LCRI would have a profoundly positive impact on public health and economic wellbeing.  
II. 
Communities where Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous people and other people of color live are 
disproportionately impacted by LSLs.  
III. 
EPA should strengthen the 2023 Proposed Rule to maximize protections for people and places at 
greatest risk for lead exposure.  
  
I. 
The LCRI would have a profoundly positive impact on public health and economic 
wellbeing.  
  
RWJF strongly supports the Administration’s commitment to replacing all LSLs. If finalized, the LCRI 
would help to realize that goal. The public health impact of the implementation of the LCRI would be 
enormous: more children thriving at home and at school, stronger and more equitable communities, and 
longer, healthier, and more productive lives.   
  
Thousands of studies have concluded that lead has wide-ranging effects on the health of young children 
and significant costs to taxpayers. Even at very low levels, lead exposure affects the brain’s ability to 
control impulses and process information. Children with lead poisoning are more likely to struggle in 
school, drop out, have encounters with the justice system, underperform in the workplace, and earn less 
throughout their lives, independent of other social and economic factors. The cost of these outcomes 
includes billions of dollars in public spending on special education, juvenile justice, and other social 
services.ii 
  
EPA’s 2024 Integrated Science Assessment for Lead found clear and consistent evidence of negative 
health effects of lead exposure among children and adults. Lead exposure is associated with decreased 
attention, increased impulsivity, and increased hyperactivity in children—effects that recent studies 
observed at blood lead levels less than or equal to 5 ug/dL. There is no evidence of a threshold for the 
observed neurodevelopmental effects. Scientists have found negative effects of lead on cognitive function 
in populations of children (ages 4–10) at blood lead levels in the range of 2–8 μg/dL. Studies show that 
cognitive effects and neurodevelopmental effects may persist into adulthood. Lead exposure in adulthood 
can negatively affect cognitive function and harm an array of organ systems, including the cardiovascular 
and renal systems.iii 
  
Although indoor plumbing fixtures and lead solder can contribute to elevated lead levels in drinking water, 
research indicates that LSLs account for the largest share of lead in drinking water.iv Studies show that 
U.S. residences with LSLs are at risk of lead exposure if corrosion control techniques are not effective at 
preventing lead from leaching from pipes and leaded fixtures into drinking water. A robust body of 
academic literature from the U.S. and Canada links lead in drinking water to increases in blood lead 
levels.v For example, one cross-sectional study of 183 children randomly selected from urban areas found 
that an increase in water lead concentrations from background levels to 15 ppb was associated with a 
nearly 14 percent jump in the share of children with estimated blood lead over 10 µg/dL.vi 

 
4 of 11 
 
  
The LCRI will meaningfully contribute to the reduction of lead exposure in the U.S. Key provisions of the 
LCRI that RWJF supports include the following:  
1. Universally mandating the replacement of LSLs over 10 years;  
2. Steady removal of lead connectors and galvanized steel lines, which present a public health 
risk;vii 
3. Reduction of the lead action level, though we believe that the action level should be further 
lowered from 10 ppb to 5 ppb as discussed in section III below;  
4. Improvements to the tap sampling protocols;  
5. Increased transparency between water systems and consumers about lead in tap water;  
6. Continuing to discourage partial LSL replacements, though as discussed in section III below, we 
believe EPA can do more in this rule to ensure the full line is replaced;   
7. The inclusion in the rule’s cost-benefit analysis of recent evidence regarding the effects of lead on 
cardiovascular disease in adults.  
  
II. 
Communities where Black, Hispanic, and Indigenous people and other people of color live 
are disproportionately impacted by lead and LSLs.  
  
Due to systemic factors discussed further below, race and ethnicity are strongly associated with children’s 
risk of exposure to lead.   
  
• 
A national survey found that Black children’s average blood lead levels were well above those of 
non-Hispanic White and Mexican-American children.viii Although the survey did not control for 
social and economic factors, other studies have shown that race and ethnicity are associated with 
elevated blood lead levels in children regardless of family income.   
• 
One study of more than 1 million blood tests from Chicago collected between 1995 and 2013 
found that, after controlling for socioeconomic factors, children from predominantly Black, and to 
a lesser extent Hispanic, neighborhoods had higher rates of lead poisoning than their White 
counterparts, even as blood lead levels fell dramatically citywide.ix 
• 
The Chicago-area Metropolitan Planning Council found that the composition of the communities 
in Illinois with 94 percent of the state’s LSLs was 65 percent Black and Latinx residents, 42 
percent Asian-American and Native American populations, and 30 percent White.x 
  
These disparate impacts by race and ethnicity are a direct consequence of racist policies and practices in 
the water and housing sectors throughout our nation’s history.   
  
• 
During the Jim Crow era, Black and Hispanic people and other people of color were 
disproportionately burdened by degraded water quality and infrastructure disinvestments through 
practices such as redlining, exclusionary zoning, and discriminatory lending practices. These 
practices enabled municipal decisions to restrict services and waterworks access for majority-
Black communities and neighborhoods. During this period, federal waterworks funding and 
services continued to decrease for communities with majority-Black populations and Indigenous 
people, which were already historically excluded from, or severely limited in accessing, federal 
investments.xi 
  
• 
After World War II, communities of color were excluded from water and sewer services through 
“under-bounding,” which was a practice of annexing White neighborhoods within a town’s 
boundaries, and then denying or limiting water and sewer services for adjacent or nearby 
communities of color.xii One study showed that Black and poor White neighborhoods received 

 
5 of 11 
 
town water and sewer services a half century or more after affluent White communities.xiii In 
subsequent decades, some White suburbs created their own private water utilities instead of 
using existing municipal ones, which reduced the revenue and market share of older, public, 
urban systems serving communities of color.    
 
• 
EPA has noted that so-called “disadvantaged communities”[1] have never received their fair share 
of federal investment. Contemporary studies show that smaller municipalities and those with 
larger populations of color are statistically less likely to receive federal water assistance.xiv 
  
III. 
EPA should strengthen the LCRI to maximize protections for people and places at greatest 
risk of lead exposure.  
  
RWJF recommends that EPA strengthen the LCRI in the following ways to better protect children and 
families from lead exposure and to more effectively advance racial and health equity.  
  
1. Require systems to pay for full LSL replacement.   
  
The replacement of LSLs is a matter of public health. Evidence shows that requiring homeowners to pay 
for the portion of the line on their property is both inequitable and a public health risk.xv Therefore, EPA 
should clarify that water systems are expected to replace the full LSL. This will likely save water utilities 
time negotiating with property owners, which will expedite replacements. Finally, EPA should require that 
utilities replace LSLs first in neighborhoods with the greatest risk of lead exposure.   
  
2. Close the “control” loophole.   
  
EPA should not allow water systems to avoid complying with the rule by claiming that they do not have 
control of a property. Clarity on this point would serve as an incentive to water systems to proactively 
uncover and address state and local legal barriers to full LSL replacement. Additionally, EPA could 
condition Safe Drinking State Revolving Fund and other drinking water funding on changes to state and 
local laws and administrative policies to clarify that water systems may replace the part of the LSL on 
private property.   
  
3. Make October 2024 the effective date of all aspects of the LCRI.   
  
EPA proposes that implementation of the LCRI would begin three years after the rule is finalized “unless 
the Administrator determines that an earlier date is practicable.” Given that EPA’s review of the current 
lead and copper rule found that leaving millions of LSLs in place would result in “generations of 
Americans being at risk of significant lead exposure through their drinking water,” RWJF strongly 
recommends that EPA make October 2024 the effective date for compliance with all aspects of the final 
rule.   
 
 
 
 
 
The Foundation’s preference is to use the term “marginalized” when referring to some neighborhoods, schools, institutions, and 
communities that have experienced historical and ongoing exclusion from equitable distribution of resources. However, the term 
“disadvantaged community” is used in this comment letter because that is the term used by EPA in the LCRI. 

 
6 of 11 
 
  
Starting implementation three years after the rule is finalized puts far too many children and families at 
risk of exposure whereas swift implementation would bring meaningful benefits to communities impacted 
by LSLs. The RWJF-funded 10 Policies Report found that removing leaded drinking water service lines 
from the homes of children born in 2018 (one birth cohort and not including the adults in these homes) 
would protect more than 350,000 children and yield $2.7 billion in future benefits for families, federal, 
state, and local governments, and the private sector.xvi 
  
It is not only in the interest of public health but also feasible for water systems to begin implementing the 
LCRI in October 2024. EPA made water systems aware in December 2021 of the agency’s intention to 
require replacement of all LSLs. As EPA notes in the LCRI, several states have already mandated full 
LSL and many cities have completed this work.   
  
Further, moving directly to the implementation of the LCRI will avoid the confusion of temporarily 
implementing some or all the provisions of the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), which are 
set to take effect in October 2024. The LCRI should replace the LCRR as the LCRI is a strengthened 
version of the LCRR and based on the latest evidence. EPA could include a year or two of “compliance 
assistance” whereby enforcement is phased in. HUD’s Office of Lead Hazard Control and Healthy Homes 
implemented such an approach when it finalized its sweeping lead safe housing rule.    
  
4. Eliminate the exceptions to the 10-year replacement timeline.   
  
RWJF recommends that the final rule does not permit exceptions to the ten-year LSL replacement 
deadline for communities with a high proportion of LSL relative to their total number of households served 
or a high total number of LSLs. Rather than offering deferred compliance deadlines to water systems in 
these communities, EPA should target grant funding and compliance assistance to enable water systems 
in these communities to complete LSL replacements within ten years. EPA could also incentivize smaller 
water systems to pursue community-led consolidation and regional partnerships to ease compliance with 
the rule’s requirements.   
  
5. Use more inclusive definitions and language that include people who rent their homes.   
  
Most of the informational requirements in the LCRI apply to “customers,” which is generally interpreted by 
EPA and water systems to mean those who receive the water bills. Wherever the LCRI refers to 
customers, it should also include those who reside in the household, regardless of whether they pay the 
water bill. Anyone residing in a home should receive information about lead test results and system-wide 
lead monitoring information. Additionally, when a water system contacts customers for access to a 
property for LSL replacement, household members should also be contacted since a renter may 
encourage the owner to participate. Newark, New Jersey allows adult occupants of a residence, including 
renters, to agree and provide access to LSLs in order to replace them. This is particularly important for 
overcoming the barrier of gaining access to buildings owned by absentee landlords.   
  
6. Strengthen the proposed requirements for schools and childcare centers.   
  
RWJF recommends that community water systems provide water filters to childcare facilities and filtration 
systems to schools while testing protocols are carried out. RWJF is aware of many communities that are 
moving to a “filter first” approach. EPA should consider whether this would be a more cost effective and 
public health protective approach than testing programs. EPA should also require community water 
systems to make public the results of the tests performed in schools.   
  

 
7 of 11 
 
7. Further lower the action level for education, filter provision, and source water monitoring 
from 10 ppb to 5 ppb.   
  
Evidence suggests that every increment of lead exposure matters and earlier action is warranted. For 
example, in the 10 Policies Report, researchers noted that EPA’s Integrated Exposure Uptake and 
Biokinetic model estimates a 0.042 µg/dL change in blood lead per 1 ppb increase in water lead. A 
Canadian study looked at cumulative lead exposure and found that for children between the ages of 1 to 
5, an increase of 1 μg/L in water lead would result in an increase of 35 percent of blood lead after 150 
days of exposure.xvii 
  
There is evidence that utilities can achieve a level of 5 ppb through optimized corrosion control, including 
EPA data cited in the LCRI, which shows that the vast majority of systems serving more than 10,000 
people would meet a 5 parts per billion standard today.xviii Furthermore, technology improvements, 
regional partnerships and consolidation, training, and the LCRI will help reduce levels over the next 
decade, making this lower action level technically feasible. Finally, as EPA points out in the LCRI, this 
level has previously been used as a trigger; the current lead and copper rule already requires optimized 
CCT when 90th percentile lead levels exceed 5 ppb. Thus, water systems already are acting at 5 ppb.   
  
In addition to lowering the action level, EPA should strengthen its oversight and enforcement efforts, 
including by requiring direct electronic reporting of monitoring results and action level exceedances to 
EPA. More rigorous enforcement should also include mandating and enforcing state reporting of 
violations, which audits have found that states vastly underreport to EPA.   
  
8. Strengthen the filter requirements.   
  
RWJF recommends that EPA require water systems to distribute filters for any exceedance of the action 
level instead of the LCRI requirement action after 3 exceedances in five years. Under EPA’s proposal, the 
requirement to distribute filters would not begin until the end of the first five-year cycle, which is 
insufficient to protect public health and could disproportionately burden disadvantaged communities that 
are more likely to experience exceedances. In addition to requiring water systems to annually notify 
households that they have an LSL, galvanized service line requiring replacement, or unknown service 
line, EPA should require water systems to provide filters and instructions for their use to households that 
have an LSL, galvanized service line requiring replacement, lead connector material, or unknown service 
line. This will help protect public health during the many years it will take to replace these materials.  
  
9. Monitor the equitable implementation of the rule.   
  
EPA should collect and report data on the implementation of the rule, including an equity analysis that 
shows the number and percent of replacements in water systems by race, ethnicity, income, and rental 
versus homeownership status. Additionally, EPA should develop a national LSL inventory where all cities 
and states report their respective inventory and progress as well as include the LSL inventory in the EPA 
EJScreen and the Climate Economic Justice Screening Tools.   
  
10. Require lead pipe replacements to be done using copper, or polypropylene when copper is 
not feasible, as new pipe materials.   
  
Plastic pipes can potentially contaminate drinking water by leaching— when pollutants seep from 
groundwater or soils through the walls of plastic pipesxix—and can release toxic chemicals into drinking 
water when exposed to wildfire temperatures.xx 
  
 

 
8 of 11 
 
Going Further: Addressing the Financing Needs of Disadvantaged Communities 
 
RWJF recommends that EPA create an ongoing source of long-term, non-competitive grants to facilitate 
implementation of the LCRI so that the lowest income customers do not have to choose between 
affordable drinking water and quality drinking water. This recommendation is a critical aspect of equitable 
implementation that RWJF believes is important for EPA to proactively address. 
 
As with most aspects of water infrastructure, it is disadvantaged communities within larger cities and 
smaller communities that will be most significantly impacted by the changes outlined in the LCRI. While 
larger cities can finance compliance with the LCRI through rate structures that are predominantly paid by 
higher-income households, disadvantaged communities do not have the economic base to implement 
similar programs. 
 
To support utilities serving disadvantaged communities in covering the cost of full LSL replacement, EPA 
could require states to account for the extent and cost of LSL replacement separately, broken down by 
population categories, which EPA has done for wastewater needs assessments. This would enable EPA 
and states to target funding for replacement costs to the smallest and poorest communities. Such funding 
could be made available through the Safe Drinking Water Act’s programs for Small and Disadvantaged 
Communities or Lead Reduction Project Program for disadvantaged communitiesxxi, a new funding 
mechanism, or by allowing states to use repayments to their Drinking Water State Revolving Funds (SRF) 
or their principal forgiveness funds. 
 
Recognizing that it may take time to set up a new funding mechanism for disadvantaged communities, 
RWJF recommends that EPA take immediate steps to modernize its SRF program—the principal source 
of funding for LSL replacement—so that it advances the Administration’s Justice 40 objectives. Many of 
RWJF’s grantee partners have experienced barriers in accessing SRF funding. While an exhaustive 
discussion of SRF reform is beyond the scope of this comment letter, RWJF makes the following high-
level recommendations to help achieve equitable implementation of the LCRI: 
 
• 
EPA should continue to promote state adoption of the definition of “disadvantaged community” 
developed by EPA and that advances Justice 40 objectives; 
• 
Prioritize loan forgiveness for disadvantaged communities; 
• 
Reduce the complexity of the application process; 
• 
Make the Intended Use Plans process more transparent, accessible, and inclusive; 
• 
Ensure that all project predevelopment expenses are recoverable through SRF; and 
• 
Ensure that environmental finance centers have the necessary financing experience to guide 
communities through the development of a full financing package given that many communities 
will likely need to activate several sources of public and private funding. 
 
We encourage EPA to work with disadvantaged communities to elevate and address these and other 
challenges to access SRF. 
 
Conclusion  
  
Where you live should not determine whether you have safe water to drink. We appreciate the opportunity 
to submit comments on the LCRI and urge EPA to move forward with a strong rule that maximizes the 
protections for the populations and places that are at greatest risk of exposure. The proposed rule goes a 
long way toward strengthening drinking water protections for children and families and promoting more 
equitable outcomes for those who have long been unjustly burdened by lead. With more aggressive 

 
9 of 11 
 
implementation timelines, elimination of loopholes and exceptions, and the other improvements noted 
above, the Administration can achieve its goal of replacing all LSLs in 10 years.   
  
Sincerely,  
   
 
  
Richard E. Besser, M.D.

National Ground Water Association 
Comments on: 
Environmental Protection Agency Proposed Regulation on 
“National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI)” 
Published on: December 6, 2023 
Comments Due:  February 5, 2024 
Document Citation: 88 FR 84878 
Code of Federal Regulations Reference: 40 CFR 141; 40 CFR 142 
Agency/Docket Numbers: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW 
Summary 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) proposes revisions to the National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act 
(SDWA). EPA proposes to require water systems to replace lead service lines, remove the lead trigger 
level, reduce the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling procedures, among other 
changes that would improve public health protection and simplify the rule relative to the 2021 Lead and 
Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). This proposed rule provides improvements in the additional following 
areas: corrosion control treatment, public education and consumer awareness, requirements for small 
systems, and sampling in schools and childcare facilities. This proposed rule aims to address potential 
disproportionate impacts of lead in drinking water in communities, including through proposed lead 
service line replacement and public education, among other aspects of the proposed rule. 
Submit Comments to Federal eRulemaking Portal: https://www.regulations.gov/ 
Electronic Link: https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2023/12/06/2023-26148/national-primary-
drinking-water-regulations-for-lead-and-copper-improvements-lcri 
National Ground Water Association Comments 
NGWA supports the EPA proposal to allow small systems to choose corrosion control, point of use 
devices or replacement of lead-bearing plumbing materials. Even though there is flexibility for small 
systems to decide what path to take for lead protection, the rule is complex necessitating assistance to 
support small systems to comply. 

 
 
Page 2 of 2 
 
Small water systems will need significant assistance in implementing the lead and copper rule in all 
major aspects. Assistance should be provided to prepare public notices, consumer notices of testing 
results within 3 days, 24-hour notice of replacement notification, communication strategies, education 
materials, recurring public education tasks, identifying and contacting consumers most at risk, 
compliance reporting, health care contact information, outreach activities and consumer confidence 
reports as well as inventorying lead service lines and regular monitoring. 
The preamble cites an EPA “Lead Service Line Replacement Accelerators” initiative to provide targeted 
technical assistance services through identification of “best practices“ to help underserved communities 
access funds from the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) and replace lead pipes that pose risks to the 
health of children and families. Best practices for small water systems should be explained and offered in 
the simplest and most direct ways possible. 
The preamble indicates that Federal funds are available to support equity including BIL funds that 
require that States provide 49 percent of their LSLR and General Supplemental capitalization grant 
amounts as additional subsidization in the form of principal forgiveness and/or grants to disadvantaged 
communities. This support should include planning for design and construction as well as for notification 
and education processes to ensure that small systems are not in violation of the regulation due to 
capacity constraints. 
Basis for National Ground Water Association Interests in this Proposed Rule 
The National Ground Water Association is the largest organization of water well contractors, scientists 
and engineers, manufacturers and distributors of services and equipment supporting the prudent 
development of groundwater. 
A concise summary of the position of the National Ground Water Association on groundwater 
protection related to sources of contamination is:  
• 
A coordinated approach by all levels of government is needed to effectively protect and manage 
groundwater quality. 
• 
Control of potential and active sources of contamination should be a national objective, 
reducing the need for remediation of groundwater.   
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule.

RE:  
Docket ID EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) 
City of Baltimore written comments 
 
 
Below for consideration is the City of Baltimore Department of Public Works’ (DPW’s) comments regarding the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements guidelines. 
 
1. Part III, Section A: EPA proposes requiring mandatory full-service line replacement of lead and galvanized 
service lines under the control of the water system regardless of the water lead level. 
 
Comment: We agree that the most conservative solution to preventing lead in drinking water is to remove all lead 
pipe; however, this solution comes at significant financial cost which has yet to be determined. If costs to replace 
lead pipe is passed onto the consumer without any financial support or resources, then that will be problematic 
for residents within the Baltimore region.  As a lower cost alternative, we recommend that lead and/or galvanized 
pipe replacement be mandated based on the lead level in the water. Lead or service line replacement should be 
required after sampling results indicate lead levels have exceeded a health-based threshold. That type of analysis 
should be considered prior to passing on costs for replacements directly to the property owner.    
 
2. Part III, Section A: EPA is proposing to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L.  
 
Comment: EPA’s proposed lead action level is arbitrary and will result in unreasonable mandates for water 
systems throughout the country. As stated in EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Revision, Part III, Section A.1, “The 
trigger level [10 µg/L] is not a health-based standard. EPA’s proposed 10 µg/L as a reasonable concentration that 
is below the action level and above the Practical Quantification Level of 5 µg/L at which to require water 
systems to take a progressive set of actions to reduce lead levels prior to an action level exceedance and to have a 
plan in place to rapidly respond if there is an action level exceedance.” Lead action levels should be health-based.  
 
3. Exhibit I: All systems must review records for information on connector materials and include lead connectors in 
the baseline inventory by the compliance date. 
 
Comment: DPW has spent significant resources over the previous 2-3 years developing our lead and galvanized 
pipe inventory, which was based on EPA’s Lead and Copper Replacement Requirement guidelines. Under LCRI, 
EPA is proposing to mandate expanding the inventory to include connector materials, which will put additional 
unknown financial burdens on DPW and other water systems. This in turn could potentially result in increased 
costs for customers. We propose that water systems update their lead/galvanized pipe inventory as information 
becomes available with no set deadline, to ensure financial resources can be fully secured to complete those 
requirements. 
 
4. Exhibit I: Systems conducting partial service line replacement must offer to replace the remaining portion of the 
service line not under their control (within 45 days for emergencies). 
 
Comment: The word “Offering” suggests that the system owner is responsible for the cost to replace the 
privately-owned portion of the service line, which is unreasonable and financially problematic. In addition to the 
financial burden borne by the system owner, the owner: 
 
a. 
Can be exposed to warranty issues and associated future repairs/costs. 
b. Allot significant staff resources to coordinate with individual property owners, which will result in 
program management/construction delays of other critical improvement projects. 
 

Page 2 of 2 
 
Federal funding that has been made available for systems owners to comply with the LCRR/LCRI requirements 
includes various restrictions/requirements such as minority/business enterprise goals, Davis-Bacon wage rates, 
Build America supplies, which precludes any type of public-private partnership (PPP). The City of Baltimore 
DPW considered a PPP model to expedite lead/galvanized service lines replacement, minimize costs and avoid 
warranty liability; however, based on discussions with state regulators and reviewing the funding requirements, it 
is apparent that the PPP model is impossible and DPW is constrained to complete the work as a typical large 
capital program. We recommend the following: 
 
a. 
Replace the work “Offering” with “Inform”. 
b. Remove the requirement for the system owner to be responsible for replacing lead/galvanized 
service lines on private property. All water improvement work on private property has been and 
should remain the responsibility of the property owner. The system owner can provide pipe 
replacement alternatives for the property owner to consider, if needed.  
c. 
Remove the restrictions/requirements for federal funding of the LCRR/LCRI.  
 
5. Exhibit I: Water systems must deliver consumer notice of lead and copper tap sampling results to consumers 
whose tap was sampled as soon as practicable but no later than 3 days after receiving the results. 
 
Comments: The LCRR/LCRI guidelines will significantly expand the number of samples that are collected and 
analyzed by the City of Baltimore DPW; therefore, the 3-day notification requirement will result in unreasonable 
staffing/notification resources for DPW and other system owners. We recommend that system owners should 
notify consumers as soon as practicable, but no later than 30 days after receiving the results.   
 
Please contact me with any questions or concerns. 
 
 
 
Best regards, 
 
 
 
 
Paul Sayan, P.E. 
 
Acting Bureau Head  
 
Bureau of Water & Wastewater 
 
Baltimore City Department of Public Works

Document ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 
 
Recipient: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)  
From: Austin Magness, Graduate Student  
Subject: Support for the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements 
Date: January 29th, 2024 
 
Executive Summary: 
This memo is intended to outline my support for the current proposed revisions to the National Drinking 
Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper and to provide additional policy options. The current 
proposal requires water systems to replace lead service lines, remove lead trigger levels, reduce the lead 
action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling procedures as well as other changes that would 
benefit human health. As previously outlined by the EPA, there are no “safe” levels of lead in drinking 
water. The EPA’s desire to pursue clean drinking water is admirable and should be pursued relentlessly 
for the betterment of all. A more effective policy addition would be to require schools and childcare 
facilities to participate in the sampling program to determine if there is any lead present in their drinking 
water. In combination, I would recommend a standardized testing requirement for uniformity. Adding 
these two additional requirements would further enhance this proposed rule to better protect our youth 
across the U.S.  
Background:  
Currently, only 24 states and the District of Columbia require their schools to test for lead or have 
programs to conduct such testing according to a recent study conducted by the University of California 
and Harvard University (PRC, 2023). This accounts for less than 50% of the United States and is 
concerning as the study highlighted that 44% of schools that were tested had one or more water 
samples with a lead concentration at or above the state’s action level (PRC, 2023). According to the same 
report, only seven states and the District of Columbia require water tests in schools (PRC, 2023). 
According to the EPA, lead in drinking water is harmful, especially for children. With that understanding, I 
find that requiring further sampling in schools and childcare facilities is imperative to ensure the 
protection of early childhood health. Using the information above, alternative policy solutions will be 
explored.  
Additional Policy Considerations:  
I. 
Sampling Program Requirement for schools and Childcare facilities 
An additional revision in the NPDWR that should be included is the requirement that all schools and 
childcare facilities recognized by the U.S. Department of Education participate in a lead water sampling 

program where the facility obtains its water source from a public system. This would set a national 
requirement for each state to implement a sampling program that would monitor and track lead in 
drinking water in consultation with the EPA for compliance. Currently, the EPA offers its three T’s toolkit 
to assist those who wish to start a lead sampling program (EPA, 2018). This could be used as a 
framework for a national program for each state to build off of.  
II. 
Standardized lead testing requirements for uniformity 
Currently, there are no standardized lead testing practices in each of the 24 states including the District 
of Columbia. Each state has its method of performing the tests with different labs analyzing the results. 
An alternative solution would be to establish a national standard established by the EPA on how to 
perform water tests, while additionally creating a national database to house the results for public 
access and transparency. Further study and discussion would need to occur before determining who 
should handle the analysis portion of the testing.   
Conclusion 
The current revision to the NPDWR is warranted and is vital to ensure safe drinking water throughout the 
country. The policy alternatives that I have offered in this memo allow for enhanced testing in schools 
and daycare facilities throughout the country to protect the health of our youth. As the EPA outlined, 
lead in drinking water is dangerous, especially for children, which highlights the importance of placing a 
priority on testing within schools and daycare facilities. The policy option of enacting a standardized 
testing method would also offer uniformity to the system and would lead to more transparency with the 
public while we pursue avenues to correct issues as they arise.
