RE: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801  
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
Aquarion Water Company provides the following comments on EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI), as described in the Federal Register / Vol. 88, No. 233 / Wednesday, December 6, 
2023 / Proposed Rules. 
 
Aquarion Water Company is an investor-owned water utility that serves a population of more than 
700,000 people in 72 cities and towns in Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New Hampshire.  
 
It should first be stated that we recognize and respect the significant effort that has been put forth by 
EPA and other contributors to develop the proposed LCRI regulation. We appreciate the opportunity to 
offer comments on the regulation. Our goal is to provide meaningful input to the regulatory process to 
assist in making the final regulation effective for protecting public health. 
 
Aquarion offers the following comment on the EPA’s proposed LCRI. 
 
1. Timely decision on compliance deadlines - The proposed LCRI moves out the compliance 
deadline for numerous requirements within the LCRR (e.g. related to service line 
disturbances, compliance monitoring plans, school and childcare sampling).  We support 
EPA’s approach of deferring compliance with many aspects of the LCRR until the compliance 
date of LCRI.  However, until the LCRI is finalized, water systems have no assurance of this 
later deadline.  We believe all stakeholders would benefit from a timely confirmation by 
EPA that the final LCRI will move the compliance date for these aspects of the LCRR to the 
compliance date of the LCRI. 
 
2. Calculation of compliance with replacement rate - The proposed LCRI specifies that the 
calculation of the number of lead service lines to be replaced each year be based on the sum 
of the number of services lines that are lead, galvanized requiring replacement (GRR), and of 
unknown material (unknowns). For water systems that initially have a high number of 
unknowns in their inventory, that calculation might result in a requirement to replace more 
than 10% of the actual lead and GRR service lines per year, particularly in the early years.  
While this will have the benefit of expediting the replacement of lead and GRR service lines, 
with the proposed 3-year rolling average replacement calculation, replacing more than 10% 
for several early years will create the risk of non-compliance in later years.   We recommend 
that EPA revise this requirement by instead requiring a cumulative annual average of 10% 
beginning in year three for replacement of LSLs. 

Aquarion Water Company Ÿ 600 Lindley Street Ÿ Bridgeport, CT 06606
aquarionwater.com
 
3. Service line disturbance requirements – customer meter replacements - The LCRI proposes 
to maintain the requirement for water systems to provide pitcher filters or point-of-use 
devices and filter replacement cartridges to last six months when a lead, GRR, or unknown 
service line is disturbed, including when an inline meter is replaced.  Considering that the 
replacement of most customer meters involves simply closing a valve on each side of the 
meter setting, leaving the service line pressurized, we recommend that EPA not require the 
provision of a filter/device when a utility replaces a customer meter if the service line is 
not drained during the process. 
4. Service line disturbance requirements – water main breaks - EPA is proposing to retain the 
requirement that following operations that cause the water to be shut off to a lead, GRR, 
or unknown service line, water systems must provide customers with flushing instructions 
before the affected line is returned to service.  Depending on the allowed/required 
methods of communication, this requirement will cause delays in returning service to 
customers after system shutdowns, such as a shutdown to repair a main break. Consider 
that this would require utilities to provide these instructions to customer at all times of day 
and night before a repaired water main could be placed back into service.    We recommend 
that EPA clarify the acceptable methods of communicating the instructions, specifically if 
methods like door hangers, a reverse911 phone call, and/or email are acceptable. 
5. Replacement of customer-owned service line on customer’s private property - The 
proposed LCRI would require water systems to replace all lead and GRR service lines, and 
any lead connectors encountered, that are “under control of” the water system. EPA is 
proposing to treat a service line as under the system's control wherever a water system has 
adequate access; however, EPA is not proposing to delineate the prerequisites or elements 
of “access” that a system would need to conduct full-service line or connector replacement 
because of the wide variation of relevant State and local laws and water tariff agreements, 
as well as the potential for these to change over time. We recommend that EPA clarify that 
one of the prerequisites of “access” be customer consent, independent of all other 
prerequisites/elements.  Asking a utility to choose between trying to perform construction 
on a non-consenting customer’s property versus accepting a violation from its regulator is 
simply not reasonable.  Both options will result in disputes that will waste resources, both 
money and time, and the former option will create an adversarial relationship between the 
utility and impacted customers. 
 
6. 
Sample reporting requirements - EPA is requesting data, analyses, and comments on the 
feasibility of requiring systems to deliver all consumer notices of lead and copper tap 
sampling results within three days of the utility receiving the results, regardless of whether 
the results exceed the lead or copper action level.  A three-day requirement will place an 
undue burden on water systems. We recommend EPA instead consider a five-business day 
requirement and limit this requirement to samples that exceed the Action Level, retaining 
the current 30-day notification for all other samples. 
 
7. 
Fire services and other non-potable service lines – We recommend that EPA remove fire 
service and other non-potable service lines from the inventory and replacement 
requirements if a utility can show that the utility has appropriate administrative safeguards 
(e.g. customer communications) to prevent potable uses off these types of service lines.  
This would allow utilities to focus attention and resources on service lines from which 
customers are drinking the water.  
 

Aquarion Water Company Ÿ 600 Lindley Street Ÿ Bridgeport, CT 06606
aquarionwater.com
 
8. Cost of replacing portion of service line not owned by the water system - EPA proposes to 
remove from the LCRI any statements from the LCR and LCRR that address how a water 
system should or should not cover the cost of replacing services lines under the control of the 
system, as well as statements about whether a water system is or is not responsible for the 
cost of full service line replacement. We would like to emphasize the value and importance 
of federal funding (particularly grant funding) to cover the cost of the customer-owned 
portion of lead and GRR service lines, especially in economically challenged service areas of 
water systems. 
9. Customer requesting sampling – Under the LCRR, systems are required to offer to sample the 
tap water for lead for any customer who requests it when there is a system-wide lead action 
level exceedance. We recommend that this requirement be limited to customers who have 
lead, GRR, or unknown service lines. 
The health and safety of the communities we serve is of the utmost importance and we hope to work 
together to ensure the safe removal of lead. We respectfully request that EPA take our comments under 
consideration when finalizing the regulation. Thank you for the opportunity to provide our comments. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Aquarion Water Company

Thank you for the opportunity to provide public comment on the EPA’s revised Lead and Copper 
Rule. I completed the EJ Griot Program hosted by Black Millennials for Flint and am the Lead 
Free Baltimore Community Organizer. I have a Masters in Environmental Health from the Johns 
Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. I am a resident of Baltimore, MD and provide these 
comments as a concerned community member, whose neighborhood is undergoing the Lead 
Service Line Inventory process as mandated by the EPA. 
There is no safe level of lead in drinking water is safe.1,2 The EPA should decrease the 
current level of remediation from 10 ppb to 5 ppb.
Lead exposure has lifelong ramifications for youth, posing cognitive and behavioral 
challenges.2,3 Due to the longterm health and wellbeing ramification of lead exposure on youth, 
the EPA should mandate testing for lead in all public schools and childcare facilities and 
enforce water filtration with a level of remediation of at most 5 ppb. 
Lead exposure to adults also has alarming health ramifications, including increased risk of 
diabetes, high blood pressure, kidney disease, and other health challenges.4  Throughout the 
United States, Black people suffer from a higher incidence of high blood pressure and diabetes. 
5,6 Health interventions for these diseases often focus on lifestyle change. The lead and copper 
rule presents an opportunity to address the systemic factors at play in the onset of disease. 
Black people, particularly Black children are known to have the highest blood lead levels in the 
United States compared with other racial groups.7,8 This positions lead poisoning at the crux of 
environmental and health injustice. 
Climate change is now, and will worsen within the next decade. Salt water intrusion is a 
pressing issue in coastal cities, as salt water is five times more corrosive to lead pipes than 
freshwater.9 In 2023, the city of New Orleans was at risk of salt water corroding pipes during the 
water scare, with the county just to the south of New Orleans, Plaquemines Parish, losing

MILWAUKEE WATER WORKS COMMENTS ON U.S. EPA’S PROPOSED 
LEAD AND COPPER RULE IMPROVEMENTS (LCRI) REGULATION 
Published on: December 6, 2023
Comments Due: February 5, 2024

Code of Federal Regulations Reference: 40 CFR 141; 40 CFR 142
Agency/Docket Numbers: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801; FRL-5423.2-01-OW
Milwaukee Water Works (MWW) herein submits formal comments on the proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) intended to revise the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulation (NPDWR) under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA). MWW 
supports the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) ongoing efforts to reduce exposure to 
lead in our communities and improve long-term public health, and appreciates the opportunity 
to provide comments that could assist in making the finalized rule as impactful as it can be. 
10-year Timeline
MWW supports the proposed 10-year timeline for replacing all lead service lines in a 
municipality, and applauds the EPA's work to incentivize the replacement of remaining lead 
service lines. 
Bipartisan Infrastructure Law funding will allow Milwaukee to make significant progress 
towards this goal. However, when BIL funding is exhausted, the costs to complete this work 
within the 10-year goal will be borne by our customers and city taxpayers, leading to rate 
increases and limiting the city's ability to invest in other urgent priorities.  
Milwaukee Water Works urges the EPA to work with Congress to allocate additional funding to 
replace lead service lines and ensure that the 10-year rule is not an unfunded mandate. 
Sampling Protocol
The maximum contaminant level goal for lead is 0 µg/L because there is no safe level of lead 
exposure. The EPA has previously set the action level above the MCLG because the EPA 
recognizes that it is not feasible to reach the MCLG in all circumstances, even with the best 
available technology or treatment approaches. MWW supports the proposed Action level 
change from 15 µg/L to 10µg/L. Changing the sampling protocol in concert with the action level 
is problematic, as there is not sufficient data of first and fifth liter sampling across the country 

Page 2
to demonstrate that this new action level is achievable for most utilities. Many utilities would 
likely be in violation of the new action level, raising the question of what actions a utility would 
be required to take to mitigate lead risks, when a separate provision of these rules already 
requires expedited replacement of lead service lines.
MWW supports the change in the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) from sampling the 
first liter to sampling the fifth liter, to better represent the water in the lead service line. MWW 
has been collecting first liter samples, in compliance with the original Lead and Copper Rule, 
for decades. While we recognize the value in continuing to collect this data and sharing it with 
customers to help them make informed decisions about their water and internal plumbing, 
MWW requests that the 90th percentile determination is made solely based on fifth liter 
sampling results for homes with a lead service line. The fifth liter results will better demonstrate 
the effectiveness of a utility’s corrosion control treatment at preventing lead leaching from 
utility-owned pipes. The first liter results are helpful for homeowners and residents to 
understand their risk of lead exposure from internal plumbing and fixtures, but are not always 
representative of the water system overall.
Customer Notification of Results
MWW makes efforts to notify customers of their lead results as soon as possible after the 
testing has been completed, but assigning a deadline of three calendar days for all samples 
regardless of concentration, as is proposed in the LCRI, is sometimes not practical. A real 
world example is if the lab sends a large batch of results to the utility late on a Friday before a 
holiday weekend. There may not be sufficient staff present to contact a dozen or more 
customers in that moment, but prioritizing the immediate contact of any customers with results 
above the action level can and must be done. MWW recommends requiring utilities to reach 
out to customers when results are above the action level within three days either electronically 
(e.g. email or text message), by phone, or hand delivery. Sending a letter in the mail is not the 
most effective method of delivering such urgent news. MWW does still recommend requiring a 
letter for confirmation and follow-up, but the timeline for this step is less critical and urgent than 
the initial contact with the customer.
While it is still important to inform customers as soon as possible of results below the action 
level, it would be more practical to allow seven days for notification in these situations. All 
modes of communication identified in the LCRI (electronic, phone, hand delivery, or mailed 
letter) should be allowed for notifying customers of results below the action level. This would 
provide the flexibility needed for utilities to prioritize notifications of the highest results during 
periods of limited staffing, holiday weekends, or unrelated emergencies, while still developing 
systems to notify all customers of results within a week at the most. Utilities should make all 
reasonable efforts to send all results within three days, but allowing a slightly longer time frame
only for samples below the action level in the regulation acknowledges the limitations that will 
occasionally exist and appropriately prioritizes resources.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0963 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
1310 L St. NW, Suite 900 • Washington, D.C. 20005 • (202) 906-8000 • clasp.org 
Michael S. Regan, Administrator

RE: RIN 2040AG16 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
Dear Administrator Regan,  
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments and input to the US Environmental 
Protection Agency (EPA) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements” (LCRI).  We are pleased to see the EPA take robust and much needed action around 
updating the rule. This proposal will pave the way for significant improvements in the health and well-
being of many across our country, and finally address decades of harm that has impacted families across 
generations.  
The Center for Law and Social Policy (CLASP) is a national, nonpartisan nonprofit advancing anti-
poverty policy solutions that disrupt structural and systemic racism and sexism and remove barriers 
blocking people from economic security and opportunity. We work at the federal and state levels, 
supporting policy and practice that makes a difference in the lives of people living in conditions of 
poverty. CLASP works to develop and implement federal, state, and local policies (in legislation, 
regulation, and implementation) that reduce poverty, improve the lives of people with low incomes, and 
create pathways to economic security for everyone. That includes directly addressing the barriers 
people face because of race, ethnicity, gender, disability, and immigration status. Through high-quality 
analysis grounded in data and on-the-ground experience, effective advocacy, a strong public voice, and 
hands-on technical assistance, CLASP develops and promotes new ideas, mobilizes others, and provides 
guidance to government leaders and advocates to help them implement strategies that improve the 
lives of people across America. CLASP works to amplify the voices of directly impacted workers and 
families and help public officials design and implement effective programs. 
CLASP does not frequently weigh in on environmental issues, but we feel compelled to 
comment on this issue because of the significant impact of lead exposure to children’s health. Lead is a 
potent neurotoxin and is particularly dangerous for the brain development of infants and young 
children. Health experts agree that any amount of lead exposure is unsafe for human health.1 Yet, up to 
22 million Americans and possibly more drink tap water served by lead pipes.2 Moreover, replacing lead 
pipes is an equity issue, as lead exposure does not impact all households evenly, with Black children and 
children living in high poverty communities particularly at risk.3 In 2021 the Centers for Disease Control 
and Prevention published a study indicating that non-Hispanic Black children were at particular risk, as 
well as children living in areas with higher-than-average poverty rates.4 But lead pipes remain 
disproportionately concentrated in low-income communities and communities of color, in part due to 
decades of federal home ownership policies that have concentrated families of color in low-income 

 
 
 
 
1310 L St. NW, Suite 900 • Washington, D.C. 20005 • (202) 906-8000 • clasp.org 
communities.56 People in these communities are more likely to live in older housing where lead 
pipelines can still be found.7 For example, a 2020 Illinois study found that 65 percent of Black residents 
lived in areas that contained 94 percent of the state’s lead service lines, while only 30 percent of white 
residents lived in those communities.8 Unlike their higher-income counterparts, residents in these 
communities cannot afford to replace the lines themselves; and in most places, landlords are not 
required to replace lead service lines or even notify renters about them.9 These factors have combined 
to create lasting disproportionate exposures to environmental health hazards for families with low 
incomes and people of color.10  
 
For these reasons, CLASP believes that a strong lead and copper rule is critical to address this 
public health crisis so everyone can access safer drinking water. CLASP would also like to make the 
following recommendations to help strengthen this proposed rule:  
  
• 
Require water utilities to cover the full cost of lead service line replacement, so we’re not 
putting that financial burden on low-income homeowners. Water systems are not required to 
pay for full lead service line replacement, potentially leaving significant cost burdens on 
individual households, and making it more difficult to reach the 100 percent replacement rate 
required under the new rule. This raises environmental justice concerns because low-income 
homeowners are often unable to afford to pay for lead pipe removal, and landlords often refuse 
to do so, meaning that too often, lower-income people continue to drink water contaminated 
by lead pipes.11 
• 
Protect renters whose landlords are unlikely to pay the cost of lead pipe replacement. In the 
rule’s current form, water systems are not held responsible for replacing pipes if the property 
owner or landlord is unable or unwilling to pay. Water systems will be allowed to claim they 
don’t “control” service lines, for example, when they require property owners to pay a 
substantial sum for full replacement and the homeowners or landlords are unable or unwilling 
to pay. Under the proposal, no replacement is required at these homes. While renters are 
entitled to notice of lead paint in homes, only a few localities have similar protections related to 
lead water pipes. 
• 
Schools and childcare centers must be meaningfully addressed. Child care centers and other 
child care settings, such as child care homes and child care offered in other community settings, 
are deeply under resourced and need additional support and funding to meaningfully address 
the issue of lead pipes in their systems. We encourage the EPA to make bolder investments and 
provide additional guidance for child care centers to help facilitate the replacement of lead 
pipes at these facilities. The EPA should minimize the burden on child care settings and schools 
so that we can maximize the impact of the lead and copper pipe rule. 
• 
Remove loopholes that prolong the replacement of lead pipes. We don’t want another 
generation of kids to be harmed by lead pipes that are contaminating their tap water. The 

 
 
 
 
1310 L St. NW, Suite 900 • Washington, D.C. 20005 • (202) 906-8000 • clasp.org 
proposal includes two provisions allowing extensions of the deadline. The first is available to 
about three to seven systems nationally with more than 80,000 to 100,000 lead service lines—
so a city like Chicago could get 40 to 50 years to replace its lead pipes.12 A second provision 
would allow around 600 to more than 2,100 water systems across the country that have a 
relatively high percentage of lead pipes to get extensions for as much as an additional decade or 
more. These provisions must be fixed; we cannot allow more generations of kids to continue 
drinking leaded water.  
• 
Encourage states, localities, and tribal governments to prioritize job quality and equitable 
workforce practices.  It’s critical that public dollars be used to create family sustaining jobs that 
are accessible to workers traditionally underrepresented in the infrastructure trades, including 
women, workers of color, and individuals with barriers to employment.  Where possible the EPA 
should encourage the use of project labor agreements, community benefits agreements, local 
hiring, and economically targeted hiring practices to increase job quality and promote equity 
and access to publicly funded jobs.  We recommend the EPA study the example of Newark, New 
Jersey’s lead pipe replacement program that models many of these recommendations.13  
The EPA’s proposed rule demonstrates a strong commitment to address the clean drinking 
water crisis in this country and ensuring that everyone has the right to safe drinking water regardless of 
their race, income, or zip code. With these additional recommendations to help strengthen the rule, we 
can ensure that tens of millions of Americans who are drinking water from systems that have significant 
lead contamination issues are finally able to see some relief. If you have any additional questions and 
would like to connect further, please contact Priya Pandey at ppandey@clasp.org.  
Best,  
 
Priya Pandey, Policy Analyst  
Center for Law and Social Policy

Re: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, NEIWPCC Comments in response to the Proposed

Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
The New England Interstate Water Pollution Control Commission (NEIWPCC) appreciates the 
opportunity to comment on behalf of the States of the Northeast1 on the U.S. Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulation for lead and copper, hereafter referred to as the Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI).  NEIWPCC requests EPA to consider the comments of our member 
states.  
 
NEIWPCC was established by an act of the United States Congress which ratified the New 
England Interstate Water Pollution Control Compact in 1947.  NEIWPCC is a regional 
commission that helps Northeast states preserve and advance water quality.2  We engage and 
convene water quality professionals and other interested parties from New England and New 
York to collaborate on drinking water, wastewater, and environmental science challenges 
across shared regions and ecosystems.   
NEIWPCC commends EPA’s effort to strengthen existing protections for lead service lines 
(LSLs).  We all agree that lead is a public health issue which needs to be addressed.  We also 
know that there are other sources of lead.  For example, lead has been found in paint, tin-lead 
solder, and telecom lines3 to name a few.  In addition, structures built before 1940 which 
constitutes a large proportion of homes in the northeast4 are expected to have lead present 
throughout the home.  The multiple sources of lead exposure compel us to holistically assess 
 
1 These comments are made by NEIWPCC on behalf of all NEIWPCC member states (the six New England states 
and New York). Our individual member states may also provide comment letters with additional noteworthy guidance and advice to consider. 
Nothing in these NEIWPCC comments is intended to limit any individual state comments. 
2 NEIWPCC member states include the six New England states and the State of New York.   
3 New York battles telecom firms over lead-sheathed lines 
4 U.S.Census Bureau’s 2019 American Community Survey 

 
–2– 
the issue. Therefore, we ask that EPA work towards making this rule a component of a more 
comprehensive effort to remediate lead present in all forms in our communities.    
Personnel Capacity 
In recent years, our member states have addressed lead public health concerns through 
several mechanisms.  Some examples include: 
1. New York enacted the “Lead Pipe Right to Know Act.” The act requires water utilities 
across the state to publicly share how many LSLs are present in their distribution 
system and where those lines are located. It also requires the New York State 
Department of Health to make an inventory of these LSLs publicly available, including 
interactive maps, to aid with replacement efforts.  From New York’s perspective, this 
will allow communities to have an informed conversation regarding LSL replacement5.  
 
2. Rhode Island enacted the “Lead Poisoning Prevention Act.” The act creates a 
replacement program for public and private LSLs, requiring they be replaced within 10 
years. The act also requires a lead risk assessment to be conducted for any home built 
prior to 2011 as part of any property transaction6. Additionally, the state passed 
legislation establishing a statewide rental registry for lead conformance certificates and 
stronger penalties for landlords found to have violated lead safety laws. Rhode Island 
hopes these actions will strengthen protections for renters and reduce the occurrence 
of childhood lead poisoning7.   
While our member states appreciate the steps EPA is taking to replace LSLs, a bigger issue for 
the states is the personnel needed to execute both the state and federal initiatives. Frankly, 
the states are having difficulties filling their current positions.  With the addition of the new 
rules, the states will need to significantly expand their staff to comply.   
Compounding this shortfall, our member states are also struggling to retain the staff they 
have. Some of the difficulties include the private sector luring trained personnel from public 
sector jobs. As a result, local and state agencies are constantly losing trained personnel.  We 
ask that EPA consider the cost impact of personnel challenges in developing the final rule. 
 
Cost 
The EPA “estimates the proposed rule would cost between $2.1 and 3.6 billion per year”, with 
costs “primarily associated with identifying and replacing [LSLs], making lead filters available, 
and changes in water treatment8.” Based on a review of the cost to comply with the more 
 
5 New York Lead Pipe Right to Know Act  
6 Lead Poisoning Prevention Act becomes law  
7 Attorney General Neronha issues guidance to Rhode Island landlords about new lead poisoning prevention laws 
8 Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements Information Webinar 

 
–3– 
stringent rule, it has become apparent that the proposed funds will fall short of the cost 
burden.    
The State of New York has replaced approximately 3,500 service lines to date and has found 
the average cost to range between $5,000-10,000 per line. With roughly half a million lines 
remaining, they estimate it could cost between $2.5-5 billion to replace all remaining service 
lines in their state alone. These estimates do not take into consideration rising cost associated 
with inflation, procurement, workforce constraints, and rising contractor costs. This is 
consistent with American Water Works Association’s (AWWA) estimated average cost to 
replace a single LSL as more than $10,0009. Currently, EPA estimates there are 9.2 million LSLs 
across the country10, meaning the total cost to replace all LSLs could exceed $90 billion. EPA 
has allocated $36 billion over a 10-year period which is $54 billion less than AWWA’s estimate 
without considering inflation.   
 
Currently $15 billion has been allocated for “[LSL] replacement projects and associated 
activities directly connected to the identification of and planning for the replacement of 
[LSLs]”. Additionally, there will be $11.7 billion in funding available through the Drinking Water 
State Revolving Loan Fund (DWSRF)11.  Systems are already facing significant challenges 
relating to per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, cybersecurity, and other infrastructure 
upgrade investments. As these initiatives are also supported by DWSRF, the available funding 
for LSL replacement could be significantly impacted. In addition, the DWSRF has earmarked 
funds for special projects which further reduces the overall availability of funds. Our states 
appreciate the funds that have been made available through BIL and DWSRF, and we ask the 
EPA to evaluate increasing the financing necessary to support this rule.   
 
Communication 
Effective communication and education will be vital to the success of the rule. Our states 
appreciate the acknowledgment of the difficulties in communicating with private entities and 
have found it to be an extremely challenging endeavor. Cooperation from homeowners has 
been difficult. Many are worried about negative effects on property values and disruptions in 
services. While EPA is proposing strategies for communication, these efforts will take time and 
demand an increase in personnel to perform outreach, tracking, and responding to public 
inquiries. We ask that EPA consider allowing state agencies, with input from their local 
stakeholders, to determine and propose a “reasonable effort” strategy.  It should be noted 
that the strategy in a rural community will differ from a strategy in a city or suburb.  We 
understand that this will require the states to determine the most effective means of 
engagement with the local populace and develop a communication tracking mechanism. 
 
9AWWA Final Report - Considerations when Costing Lead Service Line Identification and Replacement (2022) 
10 EPA 7th Report to Congress - Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment (2023) 
11 Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements Information Webinar 

 
–4– 
Additionally, the lower lead action levels and change in sampling technique, notably the 
collection of a fifth liter sample, will likely increase the number of exceedances.   Concurrently, 
the frequency of exceedance communications will also increase.  We ask the EPA to consider 
developing resources and materials for states and water systems to streamline 
communication, ensure consistent messaging, and possibly reduce the burden on drinking 
water systems. 
Corrosion Control 
 
EPA is also proposing “to further streamline the rule by deferring the optimal corrosion control 
treatment and re-optimized optimal corrosion control treatment processes for systems that 
can remove 100 percent of LSLs within five years of the date the system is triggered into the 
corrosion control treatment steps12.”  Tin-lead solder can leach from homes which contain 
copper piping.  This has the potential to increase lead concentration should the drinking water 
system eliminate/reduce their corrosion control measures. States are concerned that EPA has 
not fully evaluated this potential contamination source.  To truly eliminate lead exposure, 
consideration of issues like the presence of tin-lead solder in homes must be addressed. 
Accordingly, our member states would ask the EPA to acknowledge and address the potential 
release of lead from solder, specifically in private home plumbing, in the final rule. 
 
Disposal  
 
The estimated 9.2 million LSLs which still need to be replaced will likely generate millions of 
tons of waste which will need to be properly disposed.  “In April 2014, Flint, MI switched its 
drinking water source from water treated in Detroit to Flint River water without applying 
corrosion control. This caused lead and other metals to leach into drinking water.” The metals 
of concern included Pb, Cu, Zn, and Cd, and levels were found to decrease after LSL removal 
over long-term period13. This trend suggests that LSLs will likely leach metals of concern after 
removal. 
 
Our states are very concerned that the waste generated from the replacement of LSLs be 
appropriately disposed and managed.  For example, if the LSL waste is landfilled, metal-laden 
leachate can be generated.  Leachate will generate metal-laden sludge which can be 
reintroduced into the environment.  Accordingly, our member states would ask the EPA to 
acknowledge and address the potential legacy impact from LSL disposal in the final rule.

Michigan.” Environmental Science: Water Research & Technology, Royal Society of Chemistry, 12 Mar. 2021. - This study analyzed a suite of 
metals from water samples collected in homes from Flint, MI that had their LSLs replaced.

State of Colorado Safe Drinking Water Program Comments Concerning National
Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements Proposed
Rule
The Safe Drinking Water Program in the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment
(Colorado) is pleased to provide comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).
Colorado adopts and enforces regulations and provides assistance to public drinking water systems to
ensure that they provide safe drinking water to the public.
In general, Colorado supports the proposed LCRI and EPA’s efforts to reduce complexity in the rule
while enhancing public health protection. Colorado appreciates EPA’s improvements to the rule
involving mandatory lead service line removal and lowering the lead action level. Removing lead lines
is necessary to protect consumers from one of the leading contributors of lead exposure in drinking
water. Colorado encourages EPA to review the feedback and concerns from states and stakeholders in
order to further strengthen the public health protections for lead exposure from drinking water while
recognizing opportunities to reduce some of the burden, costs, and environmental impacts associated
with certain aspects of the LCRI.
Colorado’s comments and recommendations support a final rule that furthers the goal of reducing lead
in tap water while simplifying and clarifying what remains a complex and challenging rule for public
drinking water systems to comply with, and for state agencies to oversee. Colorado is providing
comments regarding the proposed LCRI, including but not limited to:
1.
Colorado is supportive of the lowered lead action level to 0.010 mg/L from the current 0.015
mg/L level, and the removal of the lead trigger level to improve health protection and reduce
rule complexity while improving public health protection.
2.
Colorado generally supports the proposal to allow accelerated lead service line replacement
within five years in lieu of implementing optimal corrosion control treatment. However,
Colorado believes that stronger safeguards need to be implemented to reduce lead exposure
during this five-year timeframe, such as offers to provide pitcher filters to taps with known or
suspected lead service lines, and implementation of an effective, but not necessarily optimal,
corrosion control treatment.
3.
Colorado previously commented in 2021 that EPA should add a provision to the Lead and Copper
Rule Revisions that allowed for an approach similar to that taken by Denver Water under its
variance approved by EPA. The variance took a holistic approach toward lead exposure
reduction, which EPA noted at the time of issuance as a model for the nation.The variance
approach involves:
○
Inventorying and removing lead service lines, including prioritizing Environmental
Justice in the effort,

○
Implementing corrosion control treatment, though it is not optimal, it is not
detrimental to the environment,
○
Educating the public, and
○
Providing filters to all taps with known or suspected lead service lines.
This approach is better for public health, the environment, environmental justice, and cost
effectiveness compared to moving forward with optimal corrosion control treatment in some
cases. This option should be considered again by EPA as it finalizes the Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements, especially since the proposed expedited five-year lead service line removal
provisions may be unattainable for large systems with many lead service lines.
4.
Based on previous statements from EPA indicating there would be no changes to the service line
inventory requirements, Colorado has concerns that the proposed requirement to document
connector materials places an undue burden on water systems that have been diligently
working on the existing inventory requirements for the last few years. Colorado recommends
that including connector materials in the inventory be optional, especially since the proposed
rule sets forth no new requirements to remove lead-containing connectors. Colorado views this
proposed change as an added cost and complexity for water systems and states to identify and
track connector materials, with little to no public health benefit over the existing
requirements.
5.
Additionally, Colorado believes that EPA’s proposal to reduce the time frame to notify
consumers of their individual lead tap results from 30 days to three (3) calendar days is
unwarranted with no added health benefit except in cases where elevated lead is found.
Considering weekends, holidays, and water system resources, Colorado believes the proposed
deadline will be impossible for many water systems to comply with and challenging for states
to oversee, resulting in many violations being issued and needing to be tracked to resolution.
We recommend that EPA consider a longer time frame.
6.
Finally, based on feedback from water systems across the state, Colorado understands that
service line and interior plumbing materials are not easily or legally accessible to water system
personnel in many instances. Colorado encourages EPA to consider utilizing lead plumbing
disclosures to renters and home buyers similar to the process by which lead-containing paint is
disclosed. This would help increase customer engagement, improve risk communications, and
allow for more efficient confirmation and replacement of lead plumbing materials. EPA should
deploy these mechanisms in its “whole of government” approach to reducing lead exposure.
Colorado’s specific comments in response to the proposed LCRI Section IX Request for Comment (FR
pages 85035 to 85038) are provided in the enclosed Attachment A. Colorado has also collaborated with
members of the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators (ASDWA) on providing input and is
supportive of ASDWA’s comments.
Colorado thanks you for the opportunity to provide these additional comments on this very important
subject.
Sincerely,
Nicole Rowan, P.E.
Director, Water Quality Control Division
Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment

Colorado Comments
IX. Request for Comment General Matters
1
Whether the proposed revisions to the LCRR treatment
technique are effective to prevent known or anticipated
adverse health effects to the extent feasible in accordance
with the SDWA.
Colorado supports this statement.
2
Whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the
complexity of the regulatory approach used to address lead in
drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a
treatment technique rule in section 1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA.
Specifically, EPA requests comment on ways that the proposed
LCRI could be simplified and ways that burden, including
paperwork burden, could be reduced without affecting the
ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse
health effects.
Colorado supports simplifications to the rule via removal of
the lead trigger level of 10 ppb and lowering of the lead
action level to 10 ppb.
Colorado is concerned that the "Distribution System and
Site Assessment" requirements following an individual
result above the action level are still overly complex and
burdensome to implement for systems and states. With the
lower action level and improved sampling method, there
will be a large increase in the number of sites subject to
these requirements. Tracking each high lead result for
proper follow-up will require substantial resources from
primacy agencies.
In Colorado, the majority of lead Action Level Exceedances
(ALEs) occur at systems without lead service lines. At
non-LSL sites, since the result is likely due to premise
plumbing and outside the jurisdiction of the water system,
Distribution System and Site Assessment requirements
could be best addressed within additional content
requirements of the consumer notification of lead tap
results (e.g. must include an offer to re-sample at no cost,
and explanation that switching to “lead-free” faucets can
substantially reduce lead levels in tap water). This would
be more efficient and not present an increase to public
health risk.
Colorado proposes confirmation lead sampling be utilized
to determine if a Distribution System and Site Assessment
is triggered. The results of the original and confirmation
sample can be used to rule out common sampling issues by
customers prior to additional actions.
Colorado additionally proposes that once triggered, then
the following actions be required:
-Customer notice of results and education with information
about the filters.
-If present, removal of the lead service line within 120
days or on a state-approved schedule.
-For systems serving more than 50,000 people, a Water
1

quality Parameter and corrosion treatment assessment.
Colorado’s proposal is based on the likelihood that smaller
systems with water quality and corrosion issues will
already exceed the lead action level based on five or ten
tap samples, versus a large system that takes additional
samples during the monitoring period and where localized
water quality issues can be improved through adjustments
to water age and corrosion treatment.
Additionally, Colorado recommends that EPA provide more
clarification, and flexibility for states, on the validation
steps required for non-lead service lines. This adds
complexity to the rule and substantial additional
requirements for systems and states. Colorado
recommends that EPA provide further clarifications and
examples of what sites should be included in the validation
pool. Additionally, Colorado recommends that if a water
system used a statistical method that is at least as
stringent as EPA’s, or an evidence based, state-specific
verification method, they should be allowed to meet this
requirement without further investigation.
3
Whether the proposed requirements of the rule are
enforceable and promote compliance without the need for
State or Federal enforcement action. EPA also solicits
comment on ways the rule could be modified to better
promote compliance.
Colorado agrees that the rule is enforceable, but as with
any additional requirement placed on water systems,
additional non-compliance and enforcement actions will
occur. Unless thorough and complete guidance and forms
are available to primacy agencies and water systems at the
effective date of LCRI, states and water systems will be
unprepared for the compliance challenges the LCRI
presents.
IX. Request for Comment Service Line Replacement
4
All aspects of the proposed scope of the replacement
requirements, including the criteria used to define a full

EPA should not include lead connectors as part of

during infrastructure work.
5

9
EPA also seeks comment on whether systems should be

Colorado does not support a minimum replacement rate in

10

Colorado has concerns that the replacement rate may

11
EPA is taking comment on whether States, as a condition of

Colorado does not support this requirement. Colorado

12
The overall approach and basis to offer deferred service line

Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
item.
13
Whether to require the State, as a condition of primacy, to
approve the use of the deferred deadline provision where the

feasible for a system to meet the 10-year deadline or a

Colorado does not support making this a condition of
primacy. This appears to add complexity for states by
trying to demonstrate how they would do this before the

14
Whether there are additional data on service line replacement
rates achieved by systems in proactive programs (i.e.,
excluding programs that only replace service lines in
coordination with main replacement or emergency repair).
Colorado supports the ability for states to approve a water
system’s holistic lead reduction program (e.g. EPA-granted
Dever Water Variance) when optimal treatment for lead
service lines is detrimental to the environment or there are
serious wastewater implications (e.g. orthophosphate) and
where an expedited lead service line replacement program
of five years is infeasible due to the number of lead service
lines present. This holistic approach should encompass at a
minimum: implementation of corrosion control treatment
3

that reduces lead levels, ongoing public education, free
pitcher filter availability, lead service line inventory and
replacement that prioritizes Environmental Justice during
the replacement period, and no-cost sampling upon
request. Colorado believes holistic approaches will better
protect public health while lead service lines are still
present in a system. Necessary oversight of such programs
could be guaranteed through additional 142 requirements.
15
The proposed use of a maximum threshold of 10,000 annual

Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this

Whether systems conducting deferred service line
replacement should be subject to any additional requirements

Colorado believes that requiring a statement in CCR (for

18
The requirement for systems to install a dielectric coupling
when conducting a partial replacement of an LSL or GRR to
separate the remaining LSL or GRR service line and the

Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
item.
19
The proposed requirement to ban partial lead and GRR service
line replacement unless it is conducted in accordance with
emergency or planned infrastructure work (excluding planned
infrastructure work solely for the purposes of replacing lead
and GRR service lines as part of a service line replacement
program).
Colorado does not support this requirement. This ban could
be infeasible at times. See additional comments below.
20
EPA is seeking comment on whether partial service line
replacement should be prohibited during “planned
infrastructure work” or with certain types of planned
infrastructure work.
Colorado does not support prohibition of partial service
line replacements during planned infrastructure work.
Doing LSLR during infrastructure work such as main
replacements is an efficient and cost-effective way to
replace at least a portion of the SL and since this is
planned work, allows adequate time for homeowner
outreach. If a homeowner declines, the system should still
be able to replace their portion of the line, especially if
damaged. The inference is that if the line is damaged, the
system would need to replace it with a lead line. The
proposed rule has other protective measures in place such
as requiring the addition of dielectric couplings during
partial replacements, additional flushing and risk
mitigation requirements, annual notification of
lead/GRR/unknown service lines, and notification after
change of ownership to reduce lead exposure after a
4

partial replacement. Disallowing partial replacements
during planned infrastructure work will ultimately leave
more lead service lines in place and could be technically
infeasible in some circumstances leaving systems with no
options to comply and states in a bad position as well in
terms of oversight.
21
The ability of the market to correct for potential shortages in
workers and materials to conduct service line replacement, as
well to provide sufficient quantities of filters to comply with
the service line replacement and other relevant provisions in
the proposal.
Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
item.
22
The extent to which property owner consent, if required by
State or local law or water tariff agreement, might
complicate full service line replacement and whether there
are additional measures EPA can take to facilitate access
through the LCRI.
Colorado believes that obtaining property owner consent
for access for service line verification and replacements is
a significant complicating factor for full service line
replacement. Throughout the majority of Colorado, there
are no existing local laws or water tariff agreements that
allow water systems to access private property to verify or
replace service lines. This leaves a lot of unknowns and the
potential for lead service lines to be left in the ground.
Colorado encourages the federal government to consider
expanding real estate disclosures about potential lead
hazards to include service line material information
through authorities available to the US Department of
Housing and Urban Development (HUD). This could help
increase participation in service line identification and
replacement, and improve risk communications.

IX. Request for Comment Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan
29
EPA is proposing a threshold of systems serving greater than
50,000 persons to host the inventory and plan online, which is
the required threshold under the LCRR. EPA is seeking
comment on the size threshold at which systems must host
their publicly accessible inventory, inventory summary data,

online, and whether it should be lowered relative to the LCRR

Colorado believes that setting the threshold at systems
serving greater than 10,000 persons (large and medium

could be made available online via an online file sharing
service such as Google Drive instead of a website. EPA
should provide states the authority to require online
posting of the inventory information at their discretion.
30
EPA is proposing a requirement for systems to validate the
accuracy of non-lead service lines in their inventory that were
categorized using methods other than records review or visual
inspection of at least two points along the line. EPA is
requesting comment on the number of validations required,
the proposed 95 percent confidence level approach used to
develop the number of validations required, the criteria for
which methods used to categorize non-lead service lines
should be included in the validation pool (including whether
non-lead lines categorized based on records should be subject
to validation), and the seven-year timeline for systems on a
10-year replacement deadline to complete the validation
requirements.
Colorado recommends that EPA provide additional
information and clarification on this requirement, and
allow states the authority to determine what sites need
validation since the LCRR allows for verification using
resources or information provided or required by the state.
Specifically, Colorado recommends EPA provide
clarification on:
- Whether this applies to lines that were determined to be
non-lead by way of a predictive/statistical method (e.g.,
20% verified or enough to reach 95% confidence level).
Colorado supports ASDWA’s recommendation that if a water
system used a statistical method that is at least as
stringent as EPA’s, they should be allowed to meet this
requirement without further investigation.
- If a service line was determined to be non-lead based on
being built after the lead ban, are systems required to
validate those lines?
- What about state-specific decisions for material
classification that were made under the LCRR based on
state-specific circumstances? The LCRR allows for using
"Any resource, information, or identification method
provided or required by the State to assess service line
materials." This should still apply under the LCRI and

excluded from the verification pool.
Colorado recommends the EPA not require systems to
include sites that were classified non-lead based on
records in the validation pool. This would be a large
burden for systems. Colorado recommends EPA provide
6

guidance on steps systems should take if they determine
through field evidence that records are not accurate. It is
unlikely that a service line with a record indicating
non-lead material would have later been replaced with
lead.
31
Comment on establishing a deadline for systems to identify all

Colorado recommends that EPA keep a single deadline for

32
Comment on a requirement for systems to update their

replacement.
Colorado supports this requirement. However, Colorado
does not expect that this will impact many water systems
in our state.
Colorado notes that the LCRI preamble says States would
be required to identify any State laws that pertain to a
water system's access to conduct full LSLR and notify water
systems in writing by the LCRI compliance date. States
must also notify systems within six months of the
enactment of any new or revised State law impacting
access to full service line replacement. Colorado does not
support this action if required in the final rule, unless
available State guidance can be utilized in lieu of direct
notification.
IX. Request for Comment Lead Action and Trigger Levels
33
EPA is seeking comment on the proposed lead action level of
0.010 mg/L, as well as comment and supporting data on
alternative action levels, such as 0.005 mg/L, with regards to
generally effective corrosion control treatment and
identifying systems most at risk of elevated levels of lead in
drinking water.
Colorado supports lowering the lead action level to 0.010
mg/L, but recommends the lead action level not be
lowered any further at this time. The proposed lower
action level of 0.010 mg/L represents a significant public
health improvement and reduction in rule complexity by
removing the trigger level. However, this will significantly
increase the number of action level exceedances that
occur, and the number of systems required to install OCCT,
which will be orthophosphate in the majority of cases. In
Colorado, the majority of lead action level exceedances
occur at water systems without lead service lines. For
feasibility of rule administration and compliance, and from
an environmental perspective, Colorado is concerned about
lowering the lead action level further.
34
EPA is also seeking comment on the use of the action level to
determine when additional public education is required, and
the use of the same action level for public education as for
the CCT provisions.
Colorado supports the using the same lead action level to
determine when public education is required and for CCT
provisions.
35
EPA is seeking public comment, data, and information on the
anticipated benefits and tradeoffs, including for public health
and administrative burden on systems and States, if more
small and medium systems are required to conduct a detailed
OCCT demonstration and take other actions if they exceed the
proposed action level of 0.010 mg/L or other lower values,
Colorado believes detailed OCCT demonstration efforts by
more small and medium systems will have few benefits
with the requirements to remove lead service lines over
the next 10 years of LCRI.
7

while water systems are simultaneously required to
mandatory conduct full service line replacement.
IX. Request for Comment Corrosion Control
36
The proposed determination that the CTT treatment
technique is feasible and prevents known or anticipated
adverse health effects to the extent feasible.
Colorado supports this statement, and believes that
collaboration between states and EPA in developing
guidance and training on CCT is critical and should be
prioritized by the Agency. Colorado encourages EPA to
consider an approach that allows states the ability to
approve a water system’s holistic lead reduction program
(e.g. EPA-granted Dever Water Variance) when optimal
treatment for lead service lines is detrimental to the
environment or there are serious wastewater implications
(e.g. orthophosphate) and where an expedited lead service
line replacement program of five years is infeasible due to
the number of lead service lines present (see details in
Row 14 above). Should EPA not want to include this option
within the rule directly, Colorado recommends EPA
consider granting a path forward for states and the water
system with approval from the EPA Regional Administrator.
37
Comment on whether it would be more appropriate to require
water systems to re-optimize again following an action level
exceedance regardless of meeting their optimal water quality
parameters and to provide the State with the authority to
waive this requirement.
Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment on requiring
re-optimization following an action level exceedance,
regardless of if a system is meeting optimal water quality
parameters or has previously re-optimized treatment.
38
The proposed option for a water system to delay OCCT until
after the system has replaced all of its LSLs and GRR service
lines, while the system achieves at least 20 percent removal
per year and must have no LSLs, GRR service lines, or lead
status unknown service lines remaining at the end of the
five-year period.
Colorado supports this option, especially since there are
concerns about phosphate as a downstream contaminant in
Colorado. However, Colorado recommends that stronger
safeguards should be implemented to reduce lead exposure
during this five-year timeframe, such as offers to provide
pitcher filters to taps with known or suspected lead service
lines, and implementation of an effective, but not
necessarily optimal, corrosion control treatment.
Otherwise, the proposed option could allow for lead
exposure without adequate protections for up to five
years. Colorado recommends EPA consider an approach
similar to that taken by Denver Water under its variance
approved by EPA. The variance approach involves
inventorying and removing lead service lines, implementing
corrosion control treatment, though it is not optimal,
educating the public, and providing filters to all taps with
known or suspected lead service lines. It is also possible
that lead will remain in the system through other media
such as solder, internal plumbing, and fixtures.
39
The treatment recommendation and CCT study process can
take multiple years to complete. For systems with existing
corrosion control, the system may be able to alter the existing
treatment (e.g., increase pH and/or orthophosphate dose)
without a new CCT study on a much faster timeframe rather
than waiting for study results that may recommend that same
change. EPA is requesting comment on whether there are
Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
item.
8

situations and/or conditions where existing treatment
modifications may achieve similar lead reductions rather than
delaying new treatment for two-and-a-half years while a study
is underway.
IX. Request for Comment: Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems
and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water Systems
40
EPA is proposing that small system flexibilities be limited to
CWSs serving 3,300 persons and fewer and all NTNCWSs for
the remaining compliance alternatives of point-of-use devices
and plumbing replacement. EPA is seeking comment on

system compliance flexibility provision.
Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment on small system

doesn’t control their distribution system.
41

Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment that POU devices and
plumbing replacement are not as effective as OCCT for
systems serving up to 10,000 persons
42
EPA is requesting comment on the ability and practicality of

IX. Request for Comment Public Education
43
The proposed determination that the public education
treatment technique is feasible and prevents known or
anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible.
Colorado agrees with the proposed determination.
44
Comment and supporting data on the capacity of water
systems to conduct some or all of the required public
education activities in 30 days, or another period of time that
is less than 30 or 60 days, after the end of the tap sampling
period in which a systemwide lead action level exceedance
occurs.
Colorado recommends EPA leave the deadline as 60 days
after the end of the monitoring period. The majority of
Colorado systems do not complete public education
requirements within 30 days. Colorado is uncertain
whether a shorter timeframe could be feasible but since
Tier 1 public notice is required following a lead action
level exceedance, Colorado feels there are adequate risk
communication measures in place and shortening the
public education deadline does not add additional public
health benefits.
45
Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination
that water systems are capable of providing consumer notices
of individual tap sampling results within three calendar days
of obtaining those results, regardless of whether the results
exceed the lead or copper action level, or if a longer time
frame is needed (e.g., three business days, seven calendar
days, 14 calendar days).
A three day timeframe is very tight and could be difficult
for many systems (especially small and rural systems) to
comply with, especially if it involves a weekend or holiday
or both. If a system has a lead ALE, they will be doing T1
PN already, which is resource intensive and eats into time
available to provide notice of tap sample results.
Notification of results below the action level within three
(3) days creates a false sense of urgency as well. The
shortened time frame creates additional complexity and
places a burden on states overseeing this requirement.
Because many systems will be unable to comply with the
three-day requirement, states will likely see an increased
workload with issuing violations for failure to comply, and
working with systems to return to compliance, with much
of this effort involving low lead test results.
9

Colorado recommends EPA allow at least ten (10) calendar
days to provide consumer notice of individual tap results.
46
Whether the proposed requirement for water systems to offer
lead sampling to consumers with LSLs, GRR service lines, or
unknown service lines in the notice of service line material is
effective at reducing adverse health effects.
Colorado agrees with ASDWA’s comment on offering lead
sampling. However, Colorado believes that reducing
adverse health effects at known lead and GRR sites may be
better done through notification/education about LSLR.
47
EPA is also requesting comment on the requirement for water
systems to deliver consumer-initiated test results within three
days of obtaining those results.
See above. Colorado recommends the EPA allow at least
ten (10) calendar days.
48
Whether the types and timing of outreach activities proposed
for systems failing to meet the mandatory service line
replacement rate are appropriate and whether other activities
should be considered.
ASDWA comments that the number of meetings or events
should be tailored to the demographics of the customers
and community and, for instance, one town hall meeting
would not be sufficient to reach enough customers for a
larger system. Colorado agrees with ASDWA’s comment on
types of outreach activities.
49
Whether EPA should require systems to annually notify
consumers if they are served by a lead connector, in addition
to notifications for sites with lead, GRR, or lead status
unknown service lines.
Colorado does not agree that customers must be notified
about lead connectors, since there is no requirement to
actively remove lead connectors in the LCRI. There are
also issues with notification pertaining to known lead
connectors and presumed lead connectors which would
make ongoing communication incorrect for many years.
Colorado supports a recommendation that systems
communicate about lead connectors accurately when their
presence is known.
50
Whether EPA should require additional public education
requirements to further encourage swift service line
replacement faster than the 10-year replacement deadline.
For example, should water systems that have LSLs, GRR
service lines, or unknown service lines five years after the
compliance date for the LCRI be required to increase the
frequency of the notification of service line materials from
annual to once every six months?
EPA should not require additional public education
requirements to encourage faster LSLR. The effectiveness
of this approach is uncertain. Requiring more frequent
public education after a certain time within the allowed
time frame for replacement creates mistrust and a false
sense that the system is in the wrong. States have the
ability to set shorter LSLR deadlines for systems if possible,
so if a shorter replacement time frame is feasible, then
the state can specify that.
51
EPA is seeking information and data on when a system
provides translated materials to consumers with limited
English proficiency, what resources are used to translate
materials (e.g., State resources, community organizations),
and what barriers water systems may face in providing
accurate translated materials.
Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
topic, but encourages EPA to develop translated templates
and provide the necessary tools and resources for states
and water systems.
52
Whether the Agency should require States, as a condition of
primacy, to provide translation support to water systems that
are unable to do so for public education materials to
consumers with limited English proficiency.
Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment that EPA should not
make this a condition of primacy. Many states do not have
the resources for this and this burden should not fall on the
state. The requirements to implement provisions of the
Safe Drinking Water Act should always be the responsibility
of the water systems. States are responsible for overseeing
and enforcing the requirements, not meeting them. Some
states may choose to do this, and Colorado has helped
systems with this on many occasions, but this kind of
provision would fundamentally change the Safe Drinking
10

Water Act and create some potentially unforeseen
consequences in terms of liability and other issues. This
could also become a slippery slope if applied to other
provisions in the Safe Drinking Water Act that systems fail
to do.
53
EPA is also requesting comment on additional ways to
streamline public education and associated certification
requirements (e.g., combine deadlines for systems to conduct
public education or submit information to the State).
The due dates for the public education and associated
certification requirements do not align. Colorado
recommends that EPA work with ASDWA to identify ways to
streamline deadlines for states and PWSs in the final rule.

Whether EPA should require water systems to make filters

since lead can come from faucets and fixtures. EPA needs

The proposed requirements for systems to develop a filter

plan.
11

60
Alternative requirements for systems with multiple action
level exceedances to provide filters to their consumers, such

cartridges to consumers served by an LSL, GRR service line, or
unknown service line or to all consumers, or to require

for multiple action level exceedances, after which the State

Colorado supports making filters available to all customers

IX. Request for Comment Lead Sampling in Schools and Child Care Facilities
63
Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples
and/or to sample more frequently in schools and child care
facilities.
Colorado does not recommend additional sampling or
sampling more frequently in schools and child care
facilities. Many schools and child care facilities have been
sampled and lead remediated already under state laws.
Because there is still no provision to remediate high lead in
schools and child care facilities under the proposed LCRI,
requiring additional or more frequent sampling isn't
necessarily more protective of public health.
64
The proposed provision to allow States to issue waivers to

sampling in schools and child care facilities during the
five-year period after the LCRI compliance date if the facility
was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021 but prior to the
LCRI compliance date and the sampling otherwise meets the
waiver requirements of § 141.92(h).
Colorado supports this provision.
65
Whether or not to allow States to waive the requirements of §

install POU devices and maintain them.
Colorado supports ASDWA’s comments to not create this
additional waiver as it would add a significant burden to
states and water systems.
66
The minimum requirements for States to provide a waiver
(e.g., should the waiver be limited to locations where the

Colorado has no specific comment or feedback on this
topic.
12

67
Whether EPA should require CWSs to make school and child

Colorado recommends the sampling results be made
publicly available. This aligns with requirements to make
routine tap sampling results publicly available. There is
also no requirement in the proposed LCRI for the results to
be provided to parents so this would allow them to see the

IX. Request for Comment Reporting and Recordkeeping
68
EPA is requesting comment on the expansion of the inventory
reporting to include lead connectors and non-lead service

Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment regarding optional
inclusion of lead connectors and non-lead service lines in
inventory reporting. Colorado has concerns that this
proposed requirement runs counter to previous statements
from EPA that there would be no changes to the service
line inventory requirements, and creates an undue burden
for water systems that have been diligently working on the
existing inventory requirements for the last few years. The
LCRR requirement to remove a lead connector when
encountered during infrastructure work ensures that
connectors will still be replaced over time. Colorado views
this change as an added cost to systems and states to
identify and track with little public health benefit over the
existing requirements.
69

whether EPA should consider a phased approach or alternate
approach to reduce the burden on States following the rule
compliance date.
Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment on using a phased
approach for the review of site sampling plans to reduce
the burden on states following the rule compliance date.
Requesting information, reviewing, and correcting issues
with sampling plans is time and resource intensive.
Colorado’s sample plan verification effort spanned several
years. These efforts will be further complicated by new
tier levels and the requirement to inventory connectors.
70
EPA is requesting comment on whether States should be

Colorado supports ASDWA’s comment on maintaining

IX. Request for Comment Definitions
76
EPA is seeking comment on all aspects of the proposed
definitions, and specifically the following: b. EPA is proposing
to define a two-foot maximum length of connectors. EPA
proposes that “connectors” that exceed two feet in length be
treated as a service line. EPA is requesting comment on the
defined length of a connector
Colorado supports EPA’s efforts to define what constitutes a
“connector”, but the current definition of a connector
needs to be further clarified to explicitly state that
anything over the defined length is considered a lead
service line. This will have a significant impact on what is
classified as a “galvanized requiring replacement” service
line. Additionally, the rule should specify which connectors
(i.e., only the connection to main) are required to be
included in the inventory.
Questions from within Preamble
77
A system’s existing authority to access the service line and
complete the full service line replacement might provide the
system with the legal authority to conduct the service line
replacement over the objection of the property owner or
resident. However, as some stakeholders noted, requiring
service line replacement at properties where customers
object to their replacement could create potential safety
concerns for utility staff. EPA is seeking comment on whether
the proposed LCRI should either allow systems to treat those
service lines as not under the control of the system and forego
replacement of the lines or require systems to conduct full
service line replacement in situations where the system has
legal access to conduct the full replacement but property
In situations where replacement could create potential
safety concerns for utility staff, the rule should allow
systems to treat those service lines as not under the
control of the system and forego replacement of the lines.
It is unreasonable to require utility staff to risk their safety
in situations such as this, and many water systems do not
have the legal resources to address situations where a
system has legal access to conduct the full replacement
but property owners or residents deny physical access.

owners or residents deny physical access.
78
While EPA is not proposing to establish a maximum stagnation
time in the LCRI because the Agency is concerned about
samples being invalidated solely because the sample result it
high, EPA is seeking comment and data, including modeling
and sampling data, on potential maximum stagnation times,
and specifically how stagnation times inform corrosion rates.
Colorado has no specific comment or data on this topic.
79
EPA is seeking comment about the potential inclusion of
samples from lower-priority tiers (i.e., Tiers 3 through 5) that
have a higher lead or copper concentration than samples from
Tier 1 and 2 sites for calculation of the 90th percentile for
systems that do not have a sufficient number of samples from
Tier 1 and 2 sites. Additionally, EPA is seeking comment on
whether to require systems to use samples with the highest
lead and copper concentration regardless of sampling tiers,
such as including samples from lower-priority tiers ( i.e., Tier
3 through 5) in the 90th percentile calculation for systems
that are collecting compliance samples from all Tier 1 and 2
sites.
Colorado believes that samples from non-lead service line
sites that have higher lead concentrations than samples
from lead service line sites should be included in the 90th
percentile calculation. Using the highest samples
regardless of tier level will simplify States’ process of
picking which samples to use based on tiers while still
ensuring the best public health protection.
80
A deadline for inventory completion that precedes the
deadline for mandatory service line replacement could reduce

deadline, but it would not have the advantages of a
consolidated deadline as described above. EPA seeks comment
on its rationale for the consolidated deadline approach as

service lines.
Colorado recommends that EPA keep deadlines the same

81
While water systems are required to notify consumers of
disturbances resulting from water main replacement under
these proposed requirements, EPA is also requesting comment
on whether to require distribution of filters for this type of
disturbance.
The amount of potholing many systems will have to do
might make it costly to distribute filters to every site.
Additionally, disturbances occur in many other forms not
related to water system activities as well, and it is
impossible to provide filters to every site for these types of
disturbances. Colorado does not recommend this change
unless EPA has supporting data demonstrating a significant
health benefit.

Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
I am writing on behalf of Autodesk, a leading technology provider dedicated to solving 
water challenges with hydraulic modeling and cloud technologies that drive efficiency and 
sustainability across all phases of the water asset lifecycle. We would like to express our 
support for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) and commend the 
EPA's commitment to eliminating lead contamination of drinking water. 
 
Autodesk understands that water utilities are under-resourced and struggle to respond to 
the many competing demands and challenges of providing safe drinking water to their 
communities. New digital technologies offer a tremendous opportunity to leverage 
innovative solutions to improve compliance efforts and enhance overall water 
management practices. 
 
We urge the EPA to fully embrace the potential of technology in addressing this public 
health challenge by providing proactive guidance that water providers are encouraged to 
adopt digital solutions to help them comply with the new requirements. By incorporating 
these solutions into planning and operational processes, utilities can not only meet the 
regulatory requirements more efficiently but also proactively identify and address 
potential problems to prevent future water quality issues. 
 
Below are a few specific examples of how technology can support utilities in meeting the 
new requirements, though it must be noted that there are many additional solutions on 
the market.  
 
1. Comprehensive risk analysis and rehabilitation tools that take into account the 
entire network and all the utility-owned assets. To best use taxpayer resources, 
replacement plans for lead pipes on the service lines should be incorporated into 
the overall capital plan for the utility.
