environmental justice centers around Black and frontline communities that are most impacted. 
 
The Illinois State Conference applauds EPA for proposing stronger regulations to protect communities 
from lead in drinking water.  Lead in drinking water has been a historically prevalent issue in Black 
communities.  It poses extreme risks to the health of young people, mothers, and their families.  
 
According to new research, Illinois is the second largest state to have the most lead pipes with more than 
one million still in service – Chicago alone has 400,000, according to the EPA survey released in early 
April 2023.  Florida emerged as the state with the most lead service lines in the nation, beating out Illinois 
with 1,159,300 lead pipes. 
 
As reported in Illinois, as of January 14, 2022, there were 3,852,509 service lines reported and 686,000 
known lead service lines—the number may be higher.  Children can suffer from intellectual development, 
increased attention-related behavior problems, and reduced growth and hearing loss.  The effects of 
childhood lead exposure linger for a lifetime, with cost that accrue to the state, meaning, “the people.”  
 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) reported that $22,000 is saved for every lead service 
line that is removed, a dollar figure that only accounts for adult cardiovascular deaths attributable to lead 
exposure.  Because of the known lead service lines mentioned above, the real number in Illinois may be 
higher because the composition of some 45 percent of service lines statewide is unknown—our state could 
save a staggering $15.1 billion due to reduced cardiovascular deaths alone. 
 
For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the proposed 
LCRI, such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the requirements for 

water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through lead pipes and a lower action 
level; but also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which undermine their goals and ensure 
that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened. 
 
 
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not leave Black 
communities in Illinois behind: 
 
Removing the Exceptions to the 10-year Lead Pipe Removal Mandate 
It is a fundamental injustice to communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 
or more years to fix this issue. 
 
Mandate That Water Systems Fully Pay for the Removal of Lead Service Lines 
Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted communities 
will result in mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced.  
 
Removal and replacement do not make up major proportions of utility budgets, and utilities 
should expect to maximize the use of available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-
ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize solving this crisis. 
 
Incentivize Schools to Install Filters and Ensure that Children Are Not at Risk 
Black children face an increased risk of lead exposure when compared with white children. 
EPA should move towards incentivizing the installation of filters and protecting children. 
 
Black communities and frontline communities have long suffered from disinvestment and lack of 
resources.  Past NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had 
the strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA of any 
sociodemographic characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to make 
significant changes in the lives of millions of people in Illinois, and to provide a measure of 
environmental justice to families, and we encourage this administration to build on the progress 
made in the proposed rule by strengthening the final rule further. 
 
We Respectfully Demand Advocacy and Education on This Issue 
We need robust outreach to Black and frontline communities which includes education on the 
importance of our drinking water and how lead in drinking water can affect children and adult 
lives.  Nothing else is relevant to our health and wellbeing. 
 
Sincerely, 
Theodis Pace 
  
 
 
 
 
Rose E Joshua  
 
 
Theodis Pace, President  
 
 
 
 
Rose E Joshua, Esq., President 
Illinois State Conference

Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
AIHA, the association for scientists and professionals committed to preserving and ensuring 
occupational and environmental health and safety (OEHS), appreciates the opportunity to 
provide feedback on the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed 
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. We hope you ﬁnd our feedback useful and are happy 
to answer any questions you may have. 
 
General Matters 
1. Whether the proposed revisions to the LCRR treatment technique are effective 
to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible in 
accordance with the SDWA. 
The only way to determine lead concentrations in drinking water is to test the water. The 
only way to test the body burden for lead is to test for lead concentrations in the human 
body. And any test result must accurately reﬂect actual conditions. AIHA, therefore, 
recognizes the need for lead laboratory certiﬁcation by participation and compliance with 
lead laboratory proﬁciency testing, which should be added to these regulations. 
AIHA supports EPA in proposing to lower the lead action level and eliminate the lead trigger 
level to simplify the rule and require water systems to act earlier. The current SDWA 15 ppb 
(15 µg/L) lead in water action level is not a health-based standard. AIHA believes that public 
education must play a signiﬁcant role in these proposed rules. 
Lead in the drinking water can cause long-term, permanent adverse health effects to 
exposed persons and unborn children. The extent of lead exposure from drinking water 
throughout the U.S. and the corresponding incidence of the long-term health effects from 
drinking water contaminated with low concentrations of lead is currently unknown. Funding 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 2 
for research to examine the prevalence of human injury from lead in drinking water is 
needed. 
“Lead in tap water is primarily contributed by lead service lines and lead-containing solder 
and brass in premise plumbing. Although lead was banned for service line use in 1986 in the 
United States, 6.3–9.3 million LSLs are still in use nationally.”i  
AIHA recognizes that any level of lead ingestion may cause adverse health effects. 
AIHA supports the CDC’s efforts regarding lead exposure prevention, including: 
• 
“Primary prevention is the removal of lead hazards from the environment before a 
child is lead exposed. It is the most effective way to ensure that children do not 
experience harmful long-term effects of lead exposure. 
• 
Secondary prevention includes blood lead testing1 and follow-up care and referral. It 
remains an essential safety net for children who may already be exposed to lead.”ii   
AIHA believes lead in drinking water should be established at the lowest possible or lowest 
achievable concentrations. 
Regarding school facilities, AIHA supports the participation of elementary, middle, and 
secondary schools and youth detention centers in a water sampling program. 
“The LCRR requires water systems to sample at least 20% of elementary schools and at 
least 20% of childcare facilities each year until all facilities are contacted. An elementary 
school or childcare facility may decline to have its taps sampled. The LCRR does not 
require schools or childcare facilities to sample for lead or require them to allow water 
systems to conduct sampling; however, a Community Water System (CWS) is required to 
conduct sampling at the request of any school or childcare facility within its service area. 
Water systems must be sampled at secondary schools upon the school's request. States 
may offer waivers to the school and childcare facilities sampling requirements under 
certain circumstances.”iii  
 
2. Whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the 
regulatory approach used to address lead in drinking water consistent with the 
statutory standard for a treatment technique rule in section 1412(b)(7)(A) of 
SDWA. Speciﬁcally, EPA requests comment on ways that the proposed LCRI could 
be simpliﬁed and ways that burden, including paperwork burden, could be 
reduced without affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated 
adverse health effects. 
AIHA believes that EPA especially needs to reduce any complexity of the rule and include 
provisions that support more efﬁcient implementation by city water systems while reducing 
 
1 https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/lead/prevention/testing-children-for-lead-poisoning.htm  

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 3 
lead exposure, particularly in low-income or other vulnerable populations, such as youth 
detention centers.  
For example, the proposed rule states: 
“While the LCRR used the deﬁnition of “full lead service line replacement” in subpart 
A of part 141 to specify full replacement criteria, these are substantive provisions 
that are integral to the requirements in § 141.84 (the service line inventory and 
replacement section). Including these substantive requirements in the service line 
replacement section of subpart I of part 141 instead of the deﬁnitions section of 
subpart A of part 141 should help water systems and States in implementation of 
these regulatory requirements.” 
EPA should describe the meaning more clearly so those without legal training can 
understand what this paragraph means to say regarding how these changes help water 
systems and States in the implementation of these regulatory requirements. 
Section § 141.2 contains “Deﬁnitions” 
AIHA believes the “executive summary” should provide concise operational meanings for 
“action level” and “trigger level” with how these meanings vary from the older lead in 
drinking water standard with an explanation of how these concentrations may vary. For 
example, “trigger” is found 78 times in the rule. “Action level” is found 556 times in the rule 
which carries confusion to the reader. 
 
3. Whether the proposed requirements of the rule are enforceable and promote 
compliance without the need for State or Federal enforcement action. EPA also 
solicits comment on ways the rule could be modiﬁed to better promote 
compliance. 
AIHA recommends that EPA clearly identiﬁes its enforcement policies and procedures for 
compliance with the new rule. Speciﬁcally, AIHA recommends that EPA clearly say how 
affected parties will be held accountable for lead testing and removing lead in the drinking 
water. 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 4 
Service Line Replacement 
1. All aspects of the proposed scope of the replacement requirements, including 
the criteria used to deﬁne a full service line replacement (e.g., cutting the pipe at 
abandoned properties, replacing the entire service line) and which lead sources 
are subject to replacement under the mandatory program. EPA is seeking 
comment on whether to prohibit reconnection of any disconnected LSL or GRR 
service line. EPA is requesting comment on whether the Agency should include 
lead connectors or galvanized service lines that are or were downstream of a lead 
connector as part of mandatory replacement.  
AIHA believes that EPA should not allow lead connectors or galvanized service lines as part 
of mandatory replacement. 
 
3. Whether the proposed LCRI appropriately interprets “control” for the purposes 
of the mandatory replacement provision (i.e., require systems to conduct full 
service line replacement in situations where the system has access to conduct the 
full replacement).  
AIHA believes that replacement provisions may vary according to engineering assessments 
of service lines. 
 
4. The proposed minimum replacement rate and replacement deadlines. EPA is 
seeking comment on whether it is feasible for systems across the nation to 
complete service line replacement in a shorter timeframe than ten years, such as 
in six, seven, or eight years. EPA is seeking comment on the rate construct 
approach, including how to calculate compliance with a given service line 
replacement deadline and average annual rate calculated across a rolling three-
year period. EPA also seeks comment on whether systems should be required to 
meet a minimum replacement rate in the ﬁrst three years after the compliance 
date to give States an opportunity to enforce replacement rate progress sooner 
than three years after the compliance date. EPA also seeks comment on the 
complexity of the rate construct. 
AIHA believes that each situation where service line replacement is required will be 
different, so ﬂexibility is recommended. The timeliest cost-effective approach is needed. 
AIHA recommends timely completion of lead-containing service line replacement across the 
nation.  
In cases of delayed remediation, persons affected by lead concentrations above the 
acceptable level should be notiﬁed in writing about the risks of lead exposure, the results of 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 5 
lead service line replacement feasibility studies, and the time needed for complete and 
effective remediation. 
 
5. EPA is taking comment on whether States, as a condition of primacy, or EPA 
when it is directly implementing the program, should be required to set initial 
shortened deadlines by a certain timeframe, such as no later than 60 days after 
the compliance date. 
AIHA believes shortened deadlines for program implementation may prove difﬁcult and 60 
days after the compliance date is too short. 
 
6. The overall approach and basis to offer deferred service line replacement to 
systems with a high proportion of LSLs and GRR service lines in their distribution 
system relative to their total number of households served. EPA is requesting 
comment on its proposed threshold of 0.039 average annual number of 
replacements per household served, which is used to calculate the number of 
years that systems can defer. 
AIHA does not concur with the proposed threshold of 0.039 average annual number of 
replacements per household served. Each situation may differ and a single requirement for 
the determination of replacements should be based on individual assessments. 
 
7. Whether to require the State, as a condition of primacy, to approve the use of 
the deferred deadline provision where the water system qualiﬁes for it and/or 
whether to require the State, as a condition of primacy, to assess whether it would 
be feasible for a system to meet the 10-year deadline or a shorter deadline even if 
the system meets the regulatory criteria for the deferred deadline. 
AIHA does not believe that EPA should set deferred deadlines, however, remediation 
depends on the extent of the lead contamination problem and system capabilities. 
 
10. Whether systems conducting deferred service line replacement should be 
subject to any additional requirements beyond those for systems that are not 
replacing service lines in accordance with a deferred deadline. 
AIHA believes that deferred system line replacement may result in continued unacceptable 
lead exposures. EPA should implement a system where the worst lead-containing systems 
are addressed ﬁrst. 
 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 6 
11. The requirement for systems to install a dielectric coupling when conducting a 
partial replacement of an LSL or GRR to separate the remaining LSL or GRR 
service line and the replaced service line unless the replaced service line is made 
of plastic and other recommended risk mitigation activities. 
The requirement for systems to install a dielectric coupling when conducting a partial 
replacement of an LSL or GRR to separate the remaining LSL or GRR service line is 
dependent on an engineering assessment. 
 
12. The proposed requirement to ban partial lead and GRR service line 
replacement unless it is conducted in accordance with emergency or planned 
infrastructure work (excluding planned infrastructure work solely for the 
purposes of replacing lead and GRR service lines as part of a service line 
replacement program). Additionally, EPA is seeking comment on whether partial 
service line replacement should be prohibited during “planned infrastructure 
work” or with certain types of planned infrastructure work. 
AIHA does not believe EPA should limit community alternatives for system repair or 
replacement, particularly by prohibiting partial service line replacement, or with diverse 
types of planned infrastructure work. 
 
13. The ability of the market to correct for potential shortages in workers and 
materials to conduct service line replacement, as well to provide sufﬁcient 
quantities of ﬁlters to comply with the service line replacement and other 
relevant provisions in the proposal. 
AIHA believes that constraints on designers should not be placed on lead in drinking water 
remediation efforts. 
 
14. The extent to which property owner consent, if required by State or local law 
or water tariff agreement, might complicate full service line replacement and 
whether there are additional measures EPA can take to facilitate access through 
the LCRI. 
Lead service line replacement may not completely remove lead from homes. Older homes, 
especially in low-income communities where buildings and homes older than 1986 may still 
have LSLs connecting the building's plumbing system to the main water supply line. These 
building water lines, or lead solder can deteriorate and corrode, releasing lead particles into 
the drinking water. These older homes may still present a problem with lead exposure even 
after main service line replacement.

Tap Sampling for Lead and Copper 
1. Comment on the sites included in Tier 3 and whether all of the proposed sites 
should be included in Tier 3, if additional sites should be included, or if some 
should be included in a different, lower priority tier, such as Tier 4. Speciﬁcally, 
comment on whether sites served by galvanized service lines or containing 
galvanized premise plumbing that are identiﬁed as ever being downstream of an 
LSL or lead connector should be included in the same tier as other sites with a 
current lead connector (e.g., copper service line downstream of a lead connector).  
AIHA believes that the priority of system characterization should be dependent on the 
population serviced and the level of lead-containing constituents’ and the concentration of 
lead contamination found in system service lines. 
 
3. Comment on the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to assess CCT 
performance, increase customer participation, and other relevant factors. 
AIHA believes that all alternate sampling protocols should be consistent with the best 
available science and technology and conform to standard water sampling methods. 
 
5. Comment and any relevant data on the number and tiering of samples used to 
calculate the 90th percentile lead and/or copper levels for systems with LSLs for 
purposes of assessing CCT efﬁcacy. Speciﬁcally, whether samples from non-LSL 
sites that have higher lead concentrations than samples from LSL sites should be 
included and whether these higher values should replace lower values from LSL 
sites in the 90th percentile calculation. 
AIHA believes that all service lines containing lead should be identiﬁed using the best 
available technology based on engineering studies. 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 8 
Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan 
2. In the LCRI, EPA is proposing a requirement for systems to validate the 
accuracy of non-lead service lines in their inventory that were categorized using 
methods other than records review or visual inspection of at least two points 
along the line. EPA is requesting comment on the number of validations required, 
the proposed 95 percent conﬁdence level approach used to develop the number of 
validations required, the criteria for which methods used to categorize non-lead 
service lines should be included in the validation pool (including whether non-
lead lines categorized based on records should be subject to validation), and the 
seven-year timeline for systems on a 10-year replacement deadline to complete 
the validation requirements. 
AIHA believes the EPA approach with the 95 percent conﬁdence level is reasonable. 
 
Lead Action and Trigger Levels 
1. EPA is seeking comment on the proposed lead action level of 0.010 mg/L, as well 
as comment and supporting data on alternative action levels, such as 0.005 mg/L, 
with regards to generally effective corrosion control treatment and identifying 
systems most at risk of elevated levels of lead in drinking water. 
AIHA supports the recommendations of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) where 
“drinking fountains in older schools can be an important source of lead exposure. 
Unfortunately, there are no regulations for evaluating lead contamination of school drinking 
fountains in most states.” AAP recommends that State and local governments ensure that 
drinking water fountains in schools do not exceed water lead concentration exceeding 0.001 
mg/L (1 ppb). This recommended level of lead in school fountains is an order of magnitude 
below the EPA proposed new action level (0.010 mg/L).iv 
 
2. EPA is also seeking comment on the use of the action level to determine when 
additional public education is required, and the use of the same action level for 
public education as for the CCT provisions. 
AIHA believes public education is important for all service line investigations with written 
reports of all lead drinking water concentrations. At a certain concentration, persons need 
information on blood lead levels which may need to be determined for children and those 
who are or seeking to become pregnant. 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 9 
Corrosion Control Treatment 
3. The proposed option for a water system to delay OCCT until after the system 
has replaced all of its LSLs and GRR service lines, while the system achieves at 
least 20 percent removal per year and must have no LSLs, GRR service lines, or 
lead status unknown service lines remaining at the end of the ﬁve-year period. 
AIHA believes this EPA approach is reasonable.  
 
Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small 
Community Water Systems and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water 
Systems 
2. EPA is requesting comment on the ability and practicality of point-of-use 
devices to address multiple contaminants. 
As stated in a 2022 article, 
“The biggest challenge for POU ﬁlters is their underperformance for lead removal for 
some water compositions. NSF/ANSI 53 certiﬁed POU ﬁlters have been distributed in 
cities facing lead-in-water crises, such as Washington, DC. Flint, MI, Newark, NJ, 
University Park, IL, and Benton Harbor, MI. However, ﬁeld sampling and lab tests 
have found conditions in which POU ﬁlters did not work well. High concentrations of 
particulate lead (1–45 μg Pb/L) were observed in the efﬂuent of POU ﬁlters in 
Newark, NJ. The POU ﬁlter underperformance may be caused by (1) lead particles 
remaining as stable suspensions of nanoparticles and (2) low attachment efﬁciency 
to ﬁlter media because of repulsive electrostatic interactions. 
“Another challenge is the change of efﬂuent water chemistry after stagnation in the 
POU ﬁlter. A recent study found that the pH of tap water stagnated inside POU ﬁlters 
decreased by 0.1–0.3 pH units. If an under-sink ﬁlter is used, then the stagnated 
water can be more corrosive to any downstream lead-containing solder and ﬁxtures. 
Even though POU ﬁlter deployment is usually effective for controlling lead in tap 
water, its presence poses other challenges to tap water quality. The microbial 
colonization of the ﬁlter media inside the POU device can result in increases of total 
bacteria in the ﬁlter efﬂuent following stagnation periods as short as overnight, 
which will have public health implications if pathogenic bacteria are present.”v 
Other downsides include the cost of ﬁlters and the need for frequent changing (e.g., 3-5000 
L capacity for some ﬁlters). 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 10 
Public Education 
1. The proposed determination that the public education treatment technique is 
feasible and prevents known or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent 
feasible. 
AIHA believes that public education efforts should include recommendations for blood lead 
testing as suggested by local physicians or other medical professionals. 
 
3. Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination that water 
systems are capable of providing consumer notices of individual tap sampling 
results within three calendar days of obtaining those results, regardless of 
whether the results exceed the lead or copper action level, or if a longer time 
frame is needed (e.g., three business days, seven calendar days, 14 calendar days).  
AIHA agrees with the notiﬁcation of individual results within a reasonable time with 
recommendations on when to supply this information to an individual’s medical provider. 
 
6. Whether EPA should require systems to annually notify consumers if they are 
served by a lead connector, in addition to notiﬁcations for sites with lead, GRR, or 
lead status unknown service lines. 
AIHA supports the EPA, in addition to any drinking water lead concentration results, to 
require systems to notify consumers at least annually if they are served by a lead connector 
in addition for sites with lead, GRR, or lead status unknown service lines. 
 
8. Whether EPA should require additional public education requirements to 
further encourage swift service line replacement faster than the 10-year 
replacement deadline. For example, should water systems that have LSLs, GRR 
service lines, or unknown service lines ﬁve years after the compliance date for 
the LCRI be required to increase the frequency of the notiﬁcation of service line 
materials from annual to once every six months? 
AIHA believes it is reasonable to increase the frequency of notiﬁcation of service line 
materials depending on the circumstances. 
 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 11 
9. EPA is seeking information and data on when a system provides translated 
materials to consumers with limited English proﬁciency, what resources are used 
to translate materials (e.g., State resources, community organizations), and what 
barriers water systems may face in providing accurate translated materials.  
AIHA believes training materials should be understandable to all community members and 
notes that translation services may be necessary. 
 
11. EPA is also requesting comment on additional ways to streamline public 
education and associated certiﬁcation requirements (e.g., combine deadlines for 
systems to conduct public education or submit information to the State).  
AIHA believes EPA funding should be provided and available and added to the rule for the 
development of local or under-served community public lead training programs, such as the 
OSHA Susan Harwood Training Grants program. 
 
Additional Requirements for Systems With Multiple Lead Action Level 
Exceedances 
1. Whether water systems should be required to take additional actions when the 
system exceeds the lead action level multiple times and if so, what actions are 
appropriate and feasible, and when these additional actions should be required 
under the LCRI. 
AIHA believes actions should be identiﬁed when blood lead monitoring is necessary and 
recommended for children or others where the lead action level is exceeded multiple times. 
Multiple action level exceedances should be deﬁned as month over month for a deﬁned 
number of months or a deﬁned number of months within a calendar year (e.g., three 
months). Other recommended actions could include the delivery of bulk potable water for 
distribution to affected populations. 
 
4. Whether EPA should require water systems to make ﬁlters certiﬁed to reduce 
lead and replacement cartridges, along with instructions for use, available to all 
consumers within 60 days of a system having multiple action level exceedances 
and whether there are any supporting or contrary data on whether the proposed 
ﬁlter requirement would be protective of public health. 
AIHA believes that water ﬁlters are not a long-term solution to multiple action level 
exceedance but only a stand-in until a long-term solution is implemented. 
 

 
| aiha.org 
Recommendations on LCRI Proposed Rule | Page 12 
8. Whether, in addition to the proposed requirements, EPA should provide States 
discretion to determine appropriate action following a multiple action level 
exceedance that is tailored to meet speciﬁc system needs. 
AIHA believes that EPA should provide ﬂexibility in protecting against the harmful effects of 
lead while providing States with alternatives tailored to system needs and the extent of 
action level exceedance. 
 
Lead Sampling in Schools and Child Care Facilities 
1. Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or to sample 
more frequently in schools and child care facilities. 
AIHA believes schools, youth detention facilities, and childcare facilities should take 
precedence for sampling and may need more frequent sampling depending upon an initial 
lead survey result. 
 
2. The proposed provision to allow States to issue waivers to community water 
systems from the requirement for lead sampling in schools and child care 
facilities during the ﬁve-year period after the LCRI compliance date if the facility 
was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021 but prior to the LCRI compliance date 
and the sampling otherwise meets the waiver requirements of § 141.92(h). 
AIHA believes ﬂexibility should be allowable within the LCRI while maintaining the best lead 
sampling strategy. 
 
3. Whether or not to allow States to waive the requirements of § 141.92 for CWSs in 
schools and child care facilities that use and maintain ﬁlters certiﬁed to reduce 
lead, and if so, whether the waiver should only be allowed where schools and 
child care facilities are required by State or local law to install POU devices and 
maintain them. 
Recent research has shown limitations to POU devices. These limitations must be 
understood. However, AIHA believes in some instances ﬁlters will be effective, however not 
as a long-term solution.vi 
 
5. Whether EPA should require CWSs to make school and child care facility 
sampling results publicly available, and if so, how frequently and in what 
manner. 
AIHA believes that all school and childcare facility sampling results should be publicly 
available, especially for real estate transactions.

Reporting and Recordkeeping 
1. EPA is requesting comment on the expansion of the inventory reporting to 
include lead connectors and non-lead service lines. 
AIHA recommends inventory reporting depending on an engineering study and best 
available practices. 
 
2. EPA has heard concern over the ability of States to review all required site 
sample plans and provide approvals in time for the ﬁrst tap monitoring period, 
and is requesting comment on whether EPA should consider a phased approach

AIHA believes ﬂexibility should be allowable within the LCRI while maintaining the best lead

3. EPA is requesting comment on whether States should be required to maintain 
records related to distribution system and site assessments conducted by water

AIHA believes that records of any sampling and engineering assessment related to

over time to clearly communicate trends.

About AIHA 
AIHA is the association for scientists and professionals committed to preserving and 
ensuring occupational and environmental health and safety in the workplace and 
community. Founded in 1939, we support our members with our expertise, networks, 
comprehensive education programs, and other products and services that help them 
maintain the highest professional and competency standards. More than half of AIHA’s 
nearly 8,500 members are Certiﬁed Industrial Hygienists, and many hold other professional 
designations. AIHA serves as a resource for those employed across the public and private 
sectors as well as to the communities in which they work. For more information, please visit 
www.aiha.org.

RE: 
US EPA’S Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) 
[Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801]  
 
Dear Mr. Goldberg: 
This American Petroleum Institute (API) and the American Chemistry Council (ACC) submits the following comments on 
EPA’s proposed rule for National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) (88 FR 
84878, December 6, 2023, EPA Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801), hereafter “Proposed Rule.”   
 
API represents nearly 600 companies involved in all aspects of the oil and natural gas industry (exploration, production, 
refining, marketing, and transportation). The ACC represents the leading companies engaged in the business of 
chemistry, which is a $639 billion enterprise and a key element of the nation’s economy. ACC participates on behalf of 
its members in administrative proceedings and in litigation arising from those proceedings.  Member companies of API 
and ACC have industrial facilities throughout the United States, of which some are also registered Non-Transient Non-
Community Public Water Systems (NTNCWSs).  Our membership is committed to the safety of our employees, including 
the protection of their health when consuming drinking water in the workplace.   
 
When assessing the requirements of the Proposed Rule and considering the competing priorities of the proposed PFAS 
regulations for Drinking Water, API and ACC have identified opportunities for EPA to provide additional flexibility and 
clarity to NTNCWSs.  Specifically, API and ACC request EPA allow the option for NTNCWSs to install point-of-use devices in 
lieu of lead service line (LSL) replacement for NTNCWSs and to provide bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or 
POU devices following disturbances.  API and ACC additionally request that EPA provide clear and timely guidance to all 
PWSs, including NTNCWSs on expectations associated with the final rule and the definition of Service Line.  Finally, API 
and ACC argue that EPA has underestimated the cost burden to NTNCWSs, and request that EPA consider feedback on 
assumptions that EPA has made on NTNCWSs when considering compliance alternatives. 
 
API and ACC are providing additional detail on these comments and feedback on assumptions made for NTNCWSs.  API 
and ACC encourage EPA to make appropriate revisions to the Proposed Rule, as set forth in these comments.  
 
Additional Details 

 
 
Page2 
1. EPA should allow Point-of-Use Devices in lieu of LSL replacement for NTNCWS that do not supply water to 
sensitive populations, such as schools or child-care facilities – The Proposed Rule contains Small System Flexibility 
provisions that allow NTNCWSs to leverage Point-of-Use (POU) systems in lieu of the corrosion control treatment 
requirements as described in the Proposed Rule § 141.93.  API and ACC appreciate EPA’s inclusion of Small System 
Flexibility and encourages EPA to consider additional applications for flexibility.   Specifically, API and ACC propose 
EPA allow NTNCWSs that do not supply water to sensitive populations (e.g., schools or child-care facilities) the 
option to use POU devices as an alternative to conducting Lead Service Line Inventories or Lead Service Line 
Replacements on the portion of the service line onto which the POU is installed.  This arrangement would allow 
NTNCWSs to outfit specific segments of their service lines with POU systems while replacing other lines if identified 
as LSLs.  This additional flexibility would further EPA’s objectives of the proposed rule by addressing both service 
lines and premise plumbing as potential lead sources. 
 
The Proposed Rule was issued in the same year as the proposed per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR).  The proposed PFAS NPDWR identified Granular 
Activated Carbon (GAC) and Reverse Osmosis (RO) amongst the possible treatment technologies capable of 
removing PFAS from drinking water.  GAC and RO are also identified and certifiable via NSF / ANSI standards1 for 
the removal of lead from drinking water.  Where a single solution can achieve removal of both PFAS and Lead, 
EPA should allow NTNCWSs the flexibility to use a single solution instead of both removing LSLs and adding 
treatment for PFAS. 
 
Under the Proposed Rule, systems must make annual updates to service line inventories, tracking both changes 
in service lines and connector materials and systems would be required to identify service lines of unknown 
materials.  API and ACC propose PWSs that use POU devices be exempt from the requirement to identify the 
material of connectors and unknown service lines.  A resulting LSL inventory would thus identify either the service 
line material or the presence of a POU system.  Expanding flexibility for NTNCWS compliance with the Proposed 
Rule will maintain alignment with EPA’s goals in the Proposed Rule of protection of human health and 
transparency to the NTNCWS water consumers. 
 
2. EPA should add supplying bottled water and sample validation as an option for risk mitigation after 
disturbances for NTNCWSs – EPA is maintaining the Lead and Copper Rule Revision (LCRR) requirement that water 
systems provide pitcher filters or point-of-use devices for six months following partial and full LSL replacement, 
replacement of a lead connector, and other scenarios.  At NTNCWSs that serve at workplace, employers may find 
it feasible to supply employees with bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or POU devices.  Some 
workplace environments are staged with water coolers that contain large (e.g., 5 gallon) bottles of water, in which 
case allowing continued use of that water supply would prevent waste of pitcher filters that would not be used. 
API and ACC request that the flexibility to use bottled water be added for NTNCWSs in addition to the options of 
providing pitcher filters or POU devices.   
 
EPA specified a six month period of time to provide pitcher filters or POU devices on the basis of a 2008 study2, 
which referenced that one site in the study suggested the potential for lead accumulated in the system to be 
 
1 The Proposed Rule’s provisions for use of a POU device specify that the device must be independently certified by a third party to 
meet the American National Standards Institute standard applicable to the specific type of POU unit to reduce lead in drinking water.  
EPAs’ Consumer Tool for Identifying Point of Use (POU) Drinking Water Filters Certified to Reduce Lead specifies NSF/ANSI Standard 
53.

of service line and plumbing fixtures to lead and copper rule compliance issue. AWWA Research Foundation, 523. 

 
 
Page3 
released for months following disturbance, while most detected releases in systems took place in the first several 
days following LSL replacement.  The reason why one system was impacted for a lengthy period was not specified 
in the preamble.  The source document summarized elevated lead concentrations following LSL replacement as 
occurring in many cases for the first three days after replacement.  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have the ability 
to control flushing of service lines and premise plumbing within buildings as well as the ability to conduct their 
own sampling following disturbances.   As such, industrial facilities are capable of monitoring taps.  API and ACC 
propose EPA allow NTNCWSs the flexibility to sample taps after a minimum of 96 hours following a disturbance 
and eliminate the use of mitigations upon receipt of analytical results confirming that lead concentrations are 
below the lead action level.    
 
3. Clear and timely guidance for industrial facility NTNCWSs is requested – EPA has concluded “the overwhelming 
majority of NTNCWSs that do have LSLs and Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRR) service lines are expected 
to have relatively few of these service lines requiring replacement over the proposed 10-year deadline” (88 FR 
84912).  EPA’s position is based upon several assumptions, namely: 
• 
Responses from 147 NTNCWSs to the 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey Assessment3  that 
indicated lead service lines are rarely used are representative of the 17,418 NTNCWSs in SWDIS, 
• 
Responses from three states that estimated the number of LSLs at NTNCWSs in 20174 are accurate and 
representative across the country, and 
• 
NTNCWSs have no stand-alone lead connectors and no GRR service lines since NTNCWSs are unlikely to 
replace only the upstream portion of an LSL and leave a galvanized service line in place, because they own 
the entire service, and galvanized lines have a high failure rate given age and disturbance like that 
produced by removing a section of LSL.5  
 
The assumption that few NTNCWSs have lead service lines cannot be confirmed until the October 2024 deadline 
to submit Lead Service Lines inventories.  Furthermore, piping makeup and configuration of NTNCWSs at industrial 
facilities could be influenced by the specific sector in which piping is used.  For example, the newest refinery with 
significant downstream capacity was built in 19776, prior to the 1986 amendment to the Safe Drinking Water Act 
to prohibit the use of pipes, solder, or flux that was not “lead free” in public water systems.    
 
Conducting Lead Service Line Inventories is a complex undertaking.  NTNCWSs at industrial sites that attempt to 
leverage guidance documents that are developed for Community Water Systems are left to interpret guidance 
written for systems that provide water to homes.   EPA Issued "Guidance for Developing and Maintaining a Service 
Line Inventory" in August 2022, and guidance tailored for small CWSs and NTNCWSs was not issued until June of 
2023.  While API and ACC membership appreciates that EPA developed guidance tailored for smaller systems, the 
guidance was issued after LSL inventory development was underway.  Accordingly, API and ACC request that EPA 
provide timely and clear guidance for NTNCWS with examples applicable to NTNCWSs at Industrial facilities.  
 
 
3 88 FR 84912: Regarding NTNCWSs, Needs Survey responses from 147 NTNCWSs showed LSLs are rarely used in these systems since 
132 of them did not report any lead, GRR, or unknown service lines. 
4 Economic Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement, 2023. In August 2017, EPA disseminated a questionnaire 
to nine states asking for the estimated number or percentage of NTNCWSs with one or more LSLs and the total number of LSLs in 
NTNCWSs.  EPA received responses from seven states.  Four states did not provide any estimate.  The remaining three states 
provided estimates ranging from five to zero percent.  Based upon this data, EPA assumed 2.5% of NTNCWSs would have LSLs. 
5 Economic Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement, 2023 
6 US Energy Information Administration https://www.eia.gov/tools/faqs/faq.php?id=29&t=6, accessed January 22, 2024 

 
 
Page4 
Clarity to the definition of Service Line is requested – EPA has added a definition of “Service Line” to the Proposed 
Rule, which states “Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe which 
connects the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water 
main to the outlet."  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have service lines that do not enter buildings and are used 
for purposes other than drinking or cooking.  Specifically, regulations issued by the Occupational Safety and Health 
Administration (OSHA) require potable water be used in eye wash station and safety showers; such safety devices 
can be located external or internal to buildings.   
 
EPA has the opportunity to add clarity and reduce ambiguity by specifying whether "outlet" in the definition is 
intended to mean all possible water uses or is specific to uses associated with cooking and drinking.  In § 141.154 
of the Proposed Rule, EPA provides informational statements regarding lead in drinking water, which includes the 
following language: "Before using tap water for drinking, cooking, or making baby formula, flush your pipes for 
several minutes. You can do this by running your tap, taking a shower, doing laundry or a load of dishes." API and 
ACC note EPA provides taking a shower as opposed to running the shower as an example of a means to flush lines 
and reduce exposure to lead in water used for drinking, cooking, or making baby formula.   Safety showers and 
eye washes in industrial facilities are not intended for consumption.   
 
API and ACC request EPA clarify the definition of "Service Line" as follows: “Service line, for the purpose of subpart 
I of this part only, means a portion of pipe that connects the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is 
not present, the service line connects the water main to an outlet used for cooking or drinking.".  
 
4. EPA’s assumptions for Cost Burden to NTNCWSs is an underestimate – EPA’s Economic Analysis of the Proposed 
Rule has assumed that NTNCWSs will not incur burdensome to costs to update their inventories since they own 
their own service lines and are not expected to have any unknowns.  This assumption is not accurate.  NTNCWSs 
at industrial facilities that have been developing their inventories have incurred costs to field-identify service lines 
in advance of the October 16, 2024 submission deadline.  Unknown service lines can occur through a variety of 
reasons including age of a facility and loss of drawings. Furthermore, NTNCWSs are unlikely to have customer 
meters, thus unlikely to have water meter readings or replacements as an opportunity to collect service line data.  
Further, EPA has assumed NTNCWSs are able to rely on drawings as a means to identify connectors and service 
line materials of construction; however, due to the age of some facilities, this is not consistently applicable to 
NTNCWSs. 
 
Cost will be a significant challenge in replacing all lead service lines, especially when considered alongside 
competing priorities such as PFAS removal. The average cost to fully replace a single lead service line is estimated 
to be between $6,507 and $8,519 per the Proposed Rule’s Economic Analysis; however, for NTNCWSs at Industrial 
facilities, these costs are likely higher due to line length as well as maintenance and safety practices required 
within industrial facilities and the possibility that piping may run adjacent to or through process units. While the 
federal Bipartisan Infrastructure Act has allocated funding for lead service line replacement, this funding will not 
be available to industrial facilities.  Similarly, the NTNCWSs at commercial facilities are not eligible for other 
funding mechanisms described in Section IV.G of the Proposed Rule’s preamble.  EPA should take these realities 
for NTNCWSs when considering the additional small system flexibilities proposed by API and ACC.  
 
5. Sample Tiering based on Premise Plumbing presents undue burden to Public Water Systems – The Proposed 
Rule maintains the tiering structure established by the original Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) and updated by the 
LCRR. In the Proposed Rule, EPA is proposing to adjust the definition for the highest priority tiers (Tier 1 and Tier 
2) to include sites with premise plumbing made of lead.  EPA specifies that by premise plumbing made of lead, 

 
 
Page5 
EPA means premise plumbing that consists of pure lead pipes, like the pipes used for LSLs, rather than pipes 
made from metal alloys which may contain lead content.  EPA further proposes galvanized premise plumbing to 
be an element of Tier 3. 
 
EPA has not requested that Lead Inventories include premise plumbing material construction.  Identifying the 
premise plumbing material of construction includes additional time and cost that EPA has not considered in the 
Economic Analysis.  EPA should not assume that NTNCWSs are likely to have previous knowledge of the premise 
plumbing present in buildings that are in their control.  
 
Conclusions:  
 
API and ACC appreciate the opportunity to file comments in this letter concerning the Proposed Rule.   EPA has 
requested feedback as to whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the regulatory 
approach used to address lead in drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique rule 
in section 1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA. API and ACC propose the LCRI could be simplified and burden could be reduced 
without affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects by allowing NTNCWSs 
additional flexibility as described within these comments. 
 
Please contact me at (202) 682-8399, claff@api.org, when you wish to discuss these comments or if you would like any 
additional information concerning the issues raised in these comments.  
 
Sincerely,

Re:  National Primary Drinking Water Regulations:  Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
Docket #ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Dear Assistant Administrator Fox: 
 
The Indiana Department of Environmental Management (IDEM) values the opportunity to provide 
the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) with comments on the proposed national 
rulemaking “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations:  Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements” (Federal Register Number 2023-84878 posted December 6, 2023) (hereinafter 
“Proposed Rule”).  IDEM is responsible for the daily implementation of the Safe Drinking Water 
Act (SDWA) programs in Indiana, including the federal Lead and Copper Regulations as they apply 
to the public water systems in the state of Indiana.  IDEM’s has carefully reviewed the Proposed 
Rule and provides the following comments: 
 
1. IDEM agrees with removal of the trigger level, as this will allow for a more streamlined rule 
that will be much easier to communicate to the regulated public water systems and the 
general public.  It will also make it easier to implement the rule. 
2. IDEM agrees with the changing “Find and Fix” to “Distribution System and Site 
Assessment”.  This terminology no longer implies that a water system is responsible for 
replacing plumbing inside a customer’s home. 
3. IDEM disagrees with setting a timeframe, as a condition of primacy, for setting initial 
shortened deadlines in the rule, especially if that deadline is as short as sixty (60) days after 
the compliance date while there are multiple decisions needing to be made and documented 
in a short period of time.  It will be difficult to determine if it is “feasible” for a system to 
replace lead service lines (LSLs) at a faster rate, especially when considering the availability 
of both construction crews and replacement materials when every system with lead service 
lines will be replacing their lines at the same time.  The availability of human and physical 
resources should not be a state primacy issue. 
4. IDEM recommends that EPA allow systems to do partial replacements during planned 
infrastructure work when they are unable to get cooperation from the homeowner. 

 
 
 
 
Coordinating service line replacements with main line replacements and transportation 
projects (for re-paving), etc. is already challenging with the new ten-year timeline for LSL 
replacements. Prohibiting partial replacements in these cases will only reduce the ability for 
this coordination to occur and increase costs. Additionally, there are many other 
requirements that ensure any lead exposure from partially replaced service lines will be 
mitigated (e.g., the addition of dielectric couplings and additional flushing and risk 
mitigation requirements; public communication annually about presence of LSL/galvanized 
line requiring replacement (GRR)/unknowns; notification after change of ownership, etc.).   
5. IDEM recommends allowing the state to have full discretion to extend the ten-year lead 
service line replacement deadline for any system that provides reasonable justification and 
explains why the ten-year deadline needs to be extended. There could be a number of 
legitimate reasons, such as: supply chain issues, budget constraints due to increased costs, 
homeowners not responding in a timely manner, etc. The state should be responsible for 
reviewing any extension requests made by public water systems and have the authority to 
decide if the extension can be granted.  
6. The states and public water systems will need additional guidance from EPA as to which 
types of records may be acceptable to use to list service lines as non-lead in the baseline 
inventory without requiring additional validation. 
7. IDEM would prefer to see a single compliance number at the 90th percentile (the action level 
of 10 micrograms per liter) rather than having some requirements be triggered at the action 
level and others being triggered at the Practical Quantitation Limit (PQL of 5 micrograms 
per liter). 
8. For many small public water systems, especially in areas of the country, like Indiana, with 
high alkalinity levels in source water, the only available corrosion control treatment option 
will be feeding a phosphate inhibitor.  We have many analogous systems with similar water 
quality and do not believe that every system with LSLs and an action level exceedance will 
benefit from doing a pipe-loop study, nor will they have the funding available (especially 
while also removing lead service lines) to complete this complex study without having to 
wait for a grant and/or loan funding period to determine if they can afford to complete the 
study.  For the majority of these small and medium-sized systems in Indiana, the pipe loop 
study would tell them the same thing as the current corrosion control guidance manual does 
– feed an orthophosphate-based corrosion inhibitor.  Completing and reviewing the pipe-
loop studies will create additional burdens on the resources of public water systems and 
IDEM staff. 
9. Concerning the small system flexibilities written into the proposed LCRI, IDEM 
recommends that the ability to use point of use (POU) filters should be limited to small 
systems that have ownership or control of the distribution system and premise plumbing 
within their public water system.  These systems will be able to ensure access to the POU 
devices to maintain and replace as necessary and to conduct any testing required to ensure 
they are operating properly. 
10. IDEM does not agree that it is necessary to provide translation support into any and every 
language spoken in the state as a condition of primacy for this rule.  EPA should provide 
these translations either as part of a guidance document or via a link on their website. 
11. IDEM recommends EPA change the proposed provision to allow states to issue waivers to 
community water systems from the requirement for lead sampling in schools and childcare 
facilities during the five-year period after the LCRI compliance date if the facility was 
sampled for lead after January 1, 2021. We suggest changing the sampling date to January 1, 
2014, which coincides with the Reduction of Lead in Drinking Water Act and would include 
sampling efforts that resulted from funding provided by America’s Water Infrastructure Act 
of 2018 and the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act.  

 
 
 
 
 
In addition, IDEM is in general agreeance with the comments being submitted by the Association of 
State Drinking Water Administrators (ASDWA) and the Environmental Council of States (ECOS). 
 
IDEM provides this feedback to help U.S. EPA develop further clarity in the rule itself or in 
complementary guidance, as appropriate.  If you have any questions about our comments, please 
contact our Chemical & Surface Water Compliance Section Chief, Stacy Jones at 317-234-7454 or 
sjones@idem.IN.gov.  
 
IDEM thanks you for this opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking.  We encourage 
continued collaboration with the states as the rule becomes final and implementation begins. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Martha Clark Mettler 
 
 
 
 
 
Assistant Commissioner 
 
 
 
 
 
Office of Water Quality

porƟon of the proposed rule be limited to only the porƟon of system that the uƟlity owns.

We do not believe it is feasible for systems to replace all lead and GRR service lines within ten years for the following 
reasons: 
A. UƟliƟes do not have suﬃcient funding available to fully replace all lead service lines. Only a fracƟon of the BIL 
funding for LSL replacements is forgivable; most funding through the State Revolving Fund (SRF) is available in the 
form of a loan, which uƟliƟes will need to ﬁnd money in the already Ɵght budget to pay for over Ɵme. Meanwhile, 
uƟliƟes are also struggling to ﬁnance repairs and replacements necessary for deterioraƟng infrastructure due to 
falling revenues. If uƟliƟes are forced to raise rates to pay for systemwide LSL replacements, this will harm low-
income residents who may already struggle to aﬀord uƟlity payments.  
B. The current 15 billion in BiparƟsan Infrastructure Law (BIL) funding is currently only guaranteed for 5 years.  
C. Customers in need of LSL replacement do not have the discreƟonary funding available to bear the cost of their 
privately owned porƟon. This is especially true of lower income residents, which equates to approximately 11% 
or 341,600 residents in the state of Iowa.  
D. Many uƟliƟes do not fully own the service line from main to water meter, and therefore do not have legal 
ownership or access over the full service line.  
E. Many customers are not willing to grant access to the property even if full replacement of a service line is made 
available to them at no cost. This is based on results from a nearby pilot project, Lead ReducƟon Pilot Program by 
Des Moines Water Works where only 35% of consumers have capitalized on the ongoing program oﬀerings2. 
F. Required service line replacements will lead to a sharp spike in prices for material(s) and labor, which will 
further exacerbate the diﬃculty of execuƟng service line replacement projects. 
G. NaƟonwide demand for service line replacement materials creates strain on the supply chain, leading to 
potenƟal for widespread shortages and lack of availability.

results indicate elevated lead, can this result be atributed to the corroded state of the ﬁxture? This would not be a 
reasonable assessment of Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) or of system water quality. 
Is there ﬂexibility to exclude this datapoint in the 90th percenƟle if found to be ﬁxture related?

monitoring criteria?

CONCLUSION 
In closing, the Cedar Rapids Water Division appreciates the opportunity to provide comments and ask quesƟons to the 
LCRI proposal. We have addressed the EPA’s request for speciﬁc comments and provided addiƟonal quesƟons for 
consideraƟon.  
It is important to note that CRWD also supports the eﬀort to remove lead service lines and improve water quality and 
health where feasible. As can be seen, this is an extremely complicated endeavor, and it is not an easy task on any level. 
CRWD believes the best and most eﬃcient use of systems’ limited Ɵme and resources would be to focus on property the 
system owns. Ownership varies from community to community and provides signiﬁcant complicaƟons to fulﬁlling the 
intent of this rule. In areas that have proacƟvely and eﬀecƟvely managed corrosion control to keep lead from becoming a 
signiﬁcant health risk, lead in drinking water is not at the forefront of consumer’s minds. According to the Iowa Health 
and Human Services department and many others across the naƟon, lead in drinking water is not the primary source of 
lead poisoning3. It contributes very litle even when lead poisoning is a concern.  
To review, CRWD’s primary concerns and recommendaƟons on the following issues within the proposed regulatory rule 
are listed below: 
1. Time, resources, and ownership. 
RECOMMENDATION: We believe the best and most eﬃcient use of systems’ limited Ɵme and resources would 
be to only require systems to comply on property owned by the system. 
2. Proposed declaration that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water. 
RECOMMENDATION: Reword to “Lead in drinking water is primarily from materials used in plumbing 
components associated with service lines and home plumbing. If present, lead can cause serious health 
problems, especially for pregnant women and young children. To reduce risk, it is important to remove any lead 
components. Over the next several years, water systems will be focusing on removing lead service lines from the 
system. Owners can also lessen risk by replacing any lead or downstream galvanized plumbing on or in their 
property as well as any ﬁxtures that may contain lead.” 
Not only does the proposed declaraƟon, in essence, contradict the “allowable” proposed 10 ppb lead level, it also insƟlls

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1332 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024 
 
Michael Regan
