Re:  National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements, Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Clean Water Action and Clean Water Fund respectfully submit these comments regarding the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead 
and Copper: Improvements (LCRI).   
 
Comments Related to Line Service Line Replacement 
Mandatory Replacement Requirement 
Our engagement in revisions of the Safe Drinking Water Act Lead and Copper Rule has 
emphasized the need to fully replace all lead service lines. We fully support the proposal to 
require all water systems subject to the Rule’s provisions to fully replace lead service lines 
within ten years.  We have focused on lead service lines as a critical aspect of controlling lead in 
drinking water for a number of reasons:  
 We have long known that lead can harm the developing brains of infants and 
children. Now we know that even low-level exposure contributes to cardiovascular 
disease, which widens the circle of concern. Replacing lead service lines - the largest 
source of lead in drinking where they are present – will reduce lead in drinking water 
and therefore overall lead exposure, every bit of which matters to everyone’s health. 
 

2 
 
 Because exposure to all sources of lead disproportionately burdens people of color 
and low-income people, any added exposure from lead in drinking water compounds 
this inequity. 
 Momentum toward this goal is greater than it has ever been as indicated by water 
system activities, state policy developments, Congressional interest, and EPA’s own 
proposal.  
EPA’s proposal is consistent with commitments made in the White House Lead Pipe and 
Paint Action Plan and with the findings of the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) 
review, which found that “Replacing 100 percent of lead service lines is an urgently needed 
action to protect all Americans from the most significant source of lead in drinking water 
systems.”1 
The 2021 LCRR, while not requiring mandatory lead service line replacement, suggested 
that fully replacing lead service lines would be appropriate and achievable. Inventory and 
replacement plan requirements put key aspects of a program in place. In Strategies to 
Achieve Full Lead Service Line Replacement (LSLR), an EPA document published to support 
the proposed LCRR, EPA noted that “LSLR programs can be structured in ways to overcome 
potential legal, financial, and practical challenges related to full LSLR.”2 Using lead in water 
distribution systems - a practice that began over 100 years ago - was a regrettable choice 
about which there was concern about public health risks at the time.3 EPA’s proposal 
appropriately recognizes that since full lead service line replacement is the best way to 
protect public health and is achievable, then it should be incorporated into the Rule’s 
requirements.   
 
Lead Service Line Definition 
In clarifying the definition of a “Lead Service Line,” EPA appears to have removed an 
essential sentence: “A lead service line may be owned by the water system, owned by the 
                                                
1 Review of the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), 86 Fed. 
Reg. 71574 (Dec. 17, 2021 
2Strategies to Achieve Full Lead Service Line Replacement, October 2019, EPA 810-R-19-003, page 5 
3 Rabin, Richard, The Lead Industry and Lead Water Pipes: ‘A Modest Campaign, American Journal of Public 
Health, Vol. 98, No. 9, September 2008 

3 
 
property owner, or both.”4 This is critical to protecting public health, as well as to Rule 
requirements including inventory development and full lead service line replacement. If service 
ownership is left ambiguous in EPA’s definition, then the intent of EPA’s emphasis on full 
replacement and on discouraging partial replacements throughout the proposal could be 
negated. Any ambiguity around what constitutes a lead service line and what is required to be 
included in the inventory and to be replaced is likely to undermine EPA’s overall goal of 
achieving full replacement of all lead service lines.  
 
Cost-Sharing in Replacement Programs 
We have consistently urged EPA to require water systems to cover the full cost of 
replacement regardless of ownership or whether the line is located under private or public 
property. The environmental justice review commissioned by EPA as part of the LCRR 
rulemaking process in 2019 found that presuming customers must pay for things, including 
covering part of the cost of lead service line replacement, leaves low-income people with 
inequitable access to the benefits of reducing lead in their water and puts them at 
disproportionately higher health risk.5 The environmental justice review for the current 
proposal found that replacement programs relying on cost-sharing could result in more 
replacements for high-income households, and notes other proposed provisions intended to 
counter this potential inequity. These equity provisions, intended to reduce differential impact, 
include: requiring equity considerations in replacement plans; increasing transparency by 
requiring replacement plans be public, and calculating the replacement rate on a 3-year rolling 
average to account for possible delays caused by targeting child care facilities, schools, or areas 
with higher lead exposure. We support these provisions but remain concerned that they do not 
fully counter the inequities involved in requiring customers to share the cost of replacement. 6 
 
                                                
4 40 C.F.R. §141.2  
5 Abt Associates, Environmental Justice Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, October 22, 
2019, Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2017-0300-0008 
 
6 Environmental Justice Analysis for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA, November 2023, 
pages 88-89, Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0689 

4 
 
While requiring customers to contribute has historically been a common practice, this is 
changing. Water systems are finding ways to conduct and finance replacements without 
customer contributions. Cost-sharing programs themselves create inefficiency and increased 
work for strained water system workforces. Perpetuating this antiquated approach will 
undermine the lead service line replacement and public health protection goals of the proposal.  
 
EPA proposes to “remain neutral”7 on cost-sharing, which they determine to be a 
matter of State and local law.  Yet, EPA is also “strongly encouraging customer-side 
replacement to be offered at no direct cost to the customer wherever possible to achieve 
higher customer participation rates and reduce environmental justice impacts that may result 
when customers cannot afford to replace their portion of the line.”8 This underplays the 
potential impact of requiring customers to pay for part of replacement costs. In most cases, 
customers will be able to refuse to contribute regardless of their ability to “afford” this cost, 
thus seriously limiting the ability to achieve full replacement of all lead service lines.  
 
EPA should revisit the decision that it is not within their authority to require systems to 
cover the full cost of replacement. EPA’s requirement that States and systems identify barriers 
to full replacement is a positive step to identifying where State and local laws prohibit the no-
cost sharing practices that EPA is strongly encouraging. EPA should work with States and 
systems on how to overcome these State and local impediments to protecting public health and 
meeting new SDWA requirements.  
 
Control and Access Issues 
EPA proposes to define “control” of lead service lines as legal and physical “access.”9 
This leaves unacceptable uncertainty for systems and States, and interferes with full 
replacement goals. “Access” could be interpreted in very different ways. In the proposal, EPA 
discusses the potential for customers to refuse any replacement activity on their property 
regardless of whether a customer contribution is required. This will require documentation and 
                                                
7 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), 88 Fed. Reg. 84923 
(Dec. 6, 2023) 
8 88 Fed. Reg. 84923 (Dec. 6, 2023) 
9 88 Fed. Reg. 84921 (Dec. 6, 2023) 
 

5 
 
procedures for attempting to replace the line when the property changes ownership or other 
circumstances change as EPA describes.  However, “access” could also be interpreted far more 
broadly to mean that if a system does not own a portion of the line, it lacks control and 
therefore access. This would have unacceptable consequences for full replacement and public 
health protection. For example, it could be interpreted to mean that if a system doesn’t own a 
portion of the service line that it therefore does not have access. EPA should define and clarify 
access more clearly in the regulatory requirements text to avoid this potential 
misinterpretation.  
 
Deferred Deadlines 
The deferred deadline proposal for systems with atypically high numbers of lead service 
lines formalizes an unacceptably long timeline for replacement. Because this applies only to a 
few systems, as EPA acknowledges, it should not be codified in the LCRI. EPA is already 
proposing to allow States to set a deadline of less than ten years for systems where the State 
determines if it is feasible. States should work with these systems that have atypical numbers of 
lead service lines to outline a schedule, perhaps in the form of a variance, rather than EPA 
setting a number in the LCRI. The goal of such an approach would be to avoid setting an upper 
limit that these systems might well be able to exceed, as EPA acknowledges, and to avoid 
having replacement incomplete for decades.  
 
Partial Lead Service Line Replacements 
We agree with proposals to prohibit partial replacements in most cases because of the 
potential to increase lead levels. However, EPA should do more than discourage partial 
replacements by signaling that the intention is to “virtually eliminate” the practice. A partial 
lead service line, whether it is under private or public property, is still a lead service line that 
contributes to elevated lead in drinking water. Presence of lead service lines is thus an ongoing 
public health risks and an impediment to the 100% replacement goal. Leaving part of a lead 
service line in place to ensure continued water service in the case of an emergency is 
reasonable, as long as mitigation activities are conducted and the system works to complete 

6 
 
the replacement. EPA should further restrict the exclusion for conducting partial replacements 
during planned infrastructure work that is not for the purpose of replacement.  Precisely 
because such maintenance is usually planned well ahead of time, systems should be able to 
make arrangements with customers in the event that lead service lines are encountered. As 
water systems complete lead service line inventories and update them, they will be increasingly 
more prepared to identify when routine maintenance plans are likely to encounter lead service 
lines and at which homes or buildings. Where customer cooperation is impossible, the risk 
mitigation activities that would be required for emergency repairs can be conducted and other 
requirements for this situation would continue to apply.  
A failure to reign in partial replacements to the greatest extent possible could result in 
the perpetuation of a practice that has left many partial lead service lines in place, particularly 
but not only on the “customer-owned” side or under private property. This complicates 
preparation of accurate inventories and replacement activities. A prohibition on partial 
replacements except in emergencies and special circumstances, with a goal of virtually 
eliminating this practice, is consistent with the public health protection goals of the LCRI. 
Connectors 
We support EPA’s proposal to define connectors as being no longer than two feet and to 
require any lead connectors encountered to be replaced. We continue to recommend that lead 
connectors be included in the mandatory replacement requirement not only if they are 
encountered in the course of maintenance, repair, or replacement but also if they are identified 
through the records reviews required in the Inventory provisions of the Rule. As EPA notes, lead 
connectors are included in the inventory and customers served by pipe with a lead connector 
must be notified because lead connectors can contribute to lead in drinking water.  
 
Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan 
 
We agree with EPA’s proposal to conduct record reviews in order to include lead 
connectors in the required inventories, and to identify the locations of previously replaced lead 
connectors, and to track where lead connectors are replaced in the future.   

7 
 
 
We support the proposal to require systems to identify State or local laws or water tariff 
agreements that govern access to conduct full service line replacement and for States to notify 
systems in writing of similar State or local laws or constitutional requirements. These State or 
local laws could impact systems’ ability to effectively carry out replacement requirements and 
need to be considered in development of replacement plans. This requirement can also help 
resolve confusion and lack of clarity around what, if any, impact such State and local provisions 
actually have on access and financing issues. EPA is requesting comment on whether plans 
should be updated in the case of any changes in State or local laws or other provisions that 
impact replacement plans, and we agree that updated plans should be required if these 
changes impact elements of the replacement plan.  
 
EPA requests comment on the threshold for requiring systems to host inventories, 
inventory summary data, replacement summary data, and service line replacement plans 
online. Specifically, EPA requests comment on whether such a requirement should pertain to 
systems serving more than 10,000 persons rather than the 50,000-person threshold in the 
proposal. We think it is reasonable to require online hosting for systems serving greater than 
10,000 persons since systems will have prepared these materials and submitted them to the 
State and should thus have the ability to host them online.  
 
Action Level and Trigger Level 
We support EPA’s proposal to eliminate the LCRR Trigger Level and to lower the Action 
Level to 10 μg/L. The intention of the Trigger Level, which was to promote early action to 
reduce lead levels when sampling results demonstrated elevation was a good one. However, 
having two tiers of activities based on sampling results set up a complicated process for water 
systems and States to manage and for the public to understand.  While the Action Level is not a 
health-based level and is intended to assess corrosivity and the effectiveness of any treatment, 
nonetheless increased understanding of health effects of lead at very low levels supports 
setting the Action Level lower than it was first set in the LCR.  
 
EPA should re-examine the decision not to lower the Action Level to 5 μg/L as many 
public health and other stakeholders advocate. It is difficult for those outside the drinking water 

8 
 
sector and the regulatory community to understand the justification for setting the Action Level 
based on whether it is generally demonstrative of how well corrosion control treatment is 
working.  While EPA’s estimates do indicate that an Action Level of 5 μg/L would lead to more 
exceedances, and thus more burden on implementing State agencies, it is increasingly difficult 
to explain being more stringent in avoiding lead exposure in drinking water wherever possible. 
These perceptions still matter despite the fact that the Action Level itself is not set as nor does 
it function as a health-based level. Ongoing perceptions that regulations meant to control lead 
exposure in drinking water are not sufficient does not increase customers’ confidence in their 
drinking water – an issue all stakeholders can agree is important. We are not arguing that the 
Action Level should be set based on public perception, but that given the communications 
inherent in a level that is not a health-based level and the ongoing debate around a lower 
Action Level that EPA should revisit the possibility that a lower Action Level would better 
support the overall LCRI goals. The health risk communication challenges inherent in the nature 
of the Action Level support the full lead service line replacement goals of the proposal, given 
that over time overall lead levels will go down.  
 
Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water 
Systems and Non-Transient Non-Community Water Systems 
 
EPA requests comment on limiting small system flexibility to use point-of-us devices and 
plumbing replacement as compliance alternatives to systems serving 3,300 persons and fewer. 
We agree with EPA’s proposal that these compliance alternatives in the case of Action Level 
exceedances are most appropriate for and should be limited to systems serving 3,300 persons 
or fewer.  
 
Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) 
As we noted in comments on the LCRR in 2020, EPA should ensure that the LCRI does 
not minimize and in fact emphasizes the need to consider the water quality impacts of 
increasing the use orthophosphate for corrosion control. Orthophosphate treatment is a critical 
item in our toolbox for preventing corrosion and controlling lead in drinking water, but its use 

9 
 
can have the unintended consequence of increasing phosphorus loadings to downstream 
surface waters and wastewater treatment facilities. Nutrient pollution like phosphorus can 
trigger excessive plant and algal growth in streams, lakes, reservoirs, and estuaries. Certain 
algae are toxic and can make people sick if they swim or come in contact with contaminated 
water. In extreme cases algal growth can result in “dead zones” devoid of any aquatic life. 
When harmful algal blooms (HABs) occur in streams, lakes, or reservoirs that are drinking water 
sources, it can create treatment challenges for drinking water systems. There are also economic 
impacts to nutrient pollution, both in the form of treatment costs for wastewater utilities that 
may have to meet certain Clean Water Act pollution limits for nutrients and in the form of lost 
recreation and tourism dollars when a lake, river, or beach is closed because of a toxic algal 
bloom.  
EPA’s economic analysis of the proposed LCRI concluded phosphorous entering surface 
waters from orthophosphate would be small compared to total phosphorus loads from all other 
anthropocentric sources.  Yet even a relatively small increase in total phosphorus in water 
bodies already impaired for phosphorus is problematic considering there is wide agreement 
among scientists that the frequency and distribution of algal outbreaks have increased in recent 
years.10 
Reducing all sources of nutrient pollution nationwide is a long-standing EPA priority. 
Public health protection and water quality can benefit by acknowledging the need for a holistic 
approach. Requiring full lead service line replacement, as EPA is proposing, is one element of a 
holistic approach in that over time it will reduce treatment needs and has the additional benefit 
of addressing particulate lead which is not always reduced by orthophosphate treatment.  EPA 
should also support research into innovative approaches to phosphorous management and 
continue to support advanced understanding of corrosion control practices. We do not suggest 
taking lightly the need to reduce exposure to lead at the tap, regardless of its source. We do ask 
EPA not to dismiss the need to address the unintended consequences of contributing more 
                                                
10National Office for Harmful Algal Blooms at Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, “Recent Trends: National 
Changes,” July 11, 2016, https://www.whoi.edu/redtide/regions/us-recent-trends  

10 
 
nutrient pollution to water bodies, which itself can create public health risk in drinking water11 
and impact water bodies that are already impaired or experiencing HABs.  
 
Please note that we have also joined other comments, including with Environment 
America others about schools and childcare settings and with Earthjustice and others about key 
provisions in the proposal. We thank EPA for enabling robust public participation during the 
LCRR Review and LCRI process and for consideration of these comments.

Members of the group have developed a technology that uses cell-free biosensors and a 
one-drop sample to provide an easy-to-read positive or negative result for water contaminants, 
including lead and copper. Professors Lucks and Jewett co-founded a private company, 
Stemloop, Inc., in 2019, which has developed convenient user interfaces and reliable 
manufacturing methods to scale up this biosensing technology for wider access and use. One of 
our aims in the WISE-Dx project is to develop, understand, and deploy this new technology to 
improve public policies and public health outcomes. Our overall vision is that this biotechnology 
platform will help mitigate the economic, political, and health impacts of the global water crisis 
by providing actionable information to individuals and communities that can positively impact 
their daily lives and inform mitigation strategies. As described further below, we are in the first 
stages of implementing a National Science Foundation grant, which will fund a pilot program to 
assess how easily members of the public in Chicago are able to use and interpret rapid biosensor 
tests for lead in their drinking water and whether their actions or attitudes change with respect to 
drinking water quality issues, among other research activities.1 
We submit these comments regarding the United States Environmental Protection 
Agency’s (“EPA”) proposed rule titled “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead 
and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (Dec. 6, 2023),” (the “LCRI”). To specify how 
our input can help advance EPA’s overarching goal to “achieve increased protection of 
communities from lead exposure through drinking water,”2 we have organized these comments 
using EPA’s enumerated requests for comments.  
Before responding to EPA’s enumerated questions, it is important to recognize broadly 
how the technology discussed herein can help EPA achieve another of the LCRI’s broad goals, to 
“address potential disproportionate impacts of lead in drinking water in communities, including 
through proposed lead service line replacement and public education, among other areas of the 
proposed rule.”3 Rapid biosensor testing can meaningfully move the needle on equity by granting

all communities, regardless of size and resources, an additional, affordable, and accessible tool to 
understand and tackle lead issues proactively. Rapid lead biosensor technology offers a relatively 
low cost, easy-to-use method to indicate the presence of dissolved lead in drinking water above a 
determined threshold. As elaborated below, the biosensor tests are less expensive than traditional 
laboratory sampling and operate in essentially the same manner as the home tests for Covid-19 to 
which we have all become accustomed.  In other words, biosensor tests can be accessible to many 
more people and can be used by people themselves to provide nearly immediate information. The 
implementation of this technology does not replace traditional laboratory sampling for total lead, 
but it can be used in conjunction with traditional sampling in many applications within the Safe 
Drinking Water Act (“SDWA”) regulatory framework. Biosensor technology, then, can assist 
EPA in its efforts to address disproportionate impacts that stem from lead in drinking water by 
both improving water system performance and empowering and engaging people from all 
communities.4  
Our comments respond to EPA’s request for public comment by addressing how 
innovative rapid lead testing tools can strengthen public health protections by pinpointing lead 
hazards in drinking water with greater speed, accessibility, cost-effectiveness, and overall scale. 
These user-friendly, affordable lead test kits should enable significantly expanded testing, leading 
to more efficient sampling, in schools, childcares, and residences. The real-time insights 
unlocked can enable drinking water systems to achieve faster lead service line (“LSL”) 
replacement through optimized resource allocation. Additionally, rapid testing empowers 
individuals and communities themselves to take charge of assessing lead issues, granting citizens 
visibility into lead levels at the tap to encourage mitigation actions like filter installation while 
systems undertake LSL replacement. In summary, these cutting-edge rapid test kits provide a 
dynamic new means to improve lead hazard identification, resource optimization, community 
empowerment, and risk reduction. 
I. OVERVIEW 
For EPA’s consideration, this comment provides recommendations on integrating 
innovative rapid lead testing technologies into the proposed LCRI. Major themes center on 
getting useful information about lead exposure to the public as quickly as possible and utilizing 
rapid testing kits in schools, as part of enhanced public education requirements, and as a 
complement to traditional compliance sampling.  We believe rapid lead testing technology can 
expedite and optimize the LSL replacement process. These comments are organized as direct 
responses to the EPA’s specific requests for comments.  
 
4 Sera Young & Julius Lucks, What’s Really in Your Water? Rapid at-home tests for contaminants are on the way,

First, we provide an overview of rapid lead biosensor testing technology and how it can 
be utilized by systems and consumers.  Second, after providing this context, we respond to the 
section titled “Lead Sampling in Schools and Child Care Facilities.” Here, we detail how rapid 
lead biosensors can help protect children from lead in drinking water at school.  Third, we 
provide comments regarding “Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for 
Small Community Water Systems and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water Systems,” 
discussing how utilizing rapid testing to evaluate the performance of point-of-use filtration 
devices can help guide proper maintenance and contaminant removal.  Fourth, we discuss “Public 
Education” and explore how rapid biosensor testing can enable quicker interventions and further 
expedited notification policies regarding traditional laboratory sampling results and lead 
exceedances. Then, the comments address EPA’s requests for comments regarding “Tap 
Sampling for Lead and Copper,” showcasing how rapid testing can augment traditional sampling 
approaches for assessing water quality, providing invaluable real-time insights.  The comments 
then briefly address EPA’s “Service Line Replacement” section and the renamed “distribution 
system and site assessment” requirements.  These comments conclude by commenting on the 
“Feasibility of Proposed Inventory Requirements To Support Mandatory Service Line 
Replacement” and note potential costs and benefits of implementing this technology. 
II. INTRODUCTION TO RAPID LEAD TESTING TECHNOLOGY 
With the LCRI, “‘EPA is doing what Congress charged it to do decades ago: getting the 
lead out of drinking water.  Communities demanding safe water got the attention of President 
Biden, whose administration will finally remove every lead pipe from the ground.’”5  History 
shows that this is easier said than done.  We are providing these comments to support EPA’s 
objectives in expeditiously completing this project.  Our aim is not only to contribute to the 
completion of this massive and massively important project, but also to ensure that communities 
and individuals receive timely and comprehensive information regarding their water quality 
along the way.  This becomes especially crucial given the extended duration anticipated for 
complete LSL replacement under the proposed requirements of the LCRI, particularly in the 
communities with the most lead service lines, like our hometown of Chicago.  
Though the proposed LCRI has a plethora of laudable components and policies, including 
requiring nationwide full LSL replacement and moving the lead action level closer to the health-
based goal of zero lead exposure, new water testing technologies can help further EPA’s goals

“to significantly reduce exposure to lead through drinking water” as a means to deliver important 
public health benefits.6 Integrating rapid lead biosensors into the implementation of the proposed 
LCRI will increase and accelerate public health benefits the proposed rule can deliver. 
The WISE-Dx team at Northwestern University was recently awarded a three-million 
dollar grant from the National Science Foundation to “expand [our] work making water 
insecurity challenges more visible and empowering citizens and communities to proactively test 
and understand the quality of their drinking water.”7  Please see Attachment 2 for a detailed 
summary of the work being done under this NSF grant.  The biosensor tests being developed and 
deployed in connection with this grant can detect contaminant content in water and give rapid 
results similar to the manner in which an at-home Covid test does.8  “A unique feature of the 
underlying cell-free biosensing technology is that it is accessible to diverse stakeholders—people 
from a range of ages, abilities, and backgrounds can see, touch, and operate these devices, 
creating powerful entry points for engagement and education.”9 In work under the NSF grant, we 
have strategically identified lead, copper, and per/polyfluoroalkyl substances (“PFAS”) as widely 
recognized contaminants of major concern.10  WISE-Dx members’ research is the basis of a 
pilot-stage lead biosensor product produced by the company Stemloop.11  Currently consumer-
ready rapid lead biosensor technology can identify lead in water in the range of 5-10 ppb, with 
the even lower detection limits under development, and indicates its results in a familiar two-
stripe format: one stripe in the indicator strip means the test functioned properly; two stripes 
indicate dissolved lead is present in the sampled water above the test’s threshold. Further, our 
team is developing rapid testing kits for copper and has made significant progress toward a 
similar test that can detect the presence of PFAS. 
As recently explained in the Chicago Tribune, our work underway will roll out new 
biosensor kits to 350 homes in Chicago.12 These kits will be provided for free as part of our 
study, but cost approximately $20 per test commercially, and will deliver results in just 30

becomes more efficient, we anticipate the $20 per test cost to decline significantly and quickly. 
Additionally, the current detection and reporting threshold indicates the presence of lead at 
EPA’s action level proposed in the LCRI of 10 ppb, though that the indicator threshold can be 
adjusted during manufacture. Currently, EPA estimates annual LCRI sampling costs using the 
prevailing laboratory-based protocols at approximately $170-180 million, based on its least 
expensive projections.13  Given the limited success of the LCR in eliminating lead exposure 
through drinking water, it is imperative that eligible water supplies identify and deploy more 
economical, practical, and efficient means to provide the public with information they can use to 
protect themselves and to promptly identify and eliminate lead pipes.14 
Using technology like rapid lead biosensors in conjunction with traditional lab-based lead 
sampling could facilitate systems to more efficiently meet the LCRI’s requirements and goals, 
and with faster and greater impact, because biosensing technology complements traditional lab-
based sampling.  The current laboratory-based lead sampling method can cost around $50-$150 
per test, and results take approximately two weeks from when they reach the laboratory, and in 
practice often longer than that.15  These limitations in sampling technology have contributed to 
the slow pace of LSL replacement nationwide.  For example, in issuing the original 1991 Lead 
and Copper Rule EPA expected water suppliers to be able to complete replacement of LSLs in a 
maximum of 14 years. In 2021, USEPA revised this rule to allow replacement to take 33 years 
instead of 14, citing the impracticality of the original goal given the technology available.16 
New biosensing technology is well-suited to help better pinpoint actual lead exposure 
within homes, while systems focus under the LCRI on replacing dangerous LSLs leading into 
homes. Given that lead exposure through drinking water results from LSLs in interplay with 
other factors such as internal plumbing, corrosion, fitting and valves, water chemistry, stagnation,

of lead exposure within the specific household context. This is why lower-cost, easier-to-use, and

at multiple taps in a house and/or at different times to get a more complete picture of lead risk in 
the home.  This information would allow consumers and water providers to more efficiently, 
economically, and effectively address the actual sources of lead risk.  
Integrating this technology within the implementation of the proposed LCRI will provide 
EPA, water systems and the public greater opportunities to learn about using and acting on this 
new source of water quality information.  That will not only enhance the effectiveness of the 
proposed framework, but also contribute to public health and knowledge benefits outside of the 
LCRI itself.  Even if the technology is not required to be used in the LCRI, allowing its use in 
LCRI implementation can promote the voluntary adoption of the technology beyond the LCRI’s 
specific mandates, allowing a wider range of stakeholders to harness its benefits. Though this 
technology cannot replace traditional lead sampling, principally because it currently detects only 
dissolved lead, not total or particulate lead, when the rapid lead biosensor testing and traditional 
laboratory sampling approaches are used in conjunction, it should allow for the more efficient 
and effective achievement of EPA’s goals in the LCRI. Accordingly, we have provided the below 
comments which address areas in which we believe the EPA can encourage the use of rapid 
testing technology to help reach their goals more efficiently.  
III. RESPONSES TO SPECIFC EPA REQUESTS FOR COMMENT  
 
A. Lead Sampling in Schools and Childcare Facilities: 
“1. Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or to sample more 
frequently in schools and childcare facilities.” 
Although EPA may lack the authority under a NPDWR to require schools and childcare 
facilities that are not regulated as public water systems (“PWS”) to act,18 lead biosensor tests 
could provide an additional means for non-PWS schools and childcare facilities to conduct 
voluntary lead testing and thereby have better water quality information. Improving lead testing 
in non-PWS schools and childcare facilities is essential to protecting children from lead 
contamination. Although there is no definitive nationwide count of schools and childcare 
facilities that fall outside of SDWA regulation, EPA’s data suggests that the overwhelming

According to EPA’s 2021 figures, up to over ~98% of schools and childcare facilities are not 
required to conduct lead sampling as PWS themselves.19 The fact that so many of our schools 
and childcare facilities are unregulated under the SDWA means that finding alternative ways to 
encourage or require lead testing or sampling would be a significant step toward identifying lead 
problems and protecting children from lead exposure. 
The WIIN Act in 2016 sought to address this issue by establishing the Lead Testing in 
School and Child Care Program Drinking Water grant, which was later amended to the 
Voluntary School and Child Care Lead Testing and Reduction Grant Program in 2021, to support 
and encourage voluntary lead testing in schools and child care facilities.20 According to EPA’s 
data, between October 2021 and March 2023, 10,232 schools have conducted sampling this grant 
program.21 While this is tremendous progress, given the substantial number of schools and child 
care facilities that have yet to be reached, both technological and structural innovations are 
necessary to meet the nationwide need for expanded lead testing in schools and childcare 
facilities. Rapid biosensor tests may be a valuable tool for EPA to make participation in 
voluntary lead testing more appealing and feasible for schools and childcare facilities that cannot 
be reached by EPA’s direct regulatory authority under the SDWA.  EPA should consider 
creating some incentive or allowance within the federal grant program for schools and childcare 
facilities to use rapid biosensor tests. This incentive would not necessarily have to be equivalent 
to the incentive for conducting full laboratory lead sampling; EPA could instead create an 
intermediate tier of incentives for facilities that implement rapid lead biosensors or could simply 
allow or encourage the integration of biosensors into grant proposals. 
Indeed, facilitating the distribution of rapid, low-cost tests to schools and childcare 
facilities could can deliver multiple benefits to the schools and their students. Jewett and Lucks, 
with co-authors, demonstrated the ease of use of a lead-based biosensor system in educational

We ran two pilots at CPS schools. The first was at Von Steuben High School, where

conduct more rigorous testing through traditional laboratory sampling methods.  
Beyond encouraging their use through grant programs, EPA can also integrate rapid 
biosensor tests into the proposed LCRI language itself. For example, EPA could slightly modify

sampling, like the biosensor technology here, would better equip schools to engage in voluntary 
testing and protect children.  This change to the informational requirement would be especially 
effective if schools were able to access rapid tests from their water system.  To further 
supplement these changes, EPA could also modify the actual sampling requirements to mandate 
that water systems conduct traditional laboratory sampling wherever schools identify a potential 
lead hazard through a rapid biosensor test.  One example of how EPA could do so would be to

Even if EPA may lack SDWA authority to require non-PWS school and childcare

cheaper and more user friendly, state and local authorities may be willing to mandate that 
schools and childcare facilities conduct rapid testing, even if those state or local authorities 
would be unwilling to mandate more expansive traditional laboratory sampling.  
The 2017 Illinois Lead Testing Law is a concrete example of how state laws can be a 
vital tool to keep children safe from lead and can have a broader reach than the SDWA. That 
program required public elementary schools to sample their drinking water for lead.24 Of the  
roughly 2,100 schools that reported sampling results, over 1,800 found some level of lead in their 
drinking water, including over 1,350 schools with at least one sample exceeding 5 ppb.25 Those 
schools with samples exceeding 5 ppb were required by the law to notify parents.26 As a result of 
the testing, Illinois public school administrators gained crucial information as to how widespread 
the lead problem was throughout the state, disseminated that information to parents, and were 
required to take immediate actions to mitigate risks to children, such as shutting down or 
repairing fixtures with dangerous lead levels.27 With the biosensor technology described here, 
similar state laws and programs can achieve even more impact than the 2017 Illinois law. 
Agencies in states like Illinois that already have authority to direct schools and childcare 
facilities to test could consider requiring or encouraging more and more frequent testing using 
biosensors. The lower costs and ease-of-use of rapid biosensor tests should mean that similar

B. Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small 
Community Water Systems and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water 
Systems: 
“2. EPA is requesting comment on the ability and practicality of point-of-use devices to 
address multiple contaminants.” 
In response to the EPA’s inquiry into the feasibility and practicality of point-of-use 
devices to mitigate the risk posed by multiple contaminants, it is important to consider how rapid 
lead test kits can be a significant asset in assuring the efficacy of point-of-use devices.  
First and foremost, though, rapid lead biosensors serve as an efficient, relatively low-cost 
measure to illustrate the ability and practicality of point-of-use devices by monitoring their 
effectiveness in filtering out lead. Specifically, these kits can be paired with point-of-use devices 
to assess filter performance; confirm adequate filter performance over time; and locate optimal 
water sources at which to apply point-of-use filters. Specifically, users can periodically conduct 
on-site lead analysis using these kits, providing a quick assessment of lead levels in their water. 
This is crucial for users to monitor (1) filter performance, by setting a baseline of water quality 
before the application of a point-of-use filter; (2) ongoing performance after the point-of-use 
filter is applied; and (3) the effective lifespan of the point-of-use filters, considering different 
households may use filters differently and different source water characteristics may cause filters 
to become ineffective more quickly. The rapid lead biosensors act as a proactive measure, 
enabling users to regularly monitor lead levels and ensure the ongoing effectiveness of installed 
point-of-use devices.  
Increased insight into water quality across time is crucial to address the long-recognized 
challenge of variability in lead content at a single tap over time or at different taps in the same 

 
12 
 
household.28 In other words, water from a kitchen sink may have different lead levels than water 
from a refrigerator spout in that same kitchen, and water at the same tap may exhibit different 
lead levels depending on the day or time sampled.  A key component of rapid lead biosensors is 
their ease of use and ability to provide crucial information instantaneously, allowing the kits to 
assist users in evaluating the relative lead risk of various taps within a home. This helps 
households decide whether a tap filter is needed in just one room or for the entire house or even 
to adjust which taps they use for drinking water in the first place. Biosensor tests can assist 
residents in identifying optimal water sources within their homes and guide their use of point-of-
use devices to best mitigate lead risks. 
 
Biosensors can also help illuminate the ability and practicality of point-of-use devices to 
address multiple contaminants.  Biosensors can be made to detect a range of contaminants, so 
they can help reveal benefits of point-of-use filters in preventing exposure to other contaminants 
beyond lead. Rapid biosensor tests based on the technology developed by WISE-Dx members 
have been produced and can be designed to test for the presence of a wide variety of chemicals 
that may be found in drinking water.29  The biosensor technology here has been studied with 
respect to testing for metals like lead, copper, zinc, and cadmium, but also antibiotics and other 
chemical compounds.  This means biosensor tests could confirm the efficacy of point-of-use 
devices in protecting people from a variety of chemicals that might be filtered out alongside lead 
contamination. This would demonstrate that point-of-use filters deployed to meet the LCRI 
requirements deliver even greater public health benefits.   
 
Integrating biosensors into LCRI implementation will facilitate familiarity with their 
usage and results interpretation among regulators, systems, and consumers, meaning that point-
of-use device benefits beyond lead filtration can be observed and appreciated. Notably, this 
biosensor technology is nearing the ability to analyze copper levels in a commercially viable and 
 
28 “The primary rationale for promulgating the LCR as a treatment technique rule was due to the nature of lead and 
copper contamination.  As EPA described in 1991, and is still accurate today, lead and copper do not generally occur 
in source water, but instead are introduced in drinking water by the corrosive action of water in contact with 
plumbing materials containing lead and copper.  These sources of lead and copper were and continue to be present 
in both the water system’s distribution system and in plumbing materials in homes. In 1991, EPA explained that lead 
and copper levels at the tap can be highly variable ‘due to many factors including the amount of lead and copper in 
the resident’s plumbing or in the PWS’s distribution system . . . temperature, age of plumbing components, chemical 
and physical characteristics of distributed water, and the length of time water is in contact with those materials’ (56 
FR 26473, USEPA, 1991).  EPA noted that while it is feasible to accurately measure the level of lead or copper in an 
individual sample, the inherent variability across sites and systems makes it ‘technologically infeasible to ascertain 
whether the lead or copper level at a tap at a single point in time represents effective application of the best available 
treatment technology’ (53 FR 31527, USEPA, 1988).”  National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and 
Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84906 (Dec. 6, 2023).

https://www.nature.com/articles/s41587-020-0571-7 (Jul. 6, 2020).

consumer-friendly kit, and it is under development to rapidly test for per- and polyfluoroalkyl 
substances (PFAS).30 PFAS, characterized as “forever chemicals,” are estimated to be present in 
at least 45% of the nation’s tap water, emphasizing the importance of expanding options for 
lower-cost, accessible PFAS testing.31 Given that EPA’s current proposed National Primary 
Drinking Water Regulation for certain PFAS would set Maximum Contaminant Levels based on  
analytical limits, rather than the public health imperative to eliminate PFAS exposure, ther eis 
tremendous value in facilitating new ways to measure and track PFAS at the tap.32 Increasing 
collective experience with alternative modes of water quality testing is particularly important 
given that so many Americans draw their water from unregulated private wells, water sources 
that have not been systematically tested for PFAS.33  Integrating rapid biosensor technology in 
the LCRI implementation will create opportunities for regulators, water systems, and individual 
members of the public to learn more about how to deploy this new technology most effectively 
and efficiently to address other dangerous drinking water contaminants, whether through future 
EPA regulation under the SDWA or otherwise.  
 
Rapid biosensor tests can help ground truth the efficacy of point-of-use devices, by 
measuring their effectiveness over time, and can be adapted to address other chemicals of serious 
concern. This real-time data, coupled with the broader contaminant removal capability of point-
of-use devices, empowers individuals and systems to make informed decisions about water 
quality. Biosensors enable continuous assessment of point-of-use devices and the potential to 
significantly contribute to a comprehensive water quality management strategy that goes beyond 
addressing lead contamination. For these reasons, we recommend EPA consider incentivizing or 
requiring the use of rapid lead biosensors alongside point-of-use devices.

treatment technique in preventing—or at least reducing—known or anticipated adverse health

In light of these concerns and this inaction, the integration of rapid lead testing kits could 
significantly enhance the intended impact of the public education requirements outlined by EPA 
in the LCRI. This enhancement can be realized through expediting the public notification 
process; motivating and assisting consumers in taking proactive measures to protect themselves;

authorized under the proposed LCRI. The following parts of this section will address how the 
integration of rapid lead testing can assist with these goals.  
Before turning to specific applications of rapid lead biosensors in the public education 
requirements, it is important to note that implementing the use of rapid lead biosensors could 
increase compliance costs associated with public education requirements.  However, those 
systems incurring these expenses are those with identified lead problems and these costs are 
justified by the potential public health benefits. Further, any marginal increases in public 
education costs are highly unlikely to alter the basic benefit-cost analysis of the LCRI because 
EPA’s lowest estimate of the service line replacement requirements is approximately $1.9 
billion, or 64% of EPA’s “Estimated National Total Monetized Annualized PWS Rule Costs,” 
and EPA’s projected public education costs amount to just $251 million, or 8.5%, of these same 
projected costs.36 The power of this cost comparison only increases if the LCRI’s more 
expensive cost projections are considered.  EPA’s cost analysis based on a discount rate of 7% 
show service line replacement cost estimates amounts from approximately $2.4 billion (80.7% of 
projected costs) to approximately $3.5 billion (73.2% of projected costs).37

“2. Comment and supporting data on the capacity of water systems to conduct some or all of 
the required public education activities in 30 days, or another period of time that is less than 
30 or 60 days, after the end of the tap sampling period in which a systemwide lead action level 
exceedance occurs.” 
EPA will no doubt receive comments from systems and others as to the timeframe in 
which water systems have the capacity to conduct some or all of the required public education 
activities. Regardless of whatever capacity concerns exist and are substantiated, it is crucial to 
highlight that rapid lead kits could play a significant role in providing faster, less expensive 
public education activities in the wake of an action level exceedance. In the event that systems 
express concerns about feasibility or timing, EPA should consider incorporating requirements 
related to rapid testing.  The notification regarding or distribution of biosensor tests could be 
included in the standard public education requirements.  Alternatively, requiring or allowing the 
use of biosensor tests could be made a part of any compliance flexibility mechanisms allowed in 
the final rule, such as, for example if a given water system with an action level exceedance is 
required to submit a plan for actions it will take if it seeks alternative education requirements or 
additional time to complete or education requirements.  
These public education requirements come into play when a water system surpasses the 
action level in over 10% of its compliance samples, a threshold designed to identify problems 
with the system’s corrosion control treatment (“CCT”). That action levels exceedances are meant 
to indicate system-wide issues based on a small sample size underscores the urgency of promptly 
informing all residents about the water reaching their homes in these scenarios. In this context, 
rapid biosensor tests could be distributed so consumers throughout the system could swiftly 
receive rapid test results, offering them immediate insights into their water quality. Systems 
could provide rapid lead biosensors alongside the public education materials required when the 
system exceeds the action-level. For example, § 141.85(b)(2)(i) points out that systems must 
deliver written materials within paragraph (a) of § 141.85. These requirements outline the 
necessity of apprising residents about the use of filters, the importance of running water to flush 
out lead, the need to minimize the use of hot water, clarification that boiling water does not 
diminish lead levels, appropriate cleaning methods, and additional measures to mitigate lead 
exposure. Furthermore, the proposed required notices would urge regular testing and provide 
guidance on how consumers can initiate the process to have their water tested. EPA should make 
a simple and powerful addition to these proposed requirements:  a rapid biosensor test should be 
included in the package delivering these notices. At least, information about accessible and easy-
to-use testing alternatives should be included.    
Whatever the timeframe ultimately required for the distribution of public education 
materials, the requirements for those education materials should be buttressed by inclusion of 

 
16 
 
information about rapid lead biosensors.  Better still, biosensors could be distributed as part of 
those public education efforts themselves.   
“3. Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination that water systems are 
capable of providing consumer notices of individual tap sampling results within three calendar 
days of obtaining those results, regardless of whether the results exceed the lead or copper 
action level, or if a longer time frame is needed (e.g., three business days, seven calendar days, 
14 calendar days).” 
Whatever timeframe may be feasible for systems to deliver results once samples have 
been processed at a laboratory, it is evident that systems can leverage rapid lead biosensors in 
conjunction with traditional sampling methods to provide meaningful information to consumers 
more quickly.  Acknowledging that the prompt delivery of consumer notices depends on the 
capacities of systems, integrating rapid lead testing kits emerges as a complementary solution. At 
sites where lead and copper testing is conducted, systems can distribute these rapid lead 
biosensors to residents at the same time as drawing samples for laboratory analysis; biosensor 
results will be available nearly immediately, while the residents await the more complete 
laboratory results.  
In other words, systems can conduct both tests at once. This is exactly what our team is 
researching in Chicago—we are providing pilot participants with biosensor tests during the same 
visit as when we draw water for testing at the laboratory, so consumers receive biosensor results 
instantly and the lab results when they are ready.  Our proposal here is that water systems can 
conduct rapid lead biosensor testing along with traditional sampling in just the same way. 
Consumers would be provided with same-day rapid testing results, enabling consumers to take 
steps that day to protect themselves.  Water systems themselves may benefit from knowing that a 
rapid biosensor has already detected lead in a sample heading to a laboratory; it could be marked 
for prioritized processing or could be flagged within the systems inventory or other planning 
processes, so the system is ready to proceed most efficiently once the laboratory result is 
returned. 
Because systems may comment that a three-day notification window is too short, EPA 
can require in the final LCRI this parallel use of rapid testing kits contemporaneously with 
laboratory sample collection. This would place less pressure on the three or even seven-day 
notification period because consumers would be provided with same-day notification of whether 
the dissolved lead content of their water exceeded the regulatory threshold.  Consumers can take 
steps that same day to mitigate their risks.  Further, consumers would be able to use these tests at 
multiple water-dispensing locations within their homes. 
It is crucial to highlight here that careful consideration around messaging and 
communications at each step would be needed and that this proposed parallel process would 

 
17 
 
create two distinct notifications—the first being the same-day notification provided by the rapid 
biosensor tests and the second being more detailed traditional sampling results released to 
consumers at whatever later date EPA deems feasible in this rulemaking.  Explaining the 
difference between the testing and sampling approaches would be part of the public notification 
effort and would be necessarily delivered at the time of rapid lead biosensor testing because that 
is when a resident could first see a result indicating that lead is in their drinking water.  In 
addition to explaining the differences between the two approaches, systems would need to 
highlight other important points such as the difference between dissolved and total lead, the 
possibility for lead results at the same tap to vary at different times, and the possibility for lead 
results to differ based on the time of day or the tap at which the test was conducted.  This would 
be needed to avoid potential confusion as consumers would have a better idea of how to interpret 
each test.  The pilot project WISE-Dx is conducting under the NSF grant includes developing 
and rolling out such communications with our technology and studying if and how well these 
notification communications work to transmit information meaningfully and to support consumer 
actions to protect themselves.38 EPA should consider requiring this dual approach to provide the 
most comprehensive and phased strategy to keep consumers as quickly and well-informed as 
possible about their water quality.  
“4. Whether the proposed requirement for water systems to offer lead sampling to consumers 
with LSLs, GRR service lines, or unknown service lines in the notice of service line material is 
effective at reducing adverse health effects. EPA is also requesting comment on the 
requirement for water systems to deliver consumer-initiated test results within three days of 
obtaining those results.” 
The proposed mandate to provide lead sampling to consumers with LSLs, GRR service 
lines, or unknown service lines is a pivotal component of the LCRI.  This provision ensures that 
citizens served by the most potentially dangerous service lines have the chance to be aware of 
their water quality.  However, a significant drawback in this proposal is the prolonged duration 
associated with customer-initiated lead sampling.  Requiring that systems provide an option to 
request lead sampling does not mean such requests will be fulfilled quickly.  Even beyond the 
requirement to deliver results within three days, or some other timeframe, there is the significant 
possibility that simply processing test requests and collecting samples will take a significant 
 
38 Attachment 2 – URoL:ASC: The design, development, and distribution of rapid, in-home, water quality

amount of time given the logistical complexities involved.39 It is common for turnaround times 
of consumer-initiated laboratory sampling to take between 2–4 weeks based on the time needed 
to send kits to residences, wait for the kits to be mailed back and processed by the laboratory, 
and then finally having to deliver the results back to residences.  As such, whatever EPA sets as 
the time limit to deliver results, that clock will not even begin to run for an undetermined and 
potentially unacceptably long period.  While a customer waits for their request to be processed 
and a sample or samples to be collected and tested, everyone in that home continues to drink 
water that is possibly lead contaminated.  
For example, the City of Chicago’s current customer-initiated laboratory lead testing 
program took three years to provide laboratory results confirming dangerous levels of lead at the 
undersigned faculty member’s former residence, a townhome built in 1977.  He made the initial 
request for a testing kit on October 8, 2019.  The estimated completion time provided by the City 
was 365 days. Not until December 2021 did City staff arrive at his home to visually inspect the 
service line connection within the home and draw samples for laboratory analysis, an 
appointment only scheduled after samples self-collected by the resident were analyzed and 
revealed lead above the action level.  Notification of that the results from the City-drawn samples 
indicated action level exceedances came four months later, in March of 2022.  The City only 
provided the actual laboratory results in a letter dated November, 2023.  
Given that experience in Chicago and the fact that SDWA requires the Administrator to 
identify treatment techniques that “would prevent known or anticipated adverse effects on the 
health of persons to the extent feasible,”40 EPA should require or encourage systems to provide 
rapid biosensor tests to customers who request traditional sampling. Rapid biosensor tests could 
be provided both with the required public education required after a system exceeds the action 
level, as discussed above in response to question #2 in this section, and concurrent with 
traditional laboratory sample collection when requested by a specific customer, as described 
above in response to question #3 in this section.  In either case, the combination of rapid lead 
biosensors with traditional sampling methods could feasibly mitigate a greater proportion of 
adverse health effects by promptly delivering actionable water quality information to consumers

and thus enabling them to take steps to avoid consuming or using contaminated water. This is

and “[increasing] the likelihood that the public education activities are effective in preventing

Integrating rapid biosensor tests could help maximize the potential value from the 
proposed mandate to offer lead sampling to consumers served by certain types of service lines. 
Doing so can help better mitigate adverse health effects by allowing for more opportunities for 
consumers to more quickly take steps to avoid using contaminated water. The value is further 
shown as consumers are essentially self-notified on the same day and can take the necessary 
precautions immediately. For example, parents and childcare providers can use these tests as 
they decide which water to use for preparing food, including infant formula, and beverages for 
their children.43  Rapid biosensors can be used to test water throughout homes and buildings, 
enabling residents to make the safest choices about water use even among options within a 
household.  Alternatively, if these tests demonstrate that water quality is free of dissolved lead, 
they can decide to spend money for other household needs that might otherwise be spent on 
bottled water.44

especially for the most vulnerable populations.46  Accurate and timely information about the 
presence of most contaminants is currently very difficult for most people to obtain due to both 
bureaucratic and technical reasons.  People from lower income or historically disadvantaged 
communities may be less likely to open a communication from a water system—which may be 
mistaken for a past-due bill, for example—or may have less time or fewer resources with which 
to navigate a convoluted sampling request process.  A unique feature of the biosensing 
technology is that it is accessible to diverse stakeholders—people from a range of ages, abilities, 
and backgrounds can see, touch, and operate these devices, creating powerful entry points for 
engagement and education, including the necessary engagement and education required to follow 
through with multi-step water system programs to implement customer-initiated sampling with 
laboratory analysis.  
The proposed requirement for water systems to offer customer-initiated lead sampling 
may even contribute to more extensive processing, sampling, and lab delays in the future given 
that there should be more demand for such sampling.  Those could be very natural consequences 
of EPA’s goal that the proposed requirement requiring systems to more broadly offer sampling 
“would encourage more people who are at greater risk of lead exposure to have their tap 
sampled.”47  Indeed, though increased sampling demand is part of the purpose of this 
requirement and would be a positive public health development, EPA should build strategies into 
the LCRI to address this possible effect of implementing the LCRI.  The use of lead biosensors 
as described in this section aligns with the proposed requirement and mitigates this potential 
implementation issue in that provides consumers prompt information from rapid test results even 
while they await traditional results on a timeline feasible for systems.   
While rapid lead biosensors do not substitute for traditional sampling analyzed at a 
laboratory, this new technology can address important limitations in the process for customer-
initiated tests under the proposed LCRI by delivering results on the same day. Consumers 
receive some meaningful information immediately and can act on that information even while 
they await traditional laboratory results that, if history is an indication, may lag for extremely 
long periods of time.  Accordingly, EPA should consider incorporating rapid lead biosensors in 
the LCRI provisions regarding customer-initiated sampling.

D. Tap Sampling for Lead and Copper: 
“3. Comment on the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to assess CCT performance, 
increase customer participation, and other relevant factors.” 
In assessing the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to evaluate CCT 
performance, and encourage customer participation, it is crucial to first acknowledge that the 
traditional sampling protocols established by EPA, such as water running time and sample 
collection methods, address important technical concerns.  That said, the standard sampling 
protocol also creates limitations related to logistics, timing and cost.  Here, rapid lead biosensors 
can be a valuable complement to traditional methods, enabling more testing, across different 
time and at multiple locations.  
The feasibility and cost-efficacy of using rapid lead biosensors at multiple points of use 
and at different times is important given that EPA has noted that lead content in samples can 
vary greatly based at different times, days, and fixtures, let alone across different sampling 
sites.48 For instance, in a house with a LSL, rapid tests enable testing at various faucets within 
the house, offering insights into which lines or fixtures may have elevated lead levels. This 
granular information can aid in assessing CCT efficacy, especially when determining if lead is 
originating from within the house where further optimization of CCT might not mitigate it in any 
event.  Additionally, as discussed above, rapid lead biosensors can empower consumers to 
protect themselves by providing information about relative lead levels in different water sources 
within their homes.  
“EPA is seeking feedback on other alternative sampling protocols, such as random daytime 
sampling (in which sampling sites are not predetermined and there is no minimum stagnation 
time), that could be used to assess CCT performance (See section IX.).” 
Rapid biosensor tests are well-suited for use in the event EPA pursues alternative 
sampling protocols, offering the advantage of providing quick and almost instantaneous results. 
Because biosensors react to dissolved lead and do not need to depend on specific collection 
techniques or chemical preparation, they can be easily deployed without predetermined sampling 
site and or minimum stagnation times.  It’s crucial to note again that while rapid biosensor tests, 
at this point, cannot replace traditional laboratory-based sampling, specifically because currently 
available biosensor kits do not detect particularized lead. 
 
48 “EPA noted that while it is feasible to accurately measure the level of lead or copper in an individual sample, the 
inherent variability across sites and systems makes it “technologically infeasible to ascertain whether the lead or 
copper level at a tap at a single point in time represents effective application of the best available treatment 
technology.” National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 
84878, 84906 (Dec. 6, 2023). 

 
22 
 
Rapid biosensor tests can be utilized to guide where traditional sampling may be 
necessary. For instance, if a rapid test indicates elevated lead levels, it suggests a specific need 
for more detailed traditional sampling. Ultimately, rapid biosensor tests could serve as valuable 
tools in the context of alternative sampling approaches, providing real-time information for 
assessing CCT performance and ensuring water quality compliance. 
“5. Comment and any relevant data on the number and tiering of samples used to calculate 
the 90th percentile lead and/or copper levels for systems with LSLs for purposes of assessing 
CCT efficacy. Specifically, whether samples from non-LSL sites that have higher lead 
concentrations than samples from LSL sites should be included and whether these higher 
values should replace lower values from LSL sites in the 90th percentile calculation.” 
The emerging availability of rapid biosensor tests should support EPA in requiring or 
encouraging the collection and reporting of test results from non-LSL sites that have higher lead 
concentrations than samples from LSL sites. Non-LSL sampling results exceeding the action 
level may reveal that there is an undiscovered source of lead within the system or that the site is 
actually an LSL site that was missed during the inventory process. Given the distinct information 
that could be derived from non-LSL sites with high lead levels, EPA should consider including 
in compliance calculations results exceeding action levels from non-LSL sites without displacing 
any data from LSL sites. We agree with EPA that systems should prioritize sampling LSL sites, 
and thus we support EPA’s decision to refuse to allow for substitution of non-LSL samples for 
LSL samples.  
The relevance of the rapid biosensor tests to including non-LSL site samples in 
compliance calculations is that biosensor tests make it more viable for systems to conduct more 
extensive testing of non-LSL sites. The lower cost, time, and effort that would go into testing 
non-LSL sites with rapid lead testing kits would mean that systems could conduct more non-LSL 
tests without redirecting resources to sample LSL sites. This additional information may, in some 
circumstances, act as valuable data that could supplement EPA’s proposed approach to the 90th 
percentile standard.  
One concrete way in which EPA may be able to gather more information from non-LSL 
sites—and in doing so, gain more insight into where resources are best allocated to resolve the 
most pressing lead threats to drinking water quality—is to require or encourage systems to use 
rapid biosensor tests extensively throughout the water system, even at non-LSL sites. Where the 
rapid tests flag potential lead hazards at non-LSL sites, EPA can require or encourage additional 
testing using traditional lab methods.  For example, if a customer suspects that water delivered 
by a non-LSL site is contaminated with lead, and a rapid test confirms that suspicion, it could 
make sense to prioritize—and then include in compliance calculations—traditional laboratory 
sampling at that non-LSL site.  Such as a result would merit such regulatory attention because 

 
23 
 
the presence of lead above the action level at a site the system had classified as being served by a 
non-LSL line could indicate a previously unknown lead issue within a portion of the system 
larger than the particular service line. Such a scenario could also demonstrate a potential 
oversight or error in the system’s inventory itself; rapid lead biosensors could then serve as a 
confirmation means to ensure accurate inventories under the LCRR (see also below at Section G. 
Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan).  
In other words, rapid lead biosensors can provide a cheap way to conduct an initial 
survey of lower-risk sites for which compliance sampling is not currently required and that may 
not be worth initially testing with traditional laboratory methods. EPA should consider the 
additional feasibility of acquiring non-LSL data presented by rapid lead biosensors by, for 
example, fashioning more stringent requirements for conducting and reporting the results of non-
LSL testing. 
“6. Comment on whether State authority to specify sampling locations when a system is 
conducting reduced monitoring should apply regardless of the number of taps meeting sample 
site criteria.” 
In general, we endorse the notion that giving more thoughtful consideration to the 
selection of sampling locations is a positive aspect of the LCRI. Therefore, we support this 
proposal. One enhancement to this aspect of the LCRI could be the incorporation of rapid lead 
biosensors. These kits offer a valuable solution to enhance the efficiency of water sampling 
during reduced monitoring periods. They provide nearly instantaneous results, allowing for quick 
adjustments in sampling locations for traditional lab sampling as needed. This becomes 
particularly relevant when considering the state authority’s role in specifying sampling locations, 
irrespective of the number of taps meeting sample site criteria.  
Incorporating rapid biosensor tests into state approaches to select sampling locations is 
justified due to their cost-effectiveness and efficiency.  Again, here, rapid tests would not replace 
traditional sampling but could be utilized as a screener for systems or state authorities to better 
decide where to sample, enabling state authorities to make informed decisions about sampling 
locations in real time, at a lower cost. This flexibility empowers states to efficiently target 
sampling efforts, ensuring resources are allocated where needed most.  
Therefore, we recommend that, in promulgating the final LCRI, EPA clarify the 
usefulness of alternative sampling technologies, like rapid biosensor tests, when State authorities 
exercise their powers to specify sampling locations.

E. Service Line Replacement: 
“10. Whether systems conducting deferred service line replacement should be subject to any 
additional requirements beyond those for systems that are not replacing service lines in 
accordance with a deferred deadline.” 
Systems with permission to defer service line replacement are being allowed to leave lead 
pipes in place longer, exposing people to that lead longer.  Therefore, such systems should be 
required to do everything else possible to protect people.  That is the right policy from a public 
health perspective and will incentivize systems to replace LSLs as fast as possible. 
In assessing whether systems conducting deferred service line replacement should face 
additional requirements, EPA should consider how rapid lead kits can serve as proactive 
measures that can help protect public health.  EPA can mandate that these systems, which are 
already failing to keep up with the nationwide schedule EPA has set to protect public health, 
provide residents with rapid lead testing kits. By implementing this requirement, funded by the 
systems themselves, EPA can encourage the systems to accelerate service line replacement and 
simultaneously empower consumers with immediate information about their water quality with 
which they can take prompt actions to protect themselves and their families.  
It is noteworthy that the NSF-funded research our team is in the process of launching will 
include a study of how the use of rapid lead biosensors affects people’s understandings of water 
quality problems and whether those people then take actions to related to water quality problems 
based on the rapid test results.49 Our study will pilot this technology in Chicago, one of the water 
systems anticipated to take advantage of the deferred deadlines provisions proposed in the LCRI.   
Requiring systems on deferred LSL replacement schedules implement rapid testing also 
aids those systems in understanding trends and targeting areas for more efficient public health 
interventions.  Specifically, by having real-time data from these tests, authorities can identify 
areas or communities where lead exposure risks are higher.  This is because we expect 
consumers whose biosensor tests indicate lead content above the regulatory minimum will 
request to have their tap traditionally sampled.  Additionally, biosensor results could be uploaded 
using a QR code or other easy means of reporting.  This information would then allow for more 
efficient and targeted interventions, such as coordinating blood lead level testing resources or 
point-of-use filter distribution, enabling authorities to focus their resources and efforts where 
they are most needed.  
Rapid lead biosensor tests could be a valuable tool to mitigate lead exposure risks during 
deferred service line replacement, aligning with the broader goal of safeguarding public health. 
 
49 Attachment 2 – URoL:ASC: The design, development, and distribution of rapid, in-home, water quality 
biosensors, at 9-11 (summary of WISE-Dx research provided to NSF).  

 
25 
 
As such, EPA should consider requiring systems conducting deferred service line replacement to 
utilize rapid lead biosensors in efforts to better protect public health.  
F. Distribution system and site assessment: 
“EPA is proposing to rename the LCRR's “find-and-fix” requirement to better align with the 
underlying requirements of the provision.” 
 EPA proposes to rename the LCRR “find-and-fix” provision as the “distribution system 
and site assessment” provision to better reflect the content of the requirements.50  This proposed 
nomenclature change is reasonable because it emphasizes the complicated nature of “fixing” lead 
in drinking water at a particular tap and reflects a more precise description of the regulatory 
expectations.  However, the substance of the process remains, where water systems are required 
to conduct an assessment of both the distribution system and specific sites where elevated lead 
levels are identified.  The overarching goal is still to understand and address the factors 
contributing to elevated lead levels in drinking water at a particular location and the requirement 
to consider actions to address identified issues is retained in the proposed LCRI.51  Though the 
name will change in the rule to deemphasize the “fix,” a significant challenge persists: water 
systems may lack, or perceive that they lack authorization to address elevated lead levels 
effectively, i.e. to “fix” them, if the source of lead is or may be within the home or on the 
homeowner’s property.  EPA explains that, “[f]or example, one stakeholder indicated that 
identified cause of the lead level could be a premise plumbing issue that the water system may 
not be authorized to “fix” it.52   
Rapid lead kits can help alleviate this problem by enabling water systems to sample more 
locations within a home, at lower costs, and less disruption to households, to “find” where, 
exactly, the problem is and either “fix,” it or advise the resident on how to do so.53  As
