‘fix’.” National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 
84944 (Dec. 6, 2023).

mentioned throughout these comments, rapid biosensor tests can be utilized by both systems and

language is implemented with the benefit of the most up-to-date tools.  This includes 
§ 141.82(j)(2), which provides that water systems must collect follow-up samples at any 
sampling site that exceeds the action level and that “[t]hese follow-up samples may use different 
sample volumes or different sample collection procedures to assess the source of elevated lead 
levels.”56 The current language, then, already contemplates that systems may use approaches 
other than the traditional laboratory sampling approach to “to assess the source of elevated lead 
levels.”57  EPA should explicitly endorse the use of rapid lead biosensors by water systems 
addressing this requirement. Moreover, incorporating periodic rapid biosensor testing at intervals 
after service line removal enhances the verification of lead levels and can be utilized to quickly 
show that the work was successful. This proactive approach expedites the confirmation process, 
 
likelihood that customers provide access for service line replacement.” National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84921 (Dec. 6, 2023). 
54 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84944 
(Dec. 6, 2023). 
55 “EPA expects some customers might be more willing to provide access based on sampling results. Where 
compliance sampling tests above the lead action level and is subject to the proposed distribution system and site 
assessment requirements, a system could identify the presence of a lead or GRR service line as the probable cause 
for the higher lead levels, which could increase the likelihood that customers provide access for service line 
replacement.” National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 
84878, 84921 (Dec. 6, 2023). 
56 40 C.F.R. § 141.82(j)(2). 
57 Id.  

 
27 
 
increasing confidence in work done, potentially reducing costs, and ensuring the sustained 
effectiveness of lead mitigation efforts. 
G. Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan: 
“EPA is seeking comment on all aspects of the proposed service line inventory approach.” 
 EPA has requested general comments on its service line inventory approach and 
comments on these points relate also to the section within the LCRI regarding “Feasibility of 
Proposed Inventory Requirements To Support Mandatory Service Line Replacement.” 
Specifically, our comments respond to the statement that “EPA has determined that it is feasible 
(i.e., technically possible and reasonably affordable relative to a large system) for water systems 
to create a complete and accurate inventory of service line materials by the proposed service line 
replacement deadline to support the treatment technique for mandatory service line 
replacement.”58 This section of these comments will explore the integration of rapid lead 
biosensor testing to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of LSL inventories in accordance 
with EPA’s well-founded position that “[e]stablishing an inventory of service line materials and 
identifying the location of LSLs are key steps in getting them replaced.”59 
“Service line inventories are the foundation from which water systems can take action to 
address LSLs.”60 Given that, we agree with EPA that “[l]ocating LSLs is the first and critical 
step to replacing them.”61 EPA’s inventory guidance instructs that “[p]rioritizing investigations 
of service lines that are unknown-likely lead and replacing them if found can lower costs and 
save time related to access agreements, traffic control, and field crew mobilization. This 
approach may also reduce the costs associated with false negatives (i.e., digging up a suspected 
lead line and finding that it is non-lead).”62 The rapid lead biosensing technology described 
above can help systems locate LSLs and screen for which service lines of unknown material 
merit follow-up, which will assist in developing a thorough, accurate, and actionable service line 
inventory. 
Rapid biosensor technology can assist in efficiently determining whether a service line of 
unknown material is, in fact, made of lead because a biosensor result showing lead above the 
action level would be inexpensive, easily gathered, and immediate evidence suggesting just that. 
 
58 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84933 
(Dec. 6, 2023). 
59 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Fact Sheet for Developing and Maintaining A Service Line Inventory, 
https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-06/EPA-Factsheet-Combined-06072023%20508-final.pdf (last 
accessed February 4, 2024).  
60 Id. 
61 U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Office of Water, Guidance for Developing and Maintaining a Service Line 
Inventory, EPA-816-B-22-001, https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2022-
08/Inventory%20Guidance_August%202022_508%20compliant.pdf (Aug. 2022) at 1-2.    
62 Id. at 6-7.  

 
28 
 
Rapid lead biosensor tests could be applied by single staff members, using a real-time, positive 
biosensor result to trigger bringing the larger and more equipped crews to undertake more 
intensive investigation techniques like potholing. Without knowledge of the underlying pipe 
structure, common service line investigative methods such as potholing, water quality sampling, 
and predictive modeling can be time consuming, costly, and invasive.63  Rapid lead technology 
offers a less invasive, efficient, and less expensive approach to identifying likely LSLs by 
allowing water sources to be tested in just minutes.  This could include utilizing rapid tests for 
screening purposes to identify areas where more invasive or intensive inventory techniques, such 
as potholing, might be necessary. It would then be more economical to train and equip potholing 
crews to perform LSL replacements if they are directed more efficiently and more reliably to 
more likely LSLs.  EPA already notes that “systems can save costs by replacing LSLs when 
crews find them onsite during service line investigations.”64 Further, EPA recommends that 
“[w]ater systems should select the method(s) that are best suited to their particular distribution 
system and community, considering cost, labor skill requirements, disruption to homeowners, 
overall time, and accuracy.”65  Rapid biosensors provide a new inventory tool that is less 
invasive and disruptive to homeowners, has relatively low costs, requires no skilled labor, and 
provides immediate and accurate information. 
Additionally, the incorporation of rapid lead testing can prove beneficial in identifying 
lead issues at non-LSL sites, especially considering fixtures and connectors issues. Therefore, 
using rapid lead biosensors could be a cost-effective approach to confirm the absence of lead 
exposure through drinking water at sites not served by LSLs, offering a less expensive way to 
ensure the accuracy of inventories and to protect water safety in residences where lead issues are 
not anticipated. If it is confirmed that a home is served by a non-LSL and yet a rapid biosensor 
test detects lead, systems and residents will know there is another source of lead that must be 
addressed, such as fixtures. 
Accordingly, we recommend that EPA highlight these benefits of lead biosensors in the 
service line inventory contest when promulgating the final LCRI.  EPA could also integrate these 
comments in the context of revising its LCRR Inventory Guidance, providing insights on how 
new technologies, including rapid lead testing, can enhance and streamline various aspects of the 
inventory process. 
IV. CONCLUSION 
Integrating innovative rapid biosensor technology can enhance implementation of EPA’s 
proposed LCRI across multiple facets. Our comments have focused specifically on the potential 
 
63 Id. (See generally, Chapter 5, describing benefits and drawbacks of various inventory tactics). 
64 Id. at 1-1.  
65 Id. at 5-1.  

 
29 
 
for these rapid biosensor tests to facilitate more extensive sampling in vital settings like schools 
and childcare facilities in a timely and cost-effective manner. Additionally, we discussed the 
value of rapid testing in assessing contaminant removal capabilities of point-of-use devices and 
highlighted how real-time insights from rapid testing empower quicker public health 
interventions and align with expedited notification policies. Moreover, we explored the 
applicability of rapid testing to augment alternative tap sampling approaches for dynamically 
evaluating water quality. Finally, we emphasized the benefits of leveraging rapid testing 
methodologies to expedite and streamline the identification of high-risk LSLs as well as confirm 
the absence of lead threats in residences without lead pipes. Most importantly and if deployed in 
various contexts throughout the LCRI, expanding the use and availability of rapid biosensor tests 
can empower people and communities to better know the quality of the water coming from their 
taps and take steps to protect their families and to demand action from their water providers.   
We firmly believe adoption of these recommendations in the final LCRI will significantly 
strengthen implementation of EPA’s regulatory goals regarding improved public health 
outcomes.  The time is now to leverage 21st century technologies to address this 20th century 
environmental health threat. Thank you for your attention to this important matter and please do 
not hesitate to contact me if you would like any additional information.

M A J O R  P R O F E S S I O N A L  I N T E R E S T S
I am an applied nutritional anthropologist who explores how vulnerable populations, especially women and 
children, adapt to challenges to their health and well-being. 
Keywords: Nutritional anthropology; medical anthropology; global health; international nutrition; maternal and 
child nutrition; pica; food insecurity; water insecurity; HIV; infant and young child feeding.

F I E L D  R E S E A R C H ,  B Y  T O P I C
Food and water insecurity:
We Are Water Evanston :: Evanston, IL 2020-present
A community-based participatory research project led by Citizens’ Greener Evanston to understand water 
insecurity and how water is valued in and around Evanston (https://greenerevanston.org/we-are-water). This 
resulted in an 8-part series in the local paper about water in Evanston: https://evanstonroundtable.com/
2021/09/20/we-are-water-evanston-about-this-series/
Individual Water Insecurity Experiences (IWISE) Scale :: 31 countries :: Northwestern University, UNESCO, 
Gallup World Poll 2019-present
A collaboration to refine and validate a scale to measure water insecurity at the individual level.
Household Water Insecurity Experiences (HWISE) Scale :: 26 sites worldwide :: Northwestern University — 
2016-2019
A 28-site, multi-partner collaboration to design and refine a novel cross-culturally validated household water 
insecurity scale, as well as the development of a scale implementation manual (http://sites.northwestern.edu/
hwise/). 
Health Consequences of Water Insecurity for HIV+ Women & Their Infants :: Kisumu, Kenya :: Northwestern 
University, Kenyan Medical Research Institute, and Family AIDS Care and Education Services, — 2016-present
An observational study of the consequences of water insecurity for adverse maternal and infant health outcomes 
among a cohort of HIV-infected and uninfected pregnant and lactating women in western Kenya.
Singida Nutrition and Agroecology Project :: Singida, Tanzania :: Cornell University, Northwestern University, 
Action Aid Tanzania, Nelson Mandela Agricultural Institution of Science and Technology 2014— present
We are assessing if a participatory educational intervention about nutrition, climate change, agroecology, and 
gender equity that we co-created with rural farmers in E. Africa improves women’s empowerment, food 
insecurity, and infant feeding practices in Singida, Tanzania.
Health Consequences of Food & Nutrition Insecurity for HIV+ Women & Their Infants :: Kisumu, Kenya :: 
Northwestern University, Cornell University, Kenyan Medical Research Institute,  and Family AIDS Care and 
Education Services, — 2013-present
An observational study of the role of food insecurity in adverse maternal and infant health outcomes among a 
cohort of HIV-infected and uninfected pregnant and lactating women in western Kenya. 
Food insecurity and nutritional status of patients infected with tuberculosis and HIV in Gulu, Northern 
Uganda (The FINITH Study) :: Gulu, Uganda :: Cornell University and Gulu University — 2013-2014
A cross-sectional study of the effects of food insecurity on disease and nutritional status among adult Ugandans 
infected with TB and/or HIV.
Prenatal Nutrition And Psychosocial Health Outcomes (PreNAPs) study :: Gulu, Uganda :: Cornell University 
and Gulu University — 2012-2015
A longitudinal cohort study of the effects of food insecurity on depression, stress, and gestational weight gain 
among HIV-infected and -uninfected pregnant women.

Maternal anemia care, program evaluation :: Pemba Island, Zanzibar, Tanzania : Cornell University/Zanzibar 
Ministry of Health— 2006
Conducted community surveys, focus group discussions and interviews with traditional and biomedical health 
care workers, private medicine retailers and pregnant women to understand how use of anemia medicine can be

Qualitative Researcher : Cornell University — 2003-2004
Conducted interviews and focus group discussions with nutritional education program staff as part of a USDA-

being. 
Pica
Antojitos study, the relationship between pregnancy, pica, iron status, and cognitive function :: Salinas, 
California  — 2008-2011
Primary investigator of a study of nutritional behaviors and beliefs, and their associations with iron status and 
cognitive function among pregnant Hispanic women.
Quantitative and qualitative study of non-food cravings, primary investigator :: Pemba Island, Zanzibar, 
Tanzania : Cornell University— 2004
Secured funding, hired, and trained Zanzibari fieldworkers to collect epidemiological data about consumption of 
non-food substances (pica) in 700 adults as part of a larger trial on the prevention of severe anemia (PI Rebecca 
Stoltzfus). Conducted in-depth interviews about pica (the cravings for and consumption of non-food substances) 
with community members and health care workers. Collected samples of pica substances for biochemical 
analysis.
Perceptions of anemia during pregnancy :: Pemba Island, Zanzibar, Tanzania : University of Amsterdam — 2002
Qualitative data was collected about the perceived causes, cures, and appropriateness of UNDP-supplied ferrous 
sulfate and traditional medicines for the treatment of anemia during pregnancy. Analyzed data to make 
suggestions about how traditional and biomedical treatments can be linked.

ATTACHMENT 2 
 
Comments on behalf of Northwestern University WISE-Dx Faculty Team Regarding 
EPA’s Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 

URoL:ASC: The design, development, and distribution of rapid, in-home, water quality biosensors. 
I. Broader Impacts
The global water crisis is among 
the most urgent issues of our 
time.1,2 This proposal seeks to 
address the need for action on 
water quality and water insecurity 
with three central goals, encap-
sulated in a novel methodology 
for the collaborative design (Stage 1), development (Stage 2), and distribution (Stage 3) of rapid in-home, 
water quality monitoring tests (Fig. 1): 
•
Goal 1: To design cell-free synthetic biological systems that can detect key water contami-
nants by harnessing the ‘rule of life’ of natural biological systems to sense their environment.
•
Goal 2: To develop these biological sensors into accessible diagnostic tests that permit an-
yone to rapidly assess their water quality in a simple and affordable way.
•
Goal 3: To distribute and understand the societal implications of these diagnostic tests,
including how people’s knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors related to water are impacted by the
information these biosensor tests generate.
Together, these goals help realize a new distributable biotechnology platform by harnessing the ‘rule of life’ 
of biosensing; this platform has the potential to democratize access to water quality information across 
society. In collaboration with the greater Chicagoland community, we will demonstrate the utility of this new 
approach with the detection of lead, copper, and per/polyfluoroalkyl substances, three water contaminants 
that are the subject of major public regulation and concern. Our vision is that this biotechnology platform 
will help mitigate the economic, political, and health impacts of the global water crisis by providing actiona-
ble information to individuals and communities that positively impact their daily lives and informs mitigation 
strategies. Below we describe the importance of water quality, the premise for harnessing the natural bio-
sensing abilities of cells (a ‘rule of life’) into technologies that can rapidly detect water quality, and how such 
a technology stands to make significant broader impacts for this paramount societal challenge.  
I.A. Water security is a global societal challenge. Water security exists when water is available, acces-
sible, safe, and reliable for a healthy life (Fig. 2).3-6 The billions of people globally who face problems with
one or more of these four domains experience far-reaching adverse economic, political, nutritional, and
mental and physical consequences, ranging from work absenteeism to waterborne infections, interpersonal
violence, and depressive disorders.4,7-9
Water quality (safety) is core to water in-
security and is threatened by both chemical and 
biological contaminants. The World Health Or-
ganization estimates that 2.2 billion people glob-
ally do not have access to “safely managed water” 
(i.e., water is likely to be contaminated). Water 
contamination can have both acute and lifelong 
consequences on human health and develop-
ment, economic output, and agricultural produc-
tion.2 Globally, the leading chemical contaminants 
of concern are fluoride and arsenic, but domesti-
cally there are a range of important contaminants 
including 
lead 
and 
copper10 
as 
well 
as 
per/polyfluoroalkyl substances.11 Water insecurity 
in the US is far more common than one might ex-
pect;12 nationally representative data reveal that 
~20% of adults do not drink their tap water13 and 
39.6% of Americans anticipate being harmed by 
their water in the next 2 years.14  
Figure 1. A collaborative methodology to address water quality and
insecurity with rapid, in-home water quality biosensors.

The global prevalence of experiences with water in-
security.7 (B) The four domains of water security.3,4

The ability to detect water contaminants should increase water security for the most vulnerable 
populations.15 However, limited accessibility to testing methods is a critical barrier to understanding water 
safety. Accurate and timely information about the presence of most contaminants is currently very difficult 
for most people to obtain due to both bureaucratic and technical reasons.16 Detecting most contaminants 
in drinking water requires analytical chemistry techniques that necessitate skilled operation in a centralized 
laboratory facility.17 This restriction results in tests that are costly (>$50/test) and slow (>2 weeks),18 creating 
barriers for private citizens to access this testing information. 
As an indicative example, establishing the presence of lead (Pb), a neurotoxin that causes severe, 
long-lasting harm by interrupting neurotransmission,19,20 is challenging in part because gold-standard Pb 
testing requires individuals to mail a sample to a laboratory, results take several weeks, and tests are ex-
pensive. Less-expensive ‘at-home’ Pb test kits consist of sample collection tubes and mailing envelopes, 
requiring sample mailing, processing and waiting that create the same barriers to testing.18 Other types of 
at-home tests are sold but are not validated and have documented issues with accuracy.21 A second diffi-
culty in establishing the presence of Pb in drinking water is the need to test multiple samples because many 
contaminants are released erratically in pipes.22 The EPA’s Lead and Copper rule, a regulation for a testing 
and remedial action regime related to lead and copper in municipal water, mandates representative sample 
testing by cities, but the number of sample sites is often small and there are unfortunate loopholes that 
enable municipalities and utilities to avoid remediation activities.23 With approximately 6-10 million house-
holds and 400,000 schools in the US having Pb water lines that contribute to this problem,24 easily acces-
sible and accurate testing by individuals is essential to prompt remediation action ensuring a safe and 
secure water supply. Our three-stage methodology will address this problem by creating a workflow to 
design, develop and assess the accessibility and accuracy of new water contaminant biosensors that are 
rapid, cheap, and easily used, which should increase water security for the most vulnerable populations. 
 
I.B. Understanding the rules of biological sensing has created new synthetic biology technologies 
that address the water insecurity crisis. A cell’s ability to sense and respond to changes in the environ-
ment is one of its defining attributes of life (“rule of life”). Many of these sense-and-response mechanisms 
arise from non-coding riboswitch RNAs25 or allosteric transcription factor (aTF) proteins that each bind to 
target small molecules to activate expression of a downstream gene.26,27 These regulators often control 
transport of the bound molecules out of the cell (e.g., heavy metals or antibiotics) or catabolism of the bound 
molecule into a more useful form (e.g., substrates for central carbon metabolism). Naturally derived ri-
boswitches and aTFs thus provide key components that can be repurposed for synthetic sensing systems. 
 
Decades of fundamental investigations into the mechanisms of riboswitches and aTFs have fueled 
recent innovations in synthetic biology that harness the biosensing ‘rule of life’ for the point-of-need detec-
tion of chemical species.18,21,28-40 These systems typically consist of three components: (i) a molecular bio-
sensor (riboswitch or aTF) that activates the production of a reporter system once a target compound is 
bound; (ii) a reporter system that generates a fluorescent or colorimetric output; and (iii) an in vitro reaction 
platform that contains reagents and other biological machinery needed to support the biosensing reactions 
(Fig. 3). Our team and others have shown that this approach can be used to create water diagnostics for a 
range of different compounds such as metals (e.g., lead, copper, cadmium, mercury),18,37 antibiotics and 
other drugs,18,37 personal care products,18 cleaning products,18 toxic geogenic ions,21 endocrine disrup-
tors,31,38-40 micronutrients,18,30 and other toxins (e.g. cyanuric acid).29 Lessons learned from these tests will 
have broad impacts for the design, develop-
ment, and distribution of other diagnostics like 
those we propose here.  
Cell-free synthetic biology biosensors 
have several advantages over conventional la-
boratory-based strategies. For one, they can be 
freeze-dried for cold chain-free storage, rapid 
distribution, and activation simply by rehydrating 
with the sample of interest. They can be manu-
factured cheaply, with cost-estimates <$2/test 
for many analytes when produced at scale,18 
and they do not have the biocontainment

life” into real-world water monitoring technology.

concerns of engineered whole cell biosensing approaches.15,41 For these and other reasons, developing at-
home water quality tests are an opportunity to increase the reach of synthetic biology by delivering public 
health benefits in the field of water insecurity. In this project, we propose to improve the sensitivity, accu-
racy, accessibility, and impact of water quality biosensors by merging synthetic biology and chemistry with 
the social sciences in community-driven, user-focused research. 
 
I.C. Distributing rapid biosensor tests could confer beneficial societal impacts. The proposed work 
represents a major step towards democratizing knowledge about water safety for all. Our three-stage meth-
odology merges social science and synthetic biology to overcome many of the financial and technical bar-
riers currently preventing individuals, especially those from marginalized communities, from ascertaining 
their exposure to unsafe water. Further, this work 
will study how access to biosensing technologies 
will affect the knowledge, attitudes, and behav-
iors of individuals about water quality—infor-
mation used to further refine the technologies 
and maximize their impact. While our project will 
directly interact with greater Chicago, there are 
clear benefits applicable well beyond Chicago-
land and even outside of the US (Fig. 4). 
The first is the translational nature of the proposed work, which sets it apart from other diagnostic 
development because of our inclusion of underserved groups from the outset. Of the thousands of point-
of-care diagnostics developed each year, only a tiny fraction is field-tested under “real world” conditions 
(i.e., by non-scientists).42 Even fewer studies examine how the technology shapes consumer risk and harm 
reduction. Our proposed work on technology usability (see Stage 2) and impacts on contaminant-related 
knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors (see Stage 3) will help illuminate how such tests can increase envi-
ronmental health and safety literacy across socio-economic groups.43,44 
The second is a much clearer picture of the prevalence of water quality issues that will arise from 
this work; the ease of obtaining quick and accurate results will likely greatly expand the current pool of 
individuals who test their water. Indeed, it is feasible that regular water testing can become standard prac-
tice in daycares and schools. There is wide agreement that information about the extent of water contami-
nation, of lead for example, are poorly understood. 
Third, this information would be incredibly powerful to advocate for environmental justice. Test re-
sults would be actionable evidence for garnering additional attention and resources to reduce the scourge 
of heavy metal poisoning and other contaminants of concern that are disproportionately borne by margin-
alized groups in the US. By analogy, data on blood lead levels of Flint children were instrumental for drawing 
media attention and the eventual government action. Data on drinking water could capture risks before the 
contaminant is ingested, and embodied. 
Fourth, these tests will empower people to make safer choices about the water they use. For ex-
ample, parents and childcare providers can use these tests as they decide which water to use for preparing 
food (including infant formula) and beverages for their children. If water is contaminated, they can take 
measures to reduce exposure to toxins. Alternatively, if these tests demonstrate that water quality is high, 
they can decide to spend money otherwise spent on bottled water for other household needs. 
Further, this body of work will generate critical, policy-relevant information to plan and evaluate 
interventions. For example, high levels of lead in drinking water can indicate where buried lead lines or 
fixtures are located that cannot otherwise be observed. Such information is critical for prioritizing areas to 
implement the lead line replacements laid out in the 2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. In terms of moni-
toring the impact of interventions, detection of contaminants after remediation actions indicates that removal 
was incomplete and more or different remediation action is needed.  
 
I.D. At-home water quality biosensor tests offer new ways to engage and educate diverse commu-
nities through citizen science. A unique feature of cell-free biosensing technology is that it is accessible 
to diverse stakeholders—people from a range of ages, abilities, and backgrounds can see, touch, and 
operate these devices, creating powerful entry points for engagement and education. For instance, our 
team recently developed an easily configurable education platform, called BioBits, using cell-free synthetic

on the knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors of households for water contaminants (see Section II). 
 
I.E. Assessing societal impacts of rapid, in-home, water quality biosensors. We have strategically 
identified lead,19 copper, and per/polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS)11 as widely recognized contaminants 
of major concern, where federal regulations are being reevaluated or just beginning to be written and where 
existing biosensing technologies are at distinct stages in our methodology (see Section II). As such, in 
parallel we will (i) use commercially available lead tests from Stemloop, Inc. (see Section II.C.3; Letter of 
Support) to probe the impact of distribution on knowledge, attitudes, and behaviors, (ii) develop an existing 
transcription factor-based biosensor for copper and optimize and distribute tests based on the biosensor to 
evaluate impact, and (iii) design a novel PFAS detection scheme combining both biological and chemical 
mechanisms, develop an at-home test, and distribute them to measure societal impact. We will test and 
refine the methodology in greater Chicago, the city with the most lead pipes in the US,23 with key community 
stakeholders, including Chicago civil society (e.g., Blacks in Green, Citizens for a Greener Evanston, Rotary 
International), Chicagoland water utilities (e.g., City of Chicago, Evanston Water District), and policymakers 
at the local, state, and federal level (see Letters of Support). These interactions will be facilitated through 
the development of a Community Advisory Board at the outset (see Project Management Plan) who will 
guide our activities throughout the project. This feedback will be augmented through presentations at town 
hall meetings, focus group discussions, ethnographic interviews, and field trials. As such, this proposal 
could contribute valuably to regulatory design and compliance assessment and advances the goals of 
NSF’s URoL big idea and NSF’s strategic plan by mobilizing knowledge most effectively to impact society. 
 
II. Intellectual Merit: Convergent Research Plan 
In this work, we propose developing a three-stage methodology for the collaborative design (Stage 1), 
development (Stage 2), and distribution (Stage 3) of rapid in-home, water quality monitoring tests for 
three contaminants of major concern—lead (Pb), copper (Cu), and per/polyfluoroalkyl substances 
(PFAS)—in the Chicagoland area (Fig. 6). This proposed research is oriented around the biosensing ‘rule 
of life’, the natural ability of cells to sense and respond to molecules in their environment (Section I.B).

Importantly, developing simple, af-
fordable, and rapid water quality di-
agnostics is a process that occurs 
across scales, from research on mo-
lecular-level engineering required to 
detect and report on contaminants21 
to the user-focused research on un-
derstanding how to format tests for 
usability and accessibility18 to the so-
cial science research needed to un-
derstand how the newly gathered wa-
ter quality information impacts indi-
viduals and communities through 
changes in their knowledge, atti-
tudes, and behaviors.49 Our method-
ology incorporates both technical de-
velopments in STEM (biology, chem-
istry, engineering, synthetic biology) 
and qualitative and quantitative meth-
ods from the social sciences (anthro-
pology, epidemiology) at all stages 
(Fig. 6). Importantly, each stage will incorporate the perspectives of diverse community stakeholders in an 
open and inclusive manner. One important mechanism for this community engagement will be through the 
establishment of an 8-person Community Advisory Board. Members of the Community Advisory Board will 
represent diverse stakeholder groups in the Chicago area, with an emphasis on amplifying the voices of 
groups that have experienced the most environmental injustices in Chicago, (i.e., those living along the 
industrial corridor, non-white individuals, and those living in poorer wards).50,51 
Stage 1: Technology discovery and design. Each water contaminant requires the discovery of a 
natural biosensing mechanism (a biosensing ‘rule of life’) that can be leveraged in a portable cell-free tech-
nology. From a technology perspective, we will address this need through molecular engineering to genet-
ically rewire sensors (riboswitches or aTFs) to produce easily visible outputs in response to detecting the 
specified contaminant and coupling chemistry techniques that may be needed to convert a desired con-
taminant target into a molecule that can be sensed by a biosensor. From a social science perspective, it is 
critical to understand at this early stage the perceptions about the contaminant within a target community: 
are they aware this contaminant is a priority? Do they have adequate mitigation strategies (e.g., access to 
filtration or alternative water supplies) if the contaminant is identified? Do they have community advocacy 
to enact long term change (e.g., replace aged pipe infrastructure) if contamination is found to be highly 
prevalent in their community? In this stage, we will address this need through town hall meetings in collab-
oration with the Community Advisory Board as well as through focus group discussions. 
Stage 2: Community-driven usability development. Once the technology is designed, it is para-
mount that it is usable and accessible by communities impacted by these contaminants. From a technology 
perspective, there are multiple ways that the presence of a water contaminant can be communicated to a 
user, for example through the generation of fluorescence, the creation of a visible color, or the development 
of a line on a lateral flow strip like an at-home COVID test. Developing the test can require high-throughput 
optimization to ensure the biosensors are sensitive and function robustly in the given test format, and in-
corporating sample processing steps (e.g., concentrating contaminants to amplify detection signals), and 
molecular and device engineering to achieve the indicated performance. From a social science perspective, 
we will conduct iterations of usability studies to inform the molecular and device engineering of the biosen-
sors. Participants in these studies will be asked to use different types of test formats (e.g., lateral flow, 
fluorescence) to test water samples either pre-seeded with known levels of contaminants, or control tests 
designed to produce specific output signals, to determine if participants interpreted test results accurately. 
They will then answer open-ended questions about knowledge, attitudes, and behavior (KAB) to inform 
optimization of technology features most important to users (e.g., speed of the test, simplicity of the test, 
cost of the test, etc.) and the survey design in Stage 3.

Stage 3: Community impact research through test distribution. The goal of biosensor technology 
development is to empower individuals with information about their water quality so that they can make 
decisions to improve their lives. However, this goal is not always realized with technology development.42 
From a technology perspective, ensuring the accuracy and reliability of biosensor tests is essential for use 
and impact. Technology outputs will be compared with gold-standard contaminant measurements to track 
accuracy as tests are distributed.  From a social science perspective, we will work to understand how water 
quality monitoring technologies influence KAB of users about the contaminant of interest, and the diagnostic 
developed to detect it. Key activities for Stage 3 are two surveys conducted before and after participants 
use the biosensor tests to understand key demographics, and changes in water insecurity and KAB related 
to the contaminant of interest. Findings will be communicated to participants and their communities through-
out the project in consultation with the Community Advisory Board. 
 
II.A. Background on targets for biosensing. We selected Pb, Cu, and PFAS as priority contaminants for 
several reasons: (i) severity—exposure to these molecules is linked to hundreds of thousands of deaths 
and billions of dollars per year;19,52,53 (ii) prevalence—these are some of the most widely distributed con-
taminants in the United States;7,54,55 (iii) technology suitability (see Section II.C.1).  
Lead (Pb) exposure is widely recognized as a top environmental health threat in the US, with a 
large proportion of exposure occurring through water.56 Pb toxicity disproportionately affects vulnerable and 
marginalized populations57,58 and is therefore a major environmental justice concern.59,60 Pb continues to 
be a pressing environmental health challenge in part because of the difficulty in identifying exposure (see 
Section I.A). Our inability to rapidly detect Pb has caused public health crises and perpetuated public health 
inequities, as seen in Flint,61,62 Newark,63,64 Washington DC,22,65 and Chicago.23 There is thus a great need 
for low-cost Pb tests that enable the public to test for exposure where and when there is cause to do so. 
While less recognized as an issue than Pb, Cu is also a serious contaminant of health concern in 
drinking water. In fact, allowable copper ion (Cu(II)) concentration in drinking water is addressed alongside 
lead through the EPA’s lead and copper rule (LCR). The LCR currently defines an action level of 1.3 ppm 
(0.02 µM) for copper concentration, meaning that a drinking water system must undertake mitigation strat-
egies if it finds a significant number of sources (10%) having at or above this concentration. High levels of 
copper are harmful to human health and can lead to severe illness including kidney and liver damage.66 
Test sensitivity is vitally important for proper detection of Cu exposure. 
PFAS are surfactants that contain many carbon–fluorine bonds, are environmentally persistent, 
and bioaccumulate.67 This pervasive and persistent contamination is alarming because chronic exposure 
to even low levels of these compounds is associated with thyroid disease, liver damage, high cholesterol, 
reduced immune responses, low birth weights, and several cancers. PFAS are used as water-, oil-, and 
stain-resistant barriers in thousands of consumer products (e.g., Teflon®) and are found in the blood of 
nearly all Americans,68 drinking water, surface waters, aquaculture, and agricultural products around the 
world. Heavily contaminated water would present ~1 ppb (1 μg/L) PFAS, but many communities face con-
tamination at far lower levels of 1-10 ppt (1-10 ng/L). PFAS detection now requires mass spectrometry-
based methods, which are expensive and largely unavailable to affected populations. Therefore, non-MS-
based PFAS detection at the ppt sensitivity level represents an important challenge and opportunity.  
 
II.B. Innovation. Our proposed three-stage methodology towards developing biosensor technologies is 
only possible today because of both recent technical developments in STEM (cell-free synthetic biology, 
aTF and riboswitch biosensing, chemical amplification and destruction methods) and qualitative and quan-
titative social science methodologies (ethnographic observations, interviews, surveys, participatory dissem-
ination). Integrating expertise across disciplines allows us to evaluate true societal impact of technologies 
that have emerged from URoL. Our expertise spans anthropology, biochemical engineering, chemistry, 
molecular biology, and synthetic biology. Specifically, our senior personnel span 4 NSF Directorates includ-
ing Behavioral and Economic Sciences (Young, Weinstock), Biological Sciences (Lucks, Jewett, and Ka-
rim), Mathematical and Physical Sciences (Dichtel), and Engineering (Gaillard, Lucks, Jewett, Karim), Fur-
thermore, as we develop the methodology, community stakeholders are at the core of new developments. 
Importantly, each of our contaminant targets are at different stages of our development pipeline: 
lead detection is prepared to enter Stage 3, with a commercial product that has been designed and devel-
oped; copper test development is at Stage 2, with biosensors identified and engineered into tests that 
6

function in the laboratory and have been field-tested with expert users; and PFAS detection is ready for 
Stage 1 design, with concepts for detection that combine chemistry and biosensing waiting to be tested 
(see Section II.C). As such, we can begin working on all three stages of our proposed methodology in 
parallel. Overall, the integration of multiple disciplines in this community-driven approach to develop these 
water quality tests will allow us to train students on these convergent approaches (see Section II.E). 
 
II.C. Preliminary Work. Several lines of research make our proposed work possible: 
II.C.1 Analysis of drinking water data shows major concerns about water quality both domestically 
and abroad. The co-PIs have analyzed nationally representative data about perceived drinking water safety 
from 140 countries and found that there is global concern about the safety of drinking water; 40% of Amer-
icans believe their drinking water will cause them serious harm in the next two years.69 Using data from the 
US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), Young has also demonstrated the de-
cline in Americans’ trust in drinking water following the Flint Pb crisis70 and been involved in a 2020-2021 
community-based participatory research project on water priorities in Evanston, IL.71-73 Preliminary data 
suggest that while there is substantial concern about drinking water safety, particularly from Pb pipes, res-
idents have limited knowledge on Pb testing, on Pb pipe replacements, and avoiding exposure to Pb. Eval-
uating in-home Pb biosensor tests could improve trust and safety in drinking water. 
 
II.C.2. The ROSALIND platform allows for 
design of cell-free biosensors for heavy 
metals. We have made significant progress in 
developing biosensors for Pb and Cu. Lead 
and copper are both sensed by microbes in 
nature using metal-sensing aTFs. Specifically, 
lead is detected by the ArsR/SmtB family aTF 
CadC, which is naturally found in the pI258 
plasmid within Staphylococcus aureus74 while 
copper is sensed by the aTF CsoR found in 
Mycobacterium tuberculosis.75 In prior pub-
lished work, we utilized each of these biosen-
sors in our ROSALIND platform (Section I.B) 
to create customized ROSALIND reactions 
that could detect lead or copper in water sam-
ples.18 By titrating different amounts of lead or copper into these ROSALIND reactions and measuring flu-
orescent output signals, we were able to characterize the limit of detection (LoD) of the reactions to be ~260 
ppb for lead and ~320 ppb for copper (Fig. 7). Interestingly the observed LoD for copper was less than the 
threshold set by the US EPA’s LCR, which is 1.3 ppm (1,300 ppb). By including a higher concentration of 
the CsoR protein in the reaction, we found that we could desensitize the system to achieve a tunable limit 
of detection of 1.3 ppm.18 The ROSALIND platform provides flexibility to design and develop cell-free bio-
sensors with specific attributes.  
 
II.C.3. Lead detection sensitivity has been improved 
through the commercialization of the ROSALIND 
platform by Stemloop, Inc. Lucks and Jewett co-
founded Stemloop, Inc. in 2019 to develop convenient 
user interfaces and reliable manufacturing methods to 
scale up distribution of biosensing tests. In 2022, Stem-
loop launched the  µSense product which uses 
ROSALIND reactions to detect lead at levels of 5 ppb 
or higher using a lateral flow device as a read out (Fig. 
8). In this format, users rehydrate ROSALIND reactions using a sample of their tap water, wait 15 minutes, 
then insert a lateral flow strip. Development of the lateral flow strip happens similar to an at-home COVID 
test: the presence of both the control and test band indicate that the water has > 5 ppb lead. We note that 
ROSALIND reactions are safe since they utilize DNA templates and purified proteins and do not contain

II.C.4. PFAS can be removed from water and mineralized to fluoride ions under mild conditions. The 
relevant levels for detecting PFAS in contaminated water resources are quite low, as a heavily contami-
nated water sample would contain 100-1,000 ppt PFAS. However, consumer tests will ultimately need to 
detect PFAS at levels as low as 1 ppt to be informative, which is around the current state-of-the-art for 
validated mass spectrometry-based PFAS measurements. This detection threshold remains 50 times 
higher than the 2022 EPA advisory levels for perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) of 0.04 ppt, which is beyond 
the detection limits of all available detection technologies. Two recent advances by Dichtel could enable 
low ppt level quantification of PFAS without the need for expensive mass spectrometry. First, novel adsor-
bents based on functionalized cyclodextrins remove PFAS from water and can be regenerated, resulting in 
an at-least 106-fold amplification of their concentration relative to the original water sample.76 This feature 
has led Dichtel’s cyclodextrin-based adsorbents to be used as analytical pre-concentrators commercially in 
passive water samplers77 and consumer-facing PFAS test kits that still require mass spectrometry.78 Sec-
ond, Dichtel recently discovered how to mineralize the PFAS to produce fluoride ions.79 This approach 
separates the PFAS selectively over other fluorine sources (e.g., fluoride ions) that might be present in 
water samples and is non-targeted (i.e., not just a single pollutant such as PFOA of the ~10,000 known 
PFAS compounds). Coupling this approach with RNA riboswitches could achieve sensitive PFAS detection 
without relying on expensive instruments. 
  
II.C.5. Fluoride can be sensed using RNA riboswitches. We have made 
significant progress in utilizing the natural fluoride-sensing RNA riboswitch bi-
osensor from Bacillus cereus in cell-free systems to detect fluoride.80 In prior 
published work, we discovered the RNA folding mechanism underlying fluo-
ride riboswitch function81 and used that knowledge to develop a version of the 
ROSALIND reaction platform that utilizes the riboswitch to detect fluoride in 
water samples.21 To enhance the analytical sensitivity of the platform, we uti-
lized a cell-free gene expression system that supports protein translation so 
that we could utilize an enzymatic reporter catecholase synthesized in situ 
when the riboswitch detects fluoride. Specifically, the catecholase enzyme 
cleaves a colorless compound included in the reaction into a yellow compound 
that is visible by eye and offers signal amplification because each enzyme 
synthesized can generate multiple, colored compounds. We demonstrated 
that this platform detects fluoride at 1.5 ppm, corresponding to the WHO’s 
secondary containment limit for fluoride in water49 (Fig. 9). Setting the stage 
for Aim 3, we have recently demonstrated improved sensitivity of the fluoride 
riboswitch (200 ppb) and compatibility with samples generated from PFAS destruction.

in the case of fluoride detection, non-expert users.

II.D. Technical Plan. 
II.D.1. Aim 1: Lead (Stage 3 Focus) 
Overview. Lead (Pb) biosensors have been developed and field-tested (Stages 1 and 2)18 and are ready 
for a broader distribution into communities. However, further evaluation in a “real world” setting is needed 
to ensure it can be used by non-scientists. In this aim, we will focus on assessing the societal impact (Stage 
3) of Pb tests, provided by Stemloop, Inc. (see Project Management Plan and Letter of Support). Our 
objective is to test the accuracy and interpretability of the in-home Pb test and its impacts on knowledge, 
attitudes, and preventative behaviors (KAB) about Pb in families with young children in Chicago (Fig. 11). 
Key activities for Stage 3 include two surveys, conducted before and two weeks after participants use the 
lead biosensor tests. These surveys will test Hypothesis 1, that users can correctly interpret the diagnostic 
output, and Hypothesis 2, that users will have greater knowledge about Pb and water testing, attitudes 
towards water testing will be more positive, and they will engage in more behaviors to reduce Pb exposure 
once they are aware of lead testing capabilities and contamination. 
 
Approach. We will start by re-
cruiting through community or-
ganizations and our Community 
Advisory Board with whom we 
have already been in contact 
(see 
Project 
Management 
Plan and Letters of Support). 
Cook County residents with 
young children (6 years or less, 
the window when children are 
most vulnerable to Pb tox-
icity19,82) who have an internet-
enabled laptop or cell phones 
with video conferencing capabilities, or who are willing to meet in person for testing their tap water, are 
eligible. To increase the likelihood of finding Pb exposure, we will also include housing type as an eligibility 
requirement (i.e., participants should live in a 1- or 2-unit residence built before 1984). We will sample to 
recruit across socio-economic status, gender, race, ethnicity, age, and technological literacy, with an em-
phasis on those more likely to be experiencing environmental injustice. We will again draw on community 
connections (see Letters of Support) as well as the relationships we established during the now completed 
$1.2 million NSF-funded study with community organizations and schools in 3 Chicagoland communities.  
 
 
Once participants have consented via telephone, we will conduct surveys and testing. Sample size 
calculations83 using 95% sensitivity and specificity estimates for the test, a 95% confidence interval, 5% 
precision, and 40% estimated prevalence of samples containing lead above 5 ppm based on published 
lead prevalence results58 and our target demographic area which enriches for lead pipe exposure, we cal-
culate that we need 182 samples to measure diagnostic sensitivity and specificity of the tests. Adding an 
additional 10% of tests above this estimate to account for possible imperfections of tests, loss/damage 
during shipment, or unreadable outputs, results in 200 tests, which we will conduct with 100 individuals (2 
tests/individual). Our community partners have assured us that this recruitment is feasible.

In Survey 1, we will establish key demographics, water insecurity, and knowledge, attitudes, and 
behaviors related to the contaminant of interest (Table 1).84-86 Participants will then have testing boxes 
mailed to their homes containing two µSense at-home Pb tests, two empty metal-free, acid-cleaned poly-
propylene sampling tubes for water collection, instructions, and information about Pb mitigation resources. 
Enclosed instructions will guide participants through 4 tasks (Fig. 11): Step 1) Collecting tap water samples. 
Two samples from the hot tap will be collected in polypropylene tubes in the morning, (i.e., after water has 
stood for 8-10 hours) and a second sample after water has run for 1 minute/5 liters, to maximize the chances 
of observing Pb that has leached into water sitting in pipes overnight and to approximately account for 
length of pipes in the household.87 Step 2) Using the at-home Pb test. Participants will apply the water they 
collected in Step 1 to the at-home Pb tests according to provided test kit instructions. Step 3) Reporting test 
results. Participants will take a photograph of both tests and text or email them to the study team. If the at-
home test indicates the presence of Pb, filters will be immediately provided and participants will receive 
additional information about mitigation resources and strategies. Step 4) Returning the kit and water sam-
ples. Participants will place the two samples of their tap water and all testing materials into the box and 
send it to Northwestern for gold-standard Pb testing using the pre-addressed, postage paid label.  
 
 
Once the drinking water samples are re-
ceived at Northwestern, they will be immediately fil-
tered, using acid cleaned syringe filters and stored 
acidified using trace metal grade nitric acid (HNO3). 
In most instances, we expect that Pb will be in the 0-
10 ppb range and therefore the first set of analyses 
performed will performed by transversely heated 
graphite furnace (GFAAS) atomic absorption spec-
troscopy88 using a high-resolution continuum source 
graphite furnace atomic absorption spectroscope 
(HR-CS-GFAAS)89-91 equipped with an echelle mon-

alytik Jena). This instrument has a spectral resolution 
of 2 pm at 200 nm and is therefore able to resolve 
spectral interferences from other elements/species. 
The characteristic masses corresponding to an ab-

pg for both elements using wavelengths at 324.754 
nm and 283.306 nm respectively. This corresponds 
to Pb concentrations of 300 ppt, well below the US-EPA standards. Results of the gold standard analyses 
will be communicated by telephone and in writing to participants as soon as they are available, in approxi-
mately 1-2 weeks. Participants whose water was determined to contain elevated levels of Pb (> 1 ppm) by 
laboratory analysis will be provided filters and liaised with Cook County lead mitigation resources. 
 
 
Survey 2 (S2 on Table 1) will be scheduled approximately two weeks after Survey 1.  This survey 
will cover experiences of water insecurity, the impacts of the test results on KAB, and experiences with the 
test. Study staff will also answer any questions that the participant may have about water contamination, 
including information shared as part of the results of the gold standard analyses.  
To test Hypothesis 1, that users can correctly interpret diagnostic output (i.e., the photographs of 
tests in Step 3 will match user’s interpretation of water lead content in >95% of samples), we will compare 
participants’ interpretations of the at-home Pb test to that of a trained technician. We hypothesize that the 
technician’s interpretation of the photographs will match the user’s interpretation of Pb content in >95% of 
the 200 samples; with this sample size we will be powered at a 95% confidence level.  
 
To test Hypothesis 2 about changes in Pb KAB, we will investigate differences in responses from 
Survey 1 to Survey 2 (Table 1). Knowledge will be scored based on the Chicago Lead Knowledge Test.87 
Although we could find no other studies about changes to Pb KAB, we expect to observe a 20% increase 
in knowledge based on changes in knowledge and attitudes on other topics (e.g., AIDS prevention, educa-
tion).86,92 Changes in attitudes will be determined by assessing differences in Likert responses to survey 
items about valuation of drinking water and perceived risks of Pb. We similarly expect to see a 20% increase 
in positive attitudes towards drinking water safety and Pb detection. The frequency of Pb mitigation-related

Anticipated results and alternative approaches. The primary expected outcome is an at-home test that can 
easily be used by non-scientists to determine if there is Pb in their water. Findings about its accuracy and 
impact on KAB will be communicated to participants through follow up email/mail communications, and in 
aggregate to the broader communities in consultation with the Community Advisory Board including at city 
council meetings, community meetings, and in two OpEds in Chicago newspapers, similar to those we have 
published elsewhere.94,95 Several potential limitations and problems are possible including: (i) Participant 
expectations, communication, and health: Because there is no safe limit of Pb in drinking water,9 it is critical 
that participants correctly understand the purpose and structure of this study and the results of the at-home 
Pb tests. (ii) Recruitment and follow-up challenges. To mitigate these, we are partnering with community-
based organizations to ensure the study meets community needs and is broadly advertised (see Project 
Management Plan and Letters of Support). To manage follow-up, we have designed the study to require 
no physical travel, only video and telephone calls, which will reduce some of the recognized barriers to 
continued study participation and inflated the sample size by 10% to account for missing data. (iii) Statistical 
power: Because prevalence estimates of Pb in drinking water are imprecise, prevalence estimates used in 
sample size calculations may be incorrect. If this is the case, we can consider revising the sample size 
based on the prevalence observed in this study, performing additional tests as the budget allows. (iv) Legal 
challenges: In Illinois, the Residential Real Property Act requires homeowners to disclose known issues to 
potential buyers, including the safety of the drinking water. During the process of written consent, we will 
provide information to homeowners about this requirement so that they can decide for themselves if the 
knowledge gained about potential lead exposure is worth the risk to potential real estate value. 
 
II.D.2. Aim 2: Copper (Stage 2 Focus) 
Overview. The mechanism for copper (Cu) detection using biosensors has already been identified through 
the development of the ROSALIND platform using the CsoR aTF to sense copper (Stage 1; Section II.C.3) 
and preliminary field testing has been conducted (Section II.C.3). In this aim, we will develop tests and 
perform user studies to detect copper in drinking water supplies (Stage 2). Stage 2 development will use 
ethnographic observations and interviews as well as expert-guided field testing to assess usability of copper 
biosensors. Iterations of testing with the community will lead to optimizing the usability and assessing the 
accuracy and interpretability of at-home copper sensing tests (Fig. 12). Below we describe our approach 
to Stage 2 that will be used in Aim 3 as well for PFAS. After development and user testing of the at-home 
copper tests we will assess the impact of these tests on KAB as described in Aim 1.  
 
Approach. First, we will observe users per-
forming ROSALIND reactions to understand 
how test formats can be adjusted to improve 
the user experience. Cu sensing reactions 
are developed at Northwestern and the oper-

of Stemloop’s µSense tests used in Aim 1. 
As published, these ROSALIND reactions 
can detect Cu at a threshold of 1.3 ppm and 
use fluorescence as an output, requiring a 
3D printed hand-held illuminator that we 
have developed to visualize if a specific con-
taminant is present above the threshold, indicated by high fluorescence. Though, like µSense, copper tests 
are prepared as lyophilized reactions that users rehydrate as an initial part of the test.  
 
 
Participant recruitment will occur through community organizations and our Community Advisory 
Board with whom we have already been in contact (see Letters of Support) as in Aim 1. In this usability

testing, we expect a sample size of 50 to be adequate because of the iterative design and the sample size

After obtaining informed consent, we will perform user testing interviews with participants using 
copper-sensing ROSALIND kits comprised of two tests, two water samples pre-seeded with Cu levels (0 
ppm, 2 ppm) and necessary personal protective equipment (gloves, protective eye wear) and tube stands 
to minimize exposure and spills. At a mutually agreed upon time, we will meet with participants in person 
for approximately 1.5 hours. First, participants will open the box and examine the materials while an inter-
viewer from the study team observes and answers questions. Participants will then be asked to test the 
water from the 2 vials pre-seeded with copper using 2 at-home copper tests. While the test runs (roughly 
30 minutes), the interviewer will ask about the different aspects of the testing experience, including the test 
format, application of water, clarity of the instructions, ideas for improvements, etc. They will also ask open-
ended questions about knowledge, attitudes, and behavior (KAB) as a pre-survey to Stage 3. Once the test 
has finished running, the interviewer will ask the participant to read and photograph the output from the 2 
tests; the interviewer will also read the output. At the end of the interview, the interviewer will collect all 
materials and explain the observed test results to the participant.  
 
 
Interviews will be conducted in 5 rounds of approximately 10 individuals and will be recorded, and 
extensive notes will be taken by the trained interviewer. The number of samples for which participants 
correctly read test output will be tracked by the interviewer in a spreadsheet. Notes, and if appropriate, 
audio or video clips, will be coded using Atlas.ti qualitative software99 to identify issues and themes germane 
to test development. After every round, all Investigators will meet to discuss findings from that round of data 
collection, including the accuracy with which participants read the output of the tests. The number of cor-
rectly read test results will be divided by the total number of test results read to test our hypothesis that 
participants can correctly follow instructions and interpret results generated by the final iteration of the test 
with >90% accuracy. Improvements in testing materials and instructions will then be implemented for the 
next round of interviews until no further improvements are needed. 
 
 
Next, we will test the diagnostic accuracy (sensitivity and specificity) of at-home copper sensing 
tests on real-world water samples (Stage 3), as well as the ability of non-expert users to interpret test 
results. Diagnostic accuracy and KAB will be assessed by following the approach of Aim 1 (see Table 1). 
Sample size calculations using the methods and parameters of Aim 1, adjusting for the estimated preva-
lence of Cu at detectable levels to be 20% based on historical data54,66 and accounting for our target de-
mographic, and padding with an additional 10%, results in a sample size of 400 tests that we will conduct 
with 200 participants. Notably, when use gold-standard measurements, it may be necessary to use flame 
atomic absorption spectroscopy88 (FAAS) when Cu concentrations are close to the US-EPA standard for 
drinking water. FAAS (PinAAcle 500, Perkin Elmer) has a characteristic concentration of about 50 ppb with 
a linear response up to 2.5 ppm88.  
 
Anticipated results and alternative approaches. In this aim, we anticipate collecting data on usability and 
accuracy of our copper sensing test that will inform test format and distribution. If fluorescent read outs are 
not amenable to easy interpretation, we will evaluate colorimetric detection approaches by reconfiguring 
the biosensor reactions to work in cell-free systems that use colorimetric enzymes.21,49  
 
II.D.3. Aim 3: PFAS (Stage 1 Focus) 
Overview. In this aim, we will focus on Stage 1 of our methodology by designing and testing a novel strategy 
to detect PFAS using a hybrid chemical and biological approach that: (1) captures PFAS from water sup-
plies, (2) destroys the PFAS into breakdown products including fluoride anions that can (3) be detected by 
fluoride biosensors. This “Capture-Destroy-Detect" approach is appealing for several reasons: first, the 
capture strategy allows at least a 1,000,000-fold concentration of PFAS from typical contaminated water 
samples and separates the PFAS selectively over other fluorine sources that might be present in the original 
water sample (e.g., fluoride ions in municipal drinking water). Secondly, the PFAS degradation to fluoride 
will result in multiple PFAS contaminants (of the ~10,000 known PFAS compounds) to contribute to the 
detection event, instead of just a small number of PFAS targets (e.g., only PFOA, PFOS, etc.) which further 
boosts sensitivity and will alert communities to PFAS contamination of even as-yet unidentified contami-
nants. Water samples that detect PFAS via fluoride ion detection may then be analyzed by more expensive 
methods that speciate individual PFAS as needed. After testing the design of this technology, we propose 
12
WISE-Dx LCRI Comments 
Attachment 2
12

 
to perform user testing following the approach of Aim 2 and assess the impact of these tests on KAB 
following the approach of Aim 1. Because the increased complexity of the amplification strategy and safety 
of likely reagents (e.g., DMSO, NaOH) required to detect PFAS without relying on mass spectrometry, we 
anticipate that user testing will focus on trained volunteers from project partners (e.g., Current, Water Keep-
ers) instead of all community members. 
 
Approach. We will begin by developing the 
capture-destroy-detect approach to be 
able to measure PFAS in water at the level 
of 1ppt (Fig. 13). The capture strategy is 
based on the development of newly cre-
ated sorbents by Dichtel.76 These sorbents 
consist of cyclodextrins (e.g., the active in-
gredient in Febreeze) that have been pol-
ymerized into insoluble networks that can 
be embedded in filter papers or isolated as 
powders or granular media. Previous char-
acterization of these adsorbents has 
shown that contaminants such as PFAS have rapid binding kinetics,100 permitting their use as flow through 
filtration systems. The use of these materials to collect PFAS, followed by PFAS elution from the membrane, 
has been demonstrated to enable adsorbent reuse and results in an approximately million-fold concentra-
tion amplification in preliminary experiments directed to this effort. The destroy strategy is based on mild 
reaction conditions recently discovered by the Dichtel lab to break down PFAS into secondary compounds 
(Section II.C.4).79 Importantly after breakdown, each PFAS molecule results in multiple fluoride anions 
released (e.g., 15 fluoride ions per PFOA molecule), offering further signal amplification. These released 
fluoride anions can then be used in a fluoride biosensing ROSALIND reaction to detect the resulting fluoride 
ions generated by PFAS degradation (Section II.C.5). We will focus on fluoride biosensing reactions that 
utilize bacterial cell-free transcription-translation extract systems33 to support the use of enzymatic protein 
reporter systems.21 These enzyme reporter systems have multiple turnover events creating multiple color-
imetric compounds per enzyme synthesized, thus offering additional signal amplification.21 
 
We will first develop a workflow that combines the capture-destroy-detect techniques in a serial 
procedure, using PFOA as a model PFAS compound. Based on a first target concentration of 50 ppt (50 
ng/L) PFOA water contamination, we will filter 5 L of water through 100 mg of cyclodextrin media, followed 
by elution of PFAS with 500 µL of DMSO. This solution will be input into a small volume (~100 µL of satu-
rated NaOH in H2O), and heated to 90 °C for 12 hours, to perform the deconstruction reaction. A titration 
of destruction reaction contents will be input into 25 µL fluoride-sensing ROSALIND reactions21 to detect 
fluoride. We note that our preliminary data has demonstrated that fluoride-sensing ROSALIND reactions 
can tolerate up to 2.5 % v/v of destruction reaction volume without any effect on performance.  
We will establish the viability of this procedure and then optimize each step to target detection of 1 
ppt PFOA concentrations in water samples. Areas of optimization include increasing input water flow 
through amount and decreasing elution volume in the capture step. It may also be possible to streamline 
the capture and destroy steps, such as by subjecting the PFAS-loaded adsorbent to the degradation con-
ditions without eluting the PFAS. Given that the target adsorbents do not themselves contain fluoride, their 
concomitant degradation will not produce false positives, and success in these types of strategies would 
streamline the design of an integrated PFAS test. For the detection step we will utilize RNA engineering 
strategies to increase signal amplification and thus overall sensitivity of detection to meet our target metric 
of 1.65 ppb detection (Fig. 13). We already have evidence that changing the sequence of the fluoride 
riboswitch terminator can significantly reduce OFF state (i.e., no fluoride) expression levels, allowing us to 
use an increase in fluoride biosensor DNA template which we have shown decreases the limit of detection 
from 2 ppm to 200 ppb (a factor of 100). Additional factors of increased sensitivity will come from further 
RNA engineering as well as introducing catalytic signal amplification circuits in the reactions.28 
As we optimize, we will assess detection capabilities through comparison with gold-standard test-
ing. Total fluorine and extractable organic fluorine (EOF) measurements will be made by HR-CS-GF MAS 
(molecular absorption spectroscopy) by adding a Ga(III) salt to form in the furnace the species GaF that

absorbs at 211.248 nm.101 Solid phase extraction (SPE) will be performed to concentrate the dissolved 
organic fluorine compounds (i.e., PFAS as well as herbicides and antimicrobials) using Oasis® HLB (Wa-
ters) cartridges102 and detected by mass spectrometry, which 2 ppt detection limits already established at 
Northwestern facilities. Inorganic fluorine (i.e., fluoride (F-)) will be measured by ion chromatography 
(Metrohm 930 Compact IC Flex) on filtered non acidified water samples (detection limit 10 ppb) for drinking 
waters that are expected to have optimal fluoride concentrations of ~0.7 ppm.103  
We will next develop a test kit format for the capture-destroy-detect approach to be used by non-
expert users. For capture, the test kit will contain a flow through filter, which will be integrated with a destroy 
module based on the most efficient method identified to integrate these processes. For example, a fluidic 
channel that routes DMSO through the separation media and into a vessel containing NaOH might prove 
feasible, or, if it proves feasible, performing destruction in the presence of the separation media would 
simplify this design. Either way, a portion of the fluoride-containing DMSO solution will be introduced into 
existing biosensor formats as developed in Aim 2 for copper detection. Once developed, we will conduct 
user testing of the test kit as in Aim 2, using iterations of testing, observation, and refinement until we 
develop a test that can be conducted by a similar sample size (n=50) of non-expert users. We will then 
distribute test kits and surveys as in Aim 1 to study the impact of these test kits on the KAB of users. 
Sample size calculations using the methods and parameters of Aim 1 and adjusting the estimated preva-
lence of PFAS at the levels the test is designed to detect to 80% for our target demographic104 and padding 
with an additional 10% results in a sample size of 100 tests that we will conduct with 50 participants. 
 
Anticipated results and alternative approaches. We anticipate that our capture-destroy-detect approach will 
measure PFAS in water at the level of 1 ppt because the approach presents opportunities to amplify signal 
at multiple steps. If we are unable to detect PFAS at the 1 ppt level using the strategies described above, 
we will implement additional RNA engineering strategies to boost the sensitivity of the fluoride riboswitch 
detection approach. These include screening additional naturally occurring fluoride riboswitch variants 
available from the RNA families database (RFAM).105 In addition, we can utilize a new catalytic signal am-
plification circuit being developed in the Lucks Lab called polymerase strand recycling (PSR). PSR utilizes 
toehold-mediated DNA strand displacement (TMSD) signal generation, whereby a biosensor-generated 
RNA output is used to strand displace a quenched fluorophore double stranded DNA gate, releasing the 
quencher and generating a fluorescence output. RNA polymerase then transcribes the resulting fluores-
cently labeled DNA, releasing the original RNA output for further signal generation and providing additional 
signal amplification to improve the biosensor’s sensitivity. If user testing in Stages 2 and 3 is too complicated 
for non-expert participants, we will work with our community partners to identify an alternative approach. 
For instance, we envision partnering with Chicagoland Water Utilities to conduct testing. Although we aim 
to distribute testing to community members to the greatest possible extent, the development of sensitive 
PFAS detection approaches without relying on mass spectrometry would be a major development in this 
emerging crisis 
 
II.E. Education and Outreach. Our plan for education and outreach consists of three main components: 
(i) development of curricular resources for classroom settings, (ii) undergraduate research, and (iii) a re-
search experience for teachers (see Student Training Plan). For graduate student training, we will develop 
and embed new curricular modules for existing courses at Northwestern. These modules will cover topics 
focused on teaching STEM students how to integrate social sciences perspectives and techniques in syn-
thetic biology technology development, and introducing anthropology students to synthetic biology technol-
ogies that can enable their work. Each of these modules will be set in the context of water quality. Under-
graduate research will give opportunities for early research experiences in water quality. We note that our 
proposed RET program is modeled off the NSF RET program but is not an official NSF RET site. 
 
II.F. Data Management. The proposed work will produce four fundamental types of data to be shared: (i) 
laboratory data describing biosensor development; (ii) gold standard characterization of water quality data; 
(iii) human subjects data about experiences with biosensor test use, , and knowledge, attitudes, and be-
haviors about water contamination; and (iv) outreach data including publications, handouts, lecture materi-
als, potential problem sets, team project descriptions, and learning assessment materials. (see Data Man-
agement Plan). In general, research data will be shared with participants and communities (in consultation

II.G. Timetable of Activities. Our performance plan consists of 3 aims phased across 5 years. We envision

KAB study on 50 participants (Y4-Y5), disseminate PFAS findings (Y4-Y5). 
 
II.H. Team Members, Organization, and Capabilities. The central goal of our proposal—to design, de-
velop, and distribute cell-free synthetic biology biosensors that enable individuals to assess the quality of 
their water—requires the integration of expertise across disciplines including anthropology, biology, chem-
istry, environmental sciences, and epidemiology. Our team is composed of researchers that are expert in 
these disciplines that cover multiple NSF directorates including biological sciences, engineering, mathe-
matical and physical sciences, and social, behavioral, and economic sciences; all have a track record of 
both leadership and collaboration (see Project Management Plan). A key component of our project is the 
integration of a Community Advisory Board that ensures that the local communities impacted by water 
contaminants and can benefit from this research help to co-produce the design, implementation, interpre-
tation, evaluation, and dissemination of the research. Members of the Community Advisory Board will come 
from Chicago civil society organizations, Chicagoland water utilities, and policymakers at the local, state, 
and national level (see Letters of Support and Project Management Plan).

RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)
Dear EPA:
The potential high level of lead and copper in Mississippi’s waters parallels with the high level 
of PFAS in several Mississippi counties, according to a Consumer Reports article and study 
released in August 2023.
In Jackson, a federal judge has allowed a lawsuit to move forward with about 1,000 children 
diagnosed with lead poisoning suing the city and Mississippi State Department of Health. As the 
water system there has been the subject of national headlines, some residents, and at least one 
college and a hospital, have decided to turn to private wells.
Jackson residents remain warned of lead levels over the EPA action level, but the city’s third-
party water administrator, Ted Henifin, has said his team had not found any lead pipes since it 
took over the system last fall, at least as of last month.
An investigation by Consumer Reports and Mississippi Spotlight, a collaboration of the Clarion 
Ledger and other news organizations, found detectable levels of lead in all 149 municipal and 
well water samples from all corners of Mississippi, covering all counties in the state.   
Essentially, more water testing must be conducted in all Mississippi municipalities and counties, 
not curtailed. And the water systems must pay for these tests, not the residents and/or taxpayers.
The EPA should not only incentivize the installation of filters in schools, they should also foot 
the bill – for the children.  

The MS State Conference NAACP and its leadership are willing to discuss further to resolve this 
matter. If you have any questions or concerns, Charles Taylor, Executive Director, can be 
reached at ctaylor@naacpms.org or 601-720-3517. 
Sincerely,
Charles Taylor
Executive Director 
MS State Conference NAACP

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1377 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
January 31, 2024 
 
President Joseph R. Biden, Jr. 
The White House 
1600 Pennsylvania Ave, NW

The Honorable Michael S. Regan Administrator

1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
