Dear President Biden and Administrator Regan, 
 
As representatives for communities across Wisconsin, we are very worried about lead’s 
impact on the health of our constituents. We know that no level of lead in drinking water is 
safe, and elevated blood lead levels in children are associated with hearing loss, lower IQs, 
developmental delays, behavioral changes, anxiety, and depression. This is particularly 
concerning because in some of our communities, as many as 1 in 4 children under 6 are 
considered lead poisoned. 
 
Thanks to your Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, Wisconsin is already benefiting from a more 
than $400 million investment to remove our lead pipes. That said, we need more tools to 
move faster. Based on 2022 data from our Public Service Commission, Wisconsin still has at 
least 174,637 utility-side service lines that contain lead or galvanized material, and 
181,918 customer-side service lines that contain lead or galvanized material. Even with the 
Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, Wisconsin will be approximately $600 million short to 
remove both utility-side and customer-side service lines. Additionally, we still have a lot to 
learn about the best ways to ensure we are quickly remediating lead paint and fixtures in 
our homes, schools, and childcare facilities.  
 
That’s why we appreciate the EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, which 
would put Wisconsin on a faster course toward lead remediation. These proposed 
improvements are an important opportunity to make good on your commitment to 
protecting children and families through strong investments in public health and 
environmental justice. 
 
We particularly appreciate that the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements include 100 
percent replacement requirements for water utilities within 10 years of finalization. To 
further improve the rule, we urge you to require water utilities to cover the costs of fully 
removing both utility side, and customer-side lead service lines. This will ensure that 
individuals who are already confronting the public health costs associated with lead 
poisoning do not need to cover replacement costs on their own. Additionally, unless all 
individuals are able to replace their customer-side lines, we will not be able to protect the 
entire community from lead contamination. 
 

We also appreciate that the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements include improved 
sampling, inventory, education, and notification requirements. We urge you to further build 
on these improvements by requiring public water systems to implement stronger testing 
and remediation plans for our schools and childcare facilities. This is the only way we can 
ensure Wisconsin children are fully protected. 
 
Thank you for your attention to this pressing matter. 
 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0931 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5th, 2024 
 
Re: Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for  
Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (December 6, 
2023), Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements (“LCRI” or “the Rule”). These comments are submitted by: Clean 
Wisconsin, on behalf of its members and supporters statewide; Midwest 
Environmental Advocates (MEA); and the Coalition on Lead Emergency (COLE). 
Clean Wisconsin, MEA, and COLE previously filed comments on February 12, 2020, 
in response to the Lead and Copper Rule revisions proposed by the EPA on 
November 13, 2019 (“the LCRR”), Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2017-0300. Clean 
Wisconsin and MEA further commented on July 28, 2021, in response to EPA’s 
request for comment on whether and how to revisit the LCRR, Docket ID No. 
EPA-HQ-OW-2021-0255. In those comments, we explained that the LCRR was 
woefully insufficient to address longstanding inadequacies in the Lead and Copper 
Rule. We specifically emphasized that EPA must lower the action level, require 
mandatory lead service line replacement (LSLR), and that utilities must be 
responsible for LSLR, not individual customers. The proposed LCRI mark major 
improvements on each of these issues. But there remain areas for improvement in 
EPA’s proposal. 
 
Lead Exposure in Wisconsin 
Childhood lead poisoning is a persistent public health issue that disproportionately 
harms lower-income children of color across the country.1 A recent study of blood lead 
levels in Milwaukee County children demonstrated similar findings in Wisconsin.2 
 
1 President’s Task Force on Environmental Health Risks and Safety Risks to Children, 
Federal Action Plan to Reduce Childhood Lead Exposures and Associated Health Impacts, 
December 2018.  https://ptfcehs.niehs.nih.gov/sites/niehsptfceh/files/resources/lead_action 
_plan_508.pdf (see also, https://www.cdc.gov/nceh/lead/prevention/populations.htm)

Milwaukee County Neighborhoods, 15 PLOS ONE 6 (2020).

Lead is a neurotoxin, and the health impacts of lead poisoning include damage to the 
brain and nervous systems, impaired growth, and development and behavioral 
problems.3 The effects can be long-lasting, including underperformance in school and 
increased likelihood of becoming incarcerated.4 There is also evidence that childhood 
lead exposure can cause long-term harm,5 and a recent study concluded that 
childhood lead exposure can reduce an American man’s lifespan by an average of 
almost three months.6 
While no safe blood lead level in children has been identified, the State of Wisconsin 
and the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) use blood lead reference values to identify 
children with elevated blood lead levels.7 Lead poisoning is currently defined in the 
Wisconsin Statutes as a blood lead level of 5 µg/dL or more.8 The CDC also used that 
level until late 2021, when the agency lowered its blood reference level to 3.5 µg/dL.9 
When compared to the rest of the nation, Wisconsin’s children have one of the highest 
rates of elevated blood lead levels. In 2018, the last year for which the CDC has 
published data on its website, 6.6% of the children under 6 years of age who were 
tested in Wisconsin had blood lead levels above 5 µg/dL, while nationally, only 2.6% 
of children tested exceeded that that threshold.10 Only Pennsylvania had a similar 
rate of elevated blood lead levels among its children.11 
While the percentage of tested children with elevated blood levels has fallen 
somewhat over the past several years, 2.7% of children tested in Wisconsin in 2022 
have blood lead levels above the 5 µg/dL threshold, and 5.3% of children tested have 
blood lead levels above the 3.5 µg/dL threshold.12 Moreover, some areas of the state 
have much higher instances of lead poisoning than do others. For example, in

Milwaukee County, from 2018-2021, 6.25% of the children tested had blood lead levels 
above the 5 µg/dL threshold, and in historically-redlined areas in Milwaukee’s central 
city, many census tracts have dramatically higher incidences of lead poisoning, in 
some cases affecting nearly 25% of the children tested.13 Sadly, it is likely that even 
these numbers may underestimate the scope of the problem, because many children 
vulnerable to lead exposure are not tested. 
Although drinking water is only one means of lead exposure for children, it remains 
a significant exposure pathway. The primary source of lead in drinking water is lead 
service lines (LSLs), which release lead into water on the way to the tap. A recent 
EPA Fact Sheet estimated that there are as many as 340,000 LSLs remaining in 
Wisconsin communities.14 Based on data used in a 2021 analysis by the NRDC, 
Wisconsin had more LSLs per capita than any other state in the nation—nearly 5,600 
LSLs per 1000 residents.15 Using data compiled by the Public Service Commission of 
Wisconsin, we estimate that there are approximately 244,000 service lines requiring 
removal16 statewide, including nearly 70,000 in the City of Milwaukee alone.17 
Until these LSLs are taken out of the ground and replaced with safe plumbing 
materials, Wisconsin residents remain at risk of lead poisoning. The current 
situation is especially tragic and unacceptable because the harms imposed by 
LSLs have fallen, and will continue to fall, disproportionately on some of the most 
vulnerable and disadvantaged members of our society.  
Accordingly, we applaud the EPA for the change in course proposed in the LCRI. 
Requiring the replacement of all, or nearly all, LSLs over a period of ten years is 
an important, if overdue, change in the EPA’s lead policy. While we offer a 
number of comments below that we believe would strengthen the LCRI, we must 
acknowledge this important change. 
Some Wisconsin municipalities have actively been working to remove LSLs, including 
the 10 communities chosen to participate in EPA’s Lead Service Line Replacement

Accelerator initiative, announced in January of 2023.18 While we are pleased to see 
some communities moving forward with LSL replacements (“LSLRs”), and believe 
that those efforts demonstrate the feasibility of accelerating removal, we know there 
are many more communities at risk of being left behind. The LCRI’s ambitious goal 
of removing 100% of LSLs in no more than 10 years should become a reality, but will 
be dependent on adequate funding and resources to get the job done, including 
additional funds to pay for the private-side LSL removal. 
 
Comments 
 
I. 
The LCRI’s Lead Service Line Replacement Requirements are a major 
improvement, but steps must be taken to ensure these requirements are 
expeditiously and equitably implemented.  
The LCRI’s baseline requirement that PWS’s replace all LSLs and galvanized requiring 
replacement (collectively “LSLs”) within 10 years is a generational investment in public 
health. Compared with either the longstanding approach to LSLR or the LCRR, the LCRI’s 
LSLR requirements are a vast improvement. The previous approaches would allow LSLs to 
stay in use so long as to be indefinite, a result inconsistent with the only durable, long-term 
solution to the problem of lead in drinking water: removing all LSLs. That the LCR has not 
required mandatory LSLR earlier is a fundamental failure on the part of the government to 
safeguard the people of this country. This failure has caused untold harm to some of our 
nation’s most vulnerable populations. Given this, EPA has a duty to ensure the LCRI’s LSLR 
requirements are implemented and enforced as early and quickly as possible, and in a 
manner that guarantees that those who have carried and continue to carry an unjust lead 
burden are given the full benefit of these proposed improvements. Anything less would 
perpetuate historical wrongs permitted by EPA’s past implementation of the SDWA and 
LCR.   
Accordingly, we start by recognizing why mandatory LSLR is so needful, and how the LCRI 
delivers on that need. We then comment on some areas for improvement, to address concerns 
that the LCR, once again, will benefit some communities more than others, creating 
predictable, yet entirely avoidable, environmental justice problems. 
a. Mandatory lead service line replacement is necessary and long 
overdue. 
The basis for mandatory, full LSLR is straightforward. The predominant source of lead in 
drinking water in most homes is a lead service line. Efforts short of LSLR require permanent, 
ongoing expenditures of money and staff time, and do not entirely remove lead from the 
 
18 See, https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/lead-service-line-replacement-accelerators, 
and https://www.epa.gov/water-infrastructure/lead-service-line-replacement-accelerator-
communities.  

5 
 
water. Treating water with orthophosphate or other chemicals to reduce corrosion—where 
this technique is even available—is expensive and does not remove all the lead from drinking 
water supplied by those LSLs, in any event. An approach where “optimizing” corrosion 
control technology means accepting some amount of lead in the water, when we know there 
is no safe level of lead to consume, is an oxymoron. Similarly, tap water filtration can reduce 
lead exposure significantly in the short-term, but it is another fix that requires ongoing, cost, 
maintenance, and time. Both approaches also leave open the possibility of technological or 
human error, exposing individuals, households, or even entire communities to lead in their 
tap water. The fundamental fact, now finally recognized in the LCRI, is that so long as LSLs 
remain in use anyone drinking water out of taps serviced by those lines is being exposed to 
lead or is at risk of being exposed to lead at any time. 
b. The LCRI must require as many LSLs be replaced as quickly as 
possible, while avoiding obstacles to LSLR in the most lead-burdened 
communities. 
  
i. The LCRI must set an early completion deadline with limited 
opportunities for deferred deadlines. 
The LCRI proposes a ten-year deadline for PWSs to replace their LSLs, finding this is feasible 
for the vast majority of PWSs based on observed LSLR rates in cities across America, 
including in Wisconsin, as well as the growing number of states with laws requiring LSLR. 
88 Fed. Reg. 84912. EPA also proposes two ways PWSs could be eligible for deferred deadlines 
and thus take longer than ten years to replace their LSLs, while also requiring states to set 
LSLR deadlines sooner than ten years from the rule implementation date when the state 
determines it is feasible for the PWS to do so. In sum, then, EPA is proposing a general ten-
year deadline with mechanisms for PWSs to go faster or slower, depending on PWS-specific 
characteristics. 
We concur with EPA that past and ongoing LSLR efforts are persuasive evidence that a ten-
year deadline for LSLR is feasible for almost all PWSs. However, there are many PWSs for 
which an earlier deadline, maybe much earlier, would plainly be feasible. See, e.g., 88 Fed. 
Reg. 84912 (citing Stoughton and Mayville, Wisconsin, as examples of systems that replaced 
their LSLs in a single year). EPA considers this approach in requesting comment on “whether 
it is feasible [f]or systems across the nation to complete service line replacement in a shorter 
timeframe than ten years, such as in six, seven, or eight years.” 88 Fed Reg. 84916 (emphasis 
added). 
We should all agree that the ultimate objective of the LCRI should be for LSLR to occur as 
soon as feasible, meaning that faster timelines must be required where feasible. There are at 
least two ways EPA could try to achieve this. 
First, what is currently proposed in the LCRI, EPA can set a baseline ten-year replacement 
deadline, with a requirement that states set an earlier deadline be set for PWSs that can 
feasibly replace all their LSLs in fewer than ten years. 88 Fed. Reg. 85065, proposed 40 CFR 
141.84(d)(5)(iv). 

6 
 
Second, EPA could set an earlier deadline than ten years for all PWSs, recognizing that more 
PWSs would therefore meet the eligibility criteria for deferred deadlines. 
On paper, it may look like a distinction without a difference. The only difference is that one 
approach bumps deadlines up where feasible, and the other approach pushes deadlines back 
where a ten-year deadline is not feasible. But the distinction matters. 
Consider a PWS with 90,000 LSLs. With a 10-year deadline to replace all LSLs, this PWS 
needs to replace 9,000 LSLs/year, and thus does not meet the eligibility requirement under 
for a deferred completion date for a PWS that would be required to replace more than 10,000 
LSLs per year. All things being equal, we would anticipate this PWS would be required to 
replace 900 LSLs/year for ten years.  
On an 8-year deadline for replacing LSLs, however, this same PWS would qualify for a 
deferred deadline because it would be required to replace 11,250 LSLs per year, more than 
the 10,000 LSLs per year EPA has identified as one of the deferred deadline eligibility 
criteria. Under EPA’s proposal, that deferred deadline should be set at 9 years—the amount 
of time the PWS needs at a 10,000 LSLs/year rate. 88 Fed. Reg. 85065, proposed 40 CFR 
141.84(d)(5)(v)(A).19  
Under EPA’s proposal states are required to set an earlier deadline than 10 years where 
feasible for a given PWS. 88 Fed. Reg. 85065, proposed 40 CFR 141.84(d)(5)(iv). Thus, it could 
be argued that under a ten-year default deadline the state could still direct this PWS to 
complete its LSLR within 9 years, because replacing 10,000 LSLs/year has been deemed 
feasible, and the LSLR would get done at the exact same time under both approaches.  
But EPA’s proposed LCRI does not explicitly state how a state sets that new, earlier deadline. 
Instead, it merely says:  
Where the State determines that a shortened replacement deadline is feasible for a 
water system (e.g., by considering the number of lead and galvanized requiring 
replacement service lines in a system’s inventory), the State must require the system 
to replace service lines by an earlier deadline than [otherwise] required . . . and 
establish a different minimum replacement rate[.] 
88 Fed. Reg. 85065, proposed 40 CFR 141.84(d)(5)(iv). 
This appears to give the state discretion to set an earlier deadline—or not—based on 
feasibility, with the number of LSLs to be replaced just an example of a factor to be considered 
in assessing what “feasibility” means in that context. It is not clear how quickly, if ever, a 
state agency with primacy even could accurately assess the feasibility of LSLR for each of the 
many PWSs with LSLs that need replacing. Indeed, there are entirely conceivable ways that 
PWSs could end up taking ten years to complete LSLR when, in retrospect, it could have been 
 
19 The same logic would apply to the other eligibility criteria for a deferred deadline for 
PWS with a high per capita LSLR rate proposed by EPA. As the number of years to 
complete LSLR shrinks, the number of LSLs that must be replaced per year grows, and 
thus the numerator grows while the denominator stays the same in the formula for the per 
capita criteria. (LSLs Replaced per year/Number of Households ≥ .039.)  

7 
 
completed faster, i.e. it was not required to do so by a state with primacy, either due to a 
failure to fully implement the provision due to resource constraints or political constraints, 
differing views of “feasibility, or there simply was not enough information to know at the time 
that an earlier deadline was indeed feasible. 
This is why the two approaches would likely yield different deadlines in application. One 
approach puts the burden on state agencies to make tough, discretionary calls to move 
deadlines up from a ten-year default, whereas under an earlier deadline that same agency 
simply processes requests to move deadlines back based on objective, mathematical eligibility 
criteria tethered to EPA’s feasibility findings in support of the LCRI. Wisconsin DNR would 
struggle to quickly assess the specific circumstances of each PWSs. The potential result of 
EPA’s proposed approach would thus be numerous PWSs being given 10 years to complete 
LSLR when they could feasibly have done so sooner yet were not required to do so for 
arbitrary reasons. 
This observation leads us to recommend EPA strongly consider a deadline earlier than 10 
years. Lowering the default deadline from ten-years to six, seven, or eight years, with 
deferred deadlines only for strictly eligible PWSs, would ensure that no PWS that could meet 
an earlier deadline fails to do so. Each year of earlier compliance would be extraordinarily 
helpful to the residents in that community, so avoiding unnecessary delay is imperative. 
We recognize that by setting an earlier deadline more—perhaps many more—PWSs will meet 
the eligibility criteria for deferred deadlines. It might be thought that this will increase the 
burden on states of administering the LCRI, because more deferred deadlines will need to be 
set. However, those deferred deadlines are set by objective criteria laid out in the proposed 
LCRI and should thus not be burdensome to set.  
This approach is particularly reasonable given that EPA is not proposing for the mandatory 
LSLR requirements to go into effect until early 2028. 
Alternatively, if EPA keeps the ten-year deadline, changes to the requirement for states to 
set earlier deadlines must be made to clarify what “feasible” means in that context, and to 
ensure states have the capacity to make these important determinations. 
EPA requests comment on whether “States should be required as a condition of primacy to 
set initial shortened deadlines by a certain timeframe, such as no later than 60 days after 
the compliance date ... .” 88 Fed. Reg. 84915. We agree that States should be affirmatively 
and explicitly required to set earlier deadlines for each PWS for which an earlier deadline is 
feasible, and that this could extend to being a condition for retaining primacy. 
However, as currently proposed, the LCRI does not set state agencies up to successfully set 
earlier deadlines for all PWS for which an earlier deadline is feasible, especially within as 
little as 60 days. There are at least two problems with the currently proposed LCRI in this 
regard. First, as stated above, states do not have the resources to set appropriate deadlines 
quickly and accurately for each PWS in the state. Wisconsin has over 550 municipal water 

8 
 
utilities.20 Second, because the LCRI does not create detailed criteria for setting an earlier 
deadline, it is left to a state agency’s discretion to determine what is “feasible.” That puts an 
agency in the difficult position of having to create fresh criteria and then apply them in an 
even-handed and transparent manner to hundreds of PWSs across the state.  
Given this, the LCRI should also be revised to explain with greater specificity not just when, 
but how states should determine which PWSs must meet earlier deadlines. As noted above, 
the LCRI simply lists the number of LSLs to be replaced as an example of a relevant 
consideration. That is not enough to guide state agencies in this difficult, important task. It 
will also generate transparency issues when some PWSs receive shorter timelines to complete 
LSLR than other, neighboring PWSs. If EPA instead creates clear, simple criteria that 
require an earlier deadline—just as it does for deferred deadlines—this would greatly 
alleviate the burden on state agencies like the Wisconsin DNR. Indeed, EPA could set 
numeric thresholds based on LSLs required to be replaced per year, that automatically 
trigger an expedited LSLR deadline, without entirely eliminating discretion at the state level. 
It is an option EPA should strongly consider, rather than simply leaving it to the states to 
figure out on an ad hoc basis.  
ii. The LCRI must be strengthened to ensure that mandatory 
LSLR replaces all LSLs. 
There are multiple areas where the LSLR requirement must be strengthened to decrease the 
opportunity for LSLs to stay in use and thus for lead-burdened communities to be exposed to 
lead in drinking water for a minute longer than necessary.  
The first point concerns which LSLs the water system must replace. 
The proposed LCRI would require water systems to replace all lead and GRR service 
lines, and any lead connectors encountered, that are “under control of” the water 
system. EPA is proposing to treat a service line as under the system’s control wherever 
a water system has adequate access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full 
service line replacement. 
88 Fed. Reg. 84920.  
EPA acknowledges the position of many advocates that this “under control of” qualifier 
creates a large potential loophole for PWSs to leave LSLs in the ground and, moreover, all 
LSLs are truly “under the control of” the water systems given the history of installation and 
the practical reality that the water system controls it even under private property. 88 Fed. 
Reg. 84923. While we tend to agree with those advocates that EPA could and should require 
PWSs to replace all LSLs without exceeding the bounds of SDWA, we recognize that EPA 
has considered this position and reached a different conclusion, and that recapitulating 
arguments may not be helpful at this juncture. To the extent EPA is not going to close this 
loophole and require utilities to replace the entire LSL, this requires EPA to do more to erode 
 
20 A list of estimated LSLs for each of these municipal water utilities is provided by the 
Wisconsin Public Service Commission. Available online at 
https://psc.wi.gov/Pages/ServiceType/Water/LeadServiceLine.aspx.  

9 
 
and avoid the barriers to full LSLR that this “under control of” qualifier will create. And the 
biggest barriers will be cost and property owner consent. 
On cost, Wisconsin DNR recently estimated the cost of replacing Wisconsin’s LSLs to be 
between $620-966 million.21 That same estimate projected that Wisconsin is in line to receive 
$400 million in total BIL funding to conduct LSLR. Id. This $220-566 million gap must be 
closed somehow. 
In Wisconsin, state law allows public water utilities to use ratepayer funds to provide 
financial assistance to the “owner” of a property to help pay for the cost of replacing the 
portion of the LSL on their property, so long as certain conditions are met. Wis. Stat. S. 
196.372. One of those conditions is that the municipality must have an ordinance requiring 
all owners of property with an LSL to replace it and authorizing the utility to provide 
financial assistance for this purpose. The utility cannot provide more than 50% of the cost of 
private side LSLR, and even that portion may be in the form of a (non-forgivable) loan. Any 
plan to provide financial assistance must be approved by the state Public Service 
Commission. Id.  
Thus, even in a state that has recently acted to increase the ability of utilities to socialize the 
costs of LSLR, significant barriers remain. If you are a Wisconsin resident drinking water 
provided by a PWS, the LCRI may not expedite removal of your LSL, unless you happen to 
live in a municipality that has enacted the required ordinances and gotten approval from a 
state commission. And even then, the assistance you receive may be only partial, leaving you 
with a significant bill, perhaps in the thousands of dollars, to replace an LSL that you played 
no part in putting in the ground in the first place. 
If the LCRI were to require PWSs to pay the full cost, however, communities would not be 
left behind in this way. The requirement to catalog local laws that create barriers to access, 
with the intent of putting pressure on those laws, is admirable. But we should not deceive 
ourselves that these efforts are a substitute for a requirement that PWSs pay for full LSLR.  
On consent, the LCRI acknowledges that in certain cases a property owner might be 
unavailable or unwilling to provide consent to replace the LSL on their side of the property 
line. 88 Fed. Reg. 84920. The LCRI requires PWSs to make a “reasonable effort” to secure 
this consent. 88 Fed. Reg. 84923. We understand that the LCRI proposes a series of 
reasonable steps to increase the likelihood that these barriers are weakened or removed, i.e. 
cataloging state laws that create barriers to access public education, etc. Those elements of 
the LCRI will help. In places in Wisconsin without local ordinances mandating private-side 
LSLR, the need to secure consent is an obstacle to full LSLR, particularly for those who rent 
or otherwise live in non-owner-occupied home.  
Where consent is required for LSLR, property owners, including landlords, can be an obstacle 
to complete LSLR, especially if they are absentee landlords or out of state investors, a

online at 
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lsjpmqHO32o&list=PLz1F3wus1j4waMx2rbPQUEReD
mDcngkdT&index=1&pp=iAQB.

situation increasingly common in Wisconsin.22 Under the proposed LCRI, Water systems 
must have a “strategy” for LSLR for apartments and non-owner-occupied homes (e.g. 
investment properties). However, if a property is owned by an individual or company that 
simply is not physically present in the state, then any strategy or reasonable effort to secure 
consent might fail. This is why the LCRI’s failure to require the PWS to replace the entire 
LSL is so problematic. We hope that the educational and informational requirements in the 
LCRI minimize the occurrence of this problem, because if it persists, the effects will, once 
again, be felt by vulnerable, already lead-burdened communities. 
Like many things in Wisconsin, the likelihood that a child lives in a home in which their 
family owns the property, versus rents the property, varies by race. For example, in 
Milwaukee, “fifty-seven percent of Black children live in a rented house compared with 26 
percent of white children, and 46% of Latino kids. Nineteen percent of Black children live in 
an owner-occupied house, compared to 60% of white kids, and 33% of Latinos.”23 Because 
status as a renter will likely make it harder to secure LSLR, then the disproportionate impact 
on Black and Latino children will raise significant environmental justice concerns. 
Importantly, these barriers to LSLR might persist even where funding is made available to 
the property owner, because their status as an out-of-state owner, more than reticence to pay, 
might create the practical barrier to securing consent, and thus initiating LSLR. If we look 
up ten years after the LSLR requirements go into effect and LSLs remain in use in a 
disproportionate fashion, then we will know EPA has again failed to protect the most lead-
burdened communities from harm.  
 
II. 
The LCRI Can and Should Set Earlier Compliance Dates for Some of the 
Rule’s Requirements. 
EPA is proposing that water systems covered by this rule come into compliance within three 
years of promulgation of the final rule, with some exceptions. 88 Fed. Reg. 84967. Given the 
likely promulgation date of a final rule, for many rule elements this means an initial 
compliance date no earlier than January 2028. 
This three-year post-promulgation compliance date would apply to the new mandatory LSLR 
requirements in the LCRI. EPA’s explanation for this delay is that “systems would better use 
the three-year period after promulgation of a final LCRI for program planning, including 
hiring additional staff, soliciting bids for contractors, securing grants or other types of 
funding, and continuing to improve inventories to ensure that they are better positioned to 
conduct mandatory service line replacement.” 88 Fed. Reg. 84968. This is a reasonable 
position; however, as mentioned above, this does buttress our position that a deadline to 
complete LSLR of fewer than 10-years is warranted. See supra at 7. Water systems are being 
 
22 See, e.g., John D. Johnson, Out of State Investment in Milwaukee’s Home Rental Market, 
Lubar Center for Public Policy and Civic Education, Marquette Law School (April 18, 2021), 
available online at https://law.marquette.edu/facultyblog/2021/04/out-of-state-investment-
in-milwaukees-home-rental-market/ 
23 Johnson (2021), at 5. 

11 
 
given four years of advance notice of this requirement. That long runway to get started 
justifies a default deadline to complete LSLR in less than 10 years. 
EPA then proposes several alternative compliance deadlines for specific parts of the LCRI. 
88 Fed. Reg. 848969. EPA specifically requests comment on “whether it is practicable for 
water systems to implement notification and risk mitigation provisions after full and partial 
service line replacement (§ 141.84(h)), notification of a service line disturbance (§ 141.85(g)), 
and associated reporting requirements (§ 141.90(e)(6) and (f)(6)) upon the effective date of 
the LCRI.” 88 Fed. Reg. 84968. These requirements should be implemented upon the effective 
date of the LCRI. Since these are notification and reporting requirements, they should not 
require large expenditures of money or lengthy training periods to accomplish. 
EPA also raises an alternative compliance date of 1-2 years after promulgation—as opposed 
to the default 3 years—for other areas of the LCRI beyond those just mentioned and the 
mandatory LSLR requirements. 88 Fed. Reg. 84969. It is difficult to make a blanket comment 
on some many disparate elements of the LCRI. Thus, here we merely suggest EPA should 
strongly consider moving many LCRI compliance dates up and provide a couple criteria EPA 
should use in guiding its analysis.  
First, as noted above, some requirements simply do not require significant expense to 
accomplish, either in terms of capital outlays or additional staff time or training. There is 
thus a reduced need to raise funds, finance expenditures, or otherwise budget for the 
requirement. There is also less need to schedule lengthy activities to prepare the water 
system for compliance. Where this is the case, further delay is unwarranted. 
Second, some requirements can better protect human health as soon as they go into effect, 
like the notice requirements around service line disturbance mentioned above. Delaying 
implementation of these notice requirements thus knowingly authorizes the continued use of 
inadequate notice procedures, needlessly placing people at risk. Whenever this element is 
present—immediate opportunity to avoid or reduce lead exposure—it should weigh heavily 
in favor of the earliest possible compliance deadline.  
 
III. 
Sampling Protocols  
We strongly support EPA’s proposal to require collection of first- and fifth-liter paired 
samples for lead at LSL sites and to use the higher of the two values to calculate the 90th 
percentile lead level to improve identification of higher risk sites for lead. The proposal is 
based in part on implementation data from Michigan’s revised LCR, and studies evaluating 
lead sampling data from various liters in different cities. The data suggest that using the 
higher of the first- and fifth-liter values from LSL sites will be more effective than using 
either value alone. 88 Fed. Reg. 84929-30.  
Historically, the 90th percentile lead level has been measured against regulatory action levels 
and trigger levels, to determine what treatment technologies the water system needed to 
adopt to reduce the levels of lead in the system. For example, under the current LCRR regime, 
the existing lead and copper action levels continue to determine whether a water system must 

12 
 
monitor source water, install corrosion control treatment (CCT), optimize or re-optimize 
existing CCT, replace lead service lines, or undertake a public education program. 88 Fed. 
Reg. 84939. 
 
IV. 
Lowered Action Level (AL) and Required Responses to AL Exceedances   
In the LCRI, EPA proposes to eliminate the lead trigger level of 0.010 mg/L, which was 
established by the LCRR, and to lower the lead action level (previously set at 0.015 mg/L) to 
0.010 mg/L (10 ppb). 88 Fed. Reg. 84939. Under the revised rules, EPA expects that 
eliminating the trigger level and establishing a single, lowered action level will simplify the 
rule and improve its implementation.  
While we applaud the reduction in the action level, and the commensurate reduction in public 
health risk that it should engender, we suggest that the action level could be set even lower, 
for example, at the at 0.005 mg/L24 alternative that EPA considered, and would confer even 
greater public health benefits. 
The EPA’s primary defense of its proposal to set the lead action level at 10 ppb, rather than 
at the lower alternative level, is that setting a lower action level would impose an undue 
administrative burden on States and water systems, because a lower action limit would 
require more small and medium systems (which make up the vast majority of all CWSs) to 
install optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT), and conduct detailed OCCT 
demonstrations, which must be overseen and evaluated by state employees. 
We urge EPA to consider less than 10ppb, i.e., 5ppb, because there is no safe blood lead level, 
and the lower the action limit, the more protective the rule will be of public health. But if 
EPA determines that it is not feasible to do so, then it must impose stricter additional 
regulatory requirements for multiple lead AL exceedances. 
 
V. 
Additional Requirements for Multiple Lead Action Level Exceedances 
 
The proposed rule would also impose additional regulatory requirements on systems with 
“multiple lead action level exceedances,” which is defined in the rule as a system that incurs 
three action level exceedances in a rolling five-year period. More specifically, EPA is 
proposing that systems with multiple lead action level exceedances conduct at least one 
additional systemwide public education outreach activity to raise additional awareness of the 
health effects of lead in drinking water, identify steps consumers can take to reduce their 
exposure, and provide information about how the water system is addressing the issue. The 
water system would be required to repeat the selected activity every six months until the 
system no longer meets the proposed criteria for multiple lead action level exceedances. 88 
Fed. Reg. 84954. 
 
While we agree that additional regulatory burdens should be imposed on such “repeat 
offenders,” we believe the criteria proposed to define these systems is insufficiently 
 
24 The 0.005 mg/L alternative is the practical quantification limit for lead. 

13 
 
protective. In Section IX of the proposed rule, EPA requests comments on “whether EPA 
should use three action level exceedances in a five-year period for identifying systems with 
multiple action level exceedances where additional action is warranted and, whether 
additional actions should be required sooner, or later, than the five-year period, or whether 
EPA should use a modified metric.” 
 
Requiring “three strikes” in five years before imposing additional public education 
requirements is overly lenient, particularly when each violation puts children at greater risk 
of lead poisoning.  We recommend that EPA instead define “multiple lead action level 
exceedances” as any two exceedances of the action level within a ten-year period.  
 
VI. 
Public Education and Outreach  
We strongly support the LCRI’s proposed improvements to the public education requirements 
in the Lead and Copper Rule, which will increase transparency and better inform the public 
of lead exposure and health risks. The changes notably include: 
 
proposed revisions to the mandatory lead health effects language that must be 
included in public education, public notification, and Consumer Confidence Reports 
(“CCRs”), to clarify the negative health effects of lead, including a statement that: 
“There is no safe level of lead in drinking water.” 88 Fed. Reg. 84963. 
 
a proposed requirement that water systems issue consumer notices of tap sampling 
results within three days of the system learning of the results, regardless of whether 
the results exceed the lead or copper AL. 88 Fed. Reg. 84947. (Under the LCRR, 
consumer notices only had to be delivered in three days if the tap sample exceeded the 
AL; non-exceedances could take up to 30 days. Id.  
 
a requirement that public education following a lead action level exceedance be sent 
within 60 days of the end of the tap sampling period for every lead action level 
exceedance. 88 Fed. Reg. 84950. 
 
Under the LCRI, the public education materials must be delivered “to every service 
connection address served.” Previously, the education materials only needed to be 
delivered to bill-paying customers. 88 Fed. Reg. 84951.  
 
a. EPA should require water systems to provide consumer notices 
regarding the results of testing within three days of receiving results.  
EPA proposes that PWSs must provide consumer notice of tap sampling results within three 
days of the system learning of the results, but is requesting comments on whether this 
requirement feasible. Clearly, it is feasible. First, water systems were required to deliver 
such notices within 3 days even before the LCRI, if the samples collected exceeded the AL.  
Second, under the proposed rule, water systems may deliver the notices either electronically 
(e.g., email or text message), by phone, hand delivery, by mail (postmarked within three days 
of the system learning of the results), or by another method approved by the State. 88 Fed. 
Reg. 84949.  There can be no question that this proposed requirement is feasible, and the 
final rule should impose the three day turnaround, as proposed. 
 

14 
 
b. Primacy states should be required to provide translation services to 
water systems in their jurisdictions, as a condition of retaining their 
primacy status. 
For water systems that serve a large proportion of consumers with limited English 
proficiency, the LCRI requires that public education materials include information about 
where consumers can obtain a translated copy of the materials, or translation assistance.  88 
Fed. Reg. 84949. In Section IX of the rule package, EPA requests comments on whether to 
require, as a condition of primacy for the LCRI, that states are required to provide translation 
support to water systems that are unable to comply on their own.   
Clearly, the answer is yes. To understand the health risks related to LSLs, and mitigate the 
risks facing their families, end-users of water systems need access to these public information 
materials. If they are not proficient in English, they need access to translated public 
education materials. In order to ensure that public education is provided in multiple 
languages, in order to mitigate environmental justice concerns, primacy states should be 
required to assist the water systems under their jurisdiction, by translating the public 
information materials, as needed. It would be incredibly inefficient for each individual water 
system to prepare translated materials on their own. The States, or perhaps more 
appropriately, the EPA, should provide consistent translations, and disseminate them to the 
PWSs for distribution to consumers who need them. 
 
 
VII. 
Reporting and Recordkeeping Requirements  
The LCRI also makes a number of improvements to the LCR’s reporting and recordkeeping 
requirements that we support, including reporting requirements regarding service line 
inventories, and replacement plans. In the LCRI, EPA has proposed that all systems 
conducting service line replacement must report information on their compliance with the 
proposed service line inventory and replacement requirements to the State. Each year, 
systems would be required to submit inventory summary information, including the current 
number of LSLs, GRR service lines, unknown service lines, non-lead service lines, and lead 
connectors. They would also be required to report information regarding their replacement 
programs, including the total number and street addresses of full service line replacements, 
partial service line replacements, replaced GRR service lines, and replaced lead connectors. 
Systems would also be required to certify to the State the number of service lines not replaced 
due to customer refusals for access to conduct service line replacement. EPA is also proposing 
that summary information about the inventory and service line replacement program be 
made available to the public to facilitate community tracking of system progress. 88 Fed. Reg. 
84959. 
 
a. All systems should be required to post service line inventories, and 
replacement plans, including information about the progress of 
replacement programs, online. 

15 
 
Large systems, serving greater than 50,000 persons, also have an obligation under the LCRI, 
to host their service line inventories and removal plans online, fostering even greater 
transparency and accountability, by making the inventory and plan easily accessible to the 
public. 88 Fed. Reg 85036.   In response to the EPA’s request for comment on this issue, we 
urge the agency to require online reporting of this information by ALL systems, not just the 
largest ones. Ready access to this information by the public should not be determined by the 
size of the system serving consumers. If the EPA is concerned about the administrative 
burden of imposing such a requirement on small and medium water systems, it should 
develop a publicly-available website that summarizes the information collected from all 
systems under the state reporting requirement, and make that information available to the 
public online. 
 
VIII. 
Schools and Childcare Facilities 
The underlying problem with the LCRI on this issue is that it simply does not change enough 
to improve on the LCRR, and thus is another missed opportunity to reduce lead exposure in 
places where our youngest children spend so much of their time. In this regard we reiterate 
some of the same comments we had in 2021 and again urge EPA to do better. 
The LCRI fails to require sufficient monitoring in schools and daycares. As we expressed in 
our 2021 comments, five samples per school and two per childcare facility is not enough to 
provide an accurate assessment of the lead in water risk at that school. EPA asks whether 
more samples should be required to be collected. 88 Fed. Reg. 84957. The answer is plainly 
yes. We understand that most schools and childcare facilities will not be served by a LSL and 
instead are at risk of lead from older, lead-bearing premises plumbing. Thus, checking each 
source of drinking water becomes imperative, when the risk may vary from source to source 
based on that premises plumbing.  
Similarly, the retained requirement from the LCRR for a PWS to test 20% of schools once in 
each of the first five years following rule implementation remains problematic. A single test 
allows for lead issues to be missed, providing false confidence in the school’s water safety. 
Further, the LCRI still allows schools to opt out and high schools to only be tested upon 
request, which renders these sampling requirements particularly incomplete. Schools and 
childcare centers should be tested more frequently and more than once, i.e., once every six 
months, or twice per school year.  
EPA should strongly consider requiring schools and daycares to either regularly test for lead 
in their water at all sources used for drinking water in that facility, or else require proactive 
water filtration at those sources, at least until testing is done to show lead is not an issue at 
that tap, i.e., results are lower than .001mg/L or another low standard. 
Lastly, it remains problematic that the LCRI does not mandate immediate publication of 
testing data from schools and childcare centers. EPA asks for comment on this point, 
suggesting that requiring publication of these testing results is too burdensome for water 
systems to comply with. 88 Fed. Reg. 84959. Given the interest parents have in their 
children’s health, any logistical burden associated with placing sampling results online for 

16 
 
parents to review is small by comparison. The LCRI should be revised to require publication 
of school and childcare center sampling results, with relevant contextual information, as soon 
as practicable following the sampling itself.

RE: Ensuring Safe Drinking Water at School - Proposed Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements (Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801)
EPA Administrator Michael Regan,
Thank you for proposing a 10-year deadline for water utilities to replace lead service lines.
Replacing these toxic pipes is a crucial step for protecting the public’s drinking water generally.
However, I also urge you to do more to stop lead from contaminating our kids’ water at school.
For most schools, lead in water comes from plumbing, fountains or faucets inside the school
building.
That’s why the EPA’s Lead & Copper Rule Improvements should require federally regulated
schools to replace fountains with water stations and put filters on all taps used for cooking or
drinking. The EPA should also limit lead in schools’ water to 1 part per billion, as recommended
by the American Academy of Pediatrics. And lastly, the EPA should work with state and local
officials to encourage all other schools to adopt such measures.
You have a historic opportunity to ensure safer drinking water for America. Please go the extra
mile to get the lead out.
Sincerely,

and we seek your partnership as we build on our progress to expedite the replacement process.
We applaud the EPA’s leadership in unveiling the LCRI proposal and its commitment to fully
replacing the nation’s lead pipes within 10 years. As you know, low-income communities and
communities of color are disproportionately impacted by contaminated drinking water. Even the
lowest level of lead exposure can cause emotional and behavioral issues in children and
cardiovascular and maternal health issues in adults – sometimes fatal. The presence of lead
pipes is a public health threat and an environmental justice issue, and it’s imperative that our
most impacted communities are prioritized throughout the replacement process.
While there’s a lot to praise in the LCRI proposal, there are a few key components that we urge
the agency to address in order to strengthen the rule:
Reconsider the exception to the 10-year removal mandate: Chicago would receive an
extension of 44.6 to 55.8 years to replace our lead service lines. It is unconscionable to tell
Chicago residents that they have to wait generations for safe drinking water. Although we
appreciate the flexibility we have been offered, we would like to discuss a shortened timeline
that’s coupled with adequate federal funding to complement our efforts.
Require water systems to fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: It can cost
$30,000 or more for a resident to replace a single lead service line in Chicago. Although the
Chicago Department of Water Management is exploring ways to reduce the cost of replacement
and currently offers various programs to incentivize homeowners to take on replacement, we’ve
seen in other cities that it’s less expensive, faster, and more equitable to have the utility cover
the full cost of lead service line replacement. A resident should not be denied access to safe
drinking water because of their lack of ability to pay or landlord absenteeism.
Enact strong protections for schools and childcare centers of all sizes, including filter
installation: While some smaller schools and childcare centers that are serviced by a lead
service line and/or lead fixtures may benefit from the proposed rule, larger schools and
childcare centers will be left out because the proposal’s testing program retains weak elements
from the previous rule. We urge the EPA to require comprehensive lead testing in all schools

and childcare centers and point-of-use filters to protect the health and safety of our children,
regardless of where they’re enrolled.
Reduce lead action level to 5 ppb: We applaud the agency’s step in reducing the lead action
level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb, but it’s important that we take another step and lower the action
level to 5 ppb to be on par with the drinking water standards of other countries, such as Canada
and the European Union, as well as recommendations from the medical and public health
community.
Although there is room for improvement in the LCRI proposal, we commend the EPA’s
commitment to improving drinking water protections across the nation. Chicago has benefited
from this commitment as a recipient of a $336M WIFIA loan to support our lead service line
replacement efforts. As elected officials representing a renter-dominated city, we hope you
consider our recommendations for the best way to achieve success, as we’ve seen in cities like
Newark, NJ, and ensure that our most impacted communities are prioritized.
Thank you Administrator Regan, Assistant Administrator Fox, and all EPA members involved for
your continued support and leadership.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0875 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024 
 
Ms. Radhika Fox 
Assistant Administrator Office of Water 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, D.C.  20460 
 
Re: 
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 
Dear Ms. Fox: 
 
The South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources (DANR) appreciates the 
opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. South 
Dakota supports reducing lead exposure from drinking water and increasing public health 
protection; however, the proposed rule creates a significant burden on the state programs 
responsible for implementing the revised rule and public water systems impacted by the 
proposed rule revisions. 
 
Many of South Dakota’s public water systems are defined as Small Water Systems. In general, 
small systems have limited resources. DANR is very concerned that the impacts of the proposed 
rule will be overly burdensome on these systems, resulting in lower compliance rates which will 
undermine consumer confidence. 
 
The proposed rule improvements are numerous and extremely complex. DANR offers the 
following general comments for specific issues important to South Dakota. Additionally, DANR 
request that EPA carefully consider the comments received from the Environmental Council of 
States, the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators, and the American Water Works 
Association, which are more extensive and provide greater technical detail.  
 
Distribution System and Site Assessment (DSSA): 
 
The proposed rule states that within 30 days of receiving sample results, water systems must 
collect and analyze a follow-up sample at any tap sample site that exceeds 0.010 mg/L and 
collect water quality samples at a site located within a half mile radius of that sample site. South 
Dakota is a rural state and many systems would be challenged to find a sampling location within 
a half-mile radius of the original sample location. DANR suggests that the EPA add additional 
language allowing systems to take a sample at the closest site to the original sampling site should 
one not be available within a half-mile radius.  Additionally, DANR is concerned with the lack 
of resources to train operators and regulatory staff on which components of the DSSA a water 
system will be required to complete.  
 

 
 
Filter Distribution: 
 
The proposed rule states that water systems must provide filters to their entire service area after 
the water system has had three or more action level exceedances. DANR is concerned that by 
having to provide filters to an entire service area, rather than solely to those locations with risks 
of lead and copper exceedances, which are locations with: lead or galvanized service lines 
requiring replacement or unknown service lines; customers will develop an unwarranted distrust 
in their water utility. DANR requests EPA allow states the discretion to require filters, where 
appropriate based on sampling results, data, and corrosion control.  
 
Public Notification: 
 
The proposed rule adds lead exceedances to the list of Tier 1violation’s requiring a 24-hour 
public notice. Tier 1 based exceedances have the potential to have serious adverse health effects 
on human health because of short-term exposure. DANR feels that requiring systems to public 
notice lead exceedances within 24 hours will cause implementation issues for states and water 
systems. One of the most significant issues is the current EPA method allows laboratories to hold 
onto samples after being preserved for several months after the sampling occurred. It does not 
make sense to require systems to report the sample results within 24 hours for samples that may 
have been collected many weeks or months earlier. To remedy this inconsistency, DANR 
recommends that the Tier 1 public notice requirement be changed to a Tier II public notice 
requirement. This change will permit states and water systems to properly assess the sample 
validity and allow adequate time to coordinate the appropriate public notice. If EPA is unwilling 
to change the public notice timing, then at a minimum, DANR recommends that EPA update the 
standard method to reduce the time a laboratory must analyze a sample so a water system to 
achieve timely notification of results to its customers. 
 
Required Testing in Schools and Daycares: 
 
Under the proposed rule, community water systems would be required to conduct lead sampling 
at all schools and all licensed daycares within its distribution system, excluding those constructed 
after 2014 or those facilities who have had full plumbing replacement. While we support testing 
of lead in schools and childcare facilities, the water system should not be considered the experts 
when it comes to plumbing and remediation services within the schools and daycares. This 
requirement will place a great burden upon the small water system with limited resources. 
DANR recommends that any required remediation work be the responsibility of the property 
owner and not be a burden of the public water system. Additionally, with different sampling 
requirements at schools and daycares and the continuous state of flux of daycare facilities, 
DANR has great concern regarding how sampling data from schools and daycares will be 
tracked and managed for compliance. EPA must also communicate where funding and resources 
are available to school and daycares and that they convey that information directly to these 
entities, as well as provide all templates for any public education material that is required.  
 
Data Management/Guidance/Training: 
 
Each of the changes outlined within the proposed revisions increase rather than decrease 
implementation challenges. It is imperative that a fully functional data system be in place a 
minimum of six months prior the rule effective date. Without a proper and functional means to 
manage all the data elements of the final rule, states and systems will be unable to implement or 
comply with the rule. EPA does not currently have a data system in place to manage all the data 

 
 
points required to be collected under the proposed rule. DANR requests that EPA makes 
available all database guidance on implementing the rule If a state must design its own, there will 
be substantial cost to an already stretched state budget.   
 
South Dakota is requesting that guidance documents and training be finalized and shared as soon 
as possible.  The effective date of the rule should be at least six months prior to implementation 
to allow adequate time for training. In addition, DANR requests that clarity and continuity be 
brought into the rule revisions for all applicable water systems.   
 
Corrosion Control Studies: 
 
Corrosion control requirements need to be updated to reflect clear definitions about what will be 
required in a study. Guidance and training should be provided to states on how to review 
corrosion control studies and water quality parameter testing.  
 
Funding:  
 
This proposed rule’s complex nature adds significant requirements to systems and states which 
will surpass most small systems ability to comply. This, in effect, shifts even more burden to 
state programs as they will be required to pull along systems struggling to comply. State 
programs are already stretched to the breaking point. With years of flat or rescission-based 
funding, states will be hard pressed to implement these rule revisions unless significant funding 
increases to the Public Water System Supervision grants are authorized and made available to 
states. Without additional grant funding, state programs will be unable to fully implement the 
rule without adversely impacting other core program areas which in turn reduces overall public 
health protection.   
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Mark A. McIntire, P.E. 
Drinking Water Program Administrator 
South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources

      Megan Goltz, Policy Advisor, Governor’s Office

Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
On behalf of the Brita® brand and The Clorox Company, we appreciate the opportunity to submit 
comments to the United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on the proposed revisions to 
the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper.    
 
We applaud and acknowledge the EPA’s efforts to reduce lead levels in drinking water across this 
country through the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).  Since 2020, Brita has 
worked directly with more than 100 municipalities and their community water systems to provide lead 
reducing point-of-use filtration products.  Based on our work with these communities, Brita believes that 
every lead service line (LSL) in the ground represents a risk to safe drinking water.  With an estimated 
9.2 million lead service lines (LSLs) in this country, and those lines disproportionately concentrated in 
low-income and people of color communities, we recognize the importance of EPA finalizing its 
comprehensive approach to ensure a clean water solution for all at-risk communities.   
 
The proposed LCRI puts forward several proactive initiatives to address lead exposure from LSLs in the 
country.  We were encouraged to see the LCRI include improved sampling, a lower lead action level, 
and additional protections for at-risk residents & occupants including making pitchers available in 
communities with multiple lead exceedances.  Given the known lead action level (ALE) exceedances1 
that occurs during LSLs replacement, we also strongly support the provision that requires distribution of 
a pitcher and replacement cartridges for six months after a LSL replacement to each occupant to 
ensure non-residency buildings are also protected.  However, even with these positive steps, many 
Americans will be waiting years for LSL replacements, representing a “lead action gap” for many 
residents and communities. 
 
 
1 “Detection and Evaluation of Elevated Lead Release from Service Lines: A Field Study,” Environmental Science & 
Technology, July 23, 2013 

To help the EPA achieve its goal of reducing community exposure to lead sources & improve their 
health outcomes2, Brita encourages the EPA to strengthen the LCRI’s requirements in the following 
areas to bridge the gap and accelerate the necessary protections to vulnerable residents. 
 
 
Bridging the “Lead Action Gap” 
 
To protect vulnerable residents waiting for LSL replacements and achieve the EPA’s goals of 
reducing community exposure to lead sources & improve their health outcomesError! Bookmark 
not defined., Brita encourages the EPA to adopt a proactive requirement to require distribution of 
a pitcher filter, replacement cartridges and public education about using the device to every 
occupant with a lead service line until six months after that line has been replaced. 
 
The model of proactive filter distribution and education has already been successfully deployed by the 
City of Denver, which reports 83% compliance in filter usage by residents enrolled in its Lead Reduction 
Program.  This program was even cited by the EPA as “an example for other communities across the 
country”3  Denver chose a proactive approach, meaning they distribute pitchers and filters to residents 
before a replacement, protecting them from lead while they wait their turn.   
 
Without government action that requires proactive distribution and education, we believe that residents 
will turn to bottled water once they are notified of their LSLs.  The purchase of bottled water has a 
significant environmental impact on our communities, in addition to the financial burden to residents.  
For approximately $50 a family can be protected for a year using available point-of-use filtration on the 
market vs. an average annual cost of $250-$2,700 per year for bottled water4. 
 
We believe proactive distribution of a filter provides fast response to residents with LSLs, while also 
ensuring trust with the water source as cities address exceedances and replace LSLs.  
 
For water systems and communities with lead action level exceedances, we urge the EPA to 
strengthen the pitcher filter requirement by mandating that point-of-use filtration (pitchers) go 
beyond “available” to “distributed” at no cost to residents, while also providing public 
education materials for communities using the filters.   
 
Point-of-use filtration can be a key component and bridge for residents with lead exceedances as they 
wait for their LSLs to be replaced.  The proposed rule acknowledged the unique and critical role of 
filtration for communities with lead exposure.  However, the proposed rule requires point-of-use filtration 
to be “available” to at-risk residents, which puts the burden on the at-risk resident or occupant.  Based 
on our experience with affected communities, residents that must go to a centralized location to acquire 
the filtration device rarely pickup or use those devices.  The EPA should require that filters are 
distributed to at-risk residents with accompanied education materials to ensure that residents can 
address their lead exposure as fast as possible.   
 
 
2 https://www.epa.gov/lead/final-strategy-reduce-lead-exposures-and-disparities-us-communities 
3 https://www.epa.gov/newsreleases/epa-finds-denver-waters-lead-reduction-program-effective 
4 https://www.counterpunch.org/2023/11/30/the-real-cost-of-bottled-water/ 

The LCRI proposal currently requires point-of-use filtration when communities have a lead exceedance 
(over a 5-year period), as well as during LSLs replacement.  However, every year that residents have 
an exceedance, or are waiting for the replacement, is putting the resident as risk of lead exposure.   
 
For example, systems with P90 lead level > .01 mg/L must begin using or re-optimize CCT and 
systems with 3 exceedances in a 5-year period must take more aggressive action. However, at 
this point residents have likely already been exposed to unsafe levels of lead.  
 
 
Lead Action Levels and Exceedances 
 
Action Level 
We were pleased to see that the LCRI proposed lowering the lead action level of 15-ppb to 10-ppb in 
the LCRI.  However, given the 5-ppb standard for lead in bottled water and the 5-ppb lead level 
recommended by Canada and the European Union for drinking water, Brita encourages the EPA to 
consider lowering the proposed 10-ppb to an action level of 5ppb in the final LCRI. 
 
Exceedances 
As stated by EPA, there is no safe level of lead exposure in drinking water; even low doses of lead 
pose major health risks and can take 20 years to fully dissipate from the human body 5.  As such, one 
confirmed exceedance can represent a major public health risk and crisis for a community impact. Brita 
encourages the EPA to strengthen the lead action level exceedances by requiring that if a water 
system has a test site with one exceedance, they should immediately retest for confirmation.  If 
the system has a confirmed exceedance, water systems should deliver remedies prescribed by 
the LCRI instead of waiting for 3 positive tests in a 5-year period. 
 
 
Implementation Timeline 
 
We have already seen more than 100+ communities that have proactively commenced lead service line 
replacement projects.  Given that the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) were published in 2021, 
we anticipate that many systems are preparing to replace lines as quickly as possible.  The proposed 
LCRI implementation timeline is three years following the finalization of the LCRI.  Each year residents 
wait for replacements is another year those residents are at risk from their LSLs, which delays health 
and economic benefits that can be realized sooner with quicker implementation of the rule.  As a result, 
we encourage the EPA to strengthen the implementation provisions, by decreasing the 
implementation timeline of the LCRI from 3 years to 2 years.   
 
If EPA is unable to shorten the LCRI implementation schedule, we encourage the EPA to bridge the 
timeline gap with residents by requiring the distribution of point-of-use filtration devices (pitchers) to 
impacted residents.

Filter Supply 
 
The proposed rule mentions that “stakeholders raised concerns during the proposed LCRI 
engagements about the availability of sufficient quantities in the market to meet new demand created

chain infrastructure and products to meet demand.  With our ongoing work with communities across the 
country, Brita is confident it can adequality meet the demand from the requirements put forth in 
the LCRI.  
 
 
At Brita, our focus is on Better Water, for People and the Planet.  Our mission is reaffirmed as we look 
at the levels of lead in the drinking water in many of our communities.  Point-of-use filtration (pitchers) is 
not the long-term solution for lead in drinking water, but filtration can serve as a necessary bridge for 
many residents as they wait for LSL replacements.   
 
The EPA can bridge the gap by requiring the proactive distribution of filtration, in addition to 
strengthening the lead action levels and protections, to ensure that we can deliver safer, clean, and 
lead-free drinking water to residents at risk of lead exposure.   
 
We applaud the EPA’s effort to enact a national solution to reduce the levels of lead in drinking water

EPA’s commitment to protecting people’s health has been evident in the proposed LCRI, as well as the
