Dr. Jennifer McLain 
November 15, 2022 
Page 6 of 6 
Conclusion 
 
AMWA supports the EPA in its mission to advance environmental justice and public health. We 
similarly support individual utility efforts to remove their lead service lines as quickly as 
possible, and agree that the complete removal of lead service lines is a worthy goal. However, 
achieving this critical milestone will be a complex process. The agency must recognize the 
various affordability, legal, and community trust challenges as it considers environmental justice 
in the development of the LCRI. We appreciate the opportunity to comment and ask that the 
agency fully consider and address the challenges associated with lead service line replacement. If 
you have any questions about this letter, please contact Brian Redder, AMWA’s Manager of 
Regulatory and Scientific Affairs at redder@amwa.net or Jessica Evans, AMWA’s Government 
Affairs Associate at evans@amwa.net.

Re: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0813, Federalism Consultation on Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements  
 
Dear Dr. McLain, 
 
The Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies (AMWA) welcomes the opportunity to provide 
input on EPA’s forthcoming proposed rulemaking, the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI). AMWA is an organization representing the largest publicly owned drinking water 
utilities in the US, and collectively its membership serves more than 160 million people. AMWA 
was generally supportive of the LCR Revisions (LCRR) but continues to urge EPA to consider 
the challenges associated with identifying and replacing lead service lines in future regulation.  
 
Last year, the Biden Administration announced its intention to “use every tool at its disposal to 
eliminate all lead service lines” in the next 10 years, including by “encouraging full lead service 
line (LSL) replacement and strongly discouraging partial replacement.”1 EPA subsequently 
concluded an ongoing review of the LCRR and announced its intention to “immediately begin 
development” of further revisions that would be known as the LCRI. Among the revisions that 
EPA intends to propose as part of the LCRI are requirements that “would result in the 
replacement of all LSLs as quickly as is feasible.”2 
 
AMWA reiterates its full support for advancing public health by reducing public exposure to 
lead. Additionally, AMWA asks the EPA to recognize, consider, and address the potential 
 
1 FACT SHEET: The Biden-⁠Harris Lead Pipe and Paint Action Plan, December 16, 2021. 
https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/statements-releases/2021/12/16/fact-sheet-the-biden-harris-lead-pipe- 
and-paint-action-plan/ 
2 Environmental Protection Agency. Review of the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation: Lead and Copper 
Rule Revisions (LCRR). 86 FR 71574. December 17, 2021. 
https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2021/12/17/2021-27457/review-of-the-national-primary-drinking-water- 
regulation-lead-and-copper-rule-revisions-lcrr 

 
Dr. Jennifer McLain 
December 13, 2022 
Page  2 
hurdles associated with full LSL replacements should they be mandated as part of a proposed 
LCRI rule, and to provide support for community water systems (CWS) to address these 
challenges. We summarize these potential complications in our comments below, split into 
sections matching EPA’s Federalism Consultation meeting slides.  
 
Identifying and Replacing Lead Service Lines 
 
AMWA continues to believe that any further revisions to the rule must consider the realities on 
the ground, namely, the practical challenges faced by water systems seeking to replace all 
publicly and privately-owned LSLs. These challenges are detailed in the attached comments 
previously submitted by AMWA on July 30, 2022 on the Lead and Copper Rule virtual 
engagements. Aside from the considerable cost factors and accompanying implications for water 
affordability for low-income ratepayers, a binding mandate on water systems to replace “all” 
public and privately-owned LSLs would meet the obstacle of individual homeowners who may 
refuse access to their property to replace their privately-owned LSL. The experience of AMWA 
members is that a significant portion of customers typically decline the chance to have their 
privately-owned LSL replaced, even when the cost is partially or fully subsidized, often due to 
distrust or apprehension in government. 
 
CWS and their communities also face differing circumstances and competing priorities. If EPA 
were to require water systems to replace all LSLs by a defined deadline, the agency would 
effectively be deciding, for each water system in the nation, that the removal of lead lines is the 
most important water infrastructure investment above all others to protect public health in a 
community. Realistically, water systems and communities must balance a variety of competing 
priorities such as addressing PFAS, the need to strengthen infrastructure to withstand the effects 
of climate change and extreme weather, cybersecurity risks, and the development of new 
drinking water sources in the face of long-term drought. As these communities often have 
limited resources, a revised LCR with an inflexible LSL removal mandate would require water 
systems to put these competing priorities aside – even if they pose the most pressing threats to 
public health and utility and community sustainability.  
 
AMWA also asks EPA to consider the following situation related to galvanized [pipe] requiring 
replacement service lines (GRRSL). Currently, GRRSL are defined as “a galvanized service line 
is or was at any time downstream of a lead service line or is currently downstream of a ‘Lead 
Status Unknown’ service line [emphasis added].”3 For utilities that identified LSLs many years 
ago and removed them, they will have to treat customer-side galvanized lines formerly connected 
to LSLs as though they are lead. EPA should consider, using the most up-to-date science, that 
these GRRSL are no longer a source of lead after a period of time as supported by the data.  
 
AMWA also urges EPA to consider the state of the workforce currently in the country. Many 
AMWA members struggle to find and secure individuals trained and capable of completing LSL 
 
3 40 CFR Part 141 Subpart I; https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-D/part-141/subpart-I 

 
Dr. Jennifer McLain 
December 13, 2022 
Page  3 
replacement and related work. Some states require specific qualifications, like being a licensed 
plumber, for those replacing LSL. This severely limits the ability of CWS to be proactive in 
quickly replacing LSLs. EPA should prioritize increased opportunities for training and workforce 
development to address this important issue. 
 
In addition, there are equity and environmental justice concerns associated with full LSL 
replacement that AMWA previously detailed in November 15, 2022 comments to EPA on 
environmental justice considerations in development of LCRI, also attached to this letter. Any 
increase in water rates due to LSL replacement would have a disproportionate impact on low-
income communities. Although the increase in water bills would be equal across ratepayers 
within the community, it would not be equitable as low-income households would be paying a 
larger portion of their income to fund replacements across the water system’s entire service area, 
which will include higher income households that are impacted less by the subsequent increase 
in water bills. EPA cannot expect that funds already appropriated will be enough to complete the 
entirety of LSL replacement, meaning the remainder of those costs will fall to the public.  
 
AMWA is also concerned that the varying definitions of disadvantaged communities in states 
and across the federal government will exclude larger utilities, with service areas including 
pockets of these communities, from being eligible for certain LSL replacement funds. AMWA 
urges EPA to maximize the opportunities for states and municipalities to use funds in a way that 
delivers the most benefit to low-income households and communities. Additionally, EPA should 
consider difficulties with communicating to customers who previously have replaced their own 
LSLs, at great cost to themselves, that others will now have access to full replacement costs.  
 
Tap Sampling and Compliance 
 
It’s critical that any revisions to the LCR do so with the mindset of minimizing burdens on CWS 
and their customers. Many CWS already struggle to get customers to participate in tap water 
sampling, some even offering incentives and discounts on water bills to conduct sampling. 
Increasing the amount of work associated with sampling will only deter more individuals from 
participating.  
 
EPA claims the first liter of water sampled from a tap represents issues from premise plumbing. 
While there are instances this may not be the case, any proposed rule should make it clear that 
water systems are not responsible for any premise plumbing or fixtures located inside the home, 
as this is outside of a water system’s control. By testing both these samples, it will only increase 
the number samples reaching the action/trigger levels, prompting public notifications that 
typically cause panic and worry among residents and cost CWS significant resources.  
 
Reducing Rule Complexity 
 
AMWA suggests EPA not take large actions in this rulemaking, and instead use the data 
acquired from LCRR implementation to make an informed decision during the next Six-Year 

 
Dr. Jennifer McLain 
December 13, 2022 
Page  4 
Review. Many CWS are still preparing for elements of the LCRR, like the LSL inventory, and 
the notion of major changes happening right as the compliance date nears has led to much 
confusion over what needs to be done now and in the future. The LCR is not the only major 
rulemaking EPA is currently undergoing, and CWS must weigh changes associated with LCRI, 
PFAS regulation, and MDBP revisions, all coming together around the same time.  
 
AMWA strongly suggests EPA keep the action level at 15 ppb. Lowering the action level, in 
addition to potentially including both 1st and 5th liter draws for sampling, will only increase the 
number of samples that require action, including public notification which will be a substantial 
burden on states. Increasing the number of samples that require action will divert resources away 
from other issues that may have larger public health consequences. Instead of lowering the action 
levels, AMWA urges EPA to develop and promote guidance documents that help CWS and the 
public understand the importance of lead testing, how to properly conduct lead testing at home, 
and resources available to reduce lead exposure. 
 
Having two similar parameters, like the action and trigger levels, seems to have created some 
confusion as to how they differ and what is specifically required of each of them. If a sample 
exceeds both levels, triggering both actions, the costs and time associated would be substantial. 
Additionally, the action level requires replacement of the LSL, so CWS should not have to 
evaluate their corrosion control technique (CCT) if the source of lead was removed.  
 
The association continues to oppose actions that require changing a system’s CCT based on a 
single sample that is above the action level. In some cases, an elevated level of lead discovered 
in an individual sample may often relate to lead coatings or other factors that are unique to the 
specific sampling site, and beyond the control of the water system. Requiring a water system to 
make corrosion control changes due to only one or a small number of individual samples 
exceeding the action level could provide limited benefits and expose the public to other public 
health risks such as elevated disinfection byproducts and microbial issues due to disruption of the 
pipe biofilms. 
 
Conclusion 
AMWA strongly supports individual utility efforts to remove their LSLs as quickly as possible 
and agrees that the complete removal of LSLs should be the ultimate goal. However, as outlined 
above, AMWA harbors deep reservations about any proposal that would require public water 
systems to eliminate all LSLs by a firm deadline for the reasons detailed in this letter. Any 
federal replacement mandate must reflect the reality that a community’s LSLs are often jointly 
owned by the water system and thousands of individual homeowners. Convincing all customers 
to agree to replace their LSLs can be a significant challenge for reasons ranging from disinterest 
to disillusionment and distrust of government. Without this customer consent, or a change in 
local laws, full replacement of LSLs is impossible.  

 
Dr. Jennifer McLain 
December 13, 2022 
Page  5 
Overall, the LCRI should make minimal changes to the current rule. EPA should collect data 
over the next few years to do a comprehensive assessment during the next Six-Year Review to 
identify areas that will be most effective in reducing lead exposure to the public. AMWA 
appreciates the opportunity to comment and asks that the agency fully consider and address the 
challenges associated with LSL replacement. If you have any questions about this letter, please 
contact Brian Redder, AMWA’s Manager of Regulatory and Scientific Affairs at 
redder@amwa.net.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
Thomas Dobbins 
Chief Executive Officer

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0828 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
US EPA Lead and Copper Rule Testimony
Annalisa Rocca
Jan 16, 2024
Good afternoon, thank you for the opportunity to testify before you today on the US
EPA’s proposed improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule. My name is Annalisa Rocca
and today I speak to you in my capacity as Drinking Water Manager at the Ohio
Environmental Council.
I want to start by commending the EPA and Biden-Harris administration for making
lead service line removal a priority.
Ohio is my home and is estimated to have the second largest collection of lead service
lines in the country, around 650,000 lines. The most critical element of this rule is
that it puts an end date on when lead service lines need to be removed and replaced,
for the first time. This has local advocates and impacted communities celebrating. We
also believe that the 10 year timeline is achievable for the vast majority of our cities
in Ohio.
The rule’s improvements also call for a comprehensive inventory of water service
lines, which must be updated regularly. This is critical because it will set utilities up
for the work ahead and give communities the information they have been asking for.
There are two areas of the updated rule that we would like to see strengthened to
better protect Americans. First, the rule as written, will allow utilities to forego
removing and replacing lead services in certain circumstances, such as when the
utility is not able to gain access to the property or when the property owner is unable
or unwilling to pay for the private-portion of the replacement. We urge the EPA to
work with states to address this potential loophole in the rule.
Secondly, we urge the EPA to strengthen the testing requirements for schools and
childcare centers. The proposed rule currently requires only one lead test to be
performed at five locations in each school and two locations in childcare centers. This
is problematic because lead can still be found in different faucets and fixtures,
especially in old buildings. The rule should require retesting, testing at more
locations, and that results be shared with parents and staff.

The $15 billion earmarked for lead service line replacement is an essential first step
at funding the requirements of the rule yet it is still not enough. The expected costs
associated with replacing just Cleveland, Ohio’s 185,000 lines is close to $1 billion. We
need more federal funding and a commitment from the EPA to continue to fight for
more dollars and to send them to the communities who need them most.
Every American, every Ohioan deserves clean, safe and affordable drinking water. We
thank the EPA and the Biden-Harris administration for developing an ambitious rule
that will chart the path forward to finally getting the lead out of our drinking water
delivery systems. This single rule will have measurable benefits for citizens in Ohio
and across the country.
Thank you.

Subject:  Comments on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements  
   (Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801) 
 
Dear Dr. McLain: 
 
The Connecticut Department of Public Health (CT DPH), as the State of Connecticut agency 
responsible for the Primacy of the SDWA public drinking water provisions, appreciates the time 
and resources the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) has spent on the Lead and Copper 
Rule Revisions (LCRR) and the current Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), 
which are significant rulemaking to strengthen the current Lead and Copper Rule and improve 
public health protection.  CT DPH appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the 
EPA’s Proposed LCRI and has put together comments in the attached EPA requested comments 
table and the following comments and recommendations for consideration during the pending 
review of the Proposed LCRI. 
 
1. Lead Service Line Definitions 
It is recommended that EPA defines the following as lead service line (LSL) or galvanized 
requiring replacement (GRR): 
 
Lead gooseneck, pigtail, or connector - Any components within the drinking water system 
containing lead may leach lead into the tap.  Lead goosenecks, pigtails, or connectors 
(connectors) may leach lead and flow into the tap, as happened in Tacoma Water 
https://www.thenewstribune.com/news/politics-government/article73004612.html.  In addition, 
these lead connectors may be connected to another metal of dissimilar property, which may 
increase the corrosion rate of these materials.  CT DPH supports and appreciates that EPA has 
added in the Proposed LCRI the requirement to inventory connectors and to replace lead 
connectors when replacing the downstream lead or galvanized requiring replacement (GRR) 
service lines.  CT DPH acknowledges and supports that the Proposed LCRI requires connectors 
more than 2 feet in length to be regulated as a service line.  However, lead connectors 2 feet or 

CT DPH Comments for Proposed LCRI 
February 2, 2024 
Page 2 of 7 
 
 
less that are not encountered during any work or not upstream of any lead or GRR service line 
that require replacement will remain connected to the service line and may continue to leach lead 
into the tap.  Thes lead connectors should be removed from the service lines since they are 
sources of lead to render the service lines lead free.  Therefore, CT DPH recommends that the 
lead gooseneck, pigtail, or connector be defined as LSL and subject to replacement to reduce the 
risk of lead contamination into the tap water. 
 
Galvanized service line - GRR is defined as any galvanized service line downstream of a lead 
service line currently or in the past or downstream of a lead status unknown service line, but not 
including downstream of the lead connectors, which may leach lead onto the galvanized pipe.  In 
addition, there are lead pipes encapsulated with galvanized pipe that were classified as 
galvanized pipe, not lead pipe, and studies have shown that zinc coating on galvanized pipe can 
be a significant source of lead in drinking water.  Therefore, CT DPH recommends that all 
galvanized service lines be defined as GRR subject to replacement to reduce the risk of lead 
contamination into the tap water. 
 
2. Timeline 
The regulatory changes in the Proposed LCRI lead to significant actions needed and increased 
significant regulatory compliance workloads on State agencies to implement the requirements.  The 
requirements to have all water systems submit all of the following at the same time by the 
compliance date of the final LCRI are not reasonable and prudent and will create delays for the 
review and approval of these submittals and for water systems to begin monitoring and replacement 
activities:   
 
1. Baseline service line inventories, 
 
2. LSL replacement (LSLR) plans,  
 
3. Lead and Copper compliance sampling site plans, and  
 
4. List of schools and childcare facilities.   
 
Timely approval of sampling site plans are needed for water systems to use when sampling begins in 
accordance with the final LCRI.  Sampling site plans are updated based on the most recent service 
line inventories (hence the baseline service line inventory) for the new compliance sampling 
requirements with new sampling tier criteria and sampling procedures.  Most systems initial service 
line inventory due on October 16, 2024 may have mostly unknown service lines; therefore, will need 
to continue verification to identify the material composition or validate those unknowns are not lead 
or GRR to include in the baseline service line inventory.  CT DPH strongly recommends the 
following staggering approach like the Stage 2 DBP Rule, but in a reverse order by water system 
size: 
 
I. 
Stagger submittal of the baseline service line inventories, compliance sampling site plans, 
and LSLR plans by water system size, to facilitate State review and approval before tap 
monitoring begins.  
 
a. Submit baseline service line inventories and sampling site plans: 
i. Very small water system (<500 people) - submit 1 years from the effective 
date of the final LCRI. 

CT DPH Comments for Proposed LCRI 
February 2, 2024 
Page 3 of 7 
 
 
ii. Small and medium water system – submit 2 years from the effective date of 
the final LCRI. 
iii. Large water system – submit by the compliance date (3 years from the 
effective date) of the final LCRI. 
 
b. Submit LSLR plans, if applicable: 
i. Very small water system (<500 people) – submit 1 ½ years from the effective 
date of the final LCRI. 
ii. Small and medium water system – submit 2 ½ years from the effective date of 
the final LCRI. 
iii. Large water system – submit ½ year from the compliance date of the final 
LCRI and lead and GRR service line replacement commencing one year from 
the compliance date of the final LCRI.   
 
II. 
Lead and copper compliance sampling to start in phases by water system size with 
monitoring to start 6 months after submitting the compliance sampling site plan from 
each category of system size listed in item I above; therefore: 
 
a. Allowing state agencies time for review and approval of the submitted baseline 
service line inventories and compliance sampling site plans, process including manual 
entry of each sampling site without auto migration of data capability into the Safe 
Drinking Water Information System that CT DPH uses, and set up compliance 
schedules and data tracking systems.   
 
b. Reduce the sample analysis burden and backlogs on certified laboratories for 
analyzing multiple samples from almost 1000 public water systems in CT by 
spreading out the compliance monitoring requirements into phases based on water 
system size listed in item I above.   
 
3. Sampling Waiver  
CT DPH does not support the allowance of a lead and copper sampling waiver from triennial 
monitoring to once every 9 years.  Corrosion is complex and the acute health effects of lead is a 
significant concern. It is unknown when the level of lead or copper may increase, if any part of the 
system and any service connections within the system’s distribution system contains lead 
components, such as the lead connector that is not defined as a lead service line and galvanized 
service line that is not defined as a GRR or any lead solder or lead components within the premise 
plumbing and/or fixtures.  Allowing a sampling waiver for systems to reduce monitoring to once 
every 9 years is a high risk.  CT DPH strongly recommends EPA to remove the 9-year waiver.    
 
4. Corrosion Control Treatment  
Pipe Rig/Loop - The treatment technique requirement for corrosion control treatment (CCT) 
step has a mandatory requirement for systems to conduct a pipe rig/loop corrosion control 
study with a section of the lead pipe harvested from the distribution system.  CT DPH does 
not support the requirements for systems, particularly the small and medium size systems, 
with a lead action level exceedance (ALE) to conduct pipe rig/loop corrosion control 

CT DPH Comments for Proposed LCRI 
February 2, 2024 
Page 4 of 7 
 
 
demonstration studies to identify their CCT approach.  The pipe rig/loop study is highly 
complex and challenging and a financial burden for the system to conduct.  In addition, there 
may not be many consultants/engineers nationwide who have experience or technical 
knowledge with pipe rig/loop corrosion control studies to provide services to the systems.  
Moreover, reviewing the results of the studies and determining the appropriate treatment is a 
challenging burden for State primacy agency staff who may not have the expertise on pipe 
rig/loop CCT studies to properly designate a CCT.  Systems in CT have been conducting 
desktop corrosion control studies and have been providing satisfactory results when the 
treatments are operated and maintained properly.  Desktop studies is less expensive and can 
be done in a fraction of the time needed for pipe rig/loop studies, therefore, systems can have 
the CCT installed within a year or two years using the desktop studies instead of over 5 years 
from the pipe rig/loop studies.  It is strongly recommended that EPA leave the option for pipe 
rig/loop studies to the system and the State primacy agency to determine.   
 
Re-Optimization - CT DPH disagrees with requiring systems to conduct only one re-
optimization of the optimal corrosion control treatment (OCCT) after an ALE.  Corrosion is 
very complex and changes in water quality from the source may also affect OCCT.  
Exceeding the action level with the system’s optimal water quality parameters (OWQP) 
meeting their designated values/ranges may indicate that the treatment was not truly 
optimized and the need to re-evaluate the treatment effectiveness and water quality 
parameters from the source and finished water.  CT DPH strongly recommends that EPA 
require systems to re-optimize OCCT, regardless of prior re-optimization and the system 
meeting their OWQP ranges.  In addition, the State primacy agency should have the authority 
to waive this requirement of only re-optimize once and the authority to require re-
optimization and the level of re-optimization efforts as deemed necessary. 
 
5. Deferment of Optimal Corrosion Control Treatment (OCCT) with Lead Action Level 
Exceedance (ALE) 
A water system with lead or GRR service lines exceeding the lead action level can defer the 
OCCT treatment technique requirements if the system can replace 100% of the lead or GRR 
service lines within 5 years.  The system will be required to conduct the OCCT treatment 
technique requirement if subsequent sampling period after the completion of the 100% 
service line replacement exceeded the lead action level.  CT DPH does not support delaying 
OCCT until after the system has replaced all its lead or GRR service lines with the 
accelerated 5-year replacement requirement.  With the 1st and 5th liter sampling requirements 
to represent water from the premise plumbing and the service line for systems with lead or 
GRR service lines, and with sampling from lower sampling tiers if the systems don’t have 
sufficient sampling locations from lead or GRR service line sites (tier 1 or 2 sites), the lead 
ALE may be from the premise plumbing and not from the lead or GRR service lines.  
Therefore, replacement of lead or GRR service lines will not address lead contamination 
from other sources of lead such as the premise plumbing or any portion of service line that 
contains some percentage of lead and not categorized as lead or GRR.  Consumers will be 
exposed to lead for a longer time if the systems are allowed to delay OCCT.  CT DPH 
supports the simultaneous OCCT and service line replacement requirement.   
 

CT DPH Comments for Proposed LCRI 
February 2, 2024 
Page 5 of 7 
 
 
6. Data Management 
With the significant changes in the Proposed LCRI and the complexity of the rule, in order for 
the state agencies to appropriately and comprehensively enforce the LCRI requirements, EPA 
should provide the following: 
 
I. 
Develop an inventory management system for State primacy agencies to house the service 
line inventories from water system including the ability to house updated inventories.   
II. 
Upgrade to Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS)/ Drinking Water State 
Federal Tribal Information Exchange Sytems (DWSFTIES).  Assure SDWIS or the new 
DWSFTIES is upgraded before the compliance date of the LCRI to track and calculate the 
necessary items and implement all aspects of the LCRI, which includes but is not limited to 
the following: 
a. Add a tool to track and report the # of connectors.   
b. Update sampling sites to include the new 5 tier levels and tier types.  
c. Develop a business logic engine to calculate the 90th percentile action level based 
on the new requirements of different matrixes in the LCRI, such as:

7. Resources 
The regulatory changes in the Proposed LCRI lead to significant actions needed and 
increased significant regulatory compliance workloads on State agencies to implement the 
requirements.  The amount of inventories, replacement plans, service line replacements, 
sampling site plans, tap and WQP samplings, systems with action level exceedances, OCCT, 
distribution system site assessment, assessment of WQP during sanitary survey process, 
public notification/education requirements, school and childcare facilities lead testing, 
customer consent/refusal, etc. place a significant burden on CT to comprehensively and 
effectively implement the rule with the limited staff working on the Lead and Copper Rule.  
The significant workloads generated from the LCRR and the LCRI will need at least an 
additional 15 full-time employee to implement the rule.  CT DPH strongly requests that EPA 
increase the federal funding to CT to fund staff to successfully conduct the required 
workloads from the LCRR and LCRI and adequately implement the rules.

requirements, CT DPH strongly recommends that EPA develop comprehensive decision-trees, 
flowcharts, or schematics clearly depicting the regulatory triggers, steps for CCT optimization,

notification/education requirements, public outreach activities, etc. as tools to assist State 
primacy agencies and water systems to understand the complexity of the rule.  With the 
complexity of the different matrixes for action level calculation and requirements, CT strongly 
recommends EPA to provide technical guidance on 90th percentile action level calculation to 
reduce confusion and ensure proper implementation, on customer consent and refusal to assist 
system staff with tracking and reporting customer engagement to the State primacy agencies.   
 
In addition, CT DPH strongly recommends EPA to provide technical guidance and frequent 
trainings on the following topics to help water systems, State primacy agencies, and consultants 
to understand corrosion control, corrosion control treatment (CCT), and proper operation and 
maintenance of an effective CCT to achieve optimal corrosion control: 
a. Incremental CCT training sessions from basic to advance level, with basic level 
training targeting for someone that has no or limited knowledge of corrosion control 
and corrosion chemistry.  
b. Technical guidances on different type of CCT studies and results interpretation. 
c. Technical guidances on selection of representative WQP montoring locations; 
designation of OWQP; maintain CCT or re-optimized CCT operation and 
effectiveness including potential adverse impacts from changes in source

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0830 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket

Dear Mr. Michael Goldberg: 
 
The West Virginia Municipal Water Quality Association (WVMWQA) appreciates the opportunity 
to comment on USEPA’s proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation 
(NPDWR) for lead and copper. On December 6, 2023, EPA issued for public comment further 
proposed revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), found in 40 C.F.R. § 141.80.91), known 
as the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Although the WVMWQA supports a robust 
Lead and Copper Rule, we have significant concerns, summarized below, about several of the 
proposed changes.  
 
The WVMWQA comprises public water and sewer statewide. Our members are dedicated to 
protecting public health and the environment – this includes reducing the amount of lead and 
copper present in our finished drinking water. We never seek to avoid necessary and appropriate 
requirements. Instead, we embrace such requirements and work to prioritize them and obtain the 
funding necessary to comply from the public that we serve. That said, as public utilities we must 
provide public water service in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  
 
With that perspective, we are compelled to submit these comments because the proposed LCRI 
requirements create a massive regulatory and economic obligation for both public water systems 
and their ratepayers. Adding these distribution system obligations is especially burdensome on 
top of the PFAS-related treatment obligations anticipated with EPA’s pending MCLs. Lead Service 
Line (LSL) removal is particularly challenging given the need for significant public outreach and 
interaction in relation to private laterals. US EPA estimates that there are around 9.2 million LSLs 
in the United States, which the AWWA estimates could cost over $90 billion to replace. Below we 
explain why we believe that the inventory obligation and removal of any LSLs that are found may 
be a major challenge both administratively and financially and will lead to significant conflict 
between EPA, the States, and water utilities as they struggle to define the universe of LSLs and 
complete the mandated replacements. 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2  
 
 
2 
 
I. 
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement Within 10 Years is Both Financially and 
Practically Impossible.  A Phased-In Deadline Based Upon System Lead Levels is 
Both Necessary and Appropriate 
 
The 10-Year Timeline 
 
The proposed LCRI would require water utilities to complete 100% lead service line replacement 
(LSLR) within 10 years. 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84882 (Dec. 6, 2023).  While there are alternative 
timelines for (1) systems with a high proportion of lead and GRR service lines in their distribution 
system relative to their total number of households served and (2) systems that would otherwise 
be required to replace greater than 10,000 service lines per year under the proposed 10-year 
replacement requirement, Id. at 84913, the ten-year timeframe is woefully inadequate.   
 
Anytime we talk in terms of “all” in relation to 50,000 water systems, spread across the country, 
we should pause for a reality check.  We should especially pause when a significant number of 
the LSLs to be replaced have not even been identified.  We should further pause when faced with 
a potential price tag of upwards of $100 billion dollars. 
 
EPA estimates that there are more than 50,000 water systems nationwide.  It is simply impractical 
for such a large number of systems to make significant distribution system changes in a ten-year 
period.  This is especially the case given the (1) fact that many/most of the LSLs have not been 
identified, (2) cost of such replacements, (3) need for public outreach around utility-owned LSL 
replacement, and (4) need for outreach and coordination with homeowners across the country 
regarding replacement of their customer-owned LSLs.  Such an historic and unprecedented effort 
would come during the worst period in modern history for trying to plan, finance, bid, and deliver 
projects.  There is simply not enough engineering or construction talent available to do the work 
- even if we could fund it. 
 
Many of our water systems are struggling right now with basic water availability, especially during 
the winter months.  Cold weather each of the last several winters has taken a major toll on water 
systems leading to numerous water main breaks and boil water advisories.  These have been 
especially prevalent across the southern United States and into the mid-Atlantic.  For example, 
much of the District of Columbia had a boil water notice in January of 2024 due to cold weather-
related line breaks. 
 
US EPA has for several decades made a priority of imposing incredibly expensive (and in many 
ways, counter-productive) sewer system improvement mandates on local governments 
nationwide.  As a result of this sewer-first enforcement approach, local resources have been 
forced to the sewer side, often at the expense of water utilities’ ability to raise revenue.  Those 
deferred investments are now coming home to roost for water systems.  On top of general system 
needs, thousands of water systems face historically expensive PFAS-related capital upgrades 
and incredible annual operation and maintenance costs for those facilities.  Adding a LSL 
replacement obligation over the next 10 years on top of these historic financial challenges is a 
bridge too far financially and from a project delivery perspective. 
 
A one-size-fits-all LSL removal period will have water systems with low lead levels vying for the 
same funding and engineering/contracting resources as water systems with much higher lead 
levels.  This makes no sense whatsoever. 
 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 3  
 
 
3 
 
A more logical approach to LSL replacement is for USEPA to adopt a phased approach where 
utilities with higher P90 lead levels have earlier deadlines to replace their LSLs while utilities with 
lower P90 numbers defer their replacements.  Such an approach will allow EPA, the States, and 
utilities to prioritize available federal and State grant/loan resources as well as engineering and 
construction resources to water systems with higher lead levels.    
 
We specifically recommend that the final rule authorize the states to establish phased-in deadlines 
for their water systems.  Any water system above the 10 ppb lead action level must remove their 
LSLs within 10 years of the effective date of the rule.  Utilities with P90 values below the 10 ppt 
would be prioritized based upon their levels for LSL removal, generally not to exceed a 20-year 
compliance period.   We believe that 20 years is a more realistic (albeit, still very challenging) 
compliance period.  Significantly, such an implementation period will allow water utilities to 
coordinate LSL removal with other system upgrades both getting and giving economies of scale 
to water system projects.  This will reduce the financial burden and system planning disruption 
that will otherwise result from a crude, 10-year LSL removal deadline. 
 
This phased approach, coupled with a one-third reduction in the lead action level, will ensure 
additional protection going forward for all Americans who receive public drinking water, from day 
one of the Rule’s effective date. 
 
II. 
Lead Service Line Replacement Must Only Include Public Lead Service Lines. 
 
The concept of LSL replacement must be revised to include replacement of only utility-owned 
LSLs. EPA lacks the authority to require public water utilities to replace privately-owned water 
infrastructure located on private property.  There are significant legal questions about whether 
public entities can even spend public funds for this private purpose.   
 
EPA cannot withhold credit for a public side lead service line replacement unless water systems 
undertake illegally impermissible action on private property.  EPA needs to address the legality of 
requiring public water systems to replace private lead service lines before imposing such a 
requirement in the LCRI. 
 
Rather than illegally seeking to force public water systems to make improvements to private 
indoor plumbing, EPA should give water utilities a benefit for each full LSL replacement that is 
performed.  For example, a utility could be given more time to complete LSL removals (within our 
suggested 20 year from the rule effective date compliance period) if they meet certain private side 
LSL removal goals (such as 30 or 40 percent associated with public LSL removal). 
 
We also question whether EPA’s assumed cost to implement the proposed rule has included 
private side LSL replacement costs.  If “yes,” we would like to know what EPA estimates those 
private costs to be and the basis for those estimates.   
 
Revise the Definition of “Under the Control of the Water System” to Exclude Customer-Owned 
LSLs 
 
Relatedly, we disagree with the proposed LCRI rule requirement that full LSL replacement is 
required when lines are “under the control” of the water system. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The term 
“under the control” of the water system is defined as wherever a water system has adequate 
access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full-service line replacement or 
replacement of the lead connector. Id. at 84920.  

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4  
 
 
4 
 
This definition is impermissibly overbroad.  The definition must clarify that water utilities are not 
obligated to replace customer-owned LSLs as EPA cannot legally require public utilities to make 
changes to private property. The key aspect should be ownership. The present proposed 
incentives are written for a complete replacement (with customer agreement) so that water 
systems do not get credit for LSL replacement if it doesn’t include the customer’s side. We believe 
this is an illegal provision and although we support full replacements, our members cannot be 
required to go on private property and replace indoor plumbing. Those private side replacements 
should instead be driven by federal funding efforts and partial replacements should be given the 
credit they are due, considering they take great effort and expense to identify and accomplish.  
Instead, and as noted above, water utilities should be given a benefit if they achieve a certain 
goal for customer-owned LSL replacement as part of LSL replacement of publicly-owned water 
distribution lines. 
 
Lining and Coating Service Lines Should Qualify for Extended Removal Deadlines 
 
As noted above, removing “all” LSLs in the country in ten years is a shocking financial and 
practical proposition.  Rather than requiring removal, we believe EPA should allow a range of 
effective lead reduction approaches, such as lining or coating technologies to count equally as 
LSL replacements.  At a minimum, lined or coated service lines should qualify for deferred removal 
schedules.  
 
Lined or coated service lines immediately control lead from entering drinking water. EPA’s 
inventory and full service line replacement requirements in the LCRI will impose substantial costs 
on water systems that must simultaneously investigate unknown lead status service lines and 
connectors, finance capital projects associated with replacing known or discovered lead and GRR 
service lines and lead connectors and assemble the resources and personnel to replace all the 
service lines requiring replacement. 
 
Granting water systems an additional period to complete the replacements of coated or lined 
service lines, e.g. for the service life of the coating or lining product, will lower the personnel and 
financial burdens of the LCRI on water systems while immediately reducing lead from drinking 
water as water systems will dedicate resources to those services lines most likely posing a risk of 
lead exposure. 
 
III. 
Galvanized Replacement Service Lines. 
 
Definition of “Galvanized Requiring Replacements” 
 
Under the proposed LCRI, galvanized service lines that have ever been downstream of LSL 
require replacement (GRR). 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The EPA defines galvanized requiring 
replacement service lines as a “galvanized service line that currently is or ever was downstream 
of a lead service line or is currently downstream in the direction of flow of a lead status unknown 
service line.” Id. 85054 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.2). If the water system cannot demonstrate the 
galvanized service line was never downstream of a lead line, the line is a galvanized requiring 
replacement service line. Id. 
 
The EPA’s proposed definition of GRRs is unreasonable and counterproductive.  The definition 
will likely result in water systems having to replace all galvanized service lines within the same 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5  
 
 
5 
 
10-year period they must replace LSLs.  We think the presumption that a galvanized line requires 
replacement is too strong.  Rather than requiring the water system to know that there was never 
a LSL above the galvanized line, a water utility should be able to conclude, based upon available 
information, that there is no information that there was ever a LSL above the galvanized line.  In 
those cases, the water system should be able to prioritize the lining/coating/removal of galvanized  
lines over a longer compliance period – say 20 years.  Again, the longer period is absolutely 
critical if water systems are to see economies of scale with other water distribution system work 
in conjunction with LSL and galvanized line removal.  This is especially the case for water utilities 
with P90 numbers that are well below the proposed 10 ppb action level.  We continue to believe 
that the states should be given the authority to prioritize LSL (and GRR) removal. 
 
The Lead Connector Threshold Should be 36 Inches and Unknown Connectors Assumed to Be 
36 Inches or Smaller 
 
We disagree that lead connectors greater than two feet in length should be considered service 
lines. See 88 id. at 84919, 85083. Connectors greater than 24 inches have been sold to utilities 
and the EPA does not present evidence suggesting significantly higher lead concentrations 
resulting from a lead connector that is 36 inches as opposed to 24 inches in length. If EPA is 
going to impose an arbitrary connector length, it should be at least 36 inches.  Moreover, there 
should be a presumption that connectors of unknown size and composition are less than three 
feet in length. 
 
IV. 
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes Remains a Monumental Task for Utilities. 
 
It might be one thing for EPA to impose a 10-year LSL removal requirement if we already 
understood how many LSLs there were and where they are located.  That would allow us to better 
estimate the cost of removal and time needed.  Instead, EPA is shooting blind in that they don’t 
even have the benefit of the existing LSL inventories that won’t come due until October 16, 2024.  
Almost all of those inventories will be derived using predictive tools with only a small percentage 
of LSLs actually having been ground-truthed. 
 
The fact remains that it is a spring for most water systems to meet October 16, 2024 initial 
inventory deadline.  We suspect that hundreds, if not thousands of water systems will miss the 
deadline.  It will take many years following the development of the initial deadlines to ground truth 
where LSLs actually are in each water system.   
 
Accordingly, we request that EPA clarify what, if any, inventory update requirements are 
contemplated between the initial inventory under the LCRI and baseline inventories in the 
proposed LCRI. We suggest the EPA suspend inventory updates between the two deadlines to 
allow water systems an opportunity to develop a complete and accurate baseline inventory in light 
of the substantial difficulty most water systems will have categorizing the material composition 
and location of their service lines and connectors. Alternatively, the EPA should consider 
eliminating the initial inventory requirement and allow water systems to dedicate all of their 
resources into developing complete and accurate baseline inventories available to the public by 
2027. 
 
Baseline Inventory Requirements 
 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 6  
 
 
6 
 
We request the EPA to reconsider requiring water systems to investigate connector locations and 
composition in its baseline inventory. The proposed rule would require water systems to remove 
lead connectors upon discovery. 88 Fed. Reg. at 85066 (Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.84(e)). The 
EPA’s justification for not requiring water systems to find and replace all lead connectors as part 
of the full-service line replacement requirement is that “regular progress towards lead connector 
replacement is made in coordination with other activities, such as planned infrastructure work, 
while resources are prioritized for replacement of all LSLs and GRR service lines as quickly as 
feasible.” Id. at 84919.  
 
EPA noted that most lead connectors will be replaced under the proposed rule because “all lead 
connectors that are attached to a lead or GRR service line would be replaced by the end of the 
mandatory service line replacement program.” Id. In addition, EPA “also expects that many lead 
connectors may be connected to aging water mains and likely to undergo replacement with 
routine main replacement activities in coming years,” especially because EPA estimates that any 
given lead connector “is expected to be a minimum of 41 years old by the LCRI compliance date 
in 2027” and the “average service life of cast iron, ductile iron, and asbestos-cement pipe is 40 
years.” Id. EPA thus acknowledged that water systems will encounter and replace the vast majority 
of lead connectors during routine maintenance as a result of aging infrastructure or as a result of 
its mandatory service line replacement requirements. 
 
At the same time, EPA acknowledges that short lead connectors pose a lower lead exposure risk 
than LSL and GRR service lines that are significantly longer. Id. at 84919 (“EPA expects that 
galvanized lines downstream of lead connectors may contribute less lead into drinking water than 
those that were downstream of much longer LSLs”). EPA therefore prioritized service line 
replacement. Because EPA accepts that its requirement for water systems to replace lead 
connectors upon discovery will address the vast majority of lead connectors in a water system 
and acknowledges that lead connectors pose less of a health risk than lead service lines, we 
request EPA to reconsider its decision to include connectors in the baseline inventory. 
 
Removing the investigation of connectors from the baseline inventory removes expensive and 
laborious investigations into the location and composition of connectors when those resources 
are best spent identifying, locating, and removing lead and GRR service lines. Water systems 
reporting the composition and location of encountered connectors and the number of replaced 
lead connectors will still provide valuable information to the water system and the public about 
the location and composition of connectors in a water system and the probability that lead 
connectors are present. 
 
Validation Pool Requirements 
 
The proposed regulation instructs water systems to develop a “validation pool” consisting of all 
lines categorized as non-lead minus the non-lead lines that already replaced LSL or GRR lines, 
non-lead lines already visually inspected at two points along the line, or non-lead lines with 
documentation demonstrating their composition. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84935, 85063 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 141.84(b)(5)). The rule would require water systems to randomly and visually inspect as 
many service lines in the validation pool as necessary to ensure a “95% confidence level” that the 
observed proportion of non-lead lines validated is representative of the larger validation pool 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 7  
 
 
7 
 
within ten years of the rule’s publication and seven years of submitting baseline inventories. Id.; 
Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA 815-
R-23-003 at 24-25 (Nov. 2023). 
 
The timing of this LSL/GRR inventory requirement reinforces the impracticality of the ten-year 
LSL/GRR removal requirement. 
 
EPA is currently calculating the number of visual inspections of lines necessary to ensure that 
lines categorized as non-lead are in fact non-lead by assuming a standard normal distribution and 
an “expected sample proportion” of 0.5. EPA assumed the expected sample proportion “to be 50 
percent, meaning that 50 percent of the non-lead service lines investigated are expected to be 
confirmed as non-lead.” Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements, EPA 815-R-23-003 at 25 (Nov. 2023). EPA acknowledged “this proportion will most 
likely be much higher since most non-lead lines will end up being confirmed as nonlead.” Id. EPA 
nonetheless maintained the proportion at 0.5 because, “an assumption of 0.50 provides the most 
conservative (or largest) sample size…meaning that any system validating this number of lines 
will be guaranteed to have met or exceeded the minimum number for statistical significance 
regardless of the true sample proportion.” Id. 
 
We question why EPA does not simply stick with the 95% confidence and allow each water utility’s 
consultant to develop a testing program that will achieve that level of confidence for the utility’s 
list.  Why does EPA pick a very aggressive 95th percent confidence level and then structure the 
rule to force an even higher level of confidence? 
 
The method for determining the number of visual inspections necessary is also not particularly 
well explained. At a minimum, EPA should clarify its validation calculations, e.g. what data it used, 
if any, to determine the expected sample proportion, what the relevant comparison EPA is making 
between the validated lines and the validation pool and what that significance of that comparison 
is, and where EPA derived its formulas for determining the appropriate sample size and provide 
citations. 
 
EPA should also assume in its sample proportion that water systems will correctly assess line 
status more than 50% of the time given its concurrent requirements to investigate lead status 
unknown lines. As EPA has explained the sample proportion, EPA is essentially assuming water 
systems will be no better at determining service line composition than flipping a coin. In light of 
the other significant investigation costs imposed by the rule, EPA should reconsider this 
assumption because it should significantly lower the number of validations water systems must 
make.  
 
We support EPA’s decision to exclude service lines which water systems have confirmed as non-
lead through records investigations from the validation pool. Id. at 84935, 85063.  
 
We also request the EPA to consider delaying the date the inventory validation must be submitted 
to better align with the categorization of lead status unknown service lines. Water systems must 
identify the material of all lead status unknown service lines within ten years from the compliance 
date. Id. at 85063. Conversely, the validation study must be submitted no later than ten years 

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 8  
 
 
8 
 
from the rule’s publication date or seven years from the compliance date. Id. at 85063. If water 
systems submit inventory validations before all unknown lines are categorized, then the validation 
pool will not include some lines categorized as “non-lead.” Allowing the validation to occur at least 
after all lead status unknown lines have been categorized will create a validation pool 
representative of all of the non-lead categorized service lines and provide water systems three 
more years to validate their inventories. 
 
Public Disclosure of LSL Addresses In Service Line Inventory 
 
The LCRI, like the LCRR, continues to require that a water system’s annual inventory updates be 
publicly accessible. Although the LCRR includes location identifiers (street, intersection, 
landmark, etc.) served by each LSL, the LCRI states utilities must include a street address with 
each service line and connector. Id. at 84936. We continue to disagree with the need to publicly 
publish a list of homes served by LSLs. Each home will get an annual reminder of this fact. Any 
home that tests for lead will receive its results – there is no need or clear authority for the EPA to 
mandate that this specific information must be made publicly available.  We especially think it is 
irresponsible to include unknown LSL in these lists. 
 
V. 
Lowering the Lead Action Level will be significant in many states. 
 
EPA is proposing to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L. 88 Fed. Reg. 84880 while 
eliminating the lead trigger level that was introduced under the 2021 LCRR. If the AL is exceeded, 
the system must inform the public (Tier 1 public notification within 24 hrs of learning of 
exceedance) and reduce lead exposure while concurrently working to replace all lead pipes (for 
example, installing/adjusting corrosion control treatment). Id. 
 
Lowering the Action Level from 15 ug/L to 10 ug/L will be a big deal in some states with some 
states asserting that the number of systems exceeding the new action level could double.  This 
is likely to be the case for a number of smaller systems.   
 
We take no position on the reduction in the action level.  However, we do believe that P90 
numbers should be a basis for phasing in LSL/GRR removal requirements and that the states are 
in the best position to prioritize LSL/GRR removal.  States are also in the best position to work 
with water systems to mitigate lead levels pending LSL removal.   
 
VI. 
We Disagree With the Requirement to Make Point-of-Use Filters/Pitchers Available 
to All Households After Three Action Level Exceedances.    
 
Under the LCRI, water systems with three lead action level exceedances would be required to 
conduct additional outreach to consumers and make pitcher filters or point-of-use devices certified 
to reduce lead available to all consumers. See id. at 84954.  
 
Providing such filters/pitchers will be overkill in that it will scare many residents not served by 
LSL/GRRs into thinking their tap water is not safe.  That loss of confidence can be difficult, if not 
impossible, to overcome to the long-term detriment of the residents and the utility.   
 
Moreover, distributing filters/pitchers will be a massive administrative and financial task.  The 
filters/pitchers would have to be provided to each residential and non-residential location served 
by the public water supply.   

WVMWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 9  
 
 
9 
 
We are also very concerned that residents would not properly replace the filters and could end up 
concentrating lead and copper beyond what would otherwise be present in their drinking water. 
 
VII. 
Utilities Must Be Allowed to Invalidate a Homeowner Sample That Does not Follow 
Proper Collection Procedures. 
 
Under the proposed rule, a water utility could not invalidate a homeowner’s sample even if the 
sample was not taken in accordance with LCRI requirements.  This is unacceptable.  All data 
must meet applicable QA/QC/Sampling requirements.  At a minimum, the rule should give the 
water utility the discretion to use a non-conforming sample but should not mandate the use of 
such samples. 
 
VIII. 
Water Systems Must Be Able to Select Homes From Lower Tiers Where Not Enough 
Tier 1 Homeowners Are Willing to Participate. 
 
The LCRI must clarify that water systems which, despite best, good faith efforts, cannot attract 
enough Tier 1 homeowners to participate in sampling, can use lower tier homes. 
 
Otherwise, the water system will be in non-compliance due to causes (lack of homeowner 
willingness to participate) which are beyond its control. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
Our member utilities work tirelessly to provide high quality finished drinking water for our 
customers in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  We appreciate EPA’s consideration of our 
concerns about the practicality and affordability of the requirements we object to above.  We also 
appreciate EPA’s consideration of our suggested improvements to the proposed rule.  In 
particular, we strongly believe that a final rule needs to provide additional time for LSL/GRR 
removal and that a state-directed phased approach over twenty years from the rule’s effective 
date, is warranted. 
 
Sincerely, 
       
 
F. Paul Calamita  
General Counsel

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1102 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
The Honorable Michael S. Regan, Administrator
Feb 5, 2024
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, N.W.
Washington, DC 20460
RE: Ensuring Safe Drinking Water at School - Proposed Lead and Copper Rule
Improvements (Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801)
Dear Administrator Regan,
On behalf of millions of American families, educators and concerned citizens, we urge you to
strengthen the proposed Lead & Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) to ensure safe drinking
water at schools and child care centers.
Lead contamination of drinking water is a serious, longstanding and widespread threat to public
health. A key reason this problem persists is that federal policy has only required action when
highly variable testing detects lead. To finally ensure safe drinking water for all Americans, the
EPA must transform that “test and fix” policy to one that prevents lead contamination at every
drinking water tap.
A perfect example of this preventative approach is the LCRI’s requirement that water utilities
replace all lead service lines within 10 years. These 9+ million toxic pipes are the single greatest
source of lead contamination for buildings served by them. We wholeheartedly support turning
President Biden’s goal of eliminating these lead pipes within a decade into an enforceable
reality.
We need similarly bold policies to stop lead from contaminating the water where
America’s children go to learn and play each day. Even low levels of lead can damage
children’s health - including learning disabilities, behavior problems, and more. Yet national
standards have allowed the fountains, faucets, pipes and plumbing in our schools to contain a

significant amount of lead. (Even some post-2014 faucets can cause contamination.) As a
result, lead contamination of schools’ drinking water is now widespread.
Yet for most schools and child care centers, the proposed rule only requires water systems to
offer testing (and very limited testing at that). Even federally regulated schools and child care
centers would only have to remediate taps where tests show lead concentrations at 10 parts per
billion (ppb) or more.
These proposed policies will fail to secure safe water for kids and educators. Because lead
testing is highly variable, the water from a fountain or faucet can be “highly hazardous” even if
several samples fail to detect lead. Moreover, the 10 ppb action level means that no remediation
will be required for a huge proportion of taps where some level of lead is detected. This weak
policy is also contrary to EPA’s own 3Ts Guidance, which urges schools to reduce lead levels “to
the lowest possible concentrations.”1
America’s kids and educators deserve better. Just as we must replace every lead service line,
federal policy should aim to prevent lead contamination at every tap at schools. Except where a
school district or child care facility affirmatively opts out, the LCRI should require Community
Water Systems (which serve 90% of schools) to implement one of the following options at
schools and child care facilities:
a) Prevent lead contamination at every tap, including:
1.
Filter first: Install and maintain point of use filters certified to remove lead on every tap
used for drinking water, cooking or beverage preparation. As fountains contain lead and
cannot accept filters at the point where water comes out, they should be replaced by
new water stations with filters. A growing number of jurisdictions have already adopted
some version of this “filter first” policy for schools - Including Michigan, Philadelphia,
Portland (OR) and the District of Columbia;
2.
A health-based limit on lead: Limit lead in schools’ water to 1 ppb, as recommended
by the American Academy of Pediatrics. Schools and child care centers are particularly
well-situated to meet this low lead concentration because they have full control of their
water delivery systems - all the way to the tap. Taps should be tested after filter
installation to ensure this standard is being met; and
3.
Get the lead out: To stop the cycle of lead contamination at school, new and
replacement taps and plumbing should meet the Q≤1 standard recently adopted by
California, where lead leached into water is less than or equal to 1 ppb; or
b) Test every drinking water tap at least once every 6 months, and then replace taps and install
filters whenever lead concentrations exceed 1 ppb. While not ideal, this much more robust “test
and fix” option would be more effective at reducing the likelihood of lead-contaminated water at
school than the infrequent testing and no required remediation in the proposed rule.
For the roughly 10% of schools and child care facilities that are federally regulated as
Non-Transient Non-Community Water Systems, the EPA can and should simply require the
much more protective Option a) above in the LCRI rule.
1 U.S. EPA, 3Ts for Reducing Lead in Drinking Water in Schools and Child Care Facilities (2018) at Module
4, page 36, accessed on January 10, 2024.

Right to Know: To counter the strong likelihood of a false sense of safety from inherently
variable testing, the LCRI should also require all water utilities to regularly communicate
(including online) the following to families, educators and the public regarding schools and child
care facilities: full test results showing any level of lead at each tap; that tests are variable and
can fail to detect lead; that there is no safe level of lead; prevention/remediation measures taken
at each tap; and any school districts or child care facilities opting out of their Community Water
System’s measures outlined above.
In addition to these requirements for schools and child care centers regulated as NTNCWS,
EPA should also incorporate policy changes that will better prevent lead contamination at all
other schools and child care facilities:
●
Establish a clear preference for awarding grants aimed at prevention - such as replacing
fountains with filter-equipped water stations - rather than funding more testing. Condition
grants on adhering to the Right to Know provisions outlined above.
●
Change the name of EPA’s 3 Ts Guidance to “Preventing Lead Contamination at Every
Tap” and replace its “test-and-fix” recommendations with the prevention-oriented
measures outlined above for LCR-regulated schools.
America’s children and educators need safe drinking water to thrive and be healthy. We urge the
EPA to act more boldly to get the lead out at school.
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0852 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024
The Honorable Michael S. Regan
Administrator
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
Washington, D.C. 20460
RE:
Comments: Improvements to Lead & Copper National Primary Drinking Water
Regulations, Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036
Dear Administrator Regan,
On behalf of our members and supporters, we write to express our strong support for the
proposed improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule. We urge the EPA to finalize the strong
improvements to the rule and share some additional ideas for consideration to further
strengthen the rule.
Specifically, we strongly support the 10 year timeline for a full lead service line (LSL)
replacement. As the most critical element of the rule, it puts an end date on when lead
service lines need to be removed and replaced, for the first time. Ohio has the second most
LSLs in the country, and we believe that the 10 year timeline is achievable for the majority of
our cities. Additionally, requiring water utilities to complete and regularly update a
comprehensive inventory of water service lines will help utilities to plan and scope the work
ahead and give communities more information about what materials are being used to deliver
the water to their homes.
The proposed rule’s stronger testing requirements, requiring sampling from both the first and
fifth liter of water from the tap, will ensure that more instances of elevated lead levels are
caught and that households are notified. The provision where water utilities will be required
to provide filters when there have been repeated exceedances of the action level will ensure
that citizens are better protected while waiting for their service lines to be replaced. Though,
we are concerned that the utilities are able to focus their resources most intently on actual
lead service line replacement. Thus, we recommend requiring utilities to provide filters only
to households with lead service lines or unknown materials.
There are some areas of the updated rule that we would like to see strengthened to better
protect Americans. While the updates to testing requirements in the home are stronger, we
urge the EPA to also strengthen the testing requirements for schools and childcare centers.
The proposed rule currently requires only one lead test to be performed at five locations in
each school and two locations in childcare centers. This is problematic because lead can still
be found in faucets and fixtures, especially in old buildings. We urge the agency to ensure
that the water flowing from taps and fountains in our schools and childcare centers are 100%

lead free. The rule should require retesting, testing at more locations, and that results of
those tests be shared with parents and staff.
Secondly, the rule as written, will allow utilities to forego removing and replacing lead service
lines in circumstances such as when the utility is not able to gain access to the property or
when the property owner is unable or unwilling to pay for the private-portion of the
replacement. This will disproportionately impact low-income individuals and renters who do
not have control over whether their landlord will give permission to the utilities. We urge the
EPA to strengthen the language in the rule to ensure that utilities must take every step
possible to gain access to the property and to either cover the cost of the private side of the
line or to provide financial assistance to low-income households/property owners for the
private portion of the line.
Finally, the drop in the lead action level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb is a step in the right direction,
but we know that no detectable level of lead is safe for children and adults. We urge the EPA
to consider lowering the lead action level even further to cover any detectable amount of
lead.
The $15 billion earmarked for lead service line replacement is an essential first step at
funding the requirements of the rule yet it is still not enough. The expected costs associated
with replacing the 185,000 LSLs in Cleveland, Ohio alone is close to $1 billion. Cincinnati
expects another $150-$200 million will be needed to get to 100% replacement of their
remaining LSLs. We need more federal funding and a commitment from the EPA to continue to
fight for more federal dollars and to send them to the communities who need them most.
Ohioans deserve clean, safe and affordable drinking water. We urge the EPA to finalize this
strong rule and chart the path forward to finally getting the lead entirely out of our drinking
water delivery systems.
Thank you,
Ohio Environmental Council
Ohio Lead Free Kids Coalition
The Junction Coalition
Black Environmental Leaders Action Fund

Dear Mr. Goldberg: 
The Texas Chemistry Council (TCC) submits the following comments on EPA’s proposed rule for National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) (88 FR 84878, December 6, 2023, EPA Docket ID No. EPA-
HQ-OW-2022-0801), hereafter “Proposed Rule.”   
 
TCC is a statewide trade association of chemical manufacturers representing more than 60 member companies who own 
and operate over 200 manufacturing and research facilities across Texas. The business of chemistry provides employment 
for approximately 500,000 Texans and its products are the state’s top non-energy export with more than $50 billion in 
state exports annually to customers around the world. TCC’s member companies have industrial facilities throughout the 
United States, of which some are also registered Non-Transient Non-Community Public Water Systems (NTNCWSs).  Our 
membership is committed to the safety of our employees, including the protection of their health when consuming 
drinking water in the workplace.   
 
When assessing the requirements of the Proposed Rule and considering the competing priorities of the proposed PFAS 
regulations for Drinking Water, TCC echoes the comments of the American Petroleum Institute (API) and American 
Chemistry Council (ACC) in identifying the following opportunities for EPA to provide additional flexibility and clarity to 
NTNCWSs.  Specifically, TCC requests EPA allow the option for NTNCWSs to install point-of-use devices in lieu of lead 
service line (LSL) replacement for NTNCWSs and to provide bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or POU devices 
following disturbances.  Additionally, TCC requests that EPA provide clear and timely guidance to all PWSs, including 
NTNCWSs on expectations associated with the final rule and the definition of Service Line.  Finally, TCC argues that EPA 
has underestimated the cost burden to NTNCWSs, and TCC formally requests that EPA consider feedback on assumptions 
that EPA has made on NTNCWSs when considering compliance alternatives. 
 
TCC offers the recommendations in these comments to inform EPA’s consideration in advance of any future regulatory 
action and support the separate comments submitted to this docket from API and ACC.  The following points highlight key 
elements of our detailed comments: 
• 
EPA should allow Point-of-Use Devices in lieu of LSL replacement for NTNCWS that do not supply water to 
sensitive populations, such as schools or child-care facilities. 
• 
EPA should add alternative options and sample validation as an option for risk mitigation after disturbances for 
NTNCWSs.

• 
EPA should provide clear and timely guidance for industrial facility NTNCWSs. 
• 
EPA should clarify the definition of Service Line. 
• 
EPA’s assumptions result in an underestimated Cost Burden to NTNCWSs. 
• 
Sample Tiering based on Premise Plumbing presents undue burden to Public Water Systems. 
 
TCC’s specific comments are included below.  
 
1. EPA should allow Point-of-Use Devices in lieu of LSL replacement for NTNCWS that do not supply water to 
sensitive populations, such as schools or child-care facilities – The Proposed Rule contains Small System Flexibility 
provisions that allow NTNCWSs to leverage Point-of-Use (POU) systems in lieu of the corrosion control treatment 
requirements as described in the Proposed Rule § 141.93.  TCC echoes API and ACC’s appreciation of EPA’s 
inclusion of Small System Flexibility and encourages EPA to consider additional applications for flexibility. TCC 
proposes that EPA allow any NTNCWSs regardless of sizes that do not supply water to sensitive populations (e.g., 
schools or child-care facilities) the option to use POU devices as an alternative to conducting Lead Service Line 
Inventories or Lead Service Line Replacements on the portion of the service line onto which the POU is installed.  
This arrangement would allow NTNCWSs to outfit specific segments of their service lines with POU systems while 
replacing other lines if identified as LSLs. TCC echoes the comments of API and ACC that this additional flexibility 
would further EPA’s objectives of the proposed rule by addressing both service lines and premise plumbing as 
potential lead sources. 
 
The Proposed Rule was issued in the same year as the proposed per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (PFAS NPDWR).  The proposed PFAS NPDWR identified Granular 
Activated Carbon (GAC) and Reverse Osmosis (RO) amongst the possible treatment technologies capable of 
removing PFAS from drinking water.  GAC and RO are also identified and certifiable via NSF / ANSI standards1 for 
the removal of lead from drinking water.  Where a single solution can achieve removal of both PFAS and Lead, 
EPA should allow NTNCWSs the flexibility to use a single solution instead of both removing LSLs and adding 
treatment for PFAS.  
 
Under the Proposed Rule, systems must make annual updates to service line inventories, tracking both changes 
in service lines and connector materials and systems would be required to identify service lines of unknown 
materials.  TCC proposes PWSs that use POU devices be exempt from the requirement to identify the material of 
connectors and unknown service lines.  A resulting LSL inventory would thus identify either the service line 
material or the presence of a POU system.  Expanding flexibility for NTNCWS compliance with the Proposed Rule 
will maintain alignment with EPA’s goals in the Proposed Rule of protection of human health and transparency to 
the NTNCWS water consumers. 
 
2. EPA should add alternative options and sample validation as an option for risk mitigation after disturbances for 
NTNCWSs – EPA is maintaining the Lead and Copper Rule Revision (LCRR) requirement that water systems provide 
pitcher filters or point-of-use devices for six months following partial and full LSL replacement, replacement of a 
lead connector, and other scenarios.  At NTNCWSs that serve at workplace, employers may find it feasible to 
supply employees with bottled water as an alternative to pitcher filters or POU devices.  Some workplace
