environments are staged with water coolers that contain large (e.g., 5 gallon) bottles of water, in which case 
allowing continued use of that water supply would prevent waste of pitcher filters that would not be used. API 
requests that the flexibility to use bottled water be added for NTNCWSs in addition to the options of providing 
pitcher filters or POU devices.   
 
EPA specified a six-month period of time to provide pitcher filters or POU devices on the basis of a 2008 study2, 
which referenced that one site in the study suggested the potential for lead accumulated in the system to be 
released for months following disturbance, while most detected releases in systems took place in the first several 
days following LSL replacement.  The reason why one system was impacted for a lengthy period was not specified 
in the preamble.  The source document summarized elevated lead concentrations following LSL replacement as 
occurring in many cases for the first three days after replacement.  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have the ability 
to control flushing of service lines and premise plumbing within buildings as well as the ability to conduct their 
own sampling following disturbances.   As such, industrial facilities are capable of monitoring taps.  TCC agrees 
with API’s proposal that EPA allow NTNCWSs the option to sample taps after a minimum of 96 hours following a 
disturbance and eliminate the use of mitigations upon receipt of analytical results confirming that lead 
concentrations are below the lead action level.    
 
3. Clear and timely guidance for industrial facility NTNCWSs is requested – EPA has concluded “the overwhelming 
majority of NTNCWSs that do have LSLs and Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRR) service lines are expected 
to have relatively few of these service lines requiring replacement over the proposed 10-year deadline” (88 FR 
84912).  EPA’s position is based upon several assumptions, namely: 
• 
That responses from just 147 NTNCWSs to the 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey 
Assessment3  indicating that lead service lines are rarely used are representative of all 17,418 NTNCWSs 
in the Safe Drinking Water Information System, 
• 
That responses from three states estimating the number of LSLs at NTNCWSs in 20174 are accurate and 
representative across the country, and 
• 
That NTNCWSs have no stand-alone lead connectors and no GRR service lines since NTNCWSs are unlikely 
to replace only the upstream portion of an LSL and leave a galvanized service line in place, because they 
own the entire service, and galvanized lines have a high failure rate given age and disturbance like that 
produced by removing a section of LSL.5  
 
The assumption that few NTNCWSs have lead service lines cannot be confirmed until the October 2024 deadline 
to submit Lead Service Lines inventories.  Furthermore, piping makeup and configuration of NTNCWSs at industrial 
facilities could be influenced by the specific sector in which the piping is used.      
 
Conducting Lead Service Line Inventories is a complex undertaking.  NTNCWSs at industrial sites that attempt to 
leverage guidance documents that are developed for Community Water Systems are left to interpret guidance 
 
2 Sandvig, A., Kwan, P., Kirmeyer, G., Maynard, B., Mast, D., Trussell, R.R., Trussel, S., Cantor, A., and Prescott, A. (2008). Contribution

written for systems that provide water to homes.   EPA Issued "Guidance for Developing and Maintaining a Service 
Line Inventory" in August 2022, and guidance tailored for small CWSs and NTNCWSs was not issued until June of 
2023.  TCC echoes the comments of API and ACC that, although EPA developed guidance tailored for smaller 
systems, the guidance was issued after LSL inventory development was underway.  Accordingly, TCC echoes the  
requests of API and ACC that EPA provide timely and clear guidance for NTNCWS with examples applicable to

that the “human consumption” definition does not list eyewash stations (skin absorbtion) and guidance

4. Clarity to the definition of Service Line is requested – EPA has added a definition of “Service Line” to the Proposed 
Rule, which states “Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe which 
connects the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water 
main to the outlet."  NTNCWSs at industrial facilities have service lines that do not enter buildings and are used 
for purposes other than drinking or cooking.  TCC comments that EPA has the opportunity to add clarity and reduce 
ambiguity by specifying whether outlet in the definition is intended to mean all possible water uses or is specific 
to uses associated with cooking and drinking. 
 
TCC joins API and ACC in requesting that EPA clarify the definition of "Service Line" as follows: “Service line, for 
the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe that connects the water main to the building 
inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water main to an outlet used for cooking or 
drinking."  
 
5. EPA’s assumptions for Cost Burden to NTNCWSs is an underestimate – EPA’s Economic Analysis of the Proposed 
Rule has assumed that NTNCWSs will not incur burdensome  costs to update their inventories since they own their 
own service lines and are not expected to have any unknowns.  This assumption is not accurate.  NTNCWSs at 
industrial facilities that have been developing their inventories have incurred costs to field-identify service lines 
in advance of the October 16, 2024 submission deadline.  Unknown service lines can occur through a variety of 
reasons including age of a facility and loss of drawings. Furthermore, NTNCWSs are unlikely to have customer 
meters, thus unlikely to have water meter readings or replacements as an opportunity to collect service line data.  
Further, EPA has assumed NTNCWSs are able to rely on drawings as a means to identify connectors and service 
line materials of construction; however, due to the age of some facilities, this is not consistently applicable to 
NTNCWSs. TCC proposes PWSs that use POU devices be exempt from the requirement to identify the material of 
connectors and unknown service lines and/or alternative options for connector identification if information is 
difficult to maintain in a system with no lead concerns. 
 
Cost will be a significant challenge in replacing all lead service lines, especially when considered alongside 
competing priorities such as PFAS removal. The average cost to fully replace a single lead service line is estimated 
to be between $6,507 and $8,519 per the Proposed Rule’s Economic Analysis; however, for NTNCWSs at Industrial 
facilities, these costs are likely higher due to line length maintenance and safety practices required within 
industrial facilities and the possibility that piping may run adjacent to or through process units. While the federal 
Bipartisan Infrastructure Act has allocated funding for lead service line replacement, this funding will not be 
available to industrial facilities.  Similarly, the NTNCWSs at commercial facilities are not eligible for other funding 
mechanisms described in Section IV.G of the Proposed Rule’s preamble.  EPA should consider these realities for 
NTNCWSs when considering the additional flexibilities proposed by TCC, API, and ACC.  
 

Comments of TCC on EPA Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations  
for Lead and Copper Improvements

February 5, 2024

6. Sample Tiering based on Premise Plumbing presents undue burden to Public Water Systems – The Proposed 
Rule maintains the tiering structure established by the original Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) and updated by the 
LCRR. In the Proposed Rule, EPA is proposing to adjust the definition for the highest priority tiers (Tier 1 and Tier 
2) to include sites with premise plumbing made of lead.  EPA specifies that by premise, plumbing made of lead, 
EPA means premise plumbing that consists of pure lead pipes, like the pipes used for LSLs, rather than pipes 
made from metal alloys which may contain lead content.  EPA further proposes galvanized premise plumbing to 
be an element of Tier 3. 
 
EPA has not requested that Lead Inventories include premise plumbing material construction.  TCC echoes the 
concern of API and ACC that identifying the premise plumbing material of construction includes additional time 
and cost that EPA has not considered in the Economic Analysis.  TCC joins API and ACC in commenting that EPA 
should not assume that NTNCWSs are likely to have previous knowledge of the premise plumbing present in 
buildings that are in their control.  
 
Conclusion:  
 
TCC appreciates the opportunity to file comments in this letter concerning the Proposed Rule.   EPA has requested 
feedback as to whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the regulatory approach used to 
address lead in drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique rule in section 
1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA. TCC joins API and ACC in proposing that the LCRI could be simplified and burden could be 
reduced without affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects by allowing 
NTNCWSs additional flexibility as described within these comments.

Re:  National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
        Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801  
 
Dear Docket, 
Since 1973, the Rural Community Assistance Partnership (RCAP) Incorporated has helped build capacity 
for and facilitated access to the most basic necessities in rural communities: clean, safe, and affordable 
drinking water and wastewater services. RCAP uses a locally driven approach in every state and territory 
to address various needs in rural and tribal communities, driven by a network of regional non-profit 
partners, who provide hands-on technical assistance under the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) and 
conduct in-person training on a variety of technical and regulatory topics as it relates to safe drinking 
water and sanitary wastewater disposal.  
RCAP appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
(EPA) on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). RCAP commends EPA throughout 
the last two decades for making updates to the regulation, for its focus on developing a better 
understanding of the challenging health effects of lead and copper on human health, and for 
modernizing the rule to match the demands of the 21st Century.  
We believe these improvements are a crucial step forward in safeguarding public health and addressing 
environmental concerns. The proposed enhancements underscore the agency's commitment to 
ensuring the safety of our drinking water by imposing enhanced regulations like reducing the action 
level for lead in drinking water. By focusing on reducing the concentration of this harmful metal in our 
drinking water, EPA aims to protect vulnerable populations, especially children and pregnant women, 
from the adverse health effects associated with lead exposure. The proposed improvements also include 
measures to speed up the replacement of lead pipes and enhance water monitoring and testing 
protocols. The EPA's proactive steps demonstrate a commendable dedication to advancing the well-
being of communities across the nation and fostering a cleaner and healthier environment for 
generations to come. However, RCAP believes that rural water utilities may face unique challenges in 
complying with the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. 
Based upon RCAP’s more than four decades of experience assisting small community drinking water 
systems to comply with SDWA regulations and state drinking water requirements, we offer the following 
recommendations and comments on the new LCRI released in November 2023:  
1. Aging Infrastructure: 

 
 
 
2 
 
• 
Many small rural water systems have outdated infrastructure, including pipes and 
plumbing materials that contribute to lead and copper leaching, making any new 
reduction to the action level difficult to manage or reach. 
2. Limited Financial Resources: 
• 
Small rural communities often struggle with limited finances, which makes it difficult for 
them to invest in the necessary upgrades and improvements needed to reduce lead 
levels in their water systems. Moreover, additional expenses for locating legacy pipes 
and conducting community outreach can further strain their finances. 
3. Lack of Technical Expertise: 
• 
Limited access to specialized technical knowledge and expertise may hinder small rural 
water systems from implementing effective lead reduction strategies. 
4. Inadequate Monitoring and Testing: 
• 
Limited resources may result in insufficient monitoring and testing, leading to delayed 
detection of elevated lead levels and difficulty in addressing the issue promptly once 
detected.  
5. Community Awareness: 
• 
Continued awareness and education in small communities about the risks of lead 
exposure will be required for successful lead reduction efforts. 
6. Geographic Isolation: 
• 
Rural locations may be geographically isolated, leading to challenges in accessing and 
transporting the necessary materials and equipment required for the additional 
suggested lead reduction measures.                                                                  
7. Population Decline: 
• 
Small rural communities may experience population decline, resulting in fewer 
consumers to share the financial burden of necessary improvements for lead reduction. 
8. Limited Regulatory Compliance Resources: 
• 
Smaller water systems may struggle to allocate resources for navigating and complying 
with additional EPA regulations, including National Primary Drinking Water Regulations 
for lead and copper. 
9. Seasonal Variations: 
• 
Seasonal changes, such as temperature fluctuations, can impact water chemistry and 
contribute to variations in lead and copper levels, making consistent mitigation more 
challenging for small water systems with fewer resources. 
10. Inadequate Corrosion Control: 

 
 
 
3 
 
• 
Lack of effective corrosion control measures can exacerbate the leaching of lead and 
copper from pipes and plumbing fixtures. 
11. Insufficient Data Management: 
• 
Small water systems often lack proper data management systems, which makes it 
difficult to track and analyze both legacy pipe and water quality data over time. This 
hinders effective decision-making concerning the prioritization of improvements for 
lead reduction. 
12. Limited Access to Funding Programs: 
• 
Small rural water systems already face challenges in accessing federal and state funding 
programs aimed at assisting with infrastructure improvements for lead reduction. 
Creating a lower action level and new legacy pipe guidelines will make it more 
challenging to compete with larger systems for SRF funds. 
13. Limited Area to contractual resources: 
• 
Small water systems in rural areas struggle to find contractors to develop infrastructure 
projects, due to the scope of the work and the cost of the projects, Across the nation, 
contractors are in high demand with pipeline replacement projects for large systems.  
Small utilities are unable to compete for and attract their services. Locating legacy pipes 
will add to the burden and competition for contractors, which will further increase 
costs. 
RCAP appreciates the opportunity to comment on the important proposed LCRI and we stand ready and 
willing to assist small community drinking water systems to comply with the requirements under the 
improved rule. RCAP and our network partners have the technical capability, training, and resources to 
assist small systems in compliance with this new regulation as well as assistance in the newly required 
development of lead service line (LSL) inventories. 
 
If you have any questions about these comments or would like RCAP to provide additional input on the 
rule improvements, please feel free to email me at omorales-pate@rcap.org or give me a call at (575) 
640-3386.

Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
The Northern Kentucky Water District (NKWD) respectfully submits the enclosed comments to the 
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to assist with evaluating, drafting and finalizing EPA’s Lead 
and Copper Rule Improvements (“LCRI” or “Rule”).   
 
The Lead and Copper Rule is imperative for the protection of public health, which is an important 
priority for the Northern Kentucky Water District.  NKWD supplies water to a population base of 
300,000 people through approximately 86,850 water service accounts, which include residential, 
commercial, industrial, wholesale, and government accounts.  Because portions of the NKWD water 
treatment and distribution system in service today date back to the late 1800s, NKWD is extremely 
challenged with replacing aging infrastructure while simultaneously complying with evolving 
regulations such as the proposed LCRI. 
 
While NKWD appreciates EPA’s efforts in proposing a regulation to reduce lead service lines 
throughout the United States, the proposed regulation does not accurately perceive or appropriately 
address the costs and impacts that such a regulation would create on water systems like NKWD.  
NKWD offers the following high-level concerns that are supported by our detailed comments that 
follow thereafter:  
 
I. 
Replacement is Technically and Financially Infeasible within the Ten-Year Replacement 
Timeframe without Significant Resources 
 
NKWD is concerned that because a mere handful of utilities have been able to complete lead service 
line replacement in a short window with the substantial support of significant technical and financial 
resources, that ALL utilities are expected to do the same within ten years—albeit without the same 
support, while also attempting to keep water rates “fair, just and reasonable” as required by Kentucky 
law.  This logic is similar to that of believing any team of United States NBA basketball players will 
win the Olympics just because the United States Men’s Basketball Dream Team with NBA players 
won the Olympics in 1992.  If the proposed Rule is promulgated as presently drafted, NKWD and 
similarly-situated water systems will be forced to overcome near insurmountable barriers that the 
 

Page 2 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
handful of example water systems did not face—and far more than what the 1992 Dream Team of 
Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan, and Larry Bird could have ever overcome. 
 
II. 
Unforeseen Costs and Needs are Insufficiently Considered 
 
The expected costs considered by EPA do not take into consideration the added costs for accelerating a 
service line replacement program faster than what can be accomplished by coordinating the work with water 
main replacement, not to mention the competition for resources needed to support the LCRI.   For 
example, a service line replacement may involve greater restoration than a small pavement patch repair.  In 
our service area, the roads are maintained by either one of the 33 cities, one of the 3 counties, or the State, 
and repair will require substantially larger areas of the road to be restored by milling and paving.  This 
requirement is not within our control and will significantly increase the cost to replace service lines.  Further, 
in the lead replacement cost analysis, EPA eliminated the top 25% of the surveyed costs and those higher 
costs represent real costs many utilities like NKWD will face.  
   
NKWD is in a region where a significant amount of the nation’s lead service lines are located, which 
means there will be substantial competition regionally for contractors, materials, and other resources 
in an effort to comply with the proposed regulation.  NKWD is very concerned with creating both a 
scarcity of available resources as well as driving up the costs of the resources that are available.  As a 
result, NKWD strongly suggest revisions to the proposed Rule that will make the limited resources 
available first to those most in need, meaning those consumers and water systems having the highest 
lead tap sampling results and highest socioeconomic indicators such as disadvantaged communities, 
followed later by those systems having lower lead tap sampling levels. 
 
III. 
Funding is Grossly Inadequate and at Risk 
 
While NKWD recognizes that historic funding is being provided under the Bipartisan Infrastructure 
Law (BIL), NKWD suggests substantially more federal funding be provided to cover the cost of 
service line replacement throughout the country.  As a special purpose governmental entity, NKWD 
is a water-only stand-alone utility that does not have access to revenue sources other than water rates.  
Spending on service line removal will be directly reflected in customer water bills.  In the absence of 
funding for these programs through grants or other sources, NKWD will be forced to pass the cost 
of service line replacements to our customers.  Funding service line replacements through grants will 
have the immediate benefit of removing the lead line from service, and it will keep customers, 
particularly in disadvantaged communities, from facing higher bills for their water.   
 
NKWD also strongly urges EPA to evaluate and ensure that a critical source of funding for water 
systems—governmental bonds—is financially viable and available for LCRI projects.  It is our opinion 
that the Economic Analysis (“EA”) (found at https://www.regulations.gov/document/EPA-HQ-
OW-2022-0801-0712) fails to consider the implications of requiring public water systems, many of 
which are governmental entities like NKWD, to potentially use public funds to replace and repair 
privately-owned service lines.  
 
While EPA has stated that certain funding is available to assist water systems to implement the 
LCRI—such as funding sources through the BIL—the EA did not include an adequate analysis of the 
funding sources available to public water systems to fund these replacements and repairs.  As EPA is 
aware, some funding may come from the BIL, but the BIL does not have enough funding available to 

Page 3 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
pay for all required service line replacements contemplated by this proposed Rule.  This leads public 
water systems like NKWD to raise water rates and/or be left to obtain other sources of funding such 
as drinking water state revolving funds (SRFs) and governmental bonds (or tax-exempt bonds).  Just 
like BIL funding, SRFs do not have the necessary funding to pay for all lead service line replacements 
leaving many public water systems to rely on funding through the issuance of governmental bonds.  
For example, NKWD’s 2024 Capital Improvement Fund (CIP) Plan identifies 66 separate capital 
projects.  Of these 66 projects, 63 are being funded through the issuance of governmental bonds.  
 
Like NKWD, many water systems owned, operated, or funded through governmental units rely 
heavily on governmental bonds to fund various infrastructure projects and often receive special 
funding terms because of tax-exempt status.  As a result, these bonds have lower-interest rates 
compared to bonds that are not tax-exempt. This is critical to sustain the financial viability of public 
water systems, which as mentioned above, are already financially overburdened because of aging 
infrastructure, increased regulatory obligations, and rising costs.  
 
The use of governmental bonds, however, is notably subject to various private use restrictions.  Thus, 
governmental bonds may become “private activity bonds” and public water systems could 
potentially lose their tax-exempt status if more than 10% of bond proceeds (1) are used for a 
private use, and (2) are directly or indirectly derived from payments in respect of the property, or 
borrowed money, used for a private use. See 26 U.S.C. Section 141.1  Because the governmental bond 
proceeds could possibly be used to replace private property (potentially satisfying the first threshold) 
and the private property itself remits payments to the public water system (potentially satisfying the 
second threshold), the use of governmental bonds by public water systems is potentially at risk.2  The 
proposed Rule unfortunately fails to discuss or account for this nearly universal circumstance at play 
for many public water systems like NKWD.  This is on top of state-specific limitations which restrict 
replacement of private service lines by water systems (discussed further below). 
 
In summary, NKWD acknowledges and supports EPA’s overall objective that water systems make 
regular progress towards lead service line replacement in a method that promotes public health but as 
outlined above and more herein, doing this work in a ten-year timeframe will be exceptionally 
challenging.  To this effort, NKWD makes the following comments below using the outline from 
EPA’s request for comments: 
 
General Matters  
 
1. Whether the proposed revisions to the LCRR treatment technique are effective to prevent known 
or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible in accordance with the SDWA. 
  
Response:  No Comment.

2. Whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the regulatory approach 
used to address lead in drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique 
rule in section 1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA. Specifically, EPA requests comment on ways that the 
proposed LCRI could be simplified and ways that burden, including paperwork burden, could be 
reduced without affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects.  
 
Response:  NKWD has several suggestions for reducing the burden water systems as 
outlined in the following paragraphs: 
 
First, NKWD suggests that lines used solely for the purposes of providing fire 
protection in a building (or other non-potable uses) not be included in the inventory.  
If not removed from the inventory, NKWD has approximately 650 fire protection lines 
that will need to be investigated and included.  Fire lines are typically larger than 2 
inches, which are not made of lead, so NKWD does not expect any lines used for fire 
protection systems to be made of lead or galvanized requiring replacement.  Removing 
this requirement would reduce the burden NKWD faces in complying with the 
proposed regulation.  In the unlikely event a fire line is discovered to be made of lead 
or galvanized requiring replacement, it would be reasonable to have provisions in 
place to prohibit it from ever being used to supply potable water to the building.  
NKWD suggests that this would be a proper interpretation under the Safe Water 
Drinking Act as the Act’s definitions contemplate regulating only water that is used 
for human consumption.     
 
Second, NKWD suggests documenting all previously replaced lead service lines and 
connectors not be required as these past records are not readily available and unduly 
burdensome particularly for systems that date back to the 1800s like NKWD. 
 
Third, NKWD, like other water systems, has accounts served by a “master meter” 
where after the master meter, the service line divides and segments to provide service 
to multiple facilities or spaces (e.g., trailer parks, shopping centers, wholesale water 
purchasers) or instances where a service only covers a sprinkler system or other type 
private piping system. NKWD suggests that for these illustrated instances, water 
systems only count the service line up to the master meter and not the privately owned 
water distribution or piping network.  This would align with the proposed Rule’s 
definition for service line which contemplates in its plain language a single line to the 
building inlet.   
 
Fourth, NKWD suggests simplifying public education and notification requirements 
to reduce the burden on water systems and to prevent consumers from becoming 
desensitized to repeated notices. EPA should consider creating optional 
communication templates for both mail and telephone that can be used by water 
systems when attempting to contact consumers who are affected by the LCRI 
replacement requirements. 
 
3.  Whether the proposed requirements of the rule are enforceable and promote compliance without 
the need for State or Federal enforcement action. EPA also solicits comment on ways the rule could 
be modified to better promote compliance.  

Page 5 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
 
Response:  NKWD does not believe the proposed Rule promotes compliance due to the 
aggressive deadlines and high implementation costs (see response under question 4 to the 
Service Line Replacement section below for additional information).  In short, NKWD 
does not believe the 10-year requirement alone can be met,  particularly when  the other 
expansive requirements of the proposed Rule are added.  NKWD believes extending the 
timeframes for service line replacement using one or more of the following methods would 
promote better compliance:   
 
(1) develop a phased approach based on tap sampling results; or 
 
(2) create another option for deferred replacement taking affordability into account 
such as coordination with water main replacement and asset management plans. 
 
These options would support improving public health while taking advantage of the 
opportunity for lower implementation and compliance costs, as well as addressing 
dramatically varied levels of technical and financial resources by water systems across the 
country.   
 
4. The revised definition of “connector,” including that connectors are defined as “not exceeding two 
feet.”  
 
Response:  No Comment. 
 
Service Line Replacement  
 
1. All aspects of the proposed scope of the replacement requirements, including the criteria used to 
define a full service line replacement (e.g., cutting the pipe at abandoned properties, replacing the 
entire service line) and which lead sources are subject to replacement under the mandatory program. 
EPA is seeking comment on whether to prohibit reconnection of any disconnected LSL or GRR 
service line. EPA is requesting comment on whether the Agency should include lead connectors or 
galvanized service lines that are or were downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory 
replacement.  
 
Response:  NKWD suggests that the replacement pool or replacement rate calculation 
account for the number of property owners who have failed to provide consent as the 
proposed Rule clearly indicated the water system is not required to replace any portion 
of the service line that is not in their “control.” As currently written, water systems who 
require property owner consent will be in non-compliance with the replacement rate 
and three-year rolling average simply due to property owner’s decision to refuse  
service line replacement.  As outlined in the proposed Rule, after four unsuccessful 
attempts to obtain consent, the water system should be deemed to be in full 
compliance of the LCRI.  Furthermore, NKWD suggests the proposed regulation be 
revised to remove unknowns from the replacement pool until the point the unknown 
becomes known lead, galvanized requiring replacement, or not lead.  While EPA has 
given water systems time to identify unknowns, counting unknowns to the 

Page 6 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
replacement pool eviscerates that allowance under the proposed regulation resulting 
in overburdening of the water systems.        
 
NKWD requests that the regulation clarify that systems have more than 45 days to 
replace a property owner-initiated replacement when additional time has been 
approved by the State.  This will allow water systems to comply when unique 
circumstances arise that make it infeasible to timely complete the work (i.e., extreme 
weather conditions, material availability).   
 
NKWD also suggests that water systems only be required to offer a pitcher filter or 
point-of-use device instead of mandatory distribution of these devices when:  service 
lines are partially or fully replaced; an action level is exceeded multiple times; or when 
a disturbance occurs.  This will improve the availability of these items for those that 
are most in need and will reduce the cost to the water system (and its rate payers) by 
not giving them to people who will not use them for various reasons (such as the 
particular consumer is already using an adequate water filtering device).  It is further 
recommended that EPA and the States provide a path for water system compliance in 
the event supply chain issues arise for these devices. 
 
2. Whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should be more than four times (e.g., 
five, six, or seven times).  
 
Response:  NKWD has several concerns regarding the reasonable effort to obtain 
consent: 
 
First, NKWD fears repeated communications could desensitize consumers to 
communications from the water system and cause consumers to ignore other 
communications such as boil water advisories and other priority service alerts.  Any 
more than four attempts will increase the chance for consumer indifference regarding 
our important notices.  Keeping the number at four attempts also avoids placing 
additional burden on limited water system resources.  Further, NKWD has not seen 
any information to believe that additional communications will yield substantially 
better results. 
 
Second, NKWD suggests that the requirement to offer full lead service line 
replacement to a new property owner within 6 months of change in ownership be 
modified to state “account holder” as water systems do not have a way of tracking 
changes in real property ownership.  NKWD only maintains accounts for the consumer 
procuring and using water service.  The account holder may change while the property 
owner does not (i.e., new tenant renting owner’s property) and in other situations the 
property owner may change (which NKWD would not be aware of) and the account 
holder does not (i.e., same tenant but change in property ownership).  Offering a lead 
service line replacement to each new “account holder" would reengage the process as 
envisioned by EPA without overburdening the individual water systems for 
information outside their control. 
 

Page 7 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
Third, NKWD suggests revising the “reasonable effort” requirement of two different 
methods of communication when reasonably feasible and allow for only one method 
of communication in situations approved by the States.  For instance, in many cases 
NKWD can only ascertain property ownership information from the County Clerk’s 
recorded deeds.  In those deeds, typically the only indicia of the property owner’s 
contact information is the address listed for mailings of tax bills.  When the property 
owner does not occupy the property (and thus is not an account holder), any effort to 
contact the property owner through a mailing to the listed address will not be readily 
available or successful.     
 
Fourth, NKWD is concerned about the safety of its employees or contractors and does 
not support requirements that would necessitate accessing the property to conduct 
work when consent from the property owner and occupant is not obtained.  
 
Fifth, NKWD suggests that EPA provide communication templates if a water system 
is attempting to obtain consent from a property owner. These templates should 
include two forms—one for written communication via mail and one for 
communication via telephone with the last known telephone number of the property 
owner.          
 
3. Whether the proposed LCRI appropriately interprets “control” for the purposes of the mandatory 
replacement provision (i.e., require systems to conduct full service line replacement in situations where 
the system has access to conduct the full replacement).  
 
Response:  NKWD has concerns that the proposed Rule’s requirement for control of 
private service lines extends the Agency’s reach beyond the lawful grasp under the Safe 
Drinking Water Act.  See West Virginia v. EPA, 142 S. Ct. 2587, 2609 (explaining agency 
must have ‘clear congressional authorization’ for the power it claims).  42 USCS § 300f 
(4) states that a public water system “means a system for the provision to the public of 
water for human consumption through pipes or other constructed conveyances, if such 
system has at least fifteen service connections or regularly serves at least twenty-five 
individuals.”  The Safe Drinking Water Act’s plain language definition clearly 
envisions an endpoint of the public water system at the connection point with the 
consumer.  Additionally, possession of the water itself also leaves NKWD’s ownership 
and is transferred to the customer at the point of sale which is at the point where water 
passes the meter as NKWD charges for all such water, regardless of whether it is used 
for its intended purpose (or lost due to negligence or mechanical failure). 
 
While that end point may vary between water systems, ownership of either the water 
or piping is unequivocally the logical point of connection to an water system owned 
portion of public water system under the SDWA definition. Any attempt to exert 
regulatory obligations beyond the plain reading of the Safe Drinking Water Act (and 
in contradiction of the statutory definition) puts the proposed LCRI in precarious legal 
standing.

whether it is feasible for systems across the nation to complete service line replacement in a shorter

options for completing the work, such as coordinating with planned improvements or 
conducting stand-alone service line replacement, and we have serious concerns with 
any approach.

water utilities.  The AWWA report indicates utilities spend nearly 70% to 100% more to

NKWD believes EPA’s approximately 20% difference underestimates the restoration cost 
NKWD will endure due to city ordinances in NKWD’s service area that require us to mill 
and pave the road following placement of the temporary patch.3  Because of the historic 
areas NKWD serves and the cost for extensive restoration requirements that will be borne 
by our water system, NKWD anticipates conducting service line replacement without 
water main replacement will increase the total project costs by approximately 75%.  This 
cost increase is within reason based on the information reported by other water systems 
with similar restoration requirements as referenced in AWWA’s report.  NKWD will still 
have to replace the water main at a later time and pay to mill and pave the road again.  In 
summary, the inevitable total cost to NKWD’s customers will be substantially more if lead 
service line replacement is not performed with water main replacement.

plumbing systems.  If enacted, the proposed Rule’s explanation of “substantial 
funding available” is simply illusory to NKWD as it will only provide a token portion 
of the total funding required to comply with the proposed Rule.  To alleviate these 
concerns, NKWD requests another deferment option be given so that additional time 
beyond 10 years can be granted by EPA or States that takes affordability and other

Second, while some water systems have conducted replacement of a substantial 
number of lines in a short period, this was done under different conditions than what 
EPA is mandating with the proposed LCRI.  Foremost, not every water system was 
trying to do the same work at the same time, which will undoubtedly raise prices 
because of the high demand nationally but may also create major limitations in the 
availability of supply to do the work.  Another potential unintended outcome under the 
proposed Rule is that water systems like NKWD will be faced with making hard 
decisions on which capital improvement projects to do and which ones to defer or 
scale back.  The projects that may be deferred or downsized are undoubtedly needed, 
whether it be for maintaining system reliability or for complying with various 
standards under the Safe Drinking Water Act. 
 
5. EPA is taking comment on whether States, as a condition of primacy, or EPA when it is directly 
implementing the program, should be required to set initial shortened deadlines by a certain timeframe, 
such as no later than 60 days after the compliance date.  
 

Page 11 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
Response:  NKWD does not believe setting a shortened deadline for service line 
replacement is even remotely feasible for our utility.  Due to concerns stated herein 
regarding resource availability and cost for implementation, it is recommended that 
neither the State nor EPA require shorter deadlines for any water system. 
 
6. The overall approach and basis to offer deferred service line replacement to systems with a high 
proportion of LSLs and GRR service lines in their distribution system relative to their total number 
of households served. EPA is requesting comment on its proposed threshold of 0.039 average annual 
number of replacements per household served, which is used to calculate the number of years that 
systems can defer.  
Response:  NKWD requests either the 0.039 number be reduced substantially or 
another option for a deferred replacement be considered. Specifically, a deferred 
replacement option that would allow systems to replace service lines at a rate that takes 
affordability and the potential added costs for not completing service line replacement 
with water main replacement into consideration. 
NKWD agrees with EPA’s statement that systems should conduct service line replacement 
in coordination with planned work to realize the efficiencies that can be gained.  However, 
requiring replacing all service lines within 10 years will not allow water systems such as 
NKWD to take real advantage of these efficiencies.  It will cost more to complete the work 
for service line replacement and water main replacement if done as two separate projects 
instead of one.  In addition, replacing service lines in an area and then returning later to 
replace the water main will significantly increase the total cost of infrastructure 
replacement by having to restore the pavement twice instead of once.   
 
7.  Whether to require the State, as a condition of primacy, to approve the use of the deferred deadline 
provision where the water system qualifies for it and/or whether to require the State, as a condition 
of primacy, to assess whether it would be feasible for a system to meet the 10-year deadline or a shorter 
deadline even if the system meets the regulatory criteria for the deferred deadline.  
 
Response:  No Comment. 
 
8. Whether there are additional data on service line replacement rates achieved by systems in proactive 
programs (i.e., excluding programs that only replace service lines in coordination with main 
replacement or emergency repair).  
 
Response:  No Comment. 
 
9. The proposed use of a maximum threshold of 10,000 annual service line replacements for systems 
with atypically high numbers of LSLs and GRR service lines as well as seeking comment on the 
alternate threshold of 8,000 annual service line replacements. EPA is also seeking feedback on other 
thresholds and supporting data. EPA is also seeking feedback on if there’s data available that would 
inform if the maximum threshold for annual service line replacement could increase after ten years, 
such as if replacement rates could double.  
 

Page 12 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
Response:  While 8,000 annual service line replacements is more reasonable than 
10,000, NKWD suggests the number should be substantially lower as both numbers 
are unreasonable, arbitrary and capricious.  NKWD recommends giving primacy 
States flexibility in working with water systems to develop service line replacement 
plans that consider factors that are specific to the water system. 
 
10. Whether systems conducting deferred service line replacement should be subject to any additional 
requirements beyond those for systems that are not replacing service lines in accordance with a 
deferred deadline.  
 
Response:  NKWD suggests that additional requirements not be placed on systems 
with deferred service line replacements as these systems will already be heavily 
burdened by the volume of work required.  Placing additional requirements on 
deferred programs could impede the goal of replacing service lines as quickly as 
possible. 
 
11. The requirement for systems to install a dielectric coupling when conducting a partial replacement 
of an LSL or GRR to separate the remaining LSL or GRR service line and the replaced service line 
unless the replaced service line is made of plastic and other recommended risk mitigation activities.  
 
Response:  NKWD uses dielectric coupling when conducting a partial replacement.  
NKWD suggests that EPA label dielectric coupling as a best practice in additional 
guidance it will surely make available after a final rule is promulgated.   
 
12.  The proposed requirement to ban partial lead and GRR service line replacement unless it is 
conducted in accordance with emergency or planned infrastructure work (excluding planned 
infrastructure work solely for the purposes of replacing lead and GRR service lines as part of a service 
line replacement program). Additionally, EPA is seeking comment on whether partial service line 
replacement should be prohibited during “planned infrastructure work” or with certain types of 
planned infrastructure work.  
 
Response:  NKWD will need the ability to repair or replace portions of the utility-
owned service line under emergency work to avoid a customer being without water for 
an extended period of time.  Banning partial replacements in these circumstances 
would mean the line would be out of service until a licensed plumber is able to perform 
the replacement work on the customer-owned service line.  For planned infrastructure 
work, NKWD has 268 miles of unlined cast iron water main that are over 60 years old, 
and logically these mains would have a majority of the system’s lead service lines 
connected.  With approximately 20 percent of NKWD’s total 1,300 miles of water main 
being cast iron that are already past or nearing the end of its expected service life, 
NKWD needs to continue to replace unlined cast iron mains.  Our water main 
replacement program helps to reduce non-revenue water and service disruptions 
caused by failures.  With a ban on partial replacements, refusal by any affected property 
owners to replace the portion of the service line owned by respective property owner 
could halt the entire water main replacement project.  Therefore, NKWD suggests not 
prohibiting partial service line replacements during planned infrastructure work or 

Page 13 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
emergency work as this practice will severely inhibit the replacement of aging 
infrastructure and repair of failing service lines.   
 
13. The ability of the market to correct for potential shortages in workers and materials to conduct 
service line replacement, as well to provide sufficient quantities of filters to comply with the service 
line replacement and other relevant provisions in the proposal.  
 
Response:  NKWD continues to see longer lead times post the COVID-19 Pandemic 
and as such, has concerns that the market will not be able to correct in a sufficient and 
timely manner to meet the requirements outlined in this proposed Rule, particularly 
when competing for resources with water systems regionally and nationally.  Of 
particular concern for NKWD will be the ability to get licensed  plumbers to complete 
the work as required by Kentucky Revised Statute 318.030.  Unlike Newark, New 
Jersey, who hired workers off the street and trained them to conduct service line 
replacements, Kentucky requires work on private property to be completed by a 
licensed Master Plumber.  Please note, pursuant to the Kentucky Department of 
Housing, Buildings and Construction, Division of Plumbing regulations it takes a 
minimum of four years’ experience and passing of two separate examinations to obtain 
a Master Plumber License in Kentucky. 
 
Furthermore, it appears EPA believes that the market will correct for any potential 
worker shortage.  While in the past, this may have been the case and a reasonable 
expectation, it is simply not the case in our region and a trend that appears to be 
growing nationally.  In Northern Kentucky, the Area Development District reports that 
our region currently has two (2) jobs for every one working age person available.  
Similarly at the national level, a similar labor concern has arisen as depicted in the 
report titled The Demographic Drought which is available at: https://www.datocms-
assets.com/62658/1663085587-demographic-drought-v18.pdf.  While our workforce 
limitation concerns may vary from other regions, it is a distinction which the Agency 
should consider and account for in its rule making.     
 
14. The extent to which property owner consent, if required by State or local law or water tariff 
agreement, might complicate full service line replacement and whether there are additional measures 
EPA can take to facilitate access through the LCRI.  
 
Response:  In Kentucky, NKWD does not have the legal authority to replace private 
service lines. Kentucky Administrative Regulation, 807 KAR 5:066 Section 12 lays 
ownership of service lines past the meter and meter box with the customer.  NKWD’s 
meters are located in the right-of-way (or are ordered by the Kentucky Public Service 
Commission to be relocated from an inside location to an outside location within the 
next 15 years).  After the point where NKWD’s ownership ends, NKWD, as a special 
purpose governmental entity whose statutory purpose under Kentucky Revised Statute 
74.012 is limited to furnishing public water supply, is prohibited from seizing 
ownership of the service line beyond that point in accordance with Kentucky 
Constitution Sections 10, 13 and 242. 
 

Page 14 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
Furthermore, legally funding full service line replacement, particularly private lead 
service lines, will be problematic in part due to the limitations of NKWD’s statutory 
authority as a special purpose governmental entity to only furnish the “public water 
supply.”  Additionally private service line replacement is further limited as the 
Kentucky statutory scheme limits NKWD’s ability through the Public Service 
Commission to recover rates for such expenditures.  Specifically, Kentucky Revised 
Statute 278.030 requires rates to be “fair, just and reasonable” and Kentucky Revised 
Statute 278.170 requires that rates not create any unreasonable preference or advantage 
or subject any to unreasonable prejudice or disadvantage.   
 
As mentioned above, the use of governmental bonds would likely be at risk as well.  
NKWD suggests that EPA assistance in the form of grants is the best funding source 
for NKWD and other similarly-situated water systems to minimize or clear the legal 
hurdles outlined herein and reach maximum lead service line replacement levels.

Corrosion Control Treatment  
 
1. The proposed determination that the CCT treatment technique is feasible and prevents known or 
anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible. 
 
Response:  NKWD agrees with EPA’s determination that CCT is feasible, affordable and 
prevents known or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible, but NKWD 
suggests other methods beyond those listed for CCT that may be available now or in the 
future should be considered.  NKWD is also aware that CCT, particularly the addition of 
phosphate-based corrosion inhibitors, can impact some consumers.  These consumers 
may be faced with installing, operating, and maintaining systems to treat the water to 
remove phosphorus so that it is suitable for their uses.  These consumer-borne costs were 
not considered in the economic analysis. 
 
2. Comment on whether it would be more appropriate to require water systems to re-optimize again 
following an action level exceedance regardless of meeting their optimal water quality parameters and to 
provide the State with the authority to waive this requirement. 

Page 17 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
 
Response:  If no changes to source water or treatment have been made and water systems 
are meeting their optimal water quality parameters, requiring a system to re-optimize again 
seems like an unnecessary burden and should be avoided.  NKWD supports the States 
having the authority to waive re-optimization again following an action level exceedance 
but suggests that the EPA provide additional guidance for States regarding the factors to 
consider when determining if re-optimization would be necessary. Also, if a utility has 
already done a CCT study similar to that required in the LCRI but prior to the LCRI the 
utility should not have to do another CCT if conditions have not changed.  
 
3. The proposed option for a water system to delay OCCT until after the system has replaced all of its LSLs 
and GRR service lines, while the system achieves at least 20 percent removal per year and must have no 
LSLs, GRR service lines, or lead status unknown service lines remaining at the end of the five-year period. 
 
Response: NKWD agrees with giving water systems an option to delay OCCT until after 
the system removes all of its LSLs and GRRs, and unknowns are determined to the extent 
considered practical and reasonable by the State or EPA. 
 
4. The treatment recommendation and CCT study process can take multiple years to complete. For systems 
with existing corrosion control, the system may be able to alter the existing treatment (e.g., increase pH 
and/or orthophosphate dose) without a new CCT study on a much faster timeframe rather than waiting 
for study results that may recommend that same change. EPA is requesting comment on whether there are 
situations and/or conditions where existing treatment modifications may achieve similar lead reductions 
rather than delaying new treatment for two and a-half years while a study is underway. 
 
Response: NKWD agrees that there are situations for water systems with existing corrosion 
control in which altering existing treatment may provide quicker lead reduction than the 
extra time a new CCT study would require.  NKWD recommends this be within the State’s 
authority to consider and approve.

Response: NKWD recommends removing the requirement for water systems to deliver 
educational materials to organizations such as pediatricians, obstetricians-
gynecologist and midwives, WIC and Head Start programs, etc. and that notice to the 
local Health Department along with direct notice to customers (account holders) be

3. Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination that water systems are capable of 
providing consumer notices of individual tap sampling results within three calendar days of obtaining 
those results, regardless of whether the results exceed the lead or copper action level, or if a longer 
time frame is needed (e.g., three business days, seven calendar days, 14 calendar days).  
 
Response:  While NKWD attempts to notify as soon as practical, NKWD recommends 
that notification be required within seven (7) calendar days of obtaining the results.  
This will ensure water systems will be able to comply, particularly when an influx of 
many test requests come in simultaneously and reduce the possibility of water systems 
receiving violations and associated administrative burden. Under the proposed Rule’s 
three (3) calendar days, holidays and other situations could easily result in a violation.   
 
4. Whether the proposed requirement for water systems to offer lead sampling to consumers with 
LSLs, GRR service lines, or unknown service lines in the notice of service line material is effective at 
reducing adverse health effects. EPA is also requesting comment on the requirement for water systems 
to deliver consumer-initiated test results within three days of obtaining those results.  
 
Response:  NKWD also suggest notification of individual consumer-initiated tap 
sampling results within seven (7) calendar days of obtaining the results for the reasons 
stated above in our response to question number 3 and to keep notification of results 
on the same timeline.  Having multiple notification deadlines for different types of 
samples would simply be confusing and add to the administrative burden. 
 
5. Whether the types and timing of outreach activities proposed for systems failing to meet the 
mandatory service line replacement rate are appropriate and whether other activities should be 
considered.

Lead Sampling in Schools and Child Care Facilities  
 
EPA is seeking comment on all aspects of the proposed lead sampling in schools and child care 
facilities requirements, and specifically:  
 
1. Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or to sample more frequently in 
schools and child care facilities.  
 

Page 22 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
Response:  While NKWD supports testing for lead in schools and child care facilities, 
NKWD suggests the best strategy to address lead in schools and child care facilities is 
through a holistic program implemented through the Department of Education, 
Health and Human Services, and EPA in collaboration with relevant state agencies.  
Water systems should be encouraged to assist schools and child care facilities in 
reducing lead exposure from drinking water, but not be required to conduct 
mandatory testing of these public and private facilities.  NKWD has concerns that such 
requirements step beyond NKWD’s legal authority as a special purpose governmental 
entity whose statutory purpose under Kentucky Revised Statute 74.012 is limited to 
furnishing public water supply.  Such requirements, if complied with by NKWD under 
certain circumstances may be in violation of NKWD’s limited authority and further 
considered a violation of Kentucky Constitution Sections 10, 13 and 242.    
 
Additionally, NKWD would also suggest some refinement to further minimize or 
mitigate the scope and extent of sampling.  For instance, NKWD has approximately 
86,850 water service accounts in Northern Kentucky and provides services to 175 
daycares, 69 elementary schools, 36 middle and high schools which are part of 11 
different public-school districts and multiple private schools (including 38 schools that 
are part of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Covington system).  The coordination and 
staffing that would be required, not only of NKWD but each independent school and 
school system would be substantial. 
  
2.  The proposed provision to allow States to issue waivers to community water systems from the 
requirement for lead sampling in schools and child care facilities during the five-year period after the 
LCRI compliance date if the facility was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021 but prior to the LCRI 
compliance date and the sampling otherwise meets the waiver requirements of § 141.92(h).  
 
Response:  The waiver construct is problematic as an “all or nothing” approach.  In 
lieu of or in addition to the waiver, NKWD suggests allowing sampling data from 
individual schools and child care facilities that were tested in accordance with the 
sampling requirements.  NKWD supports allowing sampling data collected from 
schools and child care facilities after January 1, 2021 but prior to LCRI compliance date 
to be eligible for submittal under the LCRI.  NKWD also suggests allowing the 
submission of earlier data going back to January 1, 2014 to coincide with the Lead 
Reduction in Drinking Water Act.  Repeating testing that has already been completed 
is not a sensible use of limited resources. 
 
3. Whether or not to allow States to waive the requirements of § 141.92 for CWSs in schools and child 
care facilities that use and maintain filters certified to reduce lead, and if so, whether the waiver should 
only be allowed where schools and child care facilities are required by State or local law to install POU 
devices and maintain them.  
 
Response:  No comment. 
 
4. The minimum requirements for States to provide a waiver (e.g., should the waiver be limited to 
locations where the filter use is required by State or local law; should the waiver be limited to locations 
where State or local law requires periodic sampling or testing to ensure proper filter use).  

Page 23 of 25 
 
February 2, 2024 
 
 
Response:  No comment. 
 
5. Whether EPA should require CWSs to make school and child care facility sampling results publicly 
available, and if so, how frequently and in what manner.  
 
Response:  NKWD suggests the school and child care facility sample results be made 
publicly available by the administrators of the school or child care facility.  Requiring 
water systems to conduct these efforts could place a large burden on the water system 
to manage the communication of the results, and water systems would not be in a 
position to communicate follow-up actions being taken by the school and child care 
facilities.  In addition, NKWD suggests notification of testing results to the school 
board and child care facility management be sufficient and that notification to each 
individual facility not be required.  Again, NKWD suggests the best strategy to address 
lead in schools and child care facilities is through a holistic program implemented 
through the Department of Education, Health and Human Services, and EPA in 
collaboration with relevant state agencies.

RE: Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Dear Sir or Madame:
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).  
The Washington Association of Sewer and Water Districts (WASWD) represents more than 180 
public water and sewer districts throughout the state, serving nearly 20% of our state’s 
population. WASWD members provide these cost-effective essential public services in the 
state’s largest population centers and in the smallest rural communities. Safe drinking water is 
a major concern to both our membership and the customers they serve.  We support strong 
protections for drinking water from the source to the tap that are furthered with the LCRI. We do 
have some concerns, however, with the proposed LCRI.
Frequency of lead service line (LSL) inventories: Annual updates are impractical as they are 
required too frequently. Particularly in areas of the country where lead service lines were 
infrequently utilized, conducting LSL inventories at this frequency would take up valuable time 
and resources that could be used for other public health issues such as PFAS.  For smaller 
utilities with few staff the frequency of the inventories is especially a real burden.  A longer time 
frame for updating inventories is warranted for these reasons.
Timeframe for compliance: Optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT) is working well in 
many jurisdictions where LSLs are present.  These systems should have extended time frames 
for replacement of LSLs since they have already taken action and made capital investments to 
control lead and copper in their water systems.  Health and safety is not at issue in these 
systems as it is in those with no OCCT, so allowing them to spread out the time and money 
needed to replace LSLs makes economic sense. 
Private service line obligations: In Exhibit 1 on page 84886 of the Register, it summarizes:
“Systems conducting partial service line replacement must offer to replace the remaining 
portion of the service line not under their control (within 45 days in emergencies)”
In some states, such as Washington, this is not legal.  Public funds cannot be spent on private 
property.  Public utilities are able to do work on private property and charge costs to the owner.  
For example, some utilities have done initial line installation and extended repayment over a 
number of years via utility billing.  However, state law does not allow the utility to force the 
owner to replace the line, or even to enter onto the property without the owner’s consent unless 

Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Page 2 of 2
900 SW 16th Street, Suite 305, Renton, Washington 98057   ▪   206.246.1299   ▪   800.244.0124   ▪   FAX: 206.246.1323   ▪   staff@waswd.org  ▪   www.waswd.org
it is recorded on the original site plans, which it would not be with older development that is 
most likely to have LSLs. This poses a significant obstacle to compliance with this provision.
Education Requirements: Required public education and its timing need to be simplified and 
scalable for different sizes of utilities.  These programs should be developed by a central 
agency, such as a state health authority, who is aware of the needs of local utilities.  It is too 
much to expect small utilities to do this on their own when they have few staff.
Funding: Funding for inventories and replacements will always be an issue. The financial 
pressures for meeting these requirements at the same time as working to meet other regulatory 
requirements are high, particularly on smaller utilities. Without ongoing federal funding, 
customers will experience rising utility rates that will be unaffordable to some, and potentially 
jeopardizing secure housing in some communities.
We appreciate the efforts of EPA in ensuring safe drinking water for all Americans.

Dear Administrator Regan,  
 
Lehigh County Authority (LCA) is a medium-sized water utility serving approximately 
200,000 people in the City of Allentown and 14 suburban municipalities throughout the Lehigh 
Valley region in eastern Pennsylvania. We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s proposed rule, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations 
for Lead and Copper: Improvements (EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801). 
 
In 2021, the EPA finalized the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR), which strengthened the 
regulatory framework initiated by the 1991 Lead and Copper Rule.  LCA supported the revisions 
in light of improved water quality and public awareness of the health impacts of lead.  While the 
LCRR made notable revisions to protecting public health, the revised rule also significantly 
increased capital and operational costs associated with complying with the regulation.  
Unfortunately, the cost of complying will undoubtedly have significant rate impacts to consumers 
across the county.  In December 2023, the EPA proposed the Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI), which further strengthens the LCRR, while also increasing the burden to 
utilities and their ratepayers.  Due to the importance of this rulemaking and significant impacts 
the regulation will have on water utilities and ratepayers, LCA is pleased to submit the following 
comments: 
 
Deadline for Completing Mandatory Service Line Replacements 
The proposed LCRI requires water systems to replace all lead and galvanized requiring replacement 
(GRR) service lines under the control of the water system within 10 years after publication of the LCRI.  

Lehigh County Authority – Public Comments 
Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2 of 5 
 
 
Every drop matters. Every customer counts. 
Accomplishing characterization and replacement within 10 years is extremely aggressive, especially for 
many large water utilities. Cities such as Allentown, PA, who can trace their public water system to the 
late 19th century, contain a disproportionate number of the nation’s lead service lines.  Based on current 
inventory data, LCA estimates approximately 13,000 service lines will need to be replaced within the 10-
year time frame.  Based on the estimated service lines that require replacement, a capital investment of 
approximately $130,000,000 will be required.  While these numbers are large, it is expected to grow even 
higher as we uncover the 16,500 unknown service lines.  When utilities are competing for contractors, 
there will undoubtedly be price escalation and logistical difficulties as water systems across the United 
States will be competing for the same construction resources (e.g. personnel, equipment, materials, etc.). 
EPA has not created a record to demonstrate such resources are available and affordable to water systems.  
Government agencies currently estimates that there are up to 10 million lead service lines in the United 
States1.  The total cost to replace these lines will exceed over $90 billion.  Additionally, the EPA has 
estimated through the 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment that the traditional 
20-year national drinking water infrastructure need is $625 billion2.  While lead service line replacements 
are included within this estimate, the funding needed to support the LCRI and other equally important 
regulations has not been adequate. To support eliminating LSLs, the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs 
Act (IIJA) included $15 billion specifically for lead service line replacement projects and associated 
activities directly connected to the identification of LSLs and planning for the replacement of LSLs.  
Utilities that are not successful in securing grants through programs such as the IIJA, will likely have to 
acquire loans, which are ultimately paid for through increases to customer rates.  This comes at a time 
where customer rates are unaffordable for many.  A recent study has shown that 17% of households spend 
more than one day each month working to pay for water services and sanitation services3.  The EPA must 
ensure funding is available for the sustainability of utilities making efforts to comply with these 
regulations. 
 
The EPA has not provided rationale behind the 10-year requirement.  A select number of examples was 
provided as a means of determining feasibility; however, their success not was not accomplished under 
the same guidelines as the proposed LCRI.  More importantly, none of the programs cited in the preamble 
accomplished the replacement program in 10 years (or anticipated achieving program goals in 10 years)

without substantial outside subsidy when the system had an appreciable number of service lines requiring 
replacement. In other words, the anticipated replacement rate and timeframe is not feasible within the 
fiscal, managerial, and technical capacity of even large systems.  EPA also has not taken into account the 
fact that there is likely to be a shortage of skilled labor to perform these replacements when all systems 
are mandated to replace them on the same timeline. A few examples of systems able to complete the work 
within a 10-year timeframe when they did not have to similarly compete for such labor does not provide a 
record supporting the feasibility of this timeframe. 
 
Replacement Rate Calculation & Inclusion of Unknown Service Lines 
In addition to the challenges associated with the 10-year deadline to replace LSLs and GRRs, the LCRI 
includes a confusing process for calculating the replacement rate due to the inclusion of service lines of 
unknown material into the equation. While utilities will strive to achieve the 10-percent replacement rate 
required to meet the 10-year deadline, this rate will be difficult to achieve when credit is given only for 
LSLs and GRRs replaced in a given year, but credit is not provided for the number of unknown service 
lines that are investigated and classified during the same period. LCA believes the tracking of unknown 
service lines should be separated from the calculation of LSLs and GRRs, so utilities have a more 
accurate way to determine how many service lines must be replaced during the course of the replacement 
period, and more accurate metrics to report to state agencies and the public.  
 
In addition, within the LCRI, EPA does not take access into account when establishing the deadlines for 
characterization of all unknown service lines or the calculation of annual replacement rate. While EPA 
recognizes the need to physically access private property with respect to service line replacement, this 
issue is not recognized when it comes to investigating service line material for inventory purposes. This 
will set many utilities up for failure in achieving compliance, as access cannot be guaranteed in all 
situations.  
 
Reporting and Notification Requirements 
The LCRI adds additional requirements to the already burdensome LCRR.  While LCA agrees that there 
are health benefits with keeping the public informed with the health impacts of lead, reporting to the state 
on individual activities should not be required.  States nor utilities are adequately staffed to prepare and 
review documents which have no added benefit to the public.  Rather, utilities should be able to provide 
documentation upon request and submit an annual certification of compliance with all applicable 
regulations.

National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements

Partial Replacement Ban 
In the LCRI, EPA is proposing to prohibit partial service line replacements unless it is conducted as part 
of an emergency repair or in coordination with planned infrastructure work, excluding planned 
infrastructure work solely for the purposes of LSL or GRR service line replacement.  While LCA agrees 
with the goal of conducting full-service line replacements, they are not always feasible.  For many water 
utilities, full-service line replacements require collaboration with property owners.  Banning partial 
replacements as a part of replacement programs impedes a utility’s ability to make incremental 
improvement by reducing at least the portion of the service line to which it has access.  While partial 
service lines replacements have been shown to increase lead levels, the EPA and states have required risk 
mitigation measures to impede the elevated lead risks associated with full and partial replacements.    
Properly installed and maintained POU filters, certified under both NSF/ANSI-53 and NSF/ANSI-42 can 
protect all populations, including pregnant women and children, by reducing lead in drinking water to 
levels that would not result in a significant increase in overall lead exposure4. Other risk mitigation 
measures are available through public education, system flushing, and post-partial-replacement lead 
testing. When properly administered, these measures can reduce risk exposure after a partial LSL 
replacement, which is preferrable over the alternative of leaving the public-side LSL in service. 
 
LCA, like most water utilities, does not have access to privately owned portions of the service line unless 
access is granted by the property owner.  By banning partial service line replacements, the EPA is 
creating situations where utilities are being required to leave lead portions in service, with the requirement 
to excavate and disturb service lines and roads again at a later date.  This has the potential to interfere and 
slow the process of completing the replacement work. 
 
Action Level Exceedance - Pitcher Filter Requirement 
The proposed rule requires water systems that exceed the action level to provide pitcher filters to all 
customers.  This requirement should be removed from the final rule as it only provides a benefit to a 
select number of customers at a significant cost.  The basis of the LCRR and LCRI is structured around 
controlling the leaching of lead from service lines.  Compliance monitoring for lead occurs at locations 
where lead is most likely to be present, but is not necessarily representative of lead levels throughout the

demonstration field study in flint, Michigan. Journal of environmental science and health. Part A, Toxic/hazardous substances & environmental 
engineering, 54(5), 484–493. https://doi.org/10.1080/10934529.2019.1611141

system.  Providing pitcher filters to customers with service lines that do not meet the requirements for 
replacement would provide little to no benefit to consumers.  The excessive funds that would be applied 
to providing filters would be better served by removing service lines meeting the removal requirements.  
LCA has over 33,500 connections in its largest system.  Complying with this requirement would 
logistically be impossible.  Locating a supply to meet the demand would not be feasible and would 
undoubtedly exceed municipal purchasing guidelines.  This would ultimately result in pitcher distribution 
delays due to the bidding and administrative process.   
 
As the infrastructure in America continues to age, water utilities struggle with maintaining affordable 
rates. The regulatory and reporting requirements, as proposed, will place additional financial and 
personnel workload burdens on utilities.   The proposed regulation is complex and implementation will be 
difficult for both water utilities and state agencies.  Effectively addressing lead exposure must be 
addressed through a collaborative approach with federal, state, and local agencies.  The responsibility is 
shared across multiple stakeholders, and not solely water utilities.
