RE:   Comments of the Alliance for the Great Lakes on Lead and Copper Rule 
 
Improvements, Docket #: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Dear Environmental Protection Agency, 
Please accept these comments submitted by the Alliance for the Great Lakes (“Alliance”) and its 
approximately 40,000 supporters on the U.S. EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements, Docket #: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 (“Proposed Rule”). The Alliance is a 
nonpartisan nonprofit working across the Great Lakes region, whose mission is to protect, 
conserve, and restore the Great Lakes, ensuring healthy water in the lakes and in our 
communities for all generations of people and wildlife. Ensuring safe, clean, and affordable 
drinking water is a pillar of the Alliance’s water advocacy. Therefore, the Alliance generally 
supports the U.S. EPA’s proposal to strengthen requirements to control lead and copper in 
drinking water – in particular the requirement to replace harmful lead service lines throughout 
the country within the next decade.  
The Great Lakes region contains by far the greatest number of lead service lines of any region in 
the country, and so has borne an especially heavy burden from this toxic legacy that is still with 
us today. Addressing lead service lines once and for all will bring huge benefits to the region by 
reducing negative impacts to childhood development and improving cardiac health. At the same 
time, the Alliance believes the Proposed Rule risks leaving the most burdened too far behind by 
allowing significant extensions of the timeframe for lead service line replacement in cities with 
the greatest number of lead service lines, including the Great Lakes cities of Chicago and 
Cleveland. This and other comments are taken up in more detail below and generally 
summarized as follows: 

 
 
2 
 
• U.S. EPA should require that systems with the greatest number of lead service lines meet 
ambitious minimum replacement rates set as a percentage of their total lead service lines, 
with such rates regularly revisited to ensure maximum feasible replacement over time. 
• U.S. EPA should further tighten the Action Level to 5 ppb to protect public health, ensure 
systems are using effective corrosion control treatment, and further promote outreach and 
education that can help spur lead service line replacement and other removal of lead from 
water systems.  
• The Alliance supports U.S. EPA’s proposed enhanced transparency measures and 
requests that U.S. EPA (a) include requirements that posted information be easily 
searchable, extractable and exportable, and (b) remove the 50,000-resident threshold for 
online provision of lead service line replacement plans.  
• The Alliance supports and suggests ways to bolster U.S. EPA’s emphasis in the Proposed 
Rule on environmental justice and civil rights obligations pertaining to lead service line 
replacement and overall Lead and Copper Rule compliance.  
The Alliance also generally supports parallel comments being submitted by Elevate, the Natural 
Resources Defense Council and Earthjustice, the Environmental Policy Innovation Center, the 
National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, the Illinois Water Justice 
Coalition, the Chicago Environmental Justice Network, and the Healing Our Waters Coalition. 
I. Timeframe for Lead Service Line Replacement 
The Alliance strongly supports U.S. EPA’s proposal to require water systems to replace their 
lead service lines within ten years. The harms of lead are well understood and the time for 
replacing lead service lines is well past. As such, the Alliance is concerned that allowing decades 
more to the systems with the most lead service lines will subject vulnerable residents to 
heightened lead levels for way too long. In addition, the Alliance questions the rationale for 
assuming that a large city like Chicago with substantial resources at its disposal can only replace 
as many lines per year as significantly smaller cities have achieved in the past. Rather than give 
some cities exceptionally long timeframes at the outset based on assumed annual replacement 
counts, the Alliance recommends requiring cities with the most lead service lines to meet an 
ambitious minimum initial replacement rate set as a percentage of the city’s total lead service 
lines at the outset, coupled with periodic review, robust technical assistance, and funding to 

 
 
3 
 
ensure that water systems meet targets as experience grows, funding increases, and supply and 
labor markets adjust.  
The Alliance is also concerned that giving cities like Chicago much longer than its suburban 
neighbors to replace lead service lines potentially increases inequities that U.S. EPA is 
committed to improving. As a Great Lakes advocate partner recently noted, setting a ten-year 
timeframe only for systems with fewer lines – including many with substantial economic 
resources – risks those systems collectively tying up limited equipment and certified workforce 
for lead service line replacement in the near term. Such resource distribution challenges from 
disparate replacement timelines could create potential shortages and even more delay for the 
systems with the most lines to replace and that are home to more low-income residents and 
residents of color. Setting more consistent timeframes for systems, and expecting cities with 
greater numbers of lines to reach ambitious annual targets, has the potential to create greater 
incentive for such cities to get out in front and secure needed resources by leveraging their 
economies of scale. It also sends a clearer and more urgent signal to supply and labor markets.  
We recognize that the same concern with being shut out of resources pertains to smaller, low-
income communities with significant proportions of residents of color located outside of large 
cities. We encourage U.S. EPA to engage with and increase the participation of these 
communities in WaterTA and with the Get the Lead Out Initiative. With subsidized assistance 
for planning and implementation, these jurisdictions could prioritize limited resources on 
securing supplies and labor, and may explore opportunities for achieving efficiencies of scale 
through coordination across water systems.  
Moreover, it is critical that Congress, U.S. EPA and state government support cities with the 
greatest number of lead service lines, as well as disadvantaged smaller communities facing 
substantial resource constraints, by ensuring that they receive funding in proportion to ambitious 
replacement goals and consistent with their proportion of vulnerable residents. As many have 
noted, the federal funding allocated for lead service line replacement to date is insufficient to 
meet the need. In addition, to the extent that cities with more lead service lines can achieve 
efficiencies by coordinating replacement with other road and water infrastructure work, and 
housing remediation, more funding will also be needed to make sure that this coordination can 
happen. U.S. EPA can play an important role in growing existing and establishing new 

 
 
4 
 
partnerships with the Department of Housing and Urban Development and Federal Emergency 
Management Agency, among other federal agencies, to incentivize and remove barriers to 
integrated funding for local infrastructure improvement goals.  
The Alliance is also concerned that some State Revolving Fund programs have been allocating 
lead service line replacement funding under existing state rules that do not ensure that funds go 
to the most vulnerable, underserved residents. We support states adopting revisions to their State 
Revolving Fund programs as soon as possible to enable more equitable distribution of funding, 
and look forward to working with community partners, state agencies, and U.S. EPA to this end. 
(See below on civil rights compliance and adding State Revolving Fund assessments to the 
special primacy requirements.) 
II. Who Bears the Costs of Lead Service Line Replacement 
The Alliance shares concerns with other advocates that allowing water systems to separately bill 
customers for replacing the portion of the service line that runs on private property runs a high 
risk of exacerbating historical inequities. We similarly believe that substantial evidence exists for 
water system control of service lines. Even if U.S. EPA finds water systems do not sufficiently 
control the entirety of the service line, thus not requiring water systems assume the full cost of 
lead service line replacement, it is critical that water systems allocate their resources in an 
equitable manner. Water systems should ensure that low-income and overburdened customers do 
not face barriers to replacement programs due to cost, and are instead prioritized for near-term 
replacement at no out-of-pocket cost to them.  
The Alliance supports U.S. EPA’s reminders throughout the proposal that federal civil rights 
obligations attach to water systems’ spending of federal funds, including awards from State 
Revolving Funds, on lead service line replacement obligations. We add that other civil rights 
laws, such as state civil rights laws and the federal Fair Housing Act, may impose obligations on 
lead service line replacement programs in addition to those under Title VI of the federal Civil 
Rights Act. Similarly, state administrators of State Revolving Fund programs are obligated to 
administer those programs consistent with Title VI. State administrators of State Revolving Fund 
programs thus are in a position to help ensure that funds for lead service line replacement do not 

 
 
5 
 
amplify inequities between water systems or within them, but instead help reduce such 
inequities.  
In addition, the Alliance believes that, regardless of U.S. EPA’s willingness to treat the entirety 
of a service line as part of the public water system, clarifying legislation at the state and/or local 
level may help local water agencies equitably meet ambitious lead service replacement timelines. 
Such legislation can significantly reduce local water agencies perceived or real exposure to 
potential litigation and clarify how a water agency will equitably fund lead service line 
replacement in its jurisdiction. Legislation should clearly delegate to local water agencies the 
authority to control service lines in their entirety, to raise local revenue needed to supplement 
federal and state funding to replace water system service lines in their jurisdiction, and to provide 
100% utility-funded lead service line replacement programs for those who qualify. While there 
are good examples of such legislation, we believe U.S. EPA should develop and/or identify 
model legislation that states and local jurisdictions can adopt to reduce barriers to achieving 
delegated authority and expediting service line replacement. Such legislation should clarify 
utility control over the water system service lines, and the utility’s authority to raise revenue 
using an equitable funding strategy. This type of targeted technical assistance in the form of 
model legislation would address significant barriers to equitably advancing ambitious lead 
service line replacement. 
III. Action Level 
The Alliance supports U.S. EPA’s proposal to strengthen the Action Level from 15 ppb to 10 
ppb, and to remove the trigger level. At the same time, the Alliance believes that a stronger 
Action Level is warranted due to the negative health impacts of lead; given systems that contain 
substantial amounts of lead-bearing fixtures; and especially if U.S. EPA allows extension of any 
timeframes for lead service line replacement beyond ten years. As is well-recognized, there is no 
safe level of lead exposure. In addition, it is the Alliance’s understanding that many water 
systems throughout the Great Lakes region had 90th percentile lead levels under the past Lead 
and Copper Rule sampling requirements that hovered in the 8 to 11 ppb range – indicating 
substantial sources of lead that were not being adequately controlled over the years. By 
tightening the action level further to 5 ppb (and with the addition of 5th draw samples to the 

 
 
6 
 
sampling regime), U.S. EPA will better ensure that these systems take steps to address their 
ongoing harmful levels of lead as they work toward lead service line replacement.  
According to U.S. EPA’s evaluation of corrosion control treatment performance in systems with 
lead service lines, nearly 40% of systems were able to achieve better than 5 ppb1, indicating that 
5 ppb is a reasonable level representative of well-implemented corrosion control treatment 
performance. U.S. EPA’s alternatives analysis also supports setting the Action Level at 5 ppb.2 
While the Alliance appreciates U.S. EPA’s desire not to impose significant administrative 
burdens on water systems (or the state agencies that support them), we are concerned that having 
low expectations for corrosion control treatment may be currently limiting water system 
operators’ understandings of complex water chemistry and corrosion control technology. 
Perpetuating low expectations by setting the Action Level at a threshold that a large majority of 
the systems are expected to meet may thus continue to hinder achieving the most effective use of 
corrosion control treatment and prevent greater learnings about the treatment technology that 
could benefit operators and the customers who rely on them.  
Strengthening the action level to 5 ppb would also have the added benefit of triggering more 
public outreach and education than an action level of 10 ppb. As noted in Section IV of these 
comments, increased outreach as a result of Action Level exceedances presents additional 
opportunities to increase public receptivity to lead service line and lead-containing home fixture 
replacement programs. Thus, further strengthening the Action Level to 5 ppb would help 
advance removal of lead from water systems.  
IV. Transparency and Accountability 
The Alliance appreciates U.S. EPA’s consideration of public education as a method of public 
health protection and thus a treatment technique that “...prevents known or anticipated adverse 
health effects ‘‘to the extent feasible...’’.3  As such, explicit requirements to improve lead health 
impact messaging4, provide materials in multiple languages5, and to make lead service line

The Alliance also supports improvements to customer notification requirements and agrees with 
U.S. EPA’s feasibility determination that the outreach requirements listed below are appropriate 
and achievable. Each notification increases customers’ exposure to lead service line replacement

A) Annual notifications to customers with known lead service lines, galvanized service lines

regardless of the lead or copper results also encourages customer system awareness.10

Requiring utilities (and States) to identify any state or local laws or water tariff agreement 
provisions that might impede adequate access to a full service line and include these access 
barriers in a publicly available lead service line replacement plan is crucial. As noted in the 
Proposed Rule, the benefits of this requirement are two-fold. First, researching legal barriers may 
elucidate legal pathways for full service line replacement previously unknown to or 
misunderstood by the utility, or identify for the utility policy changes required to service a line 
fully. Second, a utility’s perception of legal barriers to full service line replacement becomes 
public information, increasing the transparency around a utility’s processes and potentially 
enhancing public discussion around reforms.12  
 
The Proposed Rule could, however, take further steps to make transparency a priority – by 
requiring that lead service line inventories be easily searchable, extractable, and exportable. 
Additionally, the Proposed Rule requires only jurisdictions/utilities with greater than 50,000 
connections to make lead service line replacement plans and inventories accessible online.13 The 
Proposed Rule and LCRR do not provide justification for establishing this population-based 
cutoff for posting inventories online, nor reasoning for why posting lead service line replacement 
plans online presents a significant burden. The Alliance requests the requirement to make plans 
available online in an accessible format extend to all communities equally – regardless of 
community size.  
 
Engagement around lead service line replacement and the health impacts of lead exposure should 
explicitly consider successful models for engaging communities in equitable lead service line 
replacement planning. The Alliance is encouraged by U.S. EPA reiterating AWWA LSLR 
Collaborative and prior U.S. EPA findings that utility/provider partnerships with community-
based organizations are particularly effective at centering community needs in lead service line

V. Environmental Justice, Civil Rights 
The Alliance appreciates the attention that U.S. EPA gives to environmental justice and civil 
rights issues in its proposal, including the Environmental Justice Analysis for the Proposed Rule 
and discussion of Title VI obligations. Our above comments address several environmental 
justice and civil rights issues as they pertain to the Proposed Rule. We raise additional items 
here. The Environmental Justice Analysis uses a method that examines the distribution of lead 
service line burdens within water systems, looking at several city case studies.17 The Alliance 
recommends that U.S. EPA also consider inter-system environmental justice issues in this and 
future rulemaking, in addition to the intra-system frame. An inter-system frame could assess 
whether relative access to funding resources for implementation of the rule, and/or different 
regulatory timelines for replacement among water systems, might produce greater (or lesser) 
inequities in lead service line distribution across/between systems than exist at the outset of 
implementation. The assessment could then also consider ways to mitigate any such heightened 
inequities.

VI. Conclusion 
In sum, the Alliance welcomes these long-awaited improvements to the federal Lead and Copper 
Rule and encourages U.S. EPA to issue a strengthened final rule that delivers on the 
Administration’s promise of equitable 100% lead service line replacement to the country and the 
Great Lakes region.

RE: Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for 
Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) 
 
Dear Administrator Regan:  
 
On behalf of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), a non-profit professional organization 
of 67,000 primary care pediatricians, pediatric medical sub-specialists, and pediatric surgical 
specialists dedicated to the health, safety and well-being of infants, children, adolescents, and 
young adults, I am writing to commend the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) 
proposed rule entitled “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI)” (docket number: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801) and provide input on this 
proposed rule. The AAP appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on this important 
children’s health issue and urges EPA to approve the strongest rule possible.  
 
Childhood lead exposure is a critical public health issue. There is no safe level of lead exposure, 
and the health harms of lead exposure can be permanent and irreversible. A significant source 
of lead exposure for children is the drinking water systems in this country, which contribute 
significantly to the persistent public health challenge of childhood lead poisoning. Children are 
uniquely vulnerable to the lifelong and irreversible health effects lead can cause, and EPA has a 
critical role in preventing children’s exposure to lead. 
 
The EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) is an essential public health tool that is used to 
determine where certain prevention methods are needed to reduce exposure to lead in 
drinking water, and it is essential to improving the primary prevention of childhood lead 
exposure. The LCR requires drinking water systems to monitor drinking water at customer taps. 
If lead concentrations exceed an action level of 15 micrograms per liter (µg/L) in more than 10% 
of customer taps sampled, the system must undertake several corrective actions. Since the 
promulgation of the original 1991 LCR, there has been a significant reduction in lead 
concentrations in tap water, and the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) strengthened 
these efforts.i The AAP commends EPA for this significant progress in reducing lead in drinking 
water while continuing to call on the EPA to finalize an updated LCR that recognizes the 
extensive scientific evidence that there is no safe level of lead. 
 
The AAP appreciates the EPA’s proposed rule to revise the LCR and LCRR to further limit 
childhood lead exposure, especially the provisions that propose to reduce the lead action levels 
from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L to require more water systems to act sooner to control corrosion and 
provide public education. The AAP believes that these proposed revisions to the LCR and LCRR 
are an important step towards stronger protections against childhood lead poisoning from 
drinking water. Pediatricians know that there is no safe level of lead exposure, so the AAP also 
urges the EPA to adopt the strongest possible standard achievable to protect the health and 
well-being of children. 
 

The AAP provides the following comments to outline the child health risks of lead poisoning across the life 
span and provide further input on EPA’s proposed changes to the LCR and LCRR:  
 
There Is No Safe Level of Lead 
 
Lead is a potent neurotoxin that can cause permanent and irreversible damage to children. Children with 
elevated lead levels are more likely to have behavior problems, attention deficit and reading disabilities, and 
fail to graduate from high school. Elevated blood lead levels are defined as lead levels above the Centers for 
Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) “reference level” of 3.5 micrograms per deciliter.ii Low-level lead 
exposure, even at blood lead concentrations below 5 µg/dL, is a causal risk factor for diminished intellectual 
and academic abilities, higher rates of neurobehavioral disorders such as hyperactivity and attention deficits, 
and lower birth weight in children. Despite historical reductions in children’s blood lead concentrations, 
pediatric lead exposure persists, and so preventing childhood lead toxicity remains a major public health 
priority in the United States. For these reasons, primary prevention of exposure to lead is essential to address 
this major public health issue. 
 
The EPA’s proposed rule updates the LCR and LCRR with stronger requirements around testing of drinking 
water and indicated actions to address the presence of lead over certain thresholds. The proposed rule also 
appropriately revises the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L, which is a significant improvement. While 
recognizing this proposed rule as a step forward, the AAP reaffirms our position that there is no safe level of 
lead and continues to call on EPA to set an action level of 0 µg/L for lead in drinking water. The AAP commends 
EPA for revising downward the action level of 15 µg/L, which was not done in the 2021 LCRR. Given the 
permanent and harmful effects of lead exposure, the AAP calls for the final LCRI to be a health-based standard 
to adequately protect children’s health. 
 
Trigger Level 
 
The AAP strongly supports the EPA’s proposal to eliminate the “trigger level,” which is currently 10 µg/L. The 
AAP has previously opposed the trigger level, and the science of the health impacts of childhood lead exposure 
supports this proposal to eliminate this arbitrary level. The AAP believes that eliminating this trigger level will 
move more water systems to take proactive measures to thoroughly prevent lead exposure more 
expeditiously. Under the current trigger level, an exceedance of the trigger level requires additional testing, 
but not the protection of a community’s needs when their water source is found to have concerning levels of 
lead. Requiring corrosion control only after a trigger level exceedance is nothing more than a stop gap 
measure, which fails to adequately protect children that drink water from lead service lines and relies on a 
reactive approach to a neurotoxin for which the optimal approach is primary prevention of exposure.  
 
By eliminating the trigger level, any water system with continually high levels of lead, which is determined by 
having multiple lead action level exceedances, would be required to conduct additional outreach to consumers 
about lead in the drinking water and make filters certified to reduce lead available for consumers. The AAP 
commends the EPA’s proposal to eliminate the trigger level, which demonstrates that the EPA understands the 
scientific evidence that there is no safe level of lead and will not set arbitrary standards that are not based on 
science.  
 
 
 
 
 
 

Lead Service Line Replacements 
 
The AAP strongly supports EPA’s proposal to require water systems to replace all lead service lines that are 
under the control of water systems. We appreciate EPA ‘s decision to require most of these replacements to 
occur in 10 years or less, and we encourage the EPA to vigorously enforce this timeline and move water systems 
to implement these replacements as soon as possible. 
 
The AAP previously called for an immediate moratorium on all partial lead service line replacements (LSLRs), 
and we were pleased that the 2021 LCRR removed provisions allowing partial service line replacement or “test-
outs” to count towards LSLR requirements. However, the AAP was disappointed that the EPA did not explicitly 
restrict or ban partial LSLRs. Partial LSLR, which is sometimes performed to minimize the cost-of-service line 
repair by water authorities, fails to reduce lead exposure. Replacement or other maintenance work can release 
additional particles of lead, further contaminating drinking water sources in the case of partial LSLRs and 
exacerbating exposure.iii  
 
The AAP supports EPA’s proposal in this LCRI to prohibit partial service line replacements. We are concerned 
about EPA’s proposal to allow for partial service line replacements if they are “conducted as part of an 
emergency repair or in coordination with planned infrastructure work, excluding planned infrastructure work 
solely for the purposes of LSLRs.” We urge EPA to eliminate this exception or ensure it is only available in 
uniquely extenuating circumstances. 
 
Overall, the proposed LCRI is a step in the right direction, although the AAP urges EPA to consider including 
additional steps in the final LCRI to prevent all cases of partial LSLRs. For example, the cost of replacing the 
homeowner-owned portion of the LSR remains on homeowners, with the proposed rule offering only 
encouragement that water systems develop financial assistance programs for supporting consumer 
replacement of service lines. It also includes requirements to communicate LSLRs to consumers, coordinate 
with planned infrastructure to replace the entire lead service line and take risk mitigation measures in the 
event of a partial lead service line replacement. While the AAP appreciates the modest improvements outlined 
in the proposed rule, the final LCRI should require water systems to pay for replacement of customer owned 
lead service lines to ensure full LSLRs and enact a moratorium on harmful, partial LSLRs.   
 
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes 
 
The AAP supports EPA’s efforts to discover where lead pipes are located in order to replace them efficiently and 
equitably. Water systems are currently required to provide an initial inventory of their lead service lines by 
October 16, 2024. Under the proposed LCRI, all water systems would be required to regularly update their 
inventories, create a publicly available service line replacement plan, and identify the materials of all service 
lines of unknown material. The AAP believes that these requirements are reasonable and appropriate in order 
to accomplish the important goal of replacing all lead pipes for all communities.  
 
Testing Protocols & Tap Sampling 
 
For too long, it has been easy for water systems to avoid needed primary prevention interventions through 
dubious water sampling protocols that are not reflective of real-world water use. These include pre-stagnation 
flushing, the cleaning or removing of faucet aerators, and the use of narrow-mouth sample collection bottles. 
The AAP appreciates that the LCRI proposed rule continues the changes made in the 2021 LCRR proposed rule 
that made steps to improve sampling reliability by no longer allowing tap sampling instructions that 
recommend these problematic practices, as well as a requirement for collecting samples in wide-mouth 
bottles. The AAP appreciates the progress that EPA has made in improving the testing protocols and continues 

to encourage EPA to ensure that the final LCRI requires rigorous testing protocols that ensure water samples 
are reflective of how families actually use their taps, so that the samples are comparable to the water they 
drink.  
 
Testing in Schools and Child Care Facilities 
 
Facilities that serve children, such as child care facilities and schools, should be required to conduct regular, 
publicly-reported tap water sampling from multiple sources. The AAP appreciates EPA’s proposal to retain the 
requirement for community water systems to sample for lead at schools and child care facilities from multiple 
sources that was included in the 2021 LCRR. However, the final rule should require community water systems 
to conduct comprehensive sampling at all taps used for cooking or drinking in these child-serving locations. 
Under the proposed LCRI, the results of this sampling would be required to be reported to the facility and to 
the local or state health department, but not to the parents of children who may be at risk of lead exposure. 
Schools and child care facilities would make their own decisions about whether to communicate these results 
to parents. The AAP urges the EPA to finalize a rule that also requires notification to parents when their 
children may be at risk of lead exposure due to contaminated tap water in child care facilities and schools. 
Finally, EPA should continue to consider other ways to ensure that proper actions are taken to protect children 
when sampling in child care facilities and schools detects lead contamination, including ways to keep the local 
medical community informed and encouraging parents to contact their pediatrician or medical provider if 
their child is exposed to high concentrations of lead or they have questions about their child’s exposure to lead. 
 
Public Education and Outreach  
 
Public education and outreach is crucial for parents and other caregivers to know of any lead contamination in 
tap water and make choices to protect their children. The AAP commends EPA for several revisions to the LCR 
and LCRR in the proposed LCRI.  
 
The AAP supports EPA’s decision to eliminate the non-health-based discrepancy that was included in the 2021 
LCRR. The 2021 LCRR required water systems with tap water samples that surpass the lead action level to notify 
customers within 24 hours of learning the result. However, under the LCRR, for samples less than or equal to 
the action level, water systems are only required to provide consumer notice by mail within 30 days. This 
discrepancy was not health-based, since childhood exposure to drinking water under the action level of 15 μg/L 
can still lead to permanent, harmful health effects. The AAP supports EPA’s proposal to eliminate this 
discrepancy in the proposed LCRI and instead to require water systems to notify all consumers of lead tap 
sampling results within the same time frame of three calendar days after the system learns of the results, 
regardless of whether the results exceed the lead action level. However, the AAP does encourage EPA to 
consider ways to ensure that water systems are informing consumers as soon as possible and not delaying until 
three days before informing consumers. In addition, this communication should provide families sufficient 
context to understand what the testing results mean. 
 
The AAP also appreciates EPA’s efforts to ensure that all consumers, including those with limited English 
proficiency, can receive education and notification materials in their respective languages. The AAP supports 
the provisions in the LCRI which require water systems to include in public education materials ways for 
consumers to obtain a translated copy of the materials, request assistance in the appropriate language, or the 
system must provide materials translated into the appropriate language. The AAP also encourages EPA to 
continue finding ways to ensure public education materials and notifications account for language, economic, 
and technological barriers to ensure that all families are notified. The EPA should also distribute education 
materials to pediatricians and Pediatric Environmental Health Specialty Units (PEHSUs) in affected areas. 
 

Conclusion 
 
Thank you for this opportunity to comment on this critical health issue. The AAP commends the proposed LCRI 
as a major step forward toward more protective policies needed to ensure children can reach their optimal 
health and development, and we urge the EPA to adopt the strongest final rule possible. If the AAP can be of 
any further assistance, please do not hesitate to contact Zach Laris in our Washington, D.C. office at 202/347-
8600 or zlaris@aap.org.  
 
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Benjamin D. Hoffman, MD, FAAP

Credit:  CDC.gov
Lead in Faucets
Though neurotoxic effects for lead are found in both adults and young children, the 
developing brain is particularly susceptible to lead-induced harm, effects which can 
include the death of cells necessary for an organism's growth or development and 
nerve cells suffer damage or death
In 2014 high levels of lead contaminated the drinking water of Flint, Michigan, and caused serious health 
problems.  Because of this, “lead in drinking water” is now recognized as a serious nationwide issue. It varies 
across states depending on the condition of the water delivery system and how the water is treated to prevent 
corrosion. In many cities the main source of the problem is lead in “lead service lines”, the pipes that connect 
city water mains to homes. If effective corrosion control is not used by a city or if it suddenly switches to more 
corrosive water, levels of lead in drinking water can rise above EPA’s Action Level of 15 ppb.
The Environmental Defense Fund (EDF), concerned about lead in the drinking water of childcare facilities, 
conducted water testing in 11 childcare facilities serving over 1,000 children primarily from low-income families 
in Illinois, Michigan, Mississippi, and Ohio.  https://www.edf.org/health/tackling-lead-water-child-care-facilities.  
A major finding was that that lead was being released from faucets sold as “lead free”. Children were being 
exposed to lead. 
The Center for Disease Control (CDC) says no level of lead is safe for children. Cities 
that do not have lead service lines can also have this problem because it is legal to 
make and sell household faucets and pipes, called premise plumbing, that contain 
lead.
The American Academy of Pediatrics has recommended that water fountains in schools should not exceed 
lead concentrations of 1 microgram per liter (µg/L).  EDF, Environmental Working Group (EWG) and the 
National Sanitation Foundation (NSF) and were invited to join a task group of the NSF Joint Committee 
responsible for revising standard that regulates drinking water contact materials. They ultimately revised the 
standard to reduce the amount of lead allowed.   In January 2021 the national consensus standard for 
plumbing devices -NSF/ANSI/CAN 61 , required that manufacturers of faucets and fountains that dispense 
drinking water meet a limit of 1 µg/L , a limit five times more protective for lead leaching than the previous 
standard
http://blogs.edf.org/health/2020/06/18/revised-lead-leaching-limits-drinking-water-fixtures/
These industries have been given until Jan. 2024 to implement this new limit.   There are serious concerns that 
implementation should be much sooner because of children’s exposures. Many children spend half their day in 
in schools and day care centers.  EPA regulations in this area are weak.  It has been recommended that the

Environmental Protection Agency should consider revising its 3Ts guidance for schools and child care facilities

One state is not waiting for the federal limits to take effect.  In 2021 California enacted AB 100, the nation’s 
strictest limit on lead leaching from faucets - ensuring faucets and fixtures sold will be practically lead-free.  
https://smartwatermagazine.com/news/environmental-working-group-ewg/california-enacts-nations-strictest-
limit-lead-leaching-faucets “The legislation, authored by Assemblymember Chris Holden (D-Pasadena), 
requires all faucets and fixtures with potable water sold in California beginning in 2023 to leach no more than 
one microgram of lead -five times less lead than the current industry certification standard allows.
Even though brass and bronze-based plumbing materials can release dangerous levels of lead, very few 
states have enacted comprehensive regulations requiring testing and remediation of drinking water in schools.   
Fortunately, knowing that lead can be leaching from faucets and drinking fountains even in cities that do not 
have lead service lines, Washington state now requires schools to test for lead in their drinking water outlets."  
In 2021 the Governor signed HB 1139 which requires that schools test drinking water outlets for lead and 
adopt action plans if results find lead contamination exceeds 5 parts per billion.  Required remedies can 
include replacement of drinking water fixtures. Opportunities to purchase “lead free” fixture should come 
sooner rather than later.  Hopefully the new requirements in California will convince the manufacturers of 
drinking fountains and other fixtures to switch to “lead free” much sooner than the federal law requires.

To U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA),
As a nurse I’ve witnessed how Social Determinants of health can 
in6luence people’s health and quality of life. Besides economic 
instability and limited access to healthcare; environmental factors 
such as lead contaminated water can have an adverse impact on 
overall health and well-being. 
Lead is a non-biodegradable metal that is toxic to body systems.
Infants, young children, and pregnant women are vulnerable to the 
harmful effects of lead. Despite improvements in water treatment 
standards and The Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA), lead exposure 
remains a concern for vulnerable populations. Therefore, it is 
reasonable to reduce lead Maximum Contaminant Level (MCL) from 
current action Level of 0.015 mg/L to 0.010 mg/L, with the 
Maximum Contaminant Level Goals (MCLGs) of zero.
Lead found in tap water usually comes from corrosion or decay of 
older 6ixtures or from the solder that connects pipes. While 
individuals can avoid drinking lead contaminated water by using 
6ilters or purchasing drinking water from certi6ied sources, these are 
not always attainable to every household especially in low-income
families. Primary prevention in lead exposure is to remove lead 
hazards from the environment by proposing the required water 
systems to replace lead service lines.

Since a blood test is the only way to determine exposure to lead. 
Having blood lead level testing and follow-up care are secondary 
prevention. Both primary and secondary preventions can be 
implemented through public education and increase consumer 
awareness.
In conclusion, lead poisoning is preventable. Everyone drinks water 
and the interventions to ensure safe drinking water for everyone 
should be feasible. Lead MCL should be as close to zero as possible. 
Special funds should be given for total lead service line 
replacements, especially for disadvantaged communities.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0966 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
January 26, 2024 
  
Mr. Michael S. Regan  
Administrator  
Environmental Protection Agency  
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue, NW  
Washington, DC 20460  
  
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, Docket 
No. EPA–HQ–OW-2022-0801  
 
Dear Administrator Regan,  
 
On behalf of the National Association of County and City Health Officials (NACCHO), I appreciate the 
opportunity to submit comments regarding the proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA); 
(Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801). NACCHO represents the more than 3,300 local health departments 
across the country, many of which develop, promote, and engage in lead poisoning prevention efforts. 
NACCHO promotes primary prevention and works toward the removal of lead sources from the 
environment prior to exposure, particularly in water and housing, in order to prevent the potential for 
adverse effects, especially in children.  
 
NACCHO’s comments on the proposed revision are as follows:  
 
NACCHO supports EPA’s mandatory full replacement of lead services lines.  
NACCHO supports EPA’s efforts to focus on the need to identify and remove sources of lead in community 
infrastructure prior to an exposure occurring. According to EPA, an estimated 9.2 million lead service lines 
serve water to properties in communities across the U.S.1 While NACCHO is pleased to see EPA moving in 
the right direction by lowering the lead action level, as noted by EPA, there is no known safe level of lead 
exposure. Furthermore, as noted in the proposed rule, the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law appropriated $15 
billion for lead service line replacement project and associated activities. NACCHO was pleased to see the 
“Lead Service Line Replacement Accelerators” initiative, however barriers remain to access this 
opportunity. Small and low-capacity jurisdictions need grant and technical support in order to apply for and 
access the funding and resources provided by EPA. While the Federal Thriving Communities Initiative and 
Environmental Justice Thriving Communities Technical Assistance Centers Program are an important step 
towards holistic government-wide technical assistance and capacity building for all communities, more is 
needed to reach these jurisdictions equitably.   
 
Urgent and swift action must be taken to remove lead for all people in all communities. Full replacement of 
lead service lines would make the 10 ppb threshold for replacement, an arbitrary value, irrelevant. . 
NACCHO also recommends that EPA consider additional ways to lower the cost burden full lead service 
line replacement will have on local governments and homeowners and continue to invest in ongoing 
funding to ensure timely action without diverting resources from other public health priorities.   
 

 
 
 
NACCHO recommends EPA increase sampling requirements for schools and childcare facilities.  
NACCHO recommends all taps in schools and childcare facilities be tested for lead. In the U.S., children are 
particularly vulnerable to the effects of lead, which can cause permanent adverse health outcomes, 
including damage to the brain and nervous systems, slowed growth and development, learning behavior 
problems, and hearing and speech problems.2 In addition, the burden of lead poisoning falls 
disproportionately on low-income families and communities of color, with African American children more 
than two times more likely to experience lead poisoning than white children.3 The proposed revisions to the 
rule again neglects to prevent exposures by omitting a requirement to act on sampling results from schools 
and childcare facilities. NACCHO recommends that the 10 ppb action level proposed for lead in public 
drinking water also be applied to lead in drinking water at schools and childcare facilities. NACCHO also 
recommends that EPA consider the cost burden full lead service line replacement will have on local 
governments, schools, and childcare centers and develop and sustain funding sources to ensure timely 
action and prioritize the prevention of lead exposure to children.    
  
NACCHO strongly encourages EPA to explore collaborations between EPA and local health departments 
to identify optimal community engagement practices.  
NACCHO is encouraged by EPA’s public education efforts. In addition to including the contact information 
of local health departments on education materials, NACCHO recommends that EPA review established 
connections between the agency and local health departments to determine successes and areas that need 
to be improved. As more communities are notified about lead service lines, local health departments can 
play a key role in education and reinforcing related messages from national and federal partners, including 
EPA. In addition, there should be continuous opportunities for collaborations among EPA and local health 
departments to not only effectively spread messaging around lead exposure, but to also to ensure EPA has 
timely feedback about the priorities and concerns of local communities. As consumers and homeowners 
become more educated about lead service lines in their community, there will be an increased need for 
public education and response to inquiries about the health impacts of lead and how to prevent lead 
exposure.  
 
NACCHO appreciates this opportunity to comment on EPA’s efforts to improve processes and tools needed 
for a safer future. We look forward to continuing to work with you to protect the public from lead 
exposure. If you have any questions, please contact Adriane Casalotti, Chief of Government and Public 
Affairs, at acasalotti@naccho.org.   
 
Sincerely,   
  
 
Lori Tremmel Freeman, MBA  
CEO

Dear Ms. McLain: 
 
As members of WaterNow Alliance (WaterNow) and National League of Cities (NLC) we 
appreciate this opportunity to provide input on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s 
(EPA) proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) to protect public health by 
reducing lead in drinking water. WaterNow is a nonprofit network of 700+ local water leaders in 
43 states nationwide advancing sustainable, affordable, equitable, and climate resilient water 
strategies. NLC is the voice of America’s cities, towns and villages, representing more than 200 
million people nationwide.  
 
As the proposed rule states, “There is no known safe level of lead exposure.”1 Eliminating all 
lead service lines nationwide—whether publicly or privately owned—is a laudable goal, both of 
the LCRI and the Biden Administration.2 Some local governments have achieved this goal. A 
growing number are working towards it. For example, Madison, Wisconsin, was the first city to 
eliminate all lead service lines, including on both public and private property.3 Newark, New 
Jersey, completed replacement of all lead service lines in 2022.4 Denver Water has successfully 
accelerated the pace of its program to replace 64,000-84,000 lead service lines, primarily on 
private properties within its service area, at no additional cost to those property owners through 
bond financing.5  
 
Local leaders, including those that have documented successes, are confronted with a variety of 
challenges that must be overcome, such as financial constraints, affordability concerns for low-
income households, staff capacity, workforce shortages and supply chain limitations. To support 
the ability of cities to overcome these challenges, protect the health and welfare of their 
populations, and meet the LCRI requirements, we urge the federal government to provide 
sufficient funding, particularly in the form of grants, to local governments to enable them to

expand and accelerate lead service line replacements (LSLRs).  
 
We also urge EPA to establish a clear and implementable replacement requirement. Local 
leaders are committed to protecting public health and eliminating lead service lines. While the 
goal of achieving 100 percent lead pipe replacement is important, without a clear framework and 
definition, we could fall well short of the goal as a nation. This is because, as proposed, the LCRI 
only requires public water systems to replace lead service lines that are “under the control of the 
water system … .”6 The rule further specifies that:  
 
Where a water system has access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full service 
line replacement, the service line is under its control, and the water system must replace the 
service line. Where a water system does not have access to conduct full service line 
replacement, the water system is not required by this rule to replace the line…7 
A great many lead lines, possibly most of them, may fall outside of this definition. The proposed 
rule does not establish criteria for determining whether a public water system has access to 
service lines,8 leaving that decision to states and local water systems. Given the disparate needs 
and challenges facing communities, we appreciate the interest in providing flexibility for state 
and local governments. However, without additional clarity, the rule is likely to create 
implementation and compliance challenges, such as lack of understanding of which service lines 
must be replaced and when a utility has met the requirement to replace “all” service lines. 
Furthermore, requiring each locality to develop its own definition of “control” and “access” 
without additional clarity from EPA could generate a complex patchwork of differing definitions 
for when lead lines fall within the federal rule and when they do not. These varying definitions 
could lead to differing levels of public health protections in communities nationwide.  
EPA’s 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment conducted in 2021 and 
published in September 2023 considered three categories of lead service lines to estimate that 
there are 9.2 million lead service lines in the U.S.9 Our understanding is that service lines solely 
owned by the utility and service lines solely owned by the customer occur but are uncommon, 
and that the service lines over which utilities and customers share ownership is by far the most 
common. Utilities obviously have “access” to service lines that they own.  
 
The LCRI, as proposed, is unclear on whether utilities would be responsible for removing lead 
lines that are not solely owned by the utility. Put differently, because most lead service lines are 
at least partly owned by customers, and because the proposed LCRI leaves what it means to have 
“access to conduct a full service line replacement” undefined, the proposed rule may be open to 
the interpretation that many, if not most, lead service lines are exempt from the replacement 
requirement. This is a particularly acute challenge since privately owned lead lines occur more 
often in disadvantaged, environmental justice communities.10

Relying on state and local governments for a definition of “control” does not provide the needed

local water systems replace lead service lines that are partially, or completely, privately owned.11 
Thus, the proposed rule would leave a significant regulatory gap in the replacement requirement.  
To close this gap, we recommend that EPA revise the LCRI to clearly indicate that the 
replacement requirement includes replacement of lead service lines located on private property to 
the maximum extent feasible. Replacing private-side lead lines is an important component to 
meeting the goal to replace 100 percent of lead service lines nationwide. Recognizing that the 
“access” requirement may pose legal and safety concerns for local governments, as well as that 
some private property owners might not permit the access necessary for private-side service line 
replacement, we recommend that the rule establish a specific procedure to address such 
situations while maintaining flexibility to implement those procedures for local jurisdictions.   
Providing additional clarity in the LCRI about which lead service lines must be replaced will 
also help ensure that funds required to pay for public and private-side lead service line 
replacements are allocated to address this public health issue.12 Estimates for replacing lead lines 
nationwide range from $45 to $100 billion.13 These estimates far exceed the $15 billion 
investment provided by the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, the majority of which will be in the 
form of loans to local governments.

the Agency moves forward with finalizing the LCRI, further clarification and additional direct 
funding to local governments are needed to help meet the intended goal of replacing all lead 
service lines. Please reach out to Cynthia Koehler at ck@waternow.org or Carolyn Berndt at 
Berndt@nlc.org with any questions.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0916 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Water and Sewer Department
1001 11th Ave, Second Floor
Greeley, Colorado 80631
February 2, 2024
Comments on U.S. EPA’s Proposed Leand and Copper Rule Improvements:
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
The City of Greeley submits the following comments on U.S. EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI).
The Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) have 
introduced significant changes aimed at reducing lead exposure in drinking water, particularly through the 
identification and replacement of lead service lines (LSLs) and galvanized requiring replacement lines 
(GRRs). While these regulations mark a pivotal step towards safeguarding public health, certain aspects of 
their implementation raise critical feasibility concerns for water systems, especially regarding the 
calculation of annual replacement rates and the requirements for non-lead validation.
A notable challenge arises in the method used to calculate the annual replacement rate. Water systems, 
like the City of Greeley, that prioritize the removal of known LSLs and GRRs may face difficulties in 
meeting the replacement rate once only lines classified as "unknown" remain.  This method inadvertently 
penalizes systems that have been proactive in eliminating known sources of lead, giving greater weight to 
the identification of unknown lines, which may not contain lead at all. 
To address this, a revised approach should be considered. For example, the EPA could introduce a 
“verification rate” for systems that have removed all known LSLs and GRRs. Under this model, a portion of 
unknown lines must be verified annually, and LSLs or GRRs that are discovered from the “unknown” pool 
must be replaced within a year. This alternative calculation would adjust compliance metrics to incentivize 
prioritizing the removal of known sources of lead to protect public health, while also pushing systems to 
continue identifying the material of unknowns in the inventory. 
The LCRI's requirements for validating non-lead service lines present another area of concern. For 
systems employing machine learning or alternative methods for final material determination, the 
requirement for non-lead validation is logical and likely beneficial to ensure assumptions made by these 
methods are supported with visually verified data. However, systems like the City of Greeley that are 
primarily relying on historical records and visual inspections of the customer-owned portion to determine 
service line materials face a different reality. Historical records, if also corroborated by a sample verified 
through visual inspection, offer a reliable basis for identifying service line materials without the need for 
further validation. For systems that utilize historical records, mechanical excavation, and visual verification 
to identify service line material, the requirement to re-validate non-lead lines identified through historical 

records review can be costly and divert resources from addressing unknown lines and lines that contain lead. 
This is particularly true given the 7-year compliance deadline for the non-lead validation, which puts this 
requirement in direct competition for resources with addressing known sources of lead.
To ensure that systems are not burdened with multiple rounds of costly validation steps for low-risk 
properties, the EPA should consider an exemption from the non-lead validation requirements. For systems 
that do not use alternative methods alone for non-lead determination and can validate the accuracy of their 
historical records with a sample of visually verified data, an exemption from this requirement would allow 
water systems to choose the best combination of material verification methods to fit their system and offer 
more system-specific flexibility while maximizing benefits. This exemption would recognize the reliability 
of verified historical documentation, where records and physical evidence can confidently exclude the 
presence of lead.
The City of Greeley supports the EPA’s critical effort to eliminate lead exposure from drinking water 
through the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. However, refining the rule to address the practical 
challenges faced by water systems—particularly regarding the calculation for annual replacement rates and 
non-lead validation requirements—could enhance its effectiveness and fairness. By adjusting these aspects, 
the EPA would not only facilitate compliance but also ensure that efforts are optimally directed towards 
reducing lead exposure in communities nationwide.
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on water system feasibility considerations in development of 
the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements.
Sincerely,
Michaela Jackson
Water Quality and Regulatory Compliance Manager
City of Greeley, Water and Sewer Department

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0770 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Dear EPA, 
 
 
The EPA has stated that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water. A goal of the LCRI is to 
conclusively identify and replace all LSLs in the US by 2037. I applaud this effort and wish to comment on 
some of the particulars of these pending regulations.  
 
Accurate identification of lead service lines is a crucial step of this process. I am concerned that 
the current approach to identify unknown service lines could cause many service lines to be 
misidentified and left in place. Historical records can provide a useful starting place for identification of 
service lines; however many records have been lost or are inconclusive. Millions of service lines are of 
unknown material. Excavation is the gold standard for service line identification, but the costs to unearth 
non-lead service lines are prohibitively expensive and should be avoided. A two-point visual inspection 
of the service line at the meter pit would not identify lead connectors, or LSLs where the meter connects 
with a tail of another material.1 A flushed water sample measuring 2.5 ppb or higher is used in the UK 
and France to identify potential LSLs, with high positive identification rates. I propose that a two-step 
verification process be required for unknown service line identification, where both a two-point visual 
inspection and flushed sample lead is measured. In cases where the lead concentration is above 2.5 ppb 
and/or a two-point visual inspection confirms lead, the service line should be labelled as a LSL. In cases 
where the water sample is below 2.5 ppb and the two-point visual inspection returns a negative 
identification, the line should be considered non-lead. To achieve maximum effectiveness and negate 
entry into customers’ homes, the property’s hose bib could be used for water sampling. Additionally, I 
propose that a significant proportion of pre 1986 built homes with non-lead lines be tested with this 
method to achieve 95 percent confidence in the identification of non-lead service lines through records 
alone. 
I encourage the EPA to make room for new technologies to aid in water sampling. Portable, 
affordable, and easy to use water sensors with sufficient LOD could alleviate some of the burden placed 
on labs to complete water testing. New technologies are under development to this end. I would 
welcome the approval of New EPA Certified Methods as an Alternate Test Procedures for use in the field 
opposed to the requirement for all lead and copper samples to be processed in EPA certified labs. The 
new three day turnaround time will overwhelm these strapped labs. A fast track for verification and 
approval of new methods could lower costs while maintaining a high standard for positive identification 
of lead in water samples.  
Regards, 
Nick Halverson 
 
[1] Hensley K, Bosscher V, Triantafyllidou S, Lytle DA. Lead service line identification: A review of

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0763 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Dear EPA, 
 
 
The EPA has stated that there is no safe level of lead in drinking water. A goal of the LCRI is to 
conclusively identify and replace all LSLs in the US by 2037. I applaud this effort and wish to comment on 
some of the particulars of these pending regulations.  
 
Accurate identification of lead service lines is a crucial step of this process. I am concerned that 
the current approach to identify unknown service lines could cause many service lines to be 
misidentified and left in place. Historical records can provide a useful starting place for identification of 
service lines; however many records have been lost or are inconclusive. Millions of service lines are of 
unknown material. Excavation is the gold standard for service line identification, but the costs to unearth 
non-lead service lines are prohibitively expensive and should be avoided. A two-point visual inspection 
of the service line at the meter pit would not identify lead connectors, or LSLs where the meter connects 
with a tail of another material.1 A flushed water sample measuring 2.5 ppb or higher is used in the UK 
and France to identify potential LSLs, with high positive identification rates. I propose that a two-step 
verification process be required for unknown service line identification, where both a two-point visual 
inspection and flushed sample lead is measured. In cases where the lead concentration is above 2.5 ppb 
and/or a two-point visual inspection confirms lead, the service line should be labelled as a LSL. In cases 
where the water sample is below 2.5 ppb and the two-point visual inspection returns a negative 
identification, the line should be considered non-lead. To achieve maximum effectiveness and negate 
entry into customers’ homes, the property’s hose bib could be used for water sampling. Additionally, I 
propose that a significant proportion of pre 1986 built homes with non-lead lines be tested with this 
method to achieve 95 percent confidence in the identification of non-lead service lines through records 
alone. 
I encourage the EPA to make room for new technologies to aid in water sampling. Portable, 
affordable, and easy to use water sensors with sufficient LOD could alleviate some of the burden placed 
on labs to complete water testing. New technologies are under development to this end. I would 
welcome the approval of New EPA Certified Methods as an Alternate Test Procedures for use in the field 
opposed to the requirement for all lead and copper samples to be processed in EPA certified labs. The 
new three day turnaround time will overwhelm these strapped labs. A fast track for verification and 
approval of new methods could lower costs while maintaining a high standard for positive identification 
of lead in water samples.  
Regards, 
Nick Halverson

Re: Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) 
 
Dear Dr. McClain,  
 
Louisville Water appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on EPA’s proposed improvements 
to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper (LCRI). Louisville Water 
provides safe reliable drinking water to nearly a million customers in Louisville Metro and the 
surrounding counties.  Louisville Water is committed to providing the highest quality water possible; 
our water quality consistently surpasses regulatory requirements. 
 
Lead is a well-recognized national public-health concern, and we need to continue to make progress 
in eliminating lead exposure. Eliminating lead from distribution systems is a shared responsibility that 
requires collaborative efforts by water utilities and their customers as well as a cross-section of local, 
state, and federal agencies. Louisville Water serves as an active partner with state and local agencies, 
as well as other utilities and organizations to enhance lead awareness and to identify solutions to 
reducing exposure to lead in our communities, including via drinking water. As of March 2020, 
Louisville Water had removed all known utility-owned lead service lines and began the work to 
systematically investigate unknown service-line materials. In addition, Louisville Water also 
administers a program to replace customer-owned lead and galvanized service lines at no cost to the 
customer.  
 
In finalizing the LCRI, EPA has the opportunity to revise the current proposal so that it enhances the 
protection of public health, builds public confidence in tap water, allows for efficient oversight and 
enforcement, and comports with the text of the Safe Drinking Water Act. The public is best served by 
a lead and copper regulation that is practical to implement and legally sound. Water systems are ill-
served by shifting and uncertain legal requirements, which can cause systems to spend limited 
resources inefficiently. 
 
Louisville Water supports the agency’s decision to continue with a treatment technique (TT) 
approach (cf., MCL) for addressing lead contamination. While no regulatory approach is ever perfect, 
by using a TT approach EPA can provide a variety of risk-reduction strategies that more holistically 
address this complex issue.  
 
Louisville Water offers the following comments highlighting the major concerns that we would like 
EPA to address in the final rule.   

 
 
EPA must act immediately (prior to the intended promulgation of the final LCRI) to extend the 
compliance dates for the provisions of the LCRR that EPA does not intend to continue under the LCRI. 
Louisville Water and other utilities are expending significant resources to prepare to comply with the 
LCRR by October of this year, while EPA is proposing to dramatically change both the substance and 
deadlines for all but three of the LCRR requirements. Water systems have a duty to comply with 
applicable regulations and have no assurance EPA will meet its promulgation timeline nor that 
enforcement discretion will be employed should EPA not publish the final rule prior to the LCRR 
compliance dates. 
 
Louisville Water supports EPA’s efforts to prioritize lead service-line replacements. However. 
Louisville Water recommends the agency consider suspending Tier sampling requirements during the 
mandatory replacement schedule to allow systems to prioritize replacements rather than completing 
standard monitoring. Sampling resources would be better used to identify unknowns and assist 
customers with the investigation of lead sources post-replacement or post-disturbance.  
 
Louisville Water recommends the Rule provide for systems that have replaced all service lines (or 
documented refusals) in a given Tier: 1) be able to forgo monitoring requirements for that Tier; and 
2) be allowed to request reduced monitoring. 
 
Louisville Water requests that systems be provided 30 days to complete all customer notifications 
following receipt of lab results. The three-day requirement for customer notification of all sample 
results is infeasible and provides no meaningful risk-reduction benefit.  
 
Louisville Water requests more flexibility in calculating replacement rates. Flexibility should be given 
to states to work with water systems to develop a feasible rate and schedule. Additional flexibility 
should be given to water systems with large numbers of documented refusals. Based on our LSLR 
experience, systems will have a significant number of lead service lines remaining on their inventories 
beyond the ten-year replacement deadline as a result of direct customer refusals and documented 
refusals for non-responsive customers. EPA must clarify the requirements for systems that have 
significant remaining lead service lines due to refusals. Louisville Water requests that if a customer 
refuses to replace the service line after all required attempts, water systems be allowed to remove 
that site from the replacement plan and exclude the site from replacement-rate calculations.  
 
Louisville Water recommends that EPA decouple unknowns from the replacement-rate calculation to 
allow flexibility for water systems because the management of identifying unknowns is very different 
than managing the replacement of known lead service lines.  In that regard, Louisville Water requests 
that the rule include two metrics: 1) for the rate of identification of unknowns; and 2) the rate of 
replacement of lead service lines. Louisville Water recognizes that it will take years to identify all 
private-side unknowns, making it infeasible to plan and conduct full service-line replacement within 
the same timeframe. As unknowns are identified as lead service lines or galvanized requiring 
replacement (GRR) these sites would be added to the replacement rate formula. 
 
Louisville Water also recommends decoupling GRR from the replacement rate calculation since 1) the 
lead risks from GRRs are much less than the risks from lead service lines; and 2) targeted replacement 
of galvanized service lines can be very challenging to coordinate. Louisville Water suggests allowing a 

 
longer timeframe to replace GRRs (e.g., 20 years) in order that replacements can be coordinated with 
main replacement projects and more carefully managed by construction crews and inspectors.   
 
The agency must recognize that the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) is not the appropriate law for 
managing all lead in drinking water issues. EPA should remove from the Rule all requirements related 
to premise plumbing. Including premise plumbing in service-line inventories and tier sampling pools 
overly complicates the Rule and increases the likelihood of non-compliance. Requiring water systems 
to sample from sites with lead or galvanized premise materials, where there is no (or limited) access 
or control of premise plumbing is beyond the scope of the SDWA.  
 
EPA’s proposed definition of “control” and “access” is not supported by the SDWA statutory text. The 
SDWA regulates public water systems but does not provide EPA authority to regulate other entities, 
such as businesses, landlords, or private residences. Similarly, the SDWA does not give EPA authority 
over private property or other persons, and therefore cannot be used to compel removal of privately-
owned service lines or plumbing fixtures. By requiring public water systems to inventory and conduct 
service line replacements on property that is not part of the public water system, the LCRI exceeds 
the scope of EPA’s authority under the SDWA and is therefore contrary to law. 
 
Louisville Water does not support the proposed requirement to provide pitcher filters to all 
customers in the event of three consecutive Action Level exceedances. This proposed requirement 
does very little to mitigate risks or change customer behavior regarding service line replacement, 
creates more confusion around lead risk communication, and is overly burdensome and unnecessary 
considering the costs and outcome benefits of such an approach. 
 
Louisville Water generally concurs with AWWA’s comments on the draft LCRI, except where our 
perspectives differ as reflected in this letter and the attached table. 
 
Thank you for your consideration of these comments. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Peter Goodmann, Director 
Water Quality and Research
