Dear Mr. Michael Goldberg: 
 
The Association of Missouri Cleanwater Agencies (AMCA) appreciates the opportunity to 
comment on USEPA’s proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation 
(NPDWR) for lead and copper. On December 6, 2023, EPA issued for public comment further 
proposed revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), found in 40 C.F.R. § 141.80.91), known 
as the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Although AMCA supports a robust Lead and 
Copper Rule, we have significant concerns, summarized below, about several of the proposed 
changes.  
 
AMCA comprises public water and sewer statewide. Our members are dedicated to protecting 
public health and the environment – this includes reducing the amount of lead and copper present 
in our finished drinking water. We never seek to avoid necessary and appropriate requirements. 
Instead, we embrace such requirements and work to prioritize them and obtain the funding 
necessary to comply from the public that we serve. That said, as public utilities we must provide 
public water service in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  
 
With that perspective, we are compelled to submit these comments because the proposed LCRI 
requirements create a massive regulatory and economic obligation for both public water systems 
and their ratepayers. Adding these distribution system obligations is especially burdensome on 
top of the PFAS-related treatment obligations anticipated with EPA’s pending MCLs. Lead Service 
Line (LSL) removal is particularly challenging given the need for significant public outreach and 
interaction in relation to private laterals. US EPA estimates that there are around 9.2 million LSLs 
in the United States, which the AWWA estimates could cost over $90 billion to replace. Below we 
explain why we believe that the inventory obligation and removal of any LSLs that are found may 
be a major challenge both administratively and financially and will lead to significant conflict 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2  
 
 
2 
 
between EPA, the States, and water utilities as they struggle to define the universe of LSLs and 
complete the mandated replacements. 
I. 
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement Within 10 Years is Both Financially and 
Practically Impossible.  A Phased-In Deadline Based Upon System Lead Levels is 
Both Necessary and Appropriate 
 
The 10-Year Timeline 
 
The proposed LCRI would require water utilities to complete 100% lead service line replacement 
(LSLR) within 10 years. 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84882 (Dec. 6, 2023).  While there are alternative 
timelines for (1) systems with a high proportion of lead and GRR service lines in their distribution 
system relative to their total number of households served and (2) systems that would otherwise 
be required to replace greater than 10,000 service lines per year under the proposed 10-year 
replacement requirement, Id. at 84913, the ten-year timeframe is woefully inadequate.   
 
Anytime we talk in terms of “all” in relation to 50,000 water systems, spread across the country, 
we should pause for a reality check.  We should especially pause when a significant number of 
the LSLs to be replaced have not even been identified.  We should further pause when faced with 
a potential price tag of upwards of $100 billion dollars. 
 
EPA estimates that there are more than 50,000 water systems nationwide.  It is simply impractical 
for such a large number of systems to make significant distribution system changes in a ten-year 
period.  This is especially the case given the (1) fact that many/most of the LSLs have not been 
identified, (2) cost of such replacements, (3) need for public outreach around utility-owned LSL 
replacement, and (4) need for outreach and coordination with homeowners across the country 
regarding replacement of their customer-owned LSLs.  Such an historic and unprecedented effort 
would come during the worst period in modern history for trying to plan, finance, bid, and deliver 
projects.  There is simply not enough engineering or construction talent available to do the work 
- even if we could fund it. 
 
Many of our water systems are struggling right now with basic water availability, especially during 
the winter months.  Cold weather each of the last several winters has taken a major toll on water 
systems leading to numerous water main breaks and boil water advisories.  These have been 
especially prevalent across the southern United States and into the mid-Atlantic.  For example, 
much of the District of Columbia had a boil water notice in January of 2024 due to cold weather-
related line breaks. 
 
US EPA has for several decades made a priority of imposing incredibly expensive (and in many 
ways, counter-productive) sewer system improvement mandates on local governments 
nationwide.  As a result of this sewer-first enforcement approach, local resources have been 
forced to the sewer side, often at the expense of water utilities’ ability to raise revenue.  Those 
deferred investments are now coming home to roost for water systems.  On top of general system 
needs, thousands of water systems face historically expensive PFAS-related capital upgrades 
and incredible annual operation and maintenance costs for those facilities.  Adding a LSL 
replacement obligation over the next 10 years on top of these historic financial challenges is a 
bridge too far financially and from a project delivery perspective. 
 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 3  
 
 
3 
 
A one-size-fits-all LSL removal period will have water systems with low lead levels vying for the 
same funding and engineering/contracting resources as water systems with much higher lead 
levels.  This makes no sense whatsoever. 
 
A more logical approach to LSL replacement, is for USEPA to adopt a phased approach where 
utilities with higher P90 lead levels have earlier deadlines to replace their LSLs while utilities with 
lower P90 numbers defer their replacements.  Such an approach will allow EPA, the States, and 
utilities to prioritize available federal and State grant/loan resources as well as engineering and 
construction resources to water systems with higher lead levels.    
 
We specifically recommend that the final rule authorize the states to establish phased-in deadlines 
for their water systems.  Any water system above the 10 ppb lead action level must remove their 
LSLs within 10 years of the effective date of the rule.  Utilities with P90 values below the 10 ppt 
would be prioritized based upon their levels for LSL removal, generally not to exceed a 20-year 
compliance period.   We believe that 20 years is a more realistic (albeit, still very challenging) 
compliance period.  Significantly, such an implementation period will allow water utilities to 
coordinate LSL removal with other system upgrades both getting and giving economies of scale 
to water system projects.  This will reduce the financial burden and system planning disruption 
that will otherwise result from a crude, 10-year LSL removal deadline. 
 
This phased approach, coupled with a one-third reduction in the lead action level, will ensure 
additional protection going forward for all Americans who receive public drinking water, from day 
one of the Rule’s effective date. 
 
II. 
Lead Service Line Replacement Must Only Include Public Lead Service Lines. 
 
The concept of LSL replacement must be revised to include replacement of only utility-owned 
LSLs. EPA lacks the authority to require public water utilities to replace privately-owned water 
infrastructure located on private property.  There are significant legal questions about whether 
public entities can even spend public funds for this private purpose.   
 
EPA cannot withhold credit for a public side lead service line replacement unless water systems 
undertake illegally impermissible action on private property.  EPA needs to address the legality of 
requiring public water systems to replace private lead service lines before imposing such a 
requirement in the LCRI. 
 
Rather than illegally seeking to force public water systems to make improvements to private 
indoor plumbing, EPA should give water utilities a benefit for each full LSL replacement that is 
performed.  For example, a utility could be given more time to complete LSL removals (within our 
suggested 20 year from the rule effective date compliance period) if they meet certain private side 
LSL removal goals (such as 30 or 40 percent associated with public LSL removal). 
 
We also question whether EPA’s assumed cost to implement the proposed rule has included 
private side LSL replacement costs.  If “yes,” we would like to know what EPA estimates those 
private costs to be and the basis for those estimates.   
 
Revise the Definition of “Under the Control of the Water System” to Exclude Customer-Owned 
LSLs 
 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4  
 
 
4 
 
Relatedly, we disagree with the proposed LCRI rule requirement that full LSL replacement is 
required when lines are “under the control” of the water system. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The term 
“under the control” of the water system is defined as wherever a water system has adequate 
access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full-service line replacement or 
replacement of the lead connector. Id. at 84920.  
 
This definition is impermissibly overbroad.  The definition must clarify that water utilities are not 
obligated to replace customer-owned LSLs as EPA cannot legally require public utilities to make 
changes to private property. The key aspect should be ownership. The present proposed 
incentives are written for a complete replacement (with customer agreement) so that water 
systems do not get credit for LSL replacement if it doesn’t include the customer’s side. We believe 
this is an illegal provision and although we support full replacements, our members cannot be 
required to go on private property and replace indoor plumbing. Those private side replacements 
should instead be driven by federal funding efforts and partial replacements should be given the 
credit they are due, considering they take great effort and expense to identify and accomplish.  
Instead, and as noted above, water utilities should be given a benefit if they achieve a certain 
goal for customer-owned LSL replacement as part of LSL replacement of publicly-owned water 
distribution lines. 
 
Lining and Coating Service Lines Should Qualify for Extended Removal Deadlines 
 
As noted above, removing “all” LSLs in the country in ten years is a shocking financial and 
practical proposition.  Rather than requiring removal, we believe EPA should allow a range of 
effective lead reduction approaches, such as lining or coating technologies to count equally as 
LSL replacements.  At a minimum, lined or coated service lines should qualify for deferred removal 
schedules.  
 
Lined or coated service lines immediately control lead from entering drinking water. EPA’s 
inventory and full service line replacement requirements in the LCRI will impose substantial costs 
on water systems that must simultaneously investigate unknown lead status service lines and 
connectors, finance capital projects associated with replacing known or discovered lead and GRR 
service lines and lead connectors and assemble the resources and personnel to replace all the 
service lines requiring replacement. 
 
Granting water systems an additional period to complete the replacements of coated or lined 
service lines, e.g. for the service life of the coating or lining product, will lower the personnel and 
financial burdens of the LCRI on water systems while immediately reducing lead from drinking 
water as water systems will dedicate resources to those services lines most likely posing a risk of 
lead exposure. 
 
III. 
Galvanized Replacement Service Lines. 
 
Definition of “Galvanized Requiring Replacements” 
 
Under the proposed LCRI, galvanized service lines that have ever been downstream of LSL 
require replacement (GRR). 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The EPA defines galvanized requiring 
replacement service lines as a “galvanized service line that currently is or ever was downstream 
of a lead service line or is currently downstream in the direction of flow of a lead status unknown 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5  
 
 
5 
 
service line.” Id. 85054 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.2). If the water system cannot demonstrate the 
galvanized service line was never downstream of a lead line, the line is a galvanized requiring 
replacement service line. Id. 
 
The EPA’s proposed definition of GRRs is unreasonable and counterproductive.  The definition 
will likely result in water systems having to replace all galvanized service lines within the same 
10-year period they must replace LSLs.  We think the presumption that a galvanized line requires 
replacement is too strong.  Rather than requiring the water system to know that there was never 
a LSL above the galvanized line, a water utility should be able to conclude, based upon available 
information, that there is no information that there was ever a LSL above the galvanized line.  In 
those cases, the water system should be able to prioritize the lining/coating/removal of galvanized  
lines over a longer compliance period – say 20 years.  Again, the longer period is absolutely 
critical if water systems are to see economies of scale with other water distribution system work 
in conjunction with LSL and galvanized line removal.  This is especially the case for water utilities 
with P90 numbers that are well below the proposed 10 ppb action level.  We continue to believe 
that the states should be given the authority to prioritize LSL (and GRR) removal. 
 
The Lead Connector Threshold Should be 36 Inches and Unknown Connectors Assumed to Be 
36 Inches or Smaller 
 
We disagree that lead connectors greater than two feet in length should be considered service 
lines. See 88 id. at 84919, 85083. Connectors greater than 24 inches have been sold to utilities 
and the EPA does not present evidence suggesting significantly higher lead concentrations 
resulting from a lead connector that is 36 inches as opposed to 24 inches in length. If EPA is 
going to impose an arbitrary connector length, it should be at least 36 inches.  Moreover, there 
should be a presumption that connectors of unknown size and composition are less than three 
feet in length. 
 
IV. 
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes Remains a Monumental Task for Utilities. 
 
It might be one thing for EPA to impose a 10-year LSL removal requirement if we already 
understood how many LSLs there were and where they are located.  That would allow us to better 
estimate the cost of removal and time needed.  Instead, EPA is shooting blind in that they don’t 
even have the benefit of the existing LSL inventories that won’t come due until October 16, 2024.  
Almost all of those inventories will be derived using predictive tools with only a small percentage 
of LSLs actually having been ground-truthed. 
 
The fact remains that it is a spring for most water systems to meet October 16, 2024 initial 
inventory deadline.  We suspect that hundreds, if not thousands of water systems will miss the 
deadline.  It will take many years following the development of the initial deadlines to ground truth 
where LSLs actually are in each water system.   
 
Accordingly, we request that EPA clarify what, if any, inventory update requirements are 
contemplated between the initial inventory under the LCRI and baseline inventories in the 
proposed LCRI. We suggest the EPA suspend inventory updates between the two deadlines to 
allow water systems an opportunity to develop a complete and accurate baseline inventory in light 
of the substantial difficulty most water systems will have categorizing the material composition 
and location of their service lines and connectors. Alternatively, the EPA should consider 
eliminating the initial inventory requirement and allow water systems to dedicate all of their 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 6  
 
 
6 
 
resources into developing complete and accurate baseline inventories available to the public by 
2027. 
 
Baseline Inventory Requirements 
 
We request the EPA to reconsider requiring water systems to investigate connector locations and 
composition in its baseline inventory. The proposed rule would require water systems to remove 
lead connectors upon discovery. 88 Fed. Reg. at 85066 (Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.84(e)). The 
EPA’s justification for not requiring water systems to find and replace all lead connectors as part 
of the full-service line replacement requirement is that “regular progress towards lead connector 
replacement is made in coordination with other activities, such as planned infrastructure work, 
while resources are prioritized for replacement of all LSLs and GRR service lines as quickly as 
feasible.” Id. at 84919.  
 
EPA noted that most lead connectors will be replaced under the proposed rule because “all lead 
connectors that are attached to a lead or GRR service line would be replaced by the end of the 
mandatory service line replacement program.” Id. In addition, EPA “also expects that many lead 
connectors may be connected to aging water mains and likely to undergo replacement with 
routine main replacement activities in coming years,” especially because EPA estimates that any 
given lead connector “is expected to be a minimum of 41 years old by the LCRI compliance date 
in 2027” and the “average service life of cast iron, ductile iron, and asbestos-cement pipe is 40 
years.” Id. EPA thus acknowledged that water systems will encounter and replace the vast majority 
of lead connectors during routine maintenance as a result of aging infrastructure or as a result of 
its mandatory service line replacement requirements. 
 
At the same time, EPA acknowledges that short lead connectors pose a lower lead exposure risk 
than LSL and GRR service lines that are significantly longer. Id. at 84919 (“EPA expects that 
galvanized lines downstream of lead connectors may contribute less lead into drinking water than 
those that were downstream of much longer LSLs”). EPA therefore prioritized service line 
replacement. Because EPA accepts that its requirement for water systems to replace lead 
connectors upon discovery will address the vast majority of lead connectors in a water system 
and acknowledges that lead connectors pose less of a health risk than lead service lines, we 
request EPA to reconsider its decision to include connectors in the baseline inventory. 
 
Removing the investigation of connectors from the baseline inventory removes expensive and 
laborious investigations into the location and composition of connectors when those resources 
are best spent identifying, locating, and removing lead and GRR service lines. Water systems 
reporting the composition and location of encountered connectors and the number of replaced 
lead connectors will still provide valuable information to the water system and the public about 
the location and composition of connectors in a water system and the probability that lead 
connectors are present. 
 
Validation Pool Requirements 
 
The proposed regulation instructs water systems to develop a “validation pool” consisting of all 
lines categorized as non-lead minus the non-lead lines that already replaced LSL or GRR lines, 

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 7  
 
 
7 
 
non-lead lines already visually inspected at two points along the line, or non-lead lines with 
documentation demonstrating their composition. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84935, 85063 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 141.84(b)(5)). The rule would require water systems to randomly and visually inspect as 
many service lines in the validation pool as necessary to ensure a “95% confidence level” that the 
observed proportion of non-lead lines validated is representative of the larger validation pool 
within ten years of the rule’s publication and seven years of submitting baseline inventories. Id.; 
Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA 815-
R-23-003 at 24-25 (Nov. 2023). 
 
The timing of this LSL/GRR inventory requirement reinforces the impracticality of the ten-year 
LSL/GRR removal requirement. 
 
EPA is currently calculating the number of visual inspections of lines necessary to ensure that 
lines categorized as non-lead are in fact non-lead by assuming a standard normal distribution and 
an “expected sample proportion” of 0.5. EPA assumed the expected sample proportion “to be 50 
percent, meaning that 50 percent of the non-lead service lines investigated are expected to be 
confirmed as non-lead.” Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements, EPA 815-R-23-003 at 25 (Nov. 2023). EPA acknowledged “this proportion will most 
likely be much higher since most non-lead lines will end up being confirmed as nonlead.” Id. EPA 
nonetheless maintained the proportion at 0.5 because, “an assumption of 0.50 provides the most 
conservative (or largest) sample size…meaning that any system validating this number of lines 
will be guaranteed to have met or exceeded the minimum number for statistical significance 
regardless of the true sample proportion.” Id. 
 
We question why EPA does not simply stick with the 95% confidence and allow each water utility’s 
consultant to develop a testing program that will achieve that level of confidence for the utility’s 
list.  Why does EPA pick a very aggressive 95th percent confidence level and then structure the 
rule to force an even higher level of confidence? 
 
The method for determining the number of visual inspections necessary is also not particularly 
well explained. At a minimum, EPA should clarify its validation calculations, e.g. what data it used, 
if any, to determine the expected sample proportion, what the relevant comparison EPA is making 
between the validated lines and the validation pool and what that significance of that comparison 
is, and where EPA derived its formulas for determining the appropriate sample size and provide 
citations. 
 
EPA should also assume in its sample proportion that water systems will correctly assess line 
status more than 50% of the time given its concurrent requirements to investigate lead status 
unknown lines. As EPA has explained the sample proportion, EPA is essentially assuming water 
systems will be no better at determining service line composition than flipping a coin. In light of 
the other significant investigation costs imposed by the rule, EPA should reconsider this 
assumption because it should significantly lower the number of validations water systems must 
make.  
 
We support EPA’s decision to exclude service lines which water systems have confirmed as non-
lead through records investigations from the validation pool. Id. at 84935, 85063.  

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 8  
 
 
8 
 
We also request the EPA to consider delaying the date the inventory validation must be submitted 
to better align with the categorization of lead status unknown service lines. Water systems must 
identify the material of all lead status unknown service lines within ten years from the compliance 
date. Id. at 85063. Conversely, the validation study must be submitted no later than ten years 
from the rule’s publication date or seven years from the compliance date. Id. at 85063. If water 
systems submit inventory validations before all unknown lines are categorized, then the validation 
pool will not include some lines categorized as “non-lead.” Allowing the validation to occur at least 
after all lead status unknown lines have been categorized will create a validation pool 
representative of all of the non-lead categorized service lines and provide water systems three 
more years to validate their inventories. 
 
Public Disclosure of LSL Addresses In Service Line Inventory 
 
The LCRI, like the LCRR, continues to require that a water system’s annual inventory updates be 
publicly accessible. Although the LCRR includes location identifiers (street, intersection, 
landmark, etc.) served by each LSL, the LCRI states utilities must include a street address with 
each service line and connector. Id. at 84936. We continue to disagree with the need to publicly 
publish a list of homes served by LSLs. Each home will get an annual reminder of this fact. Any 
home that tests for lead will receive its results – there is no need or clear authority for the EPA to 
mandate that this specific information must be made publicly available.  We especially think it is 
irresponsible to include unknown LSL in these lists. 
 
V. 
Lowering the Lead Action Level will be significant in many states. 
 
EPA is proposing to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L. 88 Fed. Reg. 84880 while 
eliminating the lead trigger level that was introduced under the 2021 LCRR. If the AL is exceeded, 
the system must inform the public (Tier 1 public notification within 24 hrs of learning of 
exceedance) and reduce lead exposure while concurrently working to replace all lead pipes (for 
example, installing/adjusting corrosion control treatment). Id. 
 
Lowering the Action Level from 15 ug/L to 10 ug/L will be a big deal in some states with some 
states asserting that the number of systems exceeding the new action level could double.  This 
is likely to be the case for a number of smaller systems.   
 
We take no position on the reduction in the action level.  However, we do believe that P90 
numbers should be a basis for phasing in LSL/GRR removal requirements and that the states are 
in the best position to prioritize LSL/GRR removal.  States are also in the best position to work 
with water systems to mitigate lead levels pending LSL removal.   
 
VI. 
We Disagree With the Requirement to Make Point-of-Use Filters/Pitchers Available 
to All Households After Three Action Level Exceedances.    
 
Under the LCRI, water systems with three lead action level exceedances would be required to 
conduct additional outreach to consumers and make pitcher filters or point-of-use devices certified 
to reduce lead available to all consumers. See id. at 84954.  
 
Providing such filters/pitchers will be overkill in that it will scare many residents not served by 
LSL/GRRs into thinking their tap water is not safe.  That loss of confidence can be difficult, if not 
impossible, to overcome to the long-term detriment of the residents and the utility.   

AMCA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 9  
 
 
9 
 
Moreover, distributing filters/pitchers will be a massive administrative and financial task.  The 
filters/pitchers would have to be provided to each residential and non-residential location served 
by the public water supply.   
 
We are also very concerned that residents would not properly replace the filters and could end up 
concentrating lead and copper beyond what would otherwise be present in their drinking water. 
 
VII. 
Utilities Must Be Allowed to Invalidate a Homeowner Sample That Does not Follow 
Proper Collection Procedures. 
 
Under the proposed rule, a water utility could not invalidate a homeowner’s sample even if the 
sample was not taken in accordance with LCRI requirements.  This is unacceptable.  All data 
must meet applicable QA/QC/Sampling requirements.  At a minimum, the rule should give the 
water utility the discretion to use a non-conforming sample but should not mandate the use of 
such samples. 
 
VIII. 
Water Systems Must Be Able to Select Homes From Lower Tiers Where Not Enough 
Tier 1 Homeowners Are Willing to Participate. 
 
The LCRI must clarify that water systems which, despite best, good faith efforts, cannot attract 
enough Tier 1 homeowners to participate in sampling, can use lower tier homes. 
 
Otherwise, the water system will be in non-compliance due to causes (lack of homeowner 
willingness to participate) which are beyond its control. 
 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
Our member utilities work tirelessly to provide high quality finished drinking water for our 
customers in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  We appreciate EPA’s consideration of our 
concerns about the practicality and affordability of the requirements we object to above.  We also 
appreciate EPA’s consideration of our suggested improvements to the proposed rule. In 
particular, we strongly believe that a final rule needs to provide additional time for LSL/GRR 
removal and that a state-directed phased approach over twenty years from the rule’s effective 
date, is warranted. 
Sincerely, 
       
 
F. Paul Calamita  
General Counsel 
  
  
C: AMCA Members

RE: Greater Cincinnati Water Works’ (GCWW) Comments on Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI), Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
The Greater Cincinnati Water Works, a department of the City of Cincinnati, serves drinking water to 
about 1.1 million people in the Greater Cincinnati region. GCWW has an old distribution system (over 
200 years old) and has lead service lines and other sources of lead in plumbing systems that are typical 
of a system of our size and age.  
 
We appreciate the opportunity to comment on the proposed LCRI regulation. The comments that 
accompany this letter are brought forward from the perspective of a large utility that is a progressive 
leader in protecting public health, including addressing the issue of lead in water. Our comments also 
speak to our environmental and social justice concerns when implementing community solutions and to 
the known challenges that small and medium utilities face that make it harder for them to secure 
funding and implement solutions.  
 
We have experienced first-hand the cost, time, and effort that is needed to engage in full lead service 
line replacement in a meaningful way. We are extremely fortunate that we have the personnel, initial 
funding, and support from our elected officials and public that is needed to implement a lead line 
removal and public engagement program. Unfortunately, many large utilities will not have the support 
to implement such a program, and smaller and more disadvantaged systems will not have the ability to 
comply with the LCRI as proposed, leading to serious questions of environmental justice.  
 
We agree that the issue of lead in drinking water can only be solved by removing the sources of lead, 
mainly lead pipes. Doing that takes a partnership between the utility and private property owners. To 
that end we have developed an aggressive public education program about lead in the water and a 
program to remove lead service lines (LSL) that includes GCWW paying for full removals, both on the 

2 
 
public and private side. Our program has been recognized by many organizations including the 
Government Accountability Office as best in class for public water systems. In 2018 our program caught 
the attention of former EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt who visited us and spent time learning about the 
program. More information about our program can be found at our website www.lead.mygcww.org.  
 
GCWW agrees that a goal needs to be set to achieve lead line replacements. However, the required rate 
of replacement, whether in 10, 15, or 20 years, should also consider the total cost and the impact on 
water and wastewater rates. In recent years, utility bill affordability has been affecting a broader range 
of households leaving them vulnerable to shutoff and loss of water access. While we understand the 
sense of urgency and the benefits of replacing lead services lines within 10 years, a 15-year replacement 
pace would enable utilities to maintain more affordable rates than with a 10-year pace while still 
achieving complete line removal. Like our situation, many water systems will have significant challenges 
obtaining approval for the multi-year, double-digit rate increases to complete this work in 10 years.  
 
Likewise, while we agree that more lead communication is needed, significant communications 
resources need to be targeted towards encouraging customers to remove their lead service lines.  
The required broad, untargeted communications—such as costly direct mailing to the entire customer 
base—on the one hand tend to be ignored, and on the other hand run the risk of undermining public 
trust in the water utility and the water that it produces. This public confidence is critical to supporting 
rate increases needed to cover costs of the lead replacement program, utility operation, and 
investments to maintain the infrastructure into the future. Limiting messaging requirements to 
customers directly affected by a risk of lead would better target efforts and reduce the risk of excessive, 
unnecessary messaging and alarming the entire community.  
 
GCWW is concerned for small and medium size water utilities and how they will meet these 
requirements. As a large utility, we have significant concerns with completing this work in 10 years and 
we have more funding, resources, technology, and experience in strategizing, resolving large problems, 
and implementing system-wide solutions. Small and medium size utilities often do not have this same 
expertise and bonuses. In many cases, smaller systems may look to larger systems for assistance or even 
spark conversations of more regionalism to address this. More guidance and understanding of these 
additional challenges should be provided, and solutions for this should be considered and handled in a 
timeframe that extends beyond 10 years.  
 
Lastly, we are frustrated that the rule is silent on assisting utilities to address affordability and social 
justice issues. The rule acknowledges that they exist yet is silent on solutions for these problems and 
leaves it up to utilities and cities to address them on their own. The topic of service line replacement 
requirements raises several very serious questions about affordability, especially in low income and 
disadvantaged areas such as those found in many older cities such as Cincinnati. The Country has known 
for decades the differences in public health dangers for families in disadvantaged communities versus 
those living in other communities that have had more opportunities to flourish. While EPA continues to 
speak to assistance to disadvantaged communities and the need to address water system challenges in 
communities already suffering from ongoing inequities; it’s not enough to expect water systems, that do 
not have the appropriate staffing or history of community relationships, to figure this out on their own 
and act in a manner to resolve these long-lasting injustices.  It would be more helpful if guidance, 

3 
 
templates, examples, messaging, and models of how this can be achieved are made available to utilities 
to adapt in their communities to then build trust and implement solutions to directly impact social and 
environmental issues and injustices in disadvantaged communities.  
 
Thank you and please contact me if you have any questions about the attached detailed comments. 
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Cathy Bernardino Bailey
Executive Director
Greater Cincinnati Water Works

4 
 
Greater Cincinnati Water Work’s Comments on the Proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements 
 
 
 
1) Utilities need assurances of delay in LCRR requirements. 
We must stress the need for the agency to take immediate action to stay or delay the requirements 
contained in the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) except for the inventory and public notice 
requirements as proposed in this LCRI. While the intention of the Agency may be to delay most LCRR 
requirements to allow utilities to focus on getting the inventory correct, utilities need assurances that 
these requirements will actually be delayed. Absent an action from the agency, utilities must still assume 
the October 16, 2024, compliance deadline stands. Failing to meet the LCRR requirements, if they still 
stand, will result in violations which undermine the trust in both the utility and the EPA. 
 
2) A 15-year replacement rate would be more affordable and achievable. 
In the proposed LCRI, the agency proposes a 10-year replacement mandate for all water systems except 
for systems which have an extreme number or proportion of lead lines. While we agree that there needs 
to be a mandate for complete replacement, a 15-year mandate would be much more affordable for 
most systems with even a moderate number of lead lines. For GCWW, we have approximately 37,000 
lines left that are either full or partial lead lines. To replace those lines within 10 years would cost an 
estimated $200M over this time period not accounting for inflation of labor and material costs. 
Absorbing that cost in such a short time period would lead to a significant rate. Federal and state 
assistance, although appreciated, fall woefully short of this need. For example, over the five-year period 
of the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, Ohio will receive $355M in total for lead service line replacement. 
About half of that funding is in the form of loans, the rest in grants. So, in total only $177M will be 
available for water system grants. This is less than the need for Cincinnati alone. When one considers 
the needs of Cleveland, Columbus, Toledo, Akron, Dayton and the numerous other medium and small 
systems in the state, the assistance fails to meet the need. The remainder of this expense will need to 
come from water rates. Stretching this cost over a 15-year period would spread the cost over a longer 
period and reduce the rate increase per year needed to cover this cost.  
As proposed, GCWW estimates achieving full compliance by 12/31/2037 would cost approx. $16.9 
million annually in addition to our current lead line replacement program. This amount represents 
approx. 9.5% of our annual revenues. The utility is already working to increase rates for significant new 
costs such as power, wage inflation, and aging infrastructure. A 15-year compliance program would 
extend the deadline to 12/31/2042 and would lower the City’s estimated annual cost increase to $11.8 
million. In addition, scheduled rate increases from the sewer utility and other charges such as 
stormwater and trash/recycling put additional strains on the affordability of the local “water bill.” 
The additional revenue needs mentioned above only address increases for lead line replacements. Over 
the past several years utilities across the country have also experienced steep increases in chemicals, 
power, materials, and labor as well. In addition, sewer and stormwater increases continue to outpace 

5 
 
inflation and they are also reflected on the same bill as drinking water services making these bills 
unaffordable for many Americans.  
 
The EPA should also consider that these costs will be borne by utility rate payers at the same time as the 
very costly PFAS regulation will require a similar level of spending to install and operate new treatment. 
This will drive rates up even further which will make basic water and wastewater services unaffordable 
to many as well as decreasing utilities’ capacity to make the normal investments into maintaining the 
systems, resulting in a decreased reliability and increased failures in drinking water systems.  
 
In several places in the rule’s preamble, the Agency makes references to cities like Flint, Benton Harbor 
and Newark which have been able to replace lead lines at a very accelerated rate to show that 
aggressive replacement rate is possible. However, it is also worth noting that these communities 
received significant state and federal financial as well as technical assistance to accomplish their removal 
goals. This level of assistance will not be available to other utilities during the LCRI so comparisons to 
those cases are not fully applicable.  
 
GCWW is also very concerned about the availability of contractors and plumbers because of our recent 
experiences. In 2016 through 2019 we held multiple plumber and contractor outreach events, and we 
continually tried to recruit contractors to bid on our jobs. In the current one-off lead replacement 
program (single household replacement), we perform about 500 replacements per year. Even with this 
amount of work, we are only able to attract six qualified contractors to submit bids for the various 
projects in this program. In addition, we also remove lead lines as part of our robust water main 
replacement program in which we perform around 700 replacements per year. In the water main 
replacement program, we also typically see six contractors, many of which are the same as the one-off 
program. This lack of contractor capacity is a limiting factor to us being able to do more than the total 
1,200 replacements per year. Despite our recruitment efforts we have not been able to influence more 
contractors to join our program. In speaking with other utilities in Ohio and across the country, this 
experience is common. With a 10-year replacement program, we will need to perform 3,700 
replacements per year, which is more than triple our current rate. This work greatly surpasses the 
capacity of our bidding contractors.  
 
3) Customer refusals should be reduced from the inventory for all regulatory requirements if 
replacement is offered every year. 
GCWW appreciates that the Agency recognizes that some customers will refuse offers from a utility to 
replace the customer-owned portion of lead service lines even when the utility completely covers 
replacement cost. In our system, we frequently experience 30 to 50 percent of our customers are either 
unresponsive or refuse to allow us to replace their lead line even though we pay all the cost for 
replacement. We have a communications program consisting of many points of contact with the 
customer, and we handle all contracting and logistics with the replacement.  Customers only need to 
give us a right of entry to allow us access to their property and into their homes to allow us to do the 
work. We continue to look for ways to overcome this opposition, but it is clear that we will not get 100 
percent of those lead lines replaced if the customers will not cooperate.  
 

6 
 
The LCRI does recognize this limitation and does have provisions to allow customer refusals. However, it 
is not clear in the rule how those will be treated with respect to achieving the replacements over 10 
years and also in the case where utilities can avoid studying and changing corrosion control treatment if 
all replacements are accomplished in 5 years. GCWW suggests that in the situation of refusals, after so 
many attempts, the refusal is counted in another/new category and not still considered as part of the 
active inventory nor considered in the decision to change corrosion control treatment. The utility would 
continue to make annual outreach efforts after the 10-year period and offer to replace the lead service 
line when the water account is switched to a different person.  
 
4) 24 Hour notice of action level exceedance should be carefully targeted to affected customers only. 
GCWW is extremely concerned that the notice required within 24 hours of a lead action level 
exceedance will cause public concern and loss of confidence in the water if the message including the 
mode of delivery is not well targeted. It is believed that it was the intent of Congress for EPA to 
determine a level of lead “that has the potential to have serious adverse effects on human health as a 
result of short-term exposure.”  However, the 10 or 15 ppb 90th percentile is not a health-based 
standard, and this measurement is even further complicated by the fact that the Agency may change the 
calculation to include a different pool of homes than has been historically used for sampling. The 90th 
percentile level was set as a metric considering what a well operated system could achieve given a 
sample pool defined by locations with half of the locations being served by a lead service line, and half of 
the locations having leaded solder.  The Agency has not presented any data, that we are aware of, 
demonstrating that action level is a level that presents significant risk for short-term exposure. 
 
Therefore, it is imperative that the language and mode of delivery be carefully crafted to be informative, 
but not cause public panic. This is especially important in the first few years where an action level 
exceedance could more likely be caused by the change in the sampling pool than an actual change in the 
water quality.  
 
When crafting the notice and delivery requirements, we are aware and believe the Agency recognizes 
that most Tier 1 notice requirements for other contaminants are made to warn about risks that are of 
immediate, acute health consequences such as microbial pathogens or chemicals at levels that pose 
immediate public health concerns for the entire population or sub populations.  In the case of lead, 
exposure is limited to certain situations which can be defined and are not applicable to all or most of the 
population especially if sampling is performed only at locations served by lead service lines. Targeted 
notice requirements would be more effective in encouraging the affected audience to take action to 
reduce risks of lead exposure and reduce unnecessary loss of confidence in unaffected households. 
 
5) Filter distribution targeted to affected consumers avoids excessive cost and filter shortages. 
GCWW agrees that providing pitchers and filters certified to the ANSI/NSF 53 standard for lead removal 
is an appropriate precaution to protect affected consumers after a disruption in the water line such as a 
partial or full lead service line replacement. GCWW has provided certified pitcher filters for many years 
in these situations and was one of the first utilities in the country to do so. Pitcher filters are very easy 
for the consumer to use, and they are implementable in most situations.  
 

7 
 
It has also been our experience that there are a very limited number of companies that sell pitchers 
certified to remove lead (we only know of three) and we have found these filters to be difficult to 
procure in quantities that we need for some water main projects. For example, in the Fall of 2023, our 
inventory of filters was extremely low because our contracted supplier (Protect Plus with the DuPont 
filter) no longer provided filters. We then put a contract out to bid for filters and only one company 
supplied a bid. We awarded the contract to that company and even with the new contract, the bidder 
was unable to provide the quantity that we needed for several months. Because of our experience we 
are extremely concerned about the availability of filters when water utilities across the country are also 
purchasing them in large quantities under the LCRI.  
 
We have also been very frustrated that we cannot find a pitcher filter that is manufactured in the United 
States. 
 
Although we support filters for line disturbances, it is very wasteful and ineffective to provide filters to 
everyone in the event of several action level exceedances. The Agency clearly states that 10 ppb is not a 
health-related standard, rather it is a trigger to further examine corrosion control treatment. In addition, 
page 84952 of the LCRI preamble, the Agency states “EPA expects that a recommendation that all or a 
subset of consumers use a filter would lead to inconsistencies, confusion, and possibly a reduction in 
confidence in tap water even where lead is not present or remains very low.”   
 
The cost of making filters available and providing filters to everyone is exorbitant and can even exceed 
the cost-of-service line replacements. As discussed earlier, GCWW estimates achieving full compliance in 
10 years or by 12/31/2037 would cost approx. $16.9 million annually in addition to our current program. 
Under our current assumptions, the cost of pitchers and filters alone represents approximately $6.6 
million or 40% of the total program cost annually. 
 
The following table outlines the costs for supplying filters and replacement cartridges in our system with 
240,000 connections.  
 
Shown in the table, the cost of the filters and cartridges is equivalent to the cost of replacing 3,460 lead 
lines which is extraordinary considering that we estimate that we would be required to replace 3,700 
lead lines with the annual 10% removal requirement. These costs consider 1) cost of the filters and 
replacement cartridges only at near current pricing, 2) a broad assumption of administrative costs such 
as postage to mail the filters or staff time to deliver, 3) staff time administering the program and keeping 
track of the program, 4) storage/warehousing of the stock, 5) providing multiple filters and cartridges to 
apartment buildings, etc.   Considering the cost of those items, the cost of providing filters will exceed 
the cost-of-service line replacements yet provide little if any public health benefit.

Even if we were to only provide the filters/cartridges upon request, if half of our customers requested 
filters, then that would be equivalent to 1,730 lead line replacements. If a quarter of our customers 
requested filters, then that would be the equivalent of 865 lead lines replaced, etc.  
 
Clearly, the cost of this requirement greatly exceeds any health benefit and will reduce the funds that 
could otherwise be spent on service line replacement or other programs to actually improve public 
health.   
 
6) Grandfather school and childcare sampling needs to be expanded to recognize past efforts. 
In 2016, as part of our overall lead program, GCWW began an outreach and assistance program and 
offered free testing for schools and childcare facilities in our system. In our school program, we offer to 
individually meet with the school, develop a sampling plan, provide bottles for the school staff to 
sample, provide the school with the results in writing along with suggested follow-up actions and post 
the data on our website for complete transparency. The sampling plan consists of sampling every water 
outlet in the school, not just five outlets as required in the LCRI. This occurred after tours of the schools 
revealed dishes, cups, utensils, and other personal items were near many sinks, indicating regular use of 
sinks for food preparation and consumption. In our program we have worked with 109 schools. Much of 
the historic sampling at our schools was done in partnership with the State of Ohio’s Facility Commission 

9 
 
which offered a grant for schools to replace fixtures at sample locations that tested above 15 ppb and 
follow up sampling was offered after the fixture replacement.  
 
Likewise, GCWW has also reached out to licensed childcare facilities in our service area and has offered 
similar services. For childcare facility testing, GCWW encourages but does not require posting of the 
results on our website to avoid any discouragement of the facility owner to participate for fear of losing 
current or future business. Like the school sampling, we encouraged sampling out of every outlet in the 
facility, not just two as required in the LCRI. Much of this program was also performed in partnership 
with the Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (OEPA) and the Ohio Department of Jobs and Family 
Services (ODJFS) which received a WINN grant to replace fixtures that tested high for lead. Follow up 
sampling is performed after the fixtures are replaced.  
 
Because our sampling was performed at all locations in schools and childcare facilities and grants were 
available to remove problem fixtures, these schools and childcare facilities that sampled should be 
grandfathered for the purposes of the five-year testing in the LCRI. This would be an action-based 
approach to grandfathering in addition to the assumed subjective 2021 date listed in the proposed rule.  
 
GCWW is also aware of some states like Massachusetts which also performed some aggressive sampling 
in their schools proactively before even the LCRR was proposed.  
 
With respect to the grandfathering, GCWW suggests that the 2021 date be kept as a default, but that 
the states be able to grandfather back to 2014 when the Lead Contamination Control Act (LCCA) was in 
effect whenever a more active sampling was performed to identify individual fixtures that could 
contribute to lead, not just five locations per school and two per childcare facility.  It should also be 
noted that the older sampling was more likely to detect lead since the lead may not yet have been 
pacified in the fixtures that were made and installed prior to LCCA. The LCRI does not need to specify the 
exact requirements but could be left to the state to decide the criteria with some guidance that may 
suggest sampling programs that went beyond the LCRI requirements should qualify for grandfathering. 
 
7) Clearly define the service lines to exclude utility responsibility for privately owned and operated 
distribution systems.  
The definition of service lines in the LCRI reads “means a portion of a pipe which connects the water 
main to the building inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water main to 
the outlet.”  GCWW agrees that this appropriately covers both the situation where the building is 
connected directly to the water system’s main and also cases such that a water fountain in a park, etc. is 
connected to the water main. However, this definition may also open the water system’s responsibility 
to include every building on a college campus, mobile home park, apartment and condominium 
complex, some military bases etc. which is far outside of the control or access of a water system. Water 
systems do not have authority, access, control, or responsibility beyond the handoff point of where the 
utility’s main is connected to the private main. GCWW suggests that the definition also includes the idea 
that the water utility’s responsibility ends where the utility’s system connects to a private water main. 
This would still put the responsibility of the individual service line connected directly to the building or 
outlet for inventory and possible replacement, but still keep the utility out of situations that are clearly 
beyond its control and where it does not have access. 

10 
 
8) The Agency should provide health-based data for changing the action level. 
 Changing the Action Level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb is not warranted given that the rule requires the 
complete removal of all lead and GRR lines, so there is no longer a need for a trigger to require 
replacements. Further, 10 or even 15 ppb at the 90th percentile is not a health-based standard, and this 
measurement is even further complicated by the fact that the rule is making changes to the sampling 
pool and not using the higher of the 1st and 5th liter sample. The 90th percentile level was set as a metric 
considering what a well operated system could achieve given a sample pool defined by Tier 1 locations 
with half of the locations being served by a lead service line, and half of the locations having leaded 
solder. The Agency should present data demonstrating that 10 or 15 ppb is a level that presents 
significant risk for short-term exposure and data showing that the action level is achievable by drinking 
water systems practicing good corrosion control treatment. With the information and considerations 
provided to date, reducing the action level to 10 ppb with the new sampling scenario appears arbitrary 
and can have some significant impacts and costs for communities. 
 
9) Changing corrosion control treatment requirements will have high costs to industrial customers 
and will have severe impacts on wastewater treatment facilities too. 
 Given that this rule requires replacements of all lead service lines, the requirement to change corrosion 
control treatment is not necessary and will negatively impact environmental water quality by increasing 
phosphorus loading into rivers, lakes, and streams. Currently, GCWW uses pH passivation as our 
corrosion control method. This method is quite successful in minimizing lead as our 90th percentile is 
below 5 ppb. However, with the new sampling methods and the natural variability inherent with lead 
sampling and analyses, we are concerned that our 90th percentile could exceed 10 ppb at some point in 
the future until such time as we remove all our lead lines.  
 
If after the pipe loop studies and review of the data with our primacy agency we are still required to 
change to phosphate treatment, changing CCT will have high costs for GCWW customers, but will also 
severely impact our regional wastewater treatment system as the same time as the Ohio EPA has been 
ratcheting down the allowable phosphorus in their effluent.  In discussions with the Metropolitan Sewer 
District of Greater Cincinnati (MSDGC), they expect cost increases to make adjustments to their 
treatment systems and their operation to remove this excess phosphorus that we were required to add. 
Not only would this change impact MSDGC, but a change in our corrosion control would also impact a 
number of other sewer districts in our region receiving our drinking water. In addition to the changes 
that would be required by regional sewer districts, this change in chemistry will require numerous 
industries in our region to make costly changes to their own treatment and manufacturing processes in 
order to deal with the change in pH and the excess phosphate that may need to be added to the water.   
Food processors, pharmaceutical manufacturers and numerous other manufacturing facilities may be 
required to make changes to adjust the water chemistry to meet their needs.  
 
10) Certified mail is costly and ineffective as customers ignore it. 
The LCRI specifies that in the event of a utility not being able to meet its 10 percent replacement 
requirement, that the utility may have to use certified mail to communicate with customers with lead, 
GRR or unknown service lines. We agree that the customers should be mailed information, however 
sending letters by certified mail is extremely costly compared with regular mail. In addition, it has been 
our experience that certified mail is less likely to be accepted by customers. Early in our lead line 

11 
 
replacement program, GCWW would send information via certified mail to customers in our main 
replacement projects who had lead lines. The information we sent included information about lead, the 
fact that they had a lead line, and our offer of financial and project coordination assistance to remove 
their portion of the line. Many of the customers, seeing that it was a certified letter from the water 
utility, actually refused delivery presumably thinking that it was a letter compelling them to take some 
action or would result in a mandatory cost to them. Because of this, we no longer use certified mail in 
this instance.  
 
If the goal is to be able to track if a utility is sending information out, then certified mail can accomplish 
that. However, if the goal is to provide effective communication to the customer, then certified mail will 
actually reduce the effectiveness and outreach of that communication.  
 
11) Simplification of public outreach and state notifications would aid utility compliance. 
Throughout the rule, various interactions and communications are required with subsets of the public. 
The LCRI uses terms like property owners, consumers, residents, occupants, customers, etc. The use of 
so many similar terms that have similar but slightly different meanings is confusing and can lead to 
misunderstandings as to who exactly needs to be notified and when. GCWW suggests the EPA review 
the rule for consistency of terms and to find ways to reduce the number of different categories used 
throughout the document.   
 
Throughout the rule there are also many certifications and communications required from the utility to 
the state to attest that the utility accomplished various required activities. Some certifications are due 
within 24 hours, some within 30 days, some annually, some at the end of a sampling period. GCWW 
suggests that the EPA review the various required certifications and submittals and look for 
opportunities to require either fewer certifications or align the frequency of these certifications so that 
they can be combined into fewer submittals. Simplifying and combining these notifications will be of 
great assistance to both the water utilities and the state primacy agencies tasked with overseeing the 
LCRI and will reduce the administrative burden for both the primacy agencies and the utilities and will 
also reduce the number of inadvertent violations that will inevitably result from such a complex 
framework.  
 
12) Notice as property changes ownership is impractical because utilities are not aware of when 
properties change ownership. 
In 141.84(d)(3)(ii) the rule states that a utility must, as part of a “reasonable effort”, reach out to 
property owners within 6 months of change in ownership in instances where the previous owner 
refused a lead line replacement. GCWW believes that it is a good idea to reach out to new owners and it 
is common for utilities to have specific outreach when a new water account opens or a change in the 
water account owner occurs. However, utilities are not informed on property transfers and have no way 
to compel notifications except when the ownership of the water account is changed. Therefore, we 
suggest changing the notification upon ownership change to when the water account changes.  
 
End of Comments.

Subject: RE: City of Hillsboro Water Department Lead and Copper Rules Improvements (LCRI) 
Comments, (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801)  
 
Dear Mr. Burneson, 
 
The City of Hillsboro Water Department (Hillsboro Water) shares the Environmental Protection Agency’s 
(EPA’s) vision to provide more effective protection of public health by reducing exposure to lead and 
copper through drinking water. Hillsboro Water oversees three public water systems as it relates to Lead 
and Copper Rule compliance: Hillsboro (PWS 01513), Hillsboro-Butternut Creek (PWS 06274), and 
Hillsboro-Cherry Grove (PWS 00985). It is within this context that Hillsboro Water submits the following 
comments and concerns as they pertain to the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). 
Hillsboro Water supports the LCRI’s emphasis on proactive measures to reduce lead exposure. 
Specifically, the proposal to replace 100% of lead service lines within 10 years, the service line inventory 
validation requirement, and requiring utilities to include lead connectors in their inventories. Hillsboro 
Water also supports LCRI proposals that directly decrease the complexity of the LCRR such as removing 
the trigger level and setting the action level to 0.010 mg/L. Further, Hillsboro Water supports the 
proposal to decrease the small system threshold from 10,000 to 3,300 customers as this change will 
translate to greater protection of public health.  
Although Hillsboro Water supports the overall goals and specific aspects of the proposed LCRI 
mentioned above, there are several concerns about the improvements that should be addressed: 
1. Pertaining to the definition of Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRR):  
Hillsboro Water urges EPA to provide specific guidance for states and utilities that do not 
currently, nor have any record of ever having, a lead service line in their distribution system but 
that do have galvanized service lines. Specifically, what counts as evidence that a galvanized 
service line was never downstream of a lead service line? If a system has no history of ever using 
lead would that suffice? Does absence of any record that a galvanized service line had been 
replaced count? While Hillsboro Water has very few galvanized lines, many of our customers do, 
and we feel it would be burdensome and unnecessary to require customers to replace their lines 
given we have no records of ever using lead service lines. This issue does not only pertain to 
correctly classifying service lines in the inventory but has many resource-heavy implications in 
other aspects of the rule such as establishing a replacement plan, additional public outreach, 
etc. We ask that EPA add specific language to guide the discernment between a galvanized line 
and a GRR line. This scenario is not unique to Hillsboro Water but applies to many utilities across 
the Unites States who have galvanized lines but no history of LSLs. 
 

2. Pertaining to individual notification of tap sample results: 
As currently written, the proposed LCRI states that utilities would have three calendar days to 
provide customers with tap sample results. Hillsboro Water feels this short timeframe does not 
allow for flexibility with holidays, staff shortages, and other unforeseen scenarios that could 
potentially put the utility out of compliance. Hillsboro Water suggests that EPA change this to 
either three business days or five calendar days. We feel this is a reasonable timeline that 
continues to prioritize public health and promote transparency but does not put undue stress on 
utilities. 
 
3. Pertaining to including lead connectors in inventory: 
While Hillsboro Water generally supports adding lead connectors to the inventory, we request 
specific verbiage in the rule for how to approach inventorying connector materials that aren’t 
known but unlikely lead due to the utility having no records of LSLs or other lead components. 
Alternatively, what do utilities put for connector material in the inventory if they have no 
records of connector materials? Additionally, Hillsboro Water would like to see stronger 
language in the final LCRI that the EPA is not expecting utilities to physically verify connector 
materials for the inventory and outline what exactly is expected of utilities regarding this topic.  
 
4. Regarding the proposal of requiring four attempts to engage a customer with an LSL, GRR, or 
unknown service line for replacement and if customer is unresponsive, the utility must try 
again if there is a change in home ownership: 
While Hillsboro Water understands the importance of engaging customers with LSLs or GRRs, 
tracking when home ownership changes would be very burdensome and potentially impossible 
depending on how many homes a utility would be required to track. If EPA keeps this change in 
the final LCRI, Hillsboro Water highly recommends that EPA provide specific guidance on how to 
track home ownership changes and/or develop tools to help utilities fulfill this expectation.  
 
5. Pertaining to service line replacement access and expectations: 
As the proposed LCRI is written, it states that systems must replace customer-owned LSLs/GRRs 
on private property if they have the legal and physical access based on state/local law, water 
tariff agreement, or customer consent. It also clarifies that systems are not required to replace 
LSLs/GRRs when a system does not have access as a matter of law, regulation, or tariff OR 
customer consent is required for access, and it cannot be obtained. Hillsboro Water does not 
support this change in the definition of “control” as it does not seem reasonable to make states, 
local municipalities, or utilities add clauses in local laws regarding this specific situation. 
Additionally, many utilities do not use water tariff agreements (as is the case with Hillsboro 
Water). Further, if a system has legal authority to conduct a service line replacement but the 
customer denies physical access it seems unsafe to require the utility to complete the 
replacement. Hillsboro Water requests that EPA further elaborates on its expectations for 
scenarios such as the one described above. Finally, as the LCRI is currently written, it is unclear 
how the utility would classify a service line in this scenario in their inventory. Would it count as a 
replacement or be added to another category that has yet to be defined?  
 
 

6. Pertaining to adding homes with galvanized premise plumbing to Tier 3: 
How does EPA suggest that utilities identify homes with galvanized premise plumbing? Is this 
based on the service line material? Also, if a galvanized line is downstream of a connector of 
unknown material would it be considered a Tier 3 home? There needs to be further clarification 
on this topic in the final rule. Hillsboro Water does not have any Tier 1 or Tier 2 homes, meaning 
our sample pool will come from Tier 3.  
 
7. Pertaining to acceptable methods for verifying unknowns: 
Hillsboro Water requests that EPA explicitly state that a statistical approach for verifying 
unknowns be acceptable in the initial and final LCRI inventory. Hillsboro Water is utilizing the 
statistical approach to verify and classify its unknown lines and would like to be certain that this 
approach is valid and acceptable in the final rule. 
 
8. Regarding whether public water utilities should make school and childcare facility sampling 
results publicly available and if so, how frequently and in what manner: 
Hillsboro Water supports increasing public transparency but believes schools and childcare 
facilities should be responsible for sharing their own lead results publicly. Viable options for this 
outreach could be a dedicated page on the school or childcare facilities website, bulletin board 
posting, handouts, letters to parents, social media, etc on an annual basis and, when applicable, 
within 30 days of receiving lead testing results. Hillsboro Water does however support including 
additional information about lead sampling in schools and childcare facilities in the CCR to 
increase public transparency. 
 
Finally, Hillsboro Water strongly requests that the EPA delay the LCRR compliance date of October 16, 
2024, due to concerns about the feasibility of promulgating the proposed LCRI before the LCRR 
compliance date. If the EPA is unable to publish the final LCRI rule before October 16, 2024, utilities will 
be forced to comply with many rules of the LCRR that are not present in the LCRI that would be a major 
investment of time and resources that are completely unnecessary. Pushing back the LCRR compliance 
date would allow the EPA enough time to publish the LCRI while not forcing systems to spend time 
potentially preparing LCRR materials (specifically, the LSLR) in the event the EPA is unable to meet its 
expected timeline, which has historically been an issue.  
Hillsboro Water hopes that our comments help EPA develop sound rule options that further reduce risks 
posed by lead, recognizing the reality of time and resource constraints as a direct result of these 
decisions. If EPA has any questions regarding these comments, please contact Hillsboro Water at 503-
615-6702 or leadtest@hillsboro-oregon.gov. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
Jessica Dorsey 
Water Resources Senior Program Manager

RE: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI): Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
The New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments to 
the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI) under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA). EPA published the proposed rules in 
the Federal Register on December 6, 2023, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. 
 
NMED serves as a coregulator with the U.S. EPA for the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations 
(NPDWRs) and is responsible for overseeing their implementation across 1,064 active public water 
systems in New Mexico. Protecting New Mexico’s drinking water quality for present and future 
generations is fundamental to NMED’s mission. 
 
The proposed LCRI would revise the most recent lead and copper rule, the LCRR, which was promulgated 
on January 15, 2021. The U.S. EPA is proposing to require water systems to replace lead service lines, 
remove the lead trigger level, reduce the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling 
procedures, among other changes that would improve public health protection and simplify the rule 
relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). The proposed LCRI also proposes 
improvements for corrosion control treatment, public education and consumer awareness, requirements 
for small systems, and sampling in schools and childcare facilities.   
 
As mentioned in our February 11, 2020, comment letter on the Proposed Revisions to the Lead and Copper 
Rule, protecting people from health impacts of lead and copper exposure in drinking water is a priority 
for NMED. In New Mexico, there are currently 691 public water systems that must comply with the 
requirements of the LCRR and the proposed LCRI. As a public health agency, NMED supports regulatory 
changes that tackle the daunting challenges of finding and replacing lead service lines and better protect 
children and other members of the public. 
 
New Mexico is a rural state and of the 691 community water systems subject to the LCRR and LCRI, 80% 
serve populations under 1,000. Many small systems face serious challenges associated with limited 
technical, managerial, and financial capacity. The proposed LCRI will also generate a significant increase 
in the workload for NMED staff that will be required to assist our community and non-transient, non-
community water systems with these proposed rules.  

 
 
As we mentioned in our comments to the LCRR, which we re-emphasize here, it is critical that the U.S. 
EPA not underestimate the resource implications, both time, money, and overall resources in 
implementing rules such as the LCRR and LCRI.  The U.S. EPA must continue to work closely with the 
Environmental Council of the States, the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators (ASDWA), 
individual states and other key stakeholders in developing the tools and guidance that states and 
communities will rely upon for rule implementation.  
 
Many of the public water systems that are impacted by these regulatory changes, especially those in small 
and disadvantaged communities, struggle to manage the day-to-day operations of their systems. Many 
will also struggle to fully understand and implement these complex and often expensive regulatory 
requirements. This increases the technical, regulatory, and compliance responsibilities of our limited 
agency staff. 
 
NMED reiterates that the LCRI will require our department to triple or quadruple our current staff 
resources devoted to LCR implementation. Long term and permanent federal funding for Public Water 
System Supervision (PWSS) and Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) for these rules is critical.  
State drinking water primacy staff are increasingly struggling to manage the frequency and broadness of 
federal regulatory changes while also trying to assist our community and non-community water systems 
with much needed compliance and capacity challenges.  Recent regulatory determinations for the Revised 
Lead and Copper Rule, Lead and Copper Improvement, PFAS, Consumer Confidence Reports, are just a 
few of the recent changes that are required to be managed without guaranteed and specific long-term 
funding for the staffing required to manage these regulations.  
 
NMED appreciates the additional effort that the U.S. EPA is taking to ensure the effective implementation 
of this complex drinking water regulation. NMED also values the opportunity to comment on this 
regulatory revision that will ensure a safe and reliable drinking water supply for New Mexico consumers.
