Attachment 1: 
Comments on EPA’s Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
December 6, 2023 
 
Introduction 
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is proposing revisions to the National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulation (NPDWR) for lead and copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act 
(SDWA). In this document, EPA is proposing to require water systems to replace lead service lines, remove 
the lead trigger level, reduce the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling procedures, 
among other changes that would improve public health protection and simplify the rule relative to the 
2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). This proposed rule provides improvements in the additional 
following areas: corrosion control treatment, public education and consumer awareness, requirements 
for small systems, and sampling in schools and childcare facilities. EPA’s proposed rule aims to address 
potential disproportionate impacts of lead in drinking water in communities, including through proposed 
lead service line replacement and public education, among other areas of the proposed rule. 
 
The health effects of these contaminants are clear. Lead exposure causes damage to the brain and kidneys 
and can interfere with the production of red blood cells that carry oxygen to all parts of the body.  
Exposure to lead is known to present serious health risks to the brain and nervous system of children.  
Young children and infants are particularly vulnerable to the physical, cognitive, and behavioral effects of 
lead due to their sensitive developmental stages. There is no known safe level of exposure to lead.  
 
Key Concerns  
New Mexico is a rural state with 1,064 public water systems. Of the 691 community water systems subject 
to the LCRR and LCRI, 80% serve populations under 1,000. Many small systems face various challenges 
associated with limited capacity. Many of these communities are challenged with failing infrastructure 
and overall inability to effectively manage their day-to-day operations.  While the funding provided by the 
Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) and other federal grant resources provide a mechanism for 
communities to pay for projects required by LCRR and LCRI, we anticipate that many of these communities 
may be forced to choose between funding a critical piece of infrastructure such as a drinking water supply 
well, storage tank, or other critical system improvements versus funding lead service line identification 
and replacement projects.  This is because many of these small and disadvantaged communities lack the 
capacity to take on multiple large-scale projects and engage in the significant effort needed to receive 
funding through these federal grant programs.    
 
While NMED and our third-party assistance providers work tirelessly to assist communities with 
understanding and complying with regulations such as the LCRR and the LCRI and assisting these 
communities with navigating the funding requirements, much of our time is taken up by assisting 
communities with the daily challenges of keeping clean drinking water flowing in their communities.  This 
leaves communities, and NMED, with very limited time and resources to develop strategies to assist with 
service line inventories and service line replacement programs as required by the LCRR and LCRI.    
 
State Staffing and Resource Implications 
Grants to states across EPA’s portfolio must include the required long term and permanent additional 
funding to address associated costs for compliance with this proposed regulation.  As an example, LCRI 
anticipates a 10-year window for lead service line replacements, which means that state primacy agencies 
like NMED will be required to ensure public water system compliance with lead service line replacements 

2 
 
over that 10-year timeline.  While NMED is pursuing additional staffing resources with our IIJA grant set-
asides, those grants are set to expire within the next four years, leaving NMED with an additional 6+ years 
of unfunded staffing resources to implement the LCRI.  NMED agrees that the replacement of lead service 
lines, reduction of the lead action level, the enhanced public education requirements are all worthwhile, 
many states, including New Mexico rely heavily on federal grant dollars to help implement our state 
drinking water regulatory programs, specifically, the federal Public Water System Supervision (PWSS). 
Grant dollars are being stretched more thinly with increasingly complex and demanding workloads 
resulting from implemented regulations such as the Revised Total Coliform Rule, Disinfection Byproduct 
rules, Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, proposed Consumer Confidence Rule revisions and now PFAS 
regulatory determinations.  The overall resources required to effectively implement these rules have 
increased over the years; however, the permanent federal grant dollars have not kept pace with those 
resource demands.   
 
State primacy agencies like NMED are managing a significant increase in overall workloads due to 
additional factors such as the tracking and reporting requirements of the IIJA and other complex 
compliance requirements while facing retirements of technical staff and trained operators, putting states 
in the unreasonable and unsustainable position of being forced to do more with less. Additionally, recent 
Congressionally Directed Spending (CDS) has been using DWSRF capitalization grants as a mechanism to 
fund CDS community projects, further reducing and negatively impacting long standing primacy agency 
grant funding sources.  NMED encourages EPA to review ASDWA’s white paper on the Hidden 
Consequences of Congressional Directed Spending Impacts on Drinking Water Programs.  Long-term and 
permanent federal grant funding is needed to fully implement a robust drinking water program to ensure 
safe and sustainable drinking water supplies for all New Mexicans.    
 
Small Systems 
Approximately 80% of public water systems in New Mexico subject to the LCRR and LCRI, serve 
populations under 1,000 people and often operate with volunteer boards, administrators, and in some 
cases, operators. Small system compliance with the proposed LCRI will be challenging. These small 
community water systems are often disadvantaged and require a significant amount of assistance from 
our drinking water program to achieve and maintain compliance with increasingly stringent drinking water 
regulations. NMED works tirelessly to provide as much assistance to these communities as possible 
through our IIJA set-aside grant funds, however, we anticipate that the need for assistance is going to 
outpace our resources and our ability to provide the needed hands-on assistance that these communities 
will require.     
 
On top of the overall challenges of achieving compliance with these proposed regulations, NMED 
anticipates that many of our small and rural communities may have outdated or nonexistent construction 
or plumbing records which will make complying with the LCRR and LCRI lead service line identification and 
replacement requirements significantly more challenging and will require much more hands on assistance 
form our limited staff or our assistance partners.    
 
Final Considerations 
In New Mexico, public water system compliance sampling is paid by Water Conservation Fund (WCF).  The 
WCF is a state specific fee required to be paid by every public water system to support compliance with 
federal Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) sampling and analysis.  This fund has a flat yearly revenue and is 

3 
 
insufficient to cover existing water sampling costs, let alone the increased costs of compliance with the 
proposed lead and copper revisions as well as the other proposed regulatory revisions being considered 
by EPA. Many small and disadvantaged communities in New Mexico have difficulties paying into this fund.  
As a result of the LCRR, LCRI, and other federal regulatory determinations, NMED will have no choice but 
to pursue a fee increase to ensure the long-term ability for this fund to pay for the increase in compliance 
sampling requirements.  While NMED understands that this is a state specific issue, we urge EPA to take 
these issues into consideration when making these types of regulatory determinations.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0716 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---

Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper 
Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
I am writing to express my strong support for the proposed rule, National Primary 
Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI), that was 
published on December 6, 2023. I am a concerned citizen and a parent, and I have 
witnessed the devastating effects of lead exposure on the health and development of 
children and communities. I applaud the EPA’s efforts to protect public health and the 
environment from the dangers of lead in drinking water. 
I support the changes that the EPA has proposed, and I am particularly supportive of 
the following aspects of the rule: 
• The reduction of the lead action level from 0.015 mg/L to 0.010 mg/L, which 
would align with the World Health Organization’s guideline value and prevent 
up to 9,000 cases of elevated blood lead levels in children per year, according 
to the EPA’s analysis. 
• The requirement for water systems to replace all lead service lines within 10 
years, regardless of the lead levels in the water. This would eliminate the main 
source of lead in drinking water and reduce the health disparities and 
environmental injustices associated with lead exposure. The EPA has also 
proposed to provide guidance, technical assistance, and funding opportunities 
to help water systems comply with the rule and address the challenges of lead 
service line replacement. 
• The simplification of the tap sampling procedures and requirements for water 
systems, and the enhancement of the public education and consumer awareness 
efforts. These changes would improve the reliability and representativeness of 
the tap samples, and ensure that customers receive timely and accurate 
information about their water quality and the actions they can take to reduce 
their exposure to lead. 
I want to emphasize the critical importance of sharing the lead service line inventory 
and address specific data with the public, as required by the proposed rule. I believe 
that this is a crucial step to increase the transparency and accountability of the water 
systems, and to empower the customers and the communities to make informed 
decisions and take action to protect themselves and their families from lead exposure.  
The public has a right to know if their water service lines are made of lead, and where 
they are located. This information can also help the EPA, the state and primacy 

 
2 
agencies, and other stakeholders to monitor and evaluate the progress and 
effectiveness of the lead service line replacement program, and to identify and address 
any gaps or challenges that may arise. 
But moreover, the public as a whole has a right to know where the lead service lines 
are located, to facilitate community efforts to focus attention and resources on getting 
these lines replaced before they can do still more harm. 
I strongly urge the EPA and the state and primacy agencies to make the inventory of 
lead service lines and of unknown service lines, and the addresses with lead service 
lines, and with unknown service lines, publicly available to the fullest extent possible, 
and to update it at least annually. I believe that having this information public will 
help get the problem addressed faster and more equitably, especially because this 
problem has festered in the dark far too long. Here are some of the reasons why I 
think public availability of this information is essential: 
• It will increase the public awareness and demand for lead service line 
replacement. Many customers and communities may not be aware of the 
presence and the risk of lead service lines, or may not have the resources or the 
motivation to request or participate in lead service line replacement. By making 
the inventory and the addresses public, the EPA and the state and primacy 
agencies can inform and educate the public about the issue, and encourage 
them to take action and seek assistance. This will also create a sense of urgency 
and pressure for the water systems to comply with the rule and to prioritize the 
most vulnerable and affected areas. It will help states, counties and cities to 
make informed decisions about their participation in addressing this problem. 
• It will enable the public oversight and participation in the lead service line 
replacement program. The public (and journalists and environmental 
advocates) can use the inventory and the addresses to monitor and track the 
progress and the performance of the water systems and the state and primacy 
agencies in replacing the lead service lines. It will also enhance the 
accountability and the responsiveness of the water systems and the state and 
primacy agencies, and improve the quality and the efficiency of the lead service 
line replacement program. 
• It will facilitate the public access and use of the information for various 
purposes and benefits. The public can use the inventory and the addresses for 
various purposes and benefits, such as research, advocacy, 
education, journalism, or personal decision making. For example, researchers 
can use the information to conduct studies and analyses on the impact and the 
outcome of the rule, and to generate new knowledge and insights on the issue 
of lead in drinking water. Advocates can use the information to raise awareness 

 
3 
and mobilize support for the rule, and to advocate for more resources and 
policies to address the issue. Educators can use the information to teach and 
inform students and the public about the issue, and to promote environmental 
literacy and civic engagement. Customers can use the information to make 
informed choices about their water consumption and treatment, and to protect 
their health and well-being. 
• Journalists and community advocates can use the information to report on the 
progress and the challenges of the lead service line replacement program, and 
to expose any violations or misconducts by the water systems or the state and 
primacy agencies. Journalists can also use the information to conduct 
investigative and data journalism on the situations like Flint, Michigan and 
other locations that were exposing residents to high levels of lead. Journalists 
can highlight the role of the news media in identifying and exposing these 
problems, and holding the responsible parties accountable, when the public 
health community or the water companies failed to do so. For example, in Flint, 
Michigan, local and national journalists, along with a pediatrician, an engineer, 
a resident, and an EPA official, uncovered the lead crisis and the cover-up by 
the state officials, and pressured the authorities to take action and provide relief 
to the affected residents. In Newark, New Jersey, journalists from NJ Advance 
Media and NorthJersey.com, along with the environmental group NRDC, 
revealed the extent and the severity of the lead contamination in the city’s water 
supply, and challenged the city’s claims that the water was safe to drink. In 
Chicago, Illinois, journalists from the Chicago Tribune, WBEZ, and the 
Guardian exposed the city’s failure to warn residents about the potential lead 
hazards from water main replacements, and documented the health impacts and 
the lawsuits filed by the residents. In many places, journalists and 
environmental advocates have played a vital role in bringing the issue of lead in 
drinking water to the public attention, and in holding the water systems and the 
state and primacy agencies accountable for their actions or inactions. 
I understand that some parties may cite security or privacy concerns that may prevent 
the disclosure of the exact address of each service line, or the locational identifier for 
“Lead Status Unknown” service lines. But there are no persuasive reasons why such 
crucial information should continue to be hidden from the public. Water providers 
have a history of concealing or downplaying the data, and of resisting or delaying the 
actions needed to address the lead problem. They may also pressure state agencies to 
limit the availability of the information on the pretext of infrastructure security. I urge 
the EPA and the state and primacy agencies to prioritize the public interest and the 
public health benefits of sharing the lead service line inventory and specific location 
data with the public, and to overcome any security concerns with appropriate 

 
4 
safeguards and measures. I also urge the EPA and the state and primacy agencies to 
ensure that the publicly accessible inventory is updated at least annually, and that the 
customers are notified of any changes in their service line material or lead levels in 
their water. 
I appreciate the EPA’s initiative and commitment to revise the Lead and Copper Rule 
and protect public health and the environment from the dangers of lead in drinking 
water, and I strongly support its adoption and implementation. 
 
 
Michael Ravnitzky 
Silver Spring, Maryland

The NAACP State Conference of Ohio submits the following comments regarding  
the US Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary  
Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”).  
The Ohio NAACP State conference provides leadership for local branches, youth 
councils, and college chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in Ohio. 
The NAACP and its Center for Environmental and Climate Justice have a long- 
standing interest in ensuring that issues of community engagement and environ- 
mental justice center Black communities and frontline communities most impacted, 
including communities in Ohio.    
   
Ohio applauds EPA for proposing stronger regulations to protect communities from  
lead in drinking water. 
   
The Lead and Cooper rule, as it stands now, is wholly inadequate.  According to an 
article published by International Journal of Environmental Research and Public  
Health, found on the National Library of Medicine National Center for Bio- 
technology Information, researchers Deniz Yeter, Ellen Banks and Michael Aschner, 
concluded that there is a “significant nationwide racial disparity in blood Pb that has 
been documented among predominantly African-American Black children since while 
ethnic disparity for Hispanic children is no longer seen at the national level compared  
to White children since the 1990s.” Though I am aware that Hispanic children 
experience heightened blood lead levels when the neighborhood conditions and  
exposure levels are the same as Black communities.       
 
From my perusal of the articles and studies available, there seem to be an agreement  
that industrial waste and products and the lack of federal enforcement of prohibitions  
of lead product and paint use as the primary cause of lead exposure and poisoning, 
especially among Black children. In fact, Ohio is ranked second in the number of lead 
pipes.  With the available science, technology and resources in the US, a course 
correction is possible.  The modification of the lead and cooper rule is critically  
needed for this to happen.

For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the 
proposed LCRI such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the 
requirements for water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through lead 
pipes and a lower action level; but also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which 
undermine their goals and ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.   
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not leave 
black communities in Ohio behind:   
 
 
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a fundamental 
injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 or more years to 
fix this issue.   
 
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: Removal can 
cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted communities will result in 
mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced. Removal and replacement 
do not make up major proportions of utility budgets, and utilities should be expected to maximize the 
use of available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-ratepayer sources of funds to 
prioritize solving this crisis.   
 
 
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many hours there 
daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead exposure when 
compared with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing program does not differ from past 
ineffective programs, and EPA should move towards incentivizing the installation of filters and 
protecting children.   
   
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would allow for 
environmental injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline communities have long suffered 
from disinvestment and lack of resources. Past NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, 
or language spoken had the strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA 
of any sociodemographic characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to make 
significant changes in the lives of millions of people in Ohio, and to provide a measure of 
environmental justice which these families are owed, and we encourage this administration to build on 
the progress made in the proposed rule by strengthening the final rule further.

Comment Clerk: 
 
American Water Works Company, Inc. (American Water) appreciates the opportunity to provide comment 
to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) regarding its proposed revisions to the national 
primary drinking water regulation for lead and copper, known as the Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI), as described in the December 6, 2023, Federal Register (88 FR 84878). American 
Water provides drinking water and wastewater service to an estimated 14 million people in 24 states, 
including more than 300 public drinking water systems. In addition to our regulated operations, we also 
provide water and wastewater services to military installations across the country through our Military 
Services Group. We currently operate 50-year contracts at 18 military installations across the nation as 
part of the U.S. Government’s Utilities Privatization Program. Our comments are based on our extensive 
experience in designing, installing and operating treatment for groundwater and surface water, including 
treatment for lead and copper that allows us to meet state standards and implementing drinking water 
regulations across our footprint. 
 
American Water supports the U.S. EPA’s efforts to revise the Lead and Copper Rule to provide more 
effective protection of public health by further reducing the potential exposure to lead and copper in 
drinking water. The attached comments detail the areas of the proposed rule where American Water 
believes clarification or alternative approaches are needed to improve the likelihood of successful 
implementation. 
 
Although American Water consistently meets water quality lead standards across our footprint, we believe 
that removing the risk of lead service lines over time is the right thing to do for the health, safety and 
peace of mind of our customers. For this reason, for more than five years we have been implementing 
programs within our service territories to replace lead service lines across the American Water footprint. 
  
American Water supports the concept of a mandatory replacement program, rather than a triggered 
replacement program. Developing an accurate, comprehensive inventory, including identifying the 
material of service lines where the material is currently unknown, is an important first step in eliminating 
lead service lines. With respect to replacement, we believe the rule must differentiate access from control, 
and that water systems should perform full-service line replacement when they are granted access to do 
so. It is also our view that the U.S. EPA’s new rule should recognize that a lack of customer approval to 
replace a service line can lead to safety issues and additional regulatory and legal risks. We believe the 
rule should allow water systems to perform partial lead service line replacements when customers do not 
grant requested access to perform full-service line replacements.  
 

2 
 
 
As we stated in our comments related to the proposed PFAS rule, we believe all stakeholders must 
understand the costs associated with the suggested improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule. The 
cost to identify the material of all unknown service lines, validate the required subset of non-lead service 
lines, and replace all lead service lines and galvanized service lines requiring replacement within 10 years 
of the compliance date of the LCRI will require significant investment for all water systems. These costs 
will be dependent upon multiple factors, including the requirements in the final rule, and the number of 
unknown service lines identified as lead or galvanized requiring replacement (GRR).  
 
American Water appreciates the U.S. EPA’s attempt to simplify the rule. This includes retaining the 
treatment technique approach and eliminating the lead trigger level, which caused confusion when 
considered in tandem with the lead action level. However, the associated reduction in the lead action 
level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb will likely result in water systems needing to modify existing corrosion control 
treatment or install new treatment where it does not currently exist. We expect that this will create an 
additional financial burden on water systems and customers, above what is required for service line 
identification and replacement. These challenges would be significantly increased if the lead action level 
were reduced to 5 ppb. 
 
To realize the full health benefits, we believe that water systems should have the financial resources to 
help them sustain the ongoing costs that will arise from the replacement process in systems for the safety 
and benefit of customers. States should treat these expenditures for regulated utilities as federally 
mandated requirements that are recoverable in customer rates through expedited means. 
 
We believe that maintaining customer affordability is critical and the additional estimated cost of this rule 
underscores the importance of federal funding for lead service line replacement availability to all water 
systems, regardless of the type of ownership. 
 
Finally, we urge the U.S. EPA to act now to delay the compliance date for those portions of the Lead and 
Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) that are proposed to be extended by the LCRI, some of which are 
currently scheduled to take effect on October 16, 2024. Water systems are expending funds and 
resources because they cannot stop preparing to comply with the existing rule until there is certainty on 
the new, proposed changes and when they will take effect. To address this, we are requesting the U.S. 
EPA to delay the LCRR compliance date by one year for those aspects being impacted by the LCRI.  
 
In conclusion, providing safe, reliable, and affordable water service is American Water’s business, and we 
look forward to working cooperatively and collaboratively with the U.S. EPA, regulators, and policymakers 
so that the implementation of the final Lead and Copper Rule Improvements helps protect customers, 
communities, and the general public. 
 
Please direct any questions regarding these comments to my attention at 856-676-5799 or 
Lynda.DiMenna@amwater.com.  
 
Sincerely, 
Lynda DiMenna 
VP Chief Environmental and Safety Officer
