Detailed American Water Comments on  
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements  
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 2, 2024 
 
 
American Water Works Company, Inc. (American Water) appreciates the opportunity to provide comment 
to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (U.S. EPA) regarding its proposed revisions to the national 
primary drinking water regulation for lead and copper, known as the Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI), as described in the December 6, 2023, Federal Register (88 FR 84878). American 
Water provides drinking water and wastewater service to an estimated 14 million people in 24 states, 
including more than 300 public drinking water systems. In addition to our regulated operations, we also 
provide water and wastewater services to military installations across the country through our Military 
Services Group. We currently operate 50-year contracts at 18 military installations across the nation as 
part of the U.S. Government’s Utilities Privatization Program. Our comments are based on our extensive 
experience in designing, installing and operating treatment for groundwater and surface water, including 
treatment for lead and copper that allows us to meet state standards and implementing drinking water 
regulations across our footprint. 
 
 
Key Issues 
 
 
American Water highlights the following overarching comments on the proposed rule. 
• 
Compliance date – We urge the U.S. EPA to act now to delay the compliance date for those 
portions of the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) that are proposed to be extended by the 
LCRI, some of which are currently scheduled to take effect on October 16, 2024. Water systems 
are expending funds and resources because they cannot stop preparing to comply with the 
existing rule until there is certainty on the new, proposed changes and when they will take effect. 
To address this, the U.S. EPA should issue a one-year delay in the LCRR compliance date for 
those aspects being impacted by the LCRI. 
• 
Mandatory replacement – American Water supports the concept of a mandatory replacement 
program, rather than a triggered replacement program. Developing an accurate, comprehensive 
inventory, including identifying the material of service lines where the material is currently 
unknown, is an important first step in eliminating lead service lines.  
• 
Access vs. control – With respect to replacement, we believe the rule must differentiate access 
from control, and that water systems should perform full-service line replacement when they are 
granted access to do so. It is also our view that the U.S. EPA’s new rule should recognize that a 
lack of customer approval to replace a service line can lead to safety issues and additional 
regulatory and legal risks. We believe the rule should allow water systems to perform partial lead 
service line replacements when customers do not grant access to perform full-service line 
replacements.  
• 
Cost – The cost to identify the material of all unknown service lines, validate the required subset 
of non-lead service lines, and replace all lead and GRR service lines within 10 years of the 
compliance date of the LCRI will require significant investment for all water systems. These costs 
will be dependent upon multiple factors, including the requirements in the final rule, and the 
number of unknown service lines identified as lead or GRR.  
• 
Affordability – We believe that maintaining customer affordability is critical and the additional 
estimated cost of this rule underscores the importance of federal funding for lead service line 
replacement availability to all water systems, regardless of the type of ownership. 
• 
Financial resources – To realize the full health benefits, we believe that water systems should 
have the financial resources to help them sustain the ongoing costs that will arise from the 
replacement process in systems for the safety and benefit of customers. States should treat these 
expenditures for regulated utilities as federally mandated requirements that are recoverable in 
customer rates through expedited means. All water utility providers, regardless of ownership, 
must have equal access to any and all Federal and State funding. In the absence of substantial 

4 
 
 
additional federal and state funding, water systems will likely be forced to defer important water 
infrastructure investments in other areas. 
• 
Rule simplification – American Water appreciates the U.S. EPA’s attempt to simplify the rule. This 
includes retaining the treatment technique approach and eliminating the lead trigger level, which 
caused confusion when considered in tandem with the lead action level. However, the associated 
reduction in the lead action level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb will likely result in water systems needing 
to modify existing corrosion control treatment or install new treatment where it does not currently 
exist. We expect that this will create an additional financial burden on water systems and 
customers, above what is required for service line identification and replacement. These 
challenges would be significantly increased if the lead action level were reduced to 5 ppb. 
• 
Sampling and compliance determinations – The LCRI should allow greater flexibility for the 
collection of 1st and 5th liter samples at sites with lead service lines beyond the current approach 
of five consecutive 1-liter bottles and ensure the final Tier definitions are clear and able to be 
implemented. 
• 
Customer outreach and communication – The LCRI provides an opportunity to educate 
customers and increase awareness about lead in drinking water. However, the U.S. EPA must be 
sensitive to the potential unintended consequences of overcommunication and the possibility of 
customers becoming indifferent to water system outreach. Public notification is a critical tool for 
customer communication and while water systems also appreciate the value of public education, 
there needs to be an appropriate balance between the two. 
• 
Reporting requirements – The U.S. EPA should look for opportunities to streamline recordkeeping 
and reporting requirements. This would include options such as combining the public education 
requirements not related to notification of a lead action level exceedance into a single public 
education plan where water systems would develop and submit the initial plan at the LCRI 
compliance date and then certify annually that that water system had complied with the plan as 
designed. This would reduce the amount of reporting, streamlining the process and reducing the 
potential for violations.  
• 
State regulator implementation – State regulators must be required to clearly articulate the criteria 
they will use to modify any requirements in the LCRI on a system-by-system basis to allow for 
understanding and consistent application across all water systems. 
 
 

5 
 
 
Detailed Comments 
 
 
Compliance Dates (141.80) 
 
The U.S. EPA must act now to delay the compliance date for those portions of the LCRR that are 
proposed to be extended by the LCRI, some of which are currently scheduled to take effect on October 
16, 2024. This would include all aspects other than those related to initial inventory, notification of service 
line material, associated reporting requirements, and the requirement for Tier 1 public notification for a 
lead action level exceedance. Water systems are expending funds and resources because they cannot 
stop preparing to comply with the existing rule until there is certainty on the new, proposed changes and 
when they will take effect. To address this, the U.S. EPA should issue a one-year delay in the LCRR 
compliance date for those aspects being impacted by the LCRI. This would allow water systems to cease 
efforts on those activities while the LCRI is finalized with a new compliance schedule. If this new 
compliance schedule extends the compliance dates as currently proposed, the LCRI would supersede the 
one-year delay; if the new compliance schedule does not extend the compliance dates as currently 
proposed, water systems would still have one year to prepare for implementation of any provisions that 
are not extended.  
 
Water systems need time to prepare for mandatory service line replacement requirements, including 
aligning technology, hiring additional skilled staff, soliciting bids for qualified contractors (who will also 
need to potentially obtain additional staff), securing grants or other types of funding, and continuing to 
improve inventories to ensure that they are better positioned to conduct mandatory service line 
replacement. Additional time would also allow the market to correct for potential shortages in resources or 
skilled workers. 
 
Water systems will need a clear understanding of any potential changes to the LCRR compliance dates 
before U.S. EPA is ready to make any such changes in the final LCRI. For example, water systems will 
need to prepare to submit Lead Service Line Replacement Plans by October 16, 2024, in case the final 
LCRI does not extend that deadline as proposed or final promulgation of the LCRI is delayed beyond that 
date. Water systems will also need to focus on other issues such as changes to compliance sampling, 
sampling in schools and licensed childcare facilities, etc. – water systems will need to prepare in case 
there are no changes to compliance date in the final LCRI. To be effective and preclude water systems 
from performing unnecessary work, the delay in compliance date needs to be finalized as soon as 
possible.  
 
More broadly, the proposed requirement to delay the compliance date for those aspects of the LCRR that 
are being changed under the LCRI is appropriate and necessary. Having time to directly transition from 
the current LCR to the LCRI, with the above exceptions, will allow water systems and state regulators to 
focus their resources on preparing, updating, and communicating on service line inventories while having 
adequate time to understand the final LCRI requirements and then develop and execute strategies to 
comply with those requirements. This would include time to prepare for mandatory service line 
replacement requirements, including hiring additional staff, soliciting bids for contractors, securing grants 
or other types of funding, and continuing to improve inventories to ensure that they are better positioned 
to conduct mandatory service line replacement. Additional time would also allow the market to correct for 
potential shortages in resources or workers. Any approach that would accelerate implementation of the 
LCRI requirements would divert valuable resources from other implementation activities currently 
underway. 
 
 
Locating and Removing Legacy Lead Pipes (141.84) 
 
The LCRI should include requirements related to mandatory identification and removal of lead service 
lines including galvanized service lines requiring replacement (GRR). This includes developing an 
accurate, comprehensive inventory, identifying the material of unknown service lines, and a validation 
step for unknowns that were identified through means other than records review or visual verification. 
However, the inventory should not include lead connectors (i.e., lead goosenecks). 

6 
 
 
 
Inventory 
 
The LCRI should retain the requirement for the initial inventory required under the LCRR and 
development of a more robust inventory by 2037. As described in greater detail elsewhere in our 
comments, the inventory requirements should not include lead connectors. 
 
The LCRI also provides the U.S. EPA with an opportunity to clarify the scope of the inventory. The U.S. 
EPA should clarify that the inventory only applies to potable water lines and does not apply to fire 
services or water mains and the associated service lines on private property, such as those on a college 
or university campus or on a large commercial property. The U.S. EPA should explore opportunities to 
address service lines on private properties, especially those that might serve children, being sure that the 
responsibilities associated with identification and replacement are appropriately distributed. 
 
Further, the U.S. EPA should provide clarity regarding the inventory process. Specifically, the LCRI 
should clearly convey that not every service line must be manually verified to be placed into inventory. 
The final rule must allow the use of predictive modeling and other methods that will allow water systems 
to list service line materials without requiring the level of scrutiny associated with the validation process. 
That level of effort should be reserved for a subset of service lines as proposed in the rule. 
 
Validation 
 
Water systems should only be required to validate a statistically relevant subset of non-lead service lines 
in water system inventories to remedy any discrepancies that may be discovered and provide added 
confidence in the accuracy of the inventory. Completing this within the proposed deadline of seven years 
would allow water systems time to address any concerns that are identified during the process before the 
deadline for identification and replacement of all lead and GRR service lines. Water systems would be 
challenged to complete validation in less time and a shorter timeframe would not allow water systems to 
take advantage of the information gained through the inventory development process. 
 
As proposed in the LCRI, validation should be limited to those locations where the water system does not 
have a record of the identification method or technique used for an individual non-lead categorization. 
The LCRI should allow visual inspections to include excavation (i.e., potholing), viewing in a meter pit or 
at the stop box, or entering the building. Customer-provided information should qualify as one point of 
visual inspection. The U.S. EPA should not put limits on information that can be used (e.g., records older 
than a certain number of years would not be eligible for use) for identification purposes. There is no 
support for setting such limitations and doing so may only make the rule more confusing. 
 
The proposed number of sites to be used for validation that allow for a 95 percent confidence level using 
20% for systems with a lower number of service lines requiring validation to a maximum of 384 appear to 
be appropriate. Water systems will need flexibility in the distribution of the validation pool. Field 
verification requires the cooperation of property owners. In some cases, this is feasible, but in other 
cases, access to a property may be denied or there may be unsafe conditions preventing verification.  
 
The LCRI needs to address identification of lead or GRR service lines during their validation process. 
Specifically, water systems should be required to perform additional validations to achieve the 95 percent 
confidence level. Water systems should not be required to repeat the validation process in its entirety.  
 
Lead Connectors 
 
Water systems should not be required to perform a record review for lead connectors and then add lead 
connectors to the water system inventory as this will not provide the value that the U.S. EPA envisions. 
Typically lead connectors are not well specified on older service records and water systems will expend 
significant effort and associated costs with an anticipated low number of known lead connectors identified 
through the process. The resources that would be spent performing the system-wide records review 
would be better spent on other activities such as service line inventory, identification of unknowns, and 
replacement of lead and GRR service lines. Lead connectors should be replaced when they are 
encountered in the field.  

7 
 
 
 
The LCRI should also not include any requirements for water systems to identify lead connectors in the 
field for the reasons listed in the preamble. Specifically, identification of lead connectors in the field would 
require water systems to excavate the connector to visually inspect the material. Excavation efforts to 
search for lead connectors would draw funding and staffing resources from the identification and 
replacement of lead and GRR service lines, likely delaying elimination of these service lines in the 
system. Because many connectors are likely to be under paved streets, excavation will incur costs 
associated with required markouts, road opening permits, work zone safety and vehicle traffic 
management plans (including rerouting school buses and emergency services vehicles, alternate traffic 
patterns and may require limited work hours including night work in high traffic areas) and potentially 
requiring utilities to fund significant street resurfacing. These activities can be better managed during 
scheduled water main replacement programs that are well coordinated with municipalities, other 
underground utilities and DOT entities. 
 
With respect to an individual location with a sample result over the lead action level, the presence of a 
lead connector at that location can be reviewed as part of the Distribution System and Site assessment at 
the time of the investigation. 
 
GRR 
 
The LCRI should not modify the approach to GRR. This includes the LCRR determination that a 
galvanized service line after a lead connector is not GRR. Any decision to the contrary could have a 
significant impact on the overall concept of identifying and replacing all lead and GRR service lines within 
10 years and would warrant further discussion. 
 
Full Service Line Replacement and Partial Service Line Replacement 
 
Full service line replacement should be the preferred approach for the reasons listed in the preamble. The 
LCRI must recognize that, in some instances, water systems will be forced to perform partial lead service 
line replacements (e.g., emergency repairs, when the property owner refuses to provide access or 
replace their portion of the service line, etc.). Further, permits, road reconstruction and repaving or 
roadway moratoriums are often a factor in the timing of upgrading underground infrastructure. In any such 
case, partial lead service line replacements may be unavoidable, and customers must be advised 
accordingly on the steps to take to reduce their potential exposure to lead. Written documentation from 
the customer (e.g., refusal to have work performed) will not always be possible as the water system does 
not have the authority to require this action of their customer. The inventory would be updated 
accordingly. 
 
The LCRI should not place a blanket prohibition on partial service line replacements including those 
solely performed for the purposes of lead or GRR service line replacement. Water systems must have the 
ability to upgrade their infrastructure networks (reduce leaks, breaks, improve fire protection, etc.) and 
cannot have non-viable limitations on their ability to perform this work. If the utility is prevented from 
replacing mains and services in streets due to customers refusing or ignoring lead service line 
replacement outreach, then area-wide upgrades could come to a halt, which could cause cascading 
affects such as impacts to property insurance costs, an increase in water main breaks, increased boil 
water notices, reduced resiliency, etc. Infrastructure upgrade projects are well coordinated to limit street 
openings and neighborhood inconvenience, are coordinated with other buried infrastructure, and can 
have significant impacts on transportation pathways (highways, roads, bridges, river crossings and similar 
infrastructure). These are not easily rescheduled when multiple entities are involved, especially when 
entities use multiple funding sources.  
 
The U.S. EPA must also recognize that not all water systems are municipal water systems and ensure 
that the provisions of the LCRI are able to be implemented by all water systems. For instance, privately 
owned water systems do not have the authority to enact local ordinances regarding service line 
replacement, so while this may be a viable option for municipally owned water systems, it will not work for 
privately-owned water systems. Likewise, privately owned water systems have limited impact and input 
on road openings, which will impact their ability to perform replacements even if the customer has 
replaced their side. 

8 
 
 
 
The LCRI should recognize physical disconnection of a lead service line as a full replacement in those 
instances where the service line will not be put back in service, such as vacant and abandoned 
properties. Water systems should not be required to have a policy documented in writing that prohibits 
disconnected LSLs and GRR service lines from being put back into service as this would add 
unnecessary administrative burden. Further, water systems need to be able to reconnect partials where 
the customer refused to replace their side or for work performed under an emergency.  
 
The LCRI should account for instances where the water system is able to replace the majority of the lead 
or GRR service line, but not able to replace into the building due to the structure being built on a concrete 
slab, the customer not allowing access, vacant property, or it is not safe for work to be performed at the 
location. While a small portion of lead or galvanized service line will remain in such cases, the risk to the 
customer has been reduced and mitigation measures have been provided to the customer such as 
flushing taps that have not been used, only using cold water for drinking and cooking, and routinely 
cleaning their aerator. 
 
Service Line Replacement Plan 
 
The approach proposed in the LCRI to require the development of a service line replacement plan due 3 
years after LCRI is finalized will allow water systems to continue to refine service line inventories and 
more refined data as well as time for meaningful plan development. 
 
The service line replacement plan should include provisions to communicate with both the bill payer and 
the resident, if they are different and addresses for both are known, to ensure that both tenants and their 
landlords at dwellings with lead or GRR have information about the program. The LCRI should not include 
requirements on the utility to contact the “owner” since water systems may not always have this 
information. 
 
Water systems that are proposing to perform full service line replacements should not be required to 
identify or cite any State and local laws and water tariff agreements relevant to the water system’s ability 
to gain access to conduct full lead and GRR service line replacement. Any specific State or local law or 
water tariff agreement provision that requires property owner consent for replacement or cost-sharing is 
not sufficient to support the safe replacement of full lead or GRR service lines over a property owner’s 
objection. Water systems attempting to perform service line replacements without approval from the 
property owner or customer with the authority to provide it can lead to safety issues, customer 
dissatisfaction, and complaints by the customer. 
 
The U.S. EPA should be balanced in the number of outreach attempts that constitute a “reasonable 
attempt” to engage the property owner about service line replacement. This includes recognizing that 
there are numerous other outreach requirements under this proposed rule and other existing regulations. 
As such, the U.S. EPA should confirm the current proposed requirement of four attempts using two 
different methods; any increase beyond that would not be appropriate. Further, as noted above, engaging 
the property owner should be deemed complete if the outreach attempts are made to the billpayer and 
resident (if they are different), in instances where the property owner is unknown. 
 
Any requirements related to water systems attempting to gain access for full replacement again upon any 
change in property ownership, even after the systems’ replacement deadline has passed, should be 
predicated on the water system becoming aware of change of ownership. 
 
Access to Replace 
 
The LCRI should not confuse control with access. Water systems need more than the authority to replace 
a service line, they also need access from the property owner or customer with the authority to provide it. 
Water systems should perform full service line replacements where they are granted access to do so, but 
the U.S. EPA must recognize that lack of property owner or customer approval to replace a service line 
can lead to safety issues, customer dissatisfaction, and complaints. Further, the LCRI cannot include any 
requirements that would place water systems in a position to take over full responsibility for customer-
owned service lines. 

9 
 
 
 
Schedule for Replacement and Determining Progress 
 
The proposed requirement in LCRI for removal of lead and GRR service lines within 10 years of the rule 
compliance date will help improve public health protection. However, the U.S. EPA should review the 
available data to confirm the maximum anticipated number of replacements per year, currently proposed 
at 10,000 per year or 0.039 average annual number of replacements served to ensure that the final rule 
includes appropriate deferred provision levels. The examples provided in the preamble of Flint, MI and 
Newark, NJ both were exceptions where significant financial assistance was provided and approval 
processes were streamlined. The typical water system will experience more difficult processes.  
 
Additionally, any water system that qualifies for the deferred provision should qualify by rule and not 
require state approval or assessment beyond confirmation of the determination. This would reduce 
burden and avoid any real or perceived arbitrary application of state discretion. 
 
State regulators should not have the authority to shorten the timeframe for replacement. If they are to be 
provided this authority, any such determinations must be made at the compliance date, not later in the 
process, and the criteria for such determinations must be clearly articulated. This is critical to ensure fair 
and consistent application across all water systems. 
 
Progress against replacement should be determined using one calculation for determining the material of 
unknown service lines and a separate calculation for removal of lead and GRR service lines. Further, 
water systems should report the number of service line refusals when they report removal statistics, 
providing these as a separate number but including them in the overall removal percentage to allow the 
water system to ultimately get to 100% removal. These calculations must also recognize customer 
refusals for any reason, including refusal to participate in service line material identification and refusal to 
replace their portion of the service line. 
 
Sharing of Inventory Information 
 
The LCRI should simplify sharing and reporting of inventory information to reduce burden while still 
providing valuable information to customers in a transparent manner. 
 
The U.S. EPA should review the data being requested to be reported and only require that information 
that is critical for oversight. This would include numbers required to understand service line identification 
and inventory but would not include location-specific information. It is more appropriate that information at 
that level would be made available to customers and water systems would certify that has occurred on an 
annual basis. 
 
Cost and Funding 
 
The cost to identify the material of all unknown service lines, validate the required subset of non-lead 
service lines, and replace all lead and GRR service lines within 10 years of the compliance date of the 
LCRI will require significant investment for all water systems. These costs will be dependent upon multiple 
factors, including the requirements in the final rule, and the number of unknown service lines identified as 
lead or galvanized requiring replacement. States should treat these expenditures for regulated utilities as 
federally mandated requirements that are recoverable in customer rates through expedited means. 
 
All water utility providers, regardless of ownership, must have equal access to any and all Federal and 
State funding. In the absence of substantial additional federal and state funding, water systems will likely 
be forced to defer important water infrastructure investments in other areas. 
 
Mitigation 
 
The U.S. EPA should limit pitcher filter distribution under LCRI to residential customers for work 
performed on potable service lines. Pitcher filters should not be required on non-potable lines, such as 
irrigation, fire services, or for non-residential customers. Non-residential customers should still receive 

10 
 
 
instructions on steps they can take to reduce their potential exposure to lead, but distributing a filter to a 
business or restaurant is not a feasible means of reducing potential exposure to lead.  
 
Following a partial service line replacement, steps should be taken to help to reduce the risk of galvanic 
corrosion between lead and other metallic pipes. While this might include installation of a dielectric 
coupling separating the remaining lead or GRR service line and the replaced service line unless the 
replaced service line is made of plastic, the U.S. EPA should be cautious about including a specific 
solution and would be better served providing a broader statement that would allow for use of new 
technologies that may be developed in the future without the need for a rule change.  
 
The LCRI should clearly state that sampling after a full service line replacement three to six months after 
the replacement is to consist of only a 1st liter sample and that water systems are not required to offer a 
5th liter sample. Collection of the additional sample is not warranted when the full service line has been 
replaced as the 5th liter sample is intended to be representative of water in the lead service line, which no 
longer exists in this instance. 
 
 
Reducing the Lead Action Level and Eliminating the Lead Trigger Level (141.80) 
 
Eliminating the lead trigger level, which caused confusion when considered in tandem with the lead action 
level, will likely improve understanding of the requirements. However, the associated reduction in the lead 
action level from 15 ppb to 10 ppb will likely result in water systems needing to modify existing corrosion 
control treatment or install new treatment where it does not currently exist. This will be an additional 
financial burden on water systems and customers, above what is required for service line identification 
and replacement. These challenges would be significantly increased if the lead action level were reduced 
to 5 ppb. 
 
American Water performed desktop treatment reviews of 55 higher risk systems to proactively address 
systems that may be challenged in meeting a lead action level of 10 ppb. It is important to note that this 
effort did not consider the additional change to include 5th liter samples from sites with lead service lines, 
which would be anticipated to increase the number of impacted systems. Of the 55 systems evaluated, 17 
had 10% of their samples over 10 ppb and 38 had 10% over 5 ppb. Recommendations were made to 
improve approaches to corrosion control at 24 systems, 18 to install new treatment and 6 to adjust 
existing treatment. These changes will require both initial capital costs as well as ongoing operation and 
maintenance costs, which are in addition to the costs for service line identification and replacement. 
 
 
Improved Tap Sampling (141.86) 
 
1st and 5th Liter Samples 
 
The LCRI should allow greater flexibility for the collection of 1st and 5th liter samples at sites with lead 
service lines beyond the current approach of five consecutive 1-liter bottles. Specifically, the rule should 
include multiple options, which would be selected at the discretion of the utility: 
• 
Sampling in five consecutive 1-liter bottles as included in the proposed LCRI. 
• 
Sampling using wide-mouth 1-liter bottles for the 1st and 5th liter samples to be analyzed for 
compliance purposes and 1-liter plastic collection bags for the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th liter samples. 
Using commercially available plastic bags in the same way as bottles will provide greater clarity 
around the samples of importance and create greater flexibility for providing sample materials to 
the customer. In addition, plastic bags take up less space in landfills than plastic bottles and could 
be beneficially reused as planters for growing small indoor plants, which would reduce the 
number of plastic bottles that could end up in waste streams or landfills.  
• 
Sampling in two wide-mouth 1-liter bottles using a timed approach where the first sample is taken 
when the faucet is turned on and the water remains running for one (1) minute before the second 
one-liter sample is collected. The average flow rate for kitchen faucets is 1.0 to 2.2 gpm, which is 
equal to 3.79 to 8.3 liters per minute. Given that instructions are to open the tap to an average 
flow, one would expect that the flow would not be at the upper end, so requiring a second sample 
collected after 1 minute would equate to a sample that is most likely between the 5th liter and the 

11 
 
 
7th or 8th liter depending on the flow from that particular tap. A sample collected between the 5th 
and 8th liter would be expected to be representative of the lead service line in an average home, 
which is the purpose of the second sample. Using a timed approach would be easier for the 
customer to understand and execute while reducing the waste associated with shipping as no 
additional materials would be required. 
 
The U.S. EPA must recognize the need for this additional flexibility in order to engage customers to 
collect compliance samples. Many water systems already need to provide financial incentives for 
customers to agree to collect one compliance sample. We anticipate needing to increase existing 
incentive amounts when we begin asking customers to collect multiple samples under the LCRI. 
 
Definition of Tier Sites 
 
The LCRI should not include sites with premise plumbing made of lead as Tier 1 or Tier 2 sites or 
galvanized premise plumbing that is or ever was downstream of lead as Tier 3. This would constitute a 
significant change to the sample tier structure with water systems needing to complete a full inventory of 
internal plumbing at the same time they are completing their service line material inventory or they would 
risk sampling from sites at a lower tier than required. Water systems do not track internal premise 
plumbing material as a typical course of business so adding this would be a significant burden at 
additional cost that would take resources away from other activities such as service line identification and 
replacement. There may also be some instances where customers may not provide access or information 
to the utility regarding the material of their premise plumbing.  
 
With respect to galvanized service lines, sites with a service line that is a combination of lead and 
galvanized should be considered a Tier 1 or Tier 2 site for sampling purposes.  
 
As indicated elsewhere in these comments, water systems should not be required to identify and include 
lead connectors in their inventories. However, if the U.S. EPA retains that requirement in the final LCRI, a 
galvanized service line following a lead connector should be a Tier 3 sampling location and with only a 1st 
liter sample required. 
 
Sampling Frequency 
 
Water systems monitoring annually should qualify for triennial monitoring if they do not exceed the lead 
and copper action levels for three consecutive years, instead of meeting the lead trigger level for three 
consecutive years. This should not only be reserved for medium and small systems; it should also apply 
to large systems. 
 
The final LCRI should retain the proposed requirement that all systems, regardless of size, can qualify for 
triennial monitoring if they measure 90th percentile levels at or below the practical quantitation limits of 
0.005 mg/L for lead and 0.65 mg/L for copper in two consecutive six-month monitoring periods. 
 
States should not have authority to specify sample locations when a system is on reduced monitoring. 
Water systems will need flexibility when developing their sampling pools, including gaining customer 
agreement to participate.  
 
Further, if state regulators are granted the authority to require more frequent monitoring than is required 
by the rule, the state should be required to have a documented process that applies equally to all water 
systems. The process should outline when additional monitoring will be required and the criteria for a 
water system to return to routine or reduced monitoring. 
 
Determining Compliance 
 
Water systems should only use results from samples collected at sample sites in their compliance pool 
when determining compliance. Results from samples collected at other locations that might meet different 
tier locations should not be used in compliance calculations since there will not necessarily be the same 
level of understanding about the sampling that would be known with a compliance sample. Providing 
flexibility in sample volume for samples collected for purposes other than determining compliance would 

12 
 
 
be one way to avoid potential confusion and unintended impacts. Water systems would need to focus 
additional resources if additional samples outside the identified compliance sampling pool were to be 
used to determine compliance, reducing the resources available for other activities such as service line 
identification and replacement. 
 
Water systems that have attempted but were not successful in engaging customers at Tier 1 and Tier 2 
sample sites should be allowed to use lower tier sample sites to meet sampling requirements. This will 
increase in importance as water systems replace lead service lines and the Tier 1 and Tier 2 sample pool 
reduces in size. 
 
Invalidation of Samples 
 
The final LCRI should allow state regulators to invalidate samples if they are determined to be from a 
location that does not meet the sample collection criteria, such as being collected from a hose bib rather 
than from a kitchen or bathroom sink tap.  
 
Initial Sampling Requirements 
 
The final LCRI compliance schedule should include a phased-in approach to allow states, water systems, 
and laboratories to focus their efforts accordingly and not be overwhelmed with all systems performing 
monitoring at the same time. This might include an approach that the U.S. EPA has used in previous 
rules where large systems monitor in Year 1, medium systems monitor in Year 2, and small systems and 
non-community systems monitor in Year 3.  
 
 
Corrosion Control Treatment (141.81 and 141.82) 
 
Section 141.81 requires large systems that meet the proposed lower lead action level but have P90 lead 
values that exceed 5 ppb and do not employ corrosion control treatment (CCT) to perform a pipe loop 
study to assess optimal corrosion control treatment (OCCT). Large systems that do employ CCT and 
meet the lead action level but exceed 5 ppb may also be required to conduct a pipe loop study at the 
State’s discretion. Only water systems that have exceeded the lead or copper action level should be 
required to optimize or re-optimize their corrosion control treatment since results of pipe loop studies can 
be difficult to interpret when trying to discriminate between CCT alternatives that produce results that 
meet the lead action level. Further, water systems that have already re-optimized due to exceeding the 
lead action level and continuously meeting optimal water quality parameters should not be required to re-
optimize again if there are subsequent action level exceedances for the reasons listed in the preamble. 
This should include studies performed prior to promulgation of the LCRI such as those water systems 
have taken to prepare for the LCRR.  
 
Water systems, especially small systems, may be able to determine the appropriate CCT based on a 
desktop evaluation and not need to spend the additional time and money on a more intensive evaluation. 
Water systems should only be required to perform pipe loop studies in those instances where the results 
would provide meaningful information in determining the appropriate path forward; otherwise, water 
systems should be able to work with their state regulator to make an informed decision in a timely, cost-
effective manner, which will accelerate our customers receiving the benefit of the proposed change to 
corrosion control treatment. This should not be limited based on system size or the state regulator 
assessment of a water system’s technical ability to perform different types of analyses as this will result in 
unfair and inconsistent application of these requirements across all water systems. 
 
The LCRI should retain the option for water systems to defer the corrosion control treatment steps, 
including costly and complex pipe loop optimization/re-optimization studies if they can replace all lead and 
GRR service lines in their system within five years. This would allow resources to be better directed to the 
removal of lead and GRR service lines than activities related to a pipe loop study and design, 
construction, and implementation of corrosion control treatment that will take approximately the same time 
to complete. The U.S. EPA should allow some flexibility around replacement rates as the proposed rate of 
a strict 20% per year does not allow these systems time to develop and ramp up their replacement plan. 

13 
 
 
This option should also recognize customer refusals similar to refusals in the overall service line 
replacement program described previously. 
 
 
Water Quality Parameters 
 
Only water systems that have exceeded the lead action level should be required to develop and maintain 
water quality parameters. Water systems may already be performing water quality monitoring as part of 
their corrosion control strategy, but including regulatory requirements would increase the resources 
necessary to complete the activity because any missed samples or deviations from developed ranges 
would carry regulatory repercussions. Water systems should maintain the current flexibility provided 
through proactive use of water quality parameters.  
 
The U.S. EPA needs to be cognizant of the potential impact including a requirement for all medium 
systems to develop and maintain water quality parameters. This would include the amount of additional 
monitoring that would be required and the additional reporting to state regulators, which provide 
opportunities for administrative violations. The U.S. EPA should also be sure the consequence of failure 
to monitor or failure to meet established water quality parameters is commensurate with the issue. Water 
systems should be required to perform additional monitoring or make changes to bring parameters back 
within range, but water systems should not be required to increase lead and copper tap sampling unless 
there are significant concerns with water quality parameter results. 
 
With respect to Distribution System and Site Assessments, collection of water quality parameters 
provides value as part of the site assessment process, but routine monitoring at those same locations 
does not necessarily provide long-term value. Water systems choose routine monitoring locations based 
on several aspects including representativeness of the location and accessibility. Locations used for a site 
assessment may have limitations, such as only being able to access a limited number of times since it is 
another customer’s home. Requiring mandatory water quality parameter sites may drive water systems to 
use hydrants as sample locations, which are not ideal for collecting samples. 
 
 
Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems 
and Non-Transient Non-Community Water Systems 
 
The U.S. EPA needs to ensure equal public health protection at all systems and to all persons, regardless 
of the size of the system. All systems need to have the technical, financial, and managerial capability to 
design, install, and operate corrosion control treatment or explore alternatives that allow them to meet 
these responsibilities (e.g., partnerships, consolidation, etc.). 
 
Regardless of any compliance alternatives that are offered to small community water systems or non-
transient water systems, all systems should be required to remove lead service lines under LCRI. 
 
 
Public Education (141.85) 
 
Overarching 
 
The LCRI provides an opportunity to educate customers and increase awareness about lead in drinking 
water. However, the U.S. EPA must be sensitive to the potential unintended consequences of 
overcommunication and the possibility of customers becoming indifferent to water system outreach. 
Public notification is a critical tool for customer communication and while water systems also appreciate 
the value of public education, there needs to be an appropriate balance between the two.  
 
The U.S. EPA needs to be cautious on the use of different terms intended to mean people who receive, 
pay for, and drink water provided by water systems. This includes terms such as “customer,” “consumer,” 
“resident,” “landlord,” and “owner.” The U.S. EPA should clearly define these terms with consideration of 
the impact of the definitions. For instance, while the U.S. EPA may intend “consumer” to mean a tenant in 
an apartment, the word “consumer” would also include someone traveling through a town that drinks 

14 
 
 
water or a restaurant in the town. Water systems would be challenged to have any communication with 
the former and any requirements to communicate with the latter would need to be different than outreach 
to residential customers, increasing the complexity of the rule. Further, while the U.S. EPA may be using 
“owner” to differentiate between the person who is responsible for the water bill and the person living at 
the location that is drinking the water, the “owner” is not always the person who is paying the bill, which 
would mean that water systems may not have this information.  The “owner” may not even be the person 
living at the location.  The U.S. EPA should carefully consider who the rule intends to address and limit 
definitions to those categories that are clearly defined in §141.80. 
 
The U.S. EPA should review regulatory language and guidance to ensure that mandatory and 
recommended language reflects steps that customers can take to reduce their potential exposure to lead, 
not minimize their potential exposure since there could be additional steps that the customer could take 
that were not identified.  
 
The LCRI should combine the public education requirements not related to notification of a lead action 
level exceedance into a single public education plan. Water systems should be required to develop and 
submit the initial plan at the LCRI compliance date and then certify annually that that water system had 
complied with the plan as designed. This would reduce the amount of reporting, streamlining the process 
and reducing the potential for violations.  
 
Delivery of Compliance Sample Results 
 
Expedited delivery of sample results to the persons served at the tap should be reserved for those 
samples that are over the lead action level. These results should be delivered in three business days 
rather than three calendar days to account for results that are received on a Friday, especially before a 
holiday weekend. Samples that are equal to or below the lead action level should be delivered in a timely 
manner, but no later than 30 days from receipt of the results since there is no immediate action needed 
by the customer or water system. Requiring all results to be communicated within three calendar days 
would force water systems to focus resources on this activity and away from other activities required 
under LCRI or other drinking water regulations. Water systems should have the flexibility to deliver results 
to customers as described in the proposed rule including electronic delivery via e-mail, phone, hand 
delivery, and mail (based on postmarked date). 
 
Water systems should use the same communication to provide both lead and copper results if both 
analytes were sampled at the location.  
 
 
Timing of Public Education 
 
As described in the preamble, water systems that exceed the lead action level need the 60 days after the 
end of the tap sampling period to develop public education materials, consult with the state regulator and 
identify the organizations that they need to share these materials with. The final LCRI should not reduce 
this time frame. 
 
Failure to Meet Service Line Replacement Requirements 
 
Water systems that are not able to meet service line replacement requirements will need flexibility for the 
best methods for engaging their customers based on the specific communities they serve. The final LCRI 
should provide a toolbox approach that allows water systems to choose from a list of options without 
limiting larger systems by having to choose from different lists. The U.S. EPA should provide flexibility to 
water systems that is simple and easy to understand and implement to achieve the desired outcome of 
public education and engagement and avoids water systems needing to focus more on the regulatory 
requirements in order to avoid an administrative violation.  
 
Water systems should include information on their service line replacement program in the CCR 
regardless of their progress in replacing service lines. The CCR presents an opportunity to engage 
customers and increase their awareness of service line replacement. 
 

15 
 
 
Notification of Service Line Material 
 
Water systems should provide notification to customers with lead, GRR, and lead status unknown service 
lines, including steps customers can take to reduce their risk. Water systems should have the flexibility to 
use a single communication to these customers as opposed to being required to send separate letters for 
each type of service as this may be more efficient for some water systems. Water systems should provide 
instructions and contact information for customers to use if they think their service line material is 
misidentified. Water systems should not be required to include lead connectors in their inventories, so 
notification to customers with lead connectors would be a moot point.  
 
Advising customers with lead service lines, GRR service lines, or service lines of unknown material about 
the value of lead sampling would be effective at helping those customers get a better understanding of 
their water quality. Water systems should have the flexibility of working with the customer to collect the 
sample or providing the customer with a list of certified laboratories that can perform the analysis. Water 
systems that are involved in the sampling should have flexibility to determine how to collect these 
samples, especially with consideration for the potential impact on compliance sampling since there will 
not necessarily be the same level of understanding about the sampling that would be known with a 
compliance sample. Some water systems may opt to mirror the same process they use for sampling after 
a lead service line replacement while others may choose to use a different sample volume to avoid 
potential confusion and unintended impacts. Results should be delivered to customers within three 
business days for results over the action level and 30 days for all other results, which is the same 
approach that should be used for delivery of all samples. 
 
Notification about Disturbances 
 
Water systems should be required to notify customers about the disturbance related to identification of 
service line material through potholing. However, water systems should only be required to provide a 
pitcher filter designed to remove lead if the U.S. EPA is able to provide data showing that the increased 
exposure to lead warrants such activity. Pitcher filters would only be appropriate if the exposure is 
expected to be significant or long-term and is not mitigated with flushing.  
 
Other Public Education Materials 
 
Water systems with a consecutive lead action level exceedance performing public education within 60 
days of the end of the monitoring period, as opposed to within 12 months of the last education as allowed 
under the current rule, will help to ensure communities receive materials in a timely manner following 
every lead action level exceedance. 
 
Sending public education materials to both the bill-paying customer address and service connection 
address, if different, would better ensure that renters receive this important information so that they can 
decide to take any needed steps to reduce their potential exposure to lead in drinking water. The U.S. 
EPA should refrain from including requirements from providing information to the “owner” since water 
systems may not have this information. 
 
Requirements for Language Updates and Accessibility 
 
The revised mandatory health effects language captures the U.S. EPA’s effort to emphasize health risks 
to all age groups (especially fetuses, formula-fed infants, and young children), include pregnant people to 
ensure that those through which the exposure is occurring to the developing fetus are highlighted so they 
can easily identify themselves as an at-risk group, simplify the language so that it is easier for consumers 
to understand, and make the language gender neutral for greater inclusivity. The U.S. EPA should revise 
the mandatory health effects language as shown below because an adjective describing the health effects 
is not necessary [emphasis added for clarity] 
 
There is no safe level of lead in drinking water. Exposure to lead in drinking water can cause 
serious health effects in all age groups, especially pregnant people, infants (both formula-fed and 
breastfed), and young children. Some of the health effects to infants and children include 
decreases in IQ and attention span. Lead exposure can also result in new or worsened learning 

16 
 
 
and behavior problems. The children of persons who are exposed to lead before or during 
pregnancy may be at increased risk of these harmful health effects. Adults have increased risks 
of heart disease, high blood pressure, kidney or nervous system problems. Contact your health 
care provider for more information about your risks. 
 
Water systems serving a large proportion of customers with limited English proficiency need the flexibility 
of providing an informational statement in public education materials regarding the importance of the 
materials that include contact information where the customer can obtain either a translated version of the 
materials or assistance in the appropriate language. Alternatively, water systems could provide materials 
in the appropriate language directly. As indicated in the preamble, some water systems may need 
assistance from their state regulator in developing translated materials. The U.S. EPA should develop a 
compendium of these resources for water systems to use. 
 
 
Systems with Multiple Lead Action Level Exceedances (141.85(j)) 
 
Water systems that exceed the lead action level are required to take specific actions including performing 
public education to their customers. Systems are required to repeat these actions until they are in 
compliance with the requirements of the rule and are required to perform them again upon a subsequent 
exceedance. The LCRI does not need to include requirements for water systems with multiple action level 
exceedances over a specific timeframe since this would be duplicative, add confusion, and unnecessarily 
cause water systems to focus resources away from other activities such as lead service line replacement. 
 
The proposed requirement that water systems make pitcher filters available would also raise concerns 
and confusion. Making pitcher filters available implies that water systems are not responsible for the cost 
of the filters, which is likely to cause confusion and dissatisfaction with customers while requiring filters for 
all customers could lead to unnecessary additional work at additional cost without providing additional 
public health protection. System-wide filter distribution can be challenging from the logistics standpoint of 
securing the necessary filters (will not be able to be stored on site), distributing (either directly or making 
available for pickup), and having the resources to plan and execute (taking away from other activities). 
Further, the rule needs to exempt distribution to non-residential customers such as fast-food restaurants 
and department stores. 
 
If the U.S. EPA retains any requirements related to making pitcher filters available to customers in this 
section, development of a filter plan after the first multiple exceedances would be appropriate but said 
water systems should not be required to submit the plan for review and approval. Additionally, the LCRI 
must include language regarding when a water system would be able to cease the additional 
requirements that were triggered by multiple exceedances of the lead action level. Otherwise, water 
systems risk not knowing when they are able to stop the additional activities. 
 
 
Schools and Licensed Childcare Facilities (141.92) 
 
Proposed LCRI Requirements 
 
The LCRI should provide schools and licensed childcare facilities with the opportunity to be sampled for 
lead, to learn about the importance of lead testing in schools and licensed childcare facilities and take 
additional actions if they choose. The U.S. EPA should include requirements to conduct public outreach 
to schools and sample in schools and licensed childcare facilities. However, the LCRI should not include 
requirements for schools, licensed childcare facilities or water systems to remediate lead based on the 
results of sampling. Further, an action level for schools and licensed childcare facilities is not necessary 
or appropriate for the reasons listed in the preamble and the existing 3Ts guidance is appropriate for 
these facilities to use for addressing lead in their facilities. 
 
Specifically, the U.S. EPA should not require water systems take remediation actions because larger 
buildings, such as schools and licensed childcare facilities, can have a higher potential for elevated lead 
levels due to complex plumbing arrangements, the presence of lead in premise plumbing, and 
inconsistent water use patterns that can result in long stagnation times. Additionally, as described in the 

17 
 
 
preamble, sampling at schools and licensed childcare facilities is a component of the treatment technique 
rule for public education and not a reflection of the water system’s corrosion control treatment. 
 
The U.S. EPA should continue to look for opportunities to clarify rule requirements and ease interpretation 
and implementation. This includes providing exclusions for newer construction and facilities that have 
undergone full plumbing replacement. It also includes separating the requirements for public education to 
all schools and licensed childcare facilities, sampling frequency for elementary schools and licensed 
childcare facilities, and sampling frequency for secondary schools, to clarify the different requirements, 
reduce cross-references, and ease implementation.  
 
The LCRI should also recognize that water systems will often need to coordinate with school districts as 
opposed to specific schools and decisions to sample will likely be at the district level. Requiring 
responses from individual schools in those instances would not be an effective approach to rule 
implementation and would likely cause confusion and customer dissatisfaction. 
 
Proposed Waivers Requirements 
 
Results from samples collected between January 1, 2021, and the LCRI compliance date should be 
acceptable to fulfill the requirements of lead and licensed childcare sampling as required under LCRI. 
This should be allowed by rule and not require a waiver from the state regulator. 
 
Sampling should not be required in a school or licensed childcare facility that installs and maintains point-
of-use devices certified to reduce lead in drinking water at all outlets used to provide water for human 
consumption (e.g. state requirements for schools to “filter-first”). This should be allowed by the rule and 
not require a waiver from the state regulator. Further, the final LCRI should not include a filter-first 
provision because filters may not be properly maintained as described in the preamble. We also agree 
with U.S. EPA’s decision to not propose that water systems be required to provide filters to schools and 
licensed childcare facilities for the same reasons that U.S. EPA is not proposing water systems to take 
other types of lead remediation requirements. 
 
Public Information About Lead Sampling in Schools and Licensed Childcare Facilities 
 
The Consumer Confidence Report provides an opportunity for water systems to provide a statement 
indicating that schools and licensed childcare facilities are eligible to be sampled for lead and direct 
interested members of the public to contact their local school or licensed childcare facility for more 
information. Water systems should not be required to make the sampling results publicly available for the 
reasons listed in the preamble including that water systems are not in a position to discuss next steps. 
Including a statement about the eligibility of sampling will increase public transparency while directing 
interested members of the public to the appropriate people to respond to any questions. 
 
Providing results from sampling at schools and licensed childcare facilities within 30 days would be 
consistent with typical water quality reporting and also meet the U.S. EPA’s goal to get data to public 
quicker and address concerns in a timely manner.  
 
 
Other Proposed Revisions to 40 CFR Part 141  
 
Consumer Confidence Report (CCR) 
 
The Consumer Confidence Report presents an opportunity to educate customers and increase 
awareness about lead in drinking water. Including an informational statement on lead as proposed would 
be more appropriate than including the mandatory health effects language that is used in public education 
materials given the different messages that are being sent (information vs. notification of a lead action 
level exceedance). 
 
Water systems should only be required to include the mandatory lead health effects language in the CCR 
for exceedance of the lead action level. Inclusion of the lead health effects language for other reasons 
such as failing to complete required public education nor failing to sample in schools and licensed 

18 
 
 
childcare facilities is not appropriate as these events are not indicative of additional risk from lead and 
therefore do not warrant the addition of health effects language in the CCR or elsewhere. 
 
Water systems that are required to include the mandatory health effects language due to exceeding the 
lead action level or failing to meet regulatory requirements related to LCRI should not be required to also 
include the CCR information statement. Including both statements will be redundant and lead to customer 
confusion as to the reason for two similar statements. 
 
As indicated elsewhere in these comments, CCRs provide an opportunity for water systems to include: 
• 
Information about their service line replacement program 
• 
A statement in their Consumer Confidence Report indicating that schools and licensed childcare 
facilities are eligible to be sampled for lead and direct interested members of the public to contact 
their local school or licensed childcare facility for more information. Water systems should not be 
required to make the sampling results publicly available for the reasons listed in the preamble 
including that water systems are not in a position to discuss next steps. Including a statement 
about the eligibility of sampling will increase public transparency while directing interested 
members of the public to the appropriate people to respond to any questions. 
 
Public Notification Rule 
 
Tier 1 public notification should be reserved for system exceedances of the lead action level as required 
by the American Water Infrastructure Act.  
 
Definitions 
• 
Distribution system and site assessment  
o 
Revising the name from Find and Fix to Distribution System and Site Assessment more 
accurately portrays the activities that will be performed and gives recognition to the fact 
that water systems will not always find something within their control to fix for every 
elevated lead sample result. 
• 
Wide mouth bottle 
o 
The definition of wide mouth bottle should be revised to specify the inner diameter to be 
at least 40 mm. This will greatly increase the variety of wide mouth bottles available to 
purchase while maintaining the advantage of sampling into a wide mouth container.

February 8, 2024
The Honorable Michael S. Regan
Administrator
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
Washington, D.C. 20460
Dear Administrator Regan:
Thank you for your bold leadership working to address and eliminate lead in drinking water 
across our nation. In particular, the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements (LCRI) proposal in December 2023 represents a critical step forward that 
will protect public health, create jobs and ensure a better future for our children. 
As you know, lead service lines (LSLs) pose an unacceptable health threat and 
disproportionately impact lower-income neighborhoods and communities of color. Black 
children especially are more likely to live in communities with LSLs and therefore have higher 
blood lead levels and are more likely to be poisoned by lead than white children. Given that 
disadvantaged low-income communities and communities of color are at greater cumulative risk 
from lead, they must be the top funding priority. This urgent public health crisis requires 
immediate action at all levels of government, which is why we strongly support the LCRI’s 
commitment to fully replace almost all of the nation’s lead pipes within 10 years.
We also appreciate that EPA is proposing to reduce the lead action level from 15 parts per billion
(ppb) to 10 ppb. This will ensure that communities across the nation are quickly detecting and 
taking action to address lead where it poses the greatest threat to public safety. However, as we 
know, there is no safe level of lead in drinking water and we recommend that you consider 
further lowering the threshold to the lowest practicable level.  
In order to further strengthen the LCRI proposal, we urge the agency to consider some additional
important changes to the final rule. Specifically, we recommend that the agency reconsider its 
proposed provisions that would enable some water systems to drag out the process of replacing 
their lead pipes over multiple decades. While we recognize the challenges for some 
municipalities to remove thousands of lead pipes in 10 years, the proposed rule could allow 
another generation of children in many communities to be exposed to lead from their tap water. 
Some cities have been able to replace tens of thousands of lead pipes in just a few years, creating
jobs while providing enormous benefits to their communities. Recent studies show that the health
and economic benefits of removing lead pipes and reducing lead levels in tap water are more 
than 10-fold larger than the costs, and that this work can create hundreds of thousands of good-
paying jobs.  

 
As part of the replacement provisions, the final rule should clearly ensure that individual 
property owners do not have to pay for lead service line replacement. These costs should be 
covered by federal, state and local government funds intended for lead service line replacement, 
including but not limited to, public-private partnerships and funds provided in the State 
Revolving Funds, EPA grant programs and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Some water 
systems and states required, installed, encouraged and approved lead pipe use for generations, 
with no input from homeowners. When utilities charge individual property owners for lead 
service line removal, low-income homeowners are often unable to pay and the landlords of low-
income renters often refuse to pay. This particularly exposes renters, low-income people and 
people of color to higher levels of lead in their drinking water. 
There are substantial new federal funds available to assist with the replacement of lead pipes, 
including $15 billion in dedicated funding for lead pipe replacement and an additional $11.7 
billion in grants, loans and principal forgiveness through the Drinking Water State Revolving 
Fund (DWSRF) included in the Drinking Water and Wastewater Act that passed as part of the 
2021 Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. There are additional funds provided under the Small, 
Underserved, and Disadvantaged Communities and the Reducing Lead in Drinking Water grants 
programs. 
Billions of dollars remain in many state and local coffers from the 2021 American Rescue Plan 
Act that are explicitly available for full lead pipe replacement. Other federal funds that may be 
used for lead pipe replacement are provided through the existing annual DWSRF appropriations 
and the Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act. We would be pleased to work with 
you on improving access to these federal investments in replacing lead pipes and addressing 
drinking water infrastructure needs. 
We also recommend that the LCRI proposal require comprehensive testing for lead in schools 
and childcare facilities, including tribal educational centers, with incentives for water utilities 
and non-profits to install filtration stations at these facilities that can provide immediate safe 
water while taking steps to remove and replace any lead plumbing, faucets and fixtures. This 
could work in coordination with the existing Voluntary School and Child Care Lead Testing and 
Reduction Grant Program created in 2016 and further improved by the Bipartisan Infrastructure 
Law in 2021. 
 
The agency’s proposed strengthening of provisions for reporting, public education and 
notification requirements are welcome, though even more could be done to ensure the public 
receives straightforward and honest information about the risk of lead in their tap water. We 
particularly urge EPA to expand lead testing and education programs in Native American and 
Tribal communities in consultation with leaders, experts and stakeholders. EPA also should work
with other relevant agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services, the 
Department of Housing and Urban Development, the Department of Agriculture, the Department
of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense to provide guidance and prioritization for the 
removal of lead pipes in government or government-subsidized housing, including transparent 
notification of lead presence for occupants. It is inexcusable for federally funded housing to 
poison its own residents.

In addition to these improvements, the existing Lead and Copper Rule must be better enforced. 
According to EPA’s own data, there are widespread – and often underreported – violations. To 
truly improve the Lead and Copper Rule, EPA must do more to ensure that these violations are 
taken seriously and addressed. 
 
We want to thank you Administrator Regan, Assistant Administrator Fox and EPA for your 
strong and consistent dedication to tackling this important problem. We believe that together, we 
can end the lead in drinking water crisis so future generations in this country will not have to 
question the safety of the water flowing from their taps.
Sincerely,
Cory A. Booker

Re: Comments on EPA's Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
 
Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI) put forward by U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA). Elevate respectfully 
submits these comments with attention to the State of Illinois and City of Chicago, which best estimates 
suggest are home to more lead service lines (LSLs) than any other state and city in the nation, 
respectively.  
 
Elevate is a Chicago-based nonprofit that advances safe, lead-free, affordable water for all with a focus 
on childcare and facilities and environmental justice communities. Elevate’s team of project managers, 
construction crews, and problem solvers work directly with the City of Chicago, as well as Cook County 
and State of Illinois, to prioritize equity in lead service line replacement both through direct 
implementation efforts and provision of technical assistance. In addition to research, analysis, and policy 
development, Elevate is the administrator of a three-pronged program to address lead in water:  
1. LeadCare Illinois1 works in collaboration with the Illinois Department of Public Health and Illinois 
EPA to engage childcare facilities across the state to test their water for lead, and support 
childcare providers in addressing sources of lead, including navigating the LSLR process. This 
program is funded through a non-competitive WIIN grant to the state.  
2. LeadCare Cook County2 goes a step further, offering free lead service line replacement (LSLR) to 
childcare providers in suburban Cook County, including the costs of restoration (e.g. repairing 
damage to floors, walls, and lawns where necessary).    
3. LeadCare Complete3 complements the City of Chicago’s LSLR program for childcare facilities by 
offering free premise plumbing assessment, upgrades, and follow-up evaluation to ensure lead 
levels remain below 2.01 parts per billion (ppb). This program is funded through a competitive 
WIIN grant for lead-in-water mitigation at childcare facilities.      
 
We share and appreciate EPA’s commitment to protecting public health by reducing the risk of exposure 
to lead, a known neurotoxin, through drinking water. We offer the following comments on the proposed

LCRI, including discussion of positive developments in the proposed rule, areas we believe need further 
improvement, as well as additional considerations important to implementation but which may be

I. Positive developments in the LCRI  
The proposed rule changes put forward by EPA mark significant, positive improvements to the Lead and 
Copper Rule. We believe the following provisions, in particular, represent movement in the right 
direction and offer these comments and recommendations with a focus on the areas in which EPA is 
seeking input: 
 
The inclusion of both first- and fifth-liter samples in water testing is more comprehensive and 
should be conducted through sampling processes as well as after LSLR. 
By adopting the Michigan model requiring both first draw and fifth-liter sampling, the proposed LCRI will 
help ensure that testing captures water from both premise plumbing, and water that has been sitting in 
service lines. This is an improvement to both the 1991 LCR and the 2021 LCRR, each of which overlooked 
potential sources of lead in water.  
➢ We applaud EPA’s decision to adopt this sampling protocol, and to retain and strengthen the 
LCRR provision requiring ANSI certified point-of-use filtration devices following full or partial 
LSLR.4  
➢ We encourage EPA to require testing following full and partial service line replacement, not 
merely offer this service to customers.5  
 
The lower action level, reduced from 15 to 10 ppb, and a simplified rule are important steps. 
We support the LCRI provisions that reduce and simplify the lead action level, removing the confusing 
“trigger level” construct from LCRR of 2021.6 As well documented, there is no safe level of lead 
exposure. While reducing the action level from 15 ppb is a step in the right direction, 10 ppb is not 
sufficiently protective from a health standpoint, and we believe EPA’s own analysis suggests 5ppb is 
feasible, which we elaborate on in the following section.  
➢ While we recognize the practical challenges of lowering the action level, we encourage EPA to 
set an action level at ≤ 5ppb or as close to zero as possible, to the extent feasible.  
 
Increased transparency in LSL inventories and LSLR plans, and improved community 
education requirements are important developments. EPA should provide model language 
and materials to support implementation and incentivize CWS actions to meet broader policy 
goals.

➢ EPA’s initial feasibility analysis and deferral eligibility thresholds should be viewed as a starting

II. Provisions in need of further improvement 
While the proposed LCRI offers important improvements on the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions 
and the 1991 rule, there are several areas that require further attention and improvements to meet the 
policy goals of safeguarding public health from the threat of lead in drinking water. The proposed rule 
should be strengthened in the following areas: 
 
Testing and mitigation requirements for schools and childcare facilities must be expanded 
and improved.  
Regardless of building type – residential or commercial – testing should be required, not merely 
“offered” following lead service line replacement. This should be paired with education efforts, 
provision of lead-rated water filters, and aerator cleaning following replacement. For example, Elevate’s 
childcare programs follow the American Water Works Association guidelines, which include filtration 
and testing activities for a duration of six months post-replacement. The LCRI should close gaps in water 
testing requirements for childcare facilities: 
➢ EPA is seeking comment on whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or 
sample more frequently in schools and child care facilities.17 Water testing should be required at 
all cooking and drinking water sources within home- and facility-based childcares and schools, 
as opposed to only five at elementary schools and two sources at childcares.18 The presence of 
high lead levels can vary greatly from fixture to fixture and sampling only a few can result in 
missing the problematic outlets.  This is clearly demonstrated by the fact that when Chicago 
tested every cooking and drinking water source in its public elementary schools, only 2.9% of 
fixtures exceeded the 15ppb standard then utilized, but these were spread out amongst 34.6% 
of school buildings.19 Probabilistically, selecting only five fixtures to test would have missed most 
schools with a high-lead fixture. 
➢ Where the LCRI states that testing be “offered” to secondary schools, the language should be 
amended to “require” testing. While young children may be at greater risk, lead exposure is 
harmful from childhood through adolescence and adulthood. Furthermore, secondary schools 
also often serve as community hubs. Drinking water fixtures in these facilities often serve

diverse populations, including expectant and breastfeeding mothers on staff or attending as
