➢ Water system representatives should visually inspect for the presence of an LSL when on site to 
perform testing at childcares and schools, if not already completed as part of inventory efforts. 
➢ Community water systems should provide information on state resources and requirements for 
testing and mitigation. This should be provided in addition to the “3Ts” guidance for reducing

20% of facilities every year. 
➢ Testing waivers should not be allowed simply for having a filter in place. In our experience, it is

➢ As the agency responsible for testing, community water systems should check school and

changes in the location of licensed childcare facilities from month to month. 
 
While the reduced action level of 10ppb is a step in the right direction, it is insufficient.  
Removing the confusing “trigger level” construct and reducing the lead action level from 15 to 10ppb 
are improvements in the proposed LCRI. However, 10ppb is not sufficiently protective from a public 
health perspective. As EPA acknowledges, including through the Maximum Contaminant Level Goal 
(MCLG) of zero parts per billion, there is no safe level of lead in water.22 Even low levels of lead in blood 
have been shown to negatively affect children’s intelligence, development, and behavioral patterns, and 
pose health risks to adults alike.  
 
Many have recommended a maximum contaminant level of 5ppb, and the American Academy of 
Pediatrics recommended an action level of 1ppb in schools. While we recognize the challenge of 
implementing an action level lower than 10ppb, we offer the following examples of where 5ppm or 
lower has been implemented:  
• 
The Illinois Department of Children and Family Services licensing standards hold Illinois child 
care providers to a standard of 2.01ppb based upon laboratory limits of quantification and 
schools are required to sent notifications of lead levels are detected above 5ppb.23 If lead is 
detected in child care facilities, providers are required to issue notifications regarding presence 
of lead, mitigation plans, and follow-up test results.24

EPA’s analysis of systems at or below alternative lead action levels show that 37% of systems with LSLs,

and that the potential burden associated with optimized CCT and other ALEs protocols can be more 
easily overcome throughout LCRI compliance, with progress toward LSLR shifting the action level 
compliance landscape over time in favor of a lower action level.   
➢ A truly health-based standard would be zero, and we support lowering the action level as close 
to zero as is practical, at a maximum of 5ppb. EPA should embrace the lower action level, and 
work with states to address administrative challenges faced by small and medium sized systems 
to support compliance.    
 
Reporting, enforcement, and response to action level exceedances (ALEs) should be strengthened. 
While the LCRI improves upon the required response to ALEs, EPA should strengthen the public 
notification provisions by requiring water systems to immediately report ALEs to customers, state 
agencies, and EPA. 
➢ EPA should consider working with states to stand up centralized web pages or online bulletins 
where ALE information can be made publicly available as quickly and transparently as possible 
for real-time tracking and accountability and to enhance accessibility.  
➢ Additionally, EPA should clarify that ANSI lead-rated filters must be provided or delivered, not 
simply “made available” in response to multiple ALEs. This is an important step in ensuring 
equitable access to filters, creates an opportunity for additional education and touchpoints with 
residents, and clarifies ambiguity around what constitutes “availability.”29   
As noted above, the LCRI also includes enhanced communication and education requirements in 
response to ALEs and failure to meet LSLR replacement rates.  
➢ EPA should work with states to ensure this language is easily accessible in ready-to-use formats 
(e.g. template emails, door hangers, phone scripts, social media posts, slides for use in town hall

EPA must do more to accelerate full lead service line replacement by tightening up deferred 
deadlines for LSLR completion and incorporating new learning into updated feasibility 
analyses throughout LCRI implementation to accelerate LSLR in deferral-eligible communities.  
While we are sensitive to feasibility and affordability concerns, allowing deferred deadlines threatens to 
leave millions of US residents at increased risk of lead contamination and creates a system of unequal 
protection from this dangerous neurotoxin that disproportionately harms already overburdened 
communities. EPA states that it expects significant learning, market correction, and advancement in 
efficiencies throughout the implementation of the LCRI in the next decade. Offering significant 
extensions beyond the national 10-year target at the outset, before these advancements have had a 
chance to take root, is misguided.  
 
In the interest of equitable implementation, environmental justice, and public health, we urge EPA to 
tighten up the deferral criteria and deadlines, work with states to identify opportunities to accelerate 
the rate of LSLR, and direct resources to communities that face the constraints identified in the agency’s 
feasibility analysis to expedite action to replace all LSLs and protect all communities from lead 
contaminated drinking water. As it stands, the LCRI leaves residents served by the most lead-burdened 
water systems with less protection for unacceptably long periods of time. “EPA is proposing two 
eligibility criteria for systems to defer their service line replacement deadline past 10 years in 
accordance with a schedule that is feasible and prevents known or anticipated adverse health effects of 
lead to the extent feasible” (emphasis added):32 
• 
The first criterion would allow deferred replacement deadlines for systems with a high density 
of LSLs per household (>0.039) based on affordability concerns. According to EPA’s estimates, 
this would apply to some 1-4% of all U.S. water systems, or 720-2,178 community water 
systems.33

Chicagoans deserve lead-free water now, not in 50 years. EPA should work with the city and 
State of Illinois to deliver on that promise and reconsider the feasibility of accelerating LSLR 
in the nation’s most lead-burdened city.  
Allowing Chicago 40 years or longer to complete LSLR is unacceptable. City leadership has already 
committed to a more aggressive rate of LSLR than the proposed LCRI would require. This is reflected in 
statements by the current and former mayoral administration, and recent action by the city council. EPA 
references Detroit’s commitment to replacing 10,000 LSLs per year as an indicator that the city believes 
this rate is feasible. The agency should similarly take Chicago at its word and set the bar higher. EPA 
should encourage Chicago to meet or exceed its ambitious goals, not set long-term deadlines – 
especially at this early stage when supporting data is limited – that immediately disincentivize the action 
that the city has already committed to. 
 
Under Mayor Lori Lightfoot, the City of Chicago launched its LSLR program in partnership with CDM 
Smith, a global engineering firm recognized for LSLR technical and program expertise. Released in April 
2021, the City of Chicago Lead Service Line Replacement Program Report details a 25-year timeframe for 
LSLR under an aggressive replacement scenario.39 With new Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) funding, 
new state and federal funding opportunities, and increased political will in the city since the 2021

• 
In the LCRI, EPA distinguishes between emergency and planned, “proactive” LSLR, and is 
“seeking additional data on service line replacement rates achieved by systems in proactive 
programs.”45 We expect this type of information to become available as water systems begin to 
comply with the LCRI. Chicago’s Department of Water Management already reports an 
estimated 3,500-5,000 emergency repairs per year, in response to which the utility provides full 
LSLR.46 If EPA’s current assumption of 10,000 LSLRs per year as the upper limit of feasibility were 
clarified to only include planned, “proactive” LSLR, Chicago’s ability to achieve 16,000-18,000 
LSLRs per year by 2028 appears feasible under EPA’s existing feasibility logic and Chicago’s 
current plans to ramp up LSLR before the LCRI 2027 compliance date. 
• 
Throughout the LCRI and BIL implementation guidance, EPA repeatedly attempts to right-size 
expectations and assistance based on system size and capacity. We should be able to expect 
more from large systems like Chicago. EPA notes Newark’s top rate of LSLR, up to 100 lines/day 
for 4-5 days per week. EPA projects out that if Newark’s rate “had been maintained for 20 weeks 
out of the year, it would have resulted in 8,000-12,000 replacements per year.”47 EPA argues 
that this could not serve as a standard for the rest of the country because it is an outlier and 
received significant federal support, the likes of which could not be widely guaranteed 
throughout LCRI implementation.48 But with more LSLs than any other U.S. city, Chicago is also 
an outlier. We should be able to call on state and federal agencies to help accelerate LSLR and 
improve upon what is currently considered feasible. What’s more, Chicago’s Department of 
Water Management conducts work year-round, reporting replacements every month, with 
significant proportions of non-emergency replacements happening into December and in early 
spring.49 This suggests a construction calendar closer to 40 weeks, which would nearly double 
EPA‘s projection of 8,000-12,000 LSLR/year being technically possible based on Newark‘s data, 
again consistent with a rate of LSLR more than 16,000 per year in Chicago.

EPA should push cities like Chicago to do more, not less – to move faster, not slower – to protect public 
health, and back up that commitment with the tools, technical assistance, and resources to get the job 
done. Why start with conservative limits that prolong Chicagoan’s exposure to lead at the outset? 
 
EPA should close loopholes by clarifying language about service lines “under the control” of 
water systems and requiring full LSLR, at no direct cost to residents.  
We appreciate that the proposed LCRI intends to require water systems to conduct full LSLR regardless 
of property ownership, and that the LCRI would only allow full LSLR to count toward a water system’s 
overall replacement rate. However, allowing exemptions where systems claim that they do not “control” 
or do not have “access to” some portion of the service lines creates a major loophole.50 Water shutoff 
policies, the management and treatment of water supply, and local codes that dictate service line 
material all indicate that the entire lead service line is under control of the water system regardless of 
whether the soil around or above it is privately or publicly owned.  
 
Wherever possible, EPA should reject the practice of differentiating between public and private “sides” 
of a service line as a condition of responsibility for replacement, and ensure that residents do not bear 
the direct cost of LSLR. There are inherent inequities baked into the public-private construct, which the 
2021 LCRR attempted to address by requiring LSLR regardless of ownership, but which is left ambiguous 
in the proposed LCRI.51  
➢ EPA should close this loophole by amending the definition of service line to clarify that service 
lines may be owned by the water system, owned by the property owner, or both. We support 
further strengthening provisions regarding mandatory full service line replacement, as 
recommended by Neltner (2024), to affirmatively clarify criteria for determining access to 
conduct full LSLR.52 
➢ As stated above, in part I. regarding LSLR plans, EPA should provide guidance and model 
legislative language for passing or amending laws to reduce barriers to accessing LSLs as 
necessary to complete thorough, full LSLR at no direct cost to residents. This technical assistance 
and education should be provided to a range of stakeholders, including local NGOs and local TA 
providers, community water systems, and state and local decision makers.  
On the issue of cost-sharing, EPA should push to the extent of its authority to shield residents from 
direct cost of LSLR. Too often, residents are stuck paying for mistakes or outright negligence of water 
system decision makers. For example, the Chicago Municipal Code required lead service lines until it was 
federally banned in 1986, well past the point of scientific consensus that the use of lead in drinking

water poses significant health risks. Adding insult to injury, contractor quotes put the cost of LSLR for 
Chicago homeowners between $16,000 and $25,000. Requiring residents to pay for LSLR is 
fundamentally unfair, violates principles of environmental justice, and disincentivizes action to remove 
LSLs.   
➢ The provision of safe, clean, affordable drinking water is a clear case of public purpose, as is the 
equitable implementation of programs to remove harmful lead infrastructure from U.S. drinking 
water systems. EPA should examine its authority and state action under the Public Purpose 
Doctrine to require water systems to address the full service line, including any portion thar runs 
through private property, at no direct cost to customers.  
➢ If and where residents are required to directly pay for LSLR and states do not act to prevent 
direct cost-sharing, EPA should work with states and other stakeholders to audit implications for 
participation in LSLR and examine such LSLR programs from an environmental justice 
perspective, including screening for civil rights violations.  
➢ Wherever possible, incentives and prioritization should be given to promote water systems’ 
assumption of responsibility for the full service line, as we have seen in Newark, NJ, Benton 
Harbor, MI, and other communities that have embraced this best practice. This could, for 
example, be included in guidance to states regarding the treatment of LSLR projects in State 
Revolving Fund scoring criteria or distribution of principal forgiveness.  
 
EPA should clarify acceptable materials for use in LSLR, and responsible management of post-
consumer waste through the process.  
EPA should disallow the use of plastics in pipe replacement and ensure safe storage, disposal, or reuse 
of lead materials. Ensuring replacement material is safe – and for service lines of the size for which lead 
was used, that means using copper – is essential. Otherwise, we could soon be facing a similar service 
line safety issue with tremendous public health and financial costs once again. Independent researchers 
have noted a variety of health concerns about plastic water pipes, including the leaching of plastic 
additives into drinking water, the increased permeation of ground contamination into the pipes, and 
increased risk to both the water and potentially first responders in the event of fires or excess heat.53 
Material scientists have also questioned the long-term durability of plastic piping materials, especially in 
comparison to copper.  
While plastic pipes have been certified to various standards, these standards are not comprehensive 
enough to address the health concerns that have been raised.  Furthermore, while copper pipes do 
present some potential health and leaching risks, our long experience with this material means we have 
a strong understanding of these risks and how to effectively address them. The same cannot be said 
about newer plastic materials for which practical experience and comprehensive research is limited.   
 
53 As reported by Robin Lloyd, ”Replacing Lead Water Pipes with Plastic Could Raise New Safety Issues,” Scientific 
American, August 16, 2022, https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/replacing-lead-water-pipes-with-plastic-
could-raise-new-safety-issues/ 
 

 
 
 
 
16 of 17
 
➢ Replacing lead with plastic has a significant risk of being a regrettable substitution and EPA 
should use its authority and influence to ensure only the safest and most well-studied materials 
are utilized. The cost of materials is small relative to the cost of service line replacement and 
should not be a barrier to choosing the most durable, proven, and safest material.  
➢ EPA should also issue guidance with clear requirements on how to handle lead pipe materials 
once old service lines are decommissioned.  As the Agency recognizes, there is no safe level of 
lead exposure, and therefore the old lead service line is a potential hazard.  Whenever feasible, 
the decommissioned service line should be fully removed and sent to a domestic recycling 
facility which offers additional assurances regarding safe handling and maintains some degree of 
control over lead materials under EPA’s purview.   
➢ We recognize that the removal of the old service line, especially when trenchless replacement 
techniques are utilized, may be difficult or economically impractical. In such cases, the agency 
should require the utility to document and preserve documentation as to the existence and 
location of the decommissioned lead line and ensure the property owner is also made aware 
that the decommissioner line remains as a potential hazard. 
 
 
III. Additional considerations 
As stated, we support EPA action to strengthen the Lead and Copper Rule, and we are grateful for the 
opportunity to comment on the proposed LCRI. In addition to the comments on the proposed changes 
offered here, we would like to draw attention to several attendant issues associated with the successful 
implementation of LSLR nationwide:  
 
Dovetailing LCRI implementation with ongoing technical assistance (TA) efforts 
EPA is already engaged in technical assistance efforts through BIL implementation, support for 
Environmental Finance Centers (EFCs), Get the Lead Out (GLO), the WaterTA initiative and other 
activities. We are pleased to see these efforts come together in a “whole of government” approach to 
mitigate the threat of lead in drinking water. We offer the following considerations to support successful 
implementation of LCRI:  
➢ EPA should work with TA providers, states, and regional actors to encourage and coordinate 
resource sharing across communities that may compete for access to the same supplies, 
resources, and labor pool as they work to comply with the LCRI. 
➢ TA and template communications materials should be provided to support water systems in 
effectively engaging the communities they serve and securing resident participation and 
cooperation in inventorying, testing, and LSLR strategies. 
➢ As stated earlier, EPA and TA providers should be prepared to offer model policies to support 
local implementation efforts, including local ordinances or statutory language that may help 
water systems in overcoming barriers to accessing properties served by LSLs.  
➢ EPA should work with partner agencies at the state level to identify capacity needs to support 
monitoring, enforcement, and provision of TA related to LCRI compliance. This should include an 
audit of state capacity to effectively implement the associated funding and financing tools that 

 
 
 
 
17 of 17
 
EPA notes as supporting LSLR nationwide: Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation 
(WIIN) funding, Water Infrastructure Finance and Innovation Act (WIFIA), Drinking Water State 
Revolving Fund (DWSRF), and others. To the extent feasible, this assessment should be made 
publicly available.  
 
Prioritizing water affordability in LSLR funding and financing strategies 
In the LCRI, EPA identifies several federal resources available to support lead testing and LSLR. These 
include WIIN, WIFIA, DWSRF and others. Additional support may be available to align federal resources 
to support LSLR and LCRI compliance, including opportunities available through other agencies such as 
Community Development Block Grants. While we applaud existing efforts to provide resources to 
communities most in need, we would like to see a clear commitment to water affordability in the 
assessment of water system financial capacity by EPA and TA providers. 
➢ Whether through the EFCs or other channels, water systems should be directed to resources 
that can support local water affordability efforts and the development of customer assistance 
programs (CAPs). While we have significant work to do to remove lead from community water 
systems – and address a range of other pressing clean water and drinking water infrastructure 
needs – these efforts must be paired with water affordability and assistance measures.

We thank EPA for its efforts to protect public health and advancing important, actionable provisions in 
the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvement.  If we can provide additional information or 
clarification, please do not hesitate to contact Anna-Lisa Gonzales Castle, Director of Water Policy, at 
anna-lisa.castle@elevatenp.org

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0968 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 2, 2024
RE: Final Lead and Copper Rule Must Prevent Lead in Drinking Water
CleanEarth4Kids.org urges the EPA to strengthen the proposed Lead & Copper Rule
Improvements (LCRI) to protect human health and especially children from lead. As
many as 12 million lead service lines threaten the drinking water of over 20 million
people.1
We ask for the following improvements and additions to the LCRI.
●
Require all water utilities to fully replace all lead service lines within 10 years
with no exceptions at no cost to consumers. This is necessary to protect
renters and low-income homeowners.
●
Set a maximum contaminant level (MCL) at all taps TO no higher than 5 ppb
(parts per billion) as done in Canada and the European Union.23
●
Require immediate electronic test results by water utilities to a publicly
accessible database shared by the EPA and state health departments.
●
Require water utilities to test for lead from each fountain and drinking/cooking
water source in schools and childcare centers at least once every 6 months.
Any tap exceeding 5 ppb must be shut off immediately with parents and
guardians notified
●
Implement mandatory lead testing for all children at 9-12 months, 24 months
and 3 years regardless of their participation in publicly funded programs.
Require lead testing as a requirement for admission to daycare, preschool,
kindergarten, elementary and middle school to provide early detection.
There Is No Safe Level of Lead
Exposure to lead can seriously harm a child’s health, including damage to the brain
and nervous system, slowed growth and development, learning and behavior
problems, as well as hearing and speech problems.4

There is no safe level of exposure to lead according to the World Health Organization,5
Centers for Disease Control6 and the American Academy of Pediatrics.7 Lead is
especially toxic to children and unborn babies.8 Lead damages children’s brains and
nervous systems, lowers IQ, causes behavior problems, and it is linked to higher
rates of suspension and detention along with lower reading and math test scores.9,10
Most health impacts from lead exposure are lifelong and irreversible.
EPA data shows minority and low-income populations have a higher risk of lead
exposure in drinking water.11 Lead poisoning disproportionately affects communities
of color,12 with Black children having the highest concentration of lead in their blood.
According to a 2021 study, over 170 million Americans are exposed to harmful levels
of lead as children.13
Lead can harm children by damaging their brain, nervous system, delay growth and
development, and hearing and speech issues.14
Please Take Additional Actions to Stop Sources of Lead
CleanEarth4Kids.org asks the EPA to take additional actions to protect children’s
health, public health, wildlife, water, soil and our environment from toxic lead.
Eliminate and Regulate Lead in Plastics
Lead is added to plastics like pacifiers, teethers, and cups including toys.15,16 Lead
dust is released when plastics are exposed to sunlight, air, and detergent or when
recycled/destroyed.17 Lead in items like teethers, pacifiers, sippy cups18, dishes,
utensils, children's toys, jewelry, clothing19, baby food or any products used or
borrowed by children must be stopped.20
Stop Lead in Consumer Goods
Lead and other heavy metals are also found in various children’s toys, products and
playground surfaces, including synthetic turf and crumb rubber infill.21,22 Children,
birds and wildlife can be harmed by ingesting the plastic blades of grass and infill.23

Lead must not be allowed in consumer goods as children are commonly given party
favors and other items meant for adults. For example, over 60% of Mardi Gras beads
were found to contain over 100 ppm of lead and other toxins.24 25 million pounds of
these beads are used in New Orleans every year, polluting our waterways and soil.25
Additionally, along with regulations prohibiting the sale of lead containing products,
the public must be alerted that lead may be found in pottery and ceramics, including
glazes and coloring along with folk remedies.26,27
Stop the Sale, Use and Storage of Lead in Aviation Fuel
According to the FAA, leaded aviation fuel (AVGAS) is used in almost 170,000
piston-engine planes & helicopters (general aviation) in over 20,000 airports in the
US.28 Less than 1/4% of Americans are pilots for these aircraft. These planes and
helicopters cause 70% of the lead pollution in our air!29 Over 5 million people,
including over 360,000 children under the age of 5, live near at least one airport
where these aircraft fly.30
Multiple studies have shown that children who live near these airports have higher
levels of lead in their blood and most high lead emission airports are in communities
of color.31
According to EPA data, 22 of the 100 most lead polluting airports are in California.
Unleaded AVGAS is now available for all general aviation. California must take action
to stop the sale, storage and use of leaded aviation fuel.32
Lead in Second and Third Hand Tobacco Smoke
Lead is in second and third hand smoke. Secondhand smoke causes higher blood
levels in children33 and adults34 and lead in house dust is likely from thirdhand
smoke.35 California must implement strong measures to protect children from lead
exposure due to tobacco smoke. Blood lead levels were 14% higher in children living
with 1 smoker and 24% living with 2 or more smokers.36 This highlights the
importance of addressing not only direct sources of lead exposure, but also indirect
sources such as second and third hand smoke.

Re: Comments on EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements

To Whom It May Concern: 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this proposed rule. 
The mission of the NaƟonal Center for Healthy Housing (NCHH) is to secure healthy homes for all. NCHH 
is a naƟonal technical and scienƟﬁc nonproﬁt organizaƟon dedicated to developing and promoƟng 
pracƟcal measures to protect children from residenƟal environmental hazards, including lead poisoning, 
while preserving aﬀordable housing. NCHH develops scienƟﬁcally valid and pracƟcal strategies to make 
homes safe from hazards, to alert low-income families about housing-related health risks, and to help 
them protect their children. 
 
NCHH strongly supports and appreciates EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The 
changes outlined by EPA would be a signiﬁcant improvement on the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule 
Revisions (LCRR), are responsive to advocate concerns about and since the LCRR, and would pave the 
way to removing all lead service lines (LSLs) in the U.S. by ten years aŌer the compliance deadline.  
The keystone change in the LCRI, and the one we are most excited to see, is the requirement that all 
water systems move to replace all of their LSLs within ten years. In the LCRR, replacement of LSLs was 
only included as a last resort and triggered when water systems exceeded the acƟon level. The LCRI 
decouples the acƟon level – sƟll an important measure for understanding risk to residents and for 
guiding corrosion control and public noƟﬁcaƟon measures – from the replacement requirements. This is 
in line with our understanding that there is no safe level of lead exposure, that even low levels of lead 
exposure can cause harm, and that the best way to prevent childhood lead exposure is to remove 
sources of lead in our homes and environments, including our drinking water. We applaud EPA for 
aﬃrming this approach in the LCRI.  
In addiƟon to the LSL replacement requirement, we are supporƟve of many of the other elements in 
the LCRI, including but not limited to: 
• 
As noted in the proposed rule, this is the ﬁrst Ɵme EPA has included the following esƟmates 
when calculaƟng the health beneﬁts of addressing lead exposure: 
o Avoided cases of ADHD  
o Avoided cases of low birth weight 
o Avoided deaths due to cardiovascular disease. 
Including all of these outcomes, as well as IQ beneﬁts, helps EPA and advocates capture some of 
the outsized posiƟve beneﬁts that will result from compliance with the LCRI. EPA esƟmates that

between the two further demonstrates how the LCRI will be a signiﬁcant improvement over the 
LCRR in terms of boosƟng public health. 
 
We are addiƟonally appreciaƟve of EPA’s demonstraƟon of these societal beneﬁts because the

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0792 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Feb 1st, 2024
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket, 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, 
Washington, DC 20460.
RE: Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 (Lead and Copper Rule)
The Wisconsin Board for People with Developmental Disabilities (BPDD) appreciates the 
opportunity to comment on proposed revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule. Lead poisoning is 
a 100% preventable cause of Intellectual and Developmental Disabilities; every Wisconsin 
county has children poisoned by lead. BPDD has been working with state agencies and the 
legislature on policy changes that will reduce and eliminate lead exposure from lead
contaminated water and paint.
Utility and customer side lead service lines and internal lead plumbing are sources of lead 
poisoning that can be eliminated when pipes are replaced. Up to 20% of lead exposure is 
caused by drinking water. In infants, 40-60% of lead poisoning is traced to drinking water and 
tap water used in infant formula. We appreciate the rule’s 10 year timeline for complete 
replacement, which will eliminate this source of lead poisoning that has been allowed to 
continue for decades.
Lead service lines exist in Wisconsin communities across the state. Based on 2022 data from 
Wisconsin’s Public Service Commission (PSC), there is an estimated 158,000 utility lead service 
lines and 141,000 customer side lead service lines in Wisconsin, with an additional 34,000 utility 
side and 45,000 customer side lead service lines that could have lead. Cities with aging 
infrastructure and a significant amount of old stock housing—including Milwaukee, Racine, and 
Kenosha—have many lines that need replacement, and many low-income residents who often 
cannot afford to move even if they are aware of unsafe lead levels.
Wisconsin has a patchwork of existing loan programs and funding sources that can be leveraged 
to support utility and customer side lead line replacement; however, replacement progress has 
been slow due to restricted eligibility, local capacity to write and administer grants and 
contracts, workforce shortages, limited funding, match requirements, lack of knowledge about 
lead line replacement options, and competing priorities. Many of Wisconsin’s options limit the 
ability for individual property owners to self-finance remediation and do not help renters.
Despite the infusion of ARPA funds and the dedication of $15B nationally under federal 
infrastructure law for lead line replacement, additional funding will be needed to fully replace 
lead service lines in the next ten years as the final rule proposes. Existing Wisconsin programs, 
including the Safe Drinking Water Loan program and the Private Lead Service Line Replacement 

program, provide some relief to municipalities, although both are competitive programs and 
funding authority is set by the legislature through the state’s biennial budget process. 
Many communities and individual property owners may not be able to complete lead line 
replacement within a 10-year timeframe given the scale of pipes that need replacement, 
procurement and supply chain delays, and workforce shortages. An ongoing source of funding 
for lead service line replacements is needed throughout the implementation period or until the 
work is done. 
Wis. Stats. 196.372 offers a mechanism for a dedicated funding source that requires a portion 
of the water utility rate to be used for utility and customer side lead service line replacement.
Current Wis. Stats. 196.372 allows a water utility to apply to the Public Service Commission to 
raise water utility rates to provide financial assistance for complete replacement of customer 
and utility side lead service lines. The statute specifies that the water utility rate increase must 
be used solely for lead line replacement. Utilities can establish either a grant or loan program 
for customer side replacement; grants are limited to cover only 50% of the cost and loans 
cannot be forgiven. 
Several Wisconsin communities have successfully used this statute to finance complete 
replacement of their lead service lines. Some communities are concerned about the impact 
increases in water rates may have on low-income households which are often correlated with 
old stock housing served by lead pipes. In these low-income communities, affected properties 
may not have high property values and affected properties may be rental units; affected 
tenants are not eligible to apply for funding that would remove lead hazards.
We recommend EPA keep the ten-year implementation requirement. The infusion of ARPA 
and Infrastructure Act funds with existing Safe Drinking Water Loan program authority offers a 
unique opportunity over the next five years for replacement of lead service lines. To the extent 
possible, we recommend state spending be directed towards communities that have the 
most lines to replace, the highest number of low-income households by census tract data, 
and rural areas with small water utilities and lower numbers of utility rate payers.
We recommend throughout the 10-year implementation period, complete lead service line 
replacement is prioritized within the Safe Drinking Water Loan program. Replacement of 
orphan customer lead service lines should be an allowable use of Safe Drinking Water Loan 
program funds, and funding should be managed centrally such that individual property owners 
are not dependent on local water utilities to apply for funding.
After the implementation deadline, we recommend EPA require water utilities to raise water 
utility rates and use the funds generated from the rate increase to replace utility and 
customer side lead service lines until all lines have been replaced. Water utilities should be 
required to document on utility bills the rate increase, that funds are being used to replace lead 
service lines, and the number of known utility and customer service lines left to replace. These 

elevated rates and required spending on lead service line replacement should continue until 
complete replacement has been accomplished; then water utilities should be required to lower 
rates.
This rule is silent on lead paint which is the source of an estimated 80% of childhood lead 
poisoning. Lead service line replacement is important and long overdue; however, this major 
accomplishment will not be sufficient to end childhood lead poisoning. 
BPDD is charged under the federal Developmental Disabilities Assistance and Bill of Rights Act 
with advocacy, capacity building, and systems change to improve self-determination, 
independence, productivity, and integration and inclusion in all facets of community life for 
people with developmental disabilities1. 
Thank you for your consideration,
Beth Swedeen, Executive Director, 
Wisconsin Board for People with Developmental Disabilities
                                                       
1 More about BPDD https://wi-bpdd.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Legislative_Overview_BPDD.pdf .

Re:  
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI)  
Dear Sir or Madam:  
The EPA is proposing revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation for Lead and 
Copper (hereafter referred to as Lead and Copper: Improvements or LCRI) under the authority of 
the Safe Drinking Water Act. 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (Dec 6, 2023).  
Lead and copper enter drinking water mainly from corrosion of plumbing materials. 84 Fed. Reg. 
61684 (Nov 13, 2019). “Lead was widely used in plumbing materials until Congress banned its 
use in 1986, and there are an estimated 6.3 to 9.3 million homes served by lead service lines 
(LSLs) in thousands of communities nationwide…”  84 Fed. Reg. at 61685. LCRI revisions 
include updates in testing protocols, corrosion controls, acceptable lead and copper levels, 
requirements for water sampling in schools and for utilities to complete lead service line 
inventories. The most significant revision is the requirement to replace lead service lines in the 
nation within 10 years. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84878. 
The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops (USCCB) Committee on Domestic Justice and Human 
Development, Committee on Pro-Life Activities and other committees have long advocated for 
safe drinking water, including funding for lead pipe replacement in the Bipartisan Infrastructure 
Law1 and other legislation to address chemicals in drinking water that disproportionately affect 
 
1 USCCB, Letter to Congress Concerning Legislation on Infrastructure, Apr. 22, 2021, 
https://www.usccb.org/resources/letter-congress-concerning-legislation-infrastructure-april-22-2021  

 
children, expecting mothers, and the unborn.2 “[A]ccess to clean water is crucial and additional 
funding is needed to replace lead pipes nationally, ensuring that all Americans have access to 
clean water, a universal human right.”3 The LCRI details the implementation of water standards 
throughout the United States which remains a priority for the USCCB’s integral ecology policies 
for three central reasons: the importance of water for health, life and justice. 
Water, health, and life 
It is well known that that lead exposure can cause harmful health effects for all people and 
“especially pregnant people, infants, and young children (CDC, 2022a; CDC, 2022b; CDC, 
2023)… Lead exposure causes damage to the brain and kidneys and… developing fetuses, 
infants, and young children are most susceptible to the harmful health effects of lead (ATSDR, 
2020)”. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84897.4 Drinking water can account for 20 percent of an adult persons 
lead exposure and most of a child’s lead exposure comes from drinking water (absent routine 
exposure to other sources like paint or contaminated soils), whereas infants may “receive 40 to 
60 percent of their exposure to lead from drinking water used in the formula.” 88 Fed. Reg. at 
84897. 
The health and well-being of all people—especially the unborn, children, and pregnant 
mothers—is affected by the quality of drinking water. In his landmark encyclical on ecology, 
Laudato Si’, Pope Francis dedicated an entire section exclusively to the importance of water for 
the world’s peoples and the planet.5 In turn, the USCCB has continuously advocated for safe 
water standards and highlighted the connection of water with health of the most vulnerable. 
Indeed, clean water is an expression of a “culture of life.”6  
For people of faith, the stewardship of water matters not only for life on this earth but for the 
afterlife. Numerous religions throughout the world revere and respect water for its healing, 
purifying and spiritual qualities and symbolism.7 Inspired by the Jewish customs and the sacred 
scriptures with its “many connections between water and healing (cf. 2 Kings 5:8-14; Jn. 5:2-4; 
Jn. 9:6-11)” 8, Christians throughout the world use water for the sacrament of baptism, which

“signifies and actually brings about death to sin” as the baptized are “born of water and Spirit” 
(Jn 3:5) and enter “into the life of faith.”9   
Water is a source of life and salvation. As such, it is a terrible contradiction that today in 
America we quench thirst and baptize children with water poisoned with lead and copper. 
Communities of faith throughout America have an additional, faith filled reason to support 
efforts to replace lead pipes and clean our nations drinking water. Based on principles of life and 
health, the USCCB supports the ambitious requirements in the LCRI to replace LSLs, update 
testing protocols, increase testing in schools and reduce levels of water contamination. 
Water and Justice 
 
While water poisoned with lead and copper constitutes an injustice to all Americans, this 
injustice is unevenly distributed among the population. The CDC asserts that “American 
drinking water supplies are among the safest in the world,”10 and points to the early history of 
water infrastructure and treatment that delivered clean water to millions in the decades that 
followed the dawn of the nation. Installation of water infrastructure, built with cast iron and lead 
pipes, began on a major scale in the United States in the late 1800s, particularly in the larger 
cities, and continued until the 1920s and 1930s.11 In the 1920s, on a trip to New York, the 
English Catholic author G.K. Chesterton was struck by the American ideal of equality expressed 
in daily experiences, including widespread and efficient access to water.12 As such, clean water 
access was not only an expression of health and salvation, but of equality of all people.   
Can we say the same today? In the last twenty years, there have been numerous municipal water 
crises stemming from deteriorated infrastructure and exacerbated by the continued use of LSLs, 
such as in Washington D.C. in 2004 and Flint, Michigan a decade later. An American Water 
Works Association report pointed out that virtually all cast-iron pipes either already have expired 
or will expire this decade, and although lead pipes may have a slightly longer average lifespan, 
much of lead infrastructure replacement must occur within the next two decades as well.13 
America’s ailing and unrepaired infrastructure is responsible for much of the disproportionate

effect of lead exposure from drinking water on communities of color and low-income 
communities.14 
The EPA has already established that communities of color and low-income communities are 
disproportionately exposed to the risks of lead in drinking water delivered by community water 
systems. 86 Fed. Reg. 71574 (Dec. 17, 2021). In addition to higher lead exposure from water, 
communities of color and low-income communities also tend to have higher exposure to lead 
from other sources, such as paint from older housing or contaminated soil, increasing the risk of 
these populations suffering elevated blood-lead levels. Due to other disparities such as lower 
economic status and limited access to medical care, these communities face additional harms 
from lead and associated health risks, of which lead-contaminated drinking water is a significant 
contributor. 86 Fed. Reg. at 71575. 
Other challenges posed by replacement of privately owned LSLs are well addressed in the LCRI. 
The USCCB supports the restrictions on partial LSL replacement due to its adverse health 
effects, which are especially likely in low-income communities and communities of color that 
cannot pay for the private portion of the LSL replacement. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84928. We also 
recognize the need for flexibility in implementation of LSL replacement given different laws in 
each state and water district and support limited flexibility in meeting timelines for LSL when 
water utilities/systems demonstrate plans to replace LSL and that do not incur extra costs on 
ratepayers. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84926. 
We thank you for your consideration of this comment, and your work on this issue of 
tremendous importance to the health and wellbeing of all Americans, especially the most 
marginalized in our society.   
 
Respectfully submitted,

The elephant in Portland’s room: Lead and Copper Rule’s “OCCT”
27 years ago, Portland Water Bureau (PWB) forged a distinctive agreement with the
state health authority, exempting PWB from adhering to federal regulation. It was
proposed as “regulatory flexibility for compliance with the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR)”
and as “a substitute for Lead and Copper Rule requirements for Optimal Corrosion
Control Treatment (OCCT).”1997 PWB XL project
Portland Water Bureau never complied with the federal LCR regulation aimed at
“minimizing public exposure to lead in drinking water.” Jeanne Briskin,EPA. 1989 interview.
Instead, our provider created their own Lead Hazard Reduction Program (LHRP), touted
as a “model strategy for other water systems” and “a cost-savings measure.” 1997 PWB XL
In short, PWB found loopholes to circumvent LCR OCCT treatment requirements.
Even where there are supposedly no or few lead pipes (LSL, GRR, pigtails), water that
is inadequately treated for corrosion can cause serious lead contamination, as it has
here, and where it’s an ongoing problem :
“... lead corrosion of plumbing materials is inextricably linked to drinking water
corrosivity, and drinking water corrosivity is to a great degree – albeit not completely –
controlled by water utilities.
This link is the foundation of the Lead and Copper Rule.”Dr. Lambrinidou, LEAD Action News OCT 2017

Re:   COMMENTS OF THE OFFICE OF THE PEOPLE’S COUNSEL FOR THE 
DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA ON THE U.S. ENVIRONMENTAL 
PROTECTION AGENCY’S PROPOSED RULEMAKING ON NATIONAL 
PRIMARY DRINKING WATER REGULATIONS FOR LEAD AND 
COPPER 
I.  
Introduction  
The Office of the People’s Counsel (“OPC-DC” or “Office”), the statutory representative 
of District of Columbia utility ratepayers,1 respectfully submits these Comments in response to 
the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) proposed rulemaking entitled “National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements” published in the 
Federal Register on December 6, 2023.2 OPC-DC commends the EPA for its proactive steps 
toward addressing a critical public health issue – the presence of lead in our nation’s drinking 
water. OPC-DC recognizes and applauds the EPA’s commitment to enhancing the safety and 
quality of drinking water through these proposed revisions. The initiative to phase out all lead 
service lines within a decade is a testament to the agency’s dedication to public health and its 
responsiveness to the urgent need for improved water safety standards. 
 
1 D.C. Code § 34-804 (Lexis 2020). 
2 Hereafter referenced as “LCRI”. 

2 
 
The proposed revisions to the Lead & Copper Rule represent a significant advancement 
in the fight against lead contamination. Lead in drinking water poses severe health risks, 
particularly to children and pregnant women, and the EPA’s move to finally eradicate this threat 
is both timely and essential. By mandating the replacement of lead service lines and lowering the 
action level for lead in drinking water, the EPA is setting a more aggressive standard to 
strengthen public health protection. These actions will have a profound and lasting impact on 
communities across the country, including those in the District. 
II.  
Summary 
In summary, OPC-DC supports the EPA’s initiative to mandate lead service line 
replacements within ten years of issuance, as this is a critical measure for public health 
protection.  
• The proposed requirements for comprehensive service line inventories and replacement 
plans should ensure a detailed and systematic approach toward identifying and addressing 
lead pipes. OPC also applauds the proposed reduction of the lead action level to 0.010 
mg/L for its potential to significantly reduce lead exposure risks while line replacement is 
ongoing. To meet these goals while complying with White House mandates, the EPA 
must provide a balanced approach that ensures an equitable cost burden 
• However, OPC-DC recommends enhancements in public education requirements, 
emphasizing the need for inclusive, clear, and frequent communication strategies about 
the dangers of lead in water and the benefits of line replacements.  
• Addressing the feasibility of the 10% annual replacement rate, OPC-DC recommends a 
thorough market analysis to ensure adequate labor and material resources are available, 

3 
 
while also advocating for partnerships with educational institutions for workforce 
development.  
• OPC-DC supports the prohibition of partial service line replacements, except in 
emergencies or during planned infrastructure work, as it aligns with long-term public 
health objectives.  
• Lastly, OPC-DC recognizes the importance of identifying and addressing potential legal 
barriers at state and local levels to full lead service line replacement and therefore 
recommends efforts to align varied laws and regulations with the EPA’s lead and copper 
rule improvements.  
These combined efforts are crucial for a more effective, efficient, and equitable approach 
to eliminating lead exposure from drinking water. In the following comments, OPC-DC seeks to 
offer constructive feedback and recommendations that we believe will strengthen the 
effectiveness of the rule's implementation and ensure that the benefits of these crucial changes 
are realized by all residents, particularly those in the most vulnerable communities. 
 
DISCUSSION 
III.  
OPC-DC Supports Mandated Lead Service Line Replacement in an Affordable and 
Equitable Manner 
First, OPC-DC firmly endorses the EPA’s proposed 10-year replacement deadline for lead 
service lines as part of its revisions to the Lead & Copper Rule. We recognize the critical 
importance of this timeline in addressing such a pressing public health concern as the presence of 
lead in drinking water is a serious issue that poses considerable health risks, particularly to 
children and vulnerable populations. Accelerating the removal and replacement of lead service 

4 
 
lines within this concrete timeframe is not only a necessary step but also a moral imperative to 
ensure the provision of safe and clean drinking water to all residents. 
However, while OPC-DC supports this vital initiative, we are acutely aware of the 
challenges that accompany it, notably the potential for rising utility rates. Across the country, we 
are witnessing a significant increase in the cost of water services, a trend that could be further 
influenced by the financial demands of such a widespread infrastructure overhaul. Without 
significant coordinated state and federal investment, the additional costs of replacing lead service 
lines within ten years, although essential for public health, may place a substantial financial 
burden on utilities and, by extension, on consumers. 
In light of this, OPC-DC urges a balanced approach. While we advocate for the swift 
elimination of lead hazards in our water supply, we also emphasize the need to consider the 
economic impact on consumers, particularly those in lower-income brackets. This could be done 
with significant state and federal funding, sliding-scale payment options and customer rebates for 
property owners that proactively replace their lead service lines, and regular review of progress 
and adjustment of strategies as needed. It is crucial that as the nation advances toward a lead-free 
future, we also ensure that these improvements are achieved equitably, without placing undue 
financial strain on residents who can least afford the costs of these replacements. 
 
IV.  
OPC-DC Supports Service Line Inventories and Replacement Plan Requirements 
But Recommends Clear Measures to Address Environmental Justice Goals 
As the advocate for water consumers in the District of Columbia, OPC-DC is keenly 
aware of the critical importance of the EPA’s proposed requirements for water systems to 
regularly update service line inventories, develop a replacement plan, and identify all service 

5 
 
lines of unknown material by the replacement deadline. The emphasis on accurate service line 
inventories is commendable, as it forms the backbone of an effective lead pipe replacement 
strategy – especially since a large portion of DC Water’s service line inventory is of unconfirmed 
material. We support the proposed validation process to ensure inventory accuracy and believe 
that this will significantly enhance the effectiveness of replacement plans. 
The requirement for water systems to include lead connectors in their inventories and 
replace them is a vital addition, considering these connectors can be significant sources of lead 
contamination. OPC-DC applauds this thorough approach, which acknowledges and addresses 
often overlooked components of water infrastructure. 
OPC-DC also agrees with EPA’s proposal to consolidate completion deadlines for water 
systems to categorize the material of all unknown service lines with the mandatory full service 
line replacement deadline. This streamlines administrative processes by synchronizing these 
critical tasks and should help water systems more efficiently manage their resources and efforts, 
leading to smoother and more coordinated operations. 
Additionally, EPA’s expanded requirements for notification and safety procedures 
following significant disturbances to lead service lines, galvanized-requiring-replacement service 
lines, or service lines of unknown material is a step in the right direction. The proposed revision, 
which extends the requirement for notification and flushing instructions to include disturbances 
resulting from inventory efforts like potholing, better protects public health than the current rule. 
This proposed change aligns with the comprehensive approach needed to mitigate the risks 
associated with lead exposure in drinking water and acknowledges that even activities not 
directly related to repair or replacement, such as inventory assessments, can disrupt lead 
particulates and potentially elevate lead levels in the water supply. 

6 
 
However, it is crucial to recognize that lead service lines (“LSLs”) are disproportionately 
found in older, lower-income, and underserved neighborhoods where residents have the least 
ability to personally afford the replacement of LSLs. This disparity raises significant concerns 
about environmental justice and the equitable distribution of public health protections. While the 
LCRI encourages water systems to prioritize replacements in an efficient, effective, and 
equitable manner, we believe more concrete and clear measures are needed in the final rule to 
meet the environmental justice goals laid out by the Biden administration.3 
As a result, OPC-DC recommends that the EPA consider mandating prioritization 
protocols that specifically target underserved and vulnerable communities. This could include 
guidelines for water systems to identify and prioritize areas with older housing stocks, lower-
income households, and a history of neglect in infrastructure upgrades. Such protocols should be 
accompanied by adequate funding mechanisms to ensure that the financial burden of these 
necessary upgrades does not fall disproportionately on the communities that are most in need of 
these improvements. Furthermore, we suggest that the EPA provide additional guidance and 
support for public outreach and community engagement in these neighborhoods to guide local 
water utilities on best practices. This will help in building trust, ensuring transparency in the 
replacement process, and encouraging community participation, which is critical for the success 
of these initiatives. 
 
 
 
3 Executive Order 14096, Executive Order to Revitalize Our Nation’s Commitment to 
Environmental Justice for All, April 21, 2023, https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-
room/presidential-actions/2023/04/21/executive-order-on-revitalizing-our-nations-commitment-
to-environmental-justice-for-all/. 

7 
 
V.  
OPC-DC Supports the Reduction of the Lead Action Level  
OPC-DC supports EPA’s proposal to lower the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L in its 
proposed LCRI – this more stringent standard for the lead action level demonstrates a serious 
commitment by the federal government to see the eradication of lead from drinking water 
sources. Lead is a well-documented neurotoxin with no safe level of exposure, particularly 
harmful to children and pregnant persons; by setting the action level at 0.010 mg/L, the EPA is 
taking a crucial step in reducing these health risks. This move aligns with the growing body of 
scientific evidence suggesting that even low levels of lead exposure can lead to significant health 
problems, including developmental disabilities in children and various chronic cardiovascular, 
neurological, and kidney conditions in adults.4 
Furthermore, the proposal to remove the lead trigger level and directly set the action level 
at 0.010 mg/L is a proactive approach that OPC-DC endorses. This change will prompt water 
systems to initiate full-scale replacement actions sooner, rather than waiting for lead levels to 
reach higher, more dangerous thresholds. Such prompt action is essential in mitigating the risks 
associated with lead exposure and ensuring that all communities have access to safe drinking 
water. 
While we recognize that this lower action level may present challenges to water systems, 
particularly in terms of resources and logistics, the potential public health benefits far outweigh 
these challenges. It is an imperative step towards ensuring that all residents, regardless of their 
socio-economic status or geographic location, have access to safe and clean water. We encourage 
 
4 EPA, Basic Information about Lead in Drinking Water, https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-
drinking-water/basic-information-about-lead-drinking-water#health; EPA, Learn about Lead, 
https://www.epa.gov/lead/learn-about-lead  

8 
 
the EPA to provide the necessary support and guidance to water systems as they work to meet 
this new standard, ensuring that the transition is effective, efficient, and equitable. 
Additionally, EPA’s proposal to limit corrosion control requirements for systems that 
have re-optimized their corrosion control and continuously meet optimal water quality standards, 
but experience a subsequent exceedance, is a pragmatic approach to reducing costs while moving 
towards full lead line replacement. This approach acknowledges the balance between protecting 
public health and being mindful of the cost implications for ratepayers. Requiring repeated re-
optimization can lead to significant expenditures that may not proportionately contribute to 
reducing lead level exceedances – especially during system-wide lead line replacement. By 
exempting systems from re-optimizing if they have already done so effectively and are 
maintaining optimal water quality, the EPA is preventing unnecessary financial burdens on 
consumers while ensuring that resources are allocated more effectively. 
 
VI.  
OPC-DC Supports Improvements in Public Education Requirements and 
Recommends the Development of Multilingual and Culturally Sensitive Educational 
Materials 
OPC-DC recognizes the critical role of public education in tackling the issue of lead in 
our drinking water. The EPA’s push for enhanced public education campaigns is a step in the 
right direction, but these efforts must be as inclusive as possible. In major urban areas as diverse 
as the District, information about the risks of lead and the importance of service line replacement 
must be accessible to all, irrespective of language or cultural background. 
To this end, OPC-DC advocates for the development of multilingual and culturally 
sensitive educational materials. We urge the EPA to provide the necessary resources and 

9 
 
guidelines to ensure that these campaigns effectively reach every corner of our community. 
Moreover, this should be more than simply disseminating written notices; visual, social, and 
digital media is necessary to ensure that crucial information about lead exposure reaches 
everyone. This could take the form of bus station ads, notices on popular local websites, or 
television public service announcements. OPC-DC also recommends adoption of programs 
similar to DC Water’s Lead Free DC Community Activators Program, which trains local 
residents to inform residents and property owners about replacing lead service lines.5 
The EPA’s requirement for water systems to make substantial efforts to engage with 
property owners is an important aspect of these educational outreach endeavors. EPA’s proposal 
to require that there be at least four different outreach attempts, utilizing various communication 
methods, is an excellent way to ensure that this message gets through. However, it’s not just 
about reaching out; it’s about providing clear, comprehensive information about the health risks, 
the benefits of replacing service lines, and available support, especially for financial aid 
programs.  
Furthermore, in areas where the risk of lead exposure is particularly high, we believe that 
the frequency of communication needs to be increased. While annual notifications are useful, 
more regular updates — perhaps quarterly — could significantly boost public awareness and 
prompt residents to take proactive measures. Lastly, the requirement to re-engage with new 
property owners is a thoughtful strategy to ensure ongoing protection and awareness. This 
continuous engagement is particularly important in a place like D.C., where property turnover 
can be frequent. 
 
5 DC Water, DC Water and District Department of Employment Services Launch the Lead Free 
DC Community Activators Program, May 23, 2023, https://www.dcwater.com/whats-going-
on/news/dc-water-and-district-department-employment-services-launch-lead-free-dc.  

10 
 
VII.  OPC-DC is Concerned About the Feasibility of EPA’s Proposed Replacement Rate 
and Market Response  
The EPA’s proposed annual replacement rate of 10%, aiming for complete replacement 
within a decade, is a commendable and ambitious goal that reflects the urgency of this public 
health concern. However, the realization of this goal hinges on the critical factor of whether the 
labor and material markets can keep pace with this heightened demand. 
Because of the very real concern over whether adequate labor and material resources 
exists to reach these admirable goals, it is imperative that EPA undertake a comprehensive 
assessment of the current labor market’s capacity to meet this increased demand for skilled labor 
in LSL replacement. This should encompass a detailed evaluation of the availability of qualified 
workers, an understanding of the training requirements, and insights into the geographical 
distribution of these labor resources. Such an assessment is crucial to anticipate potential 
shortages and to devise effective strategies to address them.  
Moreover, while the 10% annual replacement target is praiseworthy, its practicality may 
vary significantly across different jurisdictions. It is vital to consider a range of factors, including 
the size and age of water systems, the condition of existing infrastructure, and the unique labor 
market conditions in various locales when determining compliance requirements and standards. 
A more adaptable approach, allowing for variability in the replacement rate based on these 
factors, could prove more effective than a one-size-fits-all mandate for replacement. 
Addressing potential labor shortages is a critical aspect of this initiative. OPC-DC 
advocates for the formation of partnerships with vocational schools and trade unions to foster the 
development of specialized training programs, akin to the District’s founding of the D.C. 

11 
 
Infrastructure Academy.6 Such initiatives would not only support this specific project but also 
contribute to long-term economic development and job creation within our communities. 
Collaboration with industry stakeholders and educational institutions is equally vital. These 
partnerships can spur innovative solutions to both labor and material shortages, potentially 
including apprenticeship programs, on-the-job training opportunities, and research into 
alternative materials or methodologies that could streamline the replacement process. 
Furthermore, the potential shortages in materials and filters necessary for replacement 
work represent a significant challenge. We urge the EPA to explore and establish contingency 
plans and alternative supply chains, in cooperation with other federal and state agencies and 
stakeholders, to ensure uninterrupted access to these essential resources over the next decade. 
This might involve strategies such as stockpiling critical materials or forming agreements with 
suppliers to prioritize lead replacement projects. 
 
VIII.  OPC-DC Supports the Prohibition of Partial Service Line Replacements  
OPC-DC largely supports EPA’s proposal to prohibit partial service line replacements, as 
partial replacements of LSLs have been shown to potentially increase lead levels in the short 
term due to disturbances in the pipes.7 The prohibition of such partial replacements, unless in the 
 
6 OPC-DC advocated for the establishment of the D.C. Infrastructure Academy as a condition of 
the negotiated settlement approving the District’s Pepco-Exelon merger; it is now a multi-utility 
collaborative between Pepco, Washington Gas, DC Water, Washington Metropolitan Area Transit 
Authority, University of D.C., and the District Government. See, e.g., D.C. Infrastructure 
Academy, https://dcia.dc.gov/; D.C. Office of the City Administrator, Mayor Bowser Announces

bowser-announces-negotiated-settlement-pepco-exelon-merger.  
7 Rebecca Renner, Reaction to the Solution: Lead Exposure Following Partial Service Line 
Replacement, Environ. Health Perspect., Vol. 118, Issue 5, A202-A208, May 2010, 
https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2866705/.  

12 
 
case of emergency repairs or as part of broader infrastructure work, is a prudent approach that 
will protect public health. It ensures that replacements are comprehensive and do not 
inadvertently exacerbate lead exposure risks to the public while addressing historical 
environmental injustices.8 
Additionally, the EPA’s proposed requirement for systems to provide advance notification 
to customers along with an offer to replace the customer-owned portion of the LSL is a 
commendable practice. This measure ensures transparency and allows homeowners to participate 
in complete line replacement, thereby reducing their risk of lead exposure. 
OPC-DC agrees with and supports the EPA’s exceptions for emergencies, since in urgent 
situations where partial replacements are necessary, it is vital to have clear and stringent 
guidelines to manage any potential increase in lead exposure. This approach balances the 
immediate need for repairs with the long-term goal of reducing lead exposure. 
Furthermore, the mandate for risk mitigation measures following a partial replacement, 
such as public education and the provision of pitcher filters, is an essential component of this 
rule. These measures are crucial in minimizing the immediate risks associated with disturbed 
lead pipes during and after LSL replacement. 
 
 
 
8 A recent study has shown that full lead service line replacements were less common in lower-
income, higher-minority neighborhoods under a cost-sharing program design in Washington,

IX.  
In Addressing Legal Barriers to Full Replacement, OPC-DC Recommends 
Guidance for State and Local Reform  
These improvements are vital steps towards ensuring safer drinking water for all. 
However, the intricate web of differing state and local laws poses significant challenges in 
implementing the proposed improvements to the LCRI. Across various jurisdictions, the 
diversity in statutes, constitutional provisions, local ordinances, and service agreements creates a 
complex regulatory environment. This diversity can potentially hinder the uniform 
implementation of the EPA’s plan, making it difficult to achieve the goal of safer drinking water 
on a nationwide scale. As state and local authorities navigate these changes, we recognize the 
potential conflicts that may arise within existing state and local laws and regulations; a challenge 
that the EPA’s new proposal seeks to address by requiring systems to identify potential legal 
barriers to full service line replacement. 
To navigate these challenges, OPC-DC proposes the creation of a framework that would 
guide states and localities in aligning their laws with the EPA’s LCRI requirements. It should 
include clear guidelines for water systems and state authorities to identify and assess legal 
barriers, alongside a compilation of best practices and examples from jurisdictions that have 
successfully integrated their local laws with federal regulations on lead in drinking water. 
Furthermore, we suggest that the EPA provide support for legal reforms at the state and local 
levels, aiding in resolving conflicts and facilitating compliance with the LCRI. 
Collaboration is key in this endeavor, so the affected communities must be actively 
involved in identifying and addressing these barriers. OPC-DC urges the EPA to facilitate 
partnerships between legal experts, state and local authorities, water systems, and community 
stakeholders. Through this collaboration, states and localities can explore and develop effective 

14 
 
strategies for overcoming legal barriers, pooling insights and experiences to inform more 
effective policy-making. 
 
X. Conclusion  
In conclusion, OPC-DC agrees with much of EPA’s proposed improvements to the Safe 
Drinking Water Act’s Lead & Copper Rule, however, there is still room for improvement. EPA 
should consider the implementation of OPC-DC’s recommendations to ensure that ratepayers 
who are least able to afford service line replacement are not left with the bulk of the costs. 
 
Respectfully Submitted,

Dear Administrator, 
The City of Dubuque, Iowa is hereby providing comments on the Environmental Protection 
Agency's proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), announced in the 
proposed rule at 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (Dec. 6, 2023). 
The City of Dubuque, chartered in 1837, is the oldest city in Iowa and is situated along the 
western bank of the Mississippi River, at the intersection of where Iowa meets Illinois and 
Wisconsin, and has a long history associated with lead and lead mining. Dating back to the 
17th Century, European maps document the presence of zinc-lead mines in the area. The 
City’s water services reflect the abundance of metal, as we have recorded over 5,000 lead 
and partial lead service lines.  
While we applaud the efforts to improve water quality and improve outreach to our 
customers in our communities understanding that “lead in drinking water can irreparably 
harm children and adults and disproportionately impacts those living in disadvantaged 
communities”1, there are some aspects of the proposed rule changes that may need to be 
addressed regionally, or via a strategic approach at the state or primacy agency level rather 
than a one-size fits all method. We offer the following commentary and are appreciative of 
this opportunity.  
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement within 10 years. The proposed LCRI would 
require many water systems to replace lead services lines within 10 years.  

 
Service 
People 
Integrity 
Responsibility 
Innovation 
Teamwork 
 
 
While the City of Dubuque supports EPA’s goal of completely removing lead service 
lines (“LSL(s)”) as quickly as possible, we believe establishing a 10-year timeframe for 
achieving that goal is not the optimal approach for many municipalities including 
Dubuque. The City of Dubuque is responsible for the operation and maintenance of 
the city’s public water mains but does not maintain or possess ownership of the water 
service from the public main into privately owned buildings, therefore there is 
concern that we, and many other communities not responsible for the water service 
line, would not be able to fulfill this aspect of a proposed rule. Further, a one-size fits 
all timeframe presents a challenge in economically disadvantaged communities, 
placing an undue financial burden on the whole community and potentially prevents 
other significant capital improvements from being completed in a timely manner, such 
installing treatment processes and advancing replacement groundwater wells for 
PFAS reduction, and replacing fatigued water distribution mains, storage facilities, and 
other water treatment processes. The arbitrary timeframe also omits adequate 
consideration of the city’s optimized corrosion control treatment (“OCCT”), which has 
proven to be effective in Dubuque and would continue to be successful in mitigating 
exposure to lead in drinking water during an LSL replacement program. However, if 
cities were to be granted the ability to work with their primacy agencies and develop 
a lead service line replacement program that coordinates with other necessary capital 
projects along with managing other variables such as working with private property 
owners, material availability, labor/workforce limitations,  along with continued 
successful use of OCCT, and if cities were provided with financial assistance in the 
form of a revolving fund administered by the state with significant, such as 90%, 
principal and interest forgiveness with reduced barriers to accessing the monies, or 
grant funds to provide the necessary funding to customers, it may lead to increased 
numbers of removal and replacement of lead service lines and lessen a concentrated 
burden on our communities. For reference, a recent cost estimate in the Dubuque, 
Iowa area for full lead service line replacement was $10,000 per property.  
Lead Service Lines are not to be Taxable Benefit. We are in the process of initiating a 
pilot lead service line replacement program to replace approximately 585 lead service 
lines in our community, so we are firsthand understanding the challenges and barriers 
that need to be overcome. We are moving forward with the pilot program albeit 
significantly less than the program we wanted to undertake for many reasons. One 
key reason was the significant reduction of loan forgiveness, it was dropped from 90% 
to 49%, thereby limiting our ability to leverage the available public funds to spend on 
private infrastructure lead service lines, this is also being done with very little to no 
assistance from state or federal agencies on public education materials or messaging, 
as we are committed to gaining the interest of as many private property owners as 
funds will be permit. In this process, we were informed by an alarming possibility that 
the lead service line replacement may be a taxable benefit. We urge as part of this 

 
Service 
People 
Integrity 
Responsibility 
Innovation 
Teamwork 
 
public comment period, that EPA directly address the Internal Revenue Service and 
require that publicly funded service line replacements are not taxable income for 
individual households or property owners.  
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes. The City of Dubuque is in support of this part of the rule 
and agrees knowing where lead pipes are is critical to replacing them efficiently and 
equitably. The city is prepared to provide an initial inventory of the lead service lines 
by October 16, 2024, create a publicly available service line replacement plan, and 
identify the materials of all service lines of unknown material. 
 
Public Education, Outreach and CCR. We are in support of providing greater clarity in 
the consumer confidence report and specifically, information pertaining to results 
associated with lead and copper testing. We do however request that further 
education and outreach come directly from EPA to assist state primacy agency field 
offices that are called upon to aid public water supplies in providing proven methods 
in communicating what the results mean to customers. In the current social media 
climate of “fake-news”, it is important the language, the tone, and the methods used 
to deliver results and explanation of those results is well thought out and consistent. 
This is important as the water industry looks to regain its position as a valued and 
trusted member of the community and build expertise to address questions and 
concerns from our customers. This is challenging to accomplish as many field offices 
are understaffed, as are many utilities, and so we look to the federal agency to assist 
in this matter. Regarding the provision of making point of service water filters 
available to customers, we request that a certified list of water filters be provided to 
utilities to reduce the risk of an ineffective filter being provided and rule preventing 
price-gouging be placed on water filters being provided by utilities to their customers.  
Again, we commend and acknowledge the work and advancement by EPA to present the 
proposed LCRI and recognize it is a major advancement in protecting children and adults 
from the significant, and irreversible, health effects from being exposed to lead in drinking 
water.

Dear Mr. Regan,
The first attempt to apply the lessons of the Flint Crisis ended in disappointing
Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) that would not adequately protect public
health from a preventable problem: lead poisoning. It is incumbent upon this current
administration to do everything in its power to indeed “Get the Lead Out.” This comment
on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) is informed by our
experience working with several Great Lakes communities experiencing lead in drinking
water, including Flint and Benton Harbor. Freshwater Future’s mission is to be a catalyst
for community action that strengthens policies designed to safeguard the waters of the
Great Lakes region.
A Stronger Rule - Thank You
Thank you to the leadership and everyone who contributed to the new proposed LCRI.
We are grateful for the stronger and more equitable components that integrate the
science, research, and lessons learned since before the Flint Water Crisis to improve
the 2021 LCRR. Some of the proposed improvements we are especially grateful for
include:
1. Requiring 100% full lead service line replacement (LSLR)
2. Reducing the Action Level and eliminating the Trigger Level
3. Strengthening the transparency and requirements of lead service line (LSL)
inventories and replacement plans

4. Standardizing and strengthening Public Education and Notification requirements
Feedback and Recommendations
Once adopted, the LCRI rule will have massive socioeconomic and public health
implications. Our specific recommendations are organized under the following
categories:
