of compliance, disparate impacts on environmental justice communities, and the sufficiency of 
protections in schools and childcare facilities. 
 
HCA requests EPA to reconsider available exemptions to the 10-year LSLR deadline and 
provide guidance to states in determining feasibility of a system to conduct LSLR at a faster rate 
than required by the proposed LCRI.  
 
The current LCRR, requires water systems to replace LSLs and Galvanized Requiring 
Replacement (GRR) service lines only after exceeding the lead action or trigger level. HCA 
supports the proposed LCRI mandating full replacement of LSLs and GRR service lines 
independent from tap sampling and monitoring requirements. The LCRI implements a 10-year 
compliance deadline with a minimum average annual replacement rate of 10 percent calculated 
across a rolling three-year period. EPA proposes to retain the LCRR provision that requires states 
to set a faster replacement rate where feasible for a system. HCA requests EPA provide guidance 
and clarify what factors a state should consider when determining whether it is feasible for a system 
to conduct LSLR at a faster rate and in establishing an adjusted rate.   
 
In contrast to the more stringent replacement rate imposed on systems that can feasibly replace 
LSLs at a faster rate, the LCRI proposes to allow “deferred service line replacement” deadlines for 
eligible water systems. EPA proposes to extend a deferred service line replacement deadline to 
eligible systems to which the 10-year deadline is infeasible, which includes systems that would 
have to replace more than ten thousand service lines per year. HCA asks EPA to reconsider an 
exemption potentially extending the compliance deadline for decades to systems serving 
communities with among the highest proportions of LSLs. Rather, HCA requests EPA consider 
structuring LSLR deadlines in a way which prioritizes most at risk communities and systems with 
the highest proportions of LSLs.  
 
HCA is concerned with the challenges small and rural systems will endure under the 10-year 
deadline for LSLR proposed under the LCRI considering the extensive resources that will be 
required to comply with the annual replacement rate coupled with increased costs and demand for 
labor and materials. With the exception of those systems eligible for deferred service line 
replacement, under the proposed LCRI all community water systems and non-transient non-
community water systems across the nation will be replacing LSLs within the same time frame. It 
is critical that EPA not underestimate the resource implications of the 10-year deadline, 
particularly for older, smaller, and economically disadvantaged communities.  
 
HCA suggests considering flexibility in LSLR deadlines for small systems that can demonstrate a 
low risk for lead exposure or that have already replaced a certain amount of service lines in its 
system. Because the LCRI proposes to reduce the threshold for a “small system” from those 
serving 10,000 or fewer persons to those serving 3,300 persons or fewer, flexibility would be 
limited to those systems which are significantly smaller and most likely to incur these types of 
challenges.  
 

3 
 
 
 
HCA is concerned EJ communities will not have equitable access to LSLR and be 
disproportionally affected by lead exposure. HCA requests EPA provide robust guidelines and 
minimum criteria regarding LSLR plans, including for prioritization and funding strategies.  
 
Under the LCRI, EPA proposes to remove any statement addressing how a water system should 
or should not cover the cost of replacing service lines under the control of the system and any 
statement on whether a system is or is not responsible for the cost of full-service line replacements. 
Rather, EPA strongly encourages customer-side service line replacement to be offered at no direct 
cost to the customer wherever possible. HCA is concerned that without a more explicit directive 
regarding the allocation of costs for customer-side replacements, low-income and minority 
communities will not have equitable access to LSLR and be at risk for increased lead exposure.  
 
In Harris County, 45% of households are rented with renters expected to represent the majority of 
households in the next twenty years.2  The majority of Harris County renters consist of minorities 
with approximately 36% of black households owning their homes compared to the nearly 70% of 
white households owning their home.3 Requiring customers to pay for the private-portions of 
service lines often leaves low-income homeowners and landlords unable or unwilling to pay for 
LSLR – disproportionately affecting low-income communities and communities of color resulting 
in higher risks of lead exposure from their water.4 Furthermore, many Harris County residents are 
at risk for other exposures to lead. While the exact number of homes that still contain lead-based 
paint is unknown, it is estimated that approximately 55,000 houses in Harris County outside of 
Houston were constructed before the ban on lead-based paint was enacted in 1978.5  
 
Under the LCRI, EPA proposes that a service line replacement plan consist of several elements 
which are aimed to improve the equitable outcomes of replacement, including that systems identify 
a replacement prioritization and funding strategy for conducting full service line replacement. One 
of these elements is that systems create a strategy to achieve full LSLR at rental properties to 
reduce instances in which LSLs are not replaced and create disparities in situations in which 
landlords refuse access.  
 
Considering the large proportion of Harris County residents that reside in rental properties, 
particularly those of color, HCA raises concerns regarding the allocation of costs for customer-
side portion replacements of lead and GRR service lines. EPA proposes systems be required to 
compile a LSLR plan which addresses targeting replacement of lines in environmental justice 
communities and low-income communities; however, HCA requests that EPA provide robust 
guidance on what is to be considered by systems in developing a LSLR plan specifically for those 
communities most at risk of lead exposure and limited access to LSLR. Additionally, HCA asks

that EPA provide more detailed information and education on opportunities for available funding 
to replace customer-portion service lines and that EPA make this information readily available to 
the public.  
 
HCA requests EPA to provide further guidance regarding a system’s determination of whether 
the customer-owned portion is within the system’s control. 
 
Under the proposed LCRI, systems would only be required to replace all lead and GRR service 
lines and any lead connectors encountered that are “under control” of the water system. EPA 
proposes to treat a service line as under a systems control wherever a system has adequate legal 
and physical access. HCA acknowledges that legal access will vary among state and local laws; 
however, HCA asks EPA to reconsider delineating prerequisites or elements of physical access to 
reduce the occurrence of conflicting interpretations of physical access and potential risks of 
circumventing a system’s obligation to replace service lines.   
 
HCA asks EPA to consider available incentives to increase installation of filters and increased 
testing at tap locations more frequently in schools and childcare facilities.  
 
In 2021, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services identified Texas as one of the states 
with the highest concentration of children with elevated blood lead levels.6 Houston Independent 
School District (HISD) voluntarily partnered with the Texas Commission on Environmental 
Quality (TCEQ) to test for lead in its drinking water during the 2016-2017 school year. HISD has 
approximately 194,607 students, 90% of which were reported as minorities and 59.5% as 
economically disadvantaged.7  
 
 Preliminary testing of HISD water resulted in nearly half of the district’s participating schools 
reporting lead in the water from drinking fountains, classroom faucets, and other outlets throughout 
each campus.8 Particularly concerning was the fact that ten HISD schools reported at least one site 
indicating the presence of 100 ppm of lead in the water. 9 Almost half of the district outlets that 
tested above the LCRR action level of 15 ppm were from drinking fountains.10  
 
EPA has concluded that the levels of lead measured at the tap are variable due to numerous factors 
including the individual site’s plumbing, characteristics of the water, length of time the water is in 
contact with the material, and consumer use patterns. This is particularly important when 
contemplating potential lead exposure in schools and childcare facilities considering that these 
facilities experience periods of time in which water is sparingly used allowing lead in pipes and 
other fixtures to leach into the water.

Recognizing variability in sampling, patterns of use, and susceptibility of individuals at risk at 
these facilities, HCA requests EPA to consider more stringent sampling requirements in the LCRI, 
including sampling at more taps within the facility, and more frequent sampling independent of 
sampling upon request. Furthermore, EPA should consider incentivizing schools and childcare 
facilities to engage in the installation of point of use filters to reduce risks of lead exposure.  
 
*** 
 
In conclusion, HCA supports EPA’s proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulation for lead and copper in the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements; however, 
HCA has concerns regarding the feasibility of compliance and practical implications of the 
proposed rule. HCA appreciates the work EPA has done to improve public health protections 
against lead exposure and the opportunity to comment. If you have any questions, please reach out 
to Brennan.Flannery@harriscountytx.gov.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0965 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024 
 
Ms. Radhika Fox 
Assistant Administrator Office of Water 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, D.C.  20460 
 
Re: 
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 
Dear Ms. Fox: 
 
The South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources (DANR) appreciates the 
opportunity to provide comments on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. South 
Dakota supports reducing lead exposure from drinking water and increasing public health 
protection; however, the proposed rule creates a significant burden on the state programs 
responsible for implementing the revised rule and public water systems impacted by the 
proposed rule revisions. 
 
Many of South Dakota’s public water systems are defined as Small Water Systems. In general, 
small systems have limited resources. DANR is very concerned that the impacts of the proposed 
rule will be overly burdensome on these systems, resulting in lower compliance rates which will 
undermine consumer confidence. 
 
The proposed rule improvements are numerous and extremely complex. DANR offers the 
following general comments for specific issues important to South Dakota. Additionally, DANR 
request that EPA carefully consider the comments received from the Environmental Council of 
States, the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators, and the American Water Works 
Association, which are more extensive and provide greater technical detail.  
 
Distribution System and Site Assessment (DSSA): 
 
The proposed rule states that within 30 days of receiving sample results, water systems must 
collect and analyze a follow-up sample at any tap sample site that exceeds 0.010 mg/L and 
collect water quality samples at a site located within a half mile radius of that sample site. South 
Dakota is a rural state and many systems would be challenged to find a sampling location within 
a half-mile radius of the original sample location. DANR suggests that the EPA add additional 
language allowing systems to take a sample at the closest site to the original sampling site should 
one not be available within a half-mile radius.  Additionally, DANR is concerned with the lack 
of resources to train operators and regulatory staff on which components of the DSSA a water 
system will be required to complete.  
 

 
 
Filter Distribution: 
 
The proposed rule states that water systems must provide filters to their entire service area after 
the water system has had three or more action level exceedances. DANR is concerned that by 
having to provide filters to an entire service area, rather than solely to those locations with risks 
of lead and copper exceedances, which are locations with: lead or galvanized service lines 
requiring replacement or unknown service lines; customers will develop an unwarranted distrust 
in their water utility. DANR requests EPA allow states the discretion to require filters, where 
appropriate based on sampling results, data, and corrosion control.  
 
Public Notification: 
 
The proposed rule adds lead exceedances to the list of Tier 1violation’s requiring a 24-hour 
public notice. Tier 1 based exceedances have the potential to have serious adverse health effects 
on human health because of short-term exposure. DANR feels that requiring systems to public 
notice lead exceedances within 24 hours will cause implementation issues for states and water 
systems. One of the most significant issues is the current EPA method allows laboratories to hold 
onto samples after being preserved for several months after the sampling occurred. It does not 
make sense to require systems to report the sample results within 24 hours for samples that may 
have been collected many weeks or months earlier. To remedy this inconsistency, DANR 
recommends that the Tier 1 public notice requirement be changed to a Tier II public notice 
requirement. This change will permit states and water systems to properly assess the sample 
validity and allow adequate time to coordinate the appropriate public notice. If EPA is unwilling 
to change the public notice timing, then at a minimum, DANR recommends that EPA update the 
standard method to reduce the time a laboratory must analyze a sample so a water system to 
achieve timely notification of results to its customers. 
 
Required Testing in Schools and Daycares: 
 
Under the proposed rule, community water systems would be required to conduct lead sampling 
at all schools and all licensed daycares within its distribution system, excluding those constructed 
after 2014 or those facilities who have had full plumbing replacement. While we support testing 
of lead in schools and childcare facilities, the water system should not be considered the experts 
when it comes to plumbing and remediation services within the schools and daycares. This 
requirement will place a great burden upon the small water system with limited resources. 
DANR recommends that any required remediation work be the responsibility of the property 
owner and not be a burden of the public water system. Additionally, with different sampling 
requirements at schools and daycares and the continuous state of flux of daycare facilities, 
DANR has great concern regarding how sampling data from schools and daycares will be 
tracked and managed for compliance. EPA must also communicate where funding and resources 
are available to school and daycares and that they convey that information directly to these 
entities, as well as provide all templates for any public education material that is required.  
 
Data Management/Guidance/Training: 
 
Each of the changes outlined within the proposed revisions increase rather than decrease 
implementation challenges. It is imperative that a fully functional data system be in place a 
minimum of six months prior the rule effective date. Without a proper and functional means to 
manage all the data elements of the final rule, states and systems will be unable to implement or 
comply with the rule. EPA does not currently have a data system in place to manage all the data 

 
 
points required to be collected under the proposed rule. DANR requests that EPA makes 
available all database guidance on implementing the rule If a state must design its own, there will 
be substantial cost to an already stretched state budget.   
 
South Dakota is requesting that guidance documents and training be finalized and shared as soon 
as possible.  The effective date of the rule should be at least six months prior to implementation 
to allow adequate time for training. In addition, DANR requests that clarity and continuity be 
brought into the rule revisions for all applicable water systems.   
 
Corrosion Control Studies: 
 
Corrosion control requirements need to be updated to reflect clear definitions about what will be 
required in a study. Guidance and training should be provided to states on how to review 
corrosion control studies and water quality parameter testing.  
 
Funding:  
 
This proposed rule’s complex nature adds significant requirements to systems and states which 
will surpass most small systems ability to comply. This, in effect, shifts even more burden to 
state programs as they will be required to pull along systems struggling to comply. State 
programs are already stretched to the breaking point. With years of flat or rescission-based 
funding, states will be hard pressed to implement these rule revisions unless significant funding 
increases to the Public Water System Supervision grants are authorized and made available to 
states. Without additional grant funding, state programs will be unable to fully implement the 
rule without adversely impacting other core program areas which in turn reduces overall public 
health protection.   
 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Mark A. McIntire, P.E. 
Drinking Water Program Administrator 
South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources

      Megan Goltz, Policy Advisor, Governor’s Office

Dear Mr. Goldberg, 
 
On behalf of the Water Quality Association (WQA), a not-for-profit trade association with more 
than 2,500 member companies representing the residential, commercial, and industrial water 
treatment industry, we are writing to you in support of the proposed Lead & Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI). The proposed rule is pivotal in addressing lead contamination in drinking 
water by strengthening public health protections and WQA commends the Administration for 
taking this important action. To further enhance these efforts, WQA offers its expertise to the 
EPA for developing comprehensive educational resources, guidance on lead contamination, and 
using certified water treatment systems to minimize exposure.  
 
About WQA 
Since its creation in 1974, WQA has worked tirelessly to improve water quality through 
sustainable technologies and services. As a leader in the point-of-use (POU) and point-of-entry 
(POE) drinking water treatment system industry, the association operates an ANSI National 
Accreditation Board (ANAB) accredited testing and certification laboratory that evaluates and 
certifies water treatment systems to nationally accepted voluntary standards for contaminant 
removal, including lead. WQA also offers a variety of technical skills and educational resources, 
many of which can serve as vital tools to the EPA, Utilities, and other organizations looking to 
address drinking water contaminants.  
 
WQA Comments on LCRI  
The proposed LCRI puts the U.S. on the path to dramatically reduce Americans’ exposure to this 
neurotoxin by strengthening key elements to address lead reduction in drinking water. Enabling a 
cohesive approach for water systems to locate lead service lines and improvements to tap 
sampling requirements are crucial first steps in understanding the extent of lead contamination. 
Moreover, lowering the action level to 10 µg/L for lead provides clarity and fixes a gap in the 

 
 
2375 Cabot Drive 
 
 
 
Lisle, Illinois 60532-3696 USA 
 
 
 
Phone 630-505-0160 
 
 
 
Fax 630-505-963 
https://wqa.org/ 
regulation, which may have led to a delayed response in treatment and mitigation efforts. All of 
these actions are central to ensuring that resources are allocated effectively and streamlined to 
communities that are most at risk and least equipped to address lead in their drinking water. 
WQA also applauds EPA’s emphasis on public education materials – a cornerstone to 
empowering stakeholders in understanding the nuances of lead contamination and treatment 
options.  
 
WQA supports the requirement that certified point-of-use water treatment products be made 
available to customers of water systems with multiple lead action level exceedances, so they may 
immediately reduce lead exposure while waiting for lead service lines to be replaced. WQA also 
supports the proposed rule’s flexibility, which allows small systems to continue to use alternative 
compliance mechanisms, such as certified point-of-use products. These devices are proven to be 
effective, affordable, and immediate at reducing lead in water. In some instances, point-of-entry 
filtration devices should be used as well.  
 
The EPA requested comments on several sections of the proposed rule. WQA is willing to 
provide the following insights: 
  
EPA is requesting comment on the ability of the market to correct for potential shortages: 
• The water treatment industry is ready to respond rapidly to any potential shortages 
in the services needed to address lead contamination. WQA and its members are 
already serving as a proven partner by assisting several cities in addressing lead, 
including during service line replacement. With multiple manufacturers producing 
certified water treatment products, municipalities should have a bevy of options to 
purchase large quantities of filters. The industry does not anticipate a shortage in 
supplies or labor and WQA is willing to prepare a list of certified products and 
professionals to help municipalities address lead issues.  
 
• In the years leading up to the enforcement date, the EPA should collaborate with 
WQA to strengthen technical assistance availability through workforce 
development – especially in underserved and rural areas. WQA’s professional 
certification program is prepared to provide the resources needed to educate and 
support the development of an expanded workforce to address water quality 
issues.  
 
EPA is proposing to require water systems with multiple action level exceedances to 
make filters certified to reduce lead and replacement cartridges, along with instructions 
for their use, available to all consumers.

• Third-party certified POU devices have been used in several cities (e.g., Newark, 
Pittsburgh, Kalamazoo, Benton Harbor, Eglin, and Denver) to address lead 
contamination and are success stories on how POU devices can serve a variety of 
communities immediately. WQA supports the requirement that certified POU 
devices be made available to all consumers of water systems that have multiple 
lead action level exceedances. This will allow the public to significantly mitigate 
lead exposure as an interim while finding and addressing the source of lead 
contamination in drinking water. WQA also supports the proposed rule’s 
flexibility, which allows small systems to continue to use alternative compliance 
mechanisms, such as certified POU devices. These devices have been proven to 
be an effective, affordable, and readily available solution, and water systems, 
including those that serve up to 10,000 people, should not be restricted from 
utilizing this mitigation option. 
 
• To assist with the implementation of POU filter compliance programs, the EPA 
should consider the use of Drinking Water State Revolving Funds (DWSRFs) and 
provide guidance to states.  
 
EPA is proposing to revise the regulatory language regarding filter distribution to clarify 
that water systems are required to provide filters and replacement cartridges to every 
occupancy, rather than residence.  
 
• WQA strongly supports providing certified filters and replacement cartridges to 
every occupant. Oftentimes, renters face unique challenges in accessing and 
implementing water quality measures. Unlike homeowners, they may not have the 
authority to make building infrastructure changes or install permanent fixtures. 
This shift in regulatory language will help clarify and address a historical 
unintended oversight. By emphasizing the provision of filters to every occupant, 
the EPA is taking a more inclusive approach to safeguarding public health, 
ensuring that individuals in various living arrangements benefit from lead 
exposure reduction measures. 
 
EPA proposes to determine that allowing these systems [CWSs serving 3,300 persons or 
fewer] to install point-of-use devices or conduct lead-bearing plumbing replacements is 
consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique rule. EPA is requesting 
comment, however, on whether the Agency should maintain the small system flexibility 
for CWSs serving 10,000 persons or fewer (see section IX. of this document).  
 
• Third-party certified POU devices have already been used by water systems and 
have a proven track record in effectively treating lead in drinking water. We 
encourage the EPA to continue to allow flexibility for utilizing this effective and 
affordable technology for all system sizes. As stated previously, water systems

implementation on a larger scale. This technology will continue to improve in the 
time between the finalized rule and enforcement date. WQA is also willing to 
work with its members and the EPA to provide “best practices” for 
communication and project management that will result in the successful 
deployment of this technology.  
 
EPA is seeking comment on the minimum requirements for States to provide a waiver 
(e.g., should the waiver be limited to locations where the filter use is required by State or 
local law; should the waiver be limited to locations where State or local law requires 
periodic sampling or testing to ensure proper filter use).  
 
• Filter-first approaches to school and childcare facilities are an effective and 
growing trend across the country. WQA supports a waiver for states that have laws 
that require periodic sampling or testing to ensure proper filter use and can 
subsequently minimize the burden on water systems in ensuring compliance.  
 
EPA is also requesting comment on alternative approaches following multiple lead 
action level exceedances, including requiring water systems to deliver a filter and 
replacement cartridges to every household served by the system.  
• WQA supports EPA’s approach in ensuring that every household and in the case of 
multi-unit residences, each occupant, be provided with third-party certified filters 
and replacement cartridges. To maximize effective program implementation, the 
EPA should consider increasing public awareness campaigns during lead service 
line replacement and disseminating information in a variety of media channels. 
Although stakeholders have highlighted that a portion of the filters distributed may 
go unused, WQA strongly urges the EPA to clarify that utilities and water systems 
should use “opt-out” language when distributing filters instead of requiring the 
end-user to have to “opt-in.” This will ultimately ensure that the public has 
received the necessary support to minimize lead exposure in drinking water.  
EPA is proposing to maintain the requirement that filter replacement cartridges be 
provided for six months [after service line replacement]…EPA is [also] proposing to 
require risk mitigation actions following disturbances resulting from physical action or 
vibration.

• Sediment from lead service line replacement or other disturbances (including water

even after project completion. WQA believes that filter replacement cartridges 
should be provided for a minimum of 6 months in alignment with the proposed

confirmed to be below the set AL. Moreover, as a precautionary measure, WQA

Cyst, and Volatile Organic Compounds (VOCs), in addition to lead. According to 
WQA’s online database of certified water treatment technologies, 81% of POU 
certified to remove lead are also certified to remove other contaminants. Our 
database shows some of these POU products were certified to remove or reduce 
up to 25 contaminants. 
 
EPA is also proposing requiring public education materials to explain that using a filter 
certified by an American National Standards Institute accredited certifier to reduce lead 
is effective in reducing lead levels in drinking water. EPA is proposing this change to 
ensure that consumers are made aware that filters are an effective option for reducing 
lead in drinking water.

quality issues and solutions. WQA welcomes collaboration with EPA on 
developing easily understandable guidance containing treatment options.

filters, which already contains the relevant certification bodies (e.g. WQA, 
IAPMO, NSF, etc.) and associated certification marks. Additionally, the EPA 
should consider including information on where to locate and find products, such 
as WQA’s product certification database and search tool. When navigating the 
complexities of drinking water challenges, it's paramount to recognize and

RE: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, National Primary
Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Dear Administrator Regan,
The NAACP State Conference of California-Hawaii submits the following comments
regarding the US Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary
Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”). The
California-Hawaii NAACP State Conference provides leadership for local branches,
youth councils, and college chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in
California and Hawaii. The NAACP and its Center for Environmental and Climate
Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring that issues of community
engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and frontline
communities are most impacted, including communities in California and Hawaii.
California-Hawaii NAACP State Conference applauds EPA for proposing stronger
regulations to protect communities from lead in drinking water. Lead in drinking water
has been a historically prevalent issue in Black communities, posing extreme risks to
the health of young people, mothers, and their families. In California, estimates
suggest that there are as many as 65,000 lead service lines, with Hawaii having 2,800,
threatening families across our state with exposure to a potent and irreversible
neurotoxin which, even at low levels of exposure, is linked to damage to the brain and
nervous system, learning disabilities, shorter stature, impaired hearing, and harm to
blood cells. In California, we would derive $5,557,500,000 in public health cost savings
from full lead service line replacement and $239,400,000 for Hawaii.
A significant portion of California’s drinking water infrastructure, including lead service
lines and components, is outdated and in need of replacement. In 2016, Fresno
residents were concerned about “rusty, discolored water” coming from their pipes.
Nearly 14% of children tested in one Fresno neighborhood had reported high lead
levels, 25% of schools in Fresno reported finding lead coming from their drinking water
fountains, and 40 homes had lead levels above the federal limit. Expanded testing
found an additional 300 homes had lead coming from their faucets, leading to class
action lawsuits. Fresno found that lead was leaching into their water through
corroding and unwrapped galvanized pipes.
For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong
elements of the proposed LCRI, such as the requirement for the removal of all lead
service lines in ten years, the requirements for water systems to sample both the first
and fifth liter of water passing through lead pipes and a lower action level; but also
ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which undermine their goals and

ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule
does not leave black communities in California and Hawaii behind:
●
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a
fundamental injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines
would be allowed 40 or more years to fix this issue.
●
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines:
Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on
impacted communities will result in mostly wealthy neighborhoods having
lead service lines replaced. Removal and replacement do not make up major
proportions of utility budgets, and utilities should be expected to maximize the
use of available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-ratepayer
sources of funds to prioritize solving this crisis.
●
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many
hours there daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased
risk of lead exposure when compared with white children. The proposal’s
suggested testing program does not differ from past ineffective programs,
and EPA should move towards incentivizing the installation of filters and
protecting children.
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components
would allow for environmental injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline
communities have long suffered from disinvestment and lack of resources. Past
NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had the
strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA of any
sociodemographic characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to
make significant changes in the lives of millions of people in California and Hawaii and
to provide a measure of environmental justice that these families are owed. We
encourage this administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by
strengthening the final rule further.
Respectfully,
Rick Callender
President
NAACP CA/HI State Conference

*Comments submitted to the Federal eRulemaking Portal 
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (Docket 
#: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036) 
Administrator Regan, 
The City of Thornton, Colorado (Thornton) appreciates the opportunity to partner with the EPA 
on continued improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule. As always, Thornton applauds the 
EPA’s efforts to protect public health from the risks of lead. Thornton offers the following 
comments to EPA to ensure that the proposed rule is properly informed and effective. 
1) General:  
Thornton concurs with the comments provided to the EPA by the Colorado Water Utility 
Council (CWUC). While LCRI is certainly an improvement over LCRR, there are still many 
areas that need clarification, correction, and simplification to increase compliance with 
the rule. In particular, the reporting and notification timelines are overly burdensome. 
The EPA should partner with water utilities to ensure that the rules they are 
promulgating are actually feasible to implement. Please strongly consider making the 
recommended changes proposed by CWUC.  
In general, Thornton believes that the promulgation of the LCRI (as well as LCRR) has 
been a fraught, clumsy process. It is completely unreasonable to modify rule 
requirements while utilities are in the process of working towards compliance deadlines. 
The addition of connectors to the Lead Service Line (LSL) inventory came after Thornton 
had already spent over $400,000 inventorying our system. Luckily for Thornton, the 
connector information was noted during the inventory process, but if another utility had 
not obtained that information during their inventory, they would be forced to perform 
another at considerable cost to their residents. With future rulemakings, please ensure 
you give utilities the best possible chance for compliance by looking at potential future 
requirements and reducing overlapping timeframes.  
 
2) Corrosion Control Treatment:  
Thornton has previously submitted comments to EPA against the use of ortho-
phosphate (ortho-P) as part of optimal corrosion control treatments (OCCT). Use of 
ortho-P as part of OCCT has the potential to significantly increase phosphorus loading in 

 
 
watersheds through wastewater discharges and returns from surface and groundwater 
flows from irrigated lawns. Increased phosphorus loading in the watershed will lead to 
increased occurrence of harmful algal blooms (HABs); increased HABs also leads to an 
increase in cyanotoxin occurrence, which are highly toxic compounds that the public can 
be exposed to through recreation in the watershed or through drinking water from 
utilities that are unable to effectively remove those compounds during the treatment 
process. Because of the increased health risks of cyanotoxins, if the EPA requires an 
upstream utility to implement ortho-P OCCT, they are effectively prioritizing the health 
of the upstream community over the health of Thornton’s residents.   
In Colorado, significant improvements in phosphorus loading have been realized 
through the nutrient criteria in CDPHE Regulation 85; the potential use of ortho-P for 
upstream entities’ OCCT could completely undo the progress that has been made to 
date. In addition, Thornton residents are already paying for phosphorus reduction 
through their wastewater rates (through the Metro Water Recovery district). If another 
entity within the Metro Water Recovery district is required to implement ortho-P OCCT, 
Thornton resident’s rates will increase to treat the increased ortho-P loading at Metro 
Water Recovery; Thornton has not violated the LCRI, but our residents will essentially 
and unfairly be forced to subsidize upstream OCCT. Likewise, even if Metro Water 
Recovery can fully remove the additional ortho-P loading, there is still the non-point 
source loading mentioned above that can increase cyanotoxin occurrence in Thornton’s 
drinking water reservoirs, thus necessitating costly capital improvements to Thornton’s 
water treatment plants; this is an additional undue cost burden on Thornton ratepayers 
to accommodate the impacts from upstream ortho-P OCCT.  
For these reasons, Thornton recommends that the EPA take a more holistic and multi-
barriered approach to OCCT than currently put forth in the LCRI as well as provide 
latitude in the OCCT approval process to consider downstream environmental and 
public health. Thornton maintains that when properly monitored, pH and alkalinity 
control is an effective, protective, and recommended treatment technique for reducing 
lead concentrations.  
In addition, Thornton believes that re-optimization of OCCT following an Action Level 
(AL) exceedance is a misappropriation of funds and resources that could be better 
applied elsewhere. Exceedances could be due to disruption of the distribution system 
during lead service line replacements and the number of exceedances would trend 
down as the utility progresses in their replacement project. The utility should be allowed 
to focus on LSL replacement instead of re-optimization. If the re-optimization provision 
is implemented, the EPA must grant state primacy agencies the ability to waive this 
requirement. Thornton also supports the proposed option to delay OCCT/re-
optimization until after the utility has replaced all of its LSLs. 
 

 
 
3) Service Line Replacement: 
Thornton believes that the State should have primacy on issues related to the service 
line replacement. In this section, and throughout other sections, EPA consistently 
suggests shortening timeframes and deadlines; Thornton recommends against these 
shortened timeframes. One reason Thornton recommends against tighter deadlines is 
that we still have not seen a market correction for supplies or labor since the onset of 
the COVID pandemic. Thornton does not feel that a market correction is imminent and 
believes the EPA should err on the side of caution by taking current shortages into 
account. Shortened timeframes and deadlines will strain an already overburdened 
market thus increasing prices and potentially necessitating rate increases to our 
residents. Thornton also disagrees that a maximum replacement threshold of 10,000 is 
appropriate; even 8,000 replacements annually would stretch resources too thin. While 
Thornton has not identified any LSLs or GRRs to date, we have seen supply chain and 
labor shortage issues on other projects that have resulted in increased costs and 
construction timelines not being met; the higher the EPA sets the threshold, the more 
shortages will be seen on the market and likely results in utilities unable to financially or 
timely comply with the rule. Additionally, Thornton has seen increased delays in 
construction projects due to climate change induced extreme weather. In Colorado in 
2023, we saw a late ground thaw and significant spring precipitation/flooding that 
would have reduced the replacement timeframe by a couple of months; a Colorado 
utility on a 10,000 per year replacement threshold would struggle to complete their 
replacements on that kind of reduced schedule. While Thornton agrees that LSLs should 
be replaced as quickly as possible, EPA should err on the smallest possible replacement 
threshold.  
 
4) Lead Action and Trigger Levels: 
Thornton supports the proposed lead AL of 10 ppb and does not support lowering the 
AL to 5 ppb. Thornton also agrees that special study samples, such as samples following 
LSL replacement, should not be considered in the 90th percentile calculation. As stated 
previously, Thornton suggests waiving requirements for OCCT after an AL exceedance so 
that utilities can focus on LSL replacement.  
 
5) Public Education: 
As stated previously, many of the proposed notification timeframes are overly 
burdensome. Requiring customer notification of lead results within 3 days is 
unreasonable, especially if the results are below the AL; Thornton proposes a 7-business 
day timeline for individual tap sampling results and consumer-initiated sampling results. 
The requirement for annual notification of lead connectors is unnecessary and will go on 
for too long considering connectors will only be replaced as needed. The suggestion by 

 
 
EPA to increase frequency of public education materials from annually to twice annually 
is administratively burdensome and likely takes away from the priority of replacing LSLs. 
 
6) Additional Requirements for Systems with Multiple Lead Action Level Exceedances: 
It is entirely unreasonable and unnecessary for EPA to require utilities to provide point 
of use filters to all consumers within 60 days of multiple AL exceedances. Thornton 
estimates that providing filters for all of our ~160,000 customers would exceed 
$2,000,000. It is infeasible for Thornton to receive and distribute $2 million of filters 
within 60 days. Utilities should only be required to supply filters to those consumers 
impacted by an exceedance due to LSLs, GRRs, or Unknowns. 
 
7) Reporting and Recordkeeping:  
Thornton suggests that the EPA consider allowing States to use a phased approach for 
reviewing and approving site sampling plans to reduce administrative burden. States 
should start with utilities with the highest 90th percentile results and work down from 
there. 
Thornton would like to thank the EPA for taking these and prior comments into consideration 
during the finalization of the LCRI.  
Sincerely,  
 
Caleb Owen 
Water Quality Administrator 
City of Thornton  
9500 Civic Center Dr 
Thornton, CO 80229 
caleb.owen@thorntonco.gov

Comments of the Copper Development Association to: 
 
Environmental Protection Agency 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water 
Request for Public Comment 
Proposed Revisions to the National Primary Drink Water Regulation (NPDWR) for Lead and Copper 
 
Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 (December 6, 2023) 
 
Submitted via www.regulations.gov on February 3, 2024 
 
Introduction  
 
The Copper Development Association (CDA) is the North American based not-for-profit association of the global 
copper industry, influencing the use of copper and copper alloys through research, development, and education, 
as well as technical and end-user support. 
 
The copper industry is a major contributor to U.S. economic and national security, with the metal being a key 
component in the cars and trucks (internal combustion and EV’s), water lines, building materials, industrial 
machinery, electronic hardware, consumer products, battery storage and renewable energy sources that 
individuals need to carry out their daily business. Those companies manufacturing copper alloys and related 
products as well as the copper mines, refineries, and other members of the industry are responsible for a $160 
billion economic impact to the United States, supporting nearly 400,000 jobs across the country with $31 billion in 
wages paid. The copper industry also supports local and regional economies through the creation of downstream 
employment opportunities for plumbers, electricians, automotive workers, and electronics manufacturers. 
 
We appreciate the opportunity to provide these general comments in connection with the Environmental 
Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) request for comments on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead 
and Copper: Improvements.  Overall, CDA supports the proposal and shares in the goal to eliminate harmful lead 
service lines (LSL) and galvanized requiring replacement (GRR) service lines across the country. 
 
Copper and copper alloy products have been used in water delivery applications for decades, and as such will be 
key – if not critical – construction materials and components in federally funded water infrastructure projects. 
Copper continues to be the preferred, alternate material for domestic water service and distribution for drinking, 
cooking, and sanitary purposes. Major cities have committed to using copper service lines as a safe and long-term 
solution for their communities, for example: Flint, Denver, Chicago, Newark, Fort Worth, Benton Harbor and 
Cleveland. In addition to being 100% recyclable, copper is impermeable, this means it is resilient against chemicals 
that may find it’s way into the ground can continues to protect communities. In addition, copper service lines form 
a protective coating (patina) when in contact with the water passing through it that renders it extremely resistant 
to corrosion. Based on the this, these comments focus primarily on lead and galvanized service line replacement, 
however, please consider CDA as a resource on other parts of the proposal affecting copper. 1   
 
1 For additional information on the historical use of copper in plumbing applications, as well as cost-savings over 
the life-cycle of copper products, please see:   
https://copper.org/applications/plumbing/water_service/city-officials.php 
 
 

 
 
2 
Lead & Galvanized Service Line Replacement Component – Copper Tube 
 
Water service lines, crucial for connecting buildings to the public water supply, are often outdated and made from 
lead, presenting significant health risks. As the federal government invests billions of dollars through the Inflation 
Reduction Act (IRA) and the Infrastructure Investments and Jobs Act (IIJA) toward replacements, copper service 
lines offer a safe, reliable, resilient, and sustainable alternative.  
  
The primary copper-related component in lead and galvanized service line replacement is copper water tube, 
specifically manufactured to the ASTM B88 Standard Specification for Seamless Copper Water Tube standard. For 
the majority of the estimated 12 million lead and galvanized service lines in the U.S. that will need replacement, 
this will require ASTM B88 copper tube in the sizes of ¾-inch to 1-1/2-inch, usually specified as Type K (indicating 
wall thickness).  It is worth noting that copper tube produced in North America contains high amounts of recycled 
content, estimated at 50% or higher in recent years.  Continued availability and security of post/pre-consumer 
recycled copper and copper scrap will also be of importance in the U.S. industry’s ability to meet the 
Administration’s goals in replacing lead and galvanized service lines. Members of CDA have been significant capital 
and personnel investments to meet the demand and schedule for total and full lead and galvanized service line 
replacements.  
 
 
Specific CDA Recommendation 1 – The Problem is Large and More Federal Funding is Needed 
 
Based on the EPA’s latest survey, there are approximately 9.2 million lead service lines actively providing water 
throughout the United States with the potential for an equal amount to be replaced.  An additional 2.8 million 
galvanized water pipes also need replacing.  Using some simple assumptions of average service line length would 
require approximately $45B - $56B in funding in 2019 dollars (total installed cost based on EPA’s 2019 estimate 
average of $4,700 per replacement, not just materials) for full replacement of all 12 million (Lead and Galvanized) 
service lines.  The amount needed is almost certainly higher today.  Unfortunately, to date the IIJA only provided 
for a total of $15B, to be allocated over 5 years.  
 
Additional funding is therefore necessary to support full service line replacement in lower income and underserved 
communities. It is also important to note that the $11.7B supplemental Drinking Water State Revolving Fund 
(DWSRF) is NOT guaranteed to service lines and much of it will likely be absorbed by other infrastructure projects, 
leaving a gap in funding for service line replacement. 
 
On January 16th the EPA had a virtual public hearing to comment on LCRI in which the agency shared the 
following: 
1. EPA estimates $2.1-$3.6B a year for replacement (estimate $36B for ten years for all service lines but 
that’s not enough to ensure full-service line replacement and instances where communities need longer 
time due to infrastructure readiness and updates).  
 
https://copper.org/applications/plumbing/water_service/resources/A4117_Service_Line_Right_Choice_Fact_Shee
t.pdf 
 
https://copper.org/applications/plumbing/water_service/resources/A4119_service_line_false-initial-cost-
economy-fact-sheet.pdf 
 

 
 
3 
2. Proposed EPA timing to begin to comply with LCRI is three years after the final rule. There’s also an 
extension of an additional two years if the systems need additional time for necessary capital 
improvement. That is 15 years from now or the final rule so funding will be challenging for communities 
that need it most. 
3. The health and safety impact (“ROI”) the EPA conducted for the US is estimated to be $9B in benefits a 
year to reduce lead exposure by removing lead service lines. If the US were to spend an average of $5B a 
year on LSR and GRR service line replacement the US would still benefit and be well ahead of the impact. 
 
 
Specific CDA Recommendation 2 – Full Replacement is Critical 
 
Full lead and/or galvanized service lines replacement is the best approach for safety and ensuring access to clean 
water within homes and communities long term. EPA’s approach should be in full support of “get the lead out”.  
• 
We are aligned with EPA’s statement that lining or coating technologies do NOT count as replacement and 
should not be a solution to lead exposure from service lines. 
• 
We are also aligned with EPA’s proposal that systems must give customers the chance to participate in full 
replacement (but must be funded by system) as well as provide notification and risk mitigation prior to 
infrastructure work and during emergency repair (if before is not possible). 
• 
We encourage point of use filters or water-pitcher filters only be used as a temporary solution until the 
full LSL, GRR or galvanized premise plumbing system can be replaced. Temporary use should be clearly 
defined by the EPA. Using filters as a long-term solution is not removing the problem of lead service lines. 
• 
We highly recommend that partial replacements should be temporary, and while the use of a dielectric 
fitting to reduce the potential for galvanic corrosion may address the issue short term, however these 
fittings are not suitable for underground use long term. This can result in failure and leaks in the 
connections and reduced efficacy as water deposits form over the relatively small dielectric separation 
created by the fitting. 
 
 
Specific CDA Recommendation 3 – Corrosion Control Treatment 
 
Water quality parameter adjustments are multivariate and should not be made to only consider one material in 
the system (lead) without understanding or investigating the impact of those adjustments on the other materials 
in the system. 
 
 
Further General CDA Comments 
 
• 
We commend and support EPA for including language regarding rental housing (single or multifamily) that 
full-service line replacement is mandatory to avoid owners choosing not to replace. This is a big step to 
protecting the lower income and underserved communities nationwide. 
 
• 
We understand the challenges water services may have meeting the October 2024 deadline to report all 
lead service lines, galvanized requiring replacement, and identifying unknown service material types. 
However, we believe it is the correct first step for an accurate estimate in order to address the issue, and  
to provide safe water to homes and businesses. 
 

 
 
4 
• 
We recommend EPA expands its scope to replace lead and galvanized piping systems in premise plumbing 
that are down stream of lead service lines. 
 
 
Conclusion 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to provide these comments. As noted, we are generally supportive of EPA’s 
approach and goals with the proposal and are happy to be a continued resource on the implementation of the 
Lead and Copper Rule.

To United States Environmental Protection Agency,  
 
 
Southwest Regional Water District appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the USEPA 
regarding the proposed drinking water for Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) to the 
United States Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) during this comment period of the rulemaking 
process.  Public participation is vital to making the rulemaking process successful.   
 
Southwest Regional Water District (District) is a political subdivision of the state of Ohio organized under 
Chapter 6119 of the Ohio Revised Code. The District serves safe drinking water to approximately 16,000 
customer connections within its service area, which primarily includes western Butler County, Ohio, but 
also includes parts of Hamilton, Preble and Warren Counties and Franklin and Union in Indiana. The 
District's water system includes more than 650 miles of water mains, two water production plants and 
twenty-five water storage facilities all maintained by a staff of less than 40 employees.  
 
The District would like to acknowledge the efforts the EPA has made to address the potential lead 
exposure in drinking water.  There are several positive elements in the proposed rules that the District 
supports, some impacting directly the District and others elements specific to neighboring PWSs, 
including:  
• 
Maintaining the treatment technique regulatory framework for the control of lead and copper in 
drinking water.  
 
• 
Establishing a program for lead service line replacement rather than based on triggered 
requirements.  
 
• 
Recognizing that public water systems (PWSs), specifically community water systems (CWSs), 
continue to face legal constraints outside of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SWDA) that limit our 
access to customer properties.  
 
• 
A goal of simplifying the rule for effective implementation.  
 
Phone: 513-863-0828  Fax: 513-863-5330  E-Mail: swrwd@swwater.org 

 
 
 
 
There are critical revisions to this rule that need to be addressed prior to the final version.  Without 
these modifications the District would be subject to regulations that are not legally sound as they would 
be beyond the scope of the SDWA.   
 
• 
EPA must act to immediately extend the compliance date for the provisions under the LCRR that 
will not be continued in the LCRI.  The District continues to work towards meeting the  
requirements of the LCRR, including service line inventory, tap sample monitoring, etc.  The 
District should not be expending resources on compliance requirements with no guarantee from 
EPA that the LCRI final rule will be published prior to the compliance date of the LCRR. 
 
• 
In the LCR revisions in 2000 the definition of “control” was based ownership.  With the proposed 
change of this definition, the EPA is creating access issues for the District to meet the 
requirements of the LCRI. The definition of what is “under the control” of water systems as 
described in SDWA does not include piping not owned by the water system, even when the 
actual owner uses their “control” to grant “access” to a water system.  
 
• 
The EPA needs to simplify the compliance path for systems with no or few LSLs and/or GRRSLs.  
The District has no known LSLs on the public side, which we have certified to our state agency, 
Ohio Environmental Protection Agency (OEPA) and based on predictive modeling, completed to 
comply with the LCRR deadline of October 16th, 2024, a very low probability of LSLs on the 
private side.  The proposed rule does not allow for an alternative method for PWSs, like the 
District, to have a second path to compliance that focuses primarily on (1) having a procedure 
for the rare occurrence of a LSL or GRRSL is discovered and (2) the validation study to assure the 
initial characterization of the system’s inventory is correct. 
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on these proposed rules.  Should the USEPA have 
additional questions, the District is available for discussion.  My contact information is below.  
 
Sincerely, 
 
 
 
Sarah Affrunti 
Regulatory Compliance & Safety Manager  
Southwest Regional Water District

RE: National Rural Water Association Comments on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for 
Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) - Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
Headquartered in Duncan (Oklahoma), the National Rural Water Association (NRWA) is the non-profit 
association of the federated state rural water associations with a combined membership of over 30,000 
small and rural communities. NRWA is the country's largest water utility association and the largest 
community-based environmental organization. State Rural Water Associations are non-profit 
associations governed by elected board members from the membership. Our member utilities have the 
very important public responsibility of complying with all applicable U.S. Environmental Protection 
Agency (EPA) regulations and for supplying the public with safe drinking water and sanitation every 
second of every day. 
____________________________________________________________________________________ 
 
Administrator Regan, 
 
The National Rural Water Association (NRWA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 
Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed National Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and 
Copper Improvements (LCRI). NRWA has been providing boots-on-the ground Technical Assistance to 
small rural water systems since 1976.   40% of all technical assistance that is provided by NRWA goes 
directly to disadvantaged communities. 100% of the assistance and training we provide is to 
communities with populations of 10,000 or less. NRWA’s technical experts provide practical, problem-
solving assistance that help small rural communities every day.  
NRWA shares the goal of eliminating harmful contaminants from the public’s drinking water and 
environment.  NRWA commends EPA for continuing to improve this rule to better protect public health 
while reducing complexity and burden to water systems.  The great majority of water systems regulated 
by the EPA under LCRI will be small (under 10,000 in population). Small and rural communities will have 
more difficulty complying with the new rule due to limited economies of scale and lack of technical 
expertise.  The items below reflect concerns the small, rural, and disadvantaged water systems that 
NRWA members have communicated. 
Cost and Affordability 
NRWA understands our infrastructure needs updating and in many cases replacement. Drinking water, 
wastewater and cybersecurity need significant investments. Although the federal government provides 
resources for LSL replacement, this funding is inadequate to meet the needs of our rural systems. 
Coupled with the recently proposed PFAS rule, this regulation will increase costs well beyond the 
available funding.  

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2 
 
The infrastructure law provides $55 billion to support upgrades to the nation’s water infrastructure, 
with projections speculating a cost of $30 billion to replace all lead service lines (LSLs). However, only 
$15 billion of this is dedicated to LSL replacements while the rest is being stretched by multiple demands 
particularly the $11.7 billion of general Drinking Water State Revolving Funds (DWSRF). The DWSRFs 
could support much of the replacement of LSLs, but they are also being utilized to address other 
contaminants like per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) in drinking water systems and used for 
congressionally directed spending (earmarks). Additionally, the available funding will impact fewer 
projects due to rising costs, permitting delays, and added expenses from expanded requirements under 
Davis-Bacon and Buy America when suitable components are unavailable domestically. All of this 
threatens to shift much of the cost to communities and ultimately the citizens they serve. 
Additionally, many states have struggled to spend their allocated SRF money. In a study published by 
Duke Nicolas Institute for Environmental Policy Solutions and the Environmental Policy Innovation 
Center, it is stated that “Nationwide there is $9.9 billion in SRF funding that states have not committed 
to projects.” There are many reasons why the SRF funding isn’t being spent that are not the fault of the 
state SRF staff: capacity, staffing, resources, and funding. These challenges will be compounded by the 
influx of new money, further challenging the state staff. If the administration wants to prioritize the 
removal of LSLs, we ask that EPA carefully considers opportunities to provide relief through exemptions, 
and more flexibility in conjunction with adequate funding. 
Please see the following comments in specific response to EPA’s “Request for Comment” Section IX in 
the proposed rule. 
General Matters: 
2. Whether there are additional ways EPA could reduce the complexity of the regulatory approach used to 
address lead in drinking water consistent with the statutory standard for a treatment technique rule in 
section 1412(b)(7)(A) of SDWA. Specifically, EPA requests comments on ways that the proposed LCRI could 
be simplified and ways that burden, including paperwork burden, could be reduced without affecting the 
ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects. 
Response: Finding a way to streamline the required communications, public notices, public education, 
language required in the Consumer Confidence Reports and consumer notifications would help greatly 
to reduce the burden of the proposed requirements. 
Service Line Replacement: 
2.  Whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should be more than four times (e.g., 
five, six, or seven times). 
Response: Reasonable effort should not be increased to require a quantity above 4 times.   
4.  The proposed minimum replacement rate and replacement deadlines. EPA is seeking comment on 
whether it is feasible for systems across the nation to complete service line replacement in a shorter 
timeframe than ten years, such as in six, seven, or eight years. EPA is seeking comment on the rate 
construct approach, including how to calculate compliance with a given service line replacement 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
3 
 
deadline and average annual rate calculated across a rolling three-year period. EPA also seeks comment 
on whether systems should be required to meet a minimum replacement rate in the first three years 
after the compliance date to give States an opportunity to enforce replacement rate progress sooner 
than three years after the compliance date. EPA also seeks comment on the complexity of the rate 
construct. 
Response: The proposed minimum replacement rate and replacement deadlines are too short at 10 
years – especially due to the increased requirements to gain access to the public funding made available 
for LSL replacements.  Planning, permitting and acquisition of parts in many locations will take up to 3 
years to get started.  There should be no minimum replacement requirement in the first 3 years.   
5.  EPA is taking comment on whether States, as a condition of primacy, or EPA when it is directly 
implementing the program, should be required to set initial shortened deadlines by a certain timeframe, 
such as no later than 60 days after the compliance date. 
Response: There should be no shortened deadlines.   
Tap Sampling for Lead and Copper criteria: 
1.  Comment on the sites included in Tier 3 and whether all of the proposed sites should be included in 
Tier 3, if additional sites should be included, or if some should be included in a different, lower priority 
tier, such as Tier 4. Specifically, comment on whether sites served by galvanized service lines or 
containing galvanized premise plumbing that are identified as ever being downstream of an LSL or lead 
connector should be included in the same tier as other sites with a current lead connector (e.g., copper 
service line downstream of a lead connector). 
Response: We do not support adding Tiers or changing Tier 3 sites.  Adding a requirement to use 
premise plumbing material for sampling tiers – adds a high level of complexity and would be difficult to 
achieve from private owners on private property. 
3.  Comment on the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to assess CCT performance, increase 
customer participation, and other relevant factors  
Response: WQP testing is a good indicator of CCT performance and doesn’t rely on complicated in-
house testing.  Testing can be completed at an outside hose bib.  
6.  Comment on whether State authority to specify sampling locations when a system is conducting 
reduced monitoring should apply regardless of the number of taps meeting sample site criteria. 
Response: There is already a requirement for sampling plans.  Requiring states to specify sampling 
locations adds another level of complexity which will only add a further burden on the water systems 
who already struggle to get the proper number of samples each monitoring period.    
Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan: 
1. In the LCRI, EPA is proposing a threshold of systems serving greater than 50,000 persons to host the 
inventory and plan online, which is the required threshold under the LCRR. EPA is seeking comment on 
the size threshold at which systems must host their publicly accessible inventory, inventory summary 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
4 
 
data, replacement summary data, and service line replacement plan online, and whether it should be 
lowered relative to the LCRR requirements. 
Response: 50,000 population is a good threshold to require systems to host the LSLI and plan online.  
Smaller systems are less likely to have the resources to comply with the requirement.  
2. In the LCRI, EPA is proposing a requirement for systems to validate the accuracy of non-lead service 
lines in their inventory that were categorized using methods other than records review or visual 
inspection of at least two points along the line. EPA is requesting comment on the number of validations 
required, the proposed 95 percent confidence level approach used to develop the number of validations 
required, the criteria for which methods used to categorize non-lead service lines should be included in 
the validation pool (including whether non-lead lines categorized based on records should be subject to 
validation), and the seven year timeline for systems on a 10-year replacement deadline to complete the 
validation requirements.  
Response: Non-lead lines categorized based on records review or visual inspection should stand as 
validated. EPA should carefully consider the difficulty and complexity of validation and the burden on 
smaller water systems – especially those that are privately, or community owned  
   
Corrosion Control Treatment: 
2.  Comment on whether it would be more appropriate to require water systems to re-optimize again 
following an action level exceedance regardless of meeting their optimal water quality parameters and 
to provide the State with the authority to waive this requirement. 
Response: Systems with existing CCT should be allowed to adjust (re-optimize) their treatment if they 
have an action level exceedance.  The primacy agencies should have authority and flexibility to assist 
systems to come into compliance. 
4.  The treatment recommendation and CCT study process can take multiple years to complete. For 
systems with existing corrosion control, the system may be able to alter the existing treatment (e.g., 
increase pH and/or orthophosphate dose) without a new CCT study on a much faster timeframe rather 
than waiting for study results that may recommend that same change. EPA is requesting comment on 
whether there are situations and/or conditions where existing treatment modifications may achieve 
similar lead reductions rather than delaying new treatment for two and- a-half years while a study is 
underway. 
Response: Systems with existing CCT should be allowed to alter their existing treatment to gain 
compliance with the rule without having to complete a new CCT study.   
Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems and  
Non- Transient, Non-Community Water Systems: 
1. EPA is proposing that small system flexibilities be limited to CWSs serving 3,300 persons and fewer and 
all NTNCWSs for the remaining compliance alternatives of point-of-use devices and plumbing 
replacement. EPA is seeking comment on whether the Agency should allow systems serving up to 10,000 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
5 
 
persons (or another threshold) to be eligible to use the small system compliance flexibility provision. EPA 
is also seeking information, data, and analysis on whether point-of-use devices and plumbing 
replacement are as effective as OCCT at systems serving up to 10,000 persons (or another threshold). 
Response: NRWA urges EPA to keep the small system flexibility available to systems serving < 10,000 
people.  If flexibilities are not feasible, larger water systems will naturally not use them, as such there 
doesn’t need to be additional regulations in place to keep it from happening.  As an example, Kentucky 
alone has 131 systems that serve between 3,300 and 10,000 people (29% of the State’s water systems, 
serving over half a million people, or 11% of state’s population). Of these, 114 (87%) serve populations 
with a MHI lower than the state MHI, indicating that these communities will require flexibility, financial 
assistance, and on-site technical assistance from trusted providers. 
 
Public Education 
2. Comment and supporting data on the capacity of water systems to conduct some or all of the required 
public education activities in 30 days, or another period of time that is less than 30 or 60 days, after the 
end of the tap sampling period in which a systemwide lead action level exceedance occurs. 
Response: Requiring Public EducaƟon for a lead acƟon level exceedance aŌer receipt of results in less 
than 30 days will be burdensome to small water systems.   
 
3. Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination that water systems are capable of 
providing consumer notices of individual tap sampling results within three calendar days of obtaining 
those results, regardless of whether the results exceed the lead or copper action level, or if a longer time 
frame is needed (e.g., three business days, seven calendar days, 14 calendar days). 
Response: The LCRI proposes an additional copper consumer notification and then a deadline of 3 days 
to get both Lead and  Copper Consumer Notifications to the customers.  It is important to note that the 
process of acquiring samples, delivering them to the lab, and lab processing times to the actual receipt 
of results and the calculated P90 can take as long as 6 months. Therefore, the need to rush a 3 day 
notification doesn’t make a great deal of sense and presents large burden to the small water systems – 
many of which are managed by volunteers.  It is also important to note that in many cases results 
provided by the laboratories contain errors that must be addressed before customer notification. For 
these reasons, NRWA requests this requirement be changed to at least 10 business days when the final 
rule is published.  
Additional Requirements for Systems with Multiple Lead Action Level Exceedances: 
6.  Alternative requirements for systems with multiple action level exceedances to provide filters to their 
consumers, such as requiring water systems to provide filters and replacement cartridges to consumers 
served by an LSL, GRR service line, or unknown service line or to all consumers, or to require systems to 
consult with the State upon meeting the criteria for multiple action level exceedances, after which the 
State determines the appropriate action to reduce lead exposure 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
6 
 
Response: NRWA recommends EPA consider requiring filters after multiple Action Level Exceedances for 
sites that exceeded the Action Level, buildings with LSLs or GRRs, and not necessarily the entire 
community. The service line inventory processes, new tiers, additional CCT requirements and 
assessments in the proposed LCRI reduce many risks to consumers related to lead in drinking water, 
making the requirement to provide filters to all consumers unnecessary, burdensome and unaffordable.  
Also, EPA should consider that filters can become harmful if not used and maintained properly. 
Reporting and Recordkeeping 
1. EPA is requesting comments on the expansion of the inventory reporting to include lead connectors 
and non-lead service lines. 
Response: Requiring an expansion of the inventory reporting now will require systems to “re-inventory” 
which is a huge expense.  “Updating the inventories” as systems do work in the water systems, and 
tracking any new components, would be a far more reasonable requirement.   
 
2. EPA has heard concern over the ability of States to review all required site sample plans and provide 
approvals in time for the first tap monitoring period and is requesting comment on whether EPA should 
consider a phased approach or alternate approach to reduce the burden on States following the rule 
compliance date. 
Response: Providing phased due dates would allow States to phase site plan reviews and approvals. 
 
Compliance Dates: 
1. The proposed LCRI includes a three-year implementation period following the publication of the final 
rule until the compliance date to allow States time to obtain primacy and work with systems to prepare 
to comply. It also allows systems time to plan and obtain funding for LSLR as appropriate. EPA is seeking 
comment on all aspects of the proposed LCRI compliance dates and whether it would be practicable for 
water systems to implement any of the proposed LCRI requirements earlier than three years from the 
date of final action on the proposed LCRI.  
Response: EPA should retain a three-year implementation period on all aspects of the rule. 
Thank you for the opportunity to participate and comment. NRWA is very appreciative of the agencies’ 
many public outreach opportunities. We believe our recommendations will result in a better rule once 
finalized. NRWA is ready to work with the EPA to responsibly provide safe, clean, and affordable drinking 
water in a manner that is cost effective and non-burdensome.

(charles@nrwa.org).

Re:
