Minnesota Department of Health (MDH) 
Comments 
EPA PROPOSED LEAD AND COPPER RULE IMPROVEMENTS (LCRI)  
Docket ID EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
Introduction  
MDH has implemented the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) since it was published in 1991, with 
minor revisions in 2000 and 2004, and short-term revisions in 2007. MDH staff work with water 
suppliers to ensure that systems across Minnesota meet the requirements of the LCR and LCRR, 
prepare for impending LCRI requirements and take action accordingly. MDH staff regularly 
assist water systems above and beyond existing rule requirements including helping them 
understand requirements regarding sampling, service line inventories, corrosion control, and 
water quality parameter monitoring.  In 2018, MDH also worked with stakeholders to evaluate 
the costs and benefits of eliminating lead service lines in Minnesota (see Lead in Minnesota 
Water Report at: 
https://www.health.state.mn.us/communities/environment/water/docs/leadreport.pdf ). In 
addition, MDH houses the state’s blood lead surveillance program and healthy homes programs 
which conduct lead assessments and work to reduce lead from all exposure sources.   
There is no safe level of lead. The goal of the LCR, LCRR, and LCRI is to reduce lead in drinking 
water through corrosion control and removal of lead service lines. Considerable progress has 
been made since the initial LCR, and many systems across Minnesota took action to utilize 
corrosion control and we have few exceedances in any given year. However, the science in 
understanding corrosion control and the risks for increased lead exposure due to source and 
treatment changes has improved significantly.   
Another goal of rule improvements is to reduce the regulatory burden for primacy agencies and 
water systems. The LCR, LCRR and now LCRI are the most complex SDWA rules to implement, 
and any changes will require significant training and technical assistance. Therefore, 
streamlining implementation is imperative so that the rule can be implemented and enforced 
effectively to protect public health. The LCRI, makes several improvements to the LCRR but 
there is still room for additional progress.  

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
3 
 
Single Action Level vs. Action and Trigger Levels 
MDH appreciates that the LCRI simplified and removed the separate action and trigger levels by 
creating one lower action level of 10 ppb. If values lower than 10 ppb are considered by EPA, 
then laboratory and sampling limitations must also be evaluated. For example, 5 ppb is 
currently the practical quantitative limit, and 2 ppb is common as a laboratory reporting limit. 
In general, if dropping the action level below 10 ppb is an option EPA is considering, then 
laboratory and other practical constraints must be carefully assessed before a new level is 
chosen. Further, EPA should also look forward to what the selected action level will represent 
as a data tool for evaluating corrosion control efficacy once all lead service lines are removed. 
There may be a level of lead, as measured by sampling protocols of LCR/LCRR/LCRI, that is 
beyond ability of the public water systems to be able to make corrosion control treatment 
changes that will be effective without additional action from property owners to manage 
building water quality or remove building sources or lead. Premise plumbing is beyond the 
scope of control of community PWSs.  
Lead Service Line (LSL) Inventories and Lead Service Line 
Replacement (LSLR) 
MDH generally agrees with ASDWA’s comments concerning changes to the inventories and 
service line replacements. Most states and water systems have operated under the 
interpretation that inventory data components would remain relatively untouched during the 
LCRI proposal process due to the need to turn them in by October 16, 2024. It is imperative that 
any additional inventory fields such as lead service line connector be allowed to be reported 
during subsequent updates rather than delay initial inventories.  
Removing lead service lines, regardless of action level exceedance is an important step toward 
reducing lead in drinking water long term. MDH supports increased efforts to replace lead 
service lines but would recommend that EPA include timelines for completing identification of 
any unknown service lines. 
Tap Sampling  
MDH supports first draw, one-liter samples after a six-hour stagnation period for LCRR 
compliance tap sampling and 5th liter sampling at sites with a lead service line.  MDH also 
agrees with the proposal to use wide mouth bottles and prohibit pre-stagnation flushing. MDH 
recommends that a maximum stagnation time of 18 hours be implemented and that for 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
4 
 
samples found to have exceeded 18 hours stagnation, the result could be invalidated by the 
state and a resample allowed.  
It is important that regulators understand practical concerns in implementing the current rule 
and the proposed LCRR/LCRI. Operators in Minnesota have provided many examples of 
sampling for the lead and copper rule where: 
• Customers collect at the wrong location. 
• Customers collect after point of use treatment or filter. 
• Customers fail to collect and don’t notify the system until the last minute (causing 
potential monitoring and reporting concerns or frantic rush to find a replacement 
volunteer). 
• Customers sample after long vacations or after a house has been vacant for long periods 
of time. 
• Occupational hazards and liability concerns exist, such as when operators have to 
follow-up to a residence with a dog or a resident provides a bottle containing urine or 
another unknown liquid instead of the tap sample. 
• Considerations during public health emergencies such as a pandemic when getting 
access to homes and participation in sampling becomes a greater challenge. Alternate 
assessment methods such as distribution monitoring stations may be useful as a back- 
up.  
For nontransient noncommunity public water systems, application of sample site selection 
under the LCR has been challenging since the initial implementation of the rule, for reasons 
including limited number of sample sites in some cases and the presence of point-of-use 
treatment devices in others. The latter issue may become more prominent should point-of-use 
treatment option for small systems proceed under the LCRR/LCRI.  For these reasons, MDH 
requests that EPA use the opportunity presented by the LCRR to clarify expectations for lead 
and copper sampling at nontransient noncommunity public water systems. MDH recommends 
maintaining a separate set of tiers for nontransient noncommunity systems so that the tiering 
approach is more applicable to each system classification and plumbing structure. This will 
simplify data collection and reduce confusion for these systems. Treating nontransient 
noncommunity systems as miniature community systems is not appropriate for the reality of 
how these facilities operate. 
Point-of-Use Devices 
Point of use devices are proposed to be provided by public water systems to customers under 
several areas of the LCRR/LCRI.  Situations such as an action level exceedance or following a 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
5 
 
lead service line replacement both require PWS to distribute a POU device. It is imperative that 
EPA consider the practicality of this approach and build in reasonable alternatives when POU 
devices would not be practical for the customer. Some examples include: 
• Number and amount of POU devices: some locations such as schools or businesses may 
not be able to practically use a POU provided by a PWS in these situations. A school 
cannot practically operate using a pitcher filter. Providing these facilities with flushing 
and lead test following an ALE or service line replacement may be better alternatives. 
• Not all sites are high risk for lead and would need a POU device. Limiting distribution of 
POU devices to homes based on tier, service line material, and/or building age may help 
make these requirements to target those that most need help reducing lead exposure. 
Corrosion Control Treatment 
MDH recommends that the final LCRI provide flexibility for states to approve less expensive 
corrosion control treatment (CCT) study options that can be tailored to system specific issues, 
existing practices, sources of lead and constraints. States and systems need a toolbox of options 
to take action to address lead and corrosion concerns. It is important that the EPA provide 
guidance to help systems chose the correct tool for commonly occurring treatment 
considerations. The proposed LCRI promotes pipe loops exclusively and is not practicable or 
implementable on the timelines proposed. Guidance should be developed to assist states in 
determining the appropriate options and when to use other types of study.  Analogous system 
studies should also be able to be used since we have decades of data from systems and often 
systems may be able to demonstrate that their system is analogous (similar water quality, 
distribution), particularly for those systems exploring orthophosphate as a CCT choice. States in 
conjunction with EPA could develop templates for systems to use to determine when this 
approach may be appropriate. It is also important for options such as installation of filter 
devices be available for those small systems that own and operate their entire distribution 
system when it would not be practical to install effective CCT. EPA also must consider other 
laws and regulations that impact water and wastewater systems such as phosphate limits when 
considering CCT treatment. Corrosion control inhibitors often have diminishing returns and the 
amount of phosphate added to water for CCT may contribute significantly so some phosphate 
load in some locations. 
MDH agrees that systems with ALE be required to evaluate the effectiveness of their existing 
CCT but there needs to be more flexibility to deal with systems that have more complicated 
configurations. The proposed rule assumes simple system configuration, presence of lead 
service lines, and that the conditions at the treatment plant are representative of distribution 
conditions. The requirement for pipe loop studies is inconsistent with the urgency indicated by 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
6 
 
the 24-hour public notification requirement and pipe loop studies when done properly may 
take years to completely implement and gather results. 
MDH recommends that the final LCRI clarify requirements for large systems to provide optimal 
corrosion control treatment and clearly establish timelines for systems to meet these criteria 
when they move from a medium size to a large size system.  The final LCRI or implementation 
guidance documents should include a clear table or flow-chart for CCT and CCT study 
requirements by system size. The typical process that states use is that systems submit a 
proposed recommendation and the state reviews and approves it. To reflect this process the 
“state designates” language should be revised to the “state will review and approve” for both 
OCCT and OWQP. 
The intent of corrosion control is to provide systems with a proactive way to manage 
distribution water quality to prevent corrosion. EPA’s definition of corrosion control provides 
limited regulatory authority for primacy agencies to help water systems manage distribution 
water quality issues that may affect corrosion (such as nitrification, iron, manganese, 
distribution flushing programs, and managing biological activity within the distribution system). 
MDH recommends that EPA use the LCRI to promote a proactive verses reactive approach to 
distribution water quality as a whole. This water management planning approach would allow 
systems to consider simultaneous compliance with other distribution regulations and allow for 
a true optimization of water quality. Water systems should work with their primacy agencies to 
evaluate and plan for distribution expansion, population growth/reduction, new/changes to 
source water, treatment changes etc.  
Changes in Source or Treatment 
MDH recommends that the final LCRI include more detailed and specific information for 
systems and primacy agencies on the types of changes that require review and approval of the 
primacy agency. Including a matrix of common source and treatment changes and guidance on 
the type of additional study that the state should consider requiring would be invaluable when 
communicating with CWS about the potential impacts of these changes and help systems more 
adequately plan for corrosion control studies.  It is important to clarify the level of review 
needed so that appropriate actions can be taken by both primacy agencies and systems.  Since 
source and treatment changes were the main reasons for the highly publicized lead crises in 
Washington DC, and Flint, MI having these issues addressed clearly in rule is important.  
Some questions (note that this is not a comprehensive list) that need answers in the final LCRI 
or guidance (as appropriate) include: 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
7 
 
• When does bringing on a new source or well require re-evaluation? 
• When are pipe loop studies needed? 
• Do CCT studies need to include hydraulic modeling for consecutive systems? 
• How does a downstream water system demonstrate how a change from the wholesaler 
or upstream water system will impact them? 
• Will wholesalers and consecutive water systems both have to switch back to six-month 
monitoring after changes are made? 
Small System Flexibility  
MDH supports the concept of flexible options for small systems that are proposed in the LCRI 
Many small systems face technical, financial, and management challenges. While having more 
than one option for compliance provides welcome flexibility and choice for small systems, it 
should be noted that these additional options increase the tracking burden for states. 
MDH recommends the following: 
1. Small System Size: MDH recommends that these flexibilities apply to systems falling in 
the population range of 3,300 or fewer and those point-of-use (POU) devices apply only 
to systems serving 100 or fewer.  
2. POU Devices: It should be clear in the final LCRR under what conditions POU devices will 
be allowed and what requirements for installation, ownership, and maintenance of the 
devices will be so that systems have an adequate understanding of the implications of 
that option. It should also be clear in rule that the primacy agency has the final approval 
of the use of these devices as a compliance option. 
3. Replacement of Lead-Bearing Plumbing Option: MDH recommends that the option to 
replace lead-bearing plumbing that is currently being reserved for Non-Transient Non-
Community Water Systems (NTNCWS) also be included as an option for Community 
Water Systems (CWS) at the discretion of the primacy agency. This option may allow 
small community systems to commit resources to removing sources of lead rather than 
commit resources to maintaining POU devices in perpetuity.  In addition, allowing states 
to set a timeline for the replacement to be completed would allow state to customize 
the option so that systems can better plan and budget for the replacements. 
4. Action Plan: MDH recommends that EPA develop guidance for small systems and 
NTNCWS that exceed that action level to work with states to develop their required 
action plan. This will help empower primacy agencies to help systems develop realistic 
plans and reduce time wasted on non-viable alternatives. This action plan could also 
include other measures for reducing lead and copper relating to distribution 
management (optimizing existing chemical feeds, free ammonia, chlorine residuals, 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
8 
 
corrosion control residuals, water age. An action plan that includes these steps with 
corrosion control treatment (such as orthophosphate) as a last resort. 
5. Maintaining CCT:  MDH recommends that EPA reference language from §141.81 again 
in the “Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems and Non-
Transient, Non-Community Water Systems” section emphasizing that small systems 
using the small system options under §141.93 and those which have treatment in place 
continue to operate and maintain optimal corrosion control treatment and meet any 
requirements that the state determines to be appropriate to ensure optimal corrosion 
control treatment is maintained. 
While the flexibilities in the proposal and those recommended here give systems more 
alternatives to reduce lead, small systems currently using CCT should not abandon those 
practices without approval from their state. Requiring approval will prevent systems from 
undermining their lead reduction efforts with CCT by moving to an alternative technique too 
quickly. 
Lead Testing in Schools and Childcares 
Minnesota is one of several states that already have requirements for schools and childcares to 
conduct ongoing testing for lead in drinking water. In Minnesota public and charter schools and 
child care centers must test all taps used for consumption once every 5 years. Starting in 2024, 
all testing data must begin to be reported to MDH and these facilities must remediate when 
lead is above 5 ppb. These requirements are much more stringent than the proposed 
requirements for water systems to test for lead in these facilities. 
MDH recommends that the testing proposed in the LCRI only be required if a state does not 
already have an ongoing lead testing program or that public water system testing in schools and 
childcares be limited to cases where there is an action level exceedance. 
Water quality in early care and educational facilities can be a challenge due to intermittent 
water usage patterns and ageing infrastructure. Rarely, is the public water system the 
source/cause of lead in the drinking water. EPA should work with other agencies to provide 
better guidance and if necessary, regulations regarding water management within their 
buildings to ensure maintenance of water quality.  

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
9 
 
SDWIS Data and Tracking  
MDH shares the concerns expressed by ASDWA and others that data management implications 
of the LCRR and LCRI are significant – in terms of complexity and added workload for public 
water systems and state primacy programs. 
States need to have implementation guidance for data tracking and reporting to EPA well in 
advance of implementation requirements so that data requirements are clear and complete. To 
date, LCRR guidance and date entry instructions have not fully addressed LCRR concerns and 
with LCRR deadlines approaching for PWS it is imperative that states know exactly what and 
how they will need to report data to EPA. The data shared by EPA, states, and water systems 
regarding SDWA compliance should be able to be consistent, accurate, and easily accessible to 
everyone that needs it. 
Copper 
Copper corrosion is a problem in many water systems, but the LCR treats copper as an 
orphaned child. Sampling under the LCR does not target the worst-case situations for copper 
and because copper violations are only treated as treatment technique violation it is not 
treated with the same concern as other health-based issues. In addition, copper exceedances 
tend to point toward broader distribution management issues in the system (such as 
nitrification, free ammonia in the distribution system, biological activity, high dissolved oxygen, 
etc.) which may not be addressed by the current or proposed water quality parameter 
monitoring or corrosion control studies. Unless these issues are addressed, systems may not be 
clear on the needed actions to reduce copper exposure. The majority of the LCR, LCRR, and the 
proposed LCRI deal with lead specifically and leaves out actions to take to reduce copper 
exposure. MDH recommends that EPA use the rule revision as an opportunity to clarify 
expectations for copper, including improved/expanded corrosion control considerations, 
education, and outreach for residents. Ensuring that sites with copper plumbing are included 
when a part of the distribution sampling is an important part of preventing excess copper 
exposure to those at risk. Considerations for evaluating homes with high copper levels to 
determine the cause of an elevated level should also be considered.  Additionally, EPA should 
consider copper action levels – and re-assess education materials to provide information to the 
public on levels that contribute to acute copper concerns, chronic copper concerns, and 
concerns for special populations (those with Wilson’s disease and infants). 

P R O P O S E D  L E A D  A N D  C O P P E R  R U L E  I M R O V E M E N T S  D O C K E T  I D  E P A - H Q - O W - 2 0 2 2 - 0 8 0 1 - 0 0 3 6  
10 
 
Customer Notices and Educational Materials 
MDH supports ASDWA’s comments regarding streamlining customer education and public 
notice materials. There are many new documentation requirements for materials and timing 
may overlap with other system requirements. MDH encourages EPA to streamline these 
requirements so that public water systems can clearly finish one step before having to 
complete the notification requirement. Consolidating certification and documentation to 
improve and reduce reporting requirements would also be helpful. 
Many materials EPA is requesting that systems provide to customers could be provided as a 
template. MDH encourages EPA to provide translated and accessible templates for systems to 
use as that would more efficiently ensure states are able to easily review these documents and 
reduce the burden for all systems to try to produce their own. 
The most important component of customer notice related to lead and copper are helping 
people understand their risks if they consume water containing lead and copper. Education 
components of the LCR/LCRR and LCRI are related to action level exceedances. While systems 
use these the action level to base treatment decisions and other actions, the public need to be 
able to understand relative health risks so they can make informed choices on remediation. In 
an ideal world everyone would be able to remediate all sources of lead and other 
environmental hazards but realistically the public makes choices everyday regarding which 
things to prioritize about their health. Providing better guidance to the public about the relative 
exposure risks from lead and copper is imperative to getting buy-in to remove sources of lead 
from home plumbing and helping the general public understand how they can take action at 
home or work to maintain and improve their water quality.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0869 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024  
 
Ms. Jennifer McLain 
Director 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20460 
 
RE: Proposed Rule: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID: No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Dear Ms. McLain, 
 
On behalf of the nation’s mayors, cities and counties we appreciate the opportunity to provide 
comments on the United States Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) Proposed National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) to reduce lead 
in drinking water. The Biden Administration has set an ambitious goal, which the LCRI 
advances, of removing all lead service lines across the country. We support EPA’s efforts to 
accomplish this goal, and many local governments are already taking action to address lead 
service lines (LSLs) in their communities, but we have some concerns regarding affordability 
and implementation of the proposal. 
 
Collectively, our organizations represent the nation’s 3,069 counties, 19,000 cities and the 
mayors of the 1,400 largest cities throughout the United States. Local governments serve as co-
regulators in implementing and enforcing many federal laws with states, including Safe Drinking 
Water Act programs, and our members take these responsibilities seriously. Protecting the 
health, safety and welfare of residents is a top priority for local leaders.  
 
EPA first promulgated the Lead and Copper Rule in 1991 to reduce exposure to lead in drinking 
water and implementation of this rule over the last 30 years has resulted in major improvements 
in public health. Implementing the proposed LCRI will be an unprecedented and major local 
effort to achieve national public health goals. For these reasons, it is important that EPA 
establish a regulatory program that is clear, cost-efficient and implementable for all our 
communities.  
 
Specifically, we recommend the Agency:  
● Provide additional and direct funding to local governments to reduce the financial burden 
imposed by this otherwise unfunded mandate.  

● Provide maximum implementation flexibility for local governments in the form of longer 
and alternative replacement schedules for systems facing affordability barriers, systems 
with many LSLs or for systems demonstrating sufficient corrosion control treatment. 
● Clarify the definition of when a service line is “under the control” of the water system.  
 
LCRI Overarching Concerns and Recommendations  
Below, we outline our concerns with the feasibility of the proposed rule and provide 
recommendations to address these concerns to ensure that the limited financial resources of 
local governments are used as effectively as possible toward meeting this public health goal.  
 
1. Affordability and Equity  
EPA estimates the annual cost for public water systems (PWSs) to comply with the proposed 
LCRI is between $2.9 billion and $4.8 billion, with costs primarily associated with identifying and 
removing LSLs, installing water treatment technologies and providing filters to consumers.  
However, according to the American Water Works Association, the average cost for LSL 
replacement ranges between $4,000 and $7,000 but can be upwards of $10,000 to replace a 
single LSL.1 Given that EPA’s 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment 
estimates that there are approximately 9.2 million LSLs across the country, the total cost for LSL 
replacement alone is likely to be upwards of $90 to $100 billion. Additionally, it is important to 
note that EPA’s cost analysis is calculated across 35 years, even though the bulk of the costs 
will be required in the first 10 to 13 years after the rule is finalized, resulting in a likely inaccurate 
assessment of the impact the proposed rule will have on ratepayer affordability.  
 
Because of this, we are concerned that not only has the Agency underestimated the full cost of 
compliance, but also the fiscal capacity of local governments and ratepayers to afford these 
costs. This is a critical miscalculation given that local governments fund over 98 percent of all 
capital, operations and maintenance investment in drinking water and wastewater infrastructure 
in the United States, primarily through user fees and bonds. The most recent U.S. Census data 
shows that local governments spent over $148 billion on water and wastewater in 2021 alone, 
and spent over $2.38 trillion between 1993 and 2019, not adjusted for inflation.  
 
Local leaders appreciate the historic $15 billion provided in the bipartisan Infrastructure 
Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) to address lead in drinking water. However, this figure is well 
below the projected replacement cost of $90 to $100 billion and the majority of the $15 billion 
comes in the form of loans, which local governments must pay back. Further, because the 
funding is only available through FY2026, it is uncertain if local governments will even be able to 
use this funding to comply with the proposed LCRI. Moreover, current proposals for upcoming 
federal appropriation bills drastically reduce the amount of funds available to local governments 
through the Drinking Water State Revolving Fund as funding for earmarks is being pulled from 
 
1 Considerations when Costing Lead Service Line Identification and Replacement, American Water 
Works Association, November 2022. Available at: 
https://www.awwa.org/Portals/0/AWWA/ETS/Resources/Technical%20Reports/2022%2011%2029%2007
2%20CDM%20SL%20Identification%20and%20LSLR%20Costs.pdf  

the base funding of the State Revolving Fund programs, limiting the amount of funds available 
for LSL removal efforts.  
 
Unfortunately, the historic capital stimulus provided by Congress in the IIJA falls far short of the 
cost this proposed LCRI will impose on public water systems and affordability will continue to 
represent a major barrier to reaching the public health goals of the proposed rule.  
 
Recommendation: We urge the Administration and Congress to provide additional and direct 
federal funding to local governments. We also urge EPA to match compliance schedules with 
financial assistance where it is needed. 
 
A. Individual Burden and Environmental Justice Concerns  
Given that local governments will be forced to bear the brunt of costs to comply with the 
proposed rule, EPA must understand that a rise in water rates in communities across the 
nation is a near certainty. The steep cost for utilities to comply with the LCRI will be felt 
most intensely by low-income households and the small business community. 
 
Additionally, in order for local governments and water systems to comply with the 
proposed mandatory annual replacement rates, many will likely be forced to prioritize 
customers who are able to afford the estimated thousands of dollars required for LSL 
replacement. Given the absolute priority that is needed for LSL replacement in low-
income and environmental justice communities, this dichotomy could raise serious equity 
issues.  
 
Recommendation: We strongly urge the Agency to consider the financial impact this 
proposed regulation will have on individual consumers, particularly those in 
environmental justice and disadvantaged communities. Affordability challenges 
associated with an accelerated timeline and limited financial resources will force local 
governments to pass these costs onto community ratepayers. To help alleviate this, we 
recommend the Agency consider additional funding sources and longer replacement 
schedules.  
 
B. Competing Drinking Water Priorities  
We must also note that EPA is in the process of finalizing a host of other new regulations 
impacting public water systems. Specifically, we are concerned that, in addition to the 
LCRI requirements, the Agency’s rulemakings around new drinking water standards for 
PFAS and regulating PFAS under CERCLA and RCRA will create additional unfunded 
mandates that will be unaffordable for many communities. This is on top of ongoing 
investments PWSs are already making to upgrade aging infrastructure, safeguard 
systems against attacks, increase climate sustainability and resiliency and meet other 
requirements under the Safe Drinking Water Act and Clean Water Act. 
 
As mentioned above, local governments already face a water infrastructure needs gap, 
and these additional unfunded mandates will exacerbate affordability and equity 

concerns for the many fixed- and low-income households that already spend a 
disproportionate amount of their income on water bills.  
 
Recommendation: We urge EPA to take a holistic and integrated approach to drinking 
water regulations and consider the cumulative impacts that the rules and regulations will 
have on local governments in terms of cost and compliance and implementation 
timelines. 
 
2. Implementation Challenges   
Given the number of challenges associated with the proposed LCRI, including limited financial 
resources, equity and affordability concerns, and workforce and supply chain shortages, among 
others, flexibility will be critical to ensuring local communities are able to implement and comply 
with the proposed rule. The Agency should take such factors as the preponderance of LSLs in a 
community, local market conditions, issues around gaining authority to access private property, 
liability concerns and the use of water rate revenue to remove LSLs into consideration when 
working with local communities on the implementation of the proposed LCRI.  
 
Recommendation: We urge EPA to offer additional flexibilities, including extended compliance 
deadlines, to local governments and PWSs that are managing their own local logistical 
constraints, limited resources, and competing priorities. 
A.  Replacement Schedule  
The Agency’s LCRI proposal sets a compliance deadline of ten years to replace 100 
percent of LSLs (10 percent rolling average over three years), regardless of the system’s 
measured lead level. We support the proposal to build lead service line replacements 
into a community’s capital improvement plan, rather than as a reactionary measure 
through a Maximum Contaminant Level requirement or lead exceedance. While the 
proposal includes some flexibility for a longer replacement timeframe for a very limited 
number of scenarios, ultimately, this compliance schedule is unachievable for a vast 
majority of communities and water systems.  
 
The two eligibility criteria proposed in the LCRI where a system may receive a deferred 
replacement timeline are: (1) systems with a high proportion of LSLs relative to the total 
number of households served (0.039 replacements per household per year); and (2) 
systems who would have to replace more than 10,000 LSLs per year under the 
proposed ten-year timeframe. We appreciate the Agency’s acknowledgment that many 
possible factors can influence how many LSLs a city could remove in one year - 
including market conditions, labor shortages, and even seasonal changes. However, the 
Agency’s conclusion that removing up to 10,000 LSLs a year is “technically feasible” for 
the vast majority of systems likely downplays the impact that varying limitations have on 
the ability of communities and water systems to feasibly replace that many pipes in one 
year.  

Additionally, EPA’s proposal includes a requirement that States set a shorter deadline 
for an individual water system to complete LSL replacement where “feasible,” which is 
undefined. Although well-intended, local governments and public water systems are in 
the best position to appropriately assess local factors and circumstances that strongly 
impact a system’s ability to remove LSLs within a certain timeframe. At a minimum, EPA 
should require States to consult with local governments before a determination is made 
regarding shortening the replacement schedule.  
 
Recommendation: Eligibility criteria for longer replacement deadlines should be 
expanded to offer local governments a more realistic and fiscally appropriate timeframe 
to account for practical limitations. The Agency should also consider a simpler, 
alternative compliance pathway for systems that have either demonstrated sufficient 
corrosion control treatment or have few LSLs. This would better allow communities to 
allocate their resources where they are most required and ensure that systems with 
higher need are prioritized first. Additionally, we urge the Agency to either remove the 
requirement that States set more rapid compliance deadlines or clarify under which 
specific criteria this requirement would be triggered to avoid any sudden shifts in local 
planning and implementation efforts.  
Additionally, EPA should not require local governments to replace non-potable service 
lines if there are administrative safeguards in place to prevent potable use nor require 
local governments to replace service lines on abandoned property if there are local 
provisions in place to ensure replacement before use. This would simplify the 
replacement requirement and provide additional flexibility for communities. 
B. Private Side Replacement 
Replacing LSLs is often complicated because ownership of the service line is often split 
between the public water system and privately owned property. As such, the local 
government must obtain consent from the property owner to access and replace LSLs 
on the private side of the water line. While financial concerns represent one of the most 
critical barriers to receiving customer consent to access private-side LSLs, it is not the 
only one. Local governments may struggle to obtain consent for a variety of reasons, 
including community distrust, the physically disruptive process of removing LSLs, and 
reluctance to view LSL replacement as a priority. The cooperation of private residents to 
replace pipes will greatly impact, either negatively or positively, a local governments’ 
ability to complete 100 percent replacement in compliance with the LCRI.  
The Safe Drinking Water Act defines public water systems and delineates between 
portions of the distribution system that are under the control of the PWS and portions 
that are connected to the distribution system, but are not under the control of the PWS. 
While the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) equates “control” with 
“ownership,” the proposed LCRI redefines “control” to equate it to “access.”  

However, the proposed rule fails to define “access” and what having “legal, physical 
access” means for local governments and PWSs in terms of conducting LSL 
replacement on the private side. The definition of “access” is also a function of state and 
local law, which EPA recognizes. The lack of a clear definition of “access” in the LCRI, 
as well as differing definitions of “control,” creates implementation and feasibility 
challenges for communities. For example, does legal access equate to physical access? 
What happens if the water system has legal access, but the property owner still refuses 
to consent for LSL replacement? What does having access to private property mean in 
terms of legal liability and worker safety?  
Furthermore, the proposed LCRI outlines various activities PWSs must do to obtain or 
attempt to obtain necessary access for private-side replacement. For example, under the 
proposed rule PWSs will be required to identify any State or local laws impacting a 
system’s ability to conduct LSL replacement with the idea being that the identification of 
these laws will help the water system overcome the barriers. We understand that this 
provision is intended to make obtaining access more likely, however without additional 
clarity on the definitions of “control” and “access,” this provision further adds to the 
regulatory burden and creates implementation and feasibility challenges for 
communities.   
Recommendations: EPA should provide additional clarity around the definitions of 
“control” and “access” to provide more guidance to communities and PWSs around 
conducting LSL replacement on private property. Without this clarity, local governments 
should not be held responsible for failing to replace LSLs they do not have control over 
where it is not feasible to do so.   
Further, we recommend that EPA maintain its provision in the LCRI to not require local 
governments to cover the costs associated with the replacement of privately-owned 
service lines, but still retain the option to do so. While some local governments have 
been able to subsidize private-side replacement, there may be legal issues or state 
prohibitions on using ratepayer or capital funds for private-side replacements. 
C. Lead Service Line Inventory 
Under EPA’s LCRR water systems are required to provide an initial inventory of their 
LSLs by October 16, 2024. Under the proposed LCRI, all water systems will have to 
regularly update their inventory and create a publicly available service line replacement 
plan. For unknown service lines, EPA is proposing to require that water systems 
categorize the material of all unknown service lines by the system’s applicable deadline 
for completing mandatory full service line replacement (ten years for most systems).  
Recommendation: While local governments are making progress on completing their 
inventories, changes to the LCRI can help ease the regulatory burden of this 
requirement. For example, we urge EPA to allow communities to complete the inventory 

without having to include fire services and other non-potable service lines, as well as 
abandoned properties.   
3. Risk Communication  
We recommend taking a moderate approach to risk communication so as not to cause undue 
public alarm and concern. While public information and transparency is important, informing 
customers of the existence of lead pipes can potentially raise undo public alarm if no lead is 
leaching due to proper corrosion control. Therefore, risk communication should be targeted to 
customers where there is a specific concern. LSL notification can be complex for local 
governments, and a requirement to notify customers when there is uncertainty will only make 
this process more challenging. Specifically, a 24-hour notification timeframe when there is an 
action level exceedance is unrealistic. Moreover, a 24-hour notification is usually reserved for 
acute public health emergencies such as significant outbreaks of infectious diseases or 
bioterrorist attacks where there is the potential for human health to be immediately impacted. 
Effective risk communication may require longer than 24 hours to execute, as there may be 
various administrative issues to resolve, and several business days could elapse in some 
instances. 
 
Recommendation: We urge the Agency to encourage best efforts for rapid delivery and 
notification but allow for flexibility in its requirements. 
4. Small System Flexibility  
EPA’s LCRI proposes to change the eligibility threshold for small system flexibility from water 
systems serving 10,000 people down to 3,300 people. Small systems are particularly 
constrained in their financial and staff capacity, which impacts their ability to comply with federal 
regulations.  
 
Recommendation: We recommend the Agency maintain its previous eligibility threshold of 
10,000 persons in an effort to provide maximum flexibility for local governments and in 
particular, smaller communities. Additionally, EPA should ensure that small system flexibilities 
will be available in every state, since many of the flexibilities could depend on the state granting 
them. 
 
Due to the concerns listed above, we believe additional financial resources, expanded 
compliance schedules and maximum implementation flexibility would offer the most 
realistic approach for local governments to make significant progress toward reducing 
lead in drinking water and removing 100 percent lead pipes. We urge EPA to take a 
reasonable and rational approach to compliance that recognizes local obstacles and to 
be realistic when setting goals or standards under the LCRI. 
 
On behalf of the nation’s mayors, cities and counties, thank you for considering the local 
government perspective on this important issue. As the Agency finalizes the LCRI, we look 
forward to working with you to ensure a clear, cost-effective and implementable rule. If you have 
any questions, please contact us: Judy Sheahan (USCM) at 202-861-6775 or 
jsheahan@usmayors.org; Carolyn Berndt (NLC) at 202-626-3101 or Berndt@nlc.org; or Sarah 
Gimont (NACo) at 202-942-4254 or sgimont@naco.org. 

 
Sincerely, 
 
 
    
 
 
Tom Cochran

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0971 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Comment letter on Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
Docket ID Number: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
February 5, 2024 
Michael Regan, Administrator 
Radhika Fox, Assistant Administrator, Office of Water 
Environmental Protection Agency 
 
Dear Administrator Regan and Assistant Administrator Fox, 
The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements released by the EPA take critical steps towards minimizing the 
presence of lead in drinking water across the country. However, there is no safe level of lead in drinking 
water, and we urge the EPA to further strengthen and expedite regulations that would protect the 22 
million Americans who receive their drinking water from lead service lines. 
From Chicago to Detroit to Cleveland, the Great Lakes region is home to urban and industrial centers 
with rich histories. While we admire the ingenuity, beauty, and culture of these major cities, they are 
deeply impacted by aging infrastructure that threatens the quality of drinking water and the health of 
communities. 
Out of the ten states in the country with the highest number of lead service lines, seven of them are 
Great Lakes states, and five of the Great Lakes states have exceeded the national average for the 
percent of children with lead blood levels above the Center for Disease Control’s former action level of 
5µg/dL. Lead exposure in children can harm their brains and nervous systems resulting in 
developmental, learning, and behavioral problems, while lead exposure in adults elevates risks for heart 
disease. The pervasiveness of lead service lines disproportionately impacts low-income households and 
communities of color, which are often already overburdened with other sources of pollution and from 
other lead hazards such as lead-based paint. 
Achieving 100% lead service line replacement within 10 years is a strong action that should be 
implemented across the country. Cities like Chicago should be held to the same standard; nearly 
400,000 lead service lines run through the city, heavily impacting low-income households and 
communities of color, and an analysis of residential water testing conducted between 2016-2021 found 
that one in 20 households tested exceeded the federal action levels for lead. Strong action must be 
taken to expedite the process to remove lead service lines in severely impacted communities. 
One of the limitations to this rule would place a disproportionate financial burden on impacted 
communities and result in Great Lakes cities like Chicago and Cleveland waiting decades to fully replace 
lead service lines, exposing several more generations to the health impacts of lead poisoning.  
The practice of splitting funding for lead service line replacement between utilities and water service 
customers places a financial burden on the communities that have already suffered the disproportionate 
impacts of lead service lines, from health complications to the costs of alternative water sources. We 

urge the EPA to follow the example of Michigan’s Lead and Copper Rule, and require public water 
utilities to cover the full costs of lead service replacement. 
In addition to lead service line replacement, there are additional protective steps that EPA should 
incorporate into the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements to minimize exposure to and effects of lead 
contamination. A Filter First policy is a key line of defense against lead poisoning, especially in schools 
and child care centers, and the EPA should match state policies such as Michigan’s and require the 
installation of filtered drinking water stations or filtered faucets designated for drinking water at those 
facilities.  
Finally, we applaud the progress of lowering the federal action limit from 15 parts per billion to 10 parts 
per billion. However, that adjustment alone will be insufficient in protecting people from the health 
impacts of lead exposure, and falls short of the standards set in Canada and recommendations by the EU 
for triggering action at 5 parts per billion. 
Please protect our communities from the hazards of lead contamination and take equitable and 
immediate action to get the lead out of our drinking water. 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0943 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Proposed LCRI Comments 
The City of St. Cloud (City) appreciates Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) 
engagement with stakeholders prior to finalizing the Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI). The City recognizes the improved communication, public 
education and reduction in lead exposure that this proposed rule would help to 
achieve. The City would like to specifically comment on the proposed service line 
replacement requirements.  
 
The proposed LCRI requires municipalities to replace all lead, galvanized requiring 
replacement, and unknown service lines within 10 years, but not to exceed 10,000 
replacements per year, at a rate of 10% each year. This timeline is aggressive and is a 
major cause of concern for the City for several reasons:  
 
1. While funding is available, it is structured as a reimbursement from the State.  
This means that the City has to maintain an available cash balance to cover 
the cost of replacements prior to receiving the reimbursement.  Using the City’s 
current service line inventory, the City would be required to use approximately 
10% of its’ Water Treatment operating budget to complete the required 
replacements. This will inhibit the City’s ability to complete other work, 
including maintenance and replacement of critical infrastructure to include 
towers, booster stations, mains, and hydrants, and reduce the funds available 
for emergencies and improvements. 
 
2. With all municipalities facing the same requirement, the availability of skilled 
workers to complete the replacements is a concern. The City is concerned 
about not meeting the required replacement rate due to the unavailability of 
qualified contractors.  
 
3. The current funding structure requires the City to pay for the service line 
replacement prior to receiving the reimbursement from the State. The City 
owns no part of the service line; the customer owns from the meter to the main. 
The City would be completing the agreement with and paying the contractor 
for work that is not the property of the City. This is a liability concern for the City.  
 
The City would encourage EPA and States to channel funding directly to service line 
owners, whether that is the municipality or the property owner. The owner should be the 
one completing the service contracts to have the replacement completed.

February 2, 2024 
 
The Honorable Radhika Fox 
Assistant Administrator

Submitted via https://www.regulations.gov 
 
RE: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements National Primary Drinking Water Regulations 
Docket #: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Dear Assistant Administrator Fox: 
 
The Missouri Department of Natural Resources (department) recognizes the considerable effort the  
U. S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has taken to develop the proposed rule, National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements. The proposal is a 
substantial undertaking, and it will have a significant impact on public water systems, state primacy 
agencies, and public health. We recognize the importance of our shared responsibility to protect public 
health and appreciate the opportunity to provide comments on the proposal. Please find the 
department’s comments and recommendations for improvement of the proposed rule outlined below in 
the order which the rule text occurs in 40 CFR Part 141. 
 
40 CFR § 141.2 Definitions – The definition for “connector” is a “pipe not exceeding two feet in 
length.” This will eliminate connectors in Missouri because we have no connectors that short. All 
connectors that have been visually identified have been well over two feet, especially pigtails. Two 
feet is very short, and even goosenecks in Missouri exceed this length. The department recommends 
the maximum length segment within the definition of “connector” be changed to four or five feet in 
length. This length is much more common and realistic. Also, clarification is needed for connectors 
longer than the defined length and if they will be included in the definition of a lead service line when 
found. 
 
40 CFR § 141.2 Definitions – The definitions for small and medium size systems have been reversed 
from the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR). Small system flexibilities were cited as up to 
10,000 population in the LCRR and have been changed in the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI) to 3,300 population, but the other citations for small systems in the LCRI have changed from 
3,300 to 10,000. This makes things very confusing for states and water systems. The definitions for 
small systems should be the same for all parts of the LCRI to eliminate this confusion. The department 
recommends that the small system population be identified as less than or equal to 3,300. 
 
40 CFR § 141.81(a)(1)(ii) – The option of letting the states determine if a large system needs to re-
optimize Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) if they exceed the Practical Quantitation Limit (PQL) of 
5ug/L should remain unchanged. Requiring large water systems to re-optimize if they exceed the PQL 
in every instance at this low lead level is unnecessary and should remain the decision of the state to 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 2 
 
 
either re-optimize or not on a case-by-case basis. Leaving the citation in the LCRI as proposed allows 
states the discretion to make the determination to re-optimize. 
 
40 CFR § 141.81(a)(1)(iii) – The LCRI requires large systems without CCT to complete steps and 
install Optimal Corrosion Control Treatment (OCCT). The existing Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) 
already requires all large water systems (except those who previously met the (b)(3) requirements 
under the LCR) and water systems that newly meet the large water system criteria to install CCT. So, 
there should be very few, if any, large systems that don’t already have OCCT installed and have 
Optimal Water Quality Parameters (OWQPs) determined. For water systems that increase population 
to greater than or equal to 50,001, the LCRI appears to allow these new large water systems to install 
CCT only if they exceed the PQL or copper action level, according to 40 CFR § 141.81(a)(1)(iii). All 
large water systems should install CCT and then follow the large system requirements of 40 CFR § 
141.81(a)(1). 
 
40 CFR § 141.81(a) and (b) – The department recommends the language of this section be revised to 
give states the discretion to determine re-optimization of CCT when the PQL or action level is 
exceeded. 
 
40 CFR § 141.81 –There is little or no experience in cities or states in performing or reviewing pipe-
rigs as required under step one of 40 CFR § 141.81(e). The department recommends removing pipe 
rigs from the Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) study requirements because of the lack of 
experience and the disturbance of harvesting the pipe. Harvested pipe will not keep the same 
characteristics it had before the harvest and may not respond to CCT options being considered in a test 
rig the same as in the real distribution system. 
 
40 CFR § 141.82(j)(1)(ii)(B) – The rule requires OCCT to be reviewed as part of the sanitary survey 
process. In Missouri, OCCT evaluations are performed by state review engineers and not during a 
sanitary survey. Review engineers evaluate if a new site better assesses the effectiveness of CCT, not 
inspectors on site during a sanitary survey. The department recommends the language be revised to not 
require this review to occur during sanitary survey. 
 
40 CFR § 141.84 – Connectors were not a part of the initial lead service line inventory. Including 
them now will cause water systems to re-evaluate service lines that have already been determined for a 
connector identification. Missouri requests that the rule be modified to track and replace connectors 
when found during normal operations. 
 
40 CFR § 141.84(d)(5)(iv) – States should not be required to shorten water system deadlines for 
replacement of lead and Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRR) service lines. The rate is set by the 
number of lead and GRR lines in the inventory, but the number most likely will not be known until 
several updates to the inventory are completed. This makes determination difficult because the true 
number of lead and GRR service lines have not yet been determined. By using a smaller number of 
known lead or GRR service lines for determining the deadline, the deadline will be shortened too 
much to be realistically achieved after more identifications are made. The water system could still be 
identifying service lines that need replacing after the shortened deadline passes. 
 
40 CFR § 141.84(g) – The rule allows partial replacements in emergency situations and establishes 
mitigation requirements in 141.84(h) that systems must implement when emergencies occur. Since 
mitigation requirements for partial replacements are already included in the LCRI, the department 
recommends that water systems be allowed to replace their own portion of the service line and follow 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 3 
 
 
the same mitigation efforts found in 141.84(h), when a customer refuses to replace their side of the line 
for other types of non-emergency repairs such as planned water main replacement. Water main 
replacement projects will disturb the lead or GRR service lines owned by the water system, causing a 
need to perform mitigation activities anyway, so allowing the systems to proceed with replacing their 
part of the service line when they are discovered during planned or unplanned work should be allowed 
in those situations where the customer refuses to replace their part of the line. The mitigation 
requirements for emergencies should be equally protective for non-emergency activities, and allowing 
the partial replacements will allow the system to address the part of the service line that they are 
responsible for.  
 
40 CFR § 141.85(a)(1) – The proposed rule states that Public Notice (PN) and Public Education (PE) 
materials must include language exactly as written, but 141.85(a)(1)(vii) has language for including a 
website for the water system. Some small water systems don’t have a website or even a computer. 
These systems include small water districts, subdivisions, and mobile home parks that will be unable 
to comply with this requirement. The department recommends revising the language to make the 
reference to a website applicable to only systems that have a website.   
 
40 CFR § 141.85(b)(2) – The current LCR and LCRR each have a PE requirement for 60 days after 
the end of the tap sampling period. This timeframe should remain unchanged in the LCRI. With the 
new requirements for the public notification for an action level exceedance to be completed in 24 
hours and to include health effect language and instructions on how to reduce lead in drinking water 
that are very similar to the PE requirements, the PE requirements are now an appropriate follow-up to 
the 24-hour notification and should be kept at the 60-day requirement. 
 
40 CFR § 141.85(c)(1-2) – As a state required to provide laboratory services to water systems by state 
law, supplemental sampling will cause increased costs to the laboratory and decrease laboratory 
capacity. When our water systems have provided supplemental sampling services in the past in 
response to a customer request, they have had to use a separate laboratory and their own funding to 
pay for this cost. Since supplemental sampling is part of the new rule, it would place the responsibility 
back on the state to provide this laboratory analysis, as it will now be sampling required of the system. 
Our state laboratory is set up to provide compliance sampling for determining compliance with 90th 
percentiles, but not to provide analysis to any customer of a water system who may request it. 
Analyzing these additional samples would be a burden to the state, as it would be difficult for the 
department to estimate the number of samples we would receive each year, and the level of staffing 
necessary to maintain our laboratory capacity. The department recommends the EPA revise the 
language to require systems to offer to collect samples but to not require them to analyze or pay for the 
cost of the samples. 
 
40 CFR § 141.85(d)(2) – The three-day requirement for sample result notification in the LCRI is too 
burdensome. It is an arbitrary timeframe. Results notification to customers in three days are for sample 
results below the new action level of 10ug/L. Thirty days has been appropriate in the LCR/LCRR. 
Samples above the action level require 24-hour notification for the customer collecting the sample, 
which is appropriate for this type of sample result. Keeping the 30-day requirement, as found in the 
LCR and LCRR, is still an appropriate timeframe for notification of sample results below the action 
level. 
 
40 CFR § 141.85(j)(2) – Requiring pitcher filters to be provided to all customers and not just the 
customers with LSL, GRR, and unknown service lines is an expense that can be avoided. Filters 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 4 
 
 
should be provided to targeted customers who have LSL, GRR, or unknown service lines. Customers 
with non-lead service lines should not need them. 
 
40 CFR § 141.86(b)(1) – Keeping the minimum stagnation period at six hours is good, but a 
maximum stagnation period should the added. This period should be 18 hours as found in the Three Ts 
Guidance. To solve the possible abuse of this maximum period, the chain of custody completed by the 
customer could have the stagnation time included. The water system could review the time and decide 
if the stagnation period is over the 18-hour limit and have the sample replaced before returning 
samples to the lab for analysis. This would solve the issue of having customers collect samples from 
taps that get no usage, or from a tap immediately after a week or more vacation. 
 
40 CFR § 141.86 – In general, the provisions for water systems with lead, GRR, or unknown service 
connections to return to standard monitoring (six-month sampling) will create lab capacity issues, as 
well as supply issues for the required bottle types. Missouri has used wide-mouth, one-liter bottles for 
well over ten years. We mentioned to the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators 
(ASDWA) LCRR workgroup where these bottles could be found so that systems could sample using 
the new criteria of the LCRR before the compliance date of the rule to avoid going to standard 
monitoring under that rule. This resulted in a shortage of the bottles and Missouri had to back order 
bottles several times after mentioning it. This demonstrated a serious lack of availability of the correct-
type of one-liter bottles. This will happen again for the LCRI requirements and water systems will not 
be able to comply with the rule because of the lack of availability of the proper bottle type. School and 
childcare facility sampling will also have a huge effect on lab capacity, but not bottle type since they 
will use 250ml bottles. 
 
To help curb laboratory capacity and bottle issues, staggering the implementation of the LCRI 
sampling requirements, as was done in the original LCR, is appropriate. Staggering can also occur 
through a different requirement than found in the LCR, for example by having large systems sample in 
year one, then medium systems in year two, and small systems in year three. Having almost all water 
systems begin standard monitoring in the same year will cause a huge monetary cost to our sampling 
budgets. Missouri is required to provide laboratory services to our water systems by state law. We 
currently sample about a third of our water systems each year. This is done to reduce the burden on the 
lab and spread out the cost. Sampling all systems in the same year for two monitoring periods and for 
an increased number of samples will cause a significant cost and capacity problem. We will likely 
have to contract out the work to address this increased volume of samples which will further increase 
the costs. This will be a hardship on the state to implement. 
 
40 CFR § 141.86(b)(1) – Acidification of samples after collection. The rule has always allowed 
acidification up to 14 days after collection, but this period could be increased. Lab techs and lab 
directors have stated that no matter how long a sample sits, all lead and copper adhering to the sides of 
the bottle will resolubilize in the required 18-hour period (found in EPA method 200.8). Nitric acid is 
added for two reasons, to preserve the sample and to resolubilize metals before analysis can begin. If 
EPA were to change the 14-day requirement to allow up to 30 days, it would provide greater flexibility 
to public water systems. Public water systems often try to have all their samples collected before 
submitting them for analysis. When individual customers are slow to return their samples, this can 
result in the need to have samples that were submitted by customers at an earlier date recollected due 
to being over the 14-day limit. 
 
40 CFR § 141.86(d)(2)(i) – Water systems that reduce to annual monitoring after two six-month 
monitoring periods should begin annual monitoring at the reduced number of samples, not remain on 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 5 
 
 
the standard number of samples as required in the proposed rule. Making this change, will help 
systems and states like Missouri who provide analytical services for water systems with lab capacity 
issues and associated costs. Missouri recommends keeping the annual monitoring requirements at the 
reduced number of samples. 
 
40 CFR § 141.87(b)(1)(i) – Wording in the rule indicates Table 5. The Table is labeled Table 1. The 
wording of the rule should be updated to change the reference to Table 1. 
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(1)(i) –With the new tier definitions in the LCRI, water systems now need to 
update their sample site plans/pools. The LCRI also requires systems to submit changes to these plans 
prior to sampling in the next tap sampling period. Changes to sampling sites occur regularly during the 
next tap sampling period’s sampling activities. Access to sample sites on the plan can change due to 
death, health issues, vacations, fires, weather damages, etc. without notice. Water systems are 
coordinating with private citizens to collect the samples and cannot always depend on them collecting 
samples when it needs to be done. These changes are discovered during the sampling effort and not 
before, requiring changes to be made. Water systems plan on using the same sites over and over under 
the current rule and will continue to do so until a change is required by such things as LSL 
replacement in the new rule. The LCRI also continues to have the procedure for reporting changes to 
the sample pool/site plan that occur during sampling included in 40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2)(v). For these 
reasons, requiring submittal of these plans just adds additional burden to the rule without a 
corresponding benefit. 
 
The department recommends the rule be updated to require systems to submit updates to the sampling 
plan once the sampling is completed with site changes reported as required by 40 CFR § 
141.90(a)(2)(v). This includes requirements to identify any site that was not sampled during previous 
monitoring periods and to provide an explanation of why the sites have changed. This updated plan 
can show the sites as a group that have changed during the current tap monitoring period, along with 
those that haven’t, and to report those sites expected to be used the next time sampling is required. It 
can be checked with the site changes submitted as required above and checked with the service line 
inventory to determine if the sites used met the tier requirements. The reason for this comment is that 
most changes to the plan won’t be known until sampling begins. Submitting an updated plan that will 
be accurate for a very short amount of time just before the tap sampling period begins doesn’t mean a 
lot. Best laid plans will change when sampling begins because systems cannot predict everything that 
can go wrong with site access. 
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2) – Reporting within the first 10 days following the end of each tap sampling 
period is not possible for lead and copper tap samples. As a state required to provide laboratory 
services by state law, samples collected during the last weeks or days of a sampling period cannot be 
shipped, preserved, analyzed, QAQC processed, signed off on, and reported, all within 10 days. The 
time associated with preparing results, delivery packets, and mailing time to the water system also 
must be accounted for in this short timeframe. The department normally receives our final sample 
results for a reduced monitoring tap sampling period 1.5 months after the end of the sampling period. 
This reporting requirement is possible for Water Quality Parameters (WQPs) since the current LCR 
requires reporting January 10 and July 10 for WQPs according to the end of the monitoring period. 
The department recommends that EPA change the citation in the LCRI from “sampling period” to the 
LCRI definition of “tap monitoring period.” 
 
If this citation is not corrected, the tap sampling period will be compressed, causing an increase in 
costs, laboratory capacity issues, and the loss of the entire month of September for lead and copper tap 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 6 
 
 
sampling. In our experience, it takes 1.5 months to have all samples analyzed and reported for the 
annual, triennial, and nine year reduced monitoring periods each year (June 1 through September 30). 
Backing up from October 10th, the last date samples could be submitted would be around August 20th 
of each year. Also, September is when Missouri samples our schools, because classes resume, and 
water is again being used. Sample results are then more reflective of the water being consumed. 
 
History: The definition has changed from the LCR “monitoring period” to the LCRR pre-publication 
version “monitoring period” to the Final LCRR version “tap sampling monitoring period” to the 
proposed LCRI version which changed the citation and terminology, to 40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2) and 
“tap sampling period” respectively. 
 
The end of a monitoring period and the end of a sampling period are two different things, and the rule 
requirement has changed from 10 days following the end of each applicable “monitoring period,” 
which meant every six months, annually, three years, or nine years, to “tap sampling period,” which 
means 10 days after the last day samples can be collected. 
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2)(i) – Please see the comment immediately above about Lead and Copper tap 
samples, because the response is also applicable to 1st and 5th liter sample results notification. The 
department recommends that EPA remove the 10 days after the end of the tap sampling period 
requirement for lead and copper tap sampling and return it to the requirements found in the 
LCR/LCRR, which under the LCRI is defined as the “Tap Monitoring Period.” 
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2)(ii) – The LCRI states that the water system can collect a replacement sample 
20 days after the state invalidates a sample, but it also states that documentation for each tap water lead 
and copper sample for which the water system requests invalidation be submitted within 10 days after 
the end of the tap sampling period. Our state laboratory cannot have all samples that are collected by 
the end of the tap sampling period, September 30, analyzed and reported by October 10th. Therefore, 
invalidations cannot be requested by the proposed date in the rule because not all sample results will 
have been reported. The department recommends EPA remove the requirement for requesting an 
invalidation within 10 days after the end of the tap sampling period and replace it with a requirement 
that invalidations be requested within 10 days after receipt of their sample results. 
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2)(iii) – This part of the LCRI requires the water system to notify the state in 
advance that they intend to comply with the rule. This notification seems unnecessary and adds burden 
to the rule, because it is already prescriptive in what the system must do to comply with 40 CFR § 
141.86(h)(3). The department recommends this reporting requirement be removed from the rule.  
 
40 CFR § 141.90(a)(2)(iv), 40 CFR § 141.90(h)(1), and 40 CFR § 142.15(c)(4)(iii)(A - C) – As 
mentioned above, if the results are not yet reported, the 90th percentile cannot be calculated. Missouri 
calculates most of the 90th percentiles for our water systems. If samples are collected at the end of the 
tap sampling period, including the last day, they cannot be shipped, preserved, analyzed, QAQC 
processed, signed off on, and reported by October 10th or 15th. For samples collected in September, 
Missouri cannot generate a 90th percentile and provide the results to the water system in 15 days. This 
requirement is too strict and causes implementation issues when systems sample late in the tap 
sampling period. Changing it to 60 days after the end of the tap monitoring period will fix this issue. 
 
40 CFR § 141.90 – General Comment. There are now 24 certification requirements in the LCRI. And 
although some certifications in the LCRR were changed to a requirement that the “water system must 
demonstrate,” this is effectively still a certification requirement. If those are counted, the total number 

Assistant Administrator Radhika Fox 
Page 7 
of certifications goes up to 26. Most are in 40 CFR § 141.90, but one certification is in 40 CFR § 
141.86(h). Overall, the rule has gotten more complex with these revisions, not less. To reduce the 
complexity of the rule, EPA should evaluate how to reduce the number of certifications that systems 
are required to complete and that states will need to track. 
40 CFR § 141.92 – The State of Missouri has used Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation 
(WIIN) grant funding to sample for lead at childcare facilities. Some of this sampling occurred prior to 
January 1, 2021, which is the date established in the proposed LCRI for using this data to acquire a 
waiver from sampling at childcare facilities. The department recommends EPA revise the rule to 
change this date, so that any sampling that was completed under the WIIN grants could be used to 
obtain a waiver from additional sampling. This will allow the state to save resources that would need 
to be dedicated to this effort, even though this sampling was completed already using the WIIN grant 
funds.
