Lead-lined galvanized steel service lines will be the most difficult material type to verify. Therefore, EPA 
should implement the following measures to ensure public health is protected: 
 
• 
In cities where at least one lead-lined galvanized steel service line is uncovered, all galvanized 
pipes should be assumed to be lead and categorized as such. These lines should be replaced 
regardless of their location. 
 
• 
Require water systems and contractors to check for lead lining in galvanized steel service lines by 
using handheld technology, such as x-ray fluorescence (XRF) and laser analyzers, and by visually 
inspecting the inside of service lines after they are cut. 
 
• 
Update the EPA guidance to incorporate lessons learned from Trenton Water Works and identify 
additional affected systems.  
 
VII. 
Enforcement  
Past problems with gathering comprehensive compliance data from states and water systems reinforce the 
notion that the LCRI should require that enforcement-related data be submitted electronically. 
a. Mandate electronic reporting of compliance data to ensure proper enforcement.  
Even with a reduced action level, enforcement is expected to remain weak without a universal 
requirement for water systems to report test results and violations electronically. While enforcement 
efforts typically focus on health violations, poor reporting can mask serious health issues. Past audits of 
EPA’s data found that 92% of lead-related health-based violations and 71% of lead-related 
monitoring/reporting violations were not reported to EPA by states30. This does not consider potential 
underreporting by water systems to the states. 
 
This is summarized in EPA’s 2013 National Drinking Water Compliance Report:  
 
“EPA has evaluated state and regional program data quality by conducting data verification audits and 
national data quality assessments, comparing primacy agencies’ files and records with information in 
SDWIS/FED to verify accuracy, completeness and whether appropriate compliance determinations are 
made (that is, in accordance with federal regulations). These audits and assessments have shown that 
violation data are substantially incomplete.”31 
 
Without reliable and accurate data reporting, EPA’s efforts to implement a successful LCRI may fall 
short. By maximizing existing information technology tools, EPA can improve effectiveness and 
efficiency while ensuring it has the full picture on compliance.  
 
• 
Change the current system where water systems report directly through their primacy agencies. 
Water systems should conduct mandatory electronic reporting of compliance information directly 
into a database shared by states and EPA. Direct reporting will eliminate data lags and potential 
underreporting of serious violations that pose a public relations problem. As noted in GAO’s 
2011 report, many states and water systems will only use electronic reporting if required to.

• 
Implement a modern database such as upgrading the existing Safe Drinking Water Information 
System (SDWIS) to provide the following benefits: 
o Effectiveness: the system will assess data quality, automate violation determinations, flag 
the most serious problems, and expand transparency. 
o Efficiency: save money by minimizing manual processing and data input by state 
agencies, water systems, and affected laboratories.  
 
• 
In 2015, EPA established a similar electronic reporting system for its NPDES program which 
monitors companies discharging water pollutants to surface waters. 
 
Additional Points for Consideration 
In addition to the major issues raised above, EDF recommends the following.  
 
a. Consider measures to facilitate consent for service line replacement. 
EPA should encourage water systems to engage with customers to secure access to private property for 
LSL replacement. Improvements to how water systems communicate with water customers could help 
secure access to private property for service line replacement work. A report Tapping into Success: 
Strategies for Effective Lead Service Line Replacement Communications by Elevate, found that 
persistence is key, as it often takes several touch points to convince residents to participate in a LSL 
replacement program.32  
 
The strategies and lessons learned in the report should be taken into consideration by both EPA and water 
systems. 
 
EPA should also encourage states to adopt laws that facilitate consent in environmental justice 
communities. To address negative impacts on environmental justice communities, the rule should require 
full service line replacement whenever the system is performing work in “disadvantaged communities” 
(according to relative state definitions), either as part of a replacement program or in conjunction with 
planned water infrastructure work. This could be limited to communities that are currently operating 
under or have experienced an action level exceedance in the past. Working with individual states, EPA 
should prioritize federal BIL funds for this purpose.  
 
As noted in the LCRI, states should be encouraged to adopt laws similar to those enacted by the State of 
New Jersey and the City of Newark, as highlighted below: 
 
• 
State of New Jersey: Authorized municipalities to adopt an ordinance allowing water systems to 
enter private property to conduct LSLR (P.L. 2019, c.291, enacted January 9, 2020). The state 
also authorized the replacement of LSLs on private property if the work is an environmental 
infrastructure project and funded either by loans from the New Jersey Infrastructure Bank or by 
loans issued through the Department of Environmental Protection. (P.l.2021, c.184) 
 
• 
City of Newark: Local ordinance authorized access to private property for LSLR purposes and, to 
handle instances where property owners refuse to participate, conditioned the issuance of 
certificates of occupancy and code compliance for property that is sold or transferred on proper 
LSLR.

page 10.  

 
 
15 
 
b. Reduce barriers to full service line replacement at tenant-occupied buildings.  
EPA should encourage states to adopt legislation that requires water systems to provide filters to residents 
in tenant-occupied buildings where the property owner refuses LSL replacement. For rental properties, 
section 605-870(ff)(1)(D) of the Illinois law also requires recalcitrant landlords to install lead-certified, 
point-of-use filters: 
 
“If complete repair of a lead service line cannot be completed due to denial by the property owner, the 
community water supply commencing the repair shall request the affected property owner to sign a 
waiver developed by the Department. If a property owner of a nonresidential building or residence 
operating as rental properties denies a complete lead service line replacement, the property owner shall be 
responsible for installing and maintaining point-of-use filters certified by an accredited third-party 
certification body to NSF/ANSI 53 and NSF/ANSI 42 for the reduction of lead and particulate at all 
fixtures intended to supply water for the purposes of drinking, food preparation, or making baby formula. 
The filters shall continue to be supplied by the property owner until such time that the property owner has 
affected the remaining portions of the lead service line to be replaced.”33  
 
c. Service line replacement plans should be updated regularly. 
Service line replacement plans should be seen as a “living” document, the same way inventories are used. 
Regular updating of plans is necessary to account for statutory or policy changes, updated service line 
inventory records, and lessons learned from risk communication in the affected communities. More 
specifically, most programs will be somewhat fluid as service lines of unknown composition are resolved, 
financial resources are pursued, and practical obstacles (e.g., property access) are identified and 
eventually resolved. See section 5 of the New Jersey Statute for an example.  
 
d. To ensure the accuracy of inventory data, historic records of service line composition should be 
randomly checked. 
As proposed, the service line inventory process outlined includes a validation process that requires water 
systems to confirm the accuracy of service line composition by visually inspecting a random sample of 
pipes at a minimum confidence level of 95 percent.34 The LCRI would require this by year seven of the 
replacement program. However, the rule does not take a similar approach to historic service line records. 
In keeping with the LCRR, EPA continues to assume that states are best positioned to judge the 
appropriateness and accuracy of historic records.  
 
The LCRR does not require systems to track the records, methods, and techniques they use to categorize 
individual service lines. By maintaining continuity, EPA understandably seeks to avoid complications as 
water systems seek to update their inventory while also providing flexibility for them to adopt new 
methods and technologies. However, because of the extent to which communities rely on historic records 
when developing their service line inventory, the LCRI should be amended to require a random sampling 
of that data. This measure would help maximize efficiency of that effort because the data in the service 
line inventory forms the bedrock for all service line replacement programs. 
 
e. Consider incidents of non-compliance with local policy regarding reconnections. 
Relying on state and local policy is not a sufficient mechanism to ensure residents are not unnecessarily 
exposed to lead from the reconnection of disturbed lead and GRR service lines. EPA must consider 
incidents of self-report non-compliance with local policy on reconnections. Otherwise, there is not 
enough disincentive to ensure that the LSL is not ultimately reconnected.  
 
33  Codified at 415 ILCS 5/17.12 
34 Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.84 (5)  

 
 
16 
 
 
Some existing LSL replacement contracts unrealistically expect contractors to self-report violations of 
local policy on reconnections, and related water main inspections are unlikely to cover all such instances. 
In recent years, EDF has noticed that some systems replace aging drinking water mains without 
addressing customer-owned LSLs. Homeowners often refuse to accept the water systems’ offer to replace 
the LSL because they are asked to pay a cost share to replace their portion of the line. In such cases, 
contractors may bend the customer-owned LSL out of the way when the old water main is replaced and 
then reattach it to the new main. This action could trigger a lead spike into the drinking water. Often, the 
customer is not formally notified about this possibility or its potential health impacts.  
 
For example, New York City, where the entire water service line is owned by individual property owners, 
provides a case in point. A typical water main replacement contract with the NYC Department of 
Environmental Protection (NYCDEP) includes the following provision: 
 
“If the damaged or cut water service pipe is lead, galvanized steel, or galvanized iron, the service pipe 
must not be partially replaced, but fully replaced from the main to the house control valve. If the service 
pipe was damaged, cut, or otherwise interrupted due to the Contractor’s actions or means & methods 
(including selection of shoring systems), the water service pipe will be replaced at the Contractor’s own 
cost.”35 
 
The NYCDEP does not consistently inspect customer-owned LSLs for damage before they are reattached 
or require contractors to report when damage occurs. Since they incur the cost of replacement, even if 
proper precautions are taken, it seems highly unlikely that contractors would unilaterally flag instances 
where a water service line was cut, bent, or disrupted during normal water main work. It stands to reason 
that such instances are not reported and the existing LSL or GRR is simply reconnected. Thus, EDF 
recommends that there be a general prohibition in the final rule on reconnecting such lines. 
 
Conclusion 
We ask that EPA consider our recommendations to strengthen the proposed LCRI by:  
 
• 
Modifying the definition of a service line by including: “A service line may be owned by the 
water system, owned by the property owner, or both” to explicitly include reference to ownership 
types. This change will prevent water systems from defining a service line as only the portion 
they own or is on public property.  
• 
Establishing clear criteria for determining whether a water system has “access” to conduct full 
service line replacement. This is a critical issue that could potentially undermine the goal of this 
rule, without this clarification, whether there is access is left entirely up to a water system to 
determine, which could result in a narrow definition where LSLs that are owned in part or in 
whole by a property owner are not their responsibility. 
• 
Requiring a written waiver documenting refusal of access for the purpose of full service line 
replacement. We believe that presenting this type of information signals the weight of opting out 
of LSL replacement to a property owner and forces them to consider the impacts on the residents.  
• 
Only using the proposed eligibility criteria for systems with more than 100,000 LSLs to identify 
the utilities that need more time. Communities determined to be eligible for a deferred deadline 
would be strongly encouraged to participate in the EPA’s Lead Service Line Replacement 
Accelerator Program. 
 
35 Oriental Boulevard Between Corbin Place and Pembroke Street, Manhattan Beach Area, Brooklyn 
(Volume 3 – Specifications; Project ID: BED819, Nov 5, 2021), page SW-13, subsection 10.24 

 
 
17 
 
• 
Increasing the minimum starting replacement rate threshold: Water systems can reasonably 
complete service line replacement at a faster rate than the maximum annual threshold of 10,000 
service line replacements. We recommend that the minimum starting rate is increased to 13,000 
lead and GRR service lines replaced in the first three years after promulgation of this rule.   
• 
Pursuing the strongest protections possible by lowering the lead action level to 5 ppb. 
• 
Lowering the system size threshold for mandatory online publication of service line inventory 
from 50,000 to 10,000 customers served.  
• 
Prohibiting the reconnection of lead and GRR service lines and require full lead and GRR service 
line replacement in all circumstances, except during emergency repairs. 
• 
Considering the instance of lead-lined galvanized steel service lines. 
• 
Mandating electronic reporting of compliance data to ensure proper enforcement.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1325 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801
RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements
Comments:
We believe the “full replacement” definition in the LCRI to include the property owner’s portion of a 
service line exceeds the legal authority of any such water system and the legal authority of the Safe 
Drinking Water Act.
The Safe Drinking Water Act as amended by The Safe Drinking Water Act of 1996 states in Section 1400, 
Part A, Section 1401
Section 1401.  For the purpose of this title:
(1) The term “Primary drinking water regulation” means a regulation which –
(A) Applies to public water systems;
and,
(4) Public Water System
(A)(i)  any collection, treatment, storage and distribution facilities under control 
of the operator of such system and used in primary connection with such 
system, 
In one part of the LCRI, it states that water systems replace service lines and connectors “under control 
of” that water system. In Texas, that would be the portion of the service line up to the meter. However, 
later in the LCRI, it states that the EPA has proposed “requirements and flexibilities to increase access 
and expedite full service line replacement”.   This certainly contradicts with the first portion of that 
proposed rule. 
The private, property owners portion of the service line is not owned by the public water system and 
therefore not “under the control” of the public water system.  Therefore, it is not within the legal 
authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act to regulate this portion of the private connection to the public 
water system.  If a water system is expected to replace the property owner’s portion of the service line, 
that would require an easement, and the water system now being responsible for that service line, I.e. 
“taking” ownership of it. In Texas “Taking” is defined in the Property Rights Act section 2007.002(5) as: 
(A) a governmental action that affects private real property, in whole or in part or temporarily or 
permanently, in a manner that requires the governmental entity to compensate the private real 
property owner as provided by the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States 
Constitution or Section 17 or 19, Article I, Texas Constitution.
Furthermore, the LCRI seems to push water systems to ask for changes to any legislation that would 
update property rights to meet those set forth in the LCRI. Legislation should not be a bottom-up 
requirement. Water systems have no authority to propose property rights bills in any State, or especially 
Federal legislature. 

Finally, if property owners are required to replace their portion of the service line, the EPA should 
provide a funding mechanism for property owners, similar to the CDC’s grant program for individual 
cities, that came out of the Lead-Based Paint Poisoning Act of 1971, followed by the Maternal and Child 
Health Services Block Grant Program and the Lead Contamination Control Act of 1988. Grant funding 
should be appropriated for States to allow its residents to apply for funding in order to replace their 
portion of the service line.  This proven methodology would allow the homeowner to be responsible for 
acquiring the money for private service line replacement in the form of a grant that does not 
accumulate interest nor has to be paid back to the funding agency.

RE: Proposed Rule: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: 
Improvements (LCRI), Docket ID: No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Dear Ms. McLain: 
 
WaterNow Alliance (WaterNow) commends the Biden Administration for its historic 
commitment to achieving 100% replacement of lead service lines, and we appreciate this 
opportunity to comment on the proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA–HQ–OW–
2022–0801 (LCRI).1 WaterNow is a nonprofit network of 700+ local water leaders in 43 states 
nationwide advancing sustainable, affordable, equitable, and climate resilient water strategies. As 
such, we share EPA’s goal of eliminating all lead service lines (LSLs) in 10 years or less. In this 
regard, WaterNow is particularly focused on helping water utilities and municipalities to develop 
funding and financing strategies to achieve this objective.  
 
While the LCRI is for the most part an improvement, the lack of clarity and guidance about 
whether and when water systems are required to replace LSLs on private properties risks 
undermining the goals of the revised regulation. As EPA is aware, the bulk of LSLs likely fall, at 
least in part, on private properties nationwide. The LCRI as currently drafted eliminates the 
current definition of full lead line replacement which expressly includes private property. It also 
excuses water utilities from replacing lead lines whenever the system “does not have access” to 
conduct a full lead service line replacement (LSLR), but then declines to establish criteria for 
determining when the utility has such access.  
 
In our view, the vagaries and ambiguities embedded in this approach are problematic. As drafted, 
the LCRI’s lack of clarity potentially opens the door to large exceptions to the lead service line 
replacement mandate that threaten to undermine EPA’s public health goals and the LCRI’s 
fundamental objective of 100% eradication of lead lines. For these reasons, WaterNow 
recommends the following language changes to the LCRI revisions of 40 C.F.R. sections 
141.2 (Definitions) and 141.84 (replacement requirements). Suggested edits to EPA’s proposed 
rule, and suggested strikeouts, are in red text (black text reflects the current LCRI draft 
language):

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-2268 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
EPA Public Hearing on the Proposed Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
Overview 
On January 16, 2024, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) held a virtual public 
hearing to provide an opportunity for the public to share their input on the proposed Lead and 
Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Members of the public were notified of the public hearing 
on December 6, 2023 through the Proposed LCRI Federal Register Notice and on EPA’s LCRI 
website. EPA requested that members of the public wishing to provide oral comments during 
the hearing register in advance to ensure all those interested would be able to provide their 
input to EPA. The Agency also held time during the public hearing for comments from 
unscheduled speakers. Additionally, during the public hearing, EPA recommended that all 
members of the public provide written comments on the proposed LCRI through the public 
docket. Please see Appendix A for the public hearing agenda. A recording of the meeting is 
provided on EPA’s LCRI website. 
The meeting began with a welcome by the facilitator from Ross Strategic with instructions on 
how to use the Zoom interface and access language captioning. This was followed by an 
introduction from EPA representative, Eric Burneson, Director of the Standards and Risk 
Management Division (SRMD) in the Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water (OGWDW). A 
representative from EPA’s OGWDW presented a brief overview of lead in drinking water, a 
summary of some of the key provisions in the proposed LCRI, and information on how to 
provide written comments on the proposed rule and where to find additional resources. EPA’s 
presentation can be found on EPA's LCRI website. Following EPA’s presentation, the facilitator 
opened the first public comment period. There were five public comment periods in total. 
During each public comment period, the facilitator reviewed the ground rules and logistics to 
provide public input. All speakers were given two and a half minutes to provide their oral 
comments to EPA. The oral comments are provided below in this document which is divided 
into different sections for each of the five public comment periods. Please note that the 
comments, information, and opinions provided in this document represent those of commenters 
only. At the end of the public hearing, EPA representative, Hannah Holsinger, Supervisor of the 
Regulatory Assessment and Development Branch of SRMD in OGWDW provided closing remarks 
and thanked attendees for their participation in the public hearing. 
Public Comment Period #1 
Yanna Lambrinidou (Campaign for Lead Free Water): Hello! Good morning, EPA. Good 
morning, everybody. I'm Yanna Lambrinidou, with the Campaign for Lead Free Water. I'd like to 
start by thanking you for the many welcomed improvements to the LCRR that you have 
proposed. In the interest of time, I will focus on one requirement that, although improved, is 
still strikingly deficient for no convincing reason. That is public education, what the preamble 
correctly refers to as a cornerstone treatment technique. Indeed, proper public education can 
plug the gaps in the LCR’s other three treatment techniques and bring lead in water levels at or 
very close to the MCLG of zero right away. EPA acknowledges that taps can and do dispense 
1 

lead even when utilities meet LCR requirements, lead service lines are not present, and 
standard testing detects no contamination. This means that the proposed public education 
provisions which center on lead action level exceedances, lead service lines, and standard 
testing results are both insufficient and misleading. Among other things, they miss the vast 
majority of people who drink and eat lead on a regular basis, because they have not been told 
that lead-bearing plumbing is present in almost every building, and that it places them at risk of 
exposure at any and all times. We urge you once again to overhaul public education 
requirements so that they can maximize health risk reduction benefits, meet public right-to-
know requirements, respect the fundamental EJ right to self-determination, and align with the 
statutory standard for a treatment technique rule. We've already brought to your attention 
serious deficiencies in EPA's smorgasbord of recommendations for self-protection, some of 
which can prolong and even worsen exposures. We've also called for public education that 
urges everyone to be concerned about lead in their water, and encourages the precautionary 
use of lead certified filters. EPA's claim that a filter first recommendation to everyone would 
lead to inconsistencies, confusion, and possibly a reduction in confidence in tap water is difficult 
to understand. According to a recent study by GW, for example, the provision of filters, 
together with filter training, actually increased public trust in and use of tap water. We have the 
technology. What we're missing is truthful messaging. Without it many more generations will 
continue to be unnecessarily exposed, and will continue to suffer harm without their knowledge 
or consent. Thank you. 
Madison Dennis (Plastic Pollution Coalition): Hello! Thank you to the EPA for taking steps 
to decrease the rampant water inequality in the U.S. that leaves many primarily Black, Brown, 
and low-income communities with toxic drinking water. My name is Madison Dennis, and I'm 
speaking on behalf of Plastic Pollution Coalition. We are grateful to see the proposed rule 
requiring filters be made available to communities with multiple lead level exceedances. We 
know these filters are critical to ensure families have clean drinking water, as there is no safe 
level of lead, and it will be up to 10 years before many families have their pipes replaced, and 
up to 40 years in cities like Chicago. However, the language must be strengthened to make 
filters available as soon as possible. EPA must require water systems to distribute water filters 
to customers at no cost, provide in-depth education materials on filter efficacy and 
maintenance, and reduce the number of lead action level exceedances in the time period 
needed to require filter distribution. Water systems must actively distribute water filters to 
impacted homes. Making filters available as currently mandated in the LCRI is simply not 
enough. Cities such as Denver that have actively distributed filters have seen much, much 
higher success rates by reducing the financial and time burden necessary to access the filter. 
Education materials must also be distributed on filter efficacy and filter use and maintenance. 
Community trust in water filters and accurate servicing of the filter is critical to ensure families 
don't turn to costly, polluting water bottles, or improperly use the filter resulting in exposure to 
unsafe water contaminants. The EPA must also lower the trigger event for filters. With the 
current language, communities would have to wait three years for implementation, and up to 
another five years for a water system to distribute filters, which is eight years too long. Plastic 
Pollution Coalition also calls on the EPA to recommend safe pipe materials and advise against 
dangerous alternatives, such as PVC plastic pipes. And we also support the many other groups 
calling for a reduction in the lead action level to five parts per billion, requirements for water 
systems to pay for full lead service line replacement, increased education and more to protect 
impacted communities. Thank you for your time and consideration.

Brad Cole (Chief Executive Officer, Illinois Municipal League): I'm Brad Cole, Chief 
Executive Officer of the Illinois Municipal League, which represents 1,294 cities, villages, and

2021, the state of Illinois enacted its Lead Service Line Replacement Notification Act, which 
created statutory deadlines for municipalities and community water supplies to undertake 
multiple aspects of lead service line replacement. The State Act requires owners and operators 
of those water supplies to develop complete material inventories and then implement a 
comprehensive plan for their replacement. The timeline is based on the number of lead service 
lines found within each specific municipality, with requirements to complete the work between 
15 and 50 years from the Act’s effective date. It is not a one-size-fits-all mandate like this rule.

are due in April of 2024. Annual reports are then required to be submitted to the Illinois EPA.

partner to help us, not a hindrance. This proposed rule, while well-intentioned, cannot be

plans. Thank you.

Lynn Thorp (National Campaigns Director, Clean Water Action, Clean Water Fund): 
My name is Lynn Thorpe and I'm the National Campaigns Director for Clean Water Action and 
Clean Water Fund. The Lead and Copper Rule proposal reflects the recognition that we can and 
must continue to reduce lead in drinking water. Our engagement around the Lead and Copper 
Rule updates has emphasized the need to fully replace all lead service lines. We will comment 
on other aspects of the proposal in our written comments. Fully replacing all lead service lines is 
an ambitious undertaking, and we recognize that, but the time has come. We've known a long 
time that lead can harm developing brains of infants and children, but now we know that even 
low-level exposure contributes to cardiovascular disease. This widens the circle of concern, and 
6 

so replacing lead service lines, the largest source of lead when they're present, will reduce lead 
in drinking water. It therefore overall reduces all lead exposure and every bit matters to 
people's health, as we now know. Also because of exposure to all sources lead 
disproportionately burdens people of color and low-income people, any added exposure from 
lead in drinking water compounds that inequity. And of course, lastly, momentum toward the 
goal is greater than it's ever been – and we know that from water system activities, from state 
policy developments, congressional interests, and EPA's own proposal. We've also consistently 
urged EPA to require all water systems to cover the full cost of replacement, regardless of 
ownership or whether lines under private or public property. And the Environmental Justice 
Review that EPA commissioned when doing the LCRR in 2019 found that presuming that 
customers must pay for things, including lead service line replacement costs, leaves low-income 
people with inequitable access to the benefits of reducing the lead in their water, and therefore 
puts them at disproportionately higher health risks. And requiring customers to contribute has 
been a common practice historically, but it's changing. Water systems have been finding ways 
to conduct and finance replacements without the customer contribution. We think that 
perpetuating this sort of antiquated approach will undermine the lead service line replacement 
and public health protection goals of the proposal itself. And we thank you for the opportunity 
to comment on the LCR proposal today.

this would push Chicago to a much shorter timeline of 25 years as compared to the 50 years 
proposed underneath the Lead and Copper Rule. Additionally, we need the rule to require water

Deandrah Cameron (Policy Manager, New Jersey Future): Good morning, and thank 
you. I’m on the list for later on, so I can be removed from that. My name is Deandrah Cameron. 
I'm a policy manager at New Jersey Future. We believe that every New Jerseyan deserves to 
live in a prosperous fair economy, and we promote policies for cost-effective sustainable water 
systems. The New Jersey Future played a pivotal role in crafting a comprehensive lead service 
line replacement law in New Jersey and we're proud to work with our partners across the nation 
to show collective leadership on public health issues. Two years into the implementation of the 
law, we found that a “no customer cost-share” policies are pivotal to the removal of the service 
lines to maximize efficiency and pace of lead service replacement. To ensure that all lead 
service lines are replaced, water utilities need a statutory authority to access private property, 
and they should not be allowed to charge a cost-share. LSLs are typically jointly owned. The 
water system owns a portion of the water from the main to the curb stop, and the property 
owner owns the portion from the curb stop to the home. The places across the nation with the 
highest concentration of lead service lines tend to be lower income communities and 
communities of color, dominated by rental housing. As such, many residents must rely on 
absentee property owners to even consent to make their properties available for work and to 
coordinate LSL replacements. To remove the barriers property owners pose to replacement, we 
recommend a provision that prohibits a customer cost-share and enabling all customers to 
participate in the program. The goal of replacing lead service lines within 10 years will not be 
achieved efficiently and cost effectively unless it's at no cost to the customers. Many lead 
service lines remain without sufficient funding to private side replacements. Since many families 
in disadvantaged areas cannot pay the private side replacement, in most states, water systems 
do not believe they can use BIL funds for private side replacement since they must repay the 
loan with ratepayer funds. A federal or a state statutory requirement is needed to allow water 
systems to use ratepayer funds to remove private side LSLs in the interest of public health. 
Given the option to charge property owners, it sounds fair, but it is not equitable and it is a 
consequence. Water utilities waste time on outreach, replacement process lacks coordination 
and becomes inefficient, resulting in replacements for far fewer pipes at significantly higher 
costs, and only for those who can afford it. Thank you so much for your time. We'll be sharing 
written comments with further information on this policy.

period of 30 days for public comment. State guidelines should be published at least two years 
prior to the due date for the proposed baseline inventory. State agencies should also be 
required to hold online and in-person informational events in which submission requirements 
and review parameters are clearly provided for community water system managers. Ten years 
is an ambitious goal to replace all lead service lines. Many water systems believe that they are 
already understaffed and underfunded to complete system modernization projects. Water 
13 

systems who develop system-wide modernization and capital improvement plans should have 
the opportunity to request additional time outside of the proposed 10-year timeframe to identify 
and replace lead service lines if the community water system can provide achievable deadlines 
for goal-based replacement. This method would not only allow water systems to replace lead 
service lines, but it would also allow water systems to better utilize funding for system 
modernization and service line replacement, since planning would be based on larger scale 
improvements and not more expensive isolated replacements. Identification of privately owned 
service lines of unknown materials will be challenging for utility workers and could introduce 
workers to dangerous situations. Many customer-owned service lines will need to be physically 
inspected via potholing. Since community water systems have no authority to access customer-
owned private property without authorization, this could add considerable time to service line 
inventory development. Additionally, citizens who restrict access to private property might 
become hostile toward utility workers, even before workers set foot on private property. The 
EPA should provide further guidance for how water systems are expected to access private 
property. Thank you very much.

Cara Cook (Alliance of Nurses for Healthy Environments): Thank you so much. This is Cara 
Cook, C-a-r-a C-o-o-k. I am a registered nurse and member of the Alliance of Nurses for 
Healthy Environments, the only national nursing organization focused solely on how the 
environment impacts human health. Our organization thanks EPA for acting to address public 
health concerns around lead in drinking water. We strongly urge EPA to quickly finalize the 
most thorough Lead and Copper Rule Improvements as possible. A stronger Lead and Copper 
Rule is an essential step towards reducing harm from lead exposure. There is no safe level of 
lead. Lead can affect almost every organ and system in the human body. Even at very low 
levels, lead can cause serious, irreversible damage to the developing brains and nervous 
systems of babies and young children. Children who are exposed to lead can experience lifelong 
health impacts. Lead is also long recognized to be a cause of hypertension and a risk factor for 
heart disease, stroke, and chronic kidney disease in adults. EPA’s proposed essential 
improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule are a step in the right direction for promoting public 
health for communities across the country. However, the proposed rule falls short. Our 
organization is strongly encouraging EPA to address the following measures to strengthen this 
proposal. The current proposed maximum contaminant level of 10 parts per billion is not a 
health-based standard. While lowering the level from 15 to 10 is an improvement, this lower 
level remains inadequate and still leaves many communities and children unprotected. We 
recommend lowering the MCL to one part per billion. EPA should strive for a goal of replacing 
all lead service lines within 10 years. The proposal allows some water systems to get extensions 
17 

well beyond 10 years to replace their lead pipes. This is unacceptable, and leaves many 
communities at risk. Water utilities should pay for lead service line removals rather than 
charging individuals. Residents have borne the brunt of lead contamination impacts and 
healthcare costs. It is also a health equity issue when utilities insist that individual property 
owners pay for lead service line replacement. Often low-income homeowners cannot, and 
landlords may not, pay to replace them. Communities across the country should be protected 
from exposure to lead. In closing, the Alliance of Nurses for Healthy Environments strongly 
urges the EPA to quickly finalize the most thorough Lead and Copper Rule Improvements as 
soon as possible. Thank you so much.

comments that expand upon the points made today. At the root of this proposed rulemaking is 
the goal of removing 100% of lead service lines in 10 years. AMWA appreciates EPA’s 
acknowledgement that this objective may not be universally attainable for every utility. Because 
of this, we urge the Agency to tailor the rule, allowing water systems to primarily focus on this 
vital goal. Overloading systems with multiple concurrent requirements can divert essential 
money, time, and personnel from lead service line replacement efforts. EPA, in this proposal, 
seems to equate access to private property with control of the private side of the service line.

state and federal funds to finance the private side replacement or with the entirety of the cost 
in one form or another falling on ratepayers. It is important to note that two major regulations 
under the Safe Drinking Water Act are expected to be finalized this year: this rule and the PFAS 
regulations, both with proposed three-year compliance dates for promulgation. These two 
rulemakings alone are estimated by EPA to cost up to a combined $4.8 billion annually to 
implement. In addition to complying with other regulations, there’s a pressing demand for 
water systems to modernize aging infrastructure. The escalating costs of materials and labor, 
influenced by supply chain disruptions, inflation, and workforce shortages further compound 
these challenges. These challenges are also likely to disproportionately impact low-income 
communities. Thank you again for the opportunity to speak today, and AMWA looks forward to 
providing robust and detailed written comments prior to the February 5th deadline.

Sarah Anderson (City of Columbus, Department of Public Utilities): Good afternoon. I am Sarah 
Bloom Anderson from the City of Columbus Department of Public Utilities. We provide safe 
drinking water throughout 220 square miles in Central Ohio. Through our optimized corrosion 
control plan, we have maintained an exceptionally low level of lead, well below the PQL, for 
over two decades. Columbus agrees that all lead service lines should be replaced. We also 
share the goal of replacing 100% as quickly as feasible but EPA’s determination of what is 
feasible needs another look. To protect public health, and ensure that even the most vulnerable 
among us can afford clean drinking water, we need to strategically allocate resources across the 
country to those with the most risk first. To have every public water system replace their 
service lines simultaneously in 10 years is not feasible. It will result in an artificially high 
demand for resources locally, regionally, and nationally. EPA acknowledges the demand, but 
does not adequately account for how it will affect cost, supplies, and labor overall, and thus 
feasibility. Here we will have to add staff and increase our budget by hundreds of millions of 
dollars without providing additional health benefits, because lead is already so well controlled. 
In some regions there are simply not enough contractors, plumbers, and engineers. Add to that 
the nationwide demand for supplies, and the result is skyrocketing costs. With insufficient grant 
funding, those extra costs created by this artificial demand will be borne by ratepayers. As a 
nonprofit governmental entity, municipal utilities do not make a profit, and we are funded only 
by the amount our residents pay in their water bills. Our utility is bracing for a large rate 
increase to meet the requirements of LCR, as drafted. When all is said and done, the across-
the-board 10-year requirement will burden the people that we are trying hardest to protect, the 
families already struggling to afford their water bills. EPA recognized that some systems will 
need additional time based solely on the quantity or proportion of lead service lines in the water 
system. EPA should expand the ability for an extension based on the risk of harm to decrease 
the demand on limited resources, reduce the resulting inflation of costs, and protect 
affordability, aligning feasibility with long-term affordability while protecting public health. If 
systems where lead is well controlled can roll out the replacements over an extended period, 
those costs can be more readily absorbed, thereby reducing the amount that rates will raise. 
19 

Also, competition will be lower for labor, supplies, and funding, allowing the nation to focus the 
bulk of resources on communities that have the most risk. Thank you.

important first step in eliminating lead service lines. We believe the rule must differentiate 
access from control and that water systems should perform full service line replacements when 
they are granted access. EPA’s new rules should recognize that the lack of customer approval to 
replace service lines can lead to a safety issue and additional regulatory and legal risk. We

when customers do not grant access to perform full lead service line replacements. We believe 
all stakeholders must understand the costs associated with the suggested improvements to the

replacement of all lead service lines, as well as galvanized lines where needed by 2037, will

dependent upon multiple factors, including the requirements in the final rule, the number of 
unknown service lines identified as lead or galvanized requiring replacement. We anticipate that 
the amounts for replacement are going to be significant, with the total replacement costs 
underestimated by EPA. To realize the full health benefits, we believe that the water systems 
should have financial resources to help them sustain ongoing costs that will arise from the 
replacement process in systems for the safety and benefit of the customers. States should treat

Douglas Cantor (Rutgers University): Hi, how are you doing? I am Douglas Cantor from the 
Political Science Department at Rutgers University. Thank you for having me. It is admirable 
that we are finally dropping down the Lead and Copper Rule threshold. I’m sorry, the lead 
threshold for parts per billion down to 10. It’s a standard that’s used by other governing bodies 
though other governments have their threshold even lower than that. But let’s not forget why 
this number is what it is and why it was originally set at 15. During the 1980s and 1990s, 
debates on whether or not to have this number be either an action level number or a maximum 
containment level number happened and the number to set it at was also debated as well. 
Now, key to these debates, key to those debates, was the fact that the number that was 
eventually settled on, which was an action level of 15, was based on nothing scientific. Nothing 
scientific. Everyone is in agreement that the acceptable level of lead in water is zero, from the 
scientific community to those running this meeting, who opened up this meeting with a 
statement that there is no acceptable level of lead for water. I'm grateful that this number is 
being dropped down, but let's not ignore the amount of pain, human suffering and economic 
loss that could have been prevented if, one, the number had been a maximum containment 
level number and not an action level, and two, the number had been even lower. The reason 
that 15 parts per billion was settled on was because it was determined that that was an

pipes made of safer materials within the next 10 years. This means no PVC pipes and no 
extensions beyond the 10-year deadline. Even as a lay person, I understand this really all 
comes down to a fight over who’s going to pay for updating the infrastructure. The proposed 
rule specifies that water systems must replace LSLs, which are under their control. As a result, 
water utilities companies are paving the way to claim that they do not control the portions of 
LSLs under private property. I know this because we have already received several reminders 
from our water company that pipes on our property are our financial responsibility. Ask 
yourselves though, who has the power to turn off the water? Do property owners have a choice 
to switch water utility providers? I believe there's only one equitable answer. The government 
and the water utility company should be required to fully fund complete LSL replacement, 
including connectors and any portion of the LSL under private property. When a car company 
recalls unsafe parts, that company foots the bill to ensure it does not harm its customers. I see 
no difference here except that the government should back up the water companies so that 
they can keep providing this vital resource. Furthermore, there is precedent that this 
arrangement can work. The City of Newark, New Jersey replaced over 23,000 lead service lines 
at no cost to property owners in under three years. To do this, Newark adopted an ordinance 
that mandated the replacement of lead service lines, provided full funding for the construction 
regardless of the property owner's income, and allowed the city to replace the lead line even if 
they couldn't locate the property owner to get their consent. My family lives one town over from 
Newark, so I can say, firsthand, that the city is still operating as usual over a year after they've 
finished paying for this program. So I urge you today to please protect my family and countless 
others by finalizing a rule that mandates full LSL replacement at the cost of governments and 
water systems. Thank you,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0748 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Oral Comments of Ronnie Levin on
EPA’s Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI)
January 16, 2024
I am Ronnie Levin, representing the Environmental Protection Network (EPN), a network of over 600
former EPA employees.
There are many improvements in the LCRI. We commend EPA for:
●
Expanding the regulated universe to 9 million pipes.
●
Reducing the time frame to 10 years.
●
Lowering the action level to 10 ppb. However, we suggest that the science could support a lower
action level of 5 ppb.
●
Requiring both first and fifth liter samples with the higher serving for compliance determination.
●
Requiring water systems to report home testing results to the residents within 3 days, regardless of
the levels.
●
Calculating the average annual replacement rate across a rolling three-year period.
●
Requiring disclosure and offering pipe replacement whenever there is a change in building
ownership.
We disagree with EPA’s proposal that utilities must only replace the portion of the lead service line (LSL)
that is on public property. Public water systems should exert the same effort to replace lead pipes as they do
to install or replace water meters.
●
We suggest that partial pipe replacement should be prohibited except in the direst emergencies.
●
EPA should encourage states to adopt explicit policies giving public water systems the authority to
use ratepayer funds to replace LSLs and galvanized requiring replacement service lines on private
property.
Last year, the Office of Management and Budget changed the discount rate for federal agencies to use in
cost-benefit analysis. The discount rate is now 2% and the analysis in the proposal should be updated to
incorporate this.
EPA and states need a working, formal agreement on implementation, including an underlying assumption
that reporting is accurate and complete. EPA should assert that each requirement is mandatory and that it
also constitutes compliance with this regulation. States should assert a statement of public awareness if in
compliance or not.
We believe EPA has unnecessarily omitted strengthening requirements to reduce children’s lead exposures in
schools and other child-occupied facilities. Both exposures and harms are potentially elevated there. In
schools and similar facilities, it has been demonstrated that mandatory installation of point-of-use filters on
all faucets potentially used for drinking is more efficient than implementing a testing and monitoring
program.

Finally, EPN believes that water systems will continue to underreport lead results and exceedances to the
public and primacy agency unless the regulatory language is strengthened to compel compliance. In
addition, state reporting to EPA will continue to be incomplete and late without a new Safe Drinking Water
Information System shared by EPA and the states and working agreements with states to comply with these
reporting requirements.
Thank you.

Palm Beach County Water Utilities Department (PBCWUD)  
Comments for the 
Proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for  
Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) 
Submitted to the EPA on February 5, 2024. 
Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0036 
 
 
Please reference to the particular section noted in the proposed LCRI. 
1. Definition Wide Mouth Bottle (P. 84966): 
PBCWUD Comment:  We are in agreement with the recommendation made by the Southeast 
Florida Utility Council in that:  Consideration of the practical aspects of tap sampling, including 
bottle sizes and availability is recommended. We suggest allowing a variance of +/- 3 mm in 
bottleneck size to accommodate commonly used containers. 
 
 
2. Paragraph 2 (P. 85035):  FR 84935.V.D. States: “Accurate service line inventories are essential to 
ensure replacement of all LSLs and GRR service lines. To that end, EPA is proposing to require 
water systems to validate a subset of the non-lead service lines in their inventory.”  The EPA 
continues:  “whether non-lead service lines categorized based on records should be subject to the 
validation process; and the role of the State in reviewing the inventory including the results of the 
validation process.” 
 
PBCWUD Comment:  
Record or as-built drawings should be treated as a valid method of identifying service line material 
regardless of the date of record. The purpose of Record or as-built drawings is the accurate 
documentation of what was constructed.  This process is considered a proven engineering 
practice. 
 
 
 
Please reference Section IX. (Pages FR 85035-85037) request for Comments section of the 
proposed LCRI for the remaining comments. 
 
3. General Matters:  
Paragraph 2 (P. 85035):  “Specifical1y, EPA requests comment on ways, that the proposed LCRI 
could be simplified and ways that burden, including paperwork burden, could be reduced without 
affecting the ability of the rule to prevent known or anticipated adverse health effects.” 
 
PBCWUD Comment:     
 
With PBCWUD 200,000 connections (400,000 individual service lines) the Public 
Accessibility Doc tab of the EPA template spreadsheet may become unstable due to this 
large number of records.   

 
WUD Comments:  Proposed LCRI 
 
05Feb2024 
Page 2 of 5 
 
 
Most utilities will be placing the inventory data into their GIS System so creating the 
spreadsheet solely for reporting to the EPA/State Agency is a duplication of effort and 
requires the Utility to maintain and addition document of substantial size. 
 
Submitting this information in a shape file (GIS System) will allow the data to be shared 
to the EPA in a more mobile format. 
PBCWUD Recommends:  The EPA should consider allowing Utilities to submit the Lead Service 
Line Inventory (LSLI) in either a GIS shape file or in a spreadsheet format with the technique to be 
chosen by the Utility. 
 
 
4. Service Line Replacement:  
Paragraph 2 (P. 85035):  “Whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should 
be more than four times (e.g., five, six, or seven times).” 
 
PBCWUD Comment:   
The PBCWUD considers four attempts excessive.  Four attempts means four certified mailings, 
four instances of documenting the four attempts, and four attempts equates to a delay in getting 
the project underway.  To be cost effective the contractor will work the service line replacements 
by geographical area.  Therefore, all responses in a certain geographical area must be received 
before work in that particular geographical area can start.  A delay by one address could delay the 
entire geographical area.  
 
PBCWUD Recommends:   
Reducing the number of required attempts to gain consent to replace the service line from the 
property owner to two attempts.  If the property owner does not respond, then that particular 
address no longer becomes the responsibility of the utility at that particular location. 
 
Second PBCWUD Comment:   
The proposed rule also mandates using at least two different methods for securing consent 
(84921) which places yet another administrative burden on the Utility.   
 
PBCWUD Recommends:   
That certified mail to the property owner with documented return receipt to the address provided 
by the customer and the address provided by the local county property appraiser be sufficient if 
different.   If both the customer’s and he property appraisers address is the same then the 
certified mail is required only at the single address with two attempts.

control” of the Utility but does consider that service line to be their property.  This understanding

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1095 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5th, 2024
Re: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801,
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Michael S. Regan, Administrator
US Environmental Protection Agency
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW
Washington, DC 20460
Dear Administrator Regan,
The undersigned organizations and experts dedicated to improving public health,
children’s health, and health equity submit the following comments regarding the US
Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water
Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”). The proposal makes several key
improvements in how lead in drinking water is regulated, and EPA now has the opportunity to
review and revise key provisions to ensure the final rule results in long-lasting and equitable
public health benefits.
Across the 19th and 20th centuries, millions of lead pipes were installed all over the
country. Decades later, millions of those lead pipes remain in the ground, causing dangerous
levels of lead exposure. This is why it is critically important for EPA to ensure the final Lead and
Copper Rule Improvements are as strong as possible, and will set us on the path to significantly
reducing lead exposure.
Health experts including scientists at EPA, at the Centers for Disease Control and
Prevention, and the American Academy of Pediatrics agree that there is no safe level of lead
exposure. Exposure is especially harmful for pregnant people, infants, and young children. In
children, lead exposure can cause cognitive and developmental effects like lower intelligence
quotient (IQ), learning and behavioral problems. In adults, health effects include risk of heart
disease, high blood pressure, kidney or nervous system problems, and cancer.1
These dangers also manifest as financial costs on individuals, families, and
communities. A recent Harvard School of Public Health study concluded that improved EPA
controls on lead in tap water would generate at least $9 billion in health benefits annually, in
contrast with EPA’s estimated implementation cost of $335 million dollars.2 The benefits would
include not only better health for children and adults but also less public health risks in
communities with lower wealth and Black, brown and Indigenous communities already
2https://www.hsph.harvard.edu/news/press-releases/regulations-reducing-lead-and-copper-contamination-
in-drinking-water-generate-9-billion-of-health-benefits-per-year-according-to-new-analysis/
1 EPA, Lead and Copper Rule Improvements: Proposed Rule, 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84880 (Dec. 6, 2023);
Lanphear, B. P., Rauch, S., Auinger, P., Allen, R. W., & Hornung, R. W. (2018). Low-level lead exposure
and mortality in US adults: a population-based cohort study. The Lancet. Public health, 3(4), e177–e184.

disproportionately burdened from cumulative exposure to different pollutants and more drinking
water quality violations.3
This is why it is critical for our nation’s collective public health that EPA keep strong
improvements of the proposed rule (such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service
lines in ten years, the requirements for water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of
water passing through lead pipes, and a lower lead action level) subject to ensuring those steps
forward do not have loopholes which undermine the goals of the regulation, as detailed below.
Equity-related shortcomings and unintended consequences stemming from loopholes could
derail the success of the rule and disproportionately harm the most vulnerable among us.
Accordingly, the undersigned organizations urge EPA to ensure the final rule is improved in the
following key ways:
●
Remove the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: Under the
proposal, the places with the most lead service lines would potentially have decades of
compliance extensions available. It is a fundamental injustice that communities with the
most lead service lines would be allowed extra decades to fix this issue, and it is
unnecessary to build such an exception into the proposal itself.
●
Remove the “access” loophole: The proposal claims to require removal of all lead
service lines in ten years, but it actually requires removal only of those service lines that
a utility has “access” to, and leaves it up to states, water systems and localities to
determine whether the utility has access. As a result, a water system could comply with
the new rule and still leave vast quantities of lead service lines in the ground by asserting
a lack of access.
●
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines:
Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and putting a disproportionate financial burden
on impacted homeowners and renters and will result in mostly wealthy and white
neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced, particularly when combined with the
“access” loophole.4 There are enough financing solutions, rate structures, and funding
streams available that EPA should ensure replacements be made at no direct cost to
individual consumers. This would achieve more equitable implementation and better
protect children’s health, resulting in more equitable public health outcomes.
●
Incentivize utilities to install filters in schools and child care facilities and ensure
that children who spend many hours in these settings daily are not at risk of
exposure: EPA’s proposed provisions related to protections in schools do not
meaningfully differ from the inadequate Trump administration proposal. EPA should
4 Baehler KJ, McGraw M, Aquino MJ, Heslin R, McCormick L, Neltner T. Full Lead Service Line Replacement: A Case
Study of Equity in Environmental Remediation. Sustainability. 2022; 14(1):352. https://doi.org/10.3390/su14010352
3 https://www.nrdc.org/resources/watered-down-justice

require water systems to install filters certified to remove lead or to conduct thorough,
frequent tap testing at all taps and full public disclosure for all schools and child cares
that lack such filters. Removal in these settings should be prioritized; tap testing
thereafter can then be used to identify additional sources of lead, such as plumbing
fixtures.
●
Lower the action level to 5 parts per billion: Lowering the action level from 15 to 10
ppb is an important improvement, but still less strict than the 5 ppb standard urged by
health experts, recommended by Canadian and European authorities, and applicable to
lead in bottled water in the United States. It is also far less stringent than the 1 ppb
maximum lead level that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends for children
in schools.
●
Public Education about Protection from Lead in Water: Historically, messaging from
EPA and water systems has revolved around compliance with regulations (which does
not equate with safe water) and outdated advice on how people can reduce their
exposures from lead in water. Improved public education should be an integral part of
any improved Lead and Copper Rule. It should include annual messaging about not only
the risks of contamination from lead service lines but also lead plumbing, which is
ubiquitous. It should also include information about the effectiveness of lead-certified
point of use filters as a way for families to reduce lead levels in their drinking water.
Messaging should not suggest that tested lead levels below the action level are "safe",
and emphasize that there is no safe level of lead exposure. Water systems should also
work with local health departments to distribute information about additional sources of
lead exposure, including lead-based paint hazards, lead in soil and dust, lead in food
and cosmetics, and lead in consumer products and cultural and imported products, along
with actionable steps to reduce these exposures. This messaging would be
science-based, culturally and linguistically relevant to communities served, regularly
delivered, and help avoid creating mistrust between water systems and the people who
rely on them.
●
Prevent regrettable substitutions and pollution from removed lead pipes: EPA
should require water systems to replace lead pipes with copper instead of plastics such
as polyvinyl chloride (PVC), chlorinated polyvinyl chloride (CPVC), PEX or HDPE pipes.
Plastics have known adverse impacts to human health and children's development, and
replacing one hazard with another will create a new set of health hazards for generations
to come. A harmful stew of chemicals can leach from plastic pipes into drinking water,
and these pipes are more vulnerable to thermal degradation from wildfires than copper
pipes. In addition, micro-and nanoplastics can be released from the pipes into drinking
water. Plastic pipes also put fenceline communities at risk during the production and
disposal phase, when toxic substances can be released into air and water. For example,
when PVC/CPVC pipes are incinerated, they can release highly toxic dioxins into the
environment. EPA should also address end of life considerations for lead pipes and
require that those removed are recycled in a safe and environmentally sound manner.

Lead exposure through drinking water is one of the most solvable health crises of our
time. With stronger regulations and more funding, this administration has the opportunity to
make unprecedented progress on this issue, and achieve their goal of removing all lead service
lines in ten years. EPA’s proposed rule is a meaningful departure from prior ineffective
regulations, but without being cognizant of the cumulative effects of these loopholes and blind
spots, these reachable public health goals may end up unrealized. Accordingly, we urge EPA to
implement the changes suggested above when developing the final rule in order to best protect
the health and development of all children and that of future generations. Thank you very much
for this opportunity to provide comments.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-2132 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, EPA Docket Center
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket, Mail Code 28221T
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20460
Docket ID No: EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801
As members of the New York League of Conservation Voters, we applaud your Lead and
Copper Rule Improvements proposal and encourage you to strengthen and quickly
finalize these important safeguards for our families and our drinking water. Lead is a
neurotoxin and is especially harmful to children. We know there is no safe level of lead,
but still up to 22 million people in this country drink water delivered through lead pipes.
The EPA has an incredible opportunity to once and for all get the lead out and protect
our families and communities.
The proposal includes a key provision requiring all lead pipes be replaced within 10
years, however, there are exemptions for some cities that could leave our families
exposed to lead in drinking water for decades. New York City has nearly 347,000 lead or
possible lead service lines. At least 40% of these lead pipes are in Disadvantaged
Communities, affecting roughly 738,000 people, a population equivalent to the 19th
biggest city in this country, larger than Boston, Washington DC, Baltimore, or Atlanta.
Under the EPA's proposal, lead pipe removal in NYC could go on for up to 35 years.
Ironically this would create a profound environmental injustice whereby wealthier and
whiter communities outside of New York City would be assured cleaner drinking water
decades before the city's low-income communities and communities of color. The
35-year timeline would be a disaster for families who live in these communities, and
would further delay environmental justice. We urge the EPA to close this loophole and
require that every water utility meet the 10-year deadline.
Additionally, we urge the EPA's proposed LCRI to follow examples from states like New
York that are leading the way. For instance, data from service line inventories will be
more readily available to New Yorkers than the rest of the nation thanks to city and state
actions. In NYC, service line data is released publicly every six months. Statewide, water
systems serving more than 10,000 people will be required to update their inventories
annually starting in 2025. In the area of school drinking water, in 2016 New York was the
first state in the nation to create a mandatory testing system. Currently this program is
leading the nation with triennial testing and with an action level of 5 ppb.

Finally, since there is no safe level of lead, we urge the EPA to follow the science and
get as close to 1 ppb as recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics by
reducing the action level from 15 ppb to 5 ppb. Also, paying to replace dangerous lead
pipes should not be the responsibility of the homeowner, which would put a
disproportionate burden on low-income communities and potentially exclude renters
whose landlords refuse to pay. EPA should ensure that the water utilities cover all the
costs of full lead service line replacement.
In closing, we appreciate the Biden administration's commitment to getting the lead out
of drinking water and encourage you to incorporate these important strengthening
provisions to ensure that everyone, no matter their race, income, or zip code, has access
to clean water.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0959 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024 
The Honorable Michael Regan
