FOR ELECTRONIC DELIVERY 
RE: 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements 
Docket ID#: EPA–HQ–OW-2022-0801 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
The District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority (DC Water) appreciates the opportunity 
to comment on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI or Proposed 
Rule). DC Water continues to be a strong advocate for public health and water quality 
protections for our customers. Specific to lead protections, our commitment is evidenced by 
DC Water’s Lead Free DC Program. 
While the Proposed Rule contains a number of very positive improvements, DC Water has 
concerns that the requirements, as proposed, may prove challenging to implement. We are 
particularly concerned with any potential impacts on affordability for District residents. 
DC Water hopes that the comments we have provided will assist EPA in formulating a final 
LCRI while recognizing the many competing challenges we face, including limited funding, 
aging infrastructure and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS).  
If you have any questions regarding the attached comments, please contact me. 
Sincerely, 
Jeffrey F. Thompson 
Chief Operating Officer and Executive Vice-President 
Attachment 

1 
 
District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority (DC Water) 
Comments on the U.S. EPA 
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
88 FR 84878 – Docket ID No. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
I. 
INVENTORY and REPLACEMENTS 
 
1. V.B.2. Deferred Deadlines for Mandatory Service Line Replacement 
 
There is significant concern over contractor capacity and supply chain of 
copper pipe, fittings and filters. Suggest EPA allow for water systems to apply 
for extensions due to shortage of resources. 
 
2. V.B.2. Deferred Deadlines for Mandatory Service Line Replacement 
 
Many water systems will not be able to replace all lead service lines within 13 
years.  Suggest EPA provide alternative public notification requirements for 
water systems that have active replacement programs but will not be able to 
meet the compliance deadline.   
 
3. V.B.3. Minimum Replacement Rate 
 
If a homeowner denies replacement on the private side, it should be removed 
from the calculation of percent replacement required.  
4. V.B.4. Partial Service Line Replacement 
 
According to pothole.com, approximately 11,000 traffic fatalities each year are 
a result of poor road conditions. Without the ability to perform partial 
replacements when the property owner refuses private-side replacement, 
streets will consistently be in need of repair and paving. Streets will need to be 
paved in full to avoid dangerous conditions due to spot repairs and then need 
to be dug up again with a property owner change or delay in acceptance of the 
program. Water systems cannot be expected to bear the cost of the constant 
paving and repairs to keep the roads safe.  Perhaps funding could be provided 
to Department of Transportation to repair roadways damaged by service line 
replacements. 
 
5. V.B.5 Service Line Replacement, Water System Access to Full Service Line 
 
Service line replacement plan must identify any legal requirements or water 
tariff agreement provisions that affect a system’s ability to gain access to 
conduct full service line replacement. Systems must conduct a minimum of four 
attempts to engage property owners (and renters/tenants) about conducting full 
service line replacement.  
 

2 
 
DC Water exceeds the outreach requirements with the customers to conduct 
full service line replacements. For instances in which the water system no 
access to private property and customer has repeatedly refused access, are 
there additional measures EPA can take to facilitate access to the privately 
owned service lines through the LCRI? DC Water may evaluate mandates that 
could include tenant/renter participation to grant access for full replacements. 
 
6. §141.2 Definitions - Connector or 141.84(a)(2)(i) 
 
Clarify the definition of a connector to the specific pipe materials instead of the 
"rigid" characterization.  DC Water interprets rigid as galvanized iron, brass, 
and plastic pipes but other users of the regulation could interpret differently. 
Also consider limiting the review and data collection to service lines less than 
3 inch-diameter since any larger would not have a lead connector. 
 
7. §141.2 Service Line Definition 
 
In 40 CFR 141.2, EPA defines the term Service Line to mean, "….Where the a 
building is not present, the service line connects the water main to the outlet." 
However, the term is overly broad EPA does not define or qualify the type or 
purpose of the "outlet," which can include outlets used for industrial purposes 
that do not impact human health.   To be consistent with the intent and purpose 
of the LCR, recommend revising this definition to read, "....the service line 
connects the water main to an outlet typically and usually used to provide water 
for human consumption." Please also clarify that a hydrant would not be 
considered an outlet. 
 
8. §141.84(a)(2)(ii) 
 
Reviewing records of past "connectors" is highly burdensome for many water 
systems. EPA assumed the connector review would be 75% of the effort for the 
LCRR records review, which must ignore the review of documented past 
replacements and instead only consider the existing connectors. Should EPA 
require a review of every individual past non-lead pipe replacement to 
determine the connector, a large water system would have to review individual 
field reports over tens of thousands of replacements. The benefit of the 
information from past replacements does not cover the level of effort.  DC 
Water recommends limiting the review to potentially existing lead exposure - 
connector materials to only galvanized iron service lines that are currently 
believed to exist in the system and requiring data collection from current 
maintenance activities to start by 1 year following the finalization of the rule. 
 
9. §141.84(b)(4) 
EPA should allow for water system responses to customer notification of 
incorrect categorization to include phone calls or emails to exchange 
information and potentially resolve the matter. In some cases, an inspection 

3 
 
may not always be required.  Many people believe their water service line was 
replaced during home renovations when only the internal plumbing was 
replaced. Water systems will have a significant burden visiting each of these 
sites to "inspect". In addition, "inspections" as used here is unclear - if the water 
service line is not viewable at the point-of-entry could an "inspection" be 
considered completed or is EPA requiring excavation based on a verbal report 
from a customer? The latter would cause extreme disruption to a scheduled 
program for replacements and identifying service line pipe materials in addition 
to "fairness" by unsupported verbal reports. If the customer reports a lead 
service line, then a picture of the pipe they are looking at will support their 
report. 
 
10. §141.84(d)(5) 
 
Combining the Known Lead/GRR and Unknowns to calculate the replacement 
rate creates a planning challenge. EPA should create separate replacement 
requirements for the unknown service lines.  The separation will allow water 
systems to better plan and execute without playing "catchup" because no lead 
service lines were found of the unknown group where they might have 
estimated a given percent to be lead as needed for budgeting. The three-year 
rolling average does not provide sufficient buffer for this type of catchup.   
 
11. §141.84(e) 
 
Replacement of a lead connector encountered during a water main repair will 
result in partial replacements if unable to confirm and/or replace the private side 
pipe material. The excavation to repair a water main typically reveals 6-10 ft of 
water main, which could have multiple service connections.  Coordinating and 
executing full service line replacements at the time of the water main repair is 
extremely challenging due to night repair work, need for additional crews to 
execute the service replacements, and extended water shuts for those services 
requiring replacement. The block could be planned for future water main or 
LSR by-block replacements which would more efficiently execute the work with 
respect to planning, communicating to residents, and costs (emergency work 
typically has a higher unit cost than planned by-block work).   
 
12. §141.84 Service line inventory and replacement requirements 
 
(ii) Within six months of any change in ownership of the property, the water 
system must offer full service line replacement to any new property owner and 
make a ‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain the property owner’s consent as described 
in paragraph (d)(3)(i) of this section within one year of any change in property 
ownership. If the water system is unable to obtain consent from the current 
property owner after making a ‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain it, the water system 
is not required under this rule to replace the line. This paragraph continues to 

4 
 
apply after a system completes its mandatory service line replacement 
program. 
 
Recommend EPA use the trigger of when the new owner contacts the water 
utility which will give the water utility the proper contact information. The real 
estate transaction may occur many months before the owner is reachable.  
 
Alternatively, recommend EPA requiring owners (sellers) to allow water 
systems to change their private service line prior to the change in ownership of 
the property. If replacement is not completed prior to the change in ownership, 
this approval must be transferable in the sales contract or addendum and 
agreed by the new owner. 
 
13. 141.84(h)(iv)(3) 
 
Providing written notice within 24 hours does not provide time for the water 
system to QA/QC the field reports and data entry.  Executing large service line 
replacement programs requires robust QA/QC of field data and EPA 
encouraging reduction of QA/QC to mail a letter that will not reach actual 
consumers is counterproductive. Mailing a letter to landlord with incorrect 
information can have dire consequences if one notes a service line was 
replaced and it was not.  The letter could be used to convey incorrect 
information to future tenants. 
 
II. 
WATER QUALITY SAMPLING AND OCCT AND RELATED NOTIFICATIONS 
 
1. §141.2 Definitions 
 
Recommend revising the definition of “Wide-mouth bottles” to be defined by the 
inner diameter of the bottle, which is the functional intent of the requirement, 
and specify a minimum diameter of at least 40 mm.  The revision is suggested 
to meet the intent of the regulations which is to capture all water flow from a 
fully open faucet (with the aerator on), while also balancing the need of all water 
systems to procure the bottles as many do not meet the current the definition 
of 55 mm wide.  DC Water's current sample bottle supply has an inner diameter 
of 42 mm.   
 
2. §141.81(d) 
 
EPA should not require water systems with corrosion control and have active 
lead service line replacement programs to re-optimize their corrosion control 
treatment if they have not exceeded the lead or copper action level. The effort 
is burdensome and water systems should focus their funding efforts on 
replacing service lines.  Although 141.81(f) does allow for water systems that 
will complete their lead service line replacement within five years to not 
complete the OCCT study, the duration is insufficient for larger water systems 

5 
 
that are also researching water service line pipe materials and/or have a large 
number to replace.  The new Action Level for Lead will trigger the study or 
exceedances for many water systems and the States will not have sufficient 
staffing to evaluate the studies. 
 
3. §141.86(a)(4)(iii) 
 
Tier 3 sample sites should not include homes with galvanized premise 
plumbing. The lead release from galvanized pipe scales is a different 
mechanism of release than the lead from lead service lines and lead solder, 
which is how EPA established the OCCT framework. The mechanism of 
release from the galvanized iron scales is unstable iron pipe scales. The OCCT 
treatment options focus on lead solubility, therefore the triggering of the OCCT 
studies stipulated in 141.81 does not adequately address the lead release from 
galvanized iron pipes.  While the regulation does allow States to waive the 
OCCT re-evaluation is some cases, the provision is insufficient. Most States 
will not have the expertise and time to evaluate individual system water 
chemistry to justify the waiver approval. 
 
4. §141.86(a)(4)(iii) 
 
EPA should provide a template Sample Form with the sampling instructions 
that are simple and have graphics.  The form can be used by all water systems 
and therefore reduce the water systems’ burden to create their own and the 
States’ burden to approve individual Sample Forms. 
 
5. §141.86(b)(2) 
 
EPA requires replacement of sample sites within the same compliance period 
and within “reasonable proximity” of the original site.  Water systems with lead 
service lines will be replacing these in full neighborhoods within months or a 
year.  Finding a site within “reasonable proximity” will be very challenging while 
EPA’s required lead service line replacements are being conducted.  EPA 
should recognize the competing efforts and waive this requirement for water 
systems with active lead service line replacement programs.   
 
6. §141.86(e) 
 
Inclusion of customer-requested samples should not be used for calculation of 
the 90th percentile if the water system has the required number of samples 
meeting their required Tier.  EPA states in the Preamble that the rule provides 
flexibility to the water system to adjust their customer-requested sampling 
protocol so those samples could not be included.  However, the use of different 
protocols has a negative impact on data analysis, which can be very helpful for 
a water system.  Some customers collecting under one program will be 

6 
 
confused why the method changed under another program and therefore 
undermine their trust in the water system. 
 
III. 
OUTREACH AND EDUCATION 
 
1. 40 CFR Part 141, Subpart Q.2 
 
General: Throughout the LCRI, there are references for a water system to 
provide mandatory lead health effects language and informational statements 
about lead. 
 
Recommend that EPA publishes required language and statements and not 
allow water systems revisions unless approved by EPA. This will allow for 
consistent messaging across the US. 
 
The LCR, LCRR, and LCRI have different mandatory health effect language.  
With the promulgation and effectiveness schedule proposed in the LCRI, the 
timeline of which language to use when has become unclear and needs to be 
clarified by EPA.  For example, the items of the LCRR that become effective 
10/16/24 require health effects language (e.g. the service line material 
notifications) but it is not specified if the associated 141.85 language should be 
used (or the language from the LCR or LCRI be used). 
 
2. IX. Request for Comment. Public Education (9) 
 
EPA is seeking information and data on when a system provides translated 
materials to consumers with limited English proficiency, what resources are 
used to translate materials (e.g., State resources, community organizations), 
and what barriers water systems may face in providing accurate translated 
materials.  
 
Water systems need further clarification on what “limited English proficiency” 
means.  In addition, water systems need more clarity on what documents 
should be translated. Barrier: Utilities often hire consultants or outside vendors 
to translate documents, which can be cost prohibitive for smaller water 
systems. 
 
IV. 
FUNDING 
 
1. The goal to replace all LSLs will not be achieved unless it is at no direct cost to 
customers. Without sufficient funding for the private side replacements, many 
LSLs will remain since many families in disadvantaged areas will not be able 
to pay for the private side replacement. In most states, water systems cannot 
use the portion of BIL loan money for private side replacements since they have 
to pay back the loan with ratepayer funds. A federal law is needed allowing 

7 
 
water systems to use ratepayer funds for removal of private side LSLs in the 
interest of public health and/or more grant money is needed for water systems 
to use specifically for the private side. Without LSLR free to water customers, 
the only LSLs remaining will be those in lower income areas, exacerbating the 
equity issue. 
 
2. Recent BIL grants issued indicate that funding cannot be used for partial 
replacements.  Does this mean that costs for a singular partial replacement will 
not be reimbursed or is the entire contract ineligible for funding? 
 
3. The LCRI indicates that in a review of a number of states that the inability to 
deploy user fees for private side replacement work may be more perceived 
than real.  In DC Water's context, the constraint is real. Currently, DC Water 
has a shortfall of approximately $60M to complete private side replacements 
since ratepayer funding cannot be used to complete private side replacements.  
Legislative action would be needed to change laws put in place to protect the 
ratepayer.  These laws currently prohibit use of ratepayer fees for work on 
private property. 
 
4. The LCRI indicates that in a review of a number of states that the inability to 
deploy user fees for private side replacement work may be more perceived 
than real.  In DC Water's context, the constraint is real. Currently, DC Water 
has a shortfall of approximately $60M to complete private side replacements 
since ratepayer funding cannot be used to complete private side replacements.  
Legislative action would be needed to change laws put in place to protect the 
ratepayer.  These laws currently prohibit use of ratepayer fees for work on 
private property. 
 
5. Water systems do not have the available funding to meet the LCRI 
requirements without increasing rates which must be approved by a board. The 
amount of EPA available BIL funds will not cover all water systems. To assist, 
EPA should establish and award water systems grants specifically for lead or 
GRR identification and replacement.

Re: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801,
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements
Dear Ms. Fox and Mr. Regan,
GreenLatinos is a national non-profit that convenes an active comunidad of Latino/a/e (hereafter
referred to as Latine) leaders, emboldened by the power and wisdom of our culture, united to
demand equity and dismantle racism, resourced to win our environmental, conservation, and
climate justice battles, and driven to secure our political, economic, cultural, and environmental
liberation. Founded in 2008, we provide an inclusive table at which our members establish
collaborative partnerships and networks to improve the environment and the well being of our
communities. We envision a healthy and equitable society where communities of color are
liberated from disproportionate environmental burdens, free to breathe fresh air, drink pure
water, access clean transportation and enjoy our majestic public lands, ocean, and waters. We
develop and advocate for policies and programs to advance this mission.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) recently proposed improvements to the lead
and copper rule (LCRI), which would mandate that all lead service lines be removed within the
next 10 years. This proposal, while essential to making sure communities across this country
have access to safe drinking water, still falls short of what is necessary to tackle this public
health issue.
Latines continue to lack clean and safe drinking water when compared to other demographics in
the US. A Guardian investigation in 2021 found that Latine communities are disproportionately
1
exposed to federal drinking water violations twice as much as those serving the rest of the US.
When it comes to lead exposure, Black and Latine communities are at the frontlines of the
1 Holden, E., Enders, C.,Kommenda, N., Ho, V. (2021) “More than 25m drink from the worst US water systems, with Latinos most

drinking water for all.
1.
No amount of lead in water is safe for consumption. While the EPA is proposing to
lower the lead action levels from 15 parts per billion (ppb) to 10 ppb, this level is not
protective enough. The lead action level dictates when a water system has to inform the
public and take action to reduce lead exposure while working to replace the lead pipes.
WIth this in mind, the lead action level should be reduced to 5 ppb. As mentioned
previously, our community faces elevated levels of lead exposure. More stringent lead
action levels must be set to ensure that these issues are addressed.
2.
When testing reveals lead concentrations above the lead action level, water
systems should provide free and accessible certified water filters to residents.
This distribution needs to be paired with robust community education and outreach so
people have information on the importance of filters and the lead reduction process. This
outreach should continue until lead levels are reduced.
3.
Testing needs to be required in public schools and childcare facilities. Currently,
there is no federal policy for lead testing to be required for drinking sources in public
schools and childcare facilities. Any testing done is voluntary, putting children from
underserved communities at a higher risk to lead exposure. Schools in states with large
Latine populations fail to protect children from lead exposure. Hence, it is critical that
5
this proposal requires the testing of all water outlets at schools and childcare facilities,
with prompt public disclosure of test results for all these facilities. Additionally, water
utilities, at minimum, should provide certified filters if testing reveals lead concentrations
above the lead action level, which we recommend should be set at 1 ppb for schools and

4.
Reduce the amount of exceptions to the 10-year lead service line removal
requirement. Communities should not have to pay the price of more exposure to lead
simply because there are more lead service lines in their water systems. Communities
that have higher proportions of lead service lines in their water systems should be
prioritized. Additionally, any loopholes that prevent water systems from removing the
entire lead service line should be removed, so additional burden is not placed on renters
or low-income homeowners.
5.
Water utilities and government agencies must cover the cost of replacing lead
pipes without passing the cost on to communities. Additional non-competitive grants
and funds should also be made available for water utilities and agencies who do not
have enough funding. Black and Latine communities have dealt with the consequences
of lack of maintenance of their communities’ water infrastructure for far too long;
ensuring that these communities are the first to receive funding with minimal bureautic
barriers will expedite access to clean and affordable drinking water.
6.
Ensuring language justice when informing communities. Make sure public notices
and any outreach is done in multiple languages, both on written materials and if
resources are shared in person. Currently, a large portion of the EPA’s resources are
only accessible in English. There are many languages spoken in the United States, so
providing information only in English contributes to the inaccessibility of resources and
lack of effectiveness. The Latine community is particularly vulnerable to exposure to lead
contamination, hence EPA must provide resources in multiple languages, especially as
the agency positions itself to promote environmental justice and meaningful public
engagement.
These revisions and recommendations align with the principles outlined in the Latino Climate
Justice Framework (LCJF), a policy guide to solving climate and conservation issues that
disproportionately burden Latine communities. Specifically, the imperative to invest in robust
water infrastructure and guarantee language accessibility throughout every phase of public
engagement. Endorsed by 64 organizations and backed by over 1200 individuals, the LCJF
underscores the essential requirement for equitable community policies.

Water is a human right. Inequitable access to affordable, clean water continues to impact our
community. More stringent lead standards are absolutely critical, along with sufficient funding to
ensure that lead pipes are removed and replaced both along main municipal lines as well as
lines connecting to residential living areas. Low-income and communities of color already bear a
disproportionate burden of environmental degradation; ensuring that costs for replacement of
water infrastructure, purification, and water quality monitoring are not passed on to them is
essential. Outreach of water quality issues must be accessible in order for our communities to
be better informed. We need safe drinking water for all.

RE: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements  
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
Revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) will help ensure that toxic-free drinking water is a priority 
for communities who have been excluded. Thank you for acknowledging the urgent need to replace 
lead service line pipes as soon as possible. At this stage, implementing the revisions in a way that 
prioritizes historically disadvantaged communities is crucial. 
Equity has always been at the core of the LCR's history. The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 
promulgated the LCR through the Safe Drinking Water Act to ensure that historically excluded 
communities were no longer disproportionately affected by water toxins.1 Therefore, decades later, 
any revision should ensure this goal at a basic level. 
Funding decisions could harm frontline communities  
State revolving loan funds (SRFs) will provide most of the funding avenues for this LCR 
implementation.2 In other words, states will decide where to allocate funds. If states do not prioritize 
frontline communities, these funding decisions will exacerbate existing resource decisions that have 
 
1 Lead and Copper Rule, 56 Fed. Reg. 26,548 (June 7, 1991) (codified at 40 C.F.R. § 141.84(b) (6–7)) (requiring prioritization 
for lead service line replacement based on factors including disadvantaged consumers and sensitive populations). 
2 Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84,878, 85090 n.27 (Dec. 6, 2023) (to be codified at 40 C.F.R. 
141–42), https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2023-26148/p-805. 

 
2
left Black and other historically excluded communities without funding to fix their water infrastructure 
for years. The intentional reallocation of funds away from Jackson, MS, the neglect in Flint, MI, and 
countless other examples demonstrate that funding must be directly funneled to Black and other 
frontline communities to remedy decades of disinvestment.3  
Across the country, not all governors care about equity nor do we see all state agencies supporting 
frontline communities.  Consequently, the EPA shouldn't leave a decision as important as water 
infrastructure funding for lead service line replacement to individuals who have no track record of 
helping frontline communities. Therefore, the EPA must take proactive steps to consider other avenues 
for state accountability and direct funding channels. Black and other frontline communities deserve 
detailed state guidance if states get this much power over these decisions. Additionally, the EPA should 
review state plans closely without rubber-stamping allocations. Finally, the EPA should take whatever 
steps possible in rulemaking and in guidance to incentivize water systems to explore equitable cost-
sharing mechanisms, abandoning regressive rate structures in favor of more equitable approaches, 
efficiencies in utilities’ pipe replacement programs, and other financing mechanisms to obtain funding 
for replacement in addition to SRF funds. 
Lead should not be left behind in any community 
Two provisions in the Lead Copper Rule allow exceptions to lead service line replacement within 10 
years.4 Although we recognize the EPA's purpose in extending the timeline for lead service line 
replacement in places with over 80,000 total lines, the logic contradicts the overarching objectives. It 
seems that a goal of the revisions is to “significantly reduce exposure to lead through drinking water.”5 
However, lengthening the amount of time, in some instances to over 40 years to remove lead will not 
accomplish this goal.  
A lack of enforcement of the Lead Copper Rule revisions in places with large populations will inevitably 
result in higher health risks for the individuals the rule is supposed to protect. The more service lines 
those communities have, the more likely they are to serve large populations. Places like Chicago, which 
have a large Black and people of color population, fall under this exception.6 And this extension falls 
flat for protecting frontline communities. It deprioritizes community health. Utilities and other entities 
have already neglected these service lines for decades. Why should residents have to continue to wait

for safe drinking water? The time is now to create bold and equitable provisions that include all 
vulnerable communities in solutions. 
Reducing action levels is a good idea 
Next, the revisions lower the lead in water action levels to 10 parts per billion while research clearly 
shows that lead in water is unsafe at any level.7 An action level only requires that there should be some 
measures taken for the next steps to protect human health. These measures can be as simple as 
informing the community regarding the lead in their water and creating mitigation steps. If the goal is 
to increase public awareness and mitigate harm, action levels for lead must be lowered to ensure 
broader drinking water safety.  
If the risk of lead exposure can lead to impaired cognitive development in children and increased 
cardiovascular risks in adults, the least that can be done is to mitigate the impact and increase public 
awareness. Other countries have already recognized this and set their action levels at 5 parts per 
billion, indicating the United States’ need for stricter regulations.8 Therefore, lowered action levels are 
necessary to reduce lead exposure and protect public health. 
Early public engagement and outreach are critical  
While it is important to have public comment periods, we continuously hear that many communities 
do not have EPA or water utility public education regarding how dangerous their current pipes can be 
to their health. Additionally, they lack public educational materials regarding how common lead 
exposure is. Indeed, most people do not know how dangerous lead is, whether they have lead pipes or 
lead plumbing, the types of filters that can help if they are at risk of exposure (most people are), and 
how to use such filters. We have observed that some of this is intentional misinformation from utilities 
and water systems - for example, conflating the issue to residents of compliance versus safety 
measures, to prevent raising alarm. Residents also do not understand which types of pipes are better 
and who qualifies for service line replacement. Currently, the EPA leaves much of this outreach to 
utility systems without ensuring that residents get information.9 Sadly, when residents request 
information, they often hear that due to government systems, they cannot receive additional 
assistance for public engagement. 
Specific questions should be raised to address the checks and balances needed to ensure outreach 
resonates across communities. For example:

These are the types of questions that the EPA should readily answer regarding public engagement. 
Next, most residents do not receive public engagement regarding lead in water until there are serious 
problems.10 While we appreciate that the EPA continues to share that information is available, this is

We hope that the EPA (1) holds utilities more accountable for misinformation regarding lead service

(3) increases funding specifically for local advocates who continue to share the importance of finding 
lead service lines and testing and (4) creates a stronger feedback loop with advocates to allow for 
better messaging to communities in real-time. 
Increased access to filters and water sampling  
A ten-year plan to replace service lines that contain lead is a welcome revision. However, no amount of 
lead can be safe for communities.11 Therefore, the EPA must provide more expedient mitigation and 
stopgaps to communities. Moreover, free water testing and filters should be available across the 
country without the need for multiple exceedances to action levels. Once it is clear that a service line 
has lead, residents should automatically be allowed to request filters.  
There must also be additional accountability steps that residents can take to test their water without 
waiting for utilities to share this information or test their service lines. Water testing is crucial because 
it allows communities to personally identify and address how much lead they are exposed to and take 
necessary steps to protect their health. We appreciate the recognition that tap sampling must 
improve. However, if a resident requests sampling, there should be a mechanism to do that testing and 
sampling regardless of whether the site is known to be a “lead service line site” given that this

frontline communities should have a direct line to the EPA and technical assistance centers to request 
sampling and filters. Residents should also be able to easily flag where it is not happening.    
The water system should pay for the replacement of infrastructure 
Currently, frontline communities may also be forced to assist in replacing lead service lines rather than 
the water system covering the full costs.12 Placing additional financial burdens on these communities 
further exacerbates the existing inequalities and injustices they face. Indeed, the EPA has data that 
demonstrates frontline communities are disproportionately affected by lead service lines and often 
cannot access the funds necessary to fix them.13  
As part of its commitment to prioritize vulnerable and frontline communities, the EPA cannot expect to 
be able to allow low-income homeowners to share costs. EPA must require water systems to pay for 
the costs of full lead service line replacement, and as mentioned before, there are numerous funding 
sources, alternative rate structures, financing mechanisms, and replacement efficiency programs that 
already exist and have been used in communities around the country to help ensure replacement is 
funded for everyone, not just wealthy homeowners. 
The “access and control” loophole must be removed 
Rather than a presumption that water systems, for purposes of maintenance, upkeep, replacement, 
etc., have access to a lead service line, as EPA has asserted in the past, this proposed rule presumes the 
opposite. The rule requires only lines that water systems have control of to be replaced, and control is 
largely defined as access – though access is not defined clearly. EPA instead defers to water system 
interpretation of access.14   
In the proposed rule, if a system does not have access (for example, because a homeowner does not 
want to pay 5,000 dollars for replacing their line and decides to not grant a utility permission to work, 
or because an absentee landlord cannot be reached) then the utility does not have to replace the 
line.15 Additionally, that lead line would not be a part of the calculus on whether a community has had 
all of their lead service lines replaced in ten years. Practically speaking, this means a system can claim 
they have replaced 100% of lead service lines as required by the rule and still have many lead service 
lines in people’s homes. Another practical consequence is that because there are thousands of 
systems, there is no way the EPA can ensure that local governments, state governments, and utilities 
do not game this provision by interpreting “access” as they see fit to avoid spending money on LSLR in

The location of lead service lines needs to be better understood 
As of now, the EPA has not identified all lead service lines.17 Part of the revisions is to locate legacy 
service lines. However, the EPA has still not shared whether it will be and how transparent it will be 
with communities regarding lead service lines. If the goal is to ensure that the country removes all lead 
service lines, what accountability mechanisms exist outside the EPA? How will communities know if all 
the lines are replaced within ten years if this information is unknown? While we appreciate that there 
are potentially some security considerations, this should not come at the cost of residents being 
unclear whether there are still lead service lines in their communities. 
The revisions must strengthen protections for students 
The LCR revisions finalized by the Trump administration did nothing to advance the health of children 
in schools when it comes to exposure to lead in drinking water. This proposal does not meaningfully 
differ from the Trump administration’s revisions. Like the Trump rule, the proposal requires a single 
lead test at just five locations in each school and just two locations in a childcare center, once in the 
first five years, with no mandatory retesting or required notice to parents and staff, and no general 
public notice.18  
Black children are more likely to be exposed to lead in drinking water, as well as other contaminants, 
and under this rule, they would be vulnerable to additional exposure at schools.19 To make matters 
worse, exposure at schools can be egregious because water sits still for long periods like weekends and 
school breaks20: one study found that about 82 percent of public school buildings in New York State in 
2016 reported having one or more taps that tested above 15 parts per billion,21 and the Seattle Public 
Schools tested for lead in 2004, they found an outlet with lead levels as high as 1,600 parts per 
billion.22

The solution is to not rely on testing, but to assume lead is present and dangerous and instead default

testing and public notice for schools that do not have appropriate filters, such that school systems end 
up preferring to install the filters. This approach would better protect children’s health.

To Whom It May Concern: 
Our firm represents the Louisiana Chemical Association (“LCA”). The LCA respectfully submits 
the following comments on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”)’s proposed National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (“LCRI”).  
LCA is a nonprofit Louisiana corporation, composed of seventy (70) members with over one 
hundred (100) chemical manufacturing plant sites in Louisiana. LCA was formed in 1959 to promote a 
positive business climate for chemical manufacturing that ensures long-term economic growth for its 
member companies. LCA members are committed to excellence in safety, health, security, and 
environmental performance, and to protecting our employees and surrounding communities. 
On December 6, 2023, the EPA proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulation (“NPDWR”) for lead and copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act 
(“SDWA”).1 EPA proposes to require water systems to replace lead service lines (“LSL”) and galvanized 
requiring replacement service lines (“GRR”), remove the lead trigger level, reduce the lead action level to 
0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling procedures, among other changes that are aimed at improving 
public health protection and simplifying the rule relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions 
(“the 2021 Rule”). The LCRI provides adjustments in the additional following areas: corrosion control 
treatment, public education and consumer awareness, requirements for small systems, and sampling in 
schools and childcare facilities. The EPA states that the LCRI “aims to address potential disproportionate 
 
1 National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements, 88 Fed. Reg. 84,878 (Dec. 6, 
2023) (hereafter referred to as the “LCRI”).  

February 5, 2024

impacts of lead in drinking water in communities, including through proposed lead service line 
replacement and public education, among other aspects of the proposed rule.” 
LCA appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the LCRI. LCA member companies 
operate facilities across Louisiana that depend on public water systems for reliable and constant supply of 
water for regular operations. Additionally, several member facilities maintain their own water supply 
through groundwater obtained by groundwater extraction wells or capturing and treating freshwater, 
thereby classifying them as “non-transient non-community water systems” (“NTNCWS”) within the 
definition of the LCRI. Therefore, LCA has a direct interest in providing these comments.  
COMMENTS 
I. 
Replacement of LSL and GRR for All Systems 
Under the LCRI, all systems will be required to replace LSLs and GRR service lines within ten 
years of the effective date of the LCRI.2  Additionally, the LCRI requires that systems enter an LSL 
replacement plan and that each system achieve at least a 10% annual reduction rate in service line 
replacements per year.3 The 10% reduction rate will be based on a three-year rolling average, which will 
be calculated “by taking the sum of the annual percentages of service lines replaced from year one, year 
two, and year three, then dividing that sum by three.”4 
The LCRI preamble provides that “the LCR and [the 2021 Rule] required water systems that 
exceeded the lead action or trigger levels to conduct [lead service line replacement]” (emphasis added).5 
The prior rules did not require all systems in the nation with LSLs and GRR service lines to simultaneously 
replace service lines. Rather, under the 2021 Rule, service lines that were shown to actually contribute to 
lead contamination through sampling and testing were required to be replaced.   
The LCRI defines a service line as “a portion of pipe which connects the water main to the building 
inlet. Where a building is not present, the service line connects the water main to the outlet.”6 For industrial 
facilities, this definition would include lines that connect not only buildings, but individual operations 
units within the facility to the water main.  
The replacement of service lines will cause enormous interruptions to industrial site activities not 
only due to excavation operations within the footprint of facility operations units, but also due to the 
interruption of water supply to the facility. The LCRI’s expedited timeline for LSL and GRR replacements 
further imposes a significant burden on industrial facilities without a commiserate reduction in risk to the 
public. Industrial facilities heavily rely on a consistent water supply for industrial processes, such as 
cooling operations for equipment. Facilities will have to either shut down or severely scale back operations 
 
2 LCRI, 88 Fed. Reg. 85,064. 
3 LCRI, 88 Fed. Reg. 85,064-5.  
4 LCRI, 88 Fed. Reg. 85,065. 
5 LCRI, 88 Fed. Reg. 84,911. 
6 LCRI, 88 Fed. Reg. 85,054.

in order to allow for service line replacement to take place, causing decreased production and safety 
concerns for facility personnel.  
EPA found generally that LSL replacement at NTNCWSs was “feasible.”7 But EPA did not 
expressly or thoroughly consider feasibility with respect to NTNCWSs at industrial facilities. Indeed, the 
effects of facility water line replacements on the expedited schedule proposed and the resulting 
interruptions to facility operations makes the current regulations infeasible within the definition of the 
SDWA. Specifically, “feasible” is defined in section 1412(b)(4)(D) of SDWA as “feasible with the use of 
the best technology, treatment techniques and other means which the Administrator finds, after 
examination for efficacy under field conditions and not solely under laboratory conditions, are available 
(taking cost into consideration).” As explained below, the cost considerations alone make the expedited 
10-year timeline and required replacement of all LSLs infeasible. Safety considerations and other process 
interruptions further support the infeasibility under the SDWA. Finally, EPA must provide field condition 
examinations for NTNCWs at industrial facilities to support feasibility under the definition.  
Moreover, the purpose of the LCRI is to ensure safe and lead-free drinking water. The zero-sum 
replacement requirements create undue burden on industrial-based NTNCWS without a commiserate 
benefit towards safe drinking water. Therefore, and for the reasons outlined in this section, LCA requests 
that the LCRI be amended to provide for an exemption for industrial facilities from LSL replacement 
requirements or, at the least, delayed implementation.   
A. Cost Analysis  
As stated by stakeholders in the EPA’s Small Business Advocacy Review Panel on the LCRI, 
limited workforce and shortages of materials could impede service line replacement progress, especially 
when all systems in a geographic region are conducting replacement simultaneously.8  The LCRI provides 
that the costs estimates associated with the proposal are derived from states that are currently 
implementing similar measures to replace LSL lines on a similarly expedited time frame. Basing a cost 
analysis on actual costs incurred by states implementing the proposal makes good sense. However, LCA 
comments that the states used in the analysis – namely Illinois, Michigan, New Jersey, and Rhode Island– 
are not comparable to all U.S. states. The four states are located in two regions – the Northeast and 
Midwest. Both areas are cold weather climates unlike other areas of the U.S. including the Southeast. 
States in other regions experience different climates, environments, and stressors, such as natural disasters 
unique to the regions. These naturally occurring events present complications for the replacement of LSLs. 
Weather events will limit the time that construction crews can engage in LSL replacement activities, 
thereby lengthening construction timelines and increasing costs. Additionally, lower sea levels in coastal 
areas further complicate LSL replacement when the lines cannot be accessed other than through 
excavation operations. LCA therefore requests that the costs analysis of the LCRI be revised to more 
accurately account for regional considerations that may increase the costs of LSL.

B. Funding Availability for Service Line Replacement  
 
The LCRI preamble provides that “the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (Pub. L. 117–58), 
also referred to as the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (“BIL”), included $15 billion specifically 
appropriated for lead service line replacement (“LSLR”) projects and associated activities directly 
connected to the identification of LSL and planning for the replacement of LSLs.”9  While the BIL 
provides funding for LSL replacement, the funding available is inadequate to meet the EPA’s projected 
cost of replacement. Estimates cited in the rulemaking docket project that the total cost of LSL 
replacement will be roughly $55 billion.10    
 
 
LCA has two central concerns as it relates to BIL funding. First, although LCA contends that $55 
billion is a conservative estimate, it is still far higher than the $15 billion that is available through the BIL. 
The remaining costs of LSL replacement will undoubtedly be passed on to ratepayers and, in the case of 
LCA members who may be NTNCWSs, absorbed by the facility. This is further exacerbated by the 
expedited time frame of 10 years for compliance now required under the LCRI. Although the 2021 Rule 
provided 35 years for compliance, the LCRI now shortens that time frame by 71.5%, thereby compressing 
the total costs of LSL and GRR replacements into a much shorter time window, essentially “frontloading” 
the costs for water systems. Compressing the timeline will also lead to increased costs through shortages 
of construction and plumbing labor and materials for service line replacement. And, although the LCRI 
provides for deferred deadlines for LSL replacement achievement, this deferral is only available for 
systems who are replacing greater than 10,000 LSLs.11 
 
 
Second, although EPA consistently cites the $15 billion in BIL funding throughout the LCRI as 
support for service line replacements, the LCRI is not clear how this funding would be made available to 
service line replacements for smaller and NTNCWS water systems. These systems are particularly 
vulnerable to the cost effects of the rule, because in many instances these systems may not sell the water 
they produce and therefore do not have a rate-setting mechanism to recover the costs of LSL replacements. 
LCA requests clarification on how funding will be made available through the BIL appropriation and that 
NTNCWSs be prioritized in considering funding awards under the BIL appropriation.  
 
C. Access to Industrial Facilities 
 
 
LCA objects to the LCRI insofar as it requires public water systems to enter private property and, 
in the case of LCA members, their industrial facilities, to remove LSLs. EPA specifically requests 
comment on “[t]he extent to which property owner consent, if required by State or local law or water tariff 
agreement, might complicate full service line replacement and whether there are additional measures EPA 
can take to facilitate access through the LCRI.”12 LCA members operate complex industrial sites that are 
subject to an expansive array of environmental, process, and safety regulations. To ensure compliance

with these many regulations, LCA members must closely regulate access to their industrial sites. Many 
member facilities achieve this through required safety training or pre-qualifying contractors and services 
through a pre-approved vendor list.  For LCA members that rely on public water systems for their water 
supply, requiring that industrial sites grant access to public utility companies would make LCA members 
susceptible to a host of liabilities and would place both the public water system and the industrial site 
employees at serious risk.  
 
 
During the EPA’s January 16, 2023, public hearing on the LCRI, several commenters stated that 
the access required for LSL replacement is similar to access to record readings on a metering device. 
However, to gain temporary access to record readings from a water flow metering device is a very different 
matter from extended, continuous access to engage in construction related activities and make physical 
alterations to property in order to replace service lines. The access required for LSL replacement will not 
only be extended in time, but extensive in nature.  
 
 
The proposed Section 141.84(c)(3) of the LCRI, which would apply to LCA member facilities 
who are served by a public water system, provides for the procedure through which a public water system 
may request consent from private landowners on four separate occasions before they cease attempts to 
replace the lead service line, citing examples such as phone calls, text messages, emails, and door hangers 
as means of attempts to make contact.13 Under Section IX of the LCRI preamble, the EPA further seeks 
comment on the possibility of requiring more attempts “e.g., five, six, or seven times.”14 LCA objects to 
this provision as currently written. If consent is required to replace a service line retained on private 
property, and a private owner explicitly denies consent to the public water system, then that express denial 
should be deemed sufficient to vitiate the need for further attempts. As provided in the foregoing 
discussion, industrial sites have legitimate safety concerns regarding the replacement of service lines and 
should be allowed to preserve their right to deny consent for replacement of the service lines. LCA 
recommends that the LCRI be amended to: a) provide greater clarity for how the consent provision pertains 
to industrial facilities, and b) if a private owner explicitly denies consent, that a public water system may 
cease further attempts to gain consent.  
 
D. Disconnection of Service Lines Considered as Replacements 
 
LCA supports the EPA’s proposal to count physical disconnections of service lines from the water 
supply as service line replacements if the line is not in active use. In many instances, the full extraction of 
a service line would be overly burdensome and costly and would result in no decrease to potential lead 
exposure in water supply. Thus, this option preserves a system’s ability to achieve a higher cost savings 
and a lower level of invasive intervention, particularly as it relates service lines retained by private owners.

II. 
Flexibility Provisions for Small and Non-Transient, Non-Community Water Systems 
A. Mandatory LSL and GRR Replacement 
LCA appreciates that the LCRI retains the Small System Flexibility provisions of the 2021 Rule, 
which provide relief to small systems and NTNCWS from corrosion control treatment (“CCT”) 
requirements.15 The Small System Flexibility provisions provide: 
Small community water systems serving 3,300 or fewer persons and all non-
transient non-community water systems that exceed the lead action level, 
but do not exceed the copper action level, may elect to use this provision in 
lieu of the corrosion control treatment requirements otherwise applicable to 
small systems in § 141.81(a)(3), if approved by the State.16  
Thus, the LCRI allows small and NTNCWS systems to choose one of three options as an alternative to 
CCT requirements: 1) approved corrosion control, 2) installation of point of use devices, or 3) replacement 
of lead-bearing plumbing materials.17   
Although the flexibility provisions provide relief for CCT requirements, the provisions have been 
amended to remove the exemption from the requirement to replace LSLs.  The 2021 Rule provided that 
small and NTNCWS systems may elect to replace LSL as an option to meet compliance when sampling 
results indicate an exceedance of the lead action level.18 However, the LCRI now removes this as an option 
of compliance, and instead requires NTNCWS to comply with the general requirement for total LSL 
replacement.19 LCA objects to this change. Many industrial facilities are classified as NTNCWSs, as they 
operate their own water system and maintain an independent water supply. The LCRI makes no distinction 
for the intended purpose of the water supply, instead stating that “all water systems” must replace “all” 
service lines.20 Based on the definitions in the rule, the requirement to replace LSLs applies even to parts 
of a NTNCWS that do not provide potable water, but instead transport, for instance, process water, such 
as for cooling systems, even though the intended purpose of the LCRI is to ensure safe drinking water. 
LCA requests that the LCRI be amended to provide that service lines used for the transport of water for 
the purpose of industrial process operations be excluded from the applicability of the LCRI.    
NTNCWS industrial facilities are required under the 2021 Rule to take certain protective measures 
under the Small System Flexibility provisions. EPA previously determined that these alternative options 
provided proper protections and that the options “allow water systems to select the most financially and 
technologically viable strategy that is effective in reducing lead in drinking water.”21 Industrial facilities

rely on water supply for industrial processes. To require LSL replacement at these facilities will require 
enormous resources and will disrupt facility operations and will require unit or plant outages. Anytime a 
facility or a unit is required to shut down and re-start, there are personnel, process safety, and 
environmental concerns. Thus, as noted by EPA, the flexibility provisions provided sufficient protections 
without requiring costly and unnecessary shutdown and restarts. The EPA does not sufficiently explain 
why those alternatives are now inadequate.    
The LCRI does not adequately consider the impact of LSL replacement on NTNCWSs. The LCRI 
preamble provides that only 147 NTNCWSs were surveyed on whether they had LSLs. The preamble 
assumes that “since 132 of them did not report any lead, GRR, or unknown service lines,” that therefore 
“LSLs are rarely used in these systems.”22 A sample of 147 cannot represent the total number of 
NTNCWSs, which numbers over 17,000.23 By comparison, this sample accounts for just 0.86% of all 
NTNCWSs. The LCRI simply assumes that because of the low number of LSL survey results combined 
with the fact that few NTNCWSs contain more than 1,000 service lines that “relatively few of these service 
lines [will require] replacement over the proposed 10-year deadline.” However, this is an assumption and 
does not take into account that many industrial facilities, which may be NTNCWSs, are pre-1970 
constructions and may therefore contain LSLs. Further, the number of service lines in a water system is 
not indicative of its ability to complete LSL replacement within the prescribed timeframe, as industrial 
sites are complex and any change in normal operations must be carefully planned well in advance. LCA, 
therefore, requests that LSL replacement be retained as an option under the flexibility provisions rather 
than as a requirement for NTNCWSs.  
B. Other Requirements for Water Systems 
Although the LCRI retains some of the flexibility provisions for NTNCWS compliance (see 
discussion above), it adds requirements for small and NTNCWS systems without providing sufficient 
justification. For example, the LCRI requires NTNCWS to provide consumer notices of testing results 
within 3 days of results, 24-hour notification of lead action level exceedances, notices for pipe replacement 
notifications, recurring educational programing, and identification of consumers most at risk.24 Although 
some or all of these requirements may benefit publicly owned systems, many of these requirements are 
inapplicable and unduly burdensome for industrial NTNCWs.  
1. Educational Programming  
The LCRI amends the 2021 Rule to now require that NTNCWSs engage in education and outreach 
services.25 LCA member facilities are already required to conduct rigorous training in compliance with 
numerous other environmental regulations and OSHA requirements.  However, the type of educational 
programming, outreach services, and public notices required under the LCRI are inapplicable to the nature 
of an industrial facility that maintains a water system without any paying customers or homes.  Said 
another way, additional training would not further the intent of the proposed rule because an industrial

facility-NTNCWS does not serve households and ratepayers.  LCA requests that the LCRI be revised to

2. Consumer Testing Results  
 
The LCRI provides that “water systems are required to provide consumer notice of an individual's 
lead tap sampling results from monitoring under § 141.86” and that results be provided to consumers 
“within three calendar days after the system learns of the results.”26  The LCRI also requires that sampling 
results for copper testing be provided to consumers.  LCA requests clarification of the applicability of this 
provision for NTNCWSs when the system does not have customers and does not deliver water to 
individual households.  The notification requirement, while applying to all systems, does not contemplate 
the unique circumstances of NTNCWSs, such as those at industrial facilities. LCA requests that the LCRI 
requirement for sampling results be amended to exclude NTNCWSs or, at least, to clarify how and to 
whom NTNCWSs should provide sampling result notifications.  
3. Consumer Risk Identification  
 
The LCRI requires that all water systems “[c]ontact customers who are most at risk by delivering 
education” and that if “local public health agencies provide a specific list of additional community based 
organizations serving populations at greatest risk from lead exposure (e.g., pregnant people, children), 
including organizations outside the service area of the water system, then the system must deliver 
education materials that meet the content requirements of paragraph (a) of this section to all organizations 
on the provided lists.”27 This requirement does not take account for the nature of industrial facility 
NTNCWSs who do not provide water to “customers,” or to individuals “outside the service area.” Like 
other provisions of the LCRI, the requirement for at risk customer identification is not applicable to most 
industrial-based NTNCWSs. LCA requests that the applicability of provisions for consumer risk 
identification be amended accordingly.  
III. 
LSL Inventory Creation 
The LCRI retains the 2021 Rule’s requirement that systems, including NTNCWSs and other small 
water systems, create and maintain an inventory of LSLs by October 16, 2024.28  The LCRI additionally 
requires that systems update the inventory annually.29 The LCRI preamble states that “EPA has 
determined that it is feasible (i.e., technically possible and reasonably affordable relative to a large system) 
for water systems to create a complete and accurate inventory of service line materials by the proposed 
service line replacement deadline to support the treatment technique for mandatory service line 
replacement.”30 However, EPA’s assessment was not performed for all types of water systems.

Industrial facilities, such as those maintained by LCA members, may not already maintain this

lead pipe regulations. To the extent compliance deadlines are required to be updated, the state regulators 
have the authority under approved primacy to amend the regulations as needed. EPA does not need 
separate provisions requiring assessment of the deadlines or feasibility of the deadlines as a condition of 
primacy.

On behalf of the physician and medical student members of the American Medical Association (AMA), I 
appreciate this opportunity to offer our comments in response to the Environmental Protection Agency’s 
(EPA) National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The 
AMA supports the proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation for lead and 
copper under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act.  
The adverse health effects of lead exposure are well documented and no safe blood lead threshold in 
children has been identified.1 Lead exposure during childhood causes adverse and permanent 
neurodevelopmental consequences. Even low blood lead levels have been linked to low IQ, decreased 
academic achievement, increased emotional and behavioral problems, as well as delayed physical 
development in adolescents.2 Drinking water remains an important, but often overlooked, source of 
exposure to lead, particularly for children and infants.3  
In 2016, the AMA’s House of Delegates, which is our policy-making body representing physicians, 
residents, and medical students from every state and national medical specialty, adopted Policy              
H-135.928, “Safe Drinking Water.”4 This policy closely aligns with several aspects of the EPA’s 
proposed LCRI. Specifically, the AMA is supportive of EPA’s efforts to remove and replace lead service 
lines and other leaded plumbing materials that come into contact with drinking water as quickly as
