Dear Mr. Michael Goldberg: 
 
The South Carolina Water Quality Association (SCWQA) appreciates the opportunity to comment 
on USEPA’s proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for 
lead and copper. On December 6, 2023, EPA issued for public comment further proposed 
revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), found in 40 C.F.R. § 141.80.91), known as the 
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Although the SCWQA supports a robust Lead and 
Copper Rule, we have significant concerns, summarized below, about several of the proposed 
changes.  
 
The SCWQA comprises public water and sewer statewide. Our members are dedicated to 
protecting public health and the environment – this includes reducing the amount of lead and 
copper present in our finished drinking water. We never seek to avoid necessary and appropriate 
requirements. Instead, we embrace such requirements and work to prioritize them and obtain the 
funding necessary to comply from the public that we serve. That said, as public utilities we must 
provide public water service in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  
 
With that perspective, we are compelled to submit these comments because the proposed LCRI 
requirements create a massive regulatory and economic obligation for both public water systems 
and their ratepayers. Adding these distribution system obligations is especially burdensome on 
top of the PFAS-related treatment obligations anticipated with EPA’s pending MCLs. Lead Service 
Line (LSL) removal is particularly challenging given the need for significant public outreach and 
interaction in relation to private laterals. US EPA estimates that there are around 9.2 million LSLs 
in the United States, which the AWWA estimates could cost over $90 billion to replace. Below we 
explain why we believe that the inventory obligation and removal of any LSLs that are found may 
be a major challenge both administratively and financially and will lead to significant conflict 
between EPA, the States, and water utilities as they struggle to define the universe of LSLs and 
complete the mandated replacements. 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2  
 
 
2 
 
I. 
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement Within 10 Years is Both Financially and 
Practically Impossible.  A Phased-In Deadline Based Upon System Lead Levels is 
Both Necessary and Appropriate 
 
The 10-Year Timeline 
 
The proposed LCRI would require water utilities to complete 100% lead service line replacement 
(LSLR) within 10 years. 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84882 (Dec. 6, 2023).  While there are alternative 
timelines for (1) systems with a high proportion of lead and GRR service lines in their distribution 
system relative to their total number of households served and (2) systems that would otherwise 
be required to replace greater than 10,000 service lines per year under the proposed 10-year 
replacement requirement, Id. at 84913, the ten-year timeframe is woefully inadequate and does 
not consider availability of material and human resources nationwide nor the complexity and 
legality of using water utilities to force work on private property.     
 
Anytime we talk in terms of “all” in relation to 50,000 water systems, spread across the country, 
we should pause for a reality check.  We should especially pause when a significant number of 
the LSLs to be replaced have not even been identified.  We should further pause when faced with 
a potential price tag of upwards of $100 billion dollars. 
 
EPA estimates that there are more than 50,000 water systems nationwide.  It is simply impractical 
for such a large number of systems to make significant distribution system changes in a ten-year 
period.  This is especially the case given the (1) fact that many/most of the LSLs have not been 
identified, (2) cost of such replacements, (3) need for public outreach around utility-owned LSL 
replacement, and (4) need for outreach and coordination with homeowners across the country 
regarding replacement of their customer-owned LSLs.  Such an historic and unprecedented effort 
would come during the worst period in modern history for trying to plan, finance, bid, and deliver 
projects.  There is simply not enough engineering or construction talent available to do the work 
- even if we could fund it. 
 
Many of our water systems are struggling right now with basic water availability, especially during 
the winter months.  Cold weather each of the last several winters has taken a major toll on water 
systems leading to numerous water main breaks and boil water advisories.  These have been 
especially prevalent across the southern United States and into the mid-Atlantic.  For example, 
much of the District of Columbia had a boil water notice in January of 2024 due to cold weather-
related line breaks. 
 
US EPA has for several decades made a priority of imposing incredibly expensive (and in many 
ways, counter-productive) sewer system improvement mandates on local governments 
nationwide.  As a result of this sewer-first enforcement approach, local resources have been 
forced to the sewer side, often at the expense of water utilities’ ability to raise revenue.  Those 
deferred investments are now coming home to roost for water systems.  On top of general system 
needs, thousands of water systems face historically expensive PFAS-related capital upgrades 
and incredible annual operation and maintenance costs for those facilities.  Adding a LSL 
replacement obligation over the next 10 years on top of these historic financial challenges is a 
bridge too far financially and from a project delivery perspective. 
 
A one-size-fits-all LSL removal period will have water systems with low lead levels vying for the 
same funding and engineering/contracting resources as water systems with much higher lead 
levels.  This makes no sense whatsoever. 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 3  
 
 
3 
 
 
A more logical approach to LSL replacement is for USEPA to adopt a phased approach where 
utilities with higher P90 lead levels have earlier deadlines to replace their LSLs while utilities with 
lower P90 numbers defer their replacements.  Such an approach will allow EPA, the States, and 
utilities to prioritize available federal and State grant/loan resources as well as engineering and 
construction resources to water systems with higher lead levels.    
 
We specifically recommend that the final rule authorize the states to establish phased-in deadlines 
for their water systems.  Any water system above the 10 ppb lead action level must remove their 
LSLs within 10 years of the effective date of the rule.  Utilities with P90 values below the 10 ppt 
would be prioritized based upon their levels for LSL removal, generally not to exceed a 20-year 
compliance period.   We believe that 20 years is a more realistic (albeit, still very challenging) 
compliance period.  Significantly, such an implementation period will allow water utilities to 
coordinate LSL removal with other system upgrades both getting and giving economies of scale 
to water system projects.  This will reduce the financial burden and system planning disruption 
that will otherwise result from a crude, 10-year LSL removal deadline. 
 
This phased approach, coupled with a one-third reduction in the lead action level, will ensure 
additional protection going forward for all Americans who receive public drinking water, from day 
one of the Rule’s effective date. 
 
II. 
Lead Service Line Replacement Must Only Include Public Lead Service Lines. 
 
Lead Service Line Replacement Must Consider Complexities and Legalities of Private Property 
Ownership. EPA lacks the authority to require public water utilities to replace privately-owned 
water infrastructure located on private property.  There are significant legal questions about 
whether public entities can even spend public funds for this private purpose.   
 
EPA needs to address the legality of requiring public water systems to replace private lead service 
lines before imposing such a requirement in the LCRI. 
 
Rather than illegally seeking to force public water systems to make improvements to indoor 
plumbing, EPA should give water utilities a benefit for each full LSL replacement that is performed.  
For example, a utility could be given more time to complete LSL removals (within our suggested 
20 year from the rule effective date compliance period) if they meet certain private side LSL 
removal goals (such as 30 or 40 percent associated with public LSL removal). 
 
We also question whether EPA’s assumed cost to implement the proposed rule has included 
private side LSL replacement costs.  If “yes,” we would like to know what EPA estimates those 
private costs to be and the basis for those estimates.   
 
Revise the Definition of “Under the Control of the Water System” to Exclude Customer-Owned 
LSLs. 
 
Relatedly, we disagree with the proposed LCRI rule requirement that full LSL replacement is 
required when lines are “under the control” of the water system. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The term 
“under the control” of the water system is defined as wherever a water system has adequate 
access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full-service line replacement or 
replacement of the lead connector. Id. at 84920.  

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4  
 
 
4 
 
This definition is impermissibly overbroad.  The definition must clarify that water utilities are not 
obligated to replace customer-owned LSLs as EPA cannot legally require public utilities to make 
changes to private property (including modifications to landscaping, driveways, etc. that may be 
required during replacement) on infrastructure it does not own. The key aspect should be 
ownership. The present proposed incentives are written for a complete replacement (with 
customer agreement) so that water systems do not get credit for LSL replacement if it doesn’t 
include the customer’s side. We believe this is an illegal provision and although we support full 
replacements, our members cannot be required to go on private property and replace indoor 
plumbing. Those private side replacements should instead be driven by federal funding efforts 
and partial replacements should be given the credit they are due, considering they take great 
effort and expense to identify and accomplish. Instead, and as noted above, water utilities should 
be given a benefit if they achieve a certain goal for customer-owned LSL replacement as part of 
LSL replacement of publicly-owned water distribution lines. 
 
Lining and Coating Service Lines Should Qualify for Extended Removal Deadlines 
 
As noted above, removing “all” LSLs in the country in ten years is a shocking financial and 
practical proposition.  Rather than requiring removal, we believe EPA should allow a range of 
effective lead reduction approaches, such as lining or coating technologies to count equally as 
LSL replacements.  At a minimum, lined or coated service lines should qualify for deferred removal 
schedules.  
 
Lined or coated service lines immediately control lead from entering drinking water. EPA’s 
inventory and full service line replacement requirements in the LCRI will impose substantial costs 
on water systems that must simultaneously investigate unknown lead status service lines and 
connectors, finance capital projects associated with replacing known or discovered lead and GRR 
service lines and lead connectors and assemble the resources and personnel to replace all the 
service lines requiring replacement. 
 
Granting water systems an additional period to complete the replacements of coated or lined 
service lines, e.g. for the service life of the coating or lining product, will lower the personnel and 
financial burdens of the LCRI on water systems while immediately reducing lead from drinking 
water as water systems will dedicate resources to those services lines most likely posing a risk of 
lead exposure. 
 
III. 
Galvanized Replacement Service Lines. 
 
Definition of “Galvanized Requiring Replacements” 
 
Under the proposed LCRI, galvanized service lines that have ever been downstream of LSL 
require replacement (GRR). 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The EPA defines galvanized requiring 
replacement service lines as a “galvanized service line that currently is or ever was downstream 
of a lead service line or is currently downstream in the direction of flow of a lead status unknown 
service line.” Id. 85054 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.2). If the water system cannot demonstrate the 
galvanized service line was never downstream of a lead line, the line is a galvanized requiring 
replacement service line. Id. 
 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5  
 
 
5 
 
The EPA’s proposed definition of GRRs is unreasonable and counterproductive.  The definition 
will likely result in water systems having to replace all galvanized service lines within the same 
10-year period they must replace LSLs.  We think the presumption that a galvanized line requires 
replacement is too strong.  Rather than requiring the water system to know that there was never 
a LSL above the galvanized line, a water utility should be able to conclude, based upon available 
information, that there is no information that there was ever a LSL upstream of the galvanized 
line.  In those cases, the water system should be able to prioritize the lining/coating/removal of 
galvanized  lines over a longer compliance period – say 20 years.  Again, the longer period is 
absolutely critical if water systems are to see economies of scale with other water distribution 
system work in conjunction with LSL and galvanized line removal.  This is especially the case for 
water utilities with P90 numbers that are well below the proposed 10 ppb action level.  We 
continue to believe that the states should be given the authority to prioritize LSL (and GRR) 
removal. 
 
The Lead Connector Threshold Should be 36 Inches and Unknown Connectors Assumed to Be 
36 Inches or Smaller 
 
We disagree that lead connectors greater than two feet in length should be considered service 
lines. See 88 id. at 84919, 85083. Connectors greater than 24 inches have been sold to utilities 
and the EPA does not present evidence suggesting significantly higher lead concentrations 
resulting from a lead connector that is 36 inches as opposed to 24 inches in length. If EPA is 
going to impose an arbitrary connector length, it should be at least 36 inches.  Moreover, there 
should be a presumption that connectors of unknown size and composition are less than three 
feet in length. 
 
IV. 
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes Remains a Monumental Task for Utilities. 
 
It might be one thing for EPA to impose a 10-year LSL removal requirement if we already 
understood how many LSLs there were and where they are located.  That would allow us to better 
estimate the cost of removal and time needed.  Instead, EPA is shooting blind in that they don’t 
even have the benefit of the existing LSL inventories that won’t come due until October 16, 2024.  
Almost all of those inventories will be derived using predictive tools with only a small percentage 
of LSLs actually having been ground-truthed. 
 
The fact remains that it is a spring for most water systems to meet October 16, 2024 initial 
inventory deadline.  We suspect that hundreds, if not thousands of water systems will miss the 
deadline.  It will take many years following the development of the initial deadlines to ground truth 
where LSLs actually are in each water system.   
 
Accordingly, we request that EPA clarify what, if any, inventory update requirements are 
contemplated between the initial inventory under the LCRI and baseline inventories in the 
proposed LCRI. We suggest the EPA suspend inventory updates between the two deadlines to 
allow water systems an opportunity to develop a complete and accurate baseline inventory in light 
of the substantial difficulty most water systems will have categorizing the material composition 
and location of their service lines and connectors. Alternatively, the EPA should consider 
eliminating the initial inventory requirement and allow water systems to dedicate all of their 
resources into developing complete and accurate baseline inventories available to the public by 
2027. 
 
Baseline Inventory Requirements 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 6  
 
 
6 
 
 
We request the EPA to reconsider requiring water systems to investigate connector locations and 
composition in its baseline inventory. The proposed rule would require water systems to remove 
lead connectors upon discovery. 88 Fed. Reg. at 85066 (Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.84(e)). The 
EPA’s justification for not requiring water systems to find and replace all lead connectors as part 
of the full-service line replacement requirement is that “regular progress towards lead connector 
replacement is made in coordination with other activities, such as planned infrastructure work, 
while resources are prioritized for replacement of all LSLs and GRR service lines as quickly as 
feasible.” Id. at 84919.  
 
EPA noted that most lead connectors will be replaced under the proposed rule because “all lead 
connectors that are attached to a lead or GRR service line would be replaced by the end of the 
mandatory service line replacement program.” Id. In addition, EPA “also expects that many lead 
connectors may be connected to aging water mains and likely to undergo replacement with 
routine main replacement activities in coming years,” especially because EPA estimates that any 
given lead connector “is expected to be a minimum of 41 years old by the LCRI compliance date 
in 2027” and the “average service life of cast iron, ductile iron, and asbestos-cement pipe is 40 
years.” Id. EPA thus acknowledged that water systems will encounter and replace the vast majority 
of lead connectors during routine maintenance as a result of aging infrastructure or as a result of 
its mandatory service line replacement requirements. 
 
At the same time, EPA acknowledges that short lead connectors pose a lower lead exposure risk 
than LSL and GRR service lines that are significantly longer. Id. at 84919 (“EPA expects that 
galvanized lines downstream of lead connectors may contribute less lead into drinking water than 
those that were downstream of much longer LSLs”). EPA therefore prioritized service line 
replacement. Because EPA accepts that its requirement for water systems to replace lead 
connectors upon discovery will address the vast majority of lead connectors in a water system 
and acknowledges that lead connectors pose less of a health risk than lead service lines, we 
request EPA to reconsider its decision to include connectors in the baseline inventory. 
 
Removing the investigation of connectors from the baseline inventory removes expensive and 
laborious investigations into the location and composition of connectors when those resources 
are best spent identifying, locating, and removing lead and GRR service lines. Water systems 
reporting the composition and location of encountered connectors and the number of replaced 
lead connectors will still provide valuable information to the water system and the public about 
the location and composition of connectors in a water system and the probability that lead 
connectors are present. 
 
Validation Pool Requirements 
 
The proposed regulation instructs water systems to develop a “validation pool” consisting of all 
lines categorized as non-lead minus the non-lead lines that already replaced LSL or GRR lines, 
non-lead lines already visually inspected at two points along the line, or non-lead lines with 
documentation demonstrating their composition. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84935, 85063 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 141.84(b)(5)). The rule would require water systems to randomly and visually inspect as 
many service lines in the validation pool as necessary to ensure a “95% confidence level” that the 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 7  
 
 
7 
 
observed proportion of non-lead lines validated is representative of the larger validation pool 
within ten years of the rule’s publication and seven years of submitting baseline inventories. Id.; 
Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA 815-
R-23-003 at 24-25 (Nov. 2023). 
 
The timing of this LSL/GRR inventory requirement reinforces the impracticality of the ten-year 
LSL/GRR removal requirement. 
 
EPA is currently calculating the number of visual inspections of lines necessary to ensure that 
lines categorized as non-lead are in fact non-lead by assuming a standard normal distribution and 
an “expected sample proportion” of 0.5. EPA assumed the expected sample proportion “to be 50 
percent, meaning that 50 percent of the non-lead service lines investigated are expected to be 
confirmed as non-lead.” Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements, EPA 815-R-23-003 at 25 (Nov. 2023). EPA acknowledged “this proportion will most 
likely be much higher since most non-lead lines will end up being confirmed as nonlead.” Id. EPA 
nonetheless maintained the proportion at 0.5 because, “an assumption of 0.50 provides the most 
conservative (or largest) sample size…meaning that any system validating this number of lines 
will be guaranteed to have met or exceeded the minimum number for statistical significance 
regardless of the true sample proportion.” Id. 
 
We question why EPA does not simply stick with the 95% confidence and allow each water utility’s 
consultant to develop a testing program that will achieve that level of confidence for the utility’s 
list.  Why does EPA pick a very aggressive 95th percent confidence level and then structure the 
rule to force an even higher level of confidence? 
 
The method for determining the number of visual inspections necessary is also not particularly 
well explained. At a minimum, EPA should clarify its validation calculations, e.g. what data it used, 
if any, to determine the expected sample proportion, what the relevant comparison EPA is making 
between the validated lines and the validation pool and what that significance of that comparison 
is, and where EPA derived its formulas for determining the appropriate sample size and provide 
citations. 
 
EPA should also assume in its sample proportion that water systems will correctly assess line 
status more than 50% of the time given its concurrent requirements to investigate lead status 
unknown lines. As EPA has explained the sample proportion, EPA is essentially assuming water 
systems will be no better at determining service line composition than flipping a coin. In light of 
the other significant investigation costs imposed by the rule, EPA should reconsider this 
assumption because it should significantly lower the number of validations water systems must 
make.  
 
We support EPA’s decision to exclude service lines which water systems have confirmed as non-
lead through records investigations from the validation pool. Id. at 84935, 85063.  
 
We also request the EPA to consider delaying the date the inventory validation must be submitted 
to better align with the categorization of lead status unknown service lines. Water systems must 
identify the material of all lead status unknown service lines within ten years from the compliance 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 8  
 
 
8 
 
date. Id. at 85063. Conversely, the validation study must be submitted no later than ten years 
from the rule’s publication date or seven years from the compliance date. Id. at 85063. If water 
systems submit inventory validations before all unknown lines are categorized, then the validation 
pool will not include some lines categorized as “non-lead.” Allowing the validation to occur at least 
after all lead status unknown lines have been categorized will create a validation pool 
representative of all of the non-lead categorized service lines and provide water systems three 
more years to validate their inventories. 
 
Public Disclosure of LSL Addresses In Service Line Inventory 
 
The LCRI, like the LCRR, continues to require that a water system’s annual inventory updates be 
publicly accessible. Although the LCRR includes location identifiers (street, intersection, 
landmark, etc.) served by each LSL, the LCRI states utilities must include a street address with 
each service line and connector. Id. at 84936. We continue to disagree with the need to publicly 
publish a list of homes served by LSLs. Each home will get an annual reminder of this fact. Any 
home that tests for lead will receive its results – there is no need or clear authority for the EPA to 
mandate that this specific information must be made publicly available.  We especially think it is 
irresponsible to include unknown LSL in these lists. 
 
V. 
Lowering the Lead Action Level will be significant in many states. 
 
EPA is proposing to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L. 88 Fed. Reg. 84880 while 
eliminating the lead trigger level that was introduced under the 2021 LCRR. If the AL is exceeded, 
the system must inform the public (Tier 1 public notification within 24 hrs of learning of 
exceedance) and reduce lead exposure while concurrently working to replace all lead pipes (for 
example, installing/adjusting corrosion control treatment). Id. 
 
Lowering the Action Level from 15 ug/L to 10 ug/L will be a big deal in some states with some 
states asserting that the number of systems exceeding the new action level could double.  This 
is likely to be the case for a number of smaller systems.   
 
We take no position on the reduction in the action level.  However, we do believe that P90 
numbers should be a basis for phasing in LSL/GRR removal requirements and that the states are 
in the best position to prioritize LSL/GRR removal.  States are also in the best position to work 
with water systems to mitigate lead levels pending LSL removal.   
 
VI. 
We Disagree With the Requirement to Make Point-of-Use Filters/Pitchers Available 
to All Households After Three Action Level Exceedances.    
 
Under the LCRI, water systems with three lead action level exceedances would be required to 
conduct additional outreach to consumers and make pitcher filters or point-of-use devices certified 
to reduce lead available to all consumers. See id. at 84954.  
 
Providing such filters/pitchers will be overkill in that it will scare many residents not served by 
LSL/GRRs into thinking their tap water is not safe.  That loss of confidence can be difficult, if not 
impossible, to overcome to the long-term detriment of the residents and the utility.   
 

SCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 9  
 
 
9 
 
Moreover, distributing filters/pitchers will be a massive administrative and financial task.  The 
filters/pitchers would have to be provided to each residential and non-residential location served 
by the public water supply.   
We are also very concerned that residents would not properly replace the filters and could end up 
concentrating lead and copper beyond what would otherwise be present in their drinking water. 
 
VII. 
Utilities Must Be Allowed to Invalidate a Homeowner Sample That Does not Follow 
Proper Collection Procedures. 
 
Under the proposed rule, a water utility could not invalidate a homeowner’s sample even if the 
sample was not taken in accordance with LCRI requirements.  This is unacceptable.  All data 
must meet applicable QA/QC/Sampling requirements.  At a minimum, the rule should give the 
water utility the discretion to use a non-conforming sample but should not mandate the use of 
such samples. 
 
VIII. 
Water Systems Must Be Able to Select Homes From Lower Tiers Where Not Enough 
Tier 1 Homeowners Are Willing to Participate. 
 
The LCRI must clarify that water systems which, despite best, good faith efforts, cannot attract 
enough Tier 1 homeowners to participate in sampling, can use lower tier homes. 
 
Otherwise, the water system will be in non-compliance due to causes (lack of homeowner 
willingness to participate) which are beyond its control. 
 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
Our member utilities work tirelessly to provide high quality finished drinking water for our 
customers in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  We appreciate EPA’s consideration of our 
concerns about the practicality and affordability of the requirements we object to above.  We also 
appreciate EPA’s consideration of our suggested improvements to the proposed rule.  In 
particular, we strongly believe that a final rule needs to provide additional time for LSL/GRR 
removal and that a state-directed phased approach over twenty years from the rule’s effective 
date, is warranted. 
 
Sincerely, 
       
 
F. Paul Calamita  
General Counsel

Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
EPA Office of Groundwater and Drinking Water Staff: 
Columbia County Water Utility (CCWU) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Lead 
and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). CCWU is located in Columbia County, Georgia, and is considered 
a large system, serving a population of roughly 150,000. While the Utility agrees that lead in drinking 
water is a major health issue in our country, we do have some concerns with certain proposed 
requirements. 
Our primary concern centers around the requirement for water utilities to replace lead service lines 
(LSLs) on private property. Even with a customer’s permission, water utility employees should not be on 
private property. Our employees are licensed Distribution System Operators; not licensed contractors 
nor plumbers. We realize these services could be contracted out to the appropriate parties, but the 
liability for future issues with the customer’s line will remain with the Utility. Also, working to replace all 
of the LSLs and galvanized lines requiring replacement (GRRs) at the same time across the country will 
put an undue burden on supply chains. EPA states in the proposed Rule that it believes supply chain 
issues will be resolved by the time the Rule is in effect; we respectfully disagree. The requisite materials 
will be in higher demand, potentially creating additional shortages and increasing costs. Plumbers 
installing these lines will likely raise their rates as well.  
Our second concern is funding the LSLs and GRRs. In the Economic Analysis of the Lead and Copper Rule 
Revisions (LCRR), EPA estimates the average cost of service line replacement will be $4,700 For the 
estimated 10 million lines that need replacement. We believe the estimate of 10 million may be too low. 
If prices for supplies rise due to shortages, plumbers raise their rates due to demand for work, and the 
estimate of 10 million lines is low, the currently estimated nationwide cost to replace lines of $47 billion 
dollars may fall woefully short. At present the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law has provisions for $15 billion 

 
A Community of Pride                 A County of Vision                Endless Opportunities 
 
P.O. Box 960  2140 William Few Parkway  Grovetown, GA 30813  Phone: 706‐863‐6928  Fax: 706‐868‐3473 
www.columbiacountyga.gov 
for funding. That is not adequate to cover the EPA’s projected costs and will be less adequate if the cost 
estimate is low. 
The LCRI states: “Consistent with the lack of authority to determine how water systems charge for 
services, EPA proposes to remove from the LCRI any statements from the LCR and LCRR that address 
how a water system should or should not cover the cost of replacing services lines under the control of 
the system as well as statements on whether a water system is or is not responsible for the cost of full 
service line replacement. Instead, the proposed LCRI remains neutral on this matter of State and local 
law.” CCWU supports this position. Requiring water utilities to fund the LSLs and GRRs through regular 
water rates puts an unfair burden on customers that do not have LSLs. Customers living in houses that 
do not have LSLs should not be required to pay the replacement costs for those who do. An equitable 
solution is to share the cost of LSL replacement ‐ the utility pays for the cost of its portion and the 
customer pays for the cost to replace their portion of the line.  CCWU realizes there will be low income 
households unable to bear that burden. If the Federal government wants to have fund to assist low 
income individuals with the cost of line replacement, that funding should be designed so that individuals 
are applying directly to the federal government (or state government if the funds are dispersed to the 
states) for those funds rather than burdening the water utility with administering those federal funds. 
In the LSRI, EPA is also proposing to count full service line replacements where a non‐lead service line is 
installed for use and the lead or GRR service line is disconnected from the water main or other service 
line. CCWU supports this proposal; it is better than requiring systems to dig up and remove the old lines. 
EPA is requesting comment as to whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should 
be more than four times (e.g., five, six, or seven times). CCWU believes four times with at least two 
different communication methods is adequate. 
Finally, any requirement by the EPA to replace LSLs and GRRs, and especially those LSLs and GRRs that 
are not owned by local governments such as Columbia County, violates the 10th Amendment of the 
United States Constitution. The proposed LCRI’s only response to these federalism concerns is to cite to 
the EPA’s previous requests for comments from multiple entities. This does not address the issue that 
the requirement exceeds the powers expressly given to the federal government. (Printz v. United States, 
521 U.S. 898 (1997)). 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the proposed LCRI.

Re: NACWA’s Comments on EPA’s National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI) (Docket ID: EPA-

Dear Administrator Regan: 
The National Association of Clean Water Agencies (NACWA) appreciates 
the opportunity to provide comments on the U.S. Environmental Protection 
Agency’s (EPA) proposed rulemaking to update and improve its National 
Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper published in the 
Federal Register.1 
NACWA represents the interests of 350 public clean water utilities across 
the country that everyday provide the essential services of managing 
billions of gallons of wastewater to ensure the continued protection of 
public health and the environment. Our members strongly support 
appropriate public health protections from lead exposure in drinking water 
supplies, and the proposed LCRI makes significant progress to eradicate 
lead in this regard.  
NACWA supports the comments submitted by our sister organizations, the 
American Water Works Association (AWWA) and the Association of 
Metropolitan Water Agencies (AMWA), whose members will be directly 
impacted by this proposed rulemaking. NACWA is submitting these 
comments to specifically provide input on how public clean water agencies 
may be impacted by the proposal. 
The proposed LCRI calls for replacement of all lead and service lines (LSL) 
within a decade and a very low lead action level of 10 parts per billion – 
which will require significant investment for public water utilities, well 
 
1 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (December 6, 2023). 

NACWA Comments on EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2 of 5 
exceeding the historic federal investments provided in the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL). NACWA 
has consistently urged a renewed federal commitment to greater infrastructure funding in rebuilding 
the nation’s aging infrastructure.  
While the BIL’s $15 billion allocation towards LSL replacement is helpful, it is a drop in the bucket 
compared to the total costs that will be borne by public water systems and ultimately passed along to 
individual ratepayers themselves to entirely replace all lead service lines, especially those that go 
beyond the utility main. This is not an argument against addressing lead but is a call to action to fully 
recognize the financial burden that will be placed on individual customers to meet these federal 
objectives, and a plea for greater federal investment as well as flexibility, where appropriate and 
backed by science, to help mitigate water rate increases. These are affordability challenges that 
customers will face on top of those already caused due to increased rates for needed clean water 
investments.  
How the LCRI Will Impact the Provision of Clean Water Services  
While this proposed rulemaking is poised to directly impact public water systems, there will be indirect 
impacts to downstream wastewater utilities and water quality. As NACWA noted during the previous 
Lead and Copper Rule Revisions, public water systems have always had flexibilities under the Safe 
Drinking Water Act in implementing corrosion control technologies (CCT) (e.g., alkalinity and pH 
adjustments, calcium hardness adjustments, and phosphate/silicate-based corrosion inhibitors) that 
reflected local water chemistry and site-specific needs within a given service area and watershed.  
In contrast, public water systems under this new proposal face a “one-sized-fits-all” orthophosphate 
dosing requirement that will add more phosphorus to the system and therefore require downstream 
public wastewater utilities to remove it before discharging to surface waters. Even if a public water 
system achieves complete LSL replacement, the current LCRI proposal leaves public water systems 
with no corrosion control option other than to continue orthophosphate dosing - essentially requiring 
phosphorus additions into the system in perpetuity. 
NACWA continues to recommend EPA not adopt a “one-size fits all” approach to mitigating lead by 
mandating orthophosphate as the preferred optimal CCT approach but rather continue to support the 
inherent flexibilities granted under the SDWA for drinking water utilities to make responsible, scientific 
decisions for their own facility’s CCT techniques. Or in the alternative, if a public water system 
achieves complete LSL replacement, there should be an “off-ramp” to continued orthophosphate 
dosing to a more flexible alternative. These recommendations would allow for locally appropriate 
protections and minimize excess phosphorus loading to water systems.  
Many surface waters throughout the United States face eutrophication from a variety of point and 
non-point sources. Federal and states regulatory agencies charged with carrying out the mission and 
goals of the Clean Water Act have responded to the enhanced nutrification of surface water by setting 
often-stringent numeric nutrient limits under the National Pollution Discharge Elimination System 
(NPDES) for publicly owned clean water agencies.  

NACWA Comments on EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 3 of 5 
These discharge limits require clean water agencies to significantly invest in treatment controls to 
reduce the amount of phosphorus and nitrogen discharged into surface waters. And, over the 50 years 
of the Clean Water Act (CWA), at a tremendous cost, clean water agencies have successfully 
mitigated millions of pounds of nutrients from entering surface waters and have greatly improved 
water quality for communities and the aquatic life alike that depend on clean and safe water.  
While many clean water agencies have installed nutrient removal technology to meet current water 
quality standards for phosphorus, the LCRI proposal will undoubtedly increase the quantity of 
phosphorus that downstream wastewater utilities will need to remove before discharging into surface 
waters. This will require more utilities to install nutrient controls and others to scale up their treatment 
technology. As the climate changes and water quality becomes more eutrophic in nature, it is 
inevitable that clean water utilities will face even more stringent nutrient limits to protect surface water 
quality.  
EPA Should Promote Regulatory Flexibility and Coordinate with States 
EPA estimates that anthropogenic sources deposit nearly 750 million pounds of phosphorus per year 
into surface waters, and at the high end the LCRI would contribute roughly 0.5% or 3.9 million pounds 
of the total phosphorus surface waters. EPA also asserts that the LCRI impact will be “small, relative to 
the total phosphorus load deposited annually from all other sources.”  
While EPA attempts to put the additional phosphorus loadings in perspective, it brushes over the 
simple fact that “more phosphorus in, is more phosphorus out.” In a one-water framework that is the 
result of the interconnectivity of our public water systems and wastewater treatment plants, often 
under dual ownership, there is one individual rate payer – the public. The national estimates also gloss 
over localized impacts under which certain communities will be significantly affected, based on local 
water quality conditions. And to look holistically at the impacts of the LCRI, EPA should also consider 
the increased energy demands and associated environmental impact and increased carbon footprint 
of adding, and then removing, phosphorus from our water systems. This approach may be the best 
solution in certain cases, but less so in others.   
NACWA continues to urge EPA to encourage state regulatory authorities to provide clean water 
utilities with regulatory flexibility―such as considering the development of a variance or conducting a 
use attainability analysis (UAA)―to account for increased phosphorus concentrations associated with 
the LCRI, especially where these tools are will enable clean water utilities to meet CWA permitting 
requirements. Downstream wastewater utilities, particularly those with stringent nutrient permit limits, 
will also need adequate time to assess their influent and make meaningful treatment adjustments for 
increased phosphorus concentrations coming into their systems.  
Further, EPA should help guide coordination between public water suppliers and downstream 
wastewater treatment plants when an upstream utility re-optimizes its CCT and begins adding 
orthophosphate as a treatment technique. As public water systems add orthophosphate 
concentrations to their treatment regimes, there is no requirement for upstream utilities to coordinate 
or relay their CCT techniques downstream. Knowing if, when, and how much phosphorus will be 

NACWA Comments on EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4 of 5 
added to the system and how it will impact wastewater influent will assist wastewater utilities in their 
efforts to prepare.  
Economic Analysis Misrepresents True Costs of Added Phosphorus Removal 
Given these downstream impacts of increased phosphorus loading, EPA’s economic analysis of the 
cost of phosphorus removal per pound is likely underestimated. 
As EPA notes in its proposed LCRI rulemaking, the number of POTWs with nutrient limits in NPDES 
permits is increasing over time. EPA acknowledges that 41% of the clean water utilities in the U.S. will 
likely face nutrient limits over the next 35 years. NACWA believes EPA’s growth rate estimation is 
conservative and there will likely be more utilities with nutrient limits.  
EPA derived unit costs associated with removal of $5.44 per pound of phosphorus incrementally 
added (88 Fed. Reg. 84990). NACWA believes it is impractical to standardize a single unit cost for 
removal of phosphorus because there are many variables and assumptions to consider. For example, 
some locations with more stringent permit limits have costs upwards of $13 per pound of phosphorus 
removed.  
EPA also estimates that the annual cost impacts of the LCRI to clean water utilities, at the high end, 
would be $12 million, a $5.9 million incremental increase over the baseline. NACWA believes that EPA’s 
Economic Analysis misrepresents the true costs on public clean water utilities in that it spreads the 
cost impacts over a 35-year period rather than when orthophosphate dosing begins within three years 
of the LCRI becoming final. In sum, the costs to clean water utilities will be greater in the near term, 
and much higher than the average would suggest for some utilities.  
In addition, the Economic Analysis assumes wastewater treatment plants have sufficient capacity 
already built in to manage increased loading and does not consider the added infrastructure capital 
costs that may be needed to expand capacity. In order to truly assess the cost of incremental 
phosphorus loading at upstream utilities, a life-cycle cost analysis would need to be conducted. 
Conclusion 
NACWA recognizes the critical need to address potential lead and copper contamination in drinking 
water and appreciates EPA’s efforts through the LCRI to provide needed clarity on public health 
protections from these constituents. 
However, many of NACWA’s members provide drinking water as well as clean water services and 
recognize that it is possible to provide public health protections through drinking water treatment 
without sacrificing downstream environmental and water quality.  
NACWA continues to recommend EPA not adopt a “one-size fits all” approach to mitigating lead by 
mandating orthophosphate as the preferred optimal CCT approach but rather continue to support the 
inherent flexibilities granted under the SDWA for drinking water utilities to make responsible, scientific 
decisions for their own facility’s CCT techniques. Or in the alternative, if a public water system 

NACWA Comments on EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5 of 5 
achieves complete LSL replacement, there should be an “off-ramp” to continued orthophosphate 
dosing to a more flexible alternative. In doing so, drinking water utilities can continue safeguarding 
public health while simultaneously ensuring protection of downstream water quality concerns.  
If you have any questions, please contact me by phone at 202/533-1839 or by email at 
eremmel@nacwa.org.  
Sincerely,  
 
 
 
Emily Remmel 
Senior Director, Regulatory Affairs

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0733 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
GREAT LAKES WATER AUTHORITY COMMENTS ON U.S. EPA’S PROPOSED LEAD AND COPPER 
RULE IMPROVEMENTS REGULATION  
DOCKET ID NO. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
The Great Lakes Water Authority (“GLWA”) submits the following comments on U.S. 
EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (“LCRI”) regulation establishing 
requirements to replace all lead water supply service lines within ten years, with limited 
exceptions, announced in the proposed rule at 88 Fed. Reg. 84878 (Dec. 6, 2023). GLWA’s 
comments are submitted on its behalf and in support of its 85 member communities and the 
115 communities that receive GLWA drinking water.  
The communities served by GLWA drinking water represent approximately 39% of 
Michigan’s population. While a socially and economically diverse group, included amongst 
those communities are some of the State’s oldest and most economically challenged 
municipalities. Given the broad range of communities GLWA supports, GLWA appreciates the 
opportunity to submit its comments and hopes they receive serious consideration by EPA. 
GLWA supports EPA’s goal of completely removing lead service lines (“LSL(s)”) as quickly 
as possible. At the same time, GLWA believes that setting a 10-year timeframe for achieving 
that goal is not the optimal approach, may not be feasible for older, smaller, or economically 
disadvantaged communities, and omits adequate consideration of affordability, practicability, 
and sufficiency of optimized corrosion control treatment (“OCCT”) to mitigate exposures to lead 
in drinking water while LSL replacement work proceeds.   
EPA acknowledges that lead pipes are more likely found in older cities and homes built 
before 1986. EPA also recognizes that minority households and low-income households are 
more likely to live in housing built when LSLs were more commonly used. This is clearly the case 
in GLWA’s service area, and these households are already struggling to afford their water and 
sewer utility costs. Those utility costs are already being driven upward by multiple 
requirements for Combined Sewer Overflow (CSO) and Sanitary Sewer Overflow (SSO) control, 
PFAS mitigation, phosphorus control, and many other state and federal regulatory initiatives. 
GLWA has been providing optimized OCCT to its water supplies for 23 years and has 
collected years of testing data throughout its system that demonstrates the OCCT has been 
highly effective in addressing unacceptable exposures to lead in drinking water. For these 
minority and low-income communities, continued OCCT while LSL replacement proceeds 
achieves the goal of minimizing lead exposure while LSL replacement work proceeds at a pace 
based upon and aligned with community affordability criteria rather than on an artificial 10-
year time frame. 

2 
 
GLWA recognizes and supports EPA’s overall objective to ensure that systems are 
making “regular progress” toward LSL replacement. Under the approach proposed under the 
LCRI, “regular progress” would require, with limited exception, a system to meet both minimum 
annual replacement rates and a 10-year replacement completion deadline. While that approach 
may seem logical on the surface, it inadequately accounts for the innumerable variables that 
will directly and indirectly impact its implementation. Those variables include economic 
conditions, material availability and supply chain disruptions, financial affordability, and 
labor/workforce limitations, among others. 
GLWA suggests there may be another approach that would motivate LSL replacements 
while respecting the many variables that can impact LCRI implementation. Systems that can 
demonstrate they are effectively implementing OCCT could be required to allocate a specified 
percentage of their annual operations and maintenance (“O&M”) budget to LSL replacement 
operations. Throughout the public sector, annual budgets are established with careful 
consideration of rate impacts and affordability limitations. Allocation of a specific percentage of 
budget for continued OCCT and a specific percentage for LSL would provide needed flexibility to 
water systems to decide whether to add LSL replacement costs as additional O&M expenditures 
or shift funds from other O&M (and possibly capital) projects to LSL replacement operations. It 
would also smooth out abrupt variations in cost because annual budgeted expenditures would 
remain fixed. The required percentage of the O&M budget allocated to LSL replacement could 
vary based on variables such as overall rate affordability and demonstrated effectiveness of 
OCCT. GLWA believes that the rush to replace LSLs should be tempered by consideration of 
OCCT effectiveness and system and ratepayer financial constraints. 
GLWA also suggests that EPA should consider setting an interim lead action level of 
0.012 mg/L as the State of Michigan has. This would ensure that systems with higher lead levels 
act first while allowing other systems to plan for future LSL replacement work. 
GLWA supports EPA’s mission to advance environmental justice and public health. 
GLWA similarly supports individual utility efforts to remove their LSLs as quickly as possible and 
agrees that the complete removal of LSLs is a worthy goal. However, it must be recognized that 
achieving this goal will be a complicated process. GLWA appreciates the opportunity to 
comment and asks that EPA fully consider and address the challenges associated with LSL 
replacement.  
Respectfully submitted, 
William M. Wolfson 
William M. Wolfson 
Chief Administrative and Compliance Officer

Thank you for the opportunity to comment on the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). 
The Washington Association of Sewer and Water Districts (WASWD) represents more than 180 
public water and sewer districts throughout the state, serving nearly 20% of our state’s 
population. WASWD members provide these cost-effective essential public services in the 
state’s largest population centers and in the smallest rural communities. Safe drinking water is 
a major concern to both our membership and the customers they serve. We support strong 
protections for drinking water from the source to the tap that are furthered with the LCRI. We do 
have some concerns, however, with the proposed LCRI.
Frequency of lead service line (LSL) inventories: Annual updates are impractical as they are 
required too frequently. Particularly in areas of the country where lead service lines were 
infrequently utilized, conducting LSL inventories at this frequency would take up valuable time 
and resources that could be used for other public health issues such as PFAS. For smaller 
utilities with few staff the frequency of the inventories is especially a real burden. A longer time 
frame for updating inventories is warranted for these reasons.
Timeframe for compliance: Optimized corrosion control treatment (OCCT) is working well in 
many jurisdictions where LSLs are present. These systems should have extended time frames 
for replacement of LSLs since they have already taken action and made capital investments to 
control lead and copper in their water systems. Health and safety is not at issue in these 
systems as it is in those with no OCCT, so allowing them to spread out the time and money 
needed to replace LSLs makes economic sense.

Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
Wisconsin Conservation Voters is a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization dedicated to 
engaging Wisconsinites to protect our environment. As members of Wisconsin 
Conservation Voters, we strongly support EPA's newest proposed improvements to the 
Lead and Copper Rule. These proposed improvements are an important opportunity to 
make good on the president's commitment to protecting children and families through a 
strong commitment to public health and environmental justice. 
 
Across Wisconsin, we are very worried about the serious, long-term health risks associated 
with lead contamination – and particularly how those risks can impact children. Based on 
2022 data from our Public Service Commission, Wisconsin still has at least 174,637 utility-
side service lines that contain lead or galvanized material, and 181,918 customer-side 
service lines that contain lead or galvanized material. In some Wisconsin communities, as 
many as 1 in 4 children under 6 years old are considered lead poisoned, based on blood 
lead levels that exceed 5 micrograms per deciliter. We know that no level of lead in 
drinking water is safe, and elevated blood lead levels in children are associated with 
hearing loss, lower IQs, developmental delays, behavioral changes, and emotional impacts 
like anxiety and depression. 
 
We appreciate that the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements include 100 percent 
replacement requirements for water utilities within 10 years of the rule's finalization. To 
further improve the rule, we urge you to require water utilities to cover the costs of fully 
removing both utility side, and customer-side lead lines. This will ensure that individuals 
who are already confronting the public health costs associated with lead poisoning do not 
need to cover replacement costs on their own. Unless all individuals are able to replace 
their customer-side lines, we will not be able to protect the entire community from lead 
contamination. 
 
We also appreciate that the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements include improved 
sampling, inventory, education, and notification requirements. We urge you to further build 

 
on these improvements by requiring public water systems to implement stronger testing 
and remediation plans for our schools and childcare facilities.  
 
Overall, we strongly support the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements. We urge you to 
further strengthen and finalize them as expeditiously as possible. 
 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0801 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy 
 
Comments to National Primary Drinking Water Regulations:  
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
Service Line Inventories 
The state of Michigan (Michigan) supports the requirement to inventory lead service line 
(LSL) materials on both public and private property and the proposed requirement to 
inventory lead connectors.  Michigan also supports the annual inventory update 
requirement for supplies with lead, galvanized, lead connectors, or unknown service 
lines.  Michigan supports requirements for supplies to conduct service line material 
validation activities.  Knowledge of service line materials is essential to properly 
identifying sample sites, mitigating risk, conducting service line replacement, and 
educating consumers about lead exposure.   
 
Michigan urges consideration be given to the following:   
• The definition of an LSL currently excludes lines with lead connectors, if that is 
the only portion containing lead.  However, these components contribute to lead 
exposure.  The definition of an LSL should be revised to include these 
connectors.   
• The current definition of a service line does not address supplies without water 
mains (such as a single building with a line directly from the wellhouse to the 
building); therefore, it is unclear what the inventory or service line replacement 
requirements are in these circumstances. 
• Consider providing criteria for supplies to be “grandfathered” for service line 
validation if states have existing programs in place and/or the supply can 
demonstrate an equivalent exercise has been conducted. 
• Consider allowing supplies to exclude sites from validation requirements if 
adequate controls were in place at the time of installation (for example 
ordinances that excluded installation of lead service lines and connectors) or 
were installed after lead service lines were banned. 
 
Lead Service Line Replacement (LSLR) 
Michigan strongly supports the proposed requirement to expand full lead/galvanized 
service line replacement requirements to all water supplies, regardless of 90th percentile 
values.  The only way to eliminate the risk of lead exposure from these service lines is 
to remove them, and this proposed requirement directly addresses this issue.  Michigan 
supports the “ban” on partial LSLRs. 
 
 

Page 2 of 16 
Michigan urges consideration be given to the following:   
• The cost of removing the portion of the service line on private property should 
NOT be left to the property owner.  This is an environmental justice issue.  It 
leaves those unable to afford service line replacement, and their children, at 
continued risk of exposure.  Rental property owners may choose not to invest in 
LSLR, thereby putting renters at continued risk.  The only way to ensure all 
consumers are protected from exposure to LSLs is to fully fund replacement and 
not require individual homeowners to bear the cost of replacement on private 
property.  Michigan rules require the water supply to cover the cost of full LSLR 
from the main to the home. 
• Additional consideration should be given to replacement requirements resulting 
from customer-initiated service line replacements.  Requiring replacement of the 
supply-side service line within 45 days of a customer-initiated replacement could 
create environmental justice issues by allowing those with financial means to 
have their service line replaced before those who do not; delay prioritized or 
planned work (such as replacements at sites with high lead results or vulnerable 
populations); delay infrastructure projects, some of which could include service 
line replacements; and/or result in higher per-line costs leading to fewer 
replacements overall. 
 
Sampling Protocol 
EGLE strongly supports the proposed adoption of Michigan’s 1st  AND 5th liter sampling 
protocol at sites served by an LSL and using the highest result in the 90th percentile 
calculation.  Measuring water in contact with interior plumbing AND the service line 
better represents exposure risk than relying on the 1st or 5th liter alone.  Since adopting 
this sampling protocol in 2019, Michigan has identified action level exceedances (ALE) 
that would not have otherwise been found, leading to more water supplies taking action 
to reduce lead exposure. 
 
Michigan urges consideration be given to the following:   
• The 1st /5th liter sampling protocol should be extended to sites served by lead 
connectors or galvanized requiring replacement (currently identified as Tier 3 
sites under the proposed LCRI).  These scenarios represent lead exposure risk 
from within the service line (hence the requirements to remove these service 
lines); therefore, a 5th liter sample should be collected at these locations to better 
assess lead exposure risk. 
• Requiring a different number of sites be sampled for lead versus copper may 
cause confusion and result in monitoring violations.  This added complexity may 
not be worth the limited burden-reduction.  Additionally, how should supplies 
decide which sites are analyzed for lead and copper versus lead only?  Consider 
requiring lead and copper to be analyzed at all sites. 
 
 

Page 3 of 16 
90th Percentile Calculation 
Michigan strongly supports use of the highest result of 1st/5th liter sampling in the 
90th percentile calculation for sites served by LSLs  Michigan also supports the 
clarification regarding how to calculate the 90th percentile when both Tier 1/2 and lower-
tiered sites are needed to meet sampling requirements by permitting only the highest 
and minimum needed of the lower tier be included to avoid dilution.  Michigan supports 
proposed revisions to the invalidation criteria to include invalidation of samples that 
were not collected in accordance with required sampling methodologies. 
 
Michigan urges consideration be given to the following:   
• Only the highest lead and the highest copper result from each site should be 
used for calculating the 90th percentile.  While the rule is clear that only the 
highest of the paired 1st/5th sampling is used in the 90th percentile calculation, it 
does not address situations where a site is sampled multiple times.  Each site 
should have equal weight in the calculation, which is designed to assess the 
water supply as a whole.  A 90th percentile can be skewed and misleading if one 
site is sampled more than other sites and multiple results from that site are used 
in the calculation.   
• There are numerous conditions under which samples are collected (routine 
compliance, customer-requested, post service line replacement, site 
assessments, etc.).  Be exceptionally clear in the rules which samples should 
and should not be included in the 90th percentile calculation.  With so many 
sampling events, under varying conditions, for different purposes, water supplies 
and states will have difficulty determining and/or verifying which are appropriate 
to include in the calculation.   
 
Site Selection Criteria 
Michigan generally supports the tiering criteria as proposed in the LCRI, with the 
following comments. 
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• As noted throughout, Michigan believes service lines with lead connectors should 
be considered LSLs.  That said, it is appropriate for sites where the only lead 
component is a connector to be tiered lower than other LSLs.  Therefore, if the 
suggestion to include connectors in the service line definition are incorporated 
into the final LCRI, Tier 1 and 2 sites should be clarified to exclude LSL sites 
containing only lead connectors.    
• Consider ways to mitigate the difficultly for both supplies and states to manage 
sampling plans.  While it is desirable to identify sites and submit updated plans 
prior to each sampling round, supplies often encounter new information during 
sampling rounds (identify higher risk sites, find sites no longer meet tiering 
criteria, lack of customer cooperation, etc.).  Additionally, supplies and states are 
asked to consider results of sampling conducted at sites that may not be on the 

Page 4 of 16 
plan.  Given these challenges, it can be difficult to sample only in accordance 
with a pre-submitted plan.  It is also a resource challenge for states to verify that 
all samples were collected in accordance with plans, and the issues above make 
it more difficult.  
 
Lead and Copper Tap Sampling and Water Quality Parameter (WQP) Sampling 
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• Do not separate the sampling frequency or location for lead and copper.  This will 
result in more frequent monitoring violations.  Sampling requirements are 
complex, and this adds another opportunity for confusion and missed monitoring, 
while achieving minimal burden reduction.  Additionally, if sampling more sites for 
lead than copper, how should the supply determine which sites should be 
sampled for lead only? 
• Ongoing WQP monitoring should be required for all water supplies with corrosion 
control treatment.  Small systems should not be permitted to stop WQP sampling 
during periods where the supply is at or below the action levels.   
 
Consumer Notice, Public Notification, Public Education (PE), Public Outreach 
Michigan supports faster consumer notice to homes with lead levels above the action 
level; annual notification to residents served by a lead, galvanized, or unknown service 
line; and other measures designed to educate the public about the risk of lead and 
mitigations activities.  Michigan also supports the added requirement for copper results 
to be included in consumer notice requirements. 
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• The requirement to notify the public of a lead ALE within 24 hours, while an 
excellent goal, can be difficult to achieve.  Michigan has adopted a requirement 
to provide notice within three business days.  Three business days can be 
challenging, but achievable.  Significantly shorter periods may be logistically 
difficult to achieve in all cases.  
• The United States Environmental Protection Agency (USEPA) should provide 
revised templates for outreach-related tasks, including improved language that 
can be read and understood more readily by consumers and available in 
additional languages (English, Spanish, Arabic).  Some language is complex, 
and some individuals may be unable to understand the documents, thereby 
leaving a portion of the population vulnerable.   
• The requirement to notify homeowners served by lead, galvanized, or unknown 
service lines should begin sooner.  Water supplies will have service line material 
information beginning with submittal of the October 2024 initial inventory and 
should not wait an additional three years to notify residents of their service line 
material. 
 

Page 5 of 16 
Corrosion Control Treatment 
Michigan supports the inclusion of re-optimization steps which provide a path for 
improving treatment at supplies with existing treatment in place.   
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• The alternative for supplies to replace LSL within five years in lieu of conducting 
treatment steps may be appropriate in cases where a lead ALE was due to 
5th liter sample results.  However, this option should not be permitted if results 
from 1st liter samples (premise plumbing) would have resulted in a lead ALE 
without inclusion of 5th liter results.  In these cases, the LSL was not the primary 
cause of the exceedance.  Additionally, it should be specified that this option is 
only be available for lead ALEs.   
• Corrosion control designation and re-optimization for consecutive systems can 
be challenging.  Please provide additional clarity regarding these situations, 
including the responsibilities of the seller and customer.  
• While robust pipe rig studies are desirable, it should be noted that these studies 
are relatively expensive, require a tremendous amount of technical support, and 
take several years to complete, resulting in continued exposure risk during the 
multi-year period of study and installation.   
 
Distribution system and site assessment 
Michigan supports follow-up sampling at sites testing over the lead action level and 
requiring a WQP sample be taken to assess water quality in the area. 
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• Unless the WQP sample collected near the site indicates a water quality concern 
and remains unresolved, the supply should not be required to permanently add 
the site to its routine WQP monitoring.  This will lead to an ever-
changing/expanding number of sampling sites and will be difficult to manage.   
• The provisions requiring assessment/re-assessment of corrosion control 
treatment present some concerns.  These steps imply potential corrosion control 
treatment decisions could be driven by results from one or two locations, which 
may not be appropriate for the supply as a whole.  Additionally, many supplies 
will not have corrosion control treatment and, therefore, no historical WQP data 
upon which to compare results.   
• Many states will receive hundreds of individuals results greater than the action 
level each year and the level of effort to approve hundreds of site-specific 
recommendations will require substantial resources.  Consider modifying 
required steps if follow-up sampling indicates WQPs are at expected levels, lead 
levels are below the action level, and no other concerns are present. 
 
 
 

Page 6 of 16 
School/daycare sampling 
Michigan supports lead mitigation in schools and daycare facilities.  However, 
Michigan’s experience with school sampling indicates a different approach would be 
more effective.  If the current approach is retained, Michigan supports provisions 
allowing waivers where state or local laws require that schools sample or require filter 
installation and maintenance. 
 
Michigan urges additional consideration be given to the following:   
• The proposed approach will be burdensome for supplies.  Michigan estimates 
there are nearly 9,000 licensed childcare facilities and 3,500 schools in the state.   
• Lead release is known to be unpredictable.  If schools have dozens or hundreds 
of taps, but only five are required to be sampled, the remaining taps may still 
present a lead exposure risk.  
• Sampling will result in “chasing” taps with high results, mitigating, moving to the 
next tap, mitigating, etc.   
 
School Sampling Alternative 
School testing in Michigan has shown that fixtures and adjoining brass 
appurtenances installed prior to 2014 introduce an elevated risk for leaching lead 
into water.  The way water is provided for consumptive purposes in schools 
needs to be rethought.  This is especially true since water usage patterns in 
schools is different than in homes or businesses.  Schools have many extended 
stagnation periods from being closed on weekends and holidays as well as 
prolonged breaks.  These excessive stagnation periods can cause a significant 
increase in lead levels until the water has been properly flushed.   Elementary 
schools are particularly vulnerable since the students are younger and more 
susceptible to the effects of lead.  In addition, there are often more points of 
distribution in elementary schools since there are often sinks with faucets and 
bubblers.   
 
Rather than sampling existing taps, a more wholistic approach would be to install 
certified lead reducing filters on consumptive taps.  These points of consumption 
should be limited, and all other points be restricted to non-consumptive purposes.  
The use of Hydration Stations (bottle filling stations with integrated lead reducing 
filters) allow students to fill water bottles which then could be consumed in the 
classroom.  With a reduced number of points of use, the school would have an 
easier time ensuring proper maintenance.  The increased water flow at the 
reduced points of consumption would also lead to improved water quality. 
 
This approach would be more effective in reducing lead exposure than a test-
and-see approach.  It would be cheaper in the long run as it immediately jumps 
to the inevitable end point of replacement.  The testing in schools across 
Michigan has been consistent in terms of identifying potential risks.  Testing 

Page 7 of 16 
Hydration Stations after installation to demonstrate they are effective is 
productive, while testing fixtures that are either currently failing or will inevitably 
fail is not a wise use of resources.   
 
Given the high number of schools, having supplies test them on a five-year 
rotational basis may be a significant burden.  This burden will be substantial both 
in terms of the number of samples each year and the necessary records 
maintenance to ensure a proper rotation each year.  There will also be issues 
with not testing all points of use in the schools since lead levels can vary 
significantly from fixture to fixture, even if the two fixtures are the same make, 
model and age.  The introduction of Hydration Stations or similar devices will 
restrict the number of points of consumption thus making monitoring much 
easier. 
 
Michigan recently passed legislation that requires schools and child care centers 
to install lead reducing filters at consumptive taps, post signage or render 
inoperable nonconsumptive taps, and sample filtered taps annually to 
demonstrate effectiveness. 
 
Additional Concerns 
• The USEPA should provide clarity on what constitutes a change in source or 
treatment for the purpose of evaluating corrosion control. 
• Additional clarity is needed regarding consecutive water systems.  What actions are 
expected of the customer supply if the seller makes changes to their source or 
treatment?  What actions are expected of the seller if a customer exceeds a trigger 
or action level?   
• Significant resource investment will be necessary for successful implementation of 
these very complex and impactful regulations.  The USEPA must commit to 
providing additional resources to regulating agencies in the form of funding for 
human resources, extensive guidance materials and training, significant data 
management upgrades, etc.   
• Data Management - The complexity of this rule will make implementation 
challenging for agencies and regulated entities.  The USEPA should provide robust 
data management tools before the rules take effect.  Successful and consistent 
implementation of these rules will require a functional data management system and 
final data entry instructions prior to implementation.   
• Federal Reporting - When developing data systems and federal reporting criteria, 
consider separating monitoring violations from reporting violations.  This provides 
more transparency and clarity for the public.  It is important to know whether a 
supply failed to monitor (and therefore water quality is unknown) or if the supply 
sampled as required but missed a reporting deadline. 

Page 8 of 16 
• Consider expanding funding available to water supplies to address the infrastructure 
investment necessary to meet these requirements, particularly LSLR on both public 
and private property. 
• See additional comments in the table below.  Some of the comments below have 
been addressed in this summary, while others have not.

141.2 Definitions 
Connector 
A connector is a not a fixture or a joint, but a piece of pipe used to 
connect the service line to the water main and should be 
considered a portion of the service line.  It should be clarified in 
the definitions and throughout the rule that the presence of a lead 
connector makes a service line a "lead service line" regardless of 
the material in the remainder of the service line.   
Galvanized 
Requiring 
Replacement 
Unless the definition of an LSL is revised to include lead 
connectors, this definition should be expanded to include 
galvanized service lines that are/were downstream of a lead 
connector.  Lead connectors contribute to lead accumulation in 
galvanized lines and, therefore, should be replaced.  As written, 
galvanized lines must only be replaced if they are/were 
downstream of an LSL which, as currently defined, does not 
include lead connectors. 
Newly regulated 
public water system 
Consider revising the definition to include water systems that 
were not identified as a public water supply on October 16, 2024. 
Service Line 
This definition should be revised to include connectors (see 
comment above).  Specify what constitutes a service line at 
supplies without water mains.  For example, facilities with direct 
connections from a wellhouse to a building, but without water 
mains.  Some community water supplies and many 
noncommunity water supplies fit this category.  These should be 
subject to service line inventory/replacement requirements, but as 
written, do not fit the definition of a service line.

Dear Michael Goldberg, 
 
The Portland Water Bureau in Portland, Oregon appreciates the opportunity to review and provide 
comments on the proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI).  
The Portland Water Bureau is the largest drinking water utility in Oregon, serving nearly one million 
Oregonians every day. Portland’s primary drinking water source is the highly protected Bull Run 
Watershed, the largest drinking water supply in Oregon. Portland also has a secondary groundwater 
source, which is used as an alternative or augmentation supply when needed.  
Portland currently complies with the Lead and Copper Rule through Optimized Corrosion Control 
Treatment that adjusts pH and alkalinity. Additionally, Portland is fortunate that lead service lines were 
never used in our system and all known lead connectors were removed from the system over 25 years 
ago. As a result, in Portland, the primary source of lead in water is from home plumbing, either copper 
pipes with lead solder or from brass plumbing fixtures.  
Overall, we support the EPA’s efforts to further reduce our country’s exposure to lead in drinking water 
through the increased focus on the removal of lead service lines, the greatest source of lead in drinking 
water nationwide. As a system that has never used lead service lines and has removed all known lead 
service connectors, we bring a unique perspective to these and the other proposed revisions to the rule 
in our attached comments.   
Thank you again for the opportunity to review and comment on these draft rules. If you have questions, 
you can reach me at Yone.Akagi@portlandoregon.gov or 503-823-1251.
