Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
Page 1 
Portland Water Bureau comments on the long-term revisions to the 
Lead and Copper Rule, Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
Portland’s compliance history with the current Lead and Copper Rule 
As of December 2023, Portland complies with the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR) through Optimized 
Corrosion Control Treatment (OCCT) that was installed in April 2022 and reduces corrosivity through 
pH and alkalinity adjustment. Previous to this OCCT designation, from 1997 through 2023 Portland 
complied with the LCR through a comprehensive Lead Hazard Reduction Program that included four 
components: corrosion control treatment and monitoring; a free customer lead-in-water testing and 
education program; an outreach and education program about all sources of lead; and a program that 
used US Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) grant funding to remediate lead paint 
in homes. Portland no longer operates this program but continues required treatment and monitoring 
activities as well as voluntary water testing and education programs.  
Applicability of LCR Improvements to Portland 
The following comments from the Portland Water Bureau are influenced by the fact that Portland: 
• 
is a large utility that installed corrosion control treatment (pH adjustment) in 1997;  
• 
recently completed re-optimizing pH/alkalinity corrosion control treatment (OCCT achieved in 
December 2023); 
• 
never used lead service lines; 
• 
already removed all known lead connectors; 
• 
is close to completing its initial service line inventory through a statistical inspection approach; 
• 
inspected every current Tier 1 home that is active in our regulatory sampling program to verify 
that lead solder is present; 
• 
currently follows the revised tap sampling guidelines; 
• 
has a robust free customer lead-in-water testing and education program; and 
• 
has a free lead-in-water testing program for schools and child care facilities. 
Given these, the Portland Water Bureau submits the following comments for consideration. 
Timing of rulemaking 
We strongly support EPA’s proposed compliance approach that utilities only have to comply with the 
service line inventory components of the LCRR and then implement the LCRI three years after the final 
rule is published. This approach simplifies utility implementation and will avoid confusion over what 
actions are required in this complex set of rules. We appreciate and support this thoughtful approach 
proposed by EPA.  
However, we also recognize that publishing the final rule by October 16, 2024 – 8 months from now – is 
an ambitious and aggressive timeline to review comments, decide on final changes, and send through 
the federal review and approval process. We are concerned of the consequences that utilities would 
face if EPA is not able to meet this October 16, 2024 deadline: being required at the last minute into 
complying with all components of the LCRR.  
We strongly urge EPA to take the appropriate actions to ensure that the October 16, 2024 
publication deadline is met to avoid this outcome.  
Definitions 
Overall, we appreciate EPA’s continued efforts to make definitions included in the LCR easier to read, 
interpret, and understand. Specifically, we support: 
• 
the application of plain language principles throughout the definitions section; 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 2 
• 
the creation of separate definitions for all types of service lines; 
• 
in the Galvanized Requiring Replacement definition, the clarifying edits that removed reference 
to connectors; and 
• 
in the Wide Mouth Bottle definition, the inclusion of where the 55 mm measurement applies. 
Additionally, we provide the following comments: 
In the Connector definition, we request that EPA increases the length from 2 feet to 4 feet.  
Lead connectors attached to galvanized service lines were routinely used in our system until the 
1930s and, following an order from the state to remove all lead pipes, were systematically removed in 
the 1980s and 1990s. Our records state that these lead connectors were typically 2 feet to 4 feet in 
length. We have strong concerns that the proposed definition is too limiting. It would categorize any 
lead connector over 2 feet as a lead service line and would pull us and possibly others into lead 
service line requirements, which otherwise wouldn’t apply since we have no lead service lines in our 
system. We appreciate EPA’s attempt to balance the length of connectors versus lead service lines. 
We believe that increasing that length limit to 4 feet still meets EPA’s goal while providing an 
evidence-based definition for utilities. 
We request a new definition for “premise plumbing made of lead.”  
“Premise plumbing made of lead” is a new phrase used in 141.86 in the Tier 1 criteria, and it is 
unclear in the rule language if this is inclusive of all sources of lead – lead pipe, leaded brass, lead 
solder – or if this is limited to just lead pipe. The preamble notes that the intent of this tier is to be 
limited to lead pipe. To codify this intent, we request a definition that specifies that “premise plumbing 
made of lead” only refers to lead pipes and does not include sites with lead solder or leaded brass in 
the plumbing. 
Corrosion control treatment and optimization 
We appreciate EPA’s continued work on developing corrosion control treatment (CCT) regulations that 
are effective for the large diversity of water systems in the country. As a system that recently completed 
re-optimization with pH and alkalinity adjustment, we offer the following comments. 
We request clarification on re-optimization requirements for systems with OCCT whose 90th 
percentile results are between 5 and 10 ppb.  
The proposed rule does not provide specific criteria for requiring systems with OCCT to re-optimize if 
90th percentile lead results are consistently under 10 ppb. If a system has previously completed a 
corrosion control study, implemented and deemed OCCT, has removed or never had lead service 
lines, and consistently meets the LCRI action levels for lead and copper, it should not be required to 
complete new corrosion control studies and re-optimize OCCT.   
We request allowing state primacy agencies to grant schedule extensions to implement re-
optimized OCCT that require significant infrastructure upgrades.  
The deadline to install re-optimized OCCT within 12 months after the State designates treatment will 
not be adequate for many systems to complete design, construction, and commissioning of a new 
CCT facility. For systems required to make CCT changes that involve installation of new treatment 
facilities, we suggest allowing state primacy agencies to grant a schedule extension based on the 
time needed for design and construction.  
Outside of the LCRI regulations, we strongly urge EPA continue to support research on 
developing industry guidelines for conducting CCT studies.  
Lead corrosion is complex, influenced by many factors, and can be system specific. The coupon and 
pilot scale corrosion control studies that take all these conditions into account to fully understand 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 3 
corrosion and effective treatment can vary significantly in their design. We strongly urge EPA to 
provide updated guidance to States and water systems (with and without lead service lines) for 
conducting and approving corrosion control studies.  
Distribution system and site assessment (DSSA) 
We appreciate EPA’s clarifying changes in the DSSA from the Find and Fix steps in the LCRR. 
Specifically, we support that DSSA customer samples cannot be used as part of the 90th percentile 
calculation and support the inclusion of maximum number of water quality parameter (WQP) sites that 
can be added. Additionally, we offer the following comment. 
We suggest establishing criteria to end monitoring from added WQP monitoring sites.  
For WQP sites that are added due to a regulatory tap monitoring site exceeding 10 ppb, we request 
the ability to discontinue monitoring the added WQP site after two or three subsequent tap monitoring 
rounds at the tap location are below 10 ppb, or after the lead source has been identified and removed 
(e.g., faucet replaced). 
Water quality parameter monitoring 
We request clarification to the excursion compliance requirements for WQP monitoring.  
The LCRI specifies that a system “is out of compliance…for a six-month period if it has excursions for 
any State-specified parameter on more than nine days, cumulatively, during the period.” While this is 
consistent with current requirements, we request clarification that more than one excursion in a day 
(e.g., multiple WQP sampling locations in a single day are outside of the State-specified WQP 
ranges) counts as one day in the maximum nine days in the 6-month sampling period. 
Tap sample location tiering 
Overall, we support and appreciate EPA’s efforts in applying plain language principles in the tier 
descriptions. This resulted in language that is much easier to read, understand, and interpret compared 
to the tier descriptions in the LCRR. In addition, we offer the following comments. 
In Tier 1, we request clarification for “premise plumbing made of lead.”  
As noted in our Definitions section above, we request that a definition for “premise plumbing made of 
lead” is added to clarify that this phrase refers to just lead pipes and does not include lead solder or 
leaded brass. 
In Tier 3, we recommend exercising caution with tiering galvanized lines above lead solder sites 
without further research.  
As EPA notes in the preamble, CCT is one of the treatment techniques to protect people from 
exposure to lead in water. Tap sampling at highest risk sites is the mechanism to assess that CCT is 
providing those public health protections. To achieve the maximum public health benefits, it is 
essential that the tiers defined by EPA are accurately ranked based on data. We have observed 
through the LCRR and LCRI rulemaking processes that Tier 3 has changed at each rulemaking step. 
In the LCRI, Tier 3 is prioritizing connector and galvanized sites above lead solder sites with 
extremely limited data to support this prioritization. We encourage EPA to gather more data to 
accurately prioritize sites in descending risk. 
In Portland, where we have never used lead service lines and have removed all lead connectors, we 
have well-documented evidence that lead solder is the largest contributor of lead in water for 
customers in our system. Through our extensive voluntary home testing program, we consistently see 
that homes built during the era when lead solder was commonly used – between 1970 and 1985 – 
have higher median and 90th percentile lead results compared to all other homes. Included in that 
pool of “all other homes” are thousands of homes that had lead connectors removed in the 1980s and 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 4 
1990s. The results from our home testing program do not support the idea that galvanized pipes that 
are downstream of a historic lead connector removed 30 to 40 years ago are currently a significant 
source of lead in drinking water and does not seem to justify tiering these sites over lead solder sites.  
We appreciate the research that East Bay Municipal Utility District (EBMUD) is conducting to 
understand the lead load in galvanized plumbing. Of note, their data suggests that sites with an active 
lead connector and galvanized service lines have very low levels of lead in both 1st and 5th liter 
samples (P90 <1 ppb). Additionally, they note that galvanized lines that were formerly downstream of 
lead pipe have the lowest measured lead (P90 <0.4 ppb). We support their comments that EPA 
should include a regulatory mechanism in the LCRI for utilities to conduct studies to understand the 
risk posed by galvanized lines in their system. We strongly encourage EPA to review their data and 
fund similar studies around the country to gather more data before including galvanized lines in the 
tiering. 
Because of these two findings, we cannot support the tiering of galvanized sites, and most specifically 
galvanized sites that used to have a lead connector, above lead solder sites. The intent of tiering is to 
find the worst-case scenario locations and test water at those locations to assess the effectiveness of 
the utility’s CCT. This proposed tiering for lead connector and galvanized sites goes against EPA’s 
preamble which states “that sites most likely to contain lead are prioritized for tap sampling” and may 
not provide the public health protections that are the foundation of the LCRI. We strongly urge EPA to 
gather more data about galvanized pipe and lead connector sites and take a thoughtful and data-
driven approach to adding these types of sites to the tiering.  
Tap sampling 
There are a number of elements in this section that we supported in our LCRR comments and continue 
to support in the LCRI. First is that we already conduct our 1st liter sampling according to these new 
rules and continue our support in codifying these requirements in the LCRI. Second, for utilities that do 
not have Tier 1 or Tier 2 sites, we support using all results from Tiers 3-5 to calculate the 90th 
percentile. Lastly, we support improved transparency of lead data and public health information to the 
community. We appreciate EPA’s clarification in the LCRI that utilities do not need to individually post 
tap monitoring results if those are already made available by the state. We are a large system whose 
state already posts both the individual home results as well as the 90th percentiles, and we support our 
interpretation that including links to those sites on our utility page is sufficient in complying with this 
requirement. For reference, our data are available at: 
• 
Individual home results: https://yourwater.oregon.gov/lead_copper_detail.php?pwsno=00657 
• 
90th percentile results: https://yourwater.oregon.gov/leadcopper.php?pwsno=00657  
Additionally, we offer the following comments. 
We request clarification on how utilities on annual monitoring implement standard sites for lead 
monitoring and reduced sites for copper monitoring.  
We are unclear how to implement standard sites for lead monitoring and reduced sites for copper 
monitoring when lead and copper are analyzed from the same samples and simultaneously by the 
same machine. Providing the option of reduced copper sites does not provide any efficiency or 
reduction in labor – it only provides confusion on how to implement. For a utility that collects 100 
samples, can they analyze 50 of those for lead and copper and 50 of them for only lead? What 
criteria should a utility use to choose those lead and copper homes versus only lead homes? Do we 
predetermine those homes, or conduct a random selection from the samples each monitoring round? 
If we had to apply this in Portland, we would likely run all 100 samples for both lead and copper since 
the bulk of the energy is working with customers to collect the samples and it is more straightforward 
for our lab staff to run the same analysis on all samples. A reduction of copper sites while maintaining 
lead sites would provide no benefit to us.  

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 5 
We request that non-lead service line utilities on annual monitoring be eligible for reduced sites 
for lead monitoring. 
For utilities that have no lead service lines and have demonstrated levels of lead below the action 
level, it is an undue burden to require they continue monitoring at a standard number of lead sites 
while on annual monitoring. We request that utilities who meet these criteria be able to monitor at the 
reduced number of sites.  
Service line inventory 
Portland supports EPA’s nationwide efforts in identifying and removing lead service lines from drinking 
water systems. As a utility that has never used lead service lines, historically had lead connectors, and 
is currently using a statistical inspection method to build our initial inventory, we offer the following 
comments.  
We request a waiver process for the inclusion of connectors in the baseline inventory if the 
utility has already removed all lead connectors.  
When Oregon banned lead pipes in 1985, it also required water providers to remove lead connectors 
and certify that no lead pipes exist in their system1. In 1985, Portland submitted its compliance plan to 
the state, implemented the comprehensive plan to identify and remove over 10,000 lead connectors, 
and in 1998 certified to the state that all known lead connectors were removed from the system2. 
Portland’s process to locate these lead connectors, which included tap cards, computer records, and 
field inspections, meets the criteria being used around the country today to locate lead service lines.  
We understand the EPA’s intent of including known, active lead connectors in the inventory to assess 
where they are currently located and provide residents important public health information; however, 
it is unclear how knowing where connectors used to exist is to be used by utilities or customers, 
especially since that information is not being collected for sites that used to have lead service lines. 
We anticipate that EPA has concerns about galvanized lines that used to be downstream of a lead 
connector, but as noted above in the tiering section, there is no existing evidence that these 
galvanized pipes continue to be a source of lead or that a location that once had a lead connector 
even has a galvanized service line still in use.  
Established by our evidenced-based and comprehensive removal of lead connectors decades ago, 
we request a waiver process for utilities that have removed all lead connectors from including 
connectors in their inventories. As part of this waiver, we support that these utilities would have to 
provide a statement on their website about how the utility inventoried and removed all connectors, 
similar to the required statement when a utility has certified that all service lines are non-lead. 
We request removing the connector category of “removed lead” or, at minimum, changing this 
to an optional subcategory.  
We are unclear on the intent for including “removed lead” as a category for service connectors. This 
category is inconsistent with service line categories, which do not keep track of where lead service 
lines have historically been located and removed. Additionally, we anticipate this connector category 
will create customer confusion and unnecessary alarm. From the customer perspective, it is not clear 
what actions, if any, they should take based on this information. We request that this category be 
 
1 Oregon Administrative Rule 333-061-0087(4): No lead pipe, lead goosenecks or similar appurtenances shall be 
used in the construction of any public water system and every water supplier must certify to the Authority that lead 
pipe, goosenecks or similar appurtenances do not exist within its water system. A water supplier that identifies the 
existence of lead components within its water system must submit a compliance schedule, acceptable to the 
Authority, for the removal of all lead components as described in this section. 
2 Portland’s certification that all lead connectors were removed: https://www.portland.gov/water/documents/lead-
pigtails-removed-1998/download  

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 6 
removed from the required category list. If maintained in the final rule, we recommend listing this as 
an optional subcategory – similar to how copper and plastic are optional subcategories for non-lead 
service lines. 
We request that service line inventory statistical inspections completed by utilities with no lead 
service lines be accepted for compliance with the validation requirements. 
We understand EPA’s intent with the validation process and appreciate the necessity of this step for 
some areas of the country. In Portland, we do not have lead service lines, we have a high degree of 
confidence that lead service lines have never been used in our system, and are currently using this 
same statistical inspection approach to certify with a 95% confidence that no lead service lines exist 
in our pool of unknown service lines. The intent of the validation process is the same: prove that the 
non-lead service lines that don’t have direct evidence are in fact non-lead. If non-lead service line 
utilities are already performing that statistical inspection to prove their inventory, it doesn’t make 
sense to repeat that activity. Therefore, we request that EPA allow previous statistical inspections that 
meet the validation criteria and already confirmed there are no lead service lines with 95% confidence 
be accepted for compliance with the validation requirements. Alternatively, we request EPA grant 
states the ability to provide waivers to utilities who meet these criteria. 
We request clarification that the two-point inspection as part of the validation requirement is a 
maximum of two points for the full line, regardless of ownership or split ownership.  
As the rule is written, it is not clear that the two-point inspection applies to the full line when there is 
split ownership. We request changes to the language about split ownership inspections that a 
maximum of two points are required for the full line from the main to the building.  
Public education and outreach 
Portland has extensive experience in effective public education and outreach initiatives that provides 
consumers the information they need to reduce their exposure to lead. Part of this is a successful 
results notification process where we prioritize notifications of high results by calling consumers with 
high results within one business day and then mail results letters to all consumers within a week. Over 
the past few years, we also have noted the growth of consumer preference to receive results digitally 
and meet that need by emailing digital copies of results upon request. 
We support and commend EPA’s changes to the health effects language and required CCR statement 
that increase the inclusivity of these statements. Through the LCRR comment process, Portland 
requested that these statements be changed to be gender neutral and we appreciate EPA’s 
consideration and implementation of these changes.   
In addition to this support, we offer the following comments. 
We request changing the timing of delivering lead result consumer notices to 5 business days 
for results above the practical quantitation limit (PQL) and 10 business days for results under 
the PQL.  
We support EPA’s intent to provide lead test results to consumers sooner than the current 
requirement of 30 days. However, the proposed 3 calendar days for postmarking a letter is not 
achievable. Our concerns with how to implement this proposed 3-day requirement are numerous; 
however, the largest is the fact that utility staff have zero control over when a letter is postmarked. On 
top of the uncertainty of how quickly USPS postmarks mail once it enters their facilities, outgoing 
letters from the utility first stop at a centralized mailing and delivery office that processes all official 
City of Portland mail. Utility staff cannot guarantee or verify that outgoing mail will be processed by 
the central office, delivered to USPS, and then postmarked by USPS in 3 calendar days. Instead, we 
propose 5 business days for results above the PQL and 10 business days for results below the PQL. 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 7 
This delivery timing allows utility staff to prioritize reaching out to consumers with higher results so 
that they can take actions sooner.  
We request changing the method of delivering lead result consumer notices to electronic 
delivery (email or data portal) as the default with option to request a paper copy.  
We support the proposed flexibility of notification methods when delivering lead result consumer 
notice and specifically want to highlight our support for the inclusion of “another method approved by 
State” in the LCRI. Portland customers request and expect electronic delivery of results, and this new 
flexibility allows us to meet those community needs. We strongly encourage EPA to take this a step 
further and fully modernize the consumer notification process by making electronic delivery the 
default delivery method with paper copies available upon consumer request. Electronic delivery would 
align the LCR with: 
• 
the upcoming CCR Rule revisions, which are codifying digital delivery options for the Drinking 
Water Quality Report while also requiring that paper copies are available upon request; 
• 
the medical industry, which adopted technology solutions to digitally communicate critical 
medical and health information to patients as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment 
Act of 2009; and  
• 
the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, where one purpose of the Act is to “provide for the 
dissemination of public information on a timely basis, on equitable terms, and in a manner that 
promotes the utility of the information to the public and makes effective use of information 
technology.” 
If the EPA maintains paper letters as the default notification method, this will codify a communication 
method that is decreasing in relevance, will force utilities to use a method that is not in alignment with 
consumer expectations, and is a larger burden on staff time and environmental resources. Digital 
communications are more efficient for utility staff: email is faster to put together relative to printing, 
folding, and stuffing an envelope, and has instant delivery. We acknowledge that paper letters are still 
preferred by some consumers and recommend following the CCR model of offering an easy way to 
request a paper copy. Portland suggests including the request for a paper copy of results in either the 
test kit order form or as part of the test kit materials.  
We request changes to increase efficiency and relevance in sharing lead data with public health 
agencies.  
Portland has a longstanding and successful collaboration with our county health agency and supports 
EPA’s efforts to establish and maintain these types of partnerships around the country through data 
and information sharing. We have been sending lead-in-water results to our county and state health 
agencies that investigate elevated blood lead level (EBLL) cases on a quarterly basis since 2016. 
With this deep experience and understanding of how to make these relationships successful, we offer 
the following recommendations to support success around the country: 
• 
Change delivery method from mail to email. Paper mail is an outdated business 
communication method. Email is the most common business communication practice and has a 
better chance at reaching the appropriate person who can act on the information. An email also 
allows utility staff to attach data in a digital format or spreadsheet, which is easier for health 
agency staff to receive and compare against their EBLL cases. Lastly, email delivery would 
align with our other regulatory reporting requirements, which are all completed to our regulator 
through email.  
• 
Remove regulatory bodies from this requirement to target agencies that provide EBLL 
case management or general public health services. We recognize that drinking water 
regulators across the country come in all shapes and sizes, including counties, tribal nations, 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 8 
states, and EPA. We also recognize that some regulators are in public health and some are in 
environmental protection. Because of this, we understand EPA’s intent with requiring data 
sharing with local and state public health agencies to make sure data is shared with agencies 
who are not regulators. However, regulators are already receiving utility data and providing 
regulatory oversight through other parts of the LCRI.  We believe that this section of the LCRI 
should instead focus on data sharing to support EBLL home investigations, case management, 
and other public health services. Staff conducting these activities have different data needs than 
drinking water regulators. We strongly suggest that only data that is understandable and 
actionable (e.g. home tap monitoring results) be shared with these agencies so that this is not a 
check-the-box activity but actually results in improving public health outcomes.  
• 
Remove sharing WQP data from requirements. We request that EPA clarifies the intent of 
sharing data, especially WQP data, with public health partners who are engaged in EBLL case 
management. Those data are most meaningful to utility staff and drinking water regulators and 
we fully support reporting these data to our regulators for regulatory oversight as specified in the 
reporting section of the LCRI. However, for our public health partners who have deep training in 
lead risk assessment or in the medical field, it is unclear what those staff are expected to do 
with WQP data. We do support either providing WQP data upon request or for states to post 
these data online with tap sampling results so that everyone has access to this data. 
• 
When sharing data with state health agencies, add a provision that this does not apply if 
your regulator is your state health agency. In Oregon, our drinking water regulator is part of 
the state health agency: the Oregon Health Authority. Under this proposed regulation, we would 
be required to send these data to them twice: as required here (annually by July 1) and through 
the distribution system and site assessment process. This is a duplicate effort and an undue 
burden on utility staff sending it and for regulatory staff receiving it. We request a provision be 
added that exempts utilities from repeating this reporting if their regulator is also the state health 
agency. 
• 
Maintain “another method approved by the State” provision in final rule. This provision 
allows state and utility flexibility in how to comply with this requirement in a way that is most 
meaningful to both utility staff and public health partners.  
We request clarification on the three additional outreach activities required during an 
exceedance.  
For the list of additional exceedance activities, the current LCR requires activities from three different 
types of categories (i.e. one paid ad, one PSA, and one public meeting). However, our interpretation 
of the proposed LCRI is that utilities could comply with this requirement with three activities from the 
same category (i.e. three public meetings). Is that interpretation correct? 
We request clarification on outreach to all multifamily units during an exceedance.  
One of the new LCRI provisions is to deliver a printed copy of the required exceedance public 
education materials to all multifamily units. Portland also noticed that this activity is included in the list 
of additional outreach activities. Does the required multifamily mailing also count as one of the three 
additional activities? 
Consumer Confidence Report (CCR) mandatory language 
We request additional considerations to make this statement more accessible to modern 
audiences. 
We appreciate EPA’s effort to codify the steps people can take to reduce their exposure to lead in 
water by adding them to the required CCR educational statement. Our concern with the proposed 
CCR statement is that by adding these steps in the middle, this has created a large block of text that 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 9 
creates more barriers to the information and is less accessible. Modern audiences avoid large blocks 
of text and plain language principles include using short paragraphs and bulleted lists. We 
recommend either applying these plain language principles to the final statement or allow utilities 
flexibility to format the statement as they choose, as long as all the text is present. We also strongly 
recommend coordinating with the EPA staff working on the CCR rule revisions to ensure that the 
content and the format of this statement meets the plain language goals they are trying to achieve. 
Schools and child care facilities 
We understand EPA’s intent of including schools and child care facilities in the LCRR and LCRI to 
provide comprehensive public health protection from lead in drinking water. We appreciate and support 
the continued inclusion of a waiver process for utilities where state or local rules already exist and 
continue to urge EPA to strengthen partnerships at the federal level to address all sources of lead 
exposure in schools and child care facilities. Portland has provided free lead-in-water testing to schools 
and child care facilities since 2016 and with that deep experience, offers the following comments.  
We request the 2 required samples at child cares be changed to align with 3Ts guidance.  
Many in-home child care providers only have one tap used for potable water: the kitchen sink. We are 
concerned that the LCRI requirement of testing two samples from each child care would result in 
sampling bathroom sinks or other taps not used for drinking water. This is in direct conflict with the 
3Ts guidance and the Oregon child care testing regulations, each of which specifies that facilities only 
test potable water locations. To provide consistency of testing requirements, we request that EPA 
instead adopt by reference the child care testing requirements in the 3Ts guidance. 
We request changes to the timing of notifying facilities, health departments, and state 
regulators of results.  
We have many concerns with the rolling 30-day results notification and reporting requirement, 
including delayed reporting to facilities, staff burden, and reporting redundancy. The premise of 
requiring a rolling reporting deadline for each sample or batch of samples is fundamentally not 
feasible. We agree that facilities need their results quickly and support that this results notification 
process is treated the same as other customer results notifications. However, rolling 30-day reporting 
to health agencies and the state has no precedent in other regulatory reporting and would be an 
unnecessary burden on utility staff conducting the reporting as well as the agency staff who will be 
inundated with data that will likely not be organized or even in tables. Based on our experience with 
implementing a school and child care testing program and our long partnership sharing data with local 
health agencies, we propose the following notification and reporting timelines.  
• 
Facilities: 5 business days for results above the practical quantitation limit (PQL) and 10 
business days for results under the PQL. Elementary schools and child care facilities directly 
serve a concentrated population of children, who are the most vulnerable to health impacts from 
the exposure of lead. Given that, we are curious why notification of results to these facilities has 
a much longer timeline (30 days) compared to the proposed 3-day timeline for consumer 
notices. We strongly recommend aligning delivery of results notifications for schools and child 
care facilities with the same timeline we propose for customer notifications: 5 business days for 
results above the PQL and 10 business days for results under the PQL. This will allow utilities to 
appropriately prioritize notifications to facilities with higher results so that the facility can quickly 
take actions to remove or remediate that drinking water outlet. 
• 
Local health agency: quarterly. We understand the intent of sharing these data with public 
health agencies but want to caution overburdening these staff with rolling reporting of data that 
may be challenging for them to track and manage. We currently share residential data with our 
health agency partners on a quarterly basis, which is a manageable period of data for them to 
compare against their elevated blood lead level cases. We initially tried monthly reporting, which 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 10 
ended up being too frequent. We also request that EPA clarifies what health agencies are 
intended to do with these data. In Oregon, child care providers are already required to report 
their results to their state regulator, who has oversight on the actions taken by the facility to 
remediate high results. It is unclear what additional actions EPA would expect public health 
agencies to do with this data. 
• 
State: quarterly. As noted in the public education section above, in Oregon our drinking water 
regulator is the same as our state health agency, so requiring that we report these results to 
both is duplicative. We recommend aligning health agency and state reporting so that both are 
quarterly and further recommend that reporting of results to the state be coupled with the 
certification of results notifications that are required in the reporting section below.  
• 
Waiver process for reporting. We request a reporting waiver process for systems where 
schools or child cares are regulated and required to report their results directly. In Oregon, the 
child care testing regulations require child care facilities to report their data to their state 
regulator within 10 days of receipt. Requiring a utility to send these same data to the state is 
duplicative and a waiver process would help reduce redundancy. 
We request clarification to the sampling frequency in the waiver criteria.  
In the sampling requirements and waiver criteria, EPA has not specified a sampling frequency for 
schools and child care facilities. Based on the 20% per year for elementary schools and child care 
facilities, it is implied that the sampling frequency is every 5 years; however, this 5-year frequency is 
not specified. Additionally, for secondary schools where sampling is not required, there is no implied 
frequency. We request that EPA adds a clearly defined frequency to the waiver requirements so that 
states and utilities can easily understand if current state or local testing rules meet the waiver criteria.   
Reporting 
We strongly urge EPA to continue combining reporting requirements to further streamline the reporting 
activities and reduce burden on both utility and regulator staff. The LCRI is complex with many required 
activities. We recognize it is a large task for EPA to create a reporting structure for all these activities as 
well as for regulators to receive these reports and provide utility oversight. We appreciate EPA’s efforts 
to continue simplifying the reporting burden for utility staff and provide the following comments for 
consideration. 
We request clarification on what the tap monitoring period is for consumer-requested samples, 
school and child care samples, and distribution system and site assessment samples. 
For each of these sampling initiatives, utilities are required to report monitoring data to the state within 
10 days after the monitoring period and certify the delivery of the consumer notice to the state within 
3 months after the monitoring period. However, the monitoring periods for these sampling initiatives 
are either not specified, ambiguous, or too short to meet these reporting deadlines. We provide the 
following recommendations for each of these initiatives. 
• 
Consumer-requested samples: create calendar year monitoring period. The LCRI does not 
currently specify a monitoring period for sampling conducted by consumers on a voluntary 
basis. We currently conduct annual reporting of these data to the state, which is a manageable 
frequency for utility staff to put together and for regulatory staff to review these data. 
• 
School and child care samples: create quarterly monitoring period. The LCRI currently has 
contradictory data reporting requirements outlined in the school and child care section – report 
data to the state within 30 days of receiving results – compared to the reporting section – report 
data to the state 10 days after the end monitoring period. We recommend both these sections 
are reconciled with the quarterly reporting that we recommended in our school and child care 
comments. Additionally, there is no reporting period specified for school and child care samples, 

 
Portland Water Bureau Comments on proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) 
 
 
Page 11 
which creates challenges for understanding how to comply with the 3 month certification of the 
consumer notice. We recommend utilities certify the consumer notice as part of the annual 
report of outreach and testing activities due on July 1. 
• 
Distribution system and site assessment (DSSA) samples: align reporting with state 
reporting required in Step 3 of DSSA. In steps 1 and 2 of DSSA, there is a 5-day monitoring 
period for the WQP samples and a 30-day monitoring period for the follow-up customer sample. 
Does the 10-day reporting deadline begin at the end of those 5 days and 30 days? Reporting 
results to the state on that timeline is unachievable and not feasible due to lab turnaround times. 
We recommend dropping the 10-day reporting deadline for DSSA samples and instead require 
reporting these results as part of the recommendation report submitted to the state in Step 3. 
We request the reporting timeline of consumer-requested monitoring data be changed from 10 
days to 60 days. 
We support and appreciate codifying the submission of additional monitoring data, specifically of 
consumer-requested testing results. However, as we also included in our LCRR comments, we 
continue to have strong concerns that 10 days is an insufficient time for reporting this dataset. 
Portland has an extensive customer-requested sampling program, which includes analyzing 
residential samples that were collected using one of our three sampling methods and includes 
customers from our 12 participating wholesale water provider districts. In order to organize data into a 
useful and understandable format that accurately describes the sampling method and organizes 
sample sets from the same home or building together, we require more than 10 days to compile this 
report. We request that this reporting requirement be changed to 60 days after the end of the 
calendar year for reporting all results collected the previous calendar year. 
Supporting comments from other organizations 
In addition to our comments above, we also support comments submitted by the Association of 
Metropolitan Water Agencies (AMWA) including: 
• 
AMWA’s request for the connector definition that the length is increased. 
• 
AMWA’s comment that the three-calendar day results notification is infeasible. 
• 
AMWA’s “upon request” alternative for schools and child cares and aligning testing procedures 
with 3Ts guidance. 
In summary, Portland strongly supports EPA’s effort to reduce the public’s exposure to lead in water. 
Protecting the health of children and those most vulnerable to lead is an essential task for water 
providers, and developing rules that are applicable to all water utilities around the country is a 
challenging endeavor. Thank you for providing us the opportunity to review and provide comments on 
these improvements. Portland is looking forward to seeing final rule when it is published later this year.

Dear Administrator Regan,
Attached are 8,235 comments submitted by advocates and supporters of the National Wildlife

Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements” under docket EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801.
15 - 22 million Americans are still drinking water out of lead service lines, despite the many health risks
lead poses to children, pregnant people, and adults. Most of the remaining lead pipes in the country
are concentrated in just a handful of states, and they disproportionately impact low-income
households and communities of color who are already overburdened with other sources of pollution
and lead-hazards. We appreciate the necessary improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule, but your

replaced.

and immediate action on the issue of lead contamination in drinking water. We urge you to strengthen
and advance the proposed improvements to protect our future generations from lead poisoning.

EPA must transform that "test and fix" policy to one that prevents lead contamination at every 
drinking water tap.

America's kids and educators deserve better. Just as we must replace every lead service line, 
federal policy should aim to prevent lead contamination at every tap at schools. Except where a 
school district or child care facility affirmatively opts out, the LCRI should require Community 
Water Systems (which serve 90% of schools) to implement one of the following options at 
schools and child care facilities: 
a) Prevent lead contamination at every tap, including: 
1. Filter first: Install and maintain point of use filters certified to remove lead on every 
tap used for drinking water, cooking or beverage preparation. As fountains contain 
lead and cannot accept filters at the point where water comes out, they should be 
replaced by new water stations with filters. A growing number of jurisdictions have 
already adopted some version of this "filter first" policy for schools -
Including Michigan, Philadelphia, Portland (OR) and the District of Columbia; 
2. JChealth-basedlimit on lead: Limit lead7n schools' water to T ppb, as recornmendea 
by the American Academy of Pediatrics. Schools and child care centers are 
particularly well-situated to meet this low lead concentration because they have full 
control of their water delivery systems - all the way to the tap. Taps should be tested 
after filter installation to ensure this standard is being met; and 
3. Get the lead out: To stop the cycle of lead contamination at school, new and 
replacement taps and plumbing should meet the Qs1 standard recently adopted 
by California, where lead leached into water is less than or equal to 1 ppb; or 
b) Test every drinking water tap at least once every 6 months, and then replace taps and install 
filters whenever lead concentrations exceed 1 ppb. While not ideal, this much more robust "test 
and fix" option would be more effective at reducing the likelihood of lead-contaminated water at 
school than the infrequent testing and no required remediation in the proposed rule. 
For the roughly 10% of schools and child care facilities that are federally regulated as Non-
Transient Non-Community Water Systems, the EPA can and should simply require the much 
more protective Option a) above in the LCRI rule. 
Right to Know: To counter the strong likelihood of a false sense of safety from inherently 
variable testing, the LCRI should also require a// water utilities to regularly communicate 
(including online) the following to families, educators and the public regarding schools and child 
care facilities: full test results showing any level of lead at each tap; that tests are variable and 
can fail to detect lead; that there is no safe level of lead; prevention/remediation measures taken 
at each tap; and any school districts or chilEI care--facilities opting out of their Community Water 
System's measures outlined above. 
In addition to these requirements for schools and child care centers regulated as NTNCWS, 
EPA should also incorporate policy changes that will better prevent lead contamination at all 
other schools and child care facilities: 
• Establish a clear preference for awarding grants aimed at prevention - such as replacing 
fountains with filter-equipped water stations - rather than funding more testing. 
Condition grants on adhering to the Right to Know provisions outlined above. 
• Change the name of EPA's 3 Ts Guidance to "Preventing Lead Contamination at Every 
Tap" and replace its "test-and-fix" recommendations with the prevention-oriented 
measures outlined above for LCR-regulated schools. 

America's children and educators need safe drinking water to thrive and be healthy. We urge 
the EPA to act more boldly to get the lead out at school. 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0906 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February, 5th, 2024 
Re: Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801,  
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
 
Michael Regan  
Administrator, US Environmental Protection Agency  
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20460 
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
I am writing this letter on behalf of Milwaukee Water Commons to commend the strides taken in the 
EPA’s proposed Lead and Copper Rule improvements, and to encourage this administration to further 
strengthen this proposal's impact on eliminating the threats of lead in water.  
No level of lead exposure is safe, a reality that has impacted generations of families around this country. 
In low income census blocks on the City of Milwaukee’s north and south sides more than one in four 
children under the age of six years old are considered lead poisoned. We are privileged to live along one 
of the world’s largest sources of freshwater, and yet, families still live in fear of the water coming from 
their tap because of lead infrastructure. Milwaukee’s Lead Service Line replacement program began in 
2017, and after almost 10 years of action on removing Milwaukee’s 70,000 lead service lines, there are 
still 65,000 lead service lines remaining. Enforcement of the Lead and Copper Rule is our opportunity to 
meet the urgency of the lead emergency happening in households in our city and around our country.  
We want to begin by thanking this administration for its commitment to taking steps to eliminate the 
public health hazards of lead infrastructure around the country. In particular we would like to commend 
the Environmental Protection Agency’s proposal to: 
● Enforce a 10-year replacement timeline for lead service line replacement – Milwaukee Water 
Commons has been advocating for a 10-year replacement timeline since our organization was 
founded, following input from over 1,500 residents from around Milwaukee who were calling 
for action to address the lead emergency in a single generation. We fully support this 
administration’s call to replace all of the country's lead service lines in 10 years, and are excited 
to see the EPA following through on that commitment in the proposed Lead and Copper Rule. 
● Lower the lead action level. It is a well-accepted fact that no amount of lead is safe in the 
human body. We are encouraged to see this proposal taking the regulation of our drinking 
water closer to that standard.  

● Require that communities of all sizes update their inventories of where Lead Service Lines 
exist. Milwaukee Water Commons has connected with a range of both small and large utilities 
across Wisconsin to unpack the implementation of the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, 
and we have learned that many utilities are facing significant disinvestment in the maintenance 
of water infrastructure. There are many instances around the state where communities have 
not developed a plan to approach major infrastructure replacements such as for lead service 
lines. Requiring the development of lead service line inventories will both be a major step 
towards planning for LSL removal and will help to communicate the need for funding and 
technical assistance in communities that feel underprepared to address that challenge.  
As we build momentum for lead service line replacement in the United States, both through the Lead 
and Copper Rule and the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law, it is critical that decision makers at all levels stay 
connected with organizers working on the ground to learn how regulations and programing can improve 
implementation and ensure that environmental justice is centered in both our national and local 
approach. We are joining many advocates from around the country both to celebrate the improvements 
in this proposal, and to do our part to continue to hone in on the role that federal regulation can play in 
ensuring that families are safe from lead in water. To further strengthen this proposal our organization is 
encouraging the EPA to: 
● Encourage equitable replacement of lead service lines, and take steps to eliminate the 
residential cost share for lead service lines. It is critical to ensure that residents burdened by 
the hazards of lead infrastructure do not foot the bill for removing lead service lines on their 
own. Requiring that utilities cover the cost does not mean that ratepayers will not be investing 
in the removal of their lead service lines, it means that we have the opportunity to lead with 
equity and affordability, and that residents restricted to living in housing with lead hazards by 
the limitations of their income are not held responsible for an injustice that they have been 
forced to endure. In many instances lead service lines, and lead poisoning, occur in a higher 
density in low income neighborhoods with older housing stock and a higher density of rental 
properties. For some families, the cost of replacing a lead service line could be an impossible 
hurdle. Renters may have no agency at all in whether, or how, the replacement of their lead 
service line is financed. Funding through the bipartisan infrastructure law has already made a 
commitment to ensure that disadvantaged communities are prioritized during lead service line 
replacement. It is critical that our approach to LSL removal does not exclude, or further burden, 
low income communities. To deliver on this administrations commitment to eliminating the 
threat of lead in water, LSL removal plans should be implemented with the assistance of 
principal forgiveness and utilizing affordability plans that spread the remaining cost of lead 
service lines equitably across the utility rate payer base.  
● Require lead testing for schools and incentivize filter installation at schools and childcare 
facilities. Under the current proposed rule, schools would be offered the opportunity to opt into 
testing for lead in water, but not required to do so. It is critical that we ensure children are safe 
from lead in water both at home and at school, and testing is one way to ensure that we are 
catching lead hazards and identifying solutions. One short term solution will be offering 
incentives for the installation of filtration systems at schools and child care facilities and 
ensuring that both internal and external lead plumbing are prioritized for replacement.  

● Lower the lead action level to an enforceable health-based standard of 5ppb or lower. Health 
professionals agree that no amount of lead is safe, and therefore our standards for lead in water 
should be the same. Though a 10-ppb standard is a major improvement, it is still insufficient 
compared to the calls to consider lead poisoning at 5 ppb.  
● Incentivize filter distribution as a short-term solution for all cities replacing lead service lines 
and strengthen the requirements for filter distribution to obtain compliance of local water 
systems with multiple Action Level Exceedances in 5 years. Filtration is a short-term solution to 
what has become a multigenerational emergency. Similar to national campaigns to distribute 
smoke detectors, a campaign to distribute filters can make households safer and educate 
residents on how to identify and avoid lead hazards. Especially in communities that have noted 
exceedances of the lead action level, filter distribution will build trust among the community 
that the issue is being taken seriously and grant more time for the utility to reach compliance.  
● Require a 10-year replacement timeline for the removal of all lead service lines. There are no 
exemptions for families facing the urgency of the national lead emergency, and so we believe 
that there should be no exemptions to the call for a 10-year replacement timeline.  
● Prepare additional resources through technical assistance centers to support utilities capacity 
to develop a workforce capable of replacing all lead service lines in a 10-year period. In 
addition to these regulatory changes, we want to acknowledge that the call for lead service line 
replacement within 10 years will be a tremendous effort and will require intentionality to grow 
the nation's water workforce. EPA should look critically at opportunities to support both public 
and private sector capacity to take on this ambitious proposal, by investing in technical 
assistance centers abilities to support equitable workforce development. This challenge will also 
be a major opportunity to create pathways to living wage employment for unemployed and 
underemployed individuals, eliminating barriers for women and people of color who are under-
represented in the nation's water sector.  
 
Sincerely, 
                                                  
 
   Brenda Coley   
 
 
                                   Joe Fitzgerald 
   Co-Executive Director   
 
 
        
      Policy and Advocacy Manager 
   Milwaukee Water Commons  
 
                     Milwaukee Water Commons

Re: Comments on National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements 
Dear Assistant Administrator Fox: 
Members of the Environmental Council of the States (ECOS) appreciate the opportunity to comment on 
the proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (LCRI). 
ECOS appreciates EPA’s efforts on the challenging and important work of updating the 1991 Lead and 
Copper Rule (LCR). In the following comments, ECOS encourages additional resources for states to adjust 
to the proposed LCRI requirements. ECOS suggests that U.S. EPA develop timely guidance for states on 
messaging and implementation and further engage with states on data management. ECOS also offers 
ideas for strategic targeted filter distribution and lead sampling requirements. The results of these 
revisions will affect the state and territorial water programs that will implement the changes, and ECOS 
advocates for the position of the states as a group. Please look to state letters for additional information, 
technical comments, and state-specific issues. 
Funding for Lead Service Line Replacement 
While the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law (BIL) is delivering funding that will make significant progress in 
removing lead service lines (LSL), it will not be adequate to meet the needs for lead pipe removal around 
the country. The BIL invests $15 billion towards LSL replacement through the Drinking Water State 
Revolving Fund (DWSRF). ECOS has long touted the importance of the DWSRF and continues to urge 
Congress to fully fund the DWSRF to support drinking water infrastructure improvements, including, but 
not limited to, LSL replacement. Water infrastructure improvements are critical to the provision of clean 
and safe drinking water, and are especially pressing in communities with populations disproportionally 
impacted by environmental issues. As stated in ECOS Resolution 16-5, Addressing Serious Needs 
Regarding Drinking Water and Clean Water Infrastructure Investment, ECOS supports efforts to prioritize 
efficient, affordable, and timely awards to those communities. 
Despite the historic BIL investments, additional funding is needed to meet the estimated $45 billion cost 
of replacing the country’s lead pipes, including to support increased workload for state primacy 
agencies. States and EPA should continue to work together to advocate for the additional needed 
funding to meet this critical public health goal.  
 
 
 

Environmental Council of the States 
  
 
 
Page 2 of 3 
 
Public Education and Messaging 
While the elimination of LSLs will significantly reduce the risk of lead contamination of drinking water, 
EPA should take care to continue to include the importance of effective corrosion control in its messaging 
since other potential sources of lead in drinking water remain. EPA should develop guidance and draft 
templates for various Public Education and Public Notices as soon as possible, and no later than six 
months prior to the compliance deadline. The guidance and templates will help the states and EPA more 
clearly and consistently convey information to the public. EPA should seek out examples from states on 
effective messaging to include in its guidance and templates. 
Implementation Guidance and Training 
Prompt, clear, and effective guidance and technical support will be necessary for states to successfully 
implement this rule. ECOS requests that EPA collaborate closely with states to develop and publish all 
implementation and data management guidance documents as soon as possible, and no later than six 
months prior to the rule’s effective date. Consistent with ECOS Resolution 11-8, On the Use of Guidance, 
timely guidance is necessary for states to effectively draft state regulations, update and align their data 
management systems, and implement the revised rule. 
Due to the complexity of the proposed rule, ECOS requests detailed guidance and training for both states 
and water suppliers on new requirements. Topics that states have identified that will require guidance 
and training include corrosion control treatment (CCT) optimization, re-optimization, and optimal water 
quality parameter designation; review and approval of CCT studies; the types of reports and records 
each agency needs to track and in what format; monitoring for lead in schools and childcare facilities; 
tap monitoring requirements including the stagnation requirements, acceptable sample tap 
descriptions, and criteria for state invalidation of samples; and small water system compliance flexibility. 
ECOS recommends the Office of Water work with states and ORD on developing the necessary guidance 
and training. 
Data Management 
Any new or modified rule has significant data management and resource implications. Prior to the rule’s 
effective date, states will need adequate time and resources to adjust their business processes, train 
staff, and implement new or modified data management systems. States, tribes, and EPA have adopted 
an E-Enterprise for the Environment Digital Strategy, September 2023 and provided expectations around 
operationalizing the principles of the EE Digital Strategy. Consistent with these principles and the EE 
Digital Strategy, EPA should engage with states as early as possible to enable timely development of the 
data management infrastructure and processes necessary to meet the rule’s requirements. Due to the 
modernization of the Safe Drinking Water Information System (SDWIS), state agencies need to 
understand what functionality changes will occur during the transition to the Drinking Water State-
Federal-Tribal Information Exchange System (DW-SFTIES), and on what timeline. EPA should plan to 
provide guidance and instruction to states with adequate time to plan for changes to SDWIS and to be 
able to effectively implement a new rule. ECOS also urges EPA to engage with states in identifying the 
best solution for reporting new data elements to EPA. Please see ECOS Resolution 13-4, Environmental 
Performance and Outcomes Data and Metrics, concerning additional considerations regarding the costs 
and burdens associated with new and ongoing data reporting requirements and ECOS Resolution 11-2, 
Respectful Use of Data, concerning collaborative data stewardship with joint governance processes 
related to data quality, change management, data context and presentation, testing data reporting tools, 
and data releases. ECOS also recommends EPA review existing data reporting requirements for any that 

Environmental Council of the States 
  
 
 
Page 3 of 3 
 
are obsolete or no longer necessary to minimize overall data management and reporting burden to 
states. 
Filter Distribution 
For drinking water systems with three or more Action Level Exceedances, states suggest that rather than 
having filters distributed to the entire service area, systems should be able target that distribution to 
customers with greater risk of exposure only. Those would include locations with LSL, galvanized 
requiring replacement, or unknown lines. Providing filters to customers with known, non-lead lines could 
hurt public confidence in the drinking water system, add extra cost and burden to the system, and may 
unnecessarily incur costs that divert funding from activities with the greatest environmental and public 
health benefits. ECOS recommends amending this requirement and providing states with the authority 
to require additional filter distribution at their discretion based on available sampling, data, CCT, and 
other factors.  
Lead Sampling in Schools and Childcare Facilities 
ECOS recommends EPA change the proposed provision to allow states to issue waivers to community 
water systems from the requirement for lead sampling in schools and childcare facilities during the five-
year period after the LCRI compliance date if the facility was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021. 
States suggest changing the sampling date to January 1, 2014, which coincides with the Reduction of 
Lead in Drinking Water Act and would include sampling efforts that resulted from funding from 
America’s Water Infrastructure Act of 2018 and the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation 
Act.  
 
ECOS continues to advocate for early, meaningful, and substantial state and territorial engagement as co-
regulators in EPA’s development and implementation of federal environmental statutes and related 
rules, as noted in ECOS Resolution 14-3, Federal Financial Resources for State Environmental Programs. 
ECOS asks that EPA consider the above comments in conjunction with the comments from individual 
states and those from the Association of State Drinking Water Administrators, which are more extensive 
and provide greater technical detail from state drinking water experts.  
ECOS members look forward to continuing to work with EPA to improve the protection of public health 
and the environment by reducing exposure to lead in drinking water. If you have any questions regarding 
this correspondence, please contact me at bgrumbles@ecos.org or 202-266-4920.

Ben Grumbles 
Executive Director
