Dear Sir or Madam: 
 
Subject:  Comments on Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, Docket ID No. EPA–
HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
The Alameda County Water District (ACWD) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on 
the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI). The EPA is proposing to require water systems to replace lead service lines, remove the 
lead trigger level, reduce the lead action level to 0.010 mg/L, and strengthen tap sampling 
procedures, among other changes that would improve public health protection and simplify the 
rule relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR).  As a public water utility that 
serves water to over 344,000 people in the cities of Fremont, Newark, and Union City in the San 
Francisco Bay Area, ACWD has a strong commitment to the protection of public health through 
the development of stringent and effective drinking water regulations. 
 
On December 6, 2023, EPA announced in the Federal Registry the availability for public comment 
of the proposed LCRI. Prior to this time, lead and copper were regulated under the Lead and 
Copper Rule (LCR) promulgated in 1991 - 40 CFR Part 141 Subpart I, which was subsequently 
revised by the LCR Minor Revisions in 2000, the LCR Short-Term Revisions in 2007, and the 
LCRR in 2021. 
 
ACWD supports the development of EPA’s LCRI, and requests consideration of the following 
comments: 
 
1. Lead Service Line Inventory (LSLI) 
 
a) Include Provisions in the LCRI Which Allow Other Means to Demonstrate that an 
Existing Galvanized Service Line Does Not Require Replacement.  

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Page 2 
February 5, 2024 
 
 
The LCRR defines galvanized service lines requiring replacement (GRR) as “galvanized 
service lines that are or ever were downstream of an LSL” (Lead Service Line), and the LCRI 
expands the definition of an LSL to include lead connectors. 
 
ACWD supports EPA’s goal of reducing lead exposure in drinking water by identifying and 
replacing lead service lines and agrees with the LCRI that “focusing the proposed service line 
replacements requirements on LSLs and galvanized service lines that are or were downstream 
of an LSL will allow these more significant lead sources to be eliminated as quickly as feasible, 
and with lower overall replacement program costs.”  ACWD, like many other utilities, has 
consolidated other water systems into its system throughout its long history.  As with many 
agencies, standards and detailed records for water main and service line installations did not 
exist in a retrievable format until several decades after our formation as a Community Water 
System (CWS).  Consequently, ACWD does not have records of service line materials which 
were installed prior to the establishment of standards or the maintenance of retrievable records.  
This definition of GRR would essentially require replacement of all customer-side service lines 
which are made of galvanized material unless records exist to prove otherwise.  Though 
ACWD does not have a history of installing LSLs in our service area, and through our LSLI 
efforts, ACWD has confidence that we have no existing lead service lines or existing lead 
connections in the utility-owned portions of our service area, it is impossible to confirm that a 
leaded line or connection did not exist sometime in the past, beyond the span of ACWD’s 
existing standards or records. By requiring ACWD to classify private service lines as GRR 
when explicit records do not exist to prove that the public portion of the service line “was never 
downstream” of a LSL, this provision may be interpreted to require ACWD to divert very 
significant funding, resources, and time from other priorities (including voluntary efforts to 
further optimize public health protection) toward replacing lines that were never impacted by 
an LSL. 
 
ACWD appreciates EPA’s acknowledgement within the LCRI of “scarce system and State 
resources” and requests EPA consider the development of provisions other than records to 
identify GRR services, such as institutional knowledge based on interviews and observations 
of long tenured field maintenance staff, or a defined sampling routine.  
 
The LCRI expands the LCRR definition of an LSL to include lead connectors up to two feet 
in length, for identification of GRRs.  ACWD completed an inventory of lead service line 
material in 2020, for the utility-owned portion of service lines, for compliance with California 
Senate Bills 1398 and 427, which identified no lead service lines in our service area.  The 
inventory development process included checking for the presence of lead connectors through 
means of record reviews, service line repairs/replacement records, main replacement projects, 
field verifications, and staff interviews, and no LSLs or lead connectors were discovered. This 
inventory was conducted based on the material of water mains currently in place and would 
not necessarily account for a potential lead-containing connector between a service line and a 
main which may have been replaced decades prior, and though that main replacement would 
normally include the replacement of the utility-owned portion of the service line, it would not 
have included the portion of the service line on the customer’s property.  Retaining the 

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Page 3 
February 5, 2024 
 
 
inclusion of connectors, coupled with the requirement for CWSs to demonstrate that a 
galvanized line was never downstream of a connector which may have contained lead, would 
essentially require the replacement of all galvanized customer-side service lines which were in 
place prior to a CWSs retrievable records of installation, and may also introduce the complexity 
for CWSs to reassess their already in progress or completed LSL inventories for the potential 
historical presence of previous lead connectors, which would be both resource intensive and 
conceptually challenging.  
 
ACWD requests EPA consider allowing or developing alternative means to determine if a 
galvanized service line was ever downstream of a potentially lead-containing connector, such 
as grandfathering inventory information which was collected and submitted in support of State 
LSLI requirements.  If an alternative method to determine GRRs cannot be developed, EPA 
should update the economic impact analysis to account for the associated costs of replacement 
of potentially all customer-owned portions of galvanized service lines that a CWS cannot prove 
were never downstream of a LSL, or downstream of a connector which potentially contained 
lead.   
 
b) Provide Funding Directly to Property Owners for Private Service Line Replacements. 
 
The LCRI includes requirements to replace both the utility-owned and privately owned 
portions of LSLs, and removes language included in the LCRR that addressed who would pay 
for the work of replacement.   
 
ACWD supports EPA’s goal of reducing lead exposure in drinking water through the 
replacement of LSLs.  Prior to the introduction of the LCRR, ACWD’s responsibility for 
service lines has always stopped at the water meter.  Requiring CWSs to replace the private 
portion of service lines would expose CWSs to potentially significant liability and costs.  
Replacement of private service lines cannot be assumed to be a cookie-cutter process due to 
the wide range of factors that can affect a replacement.  For example, a service line that runs 
through a grass front yard will cost less to replace than a service line that runs underneath 
concrete or pavers.  Replacing items such as concrete or pavers can result in aesthetic issues 
that the customer will demand the utility to resolve. Without clear guidance or cost caps per 
replacement, it is anticipated that replacement costs will balloon.  As a mid-sized water utility 
with a diverse customer base, ACWD’s experience attempting to utilize existing federal and 
state funding streams to support regulatory compliance has indicated that they can be difficult 
and costly for CWSs to take advantage of due to eligibility constraints or other nuances of the 
specific funding effort.  
 
ACWD requests EPA consider clarifying that property owners are responsible for replacement 
of private side service lines and offering the use of grants directly to the property owners to 
fund private service line replacements, rather than placing responsibility on CWSs to replace 
LSLs on private property. 
 
 

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Page 4 
February 5, 2024 
 
 
c) Extend Initial Inventory Submittal Deadline of October 16, 2024. 
 
The LCRI extends compliance dates in the LCRR with the exception of the LSL inventory, 
and associated notification and reporting requirements. 
 
ACWD supports EPA’s extension of the compliance deadline to implement the revisions 
included in the LCRI, and agrees that this would facilitate a more effective implementation of 
the multiple enhancements to public health protection.  The LCRR includes requirements for 
CWSs to fulfill regarding services classified as a material type of “unknown,” and to make the 
inventory publicly accessible.  Additionally, the LCRI includes provisions which may affect 
the final inventory service line classification, particularly in regard to determining GRRs.  This 
combination of provisions adds a level of complexity into current inventory efforts since it 
could be confusing for customers if a service line can be identified as galvanized non-lead 
under the requirements of the LCRR and needs to be reclassified as a GRR under the 
requirements of the LCRI.  Conversely, it would be an unnecessary use of resources to classify 
a service as “unknown” and comply with the associated requirements thereof, for a service 
which ultimately would not be a GRR. 
 
ACWD requests EPA consider extending the deadline for submission of the initial lead service 
line inventory to provide time for CWSs to accurately conduct the inventory according to the 
guidance in the LCRI and provide more consistent messaging for customers. 
 
d) Reduce Required Number of Customer Outreach Attempts for Privately Owned LSLs from 
Four to Two. 
 
The LCRI includes provision for CWSs to make a reasonable effort to obtain property owner 
consent for replacing customer-owned service lines. As proposed in the LCRI, a reasonable 
effort would include at least four customer outreach attempts using at least two different 
communication methods. 
 
ACWD is supportive of improved customer outreach.  However, four outreach attempts 
by CWSs would increase the burden without added public health benefits.   ACWD 
requests EPA take into consideration the cost and resources for CWSs and suggests the 
outreach attempts be reduced to two, as proposed under the LCRR.   
 
2. Tap Sampling for Lead and Copper 
 
a) Remove Requirement for Delivery of Lead and Copper Tap Sampling Results to Residents 
Within 3 days for Customers Below the Action Level. 
 
The LCRR includes the requirement to provide customer tap sample results within 3 days when 
the action level is exceeded.  EPA is proposing in the LCRI that CWSs deliver all consumer 
notices of lead or copper tap sampling results within three days, regardless of whether the 
results exceed the lead or copper action levels. 

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Page 5 
February 5, 2024 
 
 
ACWD supports EPA’s efforts for timely customer notification for those customers whose 
lead sample results exceed the action level.  However, the requirement of notifying customers 
with 3 days regardless of the lead results does not provide additional benefits and may not be 
consistently achievable by some agencies.  Additionally, requiring CWSs to notify all sampling 
participants, regardless of their test results, in such a short timeframe could divert CWS staff 
attention from focusing on the messaging and notifications of those customers whose test 
results exceeded the action levels.  ACWD requests EPA consider extending this time period 
to a minimum of 15 business days, for participants whose sample results are below the action 
level, to allow CWSs staff sufficient time to organize data and create customer-friendly 
notifications and education materials. Alternatively, if a shorter notification timeline is 
required, please consider allowing the initial notification to be made via phone call, text 
message, and/or email followed-up with written customer-friendly material within 30 days. 
 
3. Public Notification 
 
a) Re-evaluate or Provide Guidance for Tier 1 Messaging for 90th Percentile Results Above 
the Action Level of 0.010 mg/L. 
 
Under the LCRR, CWSs must comply with the Tier 1 public notification requirement for a 
lead action level of 0.015 mg/L.  Additionally, EPA is proposing under the LCRI that CWSs 
must comply with Tier 1 public notification requirements when sample results exceed the 
proposed revised lead action level of 0.010 mg/L.  
 
ACWD is supportive of EPA efforts to improve public notification in regard to health risks 
associated with lead in drinking water.   A Tier 1 public notification has historically been used 
for providing information to the public about drinking water hazards that pose an immediate 
risk to public health such as E. coli or nitrate.  
 
ACWD requests EPA provide messaging guidance for the Tier 1 public notifications 
associated with 90th percentile (P90) results that are above the action level such that the 
notification language is not unnecessarily alarming to customers.  The P90 value is a ranked 
value derived from sample results from selected homes that are most susceptible to lead 
contamination in drinking water.  These homes are generally not representative of the majority 
of homes in the service area.  ACWD does not have lead service lines, and it has been ACWD’s 
experience that sample results greater than the detection limit are normally associated with 
internal customer plumbing in homes that have not gone through plumbing modernization.    In 
these cases, the potential health risk may not be present for the majority of customers in the 
distribution system, who would be receiving the Tier 1 public notifications.  ACWD suggests 
that EPA consider a more targeted approach to messaging directed to the locations where 
sampling indicates that lead levels are higher than the action level.  
 
 

Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Page 6 
February 5, 2024 
 
 
4. Lead Sampling at Schools and Child Care Facilities 
 
a) Consider Expanding, from January 1, 2021, to January 1, 2017, the Timeframe for Prior 
School Lead Sampling Results to be Considered Acceptable as Part of the Initial School 
Lead Sampling. 
 
The LCRR requires CWSs to conduct lead sampling at schools and childcare facilities that 
were constructed prior to January 1, 2014, or the date the State adopted standards that meet the 
definition of lead-free in accordance with section 1417 of the Safe Drinking Water Act, 
whichever is earlier.  Initially, all elementary schools and childcare facilities would be sampled 
within 5 years of the rule compliance date and then upon request, once every five years 
afterward. The LCRI includes a provision for CWSs to attain waivers for the initial round of 
sampling provided the schools had been sampled after January 1, 2021, in acknowledgement 
that some states have enacted legislation regarding school lead sampling since the LCRR was 
promulgated.   
 
ACWD supports EPA’s goal of the reduction of exposure to lead in drinking water at schools 
and requests EPA consider expanding the date for waiver eligibility to January 1, 2017.  In 
2017, ACWD conducted outreach offering lead sampling at K-12 schools in its service area as 
required by the State of California Division of Drinking Water’s amendment to our water 
supply permit.  Between 2017 and 2019, ACWD conducted additional lead sampling at all 
public K-12 schools and preschools and child day care facilities located on public school 
properties in compliance with California Assembly Bill 746.  This sampling included five 
samples per school and was conducted according to the guidance contained in EPAs 3Ts 
Toolkit, which is the same guidance referenced in the LCRI. Additional sampling of the same 
locations using the same methodology may not provide additional health benefit.  ACWD is 
supportive of reducing exposure to lead in drinking water for children and requests that EPA 
consider amending the waiver eligibility timeframe to encompass school lead sampling 
conducted in support of the earlier legislative and regulatory efforts within California to 
minimize lead exposure for children in schools.

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
1 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
General Matters 
 
Whether the proposed revisions to the 
LCRR treatment technique are 
effective to prevent known or 
anticipated adverse health effects to 
the extent feasible in accordance with 
the SDWA. 
While the rule goes a long way to reduce lead, through requiring lead service line removal, it 
implicitly minimizes the importance of premise plumbing and other sources of lead beyond the 
service line. While there are lead service lines in use in Vermont, essentially all action level 
exceedances in the past decade of LCR implementation have been from premise plumbing or 
lead content in various appurtenances and equipment. Minimizing the role premise plumbing 
plays is counter to public health protection. 
 
As detailed below, Vermont DWGPD has concerns about the ability for a water system to cease 
monitoring for entry point and/or distribution water quality parameters, as this is the first 
indicator of excursions and likely impacts “down the line”. Continuing the entry point monitoring 
would be a good way to assess the anticipated adverse health effects early while reducing the 
burden of the distribution WQP monitoring.  
Whether there are additional ways EPA 
could reduce the complexity of the 
regulatory approach used to address 
lead in drinking water consistent with 
the statutory standard for a treatment 
technique rule in section 1412(b)(7)(A) 
of SDWA. Specifically, EPA requests 
comment on ways that the proposed 
LCRI could be simplified and ways that 
burden, including paperwork burden, 
could be reduced without affecting the 
ability of the rule to prevent known or 
anticipated adverse health effects. 
Vermont DWGPD suggests reducing, streamlining, and even eliminating some of the annual 
certifications, notifications, education, and updates that a water system is required to do as 
individual requirements. These individual steps will need to be tracked system-by-system and 
step-by-step, will likely lead to increased non-compliance, and as part of that, will erode 
consumer confidence in the product delivered. It will also mandate technical rule manager staff 
into focusing time and attention on the more administrative aspect of the rule and not the 
technical content. Vermont has limited staffing to implement these rules; so, time spent tracking 
annual notice and education is time taken away from technical and compliance assistance. 
 
The CCR is a powerful tool that can be updated to include most if not all of that information 
directed in the LCRI, but if that is the approach, it must be done using plain language and not 
complicated wording that is difficult to translate and difficult for non-industry individuals to 
understand. 
 
A streamlined inventory document, including some of the required metrics all in one place would 
also streamline the “paperwork” requirements of the regulation so that things can be tracked in 
“bunches” not individual submissions. The more individual compliance items, and with separate 
due dates, means there are more items to track for already burdened water system operators 
and state staff.

We recommend prohibiting re-connecting lead service lines once disconnected except in rare 
instances of emergency or critical need. Otherwise, EPA regulations and/or plumbing code 
should be expanded to prohibit something that is largely outside of the control of the water

linked with the individuals making those connections – the plumbers.  
 
It is a difficult argument to say that a lead line segment of 25 inches will have a dramatically 
different impact on public health than a lead connector of 23 inches; especially if that connector 
is upstream of a galvanized line.   
 
We would support making the known connectors a mandatory replacement when upstream of 
galvanized, however, the associated funding needs to be provided as discussed elsewhere in 
these comments.  A blanket mandate of replacing lead connectors within 10 years will create an 
additional burden with which water systems cannot comply readily. Without records, identifying 
a 10-inch segment of lead pipe would be very difficult to do via sequential sampling, so leeway 
needs to be given for “connector unknown” or unvalidated connectors if it becomes a mandate.

bridges for future engagement and support, however selecting an arbitrary number feels 
insufficient. We would defer to other states with more related experience to assign the correct 
number based on their experience.

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
4 
 
The proposed minimum replacement 
rate and replacement deadlines. EPA 
is seeking comment on whether it is 
feasible for systems across the nation 
to complete service line replacement 
in a shorter timeframe than ten years, 
such as in six, seven, or eight years. 
EPA is seeking comment on the rate 
construct approach, including how to 
calculate compliance with a given 
service line replacement deadline and 
average annual rate calculated across 
a rolling three-year period. EPA also 
seeks comment on whether systems 
should be required to meet a minimum 
replacement rate in the first three

States an opportunity to enforce 
replacement rate progress sooner than 
three years after the compliance date. 
EPA also seeks comment on the 
complexity of the rate construct.  
The rate approach is problematic. It does not take into account the real life demands of a water 
system operator/public works department- they read meters, they do other planned 
maintenance, they respond to breaks and leaks; in Vermont many plow roads, pave roads, 
simultaneously operate the wastewater system. They are also dealing with other complicated 
drinking water regulations such as PFAS. To say that a system can devote 100% of their attention 
to lead removal is ambitious. The preamble cites situations such as Newark, NJ and Flint, MI, 
both of which are extreme examples and national-level priorities. They were certainly all-hands-
on-deck, and we don’t say this to minimize the importance of lead removal, but in reality, most 
‘average’ water systems do not have the capacity to deploy like resources were deployed in Flint 
or Newark. 
 
In Vermont, our fifth largest community water system has been working since 2017 to inventory 
service lines with service line replacement starting in 2021, in a project fully funded by federal 
funds (pre-BIL). Granted, this includes impacts from the Covid-19 pandemic, however, they have 
also simultaneously been addressing PFAS and expanding the distribution mains considerable 
distances to add on hundreds of homes that had private wells contaminated with PFAS.  This 
demonstrates the real-world situation we are under; working with a very devoted water system 
and consultants to inventory approximately 1,500 of the 4,000+ connections and removal of just 
under 500 GRR or lead/partial lead service lines. The system is not expected to complete 
inventorying and removal of LSLs/GRR until at least 2025 or 2026. They are doing everything they 
can to complete approximately 100 line replacements per year and are working with the most 
experienced consulting firm in the State on the matter.  Much of our world, and likely other small 
states and systems are not constructed in a simple grid like large cities, so it takes more 
resources to “mobilize” and replace lines, integrate with state permitting for road construction, 
and other state and local permits.    
 
In Vermont service lines are buried 6+ feet down, so trenching/digging/pulling in new lines is 
labor intensive especially considering rocky, rural terrain, further complicated by seasonal 
limitations on work/construction season that at best runs from mid-May to mid-December. 
 
If a water system conducts partial service line replacement and all associated notice, filters, re-
sampling, etc. then that line should “count” toward the system’s rate and ultimate completion. 
The difficulty is the permitting, mobilization and digging under the road/sidewalk/right of way.

The proposed requirement to ban 
partial lead and GRR service line

While Vermont DWGPD agrees that partial replacements pose significant health risks, it is still 
removing a major source of lead which, in the long run, will be beneficial; especially if/when 
properties change ownership, and the new owners are willing to engage.  The process 
established in the rule about pre-replacement notice/education, provision of filters, post-
replacement flushing and sampling would help alleviate public health concerns directly 
following replacement.  If the goal is to remove as much lead as possible, there are safeguards in 
place, and the water system can document the owner declining to replace the private segment, 
then partial replacement should be allowed.  It cannot be done in a vacuum or without 
signoff/declining on behalf of the owner. There must be steps to satisfy to warrant the partial, not 
just that the system could not be bothered to attempt to work with the private side owner.  
The ability of the market to correct for 
potential shortages in workers and 
materials to conduct service line 
replacement, as well to provide 
sufficient quantities of filters to 
comply with the service line 
replacement and other relevant 
provisions in the proposal. 
Vermont is a rural and isolated state. It is highly likely that larger states and municipalities in the 
region will dominate the market and purchase filters, making it difficult and therefore expensive 
to obtain filters in Vermont. The assumption in the rule that manufacturers will rise to the 
challenge is ambitious.  What is more likely to happen is that systems and homeowners will turn 
to online retailers that source products internationally and may not meet the ANSI/NSF 
standards.  We have seen this with school plumbing replacements given the recent national 
prioritization of these sorts of things, kitchen spray nozzles were hard to find, so the school went 
online and, unknowingly, purchased a product that did not meet US plumbing code. 
 
If filters are a long-term option, they need to be made a “fundable” expense under the DWSRF. 
Otherwise, systems will not have the ongoing revenue to support their purchase and upkeep.  
Many small and rural water systems do not charge a sufficient water rate and operate at a break-
even budget. Purchasing, maintaining, and replacing filters will increase costs significantly for a 
small system.

Comment on the proposed updated

“bottles that are one liter in volume 
with a mouth, whose outer diameter 
measures at least 55 mm wide,” and 
specifically on the availability of 
qualifying bottles. 
Labs in Vermont have made valiant efforts since 2016 to procure and use wide-mouth bottles for 
analytic purposes. However, they report that many wide-mouth bottles do not have a 1-liter fill 
line and many that have fill lines are not truly to the full capacity of 1liter required for the analysis, 
adversely impacting the QA/QC process. The assumption that sufficient bottles will be available, 
and that they will be able to meet the 1st and 5th liter sampling is problematic based on our 
experiences since 2016. 
 
The rule is unclear about whether the 55 mm reflects the opening aperture, includes the threads, 
or the measurement with the cap on. Simply put, the internal opening should be what is 
measured and required (and adjusted from the expected 55mm external opening accordingly).

Vermont DWGPD Response 
Comment and any relevant data on the 
number and tiering of samples used to 
calculate the 90th percentile lead 
and/or copper levels for systems with 
LSLs for purposes of assessing CCT 
efficacy. Specifically, whether samples 
from non-LSL sites that have higher 
lead concentrations than samples 
from LSL sites should be included and 
whether these higher values should 
replace lower values from LSL sites in 
the 90th percentile calculation. 
The highest sample results should be used to assess the 90th percentile, regardless of tier. The 
likelihood is that in systems with insufficient Tier 1 locations these locations would represent a 
greater percentage of the system infrastructure and possible lead exposure.   
 
Not counting the highest results also creates confusion for the users who see high results, but 
they aren’t “counted”; this can lead to an education/outreach problem where it looks like the 
system or the State are covering things up. As we have learned in the last several years, 
everything pertaining to this rule needs to be easily understood and its implementation needs to 
be transparent.  
 
In the preamble there is discussion about whether any sample, including customer-requested 
sampling would be used to calculate the 90th percentile. From a workload standpoint and 
monitoring framework standpoint, it would be difficult for states to manage “random” data 
arriving at random intervals but be required to apply it toward the 90th percentile, especially 
if/when a system samples early in the monitoring period and there has been considerable work 
to assess that they did not exceed the action level, for then a random sample to arrive months 
later and require a re-review of everything and potentially changing course. This would mean tap 
notices which would need to go out within 3 days of receipt of results would all need to be 
changed if the action level is exceeded and would lead to user confusion and lack of trust.  
 
There is also concern that this could lead to more “gaming” of the system whereby a system may 
receive 10-20 more samples per monitoring period from locations that are not highest risk/Tier 1 
sites, so it would change the 90th percentile by allowing “more” samples above the action level to 
not count toward the action level.  
Comment on whether State authority 
to specify sampling locations when a 
system is conducting reduced 
monitoring should apply regardless of 
the number of taps meeting sample 
site criteria. 
What is it that EPA is attempting to address by limiting/setting the sampling locations? If it wants 
to assess those locations with the highest concentrations, then require that under reduced 
monitoring, the sampling locations include the top “X” number of locations when sampling 
under standard monitoring.  Currently the State would have difficulty asserting authority to do so, 
but this could be easily done in the final LCRI.

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801

EPA is proposing a requirement for

non-lead service lines in their

along the line. EPA is requesting

For many NTNCs the service/supply line can be visually inspected at one point.  This new 
requirement would necessitate an excavation or supplemental records review for every NTNC. 
Clarity around distinguishing between community and NTNCs should be provided since digging 
at all NTNCs state-wide is prohibitive for each system to engage and mobilize individually for a 
single or very small number of lines. If adequate records exist and a visual inspection can be 
performed at the building inlet, that should satisfy the validation requirements and this needs to 
be clarified in the rule.  
 
For community systems, there should not be a timeframe that records are considered less 
reliable, if they have been documented to be accurate within a set range of acceptance (90-95% 
for example). Vermont has many old water systems where some things have not yet changed. A 
records review should be adequate evidence for an inventory determination.  
 
Perhaps consider a validation process through which a 5% audit is performed to confirm the 
records, regardless of age or pipe material.  
 
We do not believe that including non-lead service lines, categorized based on a records review in 
the validation pool would be worthwhile. 
 
In terms of validation of non-lead lines, this directive creates a considerable burden on systems 
that may have limited or no information pertaining to its materials, especially those that were 
built post-lead ban.  Requiring 2 points of validation in a northern climate state would mean 
digging 6+ feet down to inspect portions of lines.  Also, the regulation is not clear whether it is 2 
points of validation per ownership segment or 2 in general. If 2 per segment, it would mean 
digging 3 holes per service line (assuming a visual inspection inside the building is possible for 
the fourth point of inspection). That is incredibly disruptive due to the depths at which services 
are buried in Vermont, which likely -if found lead- would lead to release.  Clarity is needed on the 
number of visual validations and those lines specifically that need to be validated.  Vermont 
DWGPD recommends creating a framework under which a system can do some truthing of their 
records and if documented to be “X%” accurate, that the rest of the inventory is assumed to be 
accurate.

Lead Action and Trigger Levels 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
14 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
EPA is seeking comment on the 
proposed lead action level of 0.010 
mg/L, as well as comment and 
supporting data on alternative action 
levels, such as 0.005 mg/L, with 
regards to generally effective corrosion 
control treatment and identifying 
systems most at risk of elevated levels 
of lead in drinking water. 
In Vermont, since 2013, there have been 254 sampling events at 117 water systems that have led 
to an action level exceedance at the 15ppb action level.  Should the action level have been 
established at 10ppb, there would have been 427 sampling events at 180 water systems that 
would trigger an action level exceedance. If the action level were 5 ppb, then 681 sampling 
events at 320 water systems would have resulted in an action level exceedance. This is in a State 
that has approximately 640 water systems subject to lead and copper sampling.  To set the 
action level at 5 ppb would require half of our water systems to install corrosion control and/or 
manage a POU filtration program. This would lead to a tremendous burden on the operators and 
water systems.  Provision of corrosion control requires a higher classification of operator and 
more on-going training for that operator.  
EPA is also seeking comment on the 
use of the action level to determine 
when additional public education is 
required, and the use of the same 
action level for public education as for 
the CCT provisions. 
Vermont DWGPD suggests using the same framework as established in the LCR – public 
education following an action level exceedance, with the potential to have a population-
dependent timeline with shorter timelines for smaller systems and longer timelines for larger 
systems.  
EPA is seeking public comment, data, 
and information on the anticipated 
benefits and tradeoffs, including for 
public health and administrative 
burden on systems and States, if more 
small and medium systems are 
required to conduct a detailed OCCT 
demonstration and take other actions 
if they exceed the proposed action 
level of 0.010 mg/L or other lower 
values, while water systems are 
simultaneously required to mandatory 
conduct full service line replacement. 
As detailed elsewhere in these comments, Vermont DWGPD is not supportive of wide-spread 
OCCT demonstrations and pipe loop studies. They are complicated, expensive, and time-
consuming projects that will likely arrive at something that a desktop analysis and comparison of 
existing water quality/situations can bring forth in a much more expedited timeline. The existing 
Optimal CCT Evaluation Technical Recommendations for Primacy Agencies and Public Water 
Systems from EPA is a very powerful document, and with minor updates, could continue to be 
the path forward for assessing OCCT and steer a system toward pH adjustment, corrosion 
inhibitor, or both. In Vermont we have only ever had one water system complete one pipe loop 
study and it was focusing on premise plumbing impacts of switching from disinfection using 
chlorine to chloramines. There is no experience in service line pipe loop studies in the State.  
Corrosion Control Treatment 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
15 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
The proposed determination that the 
CCT treatment technique is feasible 
and prevents known or anticipated 
adverse health effects to the extent 
feasible. 
 Vermont DWGPD supports the continued approach of the treatment technique triggering 
activities that the system must complete to address corrosion and the associated health effects.  
However, Vermont DWGPD does not support requiring the pipe loop studies and complicated 
CCT studies as part of the process and believe that a more expedited framework is possible and 
can be successful at addressing public health concerns, especially at small/very small systems.  
Comment on whether it would be 
more appropriate to require water 
systems to re-optimize again following 
an action level exceedance regardless 
of meeting their optimal water quality 
parameters and to provide the State 
with the authority to waive this 
requirement. 
In Vermont many of our water systems, including those that would be categorized as those with 
multiple exceedances, may already provide CCT, however, due to prolonged periods of water 
stagnation (see elsewhere in comments pertaining to setting a maximum stagnation period), for 
a corrosion inhibitor to be effective there must be routine water movement in the plumbing.  A 
system may only be able to control things at the entry point, so requiring re-optimization every 
time there is an Action Level Exceedance, in absence of other changes or excursions from 
OWQP, would only serve as a paperwork exercise.  Discretion should be afforded to those 
systems who have been deemed optimized who, without excursions, subsequently exceed the 
action level. The state should also be provided with adequate discretion to require re-
optimization regardless of past attempts so long as the state provides written rationale. 
The proposed option for a water 
system to delay OCCT until after the 
system has replaced all of its LSLs and 
GRR service lines, while the system 
achieves at least 20 percent removal 
per year and must have no LSLs, GRR 
service lines, or lead status unknown 
service lines remaining at the end of 
the five-year period. 
It is unclear what happens during this 5-year window, especially if a system continues to have 
action level exceedances. This is essentially permission to exceed and not address things, 
unless/until the system gets to the “next” step of 3 action level exceedances in a 5-year period 
and then need to provide filters.  A concern would be if the system does delay installation of 
OCCT and opt to remove LSLs, if they do not address premise plumbing that 5 years would pass, 
and the system would still have elevated lead and potentially repeated action level exceedances 
at the now lower action level.  While removing the lead/GRR services is important, a system will 
be better and have better water quality upon installation of OCCT. Waiting 5 years to say, “you 
need to install OCCT now” and then giving 2 more years or more is prolonging the situation too 
far.  

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
16 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
The treatment recommendation and 
CCT study process can take multiple 
years to complete. For systems with 
existing corrosion control, the system 
may be able to alter the existing 
treatment (e.g., increase pH and/or 
orthophosphate dose) without a new 
CCT study on a much faster timeframe 
rather than waiting for study results 
that may recommend that same 
change. EPA is requesting comment on 
whether there are situations and/or 
conditions where existing treatment 
modifications may achieve similar 
lead reductions rather than delaying 
new treatment for two-and-a-half 
years while a study is underway. 
While not attempting to minimize the importance of the corrosion control treatment process, it is 
quite easy and in Vermont we have found success with our approach, especially for our smaller 
systems. This process does not require a pipe loop study or extensive (and expensive) corrosion 
studies.  We rely on the Optimal CCT Evaluation Technical Recommendations for Primacy 
Agencies and Public Water Systems guidance published by EPA which boils things down into 
either 1) pH management, 2) corrosion inhibitor, or 3) both. To take 5-7 years on a study of pH 7.3 
water to assess how to make it less corrosive is wasting valuable time and will take a child from 
the critical developmental period from newborn to kindergarten. A corrosion inhibitor could be 
installed very quickly and then the 6-month monitoring and entry point and distribution WQP 
monitoring would clearly document whether it is working. Maybe there will be tweaks along the 
way, maybe not.  The pipe-loop study will arrive at a similar result, but perhaps many many years 
later. Because of the improvements of the LCR to date, many states are familiar with the best 
options already and could likely do a very quick desktop analysis to point to one of the three 
options identified above, in a far quicker fashion than a pipe loop study or other complicated 
piloting.  Ultimately the water will be better having had corrosion control installed, why delay that 
process? 
 
This would reduce the burden on systems and states, to have clear guidance from the experts, 
that works as a framework into which to insert data and out of which the corrosion method is 
produced.  
Compliance Alternatives for a Lead Action Level Exceedance for Small Community Water Systems and Non-Transient, Non-Community 
Water Systems 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
17 
 
EPA is proposing that small system 
flexibilities be limited to CWSs serving 
3,300 persons and fewer and all 
NTNCWSs for the remaining 
compliance alternatives of point-of-
use devices and plumbing 
replacement. EPA is seeking comment 
on whether the Agency should allow 
systems serving up to 10,000 persons 
(or another threshold) to be eligible to 
use the small system compliance 
flexibility provision. EPA is also seeking 
information, data, and analysis on 
whether point-of-use devices and 
plumbing replacement are as effective 
as OCCT at systems serving up to 
10,000 persons (or another threshold). 
Vermont DWGPD feels that a system size of 3,300 is impossible to manage under the small 
system flexibility aspect and would prefer a much lower number/threshold. Based on the 
systems of this size in Vermont, we do not see this as a viable option for a system of that size to 
oversee removal of all lead-containing infrastructure to 100% completion, nor can it manage a 
POU program of over 1,000 filters and 300+ samples annually.  
 
In Vermont a water system of 3,300 is one of our larger water systems, with large commercial 
centers, hospitals, schools, restaurants, etc. How can we be sure that every school updates 
every valve and lead-containing solder sufficiently so that the system is truly lead-free? It would 
create multiple different qualities of water throughout the system and lead to environmental and 
social justice concerns. This should be limited to systems that have access and/or ownership 
of100% of the plumbing infrastructure such as NTNCs and housing/condominium associations.   
 
Of the 5 water systems in Vermont that are just under the 3,300 population line, three of the 
systems only have a single operator. The remaining two systems have two operators. To expect 
these individuals to manage everything going on at the system, including surface water filtration 
at two of the systems, in addition to the small system flexibility requirements is not feasible.  
 
We are supportive of systems such as NTNCs which own/control their plumbing to be able to 
make plumbing changes and/or manage a POU program, but not for communities of 3,300.  
While it may seem “easier” than installing and maintaining corrosion control, it is our opinion 
that it would not be the case. As required, a system of 3,000 people would be approximately 
1,000 connections. This would require each kitchen in each living unit and every kitchen/food 
prep area in commercial areas. This is well over 1,000 filters. So, the system would need to 
replace filters on a quarterly basis, perhaps 6 months at best, based on manufacturers’ 
suggestions. For systems of this size, that is a full-time job. Then the need to sample from 1/3 of 
those locations (300+) is another full-time job. Then the burden of the deluge of data coming in to 
the state would present other workload issues. At approximately $25 per sample, 300 samples 
would mean $7,500 per year on the POU “efficacy” sampling, to say nothing for the operator’s 
time, travel to/from the lab and/or shipping of samples. This should be compared with the long-
term costs of similar sized systems providing central corrosion control.  
 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
18 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
Vermont DWGPD has concerns about systems utilizing Reverse Osmosis (RO) widespread as 
POU. If systems worked to implement RO “under sink”, it would be very impactful on the quantity 
of water needed to supply the system due to the efficiency of RO and the waste stream it creates. 
While the rule seems to favor pitcher/tap filters which would imply GAC or some sort of carbon 
adsorption, there should be quality/scarcity concerns through wide-spread RO use. 
 
In Vermont in 2019 we had a condominium association water system investigate removal of all 
lead-containing infrastructure. For a system of 31 connections (among 7 different condominium 
cluster buildings) to remove plumbing entirely in each residence kitchen and bathroom, it would 
have cost over $615,000. There are concerns that lead-containing infrastructure may be behind 
walls painted with lead paint, contain asbestos insulation or other harmful materials and 
“simply” making plumbing replacements to remove lead solder may open a pandoras box of 
other health effects while pursuing plumbing replacement. And the system will not realize the 
cost almost until they mobilize and line up contractors to do the work.  
 
We are supportive of the flexibility options where it makes sense, for NTNC systems and 
community systems with total ownership and control of its infrastructure.  

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
19 
 
Request for Comment 
Vermont DWGPD Response 
EPA is requesting comment on the 
ability and practicality of point-of-use 
devices to address multiple 
contaminants. 
Reliance on POU for multiple contaminants will in reality have a net-positive effect, however, 
without careful sampling and analysis, it may be short-lived.  In Vermont, we have naturally 
occurring iron and manganese which have documented adverse impacts on GAC filtration 
media, greatly reducing their expected lifespans. When considering multiple contaminants, it 
needs to be a site-specific analysis including periods of water use and stagnation, which can and 
will lead to filter differences, which further leads to multiple different water qualities throughout 
distribution.  There is a reason we regulate so many contaminants at the entry point; because we 
can more closely control and regulate it. We cannot regulate individual homes, we cannot be 
assured that 100% of the filters will work 100% of the time, or if the filters will even remain 
installed in some locations. POU can be seen as a short-term or stopgap measure following 
service line removal or disruption, but relying on them as permanent lead or other contaminant 
treatment is not sustainable. 
 
Additionally, central water system treatment in many water systems is an SRF-eligible expense; 
provision of POU is likely not. It would benefit the system to bond/vote/fund a central project 
once as opposed to on-going POU upkeep. 
 
What will likely happen is that the users will grow disenfranchised with the filter approach, get 
tired of the slow trickle through the filters, and end up taking the filters off or possibly more likely, 
losing patience with the water system and resort to purchasing their own bottled water.

Vermont DWGPD is supportive of the additional actions (education, filters, etc.) prescribed by

infrastructure/Tier.  When it gets to bigger systems or more diverse systems, provision of filters to 
every user may be unnecessary and as discussed elsewhere in these comments in reference to 
any other “filter first” approach, may lead to a false sense of safety, not knowing truly what else is 
in the water and what the efficacy of the filters would be.  We are concerned that poorly 
maintained filters can promote bacteriological growth (particularly in non-chlorinating systems, 
of which Vermont has many) and can also release elevated lead and other concentrated 
constituents into the water. Situations like supply chain problems and sourcing issues could 
eventually lead to greater public health concerns than the original reason the filters seek to 
address.

The importance and severity of this timeline and approach seem to be at odds with a system’s

to have these systems provide more education and filters and then eventually address the

they are doing everything “right”.

some time to have a passivating coating applied through corrosion inhibitors, so again, the

users.  The likelihood is that with education and provision of filters the users will lose all

The difficulty in a “filter first” approach like this, without knowing the water quality and water use 
patterns is that too much is left unknown, and it provides a false sense of confidence in the 
filters. There is a difference between filtering out 11ppb vs 100ppb in terms of loading on the 
filter. Without having the water quality data, schools and systems would be guessing.  
 
Vermont has required school lead sampling since 2019 and in our experience, it is difficult 
getting filters for high-velocity kitchen fixtures, especially at larger schools which essentially are 
commercial grade kitchens that need high volumes of water. Opting to put on a filter where it is 
not needed will only frustrate the kitchen staff and reducing flow from 5gpm+ to much less due 
to the “trickle” that comes out of a POU filter will likely lead to their hasty removal from use by 
on-site staff or instead changing behavior and using what may have previously been a dish or 
handwashing only sink that has a high velocity to being incorporated into cooking; something of 
which the water system would have no knowledge.

Below are other comments that were not specifically asked for /addressed in the EPA request for comments but are based on Vermont 
DWGPD’s and are being submitted for EPA’s consideration: 
Subject 
Vermont DWGPD Comment 
Non-lead validation 
EPA is proposing that systems with 1,500 or fewer non-lead service lines in their validation pools validate at 
least 20% of lines in the pool. If two points of visual inspection are required, then this may be very 
burdensome for VT’s small CWSs. As discussed elsewhere, being in a northern climate, digging potholes or 
other work to visually inspect a service line will likely mean going 6-feet or deeper, which will be cost and time 
intensive and likely create disturbances for any lead lines found.   
Gender inclusivity 
Vermont DWGPD supports changing public health language from “women” to “people” or “persons”. 
 
Abbreviations, if used, should have an explanation included. The mandatory education statement doesn't 
explain what "IQ" is. Changing the word to "intelligence" communicates the point without having to elaborate 
or assume that the reader know what an "intelligence quotient" is. 
Access/Control  
Systems are required to make an attempt to get access for full LSL upon a location’s change in ownership. 
This is an undue burden on the water system to track purchase and sales. Instead, there should be 
information included as a statement as part of the annual notice/education/certification/CCR required for 
those with lead lines who are new owners and to engage with the system personnel should they have 
questions or wish to have their portion replaced.    
Inaccurate examples – 
small system impact.  
The preamble refers to Quincy Massachusetts as a small water system and their efforts to do public 
education, website content etc.  Quincy Massachusetts serves 103,000 people and this misses the mark for 
the capabilities of a truly small system and what their capacity is. It is unclear whether EPA assessed truly 
small or very small systems, such as a mobile home park cooperative serving 27 connections. That is a 
different scope and far less capacity than Quincy, MA.   
Maximum Stagnation Time There needs to be a maximum stagnation time established in the rule. Vermont DWGPD proposes 18 hours, 
consistent with the EPA’s 3Ts based on the research and analysis that went into that publication. It is not our 
desire to lean on this number to authorize us to invalidate high sample results, but more to steer operators 
toward good sample collection and explain, in regulation, why they should not be sampling at locations that 
do not see normal operation.  It would be more beneficial to issue a violation for improper sampling 
technique than it would be to have carte blanche authority to invalidate samples. If we don’t accept samples 
taken with greater than 18-hour stagnation, the hope is that eventually they will stop sampling those 
locations.  
 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
34 
 
Subject 
Vermont DWGPD Comment 
This is a real issue and one we face in Vermont due to the residential areas surrounding ski mountains. These 
locations may be vacant for considerable portions of the year, information the operator may not be aware of, 
until the sample comes back elevated, and the sampling may not reflect normal operation. 
 
Vermont DWGPD would support for “waiving” the maximum stagnation time if occupants collect samples 
under instruction from the operator and to set a maximum number or tap sampling periods for which 
samples could be invalidated due to exceeding the stagnation period, but especially in the tightened 
situation the LCRI creates with limited ability to “test out” of needing to install OCCT, we will continue to 
chase our tails over high results due to water that sat for too long.  
9-year sampling waiver 
Vermont DWGPD does not anticipate pursuing the 9-year sampling waiver. It is too burdensome for state and 
water system staff to maintain and adhere to.  
Previously replaced lead 
connectors 
There is discussion in the preamble about systems being required to identify locations of previously replaced 
lead connectors.  This can pose a significant burden and could essentially double the time required to 
complete the initial or baseline inventory. 
 
Instead, we suggest that the definition of Galvanized Requiring Replacement be amended to include 
galvanized that is currently downstream of a lead connector or if it is unknown whether it ever was 
downstream of a lead connector. Requiring a system to inventory something that is no longer present is 
confusing and will lead to data integrity issues when we have multiple entries for each service line of past vs. 
current infrastructure. 
Filtration after OCCT 
installation 
There needs to be a better-defined “offramp” through which a system that is either lead-free and/or installs 
OCCT where they previously relied on filters to address corrosion can remove/cease use of filters.  Vermont 
DWGPD recommends an unfiltered testing protocol or study to assess efficacy of OCCT and reduction of 
lead results.  Filters can be a very effective tool, but we feel that they are not a permanent option long-term. 
There needs to be consideration of the eventuality that OCCT is required.  
Data management needs 
As with every new regulation, there is the need for detailed data management instructions. Often these come 
sometime after the final rule promulgation but given the complexity and intertwined nature of the 3 active 
rules (LCR, LCRR, LCRI), these need to be done immediately.  There is reference to reporting a lead action 
level exceedance to the EPA within 15 days of the close of the monitoring period. This is not the standard data 
submission protocol employed, so how will this need to be done? 

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
35 
 
Subject 
Vermont DWGPD Comment 
Laboratory 
Integration/improvement 
Currently many labs from which Vermont DWGPD receive data know to provide total coliform and E-coli 
positive data immediately. It may take up to 10-15 days to get completed lead/copper data. There are 
concerns with lab capacity and customer service or QA/QC capacity at laboratories to provide validated data 
to States in a very timely manner. It is confusing and misleading to require Tier 1 public notice for something 
that happened several weeks ago.  Lab availability must also consider other regulations, such as PFAS, which 
will have tremendous impacts on lab capacity. As stated elsewhere, these decisions must be made when 
assessing the capacity of the full program, not a single regulation.  
Financial impact of LSLR 
The preamble discusses that lead service line replacement is less financially impactful on a system than is 
installation of corrosion control treatment.  In Vermont we have experienced prices anywhere from $4,000 to 
$20,000 per building to replace a lead service line.  To say that this is cheaper/less impactful than installing 
corrosion control is off target. While not attempting to minimize the importance of replacing lead service 
lines, it is important to understand the context and relative prices.  If a system has only a handful of service 
lines that are on the higher end of the spectrum that we have experienced – meaning they would need to be 
re-located due to legacy trees or changes in building access etc. then it would cost more than installation of 
corrosion control, even factoring in the on-going expenditures associated with corrosion control treatment.  
Existing data 
The LCRI identifies that if a system has a second action level exceedance that the system will 
resume/complete the OCCT steps. However, there is no discussion in terms of how far to look back. Does 
this include data under the LCR? Is there a “window” in which the data is valid or invalid? Should there be a 
determination made based on the laboratory reporting level, which may have changed since 1991? 
 
Vermont DWGPD asks for clarity in how to integrate the existing rule with the future rule as it applies to 
triggers/thresholds for needing to install treatment. 
 
Additionally, during this time of transition from LCR to LCRR to LCRI, while the LCRR is still completely “valid” 
rule, there needs to be guidance or at least a determination about what happens TODAY if a system has an 
action level exceedance so that they may plot the correct course.  Does that need to be resolved under LCR 
framework, LCRR, or expected LCRI?  This is particularly impactful given the changes in small system 
flexibility eligibility and options.  When the RTCR was implemented, there was clear guidance that any 
action/activity triggered under the TCR must be resolved under the TCR framework. We have seen no such 
statements about LCR, LCRR, or LCRI implementation and especially as we approach October 16, 2024, are 
uncertain how to proceed following an action level exceedance.  

Vermont Drinking Water and Groundwater Protection Division (DWGPD) Comments – LCRI EPA Docket ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
36 
 
Subject 
Vermont DWGPD Comment 
Customer requested 
samples 
There needs to be guardrails put on the requirements for customer-requested sampling and better 
information about who pays for the analysis of the sampling.  The rule is inconsistent about when certain 
things need to or do not need to be paid for by the water system; customer-initiated sampling is one such 
item in the rule.  Water systems cannot budget for an unknown and unanticipated volume of sampling. 
Occasional sampling may be able to be absorbed into a budget, but both the operator’s time and the analytic 
costs need to be paid for.  We suggest creating a ratio of % of service lines per year as a cap that can be paid 
for by the water system, with a “not to exceed” either number of samples or cost incurred. Otherwise, if there 
is another national news story and a renewal in attention and focus, systems will be buried with requests and 
budgets will be blown, leaving the response to be first-come first-served until the budget is drained and not 
being able to consider later requests at more vulnerable locations. 
 
There are also data management concerns pertaining to sampling points/sampling locations leading to 
confusion, especially with high volumes of samples. 
Water Quality Parameter 
monitoring framework 
Vermont DWGPD disagrees with the approach established in the rule under which small/medium systems 
that are not exceeding the action level do not need to monitor and report water quality parameters.  Sampling 
for Water Quality Parameters is the only way to know outside of required Lead/Copper sampling that the 
OCCT is working. We have found that it is an effective way to “catch” an issue before it arises in LCR 
sampling, especially when a system is on reduced monitoring.  It has been our practice to require continued 
entry point WQP monitoring for any system that implements pH adjustment or a corrosion inhibitor to ensure 
on-going efficacy of treatment. We will expect to continue to do so and encourage the complicated 
framework of when a system does or does not need to collect WQP be streamlined. 
Annual notice/certification Vermont DWGPD requests a review and change to §141.90. If a system will be updating its inventory annually, 
much of the annual certification information pertaining to things like lead connectors replaced, failing to 
meet customer-initiated replacement requests, completion of customer-initiated line replacements, 
updating the # of lead lines replaced, GRR replaced, unknown identified etc. as required by this section. It 
seems cumbersome to require individual certifications when this all could be incorporated into a line item in 
an inventory.   
 
Should this be the path forward, States will need somewhere for this data to “go”, presumably SDWIS with 
easy reporting information for EPA.

Viken Detection’s Comments on U.S. EPA’s Proposed  
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements Regulation 
 
DOCKET ID NO. EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Viken Detection is a leading technology provider with a longstanding history of protecting 
children and families from lead poisoning by contact with contaminated paint. Our PB200™ 
family of handheld lead paint analyzers have been on the market since 2015 and are used 
by thousands of housing inspectors to identify the presence of lead paint on and within 
building materials.  
 
We commend the Federal government and EPA for their efforts to mandate the detection and 
remediation of lead pipes in our drinking water systems.  
 
With our background and industry expertise in lead detection and passionate mission to 
children and keeping families safe from lead poisoning, we have several recommendations 
regarding the EPA’s role in offering guidance, regulations and potential funding to facilitate 
efficient use of technology to solve this public health problem.  
 
We believe the list of recommendations below will not only ultimately benefit public health, 
but also be beneficial to technology developers, the U.S. government, and the EPA, as well as 
the end users and agencies who will have a need to leverage innovative technologies to 
identify and remediate lead service lines in their communities as quickly, efficiently, and cost-
effectively as possible. 
 
We encourage the EPA to consider the following:  
• 
Exploring technologies capable of detecting lead pipes in the water system which do 
not require costly and disruptive excavation in private and public spaces. 
• 
Preparing guidance for technology providers to ensure a clear path for bringing EPA-
sanctioned tools and methodologies to market for widespread adoption. 
• 
Setting up and facilitating the execution of testing protocols at publicly accessible 
facilities, so that technology providers can rapidly determine the efficacy of new tools 
in development. 
• 
Funding field studies aimed at understanding the best current and proposed 
methods of lead detection and how to ensure safe drinking water after interdictory 
actions. 
• 
Allowing states and municipalities to qualify for available replacement funding if they 
are actively participating in trial or research study activities aimed at detecting lead 
pipe stock and taking later action to address the findings. 
• 
Publishing the results of EPA coordinated trials to facilitate increased adoption by 
state and regional users attempting to comply with the federal requirements.

interested parties for field evaluations and potential applications for funded use case

Dear EPA Assistant Administrator for Water Radhika Fox: 
 
The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (WDNR) maintains primacy for implementation of the Safe 
Drinking Water Act (SDWA) in the state of Wisconsin. Except where noted in the letter below, WDNR is writing 
to express its strong support for the comments submitted by the Association of State Drinking Water 
Administrators (ASDWA), developed in collaboration with state drinking water primacy agencies on the 
proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI) during the public comment period between 12/05/2023 – 
2/5/2024. In addition to expressing our general support of the comments in the cover letter and Appendices A and 
B submitted by ASDWA, in the text below we highlight, expand upon, clarify, and in a few cases disagree with 
ASDWA’s comments.   
 
General Requirements and Action Levels (§ 141.80) 
 
The WDNR emphasizes its agreement with ASDWA’s recommendation that EPA dedicate additional resources to 
support state primacy agency administration of the LCRI. Throughout the ASDWA comment package, there are 
numerous requests for the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to provide clarification on rule requirements, 
and for EPA to develop and provide states with implementation support and guidance. WDNR suggests that EPA 
consider meeting with ASDWA and states to clarify the rule ahead of its final promulgation. Additionally, 
WDNR suggests that EPA collaborate with ASDWA and states to develop the recommended implementation 
guidance prior to the rule compliance date.  
 
Lead 90th percentiles should be calculated using the highest lead results, regardless of sampling site tier. It will be 
difficult for states to calculate lead 90th percentiles and for systems to understand how 90th percentiles are 
calculated if the process requires picking and choosing results based on tiers. It would also be difficult to justify to 
the public why the highest lead results are not included in the calculation. Using only the highest results from the 
required number of sampling locations will both simplify the 90th percentile calculation and better protect public 
health [§ 141.80 (c)].     
 
Definitions (§ 141.2) 
 
WDNR highlights the ASDWA requests for clarification from EPA on the definitions listed below.  
 
Clarify the definition of “connector” to indicate whether anything over the defined length (currently two feet) 
is considered a “service line”. This has a significant impact on what is considered a “galvanized requiring 
replacement service line” and should be clear in the definition.
