 
Clarify that the definition of “service line” includes systems that do not have water mains. This change would 
make the definition of “service line” consistent with Exhibit 4 on p. 8 of EPA’s 2023 Developing and 
Maintaining a Service Line Inventory: Small Entity Compliance Guide. The proposed LCRI defines a 
“service line” as a portion of pipe that connects the water main to the building inlet. By contrast, Exhibit 4 of 
EPA’s 2023 guidance shows examples of systems without water mains, where the service lines include pipes 
that deliver water from a wellhouse to a building inlet; from a pressure tank to a building inlet; and from one 
building to another building. If the proposed LCRI definition of a service line remains unchanged, most non-
transient, non-community water systems (NTNCWS) and many non-municipal community water systems 
(CWS) will not have any service lines because they do not have water mains in their distribution system. As 
such, these systems would not be subject to the any LCRI service line inventory or replacement requirements. 
Additionally, it would not be clear how to assign a tier to compliance monitoring sites based on service line 
material in systems where no service lines exist. Additionally, Wisconsin has already invested significant 
resources into inventorying pipe material that meets the EPA 2023 guidance but does not meet the definition 
of “service line” in the proposed LCRI. 
 
The WDNR emphasizes its support for the ASDWA comments below.  
 
The definition of “small water system” should be the same for all parts of the LCRI in order to eliminate 
confusion.  WDNR agrees with ASDWA that the definition should be consistent with the original lead and 
copper rule (LCR), i.e., water systems serving a population of 3,300 or fewer persons. 
 
The definition of “connector” should be increased from two feet to three feet. 
 
Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) (§ 141.81) 
 
WDNR highlights the ASDWA requests for clarification from EPA on the issues listed below.  
 
Clarify the meaning of “started to install CCT” in Exhibit 1 – FR 84890 of the Preamble which states that 
“Systems with P90 lead level > 0.010 mg/L: No CCT: Must complete CCT installation regardless of their 
subsequent P90 levels if the system has started to install CCT. " This is also an important clarification for 
when a small or medium system without corrosion control treatment that does not exceed the action levels for 
two consecutive six-month monitoring periods may stop completing the CCT steps, as it is determined by 
when the system “starts” to install OCCT. [§ 141.81(g)] 
 
Clarify how CCT and optimal water quality parameter (OWQP) requirements apply to systems that have 
installed CCT but have not previously been “deemed optimized” because they have not had an ALE.  Are all 
systems with CCT that are not currently deemed optimized expected to be deemed optimized and subject to 
OWQP requirements? If so, what is the expected timeframe for implementing this requirement? [§ 141.80 
(a)(1)(i) and §141.81] 
 
Clarify when consecutive systems are subject to OCCT and OWQP requirements at entry points where 
treatment is not added. For example, in Wisconsin, there are many water systems that do not add treatment 
but that purchase water from another water supplier that does add treatment.  Are consecutive systems 
required to monitor for their wholesaler’s OWQPs and subject to excursion violations when their wholesaler 
gets an ALE [§ 141.82(g)]?  
 
Clarify that systems with installed CCT cannot cease CCT to pursue a shorter LSL (lead service line) 
replacement schedule [§ 141.81(f)(1)(I)(A)]. 
 
Clarify § 141.81(d) and § 141.81(a) to clearly state that water systems are required to re-optimize as often as 
required by the state and remove references to one time re-optimization.  
 
Clarify that the shortened LSL replacement compliance option does not apply to systems addressing a copper 
ALE [141.81(f)].  
 
 
 

Page 3 
WDNR highlights its support for ASDWA’s request that EPA provide guidance, training and other resources in 
advance of the LCRI compliance date in the areas listed below. 
 
EPA should develop comprehensive decision-trees, flowcharts, and/or schematics clearly depicting the 
regulatory triggers and steps for CCT optimization, re-optimization, and optimal water quality parameter 
(OWQP) designation. These tools should be developed and shared with primacy agencies as soon as possible 
to aid in state rulemaking, compliance determinations, and training. With so many conditional statements and 
complexity throughout these sections, it will be difficult for primacy agency staff to communicate, administer 
and enforce these requirements without these tools.  
 
EPA, ASDWA and states should work together to develop comprehensive guidance and training on how 
states should consider the impact of proposed CCT on other drinking water contaminants, as well as how 
states should consider the impacts of proposed source and treatment changes on CCT. For example, 
Wisconsin recently received an engineering report that asserted that a systems’ designated CCT would 
increase disinfection byproduct (DBP) formation.  
 
EPA should develop CCT training and guidance covering conditions under which a system should be allowed 
to stop CCT following complete replacement of LSLs and galvanized requirement replacement (GRR) service 
lines and any steps that should be taken when this occurs. 
 
WDNR also adds emphasis to the ASDWA comment that there are situations and conditions where modifying a 
water system’s existing CCT may be more beneficial than delaying a change for two-and-a-half years while a 
system conducts a study. EPA should give states the authority to allow systems - under certain circumstances and 
with state prior approval - to make treatment changes consistent with EPA OCCT guidance to optimize CCT 
concurrently with performing a study [§ 141.81(d)]. 
 
WDNR is concerned about the proposed option that would allow water systems to delay OCCT until after the 
system has replaced all of its LSLs and GRR service lines, while the system achieves at least 20 percent removal 
per year.  In addition to the concerns expressed in the ASDWA letter, WDNR is concerned about situations where 
an ALE results from a water system’s 1st liter sample results, thereby indicating that premise plumbing, rather 
than lead service lines, could be the primary source of high lead levels in drinking water [§ 141.81(f)]. 
 
Wisconsin agrees with ASDWA that states should have the discretion to allow small systems to conduct a desktop 
CCT study, rather than always requiring systems of all sizes to conduct the pipe loop study.  However, Wisconsin 
supports requiring pipe loop studies for medium and large systems under certain conditions [§ 141.81(d) and § 
141.81(e)]. 
 
Lead Service Line Inventories and Replacement (§ 141.84) 
 
The WDNR emphasizes its support for the ASDWA comments described below.  
 
Clarify § 141.84(d)(5)(iv) to explain what factors for a state should consider when deciding whether it is 
feasible for a system to replace LSLs at a faster rate. 
 
Remove the requirement in § 141.84(a)(2)(ii)(B) for water systems to identify where lead connectors have 
been replaced in the past, and instead make the “replaced lead” connector category optional. It is more 
efficient to allow water systems to focus their time and resources on higher priority inventory and 
replacement activities such as lead service line removal and replacement, and identification and removal of 
galvanized service lines currently and formerly downstream of lead service lines. However, if connectors are 
required to be included in inventories, it would be helpful if the rule specified which connectors (i.e., only the 
connection to main) must be included in the inventory. 
 
Require all water systems update their inventory when service lines previously categorized as non-lead are 
subsequently determined to be lead or GRR, instead of leaving it to the states to determine what “additional 
actions” are appropriate to address the inaccuracy [§ 141.84 (b)(3)].  

Page 4 
 
Give states the flexibility and authority in § 141.84(b)(5)(i) & (ii) to allow a single point of inspection where 
an entire service line is under the same ownership. For example, at most NTNCWS and many non-municipal 
community water systems, all portions of all service lines are entirely owned by the water system.  Requiring 
two-point verification of these service lines would be unnecessarily burdensome and unlikely to improve 
inventory accuracy.  
 
Wisconsin disagrees with the ASDWA comment that EPA should establish a deadline for systems to identify all 
unknown service lines prior to their service line replacement deadlines. As long as all unknown service lines are 
included in a water system’s lead service line replacement plan, it does not make sense to require water systems to 
excavate twice – once to visually confirm that the service line material is lead, and a second time to remove the 
service line.  
 
Public Education and Notification (§ 141.85) 
 
WDNR emphasizes ASDWA’s request that EPA provide clarification on the issues listed below.  
 
Clarify the circumstances under which a state can grant an extension [§ 141.85(b)(7)]. Can all requirements 
be extended, or only certain requirements based on the justification provided by the water system?   
 
Clarify what is meant by the term “offer” in § 141.85(c)(1) & (2), and whether a public notice including 
content described in § 141.85(e)(3)(i)(d) would be sufficient. Additionally, EPA should clarify who is 
responsible for the cost of customer-requested sampling. 
 
WDNR also emphasizes its support for ASDWA’s request that EPA provide guidance, training and other 
resources in advance of the LCRI compliance date in the areas listed below. 
 
EPA should develop guidance and draft templates for each public education and public notice requirement in 
advance of the LCRI compliance date.  
 
EPA should establish guidance and expectations for the required filter plan under § 141.85(j). 
 
The WDNR highlights its support for the ASDWA comments listed below.  
 
The LCRI should require systems to submit a communication strategy at the start of the LCRI rule. The 
public education requirements are highly complex and developing a plan in advance will help systems avoid 
incurring violations for missing a requirement they misunderstood or did not adequately plan for. 
 
The EPA should streamline and combine post-ALE deadlines and reporting requirements, including the filter 
plans required under § 141.85 (j)(3).  Many due dates and associated certification requirements do not align. 
Recommend that EPA work with ASDWA to streamline deadlines for states and PWSs in the final rule. 
 
The EPA should keep the 60 days period after the sampling period to complete public education 
requirements; we do not think EPA should shorten this timeframe. It would be difficult for systems to 
complete all requirements and undertake the necessary printing and mailing within any shorter timeframe. 
The 60-day timeframe will also reduce the likelihood of water systems incurring a violation due to delayed 
receipt of sampling results [§ 141.85 (b)].  
 
EPA should consider giving public water systems more than three days to provide consumers with tap 
sampling results [§ 141.85 (d)]. Most small water systems in Wisconsin have limited staff with contracted 
operators responsible for multiple water systems. A three-day deadline would be difficult for small systems to 
comply with.  
 
WDNR disagrees with the ASDWA comment stating that EPA should consider not requiring public water 
systems to send public education materials to local health departments. We appreciate that the proposed LCRI 
requires notification and partnering with local public health departments when water systems exceed the lead 
action level [§ 141.85 (b) (2)]. Local public health departments play a key role in protecting public health from 
the harm posed by lead. Strong collaboration between water systems and health departments ensures effective and 
timely public education, especially for those groups most at risk. 

Page 5 
 
Compliance Monitoring (§141.86)  
The WDNR takes this opportunity to emphasize and/or elaborate on its support for the ASDWA comments 
described below.  
 
Annual monitoring requirements should be conducted at the reduced number of sites, rather than standard 
number of sites. This is both more cost-effective for water systems and more protective of public health in 
systems with fewer available Tier 1 and Tier 2 sampling locations than required number monitoring sites, as it 
reduces the likelihood that 90th percentile calculations will be diluted with the results from lower tier sites [§ 
141.86(d)(2)(i)].  
 
EPA should clarify what evidence or documentation a water system must provide to the state to prove a 
sample meets the invalidation criteria of § 141.86(f)(1)(ii). For example, what evidence or documentation is 
required when a water system claims, after receiving a high lead result, that the sample was taken from a site 
that did not meet the site selection criteria of § 141.86(a)(4). Or what evidence or documentations is required 
when a system claims a sample with a high lead result was collected in a manner that did not meet the sample 
collection criteria of § 141.86 (b)(1)?  
 
WDNR agrees with EPA’s proposal to not establish a maximum stagnation time in the LCRI because of concerns 
that samples will be invalidated solely because the sample result is high. Thus, WDNR strongly disagrees with the 
ASDWA recommendation to establish a maximum stagnation time of 18 hours. However, if EPA were to follow 
ASDWA’s recommendation and establish a stagnation time, then WDNR recommends that EPA require water 
systems report the stagnation time of every tap sampled at the time of sampling (such as on the lab slip), so that 
water systems cannot claim a site exceed the stagnation time after the fact as a justification for invalidating a 
sample with a high result.  
 
Data and Reporting (§ 141.90) 
 
The WDNR takes this opportunity to emphasize and elaborate on its support for the ASDWA comments 
described below.  
 
Reduce the number of required certifications.  This will help make the rule less complex. There are now 24 
certifications in the LCRI.   
 
A 10-day timeframe following the end of each sampling period [§ 141.90(a)(2)] for reporting for lead and 
copper tap samples, will not be feasible for many water systems to meet. Samples collected during the last 
weeks or days of a sampling period cannot be shipped, analyzed and reported in 10 days.  In Wisconsin, 
samples taken near the end of a monitoring period are typically not analyzed and reported until up 45 after the 
end of the sampling period.   
 
Allow a phased-in approach for the review and implementation of updated sampling plans in § 141.90 (a)(1). 
WDNR agrees with ASDWA that EPA should give large systems three years after the effective date of the 
final LCRI to update and obtain approval of their LCRI sampling plan. We further agree that EPA should 
allow medium and small systems four and five years respectively from the effective date of the final rule to 
update their sampling plans. Under the current rule, a high level of effort is necessary for systems to update 
their sampling plan, and significant follow-up with the system is often required before the sampling plan can 
be approved. WDNR has been working with community water systems on updating their sampling plans in 
accordance with existing lead and copper rule requirements since 2020, and this ongoing effort is still in 
progress, with approximately 90 percent complete. Under the current rule, systems have struggled to 
inventory premise plumbing material, determine the presence of a softener or filter, and assign the correct tier. 
Under the proposed LCRI, this will be further complicated by the need to inventory and consider lead 
connectors when prioritizing and assigning tiers to monitoring sites. 
 
Clarify when the 24-hour clock starts in § 141.90(j)(1). Within 24-hours of receiving results from who? What 
if results are received over the weekend or on a holiday?

Lead and Copper Rule Improvements  
 
To Whom It May Concern:  
 
On behalf of the City of Philadelphia, the Philadelphia Water Department (PWD or Department) 
appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) 
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), published at 88 Fed. Reg. 84,878 (Dec. 6, 2023). PWD 
has been a long-standing supporter of local, state, and federal efforts to minimize the levels of lead 
in drinking water and reduce the risk of lead exposure to our City’s residents.  
 
Since the promulgation of the original Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), PWD has supported and 
participated in research and studies to improve the water industry’s management and reduction of 
lead in drinking water. PWD supports the implementation of science-based policies and regulations 
that are both effective and feasible. PWD is an adamant supporter of efforts to reduce lead exposure 
through drinking water. PWD also supports EPA’s goal of removing all lead service lines across the 
country and making efforts to help our customers remove their lead service lines across Philadelphia. 
However, PWD has several concerns regarding the feasibility of the proposed rule with regards to the 
proposed timeline for completion of the service line inventory and lead service line replacement 
program, the costs of the proposed rule, the modifications to the treatment technique, and various 
other technical aspects.  
 
PWD has the following overarching comments regarding the LCRI for your consideration. These 
comments, with additional minor comments, are detailed in the following pages.  
 
1. EPA should immediately delay all Lead and Copper Rule (LCRR) requirements that are 
proposed to be delayed by the LCRI.  
2. EPA and Congress should provide additional funding for water systems to be able to complete 
the proposed service line inventory and lead service line replacement requirements.  
3. EPA’s proposed timeline for 100% lead service line replacement (LSLR) is infeasible and the 
proposed method for determining compliance with this provision is flawed.  
4. EPA’s cost analysis contains large amounts of uncertainty and is annualized over too long of 
a timeframe.  
 

 
 
 
 
 
5. EPA has not demonstrated that the proposed treatment technique is feasible under the newly 
proposed provisions.  
6. EPA should provide clarity on several aspects of the proposed sampling requirements.  
7. EPA should reduce the amount of unnecessary administrative burden on water systems.  
 
PWD appreciates the opportunity to contribute to the regulatory process through the submission of 
these comments. PWD greatly appreciates EPA’s commitment to protecting public health and 
reducing the risk of lead exposure through drinking water.  
 
Sincerely,  
 
 
Randy E. Hayman, Esq. 
Commissioner & Chief Executive Officer 
Philadelphia Water Department 
 

 
 
General 
 
1. EPA should immediately delay the LCRR provisions that LCRI proposes to delay, ensuring 
that Community Water Systems (CWS) aren’t left unprepared if the LCRI is not finalized by 
October 16, 2024. 
 
Given the very short time between the end of the proposed LCRI comment period and the 
compliance deadline for the LCRR, PWD requests that EPA immediately issue a final rule 
postponing the components of the LCRR that the LCRI proposes to delay. This will allow 
water systems to focus already limited resources on the components of the LCRR that begin 
in 2024 and allow more time for systems to receive additional and needed guidance from the 
EPA and states on implementation of the other requirements that would now be delayed. 
Without the delay, water systems are faced with the choice of allotting significant resources 
to prepare for requirements that may be delayed, or potentially face non-compliance. 
 
2. EPA needs to provide more funding to support the replacement and identification of Lead 
Service Lines (LSLs) and Galvanized Requiring Replacement (GRRs), given realistic 
replacement costs.  
 
The cost of service for PWD’s drinking water, wastewater, and stormwater improvements are 
borne by the rates and charges paid by customers. Current estimates for replacing lead 
service lines outside of existing infrastructure work in Philadelphia (i.e. not during water main 
replacement) range from approximately $12,000 to $15,000 per service line, approximately 
$6,000 higher than what EPA has estimated in the rulemaking. PWD believes that these costs 
will result in a total program cost for LSL replacement between $400 and $500 million, based 
on current estimates of LSLs and GRRs in our systems. These costs are reflective of the 
complications of doing this work in a dense urban environment, and include extensive 
restoration of sidewalk concrete, where the bulk of curb stops are located. These costs are in 
line with a 2022 American Water Works Association (AWWA) commissioned report that 
included a detailed engineering analysis of actual service line replacement programs that was 
provided to EPA during the LCRI federalism comment period1. In Philadelphia, where the 
service line is owned in entirety by the property owner, the LCRI would require PWD rate 
payers to shoulder that cost through rate increases in the absence of additional, significant 
federal investment. Rate increases are already necessary to support replacement of aging 
infrastructure and compliance with multiple new rulemakings. In conversations with the PA 
State Revolving Fund (SRF) program, PWD does not anticipate more than $5-$10 million a 
year in grant availability for this program for Philadelphia, while PWD estimates LSL 
replacement to cost $40-$50/year over a 10-year period. A lack of funding to support 
replacing LSL and GRR will only increase the cost burden on the rate payer. 
 
3. EPA should consider affordability more broadly when determining a utility’s ability to pay 
for unfunded and underfunded mandates.  
 
1 AWWA. 2022. Lead and Copper Rulemaking Improvements Rulemaking. Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0813 
(Federalism Comments). CDM Smith. Final Report. Considerations when Costing Lead Service Line Identification 
and Replacement, November 2022.   

 
 
 
PWD is faced with many obligations and regulatory initiatives that require the expenditure of  
operating and capital dollars. Current planned investments include increasing water main 
replacement targets to 42 miles per year2, increasing  planned sewer main rehabilitation to 
eight (8) miles per year2, comprehensive water and wastewater revitalization plans to renew 
and rehabilitate existing assets, a Long-Term Control Plan Update (LTCPU) Consent Order and 
Agreement (CO&A), forthcoming new NPDES permit requirements at all three Water 
Pollution Control Plants (WPCPs), forthcoming new Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System 
(MS4) permit requirements, as well as evaluating and future-proofing facilities in the face of 
major climate impacts. Beyond planned investments in existing infrastructure and imminent 
permit requirements, EPA is establishing three new rules in 2024 that will have major financial 
impacts to the Department. The first is the LCRI, which will require significant investments by 
the Department to locate and replace all LSLs and GRRs the system (The Department’s system 
includes approximately 511,000 service lines). Shortly following the draft LCRI, the EPA  
published a proposed rule to revise the aquatic life designated use and dissolved oxygen 
water quality criteria applicable to a portion of the Delaware River. This regulation will compel 
PWD to make significant capital investments at all three of the Department’s wastewater 
treatment plants to remove ammonia3. Finally, the final PFAS Maximum Contaminant Level 
(MCL) is expected to be issued this year, which is likely to propose requirements for PWD to 
install expensive PFAS treatment technologies in at least two of three large drinking water 
treatment plants. These three rules in combination will require PWD to spend billions of 
dollars in the coming years to tackle these three issues simultaneously, with minimal 
opportunities currently for federal assistance. If PWD is forced to make investment decisions 
on how to spend ratepayer dollars based on these combined rulemakings, the failure to be 
able to invest in other asset groups may risk our services and public health and safety in 
other ways. PWD concludes that EPA should take a holistic view of the regulated industry and 
consider the potential impacts of all regulations.   
 
 
Corrosion Control Treatment (CCT) 
 
4. EPA should remove requirements for large CWSs to re-optimize Corrosion Control 
Treatment (CCT) in the absence of an action level exceedance. 
 
The LCRI CCT requirements as per the proposed §141.81(a)(1)(ii - iii) include a provision 
which states that larger water systems “may be required by the state” to complete the 
re-optimized Optimized Corrosion Control Treatment (OCCT), in instances where they 
have an existing CCT strategy and a 90th percentile result that are below the action 
level. This provision should be removed from the final rule for at least three reasons. 
First, given the aggressive timeline for service line replacement, and the reduced action 
level, it does not add any practical value or additional public health protection in this 
 
2 City of Philadelphia.2023. Water and Wastewater Revenue Bonds Series 2023B, available at 
ttps://www.phila.gov/media/20231003113936/Water-and-Wastewater-Revenue-Bonds-Series-2023.pdf. 
3 See 88 Fed. Reg. 88,315 (Dec. 21, 2023). 

 
 
instance to require a system to go through re-optimization. It takes a significant amount 
of time and effort to plan and execute a valid OCCT study at a large system, and then to 
implement the results of that study. If a system has previously conducted those studies, 
there should be no reason to replicate them in absence of an action level exceedance. 
 
Second, it should also be noted that States continue to retain the authority to require 
additional action above and beyond federal law, so the inclusion of such language 
seems unnecessary. 
 
Third, this requirement will result in similar levels of confusion that were caused by the 
trigger level introduced in the LCRR. The EPA intentionally removed the trigger level to 
reduce complexity and remove the confusion caused by having two different levels 
triggering or potentially triggering different actions. The EPA should continue to avoid 
this type of complexity by not requiring actions based on 90th percentile values greater 
than the Practical Quantitation Limit (PQL) but less than the Action Level. 
 
 
Lead Service Line Replacement 
 
5. EPA should revise the definition of “control” in the LCRI. 
 
PWD agrees strongly with AWWA’s comment that EPA should return to the definition 
of “control” it adopted in the LCR revisions in 2000, that “control” is based on 
ownership. The definition of what is “under the control” of water systems as described 
in the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA) does not include piping unowned by the water 
system, even when the actual owner uses their control to grant access to a water 
system. EPA’s authorizing statute, then, does not authorize the Agency to require water 
systems to replace service lines not owned by the water system.   
 
6. EPA should consider a longer timeline for the replacement of all lead service lines. 
 
The 10-year replacement timeline for all LSLs and GRRs as per the proposed §141.84(d)(4) is 
not feasible due to financial concerns, limited resources, and competing regulatory priorities. 
The rule should provide additional mechanisms for CWSs to evaluate a longer timeline for 
their replacement schedule.  
 
With the limited federal funding available, many systems, including PWD, may need to delay 
necessary capital work and/or need to cut programs or defer maintenance in our operating 
budget to meet the 10-year timeframe, delaying necessary improvements and creating 
additional community impacts that may increase risk of service and other public health and 
safety concerns. See Comment #3, above, for more details on PWD’s other commitments and 
infrastructure needs. None of the programs highlighted within the rule text could have 
completed their replacement schedules on accelerated schedules without the additional 
external subsidies they received (See 88 Fed. Reg. at 84,912-913). It is also unlikely that those 

 
 
systems would have been able to accelerate their replacement schedules when competing 
with every other water system for contractors and consultants to complete this work.  
 
PWD is also concerned that the amount of skilled labor needed to perform these 
replacements will not be available at the level necessary to meet the established replacement 
timeframe. For instance, the Associated Builders and Contractors (ABC), an organization that 
tracks the construction industry, has found that there is an 8.5-month backlog on projects as 
of December 2023. These trends remain unchanged for the last several years, indicating that 
this problem is likely to not abate4. 
 
Additionally, PWD recommends that EPA remove the language in §141.84(c)(5)(iv). The 
entirety of this section that begins with "Shortened deadline and associated replacement 
rate” should be removed. States already have the authority to create guidance and 
regulations that are more stringent than those adopted by the EPA. Placing language in the 
LCRI proposed rule that authorizes States to establish shortened replacement schedules is 
not only unnecessary but also means many states will approach their own programs assuming 
that EPA wants them to adopt shorter replacement schedules. Given the complications with 
executing a 10-year replacement schedule, any language that intimates that shortened 
schedules can be met should be removed. 
 
7. “Unknowns” should not be included in the replacement rates. 
 
By requiring water systems to include service lines defined based on state or federal adopted 
service line inventory guidance as unknown (hereafter referred to as “Unknowns”) in the 
replacement calculations as per the proposed §141.84(d)(6)(i), EPA is forcing many utilities to 
grossly accelerate their lead service line replacement rates, especially in the early years of the 
program. Using current PWD service line information, the following example showcases the 
issues with these rate calculations. 
 
One scenario, using PWD’s estimate of lead services and assuming a baseline inventory with 
10% Unknowns in a system of 511,000 connections, exemplifies the problem of including 
Unknowns in EPA’s replacement rate calculation. PWD is currently anticipating approximately 
a 4% rate of lead and a 0.5% rate of galvanized service lines in the system. As it is currently 
written, the LCRI could require  the Department to meet a 31% replacement rate averaged 
across the first three years of compliance to meet a required replacement rate in this 
scenario. This equates to a replacement of almost 7,200 services in the first year of 
compliance, and the highest projected number of replacements required in the program at 
a time when the program is still being established, issues are being resolved, and 
contractors are being engaged and ramping up their own workforce. If the Department has 
greater than 10% Unknowns in its baseline inventory, the calculations become even more 
untenable for reasons outlined in Comment #6 above. See Table 1 below for the details 
regarding this scenario. 
 
4 ABC. 2023. ABC’s Construction Backlog Indicator Inches up in November, Contractors Remain Confident. Dec 
12,2023. 

 
 
Table 1: PWD Replacement Program with 10% Unknowns 
 
 
The requirement to include Unknown service lines in replacement rate calculations 
unnecessarily complicates LCRI compliance for many utilities. Many utilities with Unknowns 
will be forced to front-end replacements in their program, when a more sensible approach 
would be to ramp up replacement rates over the first few years as the program develops and 
the workforce adjusts. There are other ways EPA could ensure utilities are making adequate 
progress, such as: 
A. Allow utilities to define their own program metrics in their required lead 
service line replacement plan. Utilities know their individual systems, 
contractor pools, and workforces best. If a replacement plan commits to 
identifying and removing all LSLs and GRRs in the 10-year compliance period,  
this should meet the intent of the rule, especially in cases where utilities have 
low tap sampling results and OCCT in place. This is PWD’s preferred approach. 
B. Consider establishing separate rates for reducing Unknowns and removing 
known LSLs and GRRs. 
C. Completely remove Unknowns as a factor in the annual replacement pool 
calculations. 
 
At a minimum, EPA should change the replacement pool calculation to allow for a percentage 
of Unknowns to count as suspected LSLs or GRRs, based on the makeup of the systems known 
services. This will still allow utilities to plan for meeting the 10-year compliance requirements, 
while removing the potential for accelerating replacements in communities without 
document lead-in-water public health issues. 
 
8. EPA should count disconnected services toward replacement goals in instances where a

Pursuant to the proposed §141.84(d)(6)(iii)(B), a full replacement is counted where a LSL or 
GRR is disconnected from the water main. As proposed, the pipe being replaced will also have 
to be disconnected from the customer’s side of the connection. PWD supports counting
