9. EPA’s decision to allow the continued use of partial service line replacements during 
emergency or planned infrastructure work is vital to allowing utilities to complete 
necessary work to keep systems operating. 
 
PWD generally agrees with EPA that while replacing only part of a lead service line is not 
preferential, it remains a necessary industry practice. Since 2017, PWD has been replacing 
lead and galvanized service lines as a standard practice on capitally funded water main 
replacement projects. To fully replace a service line, PWD must obtain written authorization 
from the property owner, and the owner and/or resident must allow access to the property 
on the day of replacement. Because such authorization and access are not always granted, 
not all homes receive a full service line replacement. Thus, PWD supports the exemptions for 
emergency repair or planned infrastructure work as per the proposed §141.84(g). 
 
PWD’s standard practice during water main replacement is to replace all services up to the 
curb stop, so every service, regardless of material type, is partially replaced. In instances 
where PWD cannot obtain authorization and/or be granted access from the property owner 
for a full lead service line replacement, the service line is replaced up to the curb stop and a 
dielectric coupling is installed. If EPA prohibits the partial replacement of lead service lines in 
instances like this, it will complicate systems’ efforts to replace water mains. Barring a water 
system the ability to reconnect the service during planned infrastructure work would lead 
to discontinuation of service to existing inhabited structures with non-cooperating or non-
responsive property owners. Discontinuation of service in such instances creates a public 
safety and public health hazard, as well as potentially deepening environmental justice issues. 
 
10. EPA should revise notification requirements following a LSL or GRR replacement. 
 
Currently, the proposed §141.84(h)(3) would require notice be provided to “the owner of the 
affected service line, or the owner’s authorized agent … as soon as possible but no longer than 
24 hours following completion of the replacement”. In many instances, the owner does not 
occupy the premises, nor is present to receive materials. As EPA is aware, LSLs and GRRs can 
be associated with rental properties, some of which include difficult to reach absentee 
landlords. PWD agrees with leaving instructions and notification, along with risk mitigation 
measures, following a LSL or GRR replacement, with the occupants of the properties. By 
requiring notice to the owner in lieu of residents in such a timeframe detracts from getting 
that information into the hands of those who would be most impacted by the service line 
replacement (i.e. those who use the water at the property on a day-to-day basis). EPA should 
eliminate the need for expedited risk communications to property owners and focus on 
occupants first. 
 
11. EPA should remove the requirement to provide outreach for service line replacement 
following a change of ownership. 

 
 
 
Currently, the proposed §141.84(d)(3)(ii) would require water systems to offer a full 
replacement within six months of change in ownership of a property. However, this 
requirement presumes that water systems have available information on property ownership 
changes within six months. In Philadelphia, property records can take up to a year to update 
in internal systems. Additionally, even when the account holder changes on a water bill, it 
does not indicate that ownership has changed, and a lack of update to the account holder 
also does not mean ownership has not changed. In short, this requirement as written will 
put utilities in non-compliance through no fault of their own and should not be finalized. 
 
 
Lead Service Line Inventory 
 
12. The inclusion of connectors in the inventory is unnecessary and likely to create confusion 
amongst the general public. 
 
PWD agrees that requiring the replacement of connectors during planned service line 
replacement is a sound policy. When a full lead service is replaced, that replacement should 
start with the water main and, in Philadelphia’s case, generally end at the meter in the 
resident’s house. However, PWD concurs with the AWWA comment that the tracking of lead 
connectors should be an element of the system’s materials evaluation (i.e., §141.42(d) as 
referenced in proposed LCRI at §141.86(a)(i)) rather than an element of the inventory as 
described in the Proposed Rule at §141.84. Requiring utilities to inventory connectors would 
simply be cost prohibitive, as the primary way of identifying them will be through excavation, 
and given that lead connectors are not considered a primary source of lead contamination in 
drinking water. 
 
Requiring the publication of connector material in the public facing database would be 
confusing to customers and potentially harmful towards maintaining the customer’s trust. 
For instance, customers who have a known service line material, but unknown connector 
type, would be less trustful that their service line was properly identified, or was being 
accurately handled by the utility. To require notification to customers about the presence or 
potential presence of lead connectors would detract from the goals of removing lead services 
and draw customer attention away from more actionable and meaningful measures. This 
creates much more uncertainty and issues with communicating to the public, which is 
contrary to EPA’s goal in the LCRI to “simplify the rule relative to the 2021 Lead and Copper 
Rule Revisions (LCRR)”.  
 
13. EPA should strengthen the use of the validation pool for inventory validation. 
 
PWD agrees that requiring validation is a great way to ensure accuracy of information, build 
trust, and allow for the implementation of new service line identification technologies. EPA 
should consider a pathway for accepting additional verification methods that may use 
new/emerging technologies. EPA could incorporate language in the rule that allows the use 
of novel identification technologies for validation purposes, provided those technologies have 
an acceptable level of accuracy to visual verifications. 

 
 
 
Additionally, it is important that EPA clearly communicate the expectations of the validation 
study to the states, along with other expectations for inventory development and what is 
considered acceptable practice. It would be important to codify the fact that records-based 
service material determinations can be reflective of a community, neighborhood, or other 
area, and not only for each individual service line. 
 
Finally, EPA should consider proposing clear language for when water systems fail their 
initial validation study. In the table included in the proposed rule §141.84(b)(5)(ii), EPA 
correctly assesses the sample size for a validation study. However, the language is unclear as 
to a water systems’ responsibility when the validation study deviates from a 95% confidence 
interval. As such, EPA should include clearer direction, such as including a third column in the 
table that is reflective of the number of additional samples to be drawn to reassess the 
validation pool. This clarification is necessary both for water systems to adhere to and for 
states to understand how to approach an initial validation study that may not meet the 
prescribed confidence interval.  
 
14. EPA should consider simplifying inventory reporting requirements. 
 
With the inclusion of property address in the required public facing inventory, EPA should 
consider utilizing the public facing inventory as a submission to the state, along with summary 
reporting of the inventory characteristics. It would be more efficient and avoid duplication 
of effort for states and water systems to rely on the required public facing inventory, rather 
than create yet another separate deliverable to upload in various state reporting systems. 
The current requirement as outlined in §141.90(e)(8)(i) and §142.14(d)(9) is overly 
burdensome from a data transfer and data storage standpoint for states and water systems. 
A simple, summary report would be more beneficial for all parties, with all the information 
currently anticipated to be required for reporting to be publicly available through the public-
facing inventory portal. 
 
Cost/Benefit Analysis 
 
15. EPA’s cost and benefit model appears subject to large amounts of uncertainty and potential 
inaccuracy.  
 
In the development of any model, it is important to recognize that there will be uncertainty 
in the results regardless of how accurate the input data is. This inherent uncertainty can 
normally be accepted if the model can be tested against known outcomes to verify its 
accuracy. However, the uncertainty in a model’s result is made far worse when the input data 
being used is either inaccurate or not representative of the population that the model is being 
used for. With EPA’s Economic Analysis for the LCRI, the level of uncertainty associated with 
almost every single input is enough to raise significant doubt in the model’s outcome. When 
all of the uncertainty from these various inputs are combined, it makes it difficult to 
understand how this model can be trusted to accurately assess the cost of this rulemaking. 
In its economic analysis, EPA makes it clear that they are unaware of how these uncertainties 
will impact the model. To be clear, not only are the assumptions or data inputs into the model 

 
 
filled with uncertainty, but there is also additional uncertainty as to how the uncertainty of 
these assumptions and inputs will impact the model. EPA chooses to only account for a few 
of these uncertainties with high and low estimates, but this seems insufficient given the scope 
and impacts that this regulation will have on the country’s water systems. Additionally, PWD 
was unable to assess how changes to any assumptions would impact the model results 
because the model and the directions provided by EPA for using it did not work as written.  
Given the significant financial scale of this regulation, EPA should not be leaving these 
important considerations up to this level of uncertainty.   
 
16. EPA should utilize an appropriate analysis period for estimating incremental costs 
proportional to the proposed timelines of the LCRI. 
 
Under the LCRI, one of the major changes is the shortened timeline for the requirement to 
replace lead service lines. Under this proposed rule, water systems will be required to replace 
all lead service lines within 10 years of the compliance date of the regulation. EPA estimates 
that this effort will drastically reduce lead levels in drinking water and provide long term 
health benefits. EPA also estimates that the number of systems that will have lead action level 
exceedances will drastically decrease once lead service lines are removed, with only 4.3%-
8.6% of systems with no LSLs expected to have an action level exceedance compared to an 
estimated 21.1%-39.1% of systems with LSLs (Exhibit 4-5 of EPA’s Economic Analysis). With 
the requirements for service line inventories and lead service line replacements all occurring 
within 10 years and the costs associated with action level exceedances expected to 
significantly decrease after lead service lines are removed, the majority of the costs 
associated with this regulation will be borne by the water systems, states, and ratepayers 
over the first 10 years. However, despite the shortened timetable for these costly 
requirements being a cornerstone for this regulation, this shorter timeline was not carried 
forward into the economic analysis proposed by EPA.  
 
In section 4.2.3.3 of EPA’s Proposed LCRI Economic Analysis, EPA states that it utilized a 35-
year period to estimate the incremental costs of the proposed LCRI. This is explained further 
in section B.2.4 of the Appendices for this Economic Analysis, where EPA states that this 35-
year period will allow EPA to “full capture the costs of the rule since it may take over 30 years 
for many CWSs to complete their service line replacement program under the LCRR.” PWD 
would agree that a 35-year analysis period is appropriate for estimating the annualized costs 
of the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions. As such, in this economic analysis, it is appropriate for 
the baseline annualized costs to be estimated over a 35-year period. However, given the 
proposed requirements regarding lead service line replacement timelines, using a 35-year 
period to estimate the costs of the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements is incorrect . While 
water systems may be able to use debt funding for LSLR costs, under the proposed LCRI, water 
systems will bear most of the remaining costs from the LCRI in the first 10 years following the 
compliance date. By providing annualized costs over a 35-year period, EPA is drastically 
underestimating the annualized costs of this regulation. Using the equation provided in 
chapter 6 of EPA’s 2010 Guideline for Preparing Economic Analyses for calculating annualized 
values, utilizing a 35 year period rather than a 10 year period would result in a cost estimate 
that is only 42% of the actual annualized costs of the components of the rule that cannot be 
debt funded.  

 
 
 
PWD recommends that EPA update their economic analysis by calculating the incremental 
cost differences between the LCRR (with costs estimated over a 35-year period) and the LCRI 
(with costs estimated over a 10-year period) to reflect the drastic changes in regulatory 
timelines between the two regulations.   
 
17. EPA should account for the impacts of other ongoing regulatory agenda items in their 
estimations on how many systems will make changes to treatment processes over the life 
of this regulation. 
 
EPA is currently pursuing many major regulatory agenda items that directly impact public 
water systems. It is critical that EPA consider the combined impacts of these regulations, 
especially from a financial perspective. EPA should consider the impacts that each of these 
regulations will have on each other, regardless of if they are finalized, when evaluating the 
cost and benefits of these regulations. In addition to this LCRI, EPA is currently in the process 
of finalizing its landmark National Primary Drinking Water Regulation establishing a drinking 
water MCL for PFAS compounds, with the final rule being submitted to the White House’s 
Office of Management and Budget on December 15, 2023 for final interagency review. This 
PFAS rule is expected to result in one of the largest nationwide investments in water 
treatment upgrades if the proposed MCL levels are maintained in the final regulation. 
However, in section 3.3.9.3 of the cost analysis for the LCRI, EPA estimates the percentage of 
systems that will change treatment each year based on historical data and do not seem to 
consider at all the significant increase in systems making changes due to the PFAS MCL 
regulation. Under the LCRI, anytime the State deems these treatment changes “to be 
significant”,  the water system will revert to standard monitoring and be required to do 
extensive piloting and pipe loop studies to confirm the impact on lead release are minimized. 
With two of the three proposed Best Available Technologies (BATs) for PFAS treatment, 
Granular Activated Carbon (GAC) and Ion Exchange (IX), expected to potentially impact 
corrosion rates, it is likely that almost all implemented PFAS treatments will trigger these 
additional LCRI requirements.  
 
PWD recommends that EPA should consider the percentages of systems likely to make 
treatment changes due to PFAS MCL exceedances and how that would impact the costs 
associated with the LCRI requirements before and after treatment changes are implemented.  
 
 
Tap Sampling Protocol 
 
18. EPA has not demonstrated that the proposed LCRI’s treatment technique’s OCCT 
component is feasible from a technical standpoint.  
 
Through the LCRI, the EPA is proposing several changes to the rule’s treatment technique 
including lowering the action level to 10 ppb, modifying the sampling protocol for homes with 
lead service lines, and revising the sample pool for systems with lead service lines and 
galvanized requiring replacement service lines. While making all these changes, EPA has 
maintained that high-dose orthophosphate or pH/alkalinity adjustment will be the 

 
 
anticipated optimal corrosion control technology. EPA’s assessment fails to reliably 
demonstrate that the proposed corrosion control treatment technologies will enable 
systems to reliably meet the new action level under the newly proposed sampling 
requirements, especially given the large number of water systems that will need to make 
treatment changes (to meet the pending PFAS MCLs) that may affect corrosion rates.   
 
First, EPA directly states in the preamble in section E.1 that “EPA anticipates more systems 
could exceed the lead action level even when re-optimized”. If EPA is readily expecting that 
even with optimized corrosion control installed that systems will be unable to meet the newer 
action level, how can they deem that the proposed treatment technologies are effective? 
While PWD agrees with the proposed provision to not require systems to continually re-
optimize corrosion control if a system has subsequent Action Level Exceedances (ALEs) 
following initial optimization or re-optimization, there are numerous actions triggered by ALE 
that will continue to be in effect even if the ALE occurs while the system has already done its 
due diligence in installing optimized corrosion control treatment. EPA continues in section E.1 
of the preamble by stating that “EPA recognizes that there may be some instances where 
systems would be unable to meet the proposed lowered lead action level of 0.010 mg/L 
because tap water lead levels can be influenced by other factors.” This statement clearly 
demonstrates that EPA recognizes that, under the proposed conditions, there will be 
situations where systems, for reasons unrelated to corrosion control efficacy, will exceed the 
action level. This makes the proposed solution infeasible by EPA’s definition.  
 
Second, EPA has extremely limited empirical data on how many systems will or will not be 
able to meet this requirement and the feasibility of optimizing or re-optimizing corrosion 
control at these systems. EPA utilized only historic first-draw lead levels and static 
multiplicative factors to try to estimate the impacts on the change in sample methodology 
would have on systems exceeding the new action level. This method is flawed and provides a 
weak estimation at best. Under the proposed LCRI, EPA is requiring all systems to revert to 
standard monitoring as their historic data is not considered valid in demonstrating that their 
90th percentile lead levels are below the action level. If these historic first-draw lead levels 
are not valid for a system to demonstrate that it is reliably below the action level, then it is 
inconsistent for EPA to then use that same data to estimate how many systems will or will 
not be able to meet their newly proposed requirements.  
 
Finally, the inclusion of galvanized iron plumbing as a separate tier in the LCRI’s sample 
location tiering system introduces the corrosion of iron plumbing materials as a key factor in 
compliance even after all lead service lines are removed. Corrosion control treatment has 
been optimized to prevent or minimize lead release from lead service lines and leaded solder 
on copper plumbing. EPA has not demonstrated that the proposed corrosion control 
treatment strategies are able to effectively control lead release from these galvanized lines.  
 
In the preamble, EPA requests comment on the proposed action level of 0.010 mg/L and 
potential alternative action levels, such as 0.005 mg/L. PWD believes that EPA has not 
adequately demonstrated that the newly proposed action level of 0.010 mg/L is feasible 
under the proposed treatment technique and that is even more true of a more stringent 
action level, such as 0.005 mg/L. PWD recommends that EPA reassess the feasibility of this 

 
 
newly proposed action level and if it cannot effectively demonstrate this feasibility that it 
then must retain the current action level of 0.015 mg/L. It is important to not lose sight of the 
lead action level being a treatment technique and not a health-based limit. Although water 
systems should continue to maintain optimized corrosion control treatment, LSL replacement 
is the component of this updated rule that will most effectively address exposure to lead by 
completely removing this major source of lead to customer drinking water. 
 
19. EPA should select only the 1st liter or 5th liter data for LSL homes and 1st Liter data for non-
LSL homes in the calculation of 90th percentile values. 
 
In section V.A (Regulatory Approach) of the LCRI’s preamble, EPA discusses its previous 
decision to utilize a treatment technique rather than establishing an MCL for Lead. In this 
section EPA concludes that the justification for using a treatment technique is still applicable 
today and that it would maintain this regulatory approach. In this discussion, one of the 
reasons for utilizing a treatment technique is that “SDWA precludes the Agency from 
promulgating a ‘regulation that holds a [public water system] liable for conditions that are 
beyond it’s control’ and that ‘EPA posited that an MCL would not be considered ‘feasible’ if a 
significant number of water systems would be in noncompliance due to conditions outside of 
their control.’” The science is clear that uncontrolled water corrosivity, which is a condition 
that can mostly be controlled by the water system, can lead to increased metals release from 
plumbing materials, including lead-bearing materials, within customer’s homes. To this point, 
EPA states in section V.C of the LCRI’s preamble that “EPA designed the tap sampling 
requirements in the LCR primarily to evaluate the corrosion of lead and copper sources present 
in the distribution system”. PWD supports the goal of the LCR, LCRR, and LCRI to better 
understand and control the corrosion of plumbing materials to prevent exposure to these 
metals in drinking water. However, while EPA states that the goal of the tap sampling protocol 
is to assess corrosivity and that feasibility should be assessed by factors that are within the 
control of the water system, the discussion in the preamble of the LCRI suggests that the 
additional requirement to sample the 1st and 5th liter at LSL homes and using the higher value 
for compliance was implemented primarily with the goal of causing more systems to have 
90th percentile results above the action level. In section V.C, EPA describes two scenarios 
where they would expect the 1st liter sample to be higher than the 5th liter sample in homes 
with LSL. For the first scenario, a system where scale in the LSL is uncontrolled, PWD agrees 
that a system would likely see high 1st liter results, however, it would seem logical that this 
system would likely see high 5th liter results as well and the 1st liter probably wouldn’t be 
needed to cause the system to exceed the action level. For the second scenario, EPA describes 
a situation where a system has effectively formed lead scale and inhibited lead release from 
lead service lines stating that then they may find higher lead in other premise plumbing 
materials, likely in the form of particulate lead. While PWD appreciates that the situation 
described in scenario #2 is possible, if a system is effectively passivating lead release from the 
largest source of lead in a home’s plumbing, then it would seem logical that it is controlling 
the corrosivity of their water, which is the aspect of lead corrosion that is within the control 
of the water system. While PWD supports efforts to reduce and remove all sources of lead in 
plumbing materials, these legacy materials will continue to exist in various aspects of home 
plumbing that are outside the control of the water system. By requiring water systems to 
collect multiple samples from a single home and then only selecting the samples with the 

 
 
higher result with the clearly stated expectation that this will “result in more systems that will 
be required to optimize or re-optimize corrosion control treatment and provide notification 
and public education”, EPA is going against its own definition of what is feasible based on 
factors that are within the control of the water system. 
 
Further, if the goal of lead and copper tap sampling is to assess the efficacy of corrosion 
control treatment as stated, then EPA has not made it clear how the newly proposed sampling 
methodology is a more effective measurement of the effectiveness of corrosion control. In 
the LCRR, EPA stated that it was switching to 5th liter sampling for homes with LSL because 
the “data gathered from the fifth liter samples to calculate the 90th percentile is a better 
indicator of the effectiveness of corrosion control treatment in a system.” EPA should more 
definitely state why this determination has changed in terms of assessing corrosion control 
efficacy.  
 
PWD suggests that EPA maintain the finalized LCRR sampling protocol utilizing 5th liter data 
for homes with LSL and 1st liter data for homes without LSL or revert back to 1st liter data 
for all samples. EPA should clearly identify the sample they believe to be most representative 
of corrosion control efficacy and remain consistent in how tap sampling results are utilized.    
 
20. EPA should be less prescriptive in how liters 2-4 are collected in sampling protocol outlined 
in 141.86(b)(ii). 
 
PWD supports EPA in providing a clear definition of what it considers to be a “wide-mouth” 
bottle. However, in 141.86(b)(ii), EPA states that during the collection of 1st and 5th liter 
samples from homes with lead service lines that “[t]o collect a first and fifth liter paired 
sample, systems must collect tap water in five consecutively numbered, wide-mouth, one-liter 
sample bottles.” While PWD does not dispute the requirement for using wide-mouth bottles 
for the 1st and 5th liter of these consecutive sample bottles, EPA should not mandate how a 
system chooses to collect the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th liter of water so long as the three liters are 
adequately accounted for before the collection of the 5th liter sample and it is approved by its 
primacy agency. For example, PWD implemented 1st and 5th liter sampling during its 2022 LCR 
monitoring period and used two different bottle types for its sample kits. For the 1st and 5th 
liter bottles, a wide-mouth, one-liter bottle was used. However, for the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th liter 
bottles, the Department used a differently shaped one-liter bottle with a slightly smaller 
mouth. The purpose of the two different bottle types was to further reinforce to the customer 
which bottles were meant to be kept for analysis and which were to be dumped. The bottles 
for the 1st and 5th liter sample were shipped with lids while the bottles for the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th 
liter were not shipped with lids and the lids from the 1st and 5th liter bottles would not fit on 
the other three. This sample kit design was done to minimize potential confusion associated 
with collecting multiple samples. While the mouth of the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th liter bottles were 
smaller than the now prescribed 55 mm wide-mouth definition, these bottles still had 
sufficiently wide mouth that they would not inhibit sample collection from a tap running at 
full flow. This is just one example of how these sample kits can be made in different ways to 
promote sample collection accuracy given the increase in complexity with this sample 
method. Given the magnitude of samples that will have to be collected using this method, 
EPA should not restrict how systems collect liters 2 through 4 during this sample collection. 

 
 
For example, if a water system finds that it is easier to fill a 3-liter container between the 1st 
and 5th liter sample, then EPA should not restrict them from doing that.  
 
PWD suggests that the wording in 141.86(b)(ii) be updated to read “To collect a first and fifth 
liter paired sample, systems must collect the first five liters of water following the required 
stagnation period with the first and fifth liter collected in wide-mouth, one-liter sample 
bottles”.   
 
21. EPA should modify the definition of “wide-mouth bottle”.  
 
As stated, PWD supports EPA providing a clearer definition of “wide-mouth bottle”. However, 
the proposed definition may present a bottleneck around the number of available bottles for 
water systems performing lead and copper tap sampling. With the intention of this definition 
being to prevent the use of small-mouth bottles for lead and copper tap sampling, which 
would require a lower flow to accurately fill the bottle, PWD believes that EPA could still fulfill 
the spirit of this requirement with a less stringent definition of “wide-mouth”. A  less stringent 
definition would reduce the supply chain burdens in procuring these bottles. PWD suggests 
that EPA modify the proposed definition of “wide-mouth” bottle from “outer diameter at 
least 55 mm wide” to “inner diameter at least 40 mm wide”.  
 
22. EPA should clarify whether sampling requirements defined in 141.86(b)(1) now apply to 
voluntary customer sampling programs that are not included in LCR monitoring. 
 
In section 141.86(b)(1), the proposed LCRI states that all tap samples analyzed for lead and 
copper, except for those collected as part of Distribution System and Site Assessments, must 
be collected in a one-liter, wide-mouth bottle after six hours of stagnation. However, in 
section H.4 of the proposed LCRI preamble, EPA states that, in the event that a system 
exceeds the action level and must offer a “supplemental” customer requested sample 
program, “EPA is proposing to maintain flexibility for water systems to determine the sampling 
protocol for this supplemental monitoring.” PWD requests clarification on whether CWSs 
that implement a voluntary customer requested lead sampling program, without exceeding 
any action levels, would also have flexibility in the methods used for collecting these 
samples or would these systems be required to collect samples following the procedures 
described in 141.86(b)(1).  
 
In addition, if a system is required to offer a customer requested sampling program, the 
proposed LCRI would also require the system to notify the customer of the results from their 
sampling within 3 days of the system getting the results. PWD asks that EPA clarify whether 
this 3-calendar day notification would also apply for any voluntary customer requested 
sampling programs that were not established as a response to an action level exceedance, 
regardless of whether the sampling procedure specified in 141.86(b)(1) was followed. If a 
CWS offers a voluntary customer requested lead program and the proposed 3-calendar day 
result notification requirement is applied to this type of program, it will act as a disincentive 
for systems to offer this service to their consumers. This requirement will likely result in less 
free lead testing across the country so that CWSs are not putting themselves at risk of 

 
 
regulatory violation due simply to administrative issues and the burden of meeting a 3-
calendar day notification requirement.    
 
23. EPA should not include results collected outside of the regulatory monitoring program in 
water systems’ compliance calculations.  
 
EPA is requesting comment on whether samples from non-LSL homes that have higher lead 
concentrations than homes with LSL should be included in the 90th percentile calculation and 
whether these higher lead concentrations from non-LSL homes should replace lower 
concentrations from LSL homes in the calculation. PWD believes that samples that were 
collected outside of the planned compliance monitoring program should not be included 
simply because they have an elevated lead level. The goal of the compliance monitoring 
program and the accompanying sample pool are very specifically to assess the lead levels in 
homes that are most at risk to evaluate the efficacy of the corrosion control treatment at the 
water system. Auxiliary monitoring program samples are likely being collected for far 
different reasons, with different goals and requirements for participation, and would not be 
designed with the same goal of evaluating corrosion control treatment. EPA acknowledges in 
section 141.82(j)(2) of the proposed rule that including samples from site assessments in 
compliance calculations would inaccurately bias systems towards re-optimization. The same 
is true for monitoring programs such as post-lead service line replacement or disturbance 
sampling, for which monitoring is offered because of the known issue, unrelated to corrosion 
control efficacy, that replacements and disturbances can temporarily increase lead levels. 
Additionally, this requirement would disincentivize systems from offering any type of 
customer requested sampling program. In addition to the added risk of finding high lead 
levels, caused by any number of reasons unrelated to corrosion control efficacy, water 
systems would then be forced to perform far more intensive site characterization of any home 
participating in the customer requested sample program. EPA should not be taking steps to 
disincentivize water systems from offering these types of programs from their customers due 
to added risk of non-compliance. Finally, through the tiering system proposed within this 
regulation and the new proposed requirement that all homes included in the compliance 
monitoring pool be Tier 1 and Tier 2 homes, EPA is clearly stating that they believe that the 
homes best suited for evaluating the efficacy of corrosion control are those with lead service 
lines. If EPA believes that the sampling pool should be comprised of only homes with lead 
service lines, then the Agency should remain consistent in that assessment and not include 
higher values from unrelated monitoring programs with different goals; this would  increase 
the number of systems that are in a state of non-compliance, and for reasons unrelated to 
system corrosion control optimization.  
 
24. EPA should remove the requirement for water systems to provide an explanation for 
changes to their sample locations from round to round. 
 
Since the promulgation of the LCR in 1991, PWD has completed 15 distinct lead and copper 
tap monitoring periods. Lead and copper tap monitoring, unlike any other regulatory 
monitoring program, is conducted at locations that are entirely out of the control of the water 
system and the water system must rely on customers’ voluntary participation. For each of 
these monitoring periods, one of the most time consuming and difficult tasks is the 

 
 
recruitment of willing participants who meet the sampling criteria for the program. EPA 
should be making every effort to reduce the burden on water systems who are acting in good 
faith to find  qualifying homes that are willing to participate. The requirements defined in 
141.86(b)(2) state that a “water system must collect tap samples from the same sampling 
sites” and that a water system “must include an explanation of why sampling sites have 
changed” unnecessarily add administrative burden to the lead and copper tap monitoring 
programs, which are already onerous as discussed here. PWD agrees with the Pennsylvania 
Department of Environmental Protection’s comments on Docket No EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0813 
that it is not necessary for a water system to report or explain that they have sampled at a 
different location from previous monitoring rounds.  
 
During the first six (6) of PWD’s lead and copper monitoring periods, from 1992 to 1999, PWD 
was able to continue with the same pool of customers while still meeting the minimum 
number of required samples. However, over those 6 monitoring periods, the number of 
participants dropped consistently from 162 to 57. This shows that even at the beginning of 
the program it was difficult to maintain a static sampling pool for this monitoring program. In 
the monitoring periods since then, and especially since only LSL were included in the sampling 
pool in 2016, PWD has had to continually supplement its sample location pool, with new 
sampling locations comprising, on average, 41% of the sample pool each round. Over time, 
customers can stop participating for any number of reasons such as change in owner, lead 
service line replacement, or lack of interest, all of which is outside of the control of the 
water system. Due to constant issues with retaining willing, qualifying participants, PWD has 
had to introduce monetary incentives to meet the minimum number of participants. In PWD’s 
most recent monitoring period, every previous participant with a LSL was contacted via mail 
and, when available, email as part of the recruitment process. In total, 215 previous 
customers were contacted and only 77 (35%) responded to PWD’s outreach efforts, of which 
only 58 (27%) completed the sampling process. Customers who had participated in a recent 
sampling round (2019) were more likely to respond, but even that cohort only had 66% of 
participants respond. This example demonstrates a common response rate that PWD 
observes even with monetary incentives for participants. To supplement the sampling pool 
to meet 100 homes, PWD reached out to additional homes identified as having or suspected 
of having LSL to participate in this sampling program.  
 
PWD acknowledges the need for the water system to inform the State, through its sample 
siting plan, which homes are included in the sample location pool, including new locations. 
However, it is an unnecessary administrative burden for water systems to have to justify 
every change in sampling location. PWD recommends that EPA remove the requirement for 
water systems to provide an explanation of why the sample locations changed between 
monitoring periods.  
 
25. EPA should provide large water systems with lead levels consistently below the action level 
with a clear path to reduced monitoring. 
 
Under the proposed language of the LCRI, any system, regardless of size, that completes two 
consecutive 6-month monitoring periods with both rounds having a 90th percentile less than 
or equal to 5 ppb moves to triennial monitoring. If any system completes the first two 6-

 
 
month monitoring periods with both rounds having a 90th percentile less than or equal to 10 
ppb, but either round having a 90th percentile greater than 5 ppb, then the system moves to 
annual monitoring. In the event that a system falls into this second category, the current 
wording of section 141.86(d)(2) doesn’t clearly provide a mechanism by which a large system 
on annual monitoring can ever move to triennial monitoring. EPA provides a mechanism for 
small and medium water systems on annual monitoring to move to triennial monitoring if 
they complete 3 consecutive years of monitoring with no lead or copper ALE. However, this 
mechanism is not extended to large water systems with no clear justification provided. EPA 
should modify the language in this section of the regulation to include large systems. If a large 
system is on annual monitoring and demonstrates for three consecutive monitoring periods 
that its 90th percentile level is less than or equal to 10 ppb, then it would make sense to 
allow the system to move to triennial monitoring similar to small and medium systems.  
 
PWD recommends that the wording of 141.85(d)(2)(ii) be revised to “Any water system that 
does not exceed the lead and copper action levels during three consecutive years of 
monitoring (standard monitoring completed during both six-month periods of a calendar year 
will be considered one year of monitoring) may sample at the reduced number of sites for lead 
and copper in accordance with this paragraph (d) and reduce the monitoring frequency to 
triennial monitoring.” 
 
PWD recommends that the wording of 141.85(d)(2)(iii) be revised to “Any water system that 
demonstrates for two consecutive six-month or annual tap monitoring periods that its 90th 
percentile lead level calculated under 141.80(c)(3), is less than or equal to 0.005 mg/L and the 
90th percentile copper level, calculated under 141.80(c)(3), is less than or equal to 0.65 mg/L 
may sample at the reduced number of sites for lead and copper in accordance with paragraph 
(C) of this section and reduce the frequency of monitoring to triennial monitoring.” 
 
 
Action Level Exceedances 
 
26. EPA should be less prescriptive in requirements for systems with multiple action level 
exceedances. 
 
In section 141.85(j)(2), EPA mandates that a water system that has three action level 
exceedances under the newly proposed sampling protocols and action level within a five-year 
period will be required to offer pitcher filters to every consumer in their system. This section 
details five key issues related to the scale, costs, and timelines of this requirement that are 
minimized, underestimated, or not considered in both the proposed rule and the associated 
economic analysis. 
 
First, EPA estimated how many systems this would impact by evaluating stagnant first liter 
data collected from homes with and without LSL under the LCR from 2012-2020. Using static 
multipliers, EPA estimated how many of these systems would have potentially exceeded the 
lower action level of 10 ppb under the new sampling protocol where compliance is based on 
the higher lead level from the first- and fifth-liter sample at a given home. This estimation 
method compounds numerous assumptions that boil complex distributions into single 

 
 
numbers, such as the impact of only sampling from homes with LSL and collecting first and 
fifth liter samples. The level of uncertainty is unaccounted for outside of a “high” and “low” 
scenario which do not adequately account for all of the possible variation in the data. As such, 
EPA has not demonstrated effectively that it knows how many systems are likely to be 
affected by this new mandate. Additionally, with many systems reverting to standard 
monitoring, systems will be collecting samples far more frequently than in the period 
analyzed which could lead to a higher number of systems that have multiple action level 
exceedances under the newly proposed sampling method and action level.  
 
Second, from the estimation method discussed in the previous paragraph, EPA detailed which 
systems it expected to trigger this provision. However, it appears that EPA opted not to 
include the few very large systems that were estimated to trigger this provision in its cost 
analysis. The national annualized cost of this provision was estimated between $6.9M and 
$9.7M. While PWD was not estimated to be at risk of triggering this provision, there were 
multiple systems of equivalent or larger size that were. Using PWD’s size as an example, with 
a population of 1.6 million people and an average household size of 2.34, PWD can judge the 
number of consumers (defined by EPA in this provision as the number of households rather 
than services) to be approximately 685,000. Using all the same assumptions described in 
section 4.3.6.4 of the economic analysis, PWD’s annualized costs alone for this type of 
program would be between $2.2M and $3.6M. With EPA’s own analysis predicting that 
multiple systems of the same size as PWD would trigger this provision, there is no clearly 
presented reason to exclude these large systems from the economic analysis. Any very large 
water system that triggers this provision is likely to push the national costs of this provision 
well past the costs EPA suggests in the economic analysis. 
 
Third, in its economic analysis, EPA assumes that only 20% of consumers will request these 
pitcher filters. EPA has provided no justification for this assumption and if underestimated, 
would cause the cost and feasibility of this provision to be drastically underestimated. If this 
provision is triggered by a water system, the water system will have issued three separate 
Tier 1 public notifications to all of its consumers saying that it has elevated lead levels. The 
mandated health language associated with these notices, the urgency of their delivery, and 
the repeated notifications will ensure that consumers in these systems are on high alert for 
lead in drinking water.  EPA should provide more clarity about how this assumption was 
derived and how it is applicable to the proposed provision.  
 
Fourth, the requirement that this program be established within 60 days of the third action 
level exceedance is not feasible. While the system may be able to develop and provide the 
educational materials associated with this provision within this time, the materials associated 
with the pitcher filter portion of the provision cannot be procured reliably in this timeframe. 
Water systems will be required within 60 days to determine which filter to use, where to store 
these filters, how to procure them, and how to track this process. This also leaves water 
systems at the mercy of pitcher filter providers to have the necessary number of filters to 
meet the demands of this program. If PWD were to trigger this provision and following EPA’s 
assumption that 20% of consumers requested filters, then PWD would need to procure more 
than 130,000 pitcher filters within 60 days. This large demand is likely to be replicated 
elsewhere putting an extreme strain on the national availability of these pitcher filters. This 

 
 
is made worse by the fact that, with every system across the country reverting to standard 
monitoring in 2028, it is likely to create a mad dash for pitcher filters at the end of the 3rd 
standard monitoring period. EPA estimates that as many as 30% of systems will exceed the 
action level, it holds that many of those will exceed it multiple times. With many systems all 
needing to procure a large number of filters at the same time, there will be supply chain issues 
inhibiting the ability of systems to establish this program in such a short period of time. 
Skyrocketing demand and low supply will also result in individual costs of these filters rising 
significantly as manufacturers know that these systems have no choice but to purchase their 
filters.  
 
Finally, the proposed revision would require that water systems make these filters available 
to all consumers rather than those with lead service lines. This requirement will confuse 
residents who are at very little to no risk of lead exposure from their water if they do not have 
lead plumbing. If EPA maintains a version of this provision in the final rule, the focus should 
be on providing, upon request, pitcher filters to customers with lead service lines.  
 
This provision is overly prescriptive and assumes a one-size-fits-all approach will work for 
systems that are experiencing multiple action level exceedances. This provision is also likely 
to distract water systems with multiple action level exceedances from the important work of 
replacing lead service lines. EPA should instead modify the requirements for systems with 
multiple action level exceedances to review their existing corrosion control and 
replacement plans with their primacy agency and give the primacy agency the discretion to 
determine if additional actions are needed, such as this type of pitcher filter program.  
 
 
Public Education and Notification 
 
27. EPA should not overly burden water systems with strict administrative requirements 
regarding sample result notification for sample results below the proposed action level. 
 
In section 141.85(d)(1)-(4) of the proposed LCRI, EPA is proposing that all lead and copper tap 
results must be provided to consumers within 3 calendar days of receiving the results, 
regardless of the lead and copper levels at the home. While PWD understands the 
importance of timely communication of these sample results, the proposed 3 calendar day 
notification timeline is not feasible for CWSs due to both the large number of samples 
required to be collected with this notification requirement and the level of effort that would 
be required to meet this requirement.  
 
Under the proposed LCRI, medium and large CWSs will be collecting large quantities of lead 
and copper samples under various portions of the rule (e.g. Lead and Copper Tap Samples, 
Customer Requested Programs, Risk Mitigation Measure sampling following LSLR). The sheer 
number of samples that must be collected will result in the water systems having to generate 
these notices constantly and will add a significant administrative burden without a clear need 
for a faster timeline.  During the first year of LCRI compliance, PWD will be required to collect 
at least 200 paired 1st and 5th liter samples for regulatory compliance. PWD regularly collects 
approximately 100 customer requested samples per year (which will likely increase with all 

 
 
the public education required under the LCRI), and with the mandated replacement rates, 
PWD could collect as many as 2,000 post replacement samples. In total, this results in up to 
2,300 customers that will require notification on an annual basis, which equates to nearly 200 
notifications per month. The current 30-day notification requirements for results less than 
the action level is already a significant administrative challenge. However, with a 30-day 
notification timeframe, water systems are more effectively able to batch communications to 
reduce the amount of time that is needed on any single result notification. However, if the 
timeframe for providing these notifications becomes 3 calendar days, it would make this 
requirement infeasible for water systems. This burden is further exacerbated by proposed 
sample methods that require both 1st and 5th liter samples to be analyzed and results 
communicated with the customer. Depending on how the labs batch and analyze samples, 
that may result in the water system receiving results for just one of the two samples at a given 
home and then having to make two separate notifications to the customer, doubling the 
administrative burden on the system.  
 
In section V.H.3 of the preamble of the LCRI, EPA states that “Based…on the fact that water 
systems have a long history of demonstrated ability to provide consumer notices within an 
even shorter time frame of 24 hours in other contexts, water systems should be capable of 
providing these consumer notices no later than three days after the water systems learns of 
the results”. While PWD does not dispute the fact that water systems have shown the ability 
to meet 24-hour notification requirements following a Tier 1 Public notification event, this is 
not a valid comparison to routine tap sample result notifications. First, a situation triggering 
a Tier 1 PN, requiring a notification to all affected customers within 24 hours, is not a routine 
event for most water systems. An event triggering this level of notification is an all-hands-on 
deck situation in which water systems are dedicating large amounts of resources to delivering 
these notifications. This is especially true in medium to large scale systems where the 
notification has to be delivered to hundreds of thousands or millions of people. In addition, 
these types of 24-hour notifications are not routine operations and may only occur once every 
few years, if even that often. PWD has only ever had to issue one 24-hour notification since 
the promulgation of the public notification regulation. Second, the water system  distributes 
the exact same information to all affected customers for a Tier 1 PN. Conversely, lead sample 
result notifications are unique and targeted communications to each individual resident. 
These are vastly different modes of communication. Third, 24-hour notifications are typically 
reserved for acute health risks. For example, if an E. coli MCL is exceeded, a Tier 1 PN is issued 
for consumers to boil their water because consuming the water may put people at risk of 
immediate gastrointestinal illness. In the preamble, EPA justifies the 3-calendar day 
notification requirement by stating that since there is no safe level of lead exposure, even 
results that are less than the action level require immediate notification. While PWD agrees 
that there is no safe level of lead exposure, EPA has not demonstrated that water lead levels 
below the proposed action level would constitute an acute health risk. This is especially true 
when the sample results show lead below the method reporting limit. There is no justification 
for requiring a 3-day notification for a sample result that indicates that the consumer is at no 
identifiable risk of lead exposure. While PWD supports a 3-business day notification for 
sample results over the action level, as those consumers are at a greater risk of lead 
exposure, it is infeasible to extend that requirement to all sample results. This is especially 
true for sample results that do not have any detectable level of lead found. Overall, PWD 

 
 
believes it is inappropriate to compare these types of rare, high consequence situations (e.g., 
boil water notices) to routine laboratory result notifications, especially for results that are 
below the proposed action level.  
 
Finally, if water systems are forced to expend exorbitant amount of time on routine, non-
emergency notifications, then resources will be diverted away from providing effective one-
on-one public education to customers who have lead levels above the action level and are at 
higher risk of lead exposure from their water. While it is important to provide effective public 
education to all consumers, it is also important to provide more in-depth information to those 
who may have a higher risk. EPA should not put in place requirements that will inhibit a water 
system’s administrative ability to provide customers with lead levels above the action level 
more highly targeted and in-depth public education.  
 
PWD suggests that EPA implement a 3-business day notification requirement for sample 
results that have a lead level above the action level but maintain the 30-day notification 
requirement for lead levels that are below the action level.  
 
28. EPA should provide clear language that absolves water systems of any liability due to 
ineffectiveness of pitcher filters that are provided as part of mandated actions from EPA.  
 
Under the LCRI, all water systems are being mandated, under several scenarios, to provide 
customers with pitcher filters that are certified to remove lead. This mandate to provide 
commercial products in such a public-facing manner inherently implies that the water system 
is also certifying that these pitcher filters meet their lead removal claims. It is outside of the 
purview of water systems to serve as a commercial product certification entity. As such, 
EPA should develop language that water systems can use that will clearly absolve the water 
system from any potential liability associated with these filters not meeting the removal 
claims of a third-party manufacturer.  
 
29. EPA should allow more flexibility on the amount of required language in public education 
documents. 
 
In section 141.154 of the proposed rulemaking, EPA has increased the amount of required 
language through the form of both informational language and health language. The 
informational and health effects language are large blocks of text that are 254 and 115 words 
long, respectively, for a total of 369 words. This is an increase from the LCRR requirements 
which had a combined word count of 269 words. Mandating this large amount of text that 
must be used verbatim in public education materials gives water systems no flexibility in 
making effective and clear communication materials for their consumers. PWD takes great 
pride in outreach and communication efforts with customers across all facets of the water 
system. There are many ways to create effective communication materials, and, often, large 
blocks of text are not at the top of the list. By forcing water systems to present this 
information in this specific manner, it reduces that ability for the water system to innovate in 
how effectively it is providing this information.  
 

 
 
EPA should limit the amount of mandated language to as small a word count as possible and 
provide the remaining information through guidance that is left open to water systems being 
able to take that information and present it in a more effective manner.  
 
30. EPA should allow more flexibility in the order of public education materials. 
 
In section 141.85 of the proposed rule, EPA states that systems must include all the 
information detailed in sections 141.85(a)(1)(i)-(iv) in the exact order they are presented in 
the regulation and for three of these subsections with the exact wording. In mandating the 
order in which information is presented in public education, EPA is restricting the water 
systems ability to present this information in easier to understand and graphically digestible 
formats. PWD suggests that EPA provide the required information and through guidance 
suggest the general order that these topics should be covered. However, EPA should allow 
water systems, under the assumption that these systems will be acting in good faith, the 
flexibility to develop effective communication materials that convey all the required topics.  
 
 
Schools and Childcare facilities 
 
31. EPA requests comments on whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples 
and/or sample more frequently in schools and childcare facilities. 
 
EPA states in their preamble that the goal of the schools and childcare facilities is to raise 
awareness of the risks of lead plumbing in these facilities. PWD agrees that educating schools 
and childcare facilities of the risks of lead plumbing and assisting them reducing the risk of 
lead exposure provides a crucial public health benefit. However, PWD does not believe that 
the burden for providing extensive water sampling at these private, commercial businesses 
should fall solely on CWSs. Schools and large childcare facilities can have dozens, and 
sometimes over 100, potable water taps in their buildings. If EPA were to increase the 
required number of samples at these facilities to cover the entire 3T’s requirement of all 
drinking water and food preparation taps, it would significantly increase the burden and cost 
of this program. Any increase in the number of required samples would both increase the 
analysis costs associated with this program as well as the complexity in the required sample 
plans and thus the amount of time and effort the CWS will have to invest into each facility. 
EPA should also not add any additional sample types, such as 30 second flush samples, or 
require any follow up samples because of elevated lead levels within a facility. PWD believes 
that these can be provided as best practice recommendations in future guidance, but 
additional investments into these programs by a CWS should be left to the discretion of the 
CWS.  
 
In addition, EPA should not increase the frequency at which these facilities must be sampled. 
In Philadelphia, there are approximately 400 elementary schools and 1600 childcare facilities. 
At the current five-year sample window, PWD will be required to sample from 80 elementary 
schools per year and 320 childcare facilities per year. At the current rate, PWD will be required 
to facilitate sampling at an average pace of approximately 8 facilities per week. Compared to 
the standard monitoring requirements for lead and copper under LCRI, this requirement, as 

 
 
proposed, is already a much larger sampling requirement. Under standard monitoring, PWD 
will be required to collect two samples from 100 homes over two six-month monitoring 
periods for a total of 400 samples. Under the currently proposed school and childcare 
sampling requirements, PWD will be required to collect up to 1,040 samples per year. 
Increasing the sampling frequency requirements to anything shorter than 5 years will 
significantly increase the burden on CWSs and put systems at risk of failing to meet sampling 
requirements.  
 
Given the extensive number of resources that are already required of CWSs under this 
regulation, PWD believes that EPA should maintain the current proposed requirements 
regarding the number and frequency of samples collected.  
 
32. EPA should strongly emphasize the use of waivers for schools and childcare facilities that 
have previous sample results.  
 
PWD agrees with EPA that facilities with sample results meeting the minimum requirements 
of the LCRI that are collected after 1/1/2021 and prior to the LCRI compliance date should be 
exempted from the first five-year sampling cycle. While this is left to the discretion of the 
individual state, it would be beneficial to CWSs for EPA to strongly encourage states to grant 
waivers for these cases. This should be especially true for any systems that choose to start 
their school and childcare monitoring program prior to the compliance date, thereby allowing 
systems more time to complete the first five-year sample cycle as the program gets off the 
ground. Furthermore, in the EPA’s cost analysis, EPA assumes that many of the public 
elementary schools and childcare facilities will be granted waivers based on Water 
Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation (WIIN) Act grant funded sampling programs. If 
states opt to not grant waivers for these programs, then the costs associated with sampling 
school and childcare facilities will be drastically underestimated.  
 
33. EPA should not require CWSs to publicly publish the lead levels of private schools and 
private childcare facilities.  
 
Many of the schools and childcare facilities that will be sampled under the LCRI’s sampling 
program will be privately run, corporate organizations. While the CWS may be providing these 
facilities with water testing, it should not be the responsibility of the CWS to publicly share 
the information of a private corporation. It is the responsibility of the facility to disseminate 
this information to any affected parties. The EPA should not place CWSs in the middle of 
potential public health disputes between facility management and its customers (i.e. 
parents) for an issue that is driven by the privately owned plumbing within the building, 
which the water system has no ownership over. If the CWS is required to publicly share this 
data, it would likely result in the CWS having to field numerous questions from concerned 
parents and require the CWS to act as intermediary between these private facilities and their 
customers. Even in the case of public-school districts, the CWS and the public school district 
are separate entities, and it should be the responsibility of the school district to share the 
results from individual district schools.  
 

 
 
In addition, sharing this data publicly could put CWS at risk of litigation from these private 
corporations if they believe that the sharing of the results led to the loss of customers to their 
business. EPA should not place CWS in the path of potential litigation issues.  
 
PWD recommends that EPA provide communications materials that CWS can provide to 
facility owners regardless of their lead levels to help the facility owners communicate this 
issue with the parents of the facility.  
 
34. Public education requirements specified under 141.85(a)(1) are not all applicable for annual 
education provided to schools and childcare facilities.  
 
Section 141.92(c)(1) of the proposed rule specifies that the annual education that community 
water systems deliver to all schools and childcare facilities be “consistent with the content 
requirements of section 141.85(a)(1).” However, section 141.85(a)(1)(i) is written in the 
context of a water system that exceeds the lead action level system wide. The paragraph in 
section 141.92(c)(1) should specify that section 141.85(a)(1)(i) is not directly applicable for 
the purpose of annual education materials delivered to schools and childcare facilities. If a 
water system were to exceed the lead action level, all customers (including these facilities) 
would receive specific public education material for a lead action level exceedance that 
includes section 141.85(a)(1)(i) exactly as written.

Comments regarding Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
 
Michael S. Regan, Administrator  
US Environmental Protection Agency  
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC 20460  
 
 
 
 
February 5, 2024 
 
Dear Administrator Regan: 
 
We are writing as members of Project TENDR (Targeting Environmental Neuro-Development Risks), 
an alliance of scientists, health professionals, and children’s and environmental advocates 
concerned about the contributions of environmental chemicals to neurodevelopmental disorders 
such as intellectual and learning disabilities, autism spectrum disorder, and attention deficit 
hyperactivity disorder. Some of the world’s most recognized experts on the dangers of early life 
lead exposure participate in Project TENDR and published the attached consensus paper (Bellinger 
et al. 2017) to inform on and advocate for adequate protections based on decades of strong 
scientific evidence.  
 
We are writing both to express our support for the proposed National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (“LCRI”) and to encourage EPA to add further 
provisions that will do even more to reduce lead in drinking water and the harm that comes from 
that exposure.  
 
Over many decades, lead has been found to be causal in neurodevelopmental detriment for 
multiple indicators including cognitive and academic performance (Lanphear et al. 2000), 
sensorimotor development (Dietrich, et al. 1985, Bellinger et al. 1991), behavior (Needleman, et al. 
1996), and attention regulation (Davis, et al. 2004) for many populations. Moreover, scientists now 
recognize that lead does lasting harm to children even at extremely low exposure levels. In 2012, 
the National Toxicology Program concluded that blood lead concentrations below 5 µg/dL have 
adverse effects on academic achievement, IQ, and attention-related behaviors. As noted later in 
this letter, several authoritative bodies have gone further, concluding that no harmless level of lead 
exposure has been identified for children. 
Furthermore, there is growing evidence that the adverse effects of lead are most severe in Black 
and Hispanic children (Evens, et al. 2015, Amato, et al. 2013) and low-income children (Marshall, et 
al. 2020). This suggests that socioeconomic disadvantages can worsen the impact of lead exposures. 
 
The U.S. EPA has long recognized there is no safe level of lead exposure for children. Likewise, in 
2012, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) moved away from a “level of concern” 
for lead – which would imply that there is a “safe” level below which no adverse effects are 
expected to occur- to a population-based guidance level in children that represents a sample of 
children at higher blood lead levels than the rest of the children in the nation. This move was 
motivated by the fact that no safe level of lead has been found over decades of research and 
hundreds of scientific publications. The population-based guidance level, referred to as a “reference 

value,” was set at 5 µg/dL in 2012, which at the time was the 97.5 percentile of the distribution of 
blood lead levels in U.S. children.  The CDC further reduced the blood lead reference value to 3.5 
μg/dL in 2021 to reflect the population exposure trend over time (CDC, 2021). Therefore, it is urgent 
and necessary that EPA eliminate sources of environmental lead at every potential opportunity.  
 
Restrictions and phasing out of lead in gasoline, paints, and other consumer products have resulted 
in decreasing blood lead concentrations in U.S. children. But lead exposure remains a major 
preventable cause of neurodevelopmental morbidity. Protective environmental health policies, like 
this proposed rule, are necessary to prevent adverse impacts of lead exposure.  
 
Neurodevelopmental harm is particularly concerning because of its intergenerational impacts 
throughout people’s and families’ lives. (Washington HA, 2019). Neurodevelopmental impacts 
hinder school success, job readiness, language transfer to children, and are associated with 
adjudicated delinquency, lost lifetime earnings, and other life-altering effects. Therefore, it is 
appropriate that the EPA finalize this proposed rule, as it is well supported by Executive Orders 
12898 (59 FR 7629) and 14096 (88 FR 25251) that require EPA to enact policy to incorporate 
Environmental Justice into their programs and policies, and Executive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885) 
that requires EPA to enact policy to protect children from environmental health risks and safety 
risks. Reducing the amount of lead in drinking water will benefit all children but especially children 
of color and those in low-income communities that are disproportionally exposed to lead. 
 
There are six ways in which EPA should strengthen this proposed rule: 
 
Lower the action level for drinking water to 5 parts per billion: Given that there is no safe level of 
lead and the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends a 1 ppb maximum lead level for drinking 
water in schools, we propose that the current action level of 15 be reduced to 5 rather than the 10 
ppb currently in the proposed rule. The FDA limit for lead in bottled water is 5 ppb.  
 
Use incentives to help utilities and other entities lower the levels of lead in drinking water in day 
care centers and schools. These incentives should include frequent tap testing, the replacement of 
lead containing faucets and fixtures, and use of filters certified to remove lead.  
 
Prioritize the communities that have the most lead service lines instead of providing exceptions 
to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate. Other cities can replicate the success of Newark, NJ 
that replaced all 23,000 of its known lead service lines in under three years.  
 
Require that federal funding and other public financing mechanisms cover the full cost of lead 
service line replacement. As it is currently written, the rule advantages communities where 
residents own rather than rent their homes and have the financial means to pay for the lead service 
line replacement costs.  
 
Address the issue of access to private property.  EPA defines the term “lead service line” as the 
“portion of pipe that is made of lead, which connects the water main to the building inlet.” To reach 
the stated goal of removing all lead service lines, EPA must change the proposed rule’s requirement 
that utilities must only remove those service lines to which a utility has “access,” a potential 
loophole that could severely limit the number of lead service lines that are replaced.  

Prevent regrettable substitutions and pollution from removed lead pipes:  EPA should require 
water systems to replace lead pipes with copper instead of plastics such as polyvinyl chloride (PVC), 
chlorinated polyvinyl chloride (CPVC), PEX or HDPE pipes. Plastics have known adverse impacts to 
human health and children's development; replacing one hazard with another will create a new set 
of health hazards for generations to come. A harmful stew of chemicals can leach from plastic pipes 
into drinking water, and these pipes are more vulnerable to thermal degradation from wildfires 
than copper pipes. In addition, micro- and nanoplastics can be released from the pipes into drinking 
water.  Plastic pipes also put fenceline communities at risk during the production and disposal 
phase, when toxic substances can be released into air and water.  For example, when PVC/CPVC 
pipes are incinerated, they can release highly toxic dioxins into the environment. EPA should also 
address end of life considerations for lead pipes and require that those removed are recycled in a 
safe and environmentally sound manner. 
Despite notable successes in reducing the blood lead concentrations of the U.S. population in 
recent decades, lead exposure remains a major preventable cause of neurodevelopmental 
morbidity in children. A voluminous body of research documents unequivocally that no level of lead 
exposure is safe for a fetus or young child. This conclusion has been endorsed by numerous 
authoritative bodies in addition to U.S. EPA that have evaluated this evidence, including the World 
Health Organization (JECFA, 2011), the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC, 2012), 
the U.S. Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry (ATSDR, 2020), the U.S. Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA, 2023) and the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA, 2010). A stronger set of 
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements will be an important step in protecting children from harm 
and ending this public health injustice.  
 
Sincerely,

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-1123 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---

VIA THE FEDERAL eRULEMAKING PORTAL

Re: Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 – National Primary Drinking 
Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements  
To Whom It May Concern: 
The City of New York writes in connection with the Environmental Protection 
Agency’s newly proposed rule, amending 40 C.F.R. Parts 141 and 142, that will require water 
systems to replace lead service lines and make other changes in connection with drinking water.  
The City, like the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), is fully committed to the reduction 
and ultimately the elimination of lead exposure.  The City lauds the goals underlying this proposal, 
and submits the following comments for EPA’s consideration. 
Minimum Replacement Rates and Timeframe 
The most significant element of the EPA’s newly proposed rule is the requirement 
that community water systems replace all lead service lines within 10 years, at least to the extent 
that this timeframe may be read to pertain to the lead service lines that are not owned in whole or 
in part by the City.  Among other things, EPA seeks comments on whether that timeframe should 
be shorter still.  The City submits, in the strongest of terms, that it should not.  While the City 
understands the importance of reducing lead exposure and is actively engaged in the effort, the 
scale of this undertaking cannot be overstated.  The New York City Department of Environmental 
Protection (DEP) estimates that the total lead service lines and unknown service lines in the City 
is approximately 340,000.  Virtually none of these lines are owned in whole or in part by the City.  
As such, the City will not be able to meet a ten-year replacement program, much less a program 
 
 
 
HON. SYLVIA O. HINDS-RADIX 
Corporation Counsel 
THE CITY OF NEW YORK 
LAW DEPARTMENT 
100 CHURCH STREET 
NEW YORK, NY 10007 
 

 
2 
 
 
that imposes a shorter period of time.1  The City thus does not, and cannot, support a shorter 
timeframe, and urges EPA to ensure that the timeline is flexible.  The City is implementing a 
program by which it will begin replacements prior to the Lead and Copper Rule Improvements 
(LCRI) compliance date.  But no matter when we begin, the City will be unable to complete all 
replacements by 2037. 
EPA also proposes that community water systems replace 10% of their lines 
annually.  While the City will make every effort to maximize the number of service lines replaced 
annually, given funding constraints and the availability of material and qualified contractors, it is 
highly unlikely that the City will be able to replace 34,000 lines each year.  Further, the City’s 
estimate of 340,000 total service line is only an estimate.  DEP (like other utilities) does not yet 
have enough data to determine an annual replacement rate that is feasible.  The City will gather 
additional information and data in the coming years and is prepared to coordinate with the State of 
New York to develop a feasible replacement plan.  As part of the revised rule, EPA should grant 
states the authority, and the flexibility, to work with individual utilities to develop workable 
replacement plans.2  Additionally, EPA should support proactive programs, and credit utilities that 
effect replacements while performing other work. 
Inventory Requirements 
There are multiple new components related to lead service line inventory in the 
proposed rule, including those that require tracking, reporting and certification within short 
deadlines.  EPA should allow the City, and other localities, to rely, at least in part, on reliable data 
that has already been collected.  Per Local Law, DEP developed and posted an interactive map on 
“LeadFreeNYC”3 where customers can check to see if their service lines might be lead.  In addition 
to the interactive map, DEP has a database of service line materials for the City that are based on 
tapping card records.  While DEP is redeveloping its service line inventory, this is a major 
undertaking requiring funding and staffing.  In the interim, the existing database can be used for 
the initial inventory. 
The LCRI requires the material of all connectors to be included in the inventory, 
though DEP has never tracked information on connectors.  The City does not recommend requiring 
the material identification of all connectors as the effort to comply far exceeds any risk reduction 
and will only detract from the efforts to identify and replace lead service lines. 
The LCRI requires utilities to statistically validate assumptions used to classify 
non-lead service lines without actual records.  DEP can reasonably assume that after 1961 all new 
service line connectors were not lead and that all service lines reconnected under a water main job 
done after 1961 also were not lead.  DEP should be permitted to base its inventory, in part, on 
 
1 Similarly, the City does not support the imposition of shortened deadlines connected to the 
compliance date. 
2 As noted throughout this letter, the City supports granting discretion to states to implement the 
LCRI.  EPA must, however, clarify criteria a state must use to “tailor” requirements. 
3 See https://www.nyc.gov/content/leadfree/pages/maps.
