these assumptions.  Under the new rule, DEP will have to randomly select 384 properties that were 
classified as non-lead based on assumptions (and conduct a 2-point visual inspection to confirm if 
the assumptions were accurate).  The City supports this method of validation, and recognizes that, 
based on the results, DEP may be required to update its inventory to account for inaccuracies or 
weaknesses in the underlying assumptions. 
Along with the baseline inventory, the proposed rule requires community water 
systems to submit and make publicly available a service line replacement (SLR) plan in 2027.  In 
addition to the replacement cycle/time frame to complete all replacements, the plan must include 
a strategy for determining the material of unknowns, standard operating procedure (e.g., means 
and methods for procurement of materials or contractors) for conducting full replacements, 
communication strategy for full or partial replacements, flushing procedures, strategy for 
prioritization of replacements, funding strategy, communication strategy for the replacement 
plan/program, and finally the identification of any laws, regulations and/or tariff agreements that 
affect the City’s ability to gain access to conduct replacements including those that require consent 
or authorization.  This extensive information should be required for the initial plan only.  EPA 
should reduce the burden for subsequent updates by requiring updates only for regulatory or policy 
changes that impact the SLR plan.  
The Impact of Revised Definitions 
The LCRI proposes to update the mandatory lead health effects language from 
“Exposure to lead in drinking water can cause serious health effects in all age groups” to “There 
is no safe level of lead in drinking water.”  This proposed language would undermine public 
confidence in drinking water, as even with the removal of all lead service lines and the optimization 
of corrosion control, lead-containing plumbing components on premises will contribute some level 
of lead to tap water.  This language is also without precedent, even for regulated substances with 
a maximum contaminant level (MCL) and a maximum contaminant level goal (MCLG) of zero. 
While the replacement of lead service lines will improve lead levels in drinking 
water for homes with lead service lines, there will still be homes with premise plumbing (e.g., 
fixtures, solder, piping) that may contain lead.  Thus, homes with and without lead services lines 
will continue to have the potential for lead exposure.  Further, the proposed LCRI public 
notification and education materials would encourage consumers to consider bottled water as an 
alternative to tap water, without disclosing that there is an allowable 5 ppb limit of lead in bottled 
water.  While EPA is requiring point-of-use filters in the case of action level exceedances, EPA 
should also acknowledge the less stringent standards for bottled water and that increased use of 
bottled water would lead to increased detrimental environmental impacts from the production, 
distribution, and disposal of plastic bottles.  Additionally, the City’s extensive City-wide free 
residential at the tap sampling data (over 43,600 samples from the past 13 years) demonstrate that 
flushing consistently provides greater protection, with flushed samples having a P90 of 2 ppb.  
The presence of lead in premise plumbing, the potential for increased use of bottled 
water and the effectiveness of flushing at the tap must be considered in the final rule to maximize 
public health protection.  

 
4 
 
 
The City also recommends that the EPA return to the definition of “control” it 
adopted in the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) in 2000, i.e., that “control” is based on 
ownership.  The definition of what is “under the control” of water systems as described in the Safe 
Drinking Water Act (SDWA) properly excludes piping not owned by the water system.  This is a 
better, and more realistic definition of “control,” and the SDWA recognizes that control is not 
transferred even when an actual owner exercises their “control” to grant “access” to a water system. 
The EPA also proposes to revise the definition of “connector,” including that 
connectors are defined as “not exceeding two feet.”  Per the New York City Code, a connector has 
been defined for decades to have a minimum length of three feet and a maximum length of five 
feet.  As EPA provides no specific scientific basis for the proposed maximum of “two feet” other 
than a manufacturer’s specification, the City urges instead that the definition should be revised to 
“not exceeding five feet.” 
Corrosion Control and the Proposed Revised Treatment Technique 
The treatment technique, as proposed in the LCRI, includes a new sampling 
protocol for homes with lead service lines, and a revised sample pool, and it retains high-dose 
orthophosphate addition as the anticipated optimal corrosion treatment.  The LCRI also proposed 
to lower the lead action level to 10 µg/L.  The Corrosion Control Program implemented by DEP 
has enabled the City’s system to consistently comply with a lead action level of 15 µg/L; however, 
the 90th percentile compliance data have never been below a lead action level of 10 µg/L.  
Lowering the action level while incorporating lead observations from a 5th liter 
sample in compliance tap samples makes control of particulate lead more critical.  EPA has not 
provided analysis demonstrating that known corrosion control treatment (CCT) methods including 
orthophosphate can control particulate lead sufficiently for community water systems to reliably 
achieve required lead concentrations.  DEP has initiated studies to evaluate optimizing the City’s 
corrosion control treatment by increasing orthophosphate levels and our data clearly demonstrate 
that the lower action level is not achievable.  
Moreover, the results of DEP’s ongoing Optimization Corrosion Control Study 
demonstrate that increasing the orthophosphoric acid dose will not reduce the 90th percentile lead 
concentration of the 5th liter samples collected from the compliance pool with lead service lines 
below the proposed Action Level of 10 ppb (see Figures 1 and 2 below). 
 

 
5 
 
 
 
Figure 1 – Projections from Home Lead Profile Study 
 
 
 
Figure 2 – Projections using LCR Compliance Data  
 
It should be noted that the results of an on-going Home Profile Study, summarized 
in Figure 1, have a 1st liter 90th percentile lead concentration of 5 ppb, which is more than 50% 
lower than the 90th percentile lead concentration of 11 ppb that has been historically calculated for 
DEP’s compliance pool.  
The projections shown in Figure 2 are based on the percent increase in the 90th 
percentile lead concentrations established using sample data observed, when switching from 1st 
liter to the 5th liter sampling using the City’s Catskill/Delaware water supply, as collected in the 
Home Profile Study. The study results demonstrate a 270% increase in 90th percentile lead 
concentrations for an orthophosphate dose of 2 ppm.  An orthophosphate dose of 4 ppm lowers 
the 90th percentile lead increase by approximately 160%.  This reduction will not lower the 90th 
percentile lead concentration below the Action Level of 10 ppb.  

 
6 
 
 
While pH adjustment may offer some additional reduction of lead concentration, 
the 90th percentile lead concentrations will still likely be greater than the proposed Action Level. 
Also, increasing the pH to achieve this additional reduction will increase total trihalomethanes and 
result in other negative water quality impacts and compliance issues in the water system. 
Corrosion control should be assessed through a thoughtful analysis that documents 
current conditions and evaluates alternatives.  There are many instances in which making a 
corrosion control change that seems logical can have unintended consequences.  Ideally, corrosion 
control modifications will not involve major changes in corrosion control strategy, which would 
necessitate more extensive implementation timeframes.   
The LCRI proposed § 141.82(c) describes corrosion control studies broadly, and it 
is possible to prioritize analysis and data collection more efficiently than is reflected in the 
proposed rule text.  Also, and importantly, a robust training program will be needed for state and 
federal regulators, consulting engineers, and water system operators. 
The City agrees with what EPA expressed in the LCRI preamble: that expertise in 
the sector to determine CCT is limited.  The answer to this challenge is not to create a regulatory 
framework that encourages corrosion control changes without a proper analysis.   
Sampling 
The LCRI proposal returns the role of lead action level exceedances to its primary 
focus: optimizing corrosion control.  With that role in mind, the first-draw, the stagnant-water 
sample, remains the most reliable and appropriate trigger for revised corrosion control.  
EPA acknowledges in the proposed LCRI preamble, correctly, that actual lead 
occurrence is significantly impacted by other factors, in particular the amount and timing of 
ongoing water use in a structure.  Neither the 1st nor the 5th liter lead observations are representative 
of actual exposure.  Accordingly, use of a 1st liter-only protocol that does not introduce the 
additional site-to-site variability associated with 5th liter samples would be preferrable.  It also 
affords the economy of being a single sample for both lead and copper compliance data.  
EPA should not include supplemental samples collected outside of the compliance 
pool, such as samples collected in City’s Free Residential Testing Program or as part of a lead 
service line or connector replacement.  The City distributes over 10,000 lead test kits to customers 
per year as part of the Free Residential Testing program.  These customers are provided with 
sample collection instructions that do not match compliance sampling requirements, and inclusion 
of these data would not be appropriate for guiding decisions made regarding corrosion control 
treatment.  The City does not support the inclusion of supplemental sampling in the 90th percentile 
compliance calculations for lead concentration. 
Regulatory language should be revised to allow states the flexibility to direct who 
must conduct the testing (not necessarily the utility), who makes the data available, who reports 
data to the state and where data is posted.  If reporting must be included in the Consumer 

 
7 
 
 
Confidence Report (CCR), it should be minimized to providing a link to where the data are already 
provided.  Failure to conduct school sampling, meanwhile, should not be a Tier 3 violation.4 
Lead Action and Trigger Levels 
In lowering the lead action level, a lead exceedance under the LCRI at 10 μg/L will 
trigger both Tier 1 public notice and public education.  While using the action level to trigger 
public notice and public education simplifies the regulation, EPA has significantly expanded the 
public education components of the LCRR, and many of these components are now disconnected 
from the lead action level.  Additional public education requirements burden systems and would 
consume resources better applied to removing lead service lines as efficiently as is feasible. The 
following steps would simplify the public education requirements: 
• Public education requirements should apply only to homes with lead service lines 
rather than City-wide.   
• States should retain the ability to grant time extensions (beyond 60 days) for the 
delivery of public education materials.  Significant mailings outside of DEP’s 90-
day billing cycle would be required to complete public education in shorter 
timeframes; those mailings would be done at a significant cost without much 
benefit to actually reaching and educating the public.  
• Request that the property owner retain the responsibility for distributing (i.e., 
posting) public education materials in multi-family dwellings.  
• Allow more flexibility in developing public education materials.  Under the 
LCRR and newly proposed LCRI, requirements for public education brochures 
and pamphlets do not facilitate effective communication.  Additionally, the 
current regulatory text does not provide the flexibility that is needed for effective 
communication via electronic communications media, should EPA elect to 
facilitate use of a broader array of communication tools. 
Under the LCRI, educational materials must include the statement “Lead in 
drinking water is primarily from materials and parts used in service lines and in home plumbing. 
DEP is responsible for providing high quality drinking water and removing lead pipes but cannot 
control the variety of materials used in the plumbing in your home.”  This ambiguous language 
implies that DEP has the responsibility for removing all lead service lines and not just the lead 
service lines and galvanized requiring replacement service lines under its “control.” 
Following an action level exceedance, the City recommends that EPA require 
community water systems to re-optimize only once, and allowing re-optimization based on past 
CCT studies.  As the trigger for additional action (e.g., the lead action level, targeted sample pool, 
sampling protocol, exceedance calculation, and monitoring frequency) becomes more sensitive, 
 
4 The New York City Public Health Law § 1110 went into effect December 22, 2022.  Pursuant to

cycle in 2023, which will conclude in December 2025.  The DOE will test at least a third of its 
buildings every year on a cyclical basis.  These results will be collected in the window between 
January 1, 2021, and the LCRI compliance date.

further adjustments to CCT practice become more challenging.  This result is especially true for 
systems like the City’s that are facing multiple, simultaneous compliance challenges (e.g., 
Disinfection Byproducts control). 
The LCRI should not require additional actions based on multiple action level 
exceedances.  Based on the study results set forth above, DEP will not be able to comply with the 
proposed action level of 10 ppb of lead but will have few if any actions available that can feasibly 
be implemented. 
The LCRR and now the LCRI contain public education measures that inform the 
public regularly about additional risk reduction steps that individuals can take.  Because EPA is 
choosing to lower the action level, multiple exceedances, particularly in the initial implementation 
period, will simply reflect the sensitivity of the new trigger for that additional focus, not a new 
health concern.  Additional public education measures are an administrative burden that neither 
affords additional health risk reduction nor accelerates improvement in corrosion control practice. 
Receiving three violations within a rolling five-year period requires additional 
actions including making available, within 60 days, “to all consumers” American National 
Standards Institute (ANSI) accredited Point of Use (POU) devices with a six-month supply of 
cartridges, and replacement cartridges every six months thereafter.  DEP estimates needing up to 
3.35 million pitcher filters (2.63 residents per household).  To meet the filter requirement, DEP 
would be required to submit a POU filter plan to the State within 30 days to outline the operation 
of distribution facilities, delivery mechanisms for filters, and barriers to obtaining filters.  DEP 
would also be required to conduct additional community outreach, at least one activity every six 
months, which may include Town Halls, community events, phone, text, email, door hanger 
messages, use of social media, etc. 
EPA should not require water systems that exceed the lead action level multiple 
times to make filters available to all consumers (see below for a fuller discussion on this potential 
requirement).  If EPA finalizes the rule including such a requirement, it should make every effort 
to minimize the burden the multiple action level exceedances requirement places on water systems.  
For example, most systems in this situation will be exceeding the action level based on a dataset 
drawn from a subset of service line / plumbing material characteristics that are not necessarily 
typical of the lines in the service area.  Consequently, if filters were to be made available, there 
should be a focus on that subset of households rather than “all consumers.” 
Potential Requirement to Provide Filters and Replacement Cartridges 
EPA should not require water systems that exceed the lead action level multiple 
times to make filters available to all consumers.  There may be instances where filters are 
warranted, but that decision should be made based on site-specific facts by the state in 
collaboration with the community water system.  The costs of a program providing filters to all 
consumers are substantial, and these resources could be better applied to lead service line 
replacements. 
 

 
9 
 
 
In 2015, to ensure that any filters recommended or provided to residents were 
effective at removing lead from the City’s tap water, DEP undertook a study to evaluate the 
effectiveness of different brands of pitcher filters.  The brands evaluated were tested using 
certification requirements equivalent to the 2019 National Sanitation Foundation (NSF)/ANSI 53 
standard levels of less than 10 ppb lead, which translates to 93% removal if the influent lead is 150 
ppb.  
DEP tested 4 pitcher filters that are NSF/ANSI 53 certified for lead reduction, and 
three (3) not NSF/ANSI 53 certified for lead, using influent solutions of three different 
concentrations of lead: 50 ppb, 100 ppb, and 150 ppb.  The study demonstrated that the average 
lead reductions per brand ranged from 50% lead removal to 93% lead removal and only one pitcher 
filter repeatedly achieved both percentage removal above 93% and lead less than 10 ppb in filtered 
water (see Figure 3).  Additionally, a drop in lead reduction was consistently observed as the 
volume of water put through each filter increased to the 13th liter.  Filters were rated for a life 
expectancy between 20 gallons and 120 gallons, depending on the brand.  Providing a filter with 
a shorter than expected life, could result in higher lead levels to the customer even if the 
manufacturer’s specifications are followed.

residences without a service line are relatively low (90% of results are below 3 ppb in the first 
draw) and flushing for 1-2 minutes further reduces lead levels (i.e., 90% of results are 1 ppb or 
lower).  Additionally, samples collected during a New York State grant-funded pilot lead service

Complexity of Regulatory Approach, Education, and Reporting 
EPA asked if the LCRI could be simplified and any of its attendant burdens 
reduced.  DEP believes that the LCRI reporting requirements can be simplified by reducing the 
requirements to an annual submittal of the service line replacement rate, and by removing the need 
to report lead connectors in the inventory.  Annual inventory data updates would be made available 
to the public, and inventory data documentation could be reported to oversight agencies at the State 
level (in the City’s case, to the New York State Department of Health, where data could be 
maintained online and be available for State audits). 
The public education requirements could include preparation and submittal of a 
single public education plan rather than EPA’s current public education reporting requirements. 
That single plan would be subject to State review and approval prior to the first compliance date, 
and DEP would certify annually compliance with the plan as approved. 
Regarding public notice requirements, Tier 1 notifications require: Within 24 hours 
notify the State Department of Health and EPA, and provide to as large a distribution as possible 
a public notice with mandatory health effects language approved by the Department of Health; 
disseminate through press releases, radio and TV, website, social media; target/reach out to entities 
that can connect to the most vulnerable people, e.g., children and pregnant women, etc.  Then 
every 90 days, distribute more information through public education materials to all customers, 
not just homes with lead service lines, including ways to reduce risk of exposure.  As the 
notification would be citywide, many residents whose plumbing does not contain lead may believe 
there is something wrong with their water when there is not.  This will undermine public 
confidence in the quality of the water supply.  In addition to the public notification, there will be 
ongoing public education and public outreach requirements every 90 days and annually.  To the 
extent that public notification requirements remain in the final rule, EPA should allow states to 
retain flexibility to grant an extension on public notice requirements. 
City-wide, 24-hour public notification based on action level exceedance is an 
excessive requirement.  The Action Level is not a Maximum Contaminant Level, it’s the 90th 
percentile value of samples from the highest risk pool of homes, collected to capture the highest 
level of lead – not what anyone would routinely or consistently be exposed to. 
Meanwhile, the presence of lead connectors does not warrant annual customer 
notification.  DEP does not have records on connector material, and would be forced to make 
conservative generalizations, resulting in required annual notification to the majority of service 
connections.  To require notification of customers about the presence (or potential presence) of 
lead connectors would misdirect limited resources and draw customers’ attention away from 
actionable risk reduction measures.  EPA was correct in proposing the LCRI without including 
lead connectors in the definition of a lead service line, and this should be reflected in the 
notification requirements.  

 
12 
 
 
Further, the City submits that it is not practicable for water systems to implement 
notification and risk mitigation provisions after full and partial service line replacement, 
notification of a service line disturbance, and associated reporting requirements upon the effective 
date of the LCRI.  Earlier alternative compliance dates for LCRI are also not practicable such that 
water systems transition directly from LCRR to LCRI in less than three years (i.e., one or two 
years) based on the assumption that water systems would comply with the LCRR until the LCRI 
compliance date.  Regarding whether there are other LCRR provisions besides the initial inventory 
and notifications of service line material for which the October 16, 2024 compliance date should 
be retained, the City submits that the October 16, 2024 date should be retained only for those 
provisions.  Relatedly, EPA must clarify, prior to the promulgation of the final LCRI, whether the 
City must still comply with provisions of the LCRR that EPA does not intend to continue under 
the LCRI (and if so, when must the City comply). 
The LCRR and LCRI introduce a new requirement if an individual home’s Lead 
level is > 10 ppb.  DEP will be required to sample within 5 days, within ½ mile of the home, testing 
for water quality parameters, orthophosphate, pH, and alkalinity.  Additionally, the customer’s tap 
must be resampled within 30 days, and DEP must conduct an inspection.  The cause (such as non-
optimal water quality from the system or local area water quality issue) of the high lead 
concentration must be documented.  If a distribution issue – DEP would have to identify and 
implement a corrective action; if an internal condition – the property owner would have to correct 
the condition, or DEP would have to document the customer’s refusal or non-response to allowing 
the follow-up sampling.  If DEP determines that there is no cause for the high lead at the sampling 
tap, then no further action is needed.  If, however, the elevated lead is due to corrosive water, then 
DEP must address and submit recommendations to the State within 6 months.  All of these 
activities will require more resources, money and staff, and staff will need training.  
DEP needs to have discretion on Distribution System and Site Assessment (DSSA) 
sampling locations.  As part of our robust distribution monitoring program, which has supported 
our ability to provide stable corrosion control treatment, DEP uses dedicated sampling stations 
which are more than ½ mile apart.  As DEP already monitors at more than twice the required 
number of sites, we would not need to add these DSSA sites to our water quality compliance 
monitoring.  DEP needs flexibility to be able to continue to use and comply through sample stations 
which support all our compliance monitoring. 
The requirement to communicate all monitoring sample results with customers by 
mail within 3 calendar days of learning of results is not feasible in New York City.  Timely delivery 
could be assured, and paperwork burden reduced by lengthening the period to 5 business days, 
limiting expedited schedule to reporting results to customers with results greater than the lead 
action level (10 μg/L), limiting delivery to the customer who conducted the testing, and allowing 
delivery via electronic means (i.e., email, text, data portal access) when the timing of 
communication with the customer can be logged for subsequent audit. 
NYCDEP does not currently provide information about sampling or results for 
samples collected at schools or childcare centers in our CCR.  DEP does not feel that all the NYC 
schools and child-care centers should be reported in this document. The LCRI compliance 
monitoring data should only be reported in the CCR. 

 
13 
 
 
Downstream Connectors and Galvanized Service Lines 
The City does not recommend including the lead connectors or galvanized service 
lines that are or were downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory replacement.  Inventory 
and Replacement requirements should be focused on potential risk of lead exposure.  Removing 
service lines that have been abandoned or used for non-potable application such as fire service will 
not reduce lead exposure.  Moreover, New York City Plumbing Code requirements and permitting 
mechanisms prohibits their reconnection.  
Partial Service Line Replacements 
The proposed rule contemplates banning partial lead and galvanized service line 
replacement, unless they are done as part of emergency or planned infrastructure work.  EPA seeks 
comment on whether partial replacement should be prohibited when performed as part of planned 
infrastructure work.  It should not.  Article 7 of the City of New York Standard Construction 
Contract requires contractors to protect the work and neighboring properties during construction 
and to repair any damage they cause during construction.  When a contractor is intentionally 
cutting lead service lines as part of their means and methods in performing non-routine street work 
(i.e., emergency repair contract work), there should be no prohibition on cutting and reconnecting 
service lines if they cannot conduct a full-service line replacement. 
Deferred Service Line Replacement  
The City does not support imposing any additional requirements on systems 
conducting deferred service line replacements. 
Dielectric Coupling 
While the use of a dielectric coupling as described in the proposed rule is good 
practice and is consistent with established field practice, per ANSI/American Water Works 
Association C810 - Replacement and Flushing of Lead Service Lines, and the use of dielectric 
coupling should be encouraged, EPA should not require its use or suggest that it is impermissible 
to take advantage of other techniques.  SDWA regulations do not specify specific design and 
construction standards because identifying specific technologies forecloses systems’ taking 
advantage of improvements in technology.   
Obtaining Property Owner Consent 
The proposed revised rule provides that community water systems will make four 
attempts to engage property owners regarding service line replacements.  EPA requests comment 
as to whether a “reasonable effort” should be more attempts.  The City submits that four attempts 
is ample.  Four attempts already places a significant resource burden on the City and should be 
deemed sufficient to meet regulatory compliance obligations.  This element of the proposed rule 
must be considered in the context of the entire requirement.  The City will be required to contact 
hundreds of thousands of property owners to undertake replacement.  Property owners are not 
under a legal obligation to reply to this outreach, and the City’s experience with the State grant-
funded lead service line replacement program shows that property owners are unlikely to respond, 

 
14 
 
 
regardless of the number of attempts.  The City notes that the proposed regulatory text provides a 
reasonable list of communication strategies that can be utilized for these efforts. 
Potential Shortages of Workers and Materials 
The City is concerned about contractor availability and the supply of materials, 
particularly filters.  Given the contemplated national effort, there is a risk of potential shortages, 
which will impact our ability to comply with the regulations.  The regulations should reflect 
alternatives, including triggers for extending deadlines, if market corrections are not sufficient to 
address labor and material shortages. 
Modifications to Improve Compliance 
The proposed rule could be modified to better promote compliance by clarifying 
that a records-based service line material determination can be considered a relevant documented 
service line construction as included in a non-lead validation study and consistent with EPA’s 
Guidance for Developing and Maintaining a Service Line Inventory (Chapter 4).  The adequate 
demonstration of service line materials of construction must be clear not only to water systems, 
but to state and EPA enforcement staff. 
Support for American Water Works Association Comments 
It should be noted that DEP is a member of and participant in the development of 
comments from American Water Works Association (AWWA), the New York Section of AWWA, 
and the Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies.  The City supports the comments prepared 
and submitted by these organizations.   
Thank you for your consideration of the City’s comments. 
 
 
Sincerely,

Andrew J. Rauchberg 
Assistant Corporation Counsel

together and conduct due diligence to minimize lead exposure. We recognize that while significant progress has 
been made over the past several decades in reducing children’s exposure to lead in their environment, that even 
small exposures may result in detrimental health effects. The Lead and Copper Rule Improvements offer the 
opportunity to make further progress in reducing potential lead exposure from drinking water. 
Upon review, we and our organizations offer the following comments to the below key items within the proposed 
rule, and endorse the much more detailed comments being offered by the American Water Works Association. In 
addition to our comments on the substance of the proposed rule, we wish to focus your initial attention on an 
important issue of rule scheduling and compliance that should be resolved immediately. 
EPA must immediately provide regulatory clarity and certainty about LCRR requirements 
and deadlines. We support EPA’s approach of eliminating confusion and unnecessary 
expenditures of resources by deferring compliance with many aspects of the LCRR until the 
compliance date of LCRI.  However, until the LCRI is finalized, water systems have no 
assurance of what will be in it, and there is concern that even if we assume that the final rule will 
contain the deferral of LCRR deadlines, any delay in issuance leaves systems vulnerable to non- 
compliance. NEWWA will be providing training and guidance on the LCRI in upcoming courses

COMMENTS ON THE LCRI PROPOSAL: 
The following sections provide specific recommendations on the proposed rule provisions and 
responses to some of the related EPA requests for comments. A number of NEWWA members 
participated in the development of the American Water Works Association and Association of 
Metropolitan Water Agencies’ comments, and we urge you to carefully consider those as well. 
 
 
LCR AS A TREATMENT TECHNIQUE: 
NEWWA supports the continued use of the Safe Drinking Water Act’s (SDWA’s) Treatment 
Technique framework for reducing the risk of lead in drinking water. 
 
 
LEAD SERVICE LINE REPLACEMENT 
REQUIREMENTS: 
EPA has overstepped its authority in saying that access equals control: NEWWA supports 
the timely full removal of all lead service lines (LSLs1). However, we have serious concerns 
that EPA has overstepped its authority under the Safe Drinking Water Act. EPA has presented 
contorted logic in attempting to demonstrate that having an owner allow access equals actual 
control. We do not agree that this is the case. Many of our water systems are actively working 
with their customers to voluntarily replace service lines on private property, often with 
substantial local funding, but the emphasis in those programs is that participation is voluntary. 
Water systems are not asserting that they have control, but rather are requesting access from the 
owner who has control over their property. Water systems do not control customer-owned 
portions of their plumbing and therefore cannot force customers to remove lead fixtures or 
plumbing materials without major changes to terms and condition agreements and methods to 
address legal liability implications. 
Federal Funding is Essential: EPA must make additional targeted funding available if 
communities across the nation are to succeed in eliminating LSLs within a decade. NEWWA 
members have serious concerns that the federal government’s financial commitment falls far 
short of the funds needed to complete the job nationwide, and that much of EPA’s public 
rhetoric on funding deliberately understates what a small fraction of the total cost will be 
covered by current federal commitments. 
 
 
1 Unless specifically stated, for simplicity we are referring to both lead service lines and galvanized requiring 
replacement as LSL 
 Failure of the federal government to step up and provide adequate resources will either result in 
communities being unable to meet the deadlines in the LCRI, or will affect their ability to meet 

3 
 
other regulatory requirements and system maintenance needs. Proposed PFAS standards, 
suggested changes in the disinfection byproducts rules, and concerns about aged infrastructure 
will all require attention and funds at many of our member’s systems. Many systems are already 
challenged by existing state rules for PFAS, and will befurther challenged if EPA finalizes its 
PFAS rule as proposed. New England has many of the oldest water systems in the U.S., and 
much of the oldest infrastructure in need of the most resources is in our poorest communities.  
EPA’s own estimates2 of need for Drinking Water State Revolving Fund-eligible infrastructure 
projects that are necessary over the 20-year period for water systems in New England to continue 
to provide safe drinking water to the public exceeds $28 billion. Unless the federal government 
increases its support, the burden of resolving the decades or centuries old issue of lead service 
lines will be borne by our most vulnerable ratepayers. 
Accelerated Replacement and CCT: NEWWA supports EPA’s use of incentives to 
accelerate LSL replacement, particularly the provision to defer construction or re-optimization of 
corrosion control treatment if a system can replace all its LSLs within 5 years of exceeding the 
proposed new lead Action Level. Both the LCRR and the LCRI recognize that lead service lines 
represent the most significant source of lead when they are present, and emphasize this by 
requiring that salvaged lead service lines be included in any evaluation of corrosion control. 
Requiring a focus on modifying carefully balanced treatment objectives, even as LSLs 
are beinging replaced, is inappropriate. NEWWA believes that EPA has struck an 
appropriate balance with this provision of encouraging that LSL replacement be 
conducted faster. 
Ten Year Deadlines: EPA should separate the metrics for replacing LSLs from those for 
resolving lead status unknown services. The current combined 3-year rolling average metrics 
for monitoring compliance with LSL replacement and resolution of unknowns are unworkable, 
and will almost inevitably result in unavoidable non-compliance for many if not most water 
systems. Systems with many more unknowns than confirmed LSLs, which appears to be the case 
for many systems in the preliminary inventories we have seen, will quickly exhaust the pool of 
LSLs to replace. And even if that were not an issue (for example, in a system with mostly 
confirmed LSLs and relatively few unknowns), the 3-year rolling average may discourage efforts 
to initially replace LSLs quickly. Replacing or resolving more than 10 percent for several early 
years will prevent compliance in later years with the proposed 3-year rolling average mechanism. 
NEWWA recommends that EPA revise this requirement by instead requiring a cumulative 
10 percent average beginning in year three for replacement of LSLs and a separate cumulative 10 
percent average for resolving unknowns. 
 
 
2DRINKING WATER INFRASTRUCTURE NEEDS SURVEY AND ASSESSMENT 7TH REPORT TO CONGRESS – September 
2023:  https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2023-09/Seventh%20DWINSA_September2023_Final.pdf 
 
Counting Refusals: NEWWA also recommends that the final rule clarify how homes with 
LSLs where the owner has refused access to their private property and declined participation in 
the system’s LSL replacement program are accounted for in progress reporting. It is clear that 
some owners will simply refuse access, even at no cost, leaving some properties with a LSL in 

4 
 
place. EPA’s proposal provides an appropriate provision that refusal after four attempts indicates 
that the property is not within the control of the water system. What is left unclear is whether a 
system can count that towards its annual 10 percent progress, and more importantly, whether the 
system would be in compliance at the end of 10 years (or five in the case where a system is 
availing itself of the incentivized deferral of corrosion control treatment provision). The final 
rule must make it clear that the replacement obligations are only applicable to those LSLs where 
the owner has allowed access. 
Partial Replacements: NEWWA supports the provision to allow partial replacements when 
they are conducted as part of an emergency repair or in coordination with planned infrastructure 
work. While the proposed exclusion of partial replacements during planned infrastructure work 
relative to LSL replacement projects is intended to prevent systems from intentionally 
conducting partial replacements, it does not account for customer refusal and further impedes 
lead removal. If a system is implementing a LSL replacement project in a neighborhood and a 
customer refuses to participate, prohibiting a partial replacement prevents the removal of the 
public-portion of the LSL and would require remobilization and additional costs to conduct the 
replacement in the future. EPA should remove this prohibition or at a minimum include language 
permitting partial replacements in these cases. 
SYSTEMS WITH MULTIPLE ACTION LEVEL 
EXCEEDANCES: 
Requiring filters: EPA should revisit the requirement to offer filters to all customers if a 
system has multiple Action Level (AL) exceedances. With the lower proposed AL and the 
changes in sampling and reporting protocols, many systems will likely exceed the AL. Even in 
our older region, for many of the systems that have lead service lines, they account for less than 
one percent of the total number of service lines in the system. If filters are needed at all, the 
focus should be on those buildings with LSLs. Providing filters to buildings without a LSL will 
confuse the public and dilute the focus on replacing LSLs where they exist. Providing them to 
buildings with LSLs could reduce the owner’s impetus to replace the LSL. EPA should 
eliminate this provision in its entirety, or at a minimum focus the offer on only those buildings 
with LSLs. 
Availability of certified filters: There are likely to be substantial issues with availability of 
appropriately certified filters if this becomes a nationwide mandate. We have already heard from 
systems that are proactively making filters available as part of LSL investigations and 
replacements that they are having difficulty purchasing even lots of a few hundred filters, let 
alone the thousands that would be needed for larger systems if this requirement were to be 
implemented. 
 
If EPA chooses to retain any part of this requirement, it must clarify what the term “make 
filters available” means in practice, as the preamble states that the system must only make them 
available at “no direct cost” for low-income customers which implies that for all others, they 
could be offered to the customer at cost3. EPA should consider the feasibility of creating a 
national program, similar to the COVID test kit program, where EPA would directly provide 
certified filters to consumers. This would simplify the requirement and make it nationally 

5 
 
uniform. 
 
We also believe there will need to be an aggressive public outreach campaign conducted by EPA 
on the proper maintenance of POU filters. Filters need to be regularly changed to ensure that 
water quality is maintained.  Our members are concerned that improperly maintained filters 
could lead to unintended negative public health impacts due to biological growth, etc. 
 
 
SAMPLING AND RESULTS REPORTING 
REQUIREMENTS: 
Rejecting inappropriate samples: EPA should further clarify when a system can reject an 
inappropriately collected sample. The rule preamble discusses ways a system can identify and 
avoid analyzing inappropriately collected samples, but there is no parallel rule. EPA should 
either provide additional language in the rule itself, or at a minimum develop explicit 
guidance that buildings that are not currently occupied or samples with stagnation times in 
excess of 12 hours should be discarded and new samples collected. 
Sample reporting requirements: Requiring that sample results be provided to the sampler 
within three calendar days presents systems with the substantial risk of inadvertent and 
potentially unavoidable non-compliance.  Analysis and reporting of results typically takes several 
weeks from when the sample is collected - one or two additional days to provide the results is not 
a crisis. Monday holidays and shortened Friday work hours mean that when results are received 
on a Friday, there may well be no one to receive and respond to the data during that entire three-
calendar-day period.  Water system staff have many varied responsibilities to actively and safely 
manage their systems; there is not a dedicated staff person awaiting results, ready to jump into 
action to immediately generate and distribute letters. EPA should change the rule to allow at a 
minimum, 5 business days and more ideally 7 business days, and limit rapid data 
transmittal to samples over the Action Level, retaining the current 30-day notification for all 
other samples. Requiring as EPA proposes in the LCRI that all samples receive rush delivery 
notification defeats the purpose of quickly delivering elevated results. 
When a result is over the AL, water system staff should be able to prioritize directly connecting 
with and educating those samplers (and beginning the process of working with the resident to 
begin the required Distribution System and Site Assessment). 
3 This requirement is clearly distinguished for the language related to replacement of LSL or disturbances of LSL 
which requires that the system “provide filters and replacement cartridges”. 
 
Sampling schedules: EPA should consider staggering implementation of standard monitoring. 
In prior rules, EPA has staggered certain requirements for monitoring with larger systems going 
first, and smaller systems staggered behind. This allows for some lessons to be learned, and 
mitigates overload of laboratory capacity and primacy agency attention. 
Sample Collection Frequency: Systems with no LSLs with current sampling results below the 
AL that have qualified for reduced monitoring for many consecutive years should have a means 
to continue on reduced monitoring as deemed appropriate by the Primacy Agency. 

6 
 
 
 
INVENTORY REQUIREMENTS: 
EPA should remove fire services and other non-potable service lines from inventory and 
replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to prevent potable 
uses. Similarly, there has been confusion about system obligations for piping downstream of the 
recognized service line.  A service line is clearly defined as connecting the system’s main with 
the building.  Additional piping connecting buildings, or connecting buildings with 
appurtenances on private property are not service lines. It should not be the responsibility of the 
water system to try to decipher materials beyond the service line, in facilities such as trailer parks 
or office or condo complexes. 
 
EPA should remove service lines serving abandoned properties from inventory and 
replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to assure 
construction of appropriate service line materials prior to the property receiving service. If the 
system has the appropriate administrative safeguards in place, this serves no useful propose and 
diverts resources from achieving LSL replacement at occupied locations. 
 
EPA should retain the LCRR requirement that systems must only replace lead connectors as 
they are encountered. EPA should not include the replacement of connectors in the mandatory 
LSL replacement requirements because in many cases connector material records are not 
available, and field investigating all connector material in the absence of records would not be 
feasible or practical for most systems. Lead connectors should only be included in service line 
inventories for the purpose of identifying potential sampling locations, and only where existing 
records indicate their presence. 
Galvanized service lines: While NEWWA supports the inclusion of galvanized service lines 
downstream of a LSL in the inventory and replacement mandates of the proposed rule, we do 
not support the inclusion of those galvanized services that ever were downstream of a LSL or 
are currently downstream of unknown service lines in the inventory and replacement mandates. 
Including them in the mandate increases the total cost of replacement programs, with limited 
benefit. In addition, as EPA is requiring that all unknowns be resolved within 10 years, any 
galvanized service lines downstream of unknowns will be either identified as needing 
replacement because the upstream line was positively identified as lead, or the upstream service 
line will be positively identified as not lead. In the case of the latter, EPA should remove its 
requirement for systems to demonstrate that the upstream portion was never a LSL, as this is not 
possible given the previously unknown nature of the material, and instead reclassify the service 
line as non-lead and remove it from the replacement pool. 
Use of state laws or regulation prohibiting lead: EPA should be explicit that service lines 
without recorded material can be classed as non-lead if state law or regulation extant at the time 
of construction prohibited the use of lead. For example, the 1926 Maine State Law Lead Pipe 
ban should be allowed to qualify homes built in or after 1927 to be classified as Non-Lead. 
 
Simplifying Inventory Updates: Systems with online inventories should be able to simply 
notify their state primacy agency annually with summary statistics on any changes and provide 
instructions on how to access their online inventory. There is no need for these systems to 
annually re-submit the complete inventory to the state. 

7 
 
 
Validation Requirements: EPA should reconsider the content and timing of the proposed 
inventory validation requirement. The validation requirement will represent a distraction and 
unnecessary resource drag for many systems. The requirements are overly prescriptive, and the 
deadline overlaps with the most important time when systems will be working to make real 
progress at LSL replacement. Validation should only be necessary if the state primacy agency 
finds that the methods used to develop the inventory are unreliable. States should be given the 
latitude to review and approve validation work done prior to the LCRI implementation date. 
NEWWA also recommends that the validation language explicitly state that only one point on 
the private side and one point on the public side need validation. EPA should also state that 
service lines that have been identified by a record on one side of the service and physical 
inspection on the other side do not need to be included in the validation pool. 
 
 
ELIMINATION OF THE TRIGGER LEVEL AND 
LOWERING THE ACTION LEVEL 
NEWWA supports the efforts that EPA has made to slightly simplify the rule by eliminating 
the Trigger Level. However, EPA has failed to adequately analyze and document the 
synergistic impacts of lowering the Action Level, changes to the sampling site selection focusing 
on LSLs, and new sampling and reporting protocols using the highest of 1st and 5th liter samples. 
These proposed changes combined with the 24-hour public notice requirement will do 
unnecessary damage to public confidence as more systems exceed the Action Level, not because 
water quality is worse, but because the goal posts and game rules have been changed. 
 
 
OUTREACH AND EDUCATION 
REQUIREMENTS: 
Flexibility to improve coordinated outreach: EPA should carefully review all outreach 
activities for consistency, and design them as an integrated public education program. The 
outreach requirements must allow sufficient flexibility so that they can be thoughtfully 
integrated into a cohesive whole, helping consumers make good choices rather than 
unnecessarily scaring or confusing them. As currently proposed, customers in systems over the 
Action Level would receive the following outreach during a 12-month period: 
1. Two consumer confidence reports, with additional information on LSLs; 
2. an annual notice that they have a LSL or unknown (perhaps 4 additional times if their 
street is in a current LSL replacement program); 
3. exposure to the 24 hour Public Notice, and 
4. a lead education brochure with information on LSLs and replacement efforts (potentially 
twice that year). 
As part of that cohesive education program, for systems with LSLs, EPA should ensure that 
the 24-hour Public Notice template emphasizes the following: 

8 
 
1. That the samples were taken at homes with LSLs, 
2. That customers would have received information about the presence of a LSL or 
unknown, and 
3. A focus on actions the system and residents can take to replace LSLs and identify 
unknowns. 
The goal should be to encourage consumer action to permanently reduce their potential exposure 
through drinking water by replacing their LSL if they have one. 
The current 60-day delivery requirement should be retained for Public Education after an 
Action Level exceedance. Especially with all the lead-related outreach efforts described above, 
including the new 24-hour Public Notice, there is no need to unnecessarily rush delivery of the 
public education brochures. 
CORROSION CONTROL TREATMENT: 
Corrosion control treatment: Any required changes to treatment and water quality parameters 
needs to be system specific. A one size fits all approach to establishing Optimum Corrosion 
Control Treatment presents real risk to what is often a carefully crafted balancing of objectives 
for simultaneous compliance. Rule text and guidance must make this clear. 
 
 
SIMPLIFYING REQUIREMENTS FOR SYSTEMS 
WITH FEW OR NO LSLs: 
 
EPA should consider simplifying the compliance and reporting path for systems with no LSLs or 
unknowns. If a system has no identified LSLs or GRR, and no specific indication that they were 
used historically, there should be no need to conduct extensive potholing or other validation 
efforts, nor should service lines currently inventoried as unknown require risk mitigation efforts 
after disturbances. In cases where there are no known LSLs and no documented history that any 
had ever been installed, the likelihood of unknowns being lead is slight, and the primacy agency 
should have the flexibility to reduce the level of required effort. 
Systems with no LSLs and unknowns or connector updates should be able to submit a statement 
to their Primacy Agency to certify that no inventory updates are currently required. 
 
 
SCHOOL SAMPLING: 
NEWWA agrees that EPA has offered some additional flexibility for systems that have worked 
with schools and/or childcare facilities on lead testing, but believes the changes do not go far 
enough. Primacy agencies should have the flexibility to exempt (or reduce the scope of testing 
for) systems with recent past or ongoing school and childcare facility lead testing programs, even 
if they are not exactly congruent with the specific requirements in the proposed rule. 
 
 
 

9 
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to comment on this complex and important effort to further 
reduce potential lead exposures to consumers from drinking water and premise plumbing. 
 
I appreciate your consideration to this request and would be happy to discuss it should you have 
any questions. If so, please feel free to contact me at 792-2800. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Philip W. Croasdale 
 
Philip W. Croasdale, Director

RE: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements (Docket 
#: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801)  
 
 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
The Massachusetts Water Resources Authority (MWRA) appreciates the opportunity to comment 
on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA’s) proposed improvements to the Lead and 
Copper Rule (LCRI). The MWRA has been actively involved in various EPA consultation 
opportunities during each iteration of revisions to the LCR since 2004, and is pleased to be able to 
provide additional comments on the current set of proposed changes.  
 
The MWRA provides wholesale water service to 53 communities in eastern and central 
Massachusetts, serving approximately 2.5 million residents. MWRA believes that managing 
potential risks associated with lead in drinking water is a shared responsibility: MWRA, our 
customer communities, their individual retail customers, our state and federal regulators, and local, 
state and federal health officials, all share a part of the responsibility for appropriate action. With 
the implementation of modern corrosion control in 1996, MWRA has seen lead levels in those 
homes most at risk drop by almost 90 percent. MWRA communities have been removing lead 
service lines since the 1960s. In 2016 MWRA established a $100 million zero-interest loan 
program to accelerate full lead service replacement by our customer communities, and is currently 
evaluating program changes to further accelerate progress. MWRA shares EPA’s goal of 
eliminating all lead services as rapidly as practical. 
 
Our comments respond to issues affecting MWRA directly as the regional wholesaler providing 
drinking water treatment for our customer communities and on behalf of those customer 
communities on issues affecting their obligations such as sampling, consumer outreach and lead 
service line replacement. MWRA takes its collaborative role with our customer communities in 
reducing lead exposure seriously, and offers the following comments on the proposed revisions 
for your consideration. 
 

2 
 
IMPORTANT POINT FOR IMMEDIATE CONSIDERATION  
EPA must immediately provide regulatory clarity and certainty about the Lead and Copper 
Rule Revisions (LCRR) requirements and deadlines.  MWRA supports EPA’s approach of 
eliminating confusion and unnecessary expenditures of resources by deferring compliance with 
many aspects of the LCRR until the compliance date of LCRI, with the important exception of the 
inventory, associated outreach, and the 24-hour Public Notice.  However, until the LCRI is 
finalized, water systems have no assurance of what will be in it, and there is concern that even if 
we assume that the final rule will contain the planned deferral of LCRR deadlines, any delay in 
LCRI issuance leaves systems vulnerable. MWRA routinely provides training and guidance to the 
53 communities we provide drinking water service to.  We are at a loss to provide specific advice 
on whether they should continue to assume compliance with LCRR by October 2024, potentially 
wasting effort that could be better spent elsewhere, or assume that LCRI will definitely provide 
the deferral. A delay in promulgation or a change of course at EPA would put them and us at risk 
of failing to be in compliance. We understand that many of the water associations have requested 
this immediate regulatory action to provide clarity and certainty – we support their request. 
 
COMMENTS ON THE LCRI PROPOSAL:  
The following sections provide specific comments and recommendations on the proposed rule 
provisions, and related EPA requests for comments. MWRA staff participated in the development 
of the American Waterworks Association and Association of Metropolitan Water Agencies’ more 
detailed comments, and urge you to carefully consider those as well. 
 
LCR as a Treatment Technique:  
MWRA supports the continued use of the Safe Drinking Water Act’s (SDWA’s) Treatment 
Technique framework for reducing the risk of lead in drinking water.  Because the source of the 
lead is from lead service lines and lead-containing premise plumbing, the use of a Maximum 
Contaminant Level (MCL) is not feasible or appropriate.  
 
Lead Service Line Replacements:  
MWRA supports the timely full removal of all lead service lines (LSL1), and has already 
committed $100 million of our ratepayers money in interest-free loans to our member communities 
for their full removal.  MWRA remains concerned that the federal government’s financial 
commitment falls far short of the funds needed to complete the job nationwide. Failure of the 
Federal government to step up and provide adequate resources will either result in communities 
being unable to meet the deadlines in the LCRI, or will affect their ability to meet all other 
                                                           
1 Unless specifically delineated, for simplicity we are referring to both lead service lines and galvanized requiring 
replacement as LSL.  

3 
 
regulatory requirements and urgent asset management objectives.  PFAS, changes in the 
disinfection byproducts rules, and concerns about legionella will all require attention and funds at 
many of our member communities. The thousands of miles of unlined cast iron mains in 
community distribution systems will continue to age and continue to require either replacement or 
relining.  In our region, we know that much of the oldest infrastructure, in need of the most 
resources, is in our poorest communities and those historically neglected. The full cost burden of 
resolving the decades or centuries old issue of lead service lines cannot be on the backs of our 
most vulnerable ratepayers. 
EPA and the Administration must make additional targeted funding available if our 
communities and communities across the nation are to succeed at eliminating lead service lines 
within a decade.  
MWRA supports EPA’s use of incentives to accelerate LSL replacement, particularly the 
provision to defer construction or re-optimization of corrosion control treatment if a system can 
replace all its LSL within five years of exceeding the proposed new lead Action Level. Lead 
service lines represent the most significant source of lead when they are present. Both the LCRR 
and the LCRI recognize this in their requirements that lead service lines be included in any 
evaluation of corrosion control.  However, any change in treatment risks upsetting the delicate 
balance of simultaneous compliance with all other rules and water quality objectives, and in 
particular the addition of phosphate carries long term implications for both water and wastewater 
system operations, even after all LSL are replaced. MWRA believes that EPA has struck an 
appropriate balance with this provision of encouraging that the best long term solution (LSL 
replacement) be conducted faster.  
MWRA recommends that EPA restructure the metrics for replacing LSL and resolving lead 
status unknown services (hereafter referred to as unknowns). The current combined three-year 
rolling average metrics for monitoring compliance with LSL replacement and resolution of 
unknowns are unworkable, and will almost inevitably result in inadvertent and unavoidable non-
compliance. Systems with many more unknowns than confirmed LSL, which appears to be the 
case for many of our communities in the preliminary inventories we have seen, will quickly 
exhaust the pool of LSL to replace, even while they are moving forward with resolving unknowns 
on a pace designed to eliminate all of them by 10 years. And even if that were not an issue (for 
example in a system with mostly confirmed LSLs), the three-year rolling average may handicap 
efforts at replacing LSL quickly (clearly a public health goal) while still meeting the rolling three-
year requirement. Replacing or resolving more than 10 percent for several early years could 
mathematically prevent compliance in later years with the three-year rolling average. MWRA 
recommends that EPA revise the requirement by requiring a cumulative 10 percent average 
beginning in year three for replacement of LSL and a separate cumulative 10 percent average for 
resolving unknowns.  
MWRA also recommends that the final rule clarify how homes with LSL where the owner has 
refused access to their private property and declined participation in the system’s LSL replacement 
program are accounted for in annual progress reporting and determination of program completion. 
The experience of MWRA’s customer communities has clearly evidenced that some owners will 

4 
 
simply refuse to participate, even at no cost, refusing access to their property, leaving, for now, 
some properties with LSL in place. EPA’s proposal provides an appropriate provision that refusal 
after four attempts using two different methods indicates that the property is not within the control 
of the water system. What is left unclear is whether a system can count that towards its annual 10 
percent progress, and more importantly, whether the system would be in compliance at the end of 
10 years (or five in the case where a system is availing itself of the incentivized deferral of 
corrosion control treatment provision). MWRA recommends that the final rule make it clear that 
the replacement obligations are only applicable to those LSL within its control, that is, where the 
owner has allowed access.   
 
Requirements for Systems with Multiple Action Level Exceedances:  
As discussed above, MWRA supports EPA’s use of incentives to accelerate LSL replacement, 
particularly the provision to defer construction or re-optimization of corrosion control treatment 
if a system can replace all its LSL within five years of exceeding the new lead Action Level. 
MWRA recommends that EPA revisit the requirements to offer filters to all customers if the 
Action Level is exceeded three times within five years.  With the changes in sampling and 
reporting protocols and the lowered Action Level, many systems will likely exceed within the first 
18 months of rule implementation. There is no justification for offering filters to every household 
- in many cases the higher risk homes will represent only a small fraction of water users – often 
less than five percent or even less than 1 percent.  Within the MWRA region, many of our systems 
that have any number of lead service lines, have less than one percent.  The current proposal will 
create substantial confusion with all the other emphases in the LCRR and LCRI on the importance 
of replacing LSL.  Offering filters to homes without a LSL will confuse the public, imply that their 
water is not safe and dilute the focus on replacing LSL where they exist. If filters are needed at all, 
the focus should be on those homes with LSL. However, offering filters to homes with LSL could 
cause the residents to believe that the risk has been removed, impacting their understanding that 
the LSL is a detriment and taking away the impetus to participate in replacement of the LSL.  
In addition to the issue related to inappropriate messaging, there is likely to be substantial issues 
with availability of appropriately certified filters if this is a nationwide mandate. We have already 
heard from systems that are making filters available as part of LSL investigations and 
replacements, that they are having difficulty purchasing even lots of a few hundred. Needing to 
secure thousands or tens of thousands of filters at the same time that many other systems will be 
facing the same task, seems likely to result in supply chain failure. MWRA recommends that 
EPA eliminate this provision in its entirety, or at a minimum focus the offer on only those homes 
with LSL. 
If EPA chooses to retain any part of this requirement, it must clarify what the term “make 
filters available” means in practice, as the preamble states that the system must only make them 
available at “no direct cost” for low-income customers, clearly implying that for all others they 

5 
 
could be offered to the consumer at cost2. At the scale of an entire system, this requirement creates 
substantial implementation issues. For example, will the system need to conduct income 
verification, is it adequate to provide access to a commercial web site where consumer can order 
a certified filter, at their cost, for delivery to their home?   
 
Sampling and Results Reporting Requirements:  
MWRA recommends that EPA further clarify under what conditions a system can reject an 
inappropriately collected sample prior to analysis. The rule preamble provides a discussion of the 
ways a system can identify and avoid analyzing inappropriately collected samples, but there is no 
parallel rule language for systems to rely on. MWRA has had communities collect samples in 
structures that were under renovation and vacant, or after extended absences. These circumstances 
produce lead data which is not representative of typical use, and could result in inappropriate 
mandated actions. EPA should either provide additional language in the rule itself, or at a 
minimum develop explicit written guidance that buildings that are not currently occupied or 
samples with stagnation times in excess of 24 hours should be discarded prior to analysis, and new 
samples collected.  
EPA should continue to explicitly allow flexibility for consecutive systems in the design of 
sampling programs, especially those regional systems like MWRA with long standing effective 
and efficient consecutive system sampling agreements.  Such systems should be able to initially 
switch to twice-annual “standard” monitoring without necessarily having to collect the full 
“standard” number of samples.  MWRA’s current regional consecutive system sampling pool for 
a system with one source and one treatment plant includes collecting just under 600 samples per 
sampling round – six times the standard number for the largest systems.  If we were to collect the 
standard number in each of our consecutive systems, we would be collecting about 1800 samples 
per sampling round, 18 times what EPA’s own statisticians had determined was necessary for 
reliable data.  
MWRA recommends that EPA revise the sample data reporting requirements. Requiring that 
sample results be provided to the sampler within three calendar days presents systems with the 
substantial risk of inadvertent and potentially unavoidable non-compliance.  In our region, many 
systems work a short day on Fridays, and there are many Monday holidays. Results received on a 
Friday would need to provided to the sampler by Monday – but there may well have been no one 
to receive and respond to the data during that entire three calendar day period. Water system staff 
have many responsibilities to actively and safely manage their systems. In smaller systems with 
fewer staff, there is not a dedicated staff person waiting for results, ready to jump into action. 
Typically by the time a system receives lead results, at least several weeks or longer have elapsed 
from the time of sample collection.  Allowing a few additional days to deliver elevated lead results 
to ensure a reasonable likelihood of compliance is not unreasonable.  MWRA recommends two 
changes: change the rule to allow three business days (or better yet five), and limit rapid data 
                                                           
2 This requirement is clearly distinguished for the language related to replacement of LSL or disturbances of LSL 
which requires that the system “provide filters and replacement cartridges”.  

6 
 
transmittal to samples over the Action Level, retaining the current 30 days for all other samples.  
Requiring as EPA now proposes in the LCRI that all samples receive rush delivery, defeats the 
purpose of quickly delivering elevated results to the much smaller number of samplers with results 
over the Action Level.  This will reduce the likelihood that water system staff will be able to 
prioritize directly connecting with and educating those samplers with higher results (and beginning 
the process of working with the resident to begin the required Distribution System and Site 
Assessment). 
Distribution System and Site Assessment: 
MWRA recommends that EPA limit the requirement for Water Quality Parameter (WQP) 
monitoring to a single sample collected in the vicinity of any LCR tap sample with results over the 
Action Level. The current requirement to add these additional sites to a system’s permanent regular 
WQP monitoring program, in the absence of a finding that the initial sample indicated a localized 
deviation from the system corrosion control limits, adds no useful additional data, provides no 
cause for action, and adds unnecessary long term sampling burden. MWRA has piloted this 
sampling requirement over the past several years, conducting 79 assessments of water quality near 
taps sampling sites that were over the Action Level: none demonstrated that local water quality 
was outside OWQP limits.  
 
Inventory Requirements:   
MWRA recommends that EPA remove fire services and other non-potable service lines from 
inventory and replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to 
prevent potable uses. Having this as a regulatory requirement with the associated annual notices 
and its presence in the publicly available inventory list adds unnecessary confusion, and adds 
unnecessary additional system effort in developing and maintaining the inventory, without any 
public health benefit.  
 
Similarly, there has been confusion about system obligations for piping downstream of the 
recognized service line.  A service line is clearly defined as connecting the system’s main with the 
building.  Additional piping connecting buildings, or connecting buildings with appurtenances on 
private property are not service lines, and EPA must clarify this in both guidance materials and 
in EPA staff’s interactions with state primacy agency staff.  
 
MWRA recommends that EPA remove service lines serving abandoned properties from 
inventory and replacement requirements if there are appropriate administrative safeguards to 
assure installation of an appropriate new non-lead service line prior to the property receiving 
service. If the system has the appropriate administrative safeguards in place, this provision serves 
no useful propose and diverts resources from achieving LSL replacement at occupied locations.  
 
EPA should retain the LCRR requirement that systems must only replace lead connectors as they 
are encountered.  EPA should not include the replacement of connectors in the mandatory LSL 
replacement requirements because in many cases connector material records are not available, and 
field investigating all connector material in the absence of records would not be feasible or 

7 
 
practical. Lead connectors should only be included in service line inventories for the purpose of 
identifying potential sampling locations, and only where existing records indicate their presence.  
MWRA supports the inclusion of galvanized service lines downstream of a lead service line in 
the inventory and replacement mandates of the proposed rule.  
MWRA does not support the inclusion of those galvanized services downstream of “ever was” 
lead or unknown service lines in the inventory and replacement mandates. While there is a 
reasonable level of evidence that galvanized pipe downstream of a lead pipe can accumulate and 
potentially release lead, the evidence for such release long after the lead line has been replaced is 
lacking, and some studies indicate essentially no risk. Including such service lines in the mandate 
increases the total cost of replacement programs, and prolongs their duration, with limited risk 
reduction. In addition, as EPA is requiring that all unknowns be resolved within ten years, any 
galvanized service lines downstream of unknowns will be either identified as needing replacement 
because the upstream line was positively identified as lead, or positively identified as not requiring 
replacement as the upstream service line was positively identified as not lead.  
EPA should reconsider the content and timing of the new inventory validation requirement. The 
validation requirement, while seemingly an important sub task in creating a reliable inventory, 
actually will represent a distraction and unnecessary resource drag for many systems. The 
requirements are overly prescriptive, and the deadline overlaps with the most important time when 
systems will be working to make real progress at LSL replacement. Validation should only be 
necessary if the state primacy agency finds that the methods used to develop the inventory are 
demonstrably unreliable. MWRA recommends requiring this be done after the 10 year window, 
simplifying the requirements, and explicitly allowing states to review and approve validation work 
done prior to the LCRI implementation date.  
MWRA also recommends that the validation language explicitly state that only one point on the 
private side and one point on the public side need validation, and thus that validation efforts may 
only require additional research on whichever side did not have adequate quality of original data.   
 
Elimination of the Trigger Level and Lowering the Action Level  
MWRA supports the efforts that EPA has made to slightly simplify the rule by eliminating the 
Trigger Level.  However, EPA has failed to adequately analyze and document the synergistic 
impacts of lowering the Action Level, changes to the sampling site selection focusing on LSL, and 
sampling and reporting protocols using the higher of 1st and 5th liter samples. These changes 
combined with the 24-hour public notice requirement will do unnecessary damage to public 
confidence as more systems exceed the Action Level, not because water quality is worse, but 
because the goal posts and game rules have been changed.  
With the switch to LSL replacement being required of all systems, rather than only those over the 
Action Level, the importance of the Action Level in the LCR rule construct has substantially 
changed. Rather than now being the primary method for lead risk reduction in the rule, it is 
diminished in importance, and will be further diminished over time as lead service lines are 

8 
 
replaced. For most systems, going forward, the impact of the Action Level will be primarily be the 
need to find ways to manage public understanding of risks of lead. The Public Notice requirement 
is a very non-targeted public education program, broadcasting rather than narrow casting to highest 
risk homes. EPA should carefully craft the guidance for the Public Notice to focus it narrowly.  
 
Appropriately Integrated and Focused Outreach and Education Requirements:  
EPA should carefully review all outreach activities for consistency and appropriate focus, as part 
of what ought to be an integrated public education program. As currently drafted, customers will 
be in danger of zoning out from information overload, thus negating the value of all the outreach 
efforts. Consider that for systems over the Action Level, during one year, customers will be 
receiving:  
 their CCR twice, with additional information on LSL;  
 an annual notice that they have a LSL or unknown (perhaps 4 additional times if their 
neighborhood is part of that year’s LSL replacement program);  
 exposure to multiple versions of the 24 hour Public Notices (hopefully focused on LSL risk 
and replacement efforts); and  
 a lead education brochure with information on LSL and replacement efforts (potentially 
twice that year).   
In most cases, most of those receiving this deluge of information will not be the actual target 
audience, and the message will not be tailored to their circumstances. The outreach requirements 
must allow sufficient flexibility so that they can be thoughtfully integrated into a cohesive cogent 
whole.  
As part of that cohesive focused education program, for systems with LSL, EPA should ensure 
that the 24-hour Public Notice template emphasizes the following key points: that the samples 
were taken at homes with LSL, that customers would have already received information about the 
presence of a LSL or unknown, and a focus on actions the system and resident can take to identify 
and replace that LSL. The goal should be to create impetus towards our long term goal of replacing 
all LSL. The same should be considered for each of the other required elements – they should work 
together to provide context for where the highest risks are, and encourage action to permanently 
reduce their potential exposure through drinking water by replacing their LSL if they have one.  
MWRA recommends that the current 60 day requirement be retained for the delivery of Public 
Education after an Action Level exceedance. Development and execution of a well-organized, 
coordinated, and effective public education effort, including gaining primacy agency approval, and 
procuring printing and delivery services takes time.  Especially with all the lead-related 
touchpoints described above, including the new 24-hour Public Notice, there is no need to 
unnecessarily rush delivery of the public education brochures.
