Dear Administrator Regan,  
  
The NAACP State Conference of Mississippi submits the following comments regarding the US 
Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water 
Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements” (“LCRI”). The Mississippi State Conference 
NAACP provides leadership for local branches, youth councils, and college chapters for 
environmental and climate justice needs in [insert state]. The NAACP and its Center for 
Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring that issues of 
community engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and frontline 
communities most impacted, including communities throughout the State of Mississippi.    
 
The Mississippi State Conference NAACP applauds EPA for proposing stronger regulations to 
protect communities from lead in drinking water. Lead in drinking water has been a historically 
prevalent issue in Black communities, posing extreme risks to the health of young people, 
mothers, and their families. In Mississippi estimates suggest that there are as many as between 
16,000 to 48,000 lead service lines, threatening families across our state with exposure to a 
potent and irreversible neurotoxin which even at low levels of exposure is linked to damage to 
the brain and nervous system, learning disabilities, shorter stature, impaired hearing, and harm 
to blood cells. In Mississippi, we would derive between $948 million and $2.4 billion in public 
health cost savings from full lead service line replacement.  
  
The potential high level of lead and copper in Mississippi’s waters parallels with the high level of 
PFAS in several Mississippi counties, according to a Consumer Reports article and study 
released in August 2023.  
 
In Jackson, a federal judge has allowed a lawsuit to move forward with about 1,000 children 
diagnosed with lead poisoning suing the city and Mississippi State Department of Health. As the 
water system there has been the subject of national headlines, some residents, and at least one 
college and a hospital, have decided to turn to private wells.  
 
Jackson residents remain warned of lead levels over the EPA action level, but the city’s third-
party water administrator, Ted Henifin, has said his team had not found any lead pipes since it 
took over the system last fall, at least as of last month.  
 
An investigation by Consumer Reports and Mississippi Spotlight, a collaboration of the Clarion 
Ledger and other news organizations, found detectable levels of lead in all 149 municipal and 
well water samples from all corners of Mississippi, covering all counties in the state. 
 

Essentially, more water testing must be conducted in all Mississippi municipalities and counties, 
not curtailed.  And the water systems must pay for these tests, not the residents and/or 
taxpayers.  
 
The EPA should not only incentivize the installation of filters in schools, they should also foot the 
bill – for the children.

For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the 
proposed LCRI such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the 
requirements for water systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through 
lead pipes and a lower action level; but also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes 
which undermine their goals and ensure that weaker parts of the rule are strengthened.  
  
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not 
leave black communities in Mississippi behind:  
  
• 
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a 
fundamental injustice that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 
40 or more years to fix this issue.  
  
  
• 
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: 
Removal can cost thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted 
communities will result in mostly wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines 
replaced. Removal and replacement do not make up major proportions of utility budgets, and 
utilities should be expected to maximize the use of available federal water infrastructure 
funds and other non-ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize solving this crisis.  
  
  
• 
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many 
hours there daily are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead 
exposure when compared with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing program 
does not differ from past ineffective programs, and EPA should move towards incentivizing 
the installation of filters and protecting children.  
  
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would allow for 
environmental injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline communities have long

rare opportunity to make significant changes in the lives of millions of people in [state], and to

this administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by strengthening the final

including informing the LCRR and state-level LCR guidance.

We are committed to achieving a lead-free drinking water system through evidence-based
decision-making and applaud EPA for establishing a timeline for the replacement of all lead
service lines in the United States. To that end, we hereby submit the following comments
regarding EPA’s proposed modifications with the LCRI. We recognize that we are employees of
a for-profit company that provides water infrastructure analytics services to utilities. However,
these recommendations are made in the public interest, based on established best practices in
statistics and data-driven decision-making in the face of uncertainty. Further, the
consequences of our recommended changes to the rule would increase the reliability and trust
service line inventory and replacement, increase efficiency of water utility compliance efforts,
and increase public transparency.
Our comments and recommended changes to the proposed rule that follow can be
summarized as:
(1) we propose streamlining some of the process for validation of non-lead service
lines;
(2) we recommend expanding the pool of addresses for validation to include non-lead
service lines that have been determined based on historic records;
(3) we propose allowing water systems more flexibility in handling their validation of
non-lead addresses;
(4) we encourage EPA to make adjustments to its rule to make it easier for water
systems to have access and control of lead service lines for the purpose of
replacement;
(5) we request that EPA make more resources available for water systems to plan for
mandatory lead service line replacement; and
(6) We propose modifying how EPA categorizes galvanized service lines in communities
where lead-lined galvanized pipes are located.
5 American Rescue Plan Funding: A Playbook for Efficiently Getting the Lead Out. Day One Project.
https://blueconduit.com/post/day-one-whitepaper/
4“When a Representative Sample of Service Lines Reveals Zero Lead, What Can You Say?” Alice Berners-Lee

Improving validation program
A reliable lead service line inventory is the backbone of the LCRI. Visually verifying every
service line’s materials is an expensive endeavor for water systems and not the best use of
their limited resources. EPA proposes requiring water systems to validate a subset of the non-
lead service lines in their inventory to validate the reliability of the methods and assumptions
used to make those determinations. This also makes it clear for water utilities that they are not
expected to visually verify every single service line’s materials, but to adopt a science-based
methodology to determine the number and distribution of service lines to be visually verified.
We believe that this is a thoughtful and scientific approach to validate across the system
without spending time and money at every unknown service line. Our team published a white
paper that specifically addresses what water systems should do when their efforts to inspect a
representative, random set of homes does not reveal a single lead service line.6
Given the overall goal of the validation process, there are a few targeted ways that it can be
improved upon.
Better defining and communicating 95% confidence level
EPA is proposing a 95 percent confidence level approach used to develop the size of the
validation pool. We believe that this is an appropriate approach for the specific statistical
question being asked of water systems, but we are concerned that EPA guidance around
confidence levels is not clear enough. As a result, we recommend that EPA make two changes
to the LCRI.
First, the final LCRI should include the following definition for confidence level.
​
“Confidence level - how likely is it that an estimated interval will typically contain the
true value.”
Applied to the context of validating non-lead service lines in an inventory, if a water system
completes inspections at a set of addresses representative of a population of addresses
requiring validation and does not find an LSL or GRR, then it can say the following, “We can
conclude with a 95% confidence level that the true count of LSL or GRR among that population
is less than Y service lines.” The number “Y” will depend on the number of addresses
representative of the population that were actually inspected.
6 “When a Representative Sample of Service Lines Reveals Zero Lead, What Can You Say?” Alice Berners-Lee
https://blueconduit.com/post/when-a-representative-sample-of-service-lines-reveals-zero-lead-what-can-you-say/

Second, because a confidence interval does not reflect true certainty (the only way to achieve
true certainty would be to physically inspect every service line), we recommend that EPA also
require the water systems to include language around the results of the validation program in
the Consumer Confidence Reports. That language will also help water utilities correctly
communicate around the reliability of their service line inventory. It is important that EPA
provide language for water systems to use because the precise meaning of terms around
uncertainty are critical to effectively communicating the relative risk. Below is some sample
language that could be used:
“As part of the Lead and Copper Rule compliance, the water system developed a lead
service line inventory. In order to verify the reliability of service lines categorized as
non-lead, the water system is required to physically verify service line materials at a
subset. Out of all service lines considered non-lead in our system, we physically
inspected a representative sample of 200 of them and found 0 lead service lines in the
representative sample set. Based on those inspections, and a standard statistical
sample size formula, these numbers suggest there is a 95% chance that less than 1.5%
of the population of those pipes is lead. Based on those results, we will continue to
classify all of the service lines in the validation pool as ‘non-lead.’”
When a system verifies more (or less) of those non-lead service lines, the statement can
change. For instance, if they verify 300 representative service lines and find 0 are lead, then
they can conclude that less than 1.0% of the population of those pipes is lead.
Many water systems and service providers have misinterpreted and misused the “95%
confidence level” in other applications to refer to a measure of reliability around a specific
prediction at a specific service line’s material. For example, some understand 95% confidence
as a 95% certainty around a specific service line’s material relative to its predicted material,
which is not the way it is being used in this application. By adding the definition and the
language about how to communicate the results of the validation program, EPA will be able to
reduce confusion around the meaning to specific statistical phrases.
Expanding validation pool to increase inventory reliability
In the proposed rule, the ‘‘validation pool’’ of addresses to include in the subset would consist
of service lines identified as non-lead using methods other than records review or visual
inspection of at least two points on the line. We encourage EPA to include service lines
categorized based on historic records and only exclude service lines verified through visual
inspection or installation after a local lead ban from the validation pool.

From our experience working with hundreds of communities, the reliability of historic records
can be variable. In some communities, they have proven to be extremely reliable, but have
been highly unreliable in other communities. In Flint, Michigan, among the first 5,145 service
lines inspected as part of the replacement project, 1,498 of those had a historic label
indicating copper.7 Of those historic copper labels, 24% of those service lines were made of
lead. If the historic records had been trusted, those lead service lines would have remained in
the ground indefinitely. Accepting the materials on the historic records as fact without
validating their reliability can cause LSLs to be mislabeled as “non-lead.”
This is further substantiated in the work done by the Lead Free DC task force that found that
20% of historic copper labels were in fact made of lead. One of the task force's
recommendations was for DC Water to “consider statistical methods to identify areas with
copper service lines that turn out to be lead, and brass service lines that turn out to be lead or
brass.”8 Increasing the validation pool to include service lines whose materials were
determined by historic record would allow EPA to ensure that these falsely labeled copper
service lines do not fall through the cracks.
We understand that there will be communities where the historic records will prove to be
100% reliable. In that case, the verification program provides additional certainty and trust in
the records. But the risk of leaving lead service lines in the ground that were mistakenly
categorized as “non-lead” because of a historic record whose reliability was never evaluated is
too great a risk for water systems.
We believe that EPA should adopt a validation pool similar to the State of Michigan EGLE in
their Distribution System Material Inventory Process, which only excluded service lines from
the validation pool if there was a recent visual verification or the installation date for the
service line was after 1986 or a local lead ban.9
We ask that EPA consider our recommendations to improve the LCRI with the below text
revisions:

described in paragraphs (b)(2)(i) through (iii) of this section visual inspection of the pipe
exterior at a minimum of two points ( e.g., excavation, visual inspection in the meter pit or

Avoiding redundancy in inventory-building
We applaud EPA for adopting best practices in reducing uncertainty through the requirement
for water systems to verify service line materials at a representative, random subset of its
service area. This methodology has already been embraced and accepted by many state
regulators as an acceptable method for developing a service line inventory, as it leverages all

available data points to generate a best estimate for service line material.10 Many water
systems have already received approval from their state regulators to utilize methodologies
similar to the validation method outlined in the LCRI to build their service line inventory. If a
water system abides by the key principle of 95% confidence interval at a representative,
random set of inspections, it is redundant to ask a water utility that has already received
regulatory approval for such a methodology to follow a similar task, again. We encourage EPA
to include language exempting water systems that have proved their process to their state
regulatory body. We suggest the following language be adopted to the LCRI to allow for this
change:
§ 141.84 (5) (ii) The water system must confirm the service line material of a
random sample (e.g., a sample selected by use of a random number generator or
lottery method) of non-lead service lines from the validation pool. Confirmation of
service line material must be done by visual inspection of the pipe exterior at a
minimum of two points. Where ownership is shared, the water system must visually
inspect both portions of the service line. Water systems must validate at least as
many service lines as are required in the table in this paragraph. Water systems
that have already received regulatory approval from their primacy agency to meet
inventory requirements through random, representative inspections are not
required to conduct another round of inspections. The table is….
Finding Lead Service Lines or Galvanized Requiring Replacement in Validation Work
The proposed LCRI is severely lacking in specificity about what a water system should do in the
case that it locates LSL or GRR during its validation program. The goal of the validation program
is to reinforce the reliability of the service line inventory. If the validation program identifies
gaps in the service line inventory, water utilities should be required to take actions to increase
the accuracy of their inventories. Yes the preamble specifically states that water systems are
not required to do so. Failure to include concrete steps to improve inventories could undermine
the trust and reliability of the document that is the backbone of LCRI compliance.
In the case that a water utility’s validation program identifies LSL or GRR among service lines
that were previously considered non-lead, we recommend that EPA require water systems to
submit a plan to their regulators about what they will do to increase the accuracy of their
inventory, including with an independent expert not involved in the development of the initial
service line inventory, who can verify that steps are being taken to improve the inventory based
on the nature/pattern of inaccuracies.
10 “State Guidance and Predictive Modeling” BlueConduit.
https://blueconduit.com/state-guidance-and-predictive-modeling/

We propose that EPA adopt two additional steps in the case that LSL or GRR are found in the
validation group. First, state regulators should ensure that the water utility works with a
qualified outside service provider to evaluate the existing service line inventory, analyze the
results of the validation work, and make recommendations for next steps on updating the
inventory.
§ 141.84 (5) Vi. If a water system’s validation program uncovers LSL or GRR, the
primacy agency would require the water utility to take steps to improve the
accuracy of their inventory, including working with an independent entity, not
involved in creating the initial inventory, to improve and resubmit the inventory to
EPA.
Second, we recommend that EPA require water systems to include information about the
validation program in the Consumer Confidence Report to increase transparency and trust. EPA
could suggest the following text be included in the CCR to provide context to customers about
the findings and progress of the validation program.
“XYZ Water System’s service line inventory includes A number of water connections. Among
those connections, we have categorized B number as non-lead based on physical inspection
and C number as non-lead based upon other methods. In order to validate the reliability of
those alternative methods, we conducted D number of inspections at a representative subset
of addresses categorized as non-lead based on something other than a physical inspection.
Among those inspections, we found E number lead addresses among those. Based on this
result, we estimate that less than XX% of the non lead addresses actually contain lead. The
water system is taking the following steps …. to update the service line inventory.”
““As part of the Lead and Copper Rule compliance, the water system developed a lead
service line inventory. In order to verify the reliability of service lines categorized as
non-lead, the water system is required to physically verify service line materials at a
subset. Out of all service lines considered non-lead in our system, we physically
inspected a representative sample of 200 of them and found 0 lead service lines in the
representative sample set. Based on those inspections, and a standard statistical
sample size formula, these numbers suggest there is a 95% chance that less than 1.5%
of the population of those pipes is lead. Based on those results, we are working with our
state regulators to improve the accuracy of the service line inventory and complete an
updated service line inventory.”
Alternative to validation process

We applaud EPA for the process outlined in the LCRI for water systems to validate the
reliability of addresses categorized as “non-lead” in their service line inventory. However, we
believe that there are some water systems where the validation process does not have the
same benefits. We are concerned that adding a requirement for representative, randomized
inspections for water systems with a high percentage of lead service lines, at the same time
that they are replacing lead service lines all over their community will reduce the efficiency of
their process without providing much additional information gain. Furthermore, for these water
systems that are planning on replacing all of their service lines in the 10-year window required
by EPA, adding a seven-year deadline for the inspections doesn’t allow for operational
efficiencies. Therefore, we recommend that EPA allow for an alternative so that water systems
have the option to visually verify all of their service lines in 10 years OR complete the
validations on the seven-year timeline outlined in the rule.
§ 141.84 (5) (iv) (D) Water systems can opt out of the validation process by
committing to physically 100% of their service lines on the same timeline as their
lead service line replacement timeline.
Access and control to complete full service line replacement
We applaud EPA for implementing a 10-year replacement timeline for all lead service lines. We
are concerned that the issue of access and control presents a barrier to achieving the rule’s
intended effect. We appreciate the detailed analysis in the “Impact of State and Local Laws on
Service Line Replacement,” but want to impress upon EPA how essential it will be for rule
implementation to take all measures possible to facilitate access to the private side of the
service line. We are concerned that water systems and states will not work to replace the
10-year replacement requirement unless EPA makes it clearer and easier for water systems to
complete full service line replacement.
The proposed rule 1) deletes the existing references to private property in the definitions of
both “Lead Service Line” and “Full Lead Service Line Replacement” and 2) provides that full
replacement of LSLs is only required when the water system has “access” to the LSL without
setting criteria for what qualifies. Taken together, these changes create a serious ambiguity as
to whether utilities will be required to replace most of the nation’s lead lines.
We think the EPA must fix the rule. Specifically, the proposed definition of service line should
include the sentence in red below that is in the current definition of LSL.
Service line, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means a portion of pipe
which connects the water main to the building inlet. Where a building is not

present, the service line connects the water main to the outlet. Service lines may be
owned by the water system, owned by the property owner, or both.
In addition, EPA should provide more useful criteria regarding access and avoid
parenthetical examples such as “(e.g., legal access, physical access)” or stating
what it does not establish. We recommend the changes to proposed 40 C.F.R. §
141.84(d) regarding mandatory full service line replacement as follows.
(1) All water systems must replace all lead and galvanized requiring
replacement service lines under the control of the water system unless the
replacement would leave in place a partial lead service line.
(2) Where a water system has access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to
conduct full service line replacement, the service line is under its control,
and the water system must replace the service line regardless of ownership
of the line or the property it is on. Where a water system does not have
access to conduct full service line replacement, the water system is not
required by this rule to replace the line, but the water system must
document the reasons that the water system does not have access and
include any specific laws, regulations, and/or water tariff agreements that
affect the water system’s ability to gain access to conduct full replacement
of a lead service line and or a galvanized requiring replacement service line
replacement identified pursuant to paragraph (c)(1)(viii) of this section. The
water system must provide this documentation to the State pursuant to §
141.90(e)(10).
(i) This rule does not establish the criteria for determining whether a
system has access to conduct full service line replacement. The
criteria for determining whether a system has access to conduct full
service line replacement include: whether the system can safely
enter the property; whether the system can safely conduct the
replacement; and whether the system has obtained the property
owner’s consent, if consent is required for access. Presence of a lead
service line on private property does not, by itself, determine whether
a system has access to conduct full service line replacement for
purposes of this rule. Any State or local laws or water tariff
agreement requirements to gain access to conduct full service line
replacement must be identified in the service line replacement plan
as described in paragraph (c) of this section and in the notification
provided to persons served by lead, galvanized requiring
replacement, and unknown service lines as described in § 141.85(e).

(3) Where a water system has legal access pursuant to § 141.84(d)(2)(i) to
conduct full service line replacement only if property owner consent is
obtained, the water system must make a ‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain
property owner consent or written waiver documenting refusal of access for
the purpose of full lead service line replacement. If such a water system
does not obtain consent after making a ‘‘reasonable effort’’ to obtain it from
any property owner, then the water system is not required by this rule to
replace any portion of the service line at that address.
Replacement Rate Usability Tools
We are encouraged by the mandatory lead service line replacement requirement of the LCRI.
In order for water systems to understand what is required of them, EPA needs to make tools
available to water systems for them to be able to calculate and communicate their annual lead
service line replacement plans and goals. To that end, we suggest that EPA release a
spreadsheet, either connected to or separate from EPA’s service line inventory template, that
water systems can use to input information about their community and various scenarios from
year to year to understand how their mandatory lead service line requirement changes from
year to year. One of the scenarios that the calculator must be able to communicate is how a
water system’s annual replacement rate changes (or doesn’t change) based on the material
verifications of “non-lead” at service lines that were previously “unknown.”
The calculator must be user-friendly so that water systems can use it to understand their
required replacements over time and include the outputs in their lead service line replacement
plans.
In addition to the user-friendly calculator, we encourage EPA to update its lead service line
inventory template to include fields for lead connectors.
Lead-Lined Galvanized Pipes
Our team has worked in Trenton, NJ since 2020. Trenton Water Works has experienced
multiple action level exceedances in the last decade due to their galvanized service lines being
lined with lead. We appreciate that EPA noted lead-lined galvanized in the LCRI preamble, but
we believe that EPA needs to go further to ensure that lead-lined galvanized pipes or
galvanized pipes that might be lead-lined are appropriately accounted for in LCRI.

EPA should be explicit that water systems where lead-lined galvanized pipes are or have been
located, all galvanized pipes in those water systems should be categorized as lead for the
purpose of inventory and replacement.
Conclusion
In this comment, we ask that EPA consider our recommendations to improve the LCRI by:
1. EPA must take steps to make it easier for water utilities to gain access and control to
complete full service line replacement.
2. Historical records of water service line materials have varying reliability. Service lines
whose material are determined by historic records should be added to the pool of
validation addresses.
3. Water systems that locate LSL or GRR as part of their validation process should be
required to work with their primacy agency to improve the accuracy of their inventory.
4. Water systems that have a state agency-approved plan for using representative,
random inspections as part of their inventory should not be required to conduct another
set of representative, random inspections.
5. Water systems will need more tools from EPA to be able to understand and implement
the mandatory lead service line replacement.
6. Galvanized pipes in systems with lead-lined galvanized pipes should be treated as
“lead.”

Re: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper- Improvements 
(LCRI) (Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801) 
 
Dear Ms. Fox and Mr. Regan:  
Heal the Bay is an environmental non-profit organization based on the lands of the Tongva 
people with nearly 40 years of experience dedicated to making the coastal waters and watersheds 
of greater Los Angeles healthy, safe, and clean. Our team of scientists, activists, educators, and 
community advocates works tirelessly to protect the public’s health from contaminated water. 
We recognize the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) proposed Lead and Copper 
Rule Improvements (LCRI) as a step towards safer drinking water for all. Lead-contaminated 
drinking water has continuously disproportionately harmed environmental justice communities 
for more than a century and it is the responsibility of the EPA to protect these communities from 
lead exposure. Although there has been an effort to improve the rule, there are weaknesses in the 
proposed LCRI that should be addressed to ensure that everyone has access to safe drinking 
water. We respectfully recommend these changes in the new proposed LCRI: 
1. Improve testing and filtration in schools and childcare facilities. 
2.  Mandate water systems to cover costs to replace old lead pipes. 
3. Lower the Lead Action Level to below 5 parts per billion.  

 
  
 
 1444 9th Street         
       
 ph. 310-451-1500       
info@healthebay.org          
Santa Monica, CA 90401         fax 310-496-1902       
www.healthebay.org       
 
 
 
These recommendations are discussed in further detail below. 
1. Improve testing and filtration in schools and childcare facilities. 
We appreciate the provisions in the proposal to improve tap water quality testing.  However, the 
provisions need to go further and require additional testing from utilities to comprehensively test 
for lead from fountains and drinking water sources in schools and childcare facilities. Infants and 
young children are especially vulnerable to lead exposure. Lead exposure can cause infants and 
children to experience new or worsened learning and behavior problems, severe harm to mental 
and physical development, and brain damage. The rule must protect public health to the 
maximum extent possible and require utilities to test for lead in all areas where the public could 
be harmed and at a frequency that is health protective. 
 
2. Mandate water systems to cover costs to replace old lead pipes. 
The proposed LCRI would require remaining lead pipes to be removed and replaced within 10 
years. Water systems are not required to pay the cost for replacing the lead pipes. This burdens 
the individual homeowner to expense this cost, which will make it difficult for low-income 
communities to protect themselves from toxins and be in compliance. Water utilities and 
government agencies must cover the cost of replacing lead pipes without passing the cost on to 
the communities.  
 
3. Lower the Lead Action Level to below 5 parts per billion. 
Research has proven there is no safe level of lead in drinking water. While the EPA is proposing 
to lower the lead action levels from 15 parts per billion (ppb) to 10 ppb, this level is not 
protective enough. Health experts and the governments in Canada and Europe recommend a 5 
ppb lead action level, whereas the American Academy of Pediatrics recommends limiting lead in 
school water fountains to no more than 1 ppb. The lead action level dictates when a water system 
has to inform the public and take action to reduce lead exposure, but is not a health standard. We 
urge the EPA to lower the lead action alert to below 5ppb and follow the same recommendations 
as Canada, Europe, and the Academy of Pediatrics. 
Lead pipes have been prohibited for over 40 years; however, more than 9 million lead pipes 
continue to transport unsafe drinking water to predominately environmental justice communities. 

 
  
 
 1444 9th Street         
       
 ph. 310-451-1500       
info@healthebay.org          
Santa Monica, CA 90401         fax 310-496-1902       
www.healthebay.org       
 
 
 
Access to safe drinking water is a fundamental right that should be available to all, especially 
children. To better protect these communities, the proposed improvements in the Lead and 
Copper Rule need to be more stringent. It is crucial to ensure that the expenses associated with 
the replacement of water infrastructure and water quality monitoring are not transferred to 
vulnerable communities. We appreciate the EPA’s efforts for putting forth improvements to the 
LCRI and look forward to further improvements to ensure that safe drinking water is accessible 
to all communities. 
 
Sincerely,  
 
Crystal Barajas 
Senior Community Science and Outreach Coordinator

Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
The NAACP Virginia State Conference submits the following comments regarding the US Environmental 
Protection Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements” (“LCRI”). The NAACP Virginia State Conference provides leadership for local branches, youth 
councils, and college chapters for environmental and climate justice needs in Virginia. The NAACP and its 
Center for Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring that issues of 
community engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and frontline communities most 
impacted, including communities in Virginia. 
 
The NAACP Virginia State Conference applauds EPA for proposing stronger regulations to protect 
communities from lead in drinking water. Lead in drinking water has been a historically prevalent issue in Black 
communities, posing extreme risks to the health of young people, mothers, and their families.  According to a 
study by the Natural Resources Defense Council (NRDC), in Virginia, there is an estimated 187,883 lead 
service lines threatening families across our state with exposure to a potent and irreversible neurotoxin which, 
even at low levels of exposure, is linked to damage to the brain and nervous system, learning disabilities, 
shorter stature, impaired hearing, and harm to blood cells. In Virginia, we would derive $16,063,996,500 in 
public health cost savings from full lead service line replacement. 
 
Lead contamination in our state's drinking water is not just a historical issue; it's an ongoing concern that 
profoundly impacts our communities' public health, economy, and overall well-being. Throughout Virginia's 
history, we have seen the devastating consequences of lead exposure, particularly on marginalized 
communities. It is imperative that we address this issue as a priority, not only for the sake of public health but 
also for the principles of economic and environmental justice. Black families in our state should not bear the 
destructive burden of lead exposure and exposure to countless other pollutants. We must commit to equitable 
access to clean and safe drinking water, ensuring that every Virginian can enjoy a healthy and prosperous 
future, free from the harmful effects of lead and other pollutants. This commitment is not just about protecting 
our environment; it's about safeguarding the health and dignity of all our residents and fostering a more just 
and sustainable future for our state. 
 
Recently, the EPA awarded Virginia $46 million for towns and cities to replace lead water lines under the 2021 
bipartisan Infrastructure bill. According to Senator Mark Warner, the Virginia Department of Health Office of 
Drinking Water will award the funds to communities.  Some Virginia municipalities have advised residents to 
filter their water until the lines can be replaced. It is imperative that the Lead and Cooper Rule modifications 
are adopted as soon as possible.  In some instances, it will take years to replace the pipes.  In July 2022, the 
issue of lead service pipe replacement needs in Virginia was amplified by the Virginia Department of Health.  
Dr. Tony Singh, deputy director of the Office of Drinking Water reported that $1.1 million in funding from the 
Environmental Protection Agency will be used to collect and analyze 40,000 drinking water samples. What is 

 
 
PAGE 2 of 2 
 
Virginia State Conference of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People 
P.O. Box 27212 • Richmond, VA 23261 • 804.321.5678 • naacpva.org 
known as a result of years of studies conducted nationwide is that Black children and 2-3 times as likely as 
white children to have high blood lead levels. Using lead pipes one day longer is too long.   
 
For these reasons, our community members urge EPA to not only retain strong elements of the proposed 
LCRI, such as the requirement for the removal of all lead service lines in ten years, the requirements for water 
systems to sample both the first and fifth liter of water passing through lead pipes and a lower action level; but 
also ensure that those provisions do not have loopholes which undermine their goals and ensure that weaker 
parts of the rule are strengthened. 
 
Specifically, we urge EPA to consider the following changes to ensure the final rule does not leave Black 
communities in Virginia behind: 
 
§ 
Removing the exceptions to the 10-year lead pipe removal mandate: it is a fundamental injustice 
that the communities with the most lead service lines would be allowed 40 or more years to fix this 
issue. 
 
§ 
Mandate that water systems fully pay for the removal of lead service lines: Removal can cost 
thousands of dollars, and putting the financial burden on impacted communities will result in mostly 
wealthy and white neighborhoods having lead service lines replaced. Removal and replacement do not 
make up major proportions of utility budgets, and utilities should be expected to maximize the use of 
available federal water infrastructure funds and other non-ratepayer sources of funds to prioritize 
solving this crisis. 
 
§ 
Incentivize schools to install filters and ensure that children who spend many hours there daily 
are not at risk of exposure: Black children face an increased risk of lead exposure when compared 
with white children. The proposal’s suggested testing program does not differ from past ineffective 
programs, and EPA should move towards incentivizing the installation of filters and protecting children. 
 
Despite meaningful steps forward in this rule, not addressing these components would allow environmental 
injustice to persist. Black communities and frontline communities have long suffered from disinvestment and 
lack of resources. Past NAACP analysis has demonstrated that race, ethnicity, or language spoken had the 
strongest relationship to slow and inadequate enforcement of the SDWA of any sociodemographic 
characteristic analyzed. The final LCRI is a rare opportunity to make significant changes in the lives of millions 
of people in Virginia and to provide a measure of environmental justice that these families are owed, and we 
encourage this administration to build on the progress made in the proposed rule by strengthening the final rule 
further.

RE: Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI): Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
Dear Administrator Regan, 
Water District No. 1 of Johnson County, Kansas (WaterOne) is a drinking water provider in northeast 
Kansas and is the largest water provider in the state. We appreciate the opportunity to submit 
comments to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) on the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements (LCRI) under the authority of the Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA). EPA published the 
proposed rules in the Federal Register on December 6, 2023, Docket ID No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. 
In the LCRI, EPA requested comments on specific regulatory elements. In the bulleted list below, 
WaterOne provides input on key items as requested by EPA. WaterOne’s comments are provided in bold 
text. 
1. The revised definition of “connector,” including that connectors are defined as “not exceeding 
two feet.” 
a. WaterOne supports and appreciates the inclusion of the “connector” definition. This 
definition will help provide additional clarity and a definitive distinction between 
connectors and service lines that currently does not exist in the LCRR. 
2. Whether a reasonable effort to obtain property owner consent should be more than four times 
(e.g., five, six, or seven times). 
a. In our staff’s experience, reaching out to a customer more than four times would not 
yield increased results and will only add burden to the utility for time associated with 
multiple forms of contact and tracking such attempts. EPA should provide clarity on 
the amount of time necessary between attempts and amount of time after last 
attempt where customer can be labeled as “not responsive”. 
3. Comment on the sites included in Tier 3 and whether all of the proposed sites should be 
included in Tier 3, if additional sites should be included, or if some should be included in a 
different, lower priority tier, such as Tier 4. Specifically, comment on whether sites served by 
galvanized service lines or containing galvanized premise plumbing that are identified as ever 
being downstream of an LSL or lead connector should be included in the same tier as other sites 
with a current lead connector (e.g., copper service line downstream of a lead connector).    

 
 
a. For water utilities with unknown service lines and no identified lead service lines, it is 
critical that EPA clarify Galvanized Requiring Replacement as only when it has been 
positively identified as being connected to or previously connected to Lead.  Utilities 
should NOT be asked to prove a negative using the entire life history of every 
connection to the line. This practice provides no benefit to customers and significantly 
increases costs and complex logistics in numerous aspects of the LCRR/LCRI.  
4. Comment on the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to assess CCT performance, 
increase customer participation, and other relevant factors.   
a. Customer participation remains a concern in general as response rates to email and 
phone calls continue to decline and it becomes very hard to keep customers engaged 
and informed. 
5. Comment and any relevant data on the number and tiering of samples used to calculate the 90th 
percentile lead and/or copper levels for systems with LSLs for purposes of assessing CCT efficacy. 
Specifically, whether samples from non-LSL sites that have higher lead concentrations than 
samples from LSL sites should be included and whether these higher values should replace lower 
values from LSL sites in the 90th percentile calculation.   
a. More clarity is needed as to how to approach a galvanized line with unknown 
connections and what it means in terms of tier and sampling requirements. 
6. In the LCRI, EPA is proposing a threshold of systems serving greater than 50,000 persons to host 
the inventory and plan online, which is the required threshold under the LCRR. EPA is seeking 
comment on the size threshold at which systems must host their publicly accessible inventory, 
inventory summary data, replacement summary data, and service line replacement plan online, 
and whether it should be lowered relative to the LCRR requirements. 
a. Under the proposed LCRI, water utilities with unknown service lines in their inventory, 
but without any documented lead service lines, will be required to develop a Lead 
Service Line Replacement Plan and post it online. This requirement of posting a Lead 
Service Line Replacement Plan will cause customers to be concerned about a problem 
that does not or may not exist and subsequently, once all of the service lines are 
characterized, this requirement would go away. This could result in false information 
being provided to the public and potentially raise unnecessary concern.    
7. In the LCRI, EPA is proposing a requirement for systems to validate the accuracy of non-lead 
service lines in their inventory that were categorized using methods other than records review or 
visual inspection of at least two points along the line. EPA is requesting comment on the number 
of validations required, the proposed 95 percent confidence level approach used to develop the 
number of validations required, the criteria for which methods used to categorize non-lead 
service lines should be included in the validation pool (including whether non-lead lines 
categorized based on records should be subject to validation), and the seven-year timeline for 
systems on a 10-year replacement deadline to complete the validation requirements. 
a. WaterOne believes this is a reasonable request and will help ease concern over using 
methodology such as predictive modeling to support service line inventory 
development. However, predictive modeling requires that visual inspection validation 
occur on the test set that is withheld from the data set used to build the model. It 
would be important to know if these visual validations used in the development of a 

 
 
predictive model will be allowed to count toward the newly required validation 
pool.  Clarification is needed as to whether the validation pool will be in addition to 
verification performed in the process of developing a predictive model.  
8. Comment on establishing a deadline for systems to identify all unknown service lines prior to 
their service line replacement deadlines. 
a. There should be a separate service line identification deadline for utilities with NO 
documented or discovered lead service lines. Tying a deadline for identification of all 
unknowns to the service line replacement deadline does not make sense as 
demonstrated in the following example: a utility with 150,000 service lines with 15% 
of those documented as unknown would be required to replace 2,250 service lines per 
year. If the utility has zero lead service lines, establishing this replacement rate would 
put the utility out of compliance with the LCRI. For utilities with zero lead service lines, 
the deadline for identification of all unknowns should have a separate service line 
identification deadline.  
9. Comment on a requirement for systems to update their service line replacement plans if there 
are any changes, such as changes to laws and policies applicable to full service line replacement. 
a. We support this requirement.   
10. EPA is also seeking comment on the use of the action level to determine when additional public 
education is required, and the use of the same action level for public education as for the CCT 
provisions. 
a. WaterOne is concerned about the effectiveness of system-wide communication 
requirements for potentially isolated exceedances caused by private plumbing. This 
scenario would seem to increase in likelihood, given the reduced action limit of 10 
ppb. 
11. The proposed determination that the public education treatment technique is feasible and 
prevents known or anticipated adverse health effects to the extent feasible. 
a. The requirements for specific phrasing such as “IMPORTANT INFORMATION ABOUT 
LEAD IN YOUR DRINKING WATER” is misleading for system-wide public education 
efforts and creates a high potential for public distrust. Targeted communication to 
residences known to be at risk would be more appropriate.   
12. Whether the Agency should require States, as a condition of primacy, to provide translation 
support to water systems that are unable to do so for public education materials to consumers 
with limited English proficiency. 
a. State resources supporting translation of public education materials would be a 
benefit to many water systems throughout the state.   
13. EPA is also requesting comment on additional ways to streamline public education and 
associated certification requirements (e.g., combine deadlines for systems to conduct public 
education or submit information to the State). 
a. Combined/consolidated deadlines would provide significant benefit in helping water 
systems plan and prepare to meet certification requirements.  

 
 
14. Data, analyses, and comments on the proposed determination that water systems are capable of 
providing consumer notices of individual tap sampling results within three calendar days of 
obtaining those results, regardless of whether the results exceed the lead or copper action level, 
or if a longer time frame is needed ( e.g., three business days, seven calendar days, 14 calendar 
days). 
a. WaterOne owns and operates a NELAC certified laboratory and even in this position, 
believes it will be extremely challenging to meet the 3-calendar day turn around for 
sample results notifications due to the additional sampling and analysis load and 
associated logistics presented by LCRR/LCRI. We believe that 7 calendar days is a more 
achievable expectation to deliver sample results. 
15. Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or to sample more frequently in 
schools and child care facilities. 
a. If lead is absent in plumbing materials at a school, the school will not benefit from 
increased sampling frequency. However, increasing the number of samples taken at a 
school may, in some cases, have the potential to identify a faucet/fixture that requires 
remediation. The EPA clearly states that the intent of the School and Childcare 
sampling is to identify situations where the water is too corrosive. We believe that 5 
samples per school and 2 per childcare facilities would provide the intended 
results/objective of EPA.    
16. The proposed provision to allow States to issue waivers to community water systems from the 
requirement for lead sampling in schools and child care facilities during the five-year period after 
the LCRI compliance date if the facility was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021 but prior to 
the LCRI compliance date and the sampling otherwise meets the waiver requirements of 
§ 141.92(h). 
a. WaterOne serves nearly 800 school and childcare facilities that require sampling per 
the LCRR/LCRI; therefore, since 2021, we have been proactively meeting with each 
school district leadership, facility directors, and PIOs. We have also met numerous 
times with the county daycare licensing department as well as privately operated 
schools in our service area to prepare them for the LCRR sampling that was set to 
begin in October 2024. Postponing this critical sampling program to potentially begin 
in October 2027 could cause distrust and frustration from our school and childcare 
partners. We respectfully request that waivers include sampling conducted between 
October 2024 and October 2027 so long as the sampling is conducted in accordance 
with the revised sampling requirements.   
17. Whether EPA should require CWSs to make school and child care facility sampling results publicly 
available, and if so, how frequently and in what manner. 
a. Local and state health departments will have the most complete data set of school and 
childcare sample results. To keep the information consistent, and to provide a 
single/uniform entity to provide data, we believe the state should be responsible for 
choosing how to share that information and not each individual CWS. 
18. EPA is requesting comment on the expansion of the inventory reporting to include lead 
connectors and non-lead service lines. 

 
 
a. WaterOne has invested signiﬁcant Dme and resources to developing our inventory 
plaEorm as well as reviewing historical records. Changes to the inventory this late in 
the process will cause signiﬁcant re-work for public uDliDes that already have minimal 
resources. Connector materials that are shown on records can be documented in the 
inventory, but moving forward should not be a requirement but added beneﬁt.  
19. Whether there are other LCRR provisions besides the initial inventory and notifications of service 
line material for which the October 16, 2024 compliance date should be retained. 
a. We support retaining the School and Childcare sampling in accordance with the LCRR 
established timeline. 
20. EPA is proposing to define a two-foot maximum length of connectors. EPA proposes that 
“connectors” that exceed two feet in length be treated as a service line. EPA is requesting 
comment on the defined length of a connector. 
a. As previously noted, we support the addition of this clarification.  
Additionally,

would need to move forward with all LCRR requirements as published in 2021. Publishing the 
draG LCRI presents signiﬁcant changes to nearly every aspect of the LCRR; therefore, we are

Dear Administrator Regan, 
I am an Assistant Professor of Environmental Health and Engineering at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg 
School of Public Health, writing to provide feedback on the United States Environmental Protection 
Agency’s (EPA) proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). I have conducted research on 
estimating the population-level health impact of lead-contaminated drinking water, and appreciate the 
opportunity to provide public comment based on my experiences. My comments are as follows: 
 
Comment 1: Support for lead service line replacement plan over 10 years. 
 
I agree with the proposal to replace all lead service lines (LSLs) within 10 years. There is considerable 
scientific evidence showing that low-dose chronic exposure to lead-contaminated drinking water is associated 
with increased blood lead levels, which is associated with a variety of adverse health outcomes.1–8 
 
Comment 2: Alternative temporary filter programs are inadequate. 
 
The interim plan to provide filters only for areas with multiple action level (AL) exceedances is insufficient, 
especially for cities with extended LSL replacement timelines, such as Chicago. If LSLs are being replaced 
under the justification that no amount of lead in drinking water is safe, then the decision to only provide 
filters for areas with multiple AL exceedances is inconsistent with that notion. Most households with lead-
contaminated drinking water will not be served by public water systems with multiple AL exceedances, yet 
would still benefit from filters.  
 
I recommend either lowering the AL, which is not a health-based standard, or otherwise changing the 
alternative temporary filter requirement to apply to a broader subset of the population. 
 
Comment 3: Economic analyses should include preterm births. 
 
The economic analysis as proposed considers the benefits of reducing instances of low birthweight, but does 
not consider the benefits of reducing pre-term births, a similar but distinct metric. The Zhu et al. (2010) 
study used in the economic analysis reports differs from other studies in terms of estimated effect of blood 
lead level on preterm births.9 For example, Fisher et al. (2023), in a prospective cohort study, report 1.48 and 
1.71 risk ratios per 1 μg/dL increase of blood lead concentration for preterm birth and spontaneous preterm 

birth, respectively.10 Other pregnancy cohort studies also found increased risk of preterm birth from increased 
blood lead concentrations.11–15 
 
The estimated costs of preterm births are high, largely driven by increased medical expenditures for the 
newborn baby, and lost productivity in the labor market. Waitzman et al. (2016) estimate the additional cost 
of preterm births over term births to be $64,815 in 2016 dollars (approximately $83,915 in December 2023 
dollars), and the additional cost of extremely preterm births over term births to be $344,355 in 2016 dollars 
(approximately $445,852 in December 2023 dollars).16 
 
Comment 4: Economic analysis underestimates benefits due to unquantified factors. 
 
There are many benefits to LSL removal that are not included in the EPA’s economic analysis, in part because 
they are difficult to quantify without fully identified exposure-response functions. For example, lead-
contaminated water disproportionately affects racially minoritized populations.17–20 This may lead to mistrust 
in the water system, which may manifest as avoidance of tap water: Black and Hispanic households are far 
more likely to use bottled water as their primary drinking water source compared to White households.21  
 
However, bottled water is roughly 3000% more expensive than tap water, and is not necessarily safer than tap 
water, with concerns of plastic exposure and a federally established maximum lead concentration of 5 ppb for 
bottled water.22 Similarly, there are unquantified stress and mental health costs to living with poor water 
quality, for which there are no fully identified exposure-response functions.23–25 
 
Lastly, clean drinking water is a human right and one of the most basic needs for human survival and 
flourishing. Systematic denial of that right, especially in a manner that disproportionately harms racially 
minoritized and other marginalized communities, is unjust and harmful in ways that cannot be captured in 
cost-benefit analyses.  
 
Conclusion 
 
In summary, I support the EPA’s recognition of the public health threat posed by widespread lead-
contaminated drinking water. Low-level exposure at the population level may be imperceptible at the 
individual level, but can have grave public health consequences for generations to come. It is my hope that the 
EPA will continue to recognize the urgency of lead-contaminated drinking water and take expedited action to 
protect the communities most at risk. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Please feel free to contact me at bhuynh@jhu.edu should you have any questions. Thank you for your 
consideration. 
Sincerely, 
Benjamin Q. Huynh, PhD  
Department of Environmental Health & Engineering 
Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health

Dr. Jennifer McLain

Washington, DC  20009 
 
RE: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI), Docket No. EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0813 
 
Dear Dr. McLain, 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to comment on this important rulemaking. The state and territorial 
primacy agencies are co-regulators with the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) in the development 
and implementation of drinking water regulations. The primacy agencies’ collective workforce of about 
3,600 regulators works tirelessly every day to ensure that the nation’s 150,000 water systems provide 
safe drinking water every time consumers turn on the tap. Additionally, state regulators provide boots-
on-the-ground assistance to respond to emergencies and address many other compliance and 
implementation challenges.  
 
States have over 30 years of direct implementation experience with the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), 
originally published in 1991, including the minor revisions in 2000 and 2004 and the short-term revisions 
in 2007. ASDWA’s Members are also currently working to implement the service line inventory 
components of the 2021 Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) ahead of the LCRI. ASDWA’s members 
have a breadth and depth of knowledge on the details of LCR implementation that EPA should 
incorporate into the final LCRI. As EPA’s development of the LCRI continues, ASDWA’s members, as co-
regulators with EPA, need to continue to be included in efforts to ensure the final LCRI can be 
implemented in such a way that both protects public health and streamlines the overall rule complexity. 
The LCRI must be feasible to implement in order to be effective.  
 
ASDWA’s members appreciate that the Agency included some of ASDWA’s LCRI Federalism Consultation 
Recommendations in the proposed rule, including: 
• Elimination of the lead trigger level. 
• Establishment of a standardized approach for proactive lead service line replacement. 
• Renaming “find-and-fix” to “Distribution System and Site Assessment.” 
• Limiting the use of small system flexibilities to those serving populations less than 3,300. 
• Alignment of school and childcare sampling protocols with existing 3Ts Guidance. 
• Clarification of definitions of galvanized requiring replacement and connectors. 
After a review of the proposed regulatory language, ASDWA’s members have developed extensive, in-
depth comments based on over 20 hours of input via Teams Meetings from 165 state regulators across 

 
2 
 
41 states. ASDWA’s members’ most pressing concern with the proposed LCRI is the increased state 
workload, compounded by the upcoming PFAS regulation and ongoing Infrastructure Investment and 
Jobs Act (IIJA) implementation. These important new tasks under LCRI will be in addition to states’ 
current everyday activities, such as providing hands-on technical assistance to water systems, ensuring 
compliance with over 90 existing standards, system inspections, engineering reviews, operator 
certification, and much more. The proposed rule requires 38 new reviews by states, 8 new templates to 
be developed, and 5 new state-to-system consultations across various components of the LCRI. Our 
estimate of the increased burden to states is a few million additional hours each year for LCRI 
implementation. 
 
ASDWA’s updated Cost of States’ Transactions Study (CoSTS) estimates that the LCRI will place a 
significant cost and time burden on states annually, estimating that a total of 5,141,769 state staff hours 
will be needed each year, or 71% of estimated available state staff time based on the estimated 3,600 
state staff across all primacy agencies. This time burden translates to over $300 million a year for state 
implementation—more than three times the amount of PWSS funding allocated for state 
implementation for the entire Safe Drinking Water Act (SDWA.) Additionally, CoSTS estimates that the 
rule will necessitate approximately 799,115 upfront state hours, equating to about $48 million for initial 
implementation and transition to the new rule.  
 
While ASDWA’s Members are encouraged that EPA incorporated state’s feedback from the Federalism 
Consultation into the proposed rule, states still have concerns about the overall feasibility of the updated 
rule. ASDWA’s detailed comments that follow this letter contain several important recommendations 
that EPA should prioritize in the final LCRI—priority issues are outlined below.  
 
Lead Service Line Replacements  
 
ASDWA’s members applaud the Agency for requiring proactive lead service line (LSL) replacements 
nationwide, as this action will help eliminate one of the major sources of lead in drinking water. However, 
ASDWA’s members are concerned with the Agency’s implicit messaging implying that full removal of 
LSLs will eliminate the risk of lead exposure from drinking water. Premise plumbing, including legacy lead 
pipes, lead solder, and brass fixtures will continue to be a potential source of lead in drinking water and 
the importance of effective corrosion control should continue to be emphasized. This messaging needs 
to be appropriately revised as part of finalizing the LCRI. 
 
The $15 billion in LSLR funding from the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act (IIJA) is a significant first 
step towards the goal of 100% LSL removal, however, this IIJA funding will not cover the estimated $45 
billion cost to replace all LSLs nationwide. Giving that impression in the Agency’s messaging is 
problematic. Additionally, this funding is anticipated to already be distributed by the time the rule is 
effective. States, systems, and EPA will need to continue to work together to advocate wherever possible 
for additional funding to meet this critical public health need.  
 
States have a variety of concerns about the feasibility of components of the proposed rule regarding LSL 
replacements. EPA’s attempt to establish that control equals access for water systems may impact the 
enforceability of the rule requirements to conduct LSL replacements. EPA should define “control” and 
determine if control equates to ownership, rather than access, to clarify these concerns. Additionally, 
prohibiting partial LSL replacement during planned infrastructure work or repairs is not realistic. Partial 

 
3 
 
replacements may be necessary where a homeowner will not cooperate with the system, and the rule 
employs several mitigation measures that will provide sufficient notice and reduce resident risk where a 
partial replacement is necessary to conduct needed infrastructure work. States determining if a 
particular water system could replace LSLs at a faster rate than determined by rule is not feasible and 
this evaluation should not be a condition of primacy in the final LCRI. This option should be left to state 
discretion where a state implements regulations more stringent than federal regulations. 
 
Lead Service Line Inventories 
 
Additional clarification is needed in the final LCRI to ensure feasibility of the inventory requirements, 
especially the requirements for connectors. States recommend that connectors be optional in the LSL 
inventory, to ensure continuity with existing inventory requirements and the first round of inventories 
that are due October 2024. EPA should revise the proposed definition of “connector,” indicating that 
connectors are not to exceed three feet, rather than two feet, otherwise many connectors would need 
to be re-classified as LSLs. Additionally, EPA should add clarification to the definition of “connector” and 
“lead service line” explicitly outlining that any such piping over three feet is an LSL for purposes of the 
rule. Further, EPA should clarify what constitutes the “service line” and where the service line ends and 
interior plumbing begins, specifically defining the “building inlet”. Recently, there have been 
inconsistencies with defining a “lead service line” for the purposes of Drinking Water State Revolving 
Fund program funding, and ASDWA recommends that all EPA programs use the proposed LCRI definition. 
 
EPA should establish a deadline for systems to identify all unknown service lines prior to service line 
replacement deadlines, or risk systems failing to meet the LSL replacement deadline altogether.  
 
States also brought up concerns about some service line data being publicly available, and potential 
misuse of this data. EPA should give states discretion to allow location identifiers to be used in lieu of 
street addresses in some instances, such as on military installations, to address privacy and security 
concerns.   
 
Compliance Monitoring 
 
Under the updated tiering requirements, most water systems will need to adjust their compliance 
sampling sites. As such, EPA should utilize a phased approach for the review of compliance sampling 
plans and implementation by water systems, similar to the approach taken for Stage 2 Disinfectants and 
Disinfection Byproducts Rule (DBPR). ASDWA recommends that large systems begin compliance 
sampling under the new scheme starting the next standard monitoring period after the compliance date, 
medium systems one year later, and small systems two years after the compliance date. Staggering the 
compliance dates is the only solution for limited laboratory capacity, as well as capacity within the states 
to review compliance determinations.  
 
For systems collecting compliance samples from sites meeting different tier definitions, the 90th 
percentile results should be calculated based off the samples with the highest lead or copper 
concentration, regardless of the tier.  
 
EPA should also address concerns about sample invalidation and should establish a maximum stagnation 
time for compliance samples. States recommend that EPA establish more definitive guidance and clarify 

 
4 
 
issues with sample invalidation that have arisen since the inception of the rule that were not made clear 
with the 2004 Memorandum “Lead and Copper Rule – Clarification of Requirements for Collecting 
Samples and Calculating Compliance.”  
 
Corrosion Control Treatment  
 
The rule relies heavily on the use of pipe-loop corrosion control treatment studies for LSL systems that 
exceed the action level, and states strongly advise against this prescriptive approach. Pipe-loop studies 
often have diminishing returns with respect to determination of the most effective treatment approach 
and are very cost- and time-intensive. Pipe loop studies also take much longer to execute (sometimes 
years) and are much more expensive than other types of studies (i.e., desktop studies, coupon studies, 
etc.) This means that the public health protection afforded by optimal corrosion control treatment could 
be delayed. States have provided EPA with examples where pipe loop studies did not show different 
results compared to coupon studies. States also have significant concerns with the number of staff hours 
needed for the reviews and approvals of the potentially larger number of pipe-loop studies. EPA should 
offer additional flexibility in implementing corrosion control treatment, leaving the discretion to states 
to determine if pipe-loop studies should be required and allowing systems to make incremental changes 
once corrosion control treatment is installed to achieve optimization for each individual system. 
Incorporating flexibility on this aspect of the rule could benefit public health and improve feasibility for 
both water systems and states. 
 
POU Filters 
 
States have expressed concern regarding the reliance of POU filters to mitigate lead levels in the 
proposed LCRI. Specifically, filters being used as a compliance option for small systems is problematic, 
as well as the provision for systems with three or more lead Action Level Exceedances (ALE) to distribute 
filters to the entire service area, and the requirement to provide POUs to individuals served by an LSL, 
GRR or unknown following a line disturbance. Not only are there efficacy concerns regarding the 
effectiveness of the filters, but there are also concerns around implementation and ensuring use of filters 
do not increase bacteriological risk for users.  
 
EPA should limit the use of small system flexibilities in lieu of corrosion control treatment to systems 
that are either in control of their entire distribution system or to those systems with 100 percent buy in 
from the community. State experience has determined that POU filters and plumbing replacement have 
only shown to be effective in systems meeting these criteria.  
 
The proposed LCRI targets the highest risk sites for monitoring and evaluating the action level, as such, 
filters distributed after an action level exceedance should be targeted at sites that are at risk of lead 
exposure, i.e., locations with LSL, GRR, or unknowns based on the system’s inventory. Providing filters 
to consumers served by known, non-lead lines could undermine public confidence in drinking water and 
introduce unnecessary cost and risk to the water system and their consumers.  
 
School and Childcare Sampling 
 
As written, many well-established lead sampling programs would not be eligible to meet the waiver 
requirements under the proposed LCRI. EPA should change the waiver deadline for school and childcare 

 
5 
 
sampling to January 1, 2014, as EPA’s proposed date of January 1, 2021, would exclude existing state 
and local sampling programs enacted through America’s Water Infrastructure Act of 2018 (AWIA) and 
the Water Infrastructure Improvements for the Nation Act (WIIN), as well as other established programs 
implemented at the state and local level.   
 
Public Education 
 
Several new public notification requirements in the LCRR and in the proposed LCRI have not yet been 
implemented. In adding these requirements, EPA has added new reporting deadlines and certifications. 
EPA should consider streamlining the reporting deadlines down to one or two dates for when the system 
needs to provide reports or certifications to the primacy agency for review. Additionally, EPA should 
coordinate with states to develop templates prior to the compliance date of LCRI for each type of 
certification the PWS is required to submit to the primacy agency to ensure national consistency and 
clarity ahead of the compliance deadline.   
 
States agree that translating important public health information for non-English speakers is important; 
however, states have significant concerns with the considerable cost for translation services and strongly 
recommend that EPA remove the requirement for translation support to be a condition of primacy. Many 
states do not have the expertise or funds to support this effort. EPA should instead pursue a contract or 
public-private partnership to provide translation as a centralized service to water systems as needed.  
 
Implementation and Guidance 
 
ASDWA’s members recommend that EPA develop comprehensive decision-trees, flowcharts, or 
schematics clearly depicting the regulatory triggers and steps for various components of the rule, 
including for corrosion control treatment, public education, and sampling components of the rule. These 
tools should be developed and shared with primacy agencies ahead of the compliance date for the rule 
to aid in compliance determinations and training. 
 
EPA needs to expeditiously prioritize the development of LCRR and LCRI implementation guidance for 
state primacy agencies. Additionally, the LCRI needs updated data management capabilities for states to 
track requirements, particularly with LSL replacements. EPA should prioritize collaboration with states 
in implementation of the LCRR and LCRI over the next few years. Specifically, states recommend 
coordination on the following: 
• Establishing expectations around including connectors in the inventory and streamlining 
implementation of the new definitions in initial and baseline inventory efforts.  
• Developing in-depth guidance and training for the review and approval of CCT studies and CCT 
adjustments needed for source and treatment changes.  
• Addressing clarification questions regarding school and childcare facility definitions and the 
expectations for state drinking water programs to manage lists of such facilities. 
• Developing new and updating existing public education and notification templates for states and 
water systems ahead of the compliance deadline.  
• Establishing guidance for filter usage and expectations for various filter requirements.  
• Ensuring compliance tracking and schedules established by LCRR and LCRI are fully supported in 
SDWIS or DW-SFTIES, and updated data entry instructions are available ahead of the compliance 
deadline.  

 
6

input on the proposed regulation that has been synthesized into the attachments that follow:

• 
Appendix C: LCRI Cost of State Transactions Study 
ASDWA appreciates the opportunity to share states’ collective experiences to provide input on the final 
LCRI. As co-regulators with EPA, states request a continued dialogue during the rule writing process. 
States are willing to provide expertise and guidance on rule components that could be more streamlined 
and can help to identify new and innovative solutions that could address problems that have arisen 
during the last 30 years of implementation. States encourage OGWDW to confer with the Agency’s Office 
of Research and Development, and regional direct implementation staff, as well as states, in ensuring 
the LCRI is truly an improvement over the existing regulation—that it is implementable, feasible, and 
improves public health.  
 
ASDWA’s members look forward to continuing our partnership with EPA to implement the LCRI. If you 
have any questions about these comments, please feel free to reach out to me (aroberson@asdwa.org)

ﬁlters generally rely on either GAC adsorpƟon or ion

AddiƟonally, EPA repeats a manufacturer’s claim in

manufacturers’ claims regarding ﬁlter usage and 
the expected ﬁlter life for typical usage. EPA
