Dear Administrator Regan, 
 
Aqua, an Essential Utilities Company, appreciates the opportunity to comment on the 
Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI).  Aqua owns and operates 
approximately 1,500 water systems covering 8 states and 3 million people.  Aqua commends 
EPA’s efforts to improve the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions (LCRR) providing for the 
removal of all lead service lines and galvanized requiring replacement within a prescribed 
timeframe.  The following sections provide specific comments on the proposed LCRI Rule 
Revisions. 
 
Regulatory Uncertainty - Challenges in Meeting Both LCRR And LCRI 
Aqua strongly encourages that EPA act immediately (prior to the intended promulgation 
of the final LCRI) to extend the compliance dates for the provisions of the LCRR that 
EPA does not intend to continue under the LCRI. Currently, systems are expending 
resources to prepare to comply with the LCRR as it is the codified regulation requiring 
compliance by October of this year, while EPA is proposing to dramatically change both 
the content and deadlines for all but three of the LCRR requirements. Water systems 
have a duty to comply with applicable regulations and have no assurance that EPA will 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
2 
meet its promulgation timeline, nor that enforcement discretion will occur should EPA 
not publish the final rule prior to the LCRR compliance dates. 
 
Primary Focus for Inventory Should Be on Systems Known to Have LSLs and GRRSLs 
Aqua encourages EPA to further develop the LCRI to recognize in the rule structure that there 
are two categories of community water systems (CWSs) following the LCRR inventory process. 
Category 1 includes systems with known LSLs and/or GRRSLs, and Category 2 includes 
systems with low probability that LSLs and/or GRRSLs exist. 
 
The rule should not require the latter category to expend resources needlessly. Rather than 
requiring Category 2 systems to proceed through the LCRI service line replacement 
requirements as though they actually have many LSLs and GRRSLs, this group of systems 
should have a second path to compliance that focuses primarily on (1) having a protocol for 
the rare instance when a LSL or GRRSL is discovered and (2) the validation study to assure 
the initial characterization of the system’s inventory is correct. 
 
This approach incentivizes CWSs to take steps prior to the beginning of the final LCRI 
compliance window to transition to Category 2 if they are currently a Category 1 system (e.g., 
accelerate service line characterization and validation studies. 
 
REQUEST FOR COMMENTS 
 
Service Line Replacement 
Request for Comment 1: “EPA is requesting comment on whether the Agency 
should include lead connectors or galvanized service lines that are or were 
downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory replacement.” 
 
Aqua believes that EPA should not include lead connectors or galvanized service lines 
that are or were downstream of a lead connector as part of mandatory replacement. 
EPA has not demonstrated that removing GRRSLs as currently defined present a 
meaningful opportunity to reduce lead exposure. To expand the scope of the final LCRI 
to include all galvanized service lines with a definition akin to GRRSLs that includes lead 
connectors would further expand the scope of the replacement task with a less certain 
demonstrable benefit.  
 
Request for Comment 3: “Whether the proposed LCRI appropriately interprets 
“control” for the purposes of the mandatory replacement provision (i.e., require 
systems to conduct full service line replacement in situations where the system has 
access to conduct the full replacement).” 
 
EPA cannot define “control” as “access.” Such a definition of control is flawed, and not 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
3 
in keeping with the intended meaning of “control” in SDWA.  
 
Request for Comment 4: “EPA also seeks comment on the complexity of the rate 
construct.” 
 
Aqua believes that EPA should revise the proposed rolling, 3-year average replacement 
rate of 10%. The replacement rate calculation includes in the denominator: known LSLs, 
known GRRSLs, and all lead status unknown service lines (LSLUSLs). Subsequent 
calculation of the replacement rate is not an accurate reflection of program progress as 
it only credits the system for full replacements of LSLs and GRRSLs. The calculation 
should take into account progress in reducing the number of LSLs and GRRSLs, 
progress reducing LSUSLs, and service lines for which the system has completed its 
good faith effort to engage the property owner in replacement.  Otherwise, in many 
instances, utilities would be forced to fully complete its replacement program within a 
few years. 
 
If the final LCRI were to include an annual replacement rate calculation, then EPA should use a 
different approach that is both fair and easily calculated. One such option is the following: 
1. An approach based on two parallel metrics, (1) a cumulative 
percentage of LSLs and GRRSLs replaced and (2) a cumulative 
percentage of LSUSLs that are characterized. 
2. The numerator in the cumulative percentage of LSLs and GRRSLs 
replaced would be the total number of lines replaced and the 
denominator would be the sum of LSLs and GRRSLs in the initial inventory 
plus those discovered in prior years. 
 
Request for Comment 6: “The overall approach and basis to offer deferred service line 
replacement to systems with a high proportion of LSLs and GRR service lines in their 
distribution system relative to their total number of households served. EPA is 
requesting comment on its proposed threshold of 0.039 average annual number of 
replacements per household served, which is used to calculate the number of years 
that systems can defer.” 
 
It is appropriate to include a mechanism for water systems to seek an extended lead 
service line replacement program. Many systems will find replacing all LSLs and 
GRRSLs within 10 years infeasible. 
 
Request for Comment 12: “The proposed requirement to ban partial lead and GRR 
service line replacement unless it is conducted in accordance with emergency or 
planned infrastructure work (excluding planned infrastructure work solely for the 
purposes of replacing lead and GRR service lines as part of a service line replacement 
program).” 
 
EPA should not finalize a requirement to ban partial lead and GRR service line 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
4 
replacement unless it is conducted in accordance with emergency or planned 
infrastructure work. Aqua supports EPA’s goal to achieve a complete replacement. 
However, full replacement requires successful collaboration with property owners, 
which is not always possible. The LCRI proposal provides important latitude to CWSs 
and allows necessary water main infrastructure renewal and rehabilitation to occur even 
with property owners that are unable or unwilling to participate in a full lead service line 
replacement. Inclusion of this flexibility to proceed with partial replacement is essential 
for ongoing water system infrastructure maintenance and should be retained in the final 
LCRI. 
 
The decision to ban partial replacements in the instance of LSL/GRRSL replacement 
programs should be revisited more broadly in the proposed regulation. Banning partial 
replacements as a part of replacement programs impedes a CWS’s ability to make 
incremental improvement by at least reducing the portion of the service line to which it 
has access. 
 
Tap Sampling for Lead and Copper 
Request for Comment 3: “Comment on the applicability of alternate sampling protocols to  
assess CCT performance, increase customer participation, and other relevant factors.” 
 
The LCRI proposal changes multiple variables contributing to the likelihood of a lead 
action level exceedance, and the cumulative effect is not well understood. That 
combination includes: (1) drawing a 5th liter sample from a LSL sample site as well as a 1st 
liter sample, (2) using the higher of the observed lead values from the 1st and 5th liter 
samples, (3) directing compliance monitoring to structures where lead is most likely to 
be high, (4) limiting calculation of the compliance metric to the highest observed lead 
values when there is a mix of sampling tiers, and (5) retaining a compliance metric 
based on the upper-tail of the occurrence distribution (i.e., 90th percentile). So, while 
EPA rightly assumes that 90th percentiles based on the higher value from a 1st or 5th 
sample from a LSL will shift the distribution of observed 90th percentiles upward when 
such sample sites exist, the agency has not described how the proposed metric is 
better at “assessing corrosion control.” Given the long-standing practice around the 1st 
draw, stagnant water sample used in the U.S. and the difficulties encountered in the U.S. 
obtaining sufficient in-home samples, the LCR 1st draw, stagnant water sample provides 
stable point-of-departure for triggering corrosion control review in the U.S. 
 
In regard to customer participation, CWSs have worked with customers to obtain tap 
samples for purposes of LCR compliance monitoring for decades. EPA is aware that 
over the duration of the LCR’s implementation, locating occupants willing to draw 
samples as specified in the LCR has been an ongoing challenge, as has obtaining 
compliant samples. This implementation challenge will be much more severe under the 
proposed LCRI: 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
5 
1. Many CWSs currently on triennial monitoring will return to standard 
monitoring necessitating twice as many samples being acquired each 
monitoring cycle and six times more sampling cycles. For a system 
serving a population of 10,001, the Proposed Rule increases the 
minimum number of compliance samples over three years from 30 to 
360. 
2. CWSs regularly report that participation by customers under the current 
LCR requires financial renumeration of the household taking a single 
one liter first-draw, stagnant sample. CWSs routinely provide credits 
toward customer water bills, gift coupons, and cash payments to 
encourage participation in the sampling program. The amount offered 
varies with urban examples reaching $100 per sample event. Even when 
renumeration is offered, follow-through by households that agree to 
take samples and receive sample kits is typically no more than 80%. EPA 
has not sufficiently considered these costs and the associated burdens 
of running such monitoring programs when assessing the feasibility of 
the Proposed Rule. 
3. EPA proposes to expand the Tier 1 and 2 sample pools by including 
actual lead plumbing and creating Tier 3, which includes galvanized 
plumbing as well as galvanized services.  Including lead plumbing and 
galvanized plumbing in the tiering structure will substantively expand 
the pool of documentable homes for LCRI compliance monitoring. Lead 
and galvanized piping within structures has been replaced over time 
both due to failure, inadequate flow, and other changes associated with 
renovating older buildings. Finished home interiors conceal pipe 
materials behind walls and in ceilings, such that a paper record review is 
not adequate to meet EPA’s current expectations for demonstration of 
adherence to sample pool Tiers. The portions of plumbing that are most 
accessible (e.g., piping under kitchen faucet or in bathrooms) are also 
components of household plumbing most likely to have been subject to 
renovation and changes in plumbing materials. 
 
Additionally, obtaining reliably 1st and 5th liter data is challenging because: 
1. Systems currently have limited latitude under the LCR and the proposed 
LCRI to invalidate samples due to sampler error, but experience with 
obtaining 1st liter samples illustrates that further complication of a 1st and 
5th liter sample will be problematic. 
a. Current CWS quality control challenges of LCR compliance 
samples collected by customers include incomplete sample 
collection / sample loss due to inadequate sample sealing in 
transit, collection of samples from taps that are not kitchen 
faucets (or designated alternative sample taps), samples being 
drawn after prolonged stagnation especially when a monetary 
reward is provided for sampling, and inadvertent use of water 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
6 
during stagnation period. 
b. Systems that currently collect 1st and 5th liter samples find that they 
must take additional steps beyond the protocol described in 
§141.86(b)(1)(ii) to facilitate successful customer sampling. Steps 
include using sample bottles that are clearly different in size, 
shape and / or color from the 1st and 5th liter samples for collecting 
the 2nd through 4th liter samples. 
2. The current Tier 2 sample sites are favored most when Tier 1 sample sites 
are not available. The sampling protocol requires a sample from a 
building where (1) the sample represents a period of six hours or more of 
stagnation and (2) a 5th liter sample that is intended to be representative 
of the service line to the building. Obtaining samples that meet either of 
the required conditions and /or meet the intent of the 5th liter sample in an 
occupied multi- family structure is challenging. And, from a CWS’s 
compliance perspective, it is very difficult to demonstrate this to the 
satisfaction of the state. 
 
Request for Comment 4: “Comment on the proposed updated definition of wide-mouth 
bottles that is “bottles that are one liter in volume with a mouth, whose outer diameter 
measures at least 55 mm wide,” and specifically on the availability of qualifying bottles.” 
 
The reworded criteria remain difficult to source from available laboratory supply 
vendors, and thus not resolving the infeasibility of the requirement. Given the purpose 
of the requirement is to prevent the use of “small mouthed” bottles that are so narrow 
as to force the sampler to throttle the flow of water from the faucet during sample 
collection, a suggested definition is: 
“Wide-mouth bottles, for the purpose of subpart I of this part only, means bottles 
one liter in volume that have a mouth with an inside outer diameter that 
measures at least 4055 mm wide.” 
 
Service Line Inventory and Service Line Replacement Plan 
Request for Comment 3: “Comment on establishing a deadline for systems to identify 
all unknown service lines prior to their service line replacement deadlines.” 
 
EPA should not establish another compliance requirement within the treatment 
technique. A one-size-fits-all solution is not appropriate here. While each system will 
have to address service lines with inadequately characterized materials, the solution 
will be system-specific. For some systems characterizing LSUSLs will be the most 
important aspect of meeting the LCRI requirements (e.g., systems that do not have LSLs 
or GRRSLs but cannot meet LCRR documentation requirements). Other systems may 
have sufficient records available for a LSLs and GRRSLs replacement program to 
capture the remaining LSUSLs as an incidental aspect of the replacement program. 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
7 
Consequently, there is not a particular point in this proposed requirement where 
complete elimination of all LSUSLs is needed. 
 
EPA does not need to add a requirement that further constrains CWS’s approach to 
inventory and replacement program design. To the degree that states are uncertain 
whether CWSs are making adequate progress addressing service line characterization, 
there are already multiple touch points in the Proposed Rule, including (1) initial 
inventory per LCRI and subsequent inventory per LCRR, (2) LCRI service line 
replacement plan, (3) nonlead characterization validation study, (4) annual updates on 
progress of the service line replacement program, and (5) annual updates of the service 
line inventories. As the LCRR/LCRI rulemaking proceeds, implementation will occur 
during a period when there will be at least five sanitary survey cycles for CWSs subject 
to the LCR.  
 
Lead Action and Trigger Levels 
Request for Comment 1: “EPA is seeking comment on the proposed lead action level of 
0.010 mg/L, as well as comment and supporting data on alternative action levels, such 
as 0.005 mg/L, with regards to generally effective corrosion control treatment and 
identifying systems most at risk of elevated levels of lead in drinking water.” 
 
The treatment technique that EPA establishes in the final LCRI must be achievable, not 
just in some systems, but reliably across the range of likely water qualities that exist in 
the United States. EPA has not demonstrated that this is possible for an action level of 
10 µg/L and therefore there is not a convincing weight-of-evidence that a lower action 
level of 5 µg/L would be reliably achievable while simultaneously assuring compliance 
with the Stage 1 Disinfection Byproducts Rule (e.g., disinfection byproduct formation), 
Surface Water Treatment Rule (e.g., maintenance of a secondary disinfectant residual), 
or Revised Total Coliform Rule (e.g., incidence of coliform bacteria with loss of 
secondary residual), or, simultaneously managing water system infrastructure longevity 
against corrosion.  
 
Corrosion Control 
Request for Comment 3: “The proposed option for a water system to delay OCCT until 
after the system has replaced all of its LSLs and GRR service lines, while the system 
achieves at least 20 percent removal per year and must have no LSLs, GRR service 
lines, or lead status unknown service lines remaining at the end of the five-year period.” 
 
Recognizing that CWSs should not be attempting to optimize or re-optimize CCT in the 
midst of a significant transition in the materials of construction at issue, is an important 
improvement in the rule. Providing CWSs with the opportunity to remove LSLs and 
GRRSLs prior to optimization and re- optimization should be included in the final LCRI. 
As a practical matter, the standard for receiving this relief as drafted (§ 141.81(f)(1)(ii)) will 

 
762 W Lancaster Ave, Bryn Mawr, PA  19010  •  877.987.2782  •  AquaAmerica.com 
 
8 
be too challenging for systems with any appreciable number of LSLs or GRRSLs to 
achieve, in that: 
1. All LSLs and GRRSLs must be fully replaced 
2. All LSUSLs must be characterized (and replaced if LSLs or GRRSLs) 
3. Every year of the five-year period the CWS must maintain a replacement 
rate of at least 20% 
The feasibility of the provision would also be enhanced by: 
1. Removing the annual replacement target 
2. Extending the identification and replacement window to 7 years in 
keeping with the schedule for a validation study under Proposed 
Rule §141.84(b)(5)(i) 
 
Request for Comment 4: “The treatment recommendation and CCT study process can 
take multiple years to complete. For systems with existing corrosion control, the 
system may be able to alter the existing treatment (e.g., increase pH and/or 
orthophosphate dose) without a new CCT study on a much faster timeframe rather than 
waiting for study results that may recommend that same change. EPA is requesting 
comment on whether there are situations and/or conditions where existing treatment 
modifications may achieve similar lead reductions rather than delaying new treatment 
for two-and-a- half years while a study is underway.” 
 
EPA is correct, there are instances when corrosion control can, and should, be modified 
without the delay associated with a pipe rig study. That is not to say that there is a 
simple list of situations where there is a single no-regrets corrosion control solution, 
and high dose orthophosphate addition is not a panacea. Rather corrosion control 
should be assessed through a thoughtful analysis that documents current conditions 
and evaluates corrosion control options, taking into account other likely changes 
underway. In some instances, this analysis can be accomplished in days or weeks, and 
in others it will require supplemental data collection and perhaps laboratory studies 
that require weeks or months to accomplish. In the LCRI proposal §141.82(c) describes 
corrosion control studies broadly. It is possible to triage analysis and data collection 
more efficiently than is reflected in the Proposed Rule text. Ideally corrosion control 
modifications do not involve major changes in corrosion control strategy which 
necessitate more extensive implementation timeframes.

Additional Requirements for Systems with Multiple Lead Action Level Exceedances  
Request for Comment 1: “Whether water systems should be required to take 
additional actions when the system exceeds the lead action level multiple times and 
if so, what actions are appropriate and feasible, and when these additional actions 
should be required under the LCRI.” 
 
The LCRI should not require additional actions based on multiple action level 
exceedances. CWSs that are focused on assuring appropriate corrosion control and a 
smooth transition to that corrosion control strategy should not be penalized by the final 
LCRI framework. Requiring additional actions would distract from the Proposed Rule’s 
focus on optimizing corrosion control treatment. Since the purpose of the lower action 
level and related monitoring changes is to improve corrosion control, rather than 
demonstrate compliance with a health-based concentration, there is no health basis for 
requirements that distract from the intended role of the action level trigger, including 
making filters available to consumers.

The LCR and now the LCRI contain public education measures that inform the public 
regularly about additional risk reduction steps they as individuals can take. Additional 
public education measures are an administrative burden that neither (1) affords 
additional health risk reduction or (2) accelerates improving corrosion control practice.

Reporting and Recordkeeping 
Request for Comment 1: “EPA is requesting comment on the expansion of the inventory 
reporting to include lead connectors and non-lead service lines.” 
 
EPA should not require the addition of lead connectors to the inventory. As described in 
the following, the associated potential health benefit is limited and the associated 
challenges shift resources from complying with provisions that afford additional risk 
reduction. Moreover, CWSs will have just completed the inventories required under the 
LCRR and this requirement would necessitate a new round of records review and field 
investigations.  The tracking of lead connectors should be an element of the system’s 
materials evaluation (i.e., §141.42(d) as referenced in LCRI at §141.86(a)(i)) rather than an 
element of the inventory as described in the Proposed Rule at §141.84.  
 
Sections 141.90 (e)(1), (2), and (4) as proposed limit the system’s duty to report the LSLs, 
GRRSLs, and LSUSLs. This is consistent with the currently codified LCRR regulatory 
text. Because the current proposal requirements for reporting the inventory are so 
burdensome (i.e., §141.90(e)(4)), EPA should not require reporting of nonlead service 
lines,  reducing the reporting to those service lines of interest in the rule.  Also, the 
need to report should be distinguished from how a CWS may provide the inventory to 
the public. As individual property owners and occupants are accessing information 
about their service line(s), the information provided from the water system will also 
convey nonlead status in some manner.

compliance date should be retained.” 
 
EPA must act immediately (prior to the intended promulgation of the LCRI) to extend 
the compliance dates for the provisions of the LCRR that EPA does not intend to 
continue under the LCRI. Currently, systems are expending resources to comply with 
the LCRR as it is the codified regulation, while EPA is proposing to dramatically change 
both the substance and deadlines for all but three of the LCRR requirements. Water 
systems have a duty to comply and have no assurance EPA will meet it promulgation 
timeline nor that enforcement discretion will occur should EPA not publish the final 
rule prior to the LCRR compliance dates.

RE: EPA–HQ–OW–2022–0801 
 
Dear Mr. Goldberg, 
 
On behalf of the International Association of Plumbing and Mechanical Officials (the IAPMO 
Group) and Plumbing Manufacturers International (PMI), we applaud the EPA’s continued efforts 
to reduce the public’s exposure to lead through drinking water and support the advancement the 
proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements will bring towards improvement of public health 
and safety. 
 
The IAPMO Group was founded in 1926 to protect public health and safety by developing the 
world's most progressive and technically advanced plumbing, mechanical, and water efficiency 
codes and standards. A central focus of IAPMO's work is the testing and certification of products 
relied upon by our industry. Our research and testing labs are capable of testing products to more 
than 400 standards, and we provide testing to new plumbing products that enter the market 
every year. These include faucets, water filters, showerheads, piping, and many other products. 
Our rigorous testing and certification processes are recognized by ANAB (the ANSI National 
Accreditation Board) in accordance with the criteria of the International Organization for 
Standardization (ISO). In the US, IAPMO works to ensure products comply with the legal 
requirements of local plumbing codes as well as federal requirements, including those relating to 
lead in drinking water.  
 
PMI is the U.S.-based trade association representing manufacturers that provide 90 percent of 
the plumbing products sold in the United States.  Our members are industry leaders in producing 
safe, reliable, and innovative water efficient plumbing technologies. Our highly engineered 
plumbing products, sold and distributed in all 50 states, include kitchen and bathroom faucets, 
showerheads, toilets, bathtubs, urinals, sinks, drinking fountains, bottle filling stations, water 
filtration systems, pot fillers, emergency eye wash stations and showers, as well as hundreds of 
types of components, valves, and piping, all of which are key to our nation’s indoor plumbing 
systems.  PMI supports the current system of third-party certifying as required by the major 
plumbing codes adopted throughout the U.S., which requires third-party certifier marks on 

 
 
 
plumbing products and/or packaging. 
 
As such, IAPMO and PMI appreciate the opportunity to offer the following comments in response 
to the EPA’s Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI): 
 
Third-Party Certification Requirements for Products 
• Certification of products by an accredited third-party is a critical element in informing 
and providing the utmost confidence to regulators, inspectors, manufacturers, 
distributors, installers, engineers and the public that products have been tested and 
certified to the applicable standards.  The proposed LCRI language currently states that 
water filtration devices must be “certified by an American National Standards Institute 
accredited certifier.” While we applaud including the requirement of certified products, 
we recommend replacing this language with the correct technical reference to 
“American National Standards Institute (ANSI) National Accreditation Board (ANAB) 
accredited certifier” which is the accreditation body within ANSI. 
 
• Strengthening requirements for third-party certified products should continue to be a 
focus of the EPA within the LCRI and other rulemakings to reduce the public’s potential 
lead exposure from consumer products. An increasing trend of non-compliant and 
fraudulent products being sold into the market continues, particularly through e-
commerce channels, and more needs to be done so that products sold online are held 
to the same standards as brick-and-mortar retailers are. Many of these non-compliant 
products can impact consumer's health and safety, including consumer exposure from 
lead found in plumbing materials used in public water systems or residential or 
nonresidential facilities providing water for human consumption.  
 
• The EPA Office of Pesticide, under FIFRA, has treated water filtration systems that 
inhibit bacteria, viruses, and other microorganisms in drinking water as pesticides and 
pesticidal devices. IAPMO and PMI encourage EPA to modernize the enforcement of 
FIFRA as it pertains to water filtration systems and accept alternative compliance 
pathways, including acceptance of third-party testing and certification of products to 
national standards associated with performance claims.  Additionally, third-party 
certification can also help address public education efforts by providing recognizable 
certification marks on products, bringing confidence to those who are purchasing and 
installing water filtration systems, such as when used in a filter program.  
Lead in Schools and Childcare Facilities 
• While IAPMO and PMI applaud EPA in addressing lead in schools and childcare facilities, 
continued improvement is warranted.  IAPMO and PMI support protections to reduce 
lead exposure and, where lead exceedances exist, recommends any replacement or 
alternative products be third-party tested and certified by an ANAB accredited certifier 
to ensure the health and safety of the public. 
Public Education and Outreach 
• IAPMO is a nonprofit organization, committed to championing solutions that lead to 
lasting quality water and sanitation services.  IAPMO is also a leading expert in testing 
and certification for the plumbing industry. IAPMO supports providing education and 

 
 
 
public outreach, including how and where to find certified products. IAPMO houses a 
publicly available product listing database at https://pld.iapmo.org, where consumers 
can find third-party certifications for water filtration and other plumbing products 
tested to industry standards.   
• IAPMO and PMI support the continued efforts to reduce the public’s exposure to lead 
through drinking water and therefore encourage EPA to reference IAPMO’s and other 
accredited third-party provider databases within the education tool kit to ensure that, 
where a replacement product is needed, the product has been tested and certified 
accordingly.  EPA should have utilities share the EPA’s consumer tool for POU filters, 
which already contains the relevant certification bodies (e.g. WQA, IAPMO, NSF, etc.) 
and associated certification marks. Additionally, the EPA should consider including 
information on where to locate and find products. 
The EPA has made great strides towards improving the health and safety of the public to reduce 
the public’s exposure to lead through drinking water. As a leading expert in product testing and 
certification for plumbing products supplying water for human consumption, IAPMO and PMI 
support the EPA’s efforts, and we look forward to working with the EPA on the proposed LCRI. 
Please do not hesitate to contact me if you require additional information by phone at (202) 445-
7514 or via email at Dain.Hansen@IAPMO.org. 
 
Kind regards, 
 
Dain Hansen 
Executive Vice President

The IAPMO Group

The NAACP SOUTH DADE BRANCH has public comments on the US Environmental Protection 
Agency (“EPA”) proposed “National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements” (“LCRI”). The NAACP South Dade Branch advocates for the residents of Miami 
Dade County and the state of Florida on these issues.  The NAACP and its Center for 
Environmental and Climate Justice have a longstanding interest in ensuring that issues of 
community engagement and environmental justice center Black communities and frontline 
communities most impacted, including communities in Florida.  We stand with our National 
NAACP and our NAACP Florida State Conference on this issue.  
The NAACP South Dade Branch supports an EPA decision proposing stronger regulations to 
protect communities from lead in drinking water. The link to illness caused by lead is well 
documented and it has significantly and historically troubled and harmed the Black communities. 
These extreme health risks that affect our young people, our mothers, and our fathers are higher 
due to discrimination.  These negative health impacts have caused harm that spans generations 
within the community and to the Black family.  
 In Florida estimates suggest that there are as many as 200,000 lead service lines, (most likely an 
underestimation) threatening families across our state. These lead service lines expose families to 
a potent and irreversible neurotoxin which even at low levels of exposure is linked to damage to 
the brain and nervous system, learning disabilities, shorter stature, impaired hearing, mental 
impairment and harm to blood cells.    
Floridians will gain enormous benefits in public health cost savings from the full lead service line 
replacement.  This will save lives in our state and reduce the crisis in the healthcare system and 
remove the culprit, lead poisoning that has negatively impacted generations of Black women, 
children and men.   
We fully support the revisions made to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) 
for lead and copper. Access to safe and clean drinking water is a fundamental civil right that 
should be available to everyone. Unfortunately, many residents are under the impression that 
their water is safe and clean simply because it comes from the municipality. Without these federal 
regulations, municipalities might continue to disregard public safety, particularly for people of 
color by not replacing lead service lines that connect to our homes and schools. Therefore, these 
regulations need immediate implementation to prevent further harm to people of color and to 
offer solutions to the generations of people who have already been affected by lead poisoning 
and its disastrous health impacts affecting the brain, kidneys, heart and blood pressure and may 
be associated with other life-threatening diseases.

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0777 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
Re: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and
Copper: Improvements
To Whom It May Concern,
We are the Health and Environmental Justice Committee of the National Association for the
Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) Flint Branch. Our committee includes public health
and medical professionals that work to address health and environmental concerns and
inequities in the Flint and Genesee County community. Lead exposure during the Flint Water
Crisis has negatively impacted our community so we believe in the importance of strong lead
regulations that focus on prevention and mitigation via equitable approaches and policies.
We would like to provide feedback on the National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead
and Copper: Improvements, Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801. In November 2023, the US
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) released improvements to the Lead and Copper Rule
(LCR) that provide a critical step to reduce lead in drinking water over the next ten years. We
have recommendations that would strengthen these protections to prevent further exposure to
lead in environmental justice communities.
Weak lead exposure regulations fail to protect the most vulnerable populations in our
community. In Flint, the vulnerable populations include the Black and Brown community, low
income households, youth and seniors. Flint is home to approximately 80,000 residents and the
median household income is $35,000. There is a large Black and Brown community in Flint, with
56% identifying as African American. Because of sensitive periods of neurodevelopment, it is
imperative that kids are protected from the irreversible harms of lead exposure. Here in Flint,
24% of the population is under 18 years and 6.7% of the population is under 5 years. Lead
exposure is also particularly harmful for seniors age 65 and up, who make up 13% of the
population in Flint. (Census, 2023)
The EPA’s proposal for lead service line replacement is valid but we encourage more robust
systems for tracking and stringent regulation of the process across the country. There should be
consequences for water systems that do not replace the lead service lines within 10 years.
Additionally, it is recommended that lead service line replacement be an opt out procedure in
order to be inclusive and equitable in communities where communication is challenging and
households residents are not the homeowner. The replacement of lead service lines should be
completed and implemented in the most efficient, effective, and equitable way to eliminate
exposure to lead and protect public health. There should also be financial prioritization of lead
service line replacement in environmental justice communities.

The EPA’s proposal for reducing complexity and improving public health protection was fair, but
we encourage this rule to go even further to protect public health. Given that there is no safe
level of lead in drinking water, NAACP Flint Branch demands that the federal action level be
lowered from 15 ppb, not only to 10 ppb as proposed here, but to 1 ppb to provide the strongest
protection possible.
Transparency and communication are vital to maintain and build public trust which is essential
for safeguarding public health and eliminating health disparities, especially in environmental
justice communities. The EPA should have a public notification process that has diverse
communication options including digital (website, social media, radio) and in person (flyers,
church announcements, etc) to effectively educate and inform communities. Equitable
communication strategies would assist residents in lead exposure notification and alert them to
when water-related work is occurring in a timely manner.
Finally, the proposal includes a cost-benefit analysis for making improvements to the Lead and
Copper rule. As residents of Flint, we can assure you that there is no dollar amount that could
compare to the cost of human life or the irreversible harm caused by lead exposure. In
environmental justice communities all across the country, there are people who depend on the
government to put forward rules that truly protect our health and well-being no matter the cost.
In closing we appreciate you taking the time to read our comments. Please consider
incorporating stricter regulations and stronger protections for drinking water to protect the health
of the most vulnerable among us.
Sincerely,
NAACP Flint Branch #3136
Health and Environmental Justice Committee

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0833 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 5, 2024 
 
By Electronic Submission: Docket EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 
 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency  
EPA Docket Center 
Office of Ground Water and Drinking Water Docket 
Mail Code 28221T 
1200 Pennsylvania Avenue NW 
Washington, DC  20460 
 
Dear Mr. Michael Goldberg: 
 
The North Carolina Water Quality Association (NCWQA) appreciates the opportunity to comment 
on USEPA’s proposed revisions to the National Primary Drinking Water Regulation (NPDWR) for 
lead and copper. On December 6, 2023, EPA issued for public comment further proposed 
revisions to the Lead and Copper Rule (LCR), found in 40 C.F.R. § 141.80.91), known as the 
Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). Although the NCWQA supports a robust Lead and 
Copper Rule, we have significant concerns, summarized below, about several of the proposed 
changes.  
 
The NCWQA comprises public water and sewer statewide. Our members are dedicated to 
protecting public health and the environment – this includes reducing the amount of lead and 
copper present in our finished drinking water. We never seek to avoid necessary and appropriate 
requirements. Instead, we embrace such requirements and work to prioritize them and obtain the 
funding necessary to comply from the public that we serve. That said, as public utilities we must 
provide public water service in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  
 
With that perspective, we are compelled to submit these comments because the proposed LCRI 
requirements create a massive regulatory and economic obligation for both public water systems 
and their ratepayers. Adding these distribution system obligations is especially burdensome on 
top of the PFAS-related treatment obligations anticipated with EPA’s pending MCLs. Lead Service 
Line (LSL) removal is particularly challenging given the need for significant public outreach and 
interaction in relation to private laterals. US EPA estimates that there are around 9.2 million LSLs 
in the United States, which the AWWA estimates could cost over $90 billion to replace. Below we 
explain why we believe that the inventory obligation and removal of any LSLs that are found may 
be a major challenge both administratively and financially and will lead to significant conflict 
between EPA, the States, and water utilities as they struggle to define the universe of LSLs and 
complete the mandated replacements. 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 2  
 
 
2 
 
I. 
Achieving 100% Lead Pipe Replacement Within 10 Years is Both Financially and 
Practically Impossible.  A Phased-In Deadline Based Upon System Lead Levels is 
Both Necessary and Appropriate 
 
The 10-Year Timeline 
 
The proposed LCRI would require water utilities to complete 100% lead service line replacement 
(LSLR) within 10 years. 88 Fed. Reg. 84878, 84882 (Dec. 6, 2023).  While there are alternative 
timelines for (1) systems with a high proportion of lead and GRR service lines in their distribution 
system relative to their total number of households served and (2) systems that would otherwise 
be required to replace greater than 10,000 service lines per year under the proposed 10-year 
replacement requirement, Id. at 84913, the ten-year timeframe is woefully inadequate.   
 
Anytime we talk in terms of “all” in relation to 50,000 water systems spread across the country, 
we should pause for a reality check.  We should especially pause when a significant number of 
the LSLs to be replaced have not even been identified.  We should further pause when faced with 
a potential price tag of upwards of $100 billion dollars. 
 
EPA estimates that there are more than 50,000 water systems nationwide.  It is simply impractical 
for such a large number of systems to make significant distribution system changes in a ten-year 
period.  This is especially the case given the (1) fact that many/most of the LSLs have not been 
identified, (2) cost of such replacements, (3) need for public outreach around utility-owned LSL 
replacement, and (4) need for outreach and coordination with homeowners across the country 
regarding replacement of their customer-owned LSLs.  Such an historic and unprecedented effort 
would come during the worst period in modern history for trying to plan, finance, bid, and deliver 
projects.  There is simply not enough engineering or construction talent available to do the work 
- even if we could fund it. 
 
Many of our water systems are struggling right now with basic water availability, especially during 
the winter months.  Cold weather each of the last several winters has taken a major toll on water 
systems leading to numerous water main breaks and boil water advisories.  These have been 
especially prevalent across the southern United States and into the mid-Atlantic.  For example, 
much of the District of Columbia had a boil water notice in January of 2024 due to cold weather-
related line breaks. 
 
US EPA has for several decades made a priority of imposing incredibly expensive (and in many 
ways, counter-productive) sewer system improvement mandates on local governments 
nationwide.  As a result of this sewer-first enforcement approach, local resources have been 
forced to the sewer side, often at the expense of water utilities’ ability to raise revenue.  Those 
deferred investments are now coming home to roost for water systems.  On top of general system 
needs, thousands of water systems face historically expensive PFAS-related capital upgrades 
and incredible annual operation and maintenance costs for those facilities.  Adding a LSL 
replacement obligation over the next 10 years on top of these historic financial challenges is a 
bridge too far financially and from a project delivery perspective. 
 
A one-size-fits-all LSL removal period will have water systems with low lead levels vying for the 
same funding and engineering/contracting resources as water systems with much higher lead 
levels.  This makes no sense whatsoever. 
 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 3  
 
 
3 
 
A more logical approach to LSL replacement is for USEPA to adopt a phased approach where 
utilities with higher P90 lead levels have earlier deadlines to replace their LSLs while utilities with 
lower P90 numbers defer their replacements.  Such an approach will allow EPA, the States, and 
utilities to prioritize available federal and State grant/loan resources as well as engineering and 
construction resources to water systems with higher lead levels.    
 
We specifically recommend that the final rule authorize the states to establish phased-in deadlines 
for their water systems.  Any water system above the 10 ppb lead action level must remove their 
LSLs within 10 years of the effective date of the rule.  Utilities with P90 values below the 10 ppt 
would be prioritized based upon their levels for LSL removal, generally not to exceed a 20-year 
compliance period.   We believe that 20 years is a more realistic (albeit, still very challenging) 
compliance period.  Significantly, such an implementation period will allow water utilities to 
coordinate LSL removal with other system upgrades both getting and giving economies of scale 
to water system projects.  This will reduce the financial burden and system planning disruption 
that will otherwise result from a crude, 10-year LSL removal deadline. 
 
This phased approach, coupled with a one-third reduction in the lead action level, will ensure 
additional protection going forward for all Americans who receive public drinking water, from day 
one of the Rule’s effective date. 
 
II. 
Lead Service Line Replacement Must Only Include Public Lead Service Lines. 
 
The concept of LSL replacement must be revised to include replacement of only utility-owned 
LSLs. EPA lacks the authority to require public water utilities to replace privately-owned water 
infrastructure located on private property.  There are significant legal questions about whether 
public entities can even spend public funds for this private purpose.   
 
EPA cannot withhold credit for a public side lead service line replacement unless water systems 
undertake illegally impermissible action on private property.  EPA needs to address the legality of 
requiring public water systems to replace private lead service lines before imposing such a 
requirement in the LCRI. 
 
Rather than illegally seeking to force public water systems to make improvements to private 
indoor plumbing, EPA should give water utilities a benefit for each full LSL replacement that is 
performed.  For example, a utility could be given more time to complete LSL removals (within our 
suggested 20 year from the rule effective date compliance period) if they meet certain private side 
LSL removal goals (such as 30 or 40 percent associated with public LSL removal). 
 
We also question whether EPA’s assumed cost to implement the proposed rule has included 
private side LSL replacement costs.  If “yes,” we would like to know what EPA estimates those 
private costs to be and the basis for those estimates.   
 
Revise the Definition of “Under the Control of the Water System” to Exclude Customer-Owned 
LSLs 
 
Relatedly, we disagree with the proposed LCRI rule requirement that full LSL replacement is 
required when lines are “under the control” of the water system. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The term 
“under the control” of the water system is defined as wherever a water system has adequate 
access (e.g., legal access, physical access) to conduct full-service line replacement or 
replacement of the lead connector. Id. at 84920.  

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 4  
 
 
4 
 
This definition is impermissibly overbroad.  The definition must clarify that water utilities are not 
obligated to replace customer-owned LSLs as EPA cannot legally require public utilities to make 
changes to private property. The key aspect should be ownership. The present proposed 
incentives are written for a complete replacement (with customer agreement) so that water 
systems do not get credit for LSL replacement if it doesn’t include the customer’s side. We believe 
this is an illegal provision and although we support full replacements, our members cannot be 
required to go on private property and replace indoor plumbing. Those private side replacements 
should instead be driven by federal funding efforts and partial replacements should be given the 
credit they are due, considering they take great effort and expense to identify and accomplish.  
Instead, and as noted above, water utilities should be given a benefit if they achieve a certain 
goal for customer-owned LSL replacement as part of LSL replacement of publicly-owned water 
distribution lines. 
 
Lining and Coating Service Lines Should Qualify for Extended Removal Deadlines 
 
As noted above, removing “all” LSLs in the country in ten years is a shocking financial and 
practical proposition.  Rather than requiring removal, we believe EPA should allow a range of 
effective lead reduction approaches, such as lining or coating technologies to count equally as 
LSL replacements.  At a minimum, lined or coated service lines should qualify for deferred removal 
schedules.  
 
Lined or coated service lines immediately control lead from entering drinking water. EPA’s 
inventory and full service line replacement requirements in the LCRI will impose substantial costs 
on water systems that must simultaneously investigate unknown lead status service lines and 
connectors, finance capital projects associated with replacing known or discovered lead and GRR 
service lines and lead connectors and assemble the resources and personnel to replace all the 
service lines requiring replacement. 
 
Granting water systems an additional period to complete the replacements of coated or lined 
service lines, e.g. for the service life of the coating or lining product, will lower the personnel and 
financial burdens of the LCRI on water systems while immediately reducing lead from drinking 
water as water systems will dedicate resources to those services lines most likely posing a risk of 
lead exposure. 
 
III. 
Galvanized Replacement Service Lines. 
 
Definition of “Galvanized Requiring Replacements” 
 
Under the proposed LCRI, galvanized service lines that have ever been downstream of LSL 
require replacement (GRR). 88 Fed. Reg. at 84882. The EPA defines galvanized requiring 
replacement service lines as a “galvanized service line that currently is or ever was downstream 
of a lead service line or is currently downstream in the direction of flow of a lead status unknown 
service line.” Id. 85054 (proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.2). If the water system cannot demonstrate the 
galvanized service line was never downstream of a lead line, the line is a galvanized requiring 
replacement service line. Id. 
 
The EPA’s proposed definition of GRRs is unreasonable and counterproductive.  The definition 
will likely result in water systems having to replace all galvanized service lines within the same 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 5  
 
 
5 
 
10-year period they must replace LSLs.  We think the presumption that a galvanized line requires 
replacement is too strong.  Rather than requiring the water system to know that there was never 
a LSL above the galvanized line, a water utility should be able to conclude, based upon available 
information, that there is no information that there was ever a LSL above the galvanized line.  In 
those cases, the water system should be able to prioritize the lining/coating/removal of galvanized  
lines over a longer compliance period – say 20 years.  Again, the longer period is absolutely 
critical if water systems are to see economies of scale with other water distribution system work 
in conjunction with LSL and galvanized line removal.  This is especially the case for water utilities 
with P90 numbers that are well below the proposed 10 ppb action level.  We continue to believe 
that the states should be given the authority to prioritize LSL (and GRR) removal. 
 
The Lead Connector Threshold Should be 36 Inches and Unknown Connectors Assumed to Be 
36 Inches or Smaller. 
 
We disagree that lead connectors greater than two feet in length should be considered service 
lines. See 88 id. at 84919, 85083. Connectors greater than 24 inches have been sold to utilities 
and the EPA does not present evidence suggesting significantly higher lead concentrations 
resulting from a lead connector that is 36 inches as opposed to 24 inches in length. If EPA is 
going to impose an arbitrary connector length, it should be at least 36 inches.  Moreover, there 
should be a presumption that connectors of unknown size and composition are less than three 
feet in length. 
 
IV. 
Locating Legacy Lead Pipes Remains a Monumental Task for Utilities. 
 
It might be one thing for EPA to impose a 10-year LSL removal requirement if we already 
understood how many LSLs there were and where they are located.  That would allow us to better 
estimate the cost of removal and time needed.  Instead, EPA is shooting blind in that they don’t 
even have the benefit of the existing LSL inventories that won’t come due until October 16, 2024.  
Almost all of those inventories will be derived using predictive tools with only a small percentage 
of LSLs actually having been ground-truthed. 
 
The fact remains that it is a spring for most water systems to meet October 16, 2024 initial 
inventory deadline.  We suspect that hundreds, if not thousands of water systems will miss the 
deadline.  It will take many years following the development of the initial deadlines to ground truth 
where LSLs actually are in each water system.   
 
Accordingly, we request that EPA clarify what, if any, inventory update requirements are 
contemplated between the initial inventory under the LCRI and baseline inventories in the 
proposed LCRI. We suggest the EPA suspend inventory updates between the two deadlines to 
allow water systems an opportunity to develop a complete and accurate baseline inventory in light 
of the substantial difficulty most water systems will have categorizing the material composition 
and location of their service lines and connectors. Alternatively, the EPA should consider 
eliminating the initial inventory requirement and allow water systems to dedicate all of their 
resources into developing complete and accurate baseline inventories available to the public by 
2027. 
 
Baseline Inventory Requirements 
 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 6  
 
 
6 
 
We request the EPA to reconsider requiring water systems to investigate connector locations and 
composition in its baseline inventory. The proposed rule would require water systems to remove 
lead connectors upon discovery. 88 Fed. Reg. at 85066 (Proposed 40 C.F.R. § 141.84(e)). The 
EPA’s justification for not requiring water systems to find and replace all lead connectors as part 
of the full-service line replacement requirement is that “regular progress towards lead connector 
replacement is made in coordination with other activities, such as planned infrastructure work, 
while resources are prioritized for replacement of all LSLs and GRR service lines as quickly as 
feasible.” Id. at 84919.  
 
EPA noted that most lead connectors will be replaced under the proposed rule because “all lead 
connectors that are attached to a lead or GRR service line would be replaced by the end of the 
mandatory service line replacement program.” Id. In addition, EPA “also expects that many lead 
connectors may be connected to aging water mains and likely to undergo replacement with 
routine main replacement activities in coming years,” especially because EPA estimates that any 
given lead connector “is expected to be a minimum of 41 years old by the LCRI compliance date 
in 2027” and the “average service life of cast iron, ductile iron, and asbestos-cement pipe is 40 
years.” Id. EPA thus acknowledged that water systems will encounter and replace the vast majority 
of lead connectors during routine maintenance as a result of aging infrastructure or as a result of 
its mandatory service line replacement requirements. 
 
At the same time, EPA acknowledges that short lead connectors pose a lower lead exposure risk 
than LSL and GRR service lines that are significantly longer. Id. at 84919 (“EPA expects that 
galvanized lines downstream of lead connectors may contribute less lead into drinking water than 
those that were downstream of much longer LSLs”). EPA therefore prioritized service line 
replacement. Because EPA accepts that its requirement for water systems to replace lead 
connectors upon discovery will address the vast majority of lead connectors in a water system 
and acknowledges that lead connectors pose less of a health risk than lead service lines, we 
request EPA to reconsider its decision to include connectors in the baseline inventory. 
 
Removing the investigation of connectors from the baseline inventory removes expensive and 
laborious investigations into the location and composition of connectors when those resources 
are best spent identifying, locating, and removing lead and GRR service lines. Water systems 
reporting the composition and location of encountered connectors and the number of replaced 
lead connectors will still provide valuable information to the water system and the public about 
the location and composition of connectors in a water system and the probability that lead 
connectors are present. 
 
Validation Pool Requirements 
 
The proposed regulation instructs water systems to develop a “validation pool” consisting of all 
lines categorized as non-lead minus the non-lead lines that already replaced LSL or GRR lines, 
non-lead lines already visually inspected at two points along the line, or non-lead lines with 
documentation demonstrating their composition. 88 Fed. Reg. at 84935, 85063 (proposed 40 
C.F.R. § 141.84(b)(5)). The rule would require water systems to randomly and visually inspect as 
many service lines in the validation pool as necessary to ensure a “95% confidence level” that the 
observed proportion of non-lead lines validated is representative of the larger validation pool 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 7  
 
 
7 
 
within ten years of the rule’s publication and seven years of submitting baseline inventories. Id.; 
Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, EPA 815-
R-23-003 at 24-25 (Nov. 2023). 
 
The timing of this LSL/GRR inventory requirement reinforces the impracticality of the ten-year 
LSL/GRR removal requirement. 
 
EPA is currently calculating the number of visual inspections of lines necessary to ensure that 
lines categorized as non-lead are in fact non-lead by assuming a standard normal distribution and 
an “expected sample proportion” of 0.5. EPA assumed the expected sample proportion “to be 50 
percent, meaning that 50 percent of the non-lead service lines investigated are expected to be 
confirmed as non-lead.” Technical Support Document for the Proposed Lead and Copper Rule 
Improvements, EPA 815-R-23-003 at 25 (Nov. 2023). EPA acknowledged “this proportion will most 
likely be much higher since most non-lead lines will end up being confirmed as nonlead.” Id. EPA 
nonetheless maintained the proportion at 0.5 because, “an assumption of 0.50 provides the most 
conservative (or largest) sample size…meaning that any system validating this number of lines 
will be guaranteed to have met or exceeded the minimum number for statistical significance 
regardless of the true sample proportion.” Id. 
 
We question why EPA does not simply stick with the 95% confidence and allow each water utility’s 
consultant to develop a testing program that will achieve that level of confidence for the utility’s 
list.  Why does EPA pick a very aggressive 95th percent confidence level and then structure the 
rule to force an even higher level of confidence? 
 
The method for determining the number of visual inspections necessary is also not particularly 
well explained. At a minimum, EPA should clarify its validation calculations, e.g. what data it used, 
if any, to determine the expected sample proportion, what the relevant comparison EPA is making 
between the validated lines and the validation pool and what that significance of that comparison 
is, and where EPA derived its formulas for determining the appropriate sample size and provide 
citations. 
 
EPA should also assume in its sample proportion that water systems will correctly assess line 
status more than 50% of the time given its concurrent requirements to investigate lead status 
unknown lines. As EPA has explained the sample proportion, EPA is essentially assuming water 
systems will be no better at determining service line composition than flipping a coin. In light of 
the other significant investigation costs imposed by the rule, EPA should reconsider this 
assumption because it should significantly lower the number of validations water systems must 
make.  
 
We support EPA’s decision to exclude service lines which water systems have confirmed as non-
lead through records investigations from the validation pool. Id. at 84935, 85063.  
 
We also request the EPA to consider delaying the date the inventory validation must be submitted 
to better align with the categorization of lead status unknown service lines. Water systems must 
identify the material of all lead status unknown service lines within ten years from the compliance 
date. Id. at 85063. Conversely, the validation study must be submitted no later than ten years 

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 8  
 
 
8 
 
from the rule’s publication date or seven years from the compliance date. Id. at 85063. If water 
systems submit inventory validations before all unknown lines are categorized, then the validation 
pool will not include some lines categorized as “non-lead.” Allowing the validation to occur at least 
after all lead status unknown lines have been categorized will create a validation pool 
representative of all of the non-lead categorized service lines and provide water systems three 
more years to validate their inventories. 
 
Public Disclosure of LSL Addresses In Service Line Inventory 
 
The LCRI, like the LCRR, continues to require that a water system’s annual inventory updates be 
publicly accessible. Although the LCRR includes location identifiers (street, intersection, 
landmark, etc.) served by each LSL, the LCRI states utilities must include a street address with 
each service line and connector. Id. at 84936. We continue to disagree with the need to publicly 
publish a list of homes served by LSLs. Each home will get an annual reminder of this fact. Any 
home that tests for lead will receive its results – there is no need or clear authority for the EPA to 
mandate that this specific information must be made publicly available.  We especially think it is 
irresponsible to include unknown LSL in these lists. 
 
V. 
Lowering the Lead Action Level will be significant in many states. 
 
EPA is proposing to lower the lead action level from 15 µg/L to 10 µg/L. 88 Fed. Reg. 84880 while 
eliminating the lead trigger level that was introduced under the 2021 LCRR. If the AL is exceeded, 
the system must inform the public (Tier 1 public notification within 24 hrs of learning of 
exceedance) and reduce lead exposure while concurrently working to replace all lead pipes (for 
example, installing/adjusting corrosion control treatment). Id. 
 
Lowering the Action Level from 15 ug/L to 10 ug/L will be a big deal in some states with some 
states asserting that the number of systems exceeding the new action level could double.  This 
is likely to be the case for a number of smaller systems.   
 
We take no position on the reduction in the action level.  However, we do believe that P90 
numbers should be a basis for phasing in LSL/GRR removal requirements and that the states are 
in the best position to prioritize LSL/GRR removal.  States are also in the best position to work 
with water systems to mitigate lead levels pending LSL removal.   
 
VI. 
We Disagree With the Requirement to Make Point-of-Use Filters/Pitchers Available 
to All Households After Three Action Level Exceedances.    
 
Under the LCRI, water systems with three lead action level exceedances would be required to 
conduct additional outreach to consumers and make pitcher filters or point-of-use devices certified 
to reduce lead available to all consumers. See id. at 84954.  
 
Providing such filters/pitchers will be overkill in that it will scare many residents not served by 
LSL/GRRs into thinking their tap water is not safe.  That loss of confidence can be difficult, if not 
impossible, to overcome to the long-term detriment of the residents and the utility.   
 
Moreover, distributing filters/pitchers will be a massive administrative and financial task.  The 
filters/pitchers would have to be provided to each residential and non-residential location served 
by the public water supply.   

NCWQA Comments – Proposed LCRI 
February 5, 2024 
Page 9  
 
 
9 
 
We are also very concerned that residents would not properly replace the filters and could end up 
concentrating lead and copper beyond what would otherwise be present in their drinking water. 
 
VII. 
Utilities Must Be Allowed to Invalidate a Homeowner Sample That Does not Follow 
Proper Collection Procedures. 
 
Under the proposed rule, a water utility could not invalidate a homeowner’s sample even if the 
sample was not taken in accordance with LCRI requirements.  This is unacceptable.  All data 
must meet applicable QA/QC/Sampling requirements.  At a minimum, the rule should give the 
water utility the discretion to use a non-conforming sample but should not mandate the use of 
such samples. 
 
VIII. 
Water Systems Must Be Able to Select Homes From Lower Tiers Where Not Enough 
Tier 1 Homeowners Are Willing to Participate. 
 
The LCRI must clarify that water systems which, despite best, good faith efforts, cannot attract 
enough Tier 1 homeowners to participate in sampling, can use lower tier homes. 
 
Otherwise, the water system will be in non-compliance due to causes (lack of homeowner 
willingness to participate) which are beyond its control. 
 
CONCLUSION 
 
Our member utilities work tirelessly to provide high quality finished drinking water for our 
customers in an affordable and cost-effective manner.  We appreciate EPA’s consideration of our 
concerns about the practicality and affordability of the requirements we object to above.  We also 
appreciate EPA’s consideration of our suggested improvements to the proposed rule.  In 
particular, we strongly believe that a final rule needs to provide additional time for LSL/GRR 
removal and that a state-directed phased approach over twenty years from the rule’s effective 
date, is warranted. 
 
Sincerely, 
       
 
F. Paul Calamita  
General Counsel

--- COMMENT ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801-0910 AND DOCKET ID: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801 ---
February 2, 2024 
 
Mr. Michael Goldberg 
Office of Ground and Drinking Water 
U.S. Environmental Protection Agency 
Mail Code 28221T, 
200 Pennsylvania Ave, NW,  
Washington, DC 20460 
 
Re: EPA-HQ-OW-2022-0801, RIN 2040-AG16, National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead 
and Copper: Improvements (LCRI)  
 
Dear Mr. Goldberg: 
 
On behalf of AASA, The School Superintendents Association, representing more than 10,000 public 
school superintendents across the nation, I write to offer comments on the Environmental Protection 
Agency’s proposed National Primary Drinking Water Regulations for Lead and Copper: Improvements 
(LCRI).  
 
AASA recognizes that a child’s exposure to lead and copper can cause serious health effects and lower 
cognitive functioning, increase behavioral difficulties, and generally impact learning and their ability to 
be college and career ready. Children are in school roughly 7 hours a day, 180 days a year and therefore 
are at risk of being exposed to water containing lead particles as well as other environmental toxins that 
may be unknowingly present in the school building. We appreciate EPA’s efforts to eliminate lead and 
copper exposure in schools and other facilities while ensuring that the regulations are achievable and 
financially viable for school districts.   
 
Specifically, we appreciate EPA’s clarification that the requirements in § 141.92 do not apply to schools 
and childcare facilities that are regulated as NTNCWSs. As we stated in our previous comments, our 
greatest concern was the impact of new regulations on districts who operate their own system. It would 
have placed a disproportionate fiscal and administrative burden on America’s highest-poverty small and 
rural districts.  
 
That being said, NTNCWSs should still be provided the opportunity to ensure the children served by 
their systems are safe and not exposed to lead. We continue to believe that EPA should require States 
that have received Drinking Water State Revolving Fund (DWSRF) to set-aside funding specifically for 
districts that are NTNCWS and may need to engage in significant remediation efforts. These districts 
already face significant economic hardships and competing priorities for addressing problems with their 
aging facilities. Given the amount of money states have received under the Infrastructure Investment 
and Jobs Act (IIJA) and the unique requirements that may be placed on these districts because of this 
updated regulation, it is critical that they receive targeted technical assistance from the State and are 
reimbursed for any compliance option that enables them to reach the target level.  
 

For the schools and districts being served by CWSs, EPA should require CWSs to do more to minimize 
exposure to lead. We encourage CWSs to communicate to districts that beyond the 3 Ts guidance, they 
can assist with remediation efforts that districts undertake, especially filter-first prevention efforts, as 
well as other, more complicated remediation strategies. 
 
Below are our responses to the questions EPA sought feedback on regarding lead sampling in schools 
and childcare facilities.  
 
1. Whether CWSs should be required to collect more samples and/or sample more frequently in 
schools and childcare facilities.  
 
We support the proposed cadence of sampling, requiring all Community Water Systems to offer 
to test for lead in elementary schools once every five years and in secondary schools only if the 
school district requests the sampling. As new school buildings are opened every year it is 
important that districts can continue to request sampling from CWSs to ensure that these new 
taps are lead and copper free. Additional requirements should be left to the discretion of State 
and local governments who are better suited to determine the needs of communities and, more 
importantly, capable of providing the resources necessary for compliance.  
 
 
2. The proposed provision to allow States to issue waivers to community water systems from the 
requirement for lead sampling in schools and childcare facilities during the five-year period 
after the LCRI compliance date if the facility was sampled for lead after January 1, 2021 but 
prior to the LCRI compliance date and the sampling otherwise meets the waiver requirements 
of § 141.92(h).  
3. Whether or not to allow States to waive the requirements of § 141.92 for CWSs in schools and 
childcare facilities that use and maintain filters certified to reduce lead, and if so, whether the 
waiver should only be allowed where schools and child care facilities are required by State or 
local law to install POU devices and maintain them.  
4. The minimum requirements for States to provide a waiver (e.g., should the waiver be limited 
to locations where the filter use is required by State or local law; should the waiver be limited 
to locations where State or local law requires periodic sampling or testing to ensure proper 
filter use). 
 
When it comes to the question of State waivers (questions 2, 3 and 4), we are of the opinion 
that State and local discretion should take precedence on these issues. States are likely better 
positioned than EPA to administer lead testing and remediation programs because States 
can establish regulations for schools and childcare facilities that would provide for greater 
consistency of education, testing, remediation activities, and public communication across all 
schools and childcare facilities throughout a State. Additionally, States can directly apply for 
and have access to funding to support schools and childcare facilities that may not be 
available to CWSs. Therefore, States are best equipped to determine what entities can and 
cannot be exempted from testing requirements and should be entrusted with the ability to 
provide waivers to the EPA’s requirements. However, district and school administrators should 
always be provided the opportunity to have their facilities tested for lead. Any policy that allows 
a State to issue waivers to community water systems should require the consent or approval of 
the relevant district or school administration.  
 

5. Whether EPA should require CWSs to make school and childcare facility sampling results 
publicly available, and if so, how frequently and in what manner. 
 
Transparency is critical to maintaining trust between communities and their public schools. In 
this case, transparency is crucial to ensure that families know that the facilities they send their 
students to are free of any harmful toxins. School administrators are best equipped to 
determine the time and manner for communicating sampling results to the students, families, 
and communities that they serve. EPA should refrain from requiring CWSs to make sampling 
results publicly available and instead, provide resources to schools and childcare facilities 
including best practices for how to simplify and communicate results to families and 
communities.   
 
We thank you for the opportunity to provide comment on this proposed rule and look forward to 
continuing to communicate and engage with EPA over the coming months around this important issue. 
 
Sincerely, 
Sasha Pudelski 
Director of Advocacy  
AASA, The School Superintendents Association

Re: National Primary Drinking Water Regulations: Lead and Copper Rule Improvements, Docket ID
